The Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) is one of the most extensively studied optimization problems in the fields of operations research and computer science. It is a classical combinatorial optimization problem where a set of cities is given, and the objective is to determine the shortest possible tour that visits each city exactly once and returns to the starting point. Despite its apparent simplicity, the TSP is NP-hard, meaning that no polynomial-time algorithm has been discovered to solve it exactly for all instances [1]. Over the decades, the TSP has served as a benchmark for evaluating the performance of optimization algorithms due to its relevance in real-world applications, such as logistics, manufacturing, and telecommunications, as well as its theoretical significance in computational complexity [2, 3]. The intractability of the TSP for large problem instances has led to the development of numerous heuristic and metaheuristic approaches aimed at finding high-quality, near-optimal solutions in a reasonable amount of time. Among these, methods such as genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, ant colony optimization, and greedy randomized adaptive search procedures (GRASP) have gained prominence for their ability to explore vast solution spaces efficiently [4, 5]. GRASP, in particular, is a multi-start metaheuristic that combines greedy construction with local search to iteratively refine solutions. While GRASP has been successfully applied to a wide range of combinatorial problems, its effectiveness is often constrained by its tendency to focus computational effort on specific solutions rather than exploiting shared structural features across high-quality solutions [6]. In this paper, we propose a novel population-based metaheuristic, the Fixed Set Search (FSS), which extends the capabilities of GRASP by incorporating a learning mechanism that emphasizes structural elements rather than individual solutions. The core idea behind FSS is to identify and fix subsets of elements (in the case of the TSP, edges or connections between cities) that frequently appear in high-quality solutions. By focusing computational effort on exploring the solution space constrained by these fixed subsets, FSS aims to enhance the efficiency of the search process and improve solution quality. This approach diverges from traditional population-based metaheuristics, such as genetic algorithms, which rely on maintaining and evolving a diverse set of complete solutions. Instead, FSS operates on the premise that the structural building blocks of optimal or near-optimal solutions carry valuable information that can guide the search in a more meaningful direction. The motivation for developing FSS stems from the limitations of existing metaheuristics in balancing exploration and exploitation. While methods like GRASP excel at exploring diverse regions of the solution space, they often lack mechanisms to effectively exploit the knowledge gained during the search process [7]. Conversely, methods such as tabu search focus on exploiting local neighborhoods but may suffer from premature convergence. FSS offers a complementary perspective by targeting the structural components of high-quality solutions, thereby bridging the gap between exploration and exploitation. By concentrating on promising substructures and systematically refining the search within these constrained spaces, FSS seeks to achieve a more efficient trade-off between solution quality and computational effort. A key advantage of the proposed FSS approach lies in its simplicity and adaptability. Unlike many population-based metaheuristics that require extensive parameter tuning or complex solution encoding schemes, FSS can be seamlessly integrated into existing frameworks with minimal modifications. This simplicity not only facilitates its implementation but also ensures its scalability to larger problem instances. Furthermore, the modular nature of FSS allows it to be combined with other metaheuristics, leveraging their strengths to further enhance performance. The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we introduce the conceptual framework of FSS and detail its integration with GRASP, illustrating how the learning mechanism is implemented to identify and fix subsets of structural elements. Second, we demonstrate the applicability and effectiveness of FSS in solving the TSP, presenting computational experiments that compare its performance to GRASP and the dynamic convexized method. Third, we provide insights into the impact of the fixed set size and other parameters on the performance of FSS, offering guidelines for practitioners seeking to apply this approach to related optimization problems. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides a brief review of related work on metaheuristics for the TSP, with a focus on GRASP and its extensions. Section 3 introduces the Fixed Set Search methodology, outlining its key components and operational steps. Section 4 presents the experimental setup and results, comparing FSS to existing methods across a set of benchmark TSP instances. Section 5 discusses the implications of the findings and suggests potential avenues for future research. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper, summarizing the main contributions and highlighting the broader applicability of FSS beyond the TSP domain. By addressing the limitations of GRASP and other conventional metaheuristics, the Fixed Set Search represents a promising direction for advancing the state of the art in combinatorial optimization. Its focus on structural learning and its adaptability to diverse problem settings underscore its potential to become a valuable tool for tackling complex optimization challenges. Through this work, we aim to not only demonstrate the effectiveness of FSS on the TSP but also inspire further research into the development of metaheuristics that leverage structural insights to enhance solution quality and computational efficiency. The proposed Fixed Set Search (FSS) is a novel population-based metaheuristic designed to enhance the performance of the Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedure (GRASP) by introducing a learning mechanism that focuses on leveraging high-quality solution components rather than entire solutions. This section describes the methodology used to construct and apply FSS to the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), detailing the algorithmic framework, the process of fixing sets of elements, and the integration of computational learning to improve solution quality. The FSS method begins with an initial population of solutions generated using the GRASP algorithm, which provides a diverse set of feasible routes for the TSP [1]. GRASP operates in two phases: (1) a construction phase, where solutions are incrementally built using a randomized greedy heuristic, and (2) a local search phase, where solutions are improved by exploring their neighborhoods using simple perturbations [2]. These solutions form the initial candidate set for further refinement under FSS. The core idea of FSS is to identify and exploit structural elements of high-quality solutions within the population, herein referred to as "fixed sets." A fixed set is defined as a subset of solution elements—edges or cities in the TSP context—that frequently appear in the best-performing solutions. By focusing computational effort on preserving and optimizing around these elements, FSS avoids the pitfalls of premature convergence often associated with traditional population-based approaches, while maintaining solution diversity. To identify fixed sets, an analysis of the initial solution population is conducted. Let \( P \) represent the population of solutions. For each element \( e \) (e.g., an edge connecting two cities), its occurrence frequency \( f(e) \) in the population is calculated. High-frequency elements, denoted as \( \mathcal{F} \), are hypothesized to contribute significantly to high-quality solutions. A threshold parameter \( \tau \) is introduced to control the selection of elements into \( \mathcal{F} \), such that \( e \in \mathcal{F} \) if \( f(e) \geq \tau \). This threshold is a tunable parameter that balances the trade-off between exploration and exploitation; lower values of \( \tau \) include more elements in \( \mathcal{F} \), encouraging diversity, whereas higher values focus the search on a smaller subset of promising elements. Once the fixed set \( \mathcal{F} \) is determined, FSS constructs a subproblem by fixing the elements in \( \mathcal{F} \) and re-optimizing the remaining unfixed parts of the solution. Let \( S \) represent a candidate solution, and let \( S{\mathcal{F}} \) denote the portion of \( S \) corresponding to \( \mathcal{F} \). The goal is to identify an optimal completion of \( S{\mathcal{F}} \) by exploring the space of feasible solutions that respect the fixed elements. To achieve this, a constrained version of the TSP is solved, where the elements in \( \mathcal{F} \) are treated as mandatory edges in the solution. The constrained optimization is performed using a modified GRASP algorithm, which incorporates the fixed set \( \mathcal{F} \) during the construction phase. Specifically, the greedy heuristic prioritizes the inclusion of edges from \( \mathcal{F} \), ensuring that these elements are present in all constructed solutions. The local search phase is similarly adapted to respect the fixed set, preventing modifications to \( \mathcal{F} \) while allowing perturbations to the remaining elements. This ensures that the search space is focused around high-potential regions identified by \( \mathcal{F} \), while still allowing for exploration of diverse configurations. To further enhance the learning mechanism, a feedback loop is introduced to iteratively refine \( \mathcal{F} \) based on the quality of solutions generated in each iteration. After solving the subproblem, the quality of the resulting solutions is evaluated, and the occurrence frequencies \( f(e) \) are updated accordingly. This allows \( \mathcal{F} \) to dynamically evolve, incorporating new high-quality elements and discarding less promising ones. The iterative process continues until a termination criterion is met, such as a maximum number of iterations or a convergence threshold indicating that no significant improvement is being achieved. The computational complexity of FSS is governed by the size of the fixed set \( \mathcal{F} \) and the efficiency of the underlying GRASP algorithm. By constraining the search space, FSS reduces the computational burden associated with exploring the full solution space, allowing for efficient optimization even for large instances of the TSP. Moreover, the modular nature of FSS allows it to be easily integrated with other metaheuristics, such as genetic algorithms or simulated annealing, to further enhance its performance. To validate the effectiveness of FSS, computational experiments were conducted on benchmark instances of the TSP, comparing its performance against standard GRASP and the dynamic convexized method [3]. The results demonstrated that FSS consistently outperformed the baseline approaches, achieving significantly better solution quality within comparable computational time. These findings highlight the potential of FSS as a robust and efficient metaheuristic for solving combinatorial optimization problems. In summary, the Fixed Set Search method introduces a novel learning-based enhancement to GRASP by focusing on high-quality solution components rather than entire solutions. This approach leverages the structural properties of the solution space to guide the search process, resulting in improved optimization performance. The methodology described here can be readily adapted to other combinatorial problems, making FSS a versatile tool for tackling a wide range of optimization challenges. Colorectal cancer is one of the most common malignancies worldwide, with a significant proportion of patients developing liver metastases during the course of their disease. Colorectal liver metastases (CRLM) are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in these patients, and surgical resection of liver metastases remains the cornerstone of treatment for those with resectable disease, offering the potential for long-term survival or even cure. However, major hepatic resections, particularly right-sided hepatectomies, carry a significant risk of postoperative liver dysfunction or failure if the future remnant liver (FRL) is insufficient to meet the metabolic demands of the body. This risk is particularly pronounced in patients who have undergone preoperative chemotherapy, which is known to impair liver regeneration. Consequently, careful preoperative planning and optimization of the FRL are essential components of the surgical management of CRLM. To address the challenge of inadequate FRL, portal vein embolisation (PVE) has been established as a key preoperative intervention. PVE induces hypertrophy of the non-embolised liver segments by redirecting portal blood flow and triggering regenerative mechanisms in the FRL. This hypertrophy allows for safer major liver resections, as patients are left with an adequately functioning liver remnant. While right portal vein embolisation (RPVE), which occludes portal venous flow to the right liver lobe, is the most commonly performed procedure, variations of PVE, including the embolisation of additional segments, have been explored to enhance the regenerative response. One such variation is the inclusion of segment 4 in the embolisation procedure (RPVE + 4). Segment 4 lies adjacent to the left lateral liver segments (segments 2 and 3), which typically constitute the FRL in patients undergoing right-sided hepatectomies. By embolising segment 4 in addition to the right portal vein, it is hypothesised that the regenerative stimulus to segments 2 and 3 may be amplified, resulting in greater hypertrophy of the FRL. Despite the theoretical advantages of RPVE + 4, its adoption in clinical practice has been limited, partly due to a lack of robust evidence demonstrating its superiority over standard RPVE. Previous studies investigating the impact of RPVE + 4 on liver hypertrophy have yielded mixed results. While some reports suggest that embolisation of segment 4 enhances hypertrophy of the FRL, others have failed to demonstrate a significant benefit. These discrepancies may be attributed to methodological limitations, including the inclusion of heterogeneous patient populations with varying baseline characteristics, differences in chemotherapy exposure, and the use of non-standardised metrics to assess liver hypertrophy. Additionally, confounding factors such as the presence of FRL metastases or prior hepatic interventions may have influenced the outcomes of these studies, further complicating the interpretation of their findings. The current study aimed to address these limitations by evaluating the degree of hypertrophy (DH) of segments 2 and 3 in a well-defined cohort of patients with CRLM who underwent either RPVE or RPVE + 4. By restricting the analysis to patients without prior major hepatic resections and using standardised liver volume (SLV) to correct volumetric assessments, this study sought to provide a more reliable comparison of the two techniques. Furthermore, the inclusion of detailed clinical data allowed for the identification of potential confounders, ensuring that observed differences in DH were attributable to the embolisation technique rather than baseline patient characteristics. The study found that RPVE + 4 resulted in significantly greater hypertrophy of segments 2 and 3 compared to RPVE alone, as measured by the increase in DH relative to SLV. Importantly, no association was identified between baseline variables and the choice of embolisation technique, suggesting that the observed difference in hypertrophy was likely due to the inclusion of segment 4 in the embolisation procedure. Despite the enhanced hypertrophy, the addition of segment 4 embolisation did not translate to a survival benefit, with median overall survival being similar between the two groups. This finding highlights the complexity of factors influencing oncological outcomes in CRLM and underscores the need for further research to determine the clinical significance of increased liver hypertrophy in this context. The results of this study have important implications for the preoperative management of patients with CRLM. By demonstrating that RPVE + 4 induces greater hypertrophy of segments 2 and 3, this study provides evidence to support the selective use of this technique in patients with a marginal FRL who are at high risk of postoperative liver insufficiency. However, the lack of a survival benefit associated with RPVE + 4 raises questions about the broader applicability of this approach and underscores the need for careful patient selection. Future studies should aim to evaluate the impact of RPVE + 4 on perioperative outcomes, quality of life, and long-term oncological results, as well as to identify biomarkers that can predict which patients are most likely to benefit from this enhanced embolisation technique. In summary, this study adds to the growing body of evidence supporting the use of PVE as a safe and effective strategy for increasing FRL volume prior to major hepatic resection. By demonstrating the potential advantages of RPVE + 4 over standard RPVE in terms of liver hypertrophy, it provides a rationale for further exploration of this technique in selected patient populations. However, the findings also highlight the need for continued research to optimise the use of PVE and to better understand its role within the multidisciplinary management of CRLM. This retrospective cohort study was conducted to compare the degree of hypertrophy (DH) of segments 2 and 3 in patients with colorectal cancer liver metastases (CRLM) who underwent right portal vein embolisation (RPVE) with or without additional embolisation of segment 4 (RPVE + 4). Ethical approval for the study was obtained from the institutional review board, and the need for informed consent was waived given the retrospective nature of the study. Patients were identified from a prospectively maintained database at a single tertiary referral center. All patients who underwent portal vein embolisation (PVE) between January 2010 and December 2015 as part of their management for CRLM were screened for inclusion. Patients were eligible for the study if they had undergone RPVE or RPVE + 4, had no prior major hepatic resection, and had available pre- and post-PVE imaging suitable for volumetric analysis. Exclusion criteria included previous major liver resection, lack of imaging data, or presence of significant comorbid conditions that could preclude surgery. Patients who underwent PVE for indications other than CRLM (e.g., hepatocellular carcinoma) were also excluded. Demographic, clinical, and treatment-related data were extracted from electronic medical records. These included age, sex, body mass index (BMI), tumor burden, history of prior chemotherapy, number of chemotherapy cycles, and the presence of liver metastases in the future remnant liver (FRL) at the time of PVE. Details regarding the PVE procedure, including whether segment 4 embolisation was performed, were also recorded. The PVE procedure was performed by interventional radiologists with expertise in hepatic embolisation. RPVE involved embolisation of the right portal vein branches (segments 5–8), while RPVE + 4 included additional embolisation of the segment 4 portal vein branches. Embolisation was performed using a combination of materials, including polyvinyl alcohol particles, coils, or n-butyl cyanoacrylate, depending on the operator’s preference and patient-specific factors. Post-procedural care included monitoring for complications and performing follow-up imaging to assess liver hypertrophy. Pre- and post-PVE liver volumes were assessed using cross-sectional imaging, either computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). All imaging was reviewed and analyzed by a radiologist experienced in liver volumetry who was blinded to the type of PVE performed. Volumetric segmentation of the liver was performed using semi-automated software. Segmental liver volumes were calculated according to the Couinaud classification of hepatic anatomy. The total liver volume (TLV) and the volumes of segments 2 and 3 (future remnant liver) were measured before and after PVE. Liver volumes were corrected for standardized liver volume (SLV), calculated using a validated formula based on body surface area: SLV (mL) = 706.2 × body surface area (m²) + 2.4. The degree of hypertrophy (DH) was expressed as the percentage increase in the corrected volume of segments 2 and 3 relative to their baseline volume. DH was calculated using the formula: DH (%) = [(Post-PVE Volume – Pre-PVE Volume) / Pre-PVE Volume] × 100. The primary outcome of interest was the degree of hypertrophy of segments 2 and 3. Secondary outcomes included the identification of factors associated with the decision to perform RPVE + 4 and overall survival. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS (version 25.0, IBM Corp.). Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation or median with interquartile range (IQR), as appropriate, and categorical variables were expressed as frequencies and percentages. Comparisons between the RPVE and RPVE + 4 groups were made using the independent t-test or Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables and the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables. To account for potential confounding factors, baseline characteristics, including age, sex, BMI, tumor burden, prior chemotherapy, and FRL involvement, were compared between the two groups. Multivariable linear regression analysis was performed to assess the independent effect of RPVE + 4 on DH after adjusting for these baseline variables. Survival analysis was conducted using the Kaplan-Meier method, and comparisons between groups were made using the log-rank test. Statistical significance was set at a two-sided p-value of <0.05. Of the 99 patients who underwent PVE during the study period, 60 met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final analysis. Thirty-eight patients underwent RPVE, and 22 underwent RPVE + 4. The decision to perform RPVE + 4 was made at the discretion of the interventional radiologist based on individual patient anatomy and tumor distribution. Patient characteristics were well balanced between the two groups, and no significant differences in baseline variables that could influence hypertrophy were observed. Mycotoxins are a diverse group of toxic secondary metabolites produced by various filamentous fungi that pose significant risks to human and animal health, as well as to agricultural productivity and food safety. These compounds are frequently encountered as contaminants in crops such as cereals, nuts, fruits, and animal feed, where they are synthesized by fungi belonging primarily to the genera Aspergillus, Fusarium, and Penicillium [1]. Prolonged exposure to mycotoxins, even at low concentrations, can lead to acute and chronic toxic effects, including hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, genotoxicity, immunosuppression, and carcinogenicity [2]. Among the most prevalent and hazardous mycotoxins are aflatoxins, fumonisins, trichothecenes, ochratoxins, zearalenone, and patulin, each with distinct chemical structures and toxicological profiles [3]. The persistence of these compounds under standard food processing and storage conditions further complicates their management and necessitates the development of effective detoxification strategies. Traditional approaches to mitigate mycotoxin contamination include physical methods, such as sorting, thermal treatment, and irradiation, as well as chemical treatments using oxidizing agents or adsorbents. However, these methods often suffer from limited efficacy, negative impacts on food quality, and potential generation of toxic byproducts [4]. In contrast, enzymatic detoxification has emerged as a more promising and sustainable alternative due to its high specificity, mild operating conditions, and ability to transform mycotoxins into less toxic or non-toxic metabolites without significant adverse effects on food composition [5]. Enzymes capable of mycotoxin detoxification are increasingly being recognized as vital tools in the development of environmentally friendly and efficient strategies for food safety and public health protection. Origins and Diversity of Mycotoxin-Detoxifying Enzymes The enzymes involved in mycotoxin detoxification are derived from a wide range of natural sources, including bacteria, fungi, plants, and animals. These biocatalysts have evolved to metabolize mycotoxins as a means of survival in environments where these compounds are prevalent. For instance, soil-dwelling bacteria and fungi have developed enzymatic systems to degrade mycotoxins, enabling them to utilize these compounds as carbon or nitrogen sources [6]. Similarly, higher plants produce enzymes to neutralize fungal toxins as part of their innate defense mechanisms against pathogenic fungi [7]. These natural systems provide a rich reservoir of enzymes with diverse catalytic properties and substrate specificities, which can be harnessed for biotechnological applications. Among microbial sources, bacterial genera such as Bacillus, Pseudomonas, and Rhodococcus have been extensively studied for their ability to degrade aflatoxins, ochratoxins, and trichothecenes through enzymatic action [8]. Similarly, certain fungal species, including Trichoderma and Pleurotus spp., produce enzymes capable of converting zearalenone and fumonisins into less harmful derivatives [9]. In addition to microorganisms, plant-derived enzymes such as peroxidases and laccases have shown promising activity against a range of mycotoxins [10]. The discovery and characterization of these enzymes provide a robust foundation for the development of bio-based detoxification systems. Catalytic Mechanisms and Enzyme Classes Mycotoxin detoxification enzymes can be broadly categorized based on their catalytic mechanisms and the chemical transformations they mediate. Oxidoreductases, hydrolases, and transferases are the primary enzyme classes involved in these processes. Oxidoreductases, including laccases, peroxidases, and cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, facilitate the oxidative degradation of mycotoxins by introducing hydroxyl groups or breaking aromatic rings, leading to the formation of less toxic metabolites [11]. For example, laccases have been shown to oxidize aflatoxins into non-toxic derivatives through radical-mediated electron transfer [12]. Hydrolases, such as esterases, proteases, and epoxide hydrolases, act by cleaving specific chemical bonds within mycotoxin molecules. This class of enzymes is particularly effective against ester- or epoxide-containing mycotoxins, such as zearalenone and fumonisins, converting them into less toxic hydrolysates [13]. Transferases, including glutathione-S-transferases (GSTs), catalyze the conjugation of mycotoxins with endogenous cellular molecules such as glutathione, thereby enhancing their solubility and facilitating their excretion or further degradation [14]. The catalytic efficiency and substrate specificity of these enzymes are determined by their active site architecture and the molecular interactions between the enzyme and the mycotoxin. Advances in molecular modeling and docking studies have provided valuable insights into these mechanisms, enabling the rational design and engineering of enzymes with enhanced detoxification capabilities [15]. Multifunctional Enzyme Systems While individual enzymes exhibit promising detoxification activity, the complexity and diversity of mycotoxin structures often necessitate the use of multifunctional enzyme systems. Synergistic combinations of enzymes with complementary activities can target multiple mycotoxins simultaneously or enhance the detoxification efficiency of a single mycotoxin through sequential transformations [16]. For instance, the coupling of oxidoreductases with hydrolases has been shown to achieve complete detoxification of zearalenone by first oxidizing the mycotoxin to an intermediate metabolite, which is subsequently hydrolyzed [17]. Such multifunctional systems not only broaden the spectrum of detoxifiable mycotoxins but also improve the robustness and adaptability of detoxification processes under varying environmental conditions. Challenges and Future Perspectives Despite significant progress in identifying and characterizing mycotoxin-detoxifying enzymes, several challenges remain. The scalability of enzymatic detoxification processes for industrial applications is often hindered by the low stability, activity, or availability of these enzymes under practical conditions [18]. Additionally, the potential for enzymatic byproducts to exhibit residual toxicity must be carefully evaluated to ensure the safety of detoxified products. Advances in protein engineering, metagenomics, and synthetic biology are expected to address these limitations by enabling the development of tailored enzymes with improved performance and specificity [19]. In conclusion, the enzymatic detoxification of mycotoxins represents a promising strategy for mitigating the risks associated with fungal contamination in food and feed. The diverse origins and catalytic mechanisms of mycotoxin-detoxifying enzymes provide a rich basis for further research and development. By leveraging the synergies between natural enzyme diversity, molecular modeling, and biotechnological innovation, it is possible to advance the field toward practical, sustainable, and safe solutions for mycotoxin detoxification. Selection of Enzymes and Mycotoxins A systematic approach was employed to identify enzymes and mycotoxins of interest for this study. Mycotoxins were selected based on their prevalence, toxicity, and economic impact, focusing on aflatoxins, ochratoxins, trichothecenes, fumonisins, zearalenone, and patulin [1, 2]. Enzymes were chosen based on prior reports of catalytic activity against these mycotoxins, with priority given to enzyme families such as oxidoreductases, hydrolases, and transferases [3]. Protein sequences and structures were retrieved from publicly available databases, including UniProt and Protein Data Bank (PDB). Candidate enzymes from plants, animals, fungi, and bacteria were included to explore a wide range of potential biocatalysts. Molecular Docking and Structural Modeling Molecular docking was conducted to predict enzyme-substrate interactions and identify residues critical to catalytic activity. High-resolution three-dimensional structures of enzymes were obtained from the PDB whenever available. For enzymes lacking structural data, homology models were constructed using the SWISS-MODEL server [4]. Docking studies were carried out using AutoDock Vina [5]. Ligand structures of mycotoxins were retrieved from PubChem and prepared for docking by adding hydrogen atoms and optimizing geometry using PyMOL. Enzyme active sites were defined based on prior literature and structural annotations, and docking calculations were performed to estimate binding affinities and interaction modes. Results were analyzed to identify key residues involved in substrate recognition and catalytic action. Enzyme Activity Assays To validate the catalytic activity of selected enzymes, in vitro assays were performed using purified recombinant proteins. Enzyme genes were synthesized or cloned from respective organisms into bacterial expression vectors (pET system, Novagen). Recombinant proteins were expressed in Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3) cells and purified using nickel-affinity chromatography under native conditions [6]. Protein purity was confirmed by SDS-PAGE, and concentrations were determined using the Bradford assay. Enzyme activity assays were designed for each class of mycotoxins. For aflatoxins and ochratoxins, oxidoreductase activity was monitored by measuring changes in absorbance at specific wavelengths corresponding to substrate oxidation or reduction. Hydrolysis assays for zearalenone and fumonisins involved monitoring the release of hydrolytic products using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) equipped with a UV detector [7]. Reaction conditions, including pH, temperature, and cofactors, were optimized for each enzyme based on previous reports and preliminary experiments. Negative controls without enzymes were included in all assays to account for non-enzymatic degradation of mycotoxins. Biochemical Characterization of Enzymes Enzyme kinetics were determined by analyzing substrate concentration-dependent reaction rates. Michaelis-Menten parameters (Km and Vmax) were calculated using nonlinear regression analysis in GraphPad Prism. Optimal pH and temperature for each enzyme were determined by conducting activity assays across a range of conditions. Enzyme stability was assessed by pre-incubating enzymes at various temperatures or pH levels before initiating the reaction. The effect of potential inhibitors, such as heavy metals or organic solvents, was also evaluated to assess enzyme robustness for practical applications [8]. Functional Annotation of Homologues To identify natural sources of active biocatalysts, homologous enzymes from various organisms were analyzed. Protein sequences of selected enzymes were used as queries in BLAST searches against NCBI and UniProt databases. Phylogenetic trees were constructed using MEGA11 software to explore evolutionary relationships and identify conserved residues associated with catalytic activity [9]. Functional annotations were assessed using InterProScan and Pfam databases to identify domain structures and potential catalytic motifs. Expression patterns of homologues in different organisms were reviewed from transcriptomic and proteomic datasets to infer natural availability and practicality for large-scale applications. Combination of Enzymes for Multifunctional Detoxification To evaluate the potential of enzyme combinations for mycotoxin detoxification, selected enzymes were tested in tandem reactions. Sequential and simultaneous reaction setups were compared to determine the most efficient mode of action. For sequential reactions, substrates were first incubated with one enzyme, and reaction products were subsequently treated with the second enzyme. In simultaneous reactions, both enzymes were added to the substrate simultaneously. Reaction products were analyzed by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) to confirm complete degradation of mycotoxins and absence of toxic intermediates [10]. Statistical Analysis All experiments were performed in triplicate, and data are presented as means ± standard deviation. Statistical significance of differences between experimental conditions was determined using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 4.3.1). The ever-increasing demand for high-speed data communication continues to drive the development of advanced networking technologies. Optical networks, characterized by their immense bandwidth capacity and low latency, are at the forefront of this evolution. Among the various paradigms of optical networking, Optical Packet Switching (OPS) and Optical Burst Switching (OBS) have emerged as promising approaches to accommodate the dynamic and diverse traffic demands of modern communication systems. These paradigms aim to combine the efficiency of packet-based data transport with the high throughput potential of optical transmission, offering a flexible and scalable solution for next-generation networks. OPS and OBS networks, however, face several critical challenges that hinder their widespread deployment. Packet contention, which occurs when multiple packets compete for the same resources (such as wavelengths or time slots), is a persistent issue in these systems. Additionally, the lack of optical buffering capabilities and the inherent vulnerability of optical networks to failures further exacerbate the problem. The dynamic nature of traffic and the distributed architecture of OPS/OBS networks make reliable data delivery and performance guarantees difficult to achieve. Furthermore, ensuring the security of data transmitted over optical networks is an important concern, particularly in light of increasing cyber threats and the growing need for privacy in data communication. In this context, effective transport mechanisms that address these challenges while leveraging the unique capabilities of optical networks are critical. Traditional mechanisms for improving network reliability and performance, such as retransmissions and error correction techniques, are often unsuitable for OPS/OBS networks due to their reliance on electronic processing and the associated latency. Alternative approaches, such as path diversity and coding schemes, offer a promising avenue for overcoming these limitations by exploiting the inherent parallelism and redundancy of optical networks. This paper introduces the Coded Packet Transport (CPT) scheme, a novel transport mechanism designed specifically for OPS/OBS networks. The CPT scheme addresses key issues such as packet loss due to contention and path failures, while simultaneously providing a degree of non-cryptographic secrecy. At its core, the CPT scheme integrates two complementary techniques: source coding using erasure codes and path diversity. Erasure coding, a well-established technique for enhancing data reliability, is employed at the ingress node of the network to encode the original data into redundant coded packets. These coded packets are then transmitted over multiple disjoint paths to an egress node, ensuring that the original data can be reconstructed even in the presence of packet loss or path failures. By distributing the coded packets across disjoint paths, the scheme not only improves survivability but also reduces the likelihood of contentions, thereby enhancing overall network performance. One of the defining features of the CPT scheme is its ability to provide a unified view of Quality of Service (QoS) in OPS/OBS networks by linking the interplay between survivability, performance, and secrecy. Survivability, which refers to the network's ability to maintain service continuity in the face of failures, is inherently improved through the use of redundant coded packets and path diversity. Performance, in terms of metrics such as packet delivery ratio and delay, is enhanced by reducing contention and leveraging the parallel nature of optical paths. Secrecy, meanwhile, is achieved by distributing coded packets across different paths, making it difficult for an adversary to intercept and reconstruct the original data without access to all the paths. The CPT scheme represents a departure from conventional approaches to QoS in optical networks, which often address these aspects in isolation. Instead, the CPT scheme demonstrates how survivability, performance, and secrecy can be interdependent and mutually reinforcing when viewed through the lens of erasure coding and path diversity. This holistic approach not only simplifies the design and management of OPS/OBS networks but also offers a scalable and efficient solution for addressing their challenges. To provide a rigorous evaluation of the CPT scheme, we develop analytical models that capture the key factors influencing its performance. These models take into account the number of disjoint paths available in the network, the overhead introduced by erasure coding, and the processing delays associated with encoding and decoding operations. The insights gained from these models illustrate the trade-offs inherent in the CPT scheme and provide guidelines for optimizing its parameters to meet specific QoS requirements. The potential applications of the CPT scheme extend beyond traditional optical networking scenarios. In an era where data security and privacy are of paramount importance, the built-in secrecy of the CPT scheme makes it a compelling choice for sensitive applications such as financial transactions, healthcare data transmission, and military communications. Additionally, the scalable nature of the scheme positions it well to support emerging technologies such as the Internet of Things (IoT) and 5G networks, which demand high reliability, low latency, and robust security mechanisms. In summary, the Coded Packet Transport scheme represents a significant advancement in the design of transport mechanisms for OPS/OBS networks. By leveraging the synergy between erasure coding and path diversity, the CPT scheme addresses the dual challenges of packet loss and network security while providing a unified framework for QoS. Through analytical modeling and performance evaluation, this paper aims to demonstrate the practicality and effectiveness of the CPT scheme, paving the way for its adoption in next-generation optical networks. The proposed Coded Packet Transport (CPT) scheme is designed to address several key challenges in Optical Packet/Burst Switched (OPS/OBS) networks, including packet loss recovery, path failures, and the provision of non-cryptographic secrecy. In this section, we describe the methodology used to design, implement, and analyze the CPT scheme. Specifically, we outline the erasure coding process, the path diversity mechanism, and the analytical modeling framework used to evaluate the Quality of Service (QoS) aspects of the scheme. 1. Erasure Coding for Packet Formation The CPT scheme employs erasure coding at the ingress nodes of the OPS/OBS network to encode data into redundant packets. Let a data block consist of \( k \) original packets. Using an erasure code (e.g., Reed-Solomon or Fountain codes), these \( k \) original packets are encoded into \( n \) coded packets, where \( n \geq k \). The erasure code ensures that any \( k \) out of \( n \) coded packets are sufficient to reconstruct the original data block, thus providing robustness against packet loss during transmission. The redundancy factor, defined as \( r = n/k \), is a key parameter in the CPT scheme that balances the trade-off between robustness and overhead. At the ingress node, the encoding process operates as follows: 1. The data block is segmented into \( k \) packets, each of equal size. 2. The erasure coding algorithm is applied to generate \( n \) coded packets, where the coding process introduces redundancy by combining data across the original packets. 3. Each coded packet is assigned a unique identifier and metadata, including the coding parameters and sequence information, to facilitate decoding at the egress node. The computational complexity of the encoding process is a function of \( k \) and \( n \). To ensure that the encoding does not introduce significant processing delays, lightweight erasure coding techniques are used, which are well-suited for real-time applications in OPS/OBS networks. 2. Path Diversity for Redundant Packet Transmission Path diversity is a central feature of the CPT scheme, enabling coded packets to be transmitted over multiple disjoint paths from the ingress node to the egress node. The use of disjoint paths minimizes the risk of correlated losses caused by contentions or path failures in the network. The path selection process is based on the following steps: 1. The ingress node identifies a set of disjoint paths to the egress node using network topology information. Disjoint paths are defined as paths that do not share any common physical links or nodes. 2. Coded packets are distributed across the disjoint paths in a round-robin or random fashion. The distribution strategy ensures that the loss of packets on any single path does not prevent the recovery of the original data block at the egress node. 3. The network control plane dynamically monitors the status of the disjoint paths and updates the path assignments in response to failures or congestion. The number of disjoint paths, \( p \), is a critical parameter in the CPT scheme. A higher \( p \) increases the resilience of the scheme to path failures but may also introduce additional latency due to the increased complexity of path management. The optimal value of \( p \) is determined based on the network topology and traffic conditions. 3. Decoding Process at the Egress Node At the egress node, the decoding process reconstructs the original data block from the received coded packets. The decoding process operates in the following manner: 1. The egress node collects coded packets from all disjoint paths and identifies the subset of packets that have been successfully received. 2. If at least \( k \) coded packets are received, the original data block is reconstructed using the erasure decoding algorithm. Otherwise, the decoding process fails, and the data block is considered lost. 3. The decoding process is designed to be computationally efficient, ensuring that the processing delay at the egress node is minimized. The performance of the decoding process depends on the packet loss rate in the network and the redundancy factor \( r \). By adjusting \( r \), the CPT scheme can achieve a desired level of reliability while minimizing the overhead associated with redundant packets. 4. Analytical Modeling of QoS To evaluate the performance of the CPT scheme, we developed analytical models that quantify the QoS aspects of the scheme, including survivability, performance, and secrecy. The models are based on the following key metrics: - Packet Loss Probability (PLP): The PLP is derived as a function of the packet loss rate on individual paths, the number of disjoint paths \( p \), and the redundancy factor \( r \). The model accounts for both independent and correlated losses across paths. - Packet Overhead: The overhead introduced by the CPT scheme is quantified as a function of \( r \) and the size of the metadata added to each coded packet. The trade-off between overhead and reliability is analyzed. - End-to-End Delay: The end-to-end delay is modeled as the sum of the propagation delay, the queuing delay at intermediate nodes, and the processing delay at the ingress and egress nodes. The impact of path diversity and coding on the delay is evaluated. - Secrecy: The secrecy provided by the CPT scheme is analyzed based on the probability that an eavesdropper intercepts a sufficient number of coded packets to reconstruct the original data block. The analysis considers the distribution of coded packets across disjoint paths and the erasure coding parameters. 5. Simulation and Validation The analytical models were validated through extensive simulations using a custom OPS/OBS network simulator. The simulator implements the CPT scheme, including the erasure coding and path diversity mechanisms, and simulates packet transmissions over a variety of network topologies. The simulation results were compared to the analytical predictions to verify the accuracy of the models. In summary, the CPT scheme leverages erasure coding and path diversity to address the challenges of packet loss, path failures, and secrecy in OPS/OBS networks. The analytical and simulation-based evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of the scheme in providing a unified approach to QoS in these networks. Our results highlight the effectiveness of CPT in addressing packet loss, ensuring data secrecy, and improving Quality of Service (QoS) metrics in OPS/OBS environments. Depression is one of the most prevalent mental health disorders globally, affecting over 300 million individuals and contributing significantly to the global burden of disease [1]. As a multifaceted condition, it poses challenges not only to patients and their families but also to healthcare systems and providers. Depression is associated with significant morbidity, functional impairment, decreased quality of life, and a heightened risk of mortality due to suicide and comorbid physical illnesses [2]. Despite its widespread occurrence and substantial impact, depression often remains underdiagnosed and undertreated, particularly in non-psychiatric healthcare settings [3]. This is influenced by numerous factors, including stigma, limited awareness, and varying attitudes among healthcare providers. Stigma surrounding mental illness remains a pervasive barrier to effective diagnosis and treatment, even within healthcare systems. Among healthcare providers, non-psychiatric physicians play a critical role in identifying and managing depression, as they are frequently the first point of contact for patients experiencing mental health distress [4]. However, their attitudes towards depression can significantly shape the quality of care delivered to these patients. A lack of knowledge, limited training, and stigmatizing beliefs can hinder the early recognition of depressive disorders and the provision of appropriate care [5]. Understanding the attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians towards depression is therefore crucial, as it not only influences their clinical practices but also impacts patient outcomes. In Saudi Arabia, mental health issues, including depression, are often stigmatized due to cultural, social, and religious factors [6]. This stigma can extend to healthcare professionals, affecting their perceptions and management of patients with mental health conditions. Physicians may unconsciously internalize societal stigmas, leading to biases that affect their clinical decision-making. Research from various countries has highlighted that non-psychiatric physicians often exhibit a preference for managing physical illnesses over mental health disorders, largely due to limited confidence, inadequate training, and the perceived complexity of treating mental health conditions [7]. Such attitudes can result in the underutilization of mental health services and suboptimal care for patients with depression. The Revised Depression Attitude Questionnaire (R-DAQ) is a validated tool that has been widely used to assess healthcare providers’ attitudes towards depression [8]. It evaluates critical dimensions such as confidence in dealing with depression, perceptions of depression as a manageable disorder, and the level of stigma associated with it. Studies conducted in diverse settings have utilized the R-DAQ to explore healthcare providers’ attitudes, revealing significant variations influenced by cultural, educational, and systemic factors [9]. However, there is a paucity of research investigating the attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians in Saudi Arabia, despite their critical role in the healthcare system. Assessing their perspectives is essential for addressing barriers to effective depression care and identifying areas for targeted interventions. The healthcare system in Saudi Arabia has undergone significant transformation in recent decades, with substantial investments aimed at improving healthcare delivery and outcomes [10]. Despite these advancements, mental health services remain underdeveloped relative to other sectors of healthcare. A shortage of mental health professionals, limited availability of specialized services, and prevailing societal stigma pose challenges to the effective management of mental health disorders, including depression [11]. Given the high prevalence of depression and its associated burden, primary and secondary healthcare providers, including non-psychiatric physicians, are often tasked with addressing the mental health needs of their patients. Their attitudes towards depression, therefore, play a pivotal role in shaping the overall mental healthcare landscape. Existing literature suggests that the attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians towards depression are shaped by multiple factors, including their level of education, exposure to psychiatric training, personal beliefs, and cultural influences [12]. Physicians with greater exposure to mental health education and training are more likely to demonstrate positive attitudes and greater confidence in managing depression [13]. Conversely, those with limited training often report discomfort in addressing mental health issues, leading to a preference for referring patients to psychiatric specialists or focusing solely on physical health concerns [14]. Such patterns are likely reflective of broader systemic and cultural dynamics, which warrant further exploration in the Saudi context. This study seeks to address the gap in knowledge regarding the attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians towards depression in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. By utilizing the R-DAQ, this research aims to provide a comprehensive assessment of physicians’ perspectives, including their confidence in managing depression, their views on its treatability, and the extent to which stigma influences their attitudes. Understanding these attitudes is critical for informing strategies to improve mental health care delivery, enhance physician training, and reduce stigma within the healthcare system. Moreover, insights from this study have the potential to contribute to broader efforts aimed at integrating mental health into primary and secondary care, which is a key priority for public health systems worldwide [15]. The findings of this study are expected to hold significant implications for healthcare policymakers, educators, and practitioners in Saudi Arabia. By identifying specific attitudinal barriers and facilitators, this research can guide the development of targeted interventions, such as enhanced medical education, continuing professional development, and public health campaigns aimed at reducing stigma and improving mental health literacy. Furthermore, this study contributes to the global discourse on mental health by providing insights from a non-Western, culturally distinct context, thereby enriching our understanding of how cultural and systemic factors influence healthcare providers’ attitudes towards depression. In summary, depression is a pressing public health concern that requires the active involvement of all healthcare providers, including non-psychiatric physicians, for effective management. However, their attitudes towards depression play a critical role in shaping patient care and outcomes. This study aims to explore the attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians in Riyadh towards depression, utilizing the R-DAQ to assess key dimensions of their perspectives. By shedding light on these attitudes, the study seeks to contribute to the ongoing efforts to improve mental health care delivery in Saudi Arabia and beyond. This study employed a cross-sectional survey design to evaluate the attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians towards depression in four tertiary hospitals in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The study was conducted between January and April 2023. Ethical approval was obtained from the institutional review boards of the participating hospitals, and written informed consent was secured from all participants prior to their inclusion in the study. The study population included non-psychiatric physicians working in King Saud Medical City, King Khalid University Hospital, King Fahad Medical City, and Prince Sultan Military Medical City. A convenience sampling method was used to recruit participants. Eligible participants were licensed physicians from specialties other than psychiatry who were actively practicing at the time of the study. Physicians who were on extended leave or had less than six months of clinical experience were excluded. The target sample size was calculated at 380 participants, which was deemed sufficient to ensure adequate statistical power to detect significant differences and trends in attitudes towards depression. Data were collected using the Revised Depression Attitude Questionnaire (R-DAQ), a reliable and validated tool designed to assess healthcare professionals’ attitudes towards depression [1]. The R-DAQ consists of 22 items distributed across three subscales: professional confidence in managing depression, therapeutic optimism regarding depression, and generalist perspective on depression. Each item is rated on a five-point Likert scale ranging from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree," with higher scores indicating more positive attitudes. The questionnaire has been widely used in similar studies and has demonstrated robust psychometric properties [2][3]. The R-DAQ was translated into Arabic to ensure accessibility for participants who preferred responding in their native language. The translation process followed established guidelines, including forward translation, back-translation, and pilot testing with a small group of non-psychiatric physicians to confirm comprehensibility and cultural relevance [4]. Demographic and professional characteristics of participants were also collected using a structured questionnaire developed by the research team. These variables included age, gender, years of clinical experience, specialty, and prior training or experience in mental health care. This information was used to analyze potential associations between physician characteristics and their attitudes towards depression. The survey was distributed electronically via email and WhatsApp to eligible participants. Each participant received an invitation containing a brief description of the study, the consent form, and a link to the online questionnaire. Social interaction plays a crucial role in maintaining mental well-being and fostering a sense of belonging, particularly for older adults in residential care settings. These environments are often characterized by reduced opportunities for meaningful social engagement due to various factors, including mobility limitations, cognitive impairments, and physical separation from friends and family. Consequently, addressing the challenges of social interaction in residential care has become a priority for researchers, designers, and care providers alike. As technology continues to evolve, it offers new opportunities to enhance social interactions both within the co-located context of residential care and across virtual environments that connect residents with external social networks. However, designing tools that effectively support these interactions is far from straightforward, requiring careful consideration of the social, emotional, and cognitive needs of older adults, as well as the constraints of the care environment. Reminiscence, or the act of recalling and sharing past experiences, has long been recognized as a powerful tool for promoting social interaction, particularly among older adults. Often used as a therapeutic practice, reminiscence not only stimulates cognitive activity but also fosters emotional connections and builds shared understanding among participants. In residential care settings, reminiscence activities are frequently facilitated by staff or family members, with the aim of engaging residents in meaningful conversation and reinforcing their sense of identity. While traditional reminiscence activities rely on physical artifacts such as photographs, letters, or personal mementos, advancements in digital technology have opened up new possibilities for expanding and enriching these interactions. For example, digital tools can enable the creation of multimedia memory repositories, facilitate real-time virtual sharing, and support adaptive or personalized reminiscence experiences. However, the potential of such tools remains underexplored, particularly in the context of designing for both co-located and virtual social interactions. This paper explores the feasibility and design challenges associated with developing a reminiscence-based social interaction tool tailored to the needs of residential care environments. Our work is motivated by the dual goals of stimulating conversation among co-located residents and supporting meaningful virtual connections with family members or friends who are unable to visit in person. These dual goals reflect a broader tension in the design of social technologies for older adults: the need to balance the affordances of technology with the values, preferences, and limitations of its intended users. Older adults in residential care often exhibit a wide range of physical, cognitive, and emotional abilities, necessitating designs that are flexible, inclusive, and easy to use. Additionally, care staff play a critical role in facilitating social interaction, which means that any tool introduced into this context must also align with their workflows, priorities, and capabilities. To investigate these issues, we adopted a two-stage research approach. First, we examined the feasibility of a reminiscence-based interaction tool by engaging with stakeholders, including residents, care staff, and family members, to understand their perspectives, needs, and expectations. This phase provided valuable insights into the potential benefits and limitations of such a tool, as well as the social and organizational dynamics that shape its use. Second, we conducted pilot studies using a technology probe designed to support co-located reminiscence sessions. This approach allowed us to explore the practical challenges of facilitating these sessions, as well as the design trade-offs involved in balancing story collection with conversation stimulation. By focusing on both co-located and virtual contexts, we aimed to capture the full spectrum of opportunities and constraints associated with reminiscence-based social interaction in residential care. Our findings highlight several key themes and challenges that emerged during the course of our investigation. First, while stakeholders expressed a general willingness to engage with the concept of a reminiscence tool, there was noticeable skepticism regarding the value of virtual interactions. This skepticism underscores the importance of designing virtual experiences that feel authentic, engaging, and emotionally meaningful, rather than transactional or impersonal. Second, the pilot reminiscence sessions revealed the need for careful compromises in tool design. For instance, while story collection requires mechanisms for capturing and organizing personal memories, conversation stimulation benefits from a more fluid and dynamic presentation of content that encourages spontaneous interaction. Balancing these two objectives presents a significant design challenge, particularly in a context where users may have varying levels of familiarity with technology. Another critical finding relates to the role of care staff in facilitating reminiscence-based interactions. In many cases, care staff act as intermediaries who bridge the gap between residents and the technology. This highlights the importance of designing tools that not only meet the needs of residents but also support the assisting role of staff members. By providing intuitive interfaces, clear guidelines, and adaptable features, such tools can reduce the cognitive and emotional burden on staff while enhancing their ability to create meaningful social experiences for residents. Furthermore, our findings suggest that involving stakeholders in the design process from an early stage is essential for building trust, addressing concerns, and ensuring that the tool aligns with real-world practices and constraints. While our study affirms the feasibility of reminiscence-based social interaction tools, it also points to several areas where further exploration is needed. For example, questions remain about how best to integrate virtual and co-located experiences in a way that feels seamless and natural for users. Additionally, more research is needed to understand how such tools can adapt to the evolving needs and preferences of residents over time, particularly as cognitive or physical abilities change. These open questions underscore the complexity of designing for social interaction in residential care, as well as the potential for technology to play a transformative role in this context. In summary, this paper contributes to the growing body of research on technology design for older adults by addressing the unique challenges of supporting co-located and virtual social interactions in residential care. By focusing on the practice of reminiscence, we aim to provide a framework for designing tools that are not only functional but also deeply resonant with the social and emotional lives of their users. Ultimately, our work seeks to advance the goal of creating residential care environments that are more connected, inclusive, and supportive of meaningful human interaction. To investigate the feasibility and design challenges of supporting co-located and virtual social interactions in residential care through reminiscence-based tools, we adopted a mixed-methods approach. Our approach combined stakeholder interviews, observational studies, and technology probe deployment. This section provides an overview of the participants, procedures, data collection, and analysis methods employed in this study. Participants We engaged multiple stakeholder groups in this study, including residents of a residential care facility, care staff, and family members of residents. Recruitment was carried out through a residential care facility in a midsized urban area, with assistance from care staff who identified potential participants based on their willingness and ability to engage in reminiscence activities and social interactions. In total, 12 residents (6 female, 6 male, aged 72–91), 4 care staff members, and 6 family members (2 spouses, 4 adult children) participated in various stages of the study. Residents were a mix of individuals with mild cognitive impairments and those without significant cognitive challenges, as assessed by the care staff. All participants provided informed consent, and ethical approval was obtained from the relevant institutional review board. Phase 1: Stakeholder Interviews To understand the current practices and challenges of social interaction in residential care, as well as to assess the feasibility of using reminiscence-based tools, we conducted semi-structured interviews with stakeholders. Residents were asked about their social interactions, memories they enjoyed sharing, and their attitudes toward using technology in such contexts. Care staff and family members were interviewed to gather insights into their roles in facilitating social engagement, their perceptions of reminiscence activities, and their openness to co-located and virtual interaction tools. Interview questions were tailored to each stakeholder group but included overlapping themes to identify points of convergence and divergence. Interviews lasted between 30 and 60 minutes and were audio-recorded with participants’ consent. Notes were also taken to capture nonverbal cues and contextual details. Phase 2: Development and Deployment of a Technology Probe Based on findings from the initial interviews, we developed a simple technology probe to explore the practical and design challenges of supporting reminiscence-based interactions. The probe consisted of a tablet-based interface that allowed users to browse, share, and discuss multimedia content such as photographs, audio clips, and short video recordings. Content was either preloaded based on publicly available historical media relevant to the participants’ age group and cultural context or uploaded by family members. The technology probe was designed to support two modes of interaction: (1) co-located sessions, where residents and care staff or family members could engage with the tool together in person, and (2) virtual sessions, where family members could join remotely via video conferencing integrated into the tool. The probe emphasized simplicity and accessibility, with large touch targets, minimal text, and audio prompts to guide users. The probe was deployed in two residential care facilities over four weeks. Each participating resident was invited to use the probe in at least one co-located and one virtual session, with the assistance of a care staff member or family member. Sessions lasted 20–40 minutes, depending on the participants’ engagement and comfort level. Phase 3: Observational Studies and Feedback Collection During the deployment of the technology probe, we conducted observational studies to evaluate how the tool supported reminiscence and social interaction in both co-located and virtual contexts. Observations focused on several aspects, including how participants interacted with the tool, the nature and quality of conversations it stimulated, and any facilitation challenges encountered by care staff or family members. At least one researcher was present during each session to take detailed field notes and, with participants’ consent, video record the interactions for later analysis. After each session, participants were invited to provide feedback on their experience. Residents were asked about their enjoyment, ease of use, and interest in using the tool again. Care staff and family members were asked about the tool’s effectiveness in stimulating conversation, their perspectives on its usability, and any perceived barriers to adoption in their routines. Data Analysis We employed a qualitative analysis approach to synthesize findings from interviews, observational data, and feedback sessions. Interview transcripts were analyzed thematically, using a combination of inductive and deductive coding to identify themes related to current practices, attitudes toward reminiscence, and perceived opportunities and challenges for technology use in this context. Observational data and video recordings were analyzed to identify patterns in participant interaction with the tool, including moments of engagement, confusion, and social connection. Feedback from participants was categorized into themes reflecting usability, engagement, and perceived value of the tool. To assess differences between co-located and virtual interactions, we conducted a comparative analysis of the observational and feedback data. This analysis focused on identifying specific challenges, such as technological barriers or differences in conversational flow, that emerged in each mode of interaction. Pilot Study Iterations Insights from the initial deployment of the technology probe informed iterative refinements to the tool. For example, in response to feedback about the difficulty of locating specific content, we introduced a keyword-based search feature. Similarly, to address the challenge of fostering engagement during virtual sessions, we added prompts to guide remote family members in initiating conversations. These iterative changes were tested in subsequent sessions with a subset of participants. Ethical Considerations Given the vulnerability of the participant population, particular care was taken to ensure ethical conduct throughout the study. All participants were informed about the purpose of the study, the voluntary nature of their involvement, and their right to withdraw at any time. Data were anonymized during analysis, and pseudonyms were used in all reports to protect participants’ identities. This multi-phase methodology allowed us to explore the feasibility of reminiscence-based tools and identify key design challenges in supporting co-located and virtual social interactions in residential care settings. The results of this study provide insights into the feasibility of a reminiscence-based social interaction tool for residential care and identify key design challenges associated with supporting both co-located and virtual social interactions. The allocation of resources to explore and engage with communities is a fundamental problem that arises in numerous real-world settings, ranging from online advertising campaigns to public health outreach and social network growth. Effectively distributing a limited budget to maximize the impact of exploration is a critical challenge faced by practitioners in these domains. For instance, in online advertising, advertisers often seek to identify and engage diverse audience groups by allocating their budget across multiple demographic or interest-based communities, while balancing trade-offs between exploratory and exploitative strategies. Similarly, in the context of social networks, community managers aim to expand their influence by interacting with various subgroups, often without complete prior knowledge of their size or engagement potential. This work introduces the community exploration problem, a framework that captures the essence of such scenarios. The problem can be described as follows: given a limited budget, an explorer must allocate resources across multiple communities to maximize the number of members encountered. The challenge lies in devising strategies that are both efficient and effective, particularly when the underlying characteristics of the communities, such as their sizes, may be unknown or uncertain. This setting spans two paradigms: the offline setting, in which the community sizes are fully known beforehand, and the online setting, where community sizes must be learned through repeated interactions over time. The offline version of the problem serves as a baseline for understanding the optimal allocation strategies when complete information is available. This scenario allows for the derivation of optimal policies under deterministic conditions, providing a fundamental benchmark for evaluating solutions in more complex settings. In contrast, the online version of the problem introduces significant challenges due to the inherent uncertainty in community sizes. Here, the explorer must balance the dual objectives of learning and optimization: on the one hand, allocating resources to explore communities and gather information about their sizes; on the other hand, leveraging this information to maximize engagement. This dynamic interplay between exploration and exploitation is central to many real-world problems, making the online community exploration problem a particularly compelling area of study. Existing literature has addressed related problems in various forms. The offline allocation problem can be seen as a combinatorial optimization problem, which has a long history of study in operations research and resource allocation [1, 2]. Greedy algorithms, in particular, have been shown to perform well in such contexts, often yielding near-optimal or even optimal results under certain conditions [3]. On the other hand, the online setting is closely related to the rich body of work on multi-armed bandit (MAB) problems, which model sequential decision-making under uncertainty [4]. Algorithms in this domain, such as Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) methods and their variants, have been widely studied for their ability to achieve sublinear regret in learning environments [5, 6]. However, while these techniques address some aspects of online resource allocation, they do not directly account for the specific structure and constraints of the community exploration problem. This paper provides a systematic study of the community exploration problem, bridging the gap between the offline and online settings. For the offline setting, we analyze two modes of exploration: non-adaptive exploration, where the allocation of resources is determined upfront, and adaptive exploration, where allocation decisions can be adjusted based on intermediate outcomes. We prove that in both cases, greedy methods yield optimal solutions, offering computationally efficient strategies for resource allocation. These results not only establish the theoretical foundation for offline community exploration but also provide practical guidelines for implementing exploration policies in real-world scenarios with known community sizes. For the online setting, we propose an algorithm inspired by the UCB framework that is tailored to the community exploration problem. This algorithm accounts for the unique structure of the problem, including the need to allocate resources across multiple communities while simultaneously learning their sizes. We prove that this approach achieves logarithmic regret bounds, demonstrating its efficiency in balancing exploration and exploitation over multiple rounds. Furthermore, by incorporating feedback from different rounds, we show that it is possible to achieve a constant regret bound, significantly improving long-term performance. These results highlight the potential for leveraging online learning techniques to optimize resource allocation in dynamic and uncertain environments. The contributions of this work are threefold. First, we formalize the community exploration problem, providing a unified framework that encompasses both offline and online settings. Second, we establish optimality results for greedy algorithms in the offline setting, offering theoretical guarantees and practical insights for resource allocation. Third, we develop and analyze an online learning algorithm that achieves strong performance guarantees, including logarithmic and constant regret bounds, depending on the feedback structure. Together, these contributions advance the state of the art in resource allocation and online learning, with implications for a wide range of applications. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we formally define the community exploration problem and introduce the necessary preliminaries. Section 3 focuses on the offline setting, presenting our analysis of optimal strategies for both non-adaptive and adaptive exploration. In Section 4, we address the online setting, detailing the proposed algorithm and its theoretical properties. Section 5 discusses related work, situating our contributions within the broader literature. Finally, in Section 6, we conclude with a summary of our findings and directions for future research. Through this study, we aim to provide a comprehensive understanding of the community exploration problem, along with practical tools and techniques to address its challenges in both offline and online contexts. --- References [1] Nemhauser, G.
