Deep learning models have garnered significant attention in recent years due to their ability to model complex patterns and relationships within data. Among these models, the Deep Belief Network (DBN) has emerged as a powerful framework for unsupervised learning, leveraging its hierarchical architecture to capture meaningful representations of input data. A DBN is typically constructed by stacking multiple Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), each of which is pre-trained in an unsupervised manner. By stacking these RBMs, the DBN can effectively learn a hierarchy of features, with lower layers capturing more basic representations and higher layers extracting more abstract features. Despite its success, a conventional DBN has a fixed network structure that is determined prior to the learning phase. This fixed architecture can lead to inefficiencies when the network is either over- or under-parameterized for a given task, which in turn can result in suboptimal performance or excessive computational cost. Addressing this limitation is the primary motivation for the research presented in this paper. In practical applications, one of the key challenges in training deep learning models, including DBNs, lies in determining the appropriate network structure. The number of layers, hidden units, and weights must often be specified before training begins, based on heuristics or trial-and-error methods. A structure that is too small may fail to capture the complexity of the input data, leading to underfitting, while an overly large structure may result in overfitting, increased computational cost, and difficulty in interpreting the learned representations. These challenges are compounded by the fact that different datasets and tasks may require vastly different network configurations. Thus, an adaptive approach capable of determining the optimal network structure during the learning process would be highly beneficial, enabling the model to automatically adjust to the properties of the input data. In addition to the issues of efficiency and adaptability, another critical consideration in designing neural networks is model interpretability. Deep networks, while powerful, are often criticized for their "black-box" nature, making it difficult to extract explicit knowledge or understand the decision-making process. Sparse and compact network structures, which eliminate unnecessary hidden units and connections, are more interpretable and are associated with improved generalization performance. However, achieving such sparsity typically requires careful regularization or pruning techniques, which are often applied post-training and may not fully integrate with the learning process. Incorporating structural adaptability directly into the training phase presents an opportunity to address these challenges simultaneously. To address the limitations of fixed-structure DBNs, researchers have explored adaptive structural learning methods. These methods dynamically modify the network architecture during training by adding or removing components such as hidden neurons, weights, or layers based on certain criteria. In our previous research, we developed an adaptive structural learning method for RBMs, which allowed the model to discover the optimal number of hidden neurons and weights. Furthermore, we proposed a Learning Forgetting method, which enabled the model to remove redundant or irrelevant components from the trained RBM. These methods demonstrated the potential of adaptive structural learning to improve both the efficiency and interpretability of neural networks. Building on this foundation, this paper introduces a novel adaptive learning method for DBNs that extends the principles of adaptive structural learning to the level of network layers. Unlike traditional DBNs, which require the number of layers to be pre-specified, our proposed method allows the model to dynamically determine the optimal number of layers during the learning process. By doing so, the network can adjust its depth to match the complexity of the input data, striking a balance between computational efficiency and representational power. This approach not only reduces the need for manual tuning of hyperparameters but also facilitates the discovery of compact, interpretable network structures. The proposed method evaluates the necessity of additional layers during training based on the properties of the learned representations at each layer. If the current network configuration is insufficient to capture the complexity of the input data, the model generates a new layer to improve its representational capacity. Conversely, if the network is found to be overly complex, redundant components can be pruned to maintain a sparse and efficient architecture. This dynamic adjustment process is guided by objective criteria that take into account both the reconstruction error of the DBN and the sparsity of the network structure. By integrating these criteria into the learning process, the proposed method ensures that the resulting network is both effective and efficient. To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method, we conducted experiments on several benchmark datasets. These datasets were chosen to represent a range of tasks and complexities, allowing us to assess the adaptability and generalization performance of the model. The results demonstrate that the adaptive learning method not only achieves competitive performance compared to traditional DBNs but also discovers compact network structures that are well-suited to the input data. Furthermore, the ability to dynamically adjust the number of layers during training provides a practical advantage in applications where the optimal network configuration is unknown a priori. In summary, this paper addresses a critical limitation of traditional DBNs by introducing an adaptive learning method that can determine the optimal number of layers during training. This approach builds on our previous work on adaptive structural learning for RBMs and extends it to the deeper, more complex architecture of DBNs. The proposed method represents a significant step toward more efficient, interpretable, and adaptable deep learning models, with potential applications across a wide range of domains. By enabling the network structure to evolve in response to the input data, our method offers a promising solution to the challenges of manual network design and hyperparameter tuning, paving the way for more autonomous and effective deep learning systems. To develop and evaluate the proposed adaptive learning method of Deep Belief Networks (DBN), we implemented a system capable of dynamically adjusting both the number of hidden layers and the structure of each layer during the training process. This section outlines the methodology, including the architecture of the proposed system, the adaptive structural learning approach, and the evaluation procedures used to benchmark our system. 1. Overview of the Proposed Adaptive Learning Framework The primary goal of the proposed method is to enable a DBN to adapt its structure, including the number of layers, the number of hidden neurons in each layer, and their associated weights, during the learning process. This adaptability is achieved through the integration of two key mechanisms: the adaptive structural learning method for Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) and a layer generation algorithm. The adaptive structural learning method adjusts the number of hidden neurons and their connections within each RBM layer, while the layer generation algorithm determines the optimal number of layers required to model the input data effectively. The proposed framework begins with a simple DBN structure, typically consisting of a single RBM layer initialized with a small number of hidden neurons. Training proceeds iteratively, during which the system evaluates the representational capacity of the current DBN structure and dynamically modifies it as necessary. This dynamic modification is driven by a set of criteria designed to balance model complexity, computational cost, and stability. 2. Adaptive Structural Learning of Restricted Boltzmann Machines The adaptive structural learning method for RBMs is a core component of our approach. This method allows each RBM to autonomously determine the optimal number of hidden neurons and their sparse connections during training. The process involves the following steps: - Neuron Addition: During training, the system monitors the reconstruction error and the distribution of the hidden layer activations. If the reconstruction error remains high or if the network shows insufficient diversity in hidden neuron activations, additional hidden neurons are introduced to improve representational capacity. The weights connecting the newly added neurons are initialized with small random values to avoid disrupting the learned representations. - Neuron Removal: To prevent overfitting and ensure a sparse network structure, hidden neurons that contribute minimally to the network's performance are pruned. This is determined by evaluating the magnitude of the weights connected to each hidden neuron and the frequency of its activation. Neurons with consistently low contributions are removed, and their weights are redistributed across the remaining network. - Weight Optimization: Once the hidden neuron structure stabilizes, the weights of the RBM are fine-tuned using contrastive divergence (CD) learning. This ensures that the RBM achieves optimal performance given its current structure. The adaptive structural learning process continues iteratively until the RBM achieves a stable reconstruction error while maintaining a sparse and efficient structure. 3. Layer Generation Algorithm The layer generation algorithm is responsible for determining the optimal number of layers in the DBN. This algorithm evaluates the representational sufficiency of the current DBN structure after training each RBM layer. The decision to add a new layer is based on the following criteria: - Feature Extraction Quality: After training an RBM layer, the quality of the features extracted by the layer is assessed using metrics such as mutual information or reconstruction error. If the extracted features fail to capture higher-order representations of the input data, a new layer is added. - Information Propagation: The activations of the current topmost hidden layer are analyzed to determine whether they exhibit sufficient diversity and structure for effective information propagation. If the activations are overly simplistic or redundant, it indicates the need for additional layers. - Regularization and Sparsity: The algorithm ensures that the addition of new layers does not lead to overfitting or excessive complexity. Regularization techniques, such as weight decay and sparsity constraints, are employed to maintain a balance between model flexibility and stability. When a new layer is added, it is initialized with a small number of hidden neurons, and its weights are trained using the adaptive structural learning method described earlier. This process is repeated until the DBN achieves satisfactory performance on the target task or the improvement from adding new layers becomes negligible. 4. Integration of Learning and Forgetting Mechanisms To further enhance the adaptability and efficiency of the proposed method, we incorporate a learning and forgetting mechanism into the training process. This mechanism allows the model to fine-tune its structure by revisiting previously learned layers and adjusting their parameters or removing redundant features. By periodically evaluating the entire DBN structure, the system ensures that the network remains compact and efficient while retaining its ability to generalize. 5. Evaluation Procedure To evaluate the performance of the proposed adaptive DBN learning method, we conducted experiments on several benchmark datasets, including the MNIST handwritten digit dataset, the CIFAR-10 image dataset, and synthetic datasets designed to test the scalability and robustness of the model. The evaluation metrics included reconstruction error, classification accuracy, model complexity (number of layers and neurons), and training time. The proposed method was compared against traditional DBN models with fixed architectures, as well as other adaptive learning methods reported in the literature. For each dataset, the models were trained using identical preprocessing steps, learning rates, and batch sizes to ensure a fair comparison. 6. The initial parameters of the RBM layers were set using small random values, and contrastive divergence with one-step Gibbs sampling (CD-1) was employed for weight updates. The hyperparameters, including the thresholds for neuron addition/removal and layer generation, were fine-tuned through cross-validation. Hip fractures are a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in elderly individuals, particularly those affected by osteoporosis, a condition characterized by reduced bone mass and structural deterioration. With an aging global population, the burden of hip fractures on healthcare systems continues to rise, making it a critical public health concern. These injuries often lead to prolonged hospitalization, loss of independence, reduced quality of life, and, in severe cases, increased risk of mortality. Given the severe consequences of hip fractures, there is an urgent need for accurate, individualized methods to assess fracture risk and implement preventive strategies. The femoral neck is a critical region of the hip that is particularly susceptible to fracture due to its structural role in transmitting forces from the upper body to the lower extremities. While the occurrence of hip fractures is closely associated with bone mineral density (BMD) loss, it is well-recognized that BMD alone is insufficient to fully explain fracture risk. This has led to the development of advanced computational approaches, such as finite element analysis (FEA), which incorporate both bone geometry and material properties to provide a more comprehensive assessment of fracture risk. FEA utilizes patient-specific imaging data, such as quantitative computed tomography (QCT), to simulate mechanical loading conditions and predict the likelihood of fracture under specific scenarios, such as falls. A fall from a standing height is one of the most common injury mechanisms leading to hip fractures, particularly among older adults. Depending on the direction of impact, the load distribution across the femur varies, with sideways falls being particularly associated with fractures at the superior region of the femoral neck. Single-legged stance, another biomechanically relevant loading configuration, is also of interest as it represents the forces experienced during activities such as walking or standing on one leg. Understanding how fracture risk indicators (FRI) differ under these loading conditions can provide valuable insights into the mechanical vulnerabilities of the femur. Current clinical protocols for assessing hip fracture risk often rely on imaging and analysis of a single hip, typically chosen at random. However, bilateral differences in bone morphology, density, and strength have been reported in previous studies, raising concerns about the accuracy of risk assessments based on unilateral measurements. The potential for variability between the left and right femurs suggests that assessing only one side could lead to an incomplete or inaccurate prediction of fracture risk. Despite these concerns, bilateral hip assessments are not routinely performed in clinical practice, largely due to time and cost considerations. This study aims to address the knowledge gap by systematically comparing the fracture risk of left and right femurs under two distinct loading scenarios: single-legged stance and sideways falls. Using QCT-based FEA models, this research evaluates and compares FRI distributions in the femoral neck region for both femurs in a cohort of thirty anonymous patients. The study also investigates sex-based differences in FRI to explore whether women, who are more prone to osteoporosis, exhibit greater susceptibility to hip fractures compared to men. The findings of this study have significant implications for clinical practice and public health. By demonstrating the variability in fracture risk between the left and right femurs, the results highlight the importance of bilateral hip assessments in providing a more accurate prediction of fracture risk. Furthermore, understanding the sex-based differences in FRI distributions can inform targeted preventive measures and treatment strategies for high-risk populations, particularly postmenopausal women. In addition to its clinical relevance, the study contributes to the growing body of research on the biomechanics of hip fractures. By focusing on the superior and inferior regions of the femoral neck, the analysis provides insights into the specific areas most vulnerable to fracture under different loading conditions. These findings could inform the development of improved diagnostic tools, such as advanced imaging protocols or personalized FEA models, to better identify individuals at risk. This research is particularly timely given the increasing availability and accessibility of QCT imaging and computational tools. The integration of advanced imaging techniques with biomechanical modeling has the potential to revolutionize the field of fracture risk assessment, moving beyond traditional measures such as BMD to a more comprehensive evaluation of bone strength and fracture susceptibility. However, the implementation of such approaches in clinical practice requires robust evidence to support their utility and cost-effectiveness. This study provides a step in that direction by demonstrating the feasibility and clinical relevance of bilateral FEA-based fracture risk assessments. In summary, this study investigates the bilateral variations in hip fracture risk under different loading scenarios using QCT-based FEA. The results underscore the need for bilateral hip scanning to improve the accuracy of fracture risk prediction and highlight the importance of considering sex-based differences in fracture susceptibility. By addressing these critical issues, the research aims to contribute to the development of more effective strategies for preventing hip fractures in the aging population, ultimately reducing the associated healthcare costs and improving patient outcomes. The study was designed to investigate the variations in fall-induced hip fracture risk between the right and left femurs using finite element analysis (FEA) derived from quantitative computed tomography (QCT) data. Thirty subjects, comprising anonymous patients aged 65 years and older, were selected for this study. The inclusion criteria required the availability of high-quality QCT scans of both the left and right femurs, and subjects with any prior hip surgeries, implants, or pathological abnormalities affecting the femur were excluded. All patient data were anonymized, and ethical approval was obtained prior to the study. QCT imaging was performed using a standard clinical protocol to ensure consistency across all scans. The scans were acquired at a resolution sufficient to capture detailed bone geometry and density variations, with slice thicknesses of 1 mm. Calibration phantoms were included during the scans to enable conversion of Hounsfield units to bone mineral density (BMD). The QCT images were preprocessed and segmented to isolate the femoral bone structures, including cortical and trabecular regions, using commercially available image analysis software. The left and right femurs were segmented separately for each subject. Following segmentation, three-dimensional models of the femurs were generated for each individual. The models were imported into a finite element analysis software platform for simulation. The finite element meshes were constructed using tetrahedral elements, with mesh density refined in the femoral neck region to improve accuracy in the region of interest. The material properties of the bone were assigned based on the BMD values derived from the QCT data, using established density-elasticity relationships. The bone was modeled as a linear, isotropic material for simplicity, given the primary focus on comparative fracture risk between the two femurs. Two loading configurations were simulated for each femur: (1) single-legged stance and (2) sideways fall. For the single-legged stance configuration, the load was applied vertically through the femoral head, simulating the distribution of body weight during single-leg support. The magnitude of the load was scaled to represent 2.5 times the subject’s body weight, accounting for dynamic effects during normal gait. For the sideways fall configuration, the load was applied laterally to the greater trochanter, simulating the impact forces experienced during a fall from standing height. The magnitude of the lateral force was derived from published data on typical fall dynamics. In both configurations, the distal femur was fully constrained to replicate the boundary conditions at the knee joint. Fracture risk indicators (FRIs) were calculated for each loading scenario. The FRI was defined as the ratio of the maximum von Mises stress in the femoral neck to the ultimate strength of the bone at that location. The ultimate strength was estimated using empirical relationships based on local BMD. FRIs were evaluated separately for the superior and inferior regions of the femoral neck to identify regional differences in fracture susceptibility. Stress and strain distributions were mapped to visualize the areas of highest risk. To assess the variability between left and right femurs, paired analyses were conducted for each subject. FRIs were compared between the left and right femurs for both loading configurations. Statistical analysis was performed using a paired sample t-test to determine whether the differences in FRIs between the two femurs were significant. A significance level of p ≤ 0.05 was considered indicative of statistically significant variability. Additionally, subgroup analyses were conducted to examine gender-based differences in fracture risk. The FRI distributions for men and women were compared using independent sample t-tests. Data processing and statistical analyses were conducted using MATLAB and statistical software. Quality control measures were implemented throughout the process to ensure the robustness of the results. For example, mesh convergence studies were performed to verify that the finite element results were independent of mesh density. Similarly, sensitivity analyses were conducted to evaluate the impact of variations in material property assignments and loading conditions on the calculated FRIs. The results of the simulations were validated qualitatively by comparing the predicted fracture risk patterns with clinical data on common hip fracture locations. While direct experimental validation was beyond the scope of this study, the use of well-established modeling techniques and parameter choices ensured the reliability of the results. Finally, the findings were interpreted in the context of clinical practice. The potential implications for bilateral hip assessment in osteoporosis screening and fracture risk prediction were discussed, particularly in light of the observed variability in FRIs between the left and right femurs. These findings support the hypothesis that bilateral femoral assessment is essential for accurately predicting hip fracture risk and provide insights into the regions of the femoral neck most susceptible to fracture. Specifically, the sideways fall configuration resulted in markedly higher FRI values at the superior aspects of the femoral neck for both left and right femurs. The average increase in FRI at the superior surface during a sideways fall, compared to the single-legged stance, ranged from 64% to 74%. Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked genetic disorder caused by mutations in the DMD gene, which encodes the protein dystrophin, a critical component of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex responsible for maintaining the structural integrity of muscle fibers. Affecting approximately 1 in 3,500 to 5,000 live male births worldwide, DMD is characterized by progressive muscle weakness, loss of ambulation (LOA), and premature mortality due to respiratory and/or cardiac failure [1,2]. Advances in genetic diagnostics have enabled the identification of a wide spectrum of DMD mutations, with deletions, duplications, and point mutations being the most common. These molecular insights have facilitated the development of mutation-specific therapeutic approaches, such as exon-skipping strategies, aimed at restoring the dystrophin protein in affected individuals [3]. Despite these advances, the variability in disease progression and response to therapy among patients necessitates an accurate understanding of the natural history of DMD to optimize clinical trial design and outcome assessment. The natural history of DMD follows a predictable trajectory, with boys typically achieving independent ambulation during early childhood but experiencing progressive motor decline starting around the age of 6 to 8 years. This decline is often exacerbated by the loss of dystrophin, which renders muscle fibers more susceptible to damage during contraction. The NorthStar Ambulatory Assessment (NSAA), a validated, disease-specific tool, has been widely adopted to measure functional motor abilities in ambulant individuals with DMD [4]. The NSAA consists of 17 items evaluating key motor functions, such as rising from the floor, climbing stairs, and walking, with the raw scores providing a cumulative measure of motor performance. More recently, a linearized version of the NSAA has been introduced, offering improved sensitivity to motor changes over time compared to the raw scale [5]. Longitudinal studies leveraging the NSAA have provided critical insights into the typical rates of motor decline in DMD, which are essential for benchmarking therapeutic efficacy in clinical trials. One of the most significant disease-modifying strategies for DMD to date has been the use of glucocorticoids, such as prednisone and deflazacort, which have been shown to delay LOA, preserve respiratory function, and reduce scoliosis progression [6]. The mechanisms underlying the benefits of glucocorticoids in DMD are multifactorial, involving anti-inflammatory effects, stabilization of muscle membranes, and modulation of muscle regeneration [7]. However, the timing of glucocorticoid initiation remains a topic of considerable debate, with emerging evidence suggesting that earlier initiation, particularly between the ages of 3 and 5 years, may confer additional benefits in preserving motor function [8]. A systematic evaluation of the temporal effects of glucocorticoid therapy on motor outcomes is therefore critical to refining treatment guidelines and informing the design of clinical trials investigating novel therapeutic agents. In addition to pharmacological interventions, genotype-phenotype correlations have garnered increasing attention in the field of DMD research. Specific DMD mutations have been associated with differences in disease progression, which may have important implications for therapeutic targeting and stratification of clinical trial participants [9]. For example, deletions amenable to skipping exons 44 and 46 have been associated with slower rates of motor decline, whereas deletions involving exons 51 and 53 are linked to more rapid disease progression [10]. These observations underscore the need to account for genetic heterogeneity when interpreting clinical trial outcomes and developing personalized treatment strategies. The NorthStar Network, a collaborative effort among multiple centers specializing in DMD care, has established a robust platform for collecting standardized longitudinal data on motor function in DMD patients. By analyzing NSAA data from over 500 ambulant boys with DMD in the UK, as well as additional data from 172 boys in Italy, this study provides a comprehensive assessment of the factors influencing motor decline in DMD. Specifically, it evaluates the effects of early glucocorticoid initiation and genotype on NSAA trajectories and LOA. The findings have important implications for optimizing clinical trial design, particularly in terms of selecting appropriate endpoints, stratifying patient populations, and determining sample size requirements. The current study builds on prior work by incorporating a linearized NSAA scoring system, which enhances the precision and interpretability of longitudinal motor function data. Previous research has demonstrated that the raw NSAA scores, while clinically meaningful, exhibit ceiling and floor effects that may limit their sensitivity to detect subtle changes over time [11]. Linearization addresses these limitations by transforming the raw scores into a continuous scale, allowing for a more nuanced assessment of motor trajectories. By applying this methodology to one of the largest DMD cohorts studied to date, the present analysis offers novel insights into the natural history of motor decline in DMD and the modifying effects of genotype and glucocorticoid therapy. Furthermore, the study highlights the critical window of intervention in DMD, emphasizing the importance of initiating glucocorticoid therapy during early childhood to maximize motor preservation. This observation aligns with recent guidelines advocating for earlier treatment initiation but also raises questions about the long-term safety and efficacy of such an approach [12]. The data also underscore the heterogeneity in motor outcomes associated with different genotypes, reinforcing the need for personalized approaches to therapy development and trial design. These findings are particularly relevant in the context of exon-skipping therapies, which target specific DMD mutations and are currently under investigation in preclinical and clinical studies [13]. In conclusion, this study leverages longitudinal NSAA data to provide a comprehensive characterization of motor function decline in DMD, with a focus on the modifying effects of genotype and early glucocorticoid treatment. By integrating these findings into the design of clinical trials, researchers can improve the precision of endpoint selection, ensure appropriate stratification of participants, and ultimately enhance the likelihood of demonstrating therapeutic efficacy. The insights gained from this work are expected to contribute significantly to the ongoing development of effective therapies for DMD, addressing the urgent unmet needs of this patient population. Study Design and Data Sources This retrospective observational study analysed standardised clinical data collected through the NorthStar Network, a collaborative database encompassing multiple clinical centres in the United Kingdom. Data from 513 ambulant boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) were included, spanning the years 2004 to 2012. For further analyses of genotype-specific subpopulations, additional data from 172 ambulant boys with DMD were obtained from clinical centres in Italy. Ethical approval for data collection and analysis was granted by the respective institutional review boards, and consent was provided by all participants or their legal guardians in line with applicable regulations and the Declaration of Helsinki [1]. Participants Inclusion criteria for the primary cohort required a confirmed genetic diagnosis of DMD, defined as the presence of a mutation in the DMD gene leading to a frameshift or premature stop codon, and the ability to ambulate independently at the time of enrolment. Participants with significant comorbidities unrelated to DMD, prior participation in interventional clinical trials, or incomplete longitudinal follow-up were excluded. For the genotype subgroup analysis, participants were stratified based on specific deletions amenable to exons 44, 46, 51, and 53 skipping. Age at loss of ambulation (LOA) was defined as the age at which individuals became permanently wheelchair-dependent, as recorded in the clinical database. Assessment of Motor Function Motor function was assessed using the NorthStar Ambulatory Assessment (NSAA), a validated 17-item functional scale specifically designed for ambulant individuals with DMD [2]. Each item is scored on a 3-point ordinal scale (0 = unable, 1 = partial performance, 2 = full performance), yielding a raw total score ranging from 0 to 34. To facilitate statistical analysis and account for the scale's non-linear properties, raw NSAA scores were transformed into linearised scores using Rasch analysis, which has been demonstrated to improve sensitivity to changes over time [3]. The linearised NSAA scale ranges from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating better motor function. Glucocorticoid Exposure Data on glucocorticoid use were extracted from clinical records, including age at initiation, duration of use, and dosing regimens. Participants were categorised based on the age at which glucocorticoid therapy commenced: early initiation (3–5 years), late initiation (≥6 years), or no glucocorticoid therapy. Prednisone and deflazacort were the two most commonly prescribed glucocorticoids, and their use was treated as equivalent in the analysis due to their similar effects on motor function reported in previous studies [4]. Discontinuation of glucocorticoid therapy during the study period was also recorded, and these participants were censored at the time of cessation for subsequent longitudinal analyses. Statistical Analysis Descriptive statistics were used to summarise baseline characteristics of the cohort, including age distribution, NSAA scores, and genotype frequencies. For longitudinal analyses, linear mixed-effects models were employed to assess changes in motor function over time, with random intercepts and slopes to account for inter-individual variability. Age, genotype, and glucocorticoid exposure were included as fixed effects. The primary outcome was the annual rate of decline in linearised NSAA scores, expressed in units per year. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis was used to estimate median age at LOA, and the association between pre-LOA NSAA scores and time to LOA was modelled using Cox proportional hazards regression. For the genotype analysis, the UK and Italian datasets were combined to maximise statistical power. Differences in motor function trajectories between genotype subgroups were assessed using pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction to adjust for multiple testing. Statistical significance was set at p<0.05 for all analyses. Missing Data Missing data were handled using multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE), which preserves variability and reduces bias by generating multiple plausible datasets based on observed data [5]. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to confirm the robustness of the results, comparing findings from the imputed datasets with those from a complete-case analysis. Missingness was assessed to ensure it was consistent with a missing-at-random (MAR) mechanism. Software and Tools All statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 4.1.2; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). The "lme4" package was used for mixed-effects modelling [6], and the "survival" package was used for time-to-event analyses [7]. Rasch transformations for the NSAA raw scores were applied using the "TAM" package [8]. Quality Control Data integrity was ensured through systematic quality control procedures, including cross-validation of clinical records against database entries and independent verification of genetic diagnoses by certified laboratories. NSAA assessments were performed by trained physiotherapists following standardised protocols, with inter-rater reliability evaluated periodically to ensure consistency across centres. Limitations This study is subject to certain limitations inherent to its observational design, including potential confounding by unmeasured variables such as variations in physiotherapy regimens or socioeconomic factors. Additionally, the inclusion of Italian participants for the genotype analysis may introduce variability due to differences in healthcare practices, although efforts were made to harmonise data collection procedures across cohorts. The increasing reliance on digital communication systems has brought forth a critical need for mechanisms that ensure both secure and reliable data transmission. Traditionally, encryption and error correction are treated as two distinct processes, with encryption safeguarding confidentiality and error correction ensuring data reliability in noisy channels. However, this separation entails a higher computational overhead and often results in inefficiencies, particularly in resource-constrained environments. To address these challenges, joint encryption-encoding schemes have been proposed, offering an integrated approach to achieve both security and error correction in a unified framework [1]. Such schemes aim to streamline communication systems by combining encryption and encoding into a single operation, reducing computational complexity and enhancing data transmission performance. In code-based cryptography, linear codes have historically played a significant role in the design of joint encryption-encoding schemes. However, conventional linear codes, such as Reed-Solomon or Bose-Chaudhuri-Hocquenghem (BCH) codes, often require large key sizes to achieve satisfactory levels of security. This limitation becomes particularly problematic in scenarios where key storage and transmission bandwidth are constrained. Furthermore, while these codes exhibit strong error correction capabilities, they may not provide optimal performance in balancing security and reliability requirements. Low-Density Parity-Check (LDPC) codes, first introduced by Gallager [2], have emerged as a promising alternative due to their excellent error correction performance, low decoding complexity, and flexible rate adaptability. Their inherent sparsity and structured design make LDPC codes well-suited for modern communication systems, including joint encryption-encoding applications. Building on the advantages of LDPC codes, Quasi-Cyclic LDPC (QC-LDPC) codes have garnered significant interest in recent years. QC-LDPC codes represent a class of structured LDPC codes with cyclic and quasi-cyclic properties, enabling efficient hardware implementation and reduced storage requirements [3]. These codes are particularly attractive in practical systems, where computational efficiency and scalability are critical design considerations. Moreover, the structured nature of QC-LDPC codes allows for the generation of large codeword lengths with compact representations, further contributing to their suitability for joint encryption-encoding schemes. Finite geometry-based codes, such as those derived from projective and affine geometries, provide a robust foundation for designing QC-LDPC codes with desirable properties. Finite geometry offers a well-defined mathematical framework for constructing codes with high minimum distance, structured sparsity, and tunable parameters [4]. By leveraging the geometric properties of finite fields, QC-LDPC codes based on finite geometry can achieve superior error correction performance while maintaining computational efficiency. These characteristics make finite geometry-based QC-LDPC codes an ideal candidate for developing secure and reliable joint encryption-encoding systems. In this paper, we propose a novel joint encryption-encoding scheme that utilizes QC-LDPC codes based on finite geometry to address the limitations of existing approaches. Our scheme integrates the error correction capabilities of QC-LDPC codes with encryption functionality, achieving a significant reduction in key size without compromising security. Specifically, we demonstrate that the key size in our proposed scheme is only one-fifth of that required by the best-known similar systems. This reduction is attributed to the structured nature of finite geometry-based QC-LDPC codes, which allows for efficient key generation and storage. Additionally, our scheme supports a wide range of transmission rates, making it adaptable to diverse communication and cryptographic requirements. The security of the proposed scheme is rigorously analyzed against known cryptanalytic attacks targeting code-based cryptosystems. We show that the inherent structure of QC-LDPC codes, combined with the randomness introduced during encryption, provides robust protection against attacks such as information set decoding and structural recovery [5]. Furthermore, the low computational complexity of our scheme ensures that it can be implemented in real-time applications with minimal resource consumption. This paper is structured as follows. In Section 2, we provide a detailed overview of QC-LDPC codes and their construction using finite geometry. Section 3 introduces the proposed joint encryption-encoding scheme, detailing its architecture and key generation process. In Section 4, we present a comprehensive security analysis, highlighting the scheme's resilience against various cryptanalytic techniques. Section 5 evaluates the performance of the proposed scheme in terms of key size, transmission rate, and computational efficiency, providing a comparison with existing solutions. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper and outlines potential directions for future research. By addressing the dual challenges of reliability and security in a unified framework, our proposed scheme advances the state-of-the-art in joint encryption-encoding systems. The integration of QC-LDPC codes based on finite geometry not only enhances error correction performance but also achieves significant improvements in key size and computational efficiency. These contributions underscore the potential of the proposed scheme to meet the demands of modern communication and cryptographic systems, paving the way for further innovations in this domain. Preliminaries on QC-LDPC Codes Based on Finite Geometry To develop the proposed joint encryption-encoding scheme, we utilized Quasi Cyclic-Low Density Parity Check (QC-LDPC) codes derived from finite geometry. QC-LDPC codes are a subclass of LDPC codes characterized by their quasi-cyclic structure, which simplifies their encoding and decoding processes while maintaining excellent error correction performance. Specifically, the QC-LDPC codes used in this work were constructed based on finite geometries, such as projective and Euclidean geometries over finite fields. These constructions are known to yield structured parity-check matrices with favorable cyclic properties [1]. The basic structure of the parity-check matrix \(H\) was derived from incidence matrices of the chosen finite geometry. Let \(q\) denote the order of the finite field \(\mathbb{F}q\), and let the finite geometry be defined on a vector space of dimension \(m\) over \(\mathbb{F}q\). The points and lines in this geometry were mapped to the rows and columns of the matrix \(H\), ensuring that each row corresponds to a hyperplane and each column to an affine point. The resulting matrix \(H\) is sparse, possesses a quasi-cyclic structure, and exhibits a girth greater than or equal to 6, which minimizes the presence of short cycles in the associated Tanner graph. To ensure consistency with communication standards and to simplify hardware implementation, we adopted QC-LDPC codes with circulant submatrices. Each circulant submatrix was represented as a cyclically shifted identity matrix. The parameters of the code, such as the block length \(n\), code rate \(R\), and row/column weights, were carefully chosen to meet the desired trade-off between error correction performance and computational efficiency. 2. Joint Encryption-Encoding Scheme Design The joint encryption-encoding scheme integrates the cryptographic and error correction functionalities into a single unified process. The main advantage of this approach is the reduction in key size and computational overhead while simultaneously achieving security and reliability. The proposed scheme operates in three stages: key generation, encryption-encoding, and decoding. 2.1 Key Generation In the key generation stage, a secret key \(K\) was generated and distributed securely to both the transmitter and receiver. The key \(K\) was derived from a random seed and used to pseudorandomly select a permutation matrix \(P\) and an invertible scrambling matrix \(S\) over \(\mathbb{F}q\). These matrices were used to obfuscate the structure of the QC-LDPC code and to introduce cryptographic security. The public parity-check matrix \(Hp\) was constructed as: \[ Hp = S H P, \] where \(H\) is the parity-check matrix of the underlying QC-LDPC code. The matrices \(S\) and \(P\) ensure that the public matrix \(Hp\) is computationally indistinguishable from a random sparse matrix, thwarting structural attacks such as those based on the algebraic or combinatorial properties of \(H\) [2]. 2.2 Encryption-Encoding Process The encryption-encoding process was designed to simultaneously encode the message \(m\) and encrypt it into a codeword \(c\). Let \(m \in \mathbb{F}q^k\) denote the plaintext message, where \(k\) is the dimension of the code. The process is as follows: 1. Message Embedding: The plaintext \(m\) was first mapped into a binary vector \(x\) of length \(n-k\) using a systematic generator matrix \(G\) derived from the public parity-check matrix \(Hp\). This ensures that \(x\) is a valid syndrome vector for \(Hp\): \[ Hp x^T = 0. \] 2. Scrambling: The encoded vector \(x\) was then scrambled using the secret matrices \(S\) and \(P\) to produce the encrypted codeword \(c\): \[ c = S x P. \] This step ensures that the codeword \(c\) is indistinguishable from a random vector, enhancing the cryptographic strength of the system. 3. Transmission: The resulting ciphertext \(c\) was transmitted over a noisy communication channel. Due to the error-correction properties of the QC-LDPC code, the scheme is robust to bit-flip errors introduced during transmission. 2.3 Decoding At the receiver, the decoding process involved both decryption and error correction. The received vector \(y\) was first descrambled using the inverse of the secret matrices: \[ x = S^{-1} y P^{-1}. \] Subsequently, a belief propagation (BP) algorithm was employed to decode \(x\) back into the original plaintext \(m\). The BP algorithm iteratively updated the probabilities of each bit in \(x\) based on the structure of the parity-check matrix \(H\) and the received vector \(y\), achieving accurate error correction with low computational complexity [3]. 3. Security Analysis The security of the proposed scheme relies on the hardness of decoding a random binary linear code, a problem widely believed to be NP-hard. The incorporation of secret matrices \(S\) and \(P\) obfuscates the structure of the QC-LDPC code, making it resistant to structural cryptanalysis. Furthermore, the key size was reduced to approximately \(1/5\) of similar systems by leveraging the quasi-cyclic properties of QC-LDPC codes, without compromising security. The system was evaluated against known attacks, including information set decoding, algebraic attacks, and combinatorial decoding attacks, and was found to be secure under all scenarios tested. 4. Computational Complexity The computational complexity of the encryption-encoding process was analyzed in terms of matrix multiplications and syndrome computations. Due to the quasi-cyclic structure of the codes, the multiplication of circulant submatrices could be implemented efficiently using cyclic shift operations. The decoding process, dominated by the BP algorithm, exhibited linear complexity in the block length \(n\). These properties make the proposed scheme suitable for practical implementations in resource-constrained environments. References [1] MacKay, D. J. C., & Neal, R. M. (1996). On the inherent intractability of certain coding problems. IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 24(3), 384–386. [3] Richardson, T. J., & Urbanke, R. L. (2001). The capacity of low-density parity-check codes under message-passing decoding. IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 47(2), 599–618. Key Size Reduction One of the primary advantages of the proposed joint encryption-encoding scheme is the significant reduction in key size compared to existing systems. By leveraging Quasi Cyclic-Low Density Parity Check (QC-LDPC) codes constructed from finite geometry, the key size is reduced to approximately one-fifth of that required by the best-known comparable system [1]. This reduction is achieved without compromising the cryptographic security of the system. Specifically, the algebraic structure of finite geometry ensures robust cryptographic properties while maintaining a compact representation of keys. The key size reduction directly translates to lower storage requirements and improved practicality for resource-constrained environments such as Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices and embedded systems. To validate these claims, a series of simulations were performed comparing the proposed scheme with a baseline system employing classical LDPC codes for encryption-encoding. The results indicate that the proposed QC-LDPC-based scheme achieves the same level of error correction performance and security with a significantly smaller key size. This improvement is particularly beneficial for applications where memory and computational resources are limited, demonstrating that the scheme is well-suited for modern communication standards. The cortical microtubule (CMT) array is a highly dynamic and self-organizing network that plays a pivotal role in the growth and development of plant cells. Localized at the inner surface of the plasma membrane, CMTs are key regulators of cell wall deposition and the overall mechanical properties of plant cells. By guiding the deposition of cellulose microfibrils, CMTs influence cell shape, tissue architecture, and organ morphogenesis. Unlike animal cells, which rely on centrosomes to organize their microtubule arrays, plant cells utilize an acentrosomal system, where microtubules nucleate, grow, and interact in a decentralized manner. This unique organizational mode has made the plant CMT array a valuable model for studying the principles of microtubule dynamics and interactions. A defining feature of CMTs is their dynamic instability, characterized by stochastic transitions between growth and shrinkage at their plus ends. This dynamic behavior is modulated by a variety of microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs) and is critical for the establishment and maintenance of CMT arrays. In addition to intrinsic dynamic instability, CMTs interact with one another through a range of mechanisms, including bundling, severing, and polymerization-induced encounters. These interactions not only contribute to the spatial organization of the array but also influence the functional output of the CMT network, such as the control of cellulose microfibril orientation. Despite substantial progress in understanding the molecular players that regulate CMT dynamics and interactions, how the overall organization of a CMT array feeds back to influence individual microtubule behaviors remains an open question. One specific interaction of interest is encounter-based catastrophe, a phenomenon in which the growing end of a microtubule contacts another microtubule and subsequently undergoes a transition to depolymerization. This mechanism has been observed in both in vitro and in vivo systems and is thought to play a central role in shaping microtubule arrays. In plant cells, where CMTs are closely associated with the plasma membrane and are subject to frequent interactions with surrounding microtubules, encounter-based catastrophe is likely to be a major determinant of CMT organization. However, the extent to which the spatial arrangement of CMTs—ranging from highly ordered, parallel arrays to more disordered, net-like configurations—influences encounter-based catastrophe rates and microtubule dynamics as a whole is not well understood. The mechanical basis of encounter-based catastrophe adds an additional layer of complexity to the regulation of CMTs. When a growing microtubule encounters another microtubule, the outcome of the interaction depends on several factors, including the angle of contact, the structural rigidity of the microtubules, and the anchoring of the microtubules to the plasma membrane. It has been hypothesized that disordered CMT arrays, characterized by a wide range of microtubule orientations, may increase the likelihood of microtubule interactions and consequently elevate encounter-based catastrophe rates. Conversely, ordered arrays, in which microtubules are aligned in parallel, may reduce such interactions and promote sustained growth. These potential feedback mechanisms between CMT organization and individual microtubule behavior have yet to be systematically explored in plant cells. In this study, we sought to investigate the relationship between CMT array organization and encounter-based catastrophe in Arabidopsis epidermal cells. We hypothesized that disordered CMT arrays, with their mixed orientations, would lead to higher rates of encounter-based catastrophe compared to ordered arrays. Using live-cell imaging and quantitative analysis, we examined the dynamics of CMTs in cotyledon and leaf pavement cells, which exhibit varying degrees of CMT organization. We further assessed how plasma membrane anchoring and CMT pause behavior influence the likelihood of encounter-based catastrophe. Our findings reveal that encounter-based catastrophe is the predominant mechanism of CMT depolymerization in Arabidopsis epidermal cells and that its frequency is strongly influenced by the spatial arrangement of the CMT array. In addition to demonstrating the prevalence of encounter-based catastrophe, we show that disordered CMT arrays exhibit higher proportions of encounter-based catastrophe relative to free catastrophe, as well as an overall increase in catastrophe events. Microtubules in disordered arrays were more likely to pause upon encountering another microtubule, a behavior that often preceded depolymerization. Moreover, the anchoring strength of CMTs to the plasma membrane emerged as a key factor influencing encounter outcomes, with tightly anchored CMTs being more prone to undergo encounter-based catastrophe. These results suggest that the organization of the CMT array not only reflects the dynamic properties of individual microtubules but also exerts a feedback effect on their behavior through mechanical constraints and interaction opportunities. Our study provides new insights into how CMT organization influences microtubule dynamics in plant cells. By linking CMT array patterning to encounter-based catastrophe rates, we highlight a bidirectional relationship in which the collective behavior of the array shapes, and is shaped by, the dynamics of its individual components. These findings underscore the importance of considering both intrinsic microtubule dynamics and higher-order organizational features when studying the plant cytoskeleton. Furthermore, our results have implications for understanding the mechanical principles underlying acentrosomal microtubule organization, not only in plant cells but also in other systems that rely on similar mechanisms for cytoskeletal regulation. Plant Material and Growth Conditions Arabidopsis thaliana plants (Columbia-0 ecotype) were used for all experiments. Seeds were surface sterilized with 70% ethanol and 0.05% Tween-20 for 5 minutes, followed by three washes with sterile water. Sterilized seeds were plated on 1/2 Murashige and Skoog (MS) medium supplemented with 1% sucrose and 0.8% agar. Plates were stratified at 4°C in the dark for 3 days and then transferred to a growth chamber at 22°C under long-day conditions (16 h light/8 h dark). For imaging, 4- to 7-day-old seedlings were used. When specified, clasp-1 mutants were used to study the effects of microtubule anchoring on encounter-based catastrophe. Live-Cell Imaging Live-cell imaging of cortical microtubules (CMTs) was performed using epidermal cells from cotyledons and leaves. Seedlings were mounted in water between a glass slide and a coverslip with a thin layer of 1% agar to stabilize the sample. Imaging was conducted on a spinning disk confocal microscope (Andor or Yokogawa system) equipped with a 60× oil immersion objective lens (NA 1.4). GFP-tagged TUA5 (GFP-TUA5) was used to visualize microtubules. For time-lapse imaging, images were acquired at 2-second intervals for a total duration of 3–5 minutes to capture the dynamic behavior of CMTs. Imaging conditions were maintained to minimize photobleaching and photodamage. Quantification of Microtubule Catastrophes CMT catastrophe events were defined as the transition from a polymerizing or paused state to a depolymerizing state. Catastrophes were further categorized into two types: encounter-based catastrophes, which occurred when a growing CMT collided with another CMT, and free catastrophes, which occurred independently of any observable interaction. To distinguish between these, the position and timing of catastrophe events were analyzed in relation to nearby CMTs. Encounters were identified as instances where the growing tip of a CMT came into close proximity (within 0.5 μm) of another CMT and subsequently underwent catastrophe. Free catastrophes were assigned when no such encounter was observed. Measurement of CMT Ordering To assess the overall organization of CMT arrays, the angular distribution of CMTs was quantified using ImageJ with the FibrilTool plugin. The degree of ordering was calculated as the nematic order parameter (S), which ranges from 0 (completely disordered) to 1 (perfectly aligned). Ordered arrays were defined as regions with S > 0.5, while disordered arrays had S ≤ 0.5. Analysis was performed on maximum intensity projections of confocal z-stacks. Analysis of CMT Anchoring The strength of CMT anchoring to the plasma membrane was assessed qualitatively by observing the mobility of CMTs during growth and interactions. CMTs were categorized as tightly anchored if they exhibited minimal lateral movement during polymerization or depolymerization, and as weakly anchored if they displayed noticeable sliding or detachment from the membrane. To further validate these observations, clasp-1 mutant plants were used as a model for reduced microtubule anchoring. Comparisons of catastrophe rates between wild-type and clasp-1 mutants were used to assess the impact of anchoring strength on encounter-based catastrophe. Data Analysis and Statistical Methods Quantitative data on catastrophe events, encounter frequencies, and angular distributions were extracted from time-lapse images using custom MATLAB scripts and ImageJ. The proportion of encounter-based catastrophes relative to total catastrophes was calculated for each region of interest. Rates of catastrophe (Fcat) were determined as the total number of catastrophes per unit time divided by the total CMT polymerization time. To compare ordered and disordered arrays, regions of interest were manually selected based on nematic order parameter values. Statistical analyses were performed using R software. Differences between groups were evaluated using Student’s t-tests or one-way ANOVA, followed by post hoc Tukey tests, with a significance threshold of p < 0.05. Data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean. Validation of Encounter-Based Catastrophe Mechanism To test the hypothesis that encounter-based catastrophe is influenced by CMT organization, the frequency and spatial distribution of encounters were compared between ordered and disordered arrays. Encounters were further classified by the angle of interaction between CMTs. Acute-angle encounters (<45°) and wide-angle encounters (≥45°) were analyzed separately to determine their contribution to catastrophe rates. Additionally, the duration of pause events preceding depolymerization was recorded for each encounter-based catastrophe to assess the mechanistic basis of this phenomenon. Control Experiments To ensure that observed differences in catastrophe rates were not due to variations in imaging conditions or artifacts, control experiments were performed under identical imaging settings across all samples. Photobleaching was minimized by using low laser power and short exposure times. To confirm that GFP-TUA5 labeling did not alter microtubule dynamics, catastrophe rates in GFP-TUA5 lines were compared to those reported in unlabeled wild-type cells from the literature. Reproducibility and Replication All experiments were performed using at least three independent biological replicates, with a minimum of five cells analyzed per replicate. Each cell was imaged in multiple regions to capture both ordered and disordered arrays. Data from replicates were pooled for statistical analysis, and trends were validated across independent experiments to ensure reproducibility. To investigate the relationship between cortical microtubule (CMT) patterning and encounter-based catastrophe, we employed live-cell imaging in Arabidopsis cotyledon and leaf epidermal cells expressing GFP-tubulin. This approach allowed us to analyze both the spatial organization of CMT arrays and the frequency and type of catastrophe events. The results revealed a strong dependence of encounter-based catastrophe rates on CMT array organization and highlighted the role of mechanical interactions in influencing CMT dynamics. We first quantified the relative contributions of encounter-based and free catastrophe events in Arabidopsis epidermal cells. Across all observed arrays, approximately 87% of catastrophe events were encounter-based, wherein a growing CMT polymer collided with another CMT and subsequently depolymerized. The remaining catastrophes (13%) occurred in the absence of direct CMT encounters and were classified as free catastrophes. These data indicate that encounter-based catastrophe is the dominant mechanism driving CMT depolymerization in vivo. To determine whether the organization of CMT arrays influences catastrophe dynamics, we compared ordered (parallel) and disordered (mixed orientation) CMT arrays. Ordered arrays were characterized by largely parallel CMTs with a high degree of alignment, whereas disordered arrays displayed mixed orientations and intersecting CMTs. Disordered arrays exhibited significantly higher proportions of encounter-based catastrophes relative to free catastrophes compared to ordered arrays. Specifically, disordered arrays showed a 1.7-fold increase in encounter-based catastrophes. This suggests that the increased frequency of CMT intersections in disordered arrays provides more opportunities for MT-MT interactions that lead to catastrophe. In addition to differences in the relative contributions of encounter-based and free catastrophes, disordered arrays also had a higher overall frequency of catastrophe events. We calculated the catastrophe frequency (Fcat) as the number of catastrophes per unit time normalized to the total length of CMTs in the array. Disordered arrays exhibited a significantly higher Fcat than ordered arrays, consistent with the hypothesis that increased CMT interactions drive higher rates of catastrophe. This result highlights the feedback between CMT organization and individual microtubule dynamics, wherein disordered arrays promote more frequent catastrophe events, potentially contributing to further disorganization. Accommodation is the process by which the eye changes its optical power to maintain focus on objects at varying distances. This dynamic adjustment is primarily facilitated by the ciliary muscle, which alters the shape of the crystalline lens to achieve focal changes. In phakic eyes, accommodation is a well-documented phenomenon, extensively studied due to its critical role in visual function. However, the accommodative mechanism is altered in pseudophakic eyes, where the natural crystalline lens is replaced by an intraocular lens (IOL). While the IOL lacks the deformable properties of the natural lens, pilocarpine-induced accommodation has been shown to influence the position of the IOL and the geometry of the eye. Understanding these changes is important for optimizing visual outcomes in pseudophakic patients, particularly in the context of presbyopia-correcting IOLs and other advanced lens designs. Pilocarpine, a muscarinic cholinergic agonist, is commonly used to pharmacologically induce accommodation by stimulating the ciliary muscle. This agent has been extensively employed in research to investigate the accommodative response in both phakic and pseudophakic eyes. In pseudophakic eyes, where the mechanical properties of the IOL and the surrounding ocular structures differ from those of the natural lens, pilocarpine-driven accommodation provides unique insights into the dynamics of ocular biometry. Previous studies have demonstrated anterior movement of the IOL and changes in anterior chamber depth (ACD) during accommodation, underscoring the interaction between the ciliary muscle, the zonules, and the IOL. These findings raise intriguing questions about the extent to which other ocular parameters, such as vitreous length (VL) and axial length (AL), may change during accommodation in pseudophakic eyes. The axial length of the eye is a parameter of significant clinical relevance, particularly in refractive surgery, myopia progression studies, and the design of IOLs for cataract surgery. Changes in AL during accommodation have been reported in phakic eyes, with elongation attributed to forward movement of the lens and posterior displacement of the retina. However, the mechanisms underlying AL changes in pseudophakic eyes remain poorly understood. It has been hypothesized that ciliary muscle contraction during pilocarpine-induced accommodation might exert forces that influence the position of the IOL and the surrounding ocular structures, potentially leading to measurable changes in axial biometry. Despite these theoretical considerations, few studies have systematically examined AL changes in pseudophakic eyes during accommodation, and those that have are often limited by measurement techniques with insufficient precision or scan depth. Advances in optical imaging technology, particularly the development of ultra-long scan depth optical coherence tomography (UL-OCT), offer new opportunities to investigate these phenomena with unprecedented accuracy and comprehensiveness. Unlike traditional imaging modalities, UL-OCT enables high-resolution, full-length imaging of the eye, from the cornea to the retina, in a single scan. This capability allows for precise measurement of individual biometric components, including central corneal thickness (CCT), ACD, IOL thickness (IOLT), and VL, which collectively contribute to the overall AL. By leveraging this technology, it is possible to gain deeper insights into the structural changes that occur during accommodation, as well as to disentangle the contributions of different ocular components to changes in AL. In this study, we aimed to investigate the effects of pilocarpine-induced accommodation on axial biometry in pseudophakic eyes using a custom-built UL-OCT system. Specifically, we sought to quantify changes in key ocular parameters, including CCT, ACD, IOLT, VL, and AL, to better understand the accommodative response in eyes with implanted IOLs. Our study builds on previous research by employing a highly precise imaging modality, enabling us to characterize subtle changes that may have been overlooked in earlier investigations. Furthermore, by focusing on pseudophakic eyes, our findings contribute to the growing body of knowledge on the functional behavior of IOLs in response to pharmacologically induced accommodation. We hypothesized that pilocarpine-induced contraction of the ciliary muscle would result in measurable changes in ACD, VL, and AL, consistent with the mechanical effects of accommodation. Additionally, we expected that CCT and IOLT would remain stable, as these parameters are not directly influenced by accommodative forces. By testing these hypotheses, our goal was to elucidate the biomechanical interactions between the IOL and surrounding ocular structures during accommodation, thereby providing insights that may inform the design of future IOLs with enhanced accommodative properties. The results of this study have important implications for both clinical practice and research. From a clinical perspective, understanding the accommodative behavior of pseudophakic eyes is essential for optimizing refractive outcomes and managing patient expectations following cataract surgery. For example, subtle changes in AL during accommodation could influence the effective lens position (ELP) and, consequently, the refractive performance of the IOL. From a research perspective, our findings contribute to the broader understanding of how pharmacological agents like pilocarpine interact with the biomechanical properties of the eye, offering potential avenues for the development of novel therapeutic strategies to enhance accommodation in both phakic and pseudophakic patients. In summary, this study leverages the capabilities of UL-OCT to provide a detailed characterization of axial biometry during pilocarpine-induced accommodation in pseudophakic eyes. By examining changes in CCT, ACD, IOLT, VL, and AL, we aim to shed light on the structural adaptations that occur in response to ciliary muscle contraction, thereby contributing to a deeper understanding of the accommodative process in eyes with implanted IOLs. This study employed a custom-built ultra-long scan depth optical coherence tomography (UL-OCT) system to investigate changes in axial biometry of pseudophakic eyes during pilocarpine-induced accommodation. The study adhered to the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the institutional ethics committee. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to their enrollment. Participants The study included 25 healthy subjects (age range: 49 to 84 years) with pseudophakic right eyes implanted with monofocal intraocular lenses (IOLs). Inclusion criteria required clear ocular media, no ocular pathologies or previous surgeries other than cataract surgery, and the ability to provide informed consent. Subjects with any history of retinal surgery, glaucoma, macular disease, or systemic conditions affecting accommodation were excluded. All participants underwent a comprehensive ophthalmic examination, including visual acuity testing, slit-lamp biomicroscopy, and fundus examination, to ensure eligibility. Instrumentation The imaging was conducted using a custom-built UL-OCT system capable of capturing high-resolution, wide-depth scans of the entire eye. The system employed a swept-source OCT design with a central wavelength of 1060 nm, providing an axial scan depth of up to 14 mm in tissue. This configuration allowed for simultaneous imaging of the anterior segment, the IOL, and the posterior segment of the eye. The system's axial resolution was approximately 6 µm in tissue, ensuring accurate and reliable biometric measurements. Experimental Protocol Each subject was imaged under two conditions: non-accommodative (baseline) and accommodative states. For the baseline measurements, the subjects were asked to fixate on a distant target to ensure a relaxed accommodative state. Following baseline imaging, accommodation was pharmacologically induced using two drops of 0.5% pilocarpine hydrochloride administered in the right eye, with a 5-minute interval between drops. Thirty minutes after the administration of the first drop, imaging was repeated under the accommodative state. The sequence of pilocarpine administration and imaging was standardized to minimize variability across subjects. The left eye was left untreated to serve as a control, although it was not analyzed in this study. Imaging Procedure During each imaging session, participants were seated comfortably in front of the UL-OCT system and instructed to maintain steady fixation on the internal target light. The head was stabilized using a chin and forehead rest. A single trained operator performed all imaging to ensure consistency. Multiple volumetric scans were acquired for each subject to capture the entire axial length of the right eye. Care was taken to ensure proper alignment of the optical axis during image acquisition. The best-quality scan from each session, as determined by signal strength and absence of motion artifacts, was selected for analysis. Biometric Measurements Custom-developed automated image analysis software was used to process the UL-OCT data and extract biometric parameters. The following measurements were obtained: 1. Central Corneal Thickness (CCT): Measured as the distance between the anterior and posterior corneal surfaces. 2. Anterior Chamber Depth (ACD): Measured as the distance from the posterior surface of the cornea to the anterior surface of the IOL. 3. IOL Thickness (IOLT): Measured as the axial dimension of the IOL. 4. Vitreous Length (VL): Measured as the distance from the posterior surface of the IOL to the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). The axial length (AL) was calculated as the sum of the above parameters: AL = CCT + ACD + IOLT + VL. Measurements were performed twice for each parameter to ensure reproducibility, and the average values were used for analysis. Statistical Analysis All biometric data were analyzed using statistical software (SPSS, IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Paired t-tests were used to compare measurements between the non-accommodative and accommodative states. A significance level of P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The mean and standard deviation (SD) were reported for each parameter. Validation and Reproducibility To assess the reliability of the UL-OCT system and the automated measurement software, repeatability testing was performed on a subset of 10 subjects. Each subject underwent three consecutive imaging sessions under the same conditions, and the coefficients of variation (CoV) and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) were calculated for all biometric parameters. The results demonstrated high reproducibility and minimal variation (<2% CoV) for all measurements. Safety Considerations The use of pilocarpine hydrochloride was considered safe for this study population. All subjects were monitored for potential side effects, including ocular discomfort, headache, or systemic symptoms, during and after the imaging sessions. No adverse events were reported during the study. This methodological approach ensured high accuracy and reliability in the assessment of changes in axial biometry during pharmacologically induced accommodation in pseudophakic eyes. A total of 25 pseudophakic eyes from 25 healthy subjects (mean age: 65.4 ± 11.2 years; range: 49–84 years) were analyzed in this study. All participants underwent imaging in both the non-accommodative and accommodative states using the ultra-long scan depth optical coherence tomography (UL-OCT) system. The key biometric measurements included central corneal thickness (CCT), anterior chamber depth (ACD), intraocular lens thickness (IOLT), vitreous length (VL), and axial length (AL). Accommodation was pharmacologically induced with 0.5% pilocarpine hydrochloride, and biometric changes were assessed 30 minutes after the first drop of pilocarpine. In the non-accommodative state, the mean CCT was measured at 0.54 ± 0.03 mm, and this value did not exhibit a statistically significant change during accommodation (P > 0.05). Similarly, the IOLT remained stable between the non-accommodative and accommodative states, with a mean value of 0.93 ± 0.07 mm in both conditions (P > 0.05). These findings suggest that the corneal and intraocular lens thicknesses were unaffected by pilocarpine-induced accommodation. The ACD, defined as the distance from the posterior surface of the cornea to the anterior surface of the IOL, showed a statistically significant increase during accommodation. In the non-accommodative state, the mean ACD was 3.99 ± 0.37 mm, which increased to 4.07 ± 0.38 mm in the accommodative state. This represented a mean change of +0.08 ± 0.09 mm (P < 0.05). The increase in ACD indicates a posterior displacement of the IOL during accommodation, likely attributable to contraction of the ciliary muscle and changes in zonular tension. The VL, defined as the distance from the posterior surface of the IOL to the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), decreased significantly during accommodation. In the non-accommodative state, the mean VL was 18.01 ± 0.90 mm, which decreased to 17.97 ± 0.90 mm after pilocarpine administration. This represented a mean change of −0.04 ± 0.09 mm (P < 0.05).
