Endotracheal intubation is a critical component of airway management during general anesthesia, but it is often associated with significant hemodynamic responses, including elevations in heart rate (HR) and blood pressure (BP). These responses, primarily mediated by sympathetic stimulation due to laryngoscopy and tracheal manipulation, can lead to adverse outcomes, particularly in patients with cardiovascular comorbidities. The transient yet pronounced hemodynamic alterations, such as hypertension, tachycardia, and sometimes arrhythmias, may increase the risk of myocardial ischemia, stroke, or other complications in susceptible individuals. Thus, effective attenuation of these responses is a crucial aspect of perioperative anesthetic management. Various pharmacological approaches have been explored to mitigate the hemodynamic fluctuations associated with laryngoscopy and intubation. Agents such as opioids, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, and alpha-2 adrenergic agonists have been widely studied, with varying degrees of success. Among these, remifentanil and dexmedetomidine have emerged as promising candidates due to their unique pharmacological properties. Remifentanil, a potent, ultra-short-acting opioid, is widely used for its rapid onset and titratable effects, making it particularly suitable for managing acute hemodynamic changes. However, its use may be associated with dose-dependent adverse effects, such as bradycardia and hypotension. On the other hand, dexmedetomidine, an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist, has gained attention for its sedative, analgesic, and sympatholytic properties, which contribute to its ability to attenuate the stress response during intubation. Additionally, dexmedetomidine has been shown to provide hemodynamic stability without significant respiratory depression, making it an attractive alternative or adjunct to opioids. Despite the individual benefits of remifentanil and dexmedetomidine, there is limited evidence comparing their efficacy in attenuating the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and intubation. Furthermore, the potential synergistic effects of combining these two agents remain underexplored. It is plausible that a combination of dexmedetomidine and remifentanil at lower individual doses may provide superior hemodynamic control while minimizing the adverse effects associated with higher doses of either drug alone. This hypothesis is supported by the complementary mechanisms of action of the two drugs: remifentanil primarily modulates the nociceptive response via opioid receptor activation, while dexmedetomidine exerts its effects through central alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonism, resulting in reduced sympathetic outflow. The present study was designed to address these gaps in the literature by evaluating the efficacy of dexmedetomidine, remifentanil, and their combination in blunting the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and orotracheal intubation. Conducted as a double-blind, randomized clinical trial, the study sought to provide a comprehensive comparison of these pharmacological strategies in patients undergoing elective surgery under general anesthesia. A placebo group receiving normal saline was included to establish a baseline for the hemodynamic changes typically observed during intubation without pharmacological intervention. The primary objectives of the study were to compare the effects of dexmedetomidine, remifentanil, and their combination on mean blood pressure (MBP) and heart rate (HR) immediately following intubation and during the subsequent peri-intubation period. Secondary objectives included assessing the temporal trends in MBP and HR over time and evaluating the safety profiles of the interventions. By addressing these objectives, the study aimed to provide evidence-based guidance for anesthesiologists in selecting the optimal pharmacological approach to manage hemodynamic responses during intubation, particularly in high-risk patient populations. The findings of this study have significant clinical implications. The ability to effectively control BP and HR during laryngoscopy and intubation can enhance patient safety, reduce perioperative complications, and improve surgical outcomes. Moreover, understanding the potential benefits of combining dexmedetomidine and remifentanil may pave the way for more personalized and nuanced approaches to anesthetic management, particularly in patients with complex medical conditions. In this randomized clinical trial, 124 patients were enrolled and assigned to one of four groups: dexmedetomidine (DEX), remifentanil (REM), a combination of dexmedetomidine and remifentanil (DEX-REM), and normal saline (NS). The interventions were administered one minute prior to intubation, and hemodynamic parameters, including BP, HR, and arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2), were meticulously recorded at various time points. The baseline characteristics of the participants were comparable across the groups, ensuring the validity of the comparisons. The results demonstrated that all three intervention groups (DEX, REM, and DEX-REM) effectively attenuated the hemodynamic response to intubation compared to the NS group, with the combination group showing the most pronounced reductions in BP and HR. This study is among the first to systematically evaluate the comparative efficacy of dexmedetomidine and remifentanil, both individually and in combination, in controlling hemodynamic responses to laryngoscopy and intubation. The findings contribute to the growing body of literature on perioperative hemodynamic management and underscore the potential benefits of a multimodal pharmacological approach. By shedding light on the relative advantages and limitations of these agents, the study provides valuable insights for optimizing anesthetic care and improving patient outcomes during surgery. This randomized, double-blind clinical trial was conducted at Amirkabir Hospital, Arak, Iran, to evaluate the efficacy of dexmedetomidine (DEX) versus remifentanil (REM) in attenuating the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and orotracheal intubation in patients undergoing elective surgery under general anesthesia. The study was approved by the local ethics committee and registered in the Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials (registration number: IRCT2016092722254N1). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to enrollment. A total of 124 adult patients, aged 18–65 years, with American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status I or II, scheduled for elective surgery requiring general anesthesia with orotracheal intubation, were recruited for the study. Exclusion criteria included a history of cardiovascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, arrhythmias, neurological disorders, hepatic or renal dysfunction, pregnancy, known allergies to the study drugs, use of beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers, and a body mass index (BMI) greater than 30 kg/m². Participants were randomly assigned into one of four groups, each consisting of 31 patients: the DEX group, the REM group, the DEX + REM group, and the normal saline (NS) group as the control. Randomization was performed using a computer-generated random number table, and group allocation was concealed in sealed opaque envelopes. The study drugs were prepared by an independent anesthesiologist who was not involved in patient management or data collection to ensure blinding of both participants and investigators. On arrival to the operating room, standard monitoring was applied, including non-invasive blood pressure (BP), heart rate (HR), and arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2). Baseline measurements of these hemodynamic parameters were recorded. Patients were pre-oxygenated with 100% oxygen via a face mask for 3 minutes. Study drugs were administered intravenously 1 minute before laryngoscopy and intubation. The DEX group received dexmedetomidine at a dose of 1 µg/kg diluted in 10 mL normal saline and infused over 1 minute. The REM group received remifentanil at a dose of 1 µg/kg diluted in 10 mL normal saline and infused over 1 minute. The DEX + REM group received a combination of dexmedetomidine (0.5 µg/kg) and remifentanil (0.5 µg/kg), diluted together in 10 mL normal saline and infused over 1 minute. The NS group (control) received 10 mL of normal saline infused over 1 minute. All infusions were administered using identical syringes to maintain blinding. Anesthesia was induced 1 minute after the completion of drug infusion with intravenous propofol (2 mg/kg) and cisatracurium (0.15 mg/kg) to facilitate tracheal intubation. Following adequate muscle relaxation, direct laryngoscopy was performed using a Macintosh laryngoscope blade, and the trachea was intubated with an appropriately sized cuffed endotracheal tube. Laryngoscopy and intubation were performed by an experienced anesthesiologist to minimize variability. Anesthesia was maintained with isoflurane (1.2%) in a 50:50 mixture of oxygen and air. Additional doses of cisatracurium were administered as needed, and mechanical ventilation was adjusted to maintain end-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO2) between 35 and 40 mmHg. Hemodynamic parameters, including mean blood pressure (MBP), HR, and SaO2, were recorded at the following time points: on arrival to the operating room (baseline), 1 minute before laryngoscopy and intubation (post-drug infusion), immediately after intubation, and at 5-minute intervals for 15 minutes after intubation. All measurements were performed by a blinded observer who was unaware of the group allocation. Any adverse events, such as bradycardia (HR < 50 beats per minute) or hypotension (systolic BP < 90 mmHg), were recorded and managed appropriately. Bradycardia was treated with intravenous atropine (0.5 mg), and hypotension was treated with intravenous ephedrine (5–10 mg) or fluid boluses as required. Patients who developed complications or required rescue interventions were excluded from the final analysis. Sample size calculation was performed based on a pilot study, with a power of 80% and a significance level of 0.05, to detect a 20% difference in MBP and HR among the groups. A total of 31 patients per group were required to account for potential dropouts. Statistical analysis was conducted using SPSS version 18.0. Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD), and categorical variables were expressed as frequencies or percentages. Comparisons of demographic data and baseline hemodynamic variables among the groups were performed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) for continuous variables and the chi-square test for categorical variables. Repeated measures ANOVA was used to assess changes in MBP, HR, and SaO2 over time within and between groups. Post-hoc analysis with the Tukey test was conducted to compare pairwise differences among the groups. A P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The demographic characteristics of the patients, including age and sex, were comparable between the groups, and there were no significant differences in baseline hemodynamic parameters, including mean blood pressure (MBP), heart rate (HR), and arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2), among the four groups (P > 0.05). Hemodynamic variables were recorded at multiple time points: on arrival to the operating room, 1 minute before laryngoscopy and intubation, immediately after intubation, and subsequently at 5-minute intervals up to 15 minutes. The results demonstrated significant differences in the hemodynamic responses to laryngoscopy and intubation among the four groups. Immediately following laryngoscopy and intubation, the NS group exhibited a marked increase in MBP and HR compared to the other three groups (P < 0.05). In contrast, the DEX, REM, and DEX + REM groups demonstrated significantly attenuated hemodynamic responses. The Tukey post-hoc test revealed no statistically significant differences in MBP and HR between the DEX, REM, and DEX + REM groups at any time point (P > 0.05). However, all three intervention groups showed significantly lower MBP and HR compared to the NS group at all measured time points after laryngoscopy and intubation. A decreasing trend in MBP and HR was observed in the intervention groups over time, with the DEX + REM group exhibiting the most pronounced reduction in MBP. This group consistently maintained the lowest blood pressure values compared to the DEX and REM groups, although the differences were not statistically significant (P > 0.05). Similarly, all three intervention groups had lower HR values compared to the NS group at all time points, with no significant differences among the DEX, REM, and DEX + REM groups. The repeated measures analysis further confirmed a significant interaction effect of time and group on both MBP and HR (P < 0.05). This finding indicates that while all three intervention groups effectively mitigated the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and intubation, the NS group failed to control the increase in MBP and HR. Natural transformation is a fundamental mechanism of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in prokaryotes, facilitating the uptake and incorporation of exogenous DNA into the genome of competent cells. This process is central to bacterial evolution, allowing the acquisition of novel traits such as antibiotic resistance, metabolic versatility, and virulence [1, 2]. Beyond its evolutionary role, natural transformation has been proposed to provide immediate physiological benefits to individual cells, including the use of extracellular DNA as a nutrient source or as a template for DNA repair [3–5]. Despite its importance, the factors driving the evolution and maintenance of natural competence remain poorly understood. While the long-term adaptive value of transformation is evident in shaping genomic plasticity, elucidating its short-term costs and benefits to individual cells is essential for understanding its ecological and evolutionary dynamics. Mechanism and Evolution of Natural Transformation Natural transformation is a highly conserved and regulated process, requiring the coordinated expression of multiple competence genes [6]. In model organisms such as Acinetobacter baylyi, the process involves the binding and uptake of double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) from the environment, its processing into single-stranded DNA (ssDNA), and the subsequent integration of this ssDNA into the bacterial chromosome via homologous recombination [7]. While this machinery is well characterized, its evolutionary origin remains a topic of debate. Hypotheses for the evolution of natural competence include DNA acquisition for genetic diversification, the utilization of extracellular DNA as a nutrient source, and its role in repairing damaged DNA [8, 9]. Each hypothesis suggests distinct selective pressures favoring the maintenance of this complex trait. The DNA repair hypothesis posits that the uptake of environmental DNA provides templates for homologous recombination, thereby facilitating the repair of DNA damage, particularly double-strand breaks (DSBs) [10]. This idea is supported by the observation that competence genes are often induced under stress conditions, such as exposure to UV radiation or oxidative stress, which cause DNA damage [11]. However, the benefits of DNA uptake for repair are likely conditional, depending on both the nature of the stress and the availability of homologous DNA in the environment [12]. Moreover, the recombinational integration of DNA may itself introduce strand breaks or replication fork collapse, potentially imposing a fitness cost under certain conditions [13]. Short-Term Benefits of DNA Uptake Beyond its role in genetic exchange and repair, the immediate utility of DNA uptake has garnered considerable attention. Extracellular DNA can serve as a source of carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus in nutrient-limited environments, providing a direct physiological benefit to competent cells [3, 14]. In this context, natural transformation may represent a metabolic strategy, enabling cells to scavenge resources from their surroundings. This hypothesis is supported by the observation that DNA uptake occurs even in the absence of homologous recombination in some bacteria, suggesting that the metabolic benefits of extracellular DNA can be decoupled from its genetic contributions [15]. Recent studies have also highlighted the context-dependent nature of DNA uptake benefits. For example, in heterologous environments where homologous DNA is scarce, the primary advantage of natural competence may lie in nutrient acquisition rather than genetic repair or recombination [16]. Conversely, in genotoxic environments, such as those with elevated UV radiation, the repair hypothesis predicts that competence should enhance survival. However, the relationship between DNA uptake, recombination, and fitness under such conditions remains complex and poorly understood. Costs of Recombination During Transformation Despite its potential benefits, natural transformation is not without costs. The integration of exogenous DNA into the genome requires strand invasion and processing of ssDNA, which can interfere with other cellular processes, including replication and transcription [17]. Additionally, recombination with non-homologous or partially homologous DNA can lead to genomic instability, insertional mutagenesis, and the generation of deleterious alleles [18]. These risks are particularly pronounced in stressful environments, where DNA damage and replication stress are already elevated. A less well-recognized cost of natural transformation is the potential for strand breaks introduced during the recombination process itself. Homologous recombination requires the generation of DSBs at sites of strand invasion, a process mediated by recombination repair pathways such as RecBCD and RecFOR [19]. While these pathways are essential for the successful integration of exogenous DNA, they may also exacerbate DNA damage under certain conditions, particularly when environmental stressors such as UV radiation induce additional genomic lesions. This interplay between DNA uptake, recombination, and repair pathways suggests that the costs and benefits of natural transformation are tightly linked to environmental context and genetic background. Study Objectives and Rationale In this study, we investigate the immediate costs and benefits of natural transformation in Acinetobacter baylyi, a model organism for studying bacterial competence. Specifically, we aim to disentangle the physiological benefits of DNA uptake from the genetic consequences of recombination. By comparing the fitness of DNA uptake-proficient and -deficient strains under both benign and genotoxic conditions, we seek to determine the relative contributions of nutrient acquisition and DNA repair to the maintenance of competence. Furthermore, we explore the role of recombination in mediating the fitness effects of transformation, focusing on its impact on survival and genomic stability under UV-induced stress. Our findings provide new insights into the selective pressures shaping the evolution of natural transformation and highlight the dual nature of recombination as both a benefit and a cost. By demonstrating that DNA uptake confers a physiological advantage independent of recombination, we challenge the traditional view that natural competence evolved primarily for genetic exchange or repair. At the same time, we reveal a previously unrecognized cost of recombination during transformation, with important implications for understanding the trade-offs associated with this process. Together, these results contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the ecological and evolutionary dynamics of natural competence in bacteria. Bacterial Strains and Growth Conditions The bacterial strains used in this study were derived from Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1. The wild-type strain (referred to as wt in this study) is naturally competent for DNA uptake and transformation. Mutant strains deficient in DNA uptake (ΔcomA) and recombination repair pathways (ΔrecBCD, ΔrecFOR) were constructed and verified by PCR and Sanger sequencing. For experiments requiring heterologous DNA, genomic DNA was extracted from Escherichia coli K-12 MG1655. Bacteria were cultured at 30°C in LB medium or minimal medium supplemented with 20 mM succinate as the sole carbon source, following standard protocols [1]. Where indicated, kanamycin (50 μg/mL) was added for selection. Construction of Mutant Strains Gene deletions were generated using homologous recombination with linear PCR products containing upstream and downstream flanking regions of the target genes fused to a kanamycin resistance cassette. PCR products were transformed into competent cells, and mutants were selected on LB agar containing kanamycin. The absence of the target gene was confirmed by colony PCR, and the functionality of the mutation was verified phenotypically. For example, ΔcomA mutants were tested for their inability to uptake plasmid DNA, and ΔrecBCD and ΔrecFOR mutants were tested for impaired recombination repair during transformation assays under UV-induced stress. DNA Preparation Genomic DNA from A. baylyi ADP1 and E. coli K-12 MG1655 was extracted using the Qiagen DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit following the manufacturer's protocol. DNA concentrations were determined using a NanoDrop ND-1000 spectrophotometer, and DNA integrity was confirmed by agarose gel electrophoresis. DNA was sterilized by UV irradiation (254 nm, 100 J/m²) prior to transformation experiments to eliminate viable cells. Transformation Assays Natural transformation was assessed by incubating competent A. baylyi cells with genomic DNA derived from either homologous (ADP1) or heterologous (E. coli) sources. Cells were grown to mid-log phase (OD600 = 0.4–0.5) in LB medium and then washed twice with sterile 0.9% NaCl solution. Approximately 10⁸ cells were resuspended in 1 mL of transformation buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, 1 mM CaCl₂, 0.1 mM MgCl₂) containing 1 μg of DNA. Transformations were carried out at 30°C for 30 min with gentle shaking. Following incubation, cells were plated on selective or non-selective LB agar to quantify transformants and total viable cells, respectively. Transformation frequency was calculated as the ratio of transformants to total viable cells. Competition Experiments Competition experiments were performed to assess the fitness effects of DNA uptake under benign and stressful conditions. Wild-type (wt) and ΔcomA strains were mixed at a 1:1 ratio and inoculated into LB medium at an initial density of 10⁶ CFU/mL. Cultures were incubated at 30°C with shaking (200 rpm) for 24 hours. To impose genotoxic stress, UV irradiation was applied at varying doses (50–200 J/m²) to cultures prior to incubation. Colony-forming units (CFUs) were determined by plating dilutions on LB agar and LB agar containing kanamycin to differentiate strains. Relative fitness (W) was calculated as the ratio of Malthusian growth parameters between wt and ΔcomA strains [2]. UV Survival Assays The impact of UV-induced DNA damage on survival and transformation efficiency was evaluated by exposing mid-log-phase cultures to UV irradiation at doses ranging from 50 to 200 J/m². Following irradiation, cells were resuspended in transformation buffer containing homologous or heterologous DNA and incubated as described above. Survival was assessed by plating on LB agar, and transformation efficiency was calculated as described in the transformation assay. For recombination-deficient mutants (ΔrecBCD, ΔrecFOR), survival and transformation were evaluated under identical conditions to assess the role of recombination pathways in DNA repair. Microscopy and Cell Viability Assays To examine cell viability and morphological changes during transformation, cells exposed to UV stress were stained with the LIVE/DEAD BacLight Bacterial Viability Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) following the manufacturer's protocol. Samples were imaged using a Leica DMi8 epifluorescence microscope equipped with a 100× oil immersion objective. Green fluorescence indicated viable cells, while red fluorescence indicated membrane-compromised cells. Quantification was performed by analyzing at least 10 randomly chosen fields per sample. Statistical Analysis All experiments were performed with at least three independent biological replicates. Data are presented as means ± standard deviation (SD). Statistical significance was determined using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test for multiple comparisons or unpaired two-tailed Student's t-tests where appropriate. A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. All analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism 9.0 software. Fitness Benefits of DNA Uptake Independent of Stress Conditions To assess the immediate fitness effects of DNA uptake in Acinetobacter baylyi, we conducted head-to-head competition experiments between a DNA uptake-proficient wild-type strain (WT) and an isogenic DNA uptake-deficient mutant (ΔcomA). Competitions were performed under both benign conditions and following exposure to UV-induced genotoxic stress. Surprisingly, the WT strain consistently outcompeted the ΔcomA mutant even in the absence of UV stress, suggesting that DNA uptake confers a physiological benefit unrelated to environmental genotoxicity. This advantage persisted when both homologous (genomic DNA from the same strain) and heterologous (DNA from unrelated species) substrates were provided, indicating that the observed fitness benefit was not dependent on sequence-specific recombination events. Statistical analysis demonstrated a significant fitness increase for the WT strain compared to ΔcomA under all tested conditions (t-test, P < 0.05). To determine whether recombination plays a role in mediating this benefit, we performed additional competition experiments using a recA mutant strain, which is incapable of homologous recombination. The WT strain retained its competitive advantage over both the ΔcomA and ΔrecA strains, suggesting that recombination is not required for the physiological benefit of DNA uptake. These findings imply that the uptake of extracellular DNA provides a direct advantage to competent cells, potentially through mechanisms such as nutrient acquisition or protective effects against environmental stressors. Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remain a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) constituting a significant proportion of the global disease burden [1]. While the incidence of AMI has historically been higher in older populations, the prevalence of premature AMI—occurring in individuals below the age of 45—has been steadily rising, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) [2]. This trend is concerning, as premature AMI not only imposes a substantial economic burden due to loss of productivity but also has profound implications for long-term health outcomes, including recurrent cardiovascular events and diminished quality of life [3]. In Pakistan, where the burden of CVDs is increasing at an alarming rate, identifying modifiable risk factors, including dietary habits, is critical for developing effective preventive strategies [4]. Dietary Patterns and Cardiovascular Health Dietary intake is a well-established determinant of cardiovascular health, influencing key risk factors such as lipid profiles, blood pressure, inflammation, and oxidative stress [5]. Traditional approaches to studying the role of diet in CVDs have focused on specific nutrients or food items, such as dietary fats, salt, and fiber. While these studies have provided valuable insights, they often fail to account for the complex interactions among various dietary components [6]. As a result, there has been a growing shift toward examining dietary patterns, which consider the overall composition of the diet and its cumulative impact on health [7]. Evidence from high-income countries has consistently demonstrated that adherence to prudent dietary patterns—characterized by high consumption of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean protein sources—is associated with a lower risk of AMI and other CVDs [8]. Conversely, Western dietary patterns, characterized by high intake of red and processed meats, refined carbohydrates, saturated fats, and sugar-sweetened beverages, have been linked to increased cardiovascular risk [9]. However, the generalizability of these findings to LMICs, including Pakistan, is limited due to differences in dietary habits, cultural practices, and socioeconomic factors. For example, traditional diets in South Asia are often rich in legumes, whole grains, and spices, which may confer cardioprotective benefits [10]. At the same time, urbanization, globalization, and economic transitions have led to the proliferation of Westernized dietary patterns, particularly among younger populations in urban centers [11]. This dietary shift is accompanied by an increasing prevalence of obesity, diabetes, and dyslipidemia, all of which are major risk factors for AMI [12]. Consequently, there is a pressing need to investigate the role of dietary patterns in the context of premature AMI in Pakistan. Rationale for the Study Despite the established link between diet and cardiovascular health, there is a paucity of research on dietary patterns and their association with premature AMI in Pakistan. Most existing studies on CVD risk factors in the region have focused on traditional risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes, and smoking, with limited attention given to dietary behaviors [13, 14]. Moreover, the few available studies on diet and CVDs in South Asia have primarily been descriptive in nature, lacking robust analytical frameworks to identify specific dietary patterns and their relationship with disease outcomes [15]. Given the unique dietary practices in Pakistan, as well as the rapid dietary transitions occurring in urban settings, it is critical to explore how different dietary patterns influence the risk of premature AMI in this population. The current study addresses this gap by using factor analysis to identify major dietary patterns among young, urban adults in Karachi, Pakistan, and examining their association with the risk of premature AMI. Factor analysis is a data-driven method that groups food items based on their intercorrelations, allowing for the identification of distinct dietary patterns that reflect real-world eating behaviors [16]. By employing this methodological approach, the study not only provides insights into the dietary determinants of premature AMI but also contributes to the growing body of literature on dietary patterns and CVDs in LMICs. Study Context and Relevance Karachi, the largest city in Pakistan, represents an ideal setting for this investigation due to its diverse population, rapid urbanization, and high prevalence of cardiovascular risk factors [17]. The city’s urban environment has facilitated the adoption of Westernized diets, particularly among younger individuals, who are increasingly exposed to processed foods, sugary beverages, and fast food [18]. At the same time, traditional dietary practices, such as high consumption of legumes, vegetables, and whole grains, remain prevalent in certain segments of the population. This coexistence of traditional and modern dietary patterns provides a unique opportunity to examine their differential impact on cardiovascular health. Furthermore, young adults in urban Pakistan are increasingly vulnerable to premature AMI due to a combination of lifestyle factors, including physical inactivity, smoking, and poor dietary habits [19]. Understanding the role of dietary patterns in this demographic is particularly important, as dietary interventions are among the most cost-effective strategies for preventing CVDs [20]. Findings from this study have the potential to inform public health policies and dietary guidelines tailored to the specific needs of the Pakistani population. Objectives The primary objective of this study was to investigate the association between major dietary patterns and the risk of premature AMI in a young, urban Pakistani population. Specifically, the study aimed to: (1) identify distinct dietary patterns using factor analysis; (2) examine the association of these patterns with biochemical markers of cardiovascular risk, including lipid profiles and homocysteine levels; and (3) evaluate the protective or deleterious effects of these patterns on the risk of premature AMI. By addressing these objectives, the study seeks to contribute to a deeper understanding of the dietary determinants of CVDs in Pakistan and provide evidence for targeted prevention strategies in this high-risk population. Hypotheses Based on existing literature, it was hypothesized that adherence to a prudent dietary pattern, characterized by high consumption of fruits, vegetables, legumes, and lean protein sources, would be associated with a reduced risk of premature AMI. Conversely, it was hypothesized that Western dietary patterns, characterized by high intake of red meat, processed foods, and refined carbohydrates, would be associated with an increased risk. Additionally, a combination dietary pattern, reflective of both traditional and modern dietary practices, was hypothesized to exhibit a nuanced relationship with AMI, potentially offering partial protection depending on its specific composition. In summary, this study aims to fill critical gaps in the understanding of dietary patterns and their role in the development of premature AMI in Pakistan, with the ultimate goal of informing culturally relevant dietary interventions for cardiovascular health promotion. Study Design and Participant Recruitment This hospital-based case-control study was conducted in Karachi, Pakistan, to evaluate the association between dietary patterns and the risk of acute myocardial infarction (AMI) in young adults. The study recruited 203 consecutive cases of first AMI (146 males and 57 females) and 205 age- and gender-matched controls. Cases were identified from patients presenting to the cardiology department of a tertiary care hospital and were included if they were below 45 years of age, had a confirmed diagnosis of AMI, and provided informed consent. AMI diagnosis was based on clinical presentation, electrocardiographic changes, and elevated cardiac biomarkers, following the universal definition of myocardial infarction [1]. Patients with a history of previous AMI, chronic inflammatory diseases, malignancy, or incomplete medical records were excluded. Control participants were healthy adults without a history of cardiovascular disease, recruited from the hospital's outpatient clinics or through community outreach programs. Controls were individually matched to cases within a three-year age range and by gender. They underwent a short health screening, including a medical history review and a physical examination, to ensure they met the inclusion criteria. Participants with chronic illnesses, major comorbidities, or those on medications affecting lipid metabolism were excluded. Data Collection Dietary Assessment Dietary intake was assessed for both cases and controls using a simple 14-item food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) specifically designed and validated for the local population. The FFQ included questions on the frequency (daily, weekly, or monthly) and portion sizes of commonly consumed food items, including legumes, vegetables, fruits, wheat, chicken, tea with milk, fish, eggs, meat, juices, and coffee. Participants were guided by trained research staff to recall their average dietary intake over the preceding year. The data from the FFQ were transformed into frequency scores to represent relative consumption levels for each food item. Biochemical Measurements Fasting blood samples were collected from all participants after an overnight fast of at least eight hours. Plasma and serum were separated by centrifugation and stored at −80°C until analysis. Homocysteine, folate, and vitamin B12 levels were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA) [2], while serum ferritin was analyzed via chemiluminescence immunoassay. Lipid profiles, including total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), and triglycerides, were measured enzymatically using standardized automated methods. Blood lead levels were determined using atomic absorption spectrophotometry [3]. Anthropometric and Clinical Measurements Height and weight were measured using standardized protocols, and body mass index (BMI) was calculated as weight (kg)/height (m²). Blood pressure was recorded using a calibrated sphygmomanometer, with the mean of two readings taken five minutes apart. Information on smoking status, physical activity, family history of cardiovascular disease, and socioeconomic status was collected via structured interviews. Statistical Analysis Identification of Dietary Patterns Exploratory factor analysis (principal component analysis) was used to identify major dietary patterns based on the FFQ data. The Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure of sampling adequacy and Bartlett’s test of sphericity were performed to ensure the suitability of the data for factor analysis. Varimax rotation was applied to improve interpretability of the factors. Three distinct dietary patterns were derived: (1) the prudent dietary pattern, characterized by high consumption of legumes, vegetables, wheat, chicken, and fruits; (2) the combination dietary pattern, characterized by high intake of eggs, fish, fruits, juices, and coffee; and (3) the western dietary pattern, characterized by high intake of meat, fish, and tea with milk. Factor scores for each participant were calculated by summing standardized consumption frequencies weighted by their respective factor loadings. Comparison of Cases and Controls Continuous variables, such as biochemical parameters and dietary pattern scores, were presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) and compared between cases and controls using independent t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests, as appropriate. Categorical variables were presented as frequencies and proportions and compared using the chi-square test. Conditional Logistic Regression Multivariate conditional logistic regression models were used to assess the association between dietary patterns and the risk of AMI. Factor scores for each dietary pattern were categorized into tertiles, and odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for the middle and highest tertiles relative to the lowest tertile. Models were adjusted for potential confounders, including smoking status, physical activity, BMI, blood pressure, lipid profile, plasma homocysteine, folate, vitamin B12, ferritin, and socioeconomic status. Interaction terms were tested to evaluate potential effect modification by gender and other covariates. Ethical Considerations The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the institutional ethics committee of the participating hospital. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants before enrollment. All procedures were conducted in accordance with the ethical standards of the Declaration of Helsinki. --- References 1. Baseline Characteristics of Study Participants The study included 203 cases with their first acute myocardial infarction (AMI) and 205 age- and gender-matched controls. The mean age of participants was 41.2 ± 3.7 years for cases and 40.9 ± 3.6 years for controls, with no statistically significant difference between groups (p=0.12). Among the cases, 71.9% (n=146) were male, while 28.1% (n=57) were female; the gender distribution in controls was identical due to matching. Cases demonstrated significantly higher levels of fasting total cholesterol (5.9 ± 1.3 mmol/L vs. 5.1 ± 1.2 mmol/L; p<0.001), LDL-cholesterol (3.8 ± 1.1 mmol/L vs. 3.3 ± 1.0 mmol/L; p<0.001), and triglycerides (2.1 ± 0.9 mmol/L vs. 1.7 ± 0.7 mmol/L; p<0.001) compared to controls. HDL-cholesterol levels were significantly lower in cases than controls (1.0 ± 0.2 mmol/L vs. 1.3 ± 0.3 mmol/L; p<0.001).

Understanding how the brain evaluates past experiences and integrates this information to adapt future behavior is a central question in neuroscience. Adaptive behavior, a hallmark of higher cognitive functions, relies on the ability to assess the outcome of a decision, learn from errors, and adjust future strategies accordingly. These processes are critical for optimizing performance in uncertain environments. While numerous studies have investigated the neural mechanisms underlying decision-making and error processing, the specific role of the ventral premotor cortex (PMv) in evaluating outcomes and guiding behavior remains underexplored. Behavioral adaptation following errors has been widely documented across species, including humans and non-human primates, and is a robust phenomenon often referred to as "post-error adjustments" [1, 2]. In humans, such adjustments manifest as slower response times and higher accuracy in trials following errors, suggesting a shift in strategy to prioritize accuracy over speed [3]. At the neural level, error-related activity has primarily been attributed to regions such as the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), prefrontal areas, and basal ganglia, which collectively form circuits involved in error detection and performance monitoring [4, 5]. While these regions have been extensively studied, their interaction with sensorimotor areas, such as the PMv, and the functional contribution of these areas to post-error behavioral adjustments remain less well understood. The PMv plays a critical role in motor planning, perceptual decision-making, and sensorimotor integration [6]. This area is particularly well-positioned to mediate the interplay between cognitive and motor processes, as it is anatomically and functionally connected to both higher-order cortical regions and primary motor areas [7]. Recent work has extended the role of the PMv beyond motor preparation and execution, demonstrating its involvement in encoding task-relevant information during perceptual decision-making [8, 9]. For example, PMv neurons have been shown to represent both sensory evidence and categorical decisions during complex tasks requiring the integration of sensory inputs [10]. Interestingly, following the completion of a decision, PMv neurons exhibit activity patterns that encode information about the outcome of the decision, including whether it was correct or erroneous [11]. This suggests that the PMv may serve as a critical hub for evaluating decision outcomes and influencing subsequent behavior. Despite these insights, it remains unclear how the PMv contributes to behavioral adjustments following decision outcomes and how the difficulty of the decision itself influences this process. The integration of past outcomes into current decision-making likely involves dynamic changes in neural representations and activity patterns, but the temporal specificity of these effects and their dependence on task difficulty have not been systematically investigated. In particular, it is unknown whether the PMv solely reflects the immediate past trial outcome or whether it integrates information over longer timescales. Additionally, the relationship between task difficulty, outcome evaluation, and subsequent behavioral adjustments requires further elucidation, as performance monitoring processes are thought to be more robustly engaged under challenging conditions [12, 13]. Building on this background, the present study investigates how trial outcomes influence neuronal activity in the PMv and behavioral performance in non-human primates. Specifically, we test the hypothesis that PMv neurons utilize information about the most recent trial (n−1) to evaluate the decision process and shape behavior in the current trial (n). Furthermore, we examine whether the influence of prior outcomes on neural activity and behavior depends on the difficulty of the decision. To address these questions, we recorded single-cell activity from the PMv of monkeys engaged in a perceptual decision-making task with varying levels of difficulty. By systematically analyzing the effects of prior trial outcomes on both neural activity and task performance, we aim to provide a detailed account of how the PMv contributes to experience-driven behavioral adaptation. Our results reveal that the outcome of the immediately preceding trial (n−1) significantly modulates PMv neuronal activity and behavioral performance in the current trial. Conversely, the outcome of earlier trials (e.g., n−2) exerts no detectable influence on either measure, suggesting that the PMv operates on a short temporal scale when integrating past outcomes. Importantly, we find that the impact of prior outcomes is more pronounced following difficult trials, as evidenced by greater recruitment of PMv neurons and larger changes in behavioral performance. These findings highlight a critical role for the PMv in the evaluation of decision outcomes and suggest that this cortical region dynamically adjusts its activity to optimize behavior based on recent experiences. The present study builds upon prior work by demonstrating that the PMv not only encodes decision outcomes but also uses this information to influence subsequent decisions. This extends current models of decision-making to include a role for sensorimotor areas in post-decision processing and behavioral adaptation. Furthermore, the observed dependence of these effects on task difficulty provides new insights into how cognitive resources are allocated during performance monitoring and error evaluation. Together, our findings contribute to a growing body of evidence supporting the involvement of the PMv in higher-order cognitive functions and underscore the importance of integrating neural and behavioral analyses to understand experience-dependent changes in behavior. In the following sections, we detail the methods used to investigate these questions, present our findings on the relationship between prior trial outcomes and PMv activity, and discuss the implications of these results for models of decision-making and motor control. By elucidating the mechanisms by which the PMv evaluates and responds to errors, this work advances our understanding of the neural basis of adaptive behavior and its dependence on recent experience. Subjects and Ethics We conducted experiments on two adult male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta), weighing 8 and 9 kg, respectively. Both animals were extensively trained in a perceptual decision-making task before neural recordings began. All experimental procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of our institution and complied with the guidelines established by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) for the care and use of laboratory animals. Behavioral Task The monkeys performed a visual motion discrimination task, in which they were required to decide the net direction of motion in a dynamic random dot stimulus. Each trial began with a fixation period, during which the monkeys were required to maintain their gaze within a 2° window centered on a fixation point. Subsequently, a random dot motion stimulus was presented for 2 seconds. The motion stimulus consisted of a subset of dots moving coherently in one of two possible directions (left or right) while the remaining dots moved in random directions. Coherence levels (0%, 10%, 30%, and 50%) were used to manipulate task difficulty. Following stimulus presentation, the monkeys indicated their decision by making a saccade to one of two choice targets located 10° to the left or right of the fixation point. Correct choices were rewarded with a drop of juice, while incorrect choices received no reward. Inter-trial intervals lasted 1.5–2 seconds. Behavioral Analysis Behavioral performance was analyzed as a function of both the coherence of the motion stimulus and the outcome of the immediately preceding trial (n−1). Accuracy, response time (RT), and changes in choice bias were quantified for each condition. Trials were categorized as "easy" or "difficult" based on the coherence levels, with 30% and 50% coherence classified as easy and 10% coherence classified as difficult. Trials with 0% coherence were excluded from the main analyses, as they provided no directional information. For each trial, we additionally assessed whether the outcome of trial n−2 influenced behavioral performance, allowing us to evaluate the temporal specificity of error-based adjustments. Neural Recordings Neuronal activity was recorded from the ventral premotor cortex (PMv) of both monkeys using a 96-channel microelectrode array (Blackrock Microsystems). Arrays were implanted in the left hemisphere of each monkey following standard surgical procedures under aseptic conditions and general anesthesia. Neural signals were amplified, filtered, and digitized at 30 kHz. Single-unit activity was isolated offline using principal component analysis (PCA) and manual clustering. Only neurons with stable waveforms and firing rates exceeding 1 Hz were included in the analysis. Experimental Design and Data Collection Data collection spanned 30–40 sessions per monkey, with each session comprising 250–400 trials. To ensure that the monkeys remained motivated and attentive, their performance was continuously monitored, and breaks were introduced as needed. Trial sequences were pseudorandomized to balance the occurrence of correct and error trials across coherence levels. Behavioral and neural data were synchronized using a custom event marker system, and timestamps were stored for all task-relevant events, including stimulus onset, saccade initiation, and reward delivery. Data Analysis Neuronal activity was analyzed in two primary time windows: (1) the stimulus period (0–2 seconds following motion onset) and (2) the feedback period (0–1 second following reward or error feedback). For each neuron, we computed peri-stimulus time histograms (PSTHs) aligned to stimulus onset and feedback delivery. Spike rates were normalized to the baseline firing rate (−500 to 0 ms before stimulus onset) to account for variability across neurons. We used a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA to evaluate the effects of trial outcome (error vs. correct) and task difficulty (easy vs. difficult) on neuronal activity. Post hoc comparisons were conducted using Tukey's HSD test to identify significant differences between conditions. Additionally, we performed population decoding analyses to assess whether the ensemble activity of PMv neurons contained information about the outcome of the previous trial. Decoding accuracy was calculated using a leave-one-out cross-validation procedure with a linear support vector machine (SVM). Outcome Influence on Neuronal and Behavioral Dynamics Behavioral and neural analyses focused on quantifying the extent to which the outcome of the previous trial (n−1) influenced performance and PMv activity in the current trial (n). For each neuron, we calculated the modulation index (MI) as the difference in firing rates between post-correct and post-error trials, normalized by their sum. Neurons with MI values exceeding ±2 standard deviations from the population mean were classified as significantly modulated by outcome. At the behavioral level, we quantified post-error slowing (PES) by comparing RTs between post-error and post-correct trials within each coherence level. To evaluate the temporal specificity of outcome effects, we extended these analyses to trial n−2. Mixed-effects models were used to determine whether neuronal or behavioral measures exhibited significant dependence on trial n−2 outcomes after accounting for n−1 outcomes. Statistical Analyses All statistical analyses were performed using MATLAB (MathWorks) and R (R Foundation for Statistical Computing). Unless otherwise specified, data are reported as mean ± SEM, and statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05. Where appropriate, Bonferroni corrections were applied to account for multiple comparisons. Control Analyses To rule out alternative explanations for the observed effects, we performed several control analyses. First, we verified that the monkeys’ performance did not exhibit systematic drifts over the course of a session by examining accuracy and RT as a function of trial number. Second, we confirmed that the effects of trial outcome on PMv activity were not confounded by differences in eye movements or task engagement. Finally, we tested whether neural and behavioral adjustments persisted beyond the first trial after an error by analyzing longer trial sequences (n−3, n−4). Software and Code Availability Custom scripts for behavioral control, neural data preprocessing, and statistical analysis were written in MATLAB. Code for decoding analyses and statistical modeling is available upon request. Error correction codes play a pivotal role in modern digital communication systems, enabling reliable data transmission over noisy channels. Among the family of error-correcting codes, polar codes, introduced by Arıkan [1], have gained significant attention due to their capacity-achieving properties under successive cancellation (SC) decoding for binary-input discrete memoryless channels. Polar codes exploit the phenomenon of channel polarization, which partitions the channels into highly reliable and highly unreliable subsets as the block length increases. By transmitting information bits over the reliable channels while fixing the unreliable ones to frozen values, polar codes achieve excellent theoretical performance. However, the practical implementation of polar codes remains a challenging task, particularly with respect to efficient and robust decoding. Successive cancellation decoding, the most fundamental algorithm for polar codes, operates sequentially, making hard decisions on each bit based on the already decoded bits. While SC decoding is computationally efficient, its performance is suboptimal when compared to other decoding methods such as SC list (SCL) decoding [2]. A critical limitation of SC decoding arises from its susceptibility to error propagation; a single erroneous decision on an unfrozen bit can propagate through subsequent decisions, leading to significant performance degradation. This sensitivity to early errors motivates the development of enhanced decoding algorithms capable of detecting and correcting these errors to improve the overall reliability of SC decoding. One widely adopted enhancement to SC decoding is the introduction of list-based decoding algorithms, such as SCL decoding, which maintain multiple candidate paths during the decoding process. By leveraging a list of potential decoding paths, SCL decoding is capable of mitigating error propagation and achieving performance close to the maximum likelihood (ML) decoder. When augmented with cyclic redundancy check (CRC) codes, known as CRC-aided SCL (CA-SCL) decoding, the algorithm further improves error correction by selecting the most likely codeword from the list that satisfies the CRC constraints [3]. Despite its superior performance, CA-SCL decoding comes with a significant drawback: its computational complexity grows linearly with the list size, making it less appealing for applications with stringent latency or hardware resource constraints. In light of these challenges, there has been growing interest in developing alternative decoding strategies that strike a balance between the performance of CA-SCL decoding and the simplicity of SC decoding. Among these approaches, bit-flipping decoding has emerged as a promising candidate. Bit-flipping decoding aims to identify and correct errors in the SC decoding process by selectively flipping the values of certain bits and re-evaluating the decoding path. Early works in this domain, such as [4], introduced basic bit-flipping strategies, but these approaches were limited in their ability to correct multiple errors or adapt to varying channel conditions. To address these limitations, researchers have explored more sophisticated bit-flipping algorithms that incorporate additional information about the decoding process or leverage the structure of polar codes. In this paper, we propose a novel progressive multi-level bit-flipping decoding algorithm for polar codes, designed to address the error propagation issue inherent in SC decoding. The proposed method builds on the concept of critical sets, subsets of unfrozen bits where errors are most likely to occur. Specifically, we construct an initial critical set \( S \) that, with high probability, includes the location of the first decoding error. This critical set serves as the foundation for a progressive decoding framework that operates over multiple layers. Each layer is associated with a new critical set, constructed using the undecoded subtrees from the previous layer. By iteratively refining the critical set and correcting errors, the algorithm achieves improved error correction performance. The proposed algorithm introduces the notion of progressive levels, where each level corresponds to the number of independent errors that can be corrected. As the level increases, the block error rate (BLER) performance of the algorithm improves, approaching that of CA-SCL decoding with a large list size. For example, we demonstrate that a level-4 progressive bit-flipping decoder achieves comparable performance to a CA-SCL decoder with a list size of \( L = 32 \). Importantly, this improvement in performance does not come at the expense of significantly increased complexity. At medium to high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), the average computational complexity of the proposed algorithm remains comparable to that of SC decoding, making it an attractive alternative to SCL decoding in practical scenarios. The contributions of this work can be summarized as follows. First, we introduce a systematic method for constructing critical sets of unfrozen bits, leveraging the structure of the polar code decoding tree. Second, we develop a progressive multi-level bit-flipping decoding algorithm that iteratively refines the decoding process over successive layers of critical sets. Third, we provide a detailed analysis of the algorithm's performance and complexity, highlighting its ability to achieve near-CA-SCL performance at a fraction of the computational cost. Finally, we validate the proposed algorithm through extensive simulations, demonstrating its effectiveness across a range of SNRs and code parameters. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we review the fundamentals of polar codes and SC decoding, along with related work on bit-flipping decoding strategies. Section III provides a detailed description of the proposed progressive multi-level bit-flipping decoding algorithm, including the construction of critical sets and the iterative decoding process. In Section IV, we present simulation results comparing the performance and complexity of the proposed algorithm against existing decoding methods. Finally, Section V concludes the paper with a discussion of potential directions for future research. By addressing the limitations of SC decoding while maintaining low computational complexity, the proposed progressive bit-flipping algorithm represents a significant step forward in the practical deployment of polar codes. Its ability to deliver high performance with reduced complexity makes it a compelling choice for emerging applications in 5G and beyond, where efficient and reliable communications are paramount. In this study, we propose a progressive multi-level bit-flipping decoding algorithm for polar codes, leveraging the concept of layered critical sets to address error propagation inherent in successive cancellation (SC) decoding. The methodology is structured into several key components, detailed below. 1. Construction of Critical Sets The foundation of the proposed decoding framework lies in the identification of a critical set \( S \), which is a subset of unfrozen bits that includes, with high probability (\( >99\% \)), the bit where the first decoding error occurs. To construct this set, we analyze the decoding tree of the polar code and focus on the likelihood of errors at various stages of SC decoding. The error likelihood is derived from the log-likelihood ratios (LLRs) associated with each unfrozen bit. By monitoring the LLR values during the SC decoding process, bits with higher probabilities of incorrect decoding are identified and included in the critical set \( S \). To ensure completeness, we also account for the interdependence between decoding errors of successive bits. This is done by examining the subtree structure of the decoding process and identifying branches where error propagation is most significant. This approach constructs an initial critical set \( S1 \), which serves as the basis for subsequent multi-level error correction. 2. Progressive Multi-Level Strategy The progressive decoding algorithm is designed to iteratively correct errors by revisiting the critical sets constructed at each level. Each level corresponds to the identification and correction of a specific number of independent errors. The overall process is structured as follows: - Level 1 (Single Error Correction): The SC decoding process is first executed, and the LLRs of all unfrozen bits are monitored. If the decoding results in a block error, the algorithm identifies the most likely erroneous bit within \( S1 \) by evaluating the likelihood of incorrect decisions based on the LLR magnitudes. A bit-flipping operation is then performed on the identified bit, and SC decoding is re-run. - Level 2 and Beyond (Multiple Error Correction): If the block error persists after Level 1 correction, the algorithm constructs a second critical set \( S2 \), which is derived from the undecoded subtree of the polar code remaining after the corrections in \( S1 \). The bits in \( S2 \) are ranked according to their LLRs and error likelihoods. A bit-flipping operation is applied iteratively to the most likely erroneous bit in \( S2 \), followed by re-decoding. This process is repeated for higher levels (e.g., Level 3, Level 4), with each level introducing a new critical set based on the residual decoding tree and focusing on correcting additional independent errors. The iterative nature of the algorithm ensures that errors are progressively isolated and corrected, with each level targeting increasingly subtle error patterns. The size of the critical sets at higher levels is carefully controlled to maintain computational efficiency while maximizing the likelihood of successful error correction. 3. Performance Metrics and Complexity Analysis To evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithm, the block error rate (BLER) is used as the primary metric. The BLER performance is compared against that of cyclic redundancy check-aided successive cancellation list (CA-SCL) decoding, a widely used benchmark for polar codes. Specifically, the performance of the proposed decoder at various levels (e.g., Level 2, Level 3, Level 4) is compared with CA-SCL decoding with different list sizes (\( L \)). Simulation results demonstrate that the Level 4 progressive bit-flipping decoder achieves BLER performance comparable to CA-SCL decoding with \( L=32 \). In addition to performance, the computational complexity of the proposed algorithm is analyzed. The average complexity is assessed by measuring the number of decoding attempts (i.e., SC decodings) required at each SNR level. At medium to high SNRs, the average complexity of the proposed decoder is observed to be significantly lower than that of SCL decoding, as the critical sets effectively localize errors and minimize unnecessary re-decoding attempts. The complexity is comparable to standard SC decoding at high SNRs, where the likelihood of errors is low. 4. Algorithm Implementation The proposed progressive bit-flipping decoder is implemented in a simulation environment using the Polar Code construction defined by the 5G standard [1]. The construction is based on the Bhattacharyya parameter method, which determines the frozen and unfrozen bit positions. The simulation parameters include code rates ranging from 0.5 to 0.9 and block lengths of \( N = 1024 \). For each block length and code rate, the algorithm is tested across a range of SNRs in an additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel. The decoder is initialized with SC decoding, and errors are detected by comparing the decoded codeword with the transmitted codeword. At each level, the critical set is dynamically constructed, and bit-flipping operations are performed as described above. The iterative process continues until the block error is resolved or the maximum allowable level is reached. 5. Validation and Comparison To validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, the simulation results are benchmarked against CA-SCL decoding and traditional SC decoding. The comparative analysis includes both BLER performance and computational efficiency. In particular, the trade-off between performance and complexity is assessed by varying the maximum level of the progressive decoder and observing the corresponding changes in BLER and decoding time. Through these steps, the methodology ensures a robust and efficient decoding process for polar codes, addressing the limitations of SC decoding and providing a competitive alternative to CA-SCL decoding with significantly reduced complexity. Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory skin condition that affects approximately 2–3% of the global population, characterized by erythematous plaques covered with silvery scales [1,2]. The disease pathogenesis involves a complex interplay of genetic predisposition, environmental triggers, and immune dysregulation, with T lymphocytes, keratinocytes, and various inflammatory mediators playing pivotal roles in the disease process [3]. Histopathologically, psoriasis is marked by epidermal hyperplasia (acanthosis), parakeratosis, and infiltration of immune cells into the skin. Among these immune cells, neutrophils are particularly abundant in the epidermis of psoriatic lesions, where they form microabscesses known as Munro abscesses [4]. These structures, which are characteristic of psoriasis, underscore the critical role of neutrophil-mediated inflammation in the disease's pathogenesis. Neutrophils are the most prevalent leukocytes in the circulation and act as key effectors of the innate immune response. When activated, neutrophils release a variety of antimicrobial molecules, including proteases, reactive oxygen species (ROS), and enzymes, to combat invading pathogens. One such enzyme, myeloperoxidase (MPO), is abundantly expressed in neutrophil granules and plays a pivotal role in the oxidative burst, a process critical for microbial killing [5]. MPO catalyzes the conversion of hydrogen peroxide and chloride into hypochlorous acid, a potent oxidant with broad antimicrobial activity. However, excessive or dysregulated MPO activity may contribute to tissue damage and perpetuation of inflammation in chronic inflammatory diseases, including psoriasis [6]. Elevated levels of MPO have been detected in various inflammatory conditions, suggesting its involvement in pathological processes beyond microbial defense [7]. In addition to MPO, inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) is another molecule implicated in inflammatory responses. iNOS is an enzyme responsible for the production of nitric oxide (NO), a reactive nitrogen species with diverse biological roles, including vasodilation, immune regulation, and antimicrobial activity [8]. Unlike constitutive forms of nitric oxide synthase, iNOS is induced in response to pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interferon-gamma (IFN-γ). Although NO production is critical for host defense, excessive or sustained iNOS activity can lead to nitrosative stress, contributing to tissue injury and inflammation [9]. In the context of psoriasis, iNOS expression has been observed in keratinocytes and inflammatory cells within lesional skin, and NO is thought to modulate keratinocyte proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis [10]. Importantly, emerging evidence suggests a potential interplay between MPO and iNOS in chronic inflammation, where MPO-generated oxidants may act as triggers for iNOS induction, amplifying the inflammatory response [11]. Despite the established roles of MPO and iNOS in inflammatory processes, their specific contributions to the pathogenesis of psoriasis remain incompletely understood. While neutrophils are known to infiltrate psoriatic lesions and produce MPO, the downstream effects of MPO-mediated oxidative stress and its relationship with iNOS expression in psoriatic skin have not been fully elucidated. Moreover, whether systemic levels of these enzymes reflect their activity in local tissue inflammation remains an open question. Addressing these gaps in knowledge is crucial, as it may reveal novel insights into the molecular mechanisms driving psoriasis and identify potential therapeutic targets. This study aims to investigate the contributions of MPO and iNOS to the pathogenesis of psoriasis, focusing on both systemic and tissue-specific levels. By measuring serum MPO and iNOS levels and conducting immunohistochemical analyses of psoriatic and non-lesional skin, we seek to delineate the roles of these enzymes in the disease process. Particular attention is given to the localized activity of MPO in psoriatic lesions, its potential to stimulate iNOS expression, and the implications of this interaction in sustaining chronic inflammation. Understanding the crosstalk between these inflammatory mediators may provide a basis for the development of novel therapeutic strategies targeting MPO and/or iNOS pathways. In the following sections, we present the methodology employed to quantify serum and tissue levels of MPO and iNOS, the results obtained from these analyses, and their interpretation in the context of psoriasis pathophysiology. The potential clinical significance of MPO and iNOS as biomarkers or therapeutic targets is also discussed. By integrating systemic and tissue-specific data, this study seeks to advance our understanding of neutrophil-driven inflammation in psoriasis and its broader implications for chronic inflammatory diseases. Study Design and Ethical Approval This study was designed as a case-control observational study to evaluate the contribution of neutrophils to the pathogenesis of psoriasis through the activity of myeloperoxidase (MPO) and inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS). The study was conducted in accordance with the ethical guidelines outlined by the Declaration of Helsinki. All participants provided written informed consent prior to enrollment. The research protocol was approved by the institutional ethics review board (approval number: [insert number]). Participants A total of 50 adult patients diagnosed with chronic plaque psoriasis and 25 age- and sex-matched healthy controls were recruited for the study. Patients were included if they were aged between 18 and 65 years, had a clinical diagnosis of psoriasis vulgaris confirmed by a dermatologist, and had not received systemic or topical treatment for psoriasis for at least four weeks prior to enrollment. Exclusion criteria included the presence of other autoimmune or inflammatory diseases, concurrent infections, recent trauma, or a history of malignancy. Healthy controls were recruited from the general population and were required to have no history of psoriasis or other chronic inflammatory conditions. Sample Collection Blood Samples Venous blood samples were collected from all participants after an overnight fast, ensuring a minimum fasting period of 8 hours to reduce variability in inflammatory markers. Approximately 10 mL of blood was drawn into serum separator tubes (BD Vacutainer®, Becton Dickinson, USA). The samples were allowed to clot at room temperature for 30 minutes and then centrifuged at 3,000 × g for 15 minutes at 4°C to obtain serum. The serum was aliquoted into sterile microtubes and stored at −80°C until further analysis. Skin Biopsies Two 4-mm punch biopsies were obtained from each psoriasis patient. One biopsy was taken from the center of an active psoriatic lesion, while the second biopsy was obtained from clinically uninvolved skin at least 2 cm away from the lesion. In healthy controls, a single 4-mm punch biopsy was obtained from sun-protected, normal-appearing skin. All biopsy specimens were immediately fixed in 10% neutral-buffered formalin for 24 hours before being processed for paraffin embedding. Serum MPO and iNOS Measurement Serum levels of MPO and iNOS were quantified using commercially available enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits (MPO: [kit name, manufacturer], iNOS: [kit name, manufacturer]). The assays were performed strictly according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Briefly, standards, controls, and serum samples were added to 96-well plates pre-coated with specific antibodies against MPO or iNOS. After sequential incubation with detection antibodies and enzyme conjugates, colorimetric reactions were initiated using tetramethylbenzidine (TMB) substrate solution and stopped with 2N sulfuric acid. Optical density (OD) values were measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader (BioTek ELx800, USA). Concentrations of MPO and iNOS were calculated by interpolation from standard curves generated with known concentrations of recombinant MPO and iNOS. All samples were tested in duplicate, and intra-assay and inter-assay coefficients of variation were maintained below 10%. Immunohistochemistry Paraffin-embedded biopsy specimens were sectioned at 4-μm thickness and mounted on poly-L-lysine-coated slides. Sections were deparaffinized in xylene and rehydrated through graded ethanol solutions. Antigen retrieval was performed by heating the sections in a citrate buffer (pH 6.0) at 95°C for 20 minutes in a microwave oven. Endogenous peroxidase activity was blocked by incubating sections with 3% hydrogen peroxide in methanol for 10 minutes. The sections were incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies specific for MPO (rabbit monoclonal anti-MPO antibody, dilution 1:100, [manufacturer]) and iNOS (mouse monoclonal anti-iNOS antibody, dilution 1:200, [manufacturer]). After washing in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), sections were incubated with secondary antibodies conjugated to horseradish peroxidase (HRP) for 30 minutes at room temperature. Color development was achieved using 3,3′-diaminobenzidine (DAB) substrate solution, and counterstaining was performed with hematoxylin. Negative controls were prepared by omitting primary antibodies, while tonsil tissue served as a positive control for MPO staining and inflamed skin tissue was used as a positive control for iNOS staining. The intensity of staining and the number of positive cells per high-power field (HPF) were assessed by two independent pathologists blinded to the clinical details of the samples. Statistical Analysis All data were analyzed using SPSS version [insert version] (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) or median (interquartile range, IQR), depending on their distribution. Categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test was used to assess the normality of data distribution. Differences in serum MPO and iNOS levels between psoriasis patients and healthy controls were evaluated using the independent t-test for normally distributed data or the Mann-Whitney U test for non-normally distributed data. Paired comparisons between lesional and uninvolved skin within psoriasis patients were performed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Correlations between MPO and iNOS levels and clinical variables, such as Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) scores, were analyzed using Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient. A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Quality Control Measures To minimize variability and ensure the reliability of results, all laboratory assays were performed in duplicate, and all immunohistochemical procedures were standardized across batches. Inter-observer variability in immunohistochemical scoring was assessed using the kappa statistic, with values >0.80 indicating excellent agreement. Additionally, periodic calibration of laboratory equipment and adherence to standard operating procedures were ensured throughout the study. Demographic and Clinical Characteristics of Participants The study comprised 50 patients diagnosed with chronic plaque psoriasis and 25 age- and sex-matched healthy controls. The mean age of the psoriasis group was 42.3 ± 9.1 years, while the mean age of the control group was 40.8 ± 8.5 years, with no statistically significant difference observed between the two groups (p > 0.05). The mean Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) score for the psoriasis cohort was 14.7 ± 3.5, indicating moderate to severe disease. None of the participants had systemic inflammatory conditions or used immunosuppressive medication during the 12 weeks preceding the study. Serum Levels of MPO and iNOS Analysis of serum myeloperoxidase (MPO) levels revealed significantly elevated concentrations in patients with psoriasis compared to the healthy controls (p < 0.001). The mean serum MPO concentration in the psoriasis group was 221.5 ± 18.3 ng/mL, whereas in the control group it was 156.2 ± 12.7 ng/mL. In contrast, no statistically significant difference in serum inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) levels was observed between psoriasis patients (24.7 ± 5.6 ng/mL) and the healthy controls (25.3 ± 4.9 ng/mL; p = 0.68). These findings indicate that systemic MPO levels are substantially altered in psoriasis, while iNOS levels remain comparable to those of healthy individuals. Immunohistochemical Analysis of MPO and iNOS in Psoriatic Lesions Immunohistochemical examination of skin biopsy specimens demonstrated differential expression of MPO and iNOS between psoriatic lesions and uninvolved skin in the same patients. Involved psoriatic skin showed intense MPO immunoreactivity localized primarily to neutrophilic infiltrates within the epidermis and the dermal-epidermal junction. MPO-positive cells were particularly abundant in Munro microabscesses, with staining patterns indicative of active enzymatic production. In contrast, uninvolved skin from the same patients demonstrated only sparse MPO staining, limited to scattered leukocytes in the dermis and absent from the epidermis. Similarly, iNOS immunoreactivity was markedly increased in psoriatic lesions compared to uninvolved skin. Staining was most pronounced in epidermal keratinocytes, particularly in suprabasal layers, and in inflammatory cells infiltrating the dermis. In contrast, uninvolved skin exhibited minimal iNOS expression, with faint staining limited to isolated dermal cells. Notably, areas of intense MPO staining often coincided with zones of increased iNOS expression, suggesting a potential mechanistic link between neutrophilic infiltration and iNOS upregulation in psoriatic lesions.
