Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the oral tongue is one of the most common malignancies of the head and neck region, with significant morbidity and mortality worldwide. Despite advances in diagnostic and therapeutic modalities, oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma (OTSCC) continues to pose a clinical challenge due to its aggressive behavior, propensity for early metastasis, and recurrence [1, 2]. The tumor thickness (TT) of OTSCC has emerged as an important prognostic factor, influencing disease progression and the likelihood of cervical lymph node metastasis [3]. Accurate preoperative assessment of TT is therefore critical in determining the extent of surgical intervention, including the need for elective neck dissection (END) in clinically node-negative (N0) patients. The evaluation of TT in OTSCC is particularly relevant in cases of early-stage disease, classified as pT1 and pT2 tumors according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) staging system. Early-stage OTSCC is often confined to the primary site, with no clinically palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. However, despite the absence of clinically detectable nodal metastasis, occult metastases can be present in a significant proportion of patients, necessitating END to improve outcomes [4, 5]. The decision to perform END in clinically N0 patients is often debated due to the associated morbidity, such as shoulder dysfunction and sensory deficits, balanced against the potential survival benefit [6]. Tumor thickness has been proposed as a surrogate marker to guide this decision-making process, as thicker tumors are more likely to harbor occult nodal metastases [7]. Traditionally, TT has been evaluated postoperatively using histopathological measurements, which remain the gold standard. However, this approach precludes its use as a preoperative decision-making tool. Preoperative imaging modalities, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT), have been employed to estimate TT, but these techniques are often limited by high costs, lack of widespread availability, and variability in accuracy [8]. Ultrasonography (USG), on the other hand, is a non-invasive, cost-effective, and widely accessible imaging modality that has shown promise in measuring TT preoperatively in OTSCC [9]. High-resolution intraoral ultrasonography allows for real-time visualization of the tumor and surrounding tissue, enabling precise measurement of TT. Additionally, neck ultrasonography can provide valuable information on cervical nodal status, further aiding in treatment planning [10]. Despite its potential, the utility of USG in the preoperative evaluation of TT in OTSCC has not been fully validated. Limited studies have explored its reliability in comparison to histopathological findings, and there is a paucity of robust data correlating USG-derived TT measurements with nodal metastasis. The present study aims to address these gaps by assessing the statistical correlation between TT measured preoperatively by USG and TT determined via histopathological examination. Furthermore, it seeks to evaluate the predictive capacity of USG-derived TT in detecting occult cervical nodal metastasis in early-stage OTSCC. Previous research has demonstrated a strong correlation between USG-derived TT and histopathological TT in various oral cavity subsites, suggesting that USG may be a reliable modality for preoperative assessment [11]. However, these studies often include small sample sizes, heterogeneous tumor subsites, and variations in imaging protocols, limiting the generalizability of their findings. The present study focuses exclusively on early OTSCC, a subgroup of tumors with distinct clinical and pathological characteristics. By doing so, it seeks to provide more specific insights into the role of USG in this context. Another critical aspect of this study is the evaluation of TT as a predictor of occult nodal metastasis. The presence of cervical lymph node metastasis is a well-established prognostic factor in OTSCC, significantly impacting survival rates [12]. While clinical and imaging-based nodal assessment remains the standard approach, it is often inadequate for detecting small-volume or micrometastatic disease. Several studies have proposed specific TT thresholds, such as 4 mm or 5 mm, as predictive cutoffs for increased risk of occult nodal metastasis [13, 14]. However, there is considerable variability in the reported thresholds, and their applicability to clinical practice is uncertain. By correlating USG-derived TT with histopathological nodal status, this study aims to determine a reliable TT cutoff that can guide the decision for END in early OTSCC. The implications of this study are significant for clinical practice, particularly in resource-limited settings where advanced imaging modalities may not be readily available. If validated, USG could serve as a rapid, cost-effective tool for preoperative risk stratification, enabling tailored surgical management and potentially reducing the morbidity associated with overtreatment. Furthermore, the findings could contribute to the growing body of evidence supporting the integration of USG into routine diagnostic workflows for oral cancer. In summary, the present study aims to evaluate the correlation between USG-derived TT and histopathological TT in early OTSCC and to assess the predictive value of USG-derived TT in detecting occult nodal metastasis. By addressing these objectives, it seeks to establish USG as a reliable and practical tool for preoperative assessment, ultimately improving the management of early-stage OTSCC. The findings are expected to have significant implications for optimizing treatment strategies, reducing unnecessary morbidity, and improving outcomes in patients with this challenging malignancy. This prospective study was conducted over a two-year period from 2012 to 2013 in a tertiary care center following approval from the institutional ethics committee. The study population consisted of patients diagnosed with early oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma (OTSCC), classified as T1 or T2 (pT1 & pT2) tumors with clinically negative neck nodes (N0). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to inclusion in the study. A total of 24 patients were enrolled, based on the following inclusion criteria: (1) histopathologically confirmed squamous cell carcinoma of the oral tongue, (2) primary tumor classified as T1 or T2 according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) staging system, and (3) clinically negative neck node status based on physical examination and ultrasonographic evaluation. Patients with recurrent disease, prior treatment for OTSCC, or distant metastases were excluded from the study. Preoperative evaluation included a detailed clinical examination, imaging studies, and ultrasonographic tumor thickness (TT) measurement. Ultrasonographic evaluation of the primary tumor was performed using a high-frequency linear transducer (7.5–13 MHz), with the patient positioned supine and the tongue protruded to maximize exposure of the lesion. The transducer was placed gently on the tongue surface to minimize compression of the soft tissue. The depth of tumor invasion, defined as the distance from the mucosal surface to the deepest point of tumor involvement, was measured in millimeters (mm). Three independent measurements were taken for each tumor, and the mean value was recorded to minimize operator variability. Nodal evaluation was conducted preoperatively using neck ultrasonography (USG), focusing on levels I through IV of the cervical lymph nodes. Sonographic criteria for suspicious nodes included a round shape, absence of fatty hilum, hypoechoic echotexture, and short-axis diameter greater than 10 mm. All cases were clinically staged using a combination of clinical examination and imaging findings. Following histopathological confirmation of malignancy through incisional biopsy, all patients underwent surgical management, which included wide local excision of the primary tumor with adequate margins and ipsilateral elective neck dissection of levels I to IV, as per institutional protocol. Intraoperatively, the glossectomy specimens were marked and carefully oriented for uniformity of measurement. Fresh specimens were used to measure tumor thickness immediately following excision. The maximum depth of invasion was recorded using a sterile caliper. Postoperative histopathological assessment was conducted on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue sections to confirm tumor thickness and nodal status. For each specimen, tumor thickness was measured microscopically as the vertical depth from the most superficial epithelial surface to the deepest point of tumor invasion. All histopathological evaluations were performed by a single experienced pathologist to ensure consistency. The pathological nodal status was classified based on the presence or absence of metastatic deposits in the dissected lymph nodes. Occult metastases were defined as histologically confirmed metastases in lymph nodes that were clinically negative preoperatively. The primary objective of the study was to assess the correlation between tumor thickness measured by preoperative ultrasonography and histopathological measurements. Statistical correlation was evaluated using Pearson’s correlation coefficient (r), and interclass correlation coefficient (ICC) was calculated to determine the level of agreement between the two methods. A Bland-Altman plot was used to assess the agreement between ultrasonographic and histopathological measurements, with bias and 95% limits of agreement reported. The secondary objective of the study was to evaluate the predictive capacity of ultrasonographic TT in identifying patients at risk of occult cervical nodal metastasis. The association between tumor thickness and nodal metastasis was analyzed using the chi-square test. Tumor thickness thresholds for nodal metastasis risk stratification were determined by categorizing patients into groups based on TT (<4 mm or ≥4 mm) and analyzing the corresponding nodal status. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05 for all analyses, which were performed using SPSS software (version 20.0; IBM Corp., Armonk, NY). Data collection and analysis were conducted in compliance with established research guidelines. The reliability of ultrasonography as a preoperative tool for TT measurement was assessed by comparing the accuracy, reproducibility, and predictive value of ultrasonographic measurements with histopathological findings. Results were reported in terms of sensitivity, specificity, and overall correlation to highlight the practical implications of ultrasonographic evaluation in the management of early OTSCC. A total of 24 patients with early oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma (OTSCC) were included in the study. The tumor thickness (TT) was assessed preoperatively by ultrasonography (USG) and compared with histopathological measurements obtained intraoperatively and postoperatively. The primary objective was to evaluate the statistical correlation between the two measurements, while the secondary objective was to assess the predictive capacity of USG-measured TT in detecting occult nodal metastasis. The analysis demonstrated a statistically significant correlation between TT obtained by USG and histopathology. Specifically, the Pearson correlation coefficient (r) was 0.678 (P < 0.001), indicating a strong positive relationship between the two measurement methods. Additionally, the interclass correlation coefficient (ICC) was calculated to be 0.808, further corroborating the reliability of USG in estimating TT. The Bland-Altman plot revealed an average difference (bias) of -0.14637 mm between the microscopic and USG measurements, with 95% limits of agreement ranging from -4.863 mm to 4.717 mm. This indicates that while minor variations in TT measurements occurred, the majority of values fell within a clinically acceptable range. Specifically, the TT measurements obtained by USG were within 1 mm of the histopathological measurements in 37.5% of cases (9/24), within 2 mm in 29.16% of cases (7/24), and more than 2 mm in 33.3% of cases (8/24). The association between TT and nodal metastasis status was also examined. The overall rate of occult cervical nodal metastasis in the cohort was 16.6% (4/24). Notably, all cases of occult nodal metastasis were observed in patients with a TT of 4 mm or greater, as measured histopathologically. In contrast, patients with a TT less than 4 mm did not exhibit any evidence of occult nodal metastasis. This finding suggests that a TT threshold of 4 mm may be a significant predictor of nodal involvement in early OTSCC. Statistical analysis using the chi-square test confirmed a significant association between TT and pathological nodal status (P < 0.05). Furthermore, no significant correlation was observed between the pathological T stage and nodal status, highlighting the importance of TT as an independent predictor of occult metastasis. The results also underscored the practical utility of USG as a preoperative imaging modality. USG not only provided a reliable estimation of TT but also proved to be a cost-effective and noninvasive tool for guiding clinical decision-making. In particular, the identification of patients with TT less than 4 mm could potentially obviate the need for elective neck dissection in selected cases, thereby reducing surgical morbidity. First, the inherent differences in tissue states between live and excised specimens may have contributed to measurement discrepancies. Biofilm-associated infections represent a significant challenge in modern medicine due to their inherent resistance to conventional antimicrobial therapies. Biofilms, which are structured communities of microbial cells enclosed in a self-produced extracellular polymeric substance (EPS), provide a protective niche for bacteria, allowing them to evade host immune responses and resist the action of antibiotics. This resilience is particularly problematic in chronic infections, where biofilms are implicated in conditions such as endocarditis, chronic wounds, medical device-associated infections, and cystic fibrosis-related lung infections. The presence of persister cells, a dormant subpopulation of bacteria within biofilms, further complicates treatment efforts. These cells exhibit a transient tolerance to antibiotics, often surviving even high doses of antimicrobial agents, and contribute to the recalcitrant nature of biofilm infections. Consequently, there is an urgent need to identify novel strategies or adjuvants that can effectively disrupt biofilms and sensitize bacteria to antibiotic therapy. The interplay between host immune defenses and antibiotics has garnered increasing attention as a potential approach to address biofilm infections. In particular, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) – small, naturally occurring components of the innate immune system – have emerged as promising candidates for enhancing antibiotic efficacy. AMPs are produced by a wide range of organisms, including humans, insects, and plants, and exhibit broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity. Their mechanisms of action often involve disruption of bacterial membranes, modulation of bacterial metabolism, or interference with biofilm formation, making them attractive tools for combating multidrug-resistant pathogens and biofilm-associated infections. Importantly, AMPs also have the potential to target persister cells and destabilize the biofilm matrix, thereby overcoming key barriers to effective treatment. Insects, as a result of their evolutionary adaptation to diverse microbial environments, possess potent AMP complexes that are highly effective against a wide range of pathogens. The blowfly Calliphora vicina, for instance, produces an AMP complex known as FLIP7, which is composed of multiple antimicrobial agents, including defensins, cecropins, diptericins, and proline-rich peptides. This multifaceted composition allows FLIP7 to target bacteria via multiple mechanisms, reducing the likelihood of resistance development. The ability of FLIP7 to synergize with antibiotics and enhance their activity against biofilms, however, remains largely unexplored. The objective of this study was to investigate the potential of FLIP7 to improve the anti-biofilm activity of antibiotics and to elucidate the mechanisms underlying this interaction. We hypothesized that the synergistic action of FLIP7 with antibiotics could sensitize persister cells and disrupt the biofilm structure, thereby enhancing bacterial eradication. To test this, we examined the interaction of FLIP7 with antibiotics from various classes, including β-lactams, aminoglycosides, macrolides, and glycopeptides, against biofilm and planktonic cultures of clinically relevant bacterial pathogens. These pathogens included Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Acinetobacter baumannii, which are among the most common causative agents of biofilm-associated infections and are notable for their ability to resist antibiotic treatment. Using a combination of methodologies, including checkerboard assays, trimethyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) cell viability assays, crystal violet biofilm eradication assays, and microscopic analysis, we evaluated the efficacy of FLIP7 in conjunction with antibiotics. The fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) was used to quantify the degree of synergy or antagonism between FLIP7 and each antibiotic. The dose-effect relationships were analyzed to identify potential targets of FLIP7's synergistic effects, with particular attention to the role of persister cells. Additionally, the biofilm eradication assay allowed us to assess the ability of the FLIP7-antibiotic combination to disrupt biofilm structures and eliminate biofilm-embedded bacteria. Our findings demonstrate that FLIP7 exhibits significant synergy with a wide range of antibiotics, particularly those targeting cell wall synthesis (e.g., meropenem, ampicillin, vancomycin) and protein synthesis (e.g., amikacin, kanamycin, clindamycin). Notably, the synergistic effect was more pronounced in biofilm cultures compared to planktonic cells, suggesting that FLIP7's activity is particularly effective in the biofilm microenvironment. The synergistic interactions allowed for substantial reductions in the effective anti-biofilm concentrations of antibiotics, in some cases by several orders of magnitude. This reduction has important clinical implications, as it enables the use of lower antibiotic doses, potentially minimizing toxicity and the risk of resistance development. Further analysis revealed that the synergistic effect of FLIP7 was associated with its ability to sensitize persister cells and disrupt the structural integrity of the biofilm matrix. The destruction of biofilm materials was especially evident in S. aureus and E. coli biofilms, where the combination treatment led to the complete eradication of biofilm-associated bacteria. The lack of interaction between FLIP7 and polymyxin B, however, highlights the specificity of the synergistic effects and underscores the need for tailored AMP-antibiotic combinations for different clinical scenarios. The results of this study underscore the potential of FLIP7 as a powerful adjuvant for antibiotics in the treatment of biofilm-associated infections. By targeting persister cells and destabilizing biofilm structures, FLIP7 enhances the efficacy of antibiotics and addresses key challenges in the management of chronic and recalcitrant infections. These findings pave the way for further research into the clinical application of AMP-antibiotic combinations, with the ultimate goal of improving outcomes for patients suffering from biofilm-related diseases. FLIP7, the antimicrobial peptide (AMP) complex of the blowfly Calliphora vicina, was isolated from the hemolymph of bacteria-challenged maggots to evaluate its potential in enhancing the anti-biofilm activity of antibiotics. The experimental design included the preparation and characterization of FLIP7, the selection of bacterial strains and antibiotics, and the application of in vitro assays to assess the interactions between FLIP7 and antibiotics in both planktonic and biofilm conditions. Preparation of FLIP7 To obtain FLIP7, C. vicina larvae were challenged with a suspension of Escherichia coli (OD600 = 0.5) to induce an antimicrobial immune response. After 24 hours, hemolymph was collected by puncturing the larvae and centrifuging at 10,000 × g for 15 minutes at 4°C to remove hemocytes and debris. The supernatant was subjected to solid-phase extraction using C18 Sep-Pak cartridges (Waters Corporation, USA) for peptide enrichment. Eluted peptides were lyophilized, resuspended in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), and further purified by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). The resulting fraction, termed FLIP7, contained a mixture of AMPs, including defensins, cecropins, diptericins, and proline-rich peptides, as confirmed by mass spectrometry. Bacterial Strains and Growth Conditions The following bacterial strains were used: Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 29213, Escherichia coli ATCC 25922, Pseudomonas aeruginosa PAO1, Klebsiella pneumoniae ATCC 700603, and Acinetobacter baumannii ATCC 19606. Strains were grown in Mueller-Hinton Broth (MHB) at 37°C with shaking for planktonic assays and in 96-well microtiter plates to establish biofilms. Biofilms were formed by incubating bacterial suspensions (OD600 = 0.5) in MHB supplemented with 1% glucose at 37°C for 24 hours without agitation. Biofilm formation was confirmed by visual inspection and crystal violet staining. Antibiotics and Concentration Ranges The antibiotics tested included meropenem, amikacin, kanamycin, ampicillin, vancomycin, cefotaxime, clindamycin, erythromycin, chloramphenicol, oxacillin, tetracycline, ciprofloxacin, gentamicin, and polymyxin B. Stock solutions of each antibiotic were prepared in sterile water or dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) as appropriate. The working concentrations for each antibiotic were selected based on their minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) against the respective bacterial strains, determined via microdilution assays in accordance with CLSI guidelines. Checkerboard Assay for Synergy Testing Synergy between FLIP7 and antibiotics was assessed using the checkerboard method. Two-fold serial dilutions of each antibiotic were prepared in 96-well plates, and FLIP7 was added at concentrations ranging from 0.5 to 32 µg/mL. Wells were inoculated with bacterial suspensions (5 × 10⁵ CFU/mL) and incubated at 37°C for 24 hours. Bacterial viability was measured using a trimethyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC, Sigma-Aldrich) assay, in which metabolically active cells reduce TTC to formazan, producing a colorimetric signal at 490 nm. The fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) was calculated for each combination as follows: FICI = (MIC of antibiotic in combination/MIC of antibiotic alone) + (MIC of FLIP7 in combination/MIC of FLIP7 alone). Synergy was defined as FICI ≤ 0.5, additive interaction as 0.5 < FICI ≤ 1, and no interaction as FICI > 1. Biofilm Eradication Assay The anti-biofilm effects of FLIP7 and antibiotics were evaluated using the crystal violet staining method. Preformed biofilms were washed twice with PBS to remove planktonic cells and treated with antibiotics, FLIP7, or their combinations for 24 hours. After treatment, wells were washed with PBS, stained with 0.1% crystal violet for 15 minutes, and washed again to remove excess stain. The adhered dye was solubilized with 30% acetic acid, and absorbance was measured at 590 nm. Biofilm eradication was expressed as a percentage relative to untreated controls. Microscopic Analysis of Biofilms To visualize biofilm disruption, confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) was employed. Biofilms were grown on glass coverslips in 24-well plates, treated with FLIP7 and antibiotics at synergistic concentrations, and stained with the LIVE/DEAD BacLight Bacterial Viability Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Images were obtained using a Zeiss LSM 880 microscope, and the ratio of live (green) to dead (red) cells was quantified using ImageJ software. Structural integrity and thickness of the biofilms were also analyzed. Dose–Effect Curve Analysis To further understand the interaction between FLIP7 and antibiotics, dose–effect curves were generated using the Chou-Talalay method. Serial dilutions of antibiotics were combined with fixed concentrations of FLIP7, and bacterial viability was assessed as described above. The data were analyzed to identify potential targeting of persister cells, which are known to contribute to biofilm resistance. Synergistic effects were indicated by a leftward shift in the dose–effect curve of the antibiotic in the presence of FLIP7. Statistical Analysis All experiments were performed in triplicate, and data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation. Statistical significance was determined using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test for multiple comparisons. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The results of our study demonstrate the potential of the FLIP7 antimicrobial peptide (AMP) complex to enhance the anti-biofilm activity of various antibiotics. The interaction of FLIP7 with antibiotics of different classes was systematically evaluated against planktonic and biofilm cultures of Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Acinetobacter baumannii. Synergistic Activity in Biofilm Cultures Using the checkerboard assay, we observed that FLIP7 exhibited high synergy with several antibiotics when tested against biofilm cultures. The combination of FLIP7 with meropenem, amikacin, kanamycin, ampicillin, vancomycin, and cefotaxime resulted in fractional inhibitory concentration (FIC) indices of less than 0.25, indicating strong synergistic interactions. Synergy was also observed for clindamycin, erythromycin, and chloramphenicol, though at slightly higher FIC indices (0.25–0.5). Additive interactions (FIC indices between 0.5 and 1.0) were noted for oxacillin, tetracycline, ciprofloxacin, and gentamicin. Notably, no interaction was detected between FLIP7 and polymyxin B (FIC > 1.0), suggesting that the mechanism of action of polymyxin B is not enhanced by FLIP7 under these conditions. Biofilm eradication assays further supported these findings. In particular, combinations of FLIP7 with meropenem, ampicillin, cefotaxime, or vancomycin led to the complete destruction of biofilm biomass in S. aureus and E. coli cultures, as quantified by crystal violet staining and confirmed through microscopic analysis. The reduction in biofilm-associated biomass was accompanied by a marked decrease in bacterial cell viability, as determined by the trimethyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) assay. Comparison Between Planktonic and Biofilm Models Interestingly, the synergistic effects of FLIP7 and antibiotics were significantly more pronounced in biofilm cultures compared to planktonic cells of the same strains. For example, while the combination of FLIP7 and meropenem reduced the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of meropenem by approximately two-fold in planktonic S. aureus cultures, the same combination resulted in a 100-fold reduction in the effective anti-biofilm concentration. Similar trends were observed for ampicillin, cefotaxime, and vancomycin, where the effective concentrations required for biofilm eradication were reduced by 2–3 orders of magnitude when combined with FLIP7. These findings suggest that FLIP7 preferentially targets biofilm-specific mechanisms, potentially including persister cells and biofilm matrix components. Protein arginine methyltransferase 4 (PRMT4), also known as co-activator-associated arginine methyltransferase 1 (CARM1), is a member of the PRMT family of enzymes responsible for catalyzing the methylation of arginine residues on histone and non-histone proteins [1]. This post-translational modification plays a critical role in regulating diverse cellular processes, including transcriptional activation, RNA splicing, and signal transduction pathways [2]. CARM1 functions predominantly as a transcriptional co-activator by asymmetrically dimethylating histone H3 at arginine 17 (H3R17me2a) and arginine 26 (H3R26me2a), modifications that are associated with transcriptional activation and chromatin remodeling [3, 4]. In addition to histone substrates, CARM1 targets a wide array of non-histone proteins, including splicing factors such as PABP1 (poly(A)-binding protein 1) and SMB (small nuclear ribonucleoprotein-associated protein B), further underscoring its role as a key regulator of gene expression and RNA processing [5, 6]. The dysregulation of CARM1 has been implicated in various aspects of cancer biology. Overexpression or hyperactivation of CARM1 has been observed in multiple malignancies, including breast cancer, prostate cancer, and colorectal cancer, where it is frequently associated with poor prognosis and increased tumor aggressiveness [7, 8]. Mechanistic studies have demonstrated that CARM1 promotes oncogenesis through its ability to regulate transcriptional programs involved in cell proliferation, migration, and survival [9]. Moreover, the enzyme's role in modulating non-histone substrates has been linked to changes in RNA splicing patterns, further contributing to tumor progression [10]. Despite its apparent importance in cancer biology, the precise mechanisms by which CARM1 drives oncogenesis remain incompletely understood, particularly in the context of hematologic malignancies such as multiple myeloma (MM). Multiple myeloma is an incurable plasma cell malignancy characterized by clonal expansion of abnormal plasma cells within the bone marrow microenvironment [11]. Although substantial progress has been made in the development of novel therapeutic agents for MM, including proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulatory drugs, and monoclonal antibodies, the disease remains challenging to treat due to the emergence of drug resistance and disease relapse [12]. As such, there is a critical need to identify new therapeutic targets and develop innovative strategies to overcome treatment resistance in MM. Accumulating evidence suggests that epigenetic dysregulation plays a central role in MM pathogenesis. Aberrant expression and activity of various epigenetic modifiers, including histone methyltransferases and acetyltransferases, have been reported in MM and are thought to contribute to disease progression and resistance to therapy [13, 14]. However, the role of CARM1 in MM has not been extensively investigated, and the identification of selective inhibitors targeting CARM1 could provide valuable insights into its biological function and therapeutic potential in this disease. Efforts to elucidate the role of CARM1 in cancer have been limited by a lack of selective tool compounds capable of inhibiting CARM1 activity in both in vitro and in vivo settings. While several chemical probes targeting other members of the PRMT family have been developed, many of these compounds lack the selectivity and potency required to precisely interrogate CARM1-specific functions [15]. Furthermore, the development of CARM1 inhibitors suitable for in vivo use has been hindered by challenges related to pharmacokinetics, bioavailability, and off-target effects on other methyltransferases [16]. The absence of robust chemical probes has thus represented a significant barrier to understanding the biological and oncogenic roles of CARM1, as well as its potential as a therapeutic target. In this study, we report the identification and characterization of EZM2302 (also referred to as GSK3359088), a highly selective and potent small-molecule inhibitor of CARM1. To our knowledge, EZM2302 represents the first chemical probe capable of robustly inhibiting CARM1 activity in preclinical models, providing a unique opportunity to investigate the functional consequences of CARM1 inhibition in cancer. EZM2302 demonstrates nanomolar potency in biochemical assays and exhibits a high degree of selectivity against other histone methyltransferases, addressing a critical unmet need for selective CARM1 inhibitors. In vitro studies reveal that EZM2302 effectively inhibits CARM1-mediated methylation of its non-histone substrates, PABP1 and SMB, leading to significant anti-proliferative effects in MM cell lines. Importantly, oral administration of EZM2302 induces dose-dependent inhibition of CARM1 activity in vivo and displays robust anti-tumor efficacy in an MM xenograft model, providing compelling evidence for the therapeutic potential of CARM1 inhibition in MM. Here, we present a detailed characterization of EZM2302, including its biochemical properties, selectivity profile, and anti-tumor activity in both in vitro and in vivo models of MM. In addition to establishing EZM2302 as a validated chemical tool for studying CARM1 biology, our findings provide the first direct evidence implicating CARM1 in MM pathogenesis and highlight its potential as a therapeutic target in this disease. This work underscores the importance of developing selective chemical probes to investigate the functions of epigenetic regulators in cancer and offers a foundation for future studies aimed at exploring the role of CARM1 in other malignancies and disease contexts. MM cell lines were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 5,000 cells per well and treated with serial dilutions of EZM2302 for 72 hours. Western Blot Analysis To assess the effects of EZM2302 on target protein methylation, MM cells were treated with the compound for 24 hours, and cell lysates were prepared using RIPA buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors. Equal amounts of protein were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred onto polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membranes. RNA integrity was confirmed using the Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies). RNA sequencing libraries were prepared using the TruSeq Stranded mRNA Library Prep Kit (Illumina) and sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 at 50 million paired-end reads per sample. Differential gene expression analysis was performed using the DESeq2 package in R, with a false discovery rate (FDR) threshold of 0.05. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was conducted to identify pathways enriched in EZM2302-treated cells compared to controls. Recommendation systems have become a critical component of modern digital platforms, shaping user experiences in various domains such as entertainment, e-commerce, social media, and employment. By leveraging vast amounts of user interaction data, these systems provide personalized suggestions that enhance user engagement and satisfaction. Their success lies in their ability to model user preferences through sophisticated algorithms, often powered by machine learning techniques. However, as these systems are designed to learn from historical user behavior, they inevitably inherit and reflect the biases embedded in the input data. While such biases may arise naturally from societal or individual preferences, the interplay between recommendation algorithms and biased data can lead to unintended and potentially harmful consequences. One of the central challenges in studying biases in recommendation systems is understanding how these systems not only reflect existing biases but also amplify or propagate them over time. This phenomenon, often referred to as bias amplification or bias disparity, occurs when the recommendations produced by a system disproportionately favor certain groups, categories, or behaviors, exacerbating inequities present in the input data. For example, consider a job recommendation system that disproportionately suggests certain roles to specific demographic groups based on historical hiring patterns. Over time, such recommendations may reinforce stereotypes and limit opportunities for underrepresented groups, creating a feedback loop that perpetuates systemic bias. Similar concerns arise in other domains, such as music or movie recommendations, where certain genres or artists may dominate at the expense of diversity, or in e-commerce, where products from smaller vendors may be systematically underrepresented. The roots of bias disparity in recommendation systems can be traced to several factors. First, the data used to train such systems often reflects historical inequalities or skewed user behavior. For instance, in a content platform, the engagement levels with different types of content may vary across user groups, leading to imbalanced data distributions. Second, algorithmic design choices, such as optimization for accuracy or user engagement, can inadvertently favor the majority or dominant patterns in the data, further disadvantaging minority groups or less-represented items. Finally, the iterative nature of recommendation systems, where user behavior is influenced by the system's outputs, creates a feedback loop in which biases can compound over time. Despite the growing recognition of these challenges, there remains limited understanding of the precise conditions under which bias disparity arises, as well as the long-term effects of biased recommendations on user behavior and data distributions. Addressing bias disparity in recommendation systems is critical for ensuring fairness, equity, and diversity in digital platforms. While much of the existing research on fairness in machine learning has focused on classification and decision-making tasks, recommendation systems pose unique challenges due to their interactive and dynamic nature. Unlike static classification models, recommendation systems continuously influence user behavior, which in turn shapes future recommendations. This interdependence introduces complexities in measuring and mitigating bias, as interventions aimed at reducing disparity may have unintended consequences on other system objectives, such as user satisfaction or engagement. Furthermore, the definition of fairness in recommendation systems is often context-dependent, requiring careful consideration of the specific domain, stakeholders, and societal norms. In this work, we aim to contribute to the growing body of research on bias in recommendation systems by examining the phenomenon of bias disparity through both synthetic and real-world data. Specifically, we investigate the conditions under which a recommendation system exhibits bias disparity and explore the long-term effects of biased recommendations on data distributions. To this end, we develop a controlled experimental setup using synthetic data, enabling us to systematically analyze the interplay between data bias, algorithmic design, and recommendation outcomes. By isolating key factors that influence bias disparity, we gain insights into the mechanisms through which biases are amplified and identify potential strategies for mitigating their effects. As a first step toward addressing bias disparity, we also explore the use of a simple re-ranking algorithm designed to reduce disparities in recommendations. Re-ranking approaches, which modify the output of a recommendation algorithm to achieve specific objectives, have gained attention as a practical and interpretable method for incorporating fairness considerations. Our preliminary results suggest that re-ranking can be an effective tool for reducing bias disparity, although its impact on other system metrics, such as accuracy and diversity, warrants further investigation. To complement our synthetic data experiments, we conduct an initial analysis of bias disparity on real-world data, providing insights into the practical challenges and trade-offs involved in mitigating bias in operational recommendation systems. Through this study, we aim to shed light on the complex dynamics of bias disparity in recommendation systems and contribute to the development of methods for building more equitable and inclusive recommendation algorithms. While our findings are preliminary, they highlight the importance of considering bias and fairness as fundamental aspects of recommendation system design, rather than as afterthoughts or secondary objectives. As the deployment of recommendation systems continues to expand into high-stakes domains, such as hiring, education, and healthcare, addressing bias disparity will be essential for ensuring that these systems serve the needs of all users fairly and equitably. We hope that this work will inspire further research into the mechanisms, measurement, and mitigation of bias in recommendation systems, fostering a broader dialogue on the societal implications of algorithmic decision-making. To investigate the phenomenon of bias disparity in recommendation systems, we conducted a series of experiments using both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our methodology is structured into three main components: (1) data generation and preprocessing, (2) recommendation algorithms and evaluation, and (3) re-ranking for bias mitigation. Each step is described in detail below. 1. Data Generation and Preprocessing To explore bias disparity systematically, we generated synthetic datasets with controlled biases and also utilized a real-world dataset. The synthetic data allowed for precise manipulation of user preferences and item characteristics, enabling us to isolate and study specific forms of bias, while the real-world dataset provided insights into the practical implications of our findings. Synthetic Data: We simulated interaction data by creating a set of users and items, each with attribute vectors representing features such as demographic characteristics for users and categorical or numerical features for items. Each attribute was assigned a value drawn from a predefined distribution. Bias was introduced by making certain attributes (e.g., gender or region) disproportionately represented in user preferences or item popularity. For example, in one configuration, users from a particular demographic group were modeled to exhibit a preference for certain item categories, while other groups exhibited neutral preferences. This allowed us to control for the level and type of bias present in the input data. Real-World Data: For our experiments on real-world data, we used the MovieLens dataset, a widely used benchmark for recommender systems. The dataset contains user-item interaction records (e.g., ratings), along with metadata about users (e.g., age, gender) and items (e.g., genres, release year). To assess bias, we focused on demographic attributes of users and genre preferences of items. We performed preliminary preprocessing, such as filtering inactive users and rarely rated items, normalizing rating scales, and encoding categorical attributes. 2. Recommendation Algorithms and Evaluation For our experiments, we selected two widely used recommendation algorithms: matrix factorization-based collaborative filtering (CF) and neural collaborative filtering (NCF). These methods are commonly employed in recommendation systems and rely on user-item interaction data to learn latent representations of users and items. Collaborative Filtering (CF): CF is a matrix factorization approach that decomposes the user-item interaction matrix into lower-dimensional representations of users and items. We implemented a standard alternating least-squares (ALS) algorithm to optimize the latent factors. Bias in the input data is inherently learned during this factorization process, which makes CF a suitable baseline for studying bias amplification. Neural Collaborative Filtering (NCF): NCF extends traditional CF by employing deep neural networks to model non-linear interactions between users and items. We implemented an NCF model with embedding layers for users and items, followed by fully connected layers to predict interaction scores. The depth of NCF enables capturing complex patterns in data, which, as we hypothesized, could lead to varying degrees of bias disparity. Evaluation Metrics: To measure bias disparity, we defined a metric based on disparity in recommendation outcomes across groups defined by sensitive attributes (e.g., gender or user age group). Specifically, for each group, we computed the proportion of recommendations that belonged to a specific item category or attribute of interest and compared these proportions across groups. A large difference in these proportions indicates bias disparity. Additionally, we used standard recommendation metrics, such as precision, recall, and normalized discounted cumulative gain (nDCG), to assess the overall accuracy of the recommendations. 3. Re-Ranking for Bias Mitigation To address bias disparity, we implemented a re-ranking algorithm that adjusts the ranked lists of recommended items for users by incorporating fairness constraints. Our approach can be summarized as follows: Initial Recommendation Generation: The recommender system generates an initial ranked list of items for each user based on their predicted interaction scores. Fairness-Aware Re-Ranking: The re-ranking algorithm modifies the initial ranked list to ensure that the distribution of recommended items across different user groups is more balanced. Specifically, we applied a proportionality constraint that limits the over-representation of any single group or attribute in the top-k recommendations. For instance, if an item category is over-represented in the recommendations for a particular demographic group, the algorithm reduces the rank of those items to mitigate the disparity. This adjustment is guided by a fairness parameter, which controls the trade-off between accuracy and fairness. Implementation Details: The re-ranking algorithm involves solving a constrained optimization problem that minimizes the deviation from the original ranking scores while satisfying the fairness constraint. We used a greedy heuristic to approximate the solution efficiently, ensuring scalability to larger datasets. The fairness parameter was tuned experimentally to observe its effect on bias disparity and recommendation accuracy. Experimental Setup and Analysis For both synthetic and real-world datasets, we divided the data into training and test sets, ensuring that the distribution of sensitive attributes was consistent across splits. The models were trained on the training set, and recommendations were generated for the test set. Bias disparity and recommendation performance were evaluated before and after applying the re-ranking algorithm. To study the long-term effects of recommendations on data bias, we performed iterative simulations where recommendations influenced future user interactions. Specifically, we assumed that users were more likely to interact with recommended items, which, in turn, affected the training data for subsequent iterations. This allowed us to observe how bias disparity evolved over time and whether the re-ranking algorithm could mitigate bias propagation. Implementation and Reproducibility All experiments were implemented in Python using standard libraries such as NumPy, Pandas, and PyTorch. The synthetic data generation process, recommendation model implementations, and re-ranking algorithm are available in a public GitHub repository to facilitate reproducibility and further research. In summary, this methodology provides a comprehensive framework to study bias disparity in recommendation systems, evaluate its impact, and explore mitigation techniques. By combining synthetic and real-world data with state-of-the-art recommendation algorithms, we aim to provide actionable insights into the challenges and opportunities of fair recommendation design. The study of pursuit-evasion games has inspired a rich body of research at the intersection of robotics, control theory, and computational geometry. These problems typically involve one or more pursuers attempting to capture or localize one or more evaders within a specified environment, subject to constraints on their dynamics, sensing, and the geometry of the domain. Such problems are relevant to numerous applications, including surveillance, search-and-rescue, and autonomous navigation [1, 2]. In this work, we address the specific problem of capturing an omnidirectional evader using a differential drive robot (DDR) in convex environments. The DDR, a widely studied robotic platform, is characterized by constraints on its turning rate, which limits its ability to instantaneously change its motion direction. This introduces nontrivial challenges when pursuing a highly agile adversary, such as an omnidirectional evader with unrestricted movement capabilities. Background and Motivation The problem of pursuit-evasion has been studied in various domains, ranging from free-space scenarios to environments with obstacles and bounded regions. Classical results, such as the lion-and-man problem, focus on differential game-theoretic formulations in which a single pursuer attempts to capture a single evader in a continuous two-dimensional environment [3]. While these foundational studies often assume point-like agents or unrestricted motion dynamics, real-world robotic systems are subject to physical constraints that significantly affect their performance. For instance, a DDR cannot reverse its direction instantaneously or execute sharp turns due to its kinematic constraints. This limitation raises fundamental questions about whether a DDR can guarantee capture of a more agile adversary, such as an omnidirectional evader, particularly in bounded convex environments. Convex environments are of particular interest because they provide a simplified yet nontrivial setting for analyzing pursuit-evasion dynamics. The absence of concave obstacles ensures that any straight-line path between two points lies entirely within the environment, reducing the complexity of the problem while still capturing essential features of bounded pursuit domains. Despite this simplification, the interplay between the DDR's motion constraints and the evader's omnidirectional capabilities necessitates careful strategy design to ensure capture. The practical relevance of this problem is underscored by its applicability to scenarios involving mobile robots tasked with intercepting intruders or targets that exhibit high maneuverability. For example, in security applications, a DDR might patrol a convex area and attempt to intercept a fast-moving intruder. Understanding the conditions under which capture is guaranteed, as well as the strategies that enable it, is critical for designing autonomous systems with robust performance in such scenarios. Problem Statement and Challenges We consider a pursuit-evasion game played between a single DDR and a single omnidirectional evader in a two-dimensional convex environment. Both players are modeled as unit disks with identical maximum speeds. The evader has no constraints on its motion direction, allowing it to instantaneously change its velocity vector, while the DDR is subject to a bounded rate of angular velocity, reflecting the kinematic constraints of differential drive robots. The DDR successfully captures the evader if the distance between their centers becomes less than or equal to twice the radius of the disks, i.e., if a collision occurs. Conversely, the evader wins by avoiding capture indefinitely. The primary challenge in this problem stems from the asymmetry in motion capabilities. The evader's ability to change direction instantaneously gives it a distinct advantage in avoiding capture, particularly when the DDR must execute wide turns or reorient itself to follow the evader's trajectory. This asymmetry raises questions about whether the DDR can guarantee capture under all possible initial configurations and, if so, what strategies it must employ to achieve this. Another key challenge arises from the bounded nature of the convex environment. While the lack of obstacles simplifies the evader's escape options, the finite size of the domain imposes constraints on both players' trajectories. This interplay between the environment's geometry and the players' dynamics creates a rich and complex problem space that demands careful analysis. Related Work The pursuit-evasion problem has been extensively studied under various assumptions about the players' dynamics, sensing capabilities, and the environment's geometry. When both players are point agents with identical speed and unrestricted motion, strategies for guaranteeing capture are well understood, particularly in convex domains [4]. However, when the pursuer's motion is restricted by kinematic constraints, as in the case of the DDR, the problem becomes significantly more challenging. Several works have explored pursuit strategies for robots with nonholonomic constraints, such as car-like robots or differential drive systems. For example, recent studies have addressed the problem of capturing an evader in free space or environments with obstacles, often leveraging geometric or control-theoretic approaches to account for the pursuer's constraints [5, 6]. However, these studies typically focus on point-like agents or simplify the environment's geometry, leaving open questions about the DDR's ability to capture an omnidirectional evader in bounded convex domains. The specific case of omnidirectional evaders has also been studied, albeit primarily in the context of holonomic pursuers. These works often assume that the pursuer has the ability to match the evader's agility, leading to strategies that may not generalize to the DDR's constrained dynamics [7]. To the best of our knowledge, the problem of capturing an omnidirectional evader in convex environments using a DDR remains largely unexplored, particularly with respect to guaranteeing capture under all initial conditions. Contributions In this paper, we address the open problem of whether a DDR can always capture an omnidirectional evader in a bounded convex environment. We provide a rigorous analysis of the DDR's motion capabilities and derive strategies that ensure capture regardless of the initial configuration of the players. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: 1. Theoretical Guarantee of Capture: We prove that a DDR, despite its kinematic constraints, can always capture an omnidirectional evader in any convex environment when both players have equal maximum speeds. 2. Strategy Design: We design explicit pursuit strategies for the DDR that account for its bounded turning rate and the evader's omnidirectional agility. 3. Analysis of Convex Environments: We leverage the geometric properties of convex domains to analyze the interaction between the players' trajectories and the environment's boundaries. 4. Simulation Validation: We validate our theoretical results through numerical simulations, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed strategies in various configurations. By addressing these contributions, we aim to extend the understanding of pursuit-evasion dynamics for nonholonomic robots and provide actionable insights for designing robust robotic systems capable of intercepting agile targets in realistic scenarios. Problem Formulation We consider a pursuit-evasion scenario in a two-dimensional convex environment \( \mathcal{E} \subset \mathbb{R}^2 \), where the boundary of \( \mathcal{E} \), denoted as \( \partial \mathcal{E} \), is a closed, smooth, and strictly convex curve. The players in this game are a Differential Drive Robot (DDR) and an omnidirectional evader, both modeled as unit disks with radius \( r = 1 \). The DDR, represented by its center at \( pD(t) \in \mathcal{E} \), is kinematically constrained in its motion, while the evader, represented by its center at \( pE(t) \in \mathcal{E} \), has no such constraints and can instantaneously change its velocity vector. The DDR moves with a maximum speed \( v{\max} \) and is subject to a bounded turning rate \( \omega{\max} \), which defines its minimum turning radius \( R{\min} = v{\max}/\omega{\max} \). The evader also has a maximum speed \( v{\max} \), but it is capable of omnidirectional motion, allowing it to follow any trajectory with instantaneous changes in direction. Both agents are assumed to have perfect knowledge of each other’s positions and velocities at all times. The DDR’s objective is to capture the evader, which occurs when \( \|pD(t) - pE(t)\| \leq 2r \). The evader’s objective is to avoid capture indefinitely. The problem is to design a pursuit strategy for the DDR that ensures capture of the evader regardless of the evader’s strategy, under the assumption that both agents start at arbitrary initial positions \( pD(0), pE(0) \in \mathcal{E} \). --- Differential Drive Robot Model The DDR’s motion is governed by the standard kinematic equations for a differential drive system. Let \( \theta(t) \) represent the orientation of the DDR with respect to a global reference frame. The state of the DDR is defined by its position \( pD(t) = [xD(t), yD(t)]^T \) and orientation \( \theta(t) \). The control inputs are the linear velocity \( v(t) \) and the angular velocity \( \omega(t) \), with \( |v(t)| \leq v{\max} \) and \( |\omega(t)| \leq \omega{\max} \). The equations of motion are given by: \[ \dot{x}D(t) = v(t) \cos \theta(t), \quad \dot{y}D(t) = v(t) \sin \theta(t), \quad \dot{\theta}(t) = \omega(t). \] The DDR’s motion constraints impose a fundamental limitation on its ability to maneuver sharply, which must be accounted for when designing the pursuit strategy. --- Evader Model The evader is modeled as an omnidirectional agent with maximum speed \( v{\max} \). At any time \( t \), the evader can choose its velocity vector \( \mathbf{v}E(t) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \) such that \( \|\mathbf{v}E(t)\| \leq v{\max} \). The evader’s trajectory is thus unconstrained by turning radius or inertia, allowing it to exploit its higher maneuverability to evade capture. However, the evader is restricted to the convex environment \( \mathcal{E} \) and cannot cross \( \partial \mathcal{E} \). --- Pursuit Strategy High-Level Strategy Overview To overcome the DDR’s kinematic constraints and achieve capture, we employ a strategy based on the concept of "motion confinement." The DDR uses its knowledge of the environment geometry and the evader’s position to systematically reduce the evader’s available free space until capture is inevitable. The strategy consists of the following stages: 1. Boundary Confinement: The DDR positions itself to push the evader toward \( \partial \mathcal{E} \), thereby limiting the evader’s escape options. 2. Dynamic Interception: The DDR continuously adjusts its trajectory to minimize the relative distance to the evader while accounting for its turning constraints. 3. Final Capture Maneuver: Once the evader is sufficiently confined, the DDR executes a final maneuver to close the remaining distance and achieve capture. Stage 1: Boundary Confinement Using the convexity of the environment, the DDR first ensures that the evader cannot move arbitrarily far away. Given the bounded turning radius of the DDR, we define a "reachable region" \( \mathcal{R}D(t) \subset \mathcal{E} \) as the set of points that the DDR can reach within a finite time, considering its kinematic constraints. By continuously steering toward the evader’s current position \( pE(t) \) while maintaining a safe distance from \( \partial \mathcal{E} \), the DDR guarantees that the evader is either driven closer to \( \partial \mathcal{E} \) or forced to move toward regions of \( \mathcal{E} \) where the DDR has a kinematic advantage. Stage 2: Dynamic Interception As the evader’s movement becomes restricted, the DDR transitions to a dynamic interception phase. In this phase, the DDR computes an optimal control input \( (v(t), \omega(t)) \) to minimize the time-to-capture \( Tc \), defined as: \[ Tc = \min \{ t \geq 0 \mid \|pD(t) - pE(t)\| \leq 2r \}. \] This is achieved by solving a time-optimal control problem subject to the DDR’s motion constraints. Existing results in differential games [1, 2] indicate that the DDR can achieve a capture trajectory by maintaining a heading such that its motion vector is consistently directed toward the evader’s predicted position. Stage 3: Final Capture Maneuver In the final stage, the DDR exploits its proximity to the evader and the reduced maneuverability of the evader near \( \partial \mathcal{E} \). By utilizing feedback control laws that prioritize rapid heading adjustments within the bounds of \( \omega{\max} \), the DDR ensures that the evader cannot escape the shrinking capture region. Capture is guaranteed within a finite time, as the DDR's kinematic constraints are offset by the evader's diminishing available space. --- Guarantees of Capture The proposed strategy is formally validated using Lyapunov-based analysis techniques, which show that the distance \( \|pD(t) - pE(t)\| \) monotonically decreases under the DDR’s control laws. Stock market prediction has long been a subject of fascination and intense research for both academic and practical purposes. The allure of forecasting stock trends lies in its potential to generate substantial financial rewards, but this task is notoriously complex. The price movement of stocks is influenced by a multitude of factors, including market sentiment, macroeconomic indicators, geopolitical events, company-specific developments, and even unpredictable investor behaviors. These factors interact in complex ways, making financial markets highly dynamic and, in many cases, seemingly chaotic. Despite these challenges, the quest for reliable methods to predict stock trends has remained a critical pursuit, as even marginal improvements in prediction accuracy can translate into significant financial gains. Over the years, a variety of techniques have been developed to address the problem of stock market prediction. Traditional approaches, such as technical analysis and fundamental analysis, have served as mainstays in the field. Technical analysis relies on historical price patterns and statistical indicators, while fundamental analysis focuses on the intrinsic value of a stock, based on factors such as company earnings, revenue, and market position. Despite their widespread use, these methods often fail to capture the full complexity of stock price movements, especially in the face of rapidly evolving market conditions and the increasing role of non-linear influences like market sentiment. With the advent of machine learning and artificial intelligence, new approaches to stock prediction have emerged. These advanced methods leverage computational power and large-scale data to identify patterns that are difficult, if not impossible, for human analysts to discern. Among these innovations, natural language processing (NLP) has gained considerable attention in recent years. By analyzing unstructured textual data, such as financial news, earnings reports, and social media sentiment, NLP has opened new avenues for understanding the underlying forces driving stock price movements. However, while NLP has been primarily applied to textual data, its potential to analyze structured financial data, such as price charts, remains relatively underexplored. One of the most popular tools for visualizing price movements in financial markets is the Japanese candlestick chart. Candlestick charts provide a graphical representation of price data, including the open, high, low, and close (OHLC) prices for a given time period. Traders and analysts have long used Japanese candlestick patterns to identify potential market trends and reversals. These patterns, such as "hammer," "doji," and "engulfing," are believed to encapsulate valuable information about market sentiment and momentum. However, interpreting candlestick patterns is often subjective and requires considerable expertise, making it difficult to systematically integrate this information into quantitative models. This paper proposes a novel methodology that combines the principles of natural language processing and Japanese candlestick charts to improve stock trend prediction. Specifically, we introduce a framework based on the Word2Vec model, a popular NLP technique for learning vector representations of words. In our approach, we create a "language" of Japanese candlesticks by converting OHLC data into sequences of candlestick patterns, which are then treated as words. These sequences form sentences, which are used to train a Word2Vec model. By embedding candlestick patterns into a continuous vector space, the model learns to capture the nuanced relationships between patterns, similar to how it captures semantic relationships between words in traditional NLP tasks. The use of Word2Vec in this context offers several advantages. First, it provides a systematic and quantitative way to analyze candlestick patterns, reducing the subjectivity inherent in traditional technical analysis. Second, the Word2Vec model is capable of capturing contextual information, allowing it to consider the sequential nature of candlestick patterns and their relationships over time. Third, by leveraging the power of machine learning, the approach can adapt to evolving market conditions and uncover patterns that may not be apparent through manual analysis. To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method, we conducted extensive experiments on stocks from different sectors and indices. We compared the performance of the Word2Vec-based model against three well-established trading strategies: Buy & Hold, Moving Average (MA), and Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD). The experiments were carried out on three individual stocks—Apple, Microsoft, and Coca-Cola—as well as a broader set of stocks from the Russell Top 50 Index. Our results demonstrate that the Word2Vec model consistently outperformed the MA and MACD strategies in terms of average yield, and it achieved positive results in all scenarios. While the Buy & Hold strategy outperformed Word2Vec during the validation phase for the Russell Top 50 Index, it is important to note that Buy & Hold is highly sensitive to market trends and does not account for trading commissions or risk management, which were integral to our Word2Vec framework. The findings of this study highlight the potential of integrating NLP techniques with traditional financial data representations to enhance stock trend prediction. By bridging the gap between textual and numerical data, our approach provides a new perspective on how to model and interpret financial markets. Moreover, the ability of Word2Vec to generalize across different stocks and market conditions suggests that this methodology could be a valuable tool for both researchers and practitioners seeking to develop more robust trading systems. In summary, this paper introduces a novel application of NLP to the domain of stock prediction by creating a language of Japanese candlesticks and training a Word2Vec model on this data. Through extensive empirical evaluations, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in outperforming traditional trading strategies and achieving consistent positive results. By combining the interpretability of candlestick patterns with the computational power of machine learning, this study contributes to the ongoing effort to develop more sophisticated and accurate methods for navigating the complexities of financial markets.
