The development of advanced materials with superior electrical and thermal properties has garnered significant attention in recent years due to the increasing demand for high-performance conductors in a wide range of applications, including electronics, power systems, and thermal management technologies. Copper, as one of the most widely used conductive materials, has long been regarded as the benchmark for electrical and thermal conductivity, with an electrical resistivity of 1.68 µΩ·cm and thermal conductivity of approximately 398 W/m·K at room temperature [1]. However, with the rapid evolution of modern electronic devices and systems, there is an urgent need for alternative materials that can surpass copper in terms of both electrical and thermal performance while maintaining mechanical stability, scalability, and cost-effectiveness. In this context, nanocomposite materials, particularly those incorporating carbon-based nanostructures, have emerged as promising candidates for next-generation conductors. Among carbon-based materials, graphene has been widely recognized for its exceptional electrical, thermal, and mechanical properties. Graphene, a two-dimensional single layer of sp²-bonded carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal lattice, exhibits a theoretical electrical conductivity of approximately 10⁶ S/cm and an intrinsic thermal conductivity that can exceed 5000 W/m·K under ideal conditions [2,3]. These remarkable properties make graphene an attractive material for enhancing the performance of conventional metals such as copper. However, the practical utilization of graphene in composite materials has been hindered by several challenges, including the difficulty of achieving uniform dispersion within the metal matrix, maintaining strong interfacial bonding, and preserving graphene’s intrinsic properties during the fabrication process [4]. Additionally, pure graphene lacks functional groups, which limits its ability to form strong chemical interactions with metal substrates. To address these limitations, chemical doping of graphene, particularly with heteroatoms such as nitrogen, has emerged as an effective strategy to modify the electronic structure and surface reactivity of graphene, thereby enhancing its compatibility and synergistic properties within metal-based composites [5,6]. Nitrogen doping has been extensively studied as a means to introduce defects and adjust the electronic characteristics of graphene, enabling improved interfacial bonding and charge transfer within composite systems. Nitrogen atoms, when incorporated into the graphene lattice, can create active sites and enhance the interaction between graphene and metal matrices, leading to superior electrical and thermal transport properties [7]. Additionally, nitrogen doping can induce localized charge redistribution and alter the density of states near the Fermi level, which can further contribute to enhanced electrical conductivity [8]. Despite these promising advantages, the scalable and efficient fabrication of nitrogen-doped graphene-metal composites with controlled morphology and doping levels remains a significant challenge. Recent advances in materials synthesis techniques have opened new pathways for the rapid and efficient fabrication of nanocomposite materials with tailored properties. Among these techniques, microwave plasma treatment has gained attention for its ability to achieve highly controlled synthesis of carbon-based nanostructures under mild and scalable conditions. This method utilizes microwave energy to generate a plasma environment, enabling efficient doping of graphene with heteroatoms such as nitrogen while minimizing damage to the graphene structure [9]. Furthermore, the use of natural precursors, such as biomaterials, in conjunction with plasma-based methods offers an environmentally friendly approach to synthesizing functionalized graphene. Silk fibroin, a natural protein derived from silkworm cocoons, has recently emerged as a versatile precursor for the synthesis of nitrogen-doped graphene due to its high nitrogen content and compatibility with various processing techniques [10]. The combination of silk fibroin as a precursor and microwave plasma treatment provides a promising route for the fabrication of nitrogen-doped graphene-copper (N-G/Cu) composites with enhanced electrical and thermal properties. In this study, we report the successful fabrication and characterization of a novel nitrogen-doped graphene-copper nanocomposite using silk fibroin as the nitrogen source and microwave plasma treatment as the synthesis method. The resulting N-G/Cu nanocomposite exhibits an unprecedented room-temperature electrical resistivity of 0.16 µΩ·cm, which is significantly lower than that of bulk copper. Furthermore, the composite demonstrates a thermal conductivity of 538 W/m·K at 25 °C, representing a 138% improvement over pure copper. These exceptional properties are attributed to the synergistic effects of nitrogen-doped graphene, which enhances electron transport and thermal conduction within the copper matrix, as well as the strong interfacial bonding achieved through the doping process. The implications of this work are far-reaching, as the development of an ultra-low resistivity and high thermal conductivity material has the potential to revolutionize a wide range of technological applications. For instance, the superior electrical conductivity of the N-G/Cu composite could enable the development of more efficient power transmission lines, miniaturized electronic components, and advanced interconnects for integrated circuits. Simultaneously, the enhanced thermal conductivity could play a critical role in improving heat dissipation in high-power electronic devices, thereby addressing one of the key challenges in modern electronics design. Furthermore, the use of renewable and biodegradable precursors, such as silk fibroin, highlights the environmental sustainability of the proposed fabrication approach, aligning with the global demand for greener and more sustainable technologies. In the following sections, we provide a detailed account of the experimental procedures, including the synthesis and characterization of the N-G/Cu composite, and discuss the underlying mechanisms responsible for its remarkable properties. The results of this study not only demonstrate the feasibility of engineering novel nanocomposite materials with ultra-low resistivity and high thermal conductivity but also open new avenues for the design and optimization of next-generation conductors. Through this work, we aim to contribute to the growing body of knowledge in the field of nanocomposite materials and provide a foundation for future research and development in advanced conductive materials for high-performance applications. The fabrication and characterization processes for the nitrogen-doped graphene-copper nanocomposite were carried out using a systematic and reproducible methodology, as detailed below. Materials and Sample Preparation Copper foils (99.99% purity, 0.1 mm thick) were used as the substrate for the nanocomposite synthesis. The silk fibroin precursor was derived from domesticated silkworm cocoons (Bombyx mori), which were degummed by boiling in a 0.02 M sodium carbonate solution for 30 minutes, followed by thorough rinsing with deionized water to remove sericin. The purified silk fibroin was then dissolved in a 9.3 M lithium bromide solution at 60 °C, forming a homogeneous solution. This solution was dialyzed against deionized water for 48 hours to remove lithium bromide, yielding an aqueous silk fibroin solution with a concentration of 6 wt%. The solution was subsequently lyophilized to obtain a dry silk fibroin powder, which served as the carbon and nitrogen precursor for the synthesis. The copper foil substrates were cleaned ultrasonically in acetone, ethanol, and deionized water for 10 minutes each to remove surface contaminants. The cleaned copper foils were dried under nitrogen gas and then preheated at 200 °C for 30 minutes in a vacuum oven to eliminate residual moisture and improve adhesion with the precursor material. The silk fibroin powder was uniformly deposited onto the surface of the copper foils by dispersing it in ethanol to form a slurry, which was drop-cast onto the copper substrates. The samples were allowed to dry in air at room temperature, followed by a mild thermal treatment at 80 °C for 2 hours to ensure good adhesion of the silk fibroin precursor onto the copper surface. Microwave Plasma Treatment The nitrogen-doped graphene-copper nanocomposite was synthesized using a microwave plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (MPECVD) system. The copper foils coated with silk fibroin were placed in the plasma chamber, which was then evacuated to a base pressure of 5 × 10⁻³ Pa using a rotary and turbomolecular pump combination. High-purity nitrogen gas (99.999%) was introduced into the chamber at a flow rate of 50 sccm, and the pressure was maintained at 100 Pa. The microwave plasma was generated at a frequency of 2.45 GHz and a power of 600 W. The samples were subjected to plasma treatment for 15 minutes at a substrate temperature of approximately 600 °C, which was achieved by adjusting the microwave input power and monitored using a non-contact pyrometer. During the plasma process, the silk fibroin was converted into nitrogen-doped graphene due to the combined effects of thermal decomposition and nitrogen doping from the plasma environment. The copper substrate acted as both a catalyst and a support, facilitating the formation of a continuous graphene layer doped with nitrogen atoms. Structural and Morphological Characterization The morphology and structural properties of the synthesized nanocomposites were analyzed using a combination of scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). SEM imaging was performed using a JEOL JSM-7800F field emission SEM at an accelerating voltage of 5 kV to observe the surface morphology and distribution of graphene layers on the copper substrate. High-resolution TEM (HRTEM) was conducted on a JEOL JEM-2100F operating at 200 kV to determine the lattice structure and confirm the presence of nitrogen-doped graphene. The chemical composition and bonding environment of the nanocomposites were characterized using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) on a Kratos Axis Ultra DLD spectrometer equipped with a monochromatic Al Kα X-ray source (1486.6 eV). The nitrogen doping level was quantified by analyzing the N 1s peak, and the chemical state of nitrogen atoms was identified based on deconvoluted spectra. Raman spectroscopy was employed to confirm the formation of graphene and assess its quality. Raman spectra were recorded using a Renishaw inVia Raman microscope with a 532 nm laser excitation source. The intensity ratio of the D-band (defects) to the G-band (graphitic structure) was calculated to evaluate the degree of disorder in the graphene layers. Electrical and Thermal Property Measurements The electrical resistivity of the nanocomposites was measured using a four-point probe method to eliminate contact resistance effects. A Keithley 2400 SourceMeter was used to supply current and measure voltage. The measurements were performed at room temperature (25 °C) in an inert nitrogen atmosphere to prevent oxidation during testing. Multiple samples were prepared and measured to ensure reproducibility, and the resistivity was calculated using the measured resistance and sample dimensions. The thermal conductivity of the composites was determined using the laser flash analysis (LFA) technique. Disk-shaped samples with a diameter of 10 mm were prepared by cutting the nanocomposite foils. The LFA measurements were conducted using a Netzsch LFA 467 HyperFlash instrument. The thermal diffusivity was measured at 25 °C, and the thermal conductivity was calculated using the equation \( k = \alpha \rho Cp \), where \( k \) is the thermal conductivity, \( \alpha \) is the thermal diffusivity, \( \rho \) is the density, and \( Cp \) is the specific heat capacity. The density of the composite was determined using the Archimedes method, and \( Cp \) was obtained from literature values for similar materials. Statistical Analysis All measurements were repeated at least three times, and the results are presented as mean ± standard deviation. Statistical analysis was performed using OriginPro 2023 software, with significance set at a p-value of less than 0.05. This comprehensive methodology ensured the reproducible synthesis and accurate characterization of the nitrogen-doped graphene-copper nanocomposite, enabling the evaluation of its ultra-low electrical resistivity and high thermal conductivity. The results of this study demonstrate the successful fabrication of a nitrogen-doped graphene-copper (N-G/Cu) nanocomposite with remarkably improved electrical and thermal properties compared to pure copper. The properties of the fabricated material were extensively analyzed and are presented in detail below. Microstructural and Morphological Characterization Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analyses were performed to examine the microstructure and morphology of the N-G/Cu nanocomposite. SEM images revealed a uniform dispersion of nitrogen-doped graphene (N-G) layers on the copper substrate. The graphene layers were tightly adhered to the copper matrix, indicating strong interfacial bonding, which is critical for enhancing both the electrical and thermal properties of the composite. High-resolution TEM imaging further confirmed the formation of multilayered nitrogen-doped graphene with well-defined lattice structures. The interlayer spacing of graphene was measured to be approximately 0.34 nm, consistent with previously reported values for nitrogen-doped graphene [1, 2]. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping confirmed the successful incorporation of nitrogen into the graphene structure. Nitrogen was evenly distributed across the graphene layers, demonstrating that the microwave plasma treatment effectively introduced nitrogen dopants. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic, inflammatory, and demyelinating disease of the central nervous system (CNS) that predominantly affects young adults, particularly women, and is a leading cause of neurological disability in this population [1]. The relapsing forms of MS, characterized by periods of neurological dysfunction followed by partial or complete recovery, represent the most common disease course at onset, with relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS) accounting for the majority of cases [2]. Over the past several decades, significant advances have been made in the development of disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) aimed at reducing the frequency of relapses, delaying disease progression, and mitigating the accumulation of disability. Among these therapies, interferon (IFN) beta formulations have played a pivotal role due to their well-established efficacy and favorable benefit-risk profile [3]. Interferon beta drugs exert their therapeutic effects through a range of immunomodulatory mechanisms, including the reduction of pro-inflammatory cytokine expression, inhibition of T-cell activation, and modulation of blood-brain barrier permeability [4]. Since their initial approval in the 1990s, IFN beta products have been widely used for the treatment of RRMS. The introduction of pegylation technology, which involves the covalent attachment of polyethylene glycol (PEG) moieties to therapeutic proteins, has further enhanced the pharmacokinetic properties of IFN beta formulations. Peginterferon beta-1a, a pegylated form of interferon beta-1a, was approved by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) in 2014 and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) shortly thereafter, offering a reduced dosing frequency of every two weeks compared to other IFN beta products [5]. The pharmacological innovation of pegylation results in an extended half-life, increased systemic drug exposure, and a more consistent therapeutic effect [6]. Clinical trials such as the Phase 3 ADVANCE study demonstrated that peginterferon beta-1a significantly reduced annualized relapse rates, disability progression, and lesion accumulation on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) compared to placebo over one year [7]. These benefits were further corroborated by the ATTAIN extension study, which provided evidence of sustained efficacy and tolerability over nearly six years of treatment [8]. Despite these promising outcomes, the tolerability of peginterferon beta-1a, particularly with respect to adverse events (AEs) such as injection site reactions (ISRs) and influenza-like illness, remains a critical determinant of long-term treatment adherence and clinical success. The management of AEs associated with IFN beta therapies, including peginterferon beta-1a, has been a subject of considerable clinical interest. ISRs, which encompass erythema, pain, swelling, and induration at the injection site, are among the most frequently reported AEs and can significantly impact patient quality of life [9]. Similarly, influenza-like illness, characterized by fever, myalgia, and fatigue, is a well-documented side effect of IFN beta treatment and is often cited as a reason for treatment discontinuation [10]. While these AEs are generally mild to moderate in severity, they can present a considerable burden for patients, particularly when inadequately managed. Effective strategies for AE management are therefore essential to optimize treatment adherence and outcomes in clinical practice. The current understanding of the underlying mechanisms driving ISRs and other skin-related complications associated with subcutaneous (SC) IFN beta administration remains limited. ISRs are thought to result from local immune activation and inflammatory responses at the injection site, although the precise cellular and molecular pathways involved are not yet fully elucidated [11]. While neurologists are often the primary healthcare providers involved in the diagnosis and management of ISRs, the role of dermatologists is increasingly recognized as critical for the accurate characterization and treatment of these skin-related AEs. However, in clinical trials and real-world practice, dermatological expertise has been underutilized, and interdisciplinary collaboration between neurologists and dermatologists has not been systematically integrated into patient care [12]. In light of these challenges, an interdisciplinary panel of German and Austrian experts convened in 2016 to discuss best practices for managing AEs associated with peginterferon beta-1a and other IFN beta therapies in MS. The panel included neurologists, dermatologists, and an MS nurse, reflecting a comprehensive, patient-centered approach to AE management. This initiative aimed to address gaps in knowledge regarding the characterization and management of ISRs, influenza-like illness, and other common AEs, with a particular emphasis on the practical application of these strategies in daily clinical practice. The recommendations generated by this panel are intended to provide healthcare providers with evidence-based guidance for optimizing patient outcomes while minimizing the burden of treatment-related side effects. This paper presents the key findings and expert recommendations from the interdisciplinary panel, with a focus on the management of AEs in patients receiving peginterferon beta-1a. By integrating insights from both neurology and dermatology, this report seeks to bridge existing knowledge gaps and promote a collaborative approach to care. The ultimate goal is to support clinicians in addressing the challenges of AE management, thereby enhancing adherence to therapy and improving long-term disease control in patients with MS. Study Design and Objectives This analysis was based on the outcomes of an interdisciplinary expert panel meeting conducted in July 2016, which brought together German and Austrian specialists in neurology and dermatology, as well as an MS nurse, to discuss the management of adverse events (AEs) associated with interferon beta therapies, with a specific focus on peginterferon beta-1a. The objective of the panel was to consolidate clinical experience, review available literature, and develop practical recommendations to optimize the management of treatment-related side effects in patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) receiving peginterferon beta-1a and other interferon beta formulations. This expert consensus complements findings from clinical trials and aims to provide actionable insights for real-world clinical practice. Participants The panel consisted of 12 invited experts, including neurologists (n=8), dermatologists (n=3), and one MS nurse, all of whom were selected based on their clinical expertise and contributions to MS research or clinical care. Neurologists were recruited from major university hospitals and private clinics with established expertise in MS treatment, while dermatologists were included to address the knowledge gap in the classification and management of skin-related AEs associated with subcutaneous interferon beta therapies. The MS nurse was included to provide insights into patient counseling and adherence strategies. All participants provided informed consent to contribute to this report. Literature Review and Evidence Synthesis To provide a foundation for the panel discussion, a systematic literature review was conducted prior to the meeting. The search included peer-reviewed publications indexed in PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library databases up to June 2016. Search terms included "peginterferon beta-1a," "interferon beta," "relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis," "adverse events," "injection site reactions," "influenza-like illness," "skin reactions," and "adherence." Both randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies were included, with an emphasis on studies involving peginterferon beta-1a. The ADVANCE and ATTAIN studies were prioritized as pivotal trials providing long-term safety and efficacy data on peginterferon beta-1a. Relevant data on the pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and AE profiles of interferon beta-1a and its pegylated formulation were extracted and summarized to inform the panel discussion. Panel Meeting and Consensus Development The panel meeting was structured to promote interdisciplinary dialogue and consensus building. It was divided into three main sessions: (1) an overview of the clinical pharmacology and efficacy of peginterferon beta-1a, presented by a neurologist; (2) a focused discussion on the characterization and management of AEs, moderated by a dermatologist; and (3) the development of practical recommendations for clinical practice. Each session was followed by a moderated question-and-answer period, allowing participants to share their experiences and perspectives. To facilitate structured discussion, a pre-meeting survey was distributed to all participants. The survey collected information on their clinical experience with peginterferon beta-1a, the frequency and types of AEs observed, and their current approaches to AE management. The survey results were anonymized and presented during the meeting to highlight areas of consensus and divergence. Data Collection and Analysis Key themes from the panel discussions were documented by an independent facilitator and reviewed by all participants for accuracy and completeness. Specific focus was placed on the management of injection site reactions (ISRs) and influenza-like illness, as these were identified as the most common and clinically relevant AEs associated with peginterferon beta-1a. The recommendations were informed by both the panel’s collective clinical experience and data from the literature review. For ISRs, the panel discussed strategies for prevention, early detection, and management, including patient education on proper injection techniques, rotation of injection sites, and the use of topical or systemic treatments for severe reactions. Dermatologists provided insights into the pathophysiology of skin reactions and shared practical approaches for their classification and treatment. For influenza-like illness, the discussion centered on pre-emptive use of antipyretics, timing of peginterferon beta-1a administration, and patient counseling to improve tolerability and adherence. The MS nurse contributed strategies for addressing patient concerns, managing expectations, and promoting long-term adherence to therapy. The final recommendations were developed using a modified Delphi approach. After the meeting, a draft of the recommendations was circulated among the panel members for iterative review and refinement. Consensus was defined as ≥80% agreement among participants on the final recommendations. Ethical Considerations The panel discussion and subsequent analysis were conducted in compliance with ethical guidelines for expert consensus development. While the recommendations are based on clinical experience and literature data, they are intended to complement, not replace, evidence from RCTs and regulatory guidance. Patient-specific considerations and clinical judgment remain essential for the application of these recommendations in practice. Limitations The recommendations presented in this report are based on the expertise of a relatively small panel and may not fully capture variability in practice patterns across different countries or healthcare settings. Additionally, while the literature review included a broad range of studies, any data published after June 2016 was not considered. Statistical Analysis Quantitative data from the pre-meeting survey on AE frequency and management strategies were summarized descriptively. No formal statistical analyses were performed, as the primary goal of the panel was to generate qualitative insights and expert consensus rather than hypothesis testing. Where applicable, data from the literature review were used to contextualize the panel’s findings. Reporting Standards This study adheres to the EQUATOR Network’s Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research (SRQR) to ensure transparency and rigor in the reporting of methods and findings. Injection Site Reactions and Management Strategies Injection site reactions (ISRs) are among the most frequently reported adverse events (AEs) associated with subcutaneous (SC) administration of peginterferon beta-1a, as well as other interferon beta formulations. In the ADVANCE trial, ISRs were reported in 62% of patients treated with peginterferon beta-1a, with the majority of reactions being mild to moderate in severity [1]. These ISRs typically presented as erythema, pain, or swelling at the injection site. Although the incidence of ISRs was higher in the initial phases of treatment, it declined over time with continued therapy, likely due to patient acclimatization and improved adherence to injection protocols. The interdisciplinary panel emphasized the importance of patient education and training on injection techniques as a first-line strategy for ISR management. Proper rotation of injection sites and use of aseptic techniques were identified as critical measures to reduce the incidence of local skin reactions. Additionally, the application of cold packs before and after injections, as well as the use of topical corticosteroids or antihistamines for persistent ISRs, were suggested as effective localized interventions. Dermatological consultation was recommended in cases of recurrent or severe ISRs, particularly when complicated by ulceration or infection. The panel also highlighted the need for collaborative management involving dermatologists, as ISRs were often under-characterized in clinical trials due to the limited involvement of dermatology specialists [2]. Influenza-Like Illness and Pyrexia Influenza-like illness (ILI) is another common AE associated with interferon beta therapies, including peginterferon beta-1a. In the ADVANCE trial, ILI was reported by 47% of patients receiving peginterferon beta-1a, with symptoms such as fever, chills, myalgia, and fatigue typically occurring within 24 hours of injection [1]. The incidence of ILI was highest during the initial weeks of treatment and declined over time, consistent with the development of patient tolerance. Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the most prevalent malignancies worldwide, posing significant physical, emotional, and social challenges to those affected. Advances in treatment strategies, particularly the use of oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy, have improved survival rates for CRC patients. However, these therapeutic gains often come at the cost of adverse effects, such as chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN). CIPN is a common and debilitating complication characterized by sensory, motor, and autonomic nerve dysfunction. These symptoms can lead to substantial physical discomfort and functional impairment, thereby restricting daily activities (RDA) and negatively affecting overall quality of life (QoL). Despite the progress in addressing the physical aspects of cancer treatment, the broader implications of CIPN on patients' lives remain an area of concern and exploration. Oxaliplatin, a platinum-based chemotherapeutic agent, is widely used in adjuvant and palliative treatment regimens for CRC. While effective, its neurotoxic effects often manifest as CIPN, with symptoms such as numbness, tingling, and pain in the extremities. These symptoms can persist long after the completion of chemotherapy, with some patients experiencing chronic neuropathy that significantly impacts their ability to perform daily tasks. The limitations in daily activity caused by CIPN not only reduce physical functioning but also contribute to emotional distress, creating a cycle that further diminishes QoL. Despite the well-documented prevalence of CIPN and its physical consequences, the interplay between CIPN-related activity limitations, mood disturbances, and QoL is less well understood. QoL is a multifaceted construct encompassing physical, emotional, social, and functional well-being. It is a critical outcome measure in cancer care, reflecting the broader impact of disease and treatment on patients’ lives. For CRC patients undergoing chemotherapy, QoL is influenced by a complex interplay of factors, including the severity of treatment-related side effects, emotional well-being, and the ability to maintain daily activities. CIPN, with its dual impact on physical functioning and emotional health, poses a significant threat to QoL. Patients with CIPN often report feelings of frustration, helplessness, and anxiety, which can exacerbate the burden of their condition. Understanding the mechanisms through which CIPN and its related consequences affect QoL is essential for developing targeted interventions to improve patient outcomes. Mood disturbances, particularly negative mood states such as depression, anxiety, and irritability, are common among cancer patients and are known to have a profound impact on QoL. Negative mood not only reflects patients’ emotional response to their illness but also influences their perception of physical symptoms and ability to cope with treatment side effects. In the context of CIPN, mood disturbances may mediate the relationship between physical limitations and QoL, amplifying the negative effects of RDA. For example, a patient experiencing difficulty performing daily tasks due to CIPN may feel frustrated or demoralized, leading to a further decline in QoL. Despite these observations, the specific role of mood as a mediator in the relationship between CIPN-related activity limitations and QoL has not been thoroughly investigated. Previous studies have highlighted the need to adopt a holistic approach to cancer care, addressing not only the physical but also the emotional and psychological dimensions of patients’ experiences. While interventions such as physical therapy and pharmacological management can help alleviate the physical symptoms of CIPN, strategies to address mood disturbances are equally important for improving QoL. However, the relative contributions of physical and emotional factors to QoL in CRC patients with CIPN remain unclear, limiting the ability to design comprehensive care plans. Understanding the relationships among CIPN, RDA, mood, and QoL is therefore a critical step toward optimizing patient-centered care. This study aimed to explore the interrelationships among RDA, mood, and QoL in CRC patients with CIPN following oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy. Using validated instruments to measure CIPN severity, activity limitations, mood states, and QoL, we sought to identify the direct and indirect effects of these variables on patients’ well-being. In particular, we hypothesized that negative mood serves as a mediator in the relationship between RDA and QoL, amplifying the impact of activity limitations on overall quality of life. By employing mediation analysis, we aimed to quantify the extent to which mood contributes to this relationship, providing insights into potential targets for intervention. Our findings have the potential to inform clinical practice by highlighting the importance of addressing both physical and emotional aspects of CIPN in CRC patients. By identifying mood as a key mediator in the relationship between RDA and QoL, this study underscores the need for integrated care strategies that combine symptom management with psychological support. Such an approach could help patients better adapt to the challenges of CIPN, improving not only their functional outcomes but also their overall quality of life. In this context, the results of our study contribute to the growing body of evidence advocating for a patient-centered approach to cancer care, emphasizing the interconnectedness of physical, emotional, and social dimensions of health. This study employed a cross-sectional design to investigate the relationships among chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN), restriction of daily activity (RDA), mood, and quality of life (QoL) in colorectal cancer patients who had received oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy. Participants were recruited from a single oncology center specializing in the treatment of colorectal adenocarcinoma. Ethical approval for the study was obtained from the institutional review board, and all participants provided written informed consent prior to data collection. Participants The study included adult patients (≥18 years old) who had completed at least three cycles of oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy for histologically confirmed colorectal adenocarcinoma and were experiencing symptoms of CIPN. Inclusion criteria required that participants be cognitively capable of completing self-reported questionnaires and fluent in the language of the assessment tools. Patients were excluded if they had pre-existing peripheral neuropathy due to other causes (e.g., diabetes, alcohol use, or neurological disorders), a history of psychiatric conditions that could confound mood assessments, or concurrent malignancies requiring non-oxaliplatin chemotherapy. A total of 120 patients were initially screened, of whom 103 met the eligibility criteria and were enrolled in the study. Demographic and clinical information, including age, sex, cancer stage, chemotherapy regimen, and duration since completion of chemotherapy, was collected through medical record review and patient interviews. Measures Four validated instruments were used to assess CIPN, RDA, mood, and QoL: 1. Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory (NPSI): The NPSI was employed to evaluate the severity and characteristics of CIPN. This tool measures neuropathy symptoms across dimensions such as burning pain, electric shocks, and tingling sensations. Scores range from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating greater severity of CIPN symptoms. Patients were asked to recall their symptoms over the previous week. 2. Screening of Activity Limitation and Safety Awareness Scale (SALSA): RDA was assessed using the SALSA scale, which evaluates limitations in daily activities such as walking, dressing, and household tasks, as well as safety awareness in these activities. The scale generates a total score ranging from 0 to 60, with higher scores reflecting greater restriction in daily activities. 3. Profile of Mood States Short Form (POMS-SF): Negative mood was measured using the POMS-SF, which consists of six subscales: tension-anxiety, depression-dejection, anger-hostility, vigor-activity, fatigue-inertia, and confusion-bewilderment. For the purposes of this study, the total mood disturbance (TMD) score was used, with higher scores indicating greater mood disturbance. 4. Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Colorectal (FACT-C v4): QoL was assessed using the FACT-C, a colorectal cancer-specific version of the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy questionnaire. The FACT-C consists of five subdomains: physical well-being, social/family well-being, emotional well-being, functional well-being, and colorectal cancer-specific concerns. Total scores range from 0 to 136, with higher scores indicating better QoL. Procedure Patients who met the eligibility criteria were approached during routine follow-up visits at the oncology center. Those who consented to participate were provided with a packet of questionnaires comprising the NPSI, SALSA, POMS-SF, and FACT-C. A trained research assistant was available to clarify any questions or assist participants with limited literacy. Completion of the questionnaires typically required 30–40 minutes. Demographic and clinical data were collected via chart review and supplemented with patient self-report. Statistical Analysis Data were analyzed using SPSS version 25.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY). Descriptive statistics were calculated for all demographic and clinical variables, as well as for scores on the NPSI, SALSA, POMS-SF, and FACT-C. Continuous variables were reported as means and standard deviations, while categorical variables were summarized as frequencies and percentages. Bivariate correlations were examined using Pearson’s correlation coefficient to evaluate the relationships between CIPN, RDA, mood, and QoL. The strength of correlations was interpreted as follows: r = 0.10–0.29 (weak), r = 0.30–0.49 (moderate), and r ≥ 0.50 (strong). Hierarchical multiple linear regression was conducted to identify predictors of QoL, with CIPN, RDA, and mood entered as independent variables in successive steps. To assess the potential mediating role of mood in the relationship between RDA and QoL, Baron and Kenny’s mediation analysis framework was applied. This approach involves three steps: (1) testing the association between the independent variable (RDA) and the dependent variable (QoL); (2) testing the association between the independent variable (RDA) and the mediator (mood); and (3) testing whether the mediator (mood) accounts for the relationship between the independent variable (RDA) and the dependent variable (QoL). The significance of the mediation effect was further evaluated using bootstrapping with 5,000 resamples to calculate bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals. A mediation effect was considered significant if the confidence interval did not include zero. Sample Size Justification The sample size for the study was calculated based on an expected medium effect size (f² = 0.15) for the regression analysis, with a power of 0.80 and an alpha level of 0.05. Using GPower software, a minimum of 92 participants was required. To account for potential missing data, the sample size was increased to 103 participants, ensuring sufficient power for detecting significant relationships among the variables. Missing Data Incomplete responses were managed using pairwise deletion, which excluded only the specific missing data points from analyses rather than entire cases. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to confirm that the results were robust to the handling of missing data. Ethical Considerations All procedures were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and institutional ethical guidelines. Participants were assured of the confidentiality of their data, and they retained the right to withdraw from the study at any time without impacting their medical care. A total of 103 colorectal adenocarcinoma patients with chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) following oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy were included in this study. The sample consisted of patients with a mean age of 58.4 years (SD = 9.2), and the majority of participants were male (56.3%). CIPN severity, restriction of daily activity (RDA), negative mood, and quality of life (QoL) were assessed using validated instruments. The descriptive analysis demonstrated that CIPN severity was generally classified as mild to moderate (mean NPSI score = 3.82, SD = 1.11), and RDA was also mild (mean SALSA score = 22.47, SD = 6.34). Negative mood was reported at a moderate level (mean POMS-SF score = 28.16, SD = 8.72), while QoL, as measured by the FACT-C version 4, was moderately impaired (mean score = 88.92, SD = 15.53). CIPN severity was positively correlated with negative mood (r = 0.425, P < 0.001), suggesting that greater CIPN symptoms were associated with higher levels of mood disturbance. RDA was also significantly correlated with negative mood (r = 0.343, P < 0.001), indicating that greater activity limitations were associated with worse mood states. Furthermore, RDA was negatively correlated with QoL (r = -0.285, P < 0.01), showing that increased activity restrictions were linked to lower quality of life. Unilateral cerebral palsy (UCP) is one of the most common developmental disorders, characterized by motor impairments predominantly affecting one side of the body. These impairments often include diminished strength, coordination, and dexterity in the upper limb, which can significantly impact daily activities and the quality of life of children and young people with this condition. Given the critical role of upper limb function in achieving independence, significant efforts have been made to develop effective rehabilitation strategies aimed at improving motor function and participation for individuals with UCP. Despite the availability of various therapeutic approaches, limitations in accessibility, adherence, and long-term sustainability continue to pose challenges for the delivery of effective rehabilitation. One promising approach in neurorehabilitation is action observation training (AOT), which is based on the principles of motor learning and neuroplasticity. AOT involves observing goal-directed actions followed by the physical execution of these actions, leveraging the mirror neuron system to facilitate motor recovery. Evidence suggests that AOT can promote improvements in motor performance and functional outcomes by enhancing neural activity in motor-related brain regions. The application of AOT in children with UCP has shown encouraging results, particularly in improving upper limb motor function. Building on this foundation, the UPper Limb Children Action Observation Training (UPCAT) program was designed as a targeted intervention to address the specific motor challenges experienced by children with UCP. While conventional AOT interventions typically require in-person sessions in clinical or rehabilitation settings, logistical barriers, such as travel distances, cost, and time constraints, often hinder consistent participation. These challenges underscore the need for innovative solutions that can deliver effective therapy in a more accessible and sustainable manner. Advances in information and communication technologies (ICT) have opened new possibilities for remote rehabilitation, enabling the delivery of therapeutic interventions in home settings through tele-rehabilitation platforms. Such approaches not only address accessibility concerns but also have the potential to increase engagement and adherence by integrating therapy into the child’s everyday environment. In response to these opportunities, the Tele-UPCAT system has been developed as a novel ICT-based platform designed to deliver AOT remotely to children and young people with UCP. The system facilitates home-based rehabilitation by providing video sequences of goal-directed actions, followed by guided motor training of the same actions. The Tele-UPCAT system is tailored to the needs of children with UCP, incorporating sensorized objects and wearable devices for activity monitoring, which allow for the collection of quantitative data to assess therapy adherence and performance. This innovative approach seeks to combine the evidence-based principles of AOT with the flexibility and convenience of tele-rehabilitation, making therapy more accessible and potentially more effective for children with UCP and their families. The primary aim of this study is to evaluate the efficacy of the Tele-UPCAT system in improving upper limb function in children and young people with UCP. Specifically, the study will investigate whether home-based AOT delivered via Tele-UPCAT can lead to functional gains comparable to or greater than those achieved through standard care. The randomized controlled trial (RCT) design will allow for a rigorous comparison between the experimental group, which will undergo Tele-UPCAT, and a waitlist control group receiving usual care. The inclusion of a waitlist design ensures that all participants will have the opportunity to engage in the AOT intervention, addressing ethical considerations while maintaining the integrity of the trial. To comprehensively assess the impact of Tele-UPCAT, the study will employ a range of outcome measures. The primary outcome will be the Assisting Hand Assessment (AHA), a validated tool for evaluating bimanual performance in children with UCP. Secondary outcome measures will include the Melbourne Assessment 2, ABILHAND, and the Participation and Environment Measure for Children and Youth, as well as the Cerebral Palsy Quality of Life Questionnaire. These measures will capture a broad spectrum of outcomes, including motor function, participation, and quality of life, ensuring a holistic evaluation of the intervention’s effectiveness. In addition, quantitative data collected from sensorized objects and Actigraphs GXT3+ worn by participants will provide objective measures of therapy adherence and activity levels, offering valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying functional improvements. The study design includes multiple assessment points to capture both short-term and long-term effects of the intervention. Assessments will be conducted immediately before and after the intervention period, as well as at follow-up intervals of 8 and 24 weeks post-intervention. This longitudinal approach will allow for the evaluation of the durability of the observed benefits, providing critical information on the potential for sustained functional gains following Tele-UPCAT. This trial represents an important step toward addressing the unmet needs of children and young people with UCP by leveraging technology to deliver effective, home-based rehabilitation. If successful, the Tele-UPCAT system has the potential to revolutionize the delivery of upper limb rehabilitation for this population, offering a scalable and accessible solution that overcomes many of the barriers associated with traditional therapy models. By integrating evidence-based AOT principles with the convenience of tele-rehabilitation, this approach may not only improve motor outcomes but also enhance the overall quality of life for children with UCP and their families. Furthermore, the findings of this trial will contribute to the growing body of evidence supporting the use of ICT in pediatric neurorehabilitation, paving the way for future innovations in this field. The study is a randomised controlled trial designed to assess the efficacy of a home-based, tele-monitored action observation training (AOT) intervention, delivered via the Tele-UPCAT platform, for children and young people with unilateral cerebral palsy (UCP). The trial is designed with two parallel investigative arms: an experimental group receiving AOT at home and a waitlist control group receiving usual care for the same duration. The study employs an allocation-concealed and evaluator-blinded design to ensure methodological rigor and minimise bias. Participants and Recruitment The study aims to recruit 24 children and young people diagnosed with UCP, aged between 6 and 18 years, from clinical settings, rehabilitation centers, and patient advocacy organizations. Eligible participants will have a confirmed diagnosis of unilateral spastic cerebral palsy and be classified as levels I–III on the Manual Ability Classification System (MACS). Exclusion criteria include significant cognitive impairments limiting task comprehension, visual or hearing impairments that prevent engagement with the video-based training, botulinum toxin injections in the upper limb less than six months prior to enrollment, or surgical interventions in the past year. Potential participants and their families will receive detailed verbal and written information about the study, and written informed consent will be obtained from parents or legal guardians. Assent will also be obtained from children where appropriate. Participants will be randomly allocated to one of the two study arms following baseline assessments. Randomisation and Blinding Participants will be randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either the experimental or control group. Randomisation will be performed using a computer-generated random sequence by an independent researcher not involved in recruitment, data collection, or analysis. Allocation will be concealed using sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes. Outcome assessors will remain blinded to group allocation throughout the study period. Interventions The experimental group will receive the Tele-UPCAT intervention, a home-based AOT program delivered via a customised tele-rehabilitation platform. Over a three-week period, participants will engage in daily sessions, each lasting approximately 30 minutes. The intervention comprises two primary components: (1) observation of video sequences depicting goal-directed actions relevant to daily living and (2) guided physical practice of the observed actions using sensorised objects. Video content has been specifically designed to depict actions performed with the impaired upper limb and to be engaging and age-appropriate for the target population. The Tele-UPCAT system includes a user-friendly interface for video playback, monitoring of adherence, and feedback from therapists. Participants in the control group will receive usual care, which may include standard upper limb rehabilitation exercises, occupational therapy, or other interventions typically provided to children with UCP. After the initial three-week period, participants in the control group will have the opportunity to engage in the Tele-UPCAT intervention. Outcome Measures The primary outcome of the study is upper limb functional performance, as measured by the Assisting Hand Assessment (AHA), a validated tool for assessing the effectiveness of the impaired hand in bimanual activities. Secondary outcome measures will include: 1. The Melbourne Assessment of Unilateral Upper Limb Function (Melbourne Assessment 2), which evaluates quality of movement. 2. ABILHAND-Kids, a parent-reported questionnaire assessing perceived manual ability in everyday activities. 3. The Participation and Environment Measure-Children and Youth (PEM-CY), which evaluates participation in home, school, and community settings. 4. The Cerebral Palsy Quality of Life Questionnaire (CP QOL-Child), assessing health-related quality of life. 5. Quantitative measures collected from sensorised objects used during training, including movement metrics such as speed, force, and precision. 6. ActiGraph GT3X+ accelerometers worn by participants on their wrists to monitor physical activity levels during the intervention period. All outcome measures will be assessed at baseline (T0), immediately after the intervention period (T1), and at follow-up time points of 8 weeks (T2) and 24 weeks (T3) post-intervention. For the waitlist control group, an additional assessment will be conducted one week after completing the AOT intervention (T1-plus). Tele-UPCAT System and Monitoring The Tele-UPCAT platform has been designed to facilitate remote delivery of the AOT intervention while ensuring adherence and safety. The system includes video-based training modules, sensorised objects for task practice, and a tele-monitoring feature that allows therapists to track progress and provide feedback remotely. Adherence to the intervention will be monitored through automated logging of video playback and task completion data within the system. Technical support will be available to participants and their families throughout the intervention period. Data Collection and Analysis Data will be collected by trained assessors blinded to group allocation. All assessments will take place in clinical settings or at participants’ homes, depending on logistical feasibility and participant preference. Quantitative data from sensorised objects and ActiGraph accelerometers will be extracted and analysed using custom software to evaluate changes in movement patterns and physical activity levels. Statistical analysis will be conducted using an intention-to-treat approach. Baseline characteristics will be summarised and compared between groups to ensure balance. Mixed-effects models will be used to assess changes in primary and secondary outcomes over time, with group (experimental vs. control) and time (T0, T1, T2, T3) as fixed effects and participant as a random effect. Post hoc analyses will explore within-group changes and potential moderators of treatment response, such as age, severity of impairment, and baseline functional levels. Sample Size Calculation A sample size of 24 participants (12 per group) was determined based on a power calculation to detect a clinically meaningful difference in AHA scores with 80% power and a two-tailed significance level of 0.05. This calculation assumes a moderate effect size and accounts for a potential 20% dropout rate. Ethical Considerations The study has been approved by the Tuscany Paediatric Ethics Committee (protocol number 169/2016). All procedures comply with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice guidelines. Participants and their families will be informed of their right to withdraw from the study at any time without consequences for their ongoing care. This methodology ensures a robust evaluation of the efficacy and feasibility of the Tele-UPCAT intervention in improving upper limb function and quality of life in children with UCP. The results of this study demonstrate the feasibility and efficacy of the Tele-UPCAT system for delivering action observation training (AOT) at home in children with unilateral cerebral palsy (UCP). A total of 24 participants were recruited and randomly assigned to the experimental group (n=12) or the control group (n=12). All participants completed the study with no dropouts, and no adverse events were reported during the intervention period. The participant demographic and clinical characteristics at baseline (T0) were comparable between the two groups, with no significant differences observed in age, sex, or baseline functional measures, including the Assisting Hand Assessment (AHA), Melbourne Assessment 2, ABILHAND, Participation and Environment Measure-Children and Youth (PEM-CY), and Cerebral Palsy Quality of Life Questionnaire (CP QOL). Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is one of the most prevalent malignancies worldwide and represents the predominant form of primary liver cancer, accounting for a significant proportion of cancer-related mortality [1,2]. Despite advances in diagnostic and therapeutic strategies, the prognosis of HCC remains dismal, particularly in cases diagnosed at advanced stages [3]. The poor clinical outcomes are attributed to the aggressive biological behavior of HCC, including its propensity for metastasis, recurrence, and resistance to conventional therapies [4]. As such, there is an urgent need to identify novel molecular biomarkers that could facilitate early diagnosis, predict disease progression, and serve as potential therapeutic targets for patients with HCC. The dysregulation of epigenetic mechanisms is increasingly recognized as a critical driver of tumorigenesis, including HCC [5,6]. Epigenetic modifications, such as histone methylation, acetylation, and DNA methylation, play central roles in regulating gene expression and chromatin dynamics [7]. Among these, histone methylation is particularly important as it governs key biological processes such as transcriptional activation, repression, and chromatin remodeling [8]. Dysregulated histone methyltransferases (HMTs), the enzymes responsible for adding methyl groups to specific histone residues, have been implicated in the initiation and progression of various cancers, including liver malignancies [9]. Therefore, understanding the functional roles of specific HMTs in the context of HCC may offer new insights into the molecular underpinnings of the disease and provide avenues for therapeutic intervention. The SET domain-containing 1B gene (SETD1B), a member of the SET1 family of HMTs, encodes a histone methyltransferase that specifically catalyzes the methylation of histone H3 at lysine 4 (H3K4) [10]. This post-translational modification is widely recognized as a marker of transcriptional activation and is involved in regulating the expression of genes critical for cell growth, differentiation, and survival [11]. SETD1B is a component of the COMPASS (complex of proteins associated with SET1) complex, which orchestrates H3K4 methylation in a context-dependent manner [12]. While SETD1B has been implicated in various biological processes, including embryonic development, immune regulation, and neuronal function, emerging evidence suggests that it may also play a role in oncogenesis [13,14]. Dysregulated SETD1B expression has been observed in several malignancies, including colorectal cancer, gastric cancer, and glioblastoma, where it has been linked to enhanced tumor cell proliferation, invasion, and metastasis [15-17]. However, its functional significance and clinical relevance in HCC remain largely unexplored. Recent studies have highlighted the heterogeneity of HCC at the molecular level, underscoring the importance of investigating specific genetic and epigenetic alterations that drive the disease [18]. Given the established role of H3K4 methylation in promoting transcriptional activation and the potential contribution of SETD1B to tumorigenesis in other cancers, it is plausible that aberrant expression of SETD1B may influence the progression of HCC. However, the precise mechanisms by which SETD1B exerts its effects in HCC and its potential as a biomarker or therapeutic target have not been delineated. Addressing these knowledge gaps could provide critical insights into the molecular etiology of HCC and inform the development of novel diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. In addition to its putative role in transcriptional regulation, SETD1B has been implicated in pathways associated with DNA damage repair, cell cycle progression, and apoptosis [19,20]. These pathways are frequently dysregulated in HCC and contribute to hallmark features of the disease, including uncontrolled proliferation, genomic instability, and resistance to apoptosis [21]. Furthermore, high levels of SETD1B expression have been correlated with poor clinical outcomes in other cancers, suggesting that its expression may serve as a prognostic marker [22]. While preliminary data suggest that SETD1B may be upregulated in HCC, comprehensive studies examining its expression patterns, functional roles, and clinical significance are lacking. Such investigations are essential to determine whether SETD1B represents an actionable target for therapeutic intervention. To address these gaps, the present study investigates the expression of SETD1B in HCC and its association with clinicopathological features and patient outcomes. By integrating molecular analyses with clinical data, this study seeks to elucidate the role of SETD1B in HCC pathogenesis and evaluate its potential as a prognostic marker. Specifically, the expression levels of SETD1B mRNA and protein were assessed in HCC tumor tissues and matched adjacent normal tissues. The correlation between SETD1B expression and clinicopathological parameters, including tumor size, clinical stage, and liver cirrhosis, was examined. Furthermore, survival analyses were conducted to determine the prognostic significance of SETD1B expression. Finally, multivariate Cox regression analysis was performed to assess whether SETD1B serves as an independent prognostic factor. The findings of this study contribute to the growing body of evidence implicating epigenetic regulators in the progression of HCC and highlight the potential of SETD1B as a biomarker and therapeutic target. By characterizing the clinical and molecular significance of SETD1B in HCC, this research provides a foundation for future studies aimed at developing SETD1B-targeted therapies. Retinoblastoma (Rb) is the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood, with an incidence of approximately 1 in 16,000 to 18,000 live births globally [1, 2]. Advances in the treatment of retinoblastoma have significantly improved survival rates, shifting the focus of research toward reducing treatment-related morbidity and optimizing long-term quality of life for survivors [3, 4]. Among the various treatment modalities, ophthalmic artery chemosurgery (OAC) has emerged as a transformative approach for the management of intraocular retinoblastoma. This technique involves the direct delivery of chemotherapeutic agents into the ophthalmic artery, enabling high local drug concentrations while minimizing systemic exposure [5, 6]. Since its introduction, OAC has demonstrated high efficacy in tumor control and eye preservation, particularly in advanced cases or those refractory to systemic chemotherapy [7, 8]. Despite these clinical benefits, the systemic implications of OAC on broader aspects of pediatric health, particularly growth, remain poorly understood. Growth disturbances in pediatric oncology patients have primarily been documented in survivors of systemic chemotherapy, with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) serving as the most extensively studied model [9, 10]. Chemotherapeutic agents, including glucocorticoids, methotrexate, and alkylating agents, have been implicated in growth suppression through mechanisms such as hypothalamic-pituitary axis dysfunction, direct toxic effects on growth plate chondrocytes, and malnutrition during treatment [11, 12]. Furthermore, radiotherapy, particularly cranial or total body irradiation, has been strongly associated with growth impairments due to its deleterious effects on growth hormone secretion and skeletal development [13]. While these findings have provided valuable insights into the growth trajectories of pediatric cancer survivors, they primarily reflect the outcomes of systemic therapies and are not directly applicable to patients undergoing OAC, which is characterized by a more localized therapeutic approach. The limited systemic absorption of chemotherapeutic agents during OAC suggests that its impact on growth may differ from that observed with systemic chemotherapy. However, data on growth patterns in retinoblastoma patients treated with OAC remain scarce. Several studies have reported the efficacy and ocular toxicities of OAC, but its potential systemic effects, particularly on growth, have not been systematically evaluated [14, 15]. This knowledge gap is clinically significant, as growth disturbances can have long-term implications for physical health, psychosocial well-being, and overall quality of life in pediatric cancer survivors [16]. Additionally, understanding the growth trajectories of retinoblastoma patients treated with OAC is important for parental counseling and the development of tailored survivorship care plans. The current study aims to address this gap by analyzing the growth patterns of retinoblastoma patients treated with OAC at a single tertiary care center. The study includes three distinct patient groups: those who received OAC as their primary treatment ("naïve"), those who transitioned to OAC after initial systemic chemotherapy ("secondary"), and a smaller cohort who received single-agent systemic chemotherapy prior to OAC as a "bridge" strategy. This classification allows for a nuanced analysis of how prior systemic chemotherapy may influence growth outcomes in the context of subsequent OAC. Importantly, patients with confounding factors such as external radiation therapy or genetic syndromes known to affect growth were excluded to ensure the validity of the findings. In pediatric oncology, growth is typically assessed through parameters such as height, weight, and growth velocity, which reflect the complex interplay of endocrine, nutritional, and skeletal factors [17]. The study's methodology involves longitudinal tracking of these parameters during the treatment phase (short-term) and up to three years post-treatment (long-term), providing a comprehensive overview of growth trajectories. By comparing growth patterns across different treatment groups and time points, the study seeks to elucidate the potential impact of OAC on both immediate and sustained growth outcomes. Preliminary data from the study indicate that OAC does not significantly impair growth velocity during treatment or adversely affect height and weight percentiles over the long term. Specifically, the findings suggest that naïve patients tend to achieve slightly higher height and weight percentiles three years post-treatment compared to secondary patients, although the differences are not statistically significant. These results are consistent with the hypothesis that the localized nature of OAC minimizes systemic toxicity and its associated growth disturbances. Additionally, the observation that the number of OAC treatments does not correlate with growth outcomes further supports the safety profile of this modality concerning pediatric growth. The implications of these findings extend beyond retinoblastoma, as OAC represents a broader paradigm shift toward targeted therapies that prioritize tumor control while preserving systemic health. By demonstrating the absence of significant growth impairments in retinoblastoma survivors treated with OAC, this study contributes to the growing body of evidence supporting the safety and efficacy of this approach. Furthermore, the results underscore the importance of longitudinal monitoring of growth and other developmental parameters in pediatric oncology patients, even in the context of therapies with minimal systemic exposure. In summary, while the systemic impact of OAC on growth appears to be minimal, this study highlights the need for continued research to validate these findings in larger, multicenter cohorts. Future investigations should also explore the potential interactions between OAC and other factors influencing growth, such as nutritional status, physical activity, and endocrine function. By addressing these questions, we can further optimize the care of retinoblastoma survivors and ensure that advances in cancer treatment translate into improved long-term outcomes for pediatric patients. Study Design and Patient Population This study was a retrospective, single-center cohort analysis conducted at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC). The primary objective was to evaluate growth patterns in pediatric patients with retinoblastoma (Rb) treated with ophthalmic artery chemosurgery (OAC). Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval was obtained prior to the initiation of the study, and all research activities adhered to the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. Informed consent was waived due to the retrospective nature of the study. The study population consisted of 341 pediatric patients diagnosed with retinoblastoma between January 2006 and December 2016. Eligible patients were identified through the institutional database. Inclusion criteria required patients to have received OAC as part of their treatment regimen, with adequate follow-up data on growth parameters. Patients were excluded if they underwent external beam radiation therapy or had known genetic syndromes associated with growth abnormalities, such as Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome or growth hormone deficiencies. A total of 297 patients met the inclusion criteria after exclusions. Patients were categorized into three groups based on their treatment history. The "naïve" group included patients who received OAC as their sole form of chemotherapy without prior systemic treatment. The "secondary" group comprised patients who initially underwent systemic chemotherapy at external institutions but subsequently transitioned to OAC at MSKCC. A third, smaller cohort, the "bridge" group, included patients who received single-agent systemic chemotherapy as a preparatory or bridging therapy prior to OAC initiation. Due to the small sample size of the bridge group, they were excluded from subgroup analyses. Treatment Protocol OAC was administered via selective ophthalmic artery infusion under general anesthesia, as previously described in published protocols [1, 2]. Chemotherapeutic agents commonly utilized included melphalan, topotecan, and carboplatin, either as single agents or in combination, depending on tumor size, laterality, and prior treatment history. The decision regarding the number of OAC sessions was individualized, based on tumor response and patient tolerability, with most patients receiving 1–6 cycles at monthly intervals. Data Collection Patient demographics, baseline clinical characteristics, and treatment details were extracted from electronic medical records. Height and weight measurements were recorded at each monthly clinical visit during the OAC treatment phase (short-term) and annually during routine follow-up visits for up to three years post-treatment (long-term). Measurements were obtained using standardized protocols. Height was measured to the nearest 0.1 cm using a wall-mounted stadiometer, and weight was recorded to the nearest 0.1 kg using a calibrated digital scale. Body mass index (BMI) was calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared (kg/m²). All growth data were converted to age- and sex-specific percentiles using the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) growth charts [3]. Outcomes The primary outcomes were growth velocity and changes in growth percentiles for height and weight during the short-term (OAC treatment phase) and long-term (three-year follow-up period) phases. Growth velocity was calculated as the change in height (cm/year) during the OAC treatment period. Secondary outcomes included weight percentiles and BMI percentiles during both time frames. Statistical Analysis Descriptive statistics were used to summarize baseline characteristics of the study population. Continuous variables were reported as means and standard deviations (SD) or medians and interquartile ranges (IQRs), as appropriate, while categorical variables were expressed as frequencies and percentages. Growth velocity during the OAC treatment phase was compared between the naïve and secondary groups using independent samples t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests, based on data distribution. Longitudinal changes in growth percentiles for height and weight were evaluated using mixed-effects linear regression models with random intercepts to account for repeated measures within individuals. Covariates in the models included age, sex, treatment group, and number of OAC sessions. Post hoc pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni corrections were conducted where applicable. To assess the impact of prior systemic chemotherapy on long-term growth, subgroup analyses were performed comparing the naïve and secondary groups. For these analyses, height and weight percentiles at one, two, and three years post-treatment were modeled as dependent variables. Kaplan-Meier survival curves were used to estimate the proportion of patients remaining within normal growth percentiles (>5th percentile) over time, with log-rank tests comparing the two groups. Missing data for growth parameters (<5% of measurements) were assumed to be missing at random and were addressed using multiple imputation with chained equations. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to ensure robustness of the findings. Statistical significance was defined as a two-tailed p-value <0.05.
