The integration of brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) with robotic systems has garnered considerable attention in recent years, particularly for its potential to enhance the autonomy and quality of life for individuals with severe motor impairments [1,2]. These brain-controlled robots, which leverage neural signals to execute actions, represent a transformative class of assistive devices. However, optimizing the interaction between humans and robots remains a critical challenge to ensure the effectiveness, safety, and usability of such systems. Specifically, understanding how humans perceive and process robot actions at the neural level is essential for the development of adaptive control algorithms that improve the human-robot interaction (HRI) experience. One promising avenue for advancing adaptive robotic systems is the use of error-related neural signals, which reflect the human brain's response to observed or executed errors. These signals, often referred to as error-related potentials (ErrPs), have been widely studied within the context of human-human interaction and traditional human-computer interaction [3-5]. ErrPs are typically characterized by distinct event-related potential (ERP) components that are elicited when individuals detect deviations from expected outcomes, whether these deviations occur in their own actions or in the actions of external agents. While previous research has demonstrated the feasibility of decoding ErrPs during human observation of robotic errors [6,7], the robustness and generalizability of these findings in more complex and naturalistic HRI scenarios remain underexplored. Additionally, the visual and morphological characteristics of robots may modulate the neural processing underlying error observation. Studies in social robotics and psychology suggest that humans perceive humanoid robots differently from non-humanoid robots, with these differences potentially influencing cognitive and affective responses during interaction [8,9]. The uncanny valley hypothesis, for example, posits that humanoid robots that closely resemble humans can evoke discomfort or heightened attention due to their near-human likeness [10]. Conversely, non-humanoid robots may elicit less anthropomorphic attributions, potentially altering the observer's expectations and neural responses to their actions. Despite growing interest in the role of robot morphology in HRI, its impact on brain activity during robot-error observation remains poorly characterized. The present study addresses these gaps by combining electroencephalographic (EEG) recordings with machine learning techniques to investigate the neural correlates of error observation in HRI. Specifically, we sought to determine whether brain activity during the observation of robot errors could be reliably decoded from single-trial EEG data, thereby providing insights into the neural mechanisms underlying error detection in this context. Furthermore, we examined whether the type of robot—humanoid or non-humanoid—modulates neural responses to errors, as well as whether this information could be decoded from EEG signals. To achieve these objectives, we designed and implemented two complementary experimental paradigms. In Experiment I, participants observed a robotic arm perform a simple task: pouring liquid into a cup. The robot's performance was manipulated to include both correct actions, in which the liquid was poured successfully, and erroneous actions, in which some liquid was spilled. This task was selected to elicit robust error-related neural responses while minimizing task complexity and cognitive load. In Experiment II, we extended this approach by introducing two distinct robot morphologies—a humanoid robot and a non-humanoid robot—and having participants observe these robots perform a ball-grasping task. By using two robot types, we aimed to disentangle the influence of robot morphology on neural responses to error observation. To analyze the recorded EEG data, we employed a Filter Bank Common Spatial Pattern (FBCSP) pipeline, a widely used method in BCI research for feature extraction and classification of multivariate neural signals [11,12]. The FBCSP approach enables the identification of discriminative spatial and spectral patterns in EEG data, which can then be used to decode specific cognitive states or processes. In this study, we applied the FBCSP pipeline to decode two key variables: (1) the correctness of the observed robot action (correct vs. erroneous) and (2) the type of robot observed (humanoid vs. non-humanoid). By evaluating decoding performance across individual participants, we aimed to assess the feasibility and reliability of using EEG signals to infer these aspects of HRI. This work extends prior research on ErrPs and HRI in several important ways. First, while much of the existing literature has focused on error detection in self-controlled or virtual agent scenarios [13,14], our study investigates error observation in the context of physical robot actions. This distinction is crucial, as physical robots introduce unique perceptual and cognitive challenges that may influence error processing. Second, by incorporating robot morphology as a variable of interest, we provide novel insights into how anthropomorphic design features shape neural responses during HRI. Lastly, our use of high-resolution EEG recordings and advanced decoding techniques represents a methodological advancement, enabling more nuanced analyses of neural dynamics during robot-error observation. The findings of this study have significant implications for the design of brain-controlled robotic systems. If error-related neural responses can be reliably decoded in real time, they could serve as a valuable feedback signal for adaptive robotic control. For instance, integrating decoded ErrPs into robotic learning algorithms could enable robots to autonomously improve their performance by identifying and correcting errors based on the user's implicit neural feedback. Furthermore, understanding how robot morphology influences neural responses could inform the design of more effective and user-friendly robotic systems that align with human cognitive and emotional preferences. In summary, the present study aims to elucidate the neural mechanisms underlying error observation in HRI and to explore the influence of robot morphology on these processes. By leveraging advanced EEG analysis techniques, we seek to contribute to the development of adaptive and intuitive brain-controlled robotic systems that can better meet the needs of their users. The results of this research not only enhance our understanding of human cognitive responses during HRI but also provide a foundation for future innovations in assistive robotics and neuroadaptive technologies. Participants A total of 30 healthy volunteers (15 females; mean age = 25.7 ± 3.2 years) participated in the study. All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no self-reported history of neurological or psychiatric disorders. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to the experiments, and the study was approved by the appropriate ethics review board in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Experimental Design Two separate experiments were conducted to investigate differential brain responses to robot actions based on correctness and robot type. Participants completed both experiments in a randomized order, with a short break between experiments. Experiment I: Observation of Robot Arm Pouring Actions In the first experiment, participants observed a robotic arm performing a liquid-pouring task. The robot arm was programmed to either execute the task correctly (i.e., pouring liquid into a cup without spillage) or to perform the task erroneously (i.e., spilling liquid outside the cup). Each trial began with a fixation cross displayed for 1,000 ms, followed by a video (4-second duration) of the robotic arm performing the task. After the video, a blank screen appeared for 1,500 ms, during which participants were instructed to remain still and refrain from blinking to minimize artifacts. Trials were pseudo-randomized to ensure an approximately equal number of correct and erroneous actions, and participants were not informed about the sequence of events in advance. A total of 100 trials (50 correct, 50 erroneous) were presented in this experiment. Experiment II: Observation of Humanoid vs. Non-Humanoid Robots In the second experiment, participants observed two distinct robot types—a humanoid robot and a non-humanoid robotic arm—performing a ball-grabbing task. Similar to Experiment I, each robot's action was either successful (i.e., the robot successfully grabbed the ball) or unsuccessful (i.e., the robot missed the ball). The trial structure was identical to Experiment I, with a fixation cross (1,000 ms), an action video (4 seconds), and a blank screen (1,500 ms). The two robot types were visually distinct, with the humanoid robot displaying anthropomorphic features (e.g., a head and arms resembling human morphology), while the non-humanoid robot had a purely mechanical appearance. A total of 120 trials were presented in Experiment II, with an equal number of trials for each combination of robot type (humanoid vs. non-humanoid) and action outcome (successful vs. unsuccessful). EEG Recording and Preprocessing EEG signals were recorded using a 64-channel cap (Brain Products GmbH, Germany) with electrodes placed according to the international 10-20 system. The EEG data were sampled at 1,000 Hz and referenced to the Cz electrode during acquisition. Impedances were maintained below 10 kΩ for all electrodes. Vertical and horizontal electrooculogram (EOG) channels were recorded to monitor eye movements and blinks. Preprocessing was performed using MATLAB (MathWorks, USA) and the EEGLAB toolbox [1]. The continuous EEG data were bandpass-filtered between 1 and 40 Hz using a zero-phase finite impulse response (FIR) filter to remove low-frequency drifts and high-frequency noise. Line noise at 50 Hz was removed using a notch filter. The data were subsequently segmented into epochs from -500 ms to 1,500 ms relative to the onset of the action video, with a 200 ms pre-stimulus baseline. Trials containing artifacts, such as large muscle activity or excessive eye movements, were identified using automated algorithms (threshold set to ±100 μV) and manually reviewed. Artifact-contaminated trials were excluded from further analysis, resulting in an average of 93.2% of trials retained per participant. Feature Extraction and Classification To decode brain responses, we employed a Filter Bank Common Spatial Pattern (FBCSP) approach [2], which is well-suited for multivariate EEG data. First, the preprocessed EEG signals were decomposed into multiple frequency bands (theta: 4–7 Hz, alpha: 8–13 Hz, beta: 14–30 Hz, and low gamma: 31–40 Hz) using bandpass filters. For each frequency band, spatial filters were computed using the common spatial pattern (CSP) algorithm, which maximizes the variance of EEG signals for one class (e.g., correct actions) while minimizing it for the other class (e.g., erroneous actions). The spatially filtered signals were then log-transformed to obtain features representing the variance of EEG activity for each class. These features were concatenated across frequency bands and used as input to a regularized linear discriminant analysis (rLDA) classifier [3]. Separate classifiers were trained for decoding action correctness (correct vs. erroneous) and robot type (humanoid vs. non-humanoid), using a 5-fold cross-validation strategy. To ensure balanced training datasets, class labels were stratified during cross-validation. Statistical Analysis Classification performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and classification accuracy. Statistical significance was assessed using a permutation test [4] with 1,000 iterations to compare observed classification performance against chance-level performance (50%). For each participant, the null distribution was generated by shuffling class labels and recomputing classification accuracy. A p-value was obtained by calculating the proportion of permuted accuracies exceeding the observed accuracy. To investigate potential differences in decoding performance across experimental conditions, a repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) was conducted with factors of action correctness (correct vs. erroneous) and robot type (humanoid vs. non-humanoid). Post hoc pairwise comparisons were corrected for multiple comparisons using the Bonferroni method. References [1] Delorme, A., & Makeig, S. (2004). EEGLAB: An open-source toolbox for analysis of single-trial EEG dynamics. Journal of Neuroscience Methods, 134(1), 9-21. [2] Ang, K. K., Chin, Z. Y., Wang, C., & Guan, C. (2008). Filter bank common spatial pattern algorithm on BCI competition IV datasets 2a and 2b. Frontiers in Neuroscience, 6, 39. [3] Blankertz, B., Lemm, S., Treder, M., Haufe, S., & Müller, K. R. (2011). Single-trial analysis and classification of ERP components: A tutorial. NeuroImage, 56(2), 814-825. [4] Nichols, T. E., & Holmes, A. P. (2002). Nonparametric permutation tests for functional neuroimaging: A primer with examples. Human Brain Mapping, 15(1), 1-25. Behavioral Observations and Subjective Ratings During both experiments, participants were fully attentive to the robot action sequences, as confirmed by post-experiment questionnaires and the absence of prolonged eye blinks or movement artifacts in the majority of EEG recordings. Participants reported being able to discern correct from erroneous actions with ease, and several mentioned that the humanoid robot in Experiment II elicited a stronger sense of familiarity compared to the non-humanoid robot. The HIV epidemic continues to pose a significant public health challenge globally, with men who have sex with men (MSM) disproportionately affected in many regions. In Thailand, MSM remain one of the most vulnerable populations, with alarmingly high rates of HIV infection. Data collected between 2007 and 2010 revealed that one in three MSM surveyed in Bangkok was HIV positive, and modeling estimates suggest that over half of new HIV infections in Thailand are among MSM. Despite the availability of effective interventions for HIV prevention, testing, and treatment, these tools have not been adequately leveraged to curb the epidemic among this key population. Early HIV testing and counselling (HTC), coupled with prompt linkage to antiretroviral therapy (ART) for those diagnosed with HIV, is critical to achieving viral suppression and reducing onward transmission. Yet, structural barriers, stigma, and discrimination often deter MSM in Thailand from accessing these essential services. At the same time, Thailand has witnessed a rapid expansion of internet and mobile technology use, especially among MSM. Studies have shown that MSM are among the most active users of digital platforms in the country, utilizing these tools for social networking, health information-seeking, and community engagement. This widespread adoption of digital technology offers a unique and underutilized opportunity to reach and engage MSM in HIV prevention and care. Harnessing the power of online platforms to address the HIV epidemic could provide a scalable and cost-effective solution, particularly in contexts where stigma and discrimination act as significant barriers to accessing traditional healthcare services. Recognizing this potential, the Thai Red Cross AIDS Research Centre launched Adam’s Love in 2011, an innovative web-based communications strategy specifically designed to engage MSM in Thailand. The programme aimed to leverage digital platforms to promote early HIV testing and facilitate linkage to care and treatment. Adam’s Love employs a comprehensive “online-to-offline” model that integrates a dedicated website, social media platforms, and online message boards to provide accessible, confidential, and user-friendly counselling and referral services. The initiative also incorporates targeted marketing, a club membership programme offering non-monetary incentives, and collaborations with MSM-friendly clinics and private healthcare providers to ensure that services are welcoming and accessible for MSM. This multifaceted approach seeks to address the structural and psychosocial barriers that often hinder MSM from seeking timely HIV testing and care. The Adam’s Love programme represents a significant departure from traditional outreach and service delivery models, which often rely on in-person interactions and fixed-site clinics. By utilizing digital channels, Adam’s Love meets MSM where they are—online—creating a safe and anonymous space for individuals to access information, seek support, and take the first step toward HIV testing. The programme also facilitates online appointment-making and referrals to ensure that users can seamlessly transition from virtual engagement to in-person services. Importantly, Adam’s Love recognizes the need for a tailored approach that resonates with the target population, employing culturally sensitive and affirming messaging to build trust and encourage uptake. Since its launch, Adam’s Love has demonstrated impressive reach and impact. Between September 2011 and January 2015, the programme engaged 1.69 million viewers and generated over 8 million page views. During this period, an estimated 11,120 MSM received online counselling through the platform, and 8,288 MSM were referred to HTC services. Additionally, the programme facilitated referrals to STI testing services and provided treatment counselling for over 1,100 MSM living with HIV. Notably, the club membership programme, which incentivizes HIV testing participation, enrolled 1,181 MSM, 15.5% of whom were diagnosed with HIV. These findings underscore the programme’s potential to serve as an effective model for engaging MSM in HIV prevention and care using digital technology. The success of Adam’s Love has broader implications for public health strategies aimed at addressing the HIV epidemic among MSM in Thailand and beyond. As the HIV epidemic continues to evolve, innovative approaches that leverage technology and address the unique needs of key populations are essential. The “online-to-offline” recruitment model pioneered by Adam’s Love offers a scalable and replicable framework that can be adapted to other settings, particularly in regions where MSM experience stigma and discrimination or have limited access to healthcare services. This paper explores the implementation and outcomes of the Adam’s Love programme, highlighting its role in promoting early HIV testing and linkage to care among MSM in Thailand. By examining the strategies employed and the lessons learned, this study aims to provide valuable insights for public health practitioners, policymakers, and researchers working to address the HIV epidemic in key populations. Ultimately, the findings underscore the critical importance of integrating technology-based interventions into the broader HIV response to achieve the goal of ending the epidemic. The study employed a web-based communications strategy developed and implemented by the Thai Red Cross AIDS Research Centre, called Adam's Love, to increase engagement in early HIV testing and counselling (HTC) and linkage to care among gay men and other men who have sex with men (MSM) in Thailand. The programme was designed as an innovative "online-to-offline" model to leverage the high internet accessibility within this population and address barriers to traditional outreach and healthcare engagement. The methods employed are detailed below. The Adam’s Love programme was launched in September 2011 and targeted MSM through a combination of internet-based platforms and partnerships with MSM-friendly healthcare providers. Central to the programme was a dedicated and interactive website (www.adamslove.org), which provided information on HIV prevention, testing, and treatment. The website content was tailored specifically to the MSM population and included culturally appropriate visuals, testimonials, videos, and educational materials to promote awareness and reduce stigma around HIV testing and care. In addition to the website, the programme integrated multiple social media platforms, including Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube, to expand its reach and engage MSM with interactive content. Social media campaigns were designed to build a community of trust and encourage online discussions around HIV-related topics. Targeted social media advertisements and posts were used to increase visibility of the programme and drive traffic to the website. The programme also utilised web-based message boards and chat services to provide real-time online counselling by trained healthcare professionals and peer counsellors. These online counselling sessions were designed to address individual concerns, answer questions about HIV, and provide guidance on accessing HTC services. To facilitate linkage to offline services, the programme offered an online appointment booking system that allowed MSM to schedule HTC sessions at collaborating MSM-friendly clinics and private hospitals. The participating healthcare facilities were chosen based on their accessibility, confidentiality, and demonstrated sensitivity to the needs of MSM. A club membership programme was also introduced as part of the strategy to provide additional incentives for MSM to engage with HTC services. MSM enrolling in the programme received non-financial benefits, such as priority access to services, exclusive educational materials, and invitations to community events. The programme incorporated targeted marketing and promotional activities to increase awareness and uptake. These included partnerships with MSM-focused organisations, community events, and outreach activities at venues frequented by MSM, such as bars, clubs, and saunas. Online advertising was also used to target MSM with specific keywords and demographics to ensure that the programme reached the population most at risk. Data collection and monitoring were integral to the programme to evaluate its effectiveness and inform ongoing improvements. Website analytics tools were used to track engagement metrics, including the number of unique visitors, page views, and user interactions. Data from the online counselling sessions, including the number of MSM counselled and referred to services, were recorded and analysed. Collaborating clinics provided de-identified data on HTC uptake, HIV diagnoses, and linkage to care for MSM referred through the Adam’s Love platform. These data were securely stored and analysed to assess the impact of the programme in increasing access to services and identifying new HIV cases. In addition to direct service delivery, the programme established partnerships with healthcare providers to ensure that MSM referred through Adam’s Love received high-quality, stigma-free care. Training sessions were conducted for healthcare staff at participating clinics to sensitise them to the specific needs of MSM and improve the overall patient experience. This component aimed to foster a supportive and welcoming environment for MSM accessing HTC and treatment services. Throughout the implementation period from September 2011 to January 2015, the programme continuously refined its strategies based on user feedback and data analysis. Regular online surveys and focus group discussions were conducted with MSM participants to gather insights into their experiences with the programme and identify areas for improvement. Feedback from healthcare providers was also collected to optimise referral processes and service delivery. The Adam’s Love programme was ultimately designed as a sustainable and scalable intervention, with the potential to be adapted for other settings and populations. Its emphasis on integrating online platforms with offline healthcare services sought to address the unique challenges faced by MSM in accessing HTC and treatment in Thailand, while also leveraging the opportunities presented by advancements in communications technology. Between September 2011 and January 2015, the Adam's Love programme demonstrated significant success in engaging gay men and other men who have sex with men (MSM) in Thailand into early HIV testing, counselling, and treatment through its innovative communications technologies. The programme's online platform, which included a dedicated website, integrated social media, and interactive web message boards, attracted a substantial audience. During this period, the website recorded an impressive 1.69 million unique viewers and more than 8 million page views. This high level of engagement highlights the potential of technology-based strategies to effectively target populations at high risk for HIV. The programme offered online counselling, which proved to be a critical element in addressing the concerns and questions of MSM regarding HIV testing and treatment. A total of 11,120 MSM received online counselling through the platform, providing them with tailored information and support. The online counselling sessions served as a gateway to HIV testing and prevention services, helping to overcome barriers such as stigma, fear, and lack of information, which often prevent MSM from accessing traditional HIV services. One of the key outcomes of Adam's Love was its ability to successfully refer MSM to HIV testing and counselling (HTC) services. Over the study period, 8,288 MSM were referred to HTC services through the programme. The referrals were facilitated by partnerships with MSM-friendly clinics and private hospitals, ensuring that users had access to safe and nonjudgmental environments for testing. By addressing issues of accessibility and creating positive healthcare experiences, the programme encouraged more MSM to get tested for HIV. In addition to HIV testing, the programme also focused on promoting sexual health more broadly. A total of 1,223 MSM were referred to sexually transmitted infection (STI) testing services. This integration of STI testing into the programme's outreach efforts further strengthened its impact, as co-infection with STIs can increase the risk of HIV transmission and complicate treatment outcomes. By providing comprehensive sexual health services, Adam's Love addressed the broader health needs of MSM in Thailand. The programme also provided tailored advice and support for MSM living with HIV. A total of 1,112 MSM who were identified as living with HIV through the programme received counselling and guidance on accessing antiretroviral treatment (ART) and navigating care services. This aspect of the programme emphasized the importance of early initiation of treatment, which not only improves individual health outcomes but also reduces the risk of onward transmission of the virus. A unique feature of Adam's Love was its club membership programme, which provided non-financial incentives for MSM to engage with HTC services. The programme successfully recruited 1,181 MSM into the membership initiative. Participants in the club membership programme were offered benefits such as priority access to services and exclusive health-related promotions. This approach helped to build trust and foster a sense of community among participants, reinforcing their commitment to regular testing and treatment adherence. The ever-increasing demand for high data rates, ultra-low latency, and enhanced reliability in wireless communications has propelled the evolution of fifth-generation (5G) networks into heterogeneous architectures, integrating sub-6 GHz and millimeter wave (mmWave) frequency bands. These mixed-frequency networks aim to exploit the complementary characteristics of each spectrum: the robust propagation conditions and wide coverage of sub-6 GHz bands, and the high capacity and ultrawide bandwidth of mmWave bands. However, this integration introduces significant challenges, particularly concerning the effective management of radio resources amidst varying propagation conditions and blockages. One critical aspect of this challenge is the decoupling of uplink (UL) and downlink (DL) transmissions, where independent access points (APs) and frequency bands may need to be assigned for UL and DL to optimize network performance. UL/DL decoupling has emerged as a promising solution to address the disparity in propagation characteristics between sub-6 GHz and mmWave bands, particularly in cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) networks. Unlike conventional coupled transmissions, where the UL and DL share the same frequency band and AP, decoupled transmissions allow the UL and DL to operate independently, leveraging the most suitable frequency and AP for each direction. This approach is particularly advantageous in scenarios where the mmWave channel experiences severe degradation due to blockages, while the sub-6 GHz channel remains robust. Moreover, decoupling can improve spectral efficiency and reduce interference, contributing to the overall reliability and performance of the network. However, implementing efficient UL/DL decoupling in real-time networks is challenging due to the need for fast and accurate radio resource management, which must account for the dynamic and heterogeneous nature of propagation environments. Traditionally, UL/DL decoupling relies on extensive real-time measurements and centralized decision-making, which can introduce significant latency and computational overhead. Furthermore, the reliance on mmWave measurements for resource allocation can be impractical in scenarios where the mmWave channel is frequently blocked or exhibits high variability. To address these limitations, semi-blind techniques have gained attention, leveraging limited measurements and predictive algorithms to make efficient resource allocation decisions. Semi-blind approaches aim to reduce the dependence on exhaustive real-time measurements, instead relying on initial training and predictive modeling to guide decision-making. In this context, we propose a novel semi-blind UL/DL decoupling framework tailored for mixed sub-6 GHz/mmWave 5G cell-free massive MIMO networks. Our approach introduces a non-linear support vector machine (SVM) classifier trained on a minimal set of measurements, including the Rician \(K\)-factor and the downlink reference signal received power (RSRP) for both 2.6 GHz and 28 GHz frequency bands. The Rician \(K\)-factor provides a statistical representation of the user's line-of-sight (LOS) conditions, which are critical for assessing the reliability of the mmWave channel. The DL RSRP offers an additional indicator of channel quality, complementing the \(K\)-factor information. By combining these metrics, the proposed framework is capable of capturing the propagation characteristics across both frequency bands, enabling accurate and efficient resource allocation. The central innovation of our approach lies in its semi-blind operation. Unlike fully blind methods, which rely solely on predictive modeling without any prior measurements, or fully informed methods, which require continuous real-time monitoring, the semi-blind framework strikes a balance between these extremes. Following an initial activation phase, the central processing unit (CPU) gathers the necessary measurements to train the SVM classifier. Once the training is complete, the framework eliminates the need for further mmWave measurements, relying exclusively on 2.6 GHz data to predict the optimal frequency bands and APs for both UL and DL. This eliminates the computational overhead associated with continuous mmWave monitoring while maintaining high prediction accuracy. The use of machine learning, particularly the SVM classifier, is pivotal to the success of the proposed framework. SVMs are well-suited for classification tasks in high-dimensional feature spaces, making them ideal for capturing the non-linear relationships between the input features (e.g., \(K\)-factor and RSRP) and the target outputs (e.g., frequency bands and APs). Furthermore, SVMs are robust to small training datasets, which aligns with the semi-blind philosophy of minimizing measurement overhead. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed SVM-based classifier achieves an accuracy of 95% with a minimal number of training samples, underscoring its potential for practical deployment in real-world networks. The proposed framework offers several advantages over existing approaches. First, it significantly reduces the reliance on mmWave measurements, which are often unreliable in the presence of blockages or high mobility. By leveraging the relatively stable and robust propagation characteristics of sub-6 GHz bands, the framework ensures reliable resource allocation even in challenging environments. Second, the semi-blind operation minimizes the latency and computational complexity associated with continuous real-time measurements, enabling faster and more efficient decision-making. Finally, the use of machine learning introduces adaptability to dynamic network conditions, allowing the framework to generalize across a wide range of scenarios. This work contributes to the broader field of 5G network design by addressing a key challenge in mixed-frequency architectures: the efficient and reliable decoupling of UL and DL transmissions. By combining semi-blind operation with machine learning, the proposed framework offers a practical and scalable solution for radio resource management in future cell-free massive MIMO networks. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section II reviews related work on UL/DL decoupling and semi-blind techniques. Section III describes the system model and problem formulation. Section IV details the proposed SVM-based semi-blind framework. Section V presents the experimental results and analysis. Finally, Section VI concludes the paper and discusses potential directions for future research. To address the challenges of propagation imbalance and latency in mixed sub-6 GHz and millimeter wave (mmWave) 5G networks, we propose a semi-blind uplink (UL) and downlink (DL) decoupling approach based on non-linear classification methods. This section outlines the methodology adopted for implementing and validating the proposed framework, which consists of three main stages: data acquisition, classifier training, and predictive resource allocation. The proposed semi-blind UL/DL decoupling mechanism begins with an initial data acquisition phase. User equipment (UE) measurements are collected across both 2.6 GHz and 28 GHz frequency bands under varying environmental and propagation conditions. Specifically, the Rician $K$-factor and the downlink reference signal received power (RSRP) are selected as the primary features for characterizing the channel conditions. The Rician $K$-factor quantifies the ratio of power in the line-of-sight (LOS) path to the scattered multipath components, serving as a measure of the presence of LOS conditions [1]. Meanwhile, the RSRP captures the received signal strength of the downlink reference signal, reflecting the user's proximity to nearby access points (APs) and the associated path loss. Both parameters are collected for each UE at the central processing unit (CPU) to enable subsequent analysis and classification. The Rician $K$-factor measurements are obtained from the channel state information (CSI) feedback provided by the UEs, while the RSRP values are directly reported by the UEs based on the received downlink signals. Measurements are conducted across multiple APs operating in both the sub-6 GHz and mmWave bands to ensure diverse propagation conditions, including LOS-dominant scenarios, non-line-of-sight (NLOS) regions, and blockage-induced fading. To ensure robustness, the data collection is performed in a dynamic network environment characterized by user mobility and varying blockage conditions. The resulting dataset comprises a set of labeled samples, where each sample corresponds to a unique combination of the Rician $K$-factor, RSRP, and the optimal AP and frequency band for UL and DL operation. Following the data acquisition phase, the labeled dataset is used to train a non-linear support vector machine (SVM) classifier. The choice of a non-linear SVM is motivated by its ability to effectively model complex and non-linear decision boundaries in high-dimensional feature spaces [2]. Specifically, the radial basis function (RBF) kernel is employed to transform the input space into a higher-dimensional space, enabling the classifier to capture intricate relationships between the Rician $K$-factor, RSRP, and the optimal resource allocation decisions. The SVM training process involves solving a convex optimization problem that seeks to maximize the margin between the decision boundary and the nearest support vectors, thereby minimizing the classification error [3]. To train the SVM classifier, the labeled dataset is split into training and validation subsets using an 80:20 ratio. The hyperparameters of the SVM model, including the kernel coefficient (gamma) and the regularization parameter (C), are optimized via grid search with cross-validation. The grid search process systematically evaluates combinations of hyperparameter values to identify the configuration that yields the highest validation accuracy. Five-fold cross-validation is employed to reduce the risk of overfitting and ensure generalization to unseen data. The performance of the trained SVM classifier is evaluated using standard metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, and the F1 score. Once the training phase is completed, the CPU ceases the collection of mmWave band measurements to reduce overhead and computational complexity. Subsequently, the trained SVM classifier is deployed to perform blind predictions based solely on the 2.6 GHz band data. For each UE, the classifier predicts the optimal frequency bands and APs to be used for UL and DL transmission, effectively decoupling the UL and DL operations. The predicted resource allocation decisions are then communicated to the UEs and APs to facilitate fast and efficient radio resource management. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed semi-blind UL/DL decoupling mechanism, extensive simulations are conducted in a system-level simulator. The simulation environment models a cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) network with distributed APs operating in both the sub-6 GHz and mmWave bands. The network topology, user mobility patterns, and blockage conditions are designed to mirror realistic deployment scenarios. The performance of the proposed SVM-based classifier is compared to that of conventional schemes that rely on simultaneous measurements across all frequency bands, as well as to schemes that do not employ decoupling. Key performance indicators (KPIs) considered in the evaluation include the classification accuracy of the SVM model, the latency associated with resource allocation decisions, and the reliability of the UL and DL links under varying propagation conditions. Additionally, the computational complexity of the proposed approach is analyzed to assess its suitability for real-time implementation in 5G networks. The results demonstrate that the proposed classifier achieves an accuracy score of 95% with only a limited number of training samples, highlighting its efficiency and scalability. In summary, the proposed semi-blind UL/DL decoupling framework leverages a non-linear SVM classifier trained on sub-6 GHz band measurements to predict the optimal resource allocation decisions for mixed sub-6 GHz/mmWave 5G networks. By reducing the reliance on mmWave band measurements, the framework addresses the challenges of propagation imbalance and latency while enabling efficient radio resource management. The methodology outlined in this section provides a foundation for future research on machine learning-based resource allocation in cell-free massive MIMO networks. To evaluate the performance of the proposed semi-blind uplink/downlink (UL/DL) decoupling approach, we conducted a series of simulations and experiments using a mixed sub-6 GHz and millimeter wave (mmWave) 5G network model. The results presented in this section validate the efficacy of the system in terms of classification accuracy, computational efficiency, and robustness under various network conditions. Simulation Setup and Methodology The experimental setup consisted of a cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) network operating across 2.6 GHz and 28 GHz frequency bands. A total of 50 access points (APs) were randomly distributed over a 1 km² area, with 200 user equipment (UE) devices uniformly scattered across the same region. The propagation environment was modeled to include both line-of-sight (LOS) and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions, characterized by a Rician $K$-factor. The LOS condition was varied by introducing random blockages to simulate realistic urban scenarios. For each UE, the downlink (DL) reference signal received power (RSRP) values for both frequency bands, as well as the corresponding $K$-factor measurements, were collected. The proposed semi-blind approach was implemented at the central processing unit (CPU), which performed the data collection, training, and classification tasks. A non-linear support vector machine (SVM) was chosen as the classifier due to its robustness in handling non-linear decision boundaries and its ability to generalize well with limited training data. The input features for the SVM consisted of the RSRP values and $K$-factor measurements from the 2.6 GHz band, while the target labels denoted the optimal frequency and AP

Cholera, an acute diarrheal disease caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae, remains a significant global public health challenge, particularly in regions burdened by conflict, poverty, and limited access to basic health services. Despite substantial progress in controlling cholera in many parts of the world, outbreaks continue to occur with devastating consequences, especially in fragile settings where infrastructure and healthcare systems are severely compromised. Yemen has been one such example of vulnerability to cholera epidemics, with the ongoing outbreak that began in late 2016 now recognized as the largest in recorded history. As of 2018, the outbreak had resulted in more than 1.4 million suspected cases and thousands of deaths, underscoring the urgent need to understand the underlying factors driving its persistence and magnitude [1,2]. The cholera epidemic in Yemen has been exacerbated by the country’s ongoing armed conflict, which has disrupted essential services, including water supply and sanitation, and severely weakened the healthcare system. The crumbling infrastructure has left millions of Yemenis without access to safe drinking water and adequate sanitation facilities, conditions that are well-documented contributors to the transmission of cholera [3,4]. Furthermore, widespread displacement and overcrowded living conditions have created an environment conducive to the rapid spread of waterborne diseases. In such settings, identifying specific risk factors that increase susceptibility to cholera becomes critically important for informing targeted public health interventions and mitigating further spread. Previous studies on cholera outbreaks globally have highlighted several risk factors associated with the disease, including the consumption of untreated or contaminated water, poor hygiene practices, inadequate sanitation, and foodborne transmission through unsafe preparation or handling of food [5,6]. Behavioral practices, such as the failure to properly wash fruits and vegetables, have also been implicated in cholera transmission in some regions [7]. However, the unique sociocultural and environmental context of Yemen necessitates a localized investigation of risk factors to better tailor intervention strategies. For instance, the widespread consumption of khat, a culturally significant herbal stimulant, raises questions about its role in cholera transmission, particularly if it is consumed without adequate washing. Similarly, the reliance on common water sources, such as wells and water trucks, in the absence of centralized water supply systems may further compound the risk. Despite the scale and severity of the cholera outbreak in Yemen, there is a paucity of research examining specific risk factors within the local context. Most studies on cholera in Yemen have focused on epidemiological trends, case counts, and mortality rates, with limited attention given to behavioral and environmental determinants of the disease. Addressing this gap is essential for developing effective prevention and control measures tailored to the needs and circumstances of affected communities. In this regard, case-control studies provide a valuable methodological approach for identifying risk factors by comparing exposures between individuals who have contracted the disease (cases) and those who have not (controls). This study was conducted in Aden, a major urban center in Yemen that has been heavily affected by the cholera outbreak. Aden’s strategic location as a port city and its role as a hub for internal displacement and migration make it a critical area for understanding risk factors associated with cholera transmission. The study sought to investigate behavioral and environmental determinants of cholera in the ongoing outbreak, with a particular focus on practices related to water use, food preparation, and the handling of khat. By identifying modifiable risk factors, the findings aim to inform public health interventions that can reduce the burden of cholera in Yemen and other similar settings. The theoretical framework for this study draws on the established causal pathways of cholera transmission, which emphasize the interplay between environmental exposures and individual behaviors. Cholera is primarily transmitted through the fecal-oral route, with contaminated water and food serving as the main vehicles for the pathogen [8]. Inadequate sanitation infrastructure facilitates the contamination of water sources, while poor hygiene practices increase the likelihood of ingestion of the bacteria. These pathways are further influenced by sociocultural factors, such as dietary habits and traditional practices, which may vary across different regions and populations. Understanding these localized dynamics is critical for designing interventions that are both effective and culturally appropriate. In addition to contributing to the body of knowledge on cholera risk factors, this study seeks to address practical challenges in outbreak response and prevention in Yemen. The findings aim to inform public health authorities and humanitarian organizations working in the region about priority areas for intervention, such as improving access to safe drinking water, promoting hygiene education, and addressing specific practices like the washing of khat and vegetables. The results also have broader implications for cholera control in other conflict-affected settings, where similar challenges related to water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) are prevalent. In summary, this study represents a critical step toward understanding the risk factors associated with cholera in Yemen’s ongoing outbreak. By examining behavioral and environmental determinants of the disease in Aden, it seeks to provide actionable insights for reducing cholera transmission and improving public health outcomes. The findings underscore the importance of integrating epidemiological research with community-level interventions to address the root causes of cholera and build resilience against future outbreaks. A case-control study design was employed to investigate the risk factors associated with cholera during the ongoing outbreak in Yemen. The study was conducted in Aden, one of the provinces heavily affected by the outbreak, from March to June 2018. This design was chosen to compare cholera cases with community controls, enabling the identification of potential exposures and behaviors associated with the disease. The study population consisted of individuals residing in Aden during the outbreak period. Cases were defined as individuals presenting with acute watery diarrhea who tested positive for Vibrio cholerae by stool culture or rapid diagnostic testing at designated cholera treatment centers (CTCs) in Aden. All cases were confirmed by healthcare providers at the CTCs, following the World Health Organization (WHO) definition for suspected cholera cases [1]. To ensure accurate case identification, the inclusion criteria required that cases were newly diagnosed, residing in Aden for at least three months prior to the onset of symptoms, and aged 5 years or older. Individuals with chronic diarrhea or other conditions potentially mimicking cholera were excluded. Community controls were selected from the same neighborhoods as the cases in order to minimize geographical and environmental differences that could confound the results. Controls were matched to cases by age (±5 years) and sex. Eligible controls were individuals without a history of diarrhea or other gastrointestinal symptoms in the four weeks preceding the study. A ratio of 2 controls per case was used to enhance the statistical power of the study. Data collection was conducted using structured, interviewer-administered questionnaires. The questionnaire was developed based on prior research on cholera risk factors and adapted to the local context based on consultations with local public health experts. The questionnaire was pre-tested in a pilot study to ensure clarity and cultural appropriateness, and adjustments were made accordingly. Data collected included demographic information (e.g., age, sex, education level), behavioral factors (e.g., food and water consumption practices, handwashing habits, use of chlorine or soap in the household), and environmental factors (e.g., source of drinking water, sanitation facilities). Additional questions assessed recent travel history, contact with visitors from outside Aden, and practices related to khat consumption, a common local custom. Trained field staff, including public health workers and medical students, conducted the interviews. All interviewers received training in data collection techniques, ethical considerations, and the use of the study tools. Informed consent was obtained from all participants or their legal guardians prior to the interviews. For illiterate participants, the consent form was read aloud, and verbal consent was documented in the presence of a witness. Data on cholera cases were obtained from CTC records, while controls were identified through a systematic random sampling method within the communities where cases resided. To ensure random selection, field staff used a predetermined starting point within the neighborhood and selected every third household, ensuring that only one eligible individual per household was interviewed. If a selected household had no eligible participant, the next household was approached. The primary exposures of interest included water source, food preparation and consumption behaviors, hygiene practices (e.g., washing hands, fruits, vegetables, and khat), and recent travel or contact with visitors. Water sources were categorized as common-source water (e.g., water trucks, shared wells) or private-source water (e.g., household wells, bottled water). Hygiene practices were assessed based on self-reported behaviors and visual confirmation of available resources such as chlorine or soap. Behavioral factors, such as eating outside the home and washing khat before consumption, were evaluated based on participant responses. The sample size was calculated to detect an odds ratio (OR) of 2.0 for the primary exposures, assuming a prevalence of exposure of 30% among controls, with 80% power and a 95% confidence level. A case-to-control ratio of 1:2 was factored into the calculation, resulting in a minimum sample size of 59 cases and 118 controls. Data were entered and analyzed using statistical software (SPSS, version 25.0). Descriptive statistics were calculated for demographic and exposure variables. Bivariate analysis was conducted using chi-square tests to identify associations between potential risk factors and cholera. Variables with a p-value of <0.20 in the bivariate analysis were included in the multivariate logistic regression model to adjust for potential confounders. Adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated to determine the strength of association between exposures and cholera status. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Ethical approval for the study was obtained from the Ministry of Public Health and Population in Yemen and the local ethics committee in Aden. The study adhered to the ethical principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. Efforts were made to minimize any potential risks to participants, and all data were anonymized to ensure confidentiality. Participants were provided with information on cholera prevention and access to safe water and sanitation services as part of the study's community engagement efforts. In summary, this case-control study utilized a systematic approach to investigate cholera risk factors in Aden, Yemen, during the ongoing outbreak. By combining robust data collection methods with rigorous statistical analysis, the study aimed to identify modifiable risk factors to inform targeted public health interventions. In total, 59 cholera cases and 118 community controls were included in the study. Among the participants, cholera cases were identified through clinical diagnosis and laboratory confirmation, while controls were selected from the same communities as the cases but had no reported symptoms of cholera during the study period. The demographic characteristics of cases and controls were comparable, with no significant differences in age or gender distribution, ensuring that observed associations were not confounded by these variables. The bivariate analysis identified several factors significantly associated with being a cholera case. A history of travelling outside Aden Province or having visitors from outside the province was strongly associated with cholera cases (odds ratio [OR]: 3.28, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.56–6.91, p < 0.01). Eating food outside the home was also a significant risk factor (OR: 2.14, 95% CI: 1.10–4.18, p = 0.02), suggesting potential exposure to contaminated food or unhygienic preparation practices in public or commercial settings. Additionally, not washing fruits, vegetables, and khat before consumption was associated with increased odds of cholera (OR: 3.45, 95% CI: 1.81–6.57, p < 0.001). Furthermore, using water from common sources, such as shared wells or public water tanks, emerged as a significant risk factor (OR: 4.22, 95% CI: 2.14–8.32, p < 0.001). Lastly, not using chlorine or soap in household water treatment or personal hygiene practices was associated with higher odds of cholera (OR: 2.87, 95% CI: 1.42–5.78, p < 0.01). In the multivariate analysis, which controlled for potential confounders, not washing khat and the use of common-source water remained statistically significant. Participants who reported consuming khat without washing it had a significantly higher likelihood of being cholera cases (adjusted odds ratio [aOR]: 3.84, 95% CI: 1.94–7.62, p < 0.001). This finding underlines the critical role of improper hygiene practices in the transmission of cholera

The study of geometric properties of data has garnered growing interest in recent years, particularly within the fields of machine learning (ML) and knowledge discovery (KD). As the dimensionality of data increases, the so-called "curse of dimensionality" often manifests as a significant challenge, adversely affecting the performance of algorithms designed for high-dimensional spaces. This phenomenon, first introduced in early discussions on high-dimensional spaces [1], refers to the exponential growth of volume and sparsity of data points as dimensions increase. Consequently, it has implications for computational complexity, statistical estimation, and generalizability, which are central concerns in both theoretical and applied domains. The present work seeks to address this challenge by investigating the intrinsic geometry of data sets, with a focus on understanding and quantifying their intrinsic dimension using a mathematically rigorous and computationally feasible framework. The curse of dimensionality is closely connected to the phenomenon of measure concentration, a property of high-dimensional probability spaces where measures become increasingly concentrated around specific geometric structures, such as equatorial regions of spheres or thin annuli in Euclidean spaces [2,3]. This relationship has been extensively studied in the context of random matrix theory, metric measure geometry, and statistical learning theory [4]. While measure concentration provides insight into the underlying structure of high-dimensional data, its implications for the intrinsic dimensionality of data are less well understood. The concept of intrinsic dimension, broadly defined as the effective number of variables or degrees of freedom required to describe a data set, is distinct from the ambient dimension in which the data resides. For example, data points sampled from a low-dimensional manifold embedded in a high-dimensional space often exhibit intrinsic dimensionality consistent with the manifold's dimension, rather than the ambient space [5]. This observation motivates the need for computational frameworks and mathematical models that can characterize intrinsic dimensionality in a robust and algorithmically efficient manner. In this work, we adopt a geometric perspective on data sets, leveraging concepts from Gromov's metric measure geometry [6] and Pestov's axiomatic approach to intrinsic dimension [7]. Metric measure spaces, which combine a metric space structure with a measure, provide a natural framework for analyzing data sets that exhibit complex geometric and probabilistic properties. By treating a data set as a finite metric measure space, we define a precise mathematical structure that captures both the geometry of pairwise distances and the distributional properties of the data. This allows us to systematically study the intrinsic dimension of data sets, not merely as a numerical quantity but as a property derived from the interplay between the metric and measure. Furthermore, we introduce a metric and a partial order on the set of isomorphism classes of geometric data sets, enabling a comparative analysis of their structural complexity. The axiomatic approach developed in this study builds upon Pestov's foundational work [7], which posits that intrinsic dimension should satisfy a set of desirable properties, including monotonicity, stability under small perturbations, and consistency with classical notions of dimension. These axioms provide a guideline for constructing dimension functions that are both theoretically sound and practically applicable. Our proposed dimension function adheres to these principles and is computationally feasible even for large-scale data sets, making it a valuable tool for machine learning and knowledge discovery tasks. Unlike traditional dimensionality reduction techniques, such as principal component analysis or manifold learning algorithms, which aim to embed data into lower-dimensional spaces, our approach focuses on quantifying the intrinsic dimension as an inherent property of the data itself. This distinction is crucial for applications where understanding the structure of the data is as important as reducing its complexity. The contributions of this work are threefold. First, we formalize the notion of a geometric data set as a finite metric measure space and introduce mathematical tools for analyzing such objects. Second, we propose an axiomatic framework for intrinsic dimension that is compatible with the structural properties of geometric data sets. Third, we demonstrate the applicability of our framework through experiments that illustrate its adaptability to specific ML and KD algorithms. These experiments highlight the practical relevance of our model in scenarios such as clustering, anomaly detection, and feature selection, where the intrinsic dimension plays a critical role in determining algorithmic performance. Related work in the field of intrinsic dimension estimation spans a wide range of approaches, including fractal-based methods [8], correlation dimension techniques [9], and spectral methods based on eigendecompositions of graph Laplacians [10]. While these methods have achieved notable success in specific contexts, they often rely on strong assumptions about the data distribution or require computationally intensive procedures that scale poorly with data size. Our approach addresses these limitations by providing a general-purpose framework that is grounded in metric measure geometry and does not depend on restrictive assumptions about the underlying data-generating process. Moreover, the incorporation of a partial order on isomorphism classes of data sets allows for a comparative analysis of intrinsic dimension across different data sets, offering insights into their relative complexity. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review the mathematical preliminaries necessary for defining geometric data sets and their intrinsic dimensions. Section 3 introduces our axiomatic framework and derives a concrete dimension function that satisfies the desired properties. Section 4 presents experimental results demonstrating the practical utility and adaptability of our approach. Section 5 discusses implications, limitations, and potential extensions of this work. Finally, Section 6 concludes with a summary of key findings and directions for future research. By integrating concepts from metric measure geometry with computational considerations, this work aims to bridge the gap between theoretical insights and practical applications in ML and KD. The proposed framework not only advances our understanding of intrinsic dimension but also provides a foundation for developing more effective algorithms for high-dimensional data analysis. 1. For each data set, we computed the intrinsic dimension using the proposed method and compared it with established techniques, including correlation dimension [5] and maximum likelihood estimation [6]. The results were analyzed with respect to computational efficiency, robustness to noise, and alignment with theoretical expectations. 6. Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remain the leading cause of morbidity and mortality globally, with their prevalence differing significantly between premenopausal women and men of similar age. This disparity has long been attributed to the cardio-protective effects of 17β-estradiol (E2), the most biologically active estrogen in premenopausal women [1,2]. E2 exerts its protective effects through the activation of estrogen receptors (ERs), which mediate both genomic and nongenomic signaling pathways in various tissues, including the cardiovascular system [3]. The decline in E2 levels during menopause is strongly associated with an increased risk of CVDs in women, highlighting the critical role of estrogen signaling in maintaining cardiovascular health [4,5]. While estrogen replacement therapy (ERT) has been utilized as a strategy to mitigate this risk, concerns regarding its adverse effects, including an increased risk of breast cancer, thromboembolism, and stroke, have necessitated the exploration of safer alternatives [6,7]. Phytoestrogens, plant-derived compounds with structural and functional similarities to E2, have emerged as promising candidates to fulfill this need, offering potential cardio-protective benefits while circumventing the risks associated with synthetic estrogens [8]. Estrogen Receptors in Cardiomyocytes: Subtypes and Functional Roles Three major subtypes of estrogen receptors—ERα, ERβ, and G-protein-coupled estrogen receptor (GPR30)—have been identified, each playing distinct yet overlapping roles in mediating estrogen signaling in cardiomyocytes [9]. ERα and ERβ belong to the nuclear receptor superfamily and are traditionally associated with genomic signaling, wherein ligand binding induces receptor dimerization, nuclear translocation, and subsequent regulation of target gene transcription [10]. In contrast, GPR30, a membrane-bound receptor, primarily mediates nongenomic signaling by activating intracellular kinases and second messenger systems [11]. These receptors exhibit tissue-specific expression and functional differences, which contribute to the complex and multifaceted effects of E2 on the cardiovascular system. In the context of cardiomyocytes, ERα activation has been linked to the regulation of genes involved in anti-apoptotic pathways, oxidative stress reduction, and mitochondrial function, all of which contribute to enhanced cell survival under conditions of ischemic or oxidative insult [12]. Similarly, ERβ plays a critical role in modulating inflammatory responses, mitochondrial biogenesis, and calcium homeostasis, thereby supporting cardiac function during stress [13]. GPR30, on the other hand, has been implicated in the rapid activation of signaling cascades such as the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/Akt and extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) pathways, which are essential for cardiomyocyte survival and vascular homeostasis [14]. The interplay between these receptor subtypes and their downstream signaling pathways underscores the complexity of E2-mediated cardioprotection and highlights the potential for selective targeting of specific ERs to achieve therapeutic benefits. Mechanisms of E2-Mediated Cardioprotection E2 confers cardioprotection through a combination of genomic and nongenomic mechanisms, which together mitigate the deleterious effects of various cardiac insults, including ischemia-reperfusion injury, oxidative stress, and inflammation [15]. Genomic mechanisms involve the direct regulation of cardioprotective genes by ERα and ERβ. For instance, E2 has been shown to upregulate the expression of anti-apoptotic genes such as B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL-2) and downregulate pro-apoptotic genes such as BCL-2-associated X protein (BAX), thereby promoting cell survival [16]. Additionally, E2 enhances the expression of antioxidant enzymes, including superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase, which mitigate oxidative damage and preserve cardiomyocyte function [17]. Nongenomic mechanisms, mediated predominantly by GPR30 and cytoplasmic pools of ERα and ERβ, involve the rapid activation of intracellular signaling cascades. For example, E2-induced activation of the PI3K/Akt pathway promotes nitric oxide (NO) production via endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) activation, leading to improved endothelial function and reduced myocardial injury [18]. Similarly, the ERK pathway has been implicated in E2-mediated inhibition of apoptosis and enhancement of angiogenesis, processes that are critical for cardiac repair and regeneration following injury [19]. These complementary mechanisms not only protect cardiomyocytes from acute damage but also contribute to long-term cardiovascular health by maintaining vascular integrity and reducing the risk of atherosclerosis. Limitations of Estrogen Replacement Therapy and the Need for Alternatives Despite the well-established benefits of E2 in cardiovascular protection, the clinical application of ERT is fraught with challenges. Large-scale clinical trials, including the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI), have reported increased risks of adverse events, such as breast and endometrial cancer, venous thromboembolism, and stroke, particularly in older postmenopausal women [20,21]. These findings have led to a decline in the use of ERT and have prompted the search for alternative approaches to harness the beneficial effects of estrogen signaling without the associated risks. Among the various alternatives being explored, phytoestrogens have gained significant attention due to their ability to interact with ERs and mimic the effects of E2 in a tissue-specific manner [22]. Phytoestrogens as Potential Cardioprotective Agents Phytoestrogens are naturally occurring plant-derived compounds that exhibit structural similarity to E2, allowing them to bind to ERs and modulate estrogen signaling [23]. These compounds are classified into three main categories: isoflavones, lignans, and coumestans, with isoflavones being the most extensively studied for their cardiovascular effects [24]. Soy-derived isoflavones, such as genistein and daidzein, have been shown to exert anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and vasodilatory effects, which collectively contribute to improved cardiac and vascular function [25]. Unlike synthetic estrogens, phytoestrogens exhibit selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM)-like properties, preferentially activating ERβ over ERα, which may account for their reduced risk of adverse effects [26]. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that phytoestrogens confer cardioprotection through mechanisms similar to those of E2, including the activation of PI3K/Akt and ERK pathways, modulation of mitochondrial function, and regulation of oxidative stress and inflammation [27]. Clinical studies, though limited, provide preliminary evidence supporting the cardiovascular benefits of phytoestrogen supplementation, particularly in postmenopausal women [28]. However, the variability in individual responses to phytoestrogens, influenced by factors such as gut microbiota composition and genetic polymorphisms, underscores the need for further research to elucidate their mechanisms of action and optimize their therapeutic potential [29]. The recognition of E2 and ERs as critical mediators of cardioprotection has spurred significant research efforts to develop safer and more effective alternatives to ERT. Phytoestrogens represent a promising class of compounds with the potential to mimic the beneficial effects of E2 while minimizing the associated risks. A deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying phytoestrogen-mediated cardioprotection and their interaction with ER subtypes will be essential for translating these findings into clinical practice. Literature Search Strategy A comprehensive and systematic literature search was conducted to gather relevant studies addressing the roles of estrogen receptors (ERs) and phytoestrogens in cardioprotection, as well as their underlying molecular mechanisms. Peer-reviewed articles were identified using electronic databases, including PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and Embase. Search terms included combinations of “estrogen,” “estrogen receptors,” “cardiomyocytes,” “cardioprotection,” “phytoestrogens,” and “estrogen signaling pathways.” Boolean operators (AND, OR) and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) were applied to refine the results. Articles published in English from 2000 to 2023 were included to ensure the inclusion of the most recent and relevant advancements. Reference lists of selected studies were manually screened to identify additional relevant publications. Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria Studies were included if they met the following criteria: (1) original research articles, reviews, or meta-analyses focusing on the molecular mechanisms of ER-mediated cardioprotection; (2) studies involving human, animal, or cell culture models of cardiomyocytes; (3) investigations on the role of phytoestrogens as potential alternatives to estrogen and their interaction with estrogen receptors; and (4) studies exploring both genomic and nongenomic signaling pathways mediated by ERα, ERβ, or G protein-coupled estrogen receptor (GPR30). Articles were excluded if they (1) were non-peer-reviewed, (2) lacked sufficient mechanistic insights, or (3) focused exclusively on non-cardiac tissues. Experimental Models and Data Extraction To analyze the cardioprotective effects of estrogen and phytoestrogens, data from experimental and clinical studies were systematically reviewed. Emphasis was placed on studies employing in vitro cardiomyocyte models, including rodent-derived primary cardiomyocytes and immortalized cell lines such as H9c2. In vivo studies were also included, particularly those utilizing animal models of ischemia-reperfusion injury, myocardial infarction, or hypertrophy induced by pressure overload. Clinical studies were considered if they provided evidence regarding the cardioprotective effects of estrogen replacement therapy or phytoestrogen supplementation in postmenopausal women. Key data points extracted from the studies included: (1) experimental design, (2) intervention details (e.g., specific estrogen or phytoestrogen compounds, doses, and administration routes), (3) molecular markers or pathways analyzed, (4) cardiomyocyte functional outcomes (e.g., cell viability, apoptosis, oxidative stress markers, and contractility), and (5) receptor-specific effects (ERα, ERβ, and GPR30). Differential gene expression data and proteomics datasets were retrieved from publicly available repositories, including Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and PRIDE, to assess transcriptomic and proteomic changes triggered by estrogen and its analogs. Docking results were validated using in silico molecular dynamics simulations to estimate receptor-ligand interaction stability. Phytoestrogen Selection and Classification Phytoestrogens selected for this study were classified into three major categories: isoflavones (e.g., genistein, daidzein), lignans (e.g., enterolactone, enterodiol), and coumestans (e.g., coumestrol). Selection criteria for phytoestrogens included their structural similarity to 17β-estradiol, documented binding affinity for ER subtypes, and evidence of cardioprotective activity reported in prior studies. The chemical structures of selected phytoestrogens were obtained from PubChem, and their pharmacokinetic properties, including bioavailability, metabolism, and half-life, were reviewed from existing literature. In Vitro Assays for Cardioprotective Effects Cardiomyocyte viability and apoptosis assays were performed to evaluate the protective effects of phytoestrogens under oxidative stress and ischemic conditions. Primary rat neonatal cardiomyocytes were isolated following standard enzymatic dissociation protocols [1]. Cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and treated with either 17β-estradiol (positive control) or varying concentrations of phytoestrogens (1 nM–10 µM). Oxidative stress was induced using hydrogen peroxide (H2O2, 200 µM), and ischemic conditions were simulated using a hypoxia chamber with 1% oxygen for 24 hours. Cell viability was assessed using the MTT assay, while apoptosis was quantified using Annexin V/propidium iodide staining and flow cytometry. Western Blot and Real-Time PCR Analysis To determine the molecular pathways activated by estrogen and phytoestrogens, Western blot analysis and real-time PCR were performed. Protein lysates were extracted from treated cardiomyocytes, and Western blotting was conducted to detect key signaling molecules, including phosphorylated Akt, ERK1/2, and AMPK. Expression of ERα, ERβ, and GPR30 at the mRNA level was quantified using SYBR Green-based real-time PCR, with GAPDH serving as the internal reference gene. Primer sequences were designed using Primer-BLAST, and target specificity was confirmed through melt curve analysis. Statistical Analysis All data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism v9.0. Results are expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) from at least three independent experiments. Statistical significance was determined using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test for multiple comparisons. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
