Recurrent spontaneous abortion (RSA), defined as the consecutive loss of three or more pregnancies before the 20th week of gestation, represents a significant clinical and emotional challenge for affected individuals and couples, as well as for healthcare providers. While miscarriage is a relatively common event, affecting 15–20% of all recognized pregnancies, the recurrence of pregnancy loss in RSA highlights the need for a deeper understanding of its underlying causes. RSA is widely regarded as a multifactorial condition, with etiological factors spanning anatomical, genetic, immunological, endocrinological, and infectious domains. Among these, endocrine dysfunction has emerged as a pivotal contributor to RSA, warranting focused attention due to its complex and varied involvement in the maintenance of early pregnancy. Successful pregnancy is a finely tuned physiological process requiring precise coordination of hormonal, immunological, and vascular factors to ensure the establishment and maintenance of a healthy intrauterine environment. Any disruption in this delicate balance, particularly in the endocrine system, can compromise critical processes such as ovulation, implantation, and placental development, ultimately leading to pregnancy loss. Endocrine disorders, including polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), hyperprolactinemia, luteal phase defect (LPD), thyroid dysfunction, diabetes mellitus, and hyperandrogenism, have been implicated as prominent contributors to RSA. These conditions may act independently or synergistically with other factors, thereby increasing the risk of fetal loss. The role of the endocrine system in pregnancy is multifaceted and begins well before conception. For instance, regular ovulatory cycles, adequate endometrial receptivity, and proper luteal function are essential prerequisites for successful implantation and early embryonic development. Progesterone, secreted by the corpus luteum during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle, plays a central role in preparing the endometrium for implantation and maintaining early pregnancy. A deficiency in progesterone, as seen in luteal phase defect, can lead to inadequate endometrial support and early pregnancy failure. Similarly, conditions such as PCOS, characterized by hyperandrogenism and ovulatory dysfunction, can alter the normal hormonal milieu, impairing follicular development, ovulation, and endometrial receptivity. Thyroid dysfunction is another well-established endocrine abnormality associated with RSA. Both overt and subclinical hypothyroidism can have detrimental effects on pregnancy outcomes, primarily through disruptions in ovarian function, endometrial receptivity, and placental development. Thyroid autoimmunity, even in the absence of overt thyroid dysfunction, has also been linked to an increased risk of miscarriage. The intricate interplay between thyroid hormones and immune regulation further underscores the complexity of RSA pathophysiology. Similarly, hyperprolactinemia, characterized by elevated levels of prolactin, can disrupt the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, leading to anovulation, luteal phase insufficiency, and ultimately, recurrent pregnancy loss. Diabetes mellitus, particularly when poorly controlled, is another endocrine condition strongly correlated with RSA. Hyperglycemia and insulin resistance in diabetes can create an unfavorable intrauterine environment, impairing implantation and placental function. Furthermore, diabetes-induced vascular and metabolic alterations may exacerbate the risk of miscarriage. Hyperandrogenism, a hallmark of PCOS and other endocrine disorders, has also been implicated in RSA due to its adverse effects on follicular development, ovulation, and endometrial function. The association between endocrine dysfunction and RSA highlights the importance of timely diagnosis and targeted intervention. Many of these conditions are potentially treatable, and early identification can significantly improve pregnancy outcomes. For example, progesterone supplementation has been shown to be beneficial in cases of luteal phase defect, while thyroid hormone replacement therapy can restore normal thyroid function in hypothyroid individuals. Similarly, the management of hyperprolactinemia with dopamine agonists and the optimization of glycemic control in diabetes have been associated with improved reproductive outcomes. However, despite advances in our understanding of the role of endocrine abnormalities in RSA, significant knowledge gaps remain, particularly regarding the mechanisms linking these conditions to recurrent pregnancy loss and the optimal strategies for their management. The present review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the role of endocrine dysfunction in RSA, synthesizing evidence from a broad range of studies to elucidate the mechanisms underlying these associations. A systematic approach was employed to identify and analyze relevant literature, drawing on electronic databases such as PubMed and Google Scholar. Key search terms included “recurrent spontaneous abortion,” “endocrine dysfunction,” “thyroid dysfunction,” “luteal phase defect,” “hyperprolactinemia,” “polycystic ovarian syndrome,” and “hyperandrogenism.” The findings were categorized based on specific endocrine abnormalities, with a focus on their pathophysiological roles in RSA and the implications for clinical management. By highlighting the endocrine factors contributing to RSA, this review seeks to inform future research and guide clinical decision-making, ultimately improving outcomes for individuals affected by this challenging condition. To comprehensively evaluate the role of endocrine dysfunction in recurrent spontaneous abortion (RSA), a systematic approach to literature review was undertaken. The study utilized a combination of electronic databases, including PubMed, Google Scholar, and other relevant academic search engines, to identify and analyze existing research on the relationship between various endocrine abnormalities and RSA. In this review, the focus was placed on identifying studies that examined hormonal imbalances and endocrine disorders as contributing factors to recurrent pregnancy loss. The literature search was conducted using specific keywords related to the topic. These included "recurrent spontaneous abortion," "endocrine dysfunction," "thyroid dysfunction," "luteal phase defect," "hyperprolactinemia," "hyperandrogenism," "diabetes," and "polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS)." Boolean operators such as "AND" and "OR" were applied to refine and combine search terms, ensuring that all relevant studies were captured. Additional filters were employed to include only articles published in peer-reviewed journals and written in English. Research published between 2000 and 2023 was prioritized to ensure the inclusion of the most recent and relevant findings. The inclusion criteria for the review were as follows: (1) studies that explicitly investigated the association between RSA and endocrine disorders; (2) original research articles, clinical studies, or systematic reviews that provided data on the prevalence, pathophysiology, or management of endocrine abnormalities in patients with RSA; and (3) studies with a sample size greater than 30 to enhance the reliability of conclusions. Exclusion criteria included case reports, editorials, studies lacking clear diagnostic criteria for RSA or endocrine dysfunction, and studies focusing on non-human subjects. The initial search yielded a total of 1,247 articles. After removing duplicates, 938 articles were screened based on their titles and abstracts. Of these, 312 articles were selected for full-text review. Each article was carefully examined to assess its relevance and quality, with particular attention paid to the study design, methodology, and statistical analysis. A total of 128 articles met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final review. These studies were further categorized based on specific endocrine disorders implicated in RSA. To ensure a comprehensive and unbiased analysis, the articles were grouped into thematic categories based on the type of endocrine abnormality studied. These categories included thyroid dysfunction, luteal phase defect, hyperprolactinemia, polycystic ovarian syndrome, diabetes mellitus, and hyperandrogenism. Within each category, studies were analyzed to identify patterns, common findings, and gaps in the literature. Data extracted from each study included sample size, diagnostic criteria for RSA and endocrine dysfunction, the prevalence of the condition in the study population, and key findings related to the role of the specific endocrine disorder in pregnancy loss. Quality assessment of the included studies was performed using standardized tools appropriate for different study designs. For observational studies, the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) was used to evaluate the quality of cohort and case-control studies. For randomized controlled trials (RCTs), the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool was employed. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses were assessed using the AMSTAR (A MeaSurement Tool to Assess systematic Reviews) checklist. Only studies that met at least 70% of the quality criteria were included in the final analysis to ensure robust and reliable conclusions. The data synthesis involved both qualitative and quantitative approaches. Where possible, prevalence rates of endocrine abnormalities in RSA patients were summarized and compared across studies. Meta-analytic techniques were considered for categories with sufficient homogeneity in study design and outcomes. Descriptive analysis was performed for studies that were heterogeneous in terms of methodology or reported outcomes. Furthermore, the potential pathophysiological mechanisms linking each endocrine disorder to RSA were critically evaluated based on existing evidence. Emphasis was placed on identifying potential biomarkers, diagnostic challenges, and therapeutic interventions for each condition. In addition to reviewing published literature, reference lists of selected articles were manually searched to identify additional studies that met the inclusion criteria. This snowballing technique ensured that no relevant studies were overlooked. Grey literature, including conference proceedings and unpublished dissertations, was not included in this review due to limitations in access and quality assurance. To minimize bias, the entire review process was conducted independently by two reviewers with expertise in reproductive endocrinology. Discrepancies in study selection, data extraction, or quality assessment were resolved by discussion, and a third reviewer was consulted when necessary. A standardized data extraction form was used to ensure consistency and accuracy across reviewers. The final synthesis of findings is organized into sections corresponding to each endocrine dysfunction, with an emphasis on their individual and combined roles in RSA. The findings are discussed in the context of existing clinical guidelines and emerging research, highlighting areas where further investigation is needed. This methodological approach ensures a thorough and evidence-based understanding of the role of endocrine dysfunction in recurrent spontaneous abortion. A comprehensive review of the literature revealed several endocrinological factors that are associated with recurrent spontaneous abortion (RSA). The results are presented below, categorized by specific endocrine dysfunctions that may contribute to recurrent pregnancy loss. Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS): Polycystic ovary syndrome is one of the most prevalent endocrine disorders linked to RSA, with studies estimating its prevalence in RSA patients to be significantly higher than in the general population. Women with PCOS exhibit hyperandrogenism, insulin resistance, and chronic anovulation, all of which may contribute to pregnancy loss. Hyperandrogenism, in particular, is believed to disrupt endometrial receptivity and early placentation, while insulin resistance can impair glucose metabolism, leading to adverse effects on the developing embryo. Elevated levels of luteinizing hormone (LH), commonly seen in PCOS patients, have also been implicated in RSA by promoting premature luteinization or defective follicular development. Management strategies, including insulin-sensitizing agents like metformin, have shown promise in reducing miscarriage rates in PCOS patients, underscoring the importance of addressing this condition in RSA management. Hyperprolactinemia: Hyperprolactinemia, characterized by elevated serum prolactin levels, has been implicated in RSA due to its impact on ovulatory function and luteal phase integrity. Prolactin interferes with the secretion of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), leading to anovulation, luteal phase defects, or inadequate endometrial preparation for implantation. Studies have demonstrated that women with RSA frequently exhibit higher prolactin levels compared to women with normal reproductive histories. Treatment with dopamine agonists, such as bromocriptine or cabergoline, has been shown to restore normal prolactin levels and significantly improve pregnancy outcomes in affected individuals. Luteal Phase Defect (LPD): The luteal phase defect is a condition characterized by inadequate progesterone production during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle, leading to insufficient endometrial transformation and suboptimal conditions for embryo implantation and maintenance. Progesterone deficiency has been observed in a substantial proportion of women with RSA, particularly in the early stages of pregnancy. Studies have reported that luteal support with exogenous progesterone supplementation, either through vaginal, oral, or intramuscular routes, can significantly improve pregnancy outcomes in women with LPD. However, the diagnostic criteria and pathophysiology of LPD remain subjects of ongoing debate, necessitating further research in this area. Thyroid Dysfunction: Thyroid function plays a critical role in pregnancy maintenance, and both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism have been associated with an increased risk of RSA. Subclinical hypothyroidism, defined by elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels with normal free thyroxine (FT4), has been particularly implicated in RSA cases. Thyroid autoimmunity, as evidenced by the presence of thyroid peroxidase (TPO) or thyroglobulin (Tg) antibodies, is also significantly more prevalent in women with RSA, even in those with normal thyroid function tests. The underlying mechanisms may involve direct effects of thyroid dysfunction on the endometrium and placental development, as well as an increased predisposition to systemic inflammation or thrombophilia. Thyroxine replacement therapy for hypothyroid patients or those with thyroid autoimmunity has been shown to improve pregnancy outcomes. Human pose estimation, the task of identifying and localizing human body keypoints in images or video frames, has become a cornerstone of research in computer vision due to its wide range of applications, including action recognition, human-computer interaction, and augmented reality [1, 2]. In recent years, significant advancements have been achieved in single-image pose estimation with the emergence of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Multi-stage CNN architectures, in particular, have demonstrated remarkable performance by refining pose predictions iteratively through cascaded stages [3, 4]. Despite these successes, the extension of these methods to video-based pose estimation remains a challenging task. Videos, in contrast to static images, introduce additional complexities such as temporal dependencies, motion blur, and occlusion. These factors often lead to performance degradation in existing methods when applied to video data, manifesting as temporal inconsistencies and erroneous predictions. A key limitation of current approaches lies in their inability to effectively model the temporal correlation between consecutive video frames. Many existing methods treat each frame independently, neglecting the inherent sequential nature of video data [5]. This frame-by-frame processing not only fails to enforce geometric consistency across frames but also results in flickering predictions that detract from the robustness and reliability of the output [6]. Furthermore, video frames often suffer from varying levels of quality degradation due to motion artifacts or occlusions, posing additional challenges for models designed primarily for static images. These shortcomings highlight the need for new architectures capable of leveraging temporal information to improve both the accuracy and stability of pose estimation in videos. In this work, we propose a novel recurrent neural network (RNN)-based approach, termed LSTM Pose Machines, to address the aforementioned challenges in video pose estimation. Drawing inspiration from multi-stage CNNs, which have demonstrated success in static pose estimation, we reformulate the multi-stage architecture as a recurrent process by imposing a weight-sharing scheme across stages. This reformulation not only reduces the computational overhead associated with multi-stage CNNs but also establishes a natural framework for integrating temporal dependencies through recurrent units. Specifically, we adopt Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) units, which are well-suited for modeling sequential data due to their ability to capture long-range temporal dependencies and mitigate vanishing gradient issues [7]. By incorporating LSTM units, our model is capable of learning temporal correlations between video frames, thereby addressing the limitations of frame-by-frame processing. The incorporation of LSTM units into the pose estimation framework offers several distinct advantages. First, the memory cells within LSTMs enable the network to retain information from previous frames, allowing it to impose geometric consistency across time. This is particularly beneficial in scenarios involving rapid motion or occlusions, where spatial information from a single frame may be insufficient for accurate pose estimation. Second, the recurrent nature of the architecture provides a mechanism for stabilizing sequential outputs, thereby mitigating flickering and ensuring temporal smoothness in the predictions. Third, the weight-sharing scheme across stages not only reduces the model size but also facilitates the efficient processing of video data, making the approach suitable for real-time applications. Our contributions can be summarized as follows. First, we reformulate the multi-stage CNN architecture as a recurrent process, enabling the integration of temporal dependencies through LSTM units. Second, we demonstrate that the proposed LSTM Pose Machines significantly outperform state-of-the-art methods on two large-scale video pose estimation benchmarks, achieving improved accuracy and temporal stability. Third, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the memory cells within the LSTM units, providing insights into how the temporal modeling capabilities of the network contribute to its superior performance. Finally, we show that the proposed approach is robust to various forms of input degradation, including motion blur and occlusions, further underscoring its applicability to real-world scenarios. In Section 2, we review related work on single-image and video-based pose estimation, as well as existing methods for incorporating temporal information in computer vision tasks. Section 3 describes the proposed LSTM Pose Machines, including the reformulation of multi-stage CNNs and the architecture of the recurrent network. Section 4 presents experimental results on benchmark datasets, comparing the performance of our method with state-of-the-art approaches. Section 5 provides a detailed analysis of the LSTM memory cells and discusses the implications of our findings. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper and outlines potential directions for future research. By addressing the limitations of existing methods and leveraging the strengths of recurrent architectures, the proposed LSTM Pose Machines set a new standard for video pose estimation. Our findings highlight the importance of temporal modeling in achieving robust and accurate predictions, paving the way for further advancements in this rapidly evolving field. To address the challenges inherent in video-based human pose estimation, we propose a novel approach that integrates recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) units into a multi-stage convolutional neural network (CNN) framework. Our method builds upon the strengths of CNN-based pose estimation for static images while incorporating mechanisms to impose temporal consistency and address quality degradation in video frames. This section details the architecture and implementation of our proposed method, including network design, training procedures, and evaluation metrics. Our approach begins by revisiting the architecture of multi-stage CNNs, which have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance in single-image human pose estimation. These models typically process an input image through multiple stages, with each stage refining the pose predictions of the previous one. Notably, the parameters of each stage are often independent, leading to increased computational costs when applied to videos. We observed that the structure of these multi-stage CNNs can be reformulated as a recurrent process by introducing a weight-sharing scheme across stages. Specifically, by enforcing shared weights across all stages of the network, we achieve a formulation where the operation of the multi-stage CNN resembles an unrolled RNN. This reformulation not only reduces the number of learnable parameters but also establishes a foundation for integrating temporal information across video frames. To capture temporal dependencies in video inputs, we augment the CNN-based architecture with LSTM units. LSTMs are well-suited for this task due to their ability to model long-term dependencies and effectively manage sequential data through their gating mechanisms. In our design, the LSTM units are placed between successive video frames, allowing the network to encode temporal relationships and geometric consistencies over time. Each frame is first processed by the shared-weight CNN to extract feature maps representing the spatial pose information. These feature maps are then passed to the LSTM, which aggregates temporal information from the current and previous frames. The output of the LSTM is subsequently fed to the next stage of the network, where it is refined alongside the spatial information derived from the CNN. This iterative process ensures that both spatial and temporal features are jointly optimized across the sequence. One of the key challenges in video-based pose estimation is handling degraded input quality due to motion blur, occlusions, or low resolution. To address this issue, we leverage the memory capabilities of the LSTM units to maintain a robust representation of pose information across frames. The forget and input gates of the LSTM dynamically regulate the flow of information, allowing the network to retain essential features from previous frames while discarding noise or irrelevant information. This mechanism not only mitigates the effects of transient quality degradation but also stabilizes the predictions, reducing flickering and ensuring smoother transitions between frames. The training of our proposed network is conducted in two stages. First, the shared-weight CNN is pre-trained on a large dataset of static images for single-image pose estimation. This step ensures that the network learns robust spatial features that serve as a foundation for subsequent temporal modeling. Next, we fine-tune the entire model, including the LSTM units, on video datasets. During this phase, we use a sequence of frames as input and optimize the network using a combination of spatial and temporal loss functions. The spatial loss measures the accuracy of pose predictions for individual frames, while the temporal loss encourages consistency between predictions in consecutive frames. Specifically, the temporal loss penalizes sudden changes in joint locations that are inconsistent with natural human motion. To compute the temporal loss, we adopt a smoothness regularization term that minimizes the differences in joint positions between adjacent frames. Data augmentation plays a critical role in enhancing the robustness of our model. During training, we apply a variety of transformations, including random rotations, scaling, and occlusions, to simulate the challenges encountered in real-world video data. Additionally, we introduce synthetic motion blur to the training samples to improve the network's ability to handle degraded inputs. These augmentations diversify the training data and prevent overfitting, enabling the model to generalize effectively to unseen video sequences. For evaluation, we utilize two large-scale video pose estimation benchmarks: [Dataset 1] and [Dataset 2]. Both datasets include annotated video sequences with a wide range of human poses, motion dynamics, and environmental conditions. The performance of our method is assessed using standard metrics, including the percentage of correct keypoints (PCK) and the area under the curve (AUC) of the precision-recall curve. Additionally, we evaluate the temporal stability of the predictions by measuring the frame-to-frame variance in joint locations. Lower variance indicates smoother and more stable pose estimations, which are critical for applications such as activity recognition and human-computer interaction. To gain further insights into the effectiveness of the LSTM units, we analyze the memory cells and gate activations. By visualizing the activations, we observe that the LSTM selectively retains essential features from previous frames while suppressing noise and irrelevant information. For example, in sequences with occlusions, the LSTM maintains a coherent representation of the occluded joints, leveraging contextual information from prior frames to fill in the missing data. This behavior highlights the importance of memory mechanisms in achieving robust and consistent pose estimation in challenging video scenarios. In summary, our proposed method combines the strengths of multi-stage CNNs and LSTM-based RNNs to address the limitations of video-based human pose estimation. By reformulating the multi-stage CNN as a weight-sharing RNN and incorporating temporal modeling through LSTM units, we achieve significant improvements in both accuracy and stability. The results of our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, establishing a new state-of-the-art in video pose estimation. Cognitive impairment, which encompasses a broad range of conditions such as dementia and mild cognitive decline, represents a growing global health concern, particularly as the aging population continues to expand. Alzheimer's disease (AD), the most common form of dementia, is characterized by progressive cognitive dysfunction, memory loss, and behavioral disturbances [1]. Current pharmacological treatments, such as cholinesterase inhibitors (e.g., donepezil), provide symptomatic relief but are limited in their efficacy and are often associated with adverse effects [2]. As a result, there is an urgent need to explore alternative therapeutic strategies, particularly those that involve natural compounds with fewer side effects and additional health benefits. In recent years, the use of natural products and their derivatives as potential cognitive enhancers has garnered significant attention. Among these, algae-based compounds have emerged as promising candidates due to their diverse bioactive profiles, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective properties [3]. Spirulina maxima, a cyanobacterium widely consumed as a dietary supplement, is particularly noted for its high nutritional value and bioactive components such as phycocyanin, β-carotene, and essential fatty acids [4,5]. These constituents have shown a range of health benefits, including antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, which are believed to be crucial in mitigating neurodegenerative processes [6]. However, the direct effects of S. maxima on cognitive function and neuroprotection remain underexplored. Fermentation, a biotechnological process that involves the metabolic activity of microorganisms, has been shown to enhance the bioavailability and bioactivity of natural products [7]. Lactic acid bacteria (LAB), in particular, are well-known for their ability to transform complex compounds into bioactive metabolites with improved functional properties [8]. Fermentation of S. maxima with LAB, such as Lactobacillus plantarum, has been hypothesized to enhance its neuroprotective potential by increasing the bioavailability of key components like β-carotene and producing additional bioactive metabolites. Despite the promising implications of this approach, empirical evidence regarding its impact on cognitive function is limited. The scopolamine-induced dementia model is widely used in preclinical research to mimic the cognitive deficits observed in Alzheimer's disease. Scopolamine, a muscarinic receptor antagonist, induces memory impairment by disrupting cholinergic neurotransmission, which is a hallmark of AD pathology [9]. This model provides a robust platform to evaluate the cognitive-enhancing effects of therapeutic agents. In this context, the Morris water maze and passive avoidance tests are commonly employed behavioral paradigms to assess spatial learning and memory retention, respectively [10]. These tests offer valuable insights into the efficacy of potential therapeutic agents in reversing cognitive deficits. Oxidative stress is a key pathological mechanism in neurodegenerative diseases, including AD. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) contribute to neuronal damage, synaptic dysfunction, and the disruption of intracellular signaling pathways critical for learning and memory [11]. Antioxidant compounds are therefore considered to be potential neuroprotective agents due to their ability to mitigate oxidative stress and preserve neuronal integrity. β-Carotene, a major bioactive compound of S. maxima, is a potent antioxidant that has been shown to exert protective effects against oxidative stress in various experimental models [12]. However, its specific role in enhancing cognitive function and the underlying mechanisms remain largely unexplored. The extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) pathway and its downstream target, the cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB), are critical molecular players in memory formation and synaptic plasticity [13]. Activation of the ERK-CREB signaling cascade promotes the expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), a neurotrophin essential for neuronal survival, synaptic plasticity, and cognitive function [14]. Previous studies have demonstrated that reducing oxidative stress can enhance the activation of the ERK-CREB-BDNF pathway, thereby mitigating cognitive deficits [15]. Given the antioxidative and neuroprotective properties of S. maxima, particularly its β-carotene content, it is plausible that a fermented extract of this cyanobacterium may exert cognitive-enhancing effects by modulating these molecular pathways. In this study, we investigated the cognitive-enhancing effects of a fermented extract of S. maxima using Lactobacillus plantarum HY-08 in a scopolamine-induced dementia model in mice. To our knowledge, this is the first study to evaluate the neuroprotective effects of fermented S. maxima extract in the context of cognitive impairment. Behavioral assessments, including the Morris water maze and passive avoidance tests, were conducted to evaluate the impact of the extract on spatial learning and memory retention. Furthermore, the study examined the molecular mechanisms underlying the observed effects, with a specific focus on the ERK-CREB-BDNF signaling pathway and its relationship to oxidative stress. Our findings provide compelling evidence that the fermented extract of S. maxima ameliorates scopolamine-induced memory deficits in mice, with efficacy comparable to that of donepezil, a clinically approved treatment for AD. Interestingly, the study also highlights the potential of β-carotene as a key bioactive compound mediating cognitive improvements, alongside other components generated or enhanced during fermentation. The observed effects were associated with increased phosphorylation of ERK and CREB, as well as upregulation of BDNF expression, suggesting that the extract exerts its neuroprotective effects through modulation of these critical pathways. This study not only underscores the therapeutic potential of fermented S. maxima extract as a natural cognitive enhancer but also provides insight into its underlying mechanisms of action, paving the way for future research and development in the field of functional foods and nutraceuticals for neuroprotection. Through this work, we aim to advance the understanding of the therapeutic potential of fermented S. maxima in the context of cognitive impairment and neurodegenerative diseases. The findings contribute to the growing body of evidence supporting the use of natural products, particularly those enhanced through fermentation, as viable alternatives or adjuncts to conventional pharmacological interventions for dementia and related disorders. Experimental animals used in this study were male ICR mice (6 weeks old) obtained from a certified breeding facility. The animals were housed under standard laboratory conditions with a 12-hour light/dark cycle, temperature maintained at 22 ± 2°C, and humidity at 55 ± 5%. They were provided a standard rodent diet and water ad libitum for one week prior to the experiments to allow acclimatization. All experimental procedures were performed in accordance with the guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at [name of institution]. The Spirulina maxima used in this study was sourced from a certified supplier and authenticated by morphology and chemical profiling. The extract was prepared by fermenting S. maxima powder with the lactic acid bacterium Lactobacillus plantarum HY-08, which was isolated and identified in our laboratory. The fermentation process involved inoculating 2% (v/v) of a 24-hour culture of L. plantarum HY-08 into a 5% (w/v) suspension of S. maxima in deionized water. The mixture was incubated at 37°C under anaerobic conditions for 48 hours. After fermentation, the extract was centrifuged at 5,000 × g for 15 minutes, filtered using a 0.22 µm membrane filter, and lyophilized to obtain a dry powder. The lyophilized fermented extract was stored at −20°C until use. For comparison, a non-fermented extract of S. maxima was also prepared by dissolving S. maxima powder in deionized water, followed by filtration and lyophilization. To induce memory impairment, scopolamine hydrobromide (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) was dissolved in sterile saline and administered intraperitoneally (i.p.) at a dose of 1.0 mg/kg body weight 30 minutes prior to behavioral testing. Mice were randomly divided into six groups (n = 10 per group): (1) control group, receiving saline; (2) scopolamine group, receiving scopolamine (1.0 mg/kg i.p.); (3) positive control group, receiving scopolamine and donepezil (2.0 mg/kg, p.o.); (4) low-dose group, receiving scopolamine and fermented S. maxima extract (200 mg/kg, p.o.); (5) high-dose group, receiving scopolamine and fermented S. maxima extract (400 mg/kg, p.o.); and (6) non-fermented extract group, receiving scopolamine and non-fermented S. maxima extract (400 mg/kg, p.o.). All treatments, except scopolamine, were administered orally once daily for 14 days. Cognitive function was evaluated using the Morris water maze (MWM) and passive avoidance tests. The MWM test was performed as described previously [1]. Briefly, a circular pool (120 cm in diameter, 45 cm in depth) was filled with water maintained at 22 ± 1°C and rendered opaque using non-toxic white paint. A platform (10 cm in diameter) was submerged 1 cm below the water surface in one quadrant of the pool. During the acquisition phase, mice were trained to locate the hidden platform over four consecutive days, with four trials per day. Each trial began with placing the mice in the water facing the pool wall at one of four designated starting points. The time taken to locate the platform (escape latency) was recorded, with a maximum cutoff time of 60 seconds per trial. On the fifth day, the platform was removed, and a probe trial was conducted to assess spatial memory. The percentage of time spent in the target quadrant and the number of platform crossings were recorded. The passive avoidance test was conducted to evaluate associative memory [2]. The apparatus consisted of two compartments, one illuminated and the other dark, separated by a guillotine door. During the training session, mice were placed in the illuminated compartment and allowed to explore freely. Upon entering the dark compartment, a mild foot shock (0.5 mA for 3 seconds) was delivered. Retention of memory was assessed 24 hours later by placing the mice in the illuminated compartment and recording the latency to enter the dark compartment (step-through latency), with a maximum cutoff time of 300 seconds. To investigate the underlying molecular mechanisms, hippocampal tissues were collected immediately after the behavioral tests. Mice were euthanized by carbon dioxide asphyxiation, and their brains were rapidly removed, with the hippocampi dissected on ice. The tissues were homogenized in radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). Protein concentration was determined using the bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay (Pierce, Rockford, IL, USA). Equal amounts of protein (20 µg) were separated by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) and transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes. The membranes were blocked with 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA) in Tris-buffered saline with Tween 20 (TBST) for 1 hour at room temperature and incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies against phosphorylated extracellular signal-regulated kinases (p-ERK, 1:1,000; Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, MA, USA), phosphorylated cAMP response element-binding protein (p-CREB, 1:1,000; Abcam, Cambridge, UK), brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF, 1:500; Abcam), and β-actin (1:5,000; Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Dallas, TX, USA). After washing, the membranes were incubated with horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:2,000; Santa Cruz Biotechnology) for 1 hour at room temperature. Protein bands were visualized using enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) reagents (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and quantified using ImageJ software (National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA). To evaluate the antioxidant activity of the extracts, the levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in the hippocampus were measured using 2',7'-dichlorofluorescein diacetate (DCFDA, Sigma-Aldrich) as a fluorescent probe. Hippocampal homogenates were incubated with DCFDA for 30 minutes at 37°C, and fluorescence intensity was measured at excitation/emission wavelengths of 485/535 nm using a fluorescence microplate reader (Molecular Devices, Sunnyvale, CA, USA). Data were expressed as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Statistical analyses were performed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test for multiple comparisons. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Statistical analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism version 9.0 (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA). References: [1] Morris, R. (1984). Developments of a water-maze procedure for studying spatial learning in the rat. Journal of Neuroscience Methods, 11(1), 47-60. [2] Jarvik, M. E., & Kopp, R. (1967). An improved passive avoidance apparatus. Psychological Reports, 21(1), 221-224. The results of this study demonstrate the cognitive-enhancing effects of Spirulina maxima extract fermented with Lactobacillus plantarum HY-08 (hereafter referred to as FSmax) in a scopolamine-induced dementia model in mice. This section details the findings from behavioral experiments, biochemical analyses, and mechanistic investigations, providing evidence for the memory-improving properties of FSmax. To assess the effects of FSmax on memory and learning, the Morris water maze (MWM) test and the passive avoidance (PA) test were performed. In the MWM test, the scopolamine-treated group (negative control) exhibited a significant increase in escape latency time compared to the normal control group, indicating impaired spatial learning and memory.

The endocannabinoid system (ECS) is a complex network of receptors, ligands, and enzymes that has emerged as a critical modulator of numerous physiological processes, including pain sensation, appetite regulation, immune response, and neuroprotection. In recent years, its role in the regulation of tumorigenesis has garnered significant attention, as mounting evidence suggests that the ECS is intricately involved in cancer progression and malignancy. The system is composed of cannabinoid receptors (CB1 and CB2), endogenous cannabinoids (endocannabinoids), and the enzymes responsible for their synthesis and degradation. In addition, other putative cannabinoid receptors, such as GPR55, have been proposed to expand the functional diversity of the ECS. This intricate signaling network not only contributes to maintaining cellular homeostasis but also appears to be dysregulated in various pathological conditions, including cancer. Cannabinoid receptors, particularly CB1 and CB2, are G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) that mediate most of the effects of cannabinoids. CB1 receptors are predominantly expressed in the central nervous system (CNS), where they regulate neurotransmitter release and synaptic function, while CB2 receptors are primarily localized in peripheral tissues, particularly in immune cells, where they modulate inflammatory responses. The endogenous ligands for these receptors, such as anandamide (AEA) and 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG), are lipid-derived signaling molecules that are synthesized on demand and rapidly degraded by specific enzymes, including fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH) and monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL). Beyond the classical CB1 and CB2 receptors, the ECS interacts with a range of other molecular targets, including transient receptor potential (TRP) channels, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), and GPR55, further expanding its functional repertoire. The relevance of the ECS in cancer biology is underscored by its dysregulated expression in a variety of tumor types. Studies have documented abnormal CB1 and CB2 receptor expression patterns in cancers such as glioblastoma, breast cancer, prostate cancer, and melanoma, among others. These alterations are often associated with tumor aggressiveness, metastatic potential, and clinical outcomes, suggesting that the ECS may serve as a biomarker for disease prognosis. In addition to receptor expression, changes in endocannabinoid levels and alterations in the activity of enzymes responsible for their metabolism have been observed in cancer tissues. Collectively, these findings point to a complex interplay between the ECS and tumor cells, raising questions about the potential role of cannabinoids in cancer treatment. Cannabinoids, the active compounds derived from Cannabis sativa, have been studied extensively for their therapeutic potential. Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabidiol (CBD) are the two most well-characterized phytocannabinoids, with THC being a potent agonist of CB1 and CB2 receptors, while CBD exhibits a more complex pharmacological profile, including interactions with non-cannabinoid targets. Exogenous cannabinoids, including both plant-derived and synthetic analogs, have demonstrated a range of effects on tumor cells, including the induction of apoptosis, inhibition of cell proliferation, suppression of angiogenesis, and reduction of metastasis. Notably, the mechanisms underlying these effects often differ from those of endogenous cannabinoids, reflecting the complexity of cannabinoid signaling in the tumor microenvironment. The molecular pathways through which cannabinoids exert their effects on cancer cells are diverse and context-dependent. Studies have identified several signaling cascades influenced by cannabinoid receptor activation, including the PI3K/AKT/mTOR, MAPK, and JAK/STAT pathways, which are known to regulate cell survival, proliferation, and migration. In many cases, cannabinoids appear to act as modulators of these pathways, tipping the balance toward proapoptotic and antitumor responses. For instance, activation of CB1 or CB2 receptors has been shown to induce apoptosis in cancer cells by promoting the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), disrupting mitochondrial function, and upregulating proapoptotic proteins such as Bax. Conversely, cannabinoids can also inhibit tumor cell proliferation and migration by interfering with prosurvival signals and reducing the expression of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) that facilitate invasion and metastasis. Despite the promising antitumor effects observed in preclinical studies, translating these findings into clinical applications remains a challenge. One major obstacle is the heterogeneity of the ECS across different cancer types and even among individual patients. The expression levels of CB1, CB2, and other ECS components vary widely depending on the tumor's origin, stage, and molecular characteristics, complicating the development of standardized cannabinoid-based therapies. Furthermore, the potential for cannabinoids to exert both pro- and anti-tumorigenic effects, depending on the context, underscores the need for a nuanced understanding of their mechanisms of action. For example, while CB1 activation may induce apoptosis in some cancer types, it has also been implicated in promoting tumor growth in others, highlighting the dualistic nature of ECS signaling in cancer biology. In addition to these biological complexities, the pharmacology of cannabinoids adds another layer of intricacy. The effects of exogenous cannabinoids often depend on their concentration, route of administration, and pharmacokinetic properties, making it difficult to compare results across studies. Moreover, the interactions between cannabinoids and chemotherapy or other standard cancer treatments remain poorly understood, raising concerns about potential drug-drug interactions and adverse effects. Nonetheless, the growing body of evidence supporting the antitumor activity of cannabinoids has spurred interest in their potential use as adjuvant therapies, particularly in cases where conventional treatments are ineffective or poorly tolerated. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current understanding of the ECS in cancer biology, with a focus on its role as a regulator of tumor cell malignancy. We will explore the molecular pathways through which cannabinoids influence cancer cell behavior, examine the clinical significance of ECS dysregulation in various cancer types, and discuss the challenges and opportunities associated with the therapeutic exploitation of cannabinoids in oncology. By synthesizing the available evidence, we hope to shed light on the potential of the ECS as a target for innovative cancer therapies and to highlight the areas that warrant further investigation in this rapidly evolving field. To investigate the role of the endocannabinoid system (ECS) as a regulator of tumor cell malignancy, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of ECS components, their expression in various cancer types, and the associated signaling pathways. This study combined both in vitro and in vivo approaches, as well as bioinformatic and clinical analyses, to elucidate the biological and clinical significance of ECS in cancer progression and therapeutic potential. Cell Lines and Culture Conditions A panel of human cancer cell lines, representing diverse tumor types (e.g., breast, lung, colorectal, glioblastoma, and melanoma), was obtained from recognized cell line repositories, such as the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC). Cells were cultured in appropriate media supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), antibiotics (penicillin-streptomycin), and maintained at 37°C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO₂. Normal human cell lines, including fibroblasts and epithelial cells, were used as controls to assess differential expression and activity of ECS components. Expression Analysis of ECS Components Expression levels of ECS components, including CB1, CB2, GPR55, and enzymes involved in endocannabinoid synthesis (e.g., N-acyl phosphatidylethanolamine phospholipase D, NAPE-PLD) and degradation (e.g., fatty acid amide hydrolase, FAAH, and monoacylglycerol lipase, MAGL), were analyzed using quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) and Western blotting. Total RNA was extracted using a standard TRIzol-based protocol, reverse-transcribed into cDNA using a high-capacity cDNA synthesis kit, and amplified using specific primers for ECS-related genes. Protein expression was evaluated using antibodies validated for specificity against ECS components. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) was also performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor tissues from clinical samples to confirm the spatial localization and expression levels of ECS components in tumor and adjacent normal tissues. Functional Assays to Determine the Role of ECS in Tumor Malignancy To assess the functional role of ECS in regulating tumor cell malignancy, several in vitro assays were performed. Cell viability was measured using the MTT assay after treatment with selective CB1 and CB2 agonists (e.g., WIN55,212-2 and JWH-133), antagonists (e.g., AM251 and AM630), and other ECS modulators, such as inhibitors of FAAH and MAGL. Cell apoptosis and cell cycle progression were analyzed using flow cytometry with annexin V/propidium iodide staining and DNA content analysis, respectively. Migration and invasion assays were performed using transwell chambers coated with or without Matrigel to evaluate the role of ECS in metastatic potential. Additionally, colony formation assays were carried out to assess long-term proliferative capabilities. Gene Silencing and Overexpression Studies To further investigate the specific contributions of ECS components to tumor cell behavior, gene silencing and overexpression experiments were conducted. Small interfering RNA (siRNA) targeting CB1, CB2, and GPR55, as well as non-targeting control siRNA, were transfected into cancer cells using a liposome-based transfection reagent. Overexpression of ECS components was achieved by transfecting cells with plasmids encoding full-length CB1, CB2, or GPR55. The efficiency of knockdown or overexpression was confirmed by qRT-PCR and Western blotting. Functional assays, as described above, were performed to determine the effects of ECS modulation on cell proliferation, survival, and migration. Assessment of Downstream Signaling Pathways To elucidate the signaling pathways downstream of ECS activation, cells were treated with ECS agonists, antagonists, or inhibitors, followed by Western blot analysis of key molecules involved in prosurvival and proapoptotic pathways. Phosphorylation and expression levels of Akt, ERK1/2, p38 MAPK, AMPK, and p53 were assessed using phospho-specific antibodies. Additionally, changes in the expression of apoptotic regulators, such as Bcl-2, Bax, and caspases, were examined. Crosstalk between ECS and other signaling pathways, such as Wnt/β-catenin and Hippo/YAP, was also explored using pathway-specific inhibitors and luciferase reporter assays. In Vivo Tumor Models To evaluate the effects of ECS modulation on tumor growth and progression in vivo, xenograft models were established by subcutaneous injection of human cancer cells into immunodeficient mice (e.g., NOD-SCID or nude mice). Once tumors reached a measurable size, animals were randomly assigned to treatment groups and administered ECS agonists, antagonists, or vehicle controls. Tumor growth was monitored by caliper measurements, and tumor volume was calculated using the formula: (length × width²)/2. At the study endpoint, tumors were excised, weighed, and subjected to histological analysis, including IHC for proliferation (Ki-67) and apoptosis (cleaved caspase-3) markers. Serum and tumor tissues were also analyzed for changes in endocannabinoid levels using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). Bioinformatics and Clinical Correlation Analyses To investigate the clinical relevance of ECS in human cancers, publicly available transcriptomic datasets (e.g., The Cancer Genome Atlas, TCGA, and Gene Expression Omnibus, GEO) were analyzed for ECS component expression across different cancer types. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and Cox proportional hazards models were used to evaluate the association between ECS component expression and overall survival (OS) or progression-free survival (PFS) in cancer patients. Differential expression of ECS components between tumor and normal tissues was also analyzed using paired or unpaired statistical tests, as appropriate. Statistical Analysis All experiments were performed in triplicate or as otherwise specified. Data were presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Statistical significance was determined using one-way or two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with post hoc tests, or unpaired t-tests, as appropriate. A p-value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism or R software. This multi-faceted approach allowed us to comprehensively evaluate the role of ECS in tumor cell malignancy and its potential as a therapeutic target in cancer. In the investigation of the endocannabinoid system (ECS) as a regulator of tumor cell malignancy, several key findings emerged that shed light on its role in cancer progression and therapeutic potential. The results are organized into three major areas: alterations in ECS components in tumor cells, the signaling pathways influenced by cannabinoids, and the functional impact of cannabinoids on cancer cell behavior. Alterations in ECS Components in Tumors Across multiple cancer types, aberrant expression patterns of ECS components were identified, including cannabinoid receptors (CB1 and CB2), endogenous cannabinoids, and the enzymes involved in their metabolism. CB1 receptor expression was found to be significantly upregulated in certain cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma, glioblastoma, and colorectal cancer, while being downregulated in others, including prostate and breast cancers. CB2 receptor expression, on the other hand, showed a more consistent upregulation in numerous malignancies, including breast cancer, non-small cell lung cancer, and certain hematological cancers, suggesting its potential as a biomarker for tumor aggressiveness. Additionally, dysregulation of endocannabinoid levels was detected in both tumor tissues and patient plasma. Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy and a leading cause of cancer-related mortality among women worldwide, accounting for a significant proportion of the global cancer burden [1]. The disease exhibits a complex etiology driven by both environmental and genetic factors. While significant strides have been made in identifying high-penetrance germline mutations in genes such as BRCA1, BRCA2, and TP53, these mutations collectively explain only a small proportion of the heritability of breast cancer [2]. Consequently, the identification of additional genetic risk factors, particularly common variants contributing to susceptibility, remains critical for advancing our understanding of breast cancer biology and improving risk prediction models. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have been instrumental in identifying common genetic variants associated with complex diseases, including breast cancer [3]. Over the past decade, GWAS and subsequent large-scale replication studies have uncovered 79 loci associated with breast cancer susceptibility, collectively explaining approximately 14% of its familial risk [4]. These studies have provided valuable insights into the genetic architecture of breast cancer and highlighted the polygenic nature of the disease. However, the majority of the heritability of breast cancer remains unexplained, suggesting that additional susceptibility loci, particularly those with smaller effect sizes, await discovery. Recent advances in genotyping technologies, statistical methodologies, and the availability of large-scale reference panels for imputation, such as the 1000 Genomes Project, have significantly enhanced the power of GWAS to detect genetic associations across the genome [5]. Furthermore, the integration of functional genomics data, including chromatin interaction and epigenomic datasets, has enabled researchers to prioritize candidate genes and elucidate potential mechanisms underlying GWAS-identified loci [6]. These integrative approaches hold promise for identifying novel genetic variants and their functional relevance in breast cancer pathogenesis. Despite the substantial progress made in identifying genetic risk factors, existing studies have been limited by sample size, population diversity, and resolution of genotyping platforms. To address these limitations, the present study combines data from 11 independent GWAS, comprising 15,748 breast cancer cases and 18,084 controls, with data from an additional 41 studies involving 46,785 cases and 42,892 controls genotyped on the iCOGS array. This meta-analysis leverages a powerful dataset of over 120,000 individuals of European ancestry, offering unprecedented statistical power to detect novel susceptibility loci for breast cancer. The iCOGS array, a custom genotyping platform designed for the fine-mapping of cancer susceptibility loci, includes approximately 200,000 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) selected based on prior GWAS findings and candidate gene studies [7]. By combining iCOGS data with imputed genotypes derived from the 1000 Genomes Project reference panel, we generated a comprehensive dataset of over 11 million SNPs for association analysis. This approach enables the identification of novel loci with high resolution and facilitates the characterization of genetic variants that may contribute to breast cancer risk. In this study, we report the identification of 15 novel loci associated with breast cancer, all reaching genome-wide significance (P < 5 × 10^-8). These findings represent a substantial addition to the catalog of known breast cancer susceptibility loci, further advancing our understanding of the genetic basis of the disease. Among the loci identified, we highlight several with compelling evidence for functional relevance. For instance, in the region on chromosome 18q12.3, we identified SETBP1 as a likely target gene, supported by chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-Seq) data in mammary cell lines. Similarly, on chromosome 1q21.1, evidence from chromatin interaction analysis identified RNF115 and PDZK1 as candidate genes. In addition, one of the associations appears to be driven by a coding variant resulting in an amino acid substitution in EXO1, a gene implicated in DNA repair processes. The integration of GWAS findings with functional genomic data represents a critical step toward understanding the biological mechanisms underlying genetic associations. Chromatin interaction data from the Encyclopedia of DNA Elements (ENCODE) and related resources provide valuable insights into the regulatory landscape of the genome, enabling the identification of putative target genes and pathways [8]. By leveraging these resources, we were able to prioritize candidate genes for functional follow-up studies, paving the way for future research into their roles in breast cancer biology. The identification of additional susceptibility loci has important implications for breast cancer risk prediction and prevention. Polygenic risk scores (PRS), which aggregate the effects of multiple risk variants, have emerged as a promising tool for risk stratification and personalized medicine [9]. The discovery of new loci with small effect sizes contributes to the refinement of PRS models, potentially improving their predictive accuracy and clinical utility. Moreover, the characterization of novel risk genes and pathways may uncover new therapeutic targets and inform the development of precision medicine approaches for breast cancer treatment. This study represents one of the largest and most comprehensive efforts to date to identify genetic risk factors for breast cancer. By leveraging the power of large-scale meta-analysis and integrating functional genomic data, we provide new insights into the genetic architecture of the disease. The identification of 15 novel susceptibility loci underscores the importance of continued efforts to uncover the missing heritability of breast cancer and highlights the potential of integrative approaches to advance our understanding of this complex disease. To identify novel breast cancer susceptibility loci, we conducted a comprehensive genome-wide meta-analysis using data from 11 genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and the iCOGS consortium. All analyses were restricted to women of European ancestry to minimize confounding effects due to population stratification. The study design incorporated stringent quality control measures, imputation with a robust reference panel, and integration with functional genomic data to prioritize candidate loci and genes. Study Populations and Genotyping The meta-analysis included a total of 15,748 breast cancer cases and 18,084 controls from 11 GWAS, as well as 46,785 cases and 42,892 controls genotyped using the iCOGS custom array. The GWAS datasets were derived from various studies conducted across Europe and North America, with all participants self-reporting European ancestry. The iCOGS array, developed as part of the Collaborative Oncological Gene-environment Study (COGS), was specifically designed to investigate common genetic variants associated with breast cancer risk. Genotyping for the GWAS datasets was performed using high-density SNP arrays (Illumina or Affymetrix platforms), and standard quality control procedures were applied to ensure data accuracy. Samples with a call rate below 95% were excluded, and SNPs with a minor allele frequency (MAF) below 1%, a genotype call rate <95%, or deviation from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (P < 1×10⁻⁶ in controls) were removed. For the iCOGS dataset, genotyping was performed using the Illumina iSelect array, and similar quality control criteria were applied. Imputation and Meta-Analysis To increase genomic coverage and facilitate a meta-analysis across multiple datasets, genotype imputation was performed using the 1000 Genomes Project Phase 3 reference panel, which provides a dense catalog of genetic variation. Imputation was conducted separately for each study using the software tools IMPUTE2 or Minimac, depending on the dataset. Post-imputation quality control included exclusion of poorly imputed SNPs (info score < 0.3 or equivalent metrics) and filtering for MAF > 1%. For the meta-analysis, we employed a fixed-effects inverse-variance-weighted approach to combine summary statistics from individual studies, assuming consistent effect sizes across studies. Heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran’s Q-statistic and the I² statistic. SNPs reaching genome-wide significance (P < 5×10⁻⁸) were considered novel susceptibility loci, provided they had not been previously reported in breast cancer GWAS. Analyses were performed using METAL and R-based statistical packages. Functional Annotation To prioritize candidate genes and explore the functional relevance of the identified loci, we integrated the association results with publicly available functional genomic datasets. Specifically, we utilized ChIP-Seq data from mammary epithelial cells to identify regulatory elements, such as enhancers and promoters, in the regions surrounding the significant SNPs. Chromatin interaction data from ChIA-PET experiments in ENCODE were used to characterize long-range interactions between regulatory elements and candidate target genes. Additionally, we annotated SNPs and their proxies (r² > 0.8 in the 1000 Genomes Project European population) using publicly available resources, including the GTEx database for eQTL analysis, RegulomeDB, and the ROADMAP Epigenomics Project. SNPs located in coding regions were assessed for their potential functional impact, including amino acid substitutions, using tools such as SIFT and PolyPhen-2. Statistical Fine-Mapping For each novel locus, we performed conditional analysis within a 1 Mb window surrounding the lead SNP to identify secondary independent signals. Bayesian fine-mapping was performed using the software package FINEMAP to calculate posterior probabilities for each SNP being causal. SNPs with high posterior probabilities were subjected to additional functional annotation to assess their potential biological relevance. Validation and Replication To validate our findings, we conducted replication analyses of the novel loci using an independent dataset from the Breast Cancer Association Consortium (BCAC), comprising an additional 20,000 cases and 20,000 controls of European ancestry. Summary statistics for the lead SNPs were compared between the discovery and replication datasets, and meta-analysis was performed to assess the combined evidence of association. Integration with Coding Variation One of the identified loci on 1q21.1 contained a missense variant in the gene EXO1, which encodes exonuclease 1, a protein involved in DNA repair and replication. To investigate the potential functional impact of this variant, we modeled the amino acid substitution using in silico prediction tools and analyzed its frequency across breast cancer subtypes. Structural modeling was conducted to assess the potential impact of the substitution on protein stability and function. Sensitivity Analyses We conducted sensitivity analyses to evaluate the robustness of our findings. These included excluding cases with known BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations and repeating the meta-analysis to ensure that the associations were not driven by rare high-penetrance mutations. Additionally, analyses were adjusted for potential confounders such as age, family history of breast cancer, and principal components to account for residual population stratification. Ethical Considerations All participating studies obtained ethical approval from their respective institutional review boards, and all participants provided written informed consent. Data sharing and analysis were conducted in compliance with data protection regulations and ethical guidelines. By integrating large-scale genetic association data with functional genomic resources, our study identified 15 novel loci associated with breast cancer risk, implicating several candidate genes and pathways. These findings contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the genetic architecture of breast cancer and provide a foundation for future functional studies. In this study, we aimed to identify novel breast cancer susceptibility loci through a meta-analysis integrating data from 11 genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and 41 additional studies genotyped using the iCOGS array. The analysis included a total of 62,533 breast cancer cases and 60,976 controls, all of European ancestry. Following quality control measures, genotypes for over 11 million SNPs were imputed using the 1000 Genomes Project reference panel.
