Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic inflammatory disease characterized by persistent synovitis, systemic inflammation, and the progressive destruction of cartilage and bone [1]. It is associated with significant morbidity, reduced quality of life, and increased healthcare utilization, imposing substantial socio-economic burdens [2]. Over the past two decades, the management of RA has been revolutionized by the introduction of biological disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (bDMARDs). These therapies target specific immunological pathways implicated in the pathogenesis of RA, offering enhanced efficacy compared to conventional synthetic DMARDs (csDMARDs) and improving clinical, functional, and radiographic outcomes [3,4]. Among bDMARDs, tumor necrosis factor inhibitors (anti-TNFs) have been the most extensively studied and widely used. However, despite their clinical efficacy, a significant proportion of patients discontinue anti-TNF therapy due to primary or secondary inefficacy, adverse events, or other factors [5,6]. Discontinuation rates among first-line anti-TNF users have been reported to range from 30% to 50% within the first year of therapy, highlighting the need for effective second-line treatment strategies [7]. When patients fail their initial anti-TNF treatment, clinical guidelines recommend switching to either a second anti-TNF agent or a bDMARD with a different mode of action (MOA), such as interleukin-6 receptor antagonists, costimulation modulators, or B-cell depleting agents [8,9]. While the therapeutic landscape for RA has expanded considerably, evidence regarding the comparative drug survival of second-line bDMARDs remains limited. Drug survival, defined as the duration a patient remains on a specific therapy, is an important metric in chronic diseases such as RA, as it reflects both treatment efficacy and tolerability in real-world settings [10]. Furthermore, drug survival is influenced by multiple factors, including the MOA of the bDMARD, demographic and clinical characteristics of the patient population, and the presence of comorbidities [11]. Understanding these factors is critical for optimizing treatment strategies and improving outcomes for RA patients. Existing literature on second-line bDMARD therapy suggests that switching to a non-anti-TNF bDMARD may confer advantages in certain clinical scenarios, particularly in patients with a history of inadequate response to anti-TNFs [12]. For instance, studies have demonstrated that non-anti-TNF bDMARDs may exhibit superior efficacy in patients with seropositive RA or in those with specific genetic markers [13,14]. However, these findings are derived primarily from randomized controlled trials (RCTs), which often exclude patients with complex comorbidities or those receiving concurrent medications, potentially limiting their generalizability to real-world populations [15]. Observational studies using claims data or registry cohorts provide complementary insights into real-world drug survival, but these studies are often hindered by heterogeneity in study designs, short follow-up durations, and limited statistical power [16]. The choice between a second anti-TNF and a non-anti-TNF bDMARD is further complicated by the lack of consensus on whether switching within the same MOA or transitioning to a different MOA yields better outcomes. Some evidence suggests that cycling within the anti-TNF class may be effective for certain patients, particularly those who discontinued their first anti-TNF due to adverse events rather than inefficacy [17]. Conversely, switching to a non-anti-TNF bDMARD may be preferable in cases of primary inefficacy or the development of neutralizing anti-drug antibodies [18]. However, the extent to which these theoretical considerations translate into differences in real-world drug survival remains poorly understood. Another critical consideration in the management of RA is the impact of patient-related factors on treatment persistence. Age, gender, disease duration, comorbidities, and concurrent medication use have all been identified as predictors of drug discontinuation or switching in RA populations [19]. For example, higher comorbidity burdens, as measured by indices such as the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), have been associated with shorter drug survival, likely owing to increased susceptibility to adverse events and polypharmacy-related interactions [20]. Conversely, the use of concomitant csDMARDs, particularly methotrexate, has been reported to enhance drug survival, potentially by reducing immunogenicity and improving therapeutic response [21]. In this context, the present study seeks to address critical gaps in the literature by providing a comprehensive analysis of the drug survival of second-line bDMARDs in RA patients, with a particular focus on the influence of MOA. Using German claims data from 2010 to 2013, the study evaluates rates of discontinuation, re-initiation, continuation, and switching to a third bDMARD, stratified by the type of second-line therapy (anti-TNF versus non-anti-TNF). Additionally, the study identifies independent predictors of early discontinuation or switching, shedding light on patient- and treatment-related factors that influence real-world drug survival. By leveraging a large, population-based dataset, this study provides robust insights into the comparative persistence of second-line bDMARDs and highlights the clinical and demographic characteristics associated with treatment outcomes. The findings have important implications for the personalized management of RA, offering guidance on the selection of second-line therapies based on patient-specific factors and therapeutic goals. Furthermore, the study underscores the need for ongoing research to optimize treatment algorithms and improve long-term outcomes for RA patients in real-world settings. Study Design and Setting This retrospective cohort study utilized anonymized claims data from a German statutory health insurance database covering the years 2010–2013. The database includes information on demographic characteristics, outpatient and inpatient diagnoses, outpatient prescriptions, and procedures. All patients included in the study had a confirmed diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) based on the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10) code M05 or M06, recorded on at least two different occasions by a specialist during the 12 months prior to the initiation of the second biological disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (bDMARD). Patients were followed for 12 months or until death, whichever occurred first. Study Population The study population consisted of adult RA patients (aged ≥18 years) who had received at least one prescription for a first bDMARD and subsequently switched to a second bDMARD with a different active compound. Patients were excluded if they had less than 12 months of continuous enrollment in the database prior to initiating their second bDMARD or if they were enrolled in hospice or palliative care at any time during the study period. The cohort was stratified into two groups based on the mode of action of the second bDMARD: (1) anti-tumor necrosis factor (anti-TNF) therapy group, which included patients who received a second anti-TNF agent different from their first anti-TNF agent, and (2) non-anti-TNF therapy group, which included patients who switched to a bDMARD with a different mechanism of action (e.g., interleukin-6 inhibitors, B-cell depleting agents, or T-cell co-stimulation inhibitors). Baseline characteristics, including age, sex, comorbidities, and prior use of pain medications, were recorded at the time of the second bDMARD initiation. Exposure and Outcomes The primary exposure of interest was the mode of action of the second bDMARD (anti-TNF versus non-anti-TNF). The primary outcome was drug survival, defined as the time from initiation of the second bDMARD to either discontinuation (defined as a gap of more than 90 days without a prescription), switching to a third bDMARD, or the end of the follow-up period. Secondary outcomes included the rates of discontinuation without re-initiation, re-initiation of the second bDMARD after discontinuation, and switching to a third bDMARD. Covariates Potential confounding factors were identified based on clinical relevance and prior literature. These included age, sex, Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) score, and prior use of pain medications in the 12-month period preceding the initiation of the second bDMARD. The CCI was calculated based on ICD-10 codes to quantify the burden of comorbid diseases, with higher scores indicating greater comorbidity. Pain medication use was defined as the receipt of at least one prescription for a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), opioid, or acetaminophen. Statistical Analysis Descriptive statistics were used to summarize baseline characteristics of the study population. Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) or median with interquartile range (IQR), as appropriate, and categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages. Differences between the anti-TNF and non-anti-TNF groups were assessed using chi-square tests for categorical variables and t-tests or Mann–Whitney U tests for continuous variables, depending on the distribution of the data. Drug survival was analyzed using Kaplan–Meier survival curves, with log-rank tests used to compare survival distributions between groups. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models were employed to identify independent predictors of time to discontinuation or switching to a third bDMARD. Hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported. The proportional hazards assumption was tested using Schoenfeld residuals, and no significant violations were identified. To assess the robustness of the findings, sensitivity analyses were conducted by varying the definition of discontinuation (e.g., using a gap of 60 days or 120 days without a prescription) and by excluding patients who switched to a third bDMARD within the first 90 days after initiating the second bDMARD. Subgroup analyses were performed to investigate potential effect modification by age group (<65 years vs. ≥65 years) and by baseline comorbidity burden (CCI score ≤2 vs. >2). Ethical Considerations The use of anonymized claims data in this study did not require patient consent as per German data protection regulations. The study protocol was approved by an independent ethics committee and adhered to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Data Management and Software All data extraction, management, and statistical analyses were conducted using SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA). Data quality was ensured through systematic checks for completeness and consistency prior to analysis. Missing data for baseline covariates were addressed using multiple imputation techniques, assuming data were missing at random. Patient Demographics and Baseline Characteristics A total of 2,667 rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patients who had received at least one prescription for an anti-tumor necrosis factor (anti-TNF) biological disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (bDMARD) were identified in the claims dataset. Among these, 451 patients (16.9%) transitioned to a second bDMARD therapy during the study period, with 340 patients (75.4%) receiving a second anti-TNF bDMARD and 111 patients (24.6%) receiving a non-anti-TNF bDMARD. The mean age of patients was slightly higher in the non-anti-TNF group compared to the anti-TNF group (55.9 years vs. 52.6 years, respectively). No significant differences were observed between the two groups in terms of gender distribution. Treatment Persistence and Discontinuation Rates During the 12-month follow-up period, substantial differences emerged in persistence rates between patients treated with a second anti-TNF bDMARD and those treated with a non-anti-TNF bDMARD. Overall, 53.5% of patients in the anti-TNF group continued therapy without interruption, compared to 66.7% in the non-anti-TNF group, a statistically significant difference (p < 0.050). When including patients who discontinued and subsequently restarted treatment, 60% of all patients maintained therapy continuity. Discontinuation without re-initiation was observed in 14.1% of patients receiving a second anti-TNF bDMARD and in 19.8% of patients in the non-anti-TNF group, although this difference did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.179). Re-initiation rates, defined as resumption of the same second bDMARD following a period of discontinuation, were low across both groups, occurring in 3.8% of anti-TNF patients and 1.8% of non-anti-TNF patients (p = 0.387). Switching to a Third bDMARD Switching to a third bDMARD was significantly more frequent among patients who received a second anti-TNF bDMARD compared to those who received a non-anti-TNF bDMARD. Specifically, 28.8% of patients in the anti-TNF group transitioned to a third bDMARD during the follow-up period, compared to 11.7% of patients in the non-anti-TNF group (p < 0.001). Drug Survival Analysis The median drug survival time, defined as the duration of continuous use of the second bDMARD without switching or discontinuation, was longer for patients treated with non-anti-TNF bDMARDs (295 days) than for those treated with anti-TNF bDMARDs (264 days; p = 0.016). Kaplan-Meier survival curves further illustrated this difference, with non-anti-TNF patients demonstrating a more gradual decline in treatment persistence over time compared to anti-TNF patients. Factors Associated with Discontinuation or Switching Cox proportional hazards regression analysis identified several independent predictors of earlier discontinuation or switching of the second bDMARD. Prescription of an anti-TNF bDMARD as the second-line therapy was associated with a 51.2% higher risk of discontinuation or switching compared to non-anti-TNF bDMARDs (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.512; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.224–1.868). Additionally, higher comorbidity levels, as measured by the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), were associated with a modest increase in the risk of treatment discontinuation

The East Antarctic Ice Sheet (EAIS) represents the largest single reservoir of frozen freshwater on Earth, with the potential to significantly influence global sea levels under climatic perturbations. Understanding the dynamics of the EAIS during past warm climates, such as the Pliocene epoch (~5.3–2.6 Ma), is critical for constraining its sensitivity to ongoing anthropogenic warming. The Late Pliocene, in particular, is often considered a potential analogue for future climate scenarios due to atmospheric CO\(2\) levels comparable to those projected for the coming centuries, as well as global mean temperatures estimated to be 2–3 °C warmer than pre-industrial levels [1,2]. These conditions led to substantial changes in ice sheet volume and global sea levels, making the Pliocene a critical period for investigating ice sheet stability and its contributions to sea level rise. The interaction between ice sheet dynamics and climate forcings during the Pliocene is complex and remains a subject of significant scientific inquiry. In addition to direct temperature effects, atmospheric and oceanic circulation patterns, precipitation regimes, and feedback mechanisms such as albedo and ice-elevation interactions all played pivotal roles in shaping the behaviour of the EAIS. Reconstructions of past ice volume and extent, particularly during the mid-to-late Pliocene, are essential for elucidating the interplay between these factors. However, direct observational constraints on ice sheet geometry and volume during this period are sparse, particularly for interior regions of East Antarctica that are difficult to access. Consequently, cosmogenic nuclide exposure dating and ice sheet modelling have emerged as powerful complementary tools for reconstructing past ice sheet configurations and testing hypotheses about their response to climatic drivers. Cosmogenic nuclide exposure dating provides a direct means of assessing glacial history by measuring the accumulation of isotopes such as \(^{10}\)Be and \(^{26}\)Al in surface rocks exposed to cosmic rays. This method is particularly useful in Antarctica, where subaerial exposure of glacially scoured bedrock and erratic boulders can preserve a record of past ice sheet thinning or thickening. Previous studies using cosmogenic nuclides in East Antarctica have revealed evidence for both extensive glacial erosion and long-term burial beneath persistent ice cover [3–5]. These findings highlight the spatial heterogeneity of past ice sheet behaviour and underscore the need for additional data from under-sampled regions, particularly those that are sensitive to climatic and oceanic forcing, such as the Wilkes Subglacial and Aurora Basins. Numerical ice sheet models provide a complementary approach for reconstructing past ice sheet dynamics, offering the ability to simulate ice sheet responses under boundary conditions informed by paleoclimate reconstructions. When constrained by geological data, such models can provide quantitative estimates of ice volume, thickness, and extent, as well as insights into the sensitivity of these parameters to key climatic forcings [6,7]. For the Pliocene, ice sheet models have suggested that significant melting of the Wilkes Subglacial and Aurora Basins likely occurred under warm climatic conditions, with potential implications for global sea level [8]. However, the extent to which such melting was offset by thickening of the interior EAIS remains uncertain, requiring validation against empirical data from cosmogenic nuclide exposure ages and other geochronological methods. The mid-Pliocene Warm Period (MPWP; ~3.3–3.0 Ma) is of particular interest due to its relatively stable climate and well-constrained boundary conditions. Proxy records suggest that Antarctic temperatures during this interval were significantly elevated relative to the present, accompanied by reduced sea ice extent and increased moisture transport from lower latitudes [9,10]. These conditions likely drove substantial changes in ice sheet geometry, with implications for global sea level rise. Estimates of Pliocene sea level highstands range from ~10 to 30 m above present levels, with contributions from the EAIS, West Antarctic Ice Sheet (WAIS), and Greenland Ice Sheet (GIS) [11]. However, reconciling these estimates with geological and geophysical evidence for ice sheet thickness and extent remains a major challenge, particularly given the uncertainties associated with isostatic adjustment, sediment compaction, and regional tectonics. The transition from the Pliocene to the Pleistocene (~2.6 Ma) marks a key shift in Antarctic climate, characterized by the intensification of glacial-interglacial cycles and a progressive cooling trend. This transition is associated with the onset of substantial sea ice expansion, which likely altered atmospheric and oceanic circulation patterns, reducing moisture transport to the Antarctic interior and thereby influencing ice sheet mass balance [12,13]. These changes underscore the importance of understanding the feedbacks between regional climate, sea ice, and ice sheet dynamics during periods of climatic change. In this study, we present new cosmogenic nuclide exposure age data from previously unsampled regions of the East Antarctic interior, complemented by a synthesis of existing datasets. These data provide critical constraints on the timing and magnitude of ice sheet thickening during the Pliocene, offering new insights into the spatial and temporal variability of EAIS dynamics under warm climate conditions. To interpret these results in a broader context, we employ a numerical ice sheet model configured with mid-Pliocene boundary conditions, including elevated atmospheric CO\(2\) concentrations, reduced sea ice extent, and enhanced precipitation. By integrating empirical and model-based approaches, we aim to refine estimates of EAIS contributions to global sea level during the Pliocene and to improve understanding of the processes driving ice sheet behaviour under past warm climates. The results of this study have implications for both paleoenvironmental reconstructions and future projections of ice sheet stability. By elucidating the response of the EAIS to Pliocene-like climatic conditions, we aim to enhance the predictive capacity of ice sheet models under scenarios of ongoing global warming. Moreover, our findings contribute to a growing body of evidence supporting the use of the Pliocene as a natural laboratory for understanding the potential long-term impacts of current anthropogenic climate change on polar ice sheets and global sea level. This integration of geological data and numerical modelling represents a critical step toward addressing the uncertainties surrounding ice sheet-climate feedbacks and their implications for future sea level rise. Study Area and Sampling Strategy To investigate the variability of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet (EAIS) during the Plio-Pleistocene, we focused on key glaciological and geomorphic sites within the Wilkes Subglacial Basin, Aurora Subglacial Basin, and adjacent regions of the Transantarctic Mountains. These areas were selected because they are sensitive to climatic and ice sheet changes and preserve geomorphic evidence of past ice dynamics. Sampling was designed to maximize spatial and temporal coverage of bedrock and glacial erratics exposed on nunataks and high-elevation surfaces, where ice sheet erosion has been minimal since their exposure. Fieldwork targeted surfaces with clear geomorphic indicators of glacial modification, such as striations, polish, and perched erratics, to ensure robust interpretations of exposure ages. Cosmogenic Nuclide Exposure Dating To reconstruct past ice sheet thickness and dynamics, we measured in situ-produced cosmogenic ^10Be and ^26Al concentrations in quartz-bearing rock samples. These radionuclides accumulate in the uppermost few meters of Earth's crust due to interactions with cosmic rays, making them effective tracers of surface exposure [1]. Quartz-rich rock samples were collected using hammer and chisel from surfaces presumed to have been exposed by ice retreat. Sampling heights were measured relative to modern ice levels using differential GPS, with submeter vertical precision, to constrain thinning histories. Sample preparation and cosmogenic nuclide analysis followed standard protocols [2]. Rocks were crushed, sieved, and processed for quartz isolation using chemical etching techniques, including repeated treatment with hydrofluoric and nitric acids. Purified quartz was dissolved, and ^10Be and ^26Al were extracted and purified using ion chromatography. The radionuclide concentrations were measured by accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) at the PRIME Lab facility at Purdue University. In addition to field samples, process blanks were analyzed to account for background contamination, and isotope ratios were normalized to the NIST SRM-4325 standard [3]. Exposure ages were calculated using the CRONUS-Earth online calculator (v3) [4], applying production rates corrected for scaling to high latitudes and elevations [5]. We used the Lal/Stone time-dependent scaling model [6] to incorporate changes in cosmic ray flux due to geomagnetic and solar variability. Uncertainties in exposure ages were calculated by propagating errors in AMS measurements, production rate calibrations, and assumptions about erosion rates. Ice Sheet Model Simulations Numerical simulations of the EAIS were conducted using the Parallel Ice Sheet Model (PISM) [7], a thermo-mechanically coupled ice sheet model that accounts for both shallow ice and shallow shelf approximations. PISM was selected for its capacity to simulate dynamic interactions between ice flow, basal conditions, and climatic forcing. The model domain encompassed the entirety of East Antarctica, with a horizontal resolution of 5 km to resolve key subglacial basins and ice streams. Model boundary conditions for the mid-Pliocene were derived from the PRISM4 (Pliocene Research, Interpretation, and Synoptic Mapping) dataset, which provides reconstructions of atmospheric and oceanic states during the mid-Piacenzian Warm Period (~3.3–3.0 Ma) [8]. Surface temperature and precipitation fields were interpolated from PRISM4 data, while basal heat flux was prescribed using the global geothermal heat flux dataset of Shapiro and Ritzwoller [9]. Oceanic boundary conditions were parameterized based on sea surface temperature reconstructions, which were used to calculate sub-ice shelf melting rates following the parameterization of Pollard and DeConto [10]. The model was initialized with present-day ice geometry and spun up for 10,000 years under modern climatic conditions to achieve thermal and dynamical equilibrium. Following spin-up, mid-Pliocene boundary conditions were imposed, and the model was run forward for 100,000 years to simulate the response of the EAIS to sustained warmth. Sensitivity tests were conducted to assess the effects of varying subglacial hydrology and basal sliding coefficients, as well as alternative reconstructions of mid-Pliocene temperatures and precipitation. Integration of Cosmogenic and Model Data To link cosmogenic exposure ages with modeled ice sheet dynamics, we compared observed exposure age constraints on ice thinning and thickening with simulated ice surface elevations. Exposure ages were grouped by elevation bands and compared to modeled ice sheet profiles along transects through the Wilkes and Aurora Subglacial Basins. This approach allowed us to assess whether observed exposure age patterns (e.g., clustering of ages at specific elevations) were consistent with modeled ice sheet thinning histories under mid-Pliocene conditions. Modeled ice volume changes were converted to equivalent sea level contributions for direct comparison with geological reconstructions of mid-Pliocene sea level [11]. Statistical and Analytical Methods To evaluate the robustness of cosmogenic exposure ages, we conducted statistical outlier detection using the Chauvenet criterion and assessed age clustering using kernel density estimates (KDEs). KDEs were used to identify periods of significant ice thinning or stability and were compared to modeled ice surface elevation changes to validate the timing and magnitude of ice dynamics. Exposure ages were further analyzed for evidence of inheritance or post-depositional nuclide production using ^10Be/^26Al ratios, assuming a steady-state erosion model [12]. Model outputs were analyzed using a combination of spatial and temporal metrics, including spatially explicit maps of ice thickness change, basal melt rates, and velocity fields. Sea level contributions were calculated by integrating modeled ice volume above flotation. Comparisons with independent geological and geophysical data (e.g., marine sediment records, subglacial topography) were used to validate model results and refine uncertainties in mid-Pliocene ice sheet reconstructions. Limitations We acknowledge several limitations in our approach. Cosmogenic exposure dating is sensitive to assumptions about erosion rates and nuclide inheritance, which can affect exposure age interpretations. Similarly, ice sheet model simulations are contingent on the accuracy of prescribed boundary conditions, particularly reconstructions of mid-Pliocene climate and ocean states. These limitations were addressed through sensitivity tests and comparison with independent datasets but remain sources of uncertainty in our reconstructions. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the sixth most common malignancy worldwide and the fourth leading cause of cancer-related mortality, accounting for approximately 8.3% of all cancer deaths. Its high mortality rate is attributed to late-stage diagnosis, limited treatment options, and the complex interplay of underlying liver dysfunction often associated with chronic liver diseases such as cirrhosis or viral hepatitis. Current therapeutic strategies for HCC are largely determined by tumor stage, liver function, and patient performance status, with curative options such as surgical resection, liver transplantation, and thermal ablation limited to patients with early-stage disease. For intermediate and advanced stages of HCC, treatment options are more constrained, and the prognosis remains poor, highlighting the urgent need for effective therapeutic approaches to improve patient outcomes. Transcatheter hepatic arterial chemoembolization (TACE) is widely regarded as the standard of care for patients with intermediate-stage HCC who are not candidates for curative therapies. TACE involves the selective delivery of chemotherapeutic agents directly to the hepatic artery supplying the tumor, followed by embolization to occlude the blood flow, enhancing local drug concentration and inducing ischemic necrosis of the tumor. Despite its efficacy in prolonging survival compared to best supportive care, TACE is not curative, and tumor recurrence or progression is common due to residual viable tumor cells and the development of angiogenic escape mechanisms. This has driven interest in combining TACE with systemic therapies, particularly molecularly targeted agents, to enhance its therapeutic efficacy. Sorafenib, an oral multikinase inhibitor, has been a cornerstone of systemic therapy for advanced HCC since the SHARP and Asia-Pacific trials demonstrated its ability to improve overall survival (OS) compared to placebo in patients with advanced disease. Sorafenib exerts its antitumor effects by targeting multiple signaling pathways involved in tumor proliferation and angiogenesis, including the vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGFR), platelet-derived growth factor receptor (PDGFR), and RAF kinase pathways. Given its antiangiogenic properties, sorafenib has been hypothesized to inhibit the angiogenic rebound that often occurs following TACE, thereby enhancing the efficacy of locoregional therapy and potentially improving clinical outcomes. The combination of TACE and sorafenib has been extensively investigated in preclinical studies and clinical trials, with the expectation that the synergistic effects of these modalities would translate into improved outcomes for patients with HCC. Several prospective studies and randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have been conducted to evaluate the impact of this combination on key clinical endpoints, including time to disease progression (TTP) and OS. Some studies have reported promising results, suggesting that TACE combined with sorafenib prolongs TTP and delays tumor progression compared to TACE alone. However, the reported benefits in OS have been inconsistent, with several trials failing to demonstrate a significant improvement in survival outcomes. Furthermore, the combination therapy is associated with a higher incidence of sorafenib-related adverse events, such as hand-foot skin reaction (HFSR), rash, fatigue, and diarrhea, which may limit its clinical utility and negatively impact patient quality of life. To date, the findings from individual RCTs on the efficacy and safety of TACE combined with sorafenib remain inconclusive, necessitating a comprehensive evaluation of the available evidence. Meta-analysis, as a powerful statistical tool, can synthesize data from multiple studies, providing a more robust assessment of the overall effects of this combination therapy. By pooling data from high-quality, randomized, double-blind controlled trials, we can gain deeper insights into the efficacy of TACE plus sorafenib in improving TTP and OS, as well as better understand the associated risks of adverse events. In this study, we conducted a meta-analysis of four double-blind, randomized controlled trials involving a total of 877 patients with HCC from 14 countries, including China and the United States. The primary objectives were to evaluate the impact of TACE combined with sorafenib on TTP and OS compared to TACE alone, and to assess the incidence of sorafenib-related adverse events, such as HFSR, rash, fatigue, diarrhea, and nausea. We hypothesized that the combination therapy would significantly improve TTP and OS, but that these benefits would come at the cost of an increased risk of adverse events. Understanding these trade-offs is critical for informing clinical decision-making and optimizing treatment strategies for patients with HCC. Our meta-analysis revealed that while TACE combined with sorafenib significantly increased TTP compared to TACE alone (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.82; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.69–0.97; p = 0.02), it did not result in a statistically significant improvement in OS (HR: 0.97; 95% CI: 0.72–1.29; p = 0.82). These findings highlight the potential of this combination therapy to delay disease progression but underscore its limited impact on long-term survival. Additionally, we observed that the experimental groups experienced significantly higher risks of sorafenib-related adverse events, with HFSR being the most pronounced (risk ratio [RR]: 5.93; 95% CI: 2.00–17.53; p = 0.001). These adverse events are important considerations, as they may contribute to treatment discontinuation and reduced patient adherence. In light of these findings, our study provides valuable evidence on the benefits and limitations of combining TACE with sorafenib for the treatment of HCC. While the addition of sorafenib to TACE can enhance disease control by prolonging TTP, the lack of improvement in OS and the increased risk of adverse events raise critical questions about the overall clinical utility of this approach. Further research is needed to explore strategies to mitigate adverse events, refine patient selection criteria, and identify biomarkers that can predict response to combination therapy. By addressing these challenges, we can better tailor treatment approaches to meet the needs of patients with HCC and improve their outcomes in a rapidly evolving therapeutic landscape. This meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. The aim was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of transcatheter hepatic arterial chemoembolization (TACE) combined with sorafenib compared to TACE alone or TACE combined with placebo in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Specifically, the outcomes of interest were time to disease progression (TTP), overall survival (OS), and the incidence of sorafenib-related adverse events, including hand and foot skin reactions (HFSR), rash, fatigue, diarrhea, and nausea. Search Strategy A comprehensive literature search was conducted to identify relevant randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated the combination of TACE and sorafenib for the treatment of HCC. We searched PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science databases up to October 2023. The search terms included a combination of the following keywords: “transcatheter hepatic arterial chemoembolization,” “TACE,” “sorafenib,” “hepatocellular carcinoma,” “HCC,” “randomized controlled trial,” “double-blind,” “time to progression,” “overall survival,” and “adverse events.” Boolean operators (AND, OR) were used to expand or narrow the search. No language restrictions were applied. In addition to the database searches, we manually screened the reference lists of relevant studies and review articles to identify additional studies that met the inclusion criteria. Conference abstracts and unpublished studies were excluded unless sufficient data were available to assess the outcomes of interest. Eligibility Criteria Studies were included if they met the following criteria: (1) double-blind, randomized controlled trial design; (2) participants diagnosed with HCC, regardless of the underlying etiology; (3) comparison of TACE combined with sorafenib (experimental group) versus TACE with placebo or TACE alone (control group); (4) reporting of at least one of the predefined outcomes, including TTP, OS, or adverse events; and (5) sufficient data available to calculate hazard ratios (HRs), risk ratios (RRs), and confidence intervals (CIs). Studies were excluded if they were non-randomized, single-arm, observational, or case-control studies, or if they involved patients with non-HCC liver malignancies. Data Extraction Two independent reviewers (Reviewer A and Reviewer B) screened the titles and abstracts of all identified studies for eligibility. Full-text articles were subsequently reviewed for studies that appeared to meet the inclusion criteria. Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer (Reviewer C) when necessary. Data were extracted using a standardized data collection form. The following information was collected from each study: first author, publication year, study design, study location, sample size, patient demographics, intervention details (TACE protocol, sorafenib dosage, and duration), control group characteristics, primary and secondary outcomes (TTP, OS, and adverse events), and follow-up duration. If outcome data were not directly reported, we contacted the corresponding authors of the studies to request additional information. Quality Assessment The methodological quality of the included RCTs was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. This tool evaluates potential biases in seven domains: random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other biases. Each domain was rated as low, high, or unclear risk of bias. Two reviewers independently conducted the quality assessment, and disagreements were resolved through consensus or consultation with a third reviewer. Statistical Analysis All statistical analyses were performed using Review Manager (RevMan) software (version 5.4, Cochrane Collaboration). Hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were used to analyze TTP and OS, while risk ratios (RRs) with 95% CIs were calculated for adverse events. For studies that did not directly report HRs or RRs, these values were estimated from Kaplan-Meier curves or raw data using established methods. A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Heterogeneity among studies was assessed using the I² statistic, where I² values of 0%-25%, 26%-50%, 51%-75%, and >75% were interpreted as indicating low, moderate, substantial, and considerable heterogeneity, respectively. A fixed-effects model was used for analyses with low heterogeneity (I² ≤ 50%), whereas a random-effects model was applied for analyses with substantial or considerable heterogeneity (I² > 50%). Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore potential sources of heterogeneity, particularly for the risk of HFSR. Publication bias was assessed visually using funnel plots for outcomes with at least 10 included studies. Egger’s test was performed to quantitatively evaluate asymmetry in the funnel plots. Outcomes of Interest The primary outcomes of interest were TTP and OS. TTP was defined as the time from randomization to radiologic progression of HCC, as assessed by the modified Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (mRECIST). OS was defined as the time from randomization to death from any cause. Secondary outcomes included the incidence of adverse events commonly associated with sorafenib, including HFSR, rash, fatigue, diarrhea, and nausea. Sensitivity Analysis Sensitivity analyses were conducted to evaluate the robustness of the findings by excluding studies with unclear or high risk of bias in key domains (e.g., random sequence generation, allocation concealment). Additional sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the impact of individual studies on the pooled estimates by sequentially excluding each study from the analysis. Ethical Considerations As this study was a meta-analysis of published data, no ethical approval was required. However, we adhered to ethical principles for systematic reviews, including transparency, reproducibility, and proper acknowledgment of original research studies. The meta-analysis included data from four randomized, double-blind controlled trials comprising a total of 877 patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) from 14 countries. The primary outcomes assessed were time to disease progression (TTP), overall survival (OS), and the incidence of sorafenib-related adverse events. Time to Disease Progression (TTP) The pooled analysis revealed a statistically significant improvement in TTP among patients in the experimental groups (TACE plus sorafenib) compared to those in the control groups (TACE plus placebo). The hazard ratio (HR) for TTP was 0.82 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.69–0.97; p = 0.02), indicating that the combination therapy was associated with a reduced risk of disease progression. This finding suggests that sorafenib, when combined with TACE, may enhance the effectiveness of local tumor control and delay disease progression. However, it is important to note that while the improvement in TTP was significant, the magnitude of the benefit was modest. Human action recognition (HAR) is a fundamental problem in computer vision with numerous applications, including video surveillance, human-computer interaction, and healthcare monitoring. Among the various modalities used for action recognition, skeleton-based approaches have gained significant attention due to their compact representation of human motion and robustness to environmental variations such as lighting and background clutter. Skeleton-based HAR relies on the spatiotemporal relationships of human body joints to model and recognize actions effectively. Graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have emerged as a powerful tool in this domain, as they can naturally encode the non-Euclidean structure of skeleton data and capture both spatial and temporal dependencies [1, 2]. Despite their success, traditional skeleton-based HAR models are often developed under the assumption of complete and noise-free skeleton data, an assumption that does not hold in real-world scenarios. In practical applications, skeleton data captured by depth sensors or pose estimation algorithms is frequently incomplete due to occlusions, self-occlusions, or errors in estimation. Certain joints may be missing or inaccurately localized, leading to noisy and incomplete skeleton representations. These issues significantly degrade the performance of existing HAR methods, as they rely heavily on the availability of all body joints to extract discriminative features. To address this challenge, a robust HAR model must be capable of effectively handling incomplete skeletons while maintaining competitive performance on complete data. However, achieving this robustness is non-trivial, as incomplete skeletons inherently contain missing structural information, which hampers the ability of traditional models to extract representative features. Existing approaches for handling incomplete skeletons in HAR can be broadly categorized into two groups: data preprocessing and model-level adaptation. Data preprocessing methods attempt to fill in the missing information using imputation techniques such as interpolation, matrix completion, or generative models [3, 4]. While these methods can improve the quality of the input data, they often introduce additional computational costs and may fail to accurately restore the original motion patterns, especially when a significant portion of the skeleton is missing. On the other hand, model-level adaptations aim to design algorithms that are inherently robust to missing data. For instance, some methods introduce attention mechanisms to weigh more reliable joints or propose graph modifications to account for incomplete connectivity [5, 6]. Although these methods achieve some degree of robustness, their performance remains constrained by the limited exploration of discriminative features in incomplete skeletons. In this work, we propose a novel approach to address the limitations of existing methods by leveraging the concept of multi-stream learning in graph convolutional networks. Specifically, we introduce the Richly Activated Graph Convolutional Network (RA-GCN), a multi-stream GCN framework designed to robustly recognize human actions from incomplete skeletons. The key idea behind RA-GCN is to iteratively activate discriminative features from unutilized or partially utilized joints across multiple streams by leveraging class activation maps (CAMs). Unlike traditional methods that rely on a single-pass feature extraction process, RA-GCN adopts a progressive feature discovery strategy, where each stream focuses on the joints that have not been fully activated in preceding streams. This richly activated mechanism ensures that the model explores a more comprehensive set of features distributed across all available joints, thereby enhancing its robustness to missing data. The motivation for our approach comes from the observation that in skeleton-based HAR, certain joints are more informative for specific actions than others. For example, hand joints are critical for recognizing actions like "waving" or "writing," whereas leg joints may be more relevant for actions like "kicking." However, in the presence of incomplete skeletons, relying solely on a fixed set of joints can lead to suboptimal performance, as some critical joints may be missing or noisy. By dynamically activating joints based on their contribution to the class-specific discriminative features, RA-GCN can adaptively focus on the most informative parts of the skeleton, even in the presence of occlusions or missing data. The RA-GCN consists of multiple interdependent streams, each equipped with a graph convolutional module and a class activation mechanism. The first stream processes the raw skeleton data and generates initial feature representations along with CAMs that highlight the most activated joints for each action class. Subsequent streams take the CAMs as input to identify unactivated joints, which are then prioritized for feature extraction in the next stage. This iterative process not only increases the number of activated joints but also ensures that the model captures complementary features from different parts of the skeleton. By the end of the multi-stream process, the RA-GCN has effectively aggregated rich features from all available joints, leading to improved robustness and discriminative power. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed RA-GCN, we conduct extensive experiments on both complete and incomplete skeleton data. Specifically, we utilize the NTU RGB+D dataset [7], a widely used benchmark for skeleton-based HAR, to demonstrate the competitive performance of RA-GCN on complete skeletons. Furthermore, we create a synthetic occlusion dataset by randomly masking joints in the NTU RGB+D dataset to simulate various levels of missing data. Experimental results show that RA-GCN significantly alleviates performance degradation caused by incomplete skeletons, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in terms of robustness to occlusion. These findings highlight the potential of RA-GCN as a practical solution for skeleton-based HAR in real-world scenarios. In summary, the contributions of this work are threefold. First, we introduce a novel multi-stream GCN framework that iteratively activates discriminative features from unutilized joints, enabling the model to handle incomplete skeletons more effectively. Second, we propose a richly activated mechanism based on class activation maps, which dynamically identifies and prioritizes unactivated joints for feature extraction. Third, we provide comprehensive experimental validation on both complete and incomplete skeleton datasets, demonstrating the superior robustness and performance of RA-GCN compared to existing methods. By addressing the challenges posed by incomplete skeletons, this work takes an important step toward the development of more reliable and practical HAR systems. This section describes the proposed Richly Activated Graph Convolutional Network (RA-GCN) for action recognition with incomplete skeletons. The RA-GCN framework is designed to enhance robustness against missing data by leveraging a multi-stream architecture that incrementally activates and extracts discriminative features from unutilized joints. The key components of the model, including skeleton representation, network architecture, and the multi-stream activation mechanism, are detailed below. 1. Skeleton Representation The input to the RA-GCN is a sequence of human skeletons, where each skeleton is represented as a graph \( G = (V, E) \). Here, \( V = \{v1, v2, \dots, vN\} \) denotes the set of \( N \) joints in the skeleton, and \( E \) represents the edges connecting the joints based on their physical connectivity. Each joint \( vi \) is associated with a feature vector \( xi \in \mathbb{R}^C \), where \( C \) represents the number of input channels (e.g., the 3D coordinates of the joint and potentially additional attributes). The graph structure is defined by an adjacency matrix \( A \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N} \), where \( A{ij} = 1 \) if joints \( vi \) and \( vj \) are connected and \( A{ij} = 0 \) otherwise. To model temporal dynamics, the skeleton graph is extended over time, forming a spatiotemporal graph. 2. Richly Activated Graph Convolutional Network The RA-GCN framework is built upon a multi-stream graph convolutional network architecture. Each stream is designed to focus on a subset of joints that remain unactivated in previous streams, ensuring a diverse and complementary learning process. The architecture is composed of the following components: 2.1 Graph Convolutional Layers Each stream in RA-GCN employs spatial graph convolutional layers to extract features from the skeleton graph. The graph convolution operation is defined as: \[ h^{(l+1)} = \sigma \left( \sum{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \frac{1}{Z{ij}} A{ij} h^{(l)} W^{(l)} \right), \] where \( h^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times Dl} \) is the node feature matrix at layer \( l \), \( W^{(l)} \) is the trainable weight matrix, \( \mathcal{N}(i) \) represents the neighbors of joint \( vi \), \( Z{ij} \) is a normalization factor, and \( \sigma \) denotes the activation function (e.g., ReLU). Temporal graph convolutions are also incorporated to capture motion dynamics across frames. 2.2 Multi-Stream Activation Mechanism Unlike traditional GCN-based approaches that process all joints simultaneously, RA-GCN employs a sequential activation strategy using multiple streams. For each stream, the network identifies currently unactivated joints based on a class activation map (CAM) generated by the preceding stream. The CAM provides a joint-level importance score for the input action, and joints with lower activation values are designated as unactivated. This mechanism ensures that each stream learns features from previously underutilized regions of the skeleton. Formally, let \( S^k \) denote the set of joints activated by the \( k \)-th stream. These joints are determined as: \[ S^k = \{ vi \mid \mathrm{CAM}i^k > \tau^k \}, \] where \( \mathrm{CAM}i^k \) is the activation value of joint \( vi \) in stream \( k \), and \( \tau^k \) is a threshold parameter. The unactivated joints \( U^k \) for the next stream are then defined as \( U^k = V \setminus S^k \). By iteratively applying this process, the RA-GCN progressively activates and learns features from all joints, including those that might be missing or occluded in earlier streams. 2.3 Feature Fusion and Classification The feature representations learned by individual streams are fused to generate a comprehensive description of the input skeleton sequence. Let \( f^k \in \mathbb{R}^{Dk} \) denote the feature vector output by the \( k \)-th stream. The fused feature vector \( f\text{fused} \) is obtained by concatenation: \[ f\text{fused} = \mathrm{Concat}(f^1, f^2, \dots, f^K), \] where \( K \) is the total number of streams. The fused feature vector is then passed through a fully connected layer followed by a softmax activation to produce the final action class probabilities. 3. Synthetic Occlusion Strategy To evaluate the robustness of RA-GCN under incomplete skeleton data, we introduce a synthetic occlusion strategy during training and testing. Specifically, a random subset of joints is masked out in each skeleton frame, simulating real-world scenarios where sensors fail to capture certain joints due to occlusions or noise. The occluded joints are replaced with zero values or interpolated based on neighboring joints. This augmentation forces the model to rely on global and contextual information rather than individual joints, improving its generalization to incomplete skeletons. 4. Implementation Details 4.1 Training Procedure The RA-GCN is trained using a cross-entropy loss function. Let \( y \) denote the ground-truth action label and \( \hat{y} \) denote the predicted class probabilities. The loss is defined as: \[ \mathcal{L} = - \sum{c=1}^C yc \log(\hat{y}c), \] where \( C \) is the total number of action classes. The model is optimized using the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of \( 0.001 \), which is decayed by a factor of \( 0.1 \) after every 10 epochs. Batch normalization and dropout are applied after each graph convolutional layer to prevent overfitting. 4.2 Datasets The RA-GCN is evaluated on two datasets: the NTU RGB+D dataset [1], which provides complete skeleton sequences, and a synthetic occlusion dataset derived from NTU RGB+D by applying the occlusion strategy described above. The NTU RGB+D dataset includes 60 action classes and 56,880 skeleton sequences, while the synthetic dataset introduces varying levels of missing joint data. 4.3 Hyperparameter Settings The number of streams \( K \) is set to 3, and the threshold \( \tau^k \) for CAM-based activation is empirically determined as 0.5. The adjacency matrix \( A \) is normalized using the symmetric normalization technique, \( \hat{A} = D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2} \), where \( D \) is the diagonal degree matrix. --- In summary, the RA-GCN framework leverages a multi-stream architecture with CAM-based activation and feature fusion to improve the robustness of action recognition models against incomplete skeletons. Early childhood trauma is a pervasive issue with profound and long-lasting effects on mental health, interpersonal relationships, and self-perception. Research has consistently demonstrated that adverse experiences in early life—such as neglect, physical abuse, emotional maltreatment, or sexual abuse—are associated with a wide range of psychological sequelae, including post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, and dissociative symptoms [1, 2]. However, one critical yet underexplored domain of impact is the way early trauma disrupts an individual’s relationship with their own body. The body, as both a physical and symbolic entity, plays a central role in how individuals experience themselves and the world. Early trauma may fundamentally alter this relationship, leading to enduring difficulties in body experience. The concept of body experience encompasses several interrelated dimensions. Broadly, it reflects how individuals perceive, evaluate, and relate to their physical self. Key domains include body attitude, which refers to individuals’ overall evaluation of their body; body satisfaction, which captures the extent to which individuals feel content or dissatisfied with specific aspects of their physical self; and body awareness, which concerns the ability to accurately perceive and attune to bodily sensations and needs [3]. Each of these domains is shaped by developmental processes and interpersonal experiences, making them particularly vulnerable to disruption in the context of early trauma. Evidence suggests that exposure to trauma in early life disrupts the development of a coherent and positive body experience. Negative messages about the body, invasive or harmful physical experiences, and the erosion of physical safety during formative years may all contribute to a fractured relationship with the body [4]. For instance, survivors of early trauma often report feelings of shame, disgust, or detachment regarding their physical selves, which may manifest in distorted body image, chronic dissatisfaction with appearance, or difficulties interpreting bodily cues [5]. This disruption is not merely psychological; trauma may also impair the brain-body connection, impacting interoceptive awareness and the regulation of physiological states [6]. These impairments are particularly concerning given that a healthy body experience is foundational for self-esteem, emotional regulation, and overall well-being. Despite the critical role of body experience in the aftermath of trauma, relatively few studies have systematically examined the specific ways in which early trauma disrupts distinct domains of body experience. Furthermore, the relationship between body experience and other trauma-related symptoms, such as the severity of PTSD or the frequency of dissociation, remains poorly understood. Dissociation, which involves disruptions in the integration of thoughts, feelings, and bodily sensations, is particularly relevant in this context. It is a common response to trauma and may further exacerbate difficulties in maintaining a coherent and connected relationship with the body [7]. However, existing research has often treated body experience and dissociation as separate constructs, with limited attention to their potential interdependence. To address these gaps, the present study sought to systematically investigate disturbances in body experience among women with a history of early childhood trauma. Specifically, we aimed to examine three domains of body experience—body attitude, body satisfaction, and body awareness—in a clinical sample of women with complex trauma. By comparing results to a non-clinical control sample, this study provides insight into the extent to which trauma uniquely impacts each domain. Additionally, we explored whether these disturbances were associated with the severity of trauma symptoms and the frequency of dissociation, aiming to elucidate potential pathways through which trauma affects the body. Our focus on women with early childhood trauma is particularly important, given the gendered nature of trauma-related experiences and their expression. Women are disproportionately likely to experience certain forms of trauma, such as sexual abuse, and are also more likely to develop trauma-related conditions such as PTSD [8]. Furthermore, cultural and societal pressures on women’s bodies are pervasive, shaping body image and satisfaction in ways that may amplify the impact of trauma [9]. By centering women in this investigation, we aim to contribute to a nuanced understanding of how early trauma interacts with gendered experiences to shape body-related outcomes. This study builds on prior research by employing validated measures to assess body attitude, body satisfaction, and body awareness, thereby providing a comprehensive evaluation of body experience. Body attitude was assessed using the Dresden Body Image Questionnaire, a widely used tool that captures individuals’ overall evaluations of their bodies, including feelings of acceptance or aversion. Body satisfaction was measured with the Body Cathexis Scale, which evaluates contentment with specific body parts and functions. Finally, body awareness was assessed with the Somatic Awareness Questionnaire, which measures attentiveness to internal bodily sensations and physiological cues. By employing these tools, we aimed to capture a multidimensional view of body experience, recognizing that different domains may be differentially affected by trauma. To quantify the severity of trauma and dissociative symptoms, participants in the clinical sample completed the Davidson Trauma Scale and the Dissociation Experience Scale, respectively. These measures allowed us to evaluate potential associations between body experience and trauma-related symptomatology, addressing questions about whether greater symptom severity or more frequent dissociation exacerbates difficulties in body experience. The inclusion of a non-clinical comparison group further allowed us to contextualize the findings and determine the extent to which disturbances in body experience are specific to trauma rather than reflective of broader societal factors. In summary, this study sought to advance understanding of the relationship between early childhood trauma and body experience by addressing three key questions: (1) How do body attitude, body satisfaction, and body awareness differ between women with complex trauma and a non-clinical sample? (2) To what extent are these domains of body experience associated with the severity of trauma symptoms? (3) What is the relationship between body experience and dissociative symptoms? By addressing these questions, we aim to highlight the importance of assessing and addressing body-related disturbances in trauma treatment and to stimulate further research on this critical but underexamined aspect of trauma recovery. The study employed a cross-sectional design to investigate the impact of early childhood trauma on three domains of body experience—body attitude, body satisfaction, and body awareness—in a clinical sample of women with complex trauma. Furthermore, the study sought to explore the relationships between these domains of body experience and the severity of trauma symptoms as well as the frequency of dissociative symptoms. Below, the participants, measures, and procedures used in the study are described in detail. Participants The study included two distinct groups of adult women: a clinical sample of 50 female patients with a history of early childhood trauma and a non-clinical comparison group of 216 women without reported trauma history. Participants in the clinical sample were recruited from a specialized outpatient trauma therapy clinic in Germany. Eligibility criteria for this group included: (1) being female, (2) aged between 18 and 65 years, (3) a confirmed diagnosis of complex trauma-related disorders, and (4) a documented history of early childhood trauma, defined as trauma occurring before the age of 12. Exclusion criteria included active psychotic symptoms, intellectual disability, or inability to provide informed consent. Participants in the non-clinical sample were recruited through convenience sampling from the general population via online advertisements and university mailing lists. Inclusion criteria for the non-clinical group required participants to have no history of trauma or psychiatric diagnoses, as assessed through self-report. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants, and the study was approved by the local ethics committee. Measures Body attitude, body satisfaction, and body awareness were assessed using validated instruments. Body attitude was measured with the Dresden Body Image Questionnaire (DBIQ), a 35-item self-report measure designed to assess subjective attitudes toward one’s body. The DBIQ includes subscales such as body acceptance, vitality, and physical self-concept, with higher scores indicating more negative body attitudes [1]. Body satisfaction was evaluated using the Body Cathexis Scale (BCS), a 40-item questionnaire that assesses satisfaction with specific body parts and functions. Items are rated on a 5-point Likert scale, with lower scores reflecting higher dissatisfaction [2]. Body awareness was measured using the Somatic Awareness Questionnaire (SAQ), a 25-item scale designed to assess the degree to which individuals notice and attend to internal bodily sensations. Higher scores on the SAQ indicate greater body awareness [3]. All measures were translated into German and back-translated by bilingual experts to ensure linguistic and conceptual equivalence. To assess the severity of trauma symptoms, participants in the clinical sample completed the Davidson Trauma Scale (DTS), a 17-item self-report measure of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms based on DSM-IV criteria. The DTS assesses the frequency and severity of trauma-related symptoms over the past week, with higher scores indicating greater symptom severity [4]. Dissociative symptoms were measured using the Dissociation Experience Scale (DES), a 28-item self-report instrument assessing the frequency of dissociative experiences, including depersonalization, derealization, and amnesia. Scores range from 0 to 100, with higher scores reflecting more frequent dissociative symptoms [5]. Procedure Participants in the clinical sample were invited to complete the study questionnaires as part of their routine psychological assessment prior to beginning trauma-focused therapy. These assessments were administered by trained clinicians during individual sessions in a private setting. Participants were informed that their participation in the research was voluntary and that declining to participate would not affect their treatment. The non-clinical sample completed the same set of body experience measures (DBIQ, BCS, and SAQ) via an online survey platform. To ensure the validity of self-reported data, participants were required to confirm that they met the inclusion criteria for the non-clinical group. Data from incomplete surveys were excluded from the analysis. Statistical Analysis Data were analyzed using SPSS version 27.0. Descriptive statistics were calculated to summarize participant demographics and mean scores on all measures. Independent samples t-tests were conducted to compare scores on the DBIQ, BCS, and SAQ between the clinical and non-clinical groups. Effect sizes were calculated using Cohen’s d, with thresholds of 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 indicating small, medium, and large effects, respectively [6]. Within the clinical sample, Pearson correlation coefficients were computed to examine the relationships between the three domains of body experience (body attitude, body satisfaction, and body awareness) and both trauma symptom severity (DTS scores) and dissociative symptom frequency (DES scores). Correlation coefficients were interpreted based on guidelines proposed by Cohen, with values of 0.10–0.29 indicating a small correlation, 0.30–0.49 a medium correlation, and 0.50 or above a large correlation [6]. Missing data were handled using pairwise deletion to maximize the available data for each analysis. Assumptions of normality, linearity, and homoscedasticity were checked prior to conducting statistical tests. For all analyses, a p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Bonferroni correction was applied to control for multiple comparisons where appropriate. Ethical Considerations Ethical approval for the study was obtained from the institutional review board of the university affiliated with the outpatient trauma clinic. All participants provided written informed consent before participation. Confidentiality and anonymity were ensured by assigning unique numerical identifiers to participant data. Participants in the clinical sample were offered the opportunity to discuss the results of their assessments with their clinicians, while participants in the non-clinical sample were debriefed via email upon completion of the study.
