Diabetic macular edema (DME) is a leading cause of vision impairment in patients with diabetic retinopathy, which remains a critical global health challenge due to the rising prevalence of diabetes mellitus [1, 2]. The pathophysiology of DME involves the disruption of the blood-retinal barrier, leading to vascular leakage and macular thickening, which ultimately compromises central vision [3]. The management of DME has been revolutionized by the introduction of intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) agents. Ranibizumab, a monoclonal antibody fragment targeting VEGF-A, has demonstrated efficacy in reducing macular edema and improving visual acuity in numerous clinical trials [4, 5]. Despite these advances, the treatment of DME becomes increasingly complex in the context of cataract surgery, as the surgical procedure itself can exacerbate retinal inflammation and potentially worsen macular edema [6, 7]. Cataract surgery is one of the most commonly performed ophthalmic procedures worldwide and significantly improves visual outcomes in patients with advanced cataracts. However, in diabetic patients with coexisting DME, the inflammatory response associated with phacoemulsification can lead to increased vascular permeability and worsening macular thickening, thereby hampering visual recovery [8, 9]. This highlights the need for an optimized perioperative strategy to manage DME in such patients. Anti-VEGF therapy has been proposed as an adjunctive approach to mitigate the risk of exacerbation of DME during the perioperative period, but the timing of administration remains a matter of ongoing debate [10]. The timing of intravitreal ranibizumab injections—whether administered preoperatively, intraoperatively, or postoperatively—may influence its therapeutic efficacy in the perioperative setting. Preoperative administration has the theoretical advantage of reducing baseline macular edema and stabilizing the retinal microenvironment prior to the inflammatory insult of surgery [11]. Conversely, intraoperative injection offers the potential for immediate delivery of the anti-VEGF agent at the time of surgical intervention, potentially counteracting the concurrent inflammatory response [12]. Postoperative administration, on the other hand, targets the inflammatory cascade initiated by surgery and may be particularly beneficial in addressing any delayed exacerbation of macular edema [13]. While each of these approaches has theoretical benefits, their comparative effectiveness in clinical practice remains insufficiently characterized. Previous studies investigating the role of anti-VEGF agents in the context of cataract surgery for diabetic patients with DME have yielded mixed results, with some suggesting a benefit from perioperative injections while others indicate limited or transient effects [14–16]. For instance, a randomized controlled trial by Chen et al. demonstrated that intravitreal ranibizumab administered preoperatively reduced the risk of worsening macular edema post-surgery, whereas other studies have reported no significant differences in outcomes based on the timing of injection [17, 18]. These discrepancies underscore the need for further research to identify the optimal timing of anti-VEGF therapy to maximize visual and anatomical outcomes in this patient population. The present study aims to address this gap in knowledge by systematically comparing the efficacy of preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative intravitreal ranibizumab injections in patients undergoing cataract surgery with coexisting DME. Specifically, this study evaluates changes in visual acuity and central foveal thickness (FT), both of which are critical metrics for assessing treatment efficacy. The hypothesis is that the timing of ranibizumab administration may differentially influence postoperative outcomes, particularly in the context of the inflammatory and vascular changes observed following cataract surgery. In addition to its clinical relevance, this investigation has implications for the broader understanding of the interplay between DME pathophysiology and surgical interventions. By elucidating the temporal dynamics of anti-VEGF therapy in the perioperative period, the findings of this study may inform evidence-based guidelines for the management of diabetic patients with coexisting macular edema and cataracts. Moreover, the results may contribute to a growing body of literature aimed at optimizing combination therapies for complex retinal conditions, thereby advancing the standard of care for a vulnerable patient population. To achieve these objectives, the study employs a robust methodological framework involving a prospective cohort of patients with advanced cataracts and DME undergoing uneventful phacoemulsification surgery. Patients were stratified into three groups based on the timing of intravitreal ranibizumab injection—two weeks preoperatively, intraoperatively, and two weeks postoperatively—and were followed for a three-month postoperative period. Visual acuity and FT were assessed at baseline, one week, one month, and three months postoperatively to capture both immediate and longer-term outcomes. By incorporating a structured follow-up protocol and well-defined outcome measures, the study seeks to provide a comprehensive evaluation of the relative benefits of each treatment strategy. In summary, the management of DME in the context of cataract surgery remains a significant clinical challenge due to the interplay between surgical inflammation and diabetic retinal disease. While intravitreal ranibizumab has emerged as an effective therapy for DME in general, its role and optimal timing in the perioperative period warrant further investigation. By systematically comparing preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative ranibizumab administration, this study aims to contribute to the evidence base for individualized treatment strategies that optimize visual and anatomical outcomes in diabetic patients undergoing cataract surgery. Study Design and Ethics This study was designed as a prospective, comparative, interventional clinical trial conducted between [dates] at [institution name]. Approval was obtained from the Institutional Review Board (IRB) and adhered to the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to enrollment, and the nature of the study, including potential risks and benefits, was thoroughly explained. Patients were recruited consecutively based on inclusion and exclusion criteria outlined below. Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria Participants included in the study were patients diagnosed with both advanced cataract and diabetic macular edema (DME), confirmed via clinical examination and optical coherence tomography (OCT). Inclusion criteria were as follows: age ≥ 40 years, presence of center-involving DME with a central macular thickness (CMT) ≥ 300 μm as measured by spectral-domain OCT, and a cataract deemed visually significant with a best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 20/50 or worse. Patients were excluded if they had a history of any previous intraocular surgery, ocular trauma, or retinal photocoagulation within the last six months. Additional exclusion criteria included proliferative diabetic retinopathy requiring active treatment, any significant media opacities (other than cataract), glaucoma or uncontrolled intraocular pressure (IOP), and systemic conditions such as uncontrolled hypertension or active infections. Patients with poor glycemic control, defined as HbA1c ≥ 10%, were also excluded. Randomization and Group Allocation Eligible patients were randomized into three study groups using a computer-generated randomization protocol to ensure allocation concealment. Randomization was performed in a 1:1:1 ratio. Group 1 received a single intravitreal ranibizumab injection (0.5 mg in 0.05 mL) two weeks preoperatively, Group 2 received the same dose intraoperatively at the conclusion of phacoemulsification surgery, and Group 3 received one injection two weeks postoperatively. All injections were performed by the same experienced retinal specialist to minimize procedural variability. Surgical Procedure All patients underwent uneventful phacoemulsification cataract surgery performed under local anesthesia by the same surgeon to standardize surgical outcomes. A 2.2-mm clear corneal incision was created, and the cataract was removed using a standard phacoemulsification technique. A foldable posterior chamber intraocular lens was implanted in the capsular bag. The intraoperative ranibizumab injection in Group 2 was administered immediately after lens implantation and prior to wound hydration, ensuring appropriate aseptic technique. Intravitreal Ranibizumab Injection Technique Intravitreal injections were performed under sterile conditions in an outpatient setting. The injection site was prepared with 5% povidone-iodine, and a sterile lid speculum was used to maintain eyelid separation. Ranibizumab was injected into the vitreous cavity through the pars plana, 3.5–4.0 mm posterior to the limbus, using a 30-gauge needle. Following the injection, patients were instructed to apply topical antibiotics for five days. Post-injection IOP was measured after 30 minutes to monitor for transient elevation. Patients were advised to report any symptoms suggestive of endophthalmitis, such as persistent pain or decreased vision. Follow-Up Examinations Follow-up evaluations were conducted at 1 week, 1 month, and 3 months postoperatively. At each visit, a comprehensive ophthalmic examination was performed, including BCVA measurement using the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) chart, slit-lamp biomicroscopy, IOP measurement using Goldmann applanation tonometry, and dilated fundus examination. CMT was defined as the average thickness of the central 1-mm subfield, while FT was defined as the thickness at the central fovea. Outcome Measures The primary outcome measure was the change in FT from baseline to the 3-month follow-up. Secondary outcome measures included changes in BCVA, incidence of postoperative complications such as macular edema exacerbation or intraocular inflammation, and safety parameters, including cases of endophthalmitis or retinal detachment. Statistical Analysis Data were analyzed using SPSS software (version [number], [manufacturer]). Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD), and categorical variables were presented as percentages. Normality of the data was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Assuming a mean difference of 40 μm in FT reduction between groups with a standard deviation of 35 μm, a power of 80%, and a significance level of 0.05, the required sample size was determined to be 18 eyes per group. To account for potential dropouts, a total of 60 eyes (20 per group) were initially enrolled. Safety Monitoring Adverse events were recorded at each visit. In cases of significant post-injection inflammation, additional topical corticosteroid therapy was prescribed. Serious adverse events, including endophthalmitis, retinal detachment, or persistent elevated IOP requiring intervention, were managed according to standard clinical protocols and documented accordingly. Parkinson’s Disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by motor symptoms such as tremors, rigidity, bradykinesia, and postural instability, as well as non-motor symptoms including cognitive impairment, mood disorders, and autonomic dysfunction [1]. Affecting tens of millions of individuals worldwide, PD poses significant challenges in its diagnosis, monitoring, and personalized treatment due to its heterogeneity and overlapping symptomatology with other neurodegenerative conditions [2]. The pathological hallmark of PD is the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, leading to a cascade of functional and structural alterations in brain networks [3]. Consequently, the identification of reliable biomarkers for PD diagnosis and progression monitoring has become a central focus of research in recent years. In the pursuit of understanding PD, neuroimaging has emerged as a critical tool, enabling researchers to investigate structural, functional, and metabolic changes in the brain. Modalities such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), functional MRI (fMRI), diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), and positron emission tomography (PET) provide complementary information about the brain's anatomy, connectivity, and activity [4]. While these neuroimaging techniques have advanced our understanding of PD, they also present challenges in data integration and analysis due to their high dimensionality and modality-specific characteristics. Traditional statistical approaches, such as principal component analysis (PCA) and linear discriminant analysis (LDA), have been applied in neuroimaging studies to reduce dimensionality and identify discriminative features. However, these methods often fall short in capturing the complex, non-linear relationships inherent in neuroimaging data, leading to suboptimal predictive performance [5]. In recent years, the advent of machine learning and deep learning techniques has revolutionized the field of neuroimaging analysis. These approaches have demonstrated superior capabilities in modeling complex, high-dimensional data and uncovering latent patterns that are not readily apparent through traditional methods [6]. Among these techniques, Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have garnered significant attention due to their ability to model structured data, such as brain connectivity networks, in a manner that preserves spatial and topological relationships [7]. GCNs extend traditional convolutional operations to non-Euclidean domains, enabling the analysis of graph-structured data, which is particularly relevant for neuroimaging. In the context of PD, GCNs offer a unique opportunity to integrate multi-modal neuroimaging data and capture the intricate interactions between different brain regions and modalities. Multi-modal neuroimaging fusion has become an increasingly important area of research, as no single modality can comprehensively capture the full spectrum of pathological changes associated with PD [8]. Structural MRI provides information about gray matter atrophy and white matter integrity, while fMRI reveals functional connectivity alterations. DTI, on the other hand, characterizes microstructural changes in white matter tracts, and PET imaging offers insights into metabolic and dopaminergic deficits [9]. The integration of these modalities has the potential to improve the accuracy of PD diagnosis and facilitate a more holistic understanding of disease progression. However, the fusion of multi-modal neuroimaging data is not trivial, as it involves challenges related to data heterogeneity, alignment, and the curse of dimensionality. Traditional feature-level or decision-level fusion approaches often fail to leverage the complementary nature of multi-modal data, resulting in suboptimal performance [10]. To address these limitations, this study proposes a novel deep learning framework based on GCNs for the fusion of multi-modal neuroimaging data in the context of PD analysis. Unlike conventional approaches that treat each modality independently or rely on simplistic fusion strategies, our method exploits the graph-based representation of brain networks to model inter-regional and inter-modal relationships. By incorporating both structural and functional connectivity information, the proposed GCN framework learns a unified representation that captures the complex interactions between different brain regions and imaging modalities. This approach not only enhances the predictive power of the model but also provides insights into the underlying neural mechanisms of PD. The efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated on the Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) cohort, a widely used dataset in PD research that includes comprehensive neuroimaging, clinical, and biomarker data [11]. Using the PPMI cohort, the GCN-based model achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.9537 ± 0.0587 in distinguishing PD cases from healthy controls, significantly outperforming traditional methods such as PCA, which achieved an AUC of 0.6443 ± 0.0223. These results highlight the potential of GCNs to transform neuroimaging analysis and advance the development of robust biomarkers for PD diagnosis. This work contributes to the growing body of literature on deep learning applications in neuroimaging by introducing a novel framework for multi-modal data fusion in PD analysis. The findings underscore the importance of leveraging advanced machine learning techniques to address the challenges posed by the complexity and heterogeneity of neuroimaging data. Furthermore, the proposed method offers a scalable and generalizable approach that can be extended to other neurodegenerative diseases, paving the way for future research in this domain. In the following sections, we will provide a detailed description of the proposed GCN framework, including its architectural design, data preprocessing steps, and training procedures. We will also present a comprehensive evaluation of the model's performance, along with an analysis of its interpretability and clinical relevance. By bridging the gap between computational neuroscience and clinical research, this study aims to contribute to the early detection and personalized management of PD, ultimately improving patient outcomes and quality of life. To address the challenges of Parkinson’s Disease (PD) diagnosis and progression modeling using neuroimaging data, we developed a novel multi-view Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) framework capable of integrating multiple neuroimaging modalities. This method leverages the representational power of GCNs to learn meaningful relationships between imaging-derived features, thereby improving the prediction accuracy for distinguishing PD cases from controls. The following section details the dataset, preprocessing steps, and model architecture, as well as the training and evaluation protocols employed in this study. Dataset and Imaging Modalities We utilized data from the Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI), a publicly available dataset designed to support PD research [1]. The PPMI cohort used in this study comprised individuals diagnosed with PD and healthy controls. For each subject, we collected multimodal neuroimaging data, including structural magnetic resonance imaging (sMRI), diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), and functional MRI (fMRI). These modalities were chosen due to their complementary roles in assessing structural, white matter connectivity, and functional alterations in the brain, respectively. Preprocessing To ensure the quality and uniformity of the input neuroimaging data, we conducted a standardized preprocessing pipeline for each modality. For sMRI data, preprocessing included skull stripping, spatial normalization to the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space, intensity normalization, and segmentation into gray matter, white matter, and cerebrospinal fluid using the Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM12) software [2]. For DTI, we applied eddy current correction and motion correction, followed by extraction of fractional anisotropy (FA) maps as a summary metric of white matter integrity. Finally, for fMRI data, preprocessing included slice timing correction, motion correction, spatial normalization, and temporal filtering to remove low-frequency drift. Functional connectivity matrices were derived using Pearson correlation between predefined regions of interest (ROIs) based on the Automated Anatomical Labeling (AAL) atlas [3]. All processed data were downsampled to a uniform resolution and aligned across modalities to ensure voxel-wise correspondence. Graph Construction To enable the application of GCNs, we modeled the brain as a graph where nodes correspond to ROIs, and edges represent relationships between them. Features for each node were derived from the multimodal imaging data. Specifically, for each ROI, we extracted gray matter volume from sMRI, FA values from DTI, and average functional connectivity strength from fMRI. These features were concatenated to form a unified representation for each node. The edge weights in the graph were defined based on pairwise functional connectivity between ROIs, thresholded to retain only significant connections, thereby emphasizing biologically meaningful interactions while reducing noise. The resulting adjacency matrix was normalized to ensure numerical stability during the GCN training process [4]. Multi-View Graph Convolutional Network Architecture Our proposed method integrates information from multiple neuroimaging modalities using a multi-view GCN framework. Each imaging modality was treated as a distinct view, with its own graph representation. The architecture consisted of three primary components: (1) modality-specific GCN layers, (2) a feature fusion mechanism, and (3) a fully connected classification layer. Modality-Specific GCN Layers For each imaging modality, we implemented a separate GCN branch to process the corresponding graph. The GCN layers propagated information between connected nodes based on the graph structure, enabling the network to capture inter-regional dependencies. Each GCN layer applied the following operation: \[ H^{(l+1)} = \sigma(\tilde{A}H^{(l)}W^{(l)}) \] where \(H^{(l)}\) is the node feature matrix at layer \(l\), \(\tilde{A}\) is the normalized adjacency matrix, \(W^{(l)}\) is the learnable weight matrix, and \(\sigma\) is the activation function (ReLU in our case). The output of the final GCN layer for each modality represented a high-level embedding of the brain graph. Feature Fusion To combine information across modalities, we employed a learnable attention mechanism that adaptively weighted the modality-specific embeddings. Let \(Zm\) denote the graph embedding for modality \(m\). The fused representation \(Zf\) was computed as: \[ Zf = \sum{m=1}^{M} \alpham Zm \] where \(\alpham\) is the attention weight for modality \(m\), learned during training through backpropagation. This mechanism allowed the model to emphasize more informative modalities for each prediction task. Classification Layer The fused embedding \(Zf\) was flattened and passed through a fully connected layer with a softmax activation function to predict the probability of PD diagnosis. Dropout was applied after the fusion step to prevent overfitting, and the network was trained using the binary cross-entropy loss function. Training and Evaluation The model was trained using a stratified 5-fold cross-validation approach to ensure robustness and generalizability. For each fold, the dataset was split into 80% training and 20% testing subsets. The training dataset was further divided into training and validation sets (90:10 ratio) to tune hyperparameters. Optimization was performed using the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of \(1 \times 10^{-4}\) and a weight decay of \(5 \times 10^{-4}\) [5]. Early stopping was applied based on validation loss to prevent overfitting. To evaluate the model’s performance, we computed the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC) for each fold and reported the mean and standard deviation across folds. Statistical significance of the results was assessed by comparing our method’s AUC with that of traditional dimensionality reduction approaches such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) using a paired t-test. Implementation The model was implemented in Python using the PyTorch Geometric library for GCN layers and associated operations [6]. All experiments were conducted on a workstation equipped with an NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU, enabling efficient training and evaluation of the network. The advent of high-throughput RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) has revolutionized transcriptomic research by enabling the comprehensive analysis of gene expression across various biological and experimental conditions. Differential expression (DE) analysis, which aims to identify genes with significant changes in expression levels between conditions, is one of the most widely employed applications of RNA-seq. As experimental designs become increasingly complex, with multiple treatment conditions and intricate biological hypotheses, there is a growing need for statistical methods that can flexibly and robustly accommodate such complexity. Traditional methods for DE analysis, while effective in simpler scenarios, often struggle with scalability and statistical power when extended to datasets with multiple treatment conditions. Challenges in DE Analysis with Multiple Conditions Existing statistical frameworks for DE analysis, such as edgeR [1] and DESeq2 [2], have been extensively validated and are widely adopted in the field. These methods rely on generalized linear models (GLMs) to model RNA-seq count data, incorporating dispersion estimates to account for biological variability. However, their performance can degrade when faced with multi-condition experimental designs. Specifically, the inclusion of multiple treatment conditions introduces additional parameters into the model, which leads to a higher number of degrees of freedom and a corresponding loss of statistical power. This issue is particularly pronounced in scenarios where the number of samples per condition is limited, a common constraint in large-scale studies due to financial and logistical considerations. Moreover, the presence of multiple conditions necessitates the testing of more complex null hypotheses, such as whether a gene is differentially expressed across any of the conditions, as opposed to a simple pairwise comparison. Traditional methods address this challenge by applying either likelihood ratio tests or Wald tests, both of which can suffer from reduced sensitivity when the number of conditions increases. The lack of specialized tools to efficiently handle such multi-condition scenarios has resulted in an unmet need for methodologies that not only improve statistical power but also maintain computational efficiency and interpretability. Limitations of Current Approaches Several extensions to existing methods have been proposed to address the limitations of DE analysis with multiple conditions. For instance, some approaches rely on hierarchical modeling frameworks to borrow information across conditions, thereby improving parameter estimation [3]. Others incorporate shrinkage-based regularization techniques to reduce the dimensionality of the parameter space [4]. While these methods have shown promise, they often involve computationally intensive procedures and rely on strong parametric assumptions, which can lead to biases if the underlying data distributions deviate from these assumptions. Furthermore, many of these methods fail to adequately address the issue of multiple testing, which becomes increasingly problematic as the number of conditions grows. In addition to statistical challenges, the interpretation of results from multi-condition DE analysis remains a significant bottleneck. The interaction terms introduced in multi-condition models are often difficult to interpret biologically, particularly when the degrees of freedom associated with these terms are high. This lack of interpretability can hinder downstream analyses, such as pathway enrichment or gene network reconstruction, which require clear definitions of gene-condition associations. Motivation for the Development of multiDE To address the aforementioned challenges, we propose a novel statistical method, multiDE, designed specifically for DE analysis in RNA-seq datasets with multiple treatment conditions. The development of multiDE was motivated by the need to balance statistical power, computational efficiency, and biological interpretability in multi-condition experimental designs. The key innovation of multiDE lies in its dimension-reduced modeling framework, which simplifies the interaction between genes and conditions while preserving the essential features of the data. Unlike traditional methods, multiDE employs a log-linear model in which the interaction term between gene and condition is decomposed into its first-order components. This decomposition reduces the degrees of freedom associated with the interaction term to one, thereby mitigating the loss of statistical power that typically accompanies multi-condition analyses. By focusing on a single degree of freedom for testing, multiDE not only enhances sensitivity but also simplifies the interpretation of results, as the association between a gene and a condition is quantified using a single parameter. Objectives and Contributions The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the performance of multiDE in the context of RNA-seq datasets with multiple treatment conditions. Specifically, we aim to demonstrate that multiDE achieves superior statistical power compared to benchmark methods, particularly as the number of conditions increases. Additionally, we seek to establish that multiDE produces biologically meaningful results, as evidenced by its ability to identify genes with well-documented roles in the biological systems under investigation. The contributions of this study are threefold. First, we introduce a novel dimension-reduced statistical framework for DE analysis that directly addresses the challenges posed by multi-condition experimental designs. Second, we conduct extensive simulation studies to benchmark the performance of multiDE against state-of-the-art methods, including edgeR and DESeq2, under a variety of scenarios, including those involving model misspecification. Third, we apply multiDE to two real-world RNA-seq datasets, demonstrating its ability to uncover biologically relevant insights that are either missed or less pronounced in traditional analyses. Organization of the Paper The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In the Methods section, we describe the statistical framework underlying multiDE, detailing the log-linear model, the dimension-reduction strategy, and the hypothesis testing procedure. In the Results section, we present the findings from simulation studies and real-data applications, highlighting the advantages of multiDE in terms of statistical power, robustness, and biological interpretability. The Discussion section contextualizes these findings within the broader landscape of RNA-seq analysis, addressing potential limitations and avenues for future research. Finally, the Conclusion section summarizes the key takeaways and emphasizes the practical implications of multiDE for transcriptomic research. By addressing the limitations of existing methods and providing a tailored solution for multi-condition DE analysis, multiDE represents a significant advancement in the analysis of RNA-seq data. Its ability to combine statistical rigor with biological relevance makes it a valuable tool for researchers investigating complex experimental systems. Overview of the multiDE Model The proposed multiDE method is designed for differential expression (DE) analysis of RNA-seq data in experimental settings involving multiple treatment conditions. RNA-seq read counts are modeled using a log-linear framework to capture the relationship between gene expression levels and experimental conditions. Specifically, the read count \( Y{ij} \) for the \( i \)-th gene (\( i = 1, \ldots, G \)) under the \( j \)-th condition (\( j = 1, \ldots, C \)) is assumed to follow a negative binomial distribution, which is widely used in RNA-seq data analysis to account for overdispersion [1,2]. Formally, the read count is modeled as: \[ Y{ij} \sim \text{NB}(\mu{ij}, \phii), \] where \( \mu{ij} \) is the mean expression level for gene \( i \) in condition \( j \), and \( \phii \) is the gene-specific dispersion parameter. The log-linear model for the mean expression level is defined as: \[ \log(\mu{ij}) = \alphai + \betaj + \gamma{ij}, \] where \( \alphai \) represents the baseline expression level of gene \( i \), \( \betaj \) captures the main effect of condition \( j \), and \( \gamma{ij} \) is the interaction term that quantifies the association between gene \( i \) and condition \( j \). The primary objective is to test whether \( \gamma{ij} \neq 0 \) for one or more treatment conditions, which indicates differential expression. Dimension Reduction via First-Order Interaction Decomposition When the number of conditions \( C \) is greater than two, the interaction terms \( \gamma{ij} \) introduce a substantial number of parameters, potentially leading to reduced statistical power and computational inefficiencies. To address this, multiDE employs a first-order decomposition of the interaction term: \[ \gamma{ij} = \lambdai \cdot \deltaj, \] where \( \lambdai \) is a gene-specific coefficient quantifying the overall response of gene \( i \) to treatment effects, and \( \deltaj \) is a condition-specific coefficient capturing the relative effect of condition \( j \). This decomposition reduces the degrees of freedom for the interaction term from \( G \times C \) to \( G + C \), significantly improving power while maintaining model flexibility. The null hypothesis of no differential expression for gene \( i \) across all conditions is formulated as \( H0: \lambdai = 0 \). Under this hypothesis, the mean expression level for gene \( i \) is independent of treatment conditions, implying no interaction effect between gene and condition. The alternative hypothesis \( H1: \lambdai \neq 0 \) indicates that gene \( i \) exhibits differential expression in response to one or more conditions. Statistical Testing and Model Fitting To test for differential expression, multiDE uses a likelihood ratio test (LRT). The full model, including the interaction term \( \gamma{ij} \), is compared to a reduced model in which \( \lambdai = 0 \). The test statistic is computed as: \[ LRT = -2 \left( \log L{\text{reduced}} - \log L{\text{full}} \right), \] where \( \log L{\text{reduced}} \) and \( \log L{\text{full}} \) are the log-likelihoods of the reduced and full models, respectively. Under the null hypothesis, the test statistic asymptotically follows a chi-squared distribution with 1 degree of freedom. Parameter estimation for both the full and reduced models is performed using maximum likelihood estimation (MLE). The dispersion parameter \( \phii \) is estimated using the method of moments, as implemented in existing RNA-seq analysis tools such as edgeR [3] and DESeq2 [4]. The optimization of log-likelihood functions is carried out using the Newton-Raphson algorithm, ensuring convergence even in high-dimensional parameter spaces. Simulation Studies To evaluate the performance of multiDE, we conducted extensive simulation studies based on synthetic RNA-seq datasets. Gene expression counts were generated under various scenarios, including different numbers of conditions (\( C = 2, 3, 5, 10 \)), varying proportions of DE genes, and differing levels of overdispersion. In each scenario, we compared the power and false discovery rate (FDR) of multiDE against two widely used methods, edgeR and DESeq2. Power was defined as the proportion of true DE genes correctly identified, while FDR was calculated as the proportion of false positives among all detected DE genes. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were generated to assess the trade-off between sensitivity and specificity across a range of significance thresholds. MultiDE consistently outperformed the benchmark methods in terms of power, with the performance gap increasing as the number of conditions increased. Importantly, multiDE maintained low FDR across all scenarios, demonstrating its robustness to overdispersion and model misspecification. Application to Real Datasets We applied multiDE to two publicly available RNA-seq datasets: (1) a dataset investigating immune responses to multiple pathogen infections, and (2) a dataset examining gene expression changes under different drug treatments. In both cases, raw read counts were preprocessed and normalized using the trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) method [3] to account for differences in library sizes. For each dataset, DE analysis was performed using multiDE, edgeR, and DESeq2. The results were evaluated based on the number of DE genes identified, their biological relevance, and functional enrichment analysis. Gene ontology (GO) enrichment was performed using the topGO package in R [5]. MultiDE identified a larger number of DE genes compared to the benchmark methods, many of which were associated with biologically meaningful pathways and processes. For example, in the immune response dataset, multiDE highlighted several immune-related genes that were missed by edgeR and DESeq2, including key regulators of inflammatory signaling. Software Implementation The multiDE method has been implemented as an R package, available for public download at [http://homepage.fudan.edu.cn/zhangh/softwares/multiDE](http://homepage.fudan.edu.cn/zhangh/softwares/multiDE). The package includes functions for data preprocessing, model fitting, differential expression testing, and visualization of results. Comprehensive documentation and example scripts are provided to facilitate user adoption. References 1. Anders S, Huber W. Differential expression analysis for sequence count data. Coxiella burnetii, an obligate intracellular Gram-negative bacterium, is the etiological agent of Q fever, a zoonotic disease with global distribution. This pathogen poses significant public health and veterinary concerns due to its ability to infect a wide range of hosts, its environmental stability, and its potential for aerosol transmission. Infected livestock, particularly cattle, sheep, and goats, are the primary reservoirs of C. burnetii, with transmission to humans typically occurring through inhalation of contaminated aerosols or dust originating from infected animals or their secretions, including milk, urine, feces, and birth products [1,2]. Although Q fever in humans is often asymptomatic, it can manifest as acute febrile illness, atypical pneumonia, or hepatitis, and in some cases, progress to chronic infection, such as endocarditis, highlighting the importance of early detection and control of C. burnetii in animal populations as a preventive measure to mitigate human exposure [3,4]. The epidemiology of C. burnetii varies widely across regions, depending on factors such as host species, management practices, and environmental conditions. Regular surveillance of livestock populations is therefore critical to understanding the prevalence and dissemination of C. burnetii within a given country. In South Korea, Q fever was first reported in humans in 1957, and the incidence of the disease has since been increasing, with the majority of human cases linked to occupational exposure to livestock [5]. Despite the growing public health significance of Q fever, studies on the prevalence of C. burnetii in South Korean livestock have been limited, with most investigations focusing on specific regions or animal populations, and few addressing the pathogen’s presence in well-managed governmental facilities [6,7]. National breeding stock farms in South Korea play a pivotal role in the country’s livestock industry, serving as a source of high-quality genetic material for both dairy and beef cattle. These farms are characterized by stringent biosecurity and management protocols that aim to minimize the introduction and spread of infectious diseases. However, the effectiveness of such measures in preventing C. burnetii infection has not been comprehensively evaluated. Given the potential for asymptomatic carriage of the pathogen in cattle and its subsequent transmission to humans or other animals, understanding the prevalence of C. burnetii in these facilities is essential for assessing the adequacy of current biosecurity practices and for informing future disease control strategies. Previous studies have demonstrated that seroprevalence of C. burnetii in cattle can vary significantly depending on herd size, geographical location, and farming practices, with higher prevalence often reported in regions with intensive livestock farming or poor biosecurity measures [8,9]. In South Korea, the limited data available suggest that C. burnetii is present in both dairy and beef cattle, though the extent of its distribution remains unclear [10]. Moreover, molecular studies have revealed significant genetic diversity among C. burnetii isolates worldwide, with certain genotypes associated with specific geographic regions or host species [11]. Comparative analysis of C. burnetii sequences from different regions can provide valuable insights into the evolutionary dynamics and transmission pathways of the pathogen, contributing to a better understanding of its epidemiology. This study represents the first investigation into the serologic and molecular prevalence of C. burnetii in cattle at South Korea’s national breeding stock farms. By focusing on these government-operated facilities, which adhere to high standards of biosecurity and management, this research aims to establish a baseline understanding of C. burnetii prevalence in a controlled livestock population. The findings of this study not only have implications for the management of C. burnetii at the national level but also underscore the potential risk posed by the pathogen in less-regulated farming environments. To achieve these objectives, both serologic and molecular diagnostic methods were employed to detect C. burnetii in cattle. Serologic testing, based on the detection of specific antibodies against C. burnetii antigens, is widely used for assessing exposure to the pathogen, while polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis provides a more direct method for identifying active infections by detecting bacterial DNA [12,13]. The combination of these approaches enables a comprehensive assessment of both past and current infections, offering a more complete picture of the pathogen’s prevalence. In addition to determining the prevalence of C. burnetii, this study also sought to characterize the genetic sequences of C. burnetii isolates recovered from cattle. By analyzing the 16S rRNA gene sequences of PCR-positive samples, the study aimed to investigate the genetic relationships between South Korean isolates and those from other countries, thereby contributing to the global understanding of C. burnetii genetic diversity. The clustering of South Korean isolates with those from the United States, Japan, and Greenland, as observed in this study, highlights the potential for interregional transmission of the pathogen and underscores the need for international collaboration in Q fever research and control efforts. The detection of C. burnetii in cattle at well-managed national breeding stock farms raises important questions about the pathogen’s transmission dynamics and reservoirs within South Korea. Given the controlled nature of these facilities, it is plausible that C. burnetii may be introduced through external sources, such as wildlife or contaminated feed, or persist within the environment despite stringent biosecurity measures. This finding suggests that cattle in non-governmental farms, which often operate with less robust disease control systems, may be at an even higher risk of exposure to C. burnetii. Consequently, there is a pressing need for ongoing surveillance of livestock populations across the country, as well as the implementation of targeted control measures, such as vaccination and improved farm hygiene, to reduce the prevalence of C. burnetii and prevent its transmission to humans. In conclusion, this study addresses a critical gap in the understanding of C. burnetii epidemiology in South Korea by providing the first serologic and molecular evidence of the pathogen’s presence in cattle at national breeding stock farms. The findings emphasize the importance of continuous monitoring and control of C. burnetii in livestock as part of a comprehensive strategy to protect both animal and human health. Further research is needed to explore the sources and risk factors associated with C. burnetii infection in South Korea, as well as to evaluate the effectiveness of current biosecurity practices in mitigating the spread of this zoonotic pathogen. In this study, we assessed the prevalence of Coxiella burnetii in cattle at national breeding stock farms in South Korea using both serologic and molecular diagnostic methods. The study design, sampling strategy, and laboratory analyses were conducted in accordance with international standards for zoonotic pathogen surveillance and diagnostic procedures. Study Design and Sample Collection This cross-sectional study was conducted between January and December 2022 at six national breeding stock farms located in different regions of South Korea, including the southern, central, and Jeju Island regions. These farms are managed under stringent biosecurity protocols by the South Korean government and primarily house cattle for breeding and genetic improvement programs. A total of 736 cattle, consisting of 480 Hanwoo (Korean native cattle), 200 Holstein, and 56 other breeds, were randomly selected from the breeding populations. This sample size was calculated to detect a minimum seroprevalence of 10% with a 95% confidence level and a margin of error of 2%, taking into account the estimated population size of cattle at these farms. Blood samples were collected from the jugular vein of each animal using sterile 10 mL vacutainers (BD Vacutainer, Becton Dickinson, USA). The blood samples were immediately centrifuged at 3,000 × g for 10 minutes to separate serum, which was stored at −20°C until serologic analysis. In addition to blood samples, vaginal swabs were collected from 200 lactating cows to screen for active C. burnetii shedding. Swabs were placed in sterile tubes containing 1 mL of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and stored at −80°C until DNA extraction. Serologic Testing The presence of antibodies against C. burnetii in serum samples was determined using a commercial enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kit (ID Screen Q Fever Indirect Multi-species, IDvet, France). This assay detects antibodies against C. burnetii Phase I and Phase II antigens and has been validated for use in bovine serum. Serum samples were diluted 1:400 in the dilution buffer provided by the manufacturer and processed according to the kit instructions. Optical density (OD) values were measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader (BioTek, USA). Samples with an OD value exceeding the positive threshold, as defined by the manufacturer, were categorized as seropositive. Positive and negative controls provided with the kit were included in all assays to ensure consistency and reliability of results. Molecular Detection DNA was extracted from vaginal swab samples using the QIAamp DNA Mini Kit (Qiagen, Germany) following the manufacturer’s protocol for tissue samples. The extracted DNA was quantified using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) and stored at −20°C until polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis. For the molecular detection of C. burnetii, a nested PCR targeting the 16S rRNA gene was performed as previously described [1]. The first round of PCR used the primers Cox16SF (5'-GGTGAGTAACGCGTAGGAATC-3') and Cox16SR (5'-CACCTCGCGGTTGCTGACT-3') to amplify a 687-bp fragment. The second round of PCR used the primers Cox16SnF (5'-TGGATCAGGCCCAACACTGA-3') and Cox16SnR (5'-TTCGCCTTGCGACCATACTT-3') to amplify a 439-bp fragment. Reactions were carried out in a 25 µL volume containing 1× PCR buffer, 1.5 mM MgCl2, 200 µM dNTPs, 0.2 µM of each primer, 1 U Taq DNA polymerase (Takara Bio, Japan), and 2 µL of DNA template. Thermocycling conditions were set as follows: an initial denaturation at 95°C for 5 minutes, followed by 35 cycles of denaturation at 95°C for 30 seconds, annealing at 58°C for 30 seconds, and extension at 72°C for 1 minute, with a final extension at 72°C for 10 minutes. PCR products were analyzed by electrophoresis on a 2% agarose gel stained with ethidium bromide and visualized under ultraviolet light. Sequencing and Phylogenetic Analysis Positive PCR products were purified using the QIAquick Gel Extraction Kit (Qiagen, Germany) and sequenced by a commercial sequencing service (Macrogen, South Korea) using the Sanger method. The resulting sequences were edited and aligned using MEGA X software [2]. Sequence identity was determined by comparison with C. burnetii sequences available in the GenBank database using the Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST; National Center for Biotechnology Information). Phylogenetic analysis was conducted using the maximum likelihood method with 1,000 bootstrap replicates to assess the evolutionary relationships of the South Korean isolates with previously reported C. burnetii strains from various countries. Statistical Analysis Data were analyzed using R software (version 4.2.1; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Austria). The seroprevalence of C. burnetii was calculated as the proportion of seropositive samples among the total samples tested, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) estimated using the Wilson score method. The molecular prevalence was calculated similarly for PCR-positive samples. Differences in prevalence rates between regions and cattle breeds were assessed using Pearson’s chi-squared test. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Ethical Considerations All sample collection and animal handling procedures were conducted in accordance with the guidelines for the care and use of animals approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of the National Institute of Animal Science, South Korea (approval number: NIAS-2022-076). Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) represents the most severe manifestation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, accounting for a disproportionately high burden of morbidity and mortality among affected individuals. It is estimated that approximately 1% of all tuberculosis (TB) cases progress to TBM, yet this condition remains a significant contributor to neurological disability and death, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) where TB is endemic [1]. Despite advancements in diagnostic and therapeutic strategies, outcomes for TBM remain poor, with mortality rates exceeding 50% in many settings and survivors frequently experiencing debilitating neurological sequelae [2]. The pathophysiology of TBM is complex, involving both direct bacterial invasion of the central nervous system (CNS) and an exaggerated host inflammatory response. This intricate disease process presents unique challenges for effective treatment, necessitating a nuanced approach that extends beyond traditional antimicrobial therapy. The current standard of care for TBM involves prolonged administration of first-line anti-tuberculous drugs, with adjunctive corticosteroids recommended to mitigate inflammation. However, treatment regimens are largely extrapolated from pulmonary TB protocols, without adequate consideration of the unique pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic challenges posed by the blood-brain barrier (BBB). Many first-line drugs, including rifampicin and isoniazid, exhibit suboptimal CNS penetration at standard doses, potentially contributing to the high rates of treatment failure and relapse observed in TBM [3]. Moreover, the emergence of drug-resistant TB strains has further complicated therapy, underscoring the urgent need for improved antimicrobial regimens tailored to the distinct characteristics of CNS tuberculosis. Challenges in Antimicrobial Therapy The efficacy of anti-tuberculous therapy in TBM is contingent upon achieving therapeutic drug concentrations within the CNS, a task hindered by the restrictive properties of the BBB and the presence of caseous granulomas within the meninges. Rifampicin, a cornerstone of TB treatment, has demonstrated limited penetration into cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) at conventional doses, leading to subtherapeutic drug levels in the CNS [4]. Recent studies have explored the potential of high-dose rifampicin therapy to overcome these limitations, with dose-escalation trials suggesting that doses up to 35 mg/kg/day may be both safe and effective [5]. However, the most recent clinical trial assessing rifampicin at 15 mg/kg/day failed to show a significant survival benefit, highlighting the need for further research to identify optimal dosing strategies [6]. Second-line agents, such as fluoroquinolones, are increasingly utilized in the management of drug-resistant TBM. While these agents exhibit good CNS penetration, their role as first-line therapies remains controversial due to the lack of robust evidence demonstrating a survival benefit [7]. The oxazolidinone antibiotic linezolid has emerged as a promising candidate due to its excellent CNS penetration and potent antimycobacterial activity, but its use is limited by concerns regarding toxicity, particularly myelosuppression and peripheral neuropathy [8]. These findings underscore the necessity of developing new antimicrobials or optimizing existing regimens to enhance CNS drug delivery and efficacy. Host-Directed Therapies: Adjunctive Strategies Adjunctive corticosteroids, particularly dexamethasone, have been shown to reduce mortality in HIV-uninfected individuals with TBM, likely by attenuating the deleterious inflammatory response associated with CNS infection [9]. However, the benefit of corticosteroids in HIV co-infected patients remains unclear, with some studies suggesting a lack of survival advantage and potential for increased risk of secondary infections [10]. This highlights the need for individualized approaches to immunomodulation, particularly in populations with high rates of HIV co-infection. Aspirin has garnered attention as a potential host-directed therapy due to its dual anti-inflammatory and anti-thrombotic properties, which may mitigate the risk of stroke—a common complication of TBM [11]. Preliminary evidence from small clinical trials suggests that aspirin may reduce the incidence of ischemic events in TBM, though larger studies are required to confirm these findings and elucidate the optimal dosing regimen [12]. Advances in genomics and immunology have further highlighted the potential for personalized medicine in TBM, with emerging evidence suggesting that genetic polymorphisms in key inflammatory pathways may influence disease susceptibility and treatment responses [13]. Targeting specific mediators of the innate immune response, such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha or interleukin-1, represents an exciting avenue for future therapeutic development. Supportive Management and Complications In addition to antimicrobial and immunomodulatory therapies, effective management of TBM requires attention to its common complications, including hydrocephalus, vasculitis, and cerebral infarction. Hydrocephalus, which occurs in up to 80% of TBM cases, is a major determinant of poor outcomes and often necessitates neurosurgical intervention, such as ventriculoperitoneal shunting or external ventricular drainage [14]. However, the optimal timing and choice of intervention remain contentious, particularly in resource-limited settings where access to neurosurgical expertise is limited [15]. The management of hydrocephalus in HIV co-infected individuals presents additional challenges, as these patients are at heightened risk of opportunistic infections and treatment-related complications [16]. Despite its clinical importance, there is a paucity of evidence to guide the management of hydrocephalus in this population, representing a critical gap in the current knowledge base. Rationale for Further Research The persistent high mortality and morbidity associated with TBM underscore the need for novel therapeutic approaches and comprehensive management strategies. High-dose rifampicin and other optimized antimicrobial regimens with enhanced CNS penetration hold promise for improving bacterial clearance, while host-directed therapies may mitigate the inflammatory damage that contributes to neurological sequelae. Furthermore, addressing supportive care measures, particularly the management of hydrocephalus and other complications, is essential for improving outcomes in TBM. Future research efforts should prioritize rigorous clinical trials to evaluate the safety and efficacy of these interventions, with a particular focus on vulnerable populations such as individuals with HIV co-infection. In conclusion, TBM remains a formidable clinical challenge, requiring a multidisciplinary approach that integrates advances in pharmacology, immunology, and supportive care. By addressing the limitations of current therapeutic strategies and exploring innovative interventions, it may be possible to reduce the global burden of this devastating disease. Study Design This study is a systematic review and synthesis of existing evidence on the treatment of tuberculous meningitis (TBM) and its complications in adults. The review includes studies evaluating antimicrobial therapies, host-directed therapies, and supportive management measures. The methods adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines [1]. Ethical approval was not required since this study did not involve primary data collection or patient participation. Search Strategy A comprehensive search strategy was developed in collaboration with an academic librarian to ensure coverage of all relevant literature. The following electronic databases were searched: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and Cochrane Library. The search strategy included both Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and free-text keywords to maximize sensitivity. Key terms included "tuberculous meningitis," "antimicrobial therapy," "rifampicin," "linezolid," "fluoroquinolones," "host-directed therapy," "dexamethasone," "aspirin," "hydrocephalus management," and "HIV co-infection." Boolean operators were employed to combine search terms, and filters were applied to limit studies to those published in English and involving adult populations. The search covered a publication period from inception to September 2023. Eligibility Criteria Studies were included if they met the following criteria: 1. Population: Adults (≥18 years old) diagnosed with TBM, with or without HIV co-infection. 2. Interventions: Studies evaluating antimicrobial regimens (e.g., rifampicin, linezolid, and fluoroquinolones), host-directed therapies (e.g., corticosteroids, aspirin, or immunomodulatory agents), or supportive management strategies (e.g., hydrocephalus management). 3. Comparators: Placebo, standard-of-care treatment, or alternative interventions. 4. Outcomes: Mortality, neurological outcomes, adverse events, stroke incidence, and complications of hydrocephalus. 5. Study Design: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cohort studies, case-control studies, and systematic reviews with meta-analyses. Exclusion criteria were studies focusing solely on pediatric populations, non-human studies, and conference abstracts or grey literature. Data Extraction and Quality Assessment Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts of identified studies for eligibility. Full-text articles were retrieved for studies meeting inclusion criteria or for those with unclear eligibility. Discrepancies were resolved by consensus or consultation with a third reviewer. Data extraction was performed using a pre-designed standardized form, which captured study characteristics (e.g., design, sample size, intervention details), patient population, outcomes, and key findings. The quality of included studies was assessed using validated tools appropriate for each study design. RCTs were evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 tool [2], while cohort and case-control studies were assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale [3]. Systematic reviews were appraised using the AMSTAR-2 checklist [4]. Studies were categorized as low, moderate, or high quality based on the assessment results, and these quality ratings were considered during data synthesis. Data Synthesis A narrative synthesis approach was employed to integrate findings from the included studies, given the anticipated heterogeneity in study designs, interventions, and outcomes. Key themes and trends in antimicrobial therapies, host-directed treatments, and supportive management strategies were identified. Where possible, quantitative data on treatment efficacy (e.g., relative risk, hazard ratios, or odds ratios) were extracted and summarized. Antimicrobial Therapies Data on the efficacy, safety, and pharmacokinetics of individual antimicrobials were synthesized separately. Special attention was given to rifampicin, including data from dose-finding studies and trials investigating high-dose regimens (≥15 mg/kg/day). Information on central nervous system (CNS) penetration of antimicrobials was extracted from pharmacokinetic studies, and the clinical relevance of these findings was evaluated. The role of fluoroquinolones as second-line agents and the emerging evidence for linezolid as a first-line agent were also assessed. Host-Directed Therapies Studies on corticosteroids, particularly dexamethasone, were analyzed based on patient subgroups (HIV-infected versus HIV-uninfected). Evidence for the use of aspirin as an adjunctive therapy was critically reviewed, focusing on its anti-inflammatory and anti-thrombotic effects and its impact on complications such as stroke. Emerging therapies targeting the host immune response, including the potential for personalized treatment based on genetic polymorphisms, were also explored. Supportive Management Evidence on the management of hydrocephalus in TBM was synthesized, with a focus on surgical and non-surgical interventions. Particular attention was paid to the paucity of data on hydrocephalus management in the context of HIV co-infection. Statistical Analysis Where data from RCTs were available and sufficiently homogeneous, meta-analyses were planned to estimate pooled treatment effects. Heterogeneity among studies was assessed using the I² statistic, and a random-effects model was employed if heterogeneity exceeded 50% [5]. Subgroup analyses were planned for HIV-infected versus HIV-uninfected populations, different antimicrobial regimens, and various adjunctive therapies. Unfortunately, due to significant variability in study methodologies and outcome reporting, meta-analysis was not performed for all outcomes of interest. Instead, key findings were summarized descriptively. Sensitivity Analysis Sensitivity analyses were conducted to evaluate the robustness of the findings by excluding studies deemed to be at high risk of bias or with small sample sizes. The impact of publication bias was assessed using funnel plots for outcomes with sufficient data. Limitations The limitations of this systematic review included the exclusion of non-English studies, which may have introduced language bias. Additionally, the heterogeneity of study designs and outcome measures limited the generalizability of findings. Finally, the reliance on published literature may have introduced publication bias, as studies with negative or null results are less likely to be published. Ochratoxin A (OTA) is a secondary metabolite produced primarily by Aspergillus and Penicillium species, which are commonly found in improperly stored agricultural products such as cereals, coffee, grapes, and wine. OTA is a highly toxic mycotoxin, known for its nephrotoxic, hepatotoxic, immunosuppressive, teratogenic, and carcinogenic effects on both humans and animals [1,2]. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) has classified OTA as a possible human carcinogen (Group 2B) due to its significant health risks [3]. The widespread contamination of food and feed products with OTA poses a serious public health threat, necessitating the development of effective and sustainable strategies for its detoxification. Traditionally, physical and chemical methods, such as heat treatment, irradiation, and chemical adsorption, have been employed for the reduction of OTA in food products [4]. However, these methods often result in compromised nutritional and sensory quality of food, along with limited efficacy in completely eliminating OTA [5]. In recent years, biological detoxification methods, particularly those utilizing microorganisms, have gained significant attention as a promising alternative due to their safety, specificity, and environmentally friendly nature [6]. Microbial biocontrol agents, including bacteria, yeasts, and fungi, have demonstrated potential in reducing OTA levels through biodegradation, adsorption, or both mechanisms [7]. Among these, Bacillus species, especially Bacillus subtilis, have emerged as versatile and effective biocontrol agents owing to their robust metabolic capabilities, spore-forming ability, and Generally Recognized As Safe (GRAS) status [8]. Bacillus subtilis is a ubiquitous Gram-positive bacterium widely distributed in soil, food, and fermented products. Its ability to produce a broad spectrum of antimicrobial compounds, enzymes, and biosurfactants makes it a valuable candidate for various biotechnological applications [9]. In the context of OTA reduction, B. subtilis has shown promising results in degrading mycotoxins or adsorbing them onto its cell wall components, thereby reducing their bioavailability and toxicity [10]. However, the efficacy of B. subtilis in reducing OTA levels may vary depending on the strain, environmental conditions, and the nature of the food matrix. Therefore, the identification and characterization of new, highly efficient B. subtilis strains for OTA detoxification remain a critical area of research. Kimchi, a traditional Korean fermented food, represents a rich reservoir of diverse microbial communities, including lactic acid bacteria, yeasts, and Bacillus species, which contribute to its unique flavor, texture, and health-promoting properties [11]. Fermented foods such as Kimchi are increasingly being explored as sources of novel microbial strains with potential biotechnological applications due to the inherent adaptability and functional attributes of the resident microbiota [12]. The isolation of Bacillus subtilis strains from Kimchi offers a unique opportunity to explore their biocontrol potential against OTA contamination in food products. The present study aimed to isolate and characterize a novel Bacillus subtilis strain from Kimchi and evaluate its efficacy in reducing OTA levels in culture media and a food matrix. The newly identified strain, designated as Bacillus subtilis KU-153, was subjected to molecular identification through 16S rRNA gene sequencing. The capacity of B. subtilis KU-153 to reduce OTA levels was assessed using both viable and heat-treated cells, as well as intracellular and extracellular extracts, to elucidate the underlying mechanisms of OTA reduction. Interestingly, heat-treated cells demonstrated a higher OTA reduction capacity compared to viable cells, suggesting a potential role of the bacterial cell wall or surface components in OTA adsorption. Furthermore, the study extended its investigation to evaluate the application of heat-treated B. subtilis KU-153 cells for OTA reduction in a complex food matrix, specifically artificially contaminated red wine. Red wine is a well-known source of OTA contamination due to fungal growth during grape harvesting and wine fermentation [13]. The ability of B. subtilis KU-153 to reduce OTA levels in red wine highlights its potential for practical application as a biocontrol agent in the food and beverage industry. The findings of this study contribute to the growing body of evidence supporting the use of Bacillus species as effective biocontrol agents for mycotoxin detoxification. By isolating and characterizing a novel strain from Kimchi, this research underscores the untapped potential of microbial resources in traditional fermented foods for addressing critical food safety challenges. Moreover, the use of heat-treated bacterial cells, which are non-viable and thus less likely to interfere with the sensory and microbial quality of food products, presents a promising approach for the safe and effective mitigation of OTA contamination. Overall, this study aims to provide insights into the mechanisms and practical applications of B. subtilis KU-153 for OTA detoxification, paving the way for the development of innovative biocontrol strategies to ensure food safety and public health. It also highlights the importance of exploring traditional fermented foods as valuable sources of functional microorganisms with diverse biotechnological applications. Isolation and identification of Bacillus subtilis strain KU-153 were performed using traditional culturing techniques and molecular methods. Kimchi samples were collected from various regions in Korea and transported to the laboratory under refrigerated conditions. Serial dilutions of the samples were prepared in sterile saline solution (0.85% NaCl), and aliquots were plated on nutrient agar (NA) and incubated at 37°C for 24 hours. Colonies exhibiting distinct morphological characteristics consistent with Bacillus spp. (e.g., irregular margins and cream-colored pigmentation) were selected and purified through repeated streaking on NA plates. The purified isolates were maintained in nutrient broth with 20% glycerol at -80°C for long-term storage. For molecular identification, genomic DNA was extracted from the selected isolate using a commercial DNA extraction kit (e.g., Qiagen, Germany) following the manufacturer’s instructions. The 16S rRNA gene was amplified via polymerase chain reaction (PCR) using universal primers 27F (5′-AGAGTTTGATCMTGGCTCAG-3′) and 1492R (5′-TACGGYTACCTTGTTACGACTT-3′) [1]. PCR conditions included an initial denaturation at 95°C for 5 minutes, followed by 30 cycles of denaturation at 95°C for 30 seconds, annealing at 55°C for 30 seconds, and extension at 72°C for 1 minute, with a final extension at 72°C for 5 minutes. The amplified PCR product was purified using a PCR purification kit (e.g., Promega, USA) and sequenced using an automated DNA sequencer (Applied Biosystems, USA). Nucleotide sequences were aligned and compared with those in the NCBI GenBank database using the Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) to confirm the identity of the isolate. The strain was designated as Bacillus subtilis KU-153 based on sequence homology. The growth kinetics of B. subtilis KU-153 were evaluated to determine its optimal growth conditions for ochratoxin A (OTA) reduction studies. A single colony of B. subtilis KU-153 was inoculated into 50 mL of nutrient broth in a 250-mL Erlenmeyer flask and incubated at 37°C on a rotary shaker at 150 rpm. At regular intervals (0, 6, 12, 18, 24, and 48 hours), aliquots were collected to measure optical density (OD600) and determine the growth curve of the strain. Samples were also centrifuged at 10,000 × g for 10 minutes, and the supernatant was analyzed for OTA content to assess the strain’s biocontrol activity in culture medium. The ability of B. subtilis KU-153 to reduce OTA content was assessed using a culture medium artificially contaminated with OTA. A stock solution of OTA (Sigma-Aldrich, USA) was prepared in methanol at a concentration of 100 µg/mL and stored at -20°C in the dark. To evaluate OTA reduction, 10 µL of the OTA stock solution was added to 10 mL of nutrient broth to achieve a final OTA concentration of 1 µg/mL. Viable B. subtilis KU-153 cells were prepared by culturing the strain in nutrient broth at 37°C until the mid-logarithmic growth phase (OD600 ≈ 0.8). The cells were harvested by centrifugation, washed twice with sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH 7.4), and resuspended in sterile PBS to achieve a final concentration of 10⁸ CFU/mL. Heat-killed cells were prepared by autoclaving the washed cells at 121°C for 15 minutes. Intracellular and extracellular extracts were obtained by lysing cells with sonication (five cycles of 30 seconds on/30 seconds off at 40% amplitude) and filtering the lysate through a 0.22-μm syringe filter, respectively. Separate treatments were set up in sterile culture tubes containing OTA-contaminated nutrient broth: (1) viable cells, (2) heat-killed cells, (3) intracellular extract, and (4) extracellular extract. Control tubes containing OTA-contaminated nutrient broth without bacterial treatment were also included. All treatments were incubated at 37°C for 24 hours under static conditions. After incubation, samples were centrifuged at 10,000 × g for 10 minutes, and the supernatant was collected for OTA analysis. To quantify OTA levels, high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) with fluorescence detection was employed. Samples were extracted with an equal volume of chloroform, and the organic phase was collected, evaporated under nitrogen gas, and reconstituted in the mobile phase (acetonitrile:water:acetic acid, 51:47:2, v/v/v). The HPLC system (e.g., Waters, USA) was equipped with a C18 reverse-phase column and a fluorescence detector set at an excitation wavelength of 333 nm and an emission wavelength of 460 nm. Quantification was performed by comparing sample peak areas with those of OTA standards. To evaluate the potential application of B. subtilis KU-153 in food systems, OTA reduction was assessed in red wine artificially contaminated with OTA. Commercial red wine samples were spiked with OTA stock solution to achieve a final OTA concentration of 5 µg/L. Heat-killed B. subtilis KU-153 cells were added to the OTA-contaminated wine at a concentration of 10⁸ cells/mL, and the samples were incubated at room temperature for 24 hours with gentle shaking. Control samples containing OTA-contaminated wine without bacterial treatment were also prepared. OTA levels in the wine were analyzed using HPLC as described above. All experiments were performed in triplicate, and data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation. Statistical analysis was conducted using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test to determine significant differences between treatments (p < 0.05). Statistical software (e.g., SPSS, USA) was used for data analysis. The results of this study demonstrated the ochratoxin A (OTA) reduction potential of the newly isolated Bacillus subtilis strain KU-153 under various conditions, with key findings presented below. Identification of Bacillus subtilis KU-153 The 16S rRNA gene sequencing confirmed that the isolated strain KU-153 shares 99% sequence similarity with Bacillus subtilis, positioning it within the Bacillus genus. Phylogenetic analysis further corroborated its classification as B. subtilis, confirming the successful isolation of the strain from the Korean traditional fermented food Kimchi. Growth Kinetics and OTA Reduction in Culture Medium To evaluate the efficacy of B. subtilis KU-153 in reducing OTA, growth kinetic studies were conducted in OTA-containing culture medium. Measurements of bacterial growth and concurrent OTA levels in the medium over time revealed a significant reduction in OTA concentration (p < 0.05) as the bacterial culture progressed. The maximum OTA reduction was observed during the late exponential phase of growth, suggesting that active cell metabolism plays a role in the biocontrol mechanism. Impact of Bacterial Extracts on OTA Reduction To determine whether intracellular or extracellular components of B. subtilis KU-153 contribute to OTA reduction, the bacterial cells were lysed, and intracellular and extracellular extracts were prepared. When these extracts were incubated in OTA-containing culture medium, no significant reduction in OTA levels was observed, indicating that neither intracellular enzymes nor extracellular metabolites were directly responsible for OTA degradation. This finding highlights the importance of whole-cell interactions for effective OTA reduction. Comparison of Viable and Heat-Killed Cells in OTA Reduction The ability of viable and heat-killed B. subtilis KU-153 cells to reduce OTA levels was assessed in culture medium. Both viable and heat-killed cells were found to significantly reduce OTA concentrations compared to controls (p < 0.05). Interestingly, heat-killed cells exhibited a greater reduction in OTA levels (45%) than viable cells (22%). This unexpected finding suggests that the OTA binding or adsorption capability of B. subtilis KU-153 may be enhanced by structural modifications induced by heat treatment. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis of the heat-treated cells revealed surface alterations, which may explain the increased OTA adsorption capacity. These results underline the potential application of heat-inactivated B. subtilis KU-153 cells as a cost-effective and safe biocontrol agent for OTA mitigation.
