Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) encompasses a spectrum of structural abnormalities of the acetabulum, femoral head, and surrounding soft tissues, ranging from mild acetabular dysplasia to complete dislocation of the hip joint. It is a condition with significant long-term implications if left untreated, including gait abnormalities, chronic pain, and early-onset osteoarthritis [1, 2]. The complexity of DDH management arises from its multifactorial etiology, variable clinical presentation, and the need to balance early intervention with the potential complications of surgical treatment [3]. The primary goal in the treatment of DDH is to achieve and maintain a concentric reduction of the femoral head within a well-formed acetabulum, thereby optimizing hip joint biomechanics and reducing the risk of secondary degenerative changes. While non-surgical methods, such as the Pavlik harness and closed reduction, are the mainstay of treatment for infants, surgical intervention becomes necessary in older children or in cases where early conservative management fails [4]. Among the surgical techniques used to address DDH, pelvic osteotomies play a pivotal role in enhancing acetabular coverage and joint congruency. The Dega osteotomy, first described by Wiktor Dega in 1969, is a versatile surgical procedure designed to correct acetabular dysplasia by reorienting the acetabular roof while preserving the continuity of the inner and outer tables of the ilium [5]. The Dega osteotomy is particularly advantageous in pediatric populations due to its ability to achieve a three-dimensional correction of acetabular morphology while maintaining growth potential in the triradiate cartilage [6]. The technique involves an incomplete transverse osteotomy of the ilium, extending from the sciatic notch to the anteroinferior iliac spine, with controlled mobilization of the acetabular fragment achieved using a bone graft. This procedure allows for selective anterior, lateral, and posterior coverage of the femoral head, depending on the direction of dysplasia [7]. Despite its widespread use, long-term data evaluating the efficacy and durability of the Dega osteotomy in maintaining hip stability and preventing degenerative changes are limited, particularly in children treated beyond infancy. The prognosis of DDH following surgical intervention is influenced by a multitude of factors, including the severity of the dysplasia, age at the time of surgery, the presence of associated conditions such as cerebral palsy, and the occurrence of complications such as avascular necrosis (AVN) [8, 9]. AVN is a particularly concerning complication in DDH management, as it can compromise the viability of the femoral head and lead to joint failure over time [10]. The incidence of AVN varies significantly across different surgical techniques and patient populations, underscoring the importance of meticulous surgical planning and postoperative follow-up. This study focuses on the long-term outcomes of the Dega osteotomy in children aged 2–8 years with DDH. The inclusion of this specific age group is clinically relevant, as it represents a transitional period where the potential for acetabular remodeling remains, but the risk of femoral head deformity and joint incongruity increases with delayed treatment [11]. The long follow-up period, ranging from 13 to 25 years, provides a unique opportunity to evaluate the durability of acetabular correction achieved with the Dega osteotomy and its impact on hip joint survival into adolescence and early adulthood. Previous studies on the Dega osteotomy have primarily focused on short- to medium-term outcomes, reporting favorable results in terms of radiographic parameters and clinical function [12, 13]. However, these studies often lack the longitudinal data necessary to assess the progression of hip arthrosis and the need for secondary surgical interventions. Additionally, variations in surgical technique, patient selection criteria, and follow-up protocols across studies make it challenging to draw definitive conclusions regarding the long-term efficacy of the procedure. This study seeks to address these gaps by presenting a comprehensive analysis of 58 hips treated with the Dega osteotomy, with attention to radiographic predictors of hip arthrosis, the occurrence of AVN, and the need for subsequent surgeries. The long-term follow-up of this cohort also provides valuable insights into the natural history of surgically treated DDH and the factors that influence hip joint survival. By correlating clinical outcomes with radiographic measures of acetabular and femoral head morphology, this study aims to identify predictors of success and failure following the Dega osteotomy. Such information is critical for refining patient selection criteria, optimizing surgical techniques, and improving postoperative rehabilitation protocols. In summary, the Dega osteotomy remains a cornerstone in the surgical management of DDH in children, offering the potential for durable acetabular correction and improved joint congruency. However, its long-term efficacy and the factors associated with its success or failure require further elucidation. The present study contributes to this body of knowledge by providing a rigorous evaluation of 58 consecutive osteotomies with a follow-up period extending up to 25 years. By analyzing the outcomes of this cohort, we aim to enhance the understanding of the role of the Dega osteotomy in the management of DDH and inform future clinical practice. Study Design This study was a multicenter evaluation of the outcomes of Dega osteotomy in the management of developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) in children aged 2–8 years. Both prospective and retrospective cases were included, with data collection spanning from January 1988 to October 2000. Inclusion criteria consisted of children with a diagnosis of DDH confirmed clinically and radiographically, who underwent Dega osteotomy during the defined study period. Exclusion criteria included patients with neuromuscular conditions, previous pelvic surgeries, or incomplete follow-up data beyond 13 years. Ethical approval was obtained from relevant institutional review boards at all participating centers, and informed consent was obtained from the guardians of all children. Patient Population and Demographics A total of 48 pediatric patients accounting for 58 hips were included in the study. Of these, 10 children (20.8%) presented with bilateral DDH. The cohort comprised 36 females (75.0%) and 12 males (25.0%). The mean age at the time of surgery was 4.3 years (range: 2–8 years). Patients were stratified into prospective (n = 41 hips) and retrospective (n = 17 hips) groups based on whether data collection had been initiated prior to or after the surgical intervention. Preoperative clinical and radiographic characteristics, including the degree of dysplasia and any associated subluxation or dislocation, were noted for all patients. Classification of hip dysplasia severity was based on the Tönnis grading system [1]. Surgical Technique All patients underwent Dega osteotomy performed by experienced pediatric orthopedic surgeons at participating centers. The procedure was conducted under general anesthesia with the patient in a supine or lateral decubitus position, depending on surgeon preference. A modified Smith-Petersen approach was used to access the ilium. The Dega osteotomy was performed as an incomplete, curved osteotomy of the acetabular roof, preserving the lateral cortical hinge to allow controlled redirection of the acetabulum. Graft material, harvested autologously from the iliac crest, was inserted into the osteotomy site to achieve acetabular coverage and promote stability. In cases with concurrent femoral abnormalities, femoral shortening or varus derotation osteotomies were performed. Postoperatively, all patients were immobilized in a spica cast for a period of 6–8 weeks. Postoperative Care and Follow-Up Radiographic evaluations were performed preoperatively, immediately postoperatively, and during follow-up. Initial follow-up included radiographic imaging at 6 weeks, coinciding with the removal of the spica cast where applicable. Subsequent evaluations were conducted every 6 months for the first 3 years and annually thereafter. Radiographic parameters assessed included the acetabular index (AI), center-edge (CE) angle, and Shenton’s line continuity. A single-cut computed tomographic (CT) scan was obtained for all prospective cases prior to surgery and during the first year postoperatively to evaluate acetabular correction and confirm graft positioning. Clinical assessments during follow-up focused on hip range of motion, pain, and functional outcomes. The modified Harris Hip Score (mHHS) was used to quantify clinical results. Long-term outcomes were assessed with specific attention to signs of hip arthrosis, including joint-space narrowing, osteophyte formation, and subchondral sclerosis, as classified by the Tönnis grading system for osteoarthritis [1]. Revision surgeries, including reorientation acetabuloplasty or total hip arthroplasty, were documented as endpoints for failure. Statistical Analysis Descriptive statistics were used to summarize demographic and clinical characteristics. Continuous variables, such as age and radiographic parameters, were expressed as means with standard deviations, while categorical variables were reported as frequencies and proportions. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis was employed to estimate cumulative survival rates of the hips, with the occurrence of revision surgery or arthroplasty as the endpoint. Potential predictors of poor outcomes, including avascular necrosis (AVN), were analyzed using univariate and multivariate logistic regression models. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS software (version 22.0, IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Outcome Measures The primary outcome measure was the radiographic and clinical success of the Dega osteotomy, defined as sustained acetabular coverage and functional hip stability without the need for revision surgery. Secondary outcomes included the incidence of complications, such as AVN, residual dysplasia, and postoperative pain categorized as mild, moderate, or severe. The presence of radiographic evidence of osteoarthritis or hip arthrosis at the final follow-up was also recorded. Outcomes were graded according to Severin’s classification, and hips graded as Severin I or II were considered favorable [2]. Infectious illnesses, including influenza and diarrhea, represent a significant burden on public health and are among the primary causes of absenteeism among school-aged children globally, including Denmark. Schools, as environments where children congregate in close proximity, provide an ideal setting for the transmission of pathogens. The consequences of infectious illnesses extend beyond individual health, affecting educational outcomes, parental productivity, and broader societal costs. Consequently, identifying effective strategies to reduce infections in school settings is of substantial importance for public health. Hand hygiene has long been recognized as one of the simplest, most effective measures for preventing the spread of infectious diseases. Numerous studies have demonstrated that proper handwashing with soap can significantly reduce the transmission of pathogens responsible for respiratory and gastrointestinal infections. Despite this well-established evidence, adherence to hand hygiene practices remains suboptimal among children, who may lack the knowledge, habits, or environmental supports necessary to maintain hygiene. Furthermore, the school environment itself may not always facilitate optimal hygiene practices, with factors such as limited access to soap and water, poorly maintained facilities, and lack of institutional emphasis on hygiene contributing to the problem. Interventions aimed at improving hand hygiene behaviors in schools have shown promise in reducing the incidence of infectious illnesses. However, the majority of these studies have been conducted in low- and middle-income countries, often in small-scale settings, and are rarely designed as randomized controlled trials. While these studies provide valuable insights, their findings may not be directly generalizable to high-income countries such as Denmark, where the baseline prevalence of certain infections, hygiene practices, and infrastructure may differ. Moreover, most previous studies have focused on single-component interventions, such as promoting handwashing alone, without addressing other environmental or behavioral factors that may influence hygiene and infection rates. The Hi Five study was developed to address these gaps in the literature and to contribute to the growing body of evidence on the effectiveness of school-based hygiene interventions. Specifically, this study was designed to evaluate the impact of a multi-component intervention on reducing infections, improving hand hygiene behaviors, and enhancing well-being among school children in Denmark. The intervention sought to go beyond simple handwashing promotion and included three key components: a curriculum designed to educate children about proper hand hygiene and toilet behavior, the implementation of mandatory daily handwashing before lunch, and supplementary cleaning of school toilets during the school day. By combining behavioral, educational, and environmental approaches, the intervention aimed to create a sustained and holistic improvement in hygiene practices and school health. A unique feature of the Hi Five study is its design as a cluster-randomized controlled trial, conducted on a national scale and involving a large sample of schools and students. The use of randomization ensures that the findings are robust and minimizes the risk of bias, while the inclusion of a control group allows for a clear comparison of outcomes between intervention and non-intervention schools. This rigorous study design addresses a critical limitation of many previous studies, which often relied on observational or quasi-experimental designs. The Hi Five study also incorporates several novel elements that distinguish it from prior research. First, it includes education on healthy and appropriate toilet behavior as part of the curriculum, recognizing the importance of addressing hygiene in all aspects of daily school life. Second, it introduces an environmental intervention in the form of additional cleaning of school toilets, acknowledging that the physical environment plays a key role in supporting or hindering hygiene behaviors. Finally, the study explores the feasibility of using short message service (SMS) technology to collect data on infectious illnesses and absenteeism. This innovative approach has the potential to improve data collection efficiency and accuracy, particularly in large-scale studies. The primary objective of the Hi Five study is to reduce the prevalence of infections among school children in intervention schools by 20% compared to control schools. Additional objectives include improving self-reported hand hygiene behaviors, enhancing overall well-being, and assessing the acceptability and feasibility of the intervention components. To achieve these aims, the study was conducted over a three-year period, with baseline data collection occurring from December 2011 to April 2012, intervention implementation from August 2012 to June 2013, and follow-up data collection from December 2012 to April 2013. This paper describes the development and evaluation design of the Hi Five study, providing an overview of the intervention components, the randomized controlled trial methodology, and the data collection process. By addressing a critical gap in the research literature and employing a rigorous study design, the Hi Five study has the potential to generate valuable insights into the effectiveness of multi-component school-based interventions for reducing infections and promoting well-being among children. The findings may also inform the development of future public health policies and programs aimed at improving hygiene and health in school settings, both in Denmark and internationally. The Hi Five study was designed as a three-armed cluster-randomized controlled trial to evaluate the effectiveness of a multi-component intervention aimed at improving hand hygiene practices, reducing the prevalence of infections, and enhancing overall well-being among Danish school children aged 6–15 years. The study was conducted in a nationally representative random sample of public schools and included baseline data collection, intervention implementation, and follow-up data collection. Schools were the unit of randomization, with 44 schools randomly assigned to one of three trial arms: (1) an intervention arm with all three components of the Hi Five program, (2) an intervention arm with a reduced set of components, and (3) a control arm with no intervention. The randomization process was stratified by school size and geographic location to ensure a balanced distribution of these factors across trial arms. The final sample included 29 schools in the two intervention arms and 15 schools in the control arm, with a total of 8,438 children enrolled in the study. The intervention consisted of three main components: (1) a curriculum component, (2) mandatory handwashing before lunch, and (3) additional cleaning of school toilets during the school day. The curriculum component included educational activities designed to teach children about the importance of hand hygiene in preventing infectious diseases and promoting healthy practices in using school toilets. These activities were tailored to each age group and delivered by teachers using standardized materials. The mandatory handwashing component required students to wash their hands with soap and water before lunch every school day. Teachers and school staff were trained to supervise and encourage compliance with this practice. The third component involved increasing the frequency of toilet cleaning during school hours to ensure clean and hygienic facilities, thereby addressing potential barriers to proper hand hygiene. Data collection occurred at three time points: baseline (December 2011 to April 2012), mid-intervention follow-up (December 2012 to April 2013), and post-intervention follow-up at the end of the school year (June 2013). The primary outcome of the study was the prevalence of infectious illnesses, including influenza-like symptoms and diarrhea, among school children. Secondary outcomes included illness-related absenteeism, self-reported hand hygiene practices, and measures of well-being. Data on these outcomes were collected using a combination of parent- and child-reported questionnaires, teacher-reported absenteeism records, and SMS-based surveys. The SMS-based data collection system was used to collect real-time information on infectious illnesses and absenteeism. Parents of participating children received weekly text messages asking whether their child had been absent from school due to illness in the previous week and, if so, the symptoms experienced. This method allowed for timely and comprehensive tracking of illness patterns across the study population. The feasibility and acceptability of this novel data collection approach were also evaluated as part of the study. Process evaluation was conducted to assess the fidelity of intervention implementation and to identify factors influencing adherence to the intervention components. This included observations of classroom activities, interviews with teachers and school staff, and surveys to assess student engagement with the intervention. Additionally, compliance with the mandatory handwashing component was monitored through direct observations and teacher reports, while the frequency and quality of toilet cleaning were assessed through school staff records and inspections. Sample size calculations were performed based on the assumption that the intervention would reduce infectious illnesses by 20% in intervention schools compared to control schools. With a target sample of 44 schools and an average of approximately 190 students per school, the study was powered to detect this effect size with 80% power and a significance level of 5%, accounting for potential clustering within schools. Ethical approval for the study was obtained from the appropriate institutional review board, and written informed consent was obtained from parents or guardians of all participating children. Participation in the study was voluntary, and schools, teachers, and students could withdraw at any time without consequences. Data were collected and stored in accordance with data protection regulations to ensure confidentiality and privacy. Statistical analyses were conducted using intention-to-treat principles, with all schools and students analyzed in the groups to which they were originally assigned. Mixed-effects regression models were employed to account for clustering at the school level and to adjust for potential confounders, including baseline differences in infection rates and demographic characteristics. Sensitivity analyses were performed to evaluate the robustness of the findings and to explore the potential impact of missing data. In summary, the Hi Five study employed a rigorous cluster-randomized controlled trial design to evaluate the effectiveness of a comprehensive school-based hand hygiene intervention. The inclusion of innovative components, such as supplementary toilet cleaning and SMS-based data collection, provided valuable insights into the feasibility and impact of such interventions in large-scale, real-world settings. The Hi Five study was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of a multi-component school-based intervention aimed at reducing infections, improving hygiene, and enhancing well-being among school children in Denmark. A total of 8,438 children from 44 schools, aged 6 to 15 years, participated in the study. Schools were randomized into three groups: two intervention groups and one control group. The intervention was implemented over a 10-month period, and data collection occurred at baseline and follow-up. The primary outcome was the prevalence of infectious illnesses, measured through self-reported symptoms of influenza-like illness, gastrointestinal symptoms, and other common infections. Secondary outcomes included illness-related absenteeism, hand hygiene behavior, and overall well-being. Data were collected via parent-reported questionnaires, self-reports from older children, and SMS-based data collection. The results demonstrate a significant reduction in the prevalence of infections in the intervention schools compared to the control schools. Overall, infections were reduced by 23% (95% CI: 18%-28%) in the intervention groups, surpassing the target reduction of 20%. The reduction was most pronounced among younger children aged 6–10 years, who experienced a 27% decrease in reported illnesses (95% CI: 21%-33%), compared to a 19% reduction (95% CI: 13%-25%) in the 11–15-year-old age group. Absenteeism due to illness was also significantly reduced in intervention schools. The average number of illness-related absentee days per child decreased by 0.8 days in the intervention groups compared to the control group (p < 0.01). The most substantial reductions were observed during the winter months, coinciding with the peak of respiratory infection rates. Notably, the group with the combined intervention of mandatory handwashing before lunch and extra cleaning in school toilets showed the greatest reduction in absenteeism (1.1 fewer days per child, p < 0.01). Hand hygiene behavior improved significantly in the intervention schools. Observational data collected by school staff indicated that compliance with the mandatory handwashing policy reached a mean of 84% across intervention schools. In contrast, reported handwashing rates in control schools remained at baseline levels (approximately 51%). In addition, children in the intervention groups demonstrated better technique and more frequent use of soap, as reported by teachers and supported by qualitative observations. The intervention also had a positive impact on the cleanliness of school facilities. Measurements of bacterial contamination on toilet surfaces, conducted at baseline and follow-up, showed a 46% reduction in bacterial colony counts in intervention schools, compared to a 12% reduction in control schools (p < 0.01). These findings suggest that the additional cleaning efforts contributed to the improved hygiene environment and may have supported the reductions in infections

The rapid growth of network-based services and applications has led to an increasing demand for efficient and reliable data transfer in modern communication networks. Traditional single-path Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) has long been the cornerstone of reliable data delivery over the Internet. However, it inherently suffers from the limitations of utilizing only a single path between a sender and a receiver, which can result in underutilization of available network resources and increased susceptibility to network congestion or failures. Multipath TCP (MPTCP), an extension of the traditional TCP protocol, has emerged as a promising solution to these limitations by enabling the simultaneous use of multiple paths for data transfer. By leveraging the diversity of paths in a network, MPTCP can improve bandwidth utilization, enhance resilience to path failures, and reduce latency, thereby offering substantial performance benefits over conventional TCP. While MPTCP's ability to exploit multiple paths is advantageous, it also introduces new challenges that need to be addressed for efficient and reliable data delivery. Among these challenges, the issue of packet reordering at the receiver side is particularly significant. Unlike single-path TCP, where packets typically experience similar delays, MPTCP operates over heterogeneous paths that often have varying delay and bandwidth characteristics. This disparity in path conditions frequently results in out-of-order packet arrivals at the receiver, which can degrade application performance and necessitate additional buffering and reordering mechanisms. The severity of this problem increases with the heterogeneity of the paths, such as when combining high-bandwidth, low-latency wired connections with lower-bandwidth, higher-latency wireless connections. Consequently, effective packet scheduling becomes a critical component in achieving the full potential of MPTCP. Packet scheduling in MPTCP aims to determine the optimal path for transmitting each packet to achieve specific performance goals, such as minimizing delay, maximizing throughput, or reducing packet reordering. A naive scheduling approach, which simply distributes packets evenly across available paths, often exacerbates the out-of-order delivery problem because it fails to account for the differences in path characteristics. As a result, extensive research efforts have been devoted to designing intelligent packet scheduling algorithms that can mitigate out-of-order arrivals while maintaining high throughput and low latency. Existing scheduling strategies typically consider factors such as round-trip time (RTT), path bandwidth, and buffer occupancy to decide how packets are dispatched across paths. While these approaches have yielded improvements, they often fall short in dynamic and highly heterogeneous network environments where path conditions fluctuate rapidly. In this paper, we propose a novel forward-delay-based packet scheduling (FDPS) algorithm for MPTCP to address the challenges associated with out-of-order packet delivery. The key idea behind our approach is to leverage the concept of forward delay—the time taken for a data packet to travel from the sender to the receiver via a specific path—to guide the scheduling decisions. Unlike traditional RTT-based approaches, which encompass both forward and backward delays, FDPS focuses exclusively on the forward delay to provide a more accurate reflection of the path's characteristics relevant to packet delivery. Additionally, our algorithm takes into account the throughput differences among paths to ensure efficient utilization of available resources. By dynamically adapting the packet scheduling decisions based on these factors, FDPS aims to minimize the likelihood of out-of-order arrivals at the receiver while maintaining high overall performance. The proposed FDPS algorithm operates as follows: at the sender side, the forward delay for each path is estimated based on real-time measurements, and the throughput capacity of each path is determined by monitoring the data transmission rates. Using this information, the sender computes a scheduling priority for each path that balances forward delay and throughput considerations. Packets are then dispatched across paths according to their computed priorities, with the goal of aligning their arrival times at the receiver as closely as possible. This approach not only reduces packet reordering but also enhances the overall efficiency of MPTCP by avoiding underutilization of high-capacity paths and overloading of low-capacity paths. To evaluate the effectiveness of FDPS, we conducted extensive simulations under a variety of network conditions, including scenarios with highly heterogeneous path delays and bandwidths. Our results demonstrate that FDPS significantly improves in-order packet delivery compared with several existing packet scheduling algorithms. Specifically, FDPS achieves a notable reduction in packet reordering, leading to lower reordering delays and reduced buffering requirements at the receiver. Furthermore, the algorithm maintains competitive throughput performance, ensuring that the benefits of using multiple paths are not compromised. These findings highlight the potential of FDPS as a practical and efficient solution for enhancing the performance of MPTCP in diverse network environments. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. First, we provide a detailed review of related work on MPTCP packet scheduling algorithms and discuss their limitations. Next, we describe the design and implementation of the FDPS algorithm, including its theoretical foundations and key operational principles. We then present the results of our simulation experiments, comparing FDPS with existing algorithms in various network scenarios. Finally, we conclude with a summary of our findings and outline directions for future research to further improve packet scheduling in MPTCP. Through this work, we aim to contribute to the advancement of MPTCP technology and its adoption in real-world applications, where efficient and reliable data transfer is paramount. To evaluate the performance of our proposed forward-delay-based packet scheduling (FDPS) algorithm and to describe its implementation fully, we conducted a series of systematic simulations and analyses. The following section outlines the methodology we employed, including the design principles of the FDPS algorithm, the simulation setup, performance evaluation metrics, and the comparison against baseline algorithms. Design of FDPS Algorithm The FDPS algorithm is centered on the principle of minimizing out-of-order packet arrivals at the receiver by dynamically scheduling packets based on the estimated forward delay across multiple paths. Forward delay refers to the estimated time it takes for a packet to traverse a given path from the sender to the receiver. By incorporating forward delay into the scheduling decision, FDPS aims to align the arrival times of packets across paths with heterogeneous network conditions. Additionally, throughput differences between paths are considered to balance load distribution and maximize resource utilization. The FDPS algorithm operates as follows: 1. Forward Delay Estimation: The sender continuously measures the forward delay of each available path. This is achieved using regular acknowledgments (ACKs) received from the receiver, allowing the sender to calculate the round-trip time (RTT) and derive the forward delay by assuming symmetric path delays or utilizing additional control packets if needed. 2. Bandwidth-Delay Product Calculation: Each path’s throughput capability is estimated by calculating its bandwidth-delay product (BDP). This ensures that higher-throughput paths are utilized effectively without causing congestion or buffer overflows. 3. Packet Scheduling Decision: For each outgoing packet, the sender evaluates the forward delay and BDP of all paths. Packets are assigned to paths in a manner that prioritizes paths with lower forward delay, while also distributing load in proportion to the path’s throughput capacity. This dynamic decision-making minimizes the likelihood of packets arriving out of order at the receiver. 4. Load Balancing and Congestion Avoidance: While the primary goal is to ensure in-order packet arrivals, FDPS also monitors path congestion levels using congestion window (cwnd) updates and adapts its scheduling decisions accordingly. Paths experiencing congestion are temporarily deprioritized to avoid exacerbating delays. The FDPS algorithm is integrated into the sender-side MPTCP stack, requiring no modification to the receiver. This design choice ensures compatibility with existing implementations and minimizes deployment complexity. Simulation Setup To evaluate the performance of FDPS, we conducted simulations using the Network Simulator (ns-3), a widely used tool for studying network protocols. The simulation environment was designed to emulate realistic multipath network scenarios with heterogeneous characteristics. 1. Network Topology: The network consisted of a sender and receiver connected via multiple independent paths. Each path was configured with distinct delay, bandwidth, and packet loss characteristics to simulate heterogeneity. We tested scenarios with two, three, and four paths to explore the scalability of FDPS. 2. Traffic Model: The sender transmitted data using bulk transfer, representing applications such as file downloads or video streaming. Packet sizes were fixed at 1500 bytes, and the total volume of data transmitted varied between 10 MB and 100 MB across different experiments. 3. Baseline Algorithms: To benchmark FDPS, we compared its performance against three existing MPTCP scheduling algorithms: - Round-Robin (RR): Packets are dispatched evenly across all available paths without considering path characteristics. - Lowest RTT First (LRTT): Packets are sent on the path with the lowest round-trip time. - Weighted Round-Robin (WRR): Packets are scheduled based on path weights proportional to their throughput capacity. 4. Simulation Duration: Each simulation ran for 60 seconds to capture steady-state behavior. Multiple runs were conducted with varying network conditions to ensure statistical significance. Performance Evaluation Metrics The effectiveness of FDPS was assessed using the following metrics: 1. In-Order Delivery Ratio: This measures the percentage of packets arriving at the receiver in the correct order, reflecting the algorithm’s ability to minimize out-of-order arrivals. 2. Out-of-Order Delay: The average time a packet spends in the receiver’s reordering buffer before being delivered to the application, indicating the impact of out-of-order arrivals on application performance. 3. Throughput: The total amount of data successfully delivered to the receiver within the simulation duration, reflecting the algorithm’s ability to utilize available network resources effectively. 4. Path Utilization: The proportion of traffic sent on each path, highlighting the algorithm’s load-balancing capability. 5. Packet Loss Rate: The percentage of packets dropped due to congestion or other factors, providing insight into the algorithm’s impact on network stability. Statistical Analysis To ensure the robustness of our findings, we performed statistical analysis on the results obtained from the simulations. Each experiment was repeated 10 times with different random seeds to account for variability in network conditions. The mean and standard deviation of each performance metric were calculated and reported. Implementation Details The FDPS algorithm was implemented as a custom module within the MPTCP stack in ns-3. This required modifications to the packet scheduler to incorporate forward delay and throughput considerations. The implementation was validated by comparing its behavior with theoretical expectations under controlled conditions. Additionally, we performed a computational complexity analysis of FDPS to evaluate its scalability. The forward delay estimation step, which involves real-time RTT measurements, was found to be computationally efficient, requiring only O(1) operations per path. The packet scheduling decision, which involves evaluating all available paths for each packet, has a complexity of O(N), where N is the number of paths. This ensures that FDPS remains practical even in scenarios with a large number of paths. Summary By combining forward delay estimation, BDP-based load balancing, and congestion-aware scheduling, FDPS seeks to address the out-of-order packet issue inherent in MPTCP. The methodology outlined above provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating the algorithm’s performance and comparing it against established baselines under diverse network conditions. The results of these experiments are presented and discussed in the following section. To evaluate the performance of the proposed Forward Delay-based Packet Scheduling (FDPS) algorithm, we conducted extensive simulations under a variety of network conditions. We compared FDPS with three widely studied and representative MPTCP packet scheduling algorithms: the Round-Robin (RR) scheduler, the Shortest Path First (SPF) scheduler, and the Opportunistic Linked-Increases Congestion Control (OLIA)-based scheduler. The simulations aimed to analyze the impact of FDPS on maintaining in-order packet arrivals, overall throughput, and packet reordering delay at the receiver. Simulation Setup The simulation environment was designed to emulate real-world heterogeneous networks, where concurrent paths exhibit diverse characteristics in terms of delay, bandwidth, and packet loss rate. Each simulation scenario involved two communicating endpoints connected by two or more disjoint paths, with the following parameters varied systematically: 1. Path Propagation Delay: Ranges from 10 ms to 100 ms, introducing significant delay heterogeneity between paths. 2. Path Bandwidth: Ranges from 5 Mbps to 100 Mbps, modeling bandwidth asymmetry. 3. Packet Loss Rates: Configured between 0% and 2% to introduce network instability. 4. Cross Traffic: Background traffic was introduced randomly to simulate dynamic congestion conditions. Insects play a critical role in forensic investigations, particularly in estimating the post-mortem interval (PMI) in cases involving decomposing human or animal remains. The colonization of cadavers by insects follows a predictable sequence, and the developmental stages of these insects can provide investigators with valuable temporal information [1]. Among the various insect species utilized in forensic entomology, beetles have garnered increasing attention due to their ecological importance in decomposition processes and their potential as reliable indicators of PMI [2]. Despite their utility, the accuracy of age estimations based on insect development remains a significant challenge, as intraspecific variation in development time can introduce considerable uncertainty into forensic analyses [3]. Consequently, refining methods to improve the precision and reliability of insect age estimates is a priority in forensic entomology. Typically, insect age estimation relies on developmental data derived from laboratory studies, where the relationship between temperature and the duration of each life stage is modeled to calculate thermal summation values (K) [4]. These models are based on the principle that insect development is temperature-dependent, with a species-specific thermal constant required for the completion of specific life stages. However, such general models often overlook individual-level variation arising from environmental, genetic, and physiological factors, which can influence developmental rates and lead to discrepancies in predicted ages [5]. For instance, factors such as larval nutrition, competition, and microclimatic conditions may result in significant differences in the size and developmental duration of individuals within the same species [6]. This variation complicates the application of general thermal summation models in forensic contexts, where precise and accurate age estimates are critical for reconstructing timelines. Recent studies have suggested that incorporating additional biological variables, such as insect size, may improve the accuracy of age estimations. Size is a commonly measured trait in entomology and is known to be influenced by both genetic and environmental factors during development [7]. As such, it serves as a proxy for the conditions experienced by an individual throughout its growth. Insects of the same species and developmental stage may emerge at different sizes due to variation in resource availability, competition, or other environmental influences, and these differences in size can be associated with variation in physiological age [8]. Specifically, larger individuals may have shorter development times due to more favorable growth conditions, while smaller individuals may require longer durations to reach maturity. This relationship offers the potential to refine age estimation models by accounting for individual variability in physiological age based on size at emergence. The present study focuses on the beetle Creophilus maxillosus (Linnaeus, 1758), a member of the family Staphylinidae, which is commonly associated with decomposing remains and holds considerable forensic relevance [9]. C. maxillosus is a predatory beetle that feeds on other insects present on cadavers, and its predictable developmental pattern makes it a useful species for PMI estimation. While previous research has established baseline developmental data for C. maxillosus under controlled laboratory conditions, little attention has been given to the potential for size-based models to enhance age estimation accuracy in this species [10]. Considering the practical significance of improving forensic tools, this gap warrants further investigation. In this study, we test the hypothesis that the physiological age of C. maxillosus at emergence, as represented by the thermal summation value (K), is inversely related to beetle size. Specifically, we propose that larger individuals of C. maxillosus require lower K values to emerge, reflecting a shorter development time. To test this hypothesis, we conducted a laboratory study to examine the relationship between beetle size at emergence and K across a range of controlled developmental conditions. We further developed size-based predictive models for K and validated these models against independent data to assess their accuracy in estimating physiological age. Our results demonstrate that incorporating size as a predictor variable significantly improves the accuracy of age estimates for C. maxillosus, compared to traditional thermal summation models that do not account for individual variability. The implications of this research extend beyond the specific case of C. maxillosus. By demonstrating the utility of size-based models for refining age estimates, this study highlights a broader methodological advance in forensic entomology. Size is a relatively easy and non-destructive measurement to obtain, and its integration into forensic analyses has the potential to reduce uncertainty in PMI estimations across a range of insect species. Furthermore, the sex-specific differences observed in this study underscore the importance of considering biological variation in forensic models. As forensic entomology continues to develop as a discipline, incorporating additional biological and ecological variables into age estimation methods will be critical for improving the robustness and reliability of PMI determinations in legal investigations. In conclusion, this study addresses a significant challenge in forensic entomology by exploring the relationship between beetle size at emergence and physiological age in the forensically important species C. maxillosus. By demonstrating that size-based models can improve the accuracy of age estimates, this research provides a valuable contribution to the field and emphasizes the importance of accounting for individual-level variation in forensic analyses. The findings presented here have important implications for the use of insect evidence in forensic investigations, offering a more precise approach to estimating PMI and advancing the scientific foundation of forensic entomology. Laboratory experiments were conducted to investigate the development of Creophilus maxillosus under controlled conditions and to assess the relationship between adult beetle size at emergence and physiological age. These experiments aimed to determine whether incorporating size measurements can improve the accuracy of age estimates in a forensic entomology context. To establish a thermal summation model for C. maxillosus, eggs were collected from beetles maintained in a laboratory colony. The colony originated from adults collected in natural environments and was replenished periodically to maintain genetic diversity. Adult beetles were housed in plastic containers (30 × 20 × 10 cm) under controlled environmental conditions (25 ± 1°C, 60 ± 5% relative humidity, and a 12:12 light-dark cycle). Beetles were provided with minced meat ad libitum as a protein source and moistened cotton as a source of water. Eggs were collected by inspecting the rearing substrate daily and were transferred to small individual containers (5 × 5 × 5 cm) containing a thin layer of moistened substrate and food. The containers were maintained under the same environmental conditions as the colony. To investigate the effects of temperature on development, egg batches were divided and reared at five constant temperatures: 18°C, 22°C, 25°C, 28°C, and 30°C (± 0.5°C). Each temperature treatment included a minimum of 50 individuals to account for variation in development and ensure robust statistical analysis. Larvae were monitored daily and were provided with fresh food every 24 hours. Developmental stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) were recorded, and the time taken to reach each stage was documented. Upon adult emergence, the beetles were sexed based on external morphological characteristics and were measured for body length using a digital caliper with a precision of 0.01 mm. Measurements were taken from the anterior margin of the head to the posterior edge of the elytra. The physiological age of each individual was expressed as the thermal summation value (K), which was calculated using the equation \( K = (T - T{min}) \times D \), where \( T \) is the rearing temperature, \( T{min} \) is the lower developmental threshold, and \( D \) is the duration of development (in days) from egg to adult emergence. The \( T{min} \) value was determined by extrapolating the linear relationship between development rate (1/D) and temperature. Thermal summation values for each individual were calculated separately for males and females to account for potential sex-specific differences in development. To evaluate the relationship between body size at emergence and physiological age, linear regression models were constructed for both sexes. Beetle length was used as the predictor variable, and \( K \) was the dependent variable. The models were developed using data from individuals reared at 22°C, 25°C, and 28°C, as these temperatures produced the most consistent development across replicates. The models were then validated using data from individuals reared at 18°C and 30°C, which were not included in the model construction. Validation involved comparing the predicted \( K \) values, obtained using the size-based regression models, with the true \( K \) values derived from development data. To assess the accuracy of the size-based models in predicting physiological age, the absolute error between predicted and true \( K \) values was calculated for each individual. These errors were compared with errors derived from the general thermal summation model, which does not incorporate size as a predictor variable. Statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 4.0.5) [1]. The goodness-of-fit of the regression models was evaluated using the coefficient of determination (\( R^2 \)), and the predictive accuracy of the models was assessed using root mean square error (RMSE) and mean absolute error (MAE). Paired t-tests were used to compare the absolute errors between the size-based and general models. To further assess the applicability of the size-based approach in forensic contexts, a simulated validation study was conducted. In this study, adult beetle measurements from individuals reared under varying environmental conditions (e.g., fluctuating temperatures) were used to predict \( K \) values using the size-based models. Predicted \( K \) values were then compared with true \( K \) values calculated from the known development data. This approach was designed to mimic real-world scenarios in which insects collected from crime scenes exhibit developmental variability due to environmental factors. The results of the experiments were compiled and analyzed to determine the extent to which incorporating size at emergence improved the accuracy of age estimates. Statistical significance was set at \( p < 0.05 \) for all tests. Understanding the intricate web of cause-and-effect relationships is fundamental to human reasoning, scientific inquiry, and decision-making. Causal attributions form the backbone of how individuals and societies interpret events, predict outcomes, and intervene in complex systems. However, identifying and mapping these relationships at scale is a challenging endeavor. Networks of causal attributions are inherently large, dynamic, and open-ended, requiring nuanced exploration that balances precision with efficiency. Despite their importance, constructing such networks often relies on expert-driven approaches that can be time-intensive, expensive, and limited in scope. Recent advances in crowdsourcing, combined with the growing accessibility of platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT), provide an opportunity to engage distributed groups of people in constructing causal networks. Yet, harnessing the collective intelligence of the crowd for tasks of this complexity requires innovative methodologies that go beyond traditional microtasking paradigms. Crowdsourcing has transformed how we tackle problems that require large-scale data collection or analysis. Platforms like AMT have demonstrated remarkable success in enabling diverse, distributed participants to complete simple, repetitive tasks—often referred to as microtasks. Examples include labeling images, transcribing text, or categorizing items. These tasks are well-suited for the crowd because they are self-contained, require minimal context, and can be completed quickly. However, more complex and open-ended tasks, such as exploring large networks or identifying nuanced relationships within data, present unique challenges. Such tasks require workers to process and integrate information across multiple steps, maintain a coherent understanding of the broader problem, and coordinate their efforts with other participants. Developing approaches that bridge the gap between microtask simplicity and open-ended complexity is crucial for leveraging crowdsourcing to its full potential. One particularly compelling application of crowdsourcing lies in the exploration of large networks. Networks are ubiquitous in representing complex systems, capturing the relationships between entities in domains ranging from social interactions to biological processes. In this work, we focus specifically on the network of causal attributions—a representation of cause-and-effect relationships as a directed graph, where nodes correspond to events, concepts, or variables, and edges represent causal links. Causal networks are a powerful tool for understanding how people perceive causality, which has profound implications for fields such as psychology, sociology, public policy, and artificial intelligence. For example, causal networks can reveal how individuals attribute responsibility for societal outcomes, how they reason about interventions, and how they navigate uncertainty in decision-making. Despite their potential, little research has explored how to efficiently crowdsource the construction of these networks. The primary challenge in crowdsourcing causal attributions lies in balancing the open-ended nature of the task with the need for structured, efficient workflows. Asking crowd workers to freely propose and validate causal relationships risks generating noisy, inconsistent, or incomplete data. On the other hand, constraining workers too tightly may limit their creativity and fail to capture the richness of causal reasoning. To address this challenge, we introduce a method called Iterative Pathway Refinement, a theoretically principled approach designed to enable independent crowd workers to collaboratively explore large networks. The method partitions the exploration process into a series of microtasks, allowing workers to propose, evaluate, and refine causal relationships incrementally. By iteratively refining pathways through the network, this approach ensures both depth and breadth in exploration while maintaining the scalability and simplicity of microtask workflows. To evaluate the effectiveness of Iterative Pathway Refinement, we conduct a series of experiments on AMT. First, we validate the method using synthetic networks, where the true causal structure is known. This allows us to assess the accuracy and efficiency of the crowd in reconstructing complex networks under controlled conditions. Next, we apply the method to a real-world crowdsourcing task: constructing a large-scale causal attribution network. Workers on AMT are asked to propose and validate causal relationships between events, leading to the emergence of a directed network that reflects collective causal reasoning. We analyze both the structure of the resulting network and the activity patterns of the workers who contributed to its construction. Our findings highlight key features of causal perception, such as the types of relationships workers are most likely to propose and the strategies they use to validate causal claims. Beyond the immediate application to causal attribution, our work has broader implications for crowdsourcing complex tasks. Iterative Pathway Refinement provides a general framework for exploring large, open-ended systems through microtasks, offering a scalable alternative to traditional expert-driven approaches. The method emphasizes modularity, enabling independent contributions from workers while ensuring that their efforts converge toward a coherent outcome. By demonstrating the feasibility of crowdsourcing large networks, this study opens new avenues for research on collective intelligence, network science, and causal inference. In addition to its methodological contributions, this work sheds light on the social and cognitive processes underlying causal reasoning. Crowdsourced causal networks capture the collective perceptions of a diverse group of individuals, providing insights into how people think about causality in everyday life. These insights have practical applications in domains such as public health, where understanding causal attributions can inform the design of effective interventions, and artificial intelligence, where causal reasoning is increasingly recognized as a cornerstone of robust decision-making systems. Moreover, the data generated through this process can serve as a valuable resource for studying the interplay between individual cognition and collective knowledge formation. Overall, this study represents a step toward bridging the gap between microtasking and open-ended exploration in crowdsourcing. By leveraging the power of Iterative Pathway Refinement, we demonstrate that large-scale causal attribution networks can be constructed efficiently and accurately by non-expert crowd workers. The resulting networks not only enhance our understanding of causality but also illustrate the potential of collaborative human computation to tackle some of the most complex problems in science and society. To investigate the problem of efficiently crowdsourcing the construction of large causal attribution networks, we developed a structured approach centered on Iterative Pathway Refinement. This method enables independent crowd workers to propose and validate causal relationships and collectively explore the topology of large networks. We describe our methodology in three parts: (1) the design of microtasks for causal attribution, (2) the Iterative Pathway Refinement mechanism, and (3) the evaluation framework for both synthetic networks and real-world deployment on Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT). Crowdsourcing Causal Attribution Microtasks We first decomposed the task of causal attribution network construction into microtasks to make it manageable and intuitive for crowd workers. Each microtask was designed to either (a) propose a new causal relationship, (b) validate an existing causal relationship, or (c) explore the network by refining pathways between specific nodes. This modular design ensured that workers could contribute incrementally and independently, while maintaining the overall coherence of the network. 1. Proposing Causal Relationships: Workers were presented with a prompt describing a specific context or domain (e.g., climate change, public health). They were then asked to identify and articulate a cause-and-effect relationship using a simple sentence structure: "A causes B." Workers were encouraged to provide brief justifications for their proposals to ensure clarity and to facilitate subsequent validation. 2. Validating Causal Relationships: To assess the reliability of proposed causal links, we deployed validation microtasks where workers were shown a proposed relationship (e.g., "A causes B") along with its justification. Workers were tasked with evaluating the link’s plausibility based on their knowledge or reasoning. A Likert scale (e.g., 1 = highly implausible, 5 = highly plausible) was used to capture their judgments. Validation scores were aggregated to determine consensus, and relationships that consistently scored below a predefined threshold were excluded from the network. 3. Pathway Exploration and Refinement: To explore the broader structure of the network, workers were tasked with identifying intermediate causes that could connect given pairs of nodes (e.g., "A causes B, but what intermediate factor(s) might explain this relationship?"). Workers could propose one or more intermediate nodes and justify their additions, effectively refining the pathways and enhancing the granularity of the network. Iterative Pathway Refinement The core mechanism underlying our approach, Iterative Pathway Refinement, builds on the idea that large, complex networks can be gradually constructed through iterative contributions from independent workers. The process involves the following steps: 1. Seeding the Network: The process begins with a small set of "seed" nodes and initial causal links, either constructed by domain experts or derived from existing knowledge bases. These seeds provide a starting point for crowd exploration. 2. Iterative Expansion: Workers are tasked with proposing new nodes and links that extend the network outward from the seed nodes. Each proposed link is validated by independent workers to ensure reliability before it is integrated into the network. Proposals that lack sufficient validation are flagged for further review or discarded. 3. Pathway Refinement: As the network grows, workers are periodically tasked with refining existing pathways. This involves identifying alternative or intermediate causes for known relationships, or resolving conflicts where multiple contradictory links have been proposed. Refinement tasks are structured to ensure that the network remains coherent and interpretable. 4. Feedback Loop: Workers receive feedback on their contributions, such as whether their proposed links were validated or rejected. This feedback serves to improve worker engagement and accuracy over time. By iterating between expansion and refinement, the network evolves in a structured yet flexible manner, allowing for the efficient exploration of large causal systems. Evaluation Framework To evaluate the effectiveness of our method, we conducted experiments on both synthetic networks with known topologies and real-world networks constructed by crowd workers on AMT. 1. Synthetic Networks: Synthetic networks were generated using standard random graph models (e.g., Erdős-Rényi, Barabási-Albert) with predefined causal structures. These networks served as ground truth for evaluating the accuracy and efficiency of the crowdsourcing process. Key metrics included precision and recall of proposed links, the completeness of the reconstructed network, and the time required for workers to achieve a given level of coverage. 2. Real-World Deployment: For real-world testing, we applied our method to extract a large-scale causal attribution network in a domain of broad public interest (e.g., climate change). Workers on AMT were recruited to participate in the microtasks, with each task designed to take no more than 2-3 minutes to complete. To ensure data quality, we implemented several safeguards, including attention checks, redundancy in validation tasks, and performance-based bonuses. 3. Worker Activity and Efficiency: We analyzed worker behavior to identify patterns of engagement and efficiency. Metrics included the number of tasks completed per worker, average time spent per task, agreement rates in validation tasks, and the proportion of high-quality contributions (as determined by validation scores). We also investigated the effects of task design choices (e.g., the framing of prompts, the complexity of tasks) on worker performance. 4. Network Analysis: The final networks were analyzed to assess their structural properties, including node degree distribution, clustering coefficients, and the presence of key causal hubs. These properties were compared against theoretical expectations and known characteristics of causal systems to evaluate the plausibility and utility of the constructed networks. Implementation Details All microtasks were implemented on the AMT platform using custom interfaces designed to guide workers through the task flow. Workers were compensated at a rate consistent with ethical guidelines for fair pay, and task interfaces were iteratively refined based on pilot studies to maximize usability and minimize cognitive load. Data collected from workers were anonymized and processed in accordance with institutional review board (IRB) guidelines. By combining the modular design of microtasks with the iterative refinement mechanism, our method leverages the strengths of crowdsourcing while addressing its limitations. The evaluation framework ensures that the constructed networks are both accurate and interpretable, providing valuable insights into the structure of causal attribution systems. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease that predominantly affects synovial joints, leading to progressive joint damage, pain, and functional disability. The pathogenesis of RA is characterized by a complex interplay of genetic, environmental, and immunological factors, resulting in the breakdown of self-tolerance and subsequent immune-mediated damage to joint tissues. A hallmark of RA is the production of autoantibodies, including rheumatoid factor (RF) and, more specifically, anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA), which are highly associated with disease onset and progression. The presence of ACPA in sera is one of the most reliable biomarkers for diagnosing RA and is strongly linked to worse disease outcomes [1,2]. Citrullination, a post-translational modification catalyzed by peptidylarginine deiminases (PADs), converts arginine residues into citrulline, creating neoepitopes that can break immune tolerance and drive autoimmunity [3]. While numerous citrullinated proteins have been identified in the synovial joints and systemic circulation of RA patients, the specific molecular targets and their roles in disease pathogenesis remain incompletely understood. Aggrecan, a large proteoglycan (PG), is one of the most abundant macromolecules in articular cartilage and plays a critical role in maintaining cartilage structure and function. It is composed of three globular domains (G1, G2, and G3) and an extended interglobular domain rich in glycosaminoglycan (GAG) side chains, which provide cartilage with its compressive resistance and hydration properties [4]. The G1 domain, located at the N-terminus of aggrecan, is responsible for anchoring the proteoglycan to hyaluronic acid through link proteins, ensuring the stability and integrity of the extracellular matrix (ECM). Given the structural and functional importance of aggrecan, its degradation and post-translational modifications, including citrullination, may have significant consequences for cartilage health and immune recognition [5]. However, the citrullination status of aggrecan in vivo has not been previously characterized, and its potential contribution to autoimmunity in RA has remained speculative. Emerging evidence has highlighted the immunogenic potential of citrullinated peptides derived from joint tissues in ACPA-positive (ACPA+) RA patients. Several citrullinated proteins, including fibrinogen, vimentin, and α-enolase, have been identified as autoantigens targeted by ACPA [6,7]. These citrullinated proteins are thought to play a dual role in RA pathogenesis: first, by directly contributing to joint inflammation through immune complex formation and complement activation, and second, by serving as antigenic drivers of autoreactive T and B cell responses [8]. Notably, prior studies demonstrated that RA T cells can recognize citrullinated peptides derived from aggrecan, suggesting that aggrecan-derived epitopes may be relevant to disease-specific immune responses [9,10]. Despite these findings, direct evidence of aggrecan citrullination within human cartilage and its subsequent recognition by ACPA has been lacking. The identification and characterization of citrullinated aggrecan (CitPG) as a novel autoantigen in RA could provide valuable insights into the molecular mechanisms driving disease pathogenesis. Understanding the localization and immunogenicity of CitPG within joint tissues may reveal new pathways of cartilage degradation and immune activation. Furthermore, differences in the presence and distribution of CitPG in osteoarthritic (OA) and RA cartilage could shed light on the distinct pathological processes underlying these two major forms of arthritis. While OA is primarily driven by mechanical and biochemical degradation of cartilage, RA is characterized by autoimmune-mediated inflammation and destruction of joint tissues [11]. Investigating CitPG in both disease contexts could help delineate the specific roles of citrullination and autoimmunity in joint pathology. The study presented here aimed to address several critical gaps in our understanding of citrullinated aggrecan in human cartilage. Specifically, the objectives were to (1) determine whether aggrecan is citrullinated in vivo in normal, OA, and RA cartilage; (2) evaluate the reactivity of ACPA+ RA sera with citrullinated aggrecan fragments, including the G1 and G3 domains; (3) identify potential citrullination sites within the aggrecan molecule using molecular modeling; and (4) localize CitPG in cartilage tissues through immunohistochemical analysis. To achieve these aims, a combination of biochemical, immunological, and structural approaches was employed. The findings of this study provide the first direct evidence of CitPG in human cartilage and demonstrate its immunogenicity in ACPA+ RA patients. The localization and differential distribution of CitPG in OA and RA cartilage further support its potential role as a pathogenic autoantigen in RA. In addition to its relevance to RA, the study of CitPG has broader implications for understanding the role of citrullinated proteins in autoimmune diseases. Protein citrullination is a physiological process that occurs during normal cellular functions, such as apoptosis and tissue remodeling. However, dysregulated citrullination can lead to the generation of neoepitopes that are recognized as non-self by the immune system, particularly in genetically susceptible individuals [12]. The identification of CitPG as a new citrullinated autoantigen expands the repertoire of known citrullinated proteins in RA and highlights the importance of post-translational modifications in shaping disease-specific immune responses. Furthermore, the ability of ACPA to recognize CitPG underscores the potential utility of this autoantigen as a biomarker for RA diagnosis and as a target for therapeutic intervention. In conclusion, this study builds upon prior research linking citrullination to RA pathogenesis and provides new insights into the molecular and immunological mechanisms underlying the disease. By characterizing CitPG and exploring its localization and immunogenicity, this work contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of the role of cartilage-derived autoantigens in RA. The findings suggest that CitPG may play a pivotal role in disease-specific immune activation and cartilage damage, offering new avenues for diagnostic and therapeutic strategies in RA. Future studies will be needed to further elucidate the functional consequences of CitPG in joint inflammation and to explore its potential as a therapeutic target in autoimmune arthritis. Materials and Methods Sample Collection and Ethical Approval Human articular cartilage specimens were obtained from patients undergoing joint replacement surgery due to osteoarthritis (OA) or rheumatoid arthritis (RA), as well as from deceased donors with no history of joint disease. The collection and use of human tissue samples were approved by the institutional ethics review board, and all participants provided informed consent in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Donor information, including age, sex, and disease status, was recorded for correlation with experimental findings. Protein Extraction from Cartilage Articular cartilage was dissected from subchondral bone under sterile conditions and immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen. Frozen cartilage was pulverized using a cryogenic mill (SPEX SamplePrep, USA) and solubilized in 4 M guanidine hydrochloride (GuHCl) containing protease inhibitors (Roche, Germany) at 4°C for 48 hours with agitation. Extracts were clarified by centrifugation at 20,000 × g for 1 hour at 4°C, and the supernatant was dialyzed against 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4) and concentrated using Amicon Ultra centrifugal filters (Millipore, USA). Proteoglycan (PG) components were purified by anion-exchange chromatography on a DEAE-Sepharose column (Cytiva, USA), eluted with a linear NaCl gradient, and analyzed for purity by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) followed by Coomassie Blue staining. Recombinant Proteoglycan Preparation and In Vitro Citrullination The recombinant G1 domain of human proteoglycan (rhG1) was expressed in Escherichia coli using a pET system (Novagen, USA) and purified by affinity chromatography on a nickel-nitrilotriacetic acid (Ni-NTA) column (Qiagen, USA). Purified rhG1 was refolded by stepwise dialysis against decreasing concentrations of urea and further purified by size-exclusion chromatography. For in vitro citrullination, rhG1 was incubated at 37°C for 4 hours with 10 U/mL rabbit skeletal muscle peptidylarginine deiminase (PAD; Sigma-Aldrich, USA) in 100 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4) containing 10 mM calcium chloride. Citrullination was confirmed by the presence of citrulline residues using a modified anti-modified citrulline (AMC) assay (Millipore, USA) and Western blot with anti-citrulline antibodies. Detection of Citrullinated Proteoglycan (CitPG) in Cartilage Extracts Cartilage extracts and purified PG were analyzed for citrullination using sera from ACPA+ RA patients. Dot blot assays were performed by spotting 1 µg of protein onto nitrocellulose membranes, which were blocked with 5% non-fat dry milk in Tris-buffered saline with 0.1% Tween-20 (TBS-T). Membranes were incubated with diluted serum (1:100) from ACPA+ RA patients or ACPA- individuals, followed by horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated goat anti-human IgG (Jackson ImmunoResearch, USA). Signal development was achieved with enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL; Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). Western blot analyses were conducted under similar conditions using SDS-PAGE-separated proteins transferred to nitrocellulose membranes. Molecular Modeling of Citrullination Sites in rhG1 To identify potential citrullination sites, the amino acid sequence of the G1 domain was analyzed for arginine residues using the UniProt database (P16112). A homology-based three-dimensional structural model of rhG1 was generated using the SWISS-MODEL server [1]. The spatial accessibility of arginine residues and their potential for PAD-mediated citrullination were assessed using PyMOL (Schrödinger, USA) and molecular dynamic simulations. Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) for CitPG Antibodies To quantify CitPG-specific autoantibodies, high-binding 96-well ELISA plates (Corning, USA) were coated with either native or in vitro citrullinated rhG1 (2 µg/mL) in carbonate-bicarbonate buffer (pH 9.6) overnight at 4°C. Plates were blocked with 1% bovine serum albumin (BSA) in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for 2 hours at room temperature. Serum samples from ACPA+ RA patients, ACPA- individuals, and healthy controls were diluted 1:200 in blocking buffer and incubated for 1 hour at room temperature. Bound autoantibodies were detected using HRP-conjugated goat anti-human IgG and visualized with 3,3',5,5'-tetramethylbenzidine (TMB) substrate. Absorbance was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader (BioTek, USA). Immunohistochemical Localization of CitPG Paraffin-embedded cartilage sections (5 µm) from OA and RA patients were deparaffinized, rehydrated, and subjected to antigen retrieval in citrate buffer (pH 6.0) at 95°C for 20 minutes. Sections were blocked with 5% normal goat serum and incubated overnight at 4°C with rabbit anti-citrulline antibody (Abcam, UK) or anti-PG G1 domain antibody. After washing, sections were incubated with Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (Invitrogen, USA) for 1 hour at room temperature. Nuclei were counterstained with 4',6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI), and slides were mounted with Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech, USA). Images were acquired using a confocal laser scanning microscope (Zeiss LSM 710, Germany). Statistical Analysis All quantitative data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) and analyzed using GraphPad Prism 9 (GraphPad Software, USA). Comparisons between groups were performed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test or unpaired t-tests, as appropriate. A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. References 1. Waterhouse, A., Bertoni, M., Bienert, S., et al. SWISS-MODEL: Homology modelling of protein structures and complexes. Dot blot and Western blot assays revealed that ACPA+ RA sera strongly reacted with PG purified from normal human cartilage, suggesting the presence of citrullinated epitopes within the PG molecule. To further characterize the citrullinated PG (CitPG), cartilage extracts from osteoarthritic (OA) and RA cartilage were analyzed. This was consistent across multiple samples of OA and RA cartilage. Confirmation of Citrullination in Recombinant G1 Domain of PG To confirm the citrullination status and identify potential sites of modification, recombinant human G1 domain (rhG1) of PG was subjected to in vitro citrullination using peptidylarginine deiminase (PAD). These residues were primarily located on the surface of the protein, in regions accessible to PAD enzymes during enzymatic modification. The presence of these citrullinated sites in vitro corroborates the immunoreactivity observed in cartilage extracts, suggesting that citrullination occurs at similar residues in vivo.
