Centrosomes serve as the primary microtubule-organizing centers in eukaryotic cells and play critical roles in processes such as spindle assembly, chromosome segregation, and cell cycle progression. In the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the centrosome equivalent is the spindle pole body (SPB), a highly conserved, multilayered structure embedded in the nuclear envelope (NE). The duplication and insertion of the SPB into the NE are essential for proper nuclear division, ensuring the correct segregation of chromosomes during mitosis. Given the importance of this process, significant efforts have been devoted to understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying SPB duplication. However, the fine spatiotemporal organization and interplay of the numerous protein components involved in SPB assembly remain incompletely understood. The SPB is composed of approximately 18 core proteins, organized into distinct structural layers extending across the cytoplasmic and nuclear sides of the NE. These proteins work in concert to mediate SPB duplication and insertion into the NE. The duplication process occurs once per cell cycle and proceeds through several discrete steps: first, the formation of a duplication site adjacent to the existing SPB; second, the recruitment and assembly of structural and regulatory components at this site; and finally, the insertion of the newly assembled SPB into the NE. Dysregulation of any step in this process can lead to errors in chromosome segregation and genomic instability, underlying the importance of tightly coordinated centrosome duplication. Several studies have identified key molecular players involved in SPB duplication. For example, the protein Sfi1, which forms a rod-like filament, has been proposed to provide a scaffold for the assembly of new SPB components. Other proteins, such as Mps1, Spc29, and Spc42, are also critical for initiating and stabilizing SPB assembly. Additionally, membrane insertion of the SPB requires the coordinated action of proteins such as Mps2, Bbp1, and Ndc1, which are thought to bridge the SPB structure with the NE. Despite these advances, the precise temporal sequence of events and the spatial organization of these proteins during SPB duplication remain poorly defined, in part due to limitations in imaging resolution and the ability to visualize protein dynamics within the complex architecture of the SPB. To address these challenges, advanced imaging techniques are required to achieve sufficient spatial and temporal resolution to dissect the fine structure of the SPB. Super-resolution microscopy has emerged as a powerful tool for studying subcellular structures with resolution beyond the diffraction limit of conventional light microscopy. Among these methods, structured illumination microscopy (SIM) offers a significant improvement in resolution while maintaining compatibility with live-cell imaging and multicolor fluorescence. However, even with super-resolution imaging, challenges remain in interpreting complex structures such as the SPB, where densely packed proteins and overlapping signals often complicate quantitative analysis. In this study, we developed a novel imaging approach combining two-color structured illumination microscopy with single-particle averaging (SPA-SIM) to investigate the molecular architecture of the SPB during duplication. By leveraging the high spatial resolution of SIM and the statistical power of particle averaging, we achieved unprecedented clarity in visualizing the localization of SPB components. Importantly, our approach utilized endogenously expressed fluorescently tagged proteins, allowing us to study SPB duplication under physiological conditions without overexpression artifacts. Using SPA-SIM, we quantitatively analyzed the localization patterns of all 18 SPB components throughout the duplication process, providing new insights into the dynamic assembly and organization of the SPB. Our results reveal a previously unappreciated level of complexity in SPB duplication. We demonstrate that duplication begins at mitotic exit with the formation of an asymmetric Sfi1 filament, which serves as a scaffold for subsequent assembly events. This process is dependent on the kinase Mps1, which promotes the recruitment of Spc29 and Spc42 to the tip of the Sfi1 filament. Strikingly, we observed that proteins involved in membrane insertion, such as Mps2, Bbp1, and Ndc1, accumulate at the new SPB at an earlier stage than previously anticipated. This finding suggests that SPB assembly and NE insertion are not independent processes but are instead tightly coupled events during SPB duplication. Our study thus provides a revised model for SPB duplication in wild-type yeast cells, with important implications for understanding the coordination between centrosome assembly and membrane dynamics. These findings underscore the utility of SPA-SIM as a powerful tool for studying the architecture of complex macromolecular assemblies. By enabling high-resolution analysis of protein localization and dynamics, this approach provides a new framework for investigating centrosome duplication and other processes involving large protein complexes. Furthermore, our results highlight the intricate interplay between structural and regulatory components during SPB duplication, offering novel insights into the mechanisms governing centrosome biogenesis. These advances not only deepen our understanding of SPB biology in yeast but also provide a foundation for exploring centrosome duplication in higher eukaryotes, where similar principles may apply. Strains and growth conditions: Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains used in this study were derived from the S288C background and listed in Supplementary Table 1. Gene tagging with fluorescent proteins was performed using a PCR-based integration method, ensuring that tagging occurred at endogenous loci to preserve native expression levels and avoid overexpression artifacts. Cells were grown at 30°C in standard yeast complete synthetic medium (CSM) supplemented with appropriate amino acids. For imaging, early log-phase cultures were harvested at an OD600 of 0.2–0.4 to ensure optimal cell health and minimal autofluorescence interference. When necessary, cell cycle arrest was induced using 10 µg/mL α-factor or 15 µg/mL nocodazole, followed by washes with fresh medium prior to imaging. Structured illumination microscopy (SIM) and image acquisition: High-resolution imaging was performed on a custom-built structured illumination microscope equipped with a 100×/1.4 NA oil immersion objective and a high-sensitivity sCMOS camera. Two-color imaging was achieved with the use of excitation lasers at 488 nm and 561 nm for GFP and mCherry-tagged proteins, respectively, and appropriate emission filters. Multicolor images were acquired sequentially to minimize bleed-through and photo-damage. For each imaging session, a Z-stack covering the entire SPB region was captured with a step size of 120 nm to ensure comprehensive spatial information. All imaging was performed at room temperature and within 30 minutes of sample preparation to limit photobleaching and other artifacts. Single-particle averaging (SPA): To improve resolution and enhance protein localization accuracy, SPA was employed by computationally aligning and averaging multiple SPB images. For each fluorescently tagged protein, at least 200 SPB images were acquired from independent cells in asynchronous populations. Images were manually screened to select those corresponding to clearly resolved SPBs. Alignment of SPB images was performed using an iterative fitting algorithm based on maximizing cross-correlation between image pairs. Averaged images were subsequently used for quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensity and protein distribution within the SPB structure. Protein localization analysis: All 18 known SPB components were individually tagged with fluorescent proteins to assess their spatial and temporal localization during SPB duplication. Endogenously expressed GFP or mCherry fusions were used to ensure physiological relevance. For dual-color experiments, GFP-tagged proteins were paired with mCherry-tagged SPB markers, such as Spc42 or Ndc1, to facilitate comparative analyses of protein positioning. Localization patterns were classified into distinct stages of SPB duplication based on the appearance of discrete fluorescence signals at the nascent SPB site. Quantitative fluorescence intensity measurements were performed using ImageJ software, with background subtraction applied to all images to correct for cytoplasmic signal and autofluorescence. Mutant analysis and pharmacological perturbations: To dissect the roles of key SPB components, mutant strains lacking specific SPB genes (e.g., sfi1Δ, mps2Δ) or expressing temperature-sensitive alleles (e.g., mps1-1) were analyzed. For temperature-sensitive mutants, cells were grown at the permissive temperature of 25°C and shifted to the restrictive temperature of 37°C for 2 hours prior to imaging. Additionally, Mps1 kinase activity was inhibited pharmacologically using the ATP-competitive inhibitor 1NM-PP1 in strains expressing analog-sensitive mps1-as1. Cells were treated with 10 µM inhibitor for 30 minutes prior to imaging, and control cells were treated with DMSO alone. Data analysis and statistical methods: Fluorescence intensity measurements for each SPB component were normalized to the maximum intensity for that protein across all stages of SPB duplication. Statistical comparisons between wild-type and mutant strains or inhibitor-treated cells were conducted using Student’s t-test or one-way ANOVA, as appropriate. A minimum of three biological replicates were analyzed per condition, and error bars in all graphs represent standard deviations. P-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. Electron microscopy and correlation with SIM: To validate the structural interpretations derived from SPA-SIM, electron microscopy (EM) was performed on samples prepared by high-pressure freezing and freeze substitution. Ultrathin sections (70 nm) were imaged on a JEOL electron microscope at 80 kV. To correlate EM and SIM data, SPB dimensions and protein localization patterns observed by SIM were compared with corresponding structural features visualized by EM. Software and computational tools: Image processing and SPA were performed using custom-written MATLAB scripts. Localization data were visualized using Fiji/ImageJ, and statistical analyses were conducted in GraphPad Prism 9. Figures were assembled in Adobe Illustrator. All scripts and raw data are available upon request. Reproducibility and data availability: All experiments were repeated at least three times with independent biological replicates, and representative images are shown in the figures. Raw and processed imaging data, including averaged SPB images, are deposited in the Dryad repository (accession number provided in Supplementary Data). Stent implantation is a cornerstone of modern interventional cardiology, providing effective treatment for coronary artery disease (CAD) by restoring blood flow and preventing myocardial ischemia. Over the past few decades, advances in stent technology, such as the development of drug-eluting stents (DES), have significantly reduced the rates of in-stent restenosis and other complications compared to bare-metal stents. However, despite these improvements, the long-term outcomes of stent implantation remain influenced by the biological response to the stent and its surrounding vascular environment. Among these responses, neointimal hyperplasia—a proliferative process involving smooth muscle cells and extracellular matrix deposition—plays a pivotal role in the pathophysiology of restenosis and can be visualized using advanced imaging modalities. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) has emerged as a powerful intravascular imaging tool that allows for high-resolution visualization of stent struts and surrounding tissue. OCT enables detailed assessment of neointimal characteristics, including the morphology and intensity patterns of tissue around the stent struts. One specific finding detectable by OCT is the peri-strut low-intensity area (PLIA), characterized by a low-intensity signal around the stent struts surrounded by higher-intensity neointimal tissue. This distinct imaging feature has garnered attention in recent years due to its potential association with underlying biological processes, such as inflammation, lipid accumulation, and extracellular matrix remodeling. However, the clinical implications of PLIA, including its genesis, risk factors, and impact on long-term prognosis, remain poorly understood. Several studies have investigated the morphological features of neointima following stent implantation, yet the specific factors associated with the development of PLIA are not well established. It is hypothesized that the presence of PLIA may reflect localized alterations in the vascular environment, possibly influenced by systemic factors such as lipid metabolism, inflammatory processes, or patient comorbidities. Notably, elevated levels of serum lipids, including triglycerides and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), are well-recognized contributors to atherosclerotic progression and may play a role in the genesis of PLIA. Similarly, a history of cerebrovascular disease—often accompanied by systemic vascular inflammation and endothelial dysfunction—may predispose patients to distinct patterns of neointimal response. The initial clinical presentation of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and the timing of OCT evaluation relative to stent implantation may also influence the prevalence and characteristics of PLIA, reflecting the dynamic nature of vascular healing and remodeling over time. Despite its frequent occurrence, the prognostic significance of PLIA remains an area of active investigation. Previous studies have suggested that abnormal neointimal patterns observed by OCT, including PLIA, may be linked to adverse clinical outcomes such as restenosis or stent thrombosis. However, robust data on the long-term impact of PLIA on patient outcomes are lacking. In particular, whether PLIA is associated with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), including myocardial infarction, stroke, or cardiovascular death, remains unclear. Furthermore, the potential relationship between PLIA and unstable angina (UA)—a clinical manifestation of myocardial ischemia—warrants further exploration, as understanding this link could provide valuable insights into risk stratification and management strategies for patients undergoing stent implantation. To address these knowledge gaps, this study aimed to systematically evaluate the clinical characteristics, predictors, and long-term prognosis of PLIA as detected by OCT in patients who underwent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). By prospectively analyzing a cohort of patients with documented neointimal hyperplasia on OCT reexamination, we sought to identify factors associated with the development of PLIA and assess its impact on subsequent clinical outcomes. Specifically, we examined the relationship between PLIA and key parameters such as serum lipid levels, history of cerebrovascular disease, initial presentation with ACS, and stent implantation time. Additionally, we evaluated the incidence of MACEs and UA during long-term follow-up to determine whether PLIA confers an increased risk of adverse clinical events. This study provides novel insights into the pathophysiological underpinnings of PLIA and its implications for patient management following PCI. By elucidating the predictors and prognostic significance of this unique imaging feature, our findings contribute to a growing body of evidence aimed at optimizing the assessment and treatment of patients with CAD. Understanding the clinical relevance of PLIA may ultimately inform tailored therapeutic approaches to improve outcomes in this high-risk population. This study was conducted as a prospective observational analysis to evaluate the clinical characteristics and prognostic implications of peri-strut low-intensity area (PLIA) detected by optical coherence tomography (OCT) following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Patients were recruited from a single-center registry between January 2009 and December 2011 based on eligibility criteria outlined below. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants, and the study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Ethical approval for the study protocol was obtained from the institutional review board. Patients aged ≥18 years who had undergone successful PCI with stent implantation and demonstrated neointimal hyperplasia on routine follow-up OCT reexamination were included in the study. Exclusion criteria consisted of incomplete stent apposition, stent fracture, restenosis requiring revascularization at the time of OCT reexamination, or poor-quality OCT images precluding detailed analysis. Patients with significant systemic inflammatory or autoimmune diseases, end-stage renal disease, or life expectancy less than one year were also excluded. Baseline demographic and clinical data, including age, sex, body mass index (BMI), comorbid conditions (e.g., diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease), smoking status, medication history, and the initial clinical presentation (acute coronary syndrome [ACS] or stable angina), were collected at the time of index PCI. Serum levels of total cholesterol, triglycerides, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) were measured during the index hospitalization. Procedural characteristics, including the type, size, and length of the stent as well as post-procedural angiographic findings, were also recorded. OCT reexaminations were performed at 6 to 12 months post-PCI using a frequency-domain OCT system (C7-XR, St. Jude Medical, St. Paul, MN, USA). Following intracoronary administration of nitroglycerin (100–200 µg), a 0.014-inch imaging catheter was positioned distal to the stented segment, and the vessel was flushed with contrast media at a rate of 3–5 mL/s to achieve blood clearance. Automated pullback at a speed of 20 mm/s was performed to acquire cross-sectional images of the stented segment at 100-µm intervals. OCT images were analyzed offline by two independent investigators blinded to clinical and procedural data. The primary parameter of interest was the peri-strut intensity pattern of the neointima. Using image analysis software (LightLab Imaging, St. Jude Medical), the intensity of the neointimal layer surrounding each stent strut was categorized as low-intensity (PLIA) or high-intensity based on signal attenuation characteristics. PLIA was defined as a homogeneous low-signal region around stent struts with minimal or no backscattering, in contrast to the high-intensity pattern characterized by strong signal reflection. Neointimal thickness and stent coverage were also quantified. Patients were classified into two groups based on the presence or absence of PLIA. Comparative analyses of baseline demographic, clinical, and procedural characteristics were performed between the two groups to identify predictors of PLIA. Logistic regression models were used to evaluate the independent associations between clinical variables and the presence of PLIA. Variables with P < 0.10 in univariate analysis were included in multivariate models to adjust for potential confounders. Following OCT reexamination, patients who did not require immediate revascularization were enrolled in long-term follow-up. Clinical follow-up was conducted via outpatient visits or telephone interviews at least annually to assess the occurrence of adverse events. The primary outcome of interest was the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), defined as a composite of all-cause death, myocardial infarction, or target lesion revascularization. The secondary outcome was the incidence of unstable angina (UA), defined as new or worsening chest pain with evidence of myocardial ischemia but without myocardial infarction. Kaplan-Meier survival curves were constructed to evaluate the cumulative incidence of MACEs and UA during the follow-up period. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using Cox proportional hazards models to assess the association between PLIA and clinical outcomes. Subgroup analyses were performed to explore potential effect modifiers, including baseline lipid levels, diabetes status, and time since stent implantation. Statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS software (version 24.0, IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation or median (interquartile range) and were compared using the Student’s t-test or Mann-Whitney U test, as appropriate. Categorical variables were reported as frequencies and percentages and analyzed using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test. A two-tailed P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant for all analyses. Interobserver agreement for OCT image interpretation was assessed using the kappa statistic. The sample size was determined based on the expected incidence of PLIA and the anticipated event rates for MACEs and UA. Assuming an incidence of PLIA of approximately 15% and a relative hazard of 3.0 for UA in patients with PLIA, a minimum of 120 patients was required to achieve 80% power at a significance level of 0.05. To account for potential losses to follow-up, we aimed to enroll at least 130 patients. This methodology allowed for a comprehensive evaluation of the clinical characteristics, predictors, and long-term prognosis of PLIA in a well-defined cohort of patients undergoing OCT imaging after stent implantation. In this study, a total of 128 patients who underwent optical coherence tomography (OCT) reexamination following stent implantation were enrolled. Among these, peri-strut low-intensity area (PLIA) was identified in 22 patients (17.2%). The baseline clinical and procedural characteristics of the patients were analyzed to determine factors associated with the development of PLIA. Importantly, serum triglyceride levels were found to be significantly higher in patients with PLIA compared to those without PLIA (2.02 ± 1.01 mmol/L vs. 1.50 ± 0.75 mmol/L, P = 0.013). Similarly, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels were also elevated in the PLIA group (3.23 ± 1.05 mmol/L vs. 2.68 ± 0.91 mmol/L, P = 0.009). Multivariate logistic regression analysis further confirmed these associations, with serum triglycerides (odds ratio [OR]: 2.11, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.14–3.90, P = 0.017) and LDL-C (OR: 2.61, 95% CI: 1.22–5.66, P = 0.015) emerging as independent predictors of PLIA. A history of cerebrovascular disease was also significantly more prevalent in the PLIA group (36.4% vs. 3.7%, P < 0.001). Logistic regression showed a strong positive correlation between a history of cerebrovascular disease and the presence of PLIA (OR: 101.11, 95% CI: 6.54–1562.13, P < 0.001). Furthermore, the initial clinical presentation of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) was significantly associated with the development of PLIA. Patients with PLIA were more likely to have presented with ACS at the time of stent implantation compared to those without PLIA (63.6% vs. 17.6%, P < 0.001). This association was robust in multivariate analysis, with ACS exhibiting an OR of 18.77 (95% CI: 2.73–128.83, P = 0.003). Additionally, the time interval between stent implantation and OCT reexamination was found to be negatively associated with the incidence of PLIA. Patients with PLIA underwent OCT reexamination after a shorter duration post-stent implantation compared to those without PLIA (median: 6.5 months vs. 11 months, P = 0.048). Multivariate analysis indicated that longer stent implantation time was associated with a lower likelihood of PLIA (OR: 0.57, 95% CI: 0.33–0.98, P = 0.043), suggesting that the prevalence of PLIA decreases over time. During a median follow-up period exceeding 3.8 years, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), including cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, and ischemic stroke, occurred in 7 patients (7.3%). There was no significant difference in the incidence of MACEs between patients with PLIA and those without PLIA (9.1% vs. 6.9%, P = 0.712). However, the occurrence of unstable angina (UA) during follow-up was significantly higher in the PLIA group. A total of 17 patients (17.7%) experienced UA, with 5 of these cases occurring in the PLIA group. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis demonstrated a significant association between the presence of PLIA and UA (log-rank P = 0.022). Multivariate Cox proportional hazards analysis showed that PLIA was an independent predictor of UA, with a hazard ratio (HR) of 6.16 (95% CI: 1.25–30.33, P = 0.025). No significant correlations were observed between PLIA and other clinical outcomes, such as repeat revascularization or heart failure hospitalization. The ability to interact with and interpret the vast amount of visual information generated in the modern world is a fundamental challenge in many fields, including neuroscience, artificial intelligence, and human-computer interaction. One promising approach for addressing this challenge lies in the development of brain-computer interface (BCI) systems, which leverage neural signals to facilitate communication and control without the need for traditional physical input devices. Among the various paradigms employed in BCI research, the rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) paradigm has emerged as a particularly effective method for target detection tasks. This paradigm involves the rapid sequential presentation of visual stimuli, where users identify target images based on their neural responses, specifically the P300 event-related potential (ERP), a well-studied marker of cognitive processing. The P300 component is an endogenous ERP that is elicited approximately 300 milliseconds after the presentation of a target stimulus. Its amplitude and latency reflect cognitive processes such as attention and working memory, making it a reliable neural marker for detecting target stimuli in RSVP tasks. The RSVP paradigm has been widely applied in areas such as image retrieval, surveillance, and medical diagnosis due to its ability to process large quantities of visual information efficiently. However, the effectiveness of these systems is heavily dependent on the accuracy of single-trial P300 detection methods, which aim to identify target stimuli based on a single instance of neural response. While significant progress has been made in improving single-trial detection algorithms, their performance remains suboptimal due to the inherently low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of EEG data and the variability of neural responses across individuals and trials. A promising alternative to single-trial detection is the use of multitrial approaches, which aggregate neural responses across multiple presentations of the same stimulus to enhance signal quality and improve classification accuracy. Multitrial methods leverage the temporal consistency of the P300 component across repeated exposures to target stimuli, allowing for more robust detection in noisy environments. However, traditional RSVP paradigms are not inherently designed to support multitrial processing, as they typically present each image only once during a sequence. This limitation has motivated the exploration of novel RSVP paradigms that can accommodate multitrial approaches, thereby unlocking their potential for improved performance in target detection tasks. In this study, we propose a novel multirapid serial visual presentation (multi-RSVP) framework that integrates the principles of multitrial processing into the RSVP paradigm. Specifically, our approach involves the simultaneous presentation of three images, with each target image appearing three times throughout the sequence. This triple-RSVP paradigm is designed to facilitate the application of multitrial P300 classification methods by ensuring that target stimuli are encountered multiple times during a session. By enabling the aggregation of neural responses across these repeated exposures, the multi-RSVP framework aims to mitigate the limitations of single-trial detection and enhance the overall accuracy of the system. The introduction of the multi-RSVP framework addresses several critical challenges in EEG-based target detection. First, it provides a structured mechanism for leveraging multitrial processing without compromising the rapidity and efficiency of the RSVP paradigm. Second, it introduces redundancy into the stimulus presentation sequence, which can help to counteract the effects of missed detections or inconsistent neural responses. Third, it offers a flexible platform for evaluating and comparing different P300 detection algorithms, as the framework is compatible with a wide range of signal processing and machine learning techniques. Together, these features make the multi-RSVP paradigm a versatile and powerful tool for advancing the state of the art in EEG-based target detection. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, we conducted an extensive experimental study that examined its performance under various conditions. Two different P300 detection algorithms were employed to demonstrate the generalizability of the multi-RSVP paradigm and to explore its compatibility with diverse classification approaches. Our results indicate that the multi-RSVP framework consistently outperforms the standard RSVP paradigm in terms of detection accuracy, highlighting the benefits of multitrial processing for EEG-based target detection. Furthermore, the findings suggest that the triple-RSVP paradigm can serve as a foundation for future research on multitrial EEG analysis, opening new avenues for innovation in BCI systems and applications. The contributions of this study are manifold. First, we introduce the multi-RSVP framework as a novel paradigm for EEG-based target detection, providing a systematic approach to integrating multitrial processing into RSVP tasks. Second, we demonstrate the universal applicability of the framework by testing it with multiple P300 detection algorithms, thereby showcasing its robustness and versatility. Third, we present empirical evidence supporting the superiority of the multi-RSVP paradigm over traditional RSVP approaches, offering valuable insights into the design and optimization of future BCI systems. By addressing the limitations of single-trial detection and leveraging the advantages of multitrial processing, this work represents a significant step forward in the development of high-precision EEG-based target detection methods. In summary, this study introduces a novel multi-RSVP framework designed to improve the accuracy and reliability of EEG-based target detection systems. By incorporating multitrial processing into the RSVP paradigm, the proposed approach overcomes many of the challenges associated with single-trial P300 detection and paves the way for more effective and efficient BCI applications. Through rigorous experimentation and analysis, we demonstrate the potential of this framework to transform the field of EEG-based target detection and to inspire new directions in BCI research and development. The proposed multi-RSVP framework was designed to enhance the detection accuracy of target images in an EEG-based brain-computer interface (BCI) system by leveraging a triple-RSVP paradigm and multitrial P300 classification methods. This section outlines the experimental design, data acquisition, preprocessing, feature extraction, classification methods, and statistical analyses used to validate the effectiveness of this approach. Experimental Design The experiment was conducted using a triple-RSVP paradigm in which three images were presented simultaneously on-screen at a fixed presentation rate. Each image triad consisted of three distinct images, and the target image was embedded randomly within the sequence. In each trial, the target image appeared exactly three times to ensure sufficient elicitation of P300 components for multitrial detection. The stimulus presentation rate was set to 6 Hz, with each image displayed for 166 milliseconds, followed by a 34-millisecond blank screen. Participants were seated approximately 60 cm away from the display monitor in a quiet, dimly lit room. The visual stimuli, including target and non-target images, were selected from a publicly available image database to ensure diversity and eliminate bias. Participants were instructed to focus on detecting the target image and mentally respond (e.g., by counting its occurrences) whenever it appeared during the RSVP sequence. No physical responses were required to prevent motor artifacts in the EEG recordings. The study involved 20 healthy volunteers (12 males, 8 females; mean age: 26.1 ± 3.4 years), all of whom had normal or corrected-to-normal vision. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to the experiment, and the study was approved by the institutional ethical review board. EEG Data Acquisition EEG signals were recorded using a 64-channel electrode cap (based on the international 10-20 system) and amplified with a sampling rate of 1000 Hz. The impedance of all electrodes was maintained below 5 kΩ throughout the experiment. Reference and ground electrodes were placed at the left and right earlobes, respectively. Key channels, including Fz, Cz, Pz, Oz, and POz, were prioritized during the analysis as they are known to exhibit strong P300 responses. To reduce artifacts, participants were asked to minimize head and body movements during the experiment. Additional channels were used to monitor electrooculographic (EOG) signals for detecting eye blinks and saccades. Trials with excessive noise, such as those containing eye blinks or muscle artifacts, were excluded from further analysis. Preprocessing EEG data were preprocessed using a combination of open-source and in-house MATLAB scripts. The raw EEG signals were downsampled to 250 Hz and bandpass-filtered between 0.1 and 30 Hz to isolate relevant frequency components. A notch filter at 50 Hz was applied to remove power-line interference. Independent component analysis (ICA) was used to identify and remove components associated with ocular and muscular artifacts. Epoching was performed with respect to the onset of each stimulus presentation, resulting in epochs ranging from -200 milliseconds to 800 milliseconds. Baseline correction was applied using the 200-millisecond pre-stimulus interval. Any epoch with voltages exceeding ±100 μV was rejected as noisy. Feature Extraction To capture the temporal and spatial characteristics of the P300 component, features were extracted from the preprocessed EEG epochs. The analysis focused on a time window between 300 and 600 milliseconds post-stimulus, which corresponds to the typical latency of the P300 response. Spatial features were derived from key parietal and occipital electrodes, where the P300 amplitude is most prominent. Principal component analysis (PCA) was applied to reduce dimensionality while retaining the most informative features. The first few principal components were selected, accounting for 95% of the variance in the data. These features were then used as inputs to the classification algorithms. Classification Methods Two classification algorithms were employed to validate the multi-RSVP framework: a support vector machine (SVM) with a radial basis function (RBF) kernel and a convolutional neural network (CNN). Both classifiers were trained and tested on the extracted features. 1. Support Vector Machine (SVM): The SVM classifier was optimized using a grid search to identify the best hyperparameters, including the regularization parameter (C) and kernel width (γ). A 10-fold cross-validation strategy was employed to evaluate the classifier’s performance, ensuring robust and unbiased results. 2. Convolutional Neural Network (CNN): The CNN was designed with three convolutional layers followed by max-pooling layers and a fully connected layer. The input to the CNN was a matrix representation of the EEG data, preserving both temporal and spatial dimensions. The network was trained using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001 and a batch size of 32. Early stopping was implemented to prevent overfitting. For multitrial P300 detection, the outputs of single-trial classifications were aggregated across the three repetitions of the target image within each trial. A majority-vote scheme was used to determine whether a given image was classified as a target or non-target. Statistical Analyses Detection accuracy was computed for both the single-trial and multitrial settings. Paired t-tests were conducted to compare the performance of the multi-RSVP framework with that of the standard RSVP paradigm. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were also generated to evaluate the classifiers’ sensitivity and specificity. To assess the generalizability of the proposed framework, leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (LOSO-CV) was performed, where data from one participant were used for testing while data from the remaining participants were used for training. This approach provided insight into the robustness of the system across different individuals. Summary The methods described above were designed to systematically evaluate the efficacy of the multi-RSVP paradigm for EEG-based target detection. By combining the triple-RSVP design with multitrial P300 classification methods, this framework aimed to overcome the limitations of traditional single-trial approaches and achieve higher detection accuracy. The results of this study, as detailed in the following sections, demonstrate the potential of the proposed method for various BCI applications. In this study, the proposed multi-RSVP paradigm was evaluated to determine its effectiveness in improving the accuracy of EEG-based target image detection compared to the standard RSVP paradigm. The results presented here include the performance metrics of target detection, a comparison of the two P300 classification algorithms employed, and an analysis of the advantages offered by the multi-RSVP framework. To assess the performance of the system, experiments were conducted on a dataset consisting of EEG signals collected from participants exposed to both the standard RSVP paradigm and the proposed triple-RSVP paradigm. The target images were presented in the triple-RSVP paradigm such that each target appeared three times across distinct trials, allowing for multitrial P300 analysis. Two P300 detection algorithms, a stepwise linear discriminant analysis (SWLDA) classifier and a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based classifier, were implemented to evaluate their performance under the multi-RSVP framework. The study of graph classes defined by structural or combinatorial properties is a central theme in graph theory. Among the numerous properties of interest, matchings—sets of edges without common vertices—play a fundamental role due to their wide-ranging applications in combinatorics, optimization, and computer science. In particular, the class of equimatchable graphs has garnered significant attention [1, 2]. A graph is said to be equimatchable if all of its maximal matchings, i.e., matchings that cannot be extended by including additional edges, have the same cardinality. This property imposes stringent structural constraints on the graph, making equimatchable graphs an intriguing object of study. While equimatchable graphs have been investigated in general and for specific graph classes, a full characterization for claw-free graphs—graphs that do not contain a claw (a complete bipartite graph \(K{1,3}\)) as an induced subgraph—has not been established prior to this work. Claw-free graphs form a natural subclass of graphs that arises in diverse applications, including scheduling, network design, and computational biology [3, 4]. The absence of a claw as an induced subgraph implies constraints on the local structure of the graph, which often leads to useful algorithmic properties. For instance, claw-free graphs are known to admit efficient algorithms for problems that are computationally challenging in general graphs, such as computing maximum independent sets and maximum matchings [5, 6]. Despite the combinatorial richness of claw-free graphs, their interplay with the property of equimatchability has remained relatively unexplored. This paper seeks to bridge this gap by providing a complete characterization of equimatchable claw-free graphs. 1.1 Background and Related Work The notion of equimatchable graphs was first introduced in the context of matching theory, where the focus was on understanding the structural properties that ensure uniformity in the size of maximal matchings [7]. Early studies identified basic examples of equimatchable graphs, such as complete graphs and odd cycles, and established several necessary and sufficient conditions for equimatchability [7, 8]. Subsequent work extended these results to broader graph classes, including bipartite graphs, chordal graphs, and planar graphs [9, 10]. However, no comprehensive characterization of equimatchable claw-free graphs has been reported to date. Claw-free graphs, on the other hand, have been extensively studied since their introduction by Minty [11] and Sbihi [12] in the 1980s. These graphs are characterized by their exclusion of a claw—a star graph \(K{1,3}\)—as an induced subgraph. The absence of claws has profound implications for the graph's local and global structure. For instance, claw-free graphs exhibit restricted neighborhood structures, which have been exploited to design efficient algorithms for various optimization problems [5]. Beyond their algorithmic properties, claw-free graphs also generalize important graph classes, such as line graphs and certain subclasses of perfect graphs [13]. Despite this rich body of research, the interaction between the claw-free condition and equimatchability has not been systematically explored. From a computational perspective, recognizing equimatchable graphs in general is a co-NP-complete problem [14]. However, for specific graph classes, the problem becomes tractable. For example, efficient recognition algorithms are known for bipartite equimatchable graphs, split equimatchable graphs, and cacti [15]. Claw-free graphs, due to their structural restrictions, provide another promising avenue for developing efficient recognition algorithms for equimatchability. Our results not only achieve a characterization of equimatchable claw-free graphs but also lead to an efficient recognition algorithm for this class. 1.2 Contributions and Significance The main contribution of this paper is the first complete characterization of equimatchable claw-free graphs. Specifically, we identify the families of claw-free graphs that are equimatchable and provide a constructive description of their structure. Our characterization reveals that equimatchable claw-free graphs can be decomposed into a small number of well-defined graph families, each of which admits a straightforward description. This result advances the theoretical understanding of both equimatchable and claw-free graph classes and highlights unexpected connections between these two areas. In addition to the theoretical contributions, our characterization has algorithmic implications. We leverage the structural properties of equimatchable claw-free graphs to design an efficient recognition algorithm. Given a graph \(G\), the algorithm determines in polynomial time whether \(G\) is both claw-free and equimatchable. This result is significant in light of the general intractability of recognizing equimatchable graphs. Furthermore, the algorithmic framework developed in this work may be extendable to other graph classes that exhibit similar structural properties. Finally, our findings contribute to ongoing efforts to classify graph families with uniform matching properties. By focusing on claw-free graphs, we shed light on how local structural constraints, such as the absence of claws, interact with global properties like equimatchability. This interplay has potential applications in designing networks with uniform resource allocation properties and in understanding the combinatorial underpinnings of matchings in restricted graph classes. 1.3 Organization of the Paper The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we provide the necessary definitions and preliminary results that will be used throughout the paper. We formally define equimatchable graphs, claw-free graphs, and other relevant concepts, and we summarize known results that are pertinent to our work. Section 3 presents the main characterization of equimatchable claw-free graphs. We describe the structural properties of these graphs and prove their equivalence to the families identified in our characterization. Section 4 details the recognition algorithm for equimatchable claw-free graphs, including its correctness and complexity analysis. In Section 5, we discuss the implications of our results and outline potential directions for future research. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper with a summary of our contributions. 1.4 Notation and Assumptions Throughout this paper, we consider simple, finite, undirected graphs. A graph \(G = (V, E)\) consists of a vertex set \(V\) and an edge set \(E\), where each edge is a two-element subset of \(V\). For a vertex \(v \in V\), the set of neighbors of \(v\) is denoted by \(N(v)\), and the degree of \(v\) is \(|N(v)|\). A matching in \(G\) is a subset of edges such that no two edges share a vertex. A matching is maximal if it cannot be extended by adding another edge, and it is maximum if it has the largest cardinality among all matchings in \(G\). Additional notation will be introduced as needed in later sections. By addressing the characterization and recognition of equimatchable claw-free graphs, this paper aims to deepen the understanding of these two important graph properties and their interplay. We now proceed to the formal definitions and preliminary results in Section 2. --- References: 1. Lovász, L. (1987). Matching theory. 2. Plummer, M. D. (1994). To characterize claw-free equimatchable graphs, we employed a combination of structural graph theory, algorithmic techniques, and combinatorial analysis. This section outlines the methodologies and approaches used to derive the characterization, establish its correctness, and develop an efficient recognition algorithm. We present the methods in three parts: definitions and preliminary results, structural decomposition, and algorithm design. 1. Definitions and Preliminary Results We begin by defining the key concepts and notations used throughout the paper. A graph \( G = (V, E) \) is said to be equimatchable if all of its maximal matchings have the same size. A maximal matching is a matching \( M \subseteq E \) such that no edge \( e \in E \setminus M \) can be added to \( M \) while preserving the matching property. A graph is claw-free if it contains no induced subgraph isomorphic to \( K{1,3} \), the complete bipartite graph on four vertices with one vertex adjacent to the other three. We utilized several fundamental results on equimatchable and claw-free graphs to guide our work. Theorem 2.1 of [1] states that a graph is equimatchable if and only if every edge belongs to at least one maximum matching. This property, combined with the absence of claws, imposes specific structural constraints on the graph. Furthermore, claw-free graphs have been extensively studied in the context of structural graph theory [2,3], and we leveraged known results about their decomposition into simpler components, such as paths, cycles, and certain classes of special substructures. As a preliminary step, we verified that the known families of claw-free graphs, such as cycles, line graphs, and complete graphs, satisfy or fail the equimatchability condition. This verification provided baseline cases and insights for extending the characterization to more complex claw-free graphs. 2. Structural Decomposition of Claw-Free Equimatchable Graphs The characterization of claw-free equimatchable graphs required identifying the families of claw-free graphs that inherently satisfy the equimatchability property. To this end, we employed a structural decomposition approach, leveraging the fact that claw-free graphs can be decomposed into basic building blocks via operations such as clique-sums and extensions [4]. Our methodology involved the following steps: 1. Base Families Identification: We systematically examined well-known classes of claw-free graphs, including complete graphs \( Kn \), cycles \( Cn \), and line graphs of bipartite graphs. By analyzing these families, we identified the conditions under which each class satisfies equimatchability. For instance, we proved that all odd cycles \( C{2k+1} \) are equimatchable, whereas even cycles \( C{2k} \), for \( k \geq 2 \), are not. 2. Forbidden Substructure Analysis: We identified substructures that prevent a claw-free graph from being equimatchable. For example, the presence of induced claws or certain configurations of disjoint paths within the graph was shown to violate equimatchability. This analysis was guided by the principle that every edge in an equimatchable graph must belong to a maximum matching. 3. Closure Properties: We explored the closure of equimatchable claw-free graphs under common graph operations, such as edge deletions, vertex deletions, and graph unions. This exploration allowed us to infer how equimatchability is preserved or disrupted when constructing larger graphs from smaller components. 4. Recursive Construction: Using the insights obtained from the above steps, we developed recursive construction rules for generating all claw-free equimatchable graphs. Specifically, we demonstrated that any claw-free equimatchable graph can be constructed from a set of base families through a sequence of operations that preserve claw-free equimatchability. 3. Algorithm Design and Complexity Analysis Based on the structural characterization, we designed an efficient recognition algorithm to determine whether a given graph \( G \) is claw-free and equimatchable. The algorithm operates in two phases: claw-free verification and equimatchability testing. 1. Claw-Free Verification: We used the classic adjacency matrix method to check whether \( G \) contains an induced subgraph isomorphic to \( K{1,3} \). Given that a graph with \( n \) vertices and \( m \) edges can have at most \( O(n^4) \) potential induced subgraphs of size four, this step was implemented with \( O(n^4) \) worst-case complexity. However, optimizations exploiting the sparsity of typical graphs allowed for practical performance improvements. 2. Equimatchability Testing: To determine whether \( G \) is equimatchable, we employed a maximum matching algorithm, such as the Edmonds' blossom algorithm [5], to compute a maximum matching \( M \) of \( G \). We then checked whether every maximal matching of \( G \) has cardinality \( |M| \). This was achieved by iteratively computing maximal matchings through a greedy algorithm and verifying their consistency with \( |M| \). The time complexity of this phase was \( O(m n) \), dominated by the matching computations. 3. Integration and Optimization: The claw-free verification and equimatchability testing phases were integrated into a unified framework. To optimize performance, we introduced preprocessing steps to simplify the graph by removing isolated vertices, pendant edges, and redundant structures that do not affect claw-free equimatchability. 4. Validation and Correctness Proofs The correctness of our characterization and algorithm was established through rigorous proofs and experimental validation. We proved that the identified families of claw-free graphs, along with the recursive construction rules, are both necessary and sufficient to generate all claw-free equimatchable graphs. Additionally, we validated the algorithm's performance using a benchmark of synthetic and real-world graph instances, ensuring that it correctly identified claw-free equimatchable graphs with high accuracy and efficiency. Voltage-gated sodium (Nav) channels play a central role in the initiation and propagation of action potentials in excitable tissues such as neurons, cardiac myocytes, and skeletal muscle fibers. These channels are responsible for the rapid depolarization phase of the action potential, a process that requires the precise coordination of channel opening and closing in response to changes in membrane potential. Consisting of a pore-forming α-subunit and auxiliary β-subunits, Nav channels are traditionally understood to function as monomeric units, with a single α-subunit independently carrying out ion permeation and voltage-dependent gating [1,2]. While this monomeric model has provided a robust framework for decades of research, accumulating evidence from structural, biochemical, and functional studies suggests that this paradigm may not fully capture the complexity of Nav channel assembly and operation. A major cornerstone of the traditional view of Nav channel function lies in the structural organization of the α-subunit. This subunit is composed of four homologous but non-identical domains (DI–DIV), each containing six transmembrane segments (S1–S6). The S5-S6 segments from the four domains collectively form the ion-conducting pore, while the S1-S4 segments function as voltage-sensing domains (VSDs) [3]. This pseudo-tetrameric architecture has been considered sufficient for voltage sensing, gating, and ion selectivity, leading to the assumption that a single α-subunit operates independently as a functional unit. In contrast, voltage-gated potassium (Kv) channels, which share evolutionary ancestry with Nav channels, assemble as tetramers of four separate α-subunits, with individual subunits contributing to the formation of a central pore [4]. This fundamental distinction between Nav and Kv channels has shaped our understanding of their respective biophysical properties and mechanisms of action. Despite the longstanding acceptance of the monomeric Nav channel model, several observations have challenged this paradigm. First, early biochemical studies identified physical interactions between Nav α-subunits in heterologous expression systems and native tissues, though these findings were often dismissed as non-specific or irrelevant to channel function [5,6]. More recently, high-resolution structural studies using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) have revealed potential dimeric arrangements of Nav channel α-subunits in certain contexts, raising the possibility of functional dimerization [7]. Additionally, electrophysiological recordings from mutant Nav channels have demonstrated behaviors that are difficult to reconcile with a strictly monomeric gating model, such as cooperative gating kinetics and allosteric modulation between subunits [8]. These findings collectively suggest that Nav channels may form higher-order assemblies with functional significance, yet the molecular basis and physiological implications of such interactions remain poorly understood. A growing body of research on ion channel dimerization and oligomerization further supports the plausibility of Nav channel dimerization. For example, dimerization has been shown to play a critical role in the function of other ion channels, including Kv channels and cyclic nucleotide-gated channels, where inter-subunit interactions contribute to gating cooperativity and signal transduction [9,10]. In the case of Nav channels, the possibility of dimerization raises important questions about how such interactions might influence gating behavior, ion conductance, and pharmacological properties. It also raises the intriguing prospect that dimerization could represent a conserved feature of Nav channel biology, shared across different isoforms and species. In this study, we demonstrate that Nav channel α-subunits not only physically interact but also assemble and function as dimers. Using a combination of biochemical, structural, and electrophysiological approaches, we identify the specific molecular interfaces that mediate α-subunit dimerization and show that this interaction is conserved across multiple mammalian Nav channel isoforms. Furthermore, we reveal that 14-3-3 proteins, a family of regulatory adapter proteins, play a critical role in mediating the coupled gating of Nav channel dimers. The involvement of 14-3-3 proteins in this process provides a mechanistic link between dimerization and the coordinated gating dynamics observed in our functional studies. Importantly, we demonstrate that dimerization has significant biophysical and physiological consequences, including enhanced gating cooperativity and altered responses to pharmacological agents. This discovery has profound implications for our understanding of Nav channel biology. By demonstrating that Nav channels assemble and gate as dimers, our findings challenge the traditional monomeric model and provide a new framework for interpreting Nav channel function. This dimeric assembly model not only advances our understanding of the fundamental mechanisms underlying Nav channel gating but also opens new avenues for investigating the pathophysiology of sodium channelopathies—disorders caused by mutations or dysregulation of Nav channels. Examples of such conditions include epilepsy, cardiac arrhythmias, and certain forms of chronic pain, all of which have been linked to aberrant Nav channel function [11,12]. Understanding how dimerization and coupled gating contribute to channel dysfunction in these contexts could lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies targeting dimer-specific interactions or regulatory mechanisms. In the following sections, we provide a detailed characterization of Nav channel dimerization and its functional consequences. We begin by describing the experimental approaches used to identify and confirm α-subunit dimerization, including co-immunoprecipitation, crosslinking assays, and cryo-EM imaging. Next, we investigate the role of 14-3-3 proteins in mediating dimerization and coupled gating, using a combination of protein interaction studies and electrophysiological recordings. Finally, we explore the functional implications of dimerization, focusing on its effects on gating kinetics, ion permeation, and pharmacological properties. Through these investigations, we aim to provide a comprehensive understanding of Nav channel dimerization and its significance in both physiological and pathological contexts. In summary, our study challenges the traditional view of Nav channels as monomeric units, presenting compelling evidence that these channels assemble and gate as dimers. By identifying the molecular determinants of dimerization and elucidating the role of 14-3-3 proteins in coupled gating, we establish a new paradigm for Nav channel biology with broad implications for basic research and therapeutic development. Materials and Methods Cell culture and transfection HEK293T cells (American Type Culture Collection, ATCC) were cultured in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM; Gibco) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Sigma) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin (Gibco) at 37°C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO₂. Cells were passaged every 2-3 days and used at 50-80% confluency. For electrophysiological and biochemical assays, cells were transiently transfected using Lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Plasmids encoding voltage-gated sodium channel α-subunits (Nav1.1, Nav1.5, and Nav1.7) tagged with fluorescent proteins (e.g., GFP or mCherry) at their C-termini were used to facilitate visualization and interaction studies. For co-expression experiments, equimolar amounts of plasmids encoding different sodium channel variants were co-transfected. In all cases, cells were allowed to express the constructs for 24-48 hours prior to experimentation. Co-immunoprecipitation and Western blot analysis To probe physical interactions between sodium channel α-subunits, co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) assays were performed. Transfected HEK293T cells were lysed in ice-cold lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 1 mM EDTA, and protease inhibitor cocktail; Sigma). Lysates were clarified via centrifugation at 14,000 × g for 15 minutes at 4°C. Protein concentrations were normalized using the bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay (Thermo Scientific). Equal amounts of lysate were incubated with 2 µg of anti-GFP (Abcam) or anti-mCherry (Cell Signaling Technology) antibodies overnight at 4°C with gentle rotation. The immune complexes were captured using Protein A/G magnetic beads (Thermo Scientific) for 2 hours at 4°C, washed extensively with lysis buffer, and eluted in SDS sample buffer. Immunoprecipitated proteins were resolved on 4-20% gradient SDS-PAGE gels (Bio-Rad) and transferred to PVDF membranes. Western blotting was performed using specific primary antibodies (anti-Nav1.5, Alomone Labs; anti-Nav1.7, Alomone Labs) and HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (Thermo Scientific). Proteins were detected with enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL; Pierce). Fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) microscopy To confirm dimerization of sodium channel α-subunits in live cells, FRET assays were conducted. HEK293T cells transfected with GFP- and mCherry-tagged sodium channels were plated on poly-D-lysine-coated glass coverslips. FRET imaging was performed on a Zeiss LSM 880 confocal microscope equipped with a 63× oil immersion objective. Excitation of the donor fluorophore (GFP) was carried out at 488 nm, and the emission was collected at 500-550 nm. Acceptor emission (mCherry) following FRET excitation was collected at 580-650 nm. FRET efficiency was quantified using the acceptor photobleaching method, wherein mCherry was photobleached with high-intensity 561 nm laser light to disrupt FRET, and the increase in GFP fluorescence was measured. FRET efficiency was calculated as \(E = (F{post} - F{pre})/F{post}\), where \(F{pre}\) and \(F{post}\) represent GFP fluorescence before and after acceptor photobleaching, respectively. Electrophysiological recordings Whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology was performed to assess the functional properties of sodium channel dimers. HEK293T cells expressing sodium channels were plated onto glass coverslips in an extracellular solution containing 140 mM NaCl, 3 mM KCl, 2 mM CaCl₂, 1 mM MgCl₂, and 10 mM HEPES (pH 7.4, adjusted with NaOH). Patch pipettes (resistance: 3-5 MΩ) were pulled from borosilicate glass capillaries (Sutter Instruments) and filled with intracellular solution containing 140 mM CsF, 10 mM NaCl, 1 mM EGTA, and 10 mM HEPES (pH 7.3, adjusted with CsOH). Experiments were performed at room temperature using an Axopatch 200B amplifier (Molecular Devices) and digitized at 10 kHz with a Digidata 1550A system (Molecular Devices). Voltage-dependent activation and inactivation properties were assessed using standard voltage protocols. Data were analyzed using pClamp 11 software (Molecular Devices). For coupled gating analysis, the voltage dependence of activation and peak current amplitudes was compared between cells expressing single vs. co-expressed sodium channel constructs. Proximity ligation assay (PLA) To visualize the physical proximity of sodium channel α-subunits within cells, in situ PLA was performed using the Duolink® kit (Sigma). Transfected HEK293T cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 minutes, permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 for 10 minutes, and incubated with blocking solution for 1 hour at 37°C. Cells were incubated with primary antibodies specific to distinct epitopes on sodium channel α-subunits (e.g., anti-Nav1.5 and anti-Nav1.7) overnight at 4°C. Secondary antibodies conjugated to oligonucleotide probes were applied, and ligation and amplification reactions were carried out according to the manufacturer’s instructions. PLA signals were imaged using a Zeiss LSM 880 confocal microscope, and the number of PLA puncta per cell was quantified using ImageJ software. 14-3-3 protein interaction studies To investigate the role of 14-3-3 proteins in sodium channel dimerization, co-IP and pull-down assays were performed. Constructs encoding FLAG-tagged 14-3-3 isoforms were co-transfected with sodium channel α-subunits in HEK293T cells. Lysates were prepared as described above, and FLAG-tagged proteins were immunoprecipitated using anti-FLAG antibodies (Sigma). Interactions were assessed via Western blotting using sodium channel-specific antibodies. To disrupt 14-3-3 interactions, cells were treated with 20 µM BV02, a selective 14-3-3 inhibitor, for 6 hours prior to lysis. The effects of 14-3-3 inhibition on sodium channel gating were assessed electrophysiologically. Conservation analysis across sodium channel isoforms To assess the conservation of dimerization across mammalian sodium channel isoforms, cDNA constructs encoding Nav1.1, Nav1.5, and Nav1.7 were individually transfected into HEK293T cells. Co-IP, FRET, and electrophysiological analyses were performed as described above. Sequence alignment of the putative dimerization region was carried out using Clustal Omega [1]. Conservation scores were calculated to identify residues critical for dimerization. Site-directed mutagenesis was performed on conserved residues to determine their contribution to dimerization and gating. Statistical analysis All experiments were performed in biological triplicates unless otherwise stated. Data are presented as mean ± SEM. Statistical analysis was conducted using GraphPad Prism 9. Comparisons between groups were made using unpaired Student’s t-tests or one-way ANOVA with post hoc Tukey’s test, as appropriate. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Professional values are fundamental principles that guide nurses in providing ethical, high-quality, and patient-centered care. These values serve as a cornerstone for decision-making, interactions with patients, and the overall practice of nursing. They are essential not only for safeguarding patients' rights and dignity but also for maintaining the integrity and credibility of the nursing profession. In today’s complex healthcare systems, where nurses face growing ethical challenges, the recognition and application of professional values have become increasingly critical. Nurses' perspectives on these values are particularly important, as they directly influence their clinical judgments, behaviors, and the quality of care they provide [1,2]. Professional values in nursing encompass a wide array of ethical principles, such as respecting patient autonomy, maintaining confidentiality, safeguarding privacy, and advocating for patients' rights. These values also extend to broader professional responsibilities, including participation in nursing research, adherence to evidence-based practice, and involvement in shaping healthcare policies [3]. However, the extent to which individual nurses prioritize and apply these values in their daily practice can vary significantly based on personal, cultural, and organizational factors. Understanding the perspectives of clinical nurses regarding the importance of professional values is essential for identifying potential gaps in their knowledge and practice, as well as for designing effective educational interventions to address these gaps. Previous studies have highlighted the integral role that professional values play in ensuring ethical and safe patient care. For instance, adherence to professional values has been linked to improved patient outcomes, enhanced trust between nurses and patients, and greater job satisfaction among nurses themselves [4]. Moreover, professional values provide nurses with a framework for navigating ethical dilemmas, which are increasingly prevalent in modern healthcare settings due to factors such as technological advancements, resource limitations, and diverse patient populations [5]. Despite the recognized importance of professional values, studies have also reported variations in the prioritization of these values among nurses, with some ethical principles receiving less attention than others [6]. Such variations underscore the need for a deeper exploration of nurses' perspectives to better understand the factors influencing their prioritization of professional values. In the Iranian healthcare context, cultural and religious norms play a significant role in shaping nurses' ethical perspectives and practices. Islamic ethical principles, which emphasize compassion, justice, and respect for human dignity, align closely with the core values of the nursing profession [7]. However, the rapid evolution of healthcare systems in Iran, coupled with increasing ethical challenges, has highlighted the need for greater awareness and reinforcement of professional values among nurses. Studies in Iran have shown that while nurses generally demonstrate a strong commitment to ethical principles, certain aspects of professional values, such as participation in research and policy-making, are often perceived as less important [8]. These findings point to potential areas for improvement in nursing education and professional development programs. The Nursing Professional Values Scale-Revised (NPVS-R), developed by Weis and Schank, is a widely used tool for assessing nurses' perspectives on professional values. This instrument encompasses a comprehensive range of ethical principles, enabling researchers to gain insights into how nurses prioritize different aspects of professional values in their practice [9]. The NPVS-R has been adapted and validated in various cultural contexts, including Iran, where it has been translated into Persian to facilitate its use among Iranian nurses [10]. By employing this tool, researchers can identify not only the overall importance that nurses assign to professional values but also specific areas where further education or support is needed. The present study aims to investigate the importance of professional values from the perspective of clinical nurses working in educational hospitals affiliated with Kerman University of Medical Sciences in Iran. Given the critical role that nurses play in the delivery of healthcare services, understanding their views on professional values is essential for informing strategies to enhance ethical practice and patient care quality. While previous research has provided valuable insights into nurses' adherence to professional values, most studies have focused on specific ethical principles or have been conducted in limited geographical settings. This study seeks to build upon existing knowledge by providing a comprehensive assessment of professional values as perceived by clinical nurses in a diverse range of hospital settings. In addition to exploring the overall importance of professional values, this study examines the relationship between nurses' perspectives and demographic factors such as age, work experience, and participation in professional ethical training programs. Previous research has suggested that these factors may influence nurses’ ethical attitudes and behaviors [11,12]. For example, older nurses or those with more years of experience may place greater emphasis on certain professional values due to their accumulated knowledge and exposure to ethical challenges [13]. Similarly, participation in ethical training programs has been shown to enhance nurses' awareness and understanding of professional values, thereby influencing their prioritization of these principles in practice [14]. Although the findings of this study are specific to the Iranian healthcare context, they have broader implications for nursing education and practice worldwide. As healthcare systems continue to evolve, fostering a strong foundation of professional values among nurses is critical for addressing emerging ethical challenges and ensuring the delivery of high-quality, patient-centered care. The results of this study can inform the development of targeted educational programs and policies aimed at enhancing nurses' awareness and application of professional values. In summary, this study seeks to address an important gap in the literature by examining the perspectives of Iranian clinical nurses on the importance of professional values. By identifying both the strengths and areas for improvement in nurses' understanding of these values, the findings can contribute to the ongoing efforts to promote ethical practice and professional development within the nursing profession. The present study employed a cross-sectional design to evaluate the importance of professional values from the perspective of clinical nurses working in educational hospitals affiliated with Kerman University of Medical Sciences, Iran. The study was conducted in 2016 and adhered to the ethical principles of research, including obtaining informed consent from all participants and maintaining the confidentiality of their data. The target population included all clinical nurses employed in the four educational hospitals of Kerman University of Medical Sciences. These hospitals were chosen due to their role in providing both educational and clinical services, which offered a comprehensive setting for studying nurses' professional values. Inclusion criteria required participants to have a minimum of one year of clinical experience and to be actively involved in direct patient care during the study period. Nurses who were on leave or engaged in administrative roles without regular clinical responsibilities were excluded to ensure the relevance of the data to clinical practice. The sample size was calculated based on Cochran’s formula for cross-sectional studies, assuming a 95% confidence level and a margin of error of 5%. Considering an expected standard deviation of scores based on similar studies, the required sample size was determined to be 250 participants. To ensure adequate representation of nurses from all four hospitals, stratified random sampling was employed. Each hospital was considered a stratum, and the proportion of nurses sampled from each hospital was proportional to its total number of clinical nurses. Within each stratum, participants were randomly selected using a table of random numbers. Data collection was conducted using the Persian version of the Nursing Professional Values Scale-Revised (NPVS-R), originally developed by Weis and Schank. This instrument has been widely used to assess nurses’ perceptions of professional values and consists of 26 items distributed across five dimensions: caring, activism, trust, professionalism, and justice. Each item is rated on a five-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (not important) to 5 (most important), with higher scores indicating greater importance attributed to professional values. The NPVS-R has demonstrated robust reliability and validity in previous studies and was translated into Persian using a forward-backward translation method. The Persian version of the tool was validated by experts and showed good internal consistency in a pilot study conducted with 30 nurses (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.89). Prior to data collection, ethical approval was obtained from the Research Ethics Committee of Kerman University of Medical Sciences (Ethics Code: IR.KMU.REC.1395.123). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants, who were assured of the confidentiality and anonymity of their responses. Participants were informed that their participation was voluntary and that they could withdraw from the study at any time without any repercussions. The NPVS-R questionnaires were distributed to participants in person by trained research assistants during their work shifts. Research assistants provided a brief explanation of the study’s objectives and instructions for completing the questionnaire. To minimize potential response bias, participants were encouraged to complete the questionnaires individually and return them in sealed envelopes to designated drop boxes located in each hospital ward. The data collection process lasted for two months, ensuring sufficient time for all selected nurses to participate. Demographic information, including age, gender, level of education, years of work experience, and history of participation in professional ethical training programs, was also collected using a separate form. This information was used to explore potential associations between demographic variables and the importance of professional values as perceived by the nurses. Data analysis was performed using SPSS software version 21. Descriptive statistics, including means, standard deviations, frequencies, and percentages, were used to summarize the demographic characteristics of the participants and their responses to the NPVS-R items. To identify the most and least important professional values from the nurses’ perspective, the mean scores for each item were calculated and ranked. Inferential statistical analyses, including independent t-tests and one-way ANOVA, were conducted to examine differences in NPVS-R scores based on demographic variables such as age, work experience, and participation in ethical training programs. Pearson’s correlation coefficient was used to assess the relationship between continuous variables, such as age and total NPVS-R scores. A significance level of 0.05 was set for all statistical tests. To ensure the accuracy and reliability of the findings, data were subjected to rigorous quality control measures. Questionnaires with missing or incomplete responses exceeding 10% of the items were excluded from the analysis. Furthermore, double data entry was performed to minimize the risk of data entry errors. The study also included a post hoc power analysis, which confirmed that the sample size was adequate to detect statistically significant differences in NPVS-R scores across demographic subgroups. By employing the NPVS-R as a validated instrument and adopting a stratified random sampling method, this study aimed to provide a comprehensive understanding of the importance of professional values from the perspective of clinical nurses in Iran. The findings are expected to inform educational and policy interventions aimed at enhancing the professional values and ethical decision-making capabilities of nurses. The analysis of the data collected through the Persian version of the Nursing Professional Values Scale-Revised (NPVS-R) revealed a high total score for professional values among the participating clinical nurses, with a mean score of 102.57 ± 11.94 out of a possible range of 26 to 130. Specifically, “Maintaining confidentiality of patients” and “Safeguarding patients’ right to privacy” received the highest mean scores, indicating their paramount significance from the nurses’ perspective.
