Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) has revolutionized Earth observation technologies with its ability to provide high-resolution imagery independent of weather conditions and lighting. By transmitting and receiving electromagnetic signals, SAR systems generate detailed images of the Earth's surface, making them invaluable in applications such as environmental monitoring, disaster management, and military reconnaissance. However, conventional SAR imaging systems often face inherent trade-offs between imaging resolution and swath width. High-resolution SAR typically requires a narrow beam, which limits the swath coverage, while achieving wide-area coverage often necessitates a reduction in spatial resolution. This conflict has driven significant research into advanced imaging modes that can simultaneously achieve high resolution and wide swath (HRWS) capabilities [1, 2]. The sliding spotlight mode is one such advanced SAR imaging technique that addresses the HRWS challenge. In this mode, the radar antenna beam is electronically steered to follow the illuminated area, enabling extended dwell times on target areas without sacrificing swath width. This steering mechanism allows for the accumulation of more signal energy, thereby enhancing resolution while maintaining a wide imaging swath. The sliding spotlight mode combines the benefits of stripmap SAR and traditional spotlight SAR, making it a promising solution for applications requiring detailed imaging over large areas [3]. However, the complexity of data acquisition in this mode introduces unique challenges in signal processing, particularly in terms of azimuth focusing and Doppler parameter estimation. The Chinese Gaofen-3 (GF-3) satellite is China’s first civilian C-band SAR satellite with multiple imaging modes, including the sliding spotlight mode. Since its launch, GF-3 has demonstrated significant potential in providing high-quality SAR imagery for a wide range of applications. Its ability to operate in sliding spotlight mode positions it as a critical tool for HRWS imaging. However, fully exploiting the benefits of sliding spotlight mode with GF-3 requires the development of robust and efficient imaging algorithms capable of addressing the unique challenges associated with this mode. In particular, the Doppler spectrum of sliding spotlight SAR data is more complex than that of conventional imaging modes, requiring advanced techniques for accurate parameter estimation and image reconstruction. To address these challenges, this study proposes an integrated imaging scheme specifically designed for the sliding spotlight mode of the GF-3 SAR sensor. The proposed methodology employs a two-step processing approach to efficiently handle the increased data complexity and achieve well-focused images. The two-step processing approach, which separates range and azimuth processing, is particularly suited to the sliding spotlight mode as it mitigates the azimuth spectral folding phenomenon commonly encountered in HRWS imaging scenarios [4]. By resolving this issue, the proposed method ensures improved image quality and enhances the interpretability of SAR data. One of the critical components of the proposed imaging scheme is the accurate estimation of Doppler parameters. Doppler parameter estimation is essential for azimuth compression and directly affects the quality of the reconstructed image. Sliding spotlight mode presents unique challenges for Doppler parameter estimation due to the continuous steering of the antenna beam. Conventional methods for Doppler estimation may not yield sufficient accuracy in this context, necessitating the development of advanced algorithms tailored to the sliding spotlight mode. The imaging scheme presented in this paper integrates a Doppler parameter estimation algorithm that ensures high accuracy, enabling the generation of well-focused images with minimal artifacts. This study builds on previous research in the field of sliding spotlight SAR imaging and contributes to the growing body of knowledge on advanced SAR imaging techniques. Existing studies have demonstrated the potential of sliding spotlight mode for achieving HRWS capabilities, but many of these investigations have focused on airborne platforms or theoretical modeling [5, 6]. The application of sliding spotlight mode to spaceborne systems such as GF-3 introduces additional challenges, including the need to account for satellite motion and the increased complexity of the signal acquisition process. By addressing these challenges, the proposed imaging methodology bridges the gap between theoretical advancements and practical implementation, paving the way for more effective utilization of spaceborne SAR systems. The significance of this research lies in its potential to enhance the performance of the GF-3 SAR sensor in sliding spotlight mode, thereby expanding its applicability to a broader range of use cases. High-resolution and wide-swath imaging capabilities are essential for monitoring dynamic processes such as urban development, deforestation, and oceanic phenomena. Additionally, the ability to obtain well-focused images with high Doppler parameter estimation accuracy has implications for improving target detection and classification in SAR imagery. The proposed imaging scheme is designed to be computationally efficient, further increasing its utility for operational scenarios where real-time or near-real-time processing is required. In summary, this paper addresses the critical challenge of achieving HRWS imaging with the GF-3 SAR sensor in sliding spotlight mode. By proposing an integrated imaging scheme based on a two-step processing approach and an advanced Doppler parameter estimation algorithm, the study aims to provide a robust solution for well-focused image reconstruction. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 discusses the theoretical background and related work on sliding spotlight SAR imaging. Section 3 presents the proposed imaging scheme, detailing the two-step processing approach and Doppler parameter estimation algorithm. Section 4 evaluates the performance of the proposed methodology using simulated and real data from the GF-3 SAR sensor. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper with a summary of findings and recommendations for future research. Through this work, we aim to contribute to the ongoing advancement of SAR imaging technologies and promote the effective utilization of spaceborne SAR systems for Earth observation. The methodology employed in this study is designed to address the unique challenges associated with the sliding spotlight imaging mode of the Gaofen-3 (GF-3) synthetic aperture radar (SAR) sensor. The proposed approach integrates advanced signal processing techniques to achieve high-resolution and wide-swath (HRWS) imaging with well-focused results. The methods are structured into four key stages: data preprocessing, the two-step imaging algorithm, Doppler parameter estimation, and image reconstruction. Each of these is described in detail below. Data Preprocessing The initial stage of the imaging process involves the preprocessing of sliding spotlight SAR raw data to ensure compatibility with subsequent stages. The raw data, acquired by the GF-3 SAR sensor in sliding spotlight mode, exhibits nonuniform sampling in the azimuth direction due to the continuous steering of the radar beam. To address this nonuniformity, a range compression process is first applied using matched filtering. This step transforms the raw data from a two-dimensional time domain to the range-Doppler domain, facilitating further processing [1]. To mitigate the effects of system noise and clutter, a noise removal filter is applied during preprocessing. Additionally, range cell migration effects caused by the varying slant range between the SAR platform and the ground target are corrected using a range migration correction algorithm. This ensures that the signal energy remains properly aligned, preserving the integrity of the data for subsequent processing steps [2]. Two-Step Imaging Approach A two-step imaging algorithm is employed to overcome the specific challenges posed by the sliding spotlight mode, particularly the azimuth spectral folding phenomenon. The first step involves the reconstruction of the azimuth spectrum to eliminate spectral ambiguities. The sliding spotlight mode inherently causes a nonuniform Doppler history, leading to folding artifacts in the azimuth spectrum. To address this, the raw data are segmented into smaller subapertures, and a spectral reconstruction technique is applied to each segment individually. This step effectively unfolds the azimuth spectrum and ensures the preservation of high-frequency components [3]. The second step focuses on the accurate focusing of the reconstructed azimuth spectrum to generate well-focused SAR images. A time-domain backprojection algorithm is employed in this stage due to its adaptability to complex imaging geometries and ability to handle varying Doppler histories. The backprojection algorithm operates by integrating the contributions of each subaperture along the azimuth direction, ensuring high-resolution imaging across the entire swath [4]. To optimize computational efficiency, the two-step algorithm is implemented using a parallel processing framework. The raw data are divided into smaller, independent processing blocks, which are executed simultaneously on multiple computational cores. This parallelized approach significantly reduces the overall processing time while maintaining the accuracy of the resulting images. Doppler Parameter Estimation Accurate estimation of Doppler parameters is critical for achieving precise image focusing in sliding spotlight mode. The Doppler centroid and Doppler rate, which describe the frequency shift and rate of change of frequency, respectively, are estimated using an iterative method. In the first iteration, an initial estimate of the Doppler centroid is obtained by analyzing the phase history of the raw data in the range-Doppler domain. This estimate is refined iteratively by minimizing the residual phase error between the observed and predicted Doppler signatures [5]. The Doppler rate is estimated using a maximum-likelihood approach, which considers the statistical properties of the SAR signal. By maximizing the likelihood function, the algorithm identifies the Doppler rate that best aligns the azimuth frequency components, ensuring accurate focusing and reducing geometric distortions in the final image [6]. To enhance the robustness of the Doppler parameter estimation process, a multiresolution analysis is incorporated. The raw data are analyzed at multiple resolution scales, allowing the algorithm to identify and correct for potential errors caused by noise or other artifacts. This multiresolution approach improves the overall accuracy of the Doppler parameter estimates and enhances the quality of the reconstructed SAR images. Image Reconstruction The final stage of the imaging process involves the reconstruction of high-resolution SAR images using the estimated Doppler parameters and the results from the two-step imaging algorithm. The backprojection algorithm is applied once again to integrate the reconstructed azimuth spectrum with the corrected range data. This step produces a focused SAR image with high spatial resolution and a wide swath. To further enhance image quality, a postprocessing filter is applied to suppress sidelobes and improve the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). The filter design is based on the apodization technique, which modifies the amplitude of the azimuth spectrum to reduce sidelobe levels while preserving the mainlobe energy [7]. The final SAR image is georeferenced to align with a predefined geographic coordinate system. This georeferencing process is performed using the precise orbital parameters of the GF-3 SAR platform and the known imaging geometry. The resulting image is then transformed into a standard format for further analysis and interpretation. Implementation and Validation The proposed methodology was implemented using MATLAB and validated with simulated and real-world sliding spotlight SAR data acquired by the GF-3 sensor. Performance metrics, including azimuth resolution, swath width, and image focusing quality, were evaluated to assess the effectiveness of the approach. The results demonstrated that the proposed method successfully overcomes the azimuth spectral folding phenomenon, achieves high Doppler parameter estimation accuracy, and produces well-focused SAR images with HRWS characteristics. Obesity remains one of the most pressing public health challenges in developed nations, with significant implications for both individual health and broader healthcare systems. The global prevalence of obesity has risen dramatically in recent decades, contributing to a substantial burden of chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and certain types of cancer. In addition to its direct health effects, obesity exerts a considerable economic toll, increasing healthcare costs and reducing workforce productivity. Addressing this issue effectively requires a multifaceted approach that integrates prevention, early identification, and treatment strategies across multiple sectors of society. Primary care is widely recognized as a critical setting for addressing obesity, given its accessibility, continuity of care, and the trusted relationships that practitioners such as general practitioners (GPs) and practice nurses (PNs) often develop with their patients. Despite increasing policy attention on the role of primary care in managing obesity, evidence suggests that the identification and referral of adults with obesity to appropriate weight management services remains suboptimal. Many adults with obesity, particularly those with co-morbidities that are exacerbated by excess weight, are not consistently identified or referred for further support. This represents a missed opportunity to intervene early and potentially mitigate the long-term health consequences of obesity. Previous interventions aimed at improving the engagement of primary care practitioners in obesity management have yielded mixed results. While some initiatives have demonstrated modest improvements in practitioner behavior and patient outcomes, others have had limited or no impact. This inconsistency points to the complexity of the issue and suggests that successful interventions must account for a range of individual, interpersonal, and systemic factors. The primary care setting presents unique challenges for obesity management. GPs and PNs often face competing priorities during consultations, with limited time to address complex and sensitive issues such as weight. In addition, practitioners may feel inadequately trained or equipped to discuss weight management with patients, particularly in the context of stigma surrounding obesity. Patients, in turn, may be reluctant to raise the issue of weight or may perceive such discussions as judgmental or unhelpful. These dynamics are further influenced by broader systemic factors, such as the availability and accessibility of weight management services, healthcare policies, and organizational resources. Understanding the interplay between these factors is critical to designing interventions that support practitioners in effectively identifying and referring patients with obesity. Realist review offers a methodological approach well-suited to addressing this complexity. Unlike traditional systematic reviews, which focus narrowly on assessing the effectiveness of interventions, realist reviews aim to explain how and why interventions work (or fail to work) in specific contexts. By examining the underlying mechanisms of action and the contextual factors that shape outcomes, realist reviews provide a nuanced understanding of what works, for whom, in what circumstances, and why. This approach is particularly valuable in the context of obesity management interventions, where outcomes are likely to be influenced by a combination of individual, interpersonal, and institutional factors. The aim of this realist review is to develop an explanatory theory regarding interventions targeted at primary care practitioners to improve the identification and referral of adults with obesity, particularly those with weight-related co-morbidities. The review seeks to explore the mechanisms through which interventions influence practitioner behavior, the contextual factors that enable or inhibit these mechanisms, and the outcomes that result. This theory-driven approach will not only provide insights into the effectiveness of existing interventions but also inform the design of future strategies to enhance obesity management in primary care. To achieve this aim, the review draws on a range of evidence sources, including qualitative and quantitative studies, policy documents, and formal theories from disciplines such as psychology, sociology, and implementation science. In addition, scoping interviews with stakeholders involved in the planning and delivery of weight management services in Scotland have been conducted to inform the review. These stakeholders include policymakers, healthcare professionals, and service providers, whose perspectives provide valuable insights into the contextual factors shaping obesity management in primary care. Stakeholder engagement is a distinctive feature of realist review and ensures that the findings are grounded in the realities of practice. The process of developing and testing theories in this review involves several iterative stages. First, initial programme theories will be developed based on the findings of scoping interviews and a preliminary review of the literature. These theories will describe potential mechanisms of action and contextual factors relevant to interventions targeting primary care practitioners. Next, a comprehensive search of the literature will be conducted to identify studies that provide evidence to test and refine these theories. Data from the included studies will be analyzed using a context-mechanism-outcome (CMO) framework, which facilitates the identification of patterns and relationships across different contexts. Finally, the refined programme theories will be synthesized into an overarching explanatory framework that takes into account individual, interpersonal, and systemic dimensions. The findings of this review are expected to contribute to the evidence base in several important ways. First, by elucidating the mechanisms and contextual factors underlying effective interventions, the review will provide actionable insights for policymakers, healthcare providers, and researchers seeking to improve obesity management in primary care. Second, the review will highlight gaps in the existing evidence and identify priorities for future research. Finally, the explanatory framework developed through this review has the potential to inform the design of interventions that are more likely to succeed in real-world primary care settings. In conclusion, this realist review represents an innovative approach to understanding and addressing the challenges of obesity management in primary care. By focusing on the interplay between mechanisms and context, the review aims to provide a comprehensive and nuanced understanding of how interventions can support primary care practitioners in identifying and referring adults with obesity. The ultimate goal is to inform the development of more effective strategies to address this pressing public health issue, improving outcomes for individuals and reducing the broader societal burden of obesity. This study will employ a realist review methodology to explore interventions targeted at primary care practitioners to improve the identification and referral of adults with obesity to weight management services. Realist review is a theory-driven approach to evidence synthesis that seeks to explain how interventions achieve their outcomes in specific contexts by identifying and analyzing the relationships between context, mechanisms, and outcomes (CMO configurations). This method is particularly suited for addressing complex interventions where outcomes are influenced by multiple interacting factors across individual, interpersonal, and institutional levels. The review will follow a structured process informed by guidance from Pawson et al. and the RAMESES (Realist And Meta-narrative Evidence Synthesis: Evolving Standards) publication standards. The review will proceed in several iterative and overlapping stages: 1. Scoping and Stakeholder Engagement As part of the initial scoping phase, we conducted exploratory interviews with key stakeholders involved in the planning, implementation, and delivery of adult weight management services in Scotland. Stakeholders included general practitioners (GPs), practice nurses (PNs), policymakers, and service managers. These interviews provided valuable insights into current practices, challenges, and facilitators in the identification and referral of adults with obesity in primary care. Stakeholder engagement will continue throughout the review process to ensure the findings remain relevant to real-world practice and to refine emerging theories. Additionally, these interviews informed the identification of formal theories from psychology, sociology, and implementation science that may explain practitioner behavior in this context. 2. Development of Initial Programme Theory Based on insights from the scoping phase and stakeholder engagement, an initial programme theory was developed to hypothesize how and why interventions targeted at primary care practitioners might improve the identification and referral of adults with obesity. This initial theory incorporates individual-level factors (e.g., practitioner knowledge, attitudes, and skills), interpersonal factors (e.g., patient-practitioner relationships), and institutional or systems-level factors (e.g., organizational support, referral pathways, and resource availability). The initial programme theory will serve as the foundation for the subsequent stages of the review. 3. Search Strategy and Study Selection A comprehensive search strategy will be implemented to identify relevant literature. Multiple electronic databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and the Cochrane Library, will be searched for studies published in English. Grey literature, such as policy documents, reports, and conference proceedings, will also be included to capture a broad range of evidence. Search terms will be developed iteratively and will include combinations of keywords related to primary care, obesity, weight management, identification, referral, interventions, and realist review. Reference lists of included studies will be screened for additional relevant publications. Studies will be eligible for inclusion if they describe interventions aimed at improving the identification and/or referral of adults with obesity in primary care settings. Both qualitative and quantitative studies will be included, as well as mixed-methods studies. The inclusion criteria will also encompass studies that explicitly or implicitly describe the contexts, mechanisms, and outcomes of such interventions. Titles, abstracts, and full texts will be screened by two reviewers independently, with disagreements resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. 4. Data Extraction and Synthesis Data will be extracted from included studies using a standardized form, capturing information on study characteristics (e.g., setting, population, intervention details), reported outcomes, and any descriptions of contextual factors and mechanisms. The rapid advancements in automated driving (AD) technology have brought humanity closer to the prospect of autonomous vehicles (AVs) operating safely and efficiently on public roads. The motivation behind this technological pursuit stems from the substantial global challenge posed by motor vehicle accidents. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), road traffic accidents are responsible for approximately 1.3 million fatalities annually, along with millions of injuries and considerable economic losses worldwide [1]. Beyond the human cost, traffic-related issues such as congestion, pollution, and inefficiencies in urban mobility systems further underscore the need for innovative solutions. Automated driving, with its promise of reducing human error—the predominant cause of traffic accidents—has emerged as a viable approach to addressing these multifaceted challenges. While significant progress has been made in highway automation and controlled environments, urban driving remains one of the most complex and demanding applications of AD systems. Urban environments are characterized by dynamic and unpredictable scenarios involving diverse road users, such as pedestrians, cyclists, and other vehicles. Furthermore, the presence of intricate traffic patterns, traffic signals, road construction zones, and varied environmental conditions increases the difficulty of achieving reliable automation. These challenges necessitate the development of advanced perception, planning, and control systems that can operate safely under real-world conditions. The field of AD research has witnessed rapid evolution in recent years, driven by advancements in machine learning, sensor technology, and computational capabilities. Research institutions, automotive manufacturers, and technology companies have all invested heavily in designing and testing automated systems capable of navigating urban environments. For example, significant efforts have been made to improve perception systems through the fusion of data from multiple sensors, such as cameras, LiDAR, radar, and GPS, enabling vehicles to detect and track objects with high accuracy [2][3]. Similarly, motion planning and decision-making algorithms have been developed to ensure safe and efficient navigation through complex urban scenarios [4]. Despite these advancements, several technical and practical challenges continue to hinder the full deployment of AD systems in urban settings. One of the critical issues is the reliability of perception systems, particularly in handling diverse lighting conditions, occlusions, and sensor noise. Additionally, planning and control systems must operate in real time while accounting for the uncertainty in the behavior of other road users. Moreover, the integration of these components into a cohesive and robust system capable of handling edge cases—rare but critical scenarios—is an ongoing research challenge [5]. Finally, public acceptance, regulatory frameworks, and ethical considerations also play a significant role in the eventual adoption of AV technologies. In this study, we aim to address some of the aforementioned challenges by demonstrating and evaluating the performance of an AD system in a controlled urban-like environment. Specifically, we focus on the technical aspects of perception and planning, which are pivotal for the success of autonomous navigation in urban scenarios. The AD system presented in this work is built on a modified Acura RLX platform and leverages state-of-the-art sensors and algorithms for decision-making and control. Our demonstration was conducted at GoMentum Station in California, a secure testing facility that replicates urban driving conditions. This facility provided a safe environment to test the system’s capabilities while ensuring repeatability and control over the experimental conditions. The primary objective of this study was to assess the system’s ability to handle four representative urban driving scenarios: traffic lights, cross-traffic at intersections, construction zones, and pedestrian interactions. These scenarios were selected because they capture the complexity and variability inherent in urban environments, where vehicles must interact with both static infrastructure and dynamic agents. The performance of the AD system in these scenarios was evaluated based on criteria such as safety, consistency, and robustness across multiple runs. Over the course of our experiments, the system successfully completed 44 runs, covering a total of 110 kilometers of automated driving. Despite the overall reliability of the system, we observed three instances where driver intervention was required, primarily due to errors in GPS positioning rather than failures in perception or planning. These interventions highlight the importance of addressing localization and mapping challenges in urban AD systems, particularly in environments with potential signal interference or degraded GPS accuracy. Our findings demonstrate that robust and consistent behavior in urban scenarios is achievable with current technologies, but there is still considerable work to be done before such systems can be deployed on public roads. In particular, further research is needed to enhance the robustness of perception systems under challenging conditions, improve the scalability of planning algorithms, and ensure the system’s ability to handle rare and unanticipated scenarios. Additionally, the integration of redundancy and fail-safe mechanisms will be critical to achieving the level of reliability required for real-world deployment. This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides an overview of the system architecture, with a detailed description of the perception and planning modules. Section 3 outlines the experimental setup and methodology used in the demonstration at GoMentum Station. Section 4 presents the results of the study, including quantitative and qualitative evaluations of the system’s performance. Section 5 discusses the implications of our findings and identifies avenues for future research. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper by summarizing the key contributions and outlining the path forward for AD in urban environments. By presenting the design, implementation, and evaluation of an AD system in a controlled urban-like environment, this work contributes to the ongoing efforts to advance autonomous driving technologies. Our results highlight both the potential and the limitations of current approaches, providing valuable insights for researchers and practitioners working towards the goal of safe and reliable autonomous vehicles in urban settings. --- References: [1] World Health Organization, "Global Status Report on Road Safety 2018," WHO, 2018. The following subsections describe the methodology in detail. Vehicle Platform and Hardware Setup The experimental platform used in this study was a modified Acura RLX equipped with sensors and computational units to enable autonomous operation. The sensor suite included three main categories: perception sensors, localization sensors, and vehicle state sensors. For perception, two Velodyne VLP-16 LiDARs were mounted on the roof to provide 360-degree coverage, and a forward-facing long-range radar was installed in the vehicle’s grille to detect dynamic obstacles. Additionally, three RGB cameras, one forward-facing and two side-facing, were installed for high-resolution visual data capture. Localization was achieved using a high-precision GPS with Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) corrections, supplemented by an Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) for pose estimation. Vehicle state information, such as speed and steering angle, was retrieved from the Controller Area Network (CAN) bus. The computational framework consisted of an NVIDIA Drive PX2 system, optimized for real-time data processing and running all major modules of the AD system. A secondary on-board computer was used for logging sensor data to facilitate post-test analysis. A fail-safe system, including manual override functionality, was integrated to ensure driver intervention during testing if required. Software Architecture The AD system was designed as a modular software stack comprising perception, localization, planning, control, and decision-making modules. Each module was implemented in C++ or Python using the Robot Operating System (ROS) middleware for communication and data exchange between components. Perception Module The perception module was responsible for detecting and tracking objects, interpreting traffic signals, and identifying lane markings. Sensor fusion techniques were applied to combine data from LiDAR, radar, and cameras for robust object detection. A convolutional neural network (CNN), pre-trained on the COCO dataset and fine-tuned on urban driving scenarios, was used for pedestrian and vehicle detection from camera feeds. LiDAR point clouds were clustered using a Euclidean distance-based approach to detect obstacles, and radar data provided velocity estimates for dynamic objects. For traffic signal recognition, a second CNN was trained using a labeled dataset of traffic lights, segmented into red, yellow, and green states. Fusion of camera data with precise GPS coordinates allowed the system to map detected traffic lights to specific intersections in the predefined high-definition (HD) map of GoMentum Station. Lane detection was performed using a combination of visual lane detection and LiDAR reflectivity data. The Hough transform was applied to camera images to identify lane boundaries, which were further validated using reflectivity data from LiDAR. Localization and Mapping Localization relied on a combination of GPS-RTK, IMU data, and HD maps. A particle filter-based approach was implemented to fuse these inputs and estimate the vehicle’s pose with centimeter-level accuracy. The HD map of the GoMentum Station, created using offline LiDAR scans, included detailed information about road geometry, lane markings, traffic signs, and construction zones. During real-time operation, the localization system continuously matched sensor data to the HD map for accurate positioning. Planning Module The planning module consisted of two layers: behavioral planning and trajectory planning. Behavioral planning determined high-level driving decisions, such as yielding to pedestrians, stopping at red lights, and navigating construction zones. A finite state machine (FSM) was implemented to encode these behaviors, transitioning between states based on sensor inputs and predefined traffic rules. Trajectory planning generated smooth, collision-free paths for the vehicle to follow. A quintic polynomial trajectory generation algorithm was employed, incorporating constraints on curvature, acceleration, and jerk to ensure passenger comfort. Dynamic obstacles detected by the perception module were incorporated into the trajectory planning process using a velocity obstacle approach. Control Module The control module translated planned trajectories into actuator commands for steering, throttle, and braking. A model-predictive control (MPC) algorithm was employed to optimize the vehicle's motion while maintaining stability and adherence to the planned path. Feedback from vehicle state sensors was used to continuously adjust control actions in real time. Experimental Setup Testing was conducted at GoMentum Station, a 20-acre closed-course facility designed for autonomous vehicle development. The course included urban-like scenarios such as intersections with traffic lights, pedestrian crosswalks, and construction zones. A pre-defined test route spanning approximately 2.5 km per lap was used for all trials. Four specific scenarios were designed to evaluate the AD system: (1) stopping at traffic lights, (2) handling cross-traffic at intersections, (3) navigating construction zones, and (4) detecting and yielding to pedestrians. Each scenario was repeated multiple times under varying environmental conditions, including changes in lighting and slight variations in obstacle positions. Data Collection and Analysis During testing, all sensor data, vehicle state information, and module outputs were logged at a frequency of 10 Hz. Driver interventions were manually annotated, with reasons for intervention noted for post-test analysis. Performance metrics included the number of successful scenario completions, path deviation, and the frequency and nature of failures. The system’s robustness was evaluated based on the consistency of its behavior across repeated trials. Post-test analysis focused on identifying failure modes, with particular attention to cases requiring driver intervention. Sensor calibration and algorithmic improvements were made iteratively based on insights from these analyses. Safety Protocols To ensure safety, the vehicle was equipped with an emergency braking system that could override autonomous control. A safety driver was present in the vehicle during all tests, with immediate access to manual controls. Before testing, all modules underwent simulation-based validation to minimize the likelihood of errors in real-world trials. This methodology enabled a comprehensive evaluation of the AD system's capabilities and limitations in urban driving scenarios, providing insights for future development and deployment. The growing complexity and scale of computer networks in recent years have underscored the critical importance of efficient traffic analysis and prediction techniques. With the continuous evolution of networked systems, ranging from traditional enterprise environments to more dynamic architectures such as cloud computing, Internet of Things (IoT), and 5G communication networks, understanding network behavior has become indispensable. Network traffic analysis and prediction serve as fundamental approaches to ensure the security, reliability, and performance optimization of these systems. By anticipating traffic patterns, organizations can proactively mitigate risks, allocate resources efficiently, and maintain seamless communication, especially in environments with high data volumes and stringent quality of service (QoS) requirements. The importance of network traffic analysis lies in its ability to provide valuable insights into communication patterns, detect anomalies, and identify potential security threats. On the other hand, traffic prediction enables network administrators to forecast future workloads and adapt infrastructure accordingly, preventing congestion and ensuring optimal performance. Together, these techniques form the backbone of modern network management strategies, offering a proactive means to address challenges before they escalate into critical issues. Despite significant advancements in this domain, the heterogeneity and ever-changing nature of network traffic present enduring challenges, necessitating continuous research to improve the accuracy, scalability, and adaptability of existing methods. Over the last two decades, substantial progress has been made in developing innovative techniques for network traffic analysis and prediction. These methods span diverse domains, including statistical modeling, machine learning, deep learning, and data mining approaches. Traditional statistical models such as autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) and exponential smoothing have provided effective tools for modeling linear traffic patterns [1]. However, as network traffic increasingly exhibits non-linear and complex behaviors, more sophisticated techniques have gained prominence. Machine learning algorithms, such as support vector machines (SVM) and decision trees, have been widely adopted to classify and analyze traffic data, while deep learning models like recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in capturing intricate temporal and spatial dependencies [2]. Beyond statistical and machine learning techniques, data mining approaches have also played a pivotal role in the field. Frequent pattern mining, clustering, and anomaly detection techniques are often employed to extract meaningful insights from raw traffic data. These methods enable the identification of recurring patterns, segmentation of traffic into meaningful categories, and detection of outliers that may indicate potential threats or irregularities [3]. The integration of data mining techniques with predictive modeling has further enhanced the accuracy and robustness of traffic analysis systems. By leveraging large-scale data repositories, these approaches can uncover hidden relationships and predict future traffic trends with improved precision. The emergence of hybrid techniques has also contributed significantly to advancing network traffic analysis and prediction. By combining multiple methodologies, such as neural networks with statistical models or machine learning with data mining, researchers have been able to exploit the strengths of each approach while mitigating their limitations. For instance, hybrid models that integrate RNNs with ARIMA have demonstrated superior performance in capturing both linear and non-linear traffic patterns, thereby offering a more comprehensive solution for traffic prediction [4]. Similarly, ensemble methods that aggregate the outputs of multiple models have gained traction for their ability to improve prediction accuracy and reliability. Despite these advancements, several challenges persist in the domain of network traffic analysis and prediction. One of the key issues is the scalability of existing techniques when applied to large-scale networks. With the exponential growth of data generated by modern communication systems, traditional methods often struggle to process and analyze traffic efficiently in real-time. Furthermore, the dynamic nature of network traffic, characterized by sudden spikes, fluctuations, and anomalies, poses considerable difficulties for predictive models. Achieving robustness and adaptability in such scenarios remains a critical area of research. Additionally, the diversity of network environments, ranging from wired to wireless networks and from enterprise systems to IoT ecosystems, necessitates the development of customized techniques tailored to specific use cases [5]. Another major concern is the interpretability of advanced machine learning and deep learning models. While these techniques have demonstrated remarkable success in achieving high accuracy, their "black-box" nature often limits their practical applicability. Network administrators may find it challenging to trust and adopt models whose inner workings are not easily interpretable or explainable. This has prompted researchers to explore explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) approaches for network traffic analysis, aiming to strike a balance between model performance and interpretability [6]. The integration of emerging technologies, such as edge computing and software-defined networking (SDN), further adds to the complexity of the field but also opens up new avenues for innovation. Edge computing, for instance, enables the analysis of network traffic closer to the source, reducing latency and improving real-time capabilities. Similarly, SDN provides centralized control and programmability, facilitating the collection and analysis of traffic data in a more streamlined and efficient manner. The combination of these technologies with advanced analytical techniques holds great promise for addressing the challenges associated with modern network traffic management [7]. In light of these developments, this paper aims to provide a comprehensive review of existing network traffic analysis and prediction techniques. By examining the strengths, limitations, and unique features of various approaches, this study seeks to identify key trends and highlight potential areas for future research. The survey covers a wide range of methodologies, from traditional statistical models to cutting-edge machine learning and hybrid approaches, offering a holistic view of the current state of the field. Furthermore, this review investigates the application of these techniques across different network environments and use cases, shedding light on their practical implications and impact. Through this exploration, we aim to contribute to the growing body of knowledge in network traffic analysis and prediction, ultimately supporting the development of more secure, efficient, and adaptive network systems. As networks continue to evolve and expand, the insights gained from this study will serve as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners striving to address the multifaceted challenges of modern network management. To systematically review and evaluate the techniques employed in network traffic analysis and prediction, a structured methodology was adopted. This section outlines the steps undertaken to collect, analyze, and synthesize the relevant studies. The approach ensures reproducibility, comprehensiveness, and the inclusion of diverse perspectives from the existing body of literature. First, a comprehensive literature search was conducted to identify relevant studies. This search spanned peer-reviewed journals, conference proceedings, and technical reports. Indexed databases including IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, SpringerLink, Scopus, and Web of Science were queried to ensure the inclusion of high-impact publications. Keywords used in the search included “network traffic analysis,” “traffic prediction,” “neural networks in network traffic,” “data mining for network traffic,” and “linear and non-linear prediction models.” Additional keyword combinations were used to capture broader and narrower aspects of the topic, such as “time-series forecasting in network traffic,” “deep learning for traffic prediction,” and “anomaly detection in network traffic.” To refine the search results, inclusion and exclusion criteria were applied. Studies were included if they presented novel methodologies, comprehensive surveys, or significant improvements in network traffic analysis or prediction. Only studies published in English between the years 2000 and 2023 were considered to ensure relevance to current technological advancements. Exclusion criteria included articles focused solely on hardware or physical network infrastructure, as the focus of this review was limited to computational and algorithmic approaches. Duplicates and studies lacking sufficient methodological detail were also excluded. After the initial search, a total of 1,245 articles were identified. These articles were screened in two phases. In the first phase, titles and abstracts were reviewed to gauge their relevance to the research topic. This step reduced the pool to 312 articles. In the second phase, full-text reviews were conducted to ensure adherence to the inclusion criteria. At the conclusion of this process, 126 studies were selected for detailed analysis. These studies represent a diverse range of methodologies, applications, and experimental setups in network traffic analysis and prediction. The selected studies were categorized into two primary domains: network traffic analysis and network traffic prediction. Subcategories were further defined within each domain based on the specific techniques employed. For network traffic analysis, the reviewed studies were grouped into four categories: statistical approaches, machine learning techniques, data mining methods, and hybrid methods. Similarly, network traffic prediction studies were classified into linear models, non-linear models, time-series forecasting methods, and deep learning-based approaches. The categorization facilitated a systematic comparison of methodologies and their respective strengths and limitations. To extract relevant data, a standardized data extraction form was developed. This form included fields for publication details (e.g., author, year, and source), methodology, datasets used, evaluation metrics, key findings, and limitations. Special attention was given to identifying the datasets employed in the studies, as the choice of dataset significantly influences the performance and applicability of traffic analysis and prediction techniques. Both publicly available datasets, such as CAIDA, MAWI, and KDD Cup datasets, and proprietary datasets were considered. When proprietary datasets were used, efforts were made to analyze the reported characteristics of the dataset to assess their representativeness and generalizability. To ensure the reliability of the extracted information, two independent reviewers conducted the data extraction process. Discrepancies in extracted data were resolved through discussion and, when necessary, consultation with a third reviewer. This approach minimized errors and biases in data collection. The analysis of the selected studies involved both qualitative and quantitative techniques. For qualitative analysis, the methodologies employed in each study were critically examined to identify trends, challenges, and research gaps. Particular attention was paid to the assumptions underlying the proposed methods, the preprocessing steps applied to raw network traffic data, and the scalability of the techniques. For quantitative analysis, the reported performance metrics, such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, mean squared error (MSE), and root mean squared error (RMSE), were aggregated and compared. Where possible, statistical meta-analysis was performed to identify the overall effectiveness of specific techniques. To provide a comprehensive overview of the field, the strengths and limitations of various approaches were systematically compared. For example, in the domain of network traffic analysis, machine learning techniques such as support vector machines (SVM) and random forests were evaluated for their ability to detect anomalies and classify traffic patterns [1][2]. The scalability of these methods to large-scale networks was also assessed. Similarly, deep learning approaches, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), were analyzed for their ability to learn complex traffic patterns from high-dimensional data [3][4]. In the domain of traffic prediction, linear models such as autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) were compared with non-linear models, including long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, to assess their predictive accuracy and computational efficiency [5][6]. To contextualize the findings of this review, the identified techniques were mapped to various application scenarios, including network security, quality of service (QoS) optimization, and resource allocation. This mapping highlighted the practical implications of adopting specific methodologies and their potential to address real-world challenges in network management. Finally, to ensure the validity of this review, a critical appraisal of the selected studies was conducted. This appraisal considered factors such as the robustness of experimental setups, the representativeness of datasets, and the appropriateness of evaluation metrics. Studies that demonstrated rigorous experimental design and transparent reporting were given greater weight in the synthesis of findings. In summary, this review employed a systematic and rigorous methodology to identify, analyze, and synthesize a diverse range of studies in network traffic analysis and prediction. By categorizing and comparing the techniques employed in these studies, this review provides valuable insights into the state of the art and identifies promising directions for future research. The study of sequential data has become increasingly central to numerous fields, including bioinformatics, speech recognition, time-series forecasting, and computer vision. Sequences, which are ordered collections of observations or events, often encode critical temporal or structural information. A fundamental challenge in sequence analysis is the measurement of similarity or dissimilarity between sequences, as this serves as the foundation for diverse tasks such as classification, clustering, and anomaly detection. Effective sequence comparison methods are crucial for extracting meaningful insights and ensuring robust performance in downstream applications. Dynamic time warping (DTW) has long been recognized as a cornerstone technique for sequence alignment. By allowing non-linear warping of the time axis, DTW is capable of aligning sequences of differing lengths and handling temporal distortions [1]. Its ability to adaptively match sequences has led to its widespread adoption across various domains, including video analysis, image processing, and gesture recognition [2][3]. However, despite its popularity and utility, DTW suffers from a fundamental limitation: its reliance on point-to-point Euclidean distance (ED) as the basis for alignment. When matching two sequences, DTW minimizes the cumulative distance between corresponding points, but this approach is agnostic to the broader structural or semantic context of the sequences. Consequently, DTW can align points with similar coordinate values but vastly different semantic meanings, such as peaks being matched with valleys. This limitation renders DTW sensitive to noise and hampers its interpretability, particularly in applications where preserving semantic coherence is critical [4]. The inadequacy of DTW in capturing the complex dependencies and autocorrelation inherent in sequential data has motivated the exploration of alternative approaches. Recent advances in sequence modeling have underscored the importance of latent representations that encapsulate the underlying dynamics of sequences. By transforming raw observations into a latent space that encodes richer information, it becomes possible to perform more meaningful comparisons. However, methods that attempt such transformations often face challenges related to computational efficiency and scalability, particularly when dealing with long sequences or large datasets [5]. Thus, the development of sequence alignment algorithms that are both semantically interpretable and computationally efficient remains an open and pressing problem. In this paper, we propose a novel sequence alignment algorithm, dynamic state warping (DSW), which addresses the aforementioned limitations of DTW. The key innovation of DSW lies in its incorporation of latent state representations for each time point in a sequence. Unlike DTW, which directly compares raw observations, DSW first transforms each point into a latent state that encodes both the local and global autocorrelation structure of the sequence. By leveraging these state representations, DSW performs alignment in a transformed space that better reflects the semantic relationships between points. This approach ensures that alignment decisions are informed by the broader context of the sequence, resulting in alignments that are more robust to noise and more interpretable than those produced by DTW. The benefits of DSW are particularly evident in tasks such as time-series classification, where the alignment of semantically meaningful features—rather than mere coordinate values—plays a critical role in achieving high accuracy. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that DSW significantly outperforms both ED and DTW in classification tasks, with improvements observed in 70 out of 85 datasets when compared to ED and in 74 out of 85 datasets when compared to DTW. These results underscore the efficacy of DSW in capturing the intrinsic similarity between sequences. Furthermore, DSW exhibits superior scalability to long sequences, a property that is increasingly important in modern applications involving high-dimensional or temporally extended data. Another key advantage of DSW lies in its flexibility. The algorithm can be adapted to incorporate domain-specific constraints or priors, allowing it to be tailored to particular applications. For instance, in domains such as bioinformatics or speech processing, where the semantic structure of sequences may be well understood, DSW can be augmented with task-specific state encoders or similarity measures. This adaptability distinguishes DSW from traditional alignment methods, which are often constrained by rigid formulations that do not easily accommodate such modifications. While DSW represents a significant step forward, it also opens new avenues for research. The choice of state representation is a critical factor that influences the performance of DSW, and future work could explore the use of advanced state encoding techniques, such as those based on deep learning [6]. Additionally, the integration of DSW with other sequence analysis frameworks, such as dynamic Bayesian networks or recurrent neural networks, holds promise for further enhancing its representational power and applicability. In summary, dynamic state warping addresses long-standing challenges in sequence alignment by introducing a principled framework for incorporating semantic and structural context into alignment decisions. By converting raw observations into latent states and aligning sequences in this transformed space, DSW achieves higher robustness, interpretability, and scalability than traditional methods. The algorithm's strong empirical performance across a wide range of datasets highlights its potential as a powerful tool for sequence analysis. Through this work, we aim to advance the state of the art in sequence alignment and to provide a foundation for future innovations in this critical area of research. To develop Dynamic State Warping (DSW) as an effective and interpretable sequence alignment algorithm, we employed a systematic approach consisting of three key components: the extraction of latent states, the alignment mechanism based on state sequences, and the performance evaluation framework. In this section, we detail each step of the methodology, emphasizing the theoretical underpinnings, computational design, and experimental setup. Latent State Representation The core innovation of DSW lies in converting each time point in a sequence into a latent state representation that captures the temporal autocorrelation structure of the sequence. To achieve this, we adopted a feature extraction process that maps raw data points into a high-dimensional latent space. Specifically, we derived the latent states using a sliding window mechanism, where a fixed-length segment of the sequence around each point is used as input to a feature extraction model. This approach captures the local temporal context, enabling the representation of each point to incorporate information about its surrounding neighborhood. To extract the latent features, we experimented with several methods, including principal component analysis (PCA), convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and autoencoders, depending on the nature of the sequences and their domain. For most of the datasets, we utilized a simple autoencoder due to its ability to learn nonlinear patterns in the data while maintaining computational efficiency. The autoencoder was trained on the entire dataset to ensure that the learned latent representations are consistent across sequences. For datasets with known domain-specific features, we also incorporated handcrafted feature extraction techniques, such as Fourier transforms or wavelet decompositions, to enhance the semantic sensitivity of the latent states. Once the latent states were generated, each sequence was transformed into a sequence of state vectors. These latent state sequences served as the input to the alignment step. The dimensionality of the latent state space was determined empirically by balancing computational efficiency and the ability to retain sufficient information from the original sequences. Sequence Alignment via Dynamic State Warping The alignment of sequences in DSW is performed using a dynamic programming approach analogous to that of Dynamic Time Warping (DTW). However, unlike DTW, which relies solely on pointwise Euclidean distances, DSW computes the distance between state vectors in the latent space. This allows DSW to align sequences based on their underlying semantic structure, rather than their raw coordinate values. The alignment cost between two sequences, \( S1 \) and \( S2 \), is computed by constructing a cost matrix \( C \), where each element \( C(i, j) \) represents the distance between the \( i \)-th latent state of \( S1 \) and the \( j \)-th latent state of \( S2 \). The distance metric used for comparing latent states was chosen based on the characteristics of the latent space. For most experiments, we used cosine similarity and squared Euclidean distance, as these metrics were found to effectively capture the dissimilarities between state vectors. Formally, the distance between two latent states \( \mathbf{s}i \) and \( \mathbf{s}j \) was calculated as: \[ d(\mathbf{s}i, \mathbf{s}j) = ||\mathbf{s}i - \mathbf{s}j||^22 \] or \[ d(\mathbf{s}i, \mathbf{s}j) = 1 - \frac{\mathbf{s}i \cdot \mathbf{s}j}{||\mathbf{s}i|| \cdot ||\mathbf{s}j||}. \] We then used dynamic programming to compute the optimal alignment path through the cost matrix. The recurrence relation for the cumulative cost \( D(i, j) \) is as follows: \[ D(i, j) = d(\mathbf{s}i, \mathbf{s}j) + \min\{D(i-1, j), D(i, j-1), D(i-1, j-1)\}, \] where \( D(i, j) \) represents the cumulative alignment cost up to the \( i \)-th and \( j \)-th points in \( S1 \) and \( S2 \), respectively. Boundary conditions were set as \( D(0,0) = 0 \), and the alignment path was backtracked from \( D(|S1|, |S2|) \) to determine the optimal warping. Comparative Evaluation To evaluate the performance of DSW, we conducted extensive experiments on 85 benchmark datasets across diverse domains, including time-series datasets from the UCR archive, motion capture data, and image sequences. The datasets were selected to represent a wide range of sequence lengths, noise levels, and semantic complexities. We compared DSW against Euclidean distance (ED) and DTW using a one nearest neighbor (1-NN) classification framework, a standard protocol for evaluating sequence alignment methods [1]. For each dataset, we split the sequences into training and test sets, computed pairwise distances between sequences within the latent state space, and classified each test sequence based on the class of its nearest neighbor in the training set. Classification accuracy was used as the primary evaluation metric. Additionally, we analyzed the robustness of DSW to noise by introducing Gaussian noise of varying magnitudes to the test sequences and measuring the degradation in classification performance. To assess scalability, we evaluated the runtime of DSW as a function of sequence length and compared it to that of DTW. Implementation Details All experiments were implemented in Python using the NumPy and SciPy libraries for numerical computations. The autoencoder models were implemented using PyTorch, with a simple architecture comprising three fully connected layers for both the encoder and decoder. For reproducibility, we set the random seed to ensure consistent initialization of weights across runs. The hyperparameters, such as the dimensionality of the latent space and the size of the sliding window, were optimized via grid search on a validation set. In summary, the DSW methodology integrates latent state extraction and dynamic alignment to address the limitations of DTW in sequence alignment. By leveraging semantic information encoded in the latent states, DSW achieves superior classification performance, robustness to noise, and scalability, as demonstrated in our experimental results. To evaluate the performance of the proposed Dynamic State Warping (DSW) algorithm, extensive experiments were conducted across multiple datasets and domains. The results presented here focus on classification accuracy, robustness to noise, scalability to long sequences, and interpretability of the resulting alignments. For comparative analysis, DSW was benchmarked against the Euclidean Distance (ED) and Dynamic Time Warping (DTW), two well-established methods for sequence alignment and distance measurement. These datasets span a wide range of application domains, including audio, image, motion capture, and sensor readings. DSW outperformed both ED and DTW in terms of classification accuracy in the majority of cases. Specifically, DSW achieved higher accuracy than ED in 70 out of the 85 datasets and outperformed DTW in 74 datasets. A paired t-test was conducted to assess the statistical significance of the observed improvements, revealing that DSW's performance gains were significant with \( p < 0.01 \) when compared to both ED and DTW. Unlike DTW, which relies solely on point-to-point Euclidean distances, DSW aligns sequences based on their underlying semantic structures. This leads to more meaningful alignments, particularly in datasets where sequences exhibit complex or nonlinear temporal dependencies. The remarkable ability of Deinococcus radiodurans R1 to withstand extreme environmental challenges, including ionizing radiation, desiccation, and oxidative stress, has been the focus of extensive research aiming to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying its extraordinary robustness. A key factor contributing to the survival of this bacterium under such conditions is its efficient oxidative stress defense system, which encompasses a diverse array of antioxidant enzymes and repair mechanisms [1, 2]. Among these, thiol-based peroxidases, including peroxiredoxins, play a particularly critical role in counteracting the detrimental effects of reactive oxygen species (ROS) [3]. Peroxiredoxins (Prxs) are highly conserved cysteine-based peroxidases found in all domains of life. They function by reducing hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), organic peroxides, and peroxynitrite to less reactive species, thereby protecting cells from oxidative damage [4]. In addition to their canonical role as peroxidases, Prxs have been implicated in various non-enzymatic functions, such as serving as molecular chaperones and participating in redox signaling [5]. The physiological relevance of these dual functions is evident in organisms subjected to frequent oxidative stress, such as D. radiodurans, where the maintenance of redox homeostasis is essential for survival. Among the six classes of peroxiredoxins identified to date, peroxiredoxin Q (PrxQ) is distinguished by its simple structural organization and substrate specificity, as well as its widespread occurrence in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes [6]. PrxQ proteins typically contain two conserved cysteine residues, known as the peroxidatic cysteine (Cₐₚ) and the resolving cysteine (Cᵣₑₛ), which form a disulfide bond during the catalytic cycle [7]. This disulfide bond is reduced by thioredoxin or other cellular reductants, allowing the enzyme to undergo multiple catalytic cycles. The functional versatility of PrxQ proteins has been demonstrated in several bacterial species, where they contribute to stress tolerance, virulence, and metabolic regulation [8]. In D. radiodurans, the oxidative stress response is mediated by a sophisticated network of enzymes, including catalases, superoxide dismutases, and thiol-based reductases [9]. Although recent studies have identified several peroxiredoxins in this organism, their precise physiological roles remain incompletely understood. The focus of this study is DR0846, a predicted PrxQ homolog in D. radiodurans. Preliminary bioinformatics analyses have demonstrated that DR0846 contains the canonical cysteine residues characteristic of PrxQ proteins, suggesting its potential role as a thiol-based peroxidase. However, the functional characterization of this protein and its contribution to the stress tolerance of D. radiodurans have not been thoroughly investigated. The dual functionality of peroxiredoxins as both enzymatic antioxidants and molecular chaperones has garnered increasing attention in recent years. Several studies have reported that certain peroxiredoxins, including PrxQ proteins, exhibit chaperone-like activity under conditions of oxidative or heat stress [10, 11]. This dual activity is thought to be mediated by structural transitions that enable peroxiredoxins to interact with unfolded or misfolded proteins, thereby preventing aggregation and facilitating proper protein folding [12]. Such chaperone function is particularly relevant in extremophiles like D. radiodurans, where protein stability and functionality are often challenged by harsh environmental conditions. In this study, we present a detailed biochemical and functional analysis of DR0846, providing evidence for its dual role as a peroxidase and a molecular chaperone. Using recombinant protein expression and mutational analyses, we demonstrate that the conserved cysteine residues in DR0846 are essential for its enzymatic activity. Furthermore, we show that DR0846 exhibits chaperone-like activity in vitro, effectively preventing the aggregation of client proteins under heat stress. These findings are supported by phenotypic analyses of a double-deletion mutant lacking DR0846 and catalase DR1998, which reveal a marked reduction in oxidative and heat shock tolerance compared to single mutants or wild-type strains. Together, our results suggest that DR0846 plays a critical role in the stress resistance mechanisms of D. radiodurans by combining its enzymatic and chaperone functions. This work expands our understanding of the multifaceted roles of peroxiredoxins in bacterial stress responses and highlights the importance of DR0846 in the remarkable resilience of D. radiodurans. By elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying the dual functionality of DR0846, we provide new insights into the adaptive strategies employed by extremophiles to survive under oxidative and thermal stress. Moreover, the identification of DR0846 as a dual-function protein underscores the broader significance of peroxiredoxins as versatile stress response mediators across diverse biological systems. These findings pave the way for future studies exploring the potential applications of peroxiredoxins in biotechnology and synthetic biology, particularly in the development of stress-resistant microbial strains for industrial and environmental purposes. Bacterial Strains, Growth Conditions, and Mutant Construction Deinococcus radiodurans strain R1 (ATCC 13939) was utilized as the wild-type strain for all experiments. Bacteria were grown in TGY medium (1% tryptone, 0.5% yeast extract, and 0.1% glucose) at 30°C with shaking at 200 rpm unless otherwise specified. For oxidative stress assays, cultures were supplemented with hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) at varying concentrations, while heat stress experiments were conducted by incubating cultures at 50°C for defined time periods. Gene deletion mutants were constructed using homologous recombination. For the deletion of DR0846 and DR1998, upstream and downstream flanking regions of the target genes were amplified using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) with specific primers (listed in Supplementary Table 1). The amplified fragments were cloned into the pKatA plasmid to disrupt the target genes with a spectinomycin resistance cassette. The plasmid constructs were introduced into D. radiodurans via electroporation using a Bio-Rad Gene Pulser set at 2.5 kV, 25 µF, and 200 Ω. Transformants were selected on TGY agar plates containing spectinomycin (50 µg/mL). Successful gene deletions were confirmed by PCR and sequencing. A double-deletion mutant (ΔDR0846ΔDR1998) was generated by sequential gene disruption. Complementation of DR0846 was achieved by cloning the full-length gene, including its native promoter, into the shuttle vector pRADZ3, followed by transformation into the deletion mutant. 2. Protein Expression and Purification The DR0846 open reading frame was amplified by PCR and cloned into the expression vector pET-28a(+) to introduce an N-terminal His-tag. The construct was transformed into Escherichia coli BL21(DE3) cells for protein overexpression. Transformed cells were grown in LB medium containing kanamycin (50 µg/mL) at 37°C until the optical density at 600 nm (OD₆₀₀) reached 0.6, at which point protein expression was induced by adding 0.5 mM isopropyl-β-D-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG). Cultures were further incubated at 18°C for 16 hours. Cells were harvested by centrifugation at 6,000 ×g for 10 minutes at 4°C and resuspended in lysis buffer (50 mM sodium phosphate, pH 8.0, 300 mM NaCl, 10 mM imidazole). The suspension was lysed by sonication, and cell debris was removed by centrifugation at 12,000 ×g for 30 minutes. The supernatant was applied to a Ni-NTA agarose column pre-equilibrated with lysis buffer. After washing with buffer containing 20 mM imidazole, the bound protein was eluted with 250 mM imidazole. Purified protein fractions were dialyzed against 20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 100 mM NaCl, and 5% glycerol. The purity of the protein was assessed by SDS-PAGE, and protein concentration was determined using the Bradford assay [1]. 3. Peroxidase Activity Assay The peroxidase activity of DR0846 was measured using the dithiothreitol (DTT)-coupled assay [2]. Reactions were conducted in a 200 µL total volume containing 50 mM HEPES (pH 7.0), 1 mM DTT, 0.1 mM H₂O₂, and various concentrations of DR0846 (0.5–10 µM). The oxidation of DTT was monitored by measuring the decrease in absorbance at 310 nm using a microplate reader (BioTek Synergy H1). For kinetic analysis, initial reaction rates were determined at different H₂O₂ concentrations (0–500 µM), and the Michaelis-Menten parameters (Km and Vmax) were calculated by nonlinear regression using GraphPad Prism software. To verify the role of cysteine residues, site-directed mutants (Cys43Ser and Cys98Ser) were generated using the QuikChange mutagenesis kit (Agilent Technologies). The purified mutant proteins were subjected to the same peroxidase assay. Additionally, the formation of disulfide bonds was analyzed by non-reducing SDS-PAGE. 4. Molecular Chaperone Assay The chaperone activity of DR0846 was assessed using a thermal aggregation assay with citrate synthase (CS) as a substrate [3]. CS (0.15 µM) was incubated at 43°C in the presence or absence of DR0846 (molar ratios of DR0846 to CS ranging from 1:1 to 10:1) in a buffer containing 20 mM HEPES (pH 7.5) and 100 mM NaCl. Protein aggregation was monitored by measuring light scattering at 360 nm using a UV-Vis spectrophotometer (Shimadzu UV-1800). Control reactions included CS alone and CS with bovine serum albumin (BSA) as a non-chaperone control. The ability of DR0846 to suppress aggregation was quantified as a percentage reduction in light scattering. 5. Oxidative and Heat Stress Tolerance Assays Wild-type, single-deletion (ΔDR0846 and ΔDR1998), and double-deletion (ΔDR0846ΔDR1998) strains were subjected to oxidative and heat stress challenges. For oxidative stress, exponential-phase cultures (OD₆₀₀ = 0.5) were treated with 20 mM H₂O₂ and incubated at 30°C for 1 hour. Serial dilutions were plated on TGY agar, and colony-forming units (CFUs) were counted after 48 hours of incubation. For heat stress, cultures were exposed to 50°C for 30 minutes before plating and CFU enumeration. 6. Statistical significance was determined using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s multiple comparisons test. Differences were considered significant at p < 0.05.
