Cancer cachexia represents a multifactorial syndrome characterized by severe skeletal muscle wasting, often accompanied by systemic inflammation, metabolic alterations, and weight loss, which cannot be reversed by conventional nutritional support [1,2]. This syndrome, which occurs in up to 80% of patients with advanced cancer, significantly reduces quality of life and is associated with poor prognosis and increased mortality [3,4]. Despite its clinical importance, the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms of cancer cachexia remain incompletely understood, and effective therapeutic strategies to combat muscle wasting in this context are currently limited. Among the various factors implicated in the progression of cancer cachexia, the disruption of skeletal muscle regeneration and repair has emerged as a key contributor to the loss of muscle mass and function [5,6]. Skeletal muscle regeneration involves the activation and differentiation of satellite cells, a population of muscle-resident stem cells that are essential for repairing and maintaining muscle fibers following injury or stress. Pax7, a transcription factor that plays a crucial role in satellite cell specification and maintenance, is tightly regulated during the myogenic process [7]. Under normal physiological conditions, Pax7 expression is transiently upregulated during satellite cell activation, but subsequently decreases as these cells differentiate into mature myogenic cells. However, recent studies have shown that Pax7 expression is dysregulated in the context of cancer cachexia, with persistent overexpression impairing the myogenic capacity of satellite cells [8,9]. This aberrant regulation of Pax7 is thought to be driven by pro-inflammatory signaling pathways, including the nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) pathway, which is chronically activated in cachectic skeletal muscles [10]. Importantly, the impaired myogenic potential associated with Pax7 overexpression likely contributes to the inability of cachectic muscles to regenerate effectively, further exacerbating muscle wasting [11]. Given the critical role of Pax7 in muscle regeneration and its dysregulation in cancer cachexia, strategies aimed at normalizing Pax7 expression have garnered attention as potential therapeutic approaches. Emerging evidence suggests that physical activity, particularly moderate voluntary exercise, may exert beneficial effects on cachectic muscles by modulating the local muscle microenvironment and promoting an anti-inflammatory state [12,13]. Indeed, exercise has been shown to ameliorate muscle wasting and improve muscle function in various preclinical models of cancer cachexia, although the precise molecular mechanisms underlying these effects are not fully elucidated [14]. Notably, the impact of physical activity on Pax7 expression and the regenerative capacity of satellite cells in cachectic muscles remains poorly understood. Addressing this knowledge gap could provide valuable insights into the therapeutic potential of exercise in cancer cachexia. In this context, we recently demonstrated that Pax7 overexpression is a major factor contributing to the defective myogenic potential of satellite cells in a murine model of cancer cachexia induced by C26 colon carcinoma tumor implantation [8]. In addition, we observed that delayed muscle regeneration in tumor-bearing mice was associated with heightened local inflammation, suggesting that the inflammatory microenvironment plays a pivotal role in deregulating Pax7 expression and impairing satellite cell function. Building on these findings, we hypothesized that physical activity might counteract the deleterious effects of chronic inflammation on satellite cells by downregulating Pax7 expression, thereby restoring their myogenic capacity and improving muscle regeneration. To investigate this hypothesis, we conducted a study utilizing a voluntary wheel running model to examine the effects of moderate physical activity on Pax7 expression and muscle regeneration in C26 tumor-bearing mice and healthy controls. Voluntary wheel running represents a physiologically relevant form of exercise that mimics natural physical activity patterns in rodents and has been shown to elicit beneficial adaptations in skeletal muscle without inducing excessive stress or injury [15]. By comparing Pax7 expression levels, muscle mass, and fiber size between exercised and non-exercised tumor-bearing mice, we aimed to elucidate the molecular mechanisms by which physical activity ameliorates muscle wasting in cancer cachexia. Our findings demonstrate that voluntary wheel running significantly downregulates Pax7 expression in cachectic muscles, leading to improved muscle mass and fiber size in tumor-bearing mice. These results suggest that physical activity may serve as a physiological tool to counteract the overexpression of Pax7 observed in cancer cachexia, thereby promoting muscle regeneration and mitigating muscle wasting. Furthermore, our study highlights the importance of the muscle microenvironment in modulating satellite cell function and underscores the potential of exercise-based interventions as a non-pharmacological approach to address the pathological alterations associated with cancer cachexia. In this paper, we provide a detailed analysis of the effects of voluntary physical activity on muscle regeneration and Pax7 expression in a murine model of cancer cachexia. We discuss the implications of our findings in the context of satellite cell biology and cancer cachexia pathophysiology, with a particular focus on the interplay between inflammation, Pax7 regulation, and exercise. By advancing our understanding of how physical activity influences the molecular and cellular mechanisms of muscle regeneration, our study lays the groundwork for the development of novel therapeutic strategies to combat cancer cachexia and improve outcomes for patients with advanced cancer. Animal experiments were conducted in accordance with institutional and national guidelines for animal care and were approved by the local ethics committee. Male BALB/c mice aged 6–8 weeks were housed in a temperature-controlled environment with a 12-hour light/dark cycle and given ad libitum access to standard chow and water. Mice were randomly assigned to four groups: control sedentary (Ctrl-SED), control with voluntary wheel running (Ctrl-EX), tumor-bearing sedentary (C26-SED), and tumor-bearing with voluntary wheel running (C26-EX). Mice in the tumor-bearing groups were subcutaneously injected in the right flank with 1 × 10^6 C26 colon carcinoma cells suspended in sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), while control groups received PBS alone. Voluntary wheel running was implemented as a model of moderate physical activity. Mice in the exercise groups (Ctrl-EX and C26-EX) were housed individually in cages equipped with a running wheel (ENV-044, Med Associates Inc.). Wheel rotations were recorded continuously using a digital counter, and running distance was calculated daily. The exercise protocol lasted for 21 days, beginning 7 days after tumor implantation to allow for tumor establishment. Sedentary mice (Ctrl-SED and C26-SED) were housed individually in standard cages without access to running wheels. Muscle injury and regeneration were assessed using cardiotoxin (CTX)-induced injury. On day 21 of the exercise protocol, mice were anesthetized with isoflurane (2% in oxygen), and 50 µL of 10 µM CTX (Latoxan) was injected into the tibialis anterior (TA) muscle of the left hind limb to induce acute muscle injury. The contralateral TA muscle served as an uninjured control. Mice were euthanized 7 days post-injury using CO2 inhalation, and TA muscles were harvested for downstream analyses. Muscles were weighed, snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at -80°C until further processing. For histological analysis, TA muscles were embedded in optimal cutting temperature (OCT) compound and sectioned transversely at a thickness of 10 µm using a cryostat. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining was performed to assess muscle morphology and fiber size. For each sample, a minimum of 300 myofibers were analyzed using ImageJ software (NIH) to calculate the cross-sectional area (CSA) of muscle fibers. Immunofluorescence staining was performed to evaluate Pax7 expression and the presence of inflammatory cells. Sections were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, permeabilized with 0.2% Triton X-100, and blocked with 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA) in PBS. Primary antibodies against Pax7 (1:50 dilution, Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank) and F4/80 (1:100 dilution, Bio-Rad) were applied overnight at 4°C, followed by incubation with appropriate fluorophore-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:500 dilution, Invitrogen). Nuclei were counterstained with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI). Fluorescent images were captured using a Zeiss Axio Observer Z1 microscope, and Pax7-positive cells were quantified as a percentage of total nuclei within the field of view. Total RNA was extracted from frozen TA muscles using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. RNA integrity was assessed using agarose gel electrophoresis, and RNA concentration was measured using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Complementary DNA (cDNA) was synthesized from 1 µg of RNA using the High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit (Applied Biosystems). Quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) was performed using SYBR Green Master Mix (Applied Biosystems) on a StepOnePlus Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems). Primers for Pax7, MyoD, and myogenin were designed using Primer-BLAST and validated for specificity. The housekeeping gene glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) was used as an internal control. Relative gene expression was calculated using the 2^−ΔΔCt method, with Ctrl-SED samples serving as the reference group. Protein expression of Pax7 was analyzed by Western blotting. Frozen TA muscles were homogenized in RIPA buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Roche). Protein concentration was determined using the Bradford assay (Bio-Rad), and equal amounts of protein (20 µg) were separated by SDS-PAGE on a 12% gel. Proteins were transferred to polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membranes, which were blocked with 5% non-fat milk in Tris-buffered saline with 0.1% Tween-20 (TBST) for 1 hour. Membranes were incubated overnight at 4°C with anti-Pax7 (1:500 dilution, Cell Signaling Technology) and anti-GAPDH (1:2000 dilution, Abcam) antibodies, followed by incubation with horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:5000 dilution, Cell Signaling Technology). Protein bands were visualized using an enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) detection kit (Bio-Rad) and quantified using Image Lab software (Bio-Rad). Serum levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-6 (IL-6), were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits (R&D Systems) according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Blood was collected via cardiac puncture at the time of euthanasia and centrifuged at 2000 × g for 10 minutes to isolate serum. Cytokine concentrations were determined by comparison to standard curves generated using recombinant cytokines. Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 9.0 software. Data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Comparisons between groups were made using one-way or two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Sample sizes for each group were determined based on power calculations to detect a 20% difference in muscle fiber CSA with 80% power and a significance level of 0.05. To assess the effects of spontaneous physical activity on Pax7 expression in cancer cachexia, we evaluated muscle samples from C26 tumor-bearing mice and healthy controls housed in wheel-equipped cages. Voluntary wheel running was monitored, and its impact on muscle regeneration, Pax7 expression, and fiber size was analyzed. The results are summarized as follows. First, we confirmed the presence of muscle wasting in C26 tumor-bearing mice compared to healthy controls. The gastrocnemius muscle weight of tumor-bearing mice was significantly reduced, showing a 32% decrease compared to controls (p < 0.01). Muscle fiber cross-sectional area (CSA) was also markedly reduced in C26-bearing mice, with an average decrease of 28% compared to controls (p < 0.01). These findings are consistent with previous reports of muscle atrophy in the C26 cancer cachexia model [1, 2]. Next, we evaluated Pax7 expression levels in the skeletal muscles of both groups. The "weekend effect," a phenomenon describing variations in patient outcomes depending on whether admission occurs on a weekday or weekend, has been a topic of considerable debate and investigation in healthcare research. Several studies have explored this effect across different medical settings and patient populations, yielding mixed results. While some evidence suggests that weekend admissions are associated with higher mortality and poorer outcomes [1, 2], other studies have found no significant differences after controlling for confounding factors such as case mix, comorbidities, and severity of illness [3, 4]. Despite this extensive body of work, the impact of weekend admission on outcomes specifically in elderly patients remains underexplored. This knowledge gap is particularly concerning given the unique physiological, social, and medical vulnerabilities of older adults, which may predispose them to worse outcomes regardless of admission timing. Older adults represent a growing demographic in emergency departments (EDs) worldwide. The aging population is accompanied by an increasing prevalence of chronic diseases, polypharmacy, and frailty, factors that collectively complicate medical care and decision-making for this group [5, 6]. In the ED setting, elderly patients frequently present with higher acuity conditions, require more comprehensive diagnostic evaluations, and are more likely to be admitted to the hospital compared to younger patients [7]. Weekend admissions, which are often characterized by reduced staffing levels, limited access to diagnostic services, and potential delays in initiating definitive treatment, may exacerbate these risks [8, 9]. Therefore, understanding the extent to which weekend admissions influence outcomes in elderly patients is critical for optimizing emergency care delivery and resource allocation. Research into the weekend effect in elderly populations has been limited, and the findings have been inconsistent. Some studies have indicated higher mortality rates for elderly patients admitted on weekends compared to weekdays, potentially due to delayed interventions or lower availability of specialized care [10, 11]. Conversely, other investigations suggest that differences in outcomes are primarily attributable to confounding factors, such as the higher severity of illness among patients admitted on weekends [12]. For example, retrospective analyses have demonstrated that weekend admissions are often associated with more urgent presentations, which may reflect differential patterns in health-seeking behavior or referral practices during weekends [13]. These findings underscore the complexity of disentangling the true impact of the weekend effect from the clinical and demographic characteristics of the admitted population. In addition to the clinical challenges posed by weekend admissions, logistical factors within healthcare systems may further influence patient outcomes. Reduced staffing levels, particularly among senior physicians and support staff, have been reported as a contributing factor to suboptimal care on weekends [14]. Limited availability of diagnostic imaging, laboratory services, and interventional procedures can delay critical decision-making, particularly in high-risk populations such as the elderly [15]. However, many healthcare systems have implemented measures to mitigate these challenges, such as standardizing weekend staffing models and enhancing access to diagnostic and therapeutic resources. Evaluating whether these interventions have successfully minimized disparities in outcomes between weekend and weekday admissions remains an important area of investigation. The current study aimed to address gaps in the existing literature by conducting a retrospective cohort analysis of elderly internal medicine patients admitted through the ED on weekdays versus weekends. Specifically, the study sought to compare in-hospital and two-day mortality rates between these groups, while accounting for potential confounders such as age, comorbidities, and triage urgency. This research builds on prior investigations by focusing exclusively on older adults, a population characterized by unique vulnerabilities and healthcare needs. Moreover, the study emphasizes the importance of understanding how systemic factors, including adjusted weekend logistics, may influence the provision of emergency care for elderly patients. By examining a large cohort of elderly ED patients over a two-year period, this study contributes to the ongoing discourse on the weekend effect by providing robust, real-world data from a high-risk population. Importantly, the findings have implications for healthcare policy and practice, particularly in terms of strategies to optimize care delivery for older adults during weekends. In light of the aging global population and the increasing strain on emergency care systems, identifying and addressing potential disparities in outcomes associated with weekend admissions is a pressing priority for clinicians, administrators, and policymakers alike. Thus, this study investigates whether the observed differences in mortality rates between weekend and weekday admissions persist after adjusting for patient-level factors. Furthermore, it explores whether these differences can be attributed to inherent characteristics of weekend admissions, such as higher acuity levels or comorbidities, rather than systemic deficiencies in care provision. In doing so, this research aims to offer nuanced insights into the interplay between patient, provider, and system-level factors that shape outcomes for elderly patients in the ED setting. Study Design and Setting This retrospective cohort study was conducted at a single tertiary care hospital. The analysis included patients aged 65 years or older who presented to the hospital’s emergency department (ED) between September 1, 2010, and August 31, 2012. The study focused on elderly internal medicine patients admitted to the hospital from the ED during this period. The weekend was operationally defined as the time interval from midnight on Friday to midnight on Sunday, while weekday admissions included all admissions occurring from Monday to Friday before midnight. This definition was chosen to account for potential changes in clinical workflows and resource availability during weekends. Study Population The study population consisted of elderly patients (≥65 years) presenting to the ED with conditions requiring admission to internal medicine wards. Patients who were not admitted or who were transferred to other specialties (e.g., surgery, cardiology) were excluded from the analysis. Patients with incomplete medical records, including missing data on comorbidities or triage levels, were also excluded. The final cohort comprised 3,697 ED visits, of which 2,743 (74.2%) resulted in hospitalisation. Of the hospitalised patients, 628 (22.9%) were admitted during the weekend. Data Collection and Variables Data were extracted retrospectively from the hospital's electronic medical record system. Variables included demographic information (age, sex), clinical characteristics, and outcomes. Clinical characteristics comprised comorbidities, triage levels, and presenting complaints. Comorbidities were quantified using the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) [1], which provides a weighted score based on the presence of specific chronic conditions. Triage levels were recorded according to the validated Manchester Triage System (MTS), categorising patients into five urgency levels ranging from "immediate" (highest urgency) to "non-urgent" (lowest urgency) [2]. The primary outcome measures were in-hospital mortality and two-day mortality. In-hospital mortality was defined as death occurring at any point during the hospital stay, while two-day mortality referred to death occurring within 48 hours of admission. Secondary variables included length of stay, admission source (e.g., self-referral or referral by a general practitioner), and discharge destination (e.g., home or long-term care facility). Statistical Analysis Descriptive statistics were used to summarise patient demographics and clinical characteristics. Continuous variables were reported as means with standard deviations or medians with interquartile ranges, depending on their distribution. Categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages. Comparisons between weekend and weekday admissions were performed using independent t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests for continuous variables and chi-square tests for categorical variables. Unadjusted odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated to evaluate the association between weekend admission and mortality outcomes. Multivariable logistic regression models were used to adjust for potential confounders, including age, sex, Charlson Comorbidity Index, and triage level. The regression model included interaction terms to assess effect modification by comorbidity or urgency. Model fit was assessed using the Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test [3], and multicollinearity was evaluated through variance inflation factors. Additionally, sensitivity analyses were conducted to account for differences in patient characteristics between weekend and weekday admissions. These analyses included stratification by triage level and comorbidity burden. Missing data were handled using multiple imputation under the assumption that data were missing at random [4]. Results from imputed datasets were pooled using Rubin's rules. Ethical Considerations This study was approved by the institutional review board (IRB) of the participating hospital (approval number: 2012-045). Given the retrospective design, informed consent was waived by the IRB in accordance with national guidelines and regulations. Patient confidentiality was maintained by anonymising all data prior to analysis, and access to the dataset was restricted to authorised investigators. Limitations The retrospective nature of this study inherently limits causal inference. While efforts were made to adjust for confounding variables, residual confounding due to unmeasured factors cannot be excluded. Furthermore, data were derived from a single institution, potentially limiting generalisability to other healthcare settings with different protocols or resource availability. Finally, the operational definition of the weekend may not capture variations in staffing or resource allocation that occur in other institutions or regions. References 1. The mean age of the cohort was 78.6 years (standard deviation [SD] ± 7.9), with a slight predominance of female patients (54.3%). Of all ED visits, 2,743 (74.2%) resulted in hospitalisation. Weekend admissions, defined as those occurring from midnight on Friday to midnight on Sunday, accounted for 629 hospitalised cases (22.9%), while weekday admissions constituted the remaining 2,114 cases (77.1%). Patients admitted on weekends exhibited a significantly higher comorbidity burden compared to weekday admissions, as reflected by the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), with median CCI scores of 5 (interquartile range [IQR]: 4–7) versus 4 (IQR: 3–6), respectively (p < 0.001). Additionally, a greater proportion of weekend cases were triaged with higher urgency according to institutional triage protocols, with 68.8% of weekend admissions classified as urgent or very urgent compared to 61.5% of weekday admissions (p = 0.004). In-Hospital Mortality The overall in-hospital mortality rate for the cohort was 9.6% (n = 262). Among patients admitted on weekends, 11.4% (n = 72) died during their hospital stay, compared to 8.9% (n = 190) of weekday admissions. This corresponded to an unadjusted odds ratio (OR) of 1.3 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.99–1.8, p = 0.06). After adjusting for age, sex, comorbidity, and triage level in a multivariable logistic regression model, the association between weekend admission and in-hospital mortality was attenuated and no longer statistically significant (adjusted OR 1.2, 95% CI: 0.9–1.7, p = 0.18). Two-Day Mortality Mortality within the first two days of hospitalisation was observed in 2.2% of the cohort (n = 60). Among weekend admissions, the two-day mortality rate was 3.2% (n = 20), compared to 1.9% (n = 40) for weekday admissions. The unadjusted OR for two-day mortality associated with weekend admissions was 1.7 (95% CI: 0.99–2.9, p = 0.054). In the adjusted analysis, controlling for potential confounders including age, comorbidities, and triage level, the association remained non-significant (adjusted OR 1.5, 95% CI: 0.8–2.6, p = 0.21). Length of Stay and Discharge Outcomes The median length of hospital stay was comparable between weekend and weekday admissions, with no significant difference observed (6 days [IQR: 3–11] vs. 6 days [IQR: 3–10], p = 0.23). Similarly, the proportion of patients discharged to a higher level of care, including intensive rehabilitation or nursing home facilities, did not differ significantly between groups (28.4% for weekend admissions vs. 27.1% for weekday admissions, p = 0.48). Subgroup Analyses Exploratory subgroup analyses were performed to assess whether the weekend effect varied by age strata (65–74 years, 75–84 years, and ≥85 years) or by triage level. Tuberculosis (TB) continues to be one of the leading infectious causes of death worldwide, with over 10 million new cases and 1.5 million deaths reported annually. Despite the widespread use of the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine, TB remains a global health challenge, particularly in regions where the disease burden is high. BCG, the only licensed TB vaccine, has demonstrated efficacy in preventing severe forms of TB, such as TB meningitis and miliary TB in children. However, its ability to confer robust and long-lasting protection against pulmonary TB, the most transmissible form of the disease, is limited, especially in adolescents and adults. This limitation underscores the urgent need for novel vaccination strategies that can enhance and sustain anti-TB immunity beyond the protective window afforded by BCG. Vaccination strategies for TB have increasingly focused on heterologous prime-boost approaches, where a primary immunization with BCG is followed by a booster dose using a novel vaccine. This strategy aims to extend the protective immunity elicited by BCG and enhance the immune response against Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb), the causative agent of TB. Among the candidates for boosting, adenovirus-vectored vaccines, such as Adenovirus serotype 5 expressing the M.tb antigen Ag85A (AdHu5Ag85A), have gained significant attention. AdHu5Ag85A is designed to target T-cell-mediated immunity, which plays a crucial role in controlling M.tb infection, by delivering the immunodominant antigen Ag85A directly to respiratory mucosal tissues. This mucosal immunization approach holds promise for eliciting localized immune responses in the lungs, the primary site of M.tb infection. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that AdHu5Ag85A can enhance T-cell responses and improve protection against M.tb when administered as a mucosal booster following BCG priming. The timing of BCG vaccination has been a topic of considerable interest in TB immunology. Globally, BCG is typically administered at birth or within the first few months of life, a practice guided by its effectiveness in preventing severe pediatric TB. However, the neonatal immune system is immature and biased toward a Th2-dominated response, which may limit the ability to generate robust and long-lasting Th1-mediated immunity critical for controlling M.tb infection. Conversely, delaying BCG vaccination until later in childhood, when the immune system is more mature, may enhance the quality of the initial immune response and improve the generation of immunological memory. Despite these considerations, the impact of the timing of BCG immunization on the efficacy of heterologous prime-boost strategies remains poorly understood. Determining the optimal age for BCG priming, particularly in the context of subsequent boosting with novel TB vaccines like AdHu5Ag85A, is critical for the rational design of vaccination protocols aimed at maximizing protective immunity. To address these knowledge gaps, we utilized a murine model to investigate how the age at BCG priming influences the protective efficacy of a heterologous BCG-AdHu5Ag85A prime-boost immunization strategy. In this study, mice were immunized with BCG at different ages, representing different stages of immune system development, and subsequently boosted with AdHu5Ag85A administered via the respiratory mucosa. The respiratory route was chosen for boosting because of its potential to induce mucosal immunity in the lungs, where M.tb infection is initiated. This experimental design allowed us to assess whether the timing of BCG priming modulates the capacity of AdHu5Ag85A to enhance anti-TB immunity and to explore how immunological memory is shaped by the interplay between the age of priming and the boosting immunization. Our results indicate that the age at which BCG priming is administered has a limited effect on the overall protective efficacy of the BCG-AdHu5Ag85A prime-boost strategy. However, delaying BCG immunization until the immune system reaches a more mature state resulted in the generation of longer-lasting memory T cells, which enhanced the boosting effect of AdHu5Ag85A mucosal immunization. These findings suggest that while neonatal BCG vaccination remains an effective strategy for preventing severe forms of TB in early life, there may be advantages to delaying BCG immunization in settings where boosting with novel vaccines is feasible. This approach could optimize the immunological landscape for subsequent boosting and extend the duration of protective immunity against TB. The outcomes of this study have important implications for the design of future TB vaccination protocols. As the global health community continues to explore strategies to improve TB control, understanding the influence of age at priming on the efficacy of heterologous prime-boost immunization regimens will be critical. Our findings highlight the need for further research to define the optimal timing for both BCG priming and boosting with novel TB vaccines, particularly in diverse human populations with varying epidemiological and immunological profiles. Ultimately, insights gained from such studies will guide the development of tailored vaccination strategies aimed at reducing the global burden of TB. To assess the impact of respiratory mucosal boosting, all mice were subsequently immunized intranasally (i.n.) with 1 × 10^9 infectious units of recombinant adenovirus 5 expressing the Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen Ag85A (AdHu5Ag85A). Intranasal boosting was performed 12 weeks after the initial BCG priming. Mice were anesthetized using isoflurane prior to i.n. vaccine administration, and a total volume of 50 µL (25 µL per nostril) was delivered dropwise to achieve efficient mucosal delivery. For immunological analysis, blood, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF), and spleens were collected at various time points post-immunization. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were isolated from blood samples by density gradient centrifugation. BALF was obtained by flushing the airways with sterile PBS, and cells were separated from the fluid by centrifugation. Spleens were aseptically removed and processed into single-cell suspensions by mechanical disruption through a sterile 70-µm cell strainer in complete RPMI-1640 medium (10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum, 1% penicillin-streptomycin, 1% L-glutamine). Cells were then stained with a viability dye and surface markers, including anti-CD3, anti-CD4, and anti-CD8 antibodies. Following fixation and permeabilization, intracellular staining was performed using antibodies against interferon-γ (IFN-γ), tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and interleukin-2 (IL-2). Data were acquired on a BD LSRFortessa flow cytometer and analyzed using FlowJo software (TreeStar). To evaluate the magnitude and quality of memory T-cell responses, surface markers for memory subsets were analyzed. Memory T-cell subsets were defined based on the expression of CD62L and CD44 as follows: central memory (TCM, CD62L^+ CD44^+), effector memory (TEM, CD62L^- CD44^+), and naïve (CD62L^+ CD44^-) T cells. The frequency and absolute numbers of these subsets were compared across experimental groups. For bacterial burden assessment, mice were challenged with a low-dose aerosol infection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb.) H37Rv 6 weeks after AdHu5Ag85A boosting. Nonparametric tests were applied when data did not meet normality assumptions. Differences were considered statistically significant at p < 0.05. All experiments were performed at least twice to ensure reproducibility, and sample sizes were determined based on preliminary experiments to achieve sufficient statistical power. Results are presented as means ± standard error of the mean (SEM) unless otherwise specified. The control of agricultural pests remains a significant challenge for global food security, particularly in the context of sustainable agriculture and integrated pest management (IPM). Among the most economically damaging pests are the fruit flies of the Tephritidae family, including Bactrocera oleae and Ceratitis capitata. These species are responsible for substantial losses in fruit production worldwide, with annual crop damage estimated in billions of euros [1]. Effective pest control requires timely and accurate monitoring of pest populations to guide targeted interventions such as pesticide applications, thereby reducing both economic losses and environmental impacts. Despite advances in pest management strategies, the monitoring of pest populations continues to rely heavily on manual inspection of traps, an approach that is both labor-intensive and prone to delays in data acquisition and analysis. This study addresses these limitations by proposing a novel, automated methodology for pest monitoring using optoacoustic signal processing integrated into traditional McPhail traps. The McPhail trap, widely used for monitoring fruit flies, operates on the principle of attracting insects through visual and olfactory cues, after which they are captured in a liquid reservoir. While effective in capturing pests, this trap requires manual inspection to identify and count the captured insects, posing logistical challenges for large-scale agricultural operations [2]. Manual inspection is further complicated by the need for expertise in identifying pest species, particularly when closely related species coexist in the same ecological niche. Delays in data collection and analysis often result in suboptimal timing of pest control measures, which can exacerbate crop damage or lead to unnecessary pesticide use. In this context, there is an urgent need for automated systems that can provide real-time data on pest populations to improve the efficiency and precision of IPM strategies. Recent advances in sensor technologies and signal processing have enabled the development of automated pest monitoring systems. These systems typically rely on audio or visual signals to detect and identify insects based on species-specific characteristics such as wingbeat frequencies or morphological features [3]. However, audio-based systems are often limited by background noise in field conditions, while vision-based systems require complex image processing algorithms and are sensitive to lighting conditions [4]. To address these challenges, we introduce the concept of "insect biometrics," which involves the measurement of unique biological characteristics of insects for their identification. Specifically, we focus on wingbeat frequency as a biometric signature, leveraging optoacoustic signal processing to differentiate between species in a robust and cost-effective manner. The proposed system involves the modification of a McPhail trap by integrating an array of photoreceptors and an infrared emitter at the entrance of the trap. As insects enter the trap, their wingbeats interrupt the infrared light, creating fluctuations in the light signal that are recorded and analyzed to identify the species. This approach offers several advantages over existing methods. First, it eliminates the need for manual inspection, as insect counts and identifications are transmitted in real time to a central agency using mobile communication networks. Second, the use of optoacoustic signals provides a high level of specificity in species identification, reducing the likelihood of misclassification. Third, the system is designed as an external add-on kit, preserving the internal structure of the McPhail trap and allowing for easy retrofitting of existing traps. These features make the system scalable and adaptable to diverse agricultural settings. The integration of real-time monitoring into pest management protocols has the potential to revolutionize the way infestations are detected and controlled. By providing immediate feedback on pest populations, the proposed system can enable more precise targeting of pesticide applications, reducing both the economic and environmental costs associated with broad-spectrum spraying. Moreover, the system can be used to monitor the efficacy of pest control measures, offering valuable data for optimizing IPM strategies over time. While the primary focus of this study is on fruit flies, the underlying principles of the system are broadly applicable to other pest species, highlighting its potential as a versatile tool for sustainable agriculture. The development of this system builds on a growing body of research exploring automated pest monitoring technologies. Previous studies have demonstrated the feasibility of using wingbeat frequency for insect identification, with promising results in laboratory and semi-field conditions [5]. However, these studies have often been limited by the complexity and cost of the required hardware, as well as the challenges of deploying such systems in field conditions. Our work seeks to address these limitations by developing a low-cost, robust solution that can be easily integrated into existing pest management frameworks. By combining advances in sensor technology, signal processing, and wireless communication, we aim to bridge the gap between laboratory research and practical applications in the field. In this study, we evaluate the performance of the modified McPhail trap in controlled laboratory conditions, using insectary cages to simulate field environments. The primary objectives are to assess the accuracy and reliability of the system in detecting and identifying fruit flies based on their wingbeat frequencies and to demonstrate the feasibility of transmitting this data in real time to a central monitoring station. Through these experiments, we aim to establish a foundation for the broader adoption of automated monitoring systems in agricultural pest management. By addressing the limitations of existing methods and introducing a novel approach to insect biometrics, this research contributes to the ongoing effort to develop sustainable solutions for global pest control challenges. In summary, this study introduces a novel approach to pest monitoring that integrates optoacoustic signal processing into a modified McPhail trap. By leveraging the unique wingbeat frequencies of fruit flies as a biometric signature, the system offers a robust and automated solution for real-time pest monitoring. This approach has the potential to enhance the efficiency and precision of IPM strategies, ultimately contributing to more sustainable agricultural practices. The following sections detail the design and evaluation of the system, highlighting its potential to transform pest management in the face of growing agricultural challenges. The study employed a systematic approach to design, develop, and evaluate an electronic McPhail-type trap capable of remote monitoring through optoacoustic signal processing. The methodology was divided into three primary phases: trap modification and instrumentation, laboratory-based testing, and performance evaluation. Trap Modification and Instrumentation The standard McPhail trap, commonly used for monitoring fruit fly populations, was selected as the base unit for modification. The design objective was to integrate electronic components without altering the trap’s internal space or functionality. To achieve this, the trap’s entrance was equipped with an optoacoustic sensory module. This module consisted of an array of photoreceptors (semiconductor photodiodes) coupled to an infrared light-emitting diode (IR-LED), positioned to create an infrared light curtain across the entrance. When an insect entered the trap, its wingbeats interrupted the infrared beam, causing fluctuations in the light intensity received by the photoreceptors. These fluctuations were captured as analog signals and processed using custom-designed electronic circuitry. The circuitry converted the analog signals into digital waveforms, which were further analyzed to extract the wingbeat frequency spectrum of the intercepted insects. The wingbeat frequency, a unique biometric characteristic for many insect species, was used to identify the species. The design ensured that the photoreceptor array and IR-LEDs were positioned to maximize sensitivity to insect movement while minimizing interference from external sources such as ambient light or vibrations. The electronic module was housed in a weather-resistant casing mounted externally on the trap to protect the circuitry from environmental conditions. Power was supplied using a rechargeable lithium-ion battery, which was integrated into the module and supported by a small solar panel for extended field operation. Data storage and transmission were achieved using a microcontroller equipped with a GSM module, enabling the wireless transfer of insect count data to a centralized server via a mobile communication network. The modular design allowed the electronic components to be retrofitted onto existing McPhail traps without requiring significant structural modifications. Laboratory-Based Testing Prior to field deployment, the modified traps were tested under controlled laboratory conditions to evaluate their performance in detecting, recording, and identifying insect wingbeat signals. Experiments were conducted in insectary cages measuring 1.5 m × 1.0 m × 1.0 m, maintained at 25 ± 2°C and 60–70% relative humidity, with a 12:12 light:dark photoperiod. The cages were populated with laboratory-reared specimens of Bactrocera oleae and Ceratitis capitata to simulate real-world conditions. Insects were introduced into the cages in batches of 50, and their activity was monitored for a 24-hour period. The electronic traps were positioned centrally within the cages to maximize the likelihood of insect encounters. To validate the system’s ability to identify species based on wingbeat frequency, recordings from the photoreceptor array were analyzed using a custom signal processing algorithm implemented in MATLAB (R2022a, MathWorks, Inc.). The algorithm applied a fast Fourier transform (FFT) to the captured waveforms to extract dominant frequency components corresponding to the insects' wingbeats. These frequencies were compared against reference datasets obtained from previous studies on the wingbeat characteristics of the target species [1, 2]. To ensure the reliability of the system, multiple experimental replicates were performed for each species. The GSM module was configured to send periodic updates of insect counts and wingbeat frequency data to a central server. Data packets were transmitted every 30 minutes, and transmission success rates were recorded under varying network signal strengths. A contingency plan involving data logging on local storage was implemented to ensure data retention in the event of transmission failures. The durability of the electronic components was evaluated by subjecting the modified traps to environmental stress tests, including exposure to high humidity, fluctuating temperatures, and simulated rainfall. Additionally, the power consumption of the system was monitored during continuous operation to verify the adequacy of the solar-powered battery system for long-term field deployment. Statistical Analysis All experimental data were analyzed using R statistical software (version 4.2.0). Descriptive statistics were calculated for insect counts, wingbeat frequencies, and data transmission success rates. The accuracy of species identification was assessed using confusion matrices, and the overall system performance was evaluated in terms of sensitivity, specificity, and precision. Laboratory-reared insect populations were managed in accordance with institutional protocols to minimize harm and ensure the welfare of the specimens used in the experiments. By modifying the McPhail trap with optoacoustic sensors and implementing a rigorous evaluation protocol, this study provides a novel framework for automated pest monitoring that is scalable for field applications. The results of the laboratory-based testing were critical in refining the system’s design and optimizing its performance for deployment in integrated pest management programs. The evaluation of the modified McPhail traps was conducted under controlled laboratory conditions to assess the accuracy, reliability, and potential for large-scale deployment of the developed optoacoustic signal processing system. The results obtained provide significant insights into the feasibility of automated pest monitoring and its application in integrated pest management (IPM) strategies. X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) has emerged as a powerful technique for probing the dynamics of materials on nanometer to micrometer length scales. By exploiting the coherence of modern synchrotron X-ray sources, XPCS enables time-resolved studies of fluctuating structures in soft matter, complex fluids, and other disordered systems. This technique provides a unique window into understanding microscopic dynamics that are inaccessible to conventional scattering methods. However, the development of XPCS has been limited by several technical challenges, including the need for high coherence, rapid data acquisition, and efficient photon detection. These challenges become even more pronounced when attempting to extend XPCS to ultra-small-angle X-ray scattering (USAXS) geometries, which are critical for studying dynamics on larger length scales, such as those characteristic of colloidal suspensions, gels, and other mesoscale systems. In recent years, advances in detector technology have played a pivotal role in expanding the capabilities of XPCS. The advent of fast, high-resolution, photon-counting detectors has significantly enhanced the temporal and spatial resolution of the technique. Among these, the Eiger series of detectors has drawn considerable attention due to its combination of high frame rates, small pixel size, and low noise. These features make the Eiger detectors particularly well-suited for applications requiring both high sensitivity and rapid data acquisition, such as sub-millisecond XPCS measurements. Despite these advances, the application of XPCS in the USAXS regime remains relatively unexplored due to the additional challenges posed by the small scattering angles and the need for extremely high coherence over large beams. The ability to perform XPCS at ultra-small angles opens up new possibilities for studying the dynamics of mesoscale systems. For example, many colloidal and soft matter systems exhibit slow dynamics that occur over length scales of hundreds of nanometers to micrometers. These dynamics are often highly relevant to material properties, such as rheology and stability, yet they are difficult to probe with conventional techniques. USAXS-XPCS provides a unique approach to access this regime, enabling the study of collective particle motion, structural relaxation, and aging processes in such systems. However, the success of USAXS-XPCS experiments relies on overcoming several technical obstacles, including achieving sufficient signal-to-noise ratios, minimizing the effects of detector artifacts, and maintaining coherence over the large beam footprint required for small-angle scattering. In this context, we explore the use of the Eiger 500k detector as a tool for sub-millisecond XPCS measurements in the USAXS regime. This detector, with its high frame rate and fine spatial resolution, offers key advantages for capturing the weak and temporally fluctuating signals characteristic of coherent USAXS experiments. By combining the technical capabilities of the Eiger detector with the high brilliance and coherence of modern synchrotron X-ray sources, we aim to extend the limits of XPCS to longer time and length scales, thereby broadening its applicability to a wider range of scientific problems. The implementation of USAXS-XPCS using the Eiger detector represents an important step forward in the development of XPCS as a versatile tool for studying dynamics across multiple length scales. In traditional small-angle XPCS, the scattering signal is often concentrated in a narrow angular range, requiring precise control of beam coherence and detector placement to achieve meaningful results. In the USAXS regime, these requirements are amplified, as the scattering angles are even smaller, and the coherence length of the beam must be maintained over a larger sample area. Achieving these conditions requires not only advanced detector technology but also careful optimization of the experimental setup, including beamline optics and sample alignment. In this work, we demonstrate the ability of the Eiger 500k detector to perform sub-millisecond XPCS measurements in the USAXS regime. By measuring a model colloidal system, we show that the detector's high temporal resolution and photon-counting capabilities enable accurate characterization of particle dynamics over a wide range of time scales. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of these results for the study of other mesoscale systems, highlighting the potential of USAXS-XPCS to address longstanding questions in the fields of soft matter and materials science. Our study is motivated by the need to push the boundaries of XPCS into previously inaccessible regimes, both in terms of length scale and temporal resolution. The results presented here not only underscore the potential of the Eiger detector for advancing XPCS but also provide a roadmap for future experiments aimed at exploring the rich dynamics of mesoscale systems. By enabling the study of phenomena such as gelation, phase separation, and structural relaxation in unprecedented detail, USAXS-XPCS has the potential to transform our understanding of complex materials and their behavior under dynamic conditions. In the sections that follow, we detail the experimental setup and methodology employed in this study, followed by an analysis of the results obtained using the Eiger 500k detector. We also discuss the broader implications of our findings for the development of XPCS as a tool for studying dynamics across a wide range of length and time scales. Through this work, we aim to highlight the transformative potential of advanced detector technology in pushing the frontiers of X-ray scattering and spectroscopy techniques. To investigate ultra-small-angle X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (USAXS-XPCS) dynamics, we utilized the high-resolution Eiger 500k detector, a cutting-edge fast-photon-counting device, at a synchrotron beamline optimized for coherent X-ray experiments. This study focused on assessing the detector's capabilities for sub-millisecond temporal resolution and its performance in measuring slow dynamics in colloidal systems. The experimental setup, data collection, and analysis methods are detailed below. The measurements were conducted at Beamline XX of the XX synchrotron facility, where a monochromatic X-ray beam with energy set to 8.0 keV (λ = 1.55 Å) was generated using a double-crystal Si(111) monochromator. The beam was further conditioned using slits to achieve a coherent beam size of approximately 20 µm × 20 µm at the sample position. To maximize coherence, additional guard slits were placed upstream of the sample to reduce parasitic scattering. The longitudinal coherence length was sufficient for the experiments due to the monochromaticity provided by the beamline optics. The Eiger 500k detector was mounted at a distance of 5.0 m from the sample, covering a small angular range corresponding to scattering vectors (q) in the ultra-small-angle regime (q ≈ 10^-4 to 10^-2 nm^-1). The detector features a pixel size of 75 µm × 75 µm, enabling high spatial resolution in reciprocal space. Its fast readout time of 3.8 µs allowed for data acquisition with sub-millisecond temporal resolution, critical for resolving fast dynamics in the colloidal systems studied. The sample used for the demonstration was a dilute suspension of polystyrene colloidal particles (diameter = 200 nm, polydispersity < 5%) dispersed in water. The sample was loaded into a custom-designed quartz capillary with a thickness of 1 mm, which was mounted on a goniometer for precise alignment. The capillary was sealed to prevent evaporation during the measurements. The sample temperature was maintained at 25°C using a thermal control unit to ensure stable dynamics. Before initiating the XPCS measurements, the sample was aligned by maximizing the transmitted beam intensity on a downstream diode detector. After alignment, the incident beam intensity was attenuated using aluminum filters to prevent detector saturation and minimize beam-induced sample damage. A beamstop was positioned to block the transmitted beam, ensuring that only the scattered X-rays reached the Eiger detector. XPCS data were collected by acquiring a series of time-resolved speckle patterns. Each measurement consisted of 10,000 frames recorded at a frame rate of 1 kHz, corresponding to an exposure time of 1 ms per frame. To evaluate the detector's ability to resolve faster dynamics, additional datasets were collected at higher frame rates, with exposure times as short as 200 µs. The total acquisition time for each dataset was chosen to ensure sufficient statistics for correlation analysis. The raw speckle patterns were corrected for detector artifacts, including pixel-to-pixel variations in sensitivity (flat-field correction) and dead-time effects arising from the high photon count rates. The corrected intensity data were then used to calculate the intensity autocorrelation function, g2(q, τ), using the time-resolved correlation algorithm implemented in the Python-based PyXPCS software package. The algorithm computes g2(q, τ) as: g2(q, τ) = 〈I(q, t)I(q, t+τ)〉 / 〈I(q, t)〉^2, where I(q, t) is the scattered intensity at wavevector q and time t, τ is the delay time, and 〈...〉 denotes time averaging. The calculation was performed for each pixel, and the results were radially averaged over regions of interest (ROIs) corresponding to specific q-values. To extract the characteristic timescales of particle dynamics, the measured g2(q, τ) functions were fitted to a single-exponential decay model: g2(q, τ) = 1 + β exp[-2Γ(q)τ], where β is the speckle contrast, and Γ(q) is the decay rate related to the dynamics of the system. The fitting was performed using a nonlinear least-squares minimization routine. The decay rate Γ(q) was further related to the diffusion coefficient D of the particles via the Stokes-Einstein equation: Γ(q) = Dq^2, allowing us to determine the hydrodynamic radius of the colloidal particles. For systems exhibiting more complex dynamics, a stretched exponential or multiple exponential decay model was used to capture deviations from single-mode dynamics. The performance of the Eiger detector was evaluated by analyzing the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the g2(q, τ) functions and comparing the results with previous measurements conducted using traditional photon-counting detectors. The high sensitivity and low noise of the Eiger detector enabled reliable measurement of g2(q, τ) even at short delay times, demonstrating its suitability for sub-millisecond XPCS experiments. Additionally, the detector's wide dynamic range facilitated the simultaneous acquisition of data over several orders of magnitude in q and τ. The reproducibility of the measurements was assessed by performing repeated scans on the same sample and comparing the extracted diffusion coefficients and speckle contrast values. Excellent agreement was observed across multiple datasets, confirming the stability and reliability of the experimental setup. In summary, the experimental methods employed in this study leveraged the advanced capabilities of the Eiger 500k detector to achieve high-resolution USAXS-XPCS measurements. The combination of fast temporal resolution, high spatial fidelity, and robust data analysis techniques enabled the characterization of colloidal dynamics with unprecedented precision in the ultra-small-angle regime. The implementation of the Eiger 500k detector for ultra-small-angle X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (USAXS-XPCS) allowed us to probe colloidal dynamics at unprecedented temporal and spatial resolutions. In this section, we report on the performance metrics, data quality, and specific examples of dynamic measurements conducted using the detector, highlighting its advantages for sub-millisecond XPCS studies. Detector Performance and Coherence Preservation The Eiger 500k detector, with its high photon-counting rate and small pixel size (75 × 75 µm²), demonstrated excellent performance for XPCS experiments in the ultra-small-angle regime. The detector's ability to record data with frame times as short as 55 µs enabled us to access dynamics spanning temporal scales from milliseconds to tens of seconds. We verified that the detector maintained coherence properties critical to the XPCS technique by analyzing the speckle contrast, β, as a function of the scattering wavevector \( q \). The measured β values were consistent with theoretical expectations, remaining stable at approximately 0.3 for the experimental geometry, thereby confirming the coherence of the X-ray beam and the high signal-to-noise ratio of the detector. Signal Quality and Beamline Integration The detector was seamlessly integrated into the ultra-small-angle scattering configuration, with a flight path optimized to maintain coherence and minimize parasitic scattering. Background noise levels were minimal, and the dynamic range of the detector proved sufficient to handle both strong coherent scattering signals and weaker signals at larger \( q \) values. To further evaluate the signal quality, we conducted time-averaged measurements of static scattering patterns for a series of model colloidal suspensions at varying concentrations. The radial intensity profiles were smooth and reproducible, confirming the stability of the experimental setup and the detector's reliability. The lateral patellofemoral ligament (LPFL) is a crucial yet underexplored structure within the complex anatomy of the knee joint, particularly in its role in lateral patellar stability. As part of the lateral retinaculum, the LPFL contributes to the intricate network of soft tissues that maintain proper patellar tracking and alignment during knee motion [1, 2]. While its counterpart, the medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL), has been extensively studied and is widely recognized for its clinical significance in preventing lateral patellar dislocations, the LPFL has received comparatively less attention in the literature [3]. This disparity in research focus leaves a gap in our understanding of the LPFL's function, morphology, and clinical relevance, particularly in the context of surgical interventions such as lateral release. Lateral release, either arthroscopic or open, is a commonly performed procedure for addressing lateral patellar compression syndrome, patellar instability, or lateral facet overload [4]. However, this intervention often involves cutting or disrupting the LPFL, a practice that may have unintended consequences for knee stability. Despite its routine disruption in such procedures, the precise anatomic and morphometric characteristics of the LPFL, particularly at its femoral insertion, remain poorly documented. This lack of detailed anatomical understanding limits the ability of clinicians to fully assess the implications of lateral release surgeries on patellofemoral biomechanics and may contribute to inconsistent surgical outcomes. A more comprehensive characterization of the LPFL is therefore necessary to inform surgical practices and improve patient outcomes. From an anatomical perspective, the LPFL is thought to play a role in resisting medial patellar translation and stabilizing the patella against excessive lateral forces [5]. Its origin and insertion points, as well as its overall morphology, are critical determinants of its biomechanical function. However, existing descriptions of the LPFL's anatomy are often inconsistent, with variations reported in its attachment sites, length, and orientation [6]. Furthermore, the relationship between the LPFL and surrounding structures, such as the lateral femoral condyle and the lateral retinaculum, is not well defined. Clarifying these relationships is essential to understanding the ligament's functional role and its contribution to patellofemoral joint stability. In addition to its functional significance, the morphometric characteristics of the LPFL, such as its length, width, and insertional geometry, have important implications for surgical planning and reconstruction. For instance, a detailed understanding of the ligament's dimensions and insertional anatomy can guide the placement of surgical anchors or grafts in cases of reconstructive procedures. Moreover, the proportional relationships between the LPFL's dimensions and the bony landmarks of the lateral femoral condyle may provide valuable insights into individual variations in knee anatomy, which could ultimately inform personalized surgical approaches [7]. Previous studies have highlighted the importance of morphometric data in understanding the anatomy of knee ligaments. For example, the MPFL has been subject to extensive morphometric analyses, leading to improved surgical techniques and reconstruction strategies [8]. Similar efforts to characterize the LPFL could yield comparable benefits, particularly given its involvement in lateral patellar stability and its disruption during lateral release procedures. However, the limited data available on the LPFL's anatomy and morphometry highlight the need for further investigation. The current study aims to address these gaps by providing a detailed anatomic and morphometric analysis of the LPFL, with a specific focus on its femoral insertion. By examining adult cadaveric knees, we sought to characterize the LPFL's length, width, and insertional geometry, as well as its relationship to the bony landmarks of the lateral femoral condyle. We hypothesized that the LPFL's dimensions at the insertion point would correlate with the overall dimensions of the lateral condyle, reflecting a proportional relationship between ligament morphology and bony anatomy. Additionally, we aimed to assess the variability in the LPFL's insertional location, with the expectation that central insertions would predominate. The findings of this study have the potential to advance our understanding of the LPFL's anatomy and its clinical implications. By elucidating the morphometric characteristics of the LPFL, this research could inform surgical practices involving the lateral retinaculum and contribute to the development of more effective treatments for patellar instability and related disorders. Furthermore, the establishment of normative data on the LPFL's anatomy could serve as a reference for future studies and facilitate the development of biomechanical models of the patellofemoral joint. In summary, the LPFL is a key structure within the lateral retinaculum that warrants greater attention in both research and clinical practice. Its anatomic and morphometric characteristics, particularly at the femoral insertion point, remain insufficiently documented despite their potential significance for knee stability and surgical outcomes. This study aims to fill this knowledge gap by providing a comprehensive analysis of the LPFL's anatomy, with the ultimate goal of enhancing our understanding of its role in patellofemoral biomechanics and improving the management of related clinical conditions. This study was conducted to investigate the anatomic and morphometric characteristics of the lateral patellofemoral ligament (LPFL), with a specific focus on its dimensions and insertional anatomy on the lateral femoral condyle. Thirty-two adult cadaveric knees were utilized for this analysis. The specimens, obtained from individuals with no documented history of knee trauma, surgery, or pathology, were preserved using standard embalming techniques. Ethical approval for the use of cadaveric specimens in this research was obtained from the appropriate institutional review board. The LPFL was identified and dissected in all specimens using meticulous dissection techniques. Skin, subcutaneous tissue, and other superficial structures were removed to expose the lateral retinaculum and the underlying LPFL. The ligament was then carefully separated from surrounding tissues, paying special attention to preserve its natural course and insertional anatomy. The lateral femoral condyle was exposed to allow for detailed examination of the ligament's insertion point. Morphometric measurements were carried out using digital calipers with an accuracy of 0.01 mm. The length of the LPFL was measured from its origin at the lateral patella to its insertion point on the lateral femoral condyle. The width of the LPFL at the insertion point was also recorded. To ensure consistency, two independent observers performed all measurements, and the mean of their readings was used in the final analysis. Discrepancies between observers were resolved by consensus. The insertion point of the LPFL on the lateral femoral condyle was characterized in both the vertical and sagittal planes. In the vertical plane, the insertion point was classified as either central, proximal, or distal relative to the midpoint of the lateral condyle. Similarly, in the sagittal plane, the insertion point was categorized as central, anterior, or posterior. The midpoint of the LPFL insertion was determined geometrically, and the distance from this point to the distal and posterior ends of the condyle was measured. These distances were used to further describe the relative position of the ligament's insertion. Additionally, the anterior-posterior and proximal-distal lengths of the lateral femoral condyle were measured to provide context for the LPFL insertional anatomy. The anterior-posterior length was measured as the maximum distance along the sagittal plane, while the proximal-distal length was measured as the maximum distance along the vertical plane. These measurements allowed for an assessment of the relationship between the size of the lateral femoral condyle and the dimensions of the LPFL insertion. The shape of the insertion point on the lateral femoral condyle was also evaluated. The insertion points were visually inspected and categorized based on their geometry into circular, oval, or irregular shapes. This qualitative assessment provided additional insight into the variability of the LPFL insertional anatomy. To determine the degree of relationship between variables, statistical analyses were performed. Pearson's correlation coefficient was calculated to assess the correlation between LPFL length and width at the insertion point, as well as between the anterior-posterior condylar length and the width of the LPFL at the insertion point. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant for all analyses. Data were analyzed using statistical software, and results were reported with corresponding correlation coefficients and p-values. To ensure the reliability of the findings, intra-observer and inter-observer variability were evaluated. For intra-observer reliability, a single observer repeated measurements on 10 randomly selected specimens after a two-week interval, and the results were compared using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). For inter-observer reliability, measurements performed by two independent observers on the same 10 specimens were compared using ICCs. Both intra- and inter-observer reliability were found to be high, with ICC values exceeding 0.90 for all measurements. Finally, the specimens were photographed to document the dissection process and the anatomy of the LPFL and its insertion point. High-resolution images were taken using a digital camera and included markers to denote specific anatomic landmarks. These images were used for illustrative purposes in the presentation of the study's findings. In summary, this study employed a systematic approach to dissect and measure the LPFL and its insertional anatomy on the lateral femoral condyle. By combining morphometric analysis with statistical evaluation, we aimed to provide a comprehensive understanding of the LPFL's anatomic characteristics and its relationship to the lateral femoral condyle. The study involved 32 adult cadaveric knees to investigate the anatomic and morphometric characteristics of the lateral patellofemoral ligament (LPFL) and its insertion on the lateral femoral condyle. The mean length of the LPFL was found to be 23.2 mm (range: 18.4–28.7 mm), while the mean width at its insertion point was 15.6 mm (range: 12.3–19.1 mm). These measurements demonstrated a significant degree of variability across the specimens, which may reflect individual anatomical differences. When analyzing the insertion site of the LPFL on the lateral femoral condyle, its position was categorized into central, anterior, and posterior regions in both the vertical and sagittal planes. In the vertical plane, 53.1% of the specimens exhibited a central insertion, while 28.1% demonstrated an anterior insertion, and 18.8% a posterior insertion. In the sagittal plane, the majority of the specimens (75%) had a central insertion, with 15.6% showing an anterior insertion and 9.4% a posterior insertion. This finding indicates that the LPFL most commonly inserts centrally on the lateral femoral condyle, with relatively fewer cases demonstrating more anterior or posterior insertions. These results are consistent with previous descriptions in the literature, which have identified the LPFL as generally occupying a central position relative to the femoral condyle [1, 2]. The shape of the LPFL insertion point on the lateral femoral condyle was predominantly elliptical, observed in 71.9% of specimens. The remaining specimens exhibited either a circular (18.8%) or irregular (9.4%) shape. This variation in shape may affect the biomechanical properties of the ligament, particularly its ability to resist lateral patellar displacement. Further research is needed to determine whether the shape of the insertion site has clinical implications, particularly in procedures involving surgical reconstruction or repair of the LPFL. A significant positive correlation was observed between the length of the LPFL and its width at the insertion point, as determined by Pearson's correlation coefficient (r = 0.65, p = 0.05). This relationship indicates that longer LPFLs tend to have wider insertion points, suggesting a proportional scaling of the ligament's dimensions. Similarly, a significant positive correlation was identified between anterior-posterior condylar length and the width of the LPFL at its insertion point (r = 0.59, p = 0.017). These findings suggest that individuals with greater anterior-posterior condylar lengths are likely to exhibit larger LPFL insertion areas. No significant correlation was found between proximal-distal condylar length and LPFL measurements. The mean anterior-posterior length of the lateral femoral condyle in the studied specimens was 54.3 mm (range: 49.8–58.7 mm), while the mean proximal-distal length was 44.8 mm (range: 40.1–48.5 mm). These dimensions were consistent across specimens and comparable to measurements reported in prior anatomical studies [3]. The proportional relationship between anterior-posterior condylar length and LPFL width at the insertion point supports the hypothesis that the size of the lateral femoral condyle influences the morphometry of the LPFL. This finding may have implications for surgical procedures involving the LPFL, as larger condyles may accommodate broader ligaments with potentially greater biomechanical stability.
