Non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) represents a significant proportion of urothelial carcinoma cases, accounting for approximately 75% of all newly diagnosed bladder cancers [1]. The standard of care for NMIBC includes transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) followed by adjuvant intravesical therapy to reduce recurrence and progression [2]. Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) has long been established as the most effective intravesical therapy for intermediate- and high-risk NMIBC, providing both immunomodulatory and direct cytotoxic effects [3]. However, despite its efficacy, a notable proportion of patients fail BCG therapy, with recurrence or progression occurring in up to 50% of cases, depending on tumor risk stratification and patient characteristics [4,5]. For these patients, therapeutic options become limited, and clinical decision-making becomes complex. The standard recommendation for patients with high-risk NMIBC who fail BCG therapy is radical cystectomy, which offers the highest likelihood of disease eradication and long-term survival [6]. However, radical cystectomy is associated with significant morbidity and impacts on quality of life, and many patients are unwilling or unable to undergo this procedure due to advanced age, comorbidities, or personal preferences for bladder preservation [7,8]. Consequently, there is a critical need to develop effective bladder-sparing strategies for patients with BCG-unresponsive NMIBC. The search for alternative intravesical therapies to salvage bladder function in this challenging patient population has gained increasing attention. Among the agents explored are chemotherapeutic agents such as gemcitabine, docetaxel, mitomycin C, and others, either as monotherapy or in combination regimens [9,10]. Gemcitabine, a pyrimidine analog, exerts its anticancer effects by inhibiting DNA synthesis and has demonstrated efficacy and tolerability as an intravesical agent in both the adjuvant and salvage settings [11,12]. Similarly, docetaxel, a taxane-based chemotherapeutic agent that stabilizes microtubules and disrupts mitotic processes, has shown promise in NMIBC treatment, particularly in the context of BCG failure [13,14]. Both agents have favorable pharmacokinetic profiles for intravesical administration, with minimal systemic absorption and manageable toxicity profiles [15]. Building on preliminary studies of single-agent therapies, the use of dual sequential intravesical gemcitabine and docetaxel has emerged as a novel combination strategy for NMIBC patients who have failed BCG. This regimen leverages the complementary mechanisms of action of gemcitabine and docetaxel to enhance antitumor activity, with gemcitabine potentially sensitizing tumor cells to the effects of docetaxel [16]. Early reports of this sequential combination have suggested promising efficacy, with manageable adverse events, making it a compelling option for patients who are not candidates for radical cystectomy [17,18]. Despite these encouraging findings, the clinical experience with sequential intravesical gemcitabine and docetaxel remains limited, with few studies providing long-term follow-up or robust outcome data in larger cohorts. Furthermore, the optimal patient selection criteria, treatment protocol, and timing for this regimen remain areas of ongoing investigation. In particular, understanding the durability of response, recurrence-free survival, progression rates, and the potential impact on subsequent cystectomy outcomes is critical to defining its role in the NMIBC treatment paradigm. In this study, we sought to evaluate the efficacy and safety of sequential dual intravesical gemcitabine and docetaxel in a cohort of NMIBC patients who had failed prior BCG therapy. Specifically, we aimed to assess treatment success, defined as the absence of bladder cancer recurrence and avoidance of cystectomy, and to analyze the durability of response over time. By reporting our initial experience with this regimen in a real-world clinical setting, we aim to contribute to the growing body of evidence supporting alternative salvage therapies for NMIBC, particularly in the context of BCG failure or shortages. This study is particularly timely given the ongoing challenges related to BCG availability worldwide. Periodic shortages of BCG supply have created a pressing need for alternative intravesical therapies that can be reliably administered to patients with NMIBC [19]. The dual sequential gemcitabine and docetaxel regimen offers an attractive option in this regard, as both agents are widely available and relatively inexpensive compared to other emerging therapies, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors, which are currently limited to advanced or metastatic disease settings [20]. Additionally, the regimen’s tolerability profile makes it suitable for a broad range of patients, including those with significant comorbidities who may not tolerate more aggressive interventions. Here, we present our findings from a cohort of 45 patients treated with this regimen over a five-year period. We hypothesized that sequential intravesical gemcitabine and docetaxel would provide meaningful therapeutic benefit in terms of recurrence-free survival, bladder preservation, and reduction in the need for cystectomy. Furthermore, we aimed to identify factors associated with treatment success and to evaluate the safety profile of the regimen in this challenging patient population. By addressing these questions, we hope to provide valuable insights into the role of dual sequential intravesical gemcitabine and docetaxel in the salvage treatment of NMIBC and to inform clinical decision-making for patients with limited options. This study was conducted to evaluate the efficacy of sequential intravesical gemcitabine and docetaxel for the treatment of non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) in patients who either experienced Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) failure or were not candidates for radical cystectomy. A retrospective analysis was performed on patients treated at our institution between June 2009 and May 2014. Institutional review board approval was obtained prior to initiating this study, and all patients provided informed consent before undergoing treatment. Eligibility criteria included histologically confirmed NMIBC, defined as Ta, T1, or carcinoma in situ (CIS), with prior failure of BCG therapy. BCG failure was classified as either persistent or recurrent disease following at least one induction and one maintenance or re-induction course of BCG. Patients were required to have no evidence of muscle invasion, upper tract urothelial carcinoma, or metastatic disease as assessed by transurethral resection, imaging, and/or cytology. Exclusion criteria included contraindications to gemcitabine or docetaxel, active urinary tract infection, or inability to tolerate intravesical therapy. Patients were scheduled to receive six weekly intravesical instillations of sequential gemcitabine and docetaxel. Gemcitabine (1 gram reconstituted in 50 mL of sterile water) was instilled into the bladder via a urethral catheter and retained for 60 minutes. Following bladder drainage, docetaxel (37.5 mg in 50 mL of saline) was administered intravesically and retained for an additional 60 minutes. Patients were encouraged to void prior to each instillation to ensure optimal retention of the treatment agents. If tolerated, patients received the full six-week induction course. Patients who demonstrated no evidence of disease at their first post-treatment surveillance were offered maintenance therapy on a case-by-case basis, consisting of monthly instillations for up to 12 months. Baseline demographic and clinical data were collected, including age, sex, performance status, smoking history, tumor stage, grade, and prior treatment history. All patients underwent cystoscopy, urine cytology, and bladder mapping biopsies at baseline to confirm the presence and extent of disease. Surveillance was performed at three-month intervals following treatment initiation, with cystoscopy, cytology, and biopsies as clinically indicated. The primary outcome was treatment success, defined as the absence of recurrence of bladder cancer and avoidance of cystectomy. Secondary outcomes included time to recurrence, time to cystectomy, and adverse events associated with therapy. For patients who underwent cystectomy, pathologic outcomes, including margin status and lymph node involvement, were recorded. Treatment tolerability was assessed based on the number of instillations completed during induction. Adverse events were graded using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 4.0. Furthermore, the absence of a control group precluded direct comparisons with other salvage therapies. The oriental armyworm, Mythimna separata (Walker), is a significant agricultural pest with a broad host range, including cereals like maize, wheat, and rice. This polyphagous insect is noted for its migratory behavior, which enables it to disperse over long distances, often resulting in severe crop damage across large geographical regions [1]. The life cycle and ecological success of M. separata are intricately linked to its sensory systems, particularly its olfactory and mechanosensory modalities, which play crucial roles in navigation, mate selection, host plant identification, and behavioral coordination during migration [2,3]. Despite its economic importance and behavioral complexity, the neuroanatomical and functional organization of its sensory systems, especially the central projections of antennal and labial sensory neurons, remains poorly understood. Insects rely on their antennae and labial palps as primary sensory organs to detect and process environmental cues. The antennae, in particular, are equipped with a diverse array of sensory structures, including olfactory and mechanosensory sensilla, which enable the detection of volatile compounds, airflow patterns, and mechanical stimuli [4]. Similarly, the labial palps, and more specifically the labial-palp pit organ (LPO), are specialized for detecting carbon dioxide, a critical cue for locating food and mates in various insect species [5]. The sensory input from these peripheral structures is transmitted via sensory neurons to specific regions of the central nervous system (CNS), where it is integrated and processed to elicit appropriate behavioral responses. Understanding the central projections and organization of these sensory inputs is key to elucidating the neural mechanisms underlying the complex behaviors of M. separata. The antennal lobe (AL) is the primary olfactory processing center in insects and serves as the initial site of integration for sensory input from antennal olfactory neurons [6]. Within the AL, sensory axons from olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) terminate in discrete spherical structures known as glomeruli, which are organized in a stereotypical and species-specific manner [7]. The spatial arrangement of these glomeruli is thought to facilitate the segregation and processing of odorant information based on receptor specificity and input modality, supporting the insect's ability to discriminate between diverse odorant blends [8]. While the glomerular organization of the AL has been extensively studied in model insects like Drosophila melanogaster and Manduca sexta, far less is known about the structure and functional organization of the AL in migratory agricultural pests such as M. separata. In addition to the AL, the antennal mechanosensory and motor center (AMMC) represents another critical neuropil in the insect CNS that processes mechanosensory input from the antennae [9]. This region is subdivided into zones that correspond to specific antennal segments, including the scape, pedicel, and flagellum, each of which houses distinct mechanosensory structures [10]. Mechanosensory input from these regions is thought to contribute to essential behaviors such as flight stabilization, orientation, and substrate vibration detection [11]. However, the precise organization of mechanosensory axon terminals within the AMMC of M. separata and their functional relationships to motor circuits remain to be fully characterized. The labial-palp pit organ (LPO) represents a specialized olfactory structure that has garnered increasing attention for its role in detecting CO₂ and other environmental cues [5,12]. Sensory neurons from the LPO have been shown to project to specific regions of the CNS, including the AL, the gnathal ganglion (GNG), and the ventral nerve cord (VNC) in various insect species [13]. These projections suggest that LPO sensory input is integrated across multiple neural centers to mediate a range of behaviors, from feeding to flight modulation. However, the contribution of the LPO to sensory processing and behavioral control in M. separata remains poorly understood. To address these gaps, the present study employs a combination of neuroanatomical techniques, including neuronal backfills, confocal microscopy, and three-dimensional reconstructions, to map the central projections of sensory neurons from the antennae and LPO of M. separata. By examining the connectivity and spatial organization of these projections in the CNS, this study provides critical insights into the neural architecture underlying the sensory modalities of olfaction and mechanosensation in this species. Specifically, the study focuses on three key objectives: (1) characterizing the glomerular organization of the AL and its relationship to olfactory input from antennal ORNs; (2) mapping the spatial arrangement of mechanosensory projections within the AMMC and their segment-specific organization; and (3) identifying the projection patterns of LPO sensory neurons to the AL, GNG, and VNC. The findings of this study are expected to advance our understanding of the functional organization of the insect CNS, particularly in the context of sensory integration and behavioral coordination in migratory pests. By elucidating the central projection patterns of antennal and labial sensory neurons, this study also provides a foundation for future investigations into the neural mechanisms underlying olfactory-guided behaviors, mechanosensory processing, and motor control in M. separata. Moreover, the results may inform the development of novel pest management strategies targeting the sensory and neural systems of this agriculturally important species. Insect Rearing and Preparation The oriental armyworm, Mythimna separata, was reared under laboratory conditions to ensure uniformity in experimental subjects. Larvae were maintained on an artificial diet under a 16:8 h light:dark photoperiod at 25 ± 1°C and 60 ± 5% relative humidity. Adult moths of both sexes, 2–4 days post-emergence, were selected for all experiments to ensure physiological maturity. Prior to dissection, individuals were immobilized on ice for 10 minutes to reduce movement and anesthetized by chilling. The antennae and labial palps were isolated under a stereo microscope (Leica M165 C, Wetzlar, Germany), ensuring minimal damage to sensory structures during excision. Neuroanatomical Tracing To trace the central projections of sensory neurons from the antenna and labial palp, neuronal backfills were performed using fluorescent dyes. For the antennal sensory neurons, the cut end of the antennal nerve was placed into a small droplet of 4% neurobiotin tracer (Vector Labs, Burlingame, CA, USA) dissolved in 0.1 M phosphate-buffered saline (PBS; pH 7.4) or a 1% solution of dextran-conjugated tetramethylrhodamine (MW 10,000; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). Similarly, for the labial palp sensory neurons, the labial nerve was exposed and immersed in the tracer solution. Preparations were sealed with petroleum jelly (Vaseline) to prevent desiccation and incubated at 4°C for 12–16 hours. Following incubation, specimens were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde in 0.1 M PBS for 4 hours at room temperature. Fixed tissues were rinsed thoroughly in PBS, then dissected to isolate the central nervous system (CNS), including the brain, subesophageal ganglion (SOG), and ventral nerve cord (VNC). The dissected CNS tissues were subsequently processed for confocal microscopy. Immunohistochemistry and Staining To enhance visualization of neural structures, immunohistochemistry was performed. CNS samples were permeabilized in 0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS (PBST) for 1 hour and blocked in 5% normal goat serum (NGS; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) for 2 hours. Preparations were then incubated overnight at 4°C with a primary antibody against synapsin (3C11, monoclonal, 1:100; Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank, Iowa City, IA, USA) diluted in PBST containing 2% NGS. After thorough washing in PBST, tissues were incubated for 2 hours at room temperature with a secondary antibody conjugated to Alexa Fluor 488 (1:200; Thermo Fisher Scientific) to label synaptic regions. Concurrently, neurons backfilled with neurobiotin were visualized by incubating tissues with streptavidin conjugated to Alexa Fluor 568 (1:200; Thermo Fisher Scientific) in PBST for 2 hours. To identify specific antennal substructures contributing to central projections, the cut ends of the flagellum, pedicle, and scape were separately filled with neurobiotin. This approach allowed delineation of projection patterns associated with each antennal segment. After staining, samples were mounted in Vectashield antifade medium (Vector Labs) between two glass coverslips separated by spacers to prevent compression. Imaging and Confocal Microscopy Processed tissues were imaged using a Leica TCS SP8 confocal laser scanning microscope equipped with 10× and 40× oil immersion objectives. Sequential scanning was employed to avoid cross-talk between fluorophores, with excitation/emission wavelengths optimized for Alexa Fluor 488 (488/500–550 nm) and Alexa Fluor 568 (561/570–620 nm). Z-stack images were acquired at 1-μm intervals for three-dimensional reconstruction. All imaging parameters were standardized across specimens to ensure comparability. Three-Dimensional Reconstruction and Data Analysis Confocal image stacks were processed and analyzed using Amira software (Thermo Fisher Scientific) to produce three-dimensional reconstructions of neural structures. Neuropil boundaries were delineated based on synapsin immunostaining, and sensory neuron projections were traced manually within the reconstructions. The antennal lobe (AL), antennal mechanosensory and motor center (AMMC), gnathal ganglion (GNG), and thoracic ganglia were identified based on anatomical landmarks and previous descriptions in related lepidopteran species [1, 2]. Projection patterns were qualitatively assessed by comparing the spatial organization of axon terminals within each neuropil. Quantitative analyses of projection density were performed using ImageJ (National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA) to measure fluorescence intensity and terminal arborization area in selected regions of interest (ROIs). Statistical comparisons between the projection patterns of neurons originating from different antennal segments or the labial palp were conducted using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by post hoc Tukey’s tests. Validation of Staining Specificity To ensure the specificity of neurobiotin and antibody labeling, control experiments were conducted. Negative controls included omission of the primary antibody during immunostaining and substitution of neurobiotin with PBS during backfills. No significant fluorescence signal was observed in control preparations, confirming the specificity of staining protocols. Ethical Considerations All experimental procedures were conducted in accordance with institutional guidelines for the ethical treatment of insects in research. As M. separata is a pest species, no specific permits were required for its collection and use. References for Methods 1. Homberg, U., Montague, R. A., & Hildebrand, J. G. (1988). Antennal Sensory Neuron Projections The central projections of antennal sensory neurons in Mythimna separata were traced using neuroanatomical techniques, revealing their diverse and spatially segregated innervation patterns across the central nervous system. When the antennal nerve was backfilled with neurotracers, dense arborizations were observed in the antennal lobe (AL), antennal mechanosensory and motor center (AMMC), and the prothoracic and mesothoracic ganglia of the ventral nerve cord. Within the AL, the antennal sensory neurons terminated exclusively in olfactory glomeruli, consistent with the known role of this structure in processing olfactory information. Dye application to the antennal flagellum confirmed that only olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) from this segment project to the AL, as no staining was observed in other segments when the pedicle or scape were targeted. In contrast, projections to the AMMC were observed to originate from mechanosensory neurons located across all three antennal segments—flagellum, pedicle, and scape. The arrangement of these projections within the AMMC was highly organized, with distinct zones corresponding to the segmental origin of the sensory neurons. Specifically, axons from the flagellum terminated predominantly in anterior regions of the AMMC, while those from the pedicle and scape extended into posterior zones. This segregated pattern of innervation suggests functional compartmentalization within the AMMC, with anterior regions likely processing flagellar mechanosensory inputs, and posterior zones integrating signals from the more basal antennal segments. Projections to the ventral nerve cord were also detected following antennal backfills, with labeled axons terminating in the motor areas of the prothoracic and mesothoracic ganglia. These projections were predominantly associated with mechanosensory neurons, suggesting that antennal mechanosensation contributes to motor control, potentially coordinating flight behaviors. Notably, no evidence of direct olfactory input into the thoracic ganglia was observed, which indicates that olfactory signals from the antenna are processed centrally in the brain and are not directly involved in motor neuron modulation. The ability to stop a clinical trial early is a critical aspect of modern trial design, offering significant potential benefits in terms of both resource efficiency and ethical considerations. Interim analyses allow investigators to assess whether the trial should continue as planned, stop early due to convincing evidence of efficacy, or halt because the available data suggest futility. In particular, stopping for futility can save valuable time and financial resources, especially when interim results indicate that the trial is unlikely to meet its objectives. However, the choice of futility boundaries in group sequential designs remains a challenging and underexplored area, especially in trials with complex designs such as those involving multiple primary endpoints. Group sequential designs are statistical methods that allow for interim analyses while maintaining overall control of the type I error rate. These designs are particularly advantageous in trials where planning assumptions are based on limited prior evidence. For example, in trials with two primary endpoints, the power of the study is influenced not only by the effect sizes of the individual endpoints but also by their correlation. Making accurate assumptions about these parameters can be challenging, especially in early-stage clinical trials or in novel therapeutic areas. In such cases, the ability to stop early for futility becomes even more important, as it reduces the risk of continuing a trial that is unlikely to yield useful results. While the literature on group sequential designs has extensively addressed the choice of boundaries for stopping a trial early for efficacy, much less attention has been given to the selection of futility boundaries. This is a critical gap, as poorly chosen futility boundaries can have significant consequences for the performance of the trial. For instance, overly conservative futility boundaries may result in unnecessary continuation of futile trials, wasting resources and potentially exposing participants to ineffective interventions. Conversely, overly lenient boundaries may lead to the premature termination of trials that could have ultimately demonstrated efficacy, thereby compromising the scientific validity and practical utility of the results. The challenges associated with selecting appropriate futility boundaries are further compounded in the context of trials with two primary endpoints. Such trials often require the use of intersection-union tests to account for the multiplicity of hypotheses, adding an additional layer of complexity to the design. The correlation between the two endpoints and the potential for differing effect sizes further complicate the selection of futility boundaries. As a result, standard approaches to futility monitoring, such as fixed thresholds or ad hoc rules, may not be adequate for trials with multiple endpoints. Instead, a more systematic approach is needed to ensure that futility boundaries are chosen in a way that balances the competing objectives of minimizing unnecessary trial continuation, preserving statistical power, and avoiding premature termination of potentially successful trials. In this context, the development of a general method for constructing "optimal" futility boundaries is a critical step forward. Such a method would allow investigators to define futility boundaries based on predefined performance criteria, ensuring that the boundaries are tailored to the specific characteristics and objectives of the trial. By explicitly accounting for the correlation between endpoints, the proposed method offers a more nuanced approach to futility monitoring, addressing the unique challenges posed by trials with multiple primary endpoints. The primary aim of this work is to propose a general framework for constructing optimal futility boundaries in group sequential designs with two endpoints. The method is designed to maximize the probability of correctly stopping a trial in cases where the true effects are small or in opposite directions, while limiting the risk of power loss and the probability of incorrectly terminating the trial. To illustrate the utility of this approach, we apply the proposed method to a real clinical trial example and conduct extensive Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate its performance under a range of scenarios. Our results demonstrate the benefits of using optimally constructed futility boundaries, particularly in comparison to conventional approaches commonly used in practice. The proposed method not only improves the probability of making correct decisions at interim analyses but also maintains the overall integrity of the trial design. Importantly, the method is flexible enough to be adapted to a wide range of trial settings, making it a valuable tool for investigators designing trials with multiple endpoints. Despite the critical importance of futility monitoring in clinical trials, its properties are often overlooked or not rigorously assessed in practice. As a result, many trials use suboptimal futility boundaries, which can lead to inefficient use of resources, ethical concerns, and compromised scientific validity. By providing a systematic method for evaluating and selecting futility boundaries, this work addresses an important gap in the literature and offers practical guidance for investigators aiming to design efficient and reliable group sequential trials. We recommend that future studies adopt the criteria proposed here to ensure that futility boundaries are chosen in a way that aligns with the overall objectives of the trial and the specific characteristics of the endpoints being studied. To address the problem of determining optimal futility boundaries in group sequential designs for clinical trials with two primary endpoints, we developed a systematic methodology that takes into account predefined performance criteria. Our approach is based on computational simulations and theoretical considerations to balance the trade-offs between stopping a trial early for futility and ensuring sufficient power to detect clinically meaningful effects. Below, we describe the framework and key steps used to construct and evaluate these futility boundaries. First, we define the statistical setting in which the group sequential design is applied. Let \( E1 \) and \( E2 \) denote the two primary endpoints of interest, which are jointly analyzed using an intersection-union test to maintain the overall type I error rate. The test hypotheses are formulated as \( H0: \mu1 \leq \mu{1,0} \) or \( \mu2 \leq \mu{2,0} \), where \( \mu1 \) and \( \mu2 \) represent the true mean effects of \( E1 \) and \( E2 \), respectively, and \( \mu{1,0} \) and \( \mu{2,0} \) are their null values. The trial is designed to reject \( H0 \) only if both endpoints demonstrate statistically significant effects. The group sequential design allows for one or more interim analyses, with pre-specified boundaries for stopping the trial early for either efficacy or futility. Futility is assessed based on the interim data, and the decision to stop the trial is made when the observed data suggest that the probability of ultimately rejecting \( H0 \) is sufficiently low under the assumed effect sizes. To construct futility boundaries, we focus on maximizing the probability of correctly stopping for futility (when true effects are small or opposite in direction) while minimizing the probability of wrongly stopping (when true effects are clinically meaningful). Our methodology begins by specifying performance criteria for evaluating the futility boundaries. These criteria include: 1. The probability of correctly stopping for futility under a null or near-null scenario (small or no treatment effects for both endpoints). 2. The probability of wrongly stopping for futility when the true effects are in the clinically relevant range. 3. The overall power of the trial after accounting for the introduction of futility boundaries. We define a range of candidate futility boundaries based on the conditional power (CP) approach. For each interim analysis, we calculate the conditional power of rejecting \( H0 \) given the observed data and the assumed effect sizes. A futility boundary is constructed such that the trial is stopped early when the CP falls below a specified threshold \( \gamma \). The choice of \( \gamma \) is critical, as it directly influences the performance characteristics of the design. To identify the optimal futility boundary, we perform an extensive grid search over a range of \( \gamma \)-values. For each candidate boundary, we evaluate the performance criteria through Monte Carlo simulations. The simulation setup includes generating data for \( E1 \) and \( E2 \) under different scenarios, varying the true effect sizes and their correlation structure. We consider realistic scenarios based on prior clinical knowledge and assumptions used in the sample size calculation. Each simulation run involves generating interim and final data, applying the group sequential design with the candidate boundary, and recording the trial outcomes (e.g., stopping for futility, stopping for efficacy, or continuing to the final analysis). The simulations are repeated thousands of times to ensure reliable estimates of the performance metrics for each candidate boundary. The optimal futility boundary is selected as the one that maximizes the probability of correctly stopping for futility while meeting predefined thresholds for power and the probability of wrongly stopping. In addition to the conditional power approach, we also explore alternative methods for constructing futility boundaries, such as using predictive probabilities (PP) or Bayesian posterior probabilities. These alternative approaches are evaluated using the same simulation framework to compare their performance against the conditional power-based boundaries. For the Bayesian approach, we specify prior distributions for the effect sizes of \( E1 \) and \( E2 \), incorporating prior clinical knowledge where available. Predictive probabilities are calculated based on the posterior distribution of the final test statistic, given the interim data. To illustrate the application of our methodology, we apply it to a real clinical trial example with two endpoints: a continuous endpoint assessing a biomarker change and a binary endpoint measuring a clinical response. The trial involves two interim analyses and a final analysis, and the correlation between endpoints is assumed to be 0.5 based on prior studies. For this example, we use the conditional power approach to construct futility boundaries and evaluate the trial's performance under different scenarios. Finally, to assess the robustness of the selected futility boundaries, we conduct sensitivity analyses by varying key parameters, such as the assumed effect sizes, correlation between endpoints, and the sample size per group. The results of these analyses are used to confirm the generalizability of the proposed methodology. All computations and simulations were conducted using R (version 4.0.3) and the R package "gsDesign" for group sequential design implementation. Additional custom scripts were developed for simulating data under the two-endpoint setting and evaluating the performance metrics. The source code for the simulations and the real trial example is provided as supplementary material to ensure reproducibility and facilitate the application of our method to other trial designs. To evaluate the proposed method for constructing optimal futility boundaries, we applied it to several scenarios and assessed its performance using a combination of analytical derivations and Monte Carlo simulations. The focus was on maximizing the probability of correctly stopping for futility when small or opposite effects are present, while maintaining acceptable levels of power and minimizing the probability of an incorrect early stop. First, we considered a real clinical trial example involving two co-primary endpoints, where the trial design was based on a group sequential framework with two interim analyses and one final analysis. The trial’s objective was to detect an effect on both endpoints simultaneously, with the correlation between endpoints assumed to be moderate (ρ = 0.5). We compared the performance of the proposed optimal futility boundaries with commonly used approaches, such as non-binding futility boundaries based on a fixed percentage of the maximum sample size or bounds derived from conditional power calculations. In the real trial example, the proposed optimal futility boundaries demonstrated clear advantages. The probability of stopping the trial early for futility when the true effects were small or in opposite directions was significantly higher compared to conventional boundaries. Specifically, when both endpoints had effect sizes close to zero, the stopping probability increased from approximately 45% with conventional boundaries to over 70% with the proposed method. This improvement was achieved without compromising the overall power of the trial, which remained above the pre-specified level of 80%. Moreover, the probability of incorrectly stopping the trial for futility when the true effects were moderate and in the same direction was kept below 5%, aligning with the desired error control. Nitrogen (N) is a fundamental building block of life, playing a critical role in biological processes and being essential for the growth and productivity of crops and livestock. However, human activities have profoundly altered the global nitrogen cycle, resulting in an unprecedented release of reactive nitrogen (Nr)—all biologically, photochemically, and radiatively active forms of nitrogen except dinitrogen gas (N₂)—into the environment. While these transformations have supported global food security and energy production through agricultural intensification and industrial processes, they have also led to significant unintended consequences. The anthropogenic Nr inputs to the environment, primarily through fertilizer use, livestock production, fossil fuel combustion, and industrial activities, have created a suite of environmental challenges, including air and water pollution, greenhouse gas emissions, biodiversity loss, soil acidification, and eutrophication of aquatic ecosystems. These impacts not only degrade ecosystem health but also pose risks to human well-being, underscoring the urgent need to better understand and manage Nr flows in the Anthropocene. To address these challenges, the concept of the nitrogen footprint has emerged as a valuable tool. The nitrogen footprint is a consumer-based metric that quantifies the amount of Nr released to the environment as a result of an individual's or a population's lifestyle choices. It encompasses Nr losses associated with food consumption, energy use, and other activities, providing a comprehensive perspective on the efficiency of Nr use in society. By connecting personal and societal behaviors with environmental outcomes, the nitrogen footprint offers a unique lens through which to evaluate the sustainability of human lifestyles and identify opportunities to mitigate Nr losses. Australia, known for its vast landscapes, rich biodiversity, and "clean and green" image, presents an intriguing case study for nitrogen footprint analysis. The country has a relatively small population but a disproportionately large environmental impact, in part due to its resource-intensive economy and high per capita consumption patterns. Despite increasing global awareness of the environmental implications of Nr emissions, there has been limited research on Australia's nitrogen footprint and the specific factors driving its magnitude. This knowledge gap is particularly significant given Australia's heavy reliance on agriculture and fossil fuels, both of which are major sources of Nr emissions. In this study, we present the first comprehensive assessment of Australia's nitrogen footprint using the N-Calculator model, a widely recognized tool for quantifying Nr losses linked to human activities. Our analysis reveals that Australia has the largest nitrogen footprint per capita among all countries that have applied the N-Calculator framework, with an estimated value of 47 kg N cap⁻¹ yr⁻¹. This striking result highlights the central role of food and energy sectors in driving Australia's Nr emissions. Notably, approximately 69% of the national nitrogen footprint is attributed to food consumption and the associated production processes, with the remaining 31% linked to energy consumption. Among food-related contributors, beef consumption and production emerge as the dominant factors behind Australia's high nitrogen footprint. Beef production is inherently nitrogen-intensive, involving significant Nr losses at multiple stages of the supply chain, including fertilizer application for feed crops, enteric fermentation in cattle, and manure management. Australia is one of the world's largest consumers of beef on a per capita basis, and its robust beef export industry further amplifies the environmental impact of this sector. The findings underscore the need to explore dietary shifts and more sustainable livestock management practices as potential strategies to reduce Nr losses in the food system. In the energy sector, the high nitrogen footprint is predominantly driven by Australia's reliance on coal as a primary source of electricity generation. Coal combustion is a major source of nitrogen oxides (NOₓ), which contribute to air pollution, climate change, and other environmental issues. Despite the global transition toward renewable energy sources, coal remains a cornerstone of Australia's energy mix, reflecting both historical dependencies and political-economic factors. The significant contribution of coal to the nation's nitrogen footprint underscores the critical importance of accelerating the shift to cleaner energy technologies and improving energy efficiency. This study provides valuable insights into the drivers and distribution of Australia's nitrogen footprint, offering a foundation for targeted interventions to mitigate Nr losses. By highlighting the key roles of beef and coal, we identify clear opportunities for reducing Australia's nitrogen footprint through changes in dietary preferences, agricultural practices, and energy systems. Moreover, the findings contribute to the broader discourse on sustainable consumption and production, emphasizing the interconnectedness of lifestyle choices, economic structures, and environmental outcomes. The results of this assessment have implications not only for Australia but also for other nations grappling with the environmental consequences of Nr emissions. As global nitrogen flows continue to increase, understanding the drivers of nitrogen footprints in different socio-economic and environmental contexts is essential for developing effective mitigation strategies. By situating Australia's nitrogen footprint within the broader global landscape, this study highlights both the challenges and opportunities of managing reactive nitrogen in a world striving for sustainability. To conduct the first full-scale assessment of anthropogenic reactive nitrogen (Nr) loss in Australia, we employed the N-Calculator model, a widely used tool for estimating national nitrogen footprints. This model provides a consumer-based perspective by linking nitrogen use efficiency to lifestyle choices, integrating both food and energy systems. The methodology included data collection, calculation of nitrogen footprints in the food and energy sectors, and identification of key contributors to the total nitrogen footprint. Data Collection Data on food consumption, energy use, and agricultural production were gathered from publicly available national databases, peer-reviewed literature, and international reports. For food consumption, we utilized dietary intake data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). These data included average per capita consumption of various food categories such as meat, dairy, grains, fruits, and vegetables. To ensure robust estimates, we also incorporated information from Australia's National Nutrition Survey, which details dietary patterns across different demographic groups. For energy consumption, data were collected from Australia's Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW) and the International Energy Agency (IEA). These data included annual electricity generation, breakdowns of energy sources (e.g., coal, gas, renewables), and per capita energy use. Coal, as a major energy source in Australia, was given particular attention, with detailed data on its contribution to electricity generation and associated nitrogen emissions. In the agricultural sector, production data were sourced from the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences (ABARES). These data included nitrogen fertilizer application rates, livestock populations, and crop yields. Emission factors for nitrogen losses in agriculture, such as ammonia volatilization, nitrate leaching, and nitrous oxide emissions, were derived from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) guidelines and corroborated with region-specific studies. Nitrogen Footprint Calculation The N-Calculator model was adapted to the Australian context by incorporating region-specific data on nitrogen flows and losses. The model calculates the nitrogen footprint by quantifying reactive nitrogen losses across the food production-consumption chain and the energy production-consumption system. For the food sector, the nitrogen footprint was calculated using a life-cycle approach, which included nitrogen inputs during agricultural production, processing, distribution, and consumption. Reactive nitrogen losses were estimated for each food category based on nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) values, which represent the proportion of nitrogen inputs retained in edible food products. For example, beef production, known for its low NUE and high nitrogen losses, was analyzed in detail. The calculation accounted for nitrogen losses from feed crop production, manure management, and enteric fermentation. Similar calculations were applied to other food categories, such as dairy, poultry, grains, and vegetables, using corresponding NUE values and emission factors. In the energy sector, the nitrogen footprint was determined based on nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions from fossil fuel combustion. Coal-fired power plants, which dominate Australia's electricity generation, were analyzed in detail. Emission factors for NOx were obtained from the National Greenhouse and Energy Reporting Scheme (NGERS) and literature on Australian power plants. The model also considered NOx emissions from transportation, industrial energy use, and residential energy consumption. Key Contributors to the Nitrogen Footprint To identify the major contributors to Australia's nitrogen footprint, we conducted a sectoral analysis of reactive nitrogen losses. The food sector was further disaggregated into subcategories based on dietary components, and the energy sector was analyzed by energy source. Beef consumption and production emerged as the dominant contributors to the food nitrogen footprint due to high nitrogen inputs for feed crop production and low NUE. Similarly, the energy nitrogen footprint was heavily influenced by coal combustion, given its high NOx emissions and significant share in Australia's energy mix. Sensitivity Analysis A sensitivity analysis was performed to assess the robustness of our nitrogen footprint estimates. Key parameters, such as nitrogen use efficiency values, emission factors, and per capita consumption rates, were varied within plausible ranges to evaluate their impact on the overall nitrogen footprint. This analysis helped identify uncertainties and prioritize areas for intervention. Validation and Comparison To validate our findings, we compared the Australian nitrogen footprint with those of other countries that have used the N-Calculator model, including the United States, the Netherlands, and China. This benchmarking highlighted Australia's unique nitrogen footprint profile and provided context for interpreting the results. Additionally, our estimates were cross-checked against independent studies on nitrogen flows in Australia to ensure consistency. Limitations While the N-Calculator model provides a comprehensive framework for estimating nitrogen footprints, certain limitations should be noted. The model relies on average national data, which may not capture regional or demographic variations in nitrogen use and emissions. Furthermore, the analysis does not include indirect nitrogen losses associated with imported goods or international trade, which could influence the overall footprint. These limitations highlight the need for further research to refine nitrogen footprint estimates and explore mitigation strategies. No primary data collection involving human or animal subjects was conducted. By integrating detailed data on food and energy systems with the N-Calculator model, our methodology provides a comprehensive assessment of Australia's nitrogen footprint. This approach highlights the significant role of beef consumption and coal reliance in driving nitrogen losses and underscores the potential for targeted interventions to reduce nitrogen footprints through sustainable lifestyle and policy choices. Health inequalities, particularly those shaped by socioeconomic disparities, have emerged as a critical public health concern globally. These disparities often manifest in differential health outcomes across income groups, with lower socioeconomic positions consistently associated with poorer physical and mental health outcomes [1, 2]. While extensive research has documented such inequalities in diverse populations, including racial and ethnic minorities in Western countries, fewer studies have addressed health disparities among immigrant populations in East Asian contexts, particularly South Korea. This gap in the literature is surprising given the rapid demographic and social transformations in South Korea, including its transition from a historically homogenous society to one incorporating a growing immigrant population. The unique sociocultural and policy environment of South Korea provides a compelling setting for investigating the intersection of health, income, and migration. South Korea has witnessed a substantial increase in immigration over the past two decades, driven by economic globalization, labor demands, and demographic challenges such as low fertility rates and an aging population [3, 4]. Among immigrants, the category of "married immigrants"—individuals migrating to South Korea through marriage, typically with native-born South Korean spouses—has grown markedly [5]. These individuals, often women from low- and middle-income countries in Asia, face unique socioeconomic challenges that may exacerbate health inequalities, including limited access to social resources, language barriers, cultural adaptation difficulties, and systemic discrimination [6]. Despite these challenges, empirical research on the health outcomes of married immigrants in South Korea remains scarce, particularly with respect to how income-related disparities shape their physical and mental health. The few studies that have examined immigrant health in South Korea suggest that married immigrants experience significant health vulnerabilities. For instance, prior research has identified high levels of mental health distress, including depression and anxiety, among this population, often attributed to economic insecurity, social isolation, and marital dissatisfaction [7, 8]. Similarly, poor self-rated health (SRH)—a robust predictor of morbidity and mortality—has been reported among married immigrants, particularly those from lower socioeconomic backgrounds [9]. However, while these studies highlight the existence of health disparities, they rarely quantify the extent of income-related health inequalities or explore the underlying factors driving these inequalities. Such an investigation is crucial for identifying modifiable determinants and designing targeted interventions to address avoidable health disparities. Income-related health inequalities are typically measured using quantitative tools such as concentration indices, which assess the degree to which health outcomes are distributed unequally across income groups [10]. These indices, particularly when combined with decomposition analyses, offer valuable insights into the relative contributions of various sociodemographic and socioeconomic factors to overall health inequalities [11]. For instance, prior studies in other settings have demonstrated that income, employment status, and subjective social status are often the primary drivers of health inequities, while demographic factors such as age and gender may play secondary roles [12]. However, such methods have not been widely applied to the study of immigrant health in South Korea, leaving a critical gap in understanding the structural determinants of health disparities in this population. The present study aims to address this gap by examining income-related inequalities in self-reported depression and poor SRH among married immigrants in South Korea. These two health outcomes were selected because they represent complementary dimensions of health: depression as a measure of mental health and SRH as a measure of overall health status. Both are widely used in public health research and have been shown to correlate strongly with objective health indicators [13, 14]. By applying the Erreygers concentration index—a modified measure suited for bounded health variables—and decomposing inequality into its sociodemographic determinants, this study provides a nuanced understanding of how income disparities influence health among married immigrants. In addition to income, the study considers a range of other factors that may contribute to health inequalities, including subjective social status, employment status, marital satisfaction, demographic characteristics, and migration-related variables. Subjective social status, which captures an individual’s perception of their position in the social hierarchy, has been shown to independently influence health outcomes, often mediating the effects of objective income measures [15]. Employment status is another critical determinant, as stable employment not only improves material living conditions but also enhances social integration and psychological well-being [16]. Marital satisfaction, meanwhile, is particularly relevant for married immigrants, given that their migration is often tied to marriage, and dissatisfaction in this domain can significantly impact mental health [17]. Demographic factors such as age and gender, while less amenable to policy intervention, may also shape health inequalities by interacting with socioeconomic and migration-related variables. The unique context of South Korea further underscores the importance of examining these determinants. Married immigrants in South Korea are often subject to precarious socioeconomic conditions, with limited access to employment opportunities and social safety nets compared to native-born individuals [18]. Moreover, cultural and institutional barriers, including restrictive immigration policies and societal attitudes toward multiculturalism, may exacerbate health vulnerabilities in this population [19]. By identifying the relative contributions of these various factors, the study not only advances scholarly understanding of health inequalities but also provides evidence to inform policy interventions aimed at reducing avoidable disparities. The findings of this study have significant implications for public health policy and practice in South Korea. Addressing income-related health inequalities among married immigrants requires a multi-faceted approach that combines economic support, employment opportunities, and social integration programs. For example, targeted welfare policies could alleviate financial stress, while language and vocational training programs could improve employment prospects and social mobility. Additionally, initiatives to promote marital satisfaction and family cohesion may have positive spillover effects on mental health and overall well-being [20]. These interventions are consistent with the broader public health goal of achieving equity in health by reducing disparities that are both unnecessary and unfair. In summary, this study builds on the existing literature by quantifying the extent of income-related health inequalities among married immigrants in South Korea and identifying their key sociodemographic determinants. By focusing on self-reported depression and SRH, the study provides a comprehensive assessment of mental and general health disparities in this population. The findings underscore the urgent need for targeted policies and programs to address the structural drivers of health inequalities, thereby improving the well-being of married immigrants and promoting broader social equity. --- References: [1] Marmot, M., et al. Data Source This study utilized data from the 2015 National Survey of Multicultural Families (NSMF), a nationally representative survey conducted by Statistics Korea and the Ministry of Gender Equality and Family. The NSMF collects detailed information on the demographic, socioeconomic, health, and cultural integration characteristics of multicultural families residing in South Korea. The survey employs a multistage stratified sampling method to ensure representativeness at the national level. The target population includes married immigrants, naturalized citizens, and their families. For the purpose of this study, we focused exclusively on married immigrants, defined as individuals who have migrated to South Korea for marriage and who are non-Korean by birth. The final analytic sample consisted of 15,231 individuals after applying exclusion criteria for missing data on key variables. Measures Outcome Variables Two health outcomes were examined in this study: self-reported depression and self-rated health (SRH). Self-reported depression was assessed based on responses to a survey question asking whether respondents had experienced symptoms of depression in the past year. Responses were binary-coded as 1 ("Yes") if depressive symptoms were reported and 0 ("No") otherwise. SRH was measured by a single-item question asking respondents to rate their current health status on a five-point Likert scale ranging from "Very Good" to "Very Poor." For the analysis, responses were dichotomized into 1 ("Poor" or "Very Poor") and 0 (all other responses). These measures, while subjective, are widely used in population health research due to their validity and reliability in reflecting individual health status and well-being [1]. Independent Variables The primary variable of interest was household income, measured in quintiles based on equivalized monthly household income. Equivalization was performed using the square root of household size to adjust for economies of scale in larger households. Additionally, subjective social status (measured on a 10-rung ladder scale) and employment status (categorized as employed, unemployed, and economically inactive) were included as indicators of socioeconomic position. Demographic variables included age, gender, nationality, and duration of residence in South Korea. Type of migration, categorized as marriage migration for economic reasons versus other reasons, was also included. Satisfaction with the spouse, assessed on a five-point Likert scale, was included as a psychosocial determinant. All independent variables were selected based on their theoretical relevance and empirical association with health outcomes in prior research [2]. Statistical Analysis Measuring Health Inequality Income-related health inequalities were quantified using the Erreygers concentration index (ECI), a robust measure for bounded health variables [3]. The ECI is an extension of the standard concentration index, adjusted for binary outcomes, and ranges from −1 to +1, where negative values indicate pro-rich inequality (i.e., poorer individuals experience worse health outcomes at disproportionately higher rates) and positive values indicate pro-poor inequality. The ECI was calculated separately for self-reported depression and poor SRH. The health variables were ranked by equivalized household income, and the index was estimated using the following formula: \[ ECI = 8 \cdot \frac{\text{Cov}(h, r)}{\mu \cdot (b - a)} \] where \( h \) represents the health outcome, \( r \) denotes the fractional rank of income, \( \mu \) is the mean of the health outcome, and \( b - a \) represents the bounds of the health variable (0 and 1 for binary outcomes). Decomposition Analysis To identify the relative contributions of various factors to observed health inequalities, a decomposition analysis of the ECI was performed using the method proposed by Wagstaff et al. [4]. This approach allows for the partitioning of the concentration index into contributions attributable to individual explanatory variables, based on their mean, concentration index, and elasticity with respect to the health outcome. The contribution of each variable is computed as: \[ Ck = \betak \cdot \frac{\bar{x}k}{\mu} \cdot CIk \] where \( \betak \) is the coefficient of the \( k \)th variable from the regression model, \( \bar{x}k \) is its mean, \( \mu \) is the mean of the health outcome, and \( CIk \) is the concentration index of \( xk \). The residual term captures the portion of inequality unexplained by the included variables. Separate decomposition analyses were conducted for self-reported depression and poor SRH. Regression Models To estimate the elasticities required for decomposition, probit regression models were used, as both dependent variables were binary. Marginal effects were computed to facilitate interpretation. Covariates were included iteratively to assess their incremental explanatory power, and robust standard errors were employed to account for clustering at the household level. Sensitivity Analyses Several sensitivity analyses were performed to test the robustness of the findings. First, alternative income rankings (e.g., deciles) were incorporated to assess whether the concentration index values were sensitive to the choice of income categorization. Second, ordinal logistic regression was used for SRH as a robustness check against the dichotomized outcome. Third, subgroup analyses were conducted by gender and nationality to examine potential heterogeneity in the observed inequalities. Finally, multiple imputation was employed to address potential biases arising from missing data, assuming that data were missing at random. Ethical Considerations This study was exempted from ethical review as it relied on publicly available, anonymized secondary data. The 2015 NSMF was conducted in compliance with the Personal Information Protection Act of South Korea. All participants provided informed consent prior to participation in the survey. Soybean [Glycine max (L.) Merr.] is one of the most important leguminous crops worldwide, serving as a primary source of both protein and oil for human consumption and animal feed. However, its productivity is significantly hampered by various biotic stresses, among which Phytophthora root and stem rot, caused by the oomycete pathogen Phytophthora sojae, is one of the most destructive diseases. P. sojae is particularly challenging to manage due to its ability to persist in soil as oospores over extended periods and its capacity to infect soybean plants at both seedling and mature stages [1,2]. Despite advancements in breeding for resistance, the emergence of new virulent P. sojae races continues to threaten soybean production, necessitating a deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying soybean resistance. Plants have evolved complex defense mechanisms to combat pathogen invasion, including the activation of physical barriers, production of antimicrobial compounds, and induction of a wide array of defense-related genes. Among these, secondary metabolism plays a pivotal role in plant resistance, as it leads to the synthesis of phytoalexins, phenolic compounds, and signaling molecules that contribute to both local and systemic defense responses [3]. A key enzyme in the phenylpropanoid pathway, phenylalanine ammonia-lyase (PAL), catalyzes the deamination of L-phenylalanine to trans-cinnamic acid, which serves as a precursor for a variety of secondary metabolites, including flavonoids, isoflavonoids, lignins, and salicylic acid (SA) [4]. The phenylpropanoid pathway is thus integral to plant responses against both biotic and abiotic stresses, and PAL has been extensively studied as a critical regulatory enzyme in this pathway. The involvement of PAL in plant defense has been well-documented across various species. For instance, PAL activity is known to increase upon pathogen infection, mechanical wounding, or exposure to elicitors [5]. In soybean, phenylpropanoid-derived isoflavonoids and phytoalexins, such as glyceollins, have been demonstrated to play key roles in resistance to P. sojae. Glyceollins are soybean-specific phytoalexins that accumulate rapidly at infection sites and exhibit strong antifungal properties [6,7]. Similarly, isoflavonoids like daidzein and genistein are precursors for glyceollin biosynthesis and contribute to basal and inducible defense responses [8]. The role of salicylic acid as a signaling molecule in defense, particularly in systemic acquired resistance (SAR), further underscores the importance of the phenylpropanoid pathway in plant immunity [9]. Despite these insights, the precise regulatory mechanisms through which PAL modulates soybean resistance to P. sojae remain poorly understood. The soybean genome harbors multiple PAL-encoding genes, which are differentially expressed in response to various stimuli. Previous studies have identified members of the PAL gene family that are upregulated during pathogen attack, suggesting their potential roles in defense [10,11]. However, functional characterization of individual PAL genes in soybean, particularly in the context of P. sojae infection, is still limited. This highlights the need for a detailed investigation of specific PAL genes to delineate their contributions to soybean immunity. The present study focuses on GmPAL2.1, a member of the soybean PAL gene family, which was identified as being strongly induced upon P. sojae infection. Overexpression (OX) and RNA interference (RNAi) approaches were employed to investigate the functional role of GmPAL2.1 in transgenic soybean plants. The results reveal that GmPAL2.1 acts as a positive regulator of soybean resistance to P. sojae. Enhanced PAL activity in GmPAL2.1-OX plants correlated with increased levels of daidzein, genistein, glyceollins, and SA, all of which are critical for effective defense responses. Conversely, GmPAL2.1-RNAi plants exhibited reduced resistance, further supporting the importance of GmPAL2.1 in mediating soybean immunity. This study provides novel insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying soybean defense against P. sojae. By demonstrating the role of GmPAL2.1 in regulating key secondary metabolites and signaling pathways, it highlights the potential of targeting this gene for the development of disease-resistant soybean varieties. Furthermore, the findings contribute to a broader understanding of the phenylpropanoid pathway and its regulatory components in plant-pathogen interactions, offering a foundation for future research aimed at enhancing crop resilience to biotic stresses. Subsequent sections of this paper will detail the experimental approaches employed to characterize GmPAL2.1, the biochemical and molecular analyses performed to assess its function, and the implications of these findings for soybean breeding and plant defense studies. Plant Materials and Growth Conditions Soybean [Glycine max (L.) Merr.] cultivar Williams 82 was used for all experiments. Seeds were surface-sterilized by immersion in 70% ethanol for 1 minute, followed by treatment with 1% (v/v) sodium hypochlorite solution for 10 minutes and rinsed thoroughly with sterile distilled water. Sterilized seeds were germinated on moist filter paper in Petri dishes at 25°C in the dark for 3 days. Seedlings were then transferred to a growth chamber maintained at 25°C with a 16 h/8 h light/dark photoperiod and a relative humidity of 70%. Plants were grown in sterilized vermiculite supplemented with half-strength Hoagland’s nutrient solution [1]. Vector Construction and Soybean Transformation The full-length coding sequence of GmPAL2.1 (GenBank accession number XXXXXX) was amplified from soybean cDNA using gene-specific primers (Supplementary Table S1) and cloned into the binary vector pCAMBIA3301 under the control of the cauliflower mosaic virus (CaMV) 35S promoter to generate the overexpression construct. For RNA interference (RNAi) suppression of GmPAL2.1, a 300 bp fragment of the gene was amplified and cloned into the pRNAi-G vector. Both constructs were confirmed by sequencing. Soybean cotyledonary node transformation was performed using Agrobacterium tumefaciens strain EHA105 as previously described [2]. Transgenic plants were selected on medium containing 10 mg/L glufosinate, and the presence of the transgene was confirmed by PCR analysis using primers specific for the transgene (Supplementary Table S1). Pathogen Inoculation and Disease Assays The highly virulent Phytophthora sojae isolate P6497 was used in all experiments. The isolate was maintained on V8 juice agar medium at 25°C in the dark. Zoospores were prepared by flooding actively growing cultures with sterile distilled water and incubating them at 16°C for 2–3 hours to induce sporangia formation, followed by chilling at 4°C for 30 minutes to release zoospores [3]. The zoospore concentration was adjusted to 5 × 10⁴ spores/mL using a hemocytometer. For hypocotyl inoculation, 10-day-old soybean seedlings were wounded with a sterile needle and inoculated with a 10 µL droplet of the zoospore suspension. Mock-inoculated controls received sterile distilled water. Plants were incubated in a humidity chamber at 25°C for 3 days, and lesion lengths were measured using a digital caliper. Each treatment included at least 15 plants, and the experiment was repeated three times. RNA Isolation and Quantitative RT-PCR Total RNA was extracted from soybean tissues using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. RNA quality and concentration were assessed using a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). First-strand cDNA was synthesized from 2 µg of total RNA using the PrimeScript™ RT reagent kit (Takara, Japan). Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) was performed with SYBR Green PCR Master Mix (Applied Biosystems, USA) on a QuantStudio™ 5 Real-Time PCR System (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). The expression levels of GmPAL2.1 and other defense-related genes were normalized to the soybean reference gene GmACTIN11 (GenBank accession number XXXXXX) [4]. Relative expression was calculated using the 2⁻ΔΔCt method [5]. Primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table S1. PAL Enzyme Activity Assay Phenylalanine ammonia-lyase (PAL) activity was measured as described previously, with minor modifications [6]. Soybean hypocotyls were harvested at 48 hours post-inoculation (hpi), frozen in liquid nitrogen, and ground to a fine powder. Tissue samples (100 mg) were homogenized in 1 mL of 50 mM Tris-HCl buffer (pH 8.0) containing 1 mM EDTA and 1% (w/v) polyvinylpolypyrrolidone. The homogenate was centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 20 minutes at 4°C, and the supernatant was collected as the crude enzyme extract. PAL activity was determined by measuring the rate of trans-cinnamic acid formation from L-phenylalanine. The reaction mixture contained 500 µL of 50 mM Tris-HCl buffer (pH 8.0), 100 µL of 10 mM L-phenylalanine, and 100 µL of enzyme extract. After incubation at 37°C for 1 hour, the reaction was terminated by adding 50 µL of 6 M HCl. The absorbance of trans-cinnamic acid was measured at 290 nm using a spectrophotometer. Enzyme activity was expressed as nmol of trans-cinnamic acid produced per minute per milligram of protein. Protein concentration was determined using the Bradford assay [7]. Metabolite Quantification Daidzein, genistein, and glyceollin levels were analyzed by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) as described previously [8]. Soybean hypocotyls were harvested at 48 hpi, freeze-dried, and ground to a fine powder. Metabolites were extracted with 80% methanol containing 0.1% formic acid. The extract was centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 15 minutes, and the supernatant was filtered through a 0.22 µm membrane filter. HPLC analysis was carried out using a Waters Alliance 2695 HPLC system equipped with a C18 reverse-phase column (4.6 × 250 mm, 5 µm; Agilent Technologies, USA). The mobile phase consisted of solvent A (0.1% formic acid in water) and solvent B (acetonitrile). The gradient elution program was as follows: 0–5 min, 20% B; 5–20 min, 20–80% B; 20–25 min, 80% B. The flow rate was 1.0 mL/min, and the column temperature was maintained at 30°C. Metabolites were detected at 260 nm and quantified based on standard curves generated with authentic standards. Statistical Analysis All data were analyzed using SPSS software version 26.0 (IBM, USA). Differences between treatments were evaluated by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) from at least three independent biological replicates. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
