Brain tumors represent one of the most complex and challenging malignancies to treat, largely due to their unique anatomical location, cellular heterogeneity, and interactions with the surrounding microenvironment. Among these neoplasms, gliomas, meningiomas, and medulloblastomas are of particular interest due to their prevalence and clinical significance. Despite advances in surgical techniques, radiation therapy, and chemotherapeutic regimens, the prognosis for many brain tumor patients remains poor, especially for glioblastoma, which is the most aggressive subtype of gliomas [1,2]. Consequently, there is an urgent need to better understand the mechanisms underlying brain tumor growth and progression, as well as to identify novel therapeutic targets. In this regard, the tumor microenvironment (TME) has emerged as a critical area of study, with tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) occupying a central role. Macrophages are key components of the innate immune system and are widely recognized for their dual functionality in tumor biology. They exhibit remarkable plasticity, with the ability to polarize into different functional states depending on environmental cues. The classical M1 phenotype is pro-inflammatory and tumoricidal, while the alternatively activated M2 phenotype is anti-inflammatory and promotes tissue remodeling, angiogenesis, and tumor progression [3]. In the context of brain tumors, TAMs are known to predominantly adopt an M2-like phenotype, supporting tumor growth, immune evasion, and metastasis [4]. This polarization is largely driven by the tumor cells themselves, which secrete a variety of cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors that modulate TAM behavior. For example, glioblastoma cells produce colony-stimulating factor 1 (CSF-1) and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β), both of which are potent inducers of M2 polarization [5]. Similarly, hypoxic conditions within the tumor core further enhance the recruitment and M2 polarization of macrophages through hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs) [6]. The interplay between TAMs and tumor cells is not limited to polarization dynamics but extends to several critical aspects of tumor biology. One of the most well-documented roles of TAMs in brain tumors is their contribution to neoangiogenesis. Angiogenesis, the formation of new blood vessels, is essential for tumor growth as it provides the necessary oxygen and nutrients to the rapidly proliferating cancer cells. TAMs secrete pro-angiogenic factors such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), which facilitate the remodeling of the extracellular matrix and the recruitment of endothelial cells [7]. In gliomas, VEGF expression is tightly regulated by hypoxia, creating a positive feedback loop between hypoxic tumor cells and TAMs [8]. This close association between TAMs and angiogenesis underscores their importance as potential therapeutic targets. In addition to supporting angiogenesis, TAMs play a pivotal role in immune modulation within the TME. Brain tumors are notorious for their ability to evade immune surveillance, and TAMs contribute significantly to this process. By producing immunosuppressive cytokines such as interleukin-10 (IL-10) and TGF-β, TAMs inhibit the activation and function of cytotoxic T cells and natural killer (NK) cells, which are critical mediators of anti-tumor immunity [9]. Furthermore, TAMs express immune checkpoint ligands such as programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), which interact with programmed death-1 (PD-1) receptors on T cells to suppress their activity [10]. This immunosuppressive microenvironment not only facilitates tumor progression but also presents a significant obstacle to the success of immunotherapy in brain tumors. Another intriguing aspect of TAM involvement in brain tumors is their potential role in metastasis. Although brain tumors, particularly primary ones such as gliomas and meningiomas, rarely metastasize outside the central nervous system (CNS), the mechanisms underlying this phenomenon remain poorly understood. Recent evidence suggests that TAMs may contribute to the dissemination of tumor cells by promoting the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), a process that enhances the migratory and invasive properties of cancer cells [11]. Additionally, TAMs secrete chemokines such as C-C motif chemokine ligand 2 (CCL2) and CCL5, which facilitate the recruitment of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) to distant sites [12]. While these mechanisms are well-documented in peripheral tumors, their relevance to brain tumors warrants further investigation. Given the multifaceted roles of TAMs in brain tumor biology, targeting these cells represents a promising therapeutic strategy. Several approaches have been explored, including the inhibition of macrophage recruitment to the TME, reprogramming TAMs from an M2-like to an M1-like phenotype, and blocking the pro-tumorigenic factors produced by TAMs [13]. For instance, CSF-1 receptor (CSF-1R) inhibitors have shown preclinical efficacy in reducing TAM infiltration and tumor growth in glioblastoma models [14]. Similarly, therapeutic agents that block VEGF signaling or disrupt hypoxia-induced pathways have demonstrated potential in inhibiting TAM-mediated angiogenesis [15]. However, these strategies face significant challenges, including the heterogeneity of TAM populations and the potential for off-target effects. In conclusion, the role of macrophages in brain tumor growth and progression is a dynamic and complex field of study that holds significant implications for both basic and translational research. By elucidating the mechanisms by which TAMs interact with tumor cells and the broader TME, we can gain valuable insights into the pathophysiology of brain tumors and identify novel therapeutic opportunities. Future studies should focus on characterizing the heterogeneity of TAM populations, understanding the molecular drivers of macrophage polarization, and exploring the potential of TAM-targeted therapies in combination with existing treatment modalities. Such efforts will be critical in advancing our ability to combat these devastating malignancies and improve outcomes for patients with brain tumors. To investigate the role of macrophages in the growth and progression of brain tumors, such as gliomas, meningiomas, and medulloblastomas, a combination of in vitro and in vivo experiments, along with bioinformatic analyses, was employed. This study was approved by the institutional ethics committee, and all experiments adhered to the guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals and human-derived samples. Macrophage Isolation and Polarization Assays Primary macrophages were obtained from human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) collected from healthy volunteers after informed consent. PBMCs were isolated using density gradient centrifugation with Ficoll-Paque Plus (GE Healthcare). Monocytes were separated by adherence to tissue culture plates and cultured in RPMI-1640 medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 1% penicillin-streptomycin, and 1% L-glutamine. Macrophage differentiation was induced by treating monocytes with macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF, 50 ng/mL) for seven days. Polarization of macrophages was achieved by exposing M0 macrophages to either lipopolysaccharide (LPS, 100 ng/mL) and interferon-gamma (IFN-γ, 20 ng/mL) for M1 polarization, or interleukin-4 (IL-4, 20 ng/mL) and interleukin-13 (IL-13, 20 ng/mL) for M2 polarization [1]. The polarization states were confirmed through the expression of marker genes by quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) and flow cytometry. Markers such as CD86 and inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) were used for M1 macrophages, while CD206 and arginase-1 (Arg1) were utilized for M2 macrophages. Brain Tumor Cell Culture and Co-Culture Assays Human glioblastoma (U87 and LN229), medulloblastoma (DAOY), and meningioma (Ben-Men-1) cell lines were obtained from authenticated cell repositories. Cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) or RPMI-1640 supplemented with 10% FBS and antibiotics (1% penicillin-streptomycin) at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO2. For co-culture experiments, tumor cells were seeded in transwell chambers (pore size 0.4 µm) above macrophages to allow paracrine signaling without direct cell-cell contact. Co-cultures were maintained for 72 hours, after which macrophages were harvested for analysis of polarization markers, cytokine secretion, and signaling pathway activation. Hypoxia Induction To simulate the hypoxic tumor microenvironment, macrophages and tumor cells were cultured in a hypoxia chamber set at 1% oxygen for 24–48 hours. Hypoxia-inducible factor-1 alpha (HIF-1α) expression was assessed in both macrophages and tumor cells by Western blotting and immunofluorescence. The impact of hypoxia on macrophage polarization and pro-tumoral activity was evaluated through cytokine profiling and angiogenesis assays. Cytokine Profiling The supernatants from mono- and co-culture systems were collected and analyzed for cytokine secretion using a multiplex bead-based assay (Bio-Plex Pro Human Cytokine Panel, Bio-Rad). Key cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-10 (IL-10), vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β), were quantified. Data were analyzed to determine the influence of tumor cells on macrophage cytokine production and the subsequent effects on the tumor microenvironment. Neoangiogenesis Assay The role of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) in angiogenesis was assessed using a tube formation assay. Human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) were seeded on Matrigel-coated plates and treated with conditioned media derived from polarized macrophages, tumor cells, or their co-cultures. Images of tube-like structures were acquired after 6–8 hours of incubation, and quantitative analysis of total tube length and branch points was performed using ImageJ software with the Angiogenesis Analyzer plugin. Animal Studies To evaluate the role of TAMs in vivo, an orthotopic glioblastoma mouse model was established. U87 cells (5 × 10^5 cells in 5 µL of phosphate-buffered saline) were stereotactically injected into the right striatum of six- to eight-week-old immunodeficient NOD/SCID mice (n=10 per group). Mice were randomized into groups receiving either clodronate liposomes to deplete macrophages or control liposomes. Tumor growth was monitored using bioluminescence imaging, and mice were sacrificed at pre-determined endpoints for immunohistochemical analysis of TAM infiltration (Iba1 staining) and polarization (CD86 and CD206 co-staining). Circulating tumor cells were isolated from blood samples using a microfluidic device and enumerated by flow cytometry. Transcriptomic and Bioinformatic Analyses For comprehensive characterization of macrophage-tumor interactions, RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) was performed on macrophages isolated from co-culture systems and tumor tissues. Libraries were prepared using the NEBNext Ultra II RNA Library Prep Kit (New England Biolabs) and sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform. Differential gene expression analysis was conducted using DESeq2, and pathway enrichment was assessed using the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database. Single-cell RNA-seq data from public repositories were also analyzed to validate findings and identify macrophage subpopulations within human brain tumors. Statistical Analysis All experiments were performed in triplicate or with appropriate biological replicates. Data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Statistical significance was determined using Student’s t-test for two-group comparisons or one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test for multiple comparisons. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. GraphPad Prism 9.0 software was used for all statistical analyses and graph generation. [1] Sica, A., & Mantovani, A. (2012). Macrophage plasticity and polarization: in vivo veritas. Journal of Clinical Investigation, 122(3), 787-795. In this study, we investigated the role of macrophages in the growth and progression of brain tumors, focusing on gliomas, meningiomas, and medulloblastomas. Our findings demonstrate that macrophage polarization plays a pivotal role in shaping the tumor microenvironment and influencing tumor biology. A systematic analysis of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) revealed their contribution to key processes such as tumor proliferation, neoangiogenesis, immune modulation, and the potential for metastatic dissemination. Our data indicate that brain tumor cells actively regulate the polarization state of macrophages, promoting a shift toward the M2-like phenotype. This phenotype is associated with pro-tumoral activities, such as immunosuppression and tissue remodeling. Immunohistochemical analysis of glioma and meningioma specimens revealed a predominance of CD163+ and CD206+ macrophages, markers associated with the M2 phenotype, in tumor tissues compared to adjacent normal brain parenchyma (p < 0.01). In contrast, M1-polarized macrophages, characterized by CD86 and inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) expression, were relatively sparse in tumor regions. This M2 polarization was found to be enhanced by tumor-derived cytokines such as IL-10 and TGF-β, which were significantly elevated in the tumor microenvironment (p < 0.001) [1, 2]. In gliomas, we observed that TAMs contribute to tumor progression by enhancing neoangiogenesis. Using immunofluorescence staining for CD31 and VEGF in glioblastoma samples, we found that regions with high TAM infiltration had a significantly increased density of microvessels (p < 0.05). Furthermore, ex vivo co-culture experiments of glioma cells with macrophages demonstrated that tumor-derived hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF-1α) promoted the upregulation of VEGF in macrophages, suggesting a synergistic interaction between hypoxia and TAMs in promoting angiogenesis [3]. These findings were corroborated by RNA sequencing of isolated TAMs, which revealed upregulation of pro-angiogenic genes, including angiopoietin-2 and matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9), in glioma-associated macrophages compared to macrophages isolated from non-tumor brain tissue. In medulloblastomas, TAMs were found to play an immunosuppressive role by modulating T-cell responses. Flow cytometry analysis of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes demonstrated a reduction in CD8+ T-cell activity in regions with high TAM density.

Ulcerative colitis (UC), a predominant form of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), is characterized by chronic inflammation of the colonic mucosa, leading to significant morbidity and reduced quality of life. The pathophysiology of UC involves complex interactions among genetic, environmental, microbial, and immune factors, ultimately resulting in the disruption of intestinal homeostasis [1,2]. A hallmark of UC is the excessive infiltration of immune cells, particularly neutrophils, into the intestinal mucosa, which exacerbates tissue damage and perpetuates the inflammatory cycle [3]. Neutrophil transmigration across the intestinal epithelium is facilitated by pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, leading to increased epithelial damage and the release of further inflammatory mediators [4]. Although significant progress has been made in identifying molecular mechanisms underlying UC, therapeutic options remain limited and are often associated with adverse effects or incomplete disease remission [5]. Thus, there is a critical need to identify novel molecular targets that modulate inflammation and neutrophil recruitment to develop more effective and targeted therapies. Syndecan-1 (SDC1) is a transmembrane heparan sulfate proteoglycan expressed on the surface of various epithelial cells, including those of the gastrointestinal tract. Through its heparan sulfate (HS) chains, SDC1 interacts with a wide range of extracellular molecules, including growth factors, cytokines, and chemokines, thereby playing a key role in cellular signaling, adhesion, and tissue repair [6,7]. Notably, SDC1 is involved in the regulation of inflammatory processes, as it modulates cytokine gradients, immune cell recruitment, and extracellular matrix remodeling [8]. A distinctive feature of SDC1 is its ability to undergo ectodomain shedding, a process in which the extracellular domain is cleaved from the cell surface by proteases such as matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) [9]. The shed ectodomain, which retains its HS chains, acts as a soluble effector, mediating many of SDC1's biological functions in inflammation and tissue repair [10]. While the role of shed SDC1 in mediating inflammation has been well-documented, the specific contribution of membrane-anchored SDC1 to the regulation of inflammatory responses remains less understood. Recent studies have implicated SDC1 shedding in the pathogenesis of various inflammatory diseases, including IBD. Elevated levels of soluble SDC1 have been detected in the serum of patients with UC, correlating with increased disease activity and inflammation [11]. This observation suggests that SDC1 shedding may exacerbate intestinal inflammation by disrupting the homeostatic functions of membrane-anchored SDC1. Furthermore, the release of the shed ectodomain may amplify pro-inflammatory signaling cascades by interacting with cytokines and chemokines in the extracellular milieu [12,13]. However, the precise mechanisms by which suppression of SDC1 shedding modulates inflammatory pathways and neutrophil transmigration in the context of UC remain to be fully elucidated. The nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) pathway is a central regulator of inflammation and immune responses. Aberrant activation of NF-κB has been implicated in the pathogenesis of UC, where it drives the transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), IL-6, and IL-8 [14]. These cytokines, in turn, promote neutrophil recruitment and activation, thereby amplifying the inflammatory response [15]. SDC1 has been shown to influence NF-κB signaling, although the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Membrane-anchored SDC1 may attenuate NF-κB activation by sequestering pro-inflammatory mediators through its HS chains, thereby preventing their interaction with cellular receptors [16]. Alternatively, SDC1 may directly modulate intracellular signaling pathways linked to NF-κB activation. Understanding the interplay between SDC1 shedding and NF-κB signaling is critical for developing therapeutic strategies aimed at mitigating intestinal inflammation in UC. Neutrophil transmigration across the intestinal epithelium is a key pathological feature of UC. This process is regulated by chemokines such as CXCL1, which bind to the CXCR2 receptor on neutrophils, directing their migration to sites of inflammation [17]. Elevated levels of CXCL1 have been detected in the colonic mucosa of UC patients, correlating with increased neutrophil infiltration and disease severity [18]. Evidence suggests that SDC1 may influence neutrophil transmigration by modulating chemokine gradients through its HS chains. Specifically, membrane-anchored SDC1 may act as a sink for CXCL1, thereby reducing its availability for receptor-mediated signaling and limiting neutrophil recruitment [19]. The suppression of SDC1 shedding could further enhance this protective effect by maintaining the integrity of the cell surface-bound proteoglycan and its capacity to sequester chemokines. In light of these observations, our study aimed to investigate the role of membrane-anchored SDC1 in the regulation of intestinal inflammation and neutrophil transmigration in UC. We hypothesized that suppression of SDC1 shedding would attenuate inflammatory responses by modulating key signaling pathways and reducing the secretion of pro-inflammatory mediators. To test this hypothesis, we employed a cleavable-resistant SDC1 mutant plasmid to establish models in which SDC1 shedding was inhibited during inflammatory stimulation. Using these models, we examined the effects of membrane-anchored SDC1 on NF-κB activation, pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion, and neutrophil transmigration in vitro and in vivo. Furthermore, we evaluated the therapeutic potential of SDC1 shedding suppression in ameliorating colitis activity and histological disturbances in a mouse model of UC. Our findings provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying SDC1's protective effects in UC and highlight its potential as a therapeutic target for intestinal inflammation. By addressing the interplay between SDC1 shedding, NF-κB activation, and neutrophil recruitment, this study seeks to advance our understanding of the complex mechanisms driving UC pathogenesis. Moreover, the identification of novel strategies to harness the anti-inflammatory functions of membrane-anchored SDC1 may pave the way for the development of more effective and targeted therapies for UC and other inflammatory disorders. Study Design and Experimental Models Cell Cultures and Plasmid Transfection Human intestinal epithelial cells (Caco-2) were cultured in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM; Gibco, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Sigma-Aldrich, USA), 1% penicillin-streptomycin (Gibco, USA), and 2 mM L-glutamine. Cells were maintained at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO₂. To investigate the function of membrane-anchored syndecan-1 (SDC1), we generated a cleavable-resistant SDC1 mutant by site-directed mutagenesis using the QuikChange Kit (Agilent Technologies, USA). The plasmid encoding the SDC1 mutant was transfected into Caco-2 cells using Lipofectamine 3000 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), following the manufacturer’s protocol. Cells transfected with an empty vector were used as controls. Stable transfectants were selected using 1 µg/mL puromycin (InvivoGen, USA) over a period of 14 days. Induction of Inflammatory Response In Vitro To simulate intestinal inflammation, Caco-2 cells were stimulated with 1 µg/mL lipopolysaccharide (LPS; Sigma-Aldrich, USA) for 6 hours. The impact of SDC1 shedding was studied by treating cells with 10 nM phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA; Sigma-Aldrich, USA), a known inducer of ectodomain shedding. The cleavable-resistant SDC1 mutant was used to block shedding during LPS stimulation. Control cells were treated with vehicle (dimethyl sulfoxide, DMSO; Sigma-Aldrich, USA). Animal Models of Colitis Eight-week-old male C57BL/6 mice were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory (USA) and housed in pathogen-free conditions. Experimental colitis was induced using 3% (w/v) dextran sulfate sodium (DSS; molecular weight 40 kDa; MP Biomedicals, USA) dissolved in drinking water for 7 days. Mice were randomly divided into three groups: (1) DSS-only group, (2) DSS + SDC1 mutant plasmid group (delivered via adenoviral vector), and (3) healthy control group. For plasmid delivery, 10⁸ plaque-forming units (PFU) of adenoviral vectors encoding the SDC1 mutant were administered via rectal enema on days 1, 3, and 5 of the DSS treatment protocol. Control mice received adenoviral vectors encoding an empty vector. All animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at [Institution Name]. --- Molecular and Cellular Assays Syndecan-1 Shedding Assay The shedding of SDC1 from the cell surface was assessed by quantifying soluble SDC1 levels in culture supernatants using ELISA (R&D Systems, USA). Total cellular SDC1 expression was analyzed by Western blotting. Proteins from whole-cell lysates were separated on 10% SDS-PAGE gels and transferred onto PVDF membranes (Millipore, USA). Membranes were incubated with anti-SDC1 antibodies (1:1000; Cell Signaling Technology, USA) followed by horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibodies. Bands were visualized using enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL; Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) and quantified using ImageJ software (NIH, USA). NF-κB Activation Assay To examine NF-κB pathway activation, nuclear extracts were prepared from Caco-2 cells using the NE-PER Nuclear and Cytoplasmic Extraction Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). NF-κB p65 levels were quantified using an NF-κB Transcription Factor Assay Kit (Abcam, USA). Phosphorylated and total p65 protein levels were also assessed by Western blotting using specific antibodies (1:1000; Cell Signaling Technology, USA). GAPDH and histone H3 were used as cytoplasmic and nuclear loading controls, respectively. Cytokine Secretion Analysis Pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion, including TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8, was measured in cell culture supernatants and mouse serum samples using multiplex cytokine assays (Bio-Plex Pro Cytokine Assay; Bio-Rad, USA). CXCL1 levels, indicative of neutrophil chemoattraction, were quantified using a specific ELISA kit (R&D Systems, USA). Neutrophil Transmigration Assay Transwell migration assays were conducted to evaluate neutrophil transmigration. Caco-2 cells were seeded onto the apical side of 24-well Transwell inserts (pore size 3 µm; Corning, USA) and allowed to form a confluent monolayer. Human neutrophils were isolated from peripheral blood using a Ficoll-Paque gradient (GE Healthcare, USA) and labeled with carboxyfluorescein succinimidyl ester (CFSE; Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). Labeled neutrophils (1 × 10⁶ cells/well) were added to the upper chamber, and CXCL1 (100 ng/mL) was added to the lower chamber as a chemoattractant. After 4 hours of incubation, migrated neutrophils in the lower chamber were quantified using fluorescence microscopy. --- Histological and Clinical Assessment of Colitis Colon tissues harvested from mice were fixed in 10% formalin, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned at 5 µm thickness. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining was performed, and histological scoring was conducted by a blinded pathologist based on epithelial damage, crypt destruction, and inflammatory cell infiltration. Disease activity indices (DAI) were calculated daily based on body weight loss, stool consistency, and rectal bleeding [1]. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) was performed to detect SDC1 expression and neutrophil infiltration (Ly6G marker) in colonic tissues. Paraffin-embedded sections were deparaffinized, rehydrated, and subjected to antigen retrieval using citrate buffer (pH 6.0). Sections were incubated with primary antibodies against SDC1 (1:200; Abcam, UK) and Ly6G (1:200; BioLegend, USA), followed by HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies. Staining was visualized using DAB substrate (Vector Laboratories, USA). --- Statistical Analysis Data were presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) unless otherwise specified. Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 9.0 (GraphPad Software, USA). Comparisons between groups were conducted using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test for multiple comparisons. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All experiments were performed in triplicate unless otherwise stated. Elevated SDC1 Levels and Inflammatory Markers in Ulcerative Colitis Patients Serum samples from ulcerative colitis (UC) patients exhibited significantly elevated levels of syndecan-1 (SDC1) compared to healthy controls (p < 0.01). Concomitantly, these patients demonstrated increased serum concentrations of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and interleukin-8 (IL-8). Enhanced nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) pathway activation, as evidenced by increased phosphorylation of P65 (p-P65), was observed in intestinal epithelial cells derived from UC patients. Additionally, the neutrophil count in peripheral blood was significantly higher in the UC cohort compared to controls (p < 0.01), consistent with the inflammatory state associated with active disease. Suppression of SDC1 Shedding Mitigates NF-κB Activation and Pro-inflammatory Cytokine Secretion To investigate the role of membrane-bound SDC1 in modulating intestinal inflammation, we generated a cleavable-resistant SDC1 mutant plasmid to suppress SDC1 ectodomain shedding in intestinal epithelial cells. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulation of wild-type cells resulted in marked activation of the NF-κB pathway, as shown by increased p-P65 levels (p < 0.01). This activation was accompanied by upregulated secretion of TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8 into the culture supernatant. In contrast, cells transfected with the shedding-resistant SDC1 mutant exhibited a significant reduction in p-P65 expression (p < 0.01). Furthermore, secretion of TNF-α and IL-1β was reduced by 48% and 53%, respectively, in cells expressing the mutant SDC1 compared to wild-type controls (p < 0.01). Similar trends were observed for IL-6 and IL-8, with reductions of 42% and 46%, respectively (p < 0.05). These data suggest that membrane-anchored SDC1 attenuates NF-κB pathway activation and pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion in response to LPS stimulation. Matrix factorization has long been a cornerstone of data analysis, with applications spanning collaborative filtering, image processing, bioinformatics, and more. The fundamental premise of matrix factorization is the assumption that a given data matrix can be approximated by the product of two or more low-rank matrices, thereby uncovering latent structure in the underlying data. This paradigm has been particularly influential in recommendation systems, where it is often used to predict user preferences based on partially observed data, such as ratings or interactions [1, 2]. Traditional approaches to matrix factorization, including singular value decomposition (SVD) and probabilistic matrix factorization (PMF), rely on the inner product of latent feature vectors to reconstruct the observed entries. While these techniques have proven effective in a wide variety of settings, their reliance on a fixed, linear interaction function can limit their ability to capture complex nonlinear relationships inherent in real-world data. In recent years, the introduction of deep learning to matrix factorization has sparked significant interest in the research community. Neural networks, with their capacity to approximate arbitrary functions, offer a powerful means of replacing the fixed inner product with a more flexible interaction function. This shift has the potential to greatly enhance the expressiveness of matrix factorization models. For example, in collaborative filtering tasks, user-item interactions often exhibit complex, nonlinear patterns that cannot be adequately modeled using a simple inner product. By learning these interactions directly from the data, neural network-based approaches can potentially achieve superior performance relative to traditional low-rank methods [3, 4]. Furthermore, the integration of deep learning into matrix factorization opens the door to leveraging the vast array of architectural innovations, activation functions, and regularization strategies that have emerged in the broader field of neural networks. The idea of using neural networks to enhance matrix factorization is not entirely new. Early efforts, such as Neural Collaborative Filtering (NCF) [5], introduced the concept of replacing the inner product with a multi-layer feed-forward neural network. This approach demonstrated that neural networks could effectively model user-item interactions, achieving performance gains on popular recommendation benchmarks. However, these initial methods often relied on strong assumptions, such as pretraining the latent feature vectors or constraining their dimensionality. Moreover, the potential of neural network-based matrix factorization remains underexplored due to the immense flexibility of neural architectures and the challenges of optimization in such high-dimensional and non-convex settings. While techniques such as dropout, batch normalization, and advanced optimizers like Adam have become standard in deep learning, their impact on neural network matrix factorization (NNMF) has yet to be fully understood. In this work, we revisit the idea of replacing the inner product with a learned interaction function implemented as a multi-layer neural network, which we jointly optimize alongside the latent feature vectors. By alternating between optimizing the neural network parameters for fixed latent features and updating the latent features for a fixed network, we develop a framework that we term Neural Network Matrix Factorization (NNMF). Our approach is motivated by the observation that data matrices often encode highly structured and nonlinear relationships, which cannot be adequately captured by linear models. By allowing the model to learn these relationships directly from the data, NNMF offers a more flexible and expressive alternative to traditional low-rank matrix factorization. While NNMF shows promise in capturing complex interactions, it is not without limitations. Recent advances in graph-based methods for matrix completion have shown that incorporating side information, such as user and item attributes or interaction graphs, can significantly improve performance [6, 7]. These approaches exploit the structure of the underlying graph to regularize the matrix factorization and introduce inductive biases that are particularly effective in sparse data settings. As a result, they often outperform NNMF in tasks where such additional information is available. Nevertheless, NNMF remains a compelling framework for exploring the potential of deep learning in matrix factorization, particularly in scenarios where side information is unavailable or incomplete. The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we formalize the NNMF framework, providing a systematic approach to jointly learning the latent feature vectors and the neural network parameters. Second, we evaluate NNMF on a suite of benchmark datasets, comparing its performance to traditional low-rank methods and recent graph-based approaches. Third, we discuss the broader implications of NNMF, highlighting the challenges and opportunities associated with integrating deep learning into matrix factorization. By providing a comprehensive study of NNMF, we aim to establish a foundation for future research in this area, encouraging the exploration of alternative architectures, regularization techniques, and optimization strategies. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review related work on matrix factorization and neural network-based approaches. Section 3 introduces the NNMF framework, detailing its formulation and optimization procedure. Section 4 presents our experimental results, including comparisons to state-of-the-art methods and an analysis of the impact of various design choices. Section 5 discusses the limitations of NNMF and outlines potential directions for future research. Finally, we conclude in Section 6 with a summary of our findings and a reflection on the broader implications of our work. In summary, NNMF represents a promising step toward bridging the gap between traditional matrix factorization and modern deep learning techniques. By replacing the inner product with a learned interaction function, NNMF offers a flexible and expressive framework for modeling complex data relationships. While challenges remain, particularly in optimizing the model and incorporating additional information, the potential of NNMF to advance the state of the art in matrix completion and related tasks is substantial. We believe that the insights gained from this study will inspire further exploration of neural network-based approaches to matrix factorization, unlocking new opportunities for innovation in data analysis and machine learning. In this study, we propose a novel matrix factorization approach that incorporates the flexibility of neural networks to approximate the functional dependencies between rows and columns of a matrix. Our method, Neural Network Matrix Factorization (NNMF), extends the standard low-rank matrix factorization framework by replacing the conventional inner product with a feed-forward neural network. This section provides a detailed description of the methodology, including the problem formulation, model architecture, optimization procedure, and implementation details. Problem Formulation Let \( M \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n} \) denote a matrix with observed entries \( \{M{ij}\} \), where \( (i, j) \in \Omega \) represents the set of observed indices. Our goal is to recover the unobserved entries of \( M \) by approximating it as a function of latent representations associated with its rows and columns. Specifically, we aim to learn two sets of latent feature vectors, \( \{ui \in \mathbb{R}^d \}{i=1}^m \) and \( \{vj \in \mathbb{R}^d \}{j=1}^n \), for the rows and columns, respectively, and a function \( f\theta: \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R} \) parameterized by a neural network, such that: \[ M{ij} \approx f\theta(ui, vj), \quad \forall (i, j) \in \Omega. \] Here, \( f\theta \) replaces the standard inner product \( \langle ui, vj \rangle = ui^\top vj \) used in traditional matrix factorization methods [1]. Model Architecture The neural network \( f\theta \) is implemented as a multi-layer feed-forward neural network. Given the concatenated latent feature vector \( z{ij} = [ui; vj] \), the network computes: \[ f\theta(ui, vj) = f\theta(z{ij}) = hL \circ h{L-1} \circ \dots \circ h1(z{ij}), \] where \( hl(x) = \sigmal(Wl x + bl) \) represents the computation at the \( l \)-th layer, \( Wl \) and \( bl \) are the learnable weight matrix and bias vector, respectively, and \( \sigmal \) is the activation function. The final output layer uses a linear activation function to predict the scalar value \( M{ij} \), while intermediate layers use nonlinear activation functions such as ReLU or tanh to introduce flexibility. The depth \( L \), width of the layers, and activation functions are chosen based on the dataset and validation performance. Optimization Procedure The training process alternates between optimizing the neural network parameters \( \theta \) and the latent feature vectors \( \{ui, vj\} \). This alternating approach is motivated by the observation that jointly optimizing all variables can lead to convergence difficulties and poor local minima [2]. The objective function for training is the reconstruction loss over observed entries: \[ \mathcal{L}(\theta, \{ui\}, \{vj\}) = \sum{(i, j) \in \Omega} \ell(M{ij}, f\theta(ui, vj)), \] where \( \ell(\cdot, \cdot) \) is a loss function, such as the squared loss \( \ell(a, b) = (a - b)^2 \) for continuous data or the cross-entropy loss for categorical data. The optimization procedure involves the following steps: 1. Fixing the latent features and optimizing the neural network: For fixed \( \{ui\} \) and \( \{vj\} \), the parameters \( \theta \) of \( f\theta \) are updated by minimizing \( \mathcal{L} \) using stochastic gradient descent (SGD) or its variants (e.g., Adam [3]). 2. Fixing the neural network and optimizing the latent features: With \( \theta \) fixed, the latent vectors \( \{ui\} \) and \( \{vj\} \) are updated by minimizing \( \mathcal{L} \) using SGD. Gradients with respect to \( ui \) and \( vj \) are computed via backpropagation through \( f\theta \). These steps are repeated iteratively until convergence. To prevent overfitting, we apply regularization techniques such as \( \ell2 \)-penalties on \( ui \), \( vj \), and the network weights, as well as dropout in the hidden layers of the neural network [4]. Initialization and Regularization The latent feature vectors \( \{ui\} \) and \( \{vj\} \) are initialized randomly from a Gaussian distribution with zero mean and small variance. The parameters \( \theta \) of the neural network are initialized using the Xavier or He initialization method to ensure stable gradients in deep networks [5]. Regularization is applied to mitigate overfitting and improve generalization. Specifically, we include \( \ell2 \)-regularization terms in the objective function: \[ \mathcal{L}{\text{reg}} = \mathcal{L} + \lambdau \sumi \|ui\|2^2 + \lambdav \sumj \|vj\|2^2 + \lambda\theta \|\theta\|2^2, \] where \( \lambdau \), \( \lambdav \), and \( \lambda\theta \) are hyperparameters controlling the strength of regularization. Hyperparameter Selection Hyperparameters, including the dimension of latent features \( d \), the architecture of \( f\theta \) (number of layers and neurons per layer), and regularization coefficients \( \lambdau, \lambdav, \lambda\theta \), are selected through cross-validation. A grid search or Bayesian optimization can be employed to identify the optimal hyperparameter values based on validation performance. Implementation Details The proposed method is implemented in Python using PyTorch [6]. The Adam optimizer is employed for both the neural network and the latent feature updates, with a learning rate selected through preliminary experiments. Training is performed on a GPU for computational efficiency. To ensure reproducibility, we fix random seeds for all sources of randomness. Computational Complexity The computational complexity of NNMF depends on the number of observed entries \( |\Omega| \), the dimension of the latent features \( d \), and the architecture of \( f\theta \). Evaluating \( f\theta \) for each observed entry requires \( O(d + \text{size of network}) \), and the overall complexity per iteration is \( O(|\Omega| \cdot (\text{cost of forward pass})) \). While this is higher than standard matrix factorization methods, the additional flexibility of \( f\theta \) justifies the computational cost. Summary The NNMF framework replaces the inner product in matrix factorization with a neural network, enabling the model to learn more complex relationships in the data. By alternating between optimizing the network parameters and the latent features, the method effectively balances model flexibility and computational feasibility. The use of regularization and careful hyperparameter tuning further enhances the robustness of the approach. To evaluate the performance of the proposed Neural Network Matrix Factorization (NNMF) method, we conducted a series of experiments on several widely used benchmark datasets, including MovieLens-100K, Jester, and Netflix Prize. These datasets represent diverse application domains and exhibit varying levels of sparsity and intrinsic complexity, allowing us to assess the robustness and generalizability of NNMF. In all experiments, we compared NNMF with standard matrix factorization (MF) methods, such as non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) and singular value decomposition (SVD), as well as state-of-the-art

Neurologically injured patients admitted to the neurointensive care unit (NICU) present a significant challenge to critical care teams. These patients often experience complex and multifaceted pathophysiological processes that require meticulous management strategies, particularly concerning analgesia and sedation. In the broader field of critical care, recent advancements have centered around initiatives designed to reduce the duration of intensive care unit (ICU) stays, improve patient outcomes, and minimize iatrogenic harm. One such initiative is the ABCDEF bundle, a structured approach endorsed by the Society of Critical Care Medicine to facilitate early recovery and improve long-term functional outcomes for ICU patients. The bundle emphasizes several key components: assessing, preventing, and managing pain (A); conducting both spontaneous awakening trials (SATs) and spontaneous breathing trials (SBTs) (B); optimizing the choice of analgesia and sedation (C); assessing, preventing, and managing delirium (D); encouraging early mobility and exercise (E); and promoting family engagement and empowerment (F). While the ABCDEF bundle has been widely studied and implemented in general ICU populations, its application to neurologically injured patients remains less well understood. The management of pain and sedation is at the core of the ABCDEF bundle, as these elements directly influence or interact with the other components. Effective pain management is essential for improving patient comfort, minimizing agitation, and enabling early mobilization, while appropriate sedation strategies are critical to preventing over-sedation, which can lead to prolonged mechanical ventilation, delirium, and other complications. Despite the importance of these interventions, neurologically injured patients present unique challenges that complicate their implementation. The pathophysiology of neurological injury often necessitates specific considerations in the choice and titration of analgesics and sedatives, given the potential for these agents to affect intracranial pressure (ICP), cerebral perfusion, and neurological monitoring. Furthermore, the frequent need for invasive monitoring, mechanical ventilation, and immobilization in this population can hinder adherence to other components of the ABCDEF bundle, such as early mobility and family engagement. Neurologically injured patients are also at heightened risk for complications such as delirium, seizures, and secondary brain injury, all of which complicate the management of analgesia and sedation. The interplay between sedation, neurological recovery, and the ability to perform frequent and accurate neurological assessments adds an additional layer of complexity. For example, while deep sedation may sometimes be necessary to control ICP or prevent secondary brain injury, it can delay the initiation of SATs, impair the ability to evaluate neurological function, and increase the risk of long-term cognitive and functional impairments. Similarly, the use of opioid analgesics, which are often necessary to manage pain in this population, carries the risk of respiratory depression, prolonged ventilation, and difficulty weaning from sedation. These challenges highlight the need for tailored protocols that balance the competing priorities of effective analgesia and sedation with the goals of early recovery and functional optimization. The literature on analgesia and sedation strategies in the NICU is sparse, with most existing studies focusing on general ICU populations. Neurologically injured patients are often excluded from clinical trials due to their unique physiological characteristics and the perceived difficulty of standardizing interventions in this group. Consequently, there is a significant knowledge gap regarding the optimal application of analgesia and sedation protocols in the NICU. This gap has important implications for practice, as the lack of evidence-based guidelines may contribute to variability in care and suboptimal outcomes for this vulnerable population. Addressing this gap is critical for advancing the field of neurocritical care and aligning the management of neurologically injured patients with the broader goals of ICU liberation and early recovery. In this context, a systematic review of analgesia and sedation strategies in the NICU is both timely and necessary. By synthesizing the available evidence, we aim to provide a comprehensive overview of the unique challenges associated with managing analgesia and sedation in neurologically injured patients and to identify strategies that may improve outcomes in this population. Specifically, this review will evaluate the impact of the ABCDEF bundle components on key endpoints of recovery in the NICU, including time to successful discontinuation of mechanical ventilation and time to early mobility. These endpoints were chosen because they reflect critical milestones in the recovery process and are directly influenced by analgesia and sedation practices. Additionally, we will conduct a stratified analysis of subgroups of interest, such as patients with traumatic brain injury, subarachnoid hemorrhage, or ischemic stroke, to account for the heterogeneity of the neurologically injured population and provide more targeted insights. The findings of this review have the potential to inform clinical practice and guide the development of evidence-based guidelines or position statements for the management of analgesia and sedation in the NICU. By addressing the unique needs of neurologically injured patients, we hope to bridge the existing knowledge gap and contribute to the broader effort to enhance recovery and reduce iatrogenic harm in critical care. Moreover, the results of this review may serve as a foundation for future research, highlighting areas where further investigation is needed to optimize care for this challenging patient population. In summary, neurologically injured patients represent a distinct subgroup within the critical care population, with unique challenges that complicate the implementation of standardized protocols for analgesia, sedation, and early recovery. The paucity of evidence in this area underscores the need for a systematic review to evaluate the existing literature and identify strategies that can be adapted to the NICU setting. Through this work, we aim to provide critical insights that will support knowledge translation, improve clinical practice, and ultimately enhance outcomes for neurologically injured patients. This systematic review will be conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. The study protocol has been registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO), under registration number CRD42017078909. The methods described below outline the approach for systematically identifying, selecting, appraising, and synthesizing the available literature on analgesia and sedation strategies in neurointensive care unit (NICU) patients, with a focus on the components of the ABCDEF bundle and their impact on early recovery outcomes. Eligibility Criteria Studies will be included if they meet the following criteria: 1. Population: Patients with neurological injuries who required neurocritical care and were admitted to an NICU. This includes, but is not limited to, patients with traumatic brain injury, stroke, subarachnoid hemorrhage, intracerebral hemorrhage, or post-cardiac arrest hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy. 2. Intervention: Analgesia and/or sedation protocols, including strategies aligned with one or more components of the ABCDEF bundle. Specific interventions of interest include pain management protocols, sedation strategies, spontaneous awakening trials (SATs), spontaneous breathing trials (SBTs), delirium assessment/prevention/management, and early mobility protocols. 3. Comparator: Standard care, alternative protocols, or no specific protocol for analgesia and/or sedation. 4. Outcomes: Studies that report at least one of the following outcomes will be included: time to successful discontinuation of mechanical ventilation, time to early mobility, incidence of delirium, ICU length of stay, NICU length of stay, mortality, or patient and family-reported outcomes such as quality of life. 5. Study Design: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-experimental studies, cohort studies, and case-control studies will be included. Case reports, case series, narrative reviews, and editorials will be excluded. No restrictions will be placed on publication year or language. If a non-English article is identified, translation services will be used to assess eligibility and extract data. Information Sources The search strategy will include the following databases and registries: - MEDLINE (via PubMed) - EMBASE - Cochrane Library - Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) - World Health Organization (WHO) International Clinical Trials Registry Platform - National Institutes of Health Clinical Trials Registry (ClinicalTrials.gov) Reference lists of included studies and relevant systematic reviews will be hand-searched to identify additional studies. Grey literature, including conference proceedings and relevant unpublished studies, will be sought through targeted searches of key organizations' websites and professional networks. Search Strategy A comprehensive search strategy will be developed with the assistance of an experienced medical librarian. The search will consist of a combination of Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms and free-text keywords related to "neurointensive care," "analgesia," "sedation," "ABCDEF bundle," "pain management," "delirium," "early mobility," and "mechanical ventilation." Boolean operators (e.g., AND, OR) and truncation will be used to optimize the sensitivity and specificity of the search. The search strategy will be piloted and iteratively refined to ensure comprehensiveness. Study Selection All identified records will be imported into a reference management software, and duplicates will be removed. Two independent reviewers will screen titles and abstracts for eligibility. Full-text articles of potentially relevant studies will be retrieved and assessed for inclusion using the predefined eligibility criteria. Discrepancies during the screening process will be resolved through discussion between the reviewers or by consulting a third reviewer if consensus cannot be reached. The level of agreement between reviewers will be quantified using Cohen’s kappa coefficient. Data Extraction Data will be extracted independently by two reviewers using a standardized data extraction form. The form will capture the following information: - Study characteristics (author, year, country, design, sample size) - Patient characteristics (age, sex, diagnosis, severity of illness) - Intervention details (type of analgesia or sedation protocol, specific ABCDEF bundle components) - Comparator details (standard care or alternative protocols) - Outcome measures (primary and secondary outcomes, follow-up duration) - Key findings (effect sizes, statistical significance) Discrepancies in data extraction will be resolved by discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. If required, corresponding authors of included studies will be contacted for clarification or to obtain missing data. Risk of Bias Assessment The risk of bias for included studies will be assessed independently by two reviewers using appropriate tools based on study design. For RCTs, the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool 2.0 will be used, assessing domains such as randomization, allocation concealment, blinding, and outcome reporting. For non-randomized studies, the Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tool will be employed. Disagreements in the risk of bias assessment will be resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. Data Synthesis A narrative synthesis of the findings will be conducted, structured around the components of the ABCDEF bundle and the outcomes of interest. If sufficient data are available, a meta-analysis will be performed using a random-effects model to account for heterogeneity between studies. Effect estimates for dichotomous outcomes will be reported as risk ratios (RRs) or odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), while continuous outcomes will be reported as mean differences (MDs) or standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% CIs. Heterogeneity will be assessed using the I² statistic and chi-squared test. Subgroup analyses will be conducted to explore heterogeneity based on factors such as patient population (e.g., traumatic brain injury vs. stroke), intervention type (e.g., sedation protocol vs. pain management), and study design. Sensitivity analyses will be performed to assess the robustness of findings by excluding studies with high risk of bias. Reporting Bias and Confidence in Evidence Publication bias will be assessed using funnel plots if 10 or more studies are included in a meta-analysis. The overall confidence in the evidence will be evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. Ethics and Dissemination As this study involves the synthesis of previously published data, ethical approval is not required. The findings of this systematic review will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, conference presentations, and knowledge translation activities targeting key stakeholders in neurocritical care. A systematic search of the literature yielded a total of 5,432 unique records after duplicates were removed. Following title and abstract screening, 482 articles were deemed potentially relevant for full-text review. Of these, 96 studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final review. Cyanobacteria, also known as blue-green algae, are photosynthetic microorganisms that inhabit diverse environments, from freshwater bodies to extreme conditions such as hot springs, deserts, and polar regions. These organisms have gained significant attention in recent years due to their diverse bioactive compounds, which include phytonutrients, pigments, and secondary metabolites with potential applications in food, pharmaceuticals, and other industries [1]. Among their most notable bioactivities, the antioxidant properties of cyanobacteria stand out for their ability to mitigate cellular damage caused by free radicals. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) and free radicals are implicated in oxidative stress, a condition linked to various chronic diseases such as cancer, diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, and neurodegenerative disorders [2]. Natural antioxidants, particularly those from microalgae like cyanobacteria, have been explored as alternatives to synthetic antioxidants, which may pose safety concerns and environmental risks [3]. The antioxidant potential of cyanobacteria is largely attributed to their production of phenolic compounds, flavonoids, and phycobiliproteins (PBPs). Phenolic compounds and flavonoids act as primary antioxidants by donating hydrogen atoms to neutralize ROS, thereby preventing lipid peroxidation and protein or DNA damage [4]. PBPs, including phycocyanin, phycoerythrin, and allophycocyanin, are unique water-soluble pigments found in cyanobacteria that serve as accessory light-harvesting complexes in photosynthesis. In addition to their photoprotective role, PBPs exhibit antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anticancer properties, making them valuable bioactive compounds for various applications [5]. Despite their potential, the biochemical composition and antioxidant capacity of cyanobacteria are highly species-specific, necessitating further exploration of individual species to identify those with the highest bioactive content and most potent antioxidant properties. Sri Lanka, with its tropical climate and abundant freshwater ecosystems, provides a conducive environment for the growth of diverse cyanobacterial species. However, studies on the bioactive properties of cyanobacteria isolated from Sri Lankan freshwater bodies remain limited. The current global interest in sustainable and natural sources of bioactive compounds highlights the importance of bioprospecting cyanobacteria in underexplored regions like Sri Lanka [6]. Furthermore, understanding the antioxidant properties and biochemical profiles of locally isolated cyanobacterial species can contribute to their potential utilization in health-related industries, including the development of functional foods, nutraceuticals, and therapeutic agents. This study focuses on four cyanobacterial species—Oscillatoria sp., Lyngbya sp., Microcystis sp., and Spirulina sp.—isolated from freshwater bodies in Sri Lanka. These species were chosen based on their prevalence and ecological significance in freshwater ecosystems. Oscillatoria sp. and Lyngbya sp. are filamentous cyanobacteria commonly found in eutrophic waters, where they play a role in nutrient cycling and primary production [7]. Microcystis sp., a unicellular cyanobacterium often associated with harmful algal blooms, is known for its production of microcystins, which are hepatotoxins, but it also harbors bioactive compounds with antioxidant potential [8]. Spirulina sp., a filamentous and non-toxigenic cyanobacterium, is widely recognized as a superfood due to its high nutritional value and bioactive content, particularly phycocyanin and other antioxidants [9]. By analyzing the total phenolic content (TPC), total flavonoid content (TFC), antioxidant activity, phycobiliproteins, and active compounds in these cyanobacteria, this study aims to provide a comparative assessment of their bioactive potential. The antioxidant activity of cyanobacteria is typically evaluated using in vitro assays, such as the ferric reducing antioxidant power (FRAP) assay and the 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) radical scavenging assay. The FRAP assay measures the reducing power of antioxidants by their ability to reduce ferric ions (Fe3+) to ferrous ions (Fe2+), whereas the DPPH assay quantifies the ability of antioxidants to donate electrons or hydrogen atoms to stabilize the DPPH radical, resulting in a color change [10]. These assays provide complementary insights into the antioxidant mechanisms of cyanobacteria, enabling a comprehensive evaluation of their bioactive potential. In addition, Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy is employed to identify functional groups present in cyanobacterial extracts, offering insights into their chemical composition and the structural basis of their antioxidant properties [11]. Previous research has demonstrated the potential of cyanobacteria as a sustainable source of natural antioxidants. For instance, studies on Spirulina platensis have highlighted its phycocyanin content and associated antioxidant activity, which have been linked to its anti-inflammatory and hepatoprotective effects [12]. Similarly, Oscillatoria sp. and Lyngbya sp. have been reported to produce a variety of bioactive compounds, including phenolics and flavonoids, with antioxidant and antimicrobial properties [13]. However, the specific biochemical profiles and antioxidant capacities of these cyanobacteria can vary significantly depending on environmental factors, such as light intensity, nutrient availability, and water quality, as well as extraction methods and analytical techniques [14]. Therefore, region-specific studies are essential to elucidate the bioactive potential of cyanobacteria under local environmental conditions. In the present study, we aim to address the knowledge gap regarding the antioxidant properties of cyanobacteria isolated from Sri Lankan freshwater bodies. By quantifying TPC, TFC, PBPs, and antioxidant activity (FRAP and DPPH assays) in Oscillatoria sp., Lyngbya sp., Microcystis sp., and Spirulina sp., this investigation seeks to identify species with the highest bioactive potential. The use of FTIR spectroscopy further enhances our understanding of the chemical composition of these cyanobacteria, shedding light on the functional groups responsible for their antioxidant activity. The findings of this study could pave the way for the utilization of cyanobacteria as natural antioxidants in food, pharmaceutical, and industrial applications, contributing to the growing demand for sustainable and eco-friendly bioactive sources. The study was conducted to assess the antioxidant properties, total phenolic content (TPC), total flavonoid content (TFC), phycobiliproteins (PBPs), and active compounds present in four cyanobacterial species, namely Oscillatoria sp., Lyngbya sp., Microcystis sp., and Spirulina sp., isolated from freshwater bodies of Sri Lanka. The methods employed for isolation, cultivation, and analysis are described below. Sampling and Isolation of Cyanobacteria Water samples were collected from various freshwater bodies across Sri Lanka using sterile containers. The samples were transported to the laboratory in ice-cold conditions to minimize microbial changes during transit. Cyanobacterial species were isolated using the serial dilution technique followed by streak plating on BG-11 agar medium, a standard medium for cyanobacterial cultivation [1]. Plates were incubated at 28 ± 2°C in a growth chamber under a 12:12-hour light-dark photoperiod with a light intensity of 35 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹. Colonies with distinct morphological features were selected and subcultured to obtain pure isolates. Identification of species was confirmed microscopically based on morphological characteristics such as filament structure, cell dimensions, and trichome organization [2]. Four species, Oscillatoria sp., Lyngbya sp., Microcystis sp., and Spirulina sp., were selected for further analysis. Cultivation of Cyanobacteria Pure cultures of the cyanobacterial isolates were inoculated into 500 mL Erlenmeyer flasks containing 250 mL of sterile BG-11 liquid medium. Cultures were maintained under the same incubation conditions as described above. Cyanobacterial biomass was harvested after 21 days of cultivation by centrifugation at 5,000 rpm for 15 minutes and washed thrice with distilled water to remove residual medium. The biomass was then freeze-dried and stored at −20°C for subsequent analyses. Determination of Total Phenolic Content (TPC) The total phenolic content of the cyanobacterial extracts was determined using the Folin–Ciocalteu method as described by Singleton et al. [3]. Briefly, 1 mL of cyanobacterial extract (1 mg/mL in methanol) was mixed with 5 mL of Folin–Ciocalteu reagent (diluted 1:10 with distilled water) and incubated for 5 minutes. Subsequently, 4 mL of 7.5% sodium carbonate solution was added, and the mixture was incubated at room temperature for 30 minutes in the dark. Absorbance was measured at 765 nm using a UV-Vis spectrophotometer (Shimadzu, Japan). Gallic acid was used as the standard, and TPC was expressed as mg gallic acid equivalents (GAE) per gram of dry biomass. Determination of Total Flavonoid Content (TFC) The aluminum chloride colorimetric assay was employed to estimate the total flavonoid content in the cyanobacterial extracts [4]. To 1 mL of extract (1 mg/mL in methanol), 0.3 mL of 5% sodium nitrite was added and incubated for 5 minutes. Following this, 0.3 mL of 10% aluminum chloride was added, and the mixture was incubated for an additional 6 minutes. Finally, 2 mL of 1 M sodium hydroxide was added, and the total volume was adjusted to 10 mL with distilled water. The absorbance was recorded at 510 nm. Catechin was used as the standard, and TFC was expressed as mg catechin equivalents (CE) per gram of dry biomass. Ferric Reducing Antioxidant Power (FRAP) Assay The ferric reducing antioxidant power (FRAP) assay was conducted following the method described by Benzie and Strain [5]. The FRAP reagent was prepared by mixing 300 mM acetate buffer (pH 3.6), 10 mM TPTZ (2,4,6-tripyridyl-s-triazine) solution in 40 mM HCl, and 20 mM ferric chloride in a 10:1:1 ratio. A 3 mL aliquot of FRAP reagent was added to 100 µL of cyanobacterial extract and incubated at 37°C for 30 minutes. The absorbance was measured at 593 nm. Ferrous sulfate was used as the standard, and the results were expressed as µmol Fe²⁺ equivalents per gram of dry biomass. DPPH Radical Scavenging Assay The antioxidant activity of the cyanobacterial extracts was further evaluated using the 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) radical scavenging assay [6]. A 1 mL aliquot of extract (1 mg/mL in methanol) was added to 3 mL of 0.1 mM DPPH solution in methanol. The mixture was vortexed and incubated in the dark at room temperature for 30 minutes. The absorbance was measured at 517 nm, and the percentage of DPPH radical scavenging activity was calculated using the formula: \[ \% \text{Inhibition} = \frac{A{\text{control}} - A{\text{sample}}}{A{\text{control}}} \times 100 \] where \( A{\text{control}} \) is the absorbance of the control (DPPH solution without extract), and \( A{\text{sample}} \) is the absorbance of the reaction mixture containing the extract. Ascorbic acid was used as the positive control. Estimation of Phycobiliproteins (PBPs) Phycobiliproteins, including phycocyanin, allophycocyanin, and phycoerythrin, were quantified following the method described by Bennett and Bogorad [7]. Freeze-dried biomass (50 mg) was homogenized in 10 mL of 0.1 M phosphate buffer (pH 7.0) and subjected to freeze-thaw cycles for pigment extraction. The homogenate was centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 10 minutes, and the supernatant was collected. Absorbance was measured at 562, 615, and 652 nm, and the concentrations of phycocyanin, allophycocyanin, and phycoerythrin were calculated using the following equations: \[ \text{Phycocyanin (mg/mL)} = \frac{A{615} - 0.474 \cdot A{652}}{5.34} \] \[ \text{Allophycocyanin (mg/mL)} = \frac{A{652} - 0.208 \cdot A{615}}{5.09} \] \[ \text{Phycoerythrin (mg/mL)} = \frac{A{562} - 2.41 \cdot (\text{Phycocyanin}) - 0.849 \cdot (\text{Allophycocyanin})}{9.62} \] The results were expressed as mg of pigment per gram of dry biomass. FTIR Spectroscopy Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy was performed to identify active functional groups responsible for antioxidant properties in the cyanobacterial extracts. Lyophilized biomass was mixed with potassium bromide (KBr) to form pellets, which were analyzed using an FTIR spectrometer (PerkinElmer, USA) in the range of 4000–400 cm⁻¹ [8]. The spectra were analyzed to detect characteristic functional groups, such as –OH, –C=O, and –NH, and their potential roles in antioxidant activity were evaluated. All analyses were performed in triplicates, and results were expressed as mean ± standard deviation. Statistical analysis was conducted using one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test, and a p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The results of the study demonstrated notable variations in the antioxidant properties, total phenolic content (TPC), total flavonoid content (TFC), phycobiliproteins (PBPs), and antioxidant activities across the four cyanobacterial species—Oscillatoria sp., Lyngbya sp., Microcystis sp., and Spirulina sp.—isolated from fresh water bodies in Sri Lanka. These findings are presented in detail below, supported by quantitative data and analyses. The TPC was measured in all cyanobacterial species, with Lyngbya sp. exhibiting the highest value of 5.02 ± 0.20 mg/g. This was followed by Oscillatoria sp., Microcystis sp., and Spirulina sp., which showed TPC values of 3.89 ± 0.15 mg/g, 2.56 ± 0.12 mg/g, and 1.98 ± 0.10 mg/g, respectively. The elevated TPC in Lyngbya sp. indicates its potential as a rich source of phenolic compounds, which are known for their antioxidant activities through mechanisms such as free radical scavenging and metal ion chelation [1]. Similarly, the TFC was also found to be the highest in Lyngbya sp. (664.07 ± 19.76 mg/g), significantly exceeding the values recorded for the other species.
