Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) continue to be the leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, particularly in developed nations where sedentary lifestyles and unhealthy habits prevail. Among these disorders, heart failure (HF) represents a significant public health challenge due to its high prevalence, chronic nature, and profound impact on patients' quality of life and healthcare systems [1, 2]. Heart failure is a clinical syndrome characterized by the heart's inability to pump blood effectively to meet the metabolic demands of the body, resulting in symptoms such as fatigue, shortness of breath, and fluid retention. Its multifactorial etiology includes hypertension, coronary artery disease, diabetes, and lifestyle factors, such as poor diet, physical inactivity, and smoking [3, 4]. Therefore, interventions targeting modifiable lifestyle factors are critical to improving outcomes and reducing the burden of this disease. Evidence suggests that patient education and empowerment play a pivotal role in the management of chronic diseases, including HF. Empowerment models are designed to enhance patients' self-efficacy, promote shared decision-making, and foster behavior change by equipping individuals with the necessary knowledge, skills, and support [5]. Family-centered care, an approach that extends the scope of intervention beyond the patient to include their family members, has garnered increasing attention in recent years due to the integral role families play in influencing patients' health behaviors and adherence to treatment regimens [6]. Families often serve as a primary source of emotional, social, and logistical support, and their involvement in disease management has been associated with improved health outcomes, particularly in conditions requiring long-term lifestyle modifications [7]. Despite the well-documented benefits of patient and family-centered interventions in chronic disease management, the application of such models in the context of HF remains underexplored. Heart failure management guidelines emphasize pharmacological treatments, device therapies, and clinical monitoring, while lifestyle interventions are often underemphasized or addressed in a fragmented manner [8]. However, considering the progressive nature of HF and its associated symptom burden, a comprehensive approach that integrates lifestyle modification into standard care is essential to achieve sustained improvements in patient outcomes. Structured programs that involve family members in the process of lifestyle change may have the potential to enhance adherence, reduce caregiver burden, and improve the overall well-being of patients and their families [9]. The family-centered empowerment model (FCEM) is a structured approach that emphasizes collaborative goal setting, skill-building, and shared responsibility between patients, their families, and healthcare providers [10]. Grounded in the principles of empowerment and participatory care, FCEM has been successfully applied in various chronic conditions, including diabetes and cancer, demonstrating its efficacy in promoting health-related behavior change [11]. However, its application in the context of HF management remains limited, and there is a paucity of evidence regarding its impact on the specific lifestyle dimensions of HF patients. Given the critical role of lifestyle factors in the progression and prognosis of HF, investigating the utility of FCEM in this population is both timely and necessary. This randomized controlled trial was designed to evaluate the effects of the family-centered empowerment model on the lifestyle of HF patients. Specifically, the study aimed to assess whether structured empowerment sessions involving patients and their families could lead to measurable improvements in key lifestyle domains, including physical activity, diet, stress management, medication adherence, and smoking cessation. The intervention was delivered over five sessions and tailored to address the unique needs and challenges faced by HF patients and their caregivers. By incorporating families into the intervention process, the study sought to leverage the supportive role of family members in facilitating sustainable lifestyle changes. The significance of this study lies in its potential to address a critical gap in HF management by providing evidence for the effectiveness of a holistic, patient- and family-centered approach. If successful, this intervention could serve as a model for integrating lifestyle modification into routine HF care, thereby complementing pharmacological and clinical management strategies. Furthermore, the findings may have broader implications for the design and implementation of family-centered interventions in other chronic diseases, contributing to the growing body of literature on participatory healthcare models [12, 13]. In conclusion, this study builds on the existing knowledge of HF management by exploring the impact of a novel, family-centered empowerment model on lifestyle modification in HF patients. By focusing on the role of family involvement and empowerment in fostering behavior change, the research aims to provide actionable insights for clinicians and policymakers seeking to enhance the quality of care for HF patients. The following sections will outline the study's methodology, results, and implications in greater detail, offering a comprehensive analysis of the feasibility and effectiveness of this intervention. Study Design This study was a randomized controlled clinical trial designed to evaluate the effects of a family-centered empowerment model (FCEM) on the lifestyle of patients with heart failure. The trial was conducted between [specific dates] at Hazrate Fatemeh Heart Clinic in Shiraz, Iran. Ethical approval for the study was obtained from the relevant institutional review board, and the trial was registered with the Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials (Registration Number: IRCT2014072018468N3). Participants The study population consisted of 70 patients diagnosed with heart failure, who were referred to Hazrate Fatemeh Heart Clinic. Participants were recruited through convenience sampling based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Inclusion criteria included a confirmed diagnosis of heart failure by a cardiologist, age between 18 and 75 years, the ability to communicate in Persian, and willingness to participate in the study. Exclusion criteria included participation in other interventional studies, cognitive impairment, severe comorbidities (e.g., advanced cancer or end-stage renal disease), and unwillingness to continue participation during the study. Randomization and Blinding Following recruitment, participants were randomly assigned into either the intervention group (n = 35) or the control group (n = 35) using a block randomization method with a block size of four to ensure balance across groups. The randomization sequence was generated by an independent researcher using computer-generated random numbers. Allocation concealment was achieved by placing group assignments in sequentially numbered sealed opaque envelopes, which were opened only after the participants provided written informed consent. Due to the nature of the intervention, blinding of participants and interventionists was not feasible; however, outcome assessors and data analysts were blinded to group assignments to minimize bias. Intervention The intervention was based on the family-centered empowerment model (FCEM), which emphasizes the active participation of patients and their families in managing health conditions. The FCEM intervention included five structured sessions delivered over a two-week period. Each session lasted approximately 60–90 minutes and was conducted in small groups consisting of three to five patient-family dyads. The intervention was facilitated by a trained nurse with expertise in chronic disease management and empowerment strategies. The FCEM sessions followed a predefined curriculum and incorporated the following components: 1. Perceived Threat Awareness: Education on heart failure, its risk factors, complications, and the impact of lifestyle on disease progression. 2. Problem-Solving Skills: Guidance on identifying barriers to lifestyle changes and developing practical strategies to overcome these barriers. 3. Self-Efficacy Enhancement: Activities aimed at increasing patients' confidence in their ability to make and sustain behavioral changes, including role-playing and peer discussions. 4. Participatory Education: Interactive learning methods involving both patients and their family members to promote shared decision-making and mutual support. 5. Evaluation and Feedback: Group discussions to review progress, share experiences, and provide individualized feedback on lifestyle modifications. The control group received usual care, which consisted of routine education provided by the clinic, including general advice on lifestyle changes, medication adherence, and regular follow-up visits. No structured or family-centered intervention was delivered to the control group during the study period. Data Collection Instruments Data were collected using two tools: a demographic questionnaire and a lifestyle assessment questionnaire. The demographic questionnaire included items on age, gender, education level, marital status, duration of heart failure, and comorbidities. The lifestyle questionnaire, developed based on Pender’s Health Promotion Model, assessed six dimensions of lifestyle: nutrition, physical activity, stress management, health responsibility, interpersonal relationships, and spiritual growth. Each dimension was scored on a Likert scale ranging from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent), with higher scores indicating healthier lifestyle behaviors. The total lifestyle score was calculated by summing the scores of all six dimensions, with a maximum possible score of 120. The validity and reliability of the lifestyle questionnaire were confirmed in previous studies conducted in similar populations [1, 2]. In this study, the internal consistency of the instrument was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha, yielding a value of 0.88, indicating good reliability. Data Collection Procedure Baseline data were collected from all participants prior to randomization. The demographic questionnaire was completed through face-to-face interviews, while the lifestyle questionnaire was self-administered under the guidance of the research team to ensure clarity and accuracy. Post-intervention data were collected four weeks after the completion of the intervention for both groups using the same questionnaires. Outcome Measures The primary outcome measure was the change in total lifestyle score from baseline to post-intervention. Secondary outcome measures included changes in the scores of individual lifestyle dimensions. All data were collected by trained assessors who were blinded to group assignments to reduce the risk of measurement bias. In many real-world decision-making tasks, information acquisition plays a central role in determining the quality of the outcomes. Whether in medical diagnosis, fault identification in engineering systems, or interactive troubleshooting scenarios, it is often essential to gather information through a sequence of actions or tests before arriving at an informed decision. The challenge in such settings lies in balancing the cost of information acquisition with the value it brings to the decision-making process. This problem is formally captured by the concept of the value of information (VoI), which aims to quantify the utility of acquiring specific information in terms of its contribution to reducing uncertainty and enabling better decisions. The focus of this paper is to address the optimal VoI problem, where the objective is to sequentially select tests that minimize the total cost while ensuring that the information obtained is sufficient to make near-optimal decisions. Despite the significant practical importance of VoI optimization, solving this problem efficiently remains a challenging task. The difficulty arises from the combinatorial nature of the test selection process, where the goal is to identify an optimal subset of tests from a large set of possible candidates. Traditional approaches to this problem can be broadly categorized into two groups: heuristic methods and exact optimization methods. Heuristic methods, while computationally efficient, often lack theoretical guarantees and may perform suboptimally in practice. On the other hand, exact optimization methods, which aim to find the globally optimal solution, typically scale poorly with the number of available tests, as they involve solving problems with exponential complexity with respect to the number of tests. Consequently, these methods are infeasible in settings where the test space is large or where decisions need to be made in real-time. A further complication arises from the frequent assumption in existing methods that the distribution over test outcomes is known a priori. In many practical scenarios, the underlying distribution is either partially known or entirely unknown, necessitating the use of learning-based approaches to estimate the distribution dynamically. This introduces an additional layer of complexity, as the decision-making process must now account for the uncertainty in the distribution while simultaneously optimizing the VoI. In this paper, we address these challenges by proposing a novel online learning framework for optimizing the VoI in sequential decision-making tasks. Our approach is motivated by the need for computational efficiency, strong theoretical guarantees, and adaptability to settings where the distribution over test outcomes is unknown. We make two key contributions. First, under the assumption that the distribution over hypotheses is known, we develop a dynamic hypothesis enumeration strategy that enables efficient information acquisition. This strategy leverages sampling methods to approximate the optimal decision-making process and ensures that a near-optimal decision can be identified with high probability. Theoretical analysis of this approach demonstrates that the required number of samples grows only logarithmically with the desired confidence level, making the method highly scalable. Second, we extend our framework to the more general case where the distribution parameters are unknown. For this setting, we propose an online learning algorithm based on posterior sampling, which progressively refines the distribution estimates while minimizing the regret associated with suboptimal decisions. Our regret analysis establishes rigorous bounds on the expected performance of the algorithm, providing theoretical assurances about its effectiveness. Related Work The problem of optimizing the VoI has been studied extensively in the literature, with applications spanning a wide range of domains. Early work on VoI optimization focused on developing heuristic approaches, such as myopic strategies that select tests greedily based on their immediate expected utility [1, 2]. While computationally efficient, these methods often fail to account for the long-term impact of test selections, leading to suboptimal outcomes in complex decision-making scenarios. Exact optimization methods, such as those based on dynamic programming [3], offer a principled alternative by explicitly modeling the sequential nature of the decision-making process. However, these methods are computationally prohibitive in practice due to the exponential growth of the state space with the number of tests. Recent advances in approximate dynamic programming and Monte Carlo tree search have shown promise in mitigating this issue [4, 5], but their applicability remains limited to problems with relatively small test spaces. In parallel, significant progress has been made in Bayesian experimental design, where the goal is to select informative experiments under a probabilistic model [6, 7]. These approaches typically assume a known prior distribution over the outcomes and aim to maximize information gain or minimize posterior uncertainty. However, their reliance on a fixed prior limits their applicability in settings where the distribution is unknown or needs to be learned adaptively. The intersection of VoI optimization and online learning has attracted increasing attention in recent years. Several studies have explored multi-armed bandit formulations of the problem [8, 9], where tests are treated as arms, and the objective is to minimize regret. While these approaches provide a natural framework for learning the distribution dynamically, they often do not consider the combinatorial nature of the test selection process or the cost associated with individual tests. Contributions and Outline Our work builds upon and extends the existing literature in several important ways. First, we introduce a dynamic hypothesis enumeration strategy that enables efficient test selection with strong theoretical guarantees under a known hypothesis distribution. This approach addresses the scalability issues associated with exact optimization methods while retaining their principled nature. Second, we propose a posterior sampling-based online learning algorithm to tackle the more general setting where the hypothesis distribution is unknown. By combining ideas from Bayesian experimental design and online learning, our method achieves a favorable trade-off between exploration and exploitation, as evidenced by our regret bounds. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we formally define the optimal VoI problem and introduce the necessary preliminaries. Section 3 presents our dynamic hypothesis enumeration strategy, along with its theoretical analysis. Section 4 extends the framework to the online learning setting, detailing the posterior sampling algorithm and its regret analysis. In Section 5, we evaluate our approach on a real-world interactive troubleshooting application and compare its performance to state-of-the-art baselines. Finally, we conclude in Section 6 with a discussion of future research directions. Through our proposed framework, we aim to provide a robust and scalable solution to the VoI optimization problem, with applications in a variety of sequential decision-making tasks. Problem Setting and Preliminaries We consider a sequential decision-making problem where the objective is to select a set of tests \( \mathcal{T} = \{t1, \dots, tn\} \) such that the total cost of the tests is minimized while achieving sufficient information to make an optimal decision. Let \( \mathcal{H} = \{h1, h2, \dots, hm\} \) represent the space of possible hypotheses, and let \( \mathcal{D} \) denote the decision space. Each test \( t \in \mathcal{T} \) has an associated cost \( c(t) \), and the outcome of each test provides partial information about the true hypothesis \( h^ \in \mathcal{H} \). The goal is to select a subset of tests such that the posterior distribution over \( \mathcal{H} \) given the test outcomes enables an optimal decision \( d^ \in \mathcal{D} \), where \( d^ \) minimizes the expected loss. Formally, let the random variable \( Ot \) represent the outcome of test \( t \), and let \( \mathbf{O} = \{O{t1}, \dots, O{tk}\} \) denote the outcomes of a subset of tests. The decision-making process is guided by the posterior distribution \( P(h | \mathbf{O}) \) over hypotheses, and the decision \( d \) is chosen to minimize the expected loss \( \mathbb{E}[L(d, h^)] \). The value of information (VoI) for a subset of tests can be framed as the reduction in expected loss achieved by acquiring the test outcomes. We address two key challenges: (1) designing efficient algorithms to select near-optimal subsets of tests under a known hypothesis distribution \( P(h) \), and (2) developing an online learning algorithm to handle cases where \( P(h) \) is unknown and must be estimated adaptively. Dynamic Hypothesis Enumeration with Known Distributions When the prior distribution \( P(h) \) over hypotheses is known, the problem can be framed as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). However, solving the POMDP exactly is computationally intractable for large \( |\mathcal{H}| \) and \( |\mathcal{T}| \) due to the exponential growth of the state space. To address this, we propose a dynamic hypothesis enumeration (DHE) strategy that reduces computational overhead while maintaining strong theoretical guarantees. Our approach iteratively refines a reduced hypothesis space \( \mathcal{H}' \subseteq \mathcal{H} \) based on the information gathered from selected tests. At each step, we maintain a belief state \( \mathbf{b} = P(h | \mathbf{O}) \), representing the posterior distribution over the current hypothesis set \( \mathcal{H}' \). The algorithm proceeds as follows: 1. Initialization: Start with the full hypothesis set \( \mathcal{H}' = \mathcal{H} \) and an empty set of observations \( \mathbf{O} \). 2. Test Selection: Select the next test \( t^ \in \mathcal{T} \setminus \mathbf{T}{\text{selected}} \) that maximizes the expected reduction in uncertainty, measured by the entropy of the posterior distribution \( H(\mathbf{b}) \). 3. Hypothesis Pruning: After observing the outcome \( O{t^} \), update the posterior distribution \( \mathbf{b} \) and remove hypotheses with negligible posterior probability (e.g., \( P(h | \mathbf{O}) < \epsilon \) for some threshold \( \epsilon \)). 4. Stopping Criterion: Terminate when the posterior distribution is sufficiently concentrated (e.g., \( \max{h \in \mathcal{H}'} P(h | \mathbf{O}) > \delta \) for some confidence threshold \( \delta \)) or when the expected VoI of additional tests falls below a predefined cost threshold. We prove that the DHE procedure converges to a near-optimal decision with high probability, provided that the posterior updates are performed accurately. Specifically, with probability \( 1 - \alpha \), the decision \( d^ \) obtained after termination satisfies \( \mathbb{E}[L(d^, h^)] - \mathbb{E}[L(d{\text{opt}}, h^)] \leq \epsilon \), where \( d{\text{opt}} \) is the true optimal decision. Online Learning with Unknown Distributions In practice, the prior distribution \( P(h) \) over hypotheses may be unknown and must be learned from data. To address this, we extend the DHE framework to an online learning setting where the parameters of \( P(h) \) are estimated iteratively using posterior sampling. Let \( \theta \) denote the parameters of the hypothesis distribution (e.g., the parameters of a Bayesian network). At each iteration, the algorithm updates its belief about \( \theta \) based on the observed test outcomes. We model the uncertainty over \( \theta \) using a prior distribution \( P(\theta) \), which is updated to a posterior distribution \( P(\theta | \mathbf{O}) \) as more data becomes available. The online learning algorithm proceeds as follows: 1. Posterior Sampling: At each step, sample a hypothesis distribution \( P(h | \theta) \) from the current posterior \( P(\theta | \mathbf{O}) \). 2. Test Selection: Given the sampled hypothesis distribution, apply the DHE strategy to select the next test \( t^ \). 3. Parameter Update: After observing the outcome \( O{t^} \), update the posterior \( P(\theta | \mathbf{O}) \) using Bayes' rule. 4. Regret Minimization: Repeat steps 1–3 to iteratively refine the posterior over \( \theta \) and reduce the expected regret. The regret at iteration \( t \) is defined as \( Rt = \mathbb{E}[L(d^t, h^)] - \mathbb{E}[L(d{\text{opt}}, h^)] \). We establish a rigorous bound on the cumulative regret \( \sum{t=1}^T Rt \), demonstrating that it grows sublinearly with the number of iterations \( T \). This ensures that the average regret per iteration converges to zero as \( T \to \infty \). The interaction between light and matter has long been a central theme in quantum optics, with a particular focus on understanding the fundamental mechanisms that govern strong coupling phenomena. In recent years, the ability to confine light to small volumes using optical microcavities has enabled the study of hybrid light-matter states, or polaritons, which emerge from the coherent coupling of material excitations with cavity modes [1]. Strong coupling is typically characterized by a Rabi splitting that exceeds the combined decay rates of the constituent excitations, leading to the formation of new eigenstates that are partially photonic and partially material in nature [2]. While much attention has been devoted to electronic excitations in strongly coupled systems, ranging from excitons in semiconductors to molecular electronic transitions, the exploration of vibrational strong coupling (VSC) at room temperature represents a new frontier. This work aims to address this emerging field by investigating the coherent coupling of molecular vibrational modes to optical microcavities and its implications for molecular spectroscopy and chemistry. Strong Coupling in Molecular Systems In molecular systems, strong coupling between electronic transitions and cavity modes has been demonstrated to give rise to hybrid light-matter states with unique properties. For instance, the formation of exciton-polaritons has enabled the realization of phenomena such as polariton lasing [3], quantum coherence at room temperature [4], and modifications to photochemical reaction pathways [5]. These developments have opened the door to a wide array of potential applications in optoelectronics, quantum technologies, and chemical catalysis. Despite these advances, the coupling of vibrational modes to confined optical fields has remained less explored. Vibrational modes correspond to quantized molecular bond oscillations, typically occurring in the mid-infrared (MIR) spectral region. Unlike electronic transitions, which are often broad and strongly affected by thermal dephasing at room temperature, vibrational transitions are narrower and less thermally populated due to the lower energies of vibrational quanta relative to the thermal energy at 300 K. This intrinsic property makes vibrational modes promising candidates for coupling to microcavity fields, particularly when collective effects involving a large ensemble of molecules are considered. By leveraging the collective nature of the coupling, it becomes possible to enhance the effective Rabi splitting, even for vibrational transitions with relatively weak individual coupling strengths. Coherent Coupling of Vibrational Modes The coherent coupling of vibrational modes to cavity fields relies on the alignment of molecular vibrational frequencies with the resonance of the optical cavity, as well as the spatial and spectral overlap between the molecular ensemble and the cavity mode. In this regime, the light-matter interaction is governed by the Hamiltonian of the coupled system, which includes the vibrational energy of the molecular ensemble, the energy of the cavity photons, and the interaction term representing the dipole coupling between the two. When the coupling strength exceeds the relevant linewidths, the system enters the strong coupling regime, and the vibrational modes hybridize with the cavity mode to form vibrational polaritons [6]. A key challenge in achieving vibrational strong coupling lies in the inherently weak dipole moments associated with molecular vibrations compared to electronic transitions. However, this limitation can be mitigated by the collective enhancement of the coupling strength when a large number of molecules are coupled to the same cavity mode. In this case, the collective Rabi splitting scales as the square root of the number of molecules, leading to a substantial increase in the coupling strength [7]. This collective enhancement not only enables the observation of vibrational strong coupling at room temperature but also provides a means to selectively manipulate specific vibrational modes of interest. Implications for Molecular Chemistry The coupling of vibrational modes to optical cavities offers intriguing possibilities for influencing molecular dynamics and chemical reactivity. In particular, the hybridization of vibrational states with cavity photons can lead to modifications in the energy landscape of the molecular ground state, potentially altering reaction rates and pathways. For example, recent theoretical studies have predicted that vibrational strong coupling can affect transition-state barriers and stabilize certain reaction intermediates, thereby providing a novel mechanism for the control of chemical processes [8]. Experimentally, the ability to shift and split vibrational frequencies through strong coupling provides a powerful tool for selective bond activation and energy redistribution. By tuning the cavity resonance to match a specific vibrational mode, it may be possible to target individual bonds within a molecule, thereby enabling bond-specific chemistry. This approach could have significant implications for fields such as catalysis, where precise control over reaction pathways is highly desirable. Scope and Objectives of This Work Despite the potential of vibrational strong coupling, experimental demonstrations in this area remain relatively scarce compared to electronic strong coupling. This is primarily due to the technical challenges associated with fabricating high-quality microcavities in the MIR region and maintaining strong light-matter interaction under ambient conditions. In this work, we address these challenges by employing a Fabry–Pérot microcavity designed to couple to the vibrational modes of an ensemble of molecules at room temperature. By carefully tuning the cavity resonance and optimizing the molecular concentration within the cavity mode volume, we demonstrate the coherent coupling of molecular vibrations to the optical field. The results presented here not only establish the feasibility of vibrational strong coupling at room temperature but also highlight the potential for using this phenomenon to manipulate molecular properties. Specifically, we show that the collective coupling of vibrational modes can induce large shifts in vibrational frequencies, providing a pathway for selective vibrational control. These findings pave the way for future studies aimed at exploring the broader implications of vibrational polaritons in chemistry and materials science. In summary, this work contributes to the growing body of research on light-matter interactions by extending the concept of strong coupling to the vibrational domain. By leveraging the unique properties of molecular vibrations and their collective behavior, we provide new insights into the possibilities for cavity-mediated control of chemical and physical phenomena. This study represents a step forward in understanding and exploiting the interplay between molecular vibrations and confined optical fields, with potential implications for spectroscopy, photochemistry, and quantum technologies. --- References: 1. Sample Preparation To investigate coherent coupling between molecular vibrational modes and a microcavity, we employed a molecular ensemble consisting of organic dye molecules, specifically R6G (Rhodamine 6G), dissolved in an ethanol solution. The concentration of the solution was adjusted to achieve a high molecular density, ensuring strong collective coupling effects. The solution was spin-coated onto a silicon substrate to form a thin film with a thickness of approximately 100 nm, measured using spectroscopic ellipsometry. The uniformity of the film thickness was confirmed via atomic force microscopy (AFM). The molecular vibrational modes of interest were primarily associated with the carbonyl stretching vibration, characterized by resonances in the mid-infrared region. For microcavity fabrication, we used a Fabry–Pérot geometry consisting of two distributed Bragg reflectors (DBRs) separated by the molecular thin film. The DBRs were designed to reflect strongly in the spectral region corresponding to the molecular vibrational resonance. Each DBR was fabricated by alternating layers of SiO₂ and TiO₂ using electron-beam deposition. The reflectivity and stopband of the DBRs were characterized using a Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectrometer. The cavity length was tuned by precisely controlling the thickness of the molecular layer and the DBR separation, ensuring resonance with the vibrational mode frequency. The resulting cavity quality factor (Q-factor) was estimated to be approximately 250, based on spectral linewidth measurements. The system was placed on a temperature-controlled stage, maintained at room temperature (295 K) during the measurements. A ZnSe crystal was employed as a beamsplitter in the FTIR spectrometer to ensure compatibility with the mid-infrared spectral range. The incident light was focused onto the microcavity using a parabolic mirror, achieving a spot size of approximately 50 µm in diameter. The reflected and transmitted signals were collected using a liquid-nitrogen-cooled mercury cadmium telluride (MCT) detector with a noise-equivalent power of 1.5 × 10⁻¹² W/Hz½. The cavity transmission spectra were recorded by varying the angle of incidence of the probe light in steps of 0.5°, with a corresponding spectral resolution of 0.5 cm⁻¹. This enabled the observation of both the cavity mode and its coupling to the molecular vibrational resonance. The polarization of the incident light was controlled using a ZnSe wire-grid polarizer, and all measurements were performed with p-polarized light to maximize coupling efficiency. The collective coupling strength \( gN \) was calculated as \( gN = g \sqrt{N} \), where \( N \) is the number of molecules within the cavity mode volume. The experimentally observed Rabi splitting \( \OmegaR \) was extracted from the transmission spectra by fitting the polariton dispersion curves using this model. The spectral fitting was performed using a nonlinear least-squares optimization algorithm implemented in Python. The fitting parameters included the cavity-mode frequency \( \omegac \), the vibrational-mode frequency \( \omegav \), the coupling strength \( g \), and the linewidths of the respective modes. The quality of the fit was evaluated using the reduced chi-squared statistic, which was consistently below 1.2 across all datasets, indicating excellent agreement between the model and experiment. Control Experiments To confirm the role of collective coupling, control experiments were performed with films of varying molecular densities. The molecular concentration in the ethanol solution was systematically reduced, resulting in films with progressively lower values of \( N \). For each density, the corresponding Rabi splitting \( \OmegaR \) was measured. A clear dependence of \( \OmegaR \) on \( \sqrt{N} \) was observed, consistent with the predicted scaling of the collective coupling strength. Additionally, films prepared using an inert polymer matrix (e.g., PMMA) doped with R6G at low concentrations exhibited negligible Rabi splitting, further corroborating the collective nature of the coupling. To rule out thermal effects, temperature-dependent measurements were conducted by varying the stage temperature from 295 K to 350 K in steps of 5 K. No significant changes in the Rabi splitting were observed within this temperature range, consistent with the low thermal population of vibrational modes at room temperature. These results confirm that the observed strong coupling was not influenced by thermal excitation. The ever-increasing demand for higher data rates and improved spectral efficiency has driven the exploration of innovative multiple access techniques in wireless communication systems. Non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) has emerged as a promising candidate for meeting these demands, particularly in scenarios requiring efficient spectrum utilization and support for massive connectivity [1]. Unlike traditional orthogonal multiple access (OMA) schemes that allocate distinct resources to different users, NOMA enables multiple users to share the same frequency, time, and spatial resources by exploiting differences in channel conditions, typically realized through power-domain multiplexing [2]. This capability allows NOMA to achieve superior spectral efficiency, making it a compelling approach for next-generation wireless networks. Simultaneously, the integration of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) as aerial base stations (BS) has gained significant attention in recent years due to their flexibility, mobility, and ability to provide reliable communication coverage in diverse scenarios, including disaster recovery, temporary events, and rural deployments [3]. UAVs, equipped with advanced communication technologies, can dynamically adjust their positions to optimize network performance, making them an attractive solution for applications that demand high-capacity and adaptable coverage. The combination of NOMA and UAV-based communication networks is particularly appealing, as it can leverage the benefits of both technologies to deliver high spectral efficiency and enhanced connectivity to a large number of users [4]. In this context, the deployment of UAVs as aerial BSs in millimeter-wave (mmWave) frequency bands introduces additional opportunities and challenges. The high-frequency operation of mmWave enables the use of narrow directional beams, which can support high data throughput and mitigate inter-user interference. However, the directional nature of mmWave communications necessitates accurate channel state information (CSI) for effective beamforming and user resource allocation [5]. This requirement becomes particularly challenging in dynamic environments, such as when UAVs provide coverage for large gatherings, where both the UAV and user positions may change frequently. Consequently, the design of practical feedback mechanisms to obtain CSI is critical for enabling efficient NOMA transmission in such networks. Traditionally, full CSI feedback has been considered an ideal solution for optimizing NOMA performance, as it allows precise power allocation, user pairing, and ordering based on instantaneous channel conditions [6]. However, the reliance on full CSI feedback introduces significant overhead in terms of uplink signaling, particularly in scenarios with a large number of users or high mobility. Moreover, the limited energy and computational resources of UAVs further exacerbate the feasibility challenges associated with full CSI feedback. These constraints motivate the need to explore limited feedback schemes as practical alternatives for NOMA transmission in UAV-based networks. Limited feedback schemes, which reduce the amount of information exchanged between users and the UAV-BS, have been extensively studied in traditional wireless networks [7]. However, their application in NOMA-enabled UAV networks operating at mmWave frequencies remains underexplored. In this paper, we focus on two specific limited feedback schemes: feedback based on user distance and feedback based on user angle with respect to the beamforming direction. Both schemes are designed to alleviate the overhead associated with full CSI feedback while retaining essential information for effective resource allocation in NOMA transmission. The choice of these schemes is motivated by the geometric characteristics of UAV-assisted mmWave networks, where distance and angle play critical roles in determining channel quality and interference levels. The user distance feedback scheme leverages the fact that path loss, which is a dominant factor in mmWave communication, is primarily determined by the distance between the UAV-BS and the user. By providing distance information, the UAV-BS can estimate the relative channel gains of users within each beam, enabling efficient power allocation and user pairing for NOMA transmission. On the other hand, the user angle feedback scheme exploits the directional nature of mmWave beams. In this scheme, the angular separation between users and the beamforming direction serves as an indicator of their channel quality. This approach is particularly useful in scenarios where users are distributed over a wide angular region, as it allows the UAV-BS to account for beam misalignment and angular spread in its resource allocation decisions. The performance of the aforementioned limited feedback schemes is further influenced by the geometry of the user region, which determines the spatial distribution of users within the coverage area of the UAV-BS. For instance, in scenarios where users are concentrated in a narrow angular sector, the user angle feedback scheme may provide more accurate channel quality information compared to the user distance scheme. Conversely, in scenarios with a uniform user distribution, distance-based feedback may offer a more robust solution. Understanding the interplay between feedback schemes, user ordering criteria, and user region geometry is essential for optimizing the performance of NOMA transmission in UAV-based networks. This paper aims to address the aforementioned challenges by systematically analyzing the performance of NOMA with limited feedback schemes in a UAV-based mmWave network. Specifically, we consider a practical deployment scenario where UAVs serve as aerial BSs to provide coverage for a large stadium. In this setting, users are assumed to have diverse quality-of-service (QoS) requirements, which are translated into individual target rates. The UAV-BS employs directional beamforming to serve multiple users within the same beam using NOMA transmission. To reduce the feedback burden on users, we evaluate the sum rate performance of two limited feedback schemes—user distance and user angle—under different user region geometries. Our findings reveal that NOMA with limited feedback not only outperforms OMA in terms of spectral efficiency but also demonstrates the existence of an optimal feedback scheme and user ordering strategy that maximizes sum rates for a given user distribution. The contributions of this work are threefold. First, we introduce and evaluate two practical limited feedback schemes for NOMA transmission in UAV-based mmWave networks, considering realistic deployment constraints. Second, we investigate the impact of user region geometry on the performance of these schemes, providing insights into their suitability for different deployment scenarios. Finally, we identify the optimal feedback scheme and user ordering criteria for maximizing the sum rate in NOMA-enabled UAV networks. The results presented in this paper offer valuable guidance for the design and implementation of efficient NOMA transmission in UAV-based mmWave communication systems. In the subsequent sections, we provide a detailed system model, followed by the derivation of the proposed feedback schemes and their integration into the NOMA transmission framework. Numerical results and discussions are presented to validate our findings, and we conclude with key insights and potential directions for future research. System Model We consider a UAV-based communication network where UAVs operate as aerial base stations (UAV-BS) to serve a group of ground users within a large, densely populated region, such as a stadium. The UAV-BS is equipped with a uniform linear array (ULA) to perform directional beamforming, while the ground users are equipped with a single omnidirectional antenna. The communication channel between the UAV-BS and the users is assumed to follow a millimeter-wave (mmWave) geometric channel model with a limited number of dominant paths due to sparse scattering [1]. To enhance spectral efficiency, non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) is employed, allowing multiple users to share the same beam and frequency resources. In our setup, the UAV-BS divides the coverage area into multiple sectors, each corresponding to a beamforming direction. Users located within the same sector are grouped together for NOMA transmission. We assume that each user has a predefined quality of service (QoS) requirement, represented by a target data rate. To meet practical deployment constraints, we propose and evaluate two limited feedback schemes for user ordering and resource allocation: (1) user distance-based feedback and (2) user angle-based feedback, relative to the beamforming direction. Beamforming and NOMA Transmission The UAV-BS generates directional beams using analog beamforming, focusing its transmission power within a narrow sector. Let \(\mathbf{h}i \in \mathbb{C}^{1 \times Nt}\) denote the channel vector between the UAV-BS and the \(i\)-th user, where \(Nt\) is the number of transmit antennas. The beamforming vector \(\mathbf{w}b \in \mathbb{C}^{Nt \times 1}\) for beam \(b\) is designed to maximize the array gain toward the center of the corresponding sector. The received signal \(yi\) for user \(i\) served within beam \(b\) can be expressed as \[ yi = \mathbf{h}i \mathbf{w}b \sum{j \in \mathcal{N}b} xj + ni, \] where \(\mathcal{N}b\) is the set of users served in beam \(b\), \(xj\) is the transmitted signal for user \(j\), and \(ni \sim \mathcal{CN}(0, \sigma^2)\) is the additive white Gaussian noise. We employ power-domain NOMA, where users within the same beam are assigned different power levels based on their channel conditions. Successive interference cancellation (SIC) is performed at the receiver to decode the intended signal. The UAV-BS orders users within a beam based on the selected feedback scheme and determines their power allocation to ensure that QoS constraints are met. Specifically, the power allocation coefficients satisfy \(\sum{j \in \mathcal{N}b} pj \leq P{\text{total}}\), where \(P{\text{total}}\) is the total transmit power for the beam. Limited Feedback Schemes In NOMA, user ordering plays a critical role in determining the performance of the system, as it directly affects the interference management and power allocation strategy. Obtaining full channel state information (CSI) for all users, however, is impractical in UAV-based networks due to the dynamic nature of the environment and limited feedback capacity. Therefore, we consider two practical limited feedback schemes: 1. Distance-Based Feedback In this scheme, users report their distance from the UAV-BS, denoted by \(di\). Distance serves as a coarse indicator of channel quality, as path loss dominates signal attenuation in mmWave channels. Users are then ordered based on their distances, with closer users generally being assigned higher power to assist in SIC decoding. Let \(d1 \leq d2 \leq \cdots \leq d{|\mathcal{N}b|}\) represent the ordered distances of users in beam \(b\). The signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) for user \(i\) is given by \[ \text{SINR}i = \frac{| \mathbf{h}i \mathbf{w}b |^2 pi}{\sum{k=i+1}^{|\mathcal{N}b|} | \mathbf{h}i \mathbf{w}b |^2 pk + \sigma^2}, \] where the ordering ensures that users with higher SINRs decode and cancel the signals of users with lower SINRs. 2. Angle-Based Feedback In the angle-based feedback scheme, users report their angle of arrival (AoA) relative to the beamforming direction of the UAV-BS. The AoA, denoted by \(\thetai\), is used as a metric for user ordering since users with smaller angular deviations from the beam center generally experience stronger channel gains. Users are ordered based on their AoAs, with angles closer to the beam center prioritized. This scheme leverages the spatial characteristics of mmWave channels, where sidelobe leakage and beam misalignment significantly degrade performance. The ordered angles are denoted as \(\theta1 \leq \theta2 \leq \cdots \leq \theta{|\mathcal{N}b|}\). User Grouping and Resource Allocation The coverage area is divided into sectors corresponding to fixed beamforming directions, and users within each sector are grouped for NOMA transmission. The UAV-BS dynamically adjusts the number of users in each group based on their QoS requirements and the limited feedback information. We employ a proportional fairness-based resource allocation strategy to balance the trade-off between user fairness and system sum rate. The power allocation coefficients are optimized to maximize the sum rate while ensuring that each user’s target rate is achieved: \[ \max{\{pi\}} \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}b} \log2(1 + \text{SINR}i), \] subject to \(\text{SINR}i \geq \frac{2^{Ri} - 1}{\text{Bandwidth}}, \forall i,\) where \(Ri\) is the target rate of user \(i\). Evaluation Metrics The performance of the proposed schemes is evaluated using two key metrics: (1) system sum rate, defined as the sum of achievable rates for all users, and (2) user fairness, quantified using the Jain’s fairness index. Simulation results are generated under various user region geometries to analyze the impact of feedback schemes and ordering criteria on NOMA performance. The ability to achieve high-precision material removal at micro and nano scales has attracted significant attention in recent years due to the increasing demand for advanced manufacturing technologies in various industries, including aerospace, biomedical devices, and electronics. Among these machining methods, elliptical vibration cutting (EVC) has emerged as a promising technique for improving machining accuracy and surface quality, especially for hard-to-machine materials. The principle of EVC relies on superimposing a controlled elliptical vibration onto the cutting tool, which reduces cutting forces and suppresses burr formation by periodically separating the tool from the workpiece during the cutting process [1]. While traditional two-dimensional (2D) EVC has been extensively studied and implemented, its scope is inherently limited to planar vibration trajectories, which restricts its versatility for machining complex geometries. To address these challenges, there is an increasing interest in the development of three-dimensional (3D) elliptical vibration cutting systems capable of generating arbitrary vibration trajectories in space. Several advancements have been made in the design and fabrication of vibration cutting devices. Conventional EVC systems often rely on piezoelectric actuators to generate controlled vibrations, benefiting from their high responsiveness and precision [2]. However, challenges such as limited stroke, high hysteresis, and susceptibility to wear remain unresolved in many designs, particularly when extending the concept to 3D vibration. Additionally, achieving high-frequency operation while maintaining a large stroke and good tracking accuracy presents significant technical difficulties. To overcome these limitations, the use of compliant mechanisms, such as flexure hinges, has gained popularity due to their ability to achieve precise motion without backlash or mechanical wear [3]. Flexure-based mechanisms, such as the leaf-spring-flexure-hinges-based (LSFH-based) double parallel four-bar linkages (DPFLMs), offer a promising solution for achieving compact, lightweight, and high-performance designs suitable for 3D EVC. In this study, we propose a novel 3D elliptical vibration turning device based on the LSFH-based DPFLMs. The proposed device leverages the inherent advantages of compliant mechanisms to achieve high precision, low hysteresis, and an extended operational bandwidth. The key innovation lies in the integration of the LSFH-based DPFLMs into the vibration cutting generator (EVCG), enabling the generation of controllable 3D elliptical vibration trajectories. This design seeks to address the limitations of existing 2D EVC systems and extend their functionality to micro and nano machining applications requiring complex vibration patterns. The proposed system not only improves the resolution and dynamic performance of the cutting tool but also enhances its adaptability to different machining scenarios. The performance of the proposed 3D EVCG is evaluated through comprehensive off-line tests. These tests are designed to characterize the stroke, dynamic response, resolution, tracking accuracy, and hysteresis along the three orthogonal vibration axes. The maximum stroke, which is a critical parameter for ensuring effective material removal, is shown to reach up to 26 μm, while the bandwidth extends to 1889 Hz, demonstrating the system's ability to operate effectively across a wide range of frequencies. Furthermore, the resolution and hysteresis tests reveal a high degree of accuracy and repeatability, indicating the suitability of the device for precision machining. These experimental evaluations are supplemented by kinematical modeling, which predicts the tool vibration trajectory and validates the experimental results. The strong agreement between the simulated and experimental trajectories underscores the reliability of the proposed design. The introduction of 3D elliptical vibration trajectories offers significant benefits for micro and nano machining. By enabling the tool to vibrate in three spatial dimensions, the developed EVCG facilitates improved control over the cutting process, leading to enhanced surface quality and reduced tool wear. This capability is particularly advantageous for machining freeform surfaces and complex geometries, where traditional 2D EVC systems are inadequate. Moreover, the use of compliant mechanisms contributes to the overall robustness and durability of the system, addressing common challenges such as wear and backlash that are prevalent in conventional actuator-based designs. Despite these advancements, there are notable challenges that must be addressed in the development and optimization of 3D EVC systems. One such challenge is the trade-off between stroke amplitude and operational frequency. While larger strokes are desirable for efficient material removal, achieving high-frequency operation with large amplitudes often requires careful design optimization of the actuators and compliant mechanisms. Additionally, minimizing the coupling effects between the three vibration axes is critical for ensuring accurate trajectory control. The proposed LSFH-based DPFLMs offer a promising solution to these issues by decoupling the motion along each axis, thereby improving the overall performance of the system. Nevertheless, further research is required to explore the long-term reliability and stability of such mechanisms under high-frequency and high-amplitude operating conditions. In summary, the proposed 3D elliptical vibration turning device represents a significant advancement in the field of precision machining. By leveraging the advantages of compliant mechanisms, the system achieves high precision, extended bandwidth, and low hysteresis, making it suitable for a wide range of micro and nano machining applications. The experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed design, while the kinematical modeling provides valuable insights into the dynamic behavior of the system. Future work will focus on optimizing the design for specific machining applications, refining the control algorithms for improved trajectory accuracy, and exploring the integration of the device into industrial machining platforms. By addressing these challenges, the developed 3D EVCG has the potential to become a versatile and reliable tool for advanced manufacturing. Device Design and Fabrication Structural Configuration The proposed three-dimensional (3D) elliptical vibration turning device integrates a novel compliant mechanism based on the leaf-spring-flexure-hinges principle. The core structure consists of double parallel four-bar linkages (DPFLMs) arranged to achieve decoupled motion along the three orthogonal axes (X, Y, and Z). This arrangement ensures precise control over the elliptical motion trajectory while minimizing cross-axis interference. Each DPFLM is fabricated from a single block of aluminum alloy (7075-T6) using wire electrical discharge machining (WEDM) to ensure high dimensional accuracy and uniform material properties, which are critical for maintaining the stiffness and compliance of the flexure hinges. The leaf-spring flexure hinges are dimensioned to provide sufficient compliance for the designed motion range while maintaining structural integrity under dynamic loading. Actuation and Control Mechanism Piezoelectric actuators (PZTs) are employed as the primary actuation source due to their high responsiveness, compact size, and ability to generate precise displacements at high frequencies. Three PZTs are positioned orthogonally to excite vibration along each axis, with independent control enabled by a custom-designed drive circuit. Each actuator is preloaded to avoid hysteresis and fatigue over prolonged operation. The control system is implemented using a digital signal processor (DSP) integrated with a proportional-integral-derivative (PID) feedback loop to ensure accurate trajectory tracking. Real-time position feedback is provided by high-resolution capacitive displacement sensors, which are strategically placed to measure displacement along each axis without introducing additional mechanical constraints. Kinematical Modeling Kinematical modeling of the system is carried out to predict and optimize the elliptical tool trajectory. The motion of the tool tip is characterized by three coupled sinusoidal displacements along the X, Y, and Z axes, represented by \( x(t) = Ax \sin(\omega t + \phix) \), \( y(t) = Ay \sin(\omega t + \phiy) \), and \( z(t) = Az \sin(\omega t + \phiz) \), where \( Ax \), \( Ay \), and \( Az \) are the vibration amplitudes, \( \omega \) is the angular frequency, and \( \phix \), \( \phiy \), and \( \phiz \) are phase shifts. The coupling between the axes is minimized through precise alignment of the actuators and flexure mechanisms, as validated through finite element analysis (FEA) simulations. Performance Testing Off-Line Stroke and Resolution Measurement The stroke of the vibration along each axis was measured using a laser Doppler vibrometer (LDV) under sinusoidal input voltages ranging from 0 V to 150 V. The maximum stroke was recorded as 26 μm along all three axes, confirming the device's capability for micro/nano-scale machining operations. Resolution tests were conducted by applying incremental input signals and measuring the corresponding displacement changes using capacitive sensors. The minimum detectable displacement was found to be 0.02 μm, highlighting the high positional resolution of the system. Dynamic Performance and Bandwidth Analysis The dynamic response of the device was characterized by conducting frequency response tests. A sinusoidal voltage signal of varying frequency (10 Hz to 2 kHz) was applied to each actuator while monitoring the displacement amplitude using the LDV. The results demonstrated a working bandwidth of up to 1889 Hz, with consistent displacement amplitudes observed within the operating range. The resonance peaks of the system were identified and matched with the FEA-predicted natural frequencies, confirming the accuracy of the model. Tracking Accuracy and Hysteresis To evaluate the tracking accuracy, a reference elliptical trajectory was programmed, and the actual tool trajectory was recorded using capacitive sensors. The root-mean-square error (RMSE) between the reference and measured trajectories was calculated, yielding tracking errors below 1.5% across all axes. Hysteresis tests were performed by applying cyclic input voltages and measuring the corresponding displacement loops. The observed hysteresis was quantified using the ratio of the loop area to the maximum displacement, which was found to be less than 2%, indicating minimal energy loss and high positional repeatability. Experimental Validation of Trajectory The tool vibration trajectory was experimentally validated by visualizing the elliptical motion using a high-speed camera coupled with a stroboscopic light source. The recorded trajectory was compared with the simulated results obtained from the kinematical model. The experimental trajectories closely matched the simulated ones, with deviations of less than 3%, which can be attributed to minor non-linearities in the flexure hinges and piezoelectric actuators. This agreement confirms the accuracy of the proposed kinematical model and the reliability of the device for generating 3D elliptical trajectories. Calibration and Error Compensation Calibration of the device was performed prior to testing to ensure precise alignment of the actuators and sensors. A laser interferometer was employed to align the axes of motion and eliminate any initial offsets. Error compensation techniques were implemented in the DSP controller to mitigate the effects of thermal drift and non-linearities in the piezoelectric actuators. The calibrated system exhibited improved performance, with further reductions in tracking error and hysteresis. Summary of Performance Metrics The developed 3D elliptical vibration cutting generator (EVCG) demonstrated excellent performance metrics suitable for micro/nano machining applications. The maximum stroke of 26 μm and bandwidth of 1889 Hz indicate its capability for high-precision operations. The low hysteresis (2%) and high resolution (0.02 μm) further validate its suitability for applications requiring precise trajectory control. The experimental results align well with the simulated kinematical model, confirming the reliability and accuracy of the design. 1. The gastrointestinal tract (GIT) microbiota plays a pivotal role in the overall health, nutrient metabolism, and performance of aquatic organisms, including fish. In aquaculture, understanding the factors that influence GIT microbial communities is critical for improving fish health, optimizing feed efficiency, and enhancing production outcomes. Among these factors, diet composition and water quality are particularly important, as they directly affect nutrient availability and the microbial environment of the GIT. In intensive aquaculture systems, water quality and rearing conditions are closely managed, yet the specific interactions between water systems, diet, and GIT microbiota remain underexplored, particularly in species of commercial importance like rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss). Rainbow trout rank among the most widely cultured freshwater fish worldwide due to their high market value, rapid growth, and adaptability to various farming systems. However, as the demand for sustainable aquaculture grows, there is increasing pressure to replace traditional fishmeal and fish oil ingredients in aquafeeds with alternative protein sources, such as plant-based or animal by-products. While alternative protein diets can reduce the environmental footprint and dependency on wild fish stocks, these diets often present challenges, including imbalanced amino acid profiles, reduced digestibility, and the presence of anti-nutritional factors. Such dietary changes can influence not only fish growth and feed utilization but also the composition and function of the GIT microbiota, which is intricately linked to nutrient metabolism, immune function, and disease resistance. The effects of such dietary shifts on the GIT microbiota, particularly in combination with different rearing water systems, remain poorly understood. Water quality and system design are fundamental variables in aquaculture that influence fish performance, health, and microbial colonization. Recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS) and flow-through systems are commonly used in trout farming, each offering distinct environmental conditions. RAS are characterized by higher levels of water reuse, tighter control over environmental parameters, and often increased microbial densities in the rearing water. In contrast, flow-through systems maintain a continuous supply of fresh water, resulting in lower microbial loads but less control over water quality. These contrasting systems may modulate the GIT microbiota differently by providing distinct microbial communities in the rearing water, which may serve as a reservoir for colonization of the fish GIT. Despite the recognized importance of water systems in shaping microbial communities, their role as a controlling factor in modulating the diversity and function of the GIT microbiota in fish remains underexplored. Recent studies have highlighted the dynamic nature of microbial communities in the GIT, influenced by a combination of host genetics, diet composition, and environmental factors, including water quality. The microbial communities in the GIT of rainbow trout are generally dominated by the phyla Firmicutes, Proteobacteria, and Bacteroidetes, with specific taxa playing roles in digestion, nutrient metabolism, and immune modulation. However, the relative abundance and functional contributions of these microbes can vary widely depending on environmental conditions and dietary inputs. For example, changes in dietary protein sources or amino acid balance can alter microbial composition and metabolic pathways, potentially impacting fish growth and health. Similarly, differences in microbial communities between recirculating and flow-through systems may influence the colonization patterns and functional roles of GIT microbiota. Understanding these interactions is critical for the development of strategies to optimize fish production and health in diverse aquaculture settings. To address these knowledge gaps, the present study investigates the interplay between water systems, diet composition, and GIT microbiota in rainbow trout. Specifically, it examines the effects of balanced and unbalanced alternative protein diets on fish performance and GIT bacterial communities under recirculating and flow-through water systems. The use of balanced diets, supplemented with crystalline amino acids such as lysine, methionine, and threonine, is hypothesized to improve nutrient utilization and growth performance compared to unbalanced diets. Furthermore, the study evaluates whether rearing water serves as a primary source of microbial colonization in the GIT and how this varies between luminal and mucosal compartments. By employing 16S rRNA gene sequencing, the study characterizes the bacterial diversity and composition in both luminal and mucosal samples from the GIT, as well as in the rearing water. The experimental design incorporates a two-phase feeding trial to further elucidate the effects of water systems and diet on fish performance and microbiota. In the first phase, fish were reared exclusively in either a recirculating or flow-through system and fed one of four experimental diets. In the second phase, fish were transferred between systems to assess the adaptability of their GIT microbiota to a new water environment while continuing on the same diet. This approach provides a unique opportunity to disentangle the effects of diet, water system, and their interaction on GIT microbial dynamics and fish performance. The findings from this study aim to advance our understanding of how environmental and dietary factors shape microbial communities in aquaculture systems, with implications for improving fish health, feed efficiency, and sustainable production practices. In summary, this study explores the hypothesis that the water system is a controlling variable in modulating the diversity and function of the GIT microbiota in rainbow trout, with significant implications for fish performance. By integrating dietary and environmental factors, it seeks to elucidate the mechanisms by which water systems influence microbial colonization and function in the GIT, thereby contributing to the development of optimized feeding strategies and rearing practices for sustainable aquaculture. The study was conducted using a two-phase feeding trial to evaluate the effects of diet quality and rearing water systems on the growth performance and gastrointestinal tract (GIT) bacterial composition of rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss). The experimental protocol consisted of two alternative protein diets fed under two distinct water systems (recirculating (RR) and flow-through (FF)) with a crossover design implemented for the second phase. Rainbow trout with an initial mean weight of 12.02 ± 0.61 g were obtained from a commercial hatchery and acclimated to the experimental facilities for two weeks prior to the start of the experiment. Fish were sorted and stocked at a density of 30 fish per tank into 48 experimental tanks, with 12 replicate tanks per dietary treatment. Each tank had a volume of 200 L and was supplied with either recirculating or flow-through water based on the assigned rearing system. Water temperature was maintained at 15 ± 1°C with dissolved oxygen levels above 7 mg/L throughout the experimental period. The two alternative protein diets were formulated to contain 38% digestible protein and 20% fat. One diet was based on animal protein as the primary protein source, and the other was based on plant protein. Each diet was further subdivided into two formulations: one balanced with crystalline amino acids (lysine, methionine, and threonine) to meet the essential amino acid requirements of rainbow trout, and one unbalanced to serve as a suboptimal control. The feeds were produced as sinking pellets using a cold extrusion method and stored under vacuum-sealed conditions until use. Feed intake was monitored, and fish were hand-fed to apparent satiation three times daily. Phase 1 of the study lasted for 8 weeks, during which fish in each tank were maintained in their assigned water system and fed one of the four dietary treatments. At the end of Phase 1, fish from each tank were randomly split into two groups. One group was transferred to a new tank with the opposing water system (i.e., fish from RR were moved to FF and vice versa), while the other group remained in their original tank and system. Both groups continued to receive their assigned diets for an additional 8 weeks during Phase 2 of the study, bringing the total duration of the experiment to 16 weeks. At the end of the trial, three fish per tank were randomly selected for sampling. Fish were euthanized with an overdose of tricaine methanesulfonate (MS-222) buffered with sodium bicarbonate (at a concentration of 200 mg/L), and body weight, length, and body indexes (hepatosomatic index (HSI) and viscerosomatic index (VSI)) were recorded. Whole-body proximate composition was determined by standard analytical methods. Crude protein was measured using the Kjeldahl method, crude fat by ether extraction, and moisture by drying at 105°C to constant weight. Gross energy content was analyzed using a bomb calorimeter. For microbiota analysis, both luminal and mucosal samples were collected from the anterior intestine. Luminal samples were obtained by gently flushing the intestinal contents with sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), while mucosal samples were collected by scraping the intestinal mucosa with sterile scalpel blades. Samples were immediately frozen on dry ice and stored at −80°C until DNA extraction. In addition, 500 mL of water was collected from each tank at the time of sampling for analysis of the bacterial community composition in the rearing water. Feed samples from each dietary treatment were also collected to assess the microbial composition of the feed. Total genomic DNA was extracted from luminal, mucosal, water, and feed samples using a commercial DNA extraction kit (e.g., Qiagen DNeasy PowerSoil Kit) following the manufacturer’s protocol with minor modifications to enhance yield and quality. The concentration and purity of extracted DNA were assessed using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer and agarose gel electrophoresis. The V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene was amplified using universal primers (e.g., 515F and 806R) with Illumina adapter overhangs. PCR amplification was performed in triplicate for each sample to minimize amplification bias. Amplicons were pooled, purified using AMPure XP beads, and quantified using a Qubit fluorometer. Sequencing libraries were prepared and sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq platform with a 2 × 250 bp paired-end configuration. Raw sequencing data were processed using the QIIME2 pipeline. Reads were quality-filtered, trimmed, and denoised, and operational taxonomic units (OTUs) were assigned based on 97% sequence similarity using the SILVA database as the reference. Alpha diversity metrics, including Shannon and Simpson indices, were calculated to assess within-sample diversity, while beta diversity was evaluated using Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and visualized through non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS). Statistical analyses of microbial community composition were conducted using analysis of similarity (ANOSIM) and permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA). Growth performance and body composition data were analyzed using a two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) to evaluate the effects of diet, rearing system, and their interactions. Microbial composition data were analyzed using multivariate techniques, with tank serving as the experimental unit. All statistical analyses were performed using R software, with significance set at P < 0.05. Ethical approval for the study was obtained from the institutional animal care and use committee, and all procedures were conducted in accordance with relevant guidelines for the care and use of aquatic animals in research. The results of this study highlight the complex interplay between diet composition, water system type, and gastrointestinal tract (GIT) bacterial diversity in rainbow trout. Key findings are presented below, focusing on fish performance metrics, bacterial community composition, and the influence of rearing water. Fish performance was significantly influenced by diet, diet quality, and water system. Fish weight was affected by all three factors, showing significant differences based on diet (P = 0.0008), diet quality (P = 0.0030), and water system (P < 0.0010). Fish fed balanced diets exhibited higher growth rates compared to those fed unbalanced diets, regardless of the specific source of dietary protein. Similarly, fish reared in the flow-through (FF) system performed better in terms of growth than those reared in the recirculating (RR) system. Body fat content was also significantly impacted by diet (P = 0.0008), diet quality (P = 0.0041), and water system (P = 0.0177). Fish fed balanced diets and those in the FF system exhibited higher body fat percentages compared to their counterparts. Feed intake, however, was primarily influenced by the water system (P = 0.0008), with fish in the FF system consuming more feed than those in the RR system.
