Schizophrenia is a chronic and debilitating mental health disorder that significantly impacts individuals’ functioning and quality of life. Characterized by a combination of positive symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions, negative symptoms including social withdrawal and lack of motivation, and general psychopathology symptoms like anxiety and depression, schizophrenia requires long-term management and care. This disorder not only imposes a substantial burden on patients and their families but also generates significant economic costs for healthcare systems globally. Consequently, understanding the impact of schizophrenia on patients’ health-related quality of life (HRQoL) is crucial for informing clinical decision-making and resource allocation. Health utility scores, which quantify individuals’ preferences for different health states, are essential for conducting cost–utility analyses—a common type of economic evaluation used to assess healthcare interventions. These scores are typically derived from generic, preference-based measures of HRQoL, such as the five-level EuroQol five-dimensional (EQ-5D-5L) instrument and the Short Form six-dimensional (SF-6D) instrument. Both tools are widely used to generate quality-adjusted life years (QALYs), a standard metric for evaluating the cost-effectiveness of medical treatments. The EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D instruments are particularly valuable because they provide utility scores on a single index scale, enabling comparisons across different diseases and interventions. Despite their utility, direct collection of EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D data is not always feasible in clinical or research settings due to time, cost, or logistical constraints. In such cases, mapping—also referred to as cross-walking—offers a viable alternative. Mapping involves using statistical models to estimate utility scores based on other commonly collected clinical or disease-specific measures. This approach is especially relevant in the context of schizophrenia, where disease-specific instruments such as the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) are routinely used to assess symptom severity. The PANSS is a clinician-administered tool designed to evaluate the severity of positive, negative, and general psychopathology symptoms in individuals with schizophrenia. Given its widespread use in both clinical practice and research, the PANSS provides a rich source of data that can potentially be leveraged to estimate utility scores. However, there is limited evidence on how PANSS scores can be mapped onto generic utility instruments like the EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D. Furthermore, existing studies on this topic have predominantly been conducted in Western populations, leaving a significant gap in understanding how these mapping algorithms perform in non-Western contexts such as Asia. Singapore, a multicultural city-state in Southeast Asia, provides a unique setting for studying the relationship between schizophrenia symptoms and HRQoL. The country’s healthcare system is characterized by a mix of public and private funding, and there is growing interest in conducting cost–utility analyses to guide resource allocation. However, the availability of utility data for individuals with schizophrenia remains limited. Developing reliable mapping algorithms for this population would not only address this gap but also support the broader application of economic evaluations in mental health care. The current study aims to address these gaps by mapping PANSS scores onto EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D utility scores in a sample of patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorder in Singapore. Specifically, we sought to develop and validate statistical models for predicting utility scores based on PANSS subscales and patient demographics, such as age and gender. To ensure the robustness of our findings, we employed three different regression methods—ordinary least squares (OLS), censored least absolute deviations, and Tobit regression—and evaluated multiple model specifications. By providing a practical method for estimating utility scores from PANSS data, this study has the potential to benefit both clinicians and researchers. For clinicians, the mapping algorithms can serve as a tool for assessing the broader impact of schizophrenia symptoms on patients’ HRQoL, facilitating more informed treatment decisions. For researchers, the ability to estimate utility scores in the absence of direct EQ-5D-5L or SF-6D data can enhance the feasibility of conducting cost–utility analyses, ultimately supporting evidence-based policy-making in mental health care. In this paper, we present the results of our mapping study, highlighting the best-performing models for predicting EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D utility scores. We also discuss the implications of our findings for clinical practice and research, as well as the challenges and limitations associated with mapping approaches. By bridging the gap between disease-specific and generic HRQoL measures, this study contributes to the growing body of evidence on the economic evaluation of mental health interventions and underscores the importance of integrating HRQoL considerations into the care of individuals with schizophrenia. This study focused on developing mapping algorithms to predict utility scores derived from the EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D instruments using the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) in patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorder. The study was conducted in a tertiary psychiatric hospital in Singapore, and the methodology is described in detail below. Study Design and Participants A cross-sectional design was employed, and participants were recruited from adult inpatients and outpatients diagnosed with schizophrenia spectrum disorders according to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th edition (DSM-5). Inclusion criteria included being between 18 and 65 years of age, having a confirmed diagnosis of schizophrenia spectrum disorder, and being able to provide informed consent. Patients with severe cognitive impairments or comorbid neurological disorders that could interfere with their ability to complete study assessments were excluded. A total of 239 participants were recruited for this study. Sociodemographic and clinical data, including age, gender, and illness duration, were collected. The PANSS was administered to assess symptom severity, while utility scores were obtained using the EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D instruments. Ethical approval for the study was obtained from the relevant institutional review board, and all participants provided written informed consent before participation. Instruments and Measures Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) The PANSS is a clinician-rated instrument used to evaluate the severity of schizophrenia symptoms. It consists of 30 items grouped into three subscales: positive symptoms (7 items), negative symptoms (7 items), and general psychopathology (16 items). Each item is rated on a scale from 1 (absent) to 7 (extreme), with higher scores indicating greater symptom severity. For this study, the PANSS subscales were further divided into five factors based on prior literature: positive symptoms, negative symptoms, excitement, depression, and cognitive symptoms. EQ-5D-5L The EQ-5D-5L is a preference-based measure of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) developed by the EuroQol Group. It assesses five dimensions of health (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression), each rated on five levels of severity. Utility scores were derived using the Singapore-specific value set, which ranges from -0.769 to 1, with higher scores indicating better health-related quality of life. SF-6D The SF-6D is another preference-based HRQoL instrument derived from the Short Form-36 Health Survey (SF-36). It consists of six dimensions (physical functioning, role limitations, social functioning, pain, mental health, and vitality), each with 4–6 response levels. Utility scores range from 0.296 to 1, with higher scores indicating better HRQoL. In this study, the SF-6D utility scores were calculated based on an algorithm developed for the Singapore population. Statistical Analysis Mapping Approach The primary objective of this study was to develop mapping algorithms to predict EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D utility scores from PANSS scores. Three regression methods were used to model the relationship between PANSS subscales and utility scores: ordinary least squares (OLS), censored least absolute deviations (CLAD), and Tobit regression. These methods were chosen to account for the properties of utility data, which are often bounded and skewed. Model Specifications Six model specifications were tested for each regression method: 1. Total PANSS score as the independent variable. 2. Three PANSS subscales (positive, negative, and general psychopathology symptoms). 3. Five PANSS factors (positive, negative, excitement, depression, and cognitive symptoms). 4. Total PANSS score with age and gender included as covariates. 5. Three PANSS subscales with age and gender as covariates. 6. Five PANSS factors with age and gender as covariates. In total, 18 regression models (three regression methods × six model specifications) were developed for each utility measure (EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D). Model Selection Criteria The performance of the models was evaluated using the following criteria: 1. Mean absolute error (MAE) – the average absolute difference between predicted and observed utility scores. 2. Mean square error (MSE) – the average squared difference between predicted and observed utility scores. 3. R-squared (R²) – the proportion of variance in observed utility scores explained by the model. 4. Adjusted R-squared (adjusted R²) – the proportion of variance explained, adjusted for the number of predictors in the model. The model with the smallest MAE and MSE, and the largest R² and adjusted R², was selected as the best model for each utility measure. Validation To assess the robustness of the selected models, tenfold cross-validation was performed. The dataset was randomly divided into ten subsets of approximately equal size. Each subset served as the validation set once, while the remaining nine subsets were used for model training. The cross-validated MAE and MSE were reported. Software All statistical analyses were conducted using Stata version 15 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA). Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05 for all analyses. A total of 239 participants diagnosed with schizophrenia spectrum disorder were included in the study. The mean age of the sample was 39.7 years (SD = 10.3), with approximately equal representation across genders. The utility scores derived from the EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D instruments revealed mean values of 0.81 (SD = 0.16) and 0.68 (SD = 0.12), respectively. These scores indicate generally moderate-to-high health-related quality of life among the participants, though variations were observed based on the severity of symptoms as measured by the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS). For mapping PANSS scores to EQ-5D-5L utility scores, a series of regression models were tested, including ordinary least squares (OLS), censored least absolute deviations (CLAD), and Tobit regression methods. Across all models, the OLS regression approach consistently demonstrated superior performance based on the pre-specified criteria, including the smallest mean absolute error (MAE), mean square error (MSE), and the largest R² and adjusted R² values. The optimal model for predicting EQ-5D-5L utility scores included the three PANSS subscale scores—positive, negative, and general psychopathology symptoms—as well as age and gender as covariates. This model yielded an R² value of 0.42, indicating that 42% of the variance in EQ-5D-5L utility scores could be explained by the predictors. The inclusion of age and gender improved the model fit slightly but significantly, suggesting that these demographic factors play a modest role in influencing health-related quality of life in this population. The final OLS model for EQ-5D-5L had an MAE of 0.091 and an MSE of 0.015. For the SF-6D utility scores, the analyses revealed that the best-performing model was also based on the OLS regression method. In this case, the model included five PANSS subscales—positive, negative, excitement, depression, and cognitive—as predictors. This model demonstrated an R² value of 0.38, with an MAE of 0.074 and an MSE of 0.009, indicating slightly lower predictive accuracy compared to the EQ-5D-5L mapping models. The inclusion of the additional PANSS subscales in the SF-6D mapping model highlights the complexity of the SF-6D utility measure, which may capture broader dimensions of health-related quality of life influenced by factors such as mood and cognitive functioning. Unlike the EQ-5D-5L mapping model, demographic variables such as age and gender did not significantly improve the prediction of SF-6D utility scores and were therefore excluded from the final model. Comparative analyses of the three regression methods (OLS, CLAD, and Tobit) confirmed that OLS regression consistently outperformed the other two approaches for both EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D utility score predictions. While CLAD and Tobit models are often used to address issues related to the bounded nature of utility scores, their application in this study did not yield improvements in model fit or predictive accuracy. This finding suggests that, within this dataset, the linearity assumption inherent in OLS regression was appropriate and sufficient for capturing the relationship between PANSS subscale scores and utility scores. Further examination of the individual predictors within the final models revealed several important findings. For the EQ-5D-5L mapping model, all three PANSS subscales (positive, negative, and general psychopathology) were statistically significant predictors (p < 0.05), with higher scores on these subscales associated with lower predicted utility

The nucleosome is the fundamental repeating unit of chromatin, serving as the primary level of DNA organization in eukaryotic cells. It consists of approximately 147 base pairs of DNA wrapped around an octameric histone core composed of two copies each of histones H2A, H2B, H3, and H4. The nucleosome plays a critical role in regulating access to DNA for processes such as transcription, replication, and repair, and its structural and dynamic properties are crucial for maintaining genomic stability and facilitating these essential cellular functions. While the histone octamer provides a relatively stable core, the dynamics of the DNA wrapped around it, particularly at the entry and exit regions, contribute significantly to chromatin's overall behavior. These DNA dynamics are influenced by the specific composition of the histone proteins, including the incorporation of histone variants, which can confer unique structural and functional properties to nucleosomes. One such histone variant, CENP-A (centromere protein A), is a centromere-specific H3 variant that replaces canonical H3 in nucleosomes at centromeric regions. CENP-A nucleosomes are critical for centromere function and assembly of the kinetochore, the protein complex that mediates chromosome segregation during cell division. Despite being structurally similar to H3, CENP-A possesses unique biochemical and biophysical characteristics that distinguish it from canonical H3 and are essential for its role in centromere identity and function. For instance, CENP-A nucleosomes exhibit altered stability, DNA wrapping dynamics, and higher-order chromatin organization compared to their H3-containing counterparts. Understanding the molecular basis of these differences is key to unraveling how CENP-A nucleosomes contribute to centromere-specific functions and how their unique properties are exploited during cell division. Among the distinguishing features of CENP-A, its N-terminal tail and αN helix have been implicated in modulating nucleosome structure and dynamics. Notably, sequence differences between CENP-A and H3 in this region can influence interactions with DNA, chromatin-associated proteins, and higher-order chromatin architecture. In particular, the αN helix of canonical H3 contains two arginine (Arg) residues at positions that are replaced by lysine (Lys) residues in CENP-A. Arginine and lysine are both positively charged amino acids, yet they differ in size, hydrogen-bonding capacity, and interaction dynamics. These differences could have profound effects on the interaction between the histone core and the negatively charged DNA, particularly at the entry and exit regions of the nucleosome where the DNA is less tightly associated with the core and more prone to fluctuations. Indeed, the entry and exit regions of nucleosomal DNA are known to play critical roles in processes such as nucleosome remodeling, transcription factor binding, and chromatin fiber compaction, making their dynamics an important area of study. Recent advances in computational and experimental techniques have provided new insights into the impact of histone variants on nucleosome dynamics. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, in particular, have emerged as a powerful tool for investigating the detailed structural and dynamic properties of nucleosomes at atomic resolution. These simulations enable the exploration of how specific amino acid substitutions, such as those found in histone variants, affect nucleosome stability, DNA flexibility, and histone-DNA interactions. In parallel, experimental approaches such as exonuclease assays can complement computational findings by providing biochemical evidence of nucleosomal DNA accessibility and flexibility. In this study, we employed MD simulations and exonuclease III assays to investigate the dynamics of nucleosomes containing either canonical H3 or its centromere-specific variant CENP-A. Our MD simulations revealed that, while the histone core remained structurally stable for both nucleosome types, the DNA at the entry and exit regions exhibited markedly different dynamics. Specifically, the DNA associated with CENP-A nucleosomes displayed significantly larger fluctuations compared to DNA in H3 nucleosomes, suggesting increased flexibility at these regions in the presence of CENP-A. Detailed analysis of the MD trajectories highlighted the role of two key residues in the αN helix of H3—Arg81 and Arg83—that are replaced by Lys residues in CENP-A. The ability of Arg to form stable hydrogen bonds with DNA was found to be a critical factor in suppressing DNA flexibility at the entry and exit regions of H3 nucleosomes. In contrast, the substitution of Arg by Lys in CENP-A reduced the formation of such hydrogen bonds, leading to enhanced DNA dynamics. To validate these computational findings, we performed exonuclease III assays to assess the susceptibility of nucleosomal DNA to enzymatic digestion. Consistent with the simulation results, replacement of the two Arg residues in H3 with Lys residues resulted in increased endonuclease susceptibility, indicating greater accessibility and flexibility of the DNA ends. These findings suggest that the substitution of Arg by Lys in the αN helix of CENP-A contributes to the unique dynamic properties of CENP-A nucleosomes, which may be important for specific centromeric functions such as kinetochore assembly and chromosome segregation. The dynamic differences between H3 and CENP-A nucleosomes likely have important implications for chromatin organization and function in centromeric and non-centromeric regions. While canonical H3 nucleosomes are optimized for stable and compact chromatin states that restrict DNA accessibility, the increased flexibility of CENP-A nucleosomes may facilitate the specialized chromatin architecture and protein interactions required at centromeres. By elucidating the molecular basis of these differences, our study provides new insights into the structural and functional diversity of nucleosomes and highlights the importance of histone variants in regulating chromatin dynamics. To investigate the dynamics of nucleosomes containing canonical histone H3 or its centromere-specific variant CENP-A, we employed molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and biochemical assays. Below, we describe the computational and experimental methods used in this study in detail. Molecular Dynamics Simulations The structures of the canonical H3 and CENP-A nucleosomes were obtained from previously resolved crystal structures available in the Protein Data Bank (PDB). The H3 nucleosome structure (PDB ID: XXXX) and the CENP-A nucleosome structure (PDB ID: YYYY) were used as starting points for the simulations. To ensure the comparability of the two systems, both nucleosomes contained 147 base pairs of DNA, and the histone octamer was assembled with H2A, H2B, H4, and either H3 or CENP-A. Missing residues and atoms in the structures were added using the MODELLER software, and protonation states of ionizable residues were assigned based on physiological pH using PDB2PQR. The nucleosome systems were solvated in a cubic box of explicit water molecules using the TIP3P water model, with a minimum buffer distance of 12 Å between the nucleosome and the edge of the box. Sodium and chloride ions were added to neutralize the system and mimic physiological ionic strength at 150 mM. The final system contained approximately XXXX atoms for each nucleosome. MD simulations were performed using the AMBER software package with the ff14SB force field for proteins and the bsc1 force field for nucleic acids. Prior to production runs, energy minimization was conducted in two stages: first, the solvent and ions were minimized while the nucleosome was restrained, and second, the entire system was minimized without restraints. The systems were then gradually heated from 0 K to 300 K over a 50 ps period using a Langevin thermostat, followed by equilibration for 1 ns in the NPT ensemble (constant number of particles, pressure, and temperature). During equilibration, positional restraints were applied to the protein and DNA heavy atoms, which were gradually reduced. Production simulations were run for 100 ns for the H3 nucleosome system and 50 ns for the CENP-A nucleosome system, with a time step of 2 fs. Periodic boundary conditions were applied, and long-range electrostatics were treated with the Particle Mesh Ewald (PME) method. Covalent bonds involving hydrogen atoms were constrained using the SHAKE algorithm. Trajectories were saved every 10 ps for subsequent analysis. To analyze DNA flexibility, root-mean-square fluctuations (RMSF) of DNA atoms were calculated using the cpptraj module in AMBER. Hydrogen bond analysis was performed to identify interactions between basic amino acid residues in the histone αN helix and DNA at the entry and exit regions. DNA end fluctuations were analyzed by measuring the distance between the DNA terminal bases and the histone core over time. Site-Directed Mutation Simulations To assess the role of specific residues in regulating DNA flexibility, additional MD simulations were performed on mutated nucleosome systems. In the H3 nucleosome, the two arginine residues in the αN helix (ArgX and ArgY) were replaced with lysine residues to mimic their counterparts in CENP-A. Similarly, in the CENP-A nucleosome, the corresponding lysine residues were replaced with arginines. These mutations were introduced using PyMOL and confirmed by energy minimization and equilibration prior to production runs. The same simulation protocol described above was applied to these systems. Comparative analyses of hydrogen bonding and DNA dynamics were conducted to evaluate the impact of these substitutions. Exonuclease III Assays To experimentally validate the computational findings, exonuclease III digestion assays were performed to assess the flexibility of nucleosomal DNA ends. Recombinant histone octamers containing either H3 or CENP-A were reconstituted using standard protocols. Histone proteins were purified from bacterial expression systems, refolded, and assembled into octamers by salt gradient dialysis. 147 bp Widom 601 DNA, labeled with 5′-fluorescent tags, was used to reconstitute nucleosomes by salt dialysis. The nucleosome reconstitution was confirmed by native polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE). For the exonuclease III assay, nucleosome samples (approximately 50 nM) were incubated with varying concentrations of exonuclease III (New England Biolabs) at 37°C in a buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 10 mM MgCl2, and 50 mM NaCl. Aliquots were removed at specific time points (0, 5, 10, 20, and 30 minutes), and the reactions were stopped by adding EDTA to a final concentration of 20 mM. The digestion products were resolved on a 10% denaturing PAGE gel and visualized using a fluorescence imaging system. To test the effects of specific residues, mutant histone octamers were prepared by substituting the two arginine residues in H3 with lysine (H3-RXKX) or the corresponding lysine residues in CENP-A with arginine (CENP-A-KXRK). These mutant octamers were reconstituted into nucleosomes with 147 bp DNA and subjected to the same exonuclease digestion protocol. Band intensities from PAGE gels were quantified using ImageJ, and the extent of digestion was calculated as a percentage of the total DNA signal. Statistical Analysis All simulation data were processed and analyzed using Python scripts and the AMBER cpptraj module. Statistical comparisons between systems were performed using two-tailed t-tests, with p-values less than 0.05 considered statistically significant. For the exonuclease III assays, digestion rates were compared between conditions using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation from at least three independent experiments. Through this combination of molecular dynamics simulations and biochemical assays, we systematically investigated the role of arginine and lysine residues in modulating nucleosomal DNA flexibility, providing mechanistic insights into the structural and functional differences between canonical and centromeric nucleosomes. Molecular dynamics simulations were performed to investigate the structural and dynamic properties of nucleosomes containing either canonical H3 or the centromeric variant CENP-A. These simulations revealed significant differences in the behavior of the nucleosomal DNA at the entry and exit regions between the two nucleosome types. While the histone cores of both nucleosomes remained structurally stable over the simulation periods (100 ns for the H3 nucleosome and 50 ns for the CENP-A nucleosome), the DNA wrapping around the histone core exhibited notable differences in flexibility. The DNA regions nearest to the entry and exit points showed the greatest fluctuations in both nucleosome types, with the CENP-A nucleosome displaying markedly higher flexibility compared to the H3 nucleosome. Specifically, the root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF) analysis of the DNA backbone revealed that approximately 20–25 base pairs (bp) of DNA at both the entry and exit regions of the CENP-A nucleosome exhibited significantly larger fluctuations than the corresponding regions of the H3 nucleosome. Nausea and vomiting are among the most distressing adverse effects experienced by patients undergoing chemotherapy or surgical procedures that require anesthesia. These symptoms can significantly impair quality of life, delay treatment schedules, and contribute to poor clinical outcomes. To manage this, serotonin 5-hydroxytryptamine 3 (5-HT3) receptor antagonists have become a cornerstone of antiemetic therapy. These agents, such as ondansetron, dolasetron, and palonosetron, are highly effective in preventing acute and delayed chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, as well as postoperative nausea and vomiting. By selectively inhibiting 5-HT3 receptors in the gastrointestinal tract and central nervous system, these medications provide targeted symptom relief and have become standard components of antiemetic protocols. Despite their efficacy in controlling nausea and vomiting, 5-HT3 receptor antagonists are associated with potential cardiac adverse effects, raising concerns about their safety, particularly in vulnerable populations. The most frequently reported cardiac concerns include prolongation of the QT interval on the electrocardiogram (ECG), which reflects delayed ventricular repolarization and increases the risk of life-threatening arrhythmias such as torsades de pointes. Other cardiac abnormalities, such as bradycardia and conduction disturbances, have also been documented. These risks are particularly concerning for patients who already have cardiovascular comorbidities, electrolyte imbalances, or are receiving other QT-prolonging medications. Consequently, there is a critical need to balance the antiemetic benefits of 5-HT3 receptor antagonists with their potential to cause cardiac harm. Although guidelines for the use of 5-HT3 receptor antagonists often recommend ECG monitoring for patients at heightened risk of cardiac events, the clinical utility and effectiveness of such monitoring remain poorly understood. ECG monitoring is resource-intensive and may not always translate to improved patient outcomes. Furthermore, the degree to which different 5-HT3 receptor antagonists vary in their cardiac safety profiles remains unclear, with some studies suggesting that newer agents like palonosetron may have a lower propensity to cause QT prolongation compared to older agents like ondansetron and dolasetron. However, the evidence base supporting these claims is limited and often conflicting. In this context, understanding the interventions that can mitigate the cardiac risks associated with 5-HT3 receptor antagonists is of paramount importance. Identifying effective strategies to minimize cardiac harm could inform clinical practice, enhance patient safety, and optimize the use of these essential antiemetic agents. In particular, the role of ECG monitoring as a tool to detect and prevent cardiac complications requires careful evaluation. While ECG monitoring is widely used in clinical practice, its ability to meaningfully reduce the risk of adverse cardiac events in patients receiving 5-HT3 receptor antagonists has not been systematically established. Moreover, the relative safety of different 5-HT3 receptor antagonists remains an area of ongoing debate and warrants further investigation. The purpose of this systematic review was to address these critical gaps in knowledge. Specifically, we sought to identify and evaluate interventions aimed at reducing the cardiac risk associated with 5-HT3 receptor antagonists in patients undergoing chemotherapy or surgery. Given the widespread use of these agents and the potential severity of their cardiac side effects, understanding the effectiveness of interventions such as ECG monitoring is essential to guide clinical decision-making. Furthermore, by comparing the cardiac safety profiles of different 5-HT3 receptor antagonists, we aimed to provide insights into whether certain agents may offer safer alternatives for patients at high risk of cardiac complications. To achieve these objectives, we conducted a comprehensive search of the literature, examining randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomized clinical trials (NRCTs) that assessed interventions to monitor or mitigate cardiac risks associated with 5-HT3 receptor antagonists. We focused on outcomes such as arrhythmias, changes in ECG parameters (e.g., QT interval), and other markers of cardiac harm. Additionally, we assessed the overall effectiveness of ECG monitoring as an intervention to detect and manage cardiac abnormalities in this patient population. Our findings revealed a paucity of high-quality evidence addressing the cardiac safety of 5-HT3 receptor antagonists and the role of ECG monitoring. Only three studies met the inclusion criteria for this review, highlighting the limited research in this area. The studies included two RCTs and one NRCT, all of which compared the cardiac effects of different 5-HT3 receptor antagonists using ECG monitoring. While minor changes in ECG parameters were observed in some cases, these changes were generally not clinically significant, and no substantial differences were detected between the agents at the time points examined. Importantly, the overall utility of ECG monitoring remains unclear, as all included patients were subject to ECG evaluation, and no direct comparisons were made between monitored and unmonitored patients. This review underscores the urgent need for further research to better understand the cardiac safety of 5-HT3 receptor antagonists and the effectiveness of interventions such as ECG monitoring. The limited number of studies and their modest sample sizes highlight a significant evidence gap, particularly in the context of high-risk patient populations. Addressing these gaps will require well-designed clinical trials that directly evaluate the impact of ECG monitoring on patient outcomes and explore potential strategies to mitigate cardiac risks. Additionally, further exploration of the comparative safety profiles of different 5-HT3 receptor antagonists is warranted to guide the selection of antiemetic agents in clinical practice. In summary, while 5-HT3 receptor antagonists remain essential tools in the management of nausea and vomiting, their potential to cause cardiac harm necessitates a careful and evidence-based approach to their use. This systematic review provides a foundation for future research and highlights the need for targeted interventions to minimize cardiac risks in patients receiving these medications. By addressing these challenges, it may be possible to optimize the safety and efficacy of antiemetic therapy in oncology and perioperative care. This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. The protocol for the review was registered in the PROSPERO database (registration number: CRD42013003565). The following methods were employed to identify, assess, and synthesize evidence regarding interventions to mitigate the cardiac risks associated with serotonin (5-HT3) receptor antagonists in patients undergoing chemotherapy or surgery. Eligibility Criteria We included studies that met the following criteria: (1) the study population consisted of adults (≥18 years) receiving chemotherapy or undergoing surgery requiring anesthesia; (2) the intervention involved the use of serotonin (5-HT3) receptor antagonists, such as ondansetron, granisetron, dolasetron, or palonosetron, either alone or in combination with other treatments; (3) an intervention or strategy was implemented to monitor or mitigate cardiac risks, including arrhythmias or other adverse cardiac events; (4) the study reported outcomes related to cardiac function, such as electrocardiogram (ECG) findings, arrhythmia incidence, QT interval prolongation, or other cardiovascular outcomes; and (5) the study design included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized controlled trials (NRCTs), cohort studies, or case-control studies. We excluded case reports, studies in pediatric populations, studies examining serotonin receptor antagonists for non-chemotherapy or non-surgical indications, and studies without relevant cardiac outcomes. Information Sources and Search Strategy A comprehensive search strategy was developed with the assistance of a medical librarian. Electronic databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and Scopus, were searched from their inception through June 2023. Additional searches were conducted in clinical trial registries, including ClinicalTrials.gov and the World Health Organization (WHO) International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). References of included studies, relevant systematic reviews, and guidelines were hand-searched to identify additional eligible studies. The search strategy included terms related to serotonin receptor antagonists (e.g., ondansetron, granisetron, dolasetron, palonosetron), chemotherapy, cardiac adverse events (e.g., arrhythmia, QT interval, cardiac harm), and monitoring interventions (e.g., ECG). Both controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH terms) and free-text terms were used. The full search strategies for each database are provided in the supplementary material. Study Selection The records identified through the database and registry searches were imported into a reference management software, where duplicates were removed. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts for relevance based on the predefined eligibility criteria. Full-text articles of potentially eligible studies were retrieved and assessed independently by the same two reviewers. Discrepancies during both stages of screening were resolved through discussion or by consulting a third reviewer. The study selection process was documented and presented in a PRISMA flow diagram. Data Collection and Management Data from eligible studies were extracted independently and in duplicate using a standardized data extraction form. The form captured the following information: study characteristics (e.g., authors, year of publication, country, study design), participant characteristics (e.g., age, sex, clinical context), intervention details (e.g., type, dosage, and administration route of 5-HT3 receptor antagonist, cardiac monitoring or mitigation strategy), comparator details (e.g., alternative antiemetics or monitoring strategies), and outcome measures (e.g., ECG findings, arrhythmia rates, QT interval changes, and mortality). Any disagreements between reviewers were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. Risk of Bias Assessment The quality of included studies was assessed independently by two reviewers using the Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care (EPOC) group’s risk-of-bias tool. This tool evaluates bias across several domains, including random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, completeness of outcome data, selective reporting, and other potential sources of bias. For non-randomized studies, additional considerations included confounding, selection bias, and comparability of groups. Each domain was rated as low, high, or unclear risk of bias, and disagreements were resolved by discussion or a third reviewer. The overall risk of bias for each study was summarized. Data Analysis and Synthesis Due to the limited number of studies identified and heterogeneity in study designs, interventions, and outcome measures, a meta-analysis was not conducted. Instead, a narrative synthesis of the findings was performed. Results were grouped and summarized by type of intervention and cardiac outcomes. Where possible, quantitative data on cardiac outcomes, such as changes in QT interval or arrhythmia incidence, were presented alongside qualitative descriptions of study findings. Sensitivity Analysis and Subgroup Exploration Given the small number of included studies, sensitivity analyses were not performed. Subgroup analyses based on specific 5-HT3 receptor antagonists or patient populations (e.g., those with pre-existing cardiac conditions) were not feasible due to insufficient data. Assessment of Publication Bias Publication bias was not formally assessed using funnel plots or statistical tests, as the limited number of included studies precluded meaningful analysis. Reporting of Results The findings of the included studies were synthesized and reported in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Key outcomes were presented in tables, and a narrative description of the evidence was provided. Limitations of the included studies and the overall evidence base were discussed. Ethical Considerations As this study was a systematic review of previously published data, no ethical approval or informed consent was required. Following an extensive search of electronic databases, trial registries, and references, 7,637 titles and abstracts were screened for eligibility. Of these, 1,554 full-text articles were assessed, and three studies meeting the inclusion criteria were identified. The included studies consisted of two randomized clinical trials (RCTs) and one non-randomized clinical trial (NRCT). All studies investigated interventions intended to mitigate the cardiac risk associated with serotonin 5-hydroxytryptamine 3 (5-HT3) receptor antagonists in patients undergoing chemotherapy or surgery. The first RCT compared the cardiac safety profiles of palonosetron and ondansetron. Electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring was used as the primary intervention for detecting cardiac abnormalities. No significant differences were observed in ECG parameters, including PR, QT, and corrected QT (QTc) intervals, between the two drugs at 15 minutes, 24 hours, and one week post-administration. Furthermore, no clinically significant arrhythmias were reported in either group during the study period. Four deaths occurred during the trial, but the investigators determined that these were unrelated to the administration of either palonosetron or ondansetron. No additional cardiac events of concern were reported. The second RCT evaluated the cardiac effects of dolasetron compared to ondansetron in a similar patient population, with ECG monitoring again serving as the primary intervention. The study found no significant differences in cardiac outcomes or ECG parameters between the two groups at the same time intervals as the first RCT (15 minutes, 24 hours, and one week post-administration). Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a life-threatening vascular condition characterized by localized dilation of the abdominal aorta. It is a progressive disorder often associated with significant morbidity and mortality due to its potential to rupture, leading to life-threatening hemorrhage. AAA is primarily observed in the elderly population, particularly among males, and its pathogenesis involves a complex interplay of genetic, environmental, and molecular factors. Despite its clinical significance, effective pharmacological interventions are lacking, and surgical repair remains the primary treatment option for patients with large or symptomatic aneurysms. This underscores the urgent need to better understand the molecular mechanisms underlying AAA development and progression in order to identify novel therapeutic targets. AAA is widely recognized as an inflammatory vascular disorder. The pathological hallmarks of AAA include chronic inflammation, extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation, vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) apoptosis, and remodeling of the vascular wall. These processes are driven by an imbalance between proteolytic enzymes, such as matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), and their endogenous inhibitors, as well as by persistent immune activation. A growing body of evidence indicates that innate immune signaling pathways play a crucial role in orchestrating this inflammatory response. Among these, Toll-like receptors (TLRs), a family of pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), have emerged as key mediators in the recognition of tissue damage and the initiation of inflammatory cascades. However, the specific role of TLR2, a member of this receptor family, in the pathogenesis of AAA remains poorly understood. TLR2 is predominantly expressed on the surface of immune and vascular cells, including macrophages, endothelial cells, and VSMCs. It recognizes a diverse array of ligands, including both pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), which are released during tissue injury. Upon ligand binding, TLR2 activates downstream signaling pathways involving key transcription factors such as nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) and activator protein-1 (AP-1). This results in the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and other mediators that contribute to tissue remodeling and immune activation. While TLR2 signaling has been extensively studied in infectious and autoimmune diseases, its role in vascular inflammation and remodeling in the context of AAA has not been fully elucidated. Recent studies have highlighted the potential involvement of TLR2 in vascular pathologies. Elevated expression of TLR2 has been reported in human atherosclerotic plaques and is associated with increased inflammation and plaque instability. Similarly, studies in murine models of vascular injury have demonstrated that TLR2 contributes to neointimal hyperplasia and vascular remodeling. These findings suggest that TLR2 may play a pivotal role in the inflammatory processes underlying AAA. However, whether TLR2 directly contributes to the development and progression of AAA, and whether targeting TLR2 can attenuate these processes, remains an open question. In this study, we sought to investigate the role of TLR2 in the pathogenesis of AAA and to explore the therapeutic potential of TLR2 antagonism. Our findings reveal that TLR2 expression is markedly upregulated in human AAA tissues, along with its endogenous ligands, suggesting a potential role for TLR2 signaling in promoting the chronic inflammation and vascular remodeling characteristic of AAA. Using mouse models of AAA, we demonstrate that neutralization of TLR2 not only prevents the formation of AAA but also induces regression of established aneurysms. These protective effects are associated with a significant reduction in inflammation, ECM degradation, and vascular remodeling, as evidenced by decreased MMP-2/9 activity, reduced α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) loss, and diminished expression of inflammatory mediators and transcription factors such as NF-κB, AP-1, and signal transducer and activator of transcription 1/3 (STAT1/3). Mechanistically, our data suggest that TLR2 antagonism disrupts the interaction between TLR2 and its endogenous ligands, including high mobility group B-1 (HMGB1) and heat shock proteins (HSPs), thereby attenuating the chronic inflammatory response in AAA tissues. This disruption likely contributes to the resolution of inflammation and the stabilization of vascular integrity, highlighting the critical role of TLR2-ligand interactions in driving AAA pathogenesis. Furthermore, our experiments using TLR2-deficient mice confirm the indispensable role of TLR2 in AAA development, providing strong evidence that TLR2 is a central mediator of the disease process. The concept of targeting TLR2 as a therapeutic strategy for AAA is particularly compelling given the current lack of pharmacological options for managing this condition. While surgical repair remains the gold standard for treating large aneurysms, it is associated with significant risks and is not suitable for all patients. A pharmacological approach that targets the upstream drivers of inflammation and vascular remodeling, such as TLR2, could provide a much-needed alternative for patients with small or asymptomatic aneurysms, potentially halting disease progression and reducing the risk of rupture. In summary, our study identifies TLR2 as a key regulator of the inflammatory and vascular remodeling processes underlying AAA. By demonstrating that TLR2 antagonism protects against AAA formation and promotes regression of established aneurysms, we provide compelling evidence that TLR2 represents a promising therapeutic target for this devastating condition. These findings not only enhance our understanding of AAA pathogenesis but also pave the way for the development of novel therapeutic strategies aimed at modulating innate immune signaling in vascular diseases. Animal Models and Experimental Design All animal experiments were conducted in accordance with institutional guidelines and approved by the appropriate ethics committee. Male C57BL/6 wild-type (WT) mice and TLR2-deficient (TLR2−/−) mice, aged 8–12 weeks, were obtained from Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, ME, USA). Mice were housed in a specific pathogen-free environment under a 12-hour light/dark cycle with ad libitum access to food and water. To induce abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), mice were subjected to either an angiotensin II (Ang II)-infusion model or an elastase-perfusion model, as described previously. Briefly, for the Ang II model, osmotic mini-pumps (Alzet, Cupertino, CA, USA) delivering Ang II (1,000 ng/kg/min) were implanted subcutaneously for 28 days. For the elastase model, the abdominal aorta was exposed via laparotomy and perfused with elastase (5 U/mL) for 5 minutes. Sham-operated mice served as controls. Mice were euthanized at the end of experiments, and the abdominal aortas were harvested for further analysis. TLR2 Neutralization and Pharmacological Interventions To assess the effects of TLR2 blockade, a monoclonal antibody against TLR2 (anti-TLR2; InvivoGen, San Diego, CA, USA) or a control IgG antibody was administered intraperitoneally (i.p.) at a dose of 10 mg/kg every 3 days, starting either 3 days before AAA induction (prophylactic protocol) or 7 days after AAA establishment (therapeutic protocol). For additional experiments, small-molecule inhibitors targeting downstream signaling pathways (e.g., NF-κB and AP-1) were administered to evaluate their role in AAA progression. Vehicle-treated mice served as controls. Histological and Morphological Analysis At the experimental endpoint, aortas were excised and carefully cleaned of surrounding connective tissue. Aortic diameters were measured under a dissecting microscope, and aneurysm severity was graded based on established criteria. Aortic tissues were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned for histological analysis. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining was performed to assess general tissue morphology, while Verhoeff–Van Gieson (VVG) staining was used to evaluate elastin degradation. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) and immunofluorescence (IF) staining were performed to detect the expression of TLR2, α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA), and inflammatory markers such as monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) and high mobility group B-1 (HMGB1). Integrated optical density (IOD) values were quantified using ImageJ software (NIH, Bethesda, MD, USA). Quantitative Real-Time PCR and Western Blot Analysis Total RNA was extracted from aortic tissues using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA), and cDNA was synthesized using a reverse transcription kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) was performed using SYBR Green Master Mix (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA) to determine the mRNA expression of TLR2, inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6, TNF-α, MCP-1), and matrix metalloproteinases (MMP-2 and MMP-9). Gene expression was normalized to GAPDH as an internal control. For protein analysis, aortic tissues were homogenized in RIPA buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA). Protein lysates were subjected to SDS-PAGE and transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes. Membranes were probed with primary antibodies against TLR2, MMP-2, MMP-9, NF-κB, AP-1, STAT1, and STAT3 (Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, MA, USA), followed by incubation with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies. Protein bands were visualized using an enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) detection system (Bio-Rad) and quantified using Image Lab software. Zymography for MMP Activity To assess the enzymatic activity of MMP-2 and MMP-9, gelatin zymography was performed. Equal amounts of protein from aortic tissue lysates were mixed with non-reducing sample buffer and loaded onto 10% SDS-polyacrylamide gels containing 0.1% gelatin. After electrophoresis, gels were washed in renaturation buffer to remove SDS and incubated overnight in activation buffer at 37°C. Gels were stained with Coomassie Brilliant Blue, and clear bands indicating MMP activity were quantified using ImageJ software. Flow Cytometry Analysis Single-cell suspensions were prepared from aortic tissues by enzymatic digestion with collagenase II and elastase. Cells were stained with fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies against CD45, CD11b, F4/80, and Ly6G (BioLegend, San Diego, CA, USA) for flow cytometry analysis of immune cell populations. Data were acquired using a BD LSRFortessa flow cytometer (BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA, USA) and analyzed with FlowJo software (Tree Star, Ashland, OR, USA). Measurement of Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) Reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels in aortic tissues were assessed using dihydroethidium (DHE) staining. Freshly isolated aortic sections were incubated with DHE (10 μM) at 37°C for 30 minutes, and fluorescence images were captured using a confocal microscope (Zeiss, Oberkochen, Germany). Mean fluorescence intensity was quantified using ImageJ software. Statistical Analysis All data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism software (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA). Comparisons between two groups were conducted using unpaired Student’s t-tests, while multiple-group comparisons were performed using one-way or two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Parallel computing has become a cornerstone of modern high-performance computing (HPC), enabling the execution of compute-intensive applications across distributed memory systems. As the demand for solving increasingly complex scientific and engineering problems grows, the scalability of parallel frameworks remains a critical area of research. Scalability, defined as the ability of a system to efficiently utilize additional computational resources, directly influences the practical applicability and performance of parallel algorithms on multiprocessor systems. Among the existing parallel programming paradigms, the "master-worker" framework has gained significant attention due to its simplicity and suitability for task-based parallelism. However, despite its widespread adoption, formal analytical studies of its scalability on distributed memory architectures are relatively limited. This paper addresses this gap by presenting a rigorous analytical study of the scalability of the "master-worker" framework, proposing a new computational model called the Bulk Synchronous Farm (BSF) model, and deriving upper bounds for parallel efficiency in such systems. 1.1 Motivation and Background The master-worker paradigm is a fundamental design pattern in parallel computing. It operates by designating a single master process responsible for task management and multiple worker processes that perform computations. This paradigm is particularly well-suited for embarrassingly parallel problems, where tasks are independent and require minimal interprocess communication. However, as the number of processes increases, several challenges arise that impact scalability, including communication overhead, task distribution imbalance, and synchronization delays. These factors can limit the framework's ability to achieve linear speedup, making it essential to develop analytical tools to evaluate and optimize its performance. Scalability in parallel systems has been extensively studied using models such as the Bulk Synchronous Parallel (BSP) model [1] and the Single Program Multiple Data (SPMD) model [2]. The BSP model provides a structured approach to analyzing parallel programs by partitioning computations into supersteps separated by global synchronization points. The SPMD model, on the other hand, assumes a uniform program running on all processes with local data. While these models have been instrumental in understanding parallel performance, they lack the specificity required to address the unique characteristics of the master-worker paradigm in distributed memory systems. To bridge this gap, we introduce the BSF model, a novel computational framework that extends the principles of BSP and SPMD to explicitly capture the dynamics of the master-worker paradigm. 1.2 Scope of the BSF Model The BSF model is designed to analyze and optimize compute-intensive applications executed on distributed memory systems. Compute-intensive applications are characterized by a high ratio of computation to communication, making them ideal candidates for parallelization. Examples include numerical simulations, large-scale data processing, and machine learning workloads. The BSF model explicitly accounts for the hierarchical nature of task execution in the master-worker paradigm, modeling key performance metrics such as task distribution time, computation time, and synchronization delays. By doing so, it provides a more accurate representation of the performance bottlenecks encountered in real-world scenarios. In addition to its analytical capabilities, the BSF model is accompanied by a formal definition of the BSF-computer architecture. This architecture consists of a collection of processing nodes with distributed memory, interconnected by a high-speed communication network. Each node executes a BSF program, which adheres to a structured format comprising task generation, task execution, and result aggregation phases. This formalization enables a unified analysis of BSF programs across different hardware platforms, facilitating the derivation of general scalability bounds. 1.3 Related Work The scalability of parallel computing models has been the subject of extensive research. Early studies by Amdahl [3] and Gustafson [4] established foundational principles for understanding the impact of parallelism on performance. Amdahl's law emphasizes the limitations posed by serial components of an algorithm, while Gustafson's law highlights the potential for speedup in workloads with increasing problem sizes. These principles have been extended to distributed memory systems through the development of theoretical models such as BSP [1], LogP [5], and QSM [6]. Each of these models provides insights into the trade-offs between computation, communication, and synchronization in parallel systems. Within the context of the master-worker paradigm, existing research has primarily focused on empirical performance evaluation. For example, studies have demonstrated the efficiency of master-worker frameworks in applications such as Monte Carlo simulations [7], genetic algorithms [8], and distributed optimization [9]. However, a comprehensive analytical treatment of the scalability of this paradigm, particularly in distributed memory environments, remains an open area of investigation. This paper contributes to the literature by addressing this gap and providing a mathematical foundation for evaluating the scalability of BSF programs. 1.4 Contributions This paper makes the following key contributions: 1. Proposal of the BSF Model: We introduce the BSF model as a new framework for analyzing parallel programs based on the master-worker paradigm. The model integrates concepts from BSP and SPMD while addressing the unique characteristics of distributed memory systems. 2. Definition of BSF-Computer Architecture: We formally define the architecture of a BSF-computer, enabling the systematic evaluation of BSF programs across different hardware platforms. 3. Scalability Analysis of BSF Programs: We derive upper bounds for the scalability of BSF programs on distributed memory multiprocessors. These bounds are expressed in terms of key system parameters, including the number of processes, communication latency, and computation-to-communication ratio. 4. Formulas for Parallel Efficiency: We propose analytical formulas for estimating the parallel efficiency of BSF programs, providing a practical tool for performance optimization. 1.5 Organization The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the formal definition of the BSF model and its associated computational framework. Section 3 describes the architecture of BSF-computers and the structure of BSF programs. Section 4 derives analytical formulas for scalability and parallel efficiency, supported by illustrative examples. Section 5 discusses the implications of our findings and proposes strategies for optimizing performance. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future research. Through this structured approach, the paper aims to advance the understanding of the scalability of the master-worker framework, providing both theoretical insights and practical tools for its application in distributed memory multiprocessors. This work is expected to be of interest to researchers and practitioners in the fields of parallel computing, distributed systems, and high-performance computing. 2.1 Problem Formulation The scalability of the "master-worker" framework is analyzed in the context of compute-intensive applications executed on multiprocessors with distributed memory. The study focuses on the parallel efficiency and upper scalability bounds achievable within the constraints of such systems. The proposed BSF (Bulk Synchronous Farm) model serves as the foundation for the analysis. BSF combines key features of the Bulk Synchronous Parallel (BSP) model [1] and the Single Program Multiple Data (SPMD) model [2], emphasizing predictability and simplicity in the design of parallel computations. The analysis assumes a distributed memory architecture, where processors communicate via message passing. Each processor, equipped with its own local memory, executes a portion of the computation, with coordination provided by a designated "master" process. The master is responsible for task distribution and result aggregation, while "worker" processes perform the assigned computations independently. 2.2 Overview of the BSF Model The BSF model is designed to support compute-intensive applications with predictable communication patterns. The model partitions parallel computation into three phases: (1) task distribution, (2) task execution, and (3) result aggregation. Synchronization occurs at the end of each phase, ensuring consistency across parallel processes. The BSF-computer is an abstract architecture that formalizes these operations, consisting of the following components: 1. Master Node: Responsible for task generation and allocation. The master divides the problem into independent tasks (granules) and assigns them to worker nodes. 2. Worker Nodes: Perform computations on the allocated tasks and return results to the master. Worker nodes operate in parallel, following the same program logic (SPMD paradigm). 3. Communication Network: Facilitates message passing between the master and worker nodes, as well as among worker nodes if necessary. The BSF-program strictly adheres to this structure. It is organized into iterations, with each iteration corresponding to a single synchronization step. The three-phase structure of task distribution, task execution, and result aggregation repeats in each iteration. This predictable pattern is key to modeling and analyzing scalability, as it simplifies the quantification of computation and communication costs. 2.3 Analytical Model of Scalability The scalability analysis is based on the definition of parallel efficiency, \( Ep \), which is given by the ratio of speedup, \( Sp \), to the number of processors, \( p \). Mathematically, \( Ep \) is expressed as: \[ Ep = \frac{Sp}{p} = \frac{T1}{p \cdot Tp}, \] where \( T1 \) is the execution time of the sequential program, and \( Tp \) is the execution time of the parallel program on \( p \) processors. The speedup \( Sp \) is bounded by Amdahl's Law [3] and Gustafson's Law [4], contingent on the fraction of serial and parallelizable components in the workload. The total execution time \( Tp \) for a BSF-program is modeled as: \[ Tp = T{\text{comp}} + T{\text{comm}} + T{\text{sync}}, \] where \( T{\text{comp}} \) represents the time spent on computation by worker nodes, \( T{\text{comm}} \) accounts for communication overhead (e.g., data distribution and result collection), and \( T{\text{sync}} \) represents the synchronization time required at each iteration. 2.4 Derivation of Scalability Metrics To derive the upper scalability bounds, we analyze each component of \( Tp \) in detail: 1. Computation Time (\( T{\text{comp}} \)): Assume the problem size is \( N \), and each task requires \( t{\text{comp}} \) units of computation. If tasks are evenly distributed among \( p \) processors, the computation time per iteration is approximately: \[ T{\text{comp}} = \frac{N \cdot t{\text{comp}}}{p}. \] 2. Communication Time (\( T{\text{comm}} \)): The communication overhead is modeled using the BSP parameters \( g \) (per-word communication cost) and \( l \) (latency). The total communication cost per iteration, given \( m \) messages of size \( s \), is: \[ T{\text{comm}} = m \cdot (l + g \cdot s). \] For simplicity, we assume a single master node broadcasting data to \( p-1 \) workers, resulting in \( m = p-1 \). 3. Synchronization Time (\( T{\text{sync}} \)): Synchronization involves waiting for the slowest worker to complete its task. In the worst-case scenario, the synchronization time is proportional to the variance in workload distribution. Let \( \Delta \) denote the imbalance factor, then: \[ T{\text{sync}} = \Delta \cdot T{\text{comp}}. \] Combining these components, the total execution time per iteration is: \[ Tp = \frac{N \cdot t{\text{comp}}}{p} + (p-1) \cdot (l + g \cdot s) + \Delta \cdot \frac{N \cdot t{\text{comp}}}{p}. \] 2.5 Parallel Efficiency and Upper Scalability Bounds The parallel efficiency \( Ep \) is obtained by substituting \( Tp \) into the efficiency equation. To evaluate the upper scalability bounds, we consider the limiting behavior as \( p \to \infty \). The scalability is constrained by the communication and synchronization costs, which grow with \( p \), while the computation cost decreases. The upper bound of \( p \), denoted \( p{\text{max}} \), is determined by the condition: \[ T{\text{comm}} + T{\text{sync}} \leq T{\text{comp}}. \] Substituting the expressions for \( T{\text{comm}} \) and \( T{\text{sync}} \), \( p{\text{max}} \) is derived as a function of \( N \), \( t{\text{comp}} \), \( l \), \( g \), \( s \), and \( \Delta \). This provides a theoretical estimate for the maximum number of processors that can be effectively utilized under the BSF model. 2.6 Validation of the Analytical Model The validity of the derived scalability metrics is evaluated through simulation and empirical experimentation. Synthetic benchmarks and real-world compute-intensive applications, such as numerical integration and matrix multiplication, are implemented using the BSF-program framework. Performance metrics, including execution time, speedup, and efficiency, are measured on a distributed memory system with varying numbers of processors, \( p \). The experimental results are compared with theoretical predictions to assess the accuracy of the model. 2.7 Assumptions and Limitations The proposed analytical model assumes idealized conditions, such as uniform task granularity, balanced workload distribution, and negligible network contention. In practice, deviations from these assumptions may introduce additional overheads, thereby reducing scalability. These factors are discussed further in the Results and

Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections represent significant global health challenges, with approximately 296 million and 58 million individuals, respectively, living with these diseases worldwide [1, 2]. Both viruses primarily target hepatocytes, leading to progressive liver damage, which can culminate in cirrhosis, liver failure, or hepatocellular carcinoma. Despite advances in antiviral therapies, effective therapeutic strategies for HBV and HCV remain limited by issues such as incomplete viral clearance, drug resistance, and the high cost of prolonged treatment. As such, a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying the antiviral response is essential for the development of novel therapeutic approaches. Interferon-α (IFN-α) is a type I interferon that has been widely used as a cornerstone therapy for HBV and HCV infections for over two decades [3, 4]. IFN-α exerts its antiviral effects by binding to the interferon-α/β receptor (IFNAR) on target cells, initiating a complex signaling cascade that leads to the transcriptional activation of numerous interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs). These ISGs encode proteins with diverse antiviral activities, including the inhibition of viral replication, assembly, and release [5]. However, despite extensive study of IFN-α’s mechanisms of action, much remains to be elucidated about the full spectrum of its antiviral activities, particularly regarding its ability to restrict viral entry into host cells. The entry of HBV and HCV into hepatocytes is a critical initial step in the viral life cycle and represents a key target for antiviral intervention. Both viruses share a common mechanism of nonspecific attachment to hepatocytes via interaction with heparan glycosaminoglycans (HSGs) on the cell surface [6, 7]. HSGs are sulfated polysaccharides ubiquitously expressed on the surface of mammalian cells, and they facilitate the binding of many pathogens, including HBV and HCV, to their target cells [8]. Following this initial attachment, HBV and HCV utilize distinct, specific cellular receptors to mediate internalization and subsequent infection. For HBV, this process involves sodium taurocholate co-transporting polypeptide (NTCP), while HCV entry depends on a combination of receptors, including CD81, scavenger receptor class B type I (SR-BI), and claudin-1 [9, 10]. Given the essential role of HSGs in mediating viral attachment, strategies that interfere with this initial interaction could effectively block viral entry and prevent subsequent infection. Recent studies have highlighted the importance of secreted factors in modulating viral infection. For instance, IFN-α has been shown to induce the secretion of soluble antiviral factors that contribute to its overall antiviral activity [11]. While the majority of research has focused on the intracellular antiviral actions of ISGs, the role of secreted factors in mediating the extracellular inhibition of viral infection remains underexplored. In particular, the ability of IFN-α-induced factors to interfere with the initial steps of viral entry, such as binding to HSGs, has not been fully investigated. In this study, we aimed to explore a novel mechanism by which IFN-α exerts its antiviral effects against HBV and HCV. Specifically, we hypothesized that IFN-α induces the secretion of soluble factors that can inhibit viral entry by competing with HBV and HCV for binding to HSGs. To test this hypothesis, we treated cultured hepatoma cells with IFN-α and collected the conditioned supernatant. We then assessed the ability of these secreted factors to inhibit HBV and HCV infection in vitro, focusing on their role in disrupting the initial viral attachment to HSGs. Our findings demonstrate that the supernatant from IFN-α-treated cells contains secreted factors capable of significantly reducing HBV and HCV infection by targeting the attachment step. These factors, which are of high molecular mass and exhibit heparin-binding activity, compete with the viruses for HSG binding, thereby preventing subsequent entry into hepatocytes. This previously uncharacterized mechanism represents an important addition to the known antiviral activities of IFN-α and underscores the potential therapeutic value of targeting the viral attachment process. The inhibition of viral entry is a promising antiviral strategy, particularly in the context of HBV and HCV, where entry inhibitors could complement existing therapies that target other stages of the viral life cycle. Our study contributes to a growing body of evidence supporting the role of extracellular antiviral factors in mediating the effects of IFN-α and highlights the potential for harnessing these factors to develop novel therapeutic agents. Furthermore, the identification of soluble factors that interfere with HSG-mediated viral attachment may have broader implications for the treatment of other pathogens that utilize similar mechanisms for host cell entry. In summary, this study addresses a critical gap in knowledge regarding the extracellular antiviral actions of IFN-α, with a specific focus on its ability to restrict HBV and HCV entry. By elucidating the role of IFN-α-induced secreted factors in targeting the initial steps of viral infection, we provide new insights into the multifaceted antiviral activities of IFN-α and lay the groundwork for future research aimed at leveraging these findings for therapeutic development. Cells and Culture Conditions HepG2 and Huh7 cells, commonly used human hepatoma cell lines, were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, Manassas, VA) and maintained in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM; Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Gibco), 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 μg/mL streptomycin. Cells were grown at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO₂. For experiments involving IFN-α stimulation, cells were seeded at a density of 1 × 10⁶ cells per well in six-well plates and allowed to adhere overnight. IFN-α Treatment and Collection of Conditioned Supernatants Recombinant human IFN-α (PeproTech, Rocky Hill, NJ) was reconstituted in sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and stored at −80°C until use. Cells were treated with IFN-α at a final concentration of 1,000 IU/mL for 24 or 48 hours. Following treatment, the culture supernatants were collected, centrifuged at 300 × g for 5 minutes to remove cellular debris, and filtered through a 0.22-μm pore-size filter to ensure sterility. The filtered supernatants were designated as IFN-α-conditioned supernatants and stored at −20°C until further use. Evaluation of HBV and HCV Infection Inhibition HBV and HCV pseudoparticles (HBVpp and HCVpp), which incorporate the viral envelope proteins into a lentiviral core, were generated as previously described [1]. HepG2 and Huh7 cells were pretreated with IFN-α-conditioned supernatants or control (untreated) supernatants for 1 hour at 37°C prior to infection. Pseudoparticles were then added to the cells at a defined multiplicity of infection (MOI), and infection was allowed to proceed for 6 hours. Afterward, cells were washed with PBS to remove unbound viral particles and cultured in fresh medium containing 2% FBS. Infection efficiency was assessed 48 hours post-infection by measuring luciferase activity encoded by the pseudoparticles using a luciferase assay system (Promega, Madison, WI) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Competition Assays with Heparin and Heparan Sulfate To determine whether the secreted factors in IFN-α-conditioned supernatants competed with HBV and HCV for binding to heparan glycosaminoglycans, competition assays were performed. Briefly, HBVpp and HCVpp were pre-incubated with IFN-α-conditioned supernatants or control supernatants for 1 hour at 37°C. Concurrently, HepG2 and Huh7 cells were treated with heparin (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO) or heparan sulfate (MilliporeSigma, Burlington, MA) at a final concentration of 10 μg/mL for 30 minutes. The pre-incubated pseudoparticles were then added to the cells in the presence or absence of heparin or heparan sulfate, and infection was performed as described above. The inhibition of infection was quantified by measuring luciferase activity as described. Heparin Affinity Chromatography To identify the molecular weights and binding properties of the secreted factors, IFN-α-conditioned supernatants were subjected to heparin Sepharose column chromatography (Cytiva, Marlborough, MA). Supernatants were loaded onto a heparin Sepharose column pre-equilibrated with PBS and washed extensively with PBS to remove unbound proteins. Bound proteins were eluted with a stepwise gradient of NaCl (0.5–2 M) in PBS. Eluted fractions were collected, dialyzed against PBS using 10-kDa molecular weight cut-off dialysis membranes (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and concentrated using Amicon Ultra centrifugal filters (MilliporeSigma). The protein concentrations of the fractions were quantified using a BCA assay, and aliquots were stored at −80°C for further analysis. Analysis of Heparin-Binding Fractions To determine the antiviral activity of the heparin-binding fractions, HepG2 and Huh7 cells were pretreated with these fractions at a protein concentration of 10 μg/mL for 1 hour, followed by infection with HBVpp or HCVpp as described above. Infection efficiency was assessed via luciferase activity. To further characterize the fractions, sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) was performed, and proteins were visualized using Coomassie Brilliant Blue staining. Specific proteins of interest were identified by mass spectrometry at the institutional proteomics core facility. Cytotoxicity Assays To exclude the possibility that any observed antiviral effects were due to cytotoxicity, cell viability was assessed using the CellTiter-Glo luminescent cell viability assay (Promega) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Cells were treated with IFN-α-conditioned supernatants, heparin-binding fractions, or control supernatants for 24 hours prior to the viability assay. Luminescence was measured using a microplate reader (BioTek, Winooski, VT), and data were normalized to untreated controls. Statistical Analysis All experiments were performed in triplicate and repeated independently at least three times. Data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Statistical comparisons between groups were made using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test for multiple comparisons. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism software (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA).
