The study of synchronization and scheduling mechanisms in decentralized systems has garnered significant attention due to their relevance in a wide range of applications, including wireless communication networks, distributed computing, and biological systems. Among the many models proposed for achieving self-organization in such systems, pulse-coupled oscillators (PCOs) have emerged as a particularly influential framework. Originally inspired by observations of synchronous flashing in fireflies and other biological phenomena [1], PCOs capture the essence of decentralized coordination through simple, local interaction rules. These properties make them highly attractive for engineering applications where scalability, robustness, and fault tolerance are critical requirements. Despite their theoretical appeal and numerous proposed applications, the fundamental convergence properties of PCOs—especially in locally connected networks—remain incompletely understood. This gap in understanding limits the broader adoption of PCO-inspired protocols in practical systems. 1.1 Motivation and Context The synchronization of oscillators through mutual coupling has been extensively studied over the past few decades, both in natural and engineered systems [2, 3]. In the context of engineered networks, synchronization refers to the alignment of oscillator phases over time, a property that is pivotal for many applications such as time-division multiple access (TDMA) scheduling, distributed beamforming, and clock synchronization in sensor networks. Similarly, desynchronization, or the process by which oscillators achieve evenly spaced phases, has been proposed as a mechanism for decentralized scheduling in multi-access communication networks [4]. A significant body of work has explored the convergence of globally coupled PCO networks, where each oscillator interacts with all others in the network [5, 6]. In this setting, convergence to synchronous states is well understood, and the dynamics are often shown to be robust to noise, delays, and other practical considerations [7]. However, global coupling is an unrealistic assumption for many practical systems, where network connectivity is typically local, constrained by factors such as physical distance, communication range, or energy limitations. In locally connected networks, where each oscillator interacts with only a subset of the network, the dynamics of PCOs become considerably more complex. The lack of global information introduces challenges in predicting the collective behavior of the system, and simple extensions of results from globally coupled systems are no longer applicable. This is particularly true in the presence of propagation delays, which are inherent in any practical implementation and can significantly impact the stability and accuracy of the resulting synchronization or desynchronization patterns [8]. Addressing these challenges requires a deeper understanding of the interplay between network topology, coupling dynamics, and delay effects. 1.2 Related Work Several studies have investigated the behavior of PCOs in locally connected networks, but the results remain fragmented and often limited to specific cases or assumptions. For instance, synchronization in ring and lattice topologies has been analyzed in [9, 10], while desynchronization has been studied under specific coupling rules for tree and planar graphs [11]. These works provide valuable insights but do not generalize to arbitrary locally connected networks or account for realistic constraints such as propagation delays. On the other hand, bio-inspired synchronization protocols based on PCO models have been proposed and analyzed for practical applications, such as wireless sensor networks [12] and Internet-of-Things (IoT) systems [13]. These protocols often rely on heuristic design principles, with limited guarantees on convergence or performance in the presence of delays and local connectivity constraints. The lack of rigorous mathematical analysis for general network topologies restricts the adoption of these protocols in standardized communication systems. Recent advances in graph theory and distributed systems have provided tools for analyzing the convergence of decentralized protocols in complex networks. Concepts such as graph coloring, maximal cliques, and spectral properties of graphs have been leveraged to study problems of synchronization and scheduling [14, 15]. Building on these foundations, there is an opportunity to systematically address the open questions surrounding the convergence and accuracy of PCO dynamics in locally connected networks. 1.3 Contributions of this Work This paper aims to advance the understanding of PCO dynamics in locally connected networks, with a focus on both synchronization and desynchronization. Specifically, the key contributions of this work are as follows: 1. Synchronization in Locally Connected Networks: We establish almost sure convergence to synchrony for a simple case involving three nodes, which serves as a foundational result for understanding more complex network topologies. For general locally connected networks, we derive bounds on the achievable synchronization accuracy under realistic propagation delay constraints. 2. Desynchronization and Scheduling: We analyze the dynamics of PCOs in achieving desynchronization for scheduling purposes, under mild assumptions on the overlapping set of maximal cliques in the network. These results provide a pathway for designing decentralized scheduling protocols in networks with arbitrary local connectivity. 3. Propagation Delay Effects: We explicitly incorporate propagation delays into the analysis, deriving conditions under which the system achieves convergence and quantifying the impact of delays on synchronization accuracy. This addresses a critical gap in the current literature, where delays are often neglected or treated in an ad hoc manner. 4. Implications for Communication Networks: We discuss the practical implications of our theoretical results for the design of decentralized synchronization and scheduling protocols in communication networks. By providing rigorous guarantees on convergence and accuracy, we aim to bridge the gap between theoretical models and real-world applications. 1.4 Organization of the Paper The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides a detailed description of the PCO model and the associated coupling dynamics, including the formal definitions of synchronization and desynchronization. In Section 3, we present the main theoretical results on the convergence of PCOs in locally connected networks, with separate treatments for synchronization and desynchronization. Section 4 extends the analysis to incorporate propagation delays, highlighting their impact on convergence properties. Section 5 discusses the implications of our findings for the design of decentralized protocols in communication networks, along with potential directions for future research. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper with a summary of the key contributions. By addressing the open questions surrounding the convergence properties of PCOs in locally connected networks, this work aims to provide a solid theoretical foundation for the development of bio-inspired synchronization and scheduling protocols in practical systems. 2.1 Network Model and PCO Dynamics We consider a network represented as a graph \( G = (V, E) \), where \( V = \{1, 2, \ldots, N\} \) is the set of nodes and \( E \subseteq V \times V \) is the set of edges. An edge \( (i, j) \in E \) indicates that nodes \( i \) and \( j \) can directly communicate. The network is assumed to be locally connected, meaning each node is connected to a subset of \( V \), forming a neighborhood denoted as \( \mathcal{N}i = \{j \in V : (i, j) \in E\} \). The degree of local connectivity is defined by the cardinality of \( \mathcal{N}i \). Each node \( i \in V \) is modeled as a pulse-coupled oscillator (PCO) with a phase \( \phii(t) \in [0, 1) \), evolving over time. The phase dynamics are governed by a piecewise-linear function that progresses linearly in the absence of interactions, i.e., \[ \dot{\phi}i(t) = \frac{1}{T}, \quad \text{for } \phii(t) \notin \{0, 1\}, \] where \( T > 0 \) is the intrinsic period of the oscillator. When \( \phii(t) \) reaches 1, node \( i \) emits a pulse to its neighbors in \( \mathcal{N}i \) and resets its phase to 0. Upon receiving a pulse from a neighbor \( j \), the phase \( \phii(t) \) of node \( i \) is updated according to a phase response function (PRF), denoted \( f(\phii) \). The PRF is assumed to be monotonically increasing, ensuring causality and stability in the phase adjustments [1]. Propagation delays are incorporated into the model by assuming a fixed delay \( \tau{ij} > 0 \) for communication between nodes \( i \) and \( j \). Thus, the effect of a pulse emitted at time \( t \) by node \( j \) is observed by node \( i \) at time \( t + \tau{ij} \). The associated dynamics are expressed as: \[ \phii(t^+) = f(\phii(t)), \quad \text{if } \phij(t - \tau{ij}) = 1. \] 2.2 Synchronization Analysis To analyze synchronization, we define the phase difference between two nodes \( i \) and \( j \) as \( \Delta{ij}(t) = \phii(t) - \phij(t) \). The goal is to achieve phase synchronization, where \( \Delta{ij}(t) \rightarrow 0 \, (\text{mod } 1) \) for all \( (i, j) \in E \) as \( t \to \infty \). For the special case of \( N = 3 \) nodes, we establish almost sure convergence to synchronization using stochastic analysis of the phase dynamics with propagation delays. The proof leverages the properties of the PRF and the boundedness of \( \tau{ij} \), ensuring that the phase adjustments lead to convergence in finite time. Specifically, we show that the Lyapunov function \( V(\phi) = \sum{(i,j) \in E} |\Delta{ij}(t)|^2 \) decreases monotonically under the dynamics, subject to the coupling constraints. For general networks, we extend the analysis by considering the graph's local structure. Using the notion of maximal cliques, we show that synchronization within each clique is achievable under mild conditions on the delays \( \tau{ij} \). The convergence accuracy is quantified in terms of the maximum delay \( \tau\text{max} = \max{(i, j) \in E} \tau{ij} \) and the coupling strength of the PRF. The results are supported by numerical simulations that demonstrate the robustness of synchronization for varying network sizes and topologies. 2.3 Desynchronization and Scheduling Desynchronization, or the process of achieving an evenly spaced firing sequence among nodes, is analyzed in networks with overlapping maximal cliques. The desynchronization dynamics are achieved by modifying the PRF to include inhibitory coupling, such that the phase adjustment pushes nodes away from synchronous states. The updated PRF is designed as: \[ f{\text{desync}}(\phii) = \phii + \epsilon \cdot g(\Delta{ij}), \] where \( g(\cdot) \) is a continuous and bounded function that penalizes small phase differences, and \( \epsilon > 0 \) is a scaling parameter. We introduce a metric \( D(t) = \max{i,j} |\phii(t) - \phij(t)| \), which quantifies the degree of desynchronization. Using graph-theoretic tools, we prove that \( D(t) \) converges to \( 1/N \) in the limit as \( t \to \infty \), ensuring equal phase spacing. The proof assumes that the overlapping set of maximal cliques satisfies the following condition: for every pair of cliques \( Ck \) and \( Cl \), there exists at least one common node \( i \in Ck \cap Cl \). This condition ensures that desynchronization propagates across the network and prevents clustering of nodes into synchronized subgroups. 2.4 Numerical Simulations The analytical results are validated through extensive numerical simulations. The simulations are performed on networks of varying size (\( N = 10 \) to \( N = 100 \)) and topology, including random geometric graphs and grid networks. For each network, the initial phases \( \phii(0) \) are uniformly distributed in \( [0, 1) \). Synchronization and desynchronization metrics are computed over \( 10^4 \) time steps, and the results are averaged over 100 independent realizations. Propagation delays \( \tau{ij} \) are sampled from a uniform distribution \( U(0, \tau\text{max}) \), with \( \tau\text{max} \) varied in the range \( [0.01T, 0.1T] \). The PRFs for synchronization and desynchronization are selected based on standard forms in the literature [2,3], with parameters tuned to ensure convergence within a reasonable time frame. The results confirm the theoretical predictions, with synchronization errors scaling as \( O(\tau\text{max}) \) and desynchronization accuracy achieving \( 1/N \) spacing. References [1] Mirollo, R. The rapid growth of digital communication platforms and social media has profoundly transformed the way individuals interact, consume, and share information. Social media platforms like Twitter, Facebook, and Sina Weibo have emerged as central hubs for disseminating news, opinions, and personal updates, enabling individuals to reach vast audiences with unprecedented efficiency. However, this surge in connectivity and content creation has given rise to a significant challenge: information overload. The sheer volume of user-generated content available online often exceeds the attention capacity of individuals, creating an environment in which information must compete for visibility and engagement. Understanding how information spreads—or fails to spread—under such conditions is critical for optimizing communication strategies, combating misinformation, and designing better algorithms for content recommendation. Conventionally, the spread of information in social networks has been analogized to the spread of infectious diseases, where viral messages "infect" susceptible individuals who, in turn, share the information with others. This analogy has been instrumental in the development of many theoretical models, such as the Susceptible-Infected-Recovered (SIR) framework, which is widely used to study the dynamics of information diffusion. In these traditional models, the probability of an individual being "infected" (i.e., adopting or sharing a message) depends primarily on the number of interactions with others who have already adopted the message. The underlying assumption is that exposure to an idea or piece of content is sufficient to trigger its adoption, much like exposure to a virus can result in physical infection. While this analogy has proven useful in understanding certain aspects of information dissemination, it often overlooks the complexities introduced by human cognitive limitations and the competitive nature of modern information ecosystems. In reality, people are not passive recipients of information, and they do not engage with every piece of content they encounter. Instead, attention acts as a finite resource that must be allocated among competing stimuli. The rise of social media has amplified this competition, as individuals are bombarded with a constant stream of posts, messages, and notifications from their online networks. Under such conditions, the likelihood of a message being shared is not solely a function of its exposure; it is also influenced by factors such as its relevance, emotional appeal, and the user's ability to process and prioritize it amidst other competing content. This shift from an abundance of information to an overabundance introduces new dynamics into the process of information spread, necessitating a reevaluation of the traditional disease-based models. This study seeks to address these gaps by examining the mechanisms underlying information diffusion in the context of information overload. Using data from Sina Weibo, one of the largest social media platforms in China, we analyze the spread of user-generated content to uncover patterns that deviate from those predicted by classical epidemic models. Our findings reveal that the spread of popular messages often follows a mechanism distinct from the spread of diseases. Specifically, we observe that individuals with larger social networks require multiple exposures to the same message before they are likely to share it. This suggests that the probability of sharing is not merely a function of exposure frequency but also depends on the proportion of an individual’s network that has already adopted the message. Such behavior is indicative of a competitive attention environment, where the decision to share is influenced by social reinforcement and the perceived popularity of the message within one’s immediate network. To further explore these dynamics, we propose a novel fractional susceptible-infected-recovered (FSIR) model that incorporates these attention-based factors. Unlike traditional SIR models, the FSIR model posits that an individual’s probability of adopting and transmitting a message is proportional to the fraction of their social connections who have shared it. This fractional approach captures the compounding effect of social reinforcement, where repeated exposures from a significant portion of one's network increase the likelihood of adoption. Importantly, our model also accounts for the finite capacity of individuals to process information, reflecting the competitive nature of attention allocation in overloaded environments. One of the most striking implications of our analysis is the discovery of a finite epidemic threshold in real-world social networks, as predicted by the FSIR model. In classical disease epidemic models, the threshold for an outbreak is often considered to be zero in infinite networks, meaning that even a single "infected" individual can theoretically trigger widespread contagion under favorable conditions. In contrast, our findings suggest that when individuals are overwhelmed with excessive information feeds, a critical threshold must be surpassed for a message to achieve widespread dissemination. Messages that fail to meet this threshold—whether due to insufficient social reinforcement, lack of relevance, or other factors—are unlikely to gain traction, regardless of how widely they are initially broadcast. This insight has profound implications for understanding the dynamics of viral content, as well as for designing strategies to effectively disseminate important information in the face of competing attention demands. By integrating empirical observations with theoretical modeling, this study contributes to a growing body of research that seeks to move beyond simplistic analogies between information and disease. Our findings underscore the importance of considering human cognitive limitations and social reinforcement mechanisms when studying information spread in digital environments. Moreover, they highlight the need for social media platforms and content creators to adapt their strategies to the realities of information overload, ensuring that critical messages are not lost amidst the noise. In the following sections, we delve deeper into the data and methods used in our analysis, present the results of our FSIR model, and discuss the broader implications of our findings for the study of information diffusion in an increasingly connected world. To investigate the dynamics of information spread in social media under conditions of information overload, we analyzed the user-generated content in Sina Weibo, one of the largest social media platforms in China. Our approach combined empirical data analysis with theoretical modeling to uncover the mechanisms governing information contagion and the role of attention competition. Below, we detail the data collection process, the analysis techniques used, and the development of the fractional susceptible-infected-recovered (FSIR) model. Data Collection and Preprocessing We obtained anonymized datasets from Sina Weibo that consisted of user interactions over a one-month period. The dataset included public posts, reposts, and user network connections (i.e., follower and followee relationships). To ensure data quality and consistency, we filtered users who had fewer than 10 connections or who were inactive during the observation period (defined as having fewer than three interactions). We focused on a subset of messages (defined as posts or reposts) that achieved significant popularity, as measured by the number of shares exceeding a predefined threshold. Each message was timestamped, allowing us to reconstruct the temporal sequence of reposting events. Additionally, we recorded the number of connections each user had and the number of reposts they made during the observation period. To ensure robust results, we excluded interactions that involved bots or automated accounts, identified using activity patterns that deviated significantly from human behavior norms (e.g., extremely high posting frequency or lack of variability in posting times). Empirical Analysis To understand how information spreads in the network, we analyzed the temporal and structural patterns of message propagation. Specifically, we examined the relationship between a user's likelihood of sharing a message and the fraction of their neighbors who had already shared the same message. For each user-message pair, we calculated the fraction of neighbors (friends or followers in the directed network) who had previously shared the message at the time of the user's decision to repost. We then aggregated these probabilities across all users and messages to determine whether the likelihood of reposting depended on this fraction. To assess the role of attention competition, we analyzed the frequency and distribution of message exposures. For each user, we measured the total number of distinct messages encountered and the number of repeated exposures to individual messages. We further examined whether users with more connections required a greater number of exposures to a single message before choosing to share it, hypothesizing that this relationship reflects competition for limited cognitive attention. Mathematical Modeling: Fractional Susceptible-Infected-Recovered (FSIR) Model To model the observed dynamics of information spread, we developed the FSIR model, which extends the classic susceptible-infected-recovered (SIR) framework used in epidemiology. In the FSIR model, a user (or node) can exist in one of three states: susceptible (S, has not seen the message), infected (I, has seen and shared the message), or recovered (R, has seen the message but will not share it). The key innovation in the FSIR model is that the probability of a susceptible node becoming infected depends on the fraction of its neighbors who are infected, rather than the absolute number of infected neighbors. Mathematically, the infection probability for a susceptible node \( i \) is given by: \[ Pi = \beta \left( \frac{ki^I}{ki} \right)^\alpha \] where \( ki^I \) is the number of infected neighbors of node \( i \), \( ki \) is the total number of neighbors, \( \beta \) is the base infection rate, and \( \alpha \) is a tunable parameter capturing the sensitivity of infection probability to the fraction of infected neighbors. The parameter \( \alpha \) reflects the degree of attention competition: higher values of \( \alpha \) indicate that individuals require a higher fraction of their neighbors to share the message before they consider reposting it. The transition from the infected state to the recovered state occurs at a fixed rate \( \gamma \), representing the likelihood that an individual stops sharing or engaging with the message over time. Once in the recovered state, individuals do not share the message again. Model Calibration and Simulation We calibrated the parameters \( \beta \), \( \alpha \), and \( \gamma \) using the empirical data from Sina Weibo. To fit the model, we employed a least-squares optimization method to minimize the difference between the observed and simulated infection curves (i.e., the number of infected users over time for each message). We validated the model using a subset of the data not used for calibration and tested its predictive accuracy by comparing simulated outcomes with real-world observations. To simulate the FSIR dynamics, we used an agent-based model implemented on the real-world network topology extracted from the Sina Weibo dataset. At each time step, we updated the states of all nodes based on the infection and recovery probabilities. Simulations were run for multiple messages with varying initial conditions (e.g., seed nodes, initial infection rates) to explore how different factors influence the spread of information. Analysis of Epidemic Threshold To determine the epidemic threshold, we analyzed the conditions under which a message spreads to a significant fraction of the network. In contrast to traditional SIR models, where the threshold depends on the average degree of the network, the FSIR model introduces a finite threshold due to the fractional infection mechanism. We derived the critical threshold as a function of \( \beta \), \( \alpha \), and the network structure, and validated the analytical results through simulations. Statistical Analysis All analyses were performed using Python and R. Statistical significance of relationships (e.g., between repost probability and fraction of infected neighbors) was assessed using non-parametric tests, given the skewed nature of the data. Confidence intervals for model parameters were estimated using bootstrapping with 1,000 replications. Ethical Considerations The dataset used in this study was fully anonymized and complied with all relevant privacy regulations. Our analysis was conducted in accordance with ethical guidelines for social media research, ensuring that no individual user could be identified from the results. This combination of empirical analysis and modeling allowed us to uncover the unique mechanisms that govern information spread under conditions of information overload, providing insights into the interplay between network structure, attention competition, and information contagion. Neuropathic pain is a debilitating condition arising from damage or dysfunction within the nervous system and is characterized by persistent pain and hypersensitivity to normally innocuous stimuli [1]. Among the numerous chemotherapeutic agents known to induce neuropathic pain, oxaliplatin, a platinum-based chemotherapeutic commonly used in the treatment of colorectal cancer, has gained significant attention due to its adverse effects on the peripheral and central nervous systems [2]. Oxaliplatin-induced neuropathy presents clinically as cold hypersensitivity, mechanical allodynia, and paresthesia, significantly impacting the quality of life for cancer patients and often necessitating dosage reductions or discontinuation of treatment [3]. While the peripheral mechanisms of oxaliplatin-induced neuropathy have been extensively studied, increasing evidence suggests that central sensitization, particularly in the spinal dorsal horn, plays a critical role in the persistence and amplification of neuropathic pain [4]. Central sensitization refers to the increased excitability of neurons in the central nervous system (CNS), particularly in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, resulting from sustained or exaggerated synaptic input from primary afferent fibers [5]. A key hallmark of central sensitization is the enhanced glutamatergic transmission mediated by glutamate receptors in the spinal cord, including α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor subunits [6]. Specifically, the NR2B subunit of NMDA receptors and the GluR1 subunit of AMPA receptors have been implicated in synaptic plasticity and hyperexcitability associated with neuropathic pain [7]. Emerging evidence has also highlighted the role of neurotrophic factors, particularly brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), in modulating synaptic strength and promoting central sensitization in pain pathways [8]. In animal models of neuropathic pain, BDNF expression is upregulated in the spinal dorsal horn, where it facilitates glutamatergic transmission by enhancing the trafficking and phosphorylation of AMPA and NMDA receptor subunits [9]. Despite the growing understanding of these molecular and cellular contributors to oxaliplatin-induced neuropathy, effective therapeutic strategies targeting central mechanisms remain inadequately explored. Gabapentin, a structural analog of the inhibitory neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), has been widely used in the management of neuropathic pain due to its ability to modulate neuronal excitability [10]. Although its precise mechanism of action is not fully understood, gabapentin binds with high affinity to the α2δ-1 subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, thereby reducing calcium influx and subsequently decreasing the release of excitatory neurotransmitters such as glutamate in the CNS [11]. In preclinical models, gabapentin has been shown to attenuate central sensitization by modulating synaptic plasticity and reducing the expression of pain-related neurochemical mediators, including BDNF [12]. However, the efficacy of gabapentin in mitigating oxaliplatin-induced central sensitization, particularly its impact on glutamatergic transmission in the spinal dorsal horn, remains insufficiently characterized. The present study was designed to address these gaps in knowledge by investigating the role of gabapentin in modulating central sensitization induced by oxaliplatin in a rat model of neuropathic pain. Specifically, we sought to determine the alterations in glutamatergic transmission and the expression of key molecular players, including NR2B, GluR1, and BDNF, in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord following oxaliplatin administration. We hypothesized that oxaliplatin would induce significant upregulation of glutamatergic transmission and BDNF expression in the dorsal horn, contributing to mechanical allodynia. Furthermore, we postulated that gabapentin would attenuate these changes by modulating the activity of glutamate receptors and suppressing the expression of BDNF, thereby alleviating hyperreactivity to mechanical stimuli. To test these hypotheses, we employed a combination of behavioral, molecular, and electrophysiological approaches to evaluate the impact of gabapentin on oxaliplatin-induced neuropathic pain. Behavioral assessments, including mechanical allodynia testing using von Frey filaments, were used to quantify pain hypersensitivity in oxaliplatin-treated rats. Changes in the expression of NR2B, GluR1, and BDNF in the dorsal horn were analyzed using immunochemical techniques, while electrophysiological recordings were performed on spinal cord slices to investigate glutamatergic synaptic strength. Together, these methods allowed for a comprehensive evaluation of the underlying mechanisms by which gabapentin modulates central sensitization in the context of chemotherapy-induced neuropathic pain. This study builds upon previous observations of gabapentin's efficacy in other neuropathic pain models and aims to provide mechanistic insights into its potential therapeutic utility in oxaliplatin-induced neuropathy. By elucidating the interactions between gabapentin, glutamatergic signaling, and BDNF in the dorsal horn, the findings from this work may contribute to the development of more targeted and effective interventions for managing chemotherapy-induced neuropathic pain. Animals and Experimental Groups Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats (200–250 g) were obtained from a local supplier and housed in standard laboratory conditions with a 12-hour light/dark cycle, controlled temperature (22 ± 1°C), and ad libitum access to food and water. All experimental procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) and were conducted in accordance with the guidelines established by the National Institutes of Health for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. Animals were randomly divided into four groups (n = 8 per group): (1) control group receiving saline and vehicle, (2) oxaliplatin group receiving oxaliplatin and vehicle, (3) gabapentin group receiving saline and gabapentin, and (4) oxaliplatin + gabapentin group receiving both oxaliplatin and gabapentin. Drug Administration Oxaliplatin (Sigma-Aldrich, USA) was freshly prepared in 5% glucose solution and administered intraperitoneally (IP) at a dose of 5 mg/kg on day 1, as previously described [1]. Gabapentin (60 mg/kg, IP; Sigma-Aldrich, USA) or its vehicle (sterile saline) was administered once daily for 7 consecutive days, beginning immediately after the administration of oxaliplatin or saline. The doses and schedules of both drugs were selected based on prior studies demonstrating their effectiveness in inducing and alleviating neuropathic pain, respectively [2,3]. Behavioral Assessment of Mechanical Allodynia Mechanical allodynia was assessed using von Frey filaments (Stoelting Co., USA) according to the up-down method [4]. Animals were placed individually in transparent plexiglass chambers on an elevated metal mesh floor and allowed to acclimate for 30 minutes. A series of calibrated von Frey filaments (1.4–15 g) were applied perpendicularly to the plantar surface of the hind paw, with enough force to cause slight bending. Each filament was applied for 5 seconds, and a positive response was defined as a rapid paw withdrawal. Testing began with the 2 g filament, with subsequent filaments applied in increasing or decreasing order depending on the response. The 50% paw withdrawal threshold was calculated using the Dixon formula [5]. Behavioral assessments were performed on day 0 (baseline) and at 24-hour intervals following oxaliplatin administration until day 7. Western Blot Analysis of Protein Expression On day 8, animals were deeply anesthetized with sodium pentobarbital (50 mg/kg, IP) and transcardially perfused with ice-cold phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). The lumbar section (L4–L6) of the spinal cord was rapidly dissected and homogenized in RIPA lysis buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Roche, USA). Protein concentration was determined using the Bradford assay (Bio-Rad, USA). Equal amounts of protein (30 µg) were separated on 10% SDS-PAGE gels and transferred onto PVDF membranes (Millipore, USA). Membranes were blocked in 5% non-fat dry milk for 1 hour at room temperature and incubated overnight at 4°C with the following primary antibodies: anti-NR2B (1:1000, Abcam, UK), anti-GluR1 (1:1000, Millipore), anti-BDNF (1:1000, Abcam), and anti-β-actin (1:5000, Sigma-Aldrich) as a loading control. After washing, membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:5000, Cell Signaling Technology, USA) for 1 hour at room temperature. Protein bands were visualized using enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and quantified using ImageJ software (NIH, USA). Protein expression levels were normalized to β-actin and expressed as a percentage of the control group. Electrophysiological Recordings To assess glutamatergic transmission, in vitro whole-cell patch-clamp recordings were performed on lamina II neurons in spinal cord slices. On day 8, animals were anesthetized with sodium pentobarbital (50 mg/kg, IP) and decapitated. The lumbar spinal cord (L4–L6) was quickly removed and placed in ice-cold artificial cerebrospinal fluid (aCSF) containing (in mM): 124 NaCl, 2.5 KCl, 26 NaHCO₃, 1.25 NaH₂PO₄, 2 CaCl₂, 1 MgCl₂, and 10 glucose, aerated with 95% O₂/5% CO₂ (pH 7.4). Transverse spinal cord slices (400 µm thick) were prepared using a vibratome (Leica VT1200S, Germany) and transferred to a recording chamber perfused with oxygenated aCSF at 32 ± 1°C. Lamina II neurons were visually identified using an upright microscope (Olympus BX51WI, Japan) equipped with infrared differential interference contrast optics. Borosilicate glass recording pipettes (5–7 MΩ) were filled with an internal solution containing (in mM): 135 K-gluconate, 10 HEPES, 10 EGTA, 2 MgCl₂, 2 Na₂-ATP, and 0.3 Na-GTP (pH 7.2, adjusted with KOH). Spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) were recorded at a holding potential of -70 mV using a Multiclamp 700B amplifier (Molecular Devices, USA). Signals were digitized at 10 kHz and analyzed offline using Clampfit 10.7 (Molecular Devices). Amplitude and frequency of sEPSCs were compared between groups. Statistical Analysis All data were expressed as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Behavioral and electrophysiological data were analyzed using two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, followed by Tukey’s post hoc test for multiple comparisons. Western blot data were analyzed using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is one of the most common malignancies worldwide and represents a significant global health burden. It is the sixth most frequently diagnosed cancer and the third leading cause of cancer-related mortality [1]. The high incidence of HCC, especially in regions with endemic hepatitis B and C virus infections, combined with late diagnosis and limited therapeutic options, underscores the urgent need for novel therapeutic strategies to improve patient outcomes. Current treatment modalities for HCC include surgical resection, liver transplantation, locoregional therapies, and systemic agents such as tyrosine kinase inhibitors and immune checkpoint inhibitors. However, these treatments often have limited efficacy, significant side effects, or are only applicable to a subset of patients [2]. Consequently, there has been growing interest in identifying bioactive compounds from natural products with anticancer potential as alternative or adjunctive therapies. Reynoutria multiflora (Thunb.) Moldenke, commonly known as "He Shou Wu" in traditional Chinese medicine, has been extensively utilized for centuries due to its purported therapeutic properties, including anti-aging, anti-inflammatory, anti-hyperlipidemic, and anticancer effects [3]. Several studies have attributed these pharmacological activities to the plant's rich content of bioactive secondary metabolites, particularly anthraquinones, stilbenes, and flavonoids [4]. Among these, emodin (1,3,8-trihydroxy-6-methylanthraquinone), a naturally occurring anthraquinone derivative, has garnered significant attention due to its diverse biological activities, including anti-inflammatory, anti-proliferative, and pro-apoptotic effects [5]. Previous investigations into He Shou Wu extract have demonstrated its ability to inhibit the growth of various cancer cell lines, including hepatocellular carcinoma cells, and emodin has been identified as one of the primary active components responsible for these effects [6]. However, the precise molecular mechanisms underlying the anticancer activity of emodin remain incompletely understood. Emerging evidence suggests that dysregulated lipid metabolism is a hallmark of cancer and plays a critical role in tumorigenesis and progression [7]. Cancer cells exhibit altered lipid biosynthesis and uptake to support rapid proliferation, energy production, and membrane biogenesis. One of the key regulators of lipid metabolism in cancer cells is sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 (SREBP1), a transcription factor that controls the expression of enzymes involved in de novo fatty acid synthesis and desaturation, such as adenosine triphosphate citrate lyase (ACLY), acetyl-CoA carboxylase alpha (ACACA), fatty acid synthase (FASN), and stearoyl-CoA desaturase 1 (SCD1) [8]. Aberrant activation of SREBP1 has been implicated in the progression of several cancer types, including HCC, and is associated with enhanced tumor growth, metastasis, and resistance to apoptosis [9]. Thus, targeting SREBP1 and its downstream lipid metabolic pathways represents a promising therapeutic strategy for the treatment of HCC. Despite the critical role of lipid metabolism in HCC, the relationship between lipid metabolic regulation and apoptosis in cancer cells remains poorly characterized. Apoptosis, or programmed cell death, is a tightly regulated process essential for maintaining tissue homeostasis and is frequently dysregulated in cancer [10]. The intrinsic apoptotic pathway, in particular, is controlled by the balance between pro-apoptotic and anti-apoptotic members of the B-cell lymphoma 2 (Bcl-2) family of proteins and is mediated by mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization, the release of cytochrome c (CYTC), and the activation of caspase cascades [11]. Recent studies have highlighted potential crosstalk between lipid metabolism and apoptotic signaling, although the underlying mechanisms remain to be elucidated [12]. Notably, SREBP1 has been shown to influence apoptosis by modulating the expression of lipid metabolism-related genes and interacting with key apoptotic regulators [13]. These findings suggest that the anticancer effects of emodin may involve both lipid metabolic reprogramming and intrinsic apoptotic pathways. In this study, we aimed to investigate the potential role of lipid metabolism in emodin-induced apoptosis in hepatocellular carcinoma cells, focusing specifically on the involvement of SREBP1. Previous research has demonstrated that emodin exerts cytotoxic effects on HCC cells through mechanisms such as cell cycle arrest, the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and mitochondrial dysfunction [14,15]. However, the extent to which emodin modulates lipid metabolism and whether this modulation contributes to its pro-apoptotic activity have not been explored in detail. To address these gaps, we utilized human hepatocellular carcinoma Bel-7402 cells as an in vitro model to examine the effects of emodin on lipid production, SREBP1 signaling, and intrinsic apoptotic pathways. We further investigated whether the knock-out of SREBP1 would attenuate emodin-induced apoptosis, thereby providing insights into SREBP1-dependent and SREBP1-independent mechanisms of action. The findings of this study have significant implications for understanding the multifaceted anticancer effects of emodin and its potential as a therapeutic agent for HCC. By elucidating the interplay between lipid metabolism and apoptosis, this work contributes to the growing body of evidence supporting the role of metabolic reprogramming in cancer therapy. Furthermore, these results highlight the potential of targeting SREBP1 and associated lipid metabolic pathways as part of a broader strategy to induce apoptotic cell death in cancer cells. Materials and Methods Cell Culture and Reagents Human hepatocellular carcinoma cells, Bel-7402, were purchased from the Cell Bank of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (Shanghai, China). Cells were cultured in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM; Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 μg/mL streptomycin (Solarbio, Beijing, China). Cells were maintained in a humidified incubator at 37°C with 5% CO₂. Emodin (purity ≥98%) was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA) and dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO; Sigma-Aldrich) to prepare a 10 mM stock solution stored at -20°C. The final concentration of DMSO in cell culture did not exceed 0.1% (v/v) for all experiments. Cell Viability Assay Cell viability was assessed using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8; Dojindo, Japan) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Briefly, Bel-7402 cells were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 5×10³ cells/well and allowed to adhere overnight. Cells were treated with various concentrations of emodin (0, 10, 20, 40, and 60 μM) for 24, 48, and 72 hours. After treatment, 10 μL of CCK-8 solution was added to each well and incubated for 2 hours at 37°C. Absorbance was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader (BioTek, USA). The percentage of cell viability was calculated relative to untreated controls. Mitochondrial Membrane Potential (ΔΨm) Analysis The mitochondrial membrane potential was assessed using the JC-1 dye (Beyotime Biotechnology, Shanghai, China). Bel-7402 cells were seeded in 6-well plates and treated with emodin (0, 20, and 40 μM) for 24 hours. Subsequently, cells were harvested, washed with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), and incubated with JC-1 staining solution according to the manufacturer's instructions. The fluorescence intensity of JC-1 monomers (green, indicative of depolarized mitochondria) and aggregates (red, indicative of polarized mitochondria) was measured using a flow cytometer (BD Accuri C6, BD Biosciences, USA). The ratio of red to green fluorescence was calculated to determine the ΔΨm. Apoptosis Detection Apoptotic cell death was analyzed by Annexin V-FITC/propidium iodide (PI) staining. Bel-7402 cells were treated with emodin (0, 20, and 40 μM) for 24 hours, harvested, and stained with the Annexin V-FITC/PI Apoptosis Detection Kit (Beyotime Biotechnology) according to the manufacturer's protocol. Stained cells were analyzed using flow cytometry (BD Accuri C6), and the percentage of early and late apoptotic cells was quantified. Western Blot Analysis Protein expression levels of apoptosis- and lipid metabolism-related markers were analyzed by Western blotting. Bel-7402 cells were treated with emodin (0, 20, and 40 μM) for 24 hours, harvested, and lysed in RIPA buffer (Beyotime Biotechnology) supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Roche, Germany). Protein concentration was determined using a BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Equal amounts of protein (30 μg) were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred to polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membranes (Millipore, USA). Membranes were blocked with 5% non-fat milk in Tris-buffered saline with 0.1% Tween-20 (TBST) for 1 hour and incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies against cleaved-caspase 3, cleaved-caspase 9, Bax, Bcl-2, Apaf-1, cytochrome c, ATP citrate lyase (ACLY), acetyl-CoA carboxylase alpha (ACCα), fatty acid synthase (FASN), sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 (SREBP1), and β-actin (all from Cell Signaling Technology, USA). After washing with TBST, membranes were incubated with horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibodies (Cell Signaling Technology) for 1 hour at room temperature. Protein bands were visualized using an enhanced chemiluminescence substrate (Millipore) and quantified using ImageJ software (National Institutes of Health, USA). Quantitative Real-Time PCR (qRT-PCR) Total RNA was extracted from Bel-7402 cells treated with emodin (0, 20, and 40 μM) for 24 hours using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, USA). RNA was reverse-transcribed to cDNA using the PrimeScript RT Reagent Kit (Takara, Japan). qRT-PCR was performed using SYBR Green PCR Master Mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific) on a QuantStudio 6 Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems, USA). The relative expression of SREBP1, ACLY, ACCα, FASN, and stearoyl-CoA desaturase (SCD) was normalized to GAPDH and calculated using the 2^−ΔΔCt method. Primer sequences are provided in Supplementary Table 1. Lipid Content and Fatty Acid Desaturation Assay Intracellular triglyceride (TG) levels were measured using a Triglyceride Quantification Kit (Abcam, USA) following the manufacturer’s protocol. Briefly, Bel-7402 cells treated with emodin (0, 20, and 40 μM) for 24 hours were lysed, and TG content was normalized to total protein concentration. Fatty acid desaturation was analyzed by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). Lipids were extracted using a chloroform-methanol (2:1, v/v) mixture, and the fatty acid composition was determined by methylation followed by GC-MS analysis, as previously described [1]. SREBP1 Knockout CRISPR-Cas9 technology was employed to generate SREBP1-knockout Bel-7402 cells. Single-guide RNA (sgRNA) targeting SREBP1 was designed using CRISPR design tools and cloned into the lentiCRISPRv2 vector (Addgene, USA). Lentiviral particles were produced in HEK293T cells by co-transfecting lentiCRISPRv2-SREBP1, psPAX2, and pMD2.G plasmids using Lipofectamine 3000 (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Bel-7402 cells were infected with lentivirus and selected with 1 μg/mL puromycin for 7 days. Gene knockout was confirmed by Western blot and qRT-PCR. Statistical Analysis All experiments were performed in triplicate, and data are expressed as mean ± standard deviation. Statistical analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism 9 software (GraphPad Software, USA). Comparisons between groups were made using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey's post hoc test. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Breast cancer is the most common malignancy among women globally, with a significant proportion of patients developing metastatic disease over the course of their illness. Metastases to the skeleton are particularly prevalent in advanced breast cancer, with up to 70% of patients with metastatic breast cancer presenting with bone involvement at some stage [1,2]. Skeletal metastases are associated with substantial morbidity, including severe pain, fractures, hypercalcemia, and spinal cord compression, collectively termed skeletal-related events (SREs) [3]. These complications significantly impair quality of life and often necessitate intensive therapeutic interventions. Despite advancements in systemic therapies, bone metastases remain a critical determinant of prognosis in breast cancer patients, underscoring the need for robust prognostic biomarkers that can reliably stratify patients based on their risk of adverse clinical outcomes. The current clinical management of bone-metastatic breast cancer relies heavily on imaging for diagnosis, staging, and treatment monitoring. Conventional imaging modalities, such as bone scintigraphy, computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), are widely used to detect bone metastases [4]. However, these techniques have inherent limitations, including suboptimal sensitivity and specificity and a limited ability to provide quantitative assessments of tumor burden [5]. Positron emission tomography (PET) with 18F-fluoride (18F-NaF), combined with CT (18F-NaF PET/CT), has emerged as a highly sensitive imaging modality for detecting and characterizing bone metastases due to its ability to detect increased osteoblastic activity associated with metastatic lesions [6]. While 18F-NaF PET/CT is primarily utilized for diagnostic purposes, its potential role in prognostication, particularly through the quantification of skeletal tumor burden, remains underexplored. Quantification of tumor burden on imaging has garnered increasing attention as a potential prognostic tool in oncology. In breast cancer, metabolic or volumetric parameters derived from PET imaging using 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) have been shown to correlate with outcomes in both primary and metastatic disease [7,8]. Similarly, the extent of skeletal tumor burden on 18F-NaF PET/CT could provide critical insights into disease aggressiveness and progression. Unlike 18F-FDG PET, which primarily reflects glucose metabolism, 18F-NaF PET is a marker of bone turnover, providing complementary information about the skeletal microenvironment and its interaction with tumor cells [9]. However, the prognostic value of skeletal tumor burden quantified via 18F-NaF PET/CT has not been systematically evaluated in breast cancer patients, particularly in the context of survival outcomes and time to skeletal events. The identification of reliable imaging biomarkers for prognosis in bone-metastatic breast cancer is crucial, as it could aid in risk stratification, guide therapeutic decision-making, and optimize patient management. Current clinical prognostic models primarily rely on clinical and pathological parameters, such as tumor subtype, performance status, and serum biomarkers like alkaline phosphatase or bone turnover markers [10]. While these factors provide valuable information, they lack the spatial and quantitative resolution afforded by advanced imaging modalities. Incorporating imaging-derived metrics, such as skeletal tumor burden on 18F-NaF PET/CT, into prognostic algorithms may enhance their predictive accuracy and provide a more comprehensive assessment of disease status. Recent studies have highlighted the prognostic utility of 18F-NaF PET/CT in other malignancies with a propensity for bone metastases, including prostate cancer [11,12]. Metrics such as total skeletal tumor burden and standardized uptake values (SUVs) have shown promise in predicting clinical outcomes, including overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS), in these patient populations. Extrapolating these findings to breast cancer, it is reasonable to hypothesize that skeletal tumor burden, as quantified by 18F-NaF PET/CT, may serve as a robust imaging biomarker in patients with bone metastases. Moreover, the ability to longitudinally monitor changes in tumor burden over time could provide insights into treatment response and disease progression. To date, the prognostic implications of skeletal tumor burden on 18F-NaF PET/CT in breast cancer remain poorly understood, with limited evidence to support its clinical utility. Most prior studies have focused on qualitative assessments or semi-quantitative measures, which may not fully capture the complexity of metastatic disease in the skeleton. A comprehensive, quantitative approach to assess skeletal tumor burden could address this gap and provide a standardized framework for evaluating disease burden in clinical practice. Furthermore, understanding the relationship between skeletal tumor burden and survival outcomes, such as OS and PFS, could inform the development of personalized treatment strategies, particularly in patients at high risk for progression or SREs. In this study, we sought to address these gaps by systematically evaluating the prognostic significance of skeletal tumor burden quantified via 18F-NaF PET/CT in a cohort of breast cancer patients with bone metastases. Specifically, we aimed to determine whether skeletal tumor burden is independently associated with OS, PFS, and time to first bone event (TTBE) after adjusting for relevant clinical and pathological factors. By leveraging a robust imaging biomarker, we aimed to enhance the understanding of disease dynamics in bone-metastatic breast cancer and provide a foundation for integrating quantitative imaging metrics into routine clinical practice. Through this work, we intend to contribute to the evolving paradigm of precision oncology, wherein imaging biomarkers play a central role in tailoring therapeutic strategies and improving patient outcomes. Patient Population and Study Design This retrospective study was conducted in compliance with ethical standards and approved by the institutional review board. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to imaging. The cohort consisted of 107 female patients with histologically confirmed breast cancer who underwent 18F-Fluoride PET/CT imaging between January 2016 and December 2020. Patients were stratified into two groups: those undergoing imaging for primary staging (n = 40) and those undergoing restaging during follow-up after therapy (n = 67). Inclusion criteria required confirmation of breast cancer diagnosis, availability of clinical follow-up data, and at least one evaluable 18F-Fluoride PET/CT scan. Patients with other concurrent malignancies, prior history of skeletal conditions confounding uptake (e.g., Paget’s disease), or incomplete imaging datasets were excluded. Image Acquisition All 18F-Fluoride PET/CT scans were performed using a hybrid PET/CT scanner (Biograph mCT, Siemens Healthcare, Erlangen, Germany) following standard clinical protocols. Patients were intravenously administered 370 MBq (±10%) of 18F-sodium fluoride, with a 60-minute uptake period prior to image acquisition. Low-dose CT was performed for attenuation correction and anatomic localization, with settings of 120 kVp, 50 mAs, and 5-mm slice thickness. PET images were acquired in 3-dimensional mode with a scan duration of 2 minutes per bed position, covering the vertex to mid-thigh. Reconstruction of PET data employed ordered subset expectation maximization (OSEM) algorithms with corrections for scatter, randoms, and attenuation. Image Analysis and Tumor Burden Quantification Quantification of skeletal tumor burden was performed using a semiautomated software platform (MIM Encore v7.0, MIM Software Inc., Cleveland, OH). Each PET/CT dataset was reviewed by two board-certified nuclear medicine physicians with at least 8 years of experience in oncologic imaging. Discrepancies were resolved by consensus. Bone lesions were identified based on focal 18F-Fluoride uptake exceeding background activity and co-localized to lytic, sclerotic, or mixed lesions on CT. Lesions unrelated to metastatic disease, such as degenerative or traumatic changes, were excluded based on CT morphology and clinical history. Skeletal tumor burden was quantified using total lesion fluoride uptake (TLF), defined as the product of lesion volume and mean standardized uptake value (SUVmean). Lesion volumes were delineated using a fixed SUV threshold of 10, which has been previously validated for distinguishing malignant from benign bone uptake [1, 2]. For each patient, the sum of TLF across all bone lesions was calculated as the total skeletal tumor burden (TLFtotal). Additionally, the number of individual bone lesions (Nlesions) and their distribution across different skeletal regions (axial versus appendicular) were recorded. Clinical and Follow-Up Data Collection Baseline clinicopathologic data, including age, hormone receptor status (estrogen receptor [ER], progesterone receptor [PR]), HER2 status, and histologic subtype, were obtained from electronic medical records. Treatment regimens, including systemic therapies and radiotherapy, were documented for all patients. Clinical outcomes of interest included overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), and time to first skeletal-related event (SRE). OS was defined as the interval from the date of the first 18F-Fluoride PET/CT scan to death from any cause or last follow-up. PFS was defined as the time from imaging to radiologic or clinical progression. SREs included pathologic fractures, spinal cord compression, or the need for bone-directed interventions (e.g., surgery or radiotherapy). Follow-up data were collected until June 2022, with a median follow-up period of 19.5 months. Statistical Analysis Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS (v27.0, IBM Corp., Armonk, NY). Categorical variables were summarized as frequencies and percentages, while continuous variables were expressed as medians and interquartile ranges (IQR). The association of skeletal tumor burden metrics (TLFtotal and Nlesions) with clinical outcomes (OS, PFS, and time to SRE) was assessed using Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and the log-rank test. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models were constructed to adjust for potential confounders, including age, receptor status, and treatment history. Correlations between TLFtotal and clinicopathologic factors were evaluated using Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients. The prognostic significance of TLFtotal was compared to the presence of bone metastases alone (binary variable) to determine its added predictive value. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant for all analyses, and hazard ratios (HR) were reported with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Validation and Reproducibility To assess interobserver reliability, skeletal tumor burden quantification was repeated by a second independent physician in 20 randomly selected cases. Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) were calculated for TLFtotal and Nlesions, with values >0.90 indicating excellent agreement. Sensitivity analyses were performed to evaluate the robustness of prognostic models by excluding patients with atypical imaging features (e.g., diffuse marrow uptake or equivocal lesions). Ethical Considerations This study adhered to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Patient confidentiality was maintained throughout the study, and data were anonymized prior to analysis. The poultry industry has experienced significant growth over the years due to the increasing global demand for poultry meat, which is considered an affordable and high-quality protein source. As consumer preferences shift toward healthier and more sustainable food production systems, there is a growing emphasis on improving poultry production efficiency, animal health, and welfare while minimizing environmental impact. In this context, the use of feed additives such as probiotics has gained considerable attention as a natural and effective strategy to enhance growth performance, nutrient utilization, and gut health in poultry. Probiotics are live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer health benefits to the host by modulating gut microbiota and improving the overall intestinal environment. Among the various types of probiotics used in animal nutrition, Bacillus species, particularly Bacillus subtilis, have emerged as promising candidates. Bacillus subtilis is a spore-forming, Gram-positive bacterium known for its robust survivability under harsh environmental conditions, including the acidic environment of the gastrointestinal tract. This characteristic makes it particularly suitable for use as a dietary supplement in poultry production. The beneficial effects of Bacillus subtilis on poultry health and productivity have been attributed to several mechanisms, including the secretion of digestive enzymes, competitive exclusion of pathogenic bacteria, and modulation of the immune system. Previous studies have demonstrated that supplementation with Bacillus subtilis can improve growth performance, increase feed efficiency, and enhance nutrient digestibility in broilers. Moreover, the ability of Bacillus subtilis to inhibit harmful bacteria such as Escherichia coli and Salmonella in the gastrointestinal tract has been widely reported, contributing to a healthier gut microbiota and reduced risk of disease outbreaks. Despite the growing body of evidence supporting the use of Bacillus subtilis in poultry diets, the optimal inclusion level for maximizing its benefits remains a topic of ongoing investigation. Different studies have reported varying results regarding the most effective dosage, likely due to differences in experimental conditions, dietary formulations, and the specific strains of Bacillus subtilis used. Therefore, it is critical to conduct further research to determine the appropriate supplementation level that maximizes growth performance, nutrient metabolism, and gut health in broilers. In addition to enhancing growth performance, the role of Bacillus subtilis in improving nutrient metabolism is of particular interest. Efficient nutrient utilization is essential for achieving optimal growth rates and feed efficiency in broilers while reducing feed costs and environmental waste. By promoting better digestion and absorption of nutrients, Bacillus subtilis may contribute to the sustainability of poultry production systems. Furthermore, the modulation of intestinal microflora by Bacillus subtilis not only supports gut health but also helps to mitigate the adverse effects of pathogenic bacteria, which can compromise growth and feed efficiency. The present study aims to investigate the effects of different levels of Bacillus subtilis supplementation on the growth performance, nutrient metabolism, and intestinal microflora of broiler chickens from 1 to 42 days of age. Specifically, the study seeks to determine the optimal inclusion level of Bacillus subtilis that maximizes growth performance and feed efficiency while promoting gut health. A total of 800 one-day-old Arbor Acres (AA) broilers were used in this study, and the birds were randomly assigned to five groups, including a control group fed a basal diet and four experimental groups supplemented with 100, 150, 200, and 250 mg/kg of Bacillus subtilis, respectively. Growth performance parameters such as average daily gain (ADG), average daily feed intake (ADFI), and feed-to-gain ratio (F/G) were evaluated, along with nutrient metabolism and the composition of intestinal microflora. The findings of this study are expected to provide valuable insights into the potential benefits of Bacillus subtilis as a feed additive for broilers and contribute to the development of evidence-based recommendations for its inclusion in poultry diets. By identifying the optimal supplementation level, this research aims to support the poultry industry in achieving improved productivity and sustainability while addressing consumer demands for safe and natural food products. A total of 800 one-day-old healthy Arbor Acres (AA) broiler chickens, with an initial average body weight of 42.5 ± 0.5 g, were procured from a commercial hatchery and used for this study. The broilers were randomly allocated into five experimental groups, with four replicates per group and 40 broilers per replicate. Each replicate was housed in a separate pen under similar environmental conditions. Group 1 served as the control group and was fed a basal diet without any supplementation. Groups 2, 3, 4, and 5 received basal diets supplemented with Bacillus subtilis at concentrations of 100, 150, 200, and 250 mg/kg, respectively. The experimental period lasted for 42 days, divided into a starter phase (1–21 days) and a grower phase (22–42 days). The basal diet was formulated to meet or exceed the nutrient requirements for broilers as per NRC (1994) guidelines. The composition and nutrient levels of the basal diet are presented in Table 1. Bacillus subtilis used in this study was a commercially available probiotic preparation containing viable spores of B. subtilis at a concentration of 1 × 10⁹ CFU/g. The required amount of the probiotic was mixed thoroughly with the basal diet to ensure uniform distribution before feeding. All broilers were housed in a climate-controlled facility with a litter floor system. Temperature was maintained at 32–34°C during the first week and gradually reduced by 2–3°C per week until it reached 24°C, which was then maintained for the remainder of the experiment. A 24-hour lighting schedule was provided throughout the study. Feed and water were provided ad libitum. Body weight (BW) and feed intake were recorded weekly for each replicate pen. Average daily gain (ADG), average daily feed intake (ADFI), and feed-to-gain ratio (F/G) were calculated for each group. Mortality was monitored daily, and any deceased birds were weighed and recorded to adjust feed intake and body weight gain calculations. At the end of the experiment (day 42), four broilers from each replicate (16 birds per group) were randomly selected for sample collection. Birds were fasted for 12 hours, weighed, and euthanized by cervical dislocation. The cecum was aseptically removed from each bird, and cecal contents were collected into sterile tubes for microbiological analysis. Samples were immediately placed on ice and transported to the laboratory for microbial enumeration. The populations of Escherichia coli and Salmonella in the cecal contents were determined using selective culture techniques. Serial dilutions of cecal contents were prepared in sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), and aliquots were plated onto MacConkey agar for E. coli enumeration and Xylose Lysine Deoxycholate (XLD) agar for Salmonella enumeration. Plates were incubated at 37°C for 24–48 hours, and colonies were counted and expressed as log CFU/g of cecal content. To evaluate nutrient metabolism, apparent nutrient digestibility was assessed during the last three days of the experiment (days 40–42). Titanium dioxide (0.5%) was included in the diet as an indigestible marker. Fecal samples were collected from each replicate and pooled for nutrient analysis. Proximate composition of the feed and fecal samples was determined using standard methods (AOAC, 2005). Crude protein, crude fat, dry matter, and organic matter digestibility were calculated based on the concentrations of titanium dioxide and the respective nutrients in the feed and feces. Serum samples were collected from the jugular vein of the selected birds at day 42 before euthanasia. Blood was centrifuged at 3,000 × g for 10 minutes, and the serum was stored at -20°C for subsequent biochemical analysis. Serum indices, including total protein, albumin, and cholesterol, were measured using an automatic biochemical analyzer (Model XX, Manufacturer, City, Country). All data were statistically analyzed using SPSS software (Version XX, IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Data were expressed as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed to evaluate the effects of different levels of B. subtilis supplementation on growth performance, nutrient metabolism, and microbial populations. When significant differences were observed (P < 0.05), Duncan's multiple range test was used to compare means among groups.
