Pelvic adhesions are a common consequence of pelvic surgery and a recognized cause of morbidity in women of reproductive age. They contribute to chronic pelvic pain, bowel obstruction, difficult reoperation, and infertility [1,2]. After operative laparoscopy for endometriosis, adhesion reformation is frequent. Second-look laparoscopy studies report that de novo adhesion formation and reformation of existing adhesions occur in a substantial proportion of patients, even after meticulous microsurgical technique [3,4]. The ovaries are particularly vulnerable. Their raw surfaces after endometrioma excision, cauterization, or adhesiolysis readily adhere to the adjacent ovarian fossa, and the resulting adhesions may distort tubo-ovarian anatomy, impair oocyte pickup, and compromise access to follicles during oocyte retrieval [5]. Pathophysiology of postoperative adhesion formation Peritoneal injury initiates an inflammatory response with exudation of fibrin-rich fluid. Under normal circumstances, mesothelial repair and fibrinolysis, mediated largely by tissue plasminogen activator, remove this fibrinous deposit within several days. Surgical trauma, ischemia, desiccation, thermal injury, and foreign bodies reduce peritoneal fibrinolytic activity, so the fibrin matrix persists and is colonized by fibroblasts and capillaries, becoming a permanent fibrous adhesion [6,7]. Two observations are central to adhesion prevention. First, the critical period for adhesion formation is the first several days after surgery. Second, adhesions form preferentially between surfaces that are in apposition during this period [8]. Strategies that maintain separation of injured surfaces during this window therefore have a sound biological rationale. Current approaches to adhesion prevention Prevention strategies include meticulous hemostasis, minimization of tissue handling and thermal injury, copious irrigation, and minimally invasive technique [9]. Pharmacologic agents, including corticosteroids, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and fibrinolytic agents, have shown inconsistent benefit and are not recommended for routine use [10]. Barrier agents, such as oxidized regenerated cellulose, expanded polytetrafluoroethylene, and hyaluronic acid or polyethylene glycol-based gels and films, aim to separate injured surfaces physically while healing occurs. Some of these reduce the incidence or severity of adhesions in controlled trials, but evidence of improved fertility or reduced pain is limited, and cost, handling difficulty, and availability restrict their use, particularly through laparoscopic ports [11,12]. Consequently, no method reliably prevents adhesions, and the search continues for simple, inexpensive, and safe adjuncts. Temporary ovarian suspension Because adhesion formation depends on apposition of raw surfaces, elevating the ovaries away from the ovarian fossa during the critical healing period is a logical mechanical approach. Several authors have described temporary ovarian suspension (TOS) to the anterior abdominal wall or to the round ligament or uterine structures at the end of laparoscopic surgery, particularly after excision of endometriosis or ovarian drilling [13–15]. Reported techniques use a transabdominal straight needle or a suture passed through the abdominal wall under laparoscopic vision, with the ovary held anteriorly for a limited time. Suspension using absorbable material allows spontaneous release, whereas non-absorbable suture requires removal after a few days, usually by cutting a subcutaneous knot or external traction. Small series and comparative studies suggest that suspension may decrease ovarian adhesion scores at second-look laparoscopy, although data remain sparse and heterogeneous [14,16]. Despite this rationale, TOS has not been widely adopted. Reasons may include concerns about safety and the lack of standardized technique. Theoretical risks include injury to the inferior epigastric vessels or bowel during needle passage, hematoma formation, infection, ovarian ischemia or torsion, and herniation or entrapment of bowel through the suture loop with obstruction or strangulation [17]. Whether the ovaries return to their normal anatomical position after suspension is released is also a relevant question, as persistent displacement could itself impair function. The choice of suture material introduces a further practical issue. Absorbable suture eliminates the need for removal and the possibility of a retained loop, but it may lose tensile strength or be absorbed before the critical period of adhesion formation has passed. Non-absorbable suture provides predictable, sustained suspension but requires a second step for removal and carries a theoretical risk if the loop is retained. Direct comparisons of the two approaches are lacking. Rationale and aim of the present study Women with advanced endometriosis are the group most likely to benefit from effective adhesion prevention, as they typically have extensive ovarian and pelvic disease, are at high risk of adhesion reformation, and frequently seek fertility treatment. Evidence on the safety of TOS in sizeable cohorts and over a long period is needed before it can be considered a reasonable adjunct, as are data on its relationship to subsequent reproductive outcomes in patients attempting conception. We therefore report a retrospective experience of 152 patients who underwent TOS to the anterior abdominal wall at the conclusion of operative laparoscopy, performed over nearly two decades by a single surgical practice. Non-absorbable monofilament nylon suture was used in earlier cases and absorbable plain catgut in later ones. The aim of this study was to compare the two techniques with respect to safety, including intraoperative and late complications, and efficacy, assessed by ovarian position on early postoperative ultrasonography and by clinical pregnancy and delivery rates in patients conceiving without in vitro fertilization. Study design and setting We conducted a retrospective cohort study of consecutive patients who underwent temporary ovarian suspension (TOS) to the anterior abdominal wall at the conclusion of operative laparoscopy between 1998 and 2017. All procedures were performed by a single surgeon (or a surgical team trained by the senior author) at one tertiary referral center for minimally invasive gynecologic surgery and reproductive medicine. The study followed the STROBE recommendations for observational studies [1]. Institutional review board approval was obtained, and the requirement for additional consent was waived because of the retrospective design and the use of de-identified data. All patients had given written informed consent for surgery and for the use of their clinical data for research. Participants Patients were eligible if they underwent operative laparoscopy in which one or both ovaries were suspended at the end of surgery to reduce postoperative adhesion formation between the ovary and the ovarian fossa. Indications for suspension included extensive dissection or excision of the ovarian fossa peritoneum, excision of endometriomas, ovarian cystectomy, and extensive adhesiolysis. Endometriosis was staged according to the revised American Society for Reproductive Medicine classification [2]. Patients were excluded if the operative record or follow-up data were incomplete, if oophorectomy was performed on the side to be suspended, or if conversion to laparotomy occurred. A total of 152 patients met the criteria. Of these, 142 (93.4%) had advanced-stage endometriosis and 10 (6.6%) had other indications, such as pelvic adhesive disease or benign adnexal pathology. Patients were allocated by the suture material used, which reflected the period of surgery rather than randomization. Group 1 (n=78) underwent suspension with absorbable 3-0 plain catgut. Group 2 (n=74) comprised earlier patients, in whom non-absorbable 3-0 monofilament nylon was used. Surgical technique Procedures were performed under general endotracheal anesthesia using a standard multiport laparoscopic approach, with a umbilical or open-entry primary port and two or three accessory ports. Surgery consisted of complete excision or ablation of endometriosis, adhesiolysis, and restoration of normal pelvic anatomy, using sharp dissection, bipolar or laser energy, as appropriate [3]. Hemostasis was secured before suspension, and the pelvis was copiously irrigated with warmed lactated Ringer's solution. For suspension, a straight or curved needle carrying the suture was introduced percutaneously through the lower abdominal wall under direct laparoscopic vision, at a site lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, which were identified by transillumination and visualization. The needle was passed through the utero-ovarian ligament or the ovarian utero-ovarian ligament and adjacent broad ligament, avoiding the ovarian hilum and vessels, and then brought back out through the abdominal wall approximately 1 cm from the entry site, creating a loop. The ovary was elevated toward the anterior abdominal wall, away from the ovarian fossa, and the suture ends were tied over the fascia in the subcutaneous tissue, with tension adequate to hold the ovary without ischemia or tenting of the skin. The procedure was repeated contralaterally when indicated. In Group 1, the plain catgut suture was left in place to be absorbed spontaneously, which was expected within about 5–7 days. In Group 2, the nylon suture was removed in the office or on the ward after a similar interval (postoperative day 5–7) by cutting the subcutaneous knot and withdrawing the suture. In both groups the intent was suspension for the critical period of early peritoneal healing and re-epithelialization [4]. Perioperative management and follow-up Patients received standard perioperative antibiotic and thromboprophylaxis according to institutional protocol and were discharged the same day or on the first postoperative day. Analgesia was provided with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and, if required, short-course opioids. Patients were reviewed at one week, when a transvaginal ultrasound scan was performed to document ovarian position relative to the ovarian fossa and uterus, after absorption or removal of the suture. Subsequent follow-up occurred at clinic visits, through telephone contact, and from medical records. Outcome measures The primary outcome was safety, defined as the occurrence of intraoperative complications (hemorrhage from the abdominal wall or ovarian vessels, visceral injury) and late complications (wound or pelvic infection, abdominal wall hematoma, bowel herniation through the suture loop and its sequelae, including obstruction or strangulation). Complications were identified from operative notes, discharge summaries, and follow-up records. Efficacy was assessed by two measures. First, the ovarian position on transvaginal ultrasonography at one week was recorded as being in the anatomical location (ovarian fossa) or not. Second, among patients seeking fertility who conceived by non-IVF methods, we recorded clinical pregnancy (ultrasound-confirmed gestational sac) and delivery (live birth beyond 20 weeks), as proxies for restored pelvic function and reduced adhesion burden [5]. Patients who underwent IVF were excluded from pregnancy analyses because assisted conception bypasses tubo-ovarian function and could mask any effect of adhesion prevention. Second-look laparoscopy was not performed routinely, so adhesion scores were not available. Data collection Demographic and clinical variables were extracted from medical records, including age, parity, infertility history, indication and stage of disease, procedures performed, operative time, laterality of suspension, and complications. Data were entered into a secure database and verified by a second reviewer. Statistical analysis Continuous variables were summarized as mean ± standard deviation or median (interquartile range), depending on distribution assessed by the Shapiro–Wilk test, and compared with Student's t-test or the Mann–Whitney U test. Categorical variables were expressed as counts and percentages and compared with the chi-square test or Fisher's exact test when expected cell counts were below five. Complication rates were reported with exact 95% confidence intervals. Pregnancy and delivery rates were compared between groups among patients attempting non-IVF conception. A two-sided P value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed using SPSS (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY) [6]. Because of the retrospective design and non-randomized allocation, no formal sample size calculation was undertaken, and results were interpreted as exploratory. Patient characteristics A total of 152 patients underwent TOS to the anterior abdominal wall at the conclusion of operative laparoscopy between 1998 and 2017. Seventy-eight patients (Group 1) had ovarian suspension with absorbable 3-0 plain catgut, and 74 patients (Group 2) had suspension with non-absorbable 3-0 monofilament nylon. Group 2 comprised the earlier cases in the series, and absorbable suture was adopted subsequently. The indication for surgery was advanced-stage endometriosis in 142 patients (93.4%) and other indications in 10 patients (6.6%). The latter included extensive pelvic adhesions and other benign adnexal pathology. The distribution of indications was similar between groups, and most patients in both groups had stage III or IV disease according to the revised American Society for Reproductive Medicine classification [1]. Table 1 summarizes the baseline characteristics. Age, body mass index, parity, and duration of infertility did not differ significantly between groups (all P > 0.05). Procedures performed included excision or ablation of endometriosis, ovarian cystectomy for endometriomas, adhesiolysis, and, where required, excision of deep infiltrating disease. The proportion of patients with unilateral versus bilateral suspension was comparable between groups. Intraoperative and technical outcomes TOS was completed successfully in all 152 patients, with no conversions to laparotomy attributable to the suspension technique. Massive multiple-input, multiple-output (MIMO) is a key technology for fifth generation (5G) and beyond wireless networks. By equipping the base station (BS) with a large number of antennas, serving many users simultaneously on the same time-frequency resource becomes possible, yielding substantial gains in spectral and energy efficiency [1], [2]. As the number of BS antennas grows, the channel vectors of different users become increasingly orthogonal under favorable propagation, and simple linear processing such as maximum-ratio or zero-forcing (ZF) approaches the performance of optimal nonlinear schemes [3]. Small-scale fading is also averaged out, a phenomenon known as channel hardening, which relaxes the demands on scheduling and power control [4]. These benefits rely on accurate channel state information (CSI) at the BS. In time division duplex (TDD) operation, which is the favored mode for massive MIMO, CSI is acquired from uplink (UL) pilots and exploited through reciprocity for both UL detection and downlink (DL) precoding [1]. The CSI is therefore only valid for a limited period. Between the instant of channel estimation and the instant of use, the channel evolves because of user mobility and movement of scatterers. This inherent propagation and processing delay produces channel aging, in which outdated CSI degrades the effective signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio and causes inaccuracies in detection and precoding [5], [6]. The effect is particularly harmful for DL precoding, since the delay between estimation and transmission is generally longer than that for UL detection, and the interference nulling of ZF is sensitive to errors in the channel estimate. In extreme cases, only the UL may remain usable. The temporal behavior of massive MIMO channels is therefore central to assessing practical deployments, determining pilot overhead, frame structure, and the feasible mobility range. Much of the literature on mobility in massive MIMO has been theoretical. Analyses based on autoregressive channel models, Jakes' Doppler spectrum, and the associated temporal correlation have been used to derive achievable rates under aging and to design predictors or robust precoders [5]–[7]. These studies typically assume independent and identically distributed Rayleigh fading across antennas and users, and an isotropic scattering environment. Real channels deviate from these assumptions: propagation is often dominated by line-of-sight (LOS) components, scatterers are spatially clustered, and the Doppler shifts experienced across a large array may differ between antennas and between users. Such features influence how rapidly the composite channel vector decorrelates, and they cannot be fully captured by simplified models. Measurements are thus indispensable. Several massive MIMO testbeds have been developed, including the Lund University LuMaMi system [8], the Argos platform [9], and the Bristol-Lund system used in this work [10]. Measurement campaigns have studied favorable propagation, channel hardening, spatial correlation, and capacity in indoor and outdoor settings, mostly with static or nomadic users [11]–[13]. Studies of the effect of mobility on real massive MIMO channels remain comparatively scarce. Some real-time prototypes have demonstrated operation with moving terminals [8], [14], and a few measurement-based works have examined channel aging at low speeds, but a systematic characterization of temporal correlation for a large array serving multiple users in a realistic LOS environment with moving vehicles and pedestrians is lacking. In particular, it is not well understood how the array size affects the rate at which the multi-user channel must be updated, nor how it influences the rate at which power control must be refreshed. The two effects of array size are expected to work in opposite directions. On one hand, the channel vector of a user with many antennas is high dimensional, and its correlation with an earlier snapshot may fall more quickly, since small phase changes accumulate coherently across antennas and the narrower beams are more sensitive to user displacement. This suggests that CSI for precoding and detection must be refreshed more often as the array grows. On the other hand, channel hardening makes the channel gain, and hence the large-scale quantity relevant to power control, vary much more slowly, so that power control updates could be less frequent. Quantifying both effects with measured data would give system designers concrete guidance. This paper presents, to the authors' knowledge, the first measured results on the temporal behavior of a LOS massive MIMO channel with moderate mobility. Using a 100-antenna BS operating at 3.7 GHz and serving 8 users, measurements were taken in an outdoor environment with moving cars and pedestrians, with vehicle speeds up to 29 km/h. We examine the temporal correlation of the MIMO channel vector, and evaluate how the correlation, and thus the required update interval, changes with the number of BS antennas. The contributions are as follows: 1. We describe a measurement campaign with a 100-antenna array and 8 simultaneously active mobile users in a LOS scenario at 3.7 GHz. 2. We characterize the temporal correlation of the channel vector and show that, relative to an 8-antenna system, the CSI update rate for the 100-antenna system may need to increase by a factor of about 7. 3. We investigate channel hardening in time and show that, relative to a single-antenna system, the power control update rate can be reduced by at least a factor of 5. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II describes the measurement system and scenario. Section III defines the metrics used for temporal analysis. Section IV presents and discusses the results, and Section V concludes the paper. The measurements were carried out using the Lund University massive MIMO testbed (LuMaMi), a software-defined radio platform based on NI hardware and operating in TDD mode [1]. The system was configured with 100 transceiver chains connected to a 160-element dual-polarized patch antenna array, centred at 3.7 GHz with a 20 MHz bandwidth. The signal used OFDM with 2048 subcarriers, of which 1200 were active, and a subcarrier spacing of 15 kHz, similar to the LTE numerology. The frame structure comprised 10 ms frames, divided into slots in which uplink pilots and data were transmitted. The array was mounted on the exterior of a building roof at about 20 m above ground level and was oriented towards the measurement area. Measurement Scenario The campaign was conducted in an outdoor, predominantly LOS environment in an open car park area adjoining the BS building. The area contained parked cars, trees, and surrounding buildings that acted as potential scatterers. Eight single-antenna user terminals were served simultaneously. Each terminal consisted of a software-defined radio connected to an omnidirectional monopole antenna. Two groups of users were used. Some terminals were carried by pedestrians walking at approximately 3–5 km/h, while others were mounted on vehicles driven along predefined routes at speeds up to 29 km/h. In addition to the intentionally moving users, other cars and pedestrians moved in the vicinity, producing time-varying scattering. Each user was synchronized to the BS through a dedicated pilot and over-the-air time and frequency references, and their transmissions used orthogonal pilot resources (frequency-interleaved subcarriers) so that the channels of all 8 users could be estimated in each pilot symbol. Channel Estimation and Data Processing For each pilot opportunity, the least-squares estimate of the channel was obtained per subcarrier and per BS antenna. The channel for user k at time t and subcarrier f is written as the vector hk(t,f) ∈ C^{M×1}, where M = 100 is the number of active BS antennas. The channel sounding repetition interval was 0.5 ms, giving a Doppler-unambiguous sampling at the speeds considered. Using a carrier frequency fc = 3.7 GHz, the maximum Doppler shift for a 29 km/h (8.06 m/s) user is fD = v fc / c ≈ 99 Hz, which corresponds to a coherence time of approximately 0.423/fD ≈ 4.3 ms according to the usual rule of thumb [2]. Measurements were recorded in snapshots of several seconds, and the data were normalized to remove the effect of the automatic gain control and hardware calibration offsets. Reciprocity calibration was not required for the temporal analysis of the UL channel, but it is relevant for the DL interpretation of the results [3]. Temporal Correlation Metrics The temporal behaviour of the channel was quantified with two measures. First, the normalized temporal correlation coefficient of the channel vector was computed as ρk(τ) = |E[hk^H(t) hk(t+τ)]| / (E[‖hk(t)‖²]^{1/2} E[‖hk(t+τ)‖²]^{1/2}), where the expectation was approximated by averaging over time t and over the subcarriers within the measured band. This is the vector generalization of the conventional scalar autocorrelation function, and for M = 1 it reduces to the single antenna case. To determine the dependence on the number of antennas, ρk(τ) was evaluated for subsets of M = 1, 8, 20, 50, and 100 antennas, selected with different random and contiguous configurations, and the results were averaged. The channel is said to be decorrelated when ρk(τ) falls below a threshold, here 0.9 for CSI-update purposes, which corresponds to a limited loss in beamforming gain [4]. The CSI update interval was taken as the lag τ at which this threshold was crossed. Second, in order to assess the effect of the temporal variation on power control, the large-scale (average) received power was separated from the instantaneous channel gain by averaging ‖hk(t)‖² over a sliding window of 20 wavelengths in distance, following the conventional approach to separate small- and large-scale fading [5]. The change in the received power over time was then evaluated for single-antenna and multi-antenna arrays, and the time lag at which the power deviated by more than 1 dB from its initial value was recorded as the power control update interval. The channel hardening effect, whereby the fluctuation of ‖hk‖² reduces as M grows [6], was quantified through the normalized variance of the channel gain, Var(‖hk‖²)/E[‖hk‖²]². Impact on Precoding and Detection To relate the correlation results to system performance, the effect of outdated CSI was examined by applying channel estimates obtained at time t to the channel at time t+τ. For the UL, a zero-forcing (ZF) detector W = H(H^H H)^{-1} was computed from the estimated H(t) ∈ C^{M×K} with K = 8, and applied to H(t+τ). The post-detection signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) was determined for each user, and the resulting sum-rate was computed under a fixed transmit power assumption. Likewise, for the DL, a ZF precoder constructed from the outdated channel was applied under the assumption of ideal reciprocity, and the sum-rate degradation relative to the ideal, instantaneous CSI case was calculated. This allowed the CSI update rate requirements for different array sizes to be compared at a fixed performance loss. Artificial neural networks (ANNs) have become a central tool for pattern recognition, signal classification, and decision-making in embedded and edge-computing systems [1], [2]. Many of these applications are constrained by power, area, and latency budgets that conventional software implementations on general-purpose processors cannot meet. This has motivated considerable work on dedicated hardware accelerators, particularly those built on analog and mixed-signal circuits and emerging non-volatile memory devices [3], [4]. Among the many network architectures, the Probabilistic Neural Network (PNN), introduced by Specht [5], is an attractive candidate for hardware realization because it requires no iterative weight training, offers fast learning, and approximates the Bayes-optimal decision rule as the number of training samples grows. Background and Motivation A PNN is a feed-forward network with four layers: an input layer, a pattern layer, a summation layer, and an output (decision) layer. The pattern layer computes, for each stored training exemplar, a radial basis activation, typically an exponential of the distance between the input vector and the exemplar. The summation layer accumulates these activations per class and approximates the class-conditional probability density through a Parzen-window estimator [6]. The output layer selects the class with the largest estimate. Training amounts to storing the exemplars as weights, so learning is essentially a single pass. Consequently, the PNN has been applied to medical diagnosis, fault detection, speech and image recognition, and remote sensing [7]–[9]. Despite these advantages, the PNN poses two significant challenges for efficient hardware implementation. First, the pattern layer requires evaluation of an exponential function for every stored exemplar. Implementing this nonlinearity digitally demands lookup tables or iterative arithmetic units, and implementing it in analog circuitry demands transistors operated in specific regimes that are sensitive to process, voltage, and temperature variation [10]. Second, the network stores one weight vector per training sample, so memory requirements grow linearly with the training set. Fetching these weights from separate memory incurs the well-known von Neumann bottleneck, which dominates energy consumption in data-intensive inference [11]. Related Work Prior hardware PNN designs have followed several directions. FPGA and ASIC digital implementations exploit parallelism but still require substantial arithmetic resources for the exponential and for distance computation [12], [13]. Analog implementations based on translinear or subthreshold circuits realize the exponential compactly but suffer from limited precision and noise [10], [14]. Approximations of the exponential, such as piecewise-linear functions, bit-shift-based schemes, and Taylor expansions, reduce cost at the expense of classification accuracy and added control logic [15]. In parallel, threshold logic has been studied as a compact computational primitive in which a gate outputs a binary value according to whether a weighted sum of inputs exceeds a threshold [16]. Threshold gates can realize functions requiring many conventional logic gates and have been demonstrated with CMOS and memristive devices [17]. Memristors, as two-terminal non-volatile devices with tunable conductance, enable dense crossbar arrays that perform vector-matrix multiplication in place, using Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws [18], [19]. Crossbar-based accelerators have been proposed for multilayer perceptrons, convolutional networks, and associative memories [20], [21]. However, memristive devices offer only a limited number of reliably programmable conductance states, and device variability, sneak paths, and peripheral circuit overhead restrict achievable precision [22]. Efficient designs therefore require algorithms that tolerate coarse weight resolution. To our knowledge, few studies have co-designed the PNN algorithm itself with a memristive crossbar and threshold-logic nonlinearity. Proposed Approach and Contributions This paper addresses this gap by developing an approximate PNN (APNN) that is jointly suited to algorithmic accuracy and circuit efficiency. Rather than computing an exponential kernel, the APNN uses gated threshold logic to produce the pattern-layer response, replacing a transcendental function with a comparison-based operation that maps naturally onto compact circuits. The stored exemplars are held in a memristive crossbar, so that the similarity computation takes place where the weights reside and data movement is reduced. To make this mapping practical, the training weights are normalized and quantized to a small number of discrete levels, matching the limited conductance resolution of memristive devices and simplifying the peripheral circuitry. The main contributions of this work are as follows: 1. An approximate PNN formulation in which the exponential activation is replaced by gated threshold logic, with analysis of its effect on the resulting decision rule. 2. A weight normalization and quantization procedure that reduces the exemplar weights to a limited set of levels, together with an evaluation of the resulting accuracy–complexity trade-off. 3. A memristive crossbar-based circuit architecture for the APNN, covering the weight storage, similarity computation, summation, and decision stages. 4. Simulation-based evaluation on benchmark classification tasks, comparing accuracy, area, and power against conventional PNN implementations. Organization of the Paper The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews the PNN algorithm and the memristive crossbar fundamentals. Section III presents the APNN algorithm, including the threshold-logic approximation and weight quantization. Section IV describes the circuit implementation. Section V reports simulation results and discusses robustness and hardware cost. Section VI concludes the paper. Overview of the Proposed Approach The proposed approximate probabilistic neural network (APNN) retains the four-layer topology of the conventional PNN [1]: an input layer, a pattern layer, a summation layer, and an output (decision) layer. Two modifications are introduced. First, the exponential activation of each pattern neuron is replaced by a gated threshold logic function that can be realized with simple comparator circuitry. Second, the pattern-layer weights are normalized, quantized to 16 levels, and stored as memristor conductances in a crossbar array. The following subsections describe the conventional formulation, the approximation, the weight preprocessing, and the hardware mapping. Conventional PNN Formulation Let the training set contain N samples xj ∈ ℝ^d, each belonging to one of C classes. For a test vector x, the Parzen-window estimate of the class-conditional density for class c is fc(x) = (1 / (Nc (2π)^{d/2} σ^d)) Σ{j∈c} exp(−‖x − xj‖² / 2σ²), where Nc is the number of training samples in class c and σ is the smoothing parameter. The decision is ĉ = argmaxc fc(x). If the input and training vectors are normalized to unit Euclidean length, the exponent reduces to exp((x·xj − 1) / σ²), so that each pattern neuron computes an inner product zj = wj·x, with wj = xj, followed by an exponential nonlinearity [1]. The inner product is a natural fit for a memristive crossbar, whereas the exponential is costly in analog and digital hardware. The approximation therefore targets this nonlinearity. Gated Threshold Logic Activation The exponential is a monotonically increasing function of zj. Since the final decision depends only on the relative magnitudes of class sums, it is sufficient to preserve the monotonic, convex character of the activation over the relevant range rather than its exact values. The exponential is approximated by a piecewise-constant function composed of K threshold units: g(z) = Σ{k=1}^{K} ak · G(z − θk), where G(·) is the Heaviside step function, θk are ordered thresholds, and ak are non-negative increments. Each step is implemented by a comparator whose output is gated, that is, passed to the summation layer only when its threshold condition is met. Because the gates produce binary outputs, the summation layer reduces to counting or weighted accumulation of gated pulses, avoiding analog multiplication or exponentiation. The thresholds are selected by sampling the target function exp((z − 1)/σ²) on [zmin, 1] so that the increments ak follow the exponential's growth. Two placement strategies were considered: uniform spacing in z, and uniform spacing in the output of the exponential (equal-increment steps). The parameters {θk, ak} were chosen by minimizing the mean squared error between g(z) and the exponential over the empirical distribution of z values observed on training data. In the extreme case of one threshold, the network behaves as a voting scheme counting training patterns whose similarity to the input exceeds θ. Weight Normalization and Quantization Each training vector is first normalized to unit L2 norm, ensuring that inner products lie in [−1, 1] and are comparable across patterns. Features are initially rescaled to a common nonnegative range, so that all weights also lie in [0, 1], matching the positive conductance range of memristive devices. Each weight wji is then quantized uniformly to one of L = 16 levels: qji = round((L − 1) · wji) / (L − 1), which requires 4 bits per weight. The quantization step is Δ = 1/15, giving a maximum per-weight error of Δ/2. Because the quantization error is approximately zero-mean and independent across features, the error in the inner product grows sublinearly with d, and the thresholds θk are recalibrated using quantized weights so that the systematic bias is absorbed. Sixteen levels were chosen as a compromise between classification accuracy and the number of distinguishable conductance states that a practical memristor can reliably hold [2]. Memristive Crossbar Implementation The quantized weights are mapped to conductances Gji ∈ [Gmin, Gmax]: Gji = Gmin + qji (Gmax − Gmin). Input features are encoded as voltages Vi applied to the crossbar rows, and each column corresponds to a pattern neuron. By Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws, the current in column j is Ij = Σi Gji Vi, which realizes the inner product in a single step. The offset Gmin contributes a term proportional to ΣVi, which is the same for all columns and is removed with a reference column or by differential subtraction. Programming of the 16 conductance states is performed with a write-verify scheme in which voltage pulses are applied until the measured conductance falls within the tolerance band of the target level [2]. Column currents are converted to voltages by transimpedance stages and fed to the bank of gated threshold comparators. The gate outputs of all pattern neurons belonging to the same class are accumulated in the summation layer, and a winner-take-all circuit selects the class with the largest sum. Experimental Evaluation Protocol The APNN was evaluated against the conventional PNN with exact exponential activation and full-precision weights. Benchmark classification datasets were partitioned with stratified k-fold cross-validation, and σ was selected by grid search on validation folds. Ablation studies isolated the effect of (i) threshold activation alone, (ii) quantization alone, and (iii) both. The number of thresholds K and quantization levels were varied to characterize the accuracy–complexity trade-off. Circuit-level simulations incorporated device variation, modeled as multiplicative log-normal perturbations of conductance, to assess robustness. Performance was reported as classification accuracy, together with component counts and estimated power for the crossbar and comparator stages. Experimental Setup. The proposed APNN was evaluated against a conventional PNN with Gaussian (exponential) kernels on three benchmark datasets from the UCI repository [12]: Iris (4 features, 3 classes), Wine (13 features, 3 classes), and Breast Cancer Wisconsin (30 features, 2 classes). Features were min-max normalized to [0,1]. Each dataset was partitioned using stratified 10-fold cross-validation, and results are reported as mean ± standard deviation over 10 independent runs. The smoothing parameter of the conventional PNN was selected by grid search on the training folds. In the APNN, the threshold of the gated threshold logic was tuned in the same manner. Circuit-level simulations of the memristive crossbar used a device model with 16 distinguishable conductance states [8], with a stated variability of 5% in the programmed conductance unless noted otherwise. Software and circuit-level results are reported separately. Classification Accuracy. Table I summarizes classification accuracy. The conventional PNN with floating-point weights achieved 96.7 ± 3.1% on Iris, 97.2 ± 2.8% on Wine, and 96.1 ± 1.9% on Breast Cancer. The APNN with normalized weights, 16-level quantization, and gated threshold logic achieved 95.3 ± 3.5%, 95.6 ± 3.2%, and 94.9 ± 2.2%, respectively. The accuracy reduction relative to the baseline was therefore 1.2–1.6 percentage points across all datasets, which is within one standard deviation of the baseline in every case. A paired t-test across folds showed no statistically significant difference (p > 0.05) on Iris and Wine, and a marginal difference on Breast Cancer (p ≈ 0.04). These results indicate that replacing the exponential activation with a threshold-based approximation preserves the discriminative ability of the PNN to a large extent. Combinatorial optimization problems arise in a wide range of practical settings, including logistics, scheduling, network design, and manufacturing. Many of these problems are NP-hard, so exact methods are often impractical for large instances, and heuristic and metaheuristic approaches are used to obtain high quality solutions within reasonable computing time [1]. Metaheuristics provide general frameworks that guide subordinate heuristics through the search space, balancing diversification, which explores new regions, with intensification, which exploits promising ones [2]. Well-known examples include simulated annealing, tabu search, genetic algorithms, ant colony optimization, and the greedy randomized adaptive search procedure (GRASP) [3,4]. GRASP is a multi-start method in which each iteration consists of two phases: a randomized greedy construction of a solution and a local search that improves it [4]. The method is simple, has few parameters, and is easy to implement. Its main limitation is that iterations are independent. No information gathered during earlier iterations influences later ones, so the search cannot learn from the structure of good solutions already found. Several extensions have been proposed to address this, the most common being path relinking [5], which explores trajectories between elite solutions, and reactive GRASP [6], which adapts the greedy randomization parameter. Other hybrids add memory or learning components, such as bias functions in the construction phase [7] and the use of frequently occurring elements from elite solutions in the spirit of "vocabulary building" and "proximate optimality" [8]. A related line of work exploits the observation that good solutions to a combinatorial problem tend to share many common elements, often called the "big valley" structure of the landscape [9]. This suggests that high quality solutions can be found by focusing on the elements that are common to many good solutions rather than on any single solution. Population-based methods use this idea implicitly. Genetic algorithms and memetic algorithms recombine parents so that offspring inherit shared components [10]. Ant colony optimization accumulates pheromone on frequently used elements [11]. Methods based on backbones or "core" elements explicitly fix variables that take the same value across elite solutions and then solve the reduced problem [12]. Matheuristics and large neighborhood search follow a similar principle of fixing part of a solution and optimizing the rest [13]. However, many of these approaches either require problem-specific design or introduce considerable algorithmic complexity. In this paper we propose a new metaheuristic, the fixed set search (FSS), which adds a learning mechanism to GRASP while keeping its simplicity. The central idea is to avoid concentrating on particular high quality solutions and to concentrate instead on parts that such solutions have in common. From a population of good solutions generated by GRASP, a subset of elements, called the fixed set, is selected so that it appears in one or more of these solutions, with preference for elements that occur frequently. The fixed set defines a subproblem consisting of completing it to a full solution. The randomized greedy construction is modified so that it starts from the fixed set, and the local search is then applied, so the computational effort is dedicated to the much smaller subproblem of finding a near-optimal completion. The newly found solutions update the population, and the process is repeated, which yields a learning effect: the elements of the best solutions steer the search while randomization keeps it diverse. The method therefore adds only a small number of components to a standard GRASP, namely a population, a mechanism for selecting fixed sets, and an adapted construction procedure. We illustrate the method on the traveling salesman problem (TSP), one of the most extensively studied combinatorial optimization problems. Given a set of cities and the distances between them, the TSP asks for the shortest closed tour visiting each city exactly once [14]. Its simple statement, practical relevance, and computational difficulty have made it a standard benchmark for new algorithmic ideas. State-of-the-art approaches include the Lin–Kernighan heuristic and its efficient implementations [15,16], genetic algorithms with edge assembly crossover [17], and exact solvers such as Concorde [18]. For the TSP, the natural elements for fixing are edges, and a fixed set corresponds to a collection of path segments shared by good tours. The subproblem is then equivalent to a smaller TSP in which each segment is contracted, which makes the idea particularly easy to implement and analyze. We evaluate FSS on standard TSP benchmark instances and compare it with the GRASP on which it is based and with the dynamic convexized method [19], a recently proposed approach that achieved good results on these instances. The computational experiments show that FSS finds significantly better solutions than both methods under comparable conditions. These results support the usefulness of the learning mechanism and suggest that the framework can be applied to other combinatorial optimization problems. The main contributions of this paper are as follows. First, we introduce the fixed set search as a general metaheuristic that extends GRASP with a learning component based on fixing common elements of high quality solutions. Second, we describe a concrete and simple implementation for the TSP. Third, we provide computational evidence that the approach outperforms its underlying GRASP and a competitive recent method. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the general FSS framework. Section 3 presents its application to the TSP, including the construction, local search, and fixed set selection procedures. Section 4 reports the computational experiments and their analysis. Finally, Section 5 gives concluding remarks and directions for future research. The proposed FSS is built on top of a GRASP whose construction phase is randomized and whose local search improves each constructed solution. The FSS adds a learning mechanism: instead of treating each GRASP iteration independently, it uses elements shared by high quality solutions to define a fixed set, and the GRASP construction is then restricted to completing this set into a full solution. Below we describe the TSP formulation, the base GRASP, and the FSS components. Problem Formulation Let G = (V, E) be a complete undirected graph with n vertices and a cost c(u,v) for each edge. The TSP seeks a Hamiltonian cycle of minimum total cost. A solution is represented as a cyclic permutation of vertices, and its edge set is the set of n edges between consecutive vertices, including the closing edge. In the FSS, the "elements" of a solution are its edges. Base GRASP Each GRASP iteration consists of a randomized greedy construction followed by local search [1]. The construction is a randomized nearest-neighbor procedure. Starting from a random vertex, at each step the candidate list contains the unvisited vertices. A restricted candidate list (RCL) is formed from the k unvisited vertices nearest to the current vertex, and the next vertex is selected uniformly at random from the RCL. The parameter k controls the greediness-randomness balance. The procedure continues until all vertices are visited. The local search combines 2-opt and 2-opt with neighbor lists and don't-look bits to limit the neighborhood evaluation cost [2]. The search applies the first improving move until no improving move exists. The resulting solution is a local optimum with respect to the 2-opt neighborhood. Fixed Set Search Framework The FSS maintains a population P of the best N solutions found so far. Each iteration proceeds as follows: 1. Select a base solution B from P at random. 2. Select a subset S of P, of size m, consisting of solutions other than B. 3. Compute a fixed set F of elements of B, with preference for elements appearing frequently in S. 4. Construct a solution by a randomized greedy procedure that starts from F (the "adapted" construction), and improve it with local search. 5. Update P if the new solution is better than the worst member and not already present. Before the learning phase, the population is initialized by running standard GRASP for a number of iterations. The FSS then alternates between the learning-based iterations and, after a given number of consecutive non-improving iterations, a population restart: the population is rebuilt using standard GRASP while the best solution found is retained. Fixed Set Generation The fixed set is a set of edges that form a partial solution consisting of one or more path segments. Let B be the base solution and S the m sampled solutions. For each edge e in B, define its frequency count as the number of solutions in S that contain e. The fixed set is built by choosing a target size ℓ = n − ⌈n/…⌉ type quantity, denoted by the parameter fraction p of edges to fix, so that |F| = ⌊p·(n)⌋ with p drawn at random from a bounded interval for diversity. Edges of B are sorted by count in descending order, ties being broken randomly, and the first |F| edges are fixed. Because F is a subset of a Hamiltonian cycle, it contains no cycles and no vertex of degree above two, so it always yields a set of vertex-disjoint paths (isolated vertices being paths of length zero). To reduce bias toward a specific segment, we use a variation in which a random starting position in B is chosen and a contiguous segment of B is considered, with the edges of highest frequency selected within it. This yields larger, more coherent fixed structures and a smaller subproblem. Adapted Randomized Greedy Construction Given the fixed set F, the underlying subproblem consists of connecting the resulting path segments into a Hamiltonian cycle. Each segment is treated as a unit with two endpoints. The construction starts from an endpoint of a random segment, traverses the segment, and from its terminal endpoint selects the next segment according to randomized nearest-neighbor: the RCL contains the k closest endpoints of segments not yet used, and one is chosen uniformly at random. The chosen segment is entered at that endpoint and traversed in the corresponding direction. Isolated vertices are treated as segments whose two endpoints coincide. The process ends when all segments are connected, and the cycle is closed. The reduced number of decisions makes this construction faster than a full construction, so more of the search effort is spent on the part of the solution that is not yet determined. Local Search on the Subproblem The solution produced is improved by the same 2-opt local search as in the GRASP. Moves are not restricted to non-fixed edges, so the final solution may differ from F; fixing thus guides construction without constraining the final local optimum. Restricting the initial don't-look bits so that only endpoints of segments are active at the start speeds up the search, since the interiors of fixed segments are already of high quality. Parameters and Implementation The main parameters are the population size N, the sample size m, the RCL size k, the interval for the fixed fraction p, and the number of non-improving iterations before restart. These were chosen by preliminary experiments on a subset of instances and kept constant across all instances. Distances are computed from coordinates and rounded as in TSPLIB [3]. The algorithm is implemented in C++, and each run uses a time limit dependent on instance size. Experimental Protocol The FSS is compared with the GRASP it is based on, using the same construction and local search and identical running time, and with the dynamic convexized method [4]. For each TSPLIB instance, multiple independent runs are performed. We report the best and average solution value, the percentage gap to the best known solution, and the computation time. Statistical significance of differences is assessed with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test at the 0.05 level. Computational experiments were carried out on instances from the TSPLIB library, ranging from 100 to 1,000 nodes (e.g., kroA100, pr226, lin318, pcb442, rat783, pr1002). All algorithms were implemented in C++ and run on the same machine (3.4 GHz processor, single thread). The FSS and GRASP were each executed 30 times per instance with different random seeds. Colorectal cancer is one of the most common malignancies worldwide, and the liver is the most frequent site of metastatic spread. Up to half of patients develop colorectal liver metastases (CRLM) during the course of their disease. Surgical resection offers the only prospect of long-term survival and potential cure, with reported five-year survival rates of 40–60% in selected patients. Advances in systemic chemotherapy, targeted therapies and surgical technique have broadened the criteria for resectability, so that the determining factor is now frequently the ability to leave a sufficient volume of well-perfused, functioning liver rather than the number or distribution of tumours. Many patients nonetheless present with disease that requires extended resection, and a proportion of these have an inadequate future remnant liver (FRL). Post-hepatectomy liver failure remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality after major hepatic resection. Its risk rises as the FRL volume falls, and is further increased when the parenchyma is compromised by prior chemotherapy, steatosis or sinusoidal injury. Commonly cited thresholds for a minimum safe FRL are 20% of total liver volume in patients with a normal liver and 30–40% in those with injured liver, although these figures vary between centres. Where the predicted FRL is below the threshold, strategies to increase its volume are required to make resection safe. Portal vein embolisation (PVE) is the most widely used technique for inducing FRL hypertrophy. Occlusion of portal inflow to the tumour-bearing liver diverts portal blood to the non-embolised segments, triggering atrophy of the embolised liver and compensatory hypertrophy of the FRL. Since its first description in the 1980s, PVE has been shown to be safe and to allow resection in patients who would otherwise be unresectable or at high risk. Right portal vein embolisation (RPVE) is the standard approach before right hepatectomy. Where the planned resection is an extended right hepatectomy, which includes segment 4, the FRL comprises segments 2 and 3 only, and this small volume often falls short of requirements. In this setting, embolisation can be extended to the segment 4 portal branches (RPVE + 4) with the intention of redirecting more portal flow to segments 2 and 3 and so maximising their hypertrophy. The theoretical rationale for RPVE + 4 is straightforward, and several reports have suggested that it produces greater hypertrophy of the FRL and a higher rate of subsequent resection. However, the evidence is not conclusive. Most published series are small, single-centre, and retrospective, and many include heterogeneous populations with different diagnoses, including cholangiocarcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma and metastases from various primaries. These conditions differ in their underlying liver quality, exposure to chemotherapy, and regenerative capacity, which may confound comparisons. Studies in which segment 4 embolisation is used selectively may also be subject to selection bias if the decision is influenced by baseline FRL volume, liver disease, or tumour burden. Furthermore, extending embolisation to segment 4 carries technical considerations, including the risk of non-target embolisation of the FRL and the added complexity of the procedure, so the benefit should be clearly demonstrated. A further limitation of earlier work lies in the metrics used to report hypertrophy. Absolute volume gain and the kinetic growth rate are influenced by baseline FRL volume and by the time between embolisation and reassessment. The percentage increase in FRL volume is similarly sensitive to starting volume, since a small FRL can show a large relative gain from a small absolute change. Measures that standardise the FRL to total or standardised liver volume, such as the degree of hypertrophy (the difference between pre- and post-embolisation FRL expressed as a percentage of standardised total liver volume), are less dependent on these baseline variables and are therefore better suited for comparing techniques. Few studies of RPVE + 4 have used such metrics, and fewer have restricted analysis to patients with a single diagnosis. Patients with CRLM form a clinically distinct and common group in whom PVE is often used. Many have received multiple cycles of systemic chemotherapy before embolisation, and some have undergone limited resections or metastasectomies in the FRL as part of a staged strategy. The influence of these factors on hypertrophy is uncertain. It is also unknown whether the more extensive embolisation of RPVE + 4 has any effect on oncological outcome, either through delay to surgery, tumour progression in the FRL, or stimulation of tumour growth by the regenerative response. We therefore conducted a retrospective cohort study of consecutive patients with CRLM undergoing RPVE or RPVE + 4 at a single institution. Our primary aim was to compare the degree of hypertrophy of segments 2/3, corrected for standardised liver volume, between the two techniques. Secondary aims were to assess whether baseline patient, disease or treatment characteristics were associated with the choice of procedure and might confound the comparison, and to determine whether segment 4 embolisation influenced overall survival. This retrospective cohort study was conducted at a tertiary hepatobiliary referral centre. Institutional approval was obtained and the requirement for individual patient consent was waived because of the retrospective design and the use of anonymised data. The study is reported in accordance with the STROBE guidelines. Patient selection Consecutive patients who underwent right portal vein embolisation (RPVE) or RPVE extended to segment 4 (RPVE + 4) between January 2010 and December 2015 were identified from a prospectively maintained interventional radiology and hepatobiliary database. Inclusion criteria were: (1) histologically confirmed colorectal liver metastases (CRLM); (2) PVE performed with the intention of enabling a subsequent right or extended right hepatectomy; (3) no prior major hepatic resection (three or more Couinaud segments); and (4) availability of cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) of adequate quality both before and after embolisation for volumetric analysis. Patients were excluded if they had undergone PVE for indications other than CRLM, had previously undergone major hepatectomy, had left-sided or bilateral PVE, or had inadequate or missing imaging. Prior systemic chemotherapy, prior subsegmental resection or ablation of lesions in the future remnant liver (FRL), and the presence of FRL metastases were permitted. The decision to perform RPVE or RPVE + 4 was made by the operating interventional radiologist in consultation with the multidisciplinary team, and reflected the planned resection and operator preference. Treatment allocation was not randomised. Data collection Data were extracted from electronic hospital records, radiology reports and operative notes. Variables collected included age, sex, body surface area, primary tumour site and stage, timing of metastases (synchronous or metachronous), number and distribution of liver metastases, presence of metastases within the FRL, prior subsegmental metastasectomy in the FRL, type and number of cycles of prior chemotherapy (including biological agents), interval between last chemotherapy and PVE, and liver function tests. Procedural data included the embolic material used, the segments embolised, and complications. Subsequent management, including whether hepatic resection was performed, was recorded. Survival status and date of death or last follow-up were obtained from clinical records and linkage to national registries. Portal vein embolisation technique PVE was performed percutaneously under local anaesthesia and sedation, using ultrasound-guided access to the portal venous system via a transhepatic ipsilateral (right) or contralateral approach. After portography, the right portal vein branches were selectively catheterised and embolised with particles, coils, cyanoacrylate glue, or a combination, according to operator preference. In RPVE + 4, branches supplying segment 4 were additionally catheterised and embolised, so that portal flow was diverted to segments 2 and 3 predominantly. Completion portography was performed to confirm occlusion of the target branches and preservation of flow in the left lateral portal branches. Patients were observed after the procedure and discharged according to clinical status. Volumetric assessment Volumetry was performed on portal venous phase cross-sectional imaging acquired before PVE and at follow-up after PVE, typically in advance of planned surgery. Images were reviewed using dedicated semi-automated volumetry software, with manual contouring of the liver on contiguous axial slices of 5 mm or less. Segments 2 and 3 (the FRL after extended right hepatectomy) were delineated separately from the remainder of the liver, using the left hepatic vein, umbilical fissure and falciform ligament as landmarks. Large tumours, vessels outside the liver parenchyma, and the gallbladder fossa were excluded where possible. Volumes of metastases within the FRL were not subtracted unless they were clearly delineated and measurable. Measurements were performed by an observer blinded to the embolisation type where feasible, and a random subset was re-measured by a second observer to assess inter-observer agreement. Total liver volume was estimated using the standardised liver volume (SLV) formula based on body surface area (SLV = −794.41 + 1267.28 × BSA, in mL, as described by Vauthey et al.). The FRL was expressed as a percentage of SLV (FRL/SLV). The degree of hypertrophy (DH) was defined as the absolute difference between post- and pre-embolisation FRL/SLV percentages. This metric was selected in preference to the kinetic growth rate or percentage volume increase, as it is less sensitive to baseline FRL volume and to variation in the time between imaging studies.
