Mycotoxins are low-molecular-weight secondary metabolites produced mainly by filamentous fungi of the genera Aspergillus, Fusarium, Penicillium, and Alternaria. They contaminate a wide range of agricultural commodities, including cereals, nuts, spices, fruits, and animal feed, both in the field and during storage [1,2]. The Food and Agriculture Organization has estimated that a considerable share of the world's food crops is contaminated with mycotoxins at detectable levels, causing substantial economic losses and risks to human and animal health [3]. Climate change is expected to alter the geographical distribution of toxigenic fungi and the patterns of contamination, so the problem is likely to intensify [4]. Several hundred mycotoxins are known, but only a few groups are of major concern: aflatoxins, ochratoxins, trichothecenes (deoxynivalenol, T-2 toxin), zearalenone, fumonisins, patulin, and ergot alkaloids. Their toxic effects are diverse. Aflatoxin B1 is a potent hepatocarcinogen after metabolic activation to an epoxide that forms DNA adducts [5]. Ochratoxin A is nephrotoxic, immunotoxic, and possibly carcinogenic [6]. Trichothecenes inhibit eukaryotic protein synthesis by binding the ribosomal peptidyl transferase center [7]. Zearalenone mimics estrogen and disrupts reproductive function [8]. Fumonisins inhibit ceramide synthase and disturb sphingolipid metabolism [9]. Co-occurrence of several mycotoxins in one matrix is common, and additive or synergistic effects complicate risk assessment [10]. Regulatory limits for mycotoxins have been established in many countries, and strategies for preventing contamination include good agricultural practices, resistant cultivars, biocontrol, and optimized storage [11]. Once toxins are formed, however, they must be removed or inactivated. Physical and chemical methods such as sorting, milling, thermal treatment, ammonization, ozonation, and the use of adsorbents have limited efficiency. They may impair the nutritional value and organoleptic properties of the product, generate toxic residues, or lack specificity [12,13]. Adsorbents such as aluminosilicates and activated carbon work well for aflatoxins but poorly for many other toxins, including zearalenone, fumonisins, and trichothecenes, and they may bind vitamins and minerals [14]. Biological detoxification using microorganisms or their enzymes is regarded as a more promising alternative because it can be specific, mild, and environmentally friendly. Enzymatic transformation permits the conversion of mycotoxins into less toxic or nontoxic products under moderate conditions without affecting feed quality. Application of enzymes as feed additives has been recognized by regulators; in the European Union, for example, fumonisin esterase and trichothecene-detoxifying biotransforming agents have been authorized as technological additives [15]. Compared with whole-cell preparations, purified or recombinant enzymes offer defined composition, controllable dosage, and absence of undesirable microbial metabolites. The enzymes known to act on mycotoxins belong to various classes. Oxidoreductases, including laccases, peroxidases, cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, and dehydrogenases, oxidize or reduce functional groups of aflatoxins, deoxynivalenol, and other toxins [16,17]. Hydrolases such as lactonases, carboxypeptidases, esterases, and amidases cleave lactone, amide, or ester bonds in zearalenone, ochratoxin A, and fumonisins, respectively [18–20]. Transferases, such as glucosyltransferases, glutathione S-transferases, and acetyltransferases, conjugate mycotoxins with sugars, glutathione, or acetyl groups, which is the basis of plant self-protection against trichothecenes [21]. Epoxide-cleaving and de-epoxidating enzymes, including the recently described DepA/DepB system and related proteins, remove the toxophoric epoxide group of trichothecenes [22]. Despite these discoveries, the activity of many enzymes remains low, and their substrate specificity, stability, and mechanisms of action are not fully understood. Many reports describe enzymatic activity without sequence or structural information, and the metabolites formed are not always identified or tested for residual toxicity [23]. Understanding catalytic mechanisms is essential for rational selection and engineering of mycotoxin-converting enzymes. Structural studies, site-directed mutagenesis, and computational approaches, particularly molecular docking and molecular dynamics, make it possible to identify key residues in the active center, explain substrate specificity, and predict the effect of amino acid substitutions [24]. Such knowledge has already been applied to improve the thermostability and activity of zearalenone hydrolases and aflatoxin-degrading oxidases [25]. Moreover, comparison of homologous proteins from plants, animals, fungi, and bacteria can reveal the distribution of such activities in nature and suggest new, easily accessible sources of biocatalysts, including enzymes with other primary functions that show promiscuous activity toward mycotoxins [26]. Previous reviews have mainly focused on individual toxins or on microorganisms capable of detoxification, and they often present enzymes as lists of activities without analyzing the underlying chemistry [27,28]. A comprehensive analysis combining biochemical mechanisms, structural modeling, and phylogenetic distribution is still lacking. In addition, because contamination with several toxins at once is typical, the possible use of multifunctional enzyme combinations deserves attention. In this review, we summarize current data on enzymes of different classes that convert major mycotoxins, with in-depth analysis of 11 key catalytic mechanisms acting on dozens of toxins. We supplement this analysis with molecular docking of mycotoxins into enzyme active centers to clarify the details of catalysis, and we examine the occurrence of protein homologues across organisms to assess the availability of natural sources of active biocatalysts. Finally, we discuss the importance of combining enzymes with complementary specificities as antidotes for efficient detoxification of mycotoxin mixtures. Literature search and selection of enzymes. Publications on enzymatic conversion of mycotoxins were retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar covering 1990–2022. Search terms combined the names of major mycotoxins (aflatoxins, zearalenone, ochratoxin A, fumonisins, trichothecenes including deoxynivalenol and T-2 toxin, patulin, citrinin, and ergot alkaloids) with "enzyme," "biotransformation," "degradation," "detoxification," and the names of enzyme classes. Studies were included if they reported (i) a purified or recombinant enzyme, (ii) identification of reaction products, and (iii) a decrease in toxicity or a clear structural rationale for it. Studies using only whole-cell or crude-extract degradation without enzyme identification were used only for context. Enzymes were grouped by EC class and by catalytic mechanism, and 11 key mechanisms were selected for in-depth analysis on the basis of the amount of biochemical and structural data available [1,2]. Structural data and preparation of enzyme models. Three-dimensional structures of the enzymes were obtained from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) [3]. Where no experimental structure existed, models were generated with AlphaFold2 [4] and checked by pLDDT values and by comparison with templates of known structure. Crystallographic water molecules, ions not involved in catalysis, and co-crystallized ligands were removed. Hydrogen atoms were added, and protonation states of ionizable residues at pH 7.0 were assigned with PROPKA [5]. Cofactors and catalytic metal ions (e.g., Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺, FAD, heme) were retained. Structures were energy-minimized with the AMBER ff14SB force field to remove steric clashes [6]. Preparation of ligands. Structures of mycotoxins were downloaded from PubChem in SDF format [7]. Three-dimensional conformers were generated and minimized using the MMFF94 force field in Open Babel [8]. Partial charges were assigned by the Gasteiger method. Rotatable bonds were defined automatically, and ring conformations of flexible macrocycles (e.g., zearalenone) were sampled before docking. Molecular docking. Docking was performed with AutoDock Vina [9] and verified for selected complexes with SwissDock [10]. The search space was a cube of 20–25 Å centered on the catalytic residues or the cofactor-binding site, as determined from the literature and from the position of co-crystallized substrates or analogues. Exhaustiveness was set to 32, and 20 binding modes were generated per ligand. Poses were ranked by predicted binding affinity (kcal/mol) and then filtered by catalytic relevance: a pose was considered productive when the reactive group of the mycotoxin (e.g., the lactone ring of aflatoxin B1 or zearalenone, the epoxide of trichothecenes, the ester bond of ochratoxin A, the tricarballylic esters of fumonisin B1, or the C3 hydroxyl of deoxynivalenol) lay within 3.5–4.5 Å of the catalytic nucleophile, metal ion, or redox cofactor and in a geometry consistent with the proposed mechanism. The docking protocol was validated by redocking native ligands where available, and a root-mean-square deviation below 2.0 Å was regarded as acceptable. Interactions were analyzed with LigPlot+ [11] and PLIP [12], and images were produced with PyMOL [13]. Analysis of catalytic mechanisms. For each of the 11 mechanisms (hydrolysis of lactone, ester, and amide bonds; epoxide opening or de-epoxidation; oxidation by oxidases, laccases, and peroxidases; P450-mediated hydroxylation; dehydrogenation and reduction; glucosylation and other conjugation reactions; sulfation; glutathione transfer; amine oxidation; and decarboxylation or ring cleavage, as applicable), reaction schemes were assembled from published product identification by LC–MS and NMR. Catalytic residues were assigned from site-directed mutagenesis data and conserved motifs in the Pfam and InterPro databases [14,15]. Docking results were interpreted against these data to assess the plausibility of the proposed mechanisms. Homology and distribution analysis. To evaluate the prevalence of potential biocatalysts in nature, amino acid sequences of the characterized enzymes were used as queries in BLASTp and PSI-BLAST searches against the NCBI nonredundant and UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot databases [16,17]. Hits with E-value < 1×10⁻⁵, sequence identity ≥ 30%, and query coverage ≥ 70% were retained, and the presence of catalytic residues and conserved motifs was verified. Homologues were sorted by taxonomic domain and kingdom (bacteria, fungi, plants, animals) using NCBI Taxonomy. Multiple sequence alignments were built with MAFFT [18] or Clustal Omega [19] and phylogenetic trees were inferred with maximum likelihood in IQ-TREE [20] with 1000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates. Trees were visualized in iTOL [21]. Subcellular localization and signal peptides were predicted with SignalP and DeepLoc to judge the suitability of homologues for recombinant production [22]. Assessment of practical potential. Enzymes were compared by reported specific activity, Km and kcat, pH and temperature optima, thermostability, cofactor requirements, and the toxicity of the products, based on data from the original publications. Suitability for feed and food processing was judged by activity under gastrointestinal or processing conditions and by the possibility of heterologous expression. Combinations of enzymes acting on different functional groups or different mycotoxins were examined by analyzing compatibility of reaction conditions and cofactor regeneration [23]. Data handling. Quantitative values were extracted manually from the original papers and harmonized to common units. Where several studies reported conflicting values, the ranges are provided. No new experimental toxicity tests were carried out; the toxicity of transformation products was taken from published cell-based, animal, or receptor-binding assays. Eleven enzyme mechanisms were identified that act on the major mycotoxin groups: aflatoxins, ochratoxins, zearalenone, trichothecenes, fumonisins, patulin, and others. They are grouped below by catalytic chemistry. Docking results and the distribution of homologues across taxa follow. Hydrolytic mechanisms. Lactonases (α/β-hydrolase fold) open the macrocyclic lactone ring of zearalenone (ZEN). ZHD101 from Clonostachys rosea is the best-characterized example [1,2]. It uses a Ser–His–Asp catalytic triad. The nucleophilic serine attacks the lactone carbonyl, forming an acyl-enzyme intermediate, which water then hydrolyzes. The product, a decarboxylated and non-estrogenic compound, loses affinity for estrogen receptors [2]. Carboxypeptidases and amidohydrolases cleave the amide bond of ochratoxin A (OTA) to give non-toxic ochratoxin α and L-phenylalanine. Carboxypeptidase A and the bacterial amidohydrolases ADH3 and ADH2 are representative [3,4]. In these enzymes a zinc ion polarizes the amide carbonyl and activates a water molecule. Carboxylesterases and fumonisin esterases (FumD) remove the tricarballylic acid side chains of fumonisin B1 (FB1), yielding hydrolyzed FB1, which is less toxic, though not completely inert [5,6]. Epoxide hydrolases were also reported to open the epoxide ring of aflatoxin B1 (AFB1) metabolites and trichothecenes, but activity toward the trichothecene 12,13-epoxide remains limited [7]. Oxidative mechanisms. Laccases, with four copper atoms, oxidize the phenolic groups of AFB1, ZEN, and OTA, often with redox mediators [8]. They generate radical intermediates that couple or fragment, and the products show reduced toxicity. Manganese peroxidases and versatile peroxidases act on aflatoxins through a similar one-electron mechanism [9]. Aflatoxin-degrading reductases from the dehydrogenase/reductase family (such as AFO from Armillaria tabescens) oxidize the furan ring of AFB1 [10]. Cytochrome P450 monooxygenases hydroxylate or epoxidize aflatoxins, ZEN, and trichothecenes. This route can detoxify, but for AFB1 it produces the highly toxic 8,9-epoxide, so the choice of enzyme matters [11]. Quinone-dependent dehydrogenases (such as Devosia PQQ-dependent dehydrogenase) oxidize the C3 hydroxyl of deoxynivalenol (DON) to 3-keto-DON, which is far less toxic. Subsequent reduction by aldo-keto reductases yields 3-epi-DON [12,13]. Conjugation and transferase mechanisms. UDP-glucosyltransferases from plants (such as barley HvUGT13248) transfer glucose to the C3 hydroxyl of DON and to ZEN, forming glucosides [14]. These conjugates are less toxic but can be hydrolyzed back in the gut, a notable limitation. Glutathione S-transferases

Optical packet switching (OPS) and optical burst switching (OBS) have emerged as promising paradigms for exploiting the enormous bandwidth of wavelength-division multiplexed (WDM) fiber while avoiding the inefficiency of statically provisioned lightpaths. By switching data units entirely in the optical domain, these architectures promise fine-grained statistical multiplexing and flexible bandwidth utilization. However, the absence of practical optical random access memory and the limited availability of wavelength converters and fiber delay lines make contention resolution a fundamental problem. When two or more packets or bursts compete for the same output wavelength at the same time, one or more must be dropped, deflected, or delayed by scarce resources. Consequently, loss caused by contention is a dominant impairment in OPS/OBS networks, and it can occur even at moderate loads. Conventional approaches to this problem fall into several categories. Switch-level techniques such as wavelength conversion, fiber delay line buffering, and deflection routing reduce contention but increase hardware cost, complexity, or out-of-order delivery. Network-level techniques such as load balancing and traffic engineering reduce the likelihood of contention but cannot eliminate it. Finally, end-to-end retransmission, as in TCP, recovers lost data but incurs a delay of at least one round-trip time per recovery, which is costly in high-speed wide-area optical networks where the bandwidth-delay product is large. Moreover, retransmission interacts poorly with bursty loss: a single dropped burst may carry data from many flows, and the resulting synchronized retransmissions and congestion window reductions can severely degrade throughput. A second class of impairments concerns survivability. Fiber cuts and node failures in optical networks can disrupt enormous volumes of traffic. Protection schemes such as dedicated 1+1 or shared backup paths provide resilience, but they typically reserve substantial spare capacity and are designed separately from the mechanisms that handle contention loss. Likewise, secrecy is usually treated as an independent concern addressed by cryptography at higher layers, which requires key management and computational processing that may be difficult at optical line rates. In consequence, performance, survivability, and secrecy are traditionally engineered in isolation, even though they all concern how data traverse the network and how much redundancy is introduced. In this paper we present the Coded Packet Transport (CPT) scheme, which addresses these three concerns with a single mechanism. The core idea combines source coding by erasure codes with path diversity. At the ingress node of the OPS/OBS network, a block of data is encoded with an erasure code, producing a larger set of coded packets such that the original data can be reconstructed from any sufficiently large subset of them. The coded packets are then distributed over multiple link- or node-disjoint paths to the egress node, where the data are decoded as soon as enough coded packets arrive. Loss of some coded packets, whether through contention at intermediate nodes or through the failure of an entire path, can thus be tolerated without retransmission, and without the dedicated spare capacity required by conventional protection. Because redundancy is spread across paths and is used both for loss recovery and failure recovery, the same overhead serves performance and survivability objectives. The same structure yields a degree of secrecy that does not rely on cryptographic computation. Since no single path carries enough coded packets to reconstruct the original data, an adversary who taps or compromises a limited number of links or paths obtains only partial information. With suitable coding and path allocation, the information available to such an eavesdropper can be made insufficient for recovering the data. This form of secrecy is non-cryptographic in that it derives from the coding and dispersion of data rather than from computational hardness assumptions, and it can complement encryption where stronger guarantees are required. CPT thereby offers a unified view of Quality of Service (QoS) in OPS/OBS networks. The number of disjoint paths, the amount of redundancy, and the processing delay of encoding and decoding act as common design parameters that jointly determine loss probability, resilience to failures, and resistance to eavesdropping. Increasing the number of paths improves the tolerance to individual path failures and reduces the information exposed on any one path, but it may require longer alternative routes and more complex ingress and egress processing. Increasing redundancy improves loss recovery but consumes bandwidth. Larger coding blocks improve coding efficiency but add delay in assembling, encoding, and decoding. Understanding these tradeoffs requires a model that captures their interaction rather than treating each metric separately. The contributions of this paper are as follows. First, we define the CPT architecture, including the roles of ingress and egress nodes, the assembly of coded packets, and their assignment to disjoint paths. Second, we develop analytical models that characterize how the QoS aspects of CPT, namely survivability, performance, and secrecy, depend on the number of disjoint paths, the packet overhead introduced by coding, and the processing delay. Third, we use these models to illustrate the design tradeoffs and to show that CPT can achieve substantial reductions in loss and meaningful secrecy at modest overhead compared with retransmission-based and protection-based approaches. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on contention resolution, protection, and coding in optical networks. Section III describes the CPT scheme. Section IV presents the analytical models for survivability, performance, and secrecy. Section V presents numerical results and discusses design implications, and Section VI concludes the paper. We consider an OPS/OBS network modeled as a graph in which an ingress node s and an egress node d are connected by a set of node-disjoint (or at least link-disjoint) paths. The CPT scheme operates between these two nodes. We first describe the coding and transmission procedure, then the analytical models for loss recovery, survivability, secrecy, and delay. Coding and Transmission. At the ingress node, incoming client data destined for d are aggregated into a block of k equal-length data packets (or bursts, in the OBS case; we use "packet" for both). Padding is added if necessary. An (n,k) maximum-distance-separable (MDS) erasure code, such as a Reed-Solomon code over GF(2^m), is applied symbol-wise across the k packets to generate n ≥ k coded packets, so that any k of the n coded packets suffice to reconstruct the block. The code rate is r = k/n and the packet overhead is (n−k)/k. Each coded packet carries a header with a block identifier, an index within the block, and the coefficients identifying its encoding vector, enabling decoding without extra signaling. The n coded packets are distributed over m disjoint paths, m ≤ n, with ni packets assigned to path i and Σni = n. Unless stated otherwise, we assume a uniform allocation ni = n/m. The egress node collects coded packets of each block, and once k distinct packets have arrived it decodes the block and delivers the original packets. Packets arriving after decoding are discarded. A decoding timer bounds the waiting time; if fewer than k packets arrive before expiry, the block is declared lost (or, in a hybrid variant, the missing packets are handled by higher-layer retransmission). Loss Model. Contention loss on path i is modeled as independent packet drops with probability pi, the end-to-end loss probability along that path. For an H-hop path with per-hop blocking probability b (e.g., from an Erlang-type model for bufferless OBS links), pi = 1 − (1−b)^H. Independence across disjoint paths is justified by the absence of shared links; within a path, losses are treated as independent as a first approximation. With uniform p, the number of received packets is binomial, and the block loss probability is Pblock = Σ{j=0}^{k−1} C(n,j)(1−p)^j p^(n−j). For heterogeneous paths, the distribution of received packets is the convolution of the per-path binomial distributions, computed numerically. We evaluate the residual packet loss rate as Pblock scaled by the expected fraction of data packets lost given a block failure, and compare it against the uncoded baseline, whose loss probability is p. Survivability Model. Each path i fails entirely with probability fi, representing a link or node failure, independently of the others. Conditioned on the set S of surviving paths, packets on those paths experience contention loss as above. The block delivery probability is Psucc = ΣS Π{i∈S}(1−fi) Π{i∉S} fi · P(received ≥ k | S). With uniform allocation, the code survives any failure of up to ⌊(n−k)/(n/m)⌋ paths in the absence of contention. We therefore examine the trade-off between m and the redundancy n−k: increasing m limits the fraction of packets lost to a single failure, while a larger overhead raises network load, and thus b. We capture this coupling by letting the offered load per link scale with n/k, so that b = b(ρ·n/k) and the loss and survivability models are solved jointly via fixed-point iteration. Secrecy Model. CPT provides non-cryptographic secrecy by ensuring that an adversary tapping a subset of paths cannot recover the data. We assume an eavesdropper who can observe up to w of the m paths, chosen randomly or adversarially. Because an MDS code requires k packets for decoding, the adversary reconstructs the block only if the number of intercepted packets reaches k. For uniform allocation, the adversary succeeds if w·n/m ≥ k. We define the secrecy probability as the probability that fewer than k distinct coded packets are intercepted, accounting for packet loss on tapped paths. To strengthen secrecy beyond the threshold property, the code may use a non-systematic generator matrix so that no individual packet exposes plaintext, and, when desired, an all-or-nothing preprocessing step so that partial information about the block is not leaked. The tension with survivability is evident: a higher n/k favors recovery but lowers the number of paths the adversary needs to tap. We quantify this using a joint measure of survivability and secrecy across (n,k,m). Delay Model. End-to-end block delay consists of encoding time Tenc, aggregation time Tagg (waiting for k packets), transmission and propagation along each path, differential path delay, and decoding time Tdec. Encoding and decoding times are modeled as proportional to k(n−k) symbol operations per packet length, with a hardware-dependent constant. Propagation delay on path i is Di = Li/v, where Li is path length and v is the propagation speed. The block is decodable at the arrival of the k-th packet, so the delivery delay is the k-th order statistic of the arrival times of surviving packets. Longer alternative paths thus increase delay, and the decoding timer is set to the maximum differential delay plus a margin. Reordering buffer size at the egress is estimated from the product of the data rate and the maximum differential delay. Evaluation. We evaluate the models numerically for representative parameters, varying m, n, k, p, and f, and report loss probability, survivability, secrecy probability, and delay. Closed-form expressions are validated against Monte Carlo simulation of the same stochastic assumptions, using 10^6 blocks per point. We evaluated CPT analytically and by numerical computation. Unless stated otherwise, a block of k source packets is expanded into n = k + r coded packets, which are distributed over m disjoint paths between ingress and egress nodes. The code is assumed maximum-distance-separable (MDS), so any k of the n coded packets suffice for recovery. Each path is modeled as an independent loss channel with contention loss probability p, and path failure occurs independently with probability q. Code rate is R = k/n, and packet overhead is (n−k)/k. Loss recovery under contention. The residual block loss probability is the probability that fewer than k of n coded packets arrive. With independent losses it is a binomial tail. Without coding (n = k), the block loss probability is 1−(1−p)^k, which grows nearly linearly with block size for small p. With coding, the residual loss falls sharply once the overhead exceeds the expected loss fraction. At p = 10^-2 and k = 10, a single redundant packet (overhead 10%) reduces block loss from about 9.6×10^-2 to about 4.3×10^-3, and two redundant packets reduce it to about 1.1×10^-4. Each additional redundant packet gives roughly a one-to-two order of magnitude improvement at low p, with diminishing returns as the residual loss approaches the floor

Depression is among the most prevalent mental disorders worldwide and a leading contributor to the global burden of disease. The World Health Organization estimates that more than 300 million people live with depression, and the condition is a major cause of disability, reduced productivity, and premature mortality through suicide and comorbid medical illness [1,2]. Its burden is not confined to psychiatric settings. Depression frequently coexists with chronic physical conditions such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease, cancer, and chronic pain, where it worsens prognosis, reduces adherence to treatment, and increases healthcare utilisation [3,4]. Consequently, patients with depression commonly present first to non-psychiatric clinicians, who are often the only professionals they encounter. Depression in primary and non-psychiatric care Because mental health specialists are scarce in many countries, integration of mental healthcare into general medical services is a central strategy for narrowing the treatment gap [5]. Non-psychiatric physicians, including family physicians, internists, surgeons, and other specialists, are therefore expected to recognise depressive symptoms, initiate first-line treatment, and refer appropriately. Evidence nonetheless indicates that depression is under-recognised and under-treated in these settings, with a substantial proportion of cases going undetected or receiving inadequate management [6,7]. The reasons are multifactorial and include time constraints, limited training in mental health, the somatic presentation of depression, and patient reluctance to disclose psychological distress. Clinician attitudes are an additional and potentially modifiable determinant. Physicians who regard depression as untreatable, as a personal weakness, or as outside their professional remit may be less likely to screen, to diagnose, or to engage patients in management [8]. Stigma and attitudes among health professionals Stigma towards mental illness is well documented in the general population, and health professionals are not immune to it [9]. Negative attitudes among clinicians may manifest as pessimism about prognosis, social distancing, diagnostic overshadowing, or reluctance to treat, and they may compound the self-stigma experienced by patients and discourage help-seeking [10]. Non-psychiatric physicians may be particularly susceptible, given their more limited exposure to psychiatric education and practice. Studies from Europe, Asia, and elsewhere have reported variable levels of confidence, optimism, and professional comfort among general practitioners and hospital doctors in managing depression, with training and experience repeatedly associated with more favourable attitudes [11,12]. Assessing these attitudes is therefore a prerequisite for designing educational and service interventions. Measuring attitudes: the Revised Depression Attitude Questionnaire The Depression Attitude Questionnaire (DAQ) was developed to assess professionals' views on depression, and was subsequently revised and psychometrically validated as the Revised Depression Attitude Questionnaire (R-DAQ) [13]. The R-DAQ is a 20-item instrument that captures multiple dimensions, including generalist perspectives on managing depression, professional confidence, optimism or pessimism about prognosis, beliefs about the identification of depression, and perceived professional boundaries between physical and mental health care. It has been applied across diverse professional groups and cultural contexts, which facilitates cross-study comparison [14,15]. The Saudi context In Saudi Arabia, mental disorders constitute a considerable public health concern. National survey data suggest that a substantial share of the population experiences a mental disorder at some point in life, with major depressive disorder among the most common, yet only a minority seek or receive treatment [16]. Cultural and religious interpretations of mental distress, concerns about family reputation, and fear of social labelling continue to contribute to stigma and delayed help-seeking [17]. The Saudi healthcare system has taken steps to expand mental health services, including through national mental health strategies and efforts to integrate mental health into primary care [18]. The success of such integration depends heavily on the preparedness and attitudes of the non-psychiatric workforce. Existing Saudi studies of attitudes towards depression and mental illness have largely focused on primary care physicians, medical students, or the general public, and have often been restricted to single institutions or regions [19,20]. Less is known about the attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians working across specialties in large tertiary hospitals in the capital, Riyadh, where complex patients with comorbid physical and mental illness are frequently managed and where many trainees receive their education. Evidence from this group is needed to identify training needs and to inform referral pathways and collaborative care models. Aim and significance of the study This study aimed to investigate the attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians towards depression in four tertiary centres in Riyadh using the R-DAQ. It further sought to examine how these attitudes relate to professional characteristics, including specialty, seniority, and clinical experience, where such factors may shape confidence and willingness to manage depression. By characterising optimism, confidence, and perceived professional roles within this population, the study provides locally relevant evidence to guide undergraduate and postgraduate mental health education, to support the integration of mental health into general hospital care, and to contribute to efforts to reduce stigma within the medical profession itself. Study design and setting A descriptive, cross-sectional, questionnaire-based survey was conducted between [month/year] and [month/year] in four tertiary care centres in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The centres were selected because they are large teaching hospitals with broad specialty coverage and receive referrals from across the central region. The study followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines for cross-sectional studies [1]. Study population and eligibility The target population comprised non-psychiatric physicians working at the participating centres. Eligible participants were consultants, specialists, residents, and medical interns/registrars from any non-psychiatric specialty (e.g., internal medicine, family medicine, surgery, paediatrics, obstetrics and gynaecology, emergency medicine, and their subspecialties) who were in active clinical practice during the data collection period. Psychiatrists and psychiatry residents were excluded because the study focused on attitudes among clinicians without specialist mental health training. Physicians who were on extended leave or who declined to take part were also excluded. Sample size and sampling technique The required sample size was calculated using the formula for estimating a single proportion, n = Z²P(1−P)/d², assuming a 95% confidence level (Z = 1.96), an expected proportion of 50% to maximise variance, and a margin of error of 5%. This yielded a minimum of 384 respondents. A finite population correction was considered based on the estimated number of eligible physicians across the four centres. The target was inflated to account for incomplete responses. A convenience sampling approach with quota allocation proportional to each centre's physician workforce was used to distribute questionnaires. In total, 380 completed questionnaires were included in the final analysis. Study instrument Data were collected using a self-administered questionnaire consisting of two parts. Part 1: Sociodemographic and professional characteristics. This section captured age, gender, nationality, marital status, specialty, professional rank, years of clinical experience, and primary workplace. It also asked about prior training in mental health or depression management, personal or family history of depression, and previous experience treating patients with depression. Part 2: Revised Depression Attitude Questionnaire (R-DAQ). Attitudes towards depression were measured using the R-DAQ, developed by Haddad and colleagues from the original Depression Attitude Questionnaire [2,3]. The R-DAQ comprises 20 items rated on a five-point Likert scale from "strongly disagree" (1) to "strongly agree" (5). Its validated factor structure includes five subscales: (i) professional confidence in managing depression, (ii) professional identification and therapeutic optimism or pessimism, (iii) generalist perspective on depression (that depression is a condition managed within general clinical practice), (iv) the perception that depression is difficult to identify or distinguish from normal distress, and (v) the perception of depression as a mental disorder with a biological or psychosocial aetiology [3]. Positively and negatively worded items were scored accordingly, with reverse scoring applied where required so that higher scores consistently reflected the construct measured by each subscale. The instrument has shown acceptable reliability and construct validity in studies of general practitioners and other clinicians across several countries [3,4]. The questionnaire was provided in English, which is the language of medical education and practice in Saudi Arabia, and permission to use the instrument was obtained from the authors. Internal consistency in the present sample was assessed using Cronbach's alpha for the total scale and subscales, with values ≥0.70 considered acceptable. Pilot testing Before the main survey, the questionnaire was piloted among about 20 physicians not included in the final sample to evaluate clarity, completion time, and feasibility. No major modifications were required, and pilot data were excluded from the analysis. Data collection procedure Following institutional approvals, trained data collectors visited clinical departments and distributed the questionnaires, either on paper or through a secure online link (according to departmental preference). Participants received an information sheet describing the purpose of the study, the voluntary nature of participation, and assurances of anonymity. Completion of the questionnaire was taken as implied consent. No personal identifiers were collected, and completed forms were stored securely, accessible only to the research team. Reminders were issued at one-week and two-week intervals to improve the response rate. Variables and outcome measures The primary outcome was the attitude towards depression, expressed as the total R-DAQ score and the five subscale scores. Attitudes were interpreted according to published scoring guidance, with higher subscale scores indicating greater confidence, more therapeutic optimism, stronger generalist orientation, greater perceived difficulty in identification, or stronger endorsement of a mental disorder model, respectively [3]. Independent variables included demographic and professional characteristics, specialty, previous training, and personal or family exposure to depression. Statistical analysis Data were entered and analysed using IBM SPSS Statistics (version [XX]) [5]. Data were screened for missing values and outliers. Categorical variables were summarised as frequencies and percentages, and continuous variables as means with standard deviations or medians with interquartile ranges, depending on distribution, which was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test and visual inspection of histograms. Item-level responses were described as the proportion agreeing (agree/strongly agree), neutral, or disagreeing (disagree/strongly disagree). Associations between R-DAQ scores and participant characteristics were examined using independent-samples t-tests or Mann–Whitney U tests for two groups, and one-way ANOVA or Kruskal–Wallis tests for three or more groups, with post hoc comparisons adjusted using the Bonferroni correction. Associations between categorical variables were tested using the chi-square or Fisher's exact test. Pearson or Spearman correlation coefficients were used for continuous variables such as age and years of experience. Multiple linear regression was used to identify independent predictors of R-DAQ subscale scores, including variables with p < 0.20 in bivariate analysis. Statistical significance was set at a two-tailed p-value < 0.05, and 95% confidence intervals were reported where appropriate. Ethical considerations The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Institutional Review Board of each participating centre (approval numbers [XX]). The study adhered to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki [6]. Participation was voluntary, responses were anonymous and confidential, and participants could withdraw at any time before submission without consequence. Data were used solely for research purposes. Participant characteristics Of the 450 questionnaires distributed across the four tertiary centres, 380 were returned complete and included in the analysis (response rate 84.4%). Respondents had a mean age of 34.6 years (SD = 8.2; range 25–62), and 231 (60.8%) were male. Saudi nationals accounted for 248 participants (65.3%). By professional grade, 142 (37.4%) were consultants or specialists, 118 (31.1%) were residents, and 120 (31.6%) were general practitioners or interns. The largest specialty groups were internal medicine (n = 87, 22.9%), surgery (n = 71, 18.7%), family medicine (n = 64, 16.8%), paediatrics (n = 52, 13.7%) and obstetrics and gynaecology (n = 41, 10.8%); the remainder were from other specialties. Mean clinical experience was 9.1 years (SD = 7.4). A total of 169 respondents (44.5%) reported previous training in mental health, and 214 (56.3%) reported that they regularly managed patients with depression. Internal consistency of the Revised Depression Attitude Questionnaire (R-DAQ) was acceptable (Cronbach's α = 0.78 for the full scale), in line with previous validations [1,2]. Social isolation and loneliness are persistent concerns for older adults living in residential care. Moving into a care home often means leaving behind familiar places, routines, and social circles, while declining health and mobility limit opportunities to maintain existing relationships or form new ones. Loneliness among older adults has been linked to depression, cognitive decline, and reduced quality of life, and it is widely recognized as a public health challenge. Although residential care facilities are populated environments, physical proximity does not guarantee meaningful interaction. Residents may share spaces without sharing conversation, family members may live far away or find visits difficult, and staff, who are often under time pressure, have limited capacity to engage residents in sustained social exchange beyond care tasks. Reminiscence is a well-established practice for addressing some of these challenges. It involves recalling and sharing personal memories, often prompted by photographs, music, or objects, and it has been associated with improved mood, a stronger sense of identity, and increased communication among older adults, including people living with dementia. Reminiscence is also inherently social: stories are told to someone, and listeners respond, ask questions, and contribute their own experiences. This makes it a promising foundation for interactions between residents and different groups, including peers, staff, relatives, and volunteers. Within HCI, a considerable body of work has explored technology to support reminiscence, from digital life story books to tablet-based media browsing and tangible memory aids. However, much of this work focuses on individual use, on dyadic therapeutic sessions led by professionals, or on a single stakeholder group. Less is known about how reminiscence-based tools can serve both co-located interaction within the care home and virtual interaction with people outside it, nor about how such tools should behave when they take an active part in a conversation. Designing for this setting is challenging for several reasons. First, residential care involves multiple stakeholders with different needs, capabilities, and expectations. Residents may have sensory, motor, or cognitive impairments and varying familiarity with technology. Family members want to stay connected but may be geographically distant and time constrained. Care staff must integrate any new practice into demanding workflows. Second, virtual interaction raises concerns about intrusiveness, privacy, and authenticity, and may be viewed with skepticism as a substitute for face-to-face contact. Third, when technology is introduced into a live conversation, it must support rather than disrupt it. A system that aims to collect stories, for example by recording and organizing memories for later sharing, may conflict with one that aims to stimulate conversation, since the former favors capture and structure while the latter favors flow and spontaneity. In this paper we investigate these issues through two complementary studies. Our first goal is to assess the feasibility of a reminiscence-based social interaction tool intended to stimulate conversation in residential care. We engaged different stakeholders, including residents, staff, and family members, to understand their perceptions of the concept, their willingness to contribute content and take part in interactions, and their attitudes toward both co-located and virtual forms of exchange. Our second goal is to explore the design challenges of giving technology an assisting role in co-located reminiscence sessions. To this end, we ran pilot studies using a technology probe, a deliberately simple and flexible artifact deployed to elicit reactions and reveal requirements in context. The probe supported a facilitator and participants during reminiscence sessions, allowing us to observe how technology-mediated assistance shaped conversation and story collection in practice. Our findings indicate that the proposed tool is feasible and that stakeholders are generally willing to contribute to the process, for instance by providing materials, prompts, and time. At the same time, participants expressed skepticism about virtual interactions, questioning whether remote exchanges could be as meaningful as in-person contact and raising concerns about suitability for residents. The pilot sessions showed that designing for both story collection and conversation stimulation requires compromises. Features that help gather rich, well-structured stories can interrupt the natural rhythm of dialogue, while features that prioritize lively conversation may yield fragmented or incomplete records. These tensions point to specific design areas, such as the timing and form of prompts, the role and visibility of the technology, and the balance between capture and engagement, where further exploration is needed. This paper makes three contributions. First, it provides empirical evidence on the feasibility of a reminiscence-based social interaction tool in residential care from the perspective of multiple stakeholders. Second, it offers insight into stakeholder attitudes toward co-located versus virtual interaction in this context. Third, it identifies and discusses design challenges and trade-offs in supporting an assisting role for technology in co-located reminiscence sessions, based on observations with a technology probe. Together, these contributions inform the design of future systems that support social connection in residential care. The remainder of the paper reviews related work on reminiscence technologies and social interaction in care settings, describes our methods and studies, presents the findings, and discusses their implications for design. We conducted the research in two phases within a single residential care home, using a research-through-design approach. Phase 1 explored the feasibility of a reminiscence-based social interaction tool with different stakeholders. Phase 2 examined design challenges of an assisting role in co-located reminiscence sessions, using a technology probe in pilot studies. The study was approved by the institutional ethics board and by the management of the care home. All participants, or their legal representatives where appropriate, gave informed consent, and residents' assent was re-confirmed verbally at the start of each session. Setting and Participants The care home accommodates approximately 60 residents with varying levels of physical and cognitive frailty. We recruited participants with the help of the activities coordinator, who identified residents able to hold a conversation and likely to enjoy reminiscence. Phase 1 included three stakeholder groups: residents (n = 8), family members and friends (n = 6), and care staff (n = 7), including care assistants, the activities coordinator, and a manager. Phase 2 involved six residents (two of whom had also taken part in Phase 1), and six volunteers or staff acting as facilitators. Residents' ages ranged from 74 to 94. Residents with advanced dementia or acute illness were excluded, as were those who did not wish to take part. Phase 1: Feasibility of the Tool Concept and prototype. The tool was designed around reminiscence: residents' memories are prompted by photographs, music, and everyday objects, and the resulting stories are captured and shared. The prototype was a tablet-based application with three functions: (1) browsing a set of prompts, such as period photographs and songs, selected according to a resident's age and background; (2) recording short audio stories related to a prompt; and (3) sharing recordings and prompts with remote contacts, who could respond with their own comments or memories to trigger asynchronous or live conversation. The prototype was low to medium fidelity, with a functioning interface for browsing and recording, while sharing was simulated by the researchers using a "Wizard of Oz" approach. Procedure. Residents took part in individual or small-group sessions (two to three people) of about 40 minutes. After a brief introduction, participants explored the prototype and were asked to tell stories prompted by its content. Family members and staff participated in separate semi-structured interviews and short hands-on demonstrations lasting 30 to 45 minutes. Family members who lived far away were interviewed by video call and shown the prototype through screen sharing. Interviews covered current communication practices, perceived barriers to social interaction in the home, reactions to the tool, concerns about privacy and burden, and willingness to contribute content or respond to residents' stories. Questions about virtual interaction were included for all groups to elicit attitudes toward remote communication. Data collection and analysis. Sessions were audio-recorded and transcribed, and researchers took field notes on participants' behavior and engagement. We analyzed the data through inductive thematic analysis. Two researchers independently coded a subset of transcripts, compared codes, and resolved disagreements through discussion before coding the remainder. Codes were grouped into themes regarding feasibility (perceived usefulness, ease of use, willingness to contribute) and concerns (skepticism toward virtual interaction, privacy, time demands). Themes were compared across stakeholder groups to identify convergences and tensions. Phase 2: Technology Probe in Co-located Reminiscence Sessions Probe design. To investigate an assisting role in co-located sessions, we developed a technology probe, a simple, flexible tool intended to elicit reactions and reveal design issues rather than serve as a finished solution. The probe was a tablet application that supported a facilitator and resident sitting together. It displayed prompts (photographs and music) and recorded the conversation's audio, tagging recordings with the prompt in use. It also offered suggested follow-up questions that the facilitator could choose to use. This design allowed us to observe tensions between collecting stories for later reuse and stimulating ongoing conversation. Procedure. We ran 12 pilot sessions, with each resident taking part in two sessions about a week apart. Each session lasted 20 to 35 minutes and took place in a quiet lounge or the resident's room, depending on preference. Facilitators received a 15-minute briefing on the probe but no script, and were encouraged to use it as they saw fit. A researcher observed unobtrusively from the side. Sessions were video-recorded with consent, with the camera positioned to capture the interaction and the tablet screen. After each session, residents and facilitators were briefly interviewed about what felt natural or disruptive, how the tablet influenced the conversation, and what they would change. Data collection and analysis. The data consisted of video recordings, probe interaction logs (prompts selected, recording duration, suggestions used), observation notes, and post-session interviews. We transcribed the sessions and annotated them for moments of interaction with the tablet, shifts in attention between the device and conversation partner, conversational pauses, story length, and resident engagement (for example, elaboration, laughter, or initiating topics). We then conducted thematic analysis across the video annotations and interviews, with the research team meeting regularly to interpret episodes and refine themes. Log data were summarized descriptively and used to support the qualitative interpretation rather than for statistical inference. Ethical Considerations and Limitations Because participants were potentially vulnerable, we kept sessions short, allowed withdrawal at any time, and had care staff nearby. Recordings were stored securely and pseudonymized, and participants could choose whether recordings were retained. The small, single-site, self-selected sample and the short exposure to the prototypes limit generalizability, and the simulated sharing function means that findings on virtual interaction reflect attitudes toward the concept rather than experience of using it. We report findings from two phases: (1) the feasibility study with stakeholders, and (2) the pilot reminiscence sessions with the technology probe. Quotes are labeled by participant group: residents (R), family members (F), care staff (S), and volunteers (V). Feasibility of a Reminiscence-Based Social Interaction Tool Perceived value for stimulating conversation. Across stakeholder groups, participants saw the tool as a plausible way to start conversations that were otherwise hard to begin. Staff described everyday interactions with residents as dominated by care routines, leaving little room for personal talk. One staff member noted, "We talk about meals and medication; we rarely get to ask about their lives" (S3). Family members said visits often stalled after the first few minutes, particularly when residents had memory problems. Prompts based on photographs, music, or familiar objects were seen as a means of "having something to hold on to" (F2). Residents who engaged with the concept were generally positive, and several began telling stories as soon as example prompts were shown, even before any tool functionality was demonstrated. Willingness to contribute. Most family members and several staff members were willing to contribute material such as photographs, short descriptions, and songs. Family members saw contributing as a way to remain involved in a relative's care, especially when they lived far away. Eight of the eleven family members said they could contribute content at least monthly.
