Community structures are ubiquitous in real-world networks, and exploiting them is central to many applications. Consider online advertising: an advertiser who wants to promote a product may purchase advertising slots on different platforms or websites, each of which attracts a distinct community of users. The advertiser has a limited budget and must decide how to allocate it across communities so as to reach as many distinct users as possible. A similar scenario arises when a sales representative visits organizations, when a researcher recruits participants from different groups, or when a marketer sends promotions through different social channels. In each case, an explorer allocates a limited budget among communities, each exploration reaches a member of a community, and the objective is to maximize the number of distinct members met. Because the same member may be encountered repeatedly, the problem exhibits diminishing returns, and the allocation must balance exploring large communities against avoiding redundant encounters. We formalize this setting as the community exploration problem. There are several disjoint communities, and the explorer has a budget of exploration opportunities. Each exploration of a community returns a member drawn uniformly at random from it. The explorer wishes to maximize the expected number of distinct members met. We study two variants. In non-adaptive exploration, the allocation of the budget across communities is fixed in advance. In adaptive exploration, the explorer observes the outcome of each exploration, such as whether the encountered member is new, and uses this information to choose the next community to explore. We further consider the problem in two regimes: an offline regime where community sizes are known, and an online regime where sizes are unknown and must be learned through repeated rounds of exploration. The problem is related to several lines of work but differs from each. Classical resource allocation and budgeted maximization problems often admit constant-factor approximations through greedy algorithms, relying on submodularity [1, 2]. The expected number of distinct members is a concave-like function of the allocation to each community, suggesting that greedy methods should perform well, but it is unclear whether they achieve exact optimality. Adaptive submodularity [3] provides guarantees for adaptive greedy policies, yet typically yields approximation ratios rather than optimality. The problem also resembles the coupon collector problem [4] and species richness estimation [5], where one samples with replacement to discover distinct items, but these works do not consider allocating a budget across multiple populations to maximize coverage. On the online side, our setting is connected to multi-armed bandits [6, 7] and especially combinatorial multi-armed bandits [8, 9, 10], in which a learner selects a set of base arms and receives semi-bandit feedback. The unknown community sizes play the role of unknown parameters, and the reward is a nonlinear function of both the sizes and the allocation. However, the feedback here has a distinctive structure: the observations are collisions among sampled members, from which sizes must be inferred, and standard analyses do not directly apply. Our contributions are as follows. First, for the offline setting with known community sizes, we show that the greedy algorithm is optimal for non-adaptive exploration. The key is to prove that the marginal gain of allocating an additional exploration to a community is decreasing in the number of explorations already allocated, so that incremental selection of the largest marginal gain yields a globally optimal allocation. For adaptive exploration, we prove that the greedy policy, which at each step explores the community with the largest expected probability of yielding a new member, is also optimal. This result is stronger than the approximation guarantees usually available for adaptive submodular problems. We also compare the adaptive and non-adaptive optima, quantifying the benefit of adaptivity. Second, for the online setting in which community sizes are unknown, we consider a multi-round game where in each round the explorer allocates a budget, observes the members met, and updates estimates of the sizes. We propose an upper-confidence-bound-style algorithm that builds confidence intervals for the community sizes from the collisions observed within each round and plays the offline greedy solution against optimistic estimates. We prove that this algorithm achieves a regret bound that is logarithmic in the number of rounds, for both the non-adaptive and adaptive versions. Our analysis handles the nonlinearity of the reward and the dependence between estimation error and allocation. Third, we show that regret can be reduced substantially by combining feedback across rounds. Because members encountered in different rounds can be matched, the collisions among all previously observed members provide far more information about community sizes than the collisions within a single round. Exploiting this, we design an algorithm whose regret is bounded by a constant independent of the number of rounds. To our knowledge, this is a rare case in combinatorial bandits in which constant regret is achievable without special assumptions on the reward gap, and it arises from the structure of the feedback. Finally, we complement the theory with experiments on synthetic data and real-world data, which confirm that greedy allocations match optimal values, that the proposed algorithms attain the predicted regret behavior, and that cross-round feedback yields markedly lower regret. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the model and notation. Section 3 analyzes the offline problem for non-adaptive and adaptive exploration. Section 4 presents the online learning algorithms and their regret bounds. Section 5 reports experiments, Section 6 reviews related work in more detail, and Section 7 concludes. We consider a set of m communities C1,...,Cm with sizes n1,...,nm, which are unknown in the online setting. An explorer has a budget of K total explorations. Each exploration of community Ci returns a member sampled uniformly at random with replacement from Ci. The goal is to allocate the budget so as to maximize the expected number of distinct members met. We study non-adaptive and adaptive strategies in the offline setting, then online learning over multiple rounds. Problem Formulation. A non-adaptive allocation is a vector k = (k1,...,km) with sum ki = K, fixed before any exploration. Exploring Ci ki times meets each member with probability 1-(1-1/ni)^{ki}, so the expected number of distinct members is f(k) = sumi ni [1-(1-1/ni)^{ki}]. An adaptive strategy chooses the next community to explore based on the members observed so far, and its value is the expectation over the randomness of the observations. We also consider a variant in which each community has a weight wi, representing the value of meeting one of its members, so the objective becomes sumi wi ni [1-(1-1/ni)^{ki}]. Offline Non-Adaptive Optimization. Define the marginal gain of the t-th exploration of Ci as Δi(t) = wi(1-1/ni)^{t-1}. This is strictly decreasing in t, so f is separable and concave in each ki. The greedy algorithm starts from k = 0 and, at each of K steps, increments the ki with the largest current marginal gain Δi(ki+1). Because the marginal gains are monotonically decreasing, this resembles the classical resource-allocation problem with separable concave objectives [1,2]. We prove optimality by an exchange argument: if an optimal allocation differs from the greedy one, there exist i and j with ki > gi and kj < gj (where g is the greedy allocation). Moving one exploration from i to j does not decrease the objective, and repeating this transforms the optimal solution into the greedy one. Implementation with a priority queue takes O(K log m) time. Offline Adaptive Optimization. In the adaptive setting, the state after some explorations is the number of distinct members already met in each community. If di members of Ci have been met, the next exploration of Ci yields a new member with probability (ni-di)/ni, so the expected immediate reward is wi(ni-di)/ni. The adaptive greedy policy always explores the community with the highest current expected reward. We show optimality by induction on the remaining budget, using dynamic programming over states. The key lemma is that the value function is separable across communities and that the one-step reward of a community depends only on its own state and is nonincreasing in di, which is stochastically nondecreasing in the number of explorations. Hence an index policy is optimal, in the spirit of Gittins-type results [3]. We further show that the adaptive optimum is at least as large as the non-adaptive optimum, and we quantify the adaptivity gap on instances with differing sizes. Online Learning Setting. The sizes ni are unknown. The game proceeds over T rounds; in each round the explorer allocates a budget K and observes the members encountered. Members have identifiers, so repeated encounters are detectable. Performance is measured by the cumulative regret relative to the optimal offline allocation computed with true sizes, or, for computational tractability, an approximation-free comparison since greedy is exactly optimal. Estimating Community Sizes. Within a round, if Ci is explored ki times, the number of collisions (pairs of explorations returning the same member) provides an unbiased estimate of 1/ni, since each pair collides with probability 1/ni. Let the pair-collision statistic be Xi = sum over pairs s<t of 1{s-th and t-th draws coincide}, so E[Xi] = C(ki,2)/ni. We estimate ni by the inverse of the empirical collision rate accumulated over rounds. Using Hoeffding-type inequalities for U-statistics [4], we derive confidence radii for the estimate of 1/ni that shrink as the number of sampled pairs grows. Upper Confidence Bound Algorithm (CUCB-style). In round t, for each community we compute an optimistic estimate of its size (or equivalently of its marginal gain) by adding a confidence radius of order sqrt(log t / Ni(t)), where Ni(t) counts accumulated pairs. We then run the offline greedy algorithm on the optimistic parameters to pick the allocation. This follows the combinatorial upper-confidence framework [5,6]. We establish a regret bound of O(log T) by showing that the objective is Lipschitz in the parameters with respect to the allocation and that suboptimal allocations are chosen only when the confidence intervals remain wide, which can occur O(log T) times. Gap-dependent constants depend on the smallest loss from deviating from the optimal allocation. Combining Feedback Across Rounds. The first algorithm uses only within-round collisions. Because members are identifiable across rounds, we can instead pool all draws from Ci over all rounds into a single sample and count collisions among all pairs. This yields an estimator whose accuracy improves quadratically in the total number of draws, rather than linearly in the number of rounds. Under the mild assumption that every community with positive greedy allocation is explored at least a fixed number of times per round, the estimation error decays fast enough that the sum of the failure probabilities converges. We then show that, after a finite number of rounds independent of T, the algorithm identifies the optimal allocation with high probability and incurs only a constant expected regret thereafter. A union bound over communities and a careful treatment of dependencies among pooled pairs [4] complete the argument. Analysis Tools. Proofs rely on concavity and exchange arguments for offline results, concentration inequalities for U-statistics for estimation, and regret decomposition by counting rounds with suboptimal choices for online results. Throughout we assume ni ≥ 2 and a bounded maximum size. We evaluate the theoretical guarantees established for the community exploration problem and complement them with numerical experiments. Throughout, there are m communities with sizes n1,…,nm, a total budget K, and an explorer who in each exploration step selects a community and meets a member drawn uniformly at random with replacement. The objective is the expected number of distinct members met. Offline optimization: non-adaptive exploration. We first consider the setting in which the allocation (k1,…,km) with Σki = K must be fixed in advance. The expected number of distinct members is Σi ni(1−(1−1/ni)^{ki}). Each term is concave in ki, and the marginal gain of the k-th exploration of community i is (1−1/ni)^{k−1}, which is decreasing in k. Consequently, the greedy algorithm, which repeatedly assigns one unit of budget to the community with the largest marginal gain, returns an optimal allocation. This result holds for arbitrary community sizes. The computational cost is O(K log m) with a priority queue.

Atherosclerosis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory disease of the arterial wall characterized by lipid deposition, endothelial dysfunction, and the progressive formation of fibrofatty plaques. It underlies most cases of myocardial infarction, stroke, and peripheral artery disease, which together make cardiovascular disease the leading cause of death worldwide. Elevated plasma total cholesterol (TC) and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) are well-established drivers of plaque initiation. Retention and oxidative modification of LDL in the subendothelial space trigger monocyte recruitment, foam cell formation, and sustained inflammation. Statins and other lipid-lowering drugs are effective, but adverse effects, incomplete risk reduction, and cost motivate the search for safe dietary strategies that can prevent or slow the early stages of the disease. Tea, prepared from the leaves of Camellia sinensis, is among the most widely consumed beverages in the world. Its principal bioactive constituents are polyphenols, mainly catechins such as (−)-epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG), (−)-epigallocatechin, (−)-epicatechin-3-gallate, and (−)-epicatechin, along with theaflavins and thearubigins in fermented teas. Epidemiological studies have associated habitual tea consumption with a lower risk of coronary heart disease and stroke. Experimental studies in animals and humans have reported that tea polyphenols (TPs) lower plasma lipids, reduce oxidative stress, improve endothelial function, and attenuate inflammation. Nevertheless, the mechanisms are not fully explained. A notable obstacle is the low bioavailability of tea catechins: only a small proportion of ingested polyphenols is absorbed in the small intestine, and the majority reaches the colon, where it interacts with resident microbes. This observation suggests that the gut microbiota may be an important mediator of the biological effects of TPs. The human and murine gut harbor trillions of microorganisms that influence host nutrient metabolism, immune development, and inflammatory tone. Alterations in microbial composition, termed dysbiosis, have been linked to obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. Gut microbes contribute to AS through several routes. Bacterial lipopolysaccharide translocating across a compromised intestinal barrier can drive metabolic endotoxemia and low-grade systemic inflammation. Microbial metabolism of dietary choline and carnitine generates trimethylamine N-oxide, which promotes foam cell formation and atherosclerosis. Microbial transformation of bile acids and production of short-chain fatty acids influence cholesterol homeostasis and host immunity. Gut bacterial DNA has even been detected within atherosclerotic plaques, and germ-free and antibiotic-treated animal models show altered lipid metabolism and plaque development, supporting a causal role for the microbiota. Dietary polyphenols and gut microbes influence one another bidirectionally. Microbes hydrolyze and ferment polyphenols into smaller phenolic acids and other metabolites that are more readily absorbed and often more bioactive than the parent compounds. Conversely, polyphenols can act as prebiotic-like substrates, selectively enhancing the growth of beneficial bacteria while inhibiting pathogens. Among the beneficial genera, Bifidobacterium is of particular interest. Bifidobacteria are Gram-positive, anaerobic, saccharolytic bacteria that are dominant members of the healthy gut and are widely used as probiotics. They help maintain intestinal barrier integrity, suppress colonization by pathogens, limit endotoxin leakage, modulate immune responses, and can assimilate cholesterol and deconjugate bile salts. Some trials and animal studies indicate that certain Bifidobacterium strains reduce serum cholesterol and inflammatory markers and slow the progression of AS. High-fat feeding, by contrast, is commonly reported to reduce intestinal bifidobacteria, a change associated with increased gut permeability and metabolic disturbance. Several studies have shown that tea extracts or polyphenols can increase bifidobacteria and other beneficial taxa in vitro and in vivo, but few have examined whether such changes are connected with the development of AS. The apolipoprotein E-deficient (ApoE−/−) mouse is a well-accepted model of AS. Lacking ApoE, which is essential for clearance of lipoprotein remnants, these animals develop marked hypercholesterolemia and spontaneous lesions resembling those of humans, and lesion development is accelerated by a high-fat diet (HFD). The model has been used to examine dietary and microbial influences on plaque formation, and it is suitable for studying early lesions, when interventions are most likely to be effective. Although TPs have been reported to be anti-atherogenic and to alter the gut microbiota, limited information is available on whether modulation of specific intestinal bacteria, such as bifidobacteria, accompanies and relates to the protective effect of TPs on early plaque formation. Most existing work has focused on lipid-lowering and antioxidant effects of TPs without considering the microbial community, or has described microbial changes without relating them to a vascular outcome. Quantitative assessment of intestinal bifidobacteria alongside plaque measurements within the same animals could help determine whether the two are linked. Therefore, the present study was designed to investigate the effects of different doses of TPs, supplied in drinking water, on serum lipid profiles, early aortic atherosclerotic lesion formation, and the abundance of intestinal Bifidobacteria in HFD-fed ApoE−/− mice. We further analyzed the correlation between bifidobacterial copy number and the plaque area/lumen area ratio to evaluate whether the proliferation of bifidobacteria may partly account for the anti-atherosclerotic effect of TPs. Animals and housing Fifty male C57BL/6 ApoE−/− mice (6 weeks old, 18–20 g) were obtained from a certified laboratory animal supplier. Mice were housed under specific pathogen-free conditions (22 ± 2 °C, 50–60% humidity, 12 h light/dark cycle) with free access to food and water. After a one-week acclimatization period on standard chow, animals were randomized by body weight into five groups (n = 10/group). All procedures followed national guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals and were approved by the institutional animal ethics committee. Diets and tea polyphenol treatment The control group (CK) received a normal chow diet and plain drinking water. The remaining four groups received a high-fat diet (HFD; 21% fat, 0.15% cholesterol, w/w). One HFD group received plain drinking water (HFD), and the other three received the HFD with tea polyphenols (TPs) dissolved in drinking water at low (TP-L, 0.1%), medium (TP-M, 0.2%), and high (TP-H, 0.4%) concentrations (w/v). The TP preparation was a commercial extract containing more than 98% total polyphenols, of which catechins accounted for over 70% (epigallocatechin gallate being the major component), as verified by HPLC. TP solutions were freshly prepared and replaced every two days to limit oxidation, and were protected from light. Water and food intake were measured twice weekly per cage, and body weight was recorded weekly. The intervention lasted 16 weeks. Sample collection At the end of the intervention, mice were fasted for 12 h. Fresh fecal pellets were collected, immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80 °C. Mice were then anesthetized, and blood was collected by retro-orbital puncture or cardiac puncture. Serum was separated by centrifugation (3000 × g, 15 min, 4 °C) and stored at −80 °C. Mice were euthanized by cervical dislocation under anesthesia. The heart with the aortic root was removed, rinsed in cold phosphate-buffered saline, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, and embedded. Cecal contents were collected and frozen at −80 °C for microbial analysis. Serum lipid analysis Serum total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides (TG), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) were measured with commercial enzymatic kits on an automatic biochemical analyzer according to the manufacturers' instructions. Histological assessment of atherosclerotic lesions Hearts were embedded in optimal cutting temperature compound, and serial 8 µm cryosections of the aortic root were cut starting from the appearance of the aortic valve leaflets. Sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and with Oil Red O to visualize lipid deposition. Images were captured under a light microscope with a digital camera and analyzed with Image-Pro Plus software by an observer blinded to group allocation. For each animal, the plaque area (PA) and lumen area (LA) were measured in at least five sections, and the PA/LA ratio was calculated as an index of early atherosclerotic lesion development; the mean value per animal was used for statistical analysis. Fecal DNA extraction Total bacterial DNA was extracted from approximately 200 mg of feces or cecal contents using a commercial stool DNA extraction kit with a bead-beating step, following the manufacturer's protocol. DNA concentration and purity were assessed with a spectrophotometer (A260/A280), and integrity was checked by 1% agarose gel electrophoresis. DNA was stored at −20 °C until use. Quantification of intestinal Bifidobacteria by real-time PCR Intestinal Bifidobacteria (IB) were quantified by SYBR Green quantitative PCR targeting the 16S rRNA gene using genus-specific primers (Bifidobacterium: forward 5′-CGCGTCYGGTGTGAAAG-3′, reverse 5′-CCCCACATCCAGCATCCA-3′). Total bacteria were quantified with universal primers as a reference. Reactions (20 µL) contained 10 µL of 2× SYBR Green master mix, 0.4 µM of each primer, 2 µL of template DNA, and nuclease-free water. Cycling conditions were 95 °C for 5 min, followed by 40 cycles of 95 °C for 15 s and 60 °C for 30 s, with a subsequent melting-curve analysis to confirm amplification specificity. Standard curves were generated from 10-fold serial dilutions of a plasmid containing the cloned Bifidobacterium 16S rRNA gene fragment, and the copy number in each sample was calculated from the curve. Results were expressed as log10 16S rRNA gene copies per gram of feces. All samples were run in triplicate, with negative controls included in each run. Statistical analysis Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation. Normality and homogeneity of variance were tested before analysis. Differences among groups were assessed by one-way analysis of variance followed by the least significant difference or Tukey post hoc test; Kruskal–Wallis testing was used where assumptions were not met. Dose dependency of the TP effect on IB copy numbers was evaluated by trend analysis across the TP dose groups. Associations between IB copy numbers and the PA/LA ratio, as well as serum lipid parameters, were examined using Pearson or Spearman correlation coefficients as appropriate. Analyses were performed with SPSS software, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant, with P < 0.01 considered highly significant. Body weight, food intake and serum lipid profiles Over the 16-week intervention, mice in all HFD-fed groups gained more body weight than those in the CK group. Body weight did not differ significantly between the HFD group and the TP-supplemented groups (P > 0.05), although the high-dose TP group tended to show lower final body weight than the HFD group. Food intake and water consumption were similar across the HFD-fed groups, indicating that TP supplementation did not noticeably affect palatability or energy intake. The HFD markedly altered the serum lipid profile relative to the CK group. Total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides (TG) and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) were significantly higher in the HFD group (P < 0.01), whereas high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) was not significantly changed. TP supplementation significantly reduced TC and LDL-C compared with the HFD group (P < 0.05), and the reductions were larger at higher TP doses. Serum TG showed a downward trend with TP treatment, but the difference did not reach significance in the low-dose group. HDL-C tended to be higher in the TP groups, though this was not statistically significant. Consequently, the LDL-C/HDL-C ratio was lower in the TP-treated groups than in the HFD group. Atherosclerotic lesion formation Histological examination of aortic root sections stained with hematoxylin and eosin showed clear differences among groups. The CK group displayed an intact intima with no obvious plaque. In contrast, the HFD group showed pronounced early lesions, characterized by subendothelial lipid deposition, foam cell accumulation and thickened intima protruding into the lumen. Lesions in the TP-supplemented groups were visibly smaller and had fewer foam cells, with relatively preserved vessel wall architecture. Quantitative analysis confirmed these observations. The ratio of plaque area to lumen area (PA/LA) was significantly higher in the HFD group than in the CK group (P < 0.01). TP supplementation reduced the PA/LA ratio in a dose-dependent manner, and all TP groups differed significantly from the HFD group (P < 0.01). The high-dose group showed the lowest PA/LA ratio among the HFD-fed animals, although it remained above that of the CK group. Intestinal Bifidobacteria Copies of Bifidobacteria (IB) 16S rRNA genes in fecal and cecal contents were quantified by real-time quantitative PCR. Convex optimization is one of the great success stories of theoretical computer science and applied mathematics: convex functions can be minimized in polynomial time using only function evaluations or subgradients, via the ellipsoid method [Khachiyan; Grötschel, Lovász, Schrijver], cutting-plane methods [Vaidya; Lee, Sidford, Wong], and gradient-based schemes [Nesterov]. Yet many objectives encountered in practice, such as those arising in training neural networks, matrix factorization, and learning dynamical systems, are not convex, even though simple local methods often succeed on them. This has motivated the search for structural conditions weaker than convexity that still permit provable global optimization. Examples include quasiconvexity, invexity, the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition, and weak or "one-point" convexity [Hardt, Ma, Recht; Kleinberg et al.; Karimi et al.]. In this paper we study one such class: star-convex functions. A function f is star-convex about a point x if, for every x in the domain and every λ in [0,1], f(λx + (1−λ)x) ≤ λ f(x) + (1−λ) f(x). Equivalently, f is convex along every line segment through x, though not necessarily along other segments. If x is a global minimizer, this says that f lies below the chord joining any point to the optimum. Convex functions are star-convex about every minimizer, but star-convex functions may be highly non-convex: they may be nonsmooth, may have many nonglobal stationary points or plateaus away from x, and need not even be continuous away from x. Star-convexity has been observed empirically in the loss landscapes of neural networks along optimization trajectories [Zhou et al.], and it has been proposed as a explanation for the success of stochastic gradient descent in such settings. Prior work. The most closely related result is that of Nesterov and Polyak [2006], who analyze a cubic-regularized Newton method and show that it finds approximate minimizers of star-convex functions with Lipschitz continuous Hessian. Their guarantee has mild dependence on the dimension but depends exponentially on the number of requested digits of accuracy, i.e., it is polynomial only in 1/ε rather than in log(1/ε). Moreover, it requires second-order smoothness, which excludes many natural star-convex functions. Lee and Valiant's question, which we address, is whether star-convex functions can be optimized in time polynomial in log(1/ε) without any smoothness assumption. Gradient-based methods are poorly suited to this goal. We show that there is a family of star-convex functions for which gradients, at essentially every point, provably reveal no information about the location of the global optimum: local derivative information can be arbitrarily misleading, since star-convexity constrains the function only along rays through the unknown optimum, and a perturbation supported away from these rays can be introduced without violating the definition. Standard variants of gradient descent, including those with momentum or adaptive step sizes, therefore cannot succeed in general, and any successful algorithm must use information of a different kind. Our contribution. We give a randomized algorithm that minimizes any star-convex function that is Lebesgue measurable and bounded on a region about the origin, using only function evaluations and running in time polynomial in the dimension n and in log(1/ε). No continuity, differentiability, or Lipschitz condition is needed. The measurability assumption is only to ensure that the sets we sample from are well-defined, and it admits a large set of pathological functions that are discontinuous almost everywhere except at the optimum. The algorithm is a cutting-plane method in which the cuts are constructed from function values alone. Given a current feasible region known to contain a global optimum, we must find a hyperplane that separates the optimum from a constant fraction of the region's volume. For convex functions, a subgradient supplies such a hyperplane. For star-convex functions, no such oracle is available, and we instead estimate it by random sampling. The key idea is counterintuitive: the algorithm must evaluate the function outside the feasible region. Star-convexity implies that if a point y in the feasible region has f(y) larger than f at a point z, then information about the optimum's location can be inferred from points along rays through z. By extrapolating along rays beyond the feasible region, we obtain inequalities that are valid because of star-convexity, and which let us certify that a half-space cannot contain a point better than those already observed. We show that with a polynomial number of random samples, one such cut succeeds with constant probability, and that repeated cuts shrink the feasible volume geometrically, giving the claimed dependence on log(1/ε). Our dimension dependence is worse than that of Nesterov and Polyak, and we do not claim it to be optimal. The trade-off is that we obtain exponentially better dependence on accuracy while eliminating the smoothness requirement entirely. Organization. Section 2 introduces notation and basic properties of star-convex functions, including the lower bounds for gradient-based methods. Section 3 presents the cut-finding procedure and its analysis. Section 4 combines it with a volume-reduction argument to obtain the optimization algorithm and handle measurability and boundedness. Section 5 discusses extensions and open problems. We view these results as a step toward understanding optimization beyond convexity and local gradient methods. We consider minimizing a function f: R^n → R that is star-convex about a minimizer x, meaning f(αx + (1−α)x) ≤ αf(x) + (1−α)f(x) for all x and α∈[0,1]. We assume f is Lebesgue measurable and bounded on a ball B(0,R) containing x, with |f| ≤ M there. No continuity, differentiability, or convexity is assumed. Access to f is through a zeroth-order oracle. The goal is to output a point x with f(x) − f(x) ≤ ε using a number of evaluations polynomial in n, log(MR/ε), and log(1/δ), where δ is the failure probability. Overview. The method is a cutting-plane scheme in the spirit of the center-of-gravity and ellipsoid methods [Grötschel et al., 1988; Bertsimas and Vempala, 2004], maintaining a convex set K ⊇ {x : f(x) ≤ f(x) + ε} ∩ B(0,R). Each iteration must produce a halfspace that excludes a constant fraction of the volume of K while retaining a near-optimal point. Since f carries no gradient or subgradient information (we show in the lower-bound section that gradients may be uninformative), the halfspace must be inferred from function values alone. Star-convexity and sublevel sets. Let Lt = {x : f(x) ≤ t}. Star-convexity implies that if x ∈ Lt then every point on the segment [x, x] has value at most max(t, f(x)) and indeed at most a convex combination of f(x) and f(x). Hence each sublevel set Lt with t ≥ f(x) is star-shaped about x, though not necessarily convex. The key consequence is that along any ray from x, the function restricted to the ray lies below the chord to f(x) at the origin of the ray; thus g(s)=f(x+su) satisfies that (g(s)−f(x))/s is nondecreasing in s. Equivalently, if f(y) > t at some point y, then every point beyond y on the ray from x through y has value > t. This monotonicity is the only structural property we use. Cut from a pair of points. Suppose we query points p and q = p + τ(p − c) lying on a line through a candidate point c, with q outside the current region. If f(q) < f(p) cannot hold with x behind... more precisely, the monotonicity above shows that if x lies on the line through p and q on the side of p opposite q, then f(p) ≤ max(f(q), f(x)) and in fact f(p) − f(x) ≤ (1−α)(f(q) − f(x)) for the corresponding α. Violations of this inequality certify that x is not on that side. Our cuts are certificates of this kind, but a single line only constrains x when it nearly passes through x, which is unlikely for random lines. We therefore aggregate many lines. Randomized cut procedure. Fix the current set K with centroid z, approximated by averaging samples from K obtained via hit-and-run random walks [Lovász and Vempala, 2006]. Draw points x1,…,xm approximately uniformly from K. For a threshold t, let St = {xi : f(xi) ≤ t}, and let t be the median of observed values. The sublevel set Lt is star-shaped about x, but unlike in the convex case its centroid need not give a separating hyperplane. Instead, we use the following outward probing: for each sampled xi with f(xi) > t, we evaluate f at points xi + s(xi − z) outside K, for s in a geometric grid up to a radius covering B(0,R). By monotonicity, a large value outside K implies large values on the ray beyond, and a small value outside implies via star-convexity that the segment from x to that point lies in a low sublevel set. Outside evaluations are therefore informative about the cone structure of Lt seen from x, which cannot be learned from inside K alone. Using these values we estimate, for each direction u, the radial extent ρt(u) of the star body Lt around z up to a multiplicative grid error. We then define a direction w as the empirical mean of directions ui of the sampled points with f(xi) ≤ t, weighted by estimated extent, and cut with the halfspace {x : ⟨w, x − z⟩ ≤ 0}, subject to a verification step: we test by further sampling whether the halfspace retains at least a (1/2 − 1/poly(n)) fraction of Lt∩K measured in volume. If verification fails, we replace t by a lower level and repeat. Measurability guarantees that volumes of sublevel sets are well defined, so the sampling estimates converge by standard concentration (Hoeffding) bounds without regularity assumptions. Progress measure. Let K0 = B(0,R). Define for ε the set Gε = {x+ (ε/(2M))(x − x) : x ∈ K0}, a scaled copy of K0 about x that, by star-convexity, consists of points with f ≤ f(x) + ε. Its volume is (ε/2M)^n vol(K0). Each cut preserves Gε with high probability and shrinks vol(K) by a constant factor (1−1/e-type bound, degraded slightly by sampling error). After N = O(n log(MR/ε)) iterations, vol(K) < vol(Gε), contradicting containment unless the process has already sampled a point of Gε. We return the best sampled point. Complexity. Each iteration uses m = poly(n, log(1/δ)) samples, each costing O(n^3) walk steps after rounding [Lovász and Vempala, 2006], plus O(log(MR/ε)) outward probes per sample. A union bound over iterations yields overall failure probability δ. The total number of evaluations is polynomial in n and log(1/ε), in contrast to the exp(1/ε)-type dependence of the cubic-regularization approach of Nesterov and Polyak [2006]. Lower-bound construction. To show gradients are uninformative, we build star-convex functions whose gradients, wherever they exist, are independent of the location of x, by superposing oscillating radial perturbations on a cone-shaped base function. This is detailed in the following section. We present our main results on optimizing star-convex functions, followed by the lower bound on gradient information and a discussion of the cutting-plane subroutine on which the algorithm rests. We write ε for the requested additive accuracy and assume f takes values in an interval of length at most B on this ball. Main theorem. Our principal result is a randomized algorithm that, given only evaluation access to f, outputs a point x̂ with f(x̂) ≤ f(x) + ε with probability at least 1 − δ. The algorithm uses a number of function evaluations and arithmetic operations that is polynomial in n, log(1/δ), and log(BR/ε)-type quantities, i.e. polynomial in the number of requested digits of accuracy. Formally, we show that the number of evaluations is O(poly(n) · log(BR/ε) · log(1/δ)). No smoothness, differentiability, or continuity is assumed. Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder in which autoantibodies, most commonly against the acetylcholine receptor (AChR) and less often against muscle-specific tyrosine kinase (MuSK) or lipoprotein-related protein 4, impair neuromuscular transmission. The clinical hallmark is fluctuating, fatigable weakness of ocular, bulbar, limb, and respiratory muscles. Advances in immunotherapy, thymectomy, and intensive care have greatly improved survival, and most patients now live for decades with the disease. As a consequence, long-term treatment-related complications have become an increasingly important determinant of outcome and quality of life. Oral glucocorticoids remain the mainstay of immunosuppressive treatment for MG. Prednisolone is effective in inducing remission or marked improvement in a large proportion of patients, and in Japan it is used in a higher proportion of patients than in many Western countries. Clinical practice has also shifted toward the use of glucocorticoids in patients with ocular and mild generalized disease, with the aim of achieving "minimal manifestations" of disease. Treatment is often prolonged, and many patients receive low to moderate doses for years. Although this strategy controls symptoms, it exposes patients to the well-known adverse effects of long-term glucocorticoid exposure, including diabetes, hypertension, infection, cataract, weight gain, and bone loss. Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis (GIO) is the most common form of secondary osteoporosis and a major cause of fragility fractures. Glucocorticoids reduce bone formation by suppressing osteoblast differentiation and promoting osteoblast and osteocyte apoptosis, while transiently increasing osteoclast-mediated resorption. They also reduce intestinal calcium absorption, increase renal calcium excretion, and affect gonadal hormones. Fracture risk rises rapidly after the start of therapy, may occur at bone mineral density (BMD) values higher than those seen in postmenopausal osteoporosis, and depends on both dose and duration of treatment. Guidelines from the American College of Rheumatology and the Japanese Society for Bone and Mineral Research recommend fracture risk assessment and preventive treatment, such as bisphosphonates, in patients receiving prolonged glucocorticoid therapy. Despite this, adherence to such guidelines is often incomplete in clinical practice, especially outside rheumatology. Patients with MG may be particularly vulnerable to GIO and its consequences. First, the disease itself causes muscle weakness and reduced physical activity, which can lead to disuse-related bone loss and an increased risk of falls. Second, bulbar involvement and dysphagia may impair nutrition and intake of calcium and vitamin D, and ocular or bulbar symptoms can limit outdoor activity and sun exposure. Third, MG predominantly affects young women and older adults, populations already at risk of low bone mass, and a substantial proportion of patients are postmenopausal women. Fourth, thymectomy, anticholinesterase drugs, and other immunosuppressants may influence bone metabolism or fracture risk through mechanisms that are incompletely understood. Finally, fractures in patients with limited muscle strength may lead to prolonged immobilization, with a risk of further deconditioning, myasthenic worsening, and loss of independence. Fractures may therefore have a disproportionate effect on daily functioning in MG. Surprisingly, few studies have examined osteoporosis and fractures in patients with MG. Some reports have suggested a reduction in BMD in patients treated with glucocorticoids, but sample sizes were small, fracture outcomes were rarely assessed, and the relationship with disease severity was not clearly defined. Population-based analyses of fracture risk in MG have given inconsistent results. In addition, it remains unclear whether the cumulative duration of glucocorticoid therapy, the daily dose, or the activity of the MG itself is the dominant determinant of fracture in this population. These distinctions matter, because current treatment strategies aim at reducing the dose of prednisolone while maintaining disease control, and because disease severity itself may be a modifiable target. Moreover, little is known about the impact of osteoporotic fractures on patient-reported outcomes in MG. Health-related quality of life is now recognized as an important endpoint in MG, and disease-specific instruments such as the 15-item Myasthenia Gravis Quality of Life scale (MG-QOL15) capture the burden of symptoms and functional limitation from the patient's perspective. Whether fractures add to this burden, and in which domains, has not been systematically examined. Such information would help clinicians and policy makers judge the importance of routine screening and prevention of osteoporosis in patients with MG. To address these gaps, we conducted a multicenter cross-sectional survey of patients with MG followed at six centers in Japan. We collected detailed information on clinical features of MG, glucocorticoid exposure, history of osteoporotic fractures, bone turnover markers, BMD, and radiological findings, and we assessed quality of life with the MG-QOL15. Our aims were to determine the prevalence of osteoporotic fractures among patients receiving glucocorticoids, to identify clinical factors associated with fractures, including the duration and dose of prednisolone and measures of MG severity, and to evaluate the relationship between fractures and quality of life. We hypothesized that fractures in patients with MG would be associated with longer glucocorticoid exposure and greater disease severity, and that they would worsen activities of daily living. We conducted a multicenter cross-sectional survey at six medical centers in Japan (university hospitals and neuromuscular referral centers) between April and July 2012. Consecutive patients with MG who attended the outpatient clinics during this period were invited to participate. The study was approved by the ethics committee of each participating institution and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. All participants provided written informed consent. Participants Eligible patients were those with a diagnosis of MG based on typical fluctuating muscle weakness together with at least one of the following: positive serum anti-acetylcholine receptor (AChR) or anti-muscle-specific tyrosine kinase (MuSK) antibodies, a decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation, or a positive edrophonium test. Patients were included if they were aged 18 years or older and had been followed at the participating center for at least 6 months. Patients were excluded if they had other conditions known to affect bone metabolism substantially, such as primary hyperparathyroidism, hyperthyroidism not controlled by treatment, chronic renal failure requiring dialysis, or malignancy with bone metastasis, or if they were unable to provide informed consent or complete the questionnaires. In total, 363 patients were enrolled. Clinical data collection Clinical information was collected by treating neurologists using a standardized case report form and by review of medical records. Data included sex, age, height, weight, body mass index (BMI), age at onset, disease duration, antibody status, presence of thymoma, and history of thymectomy. Disease severity at the time of the survey was classified according to the Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America (MGFA) clinical classification, and the quantitative MG (QMG) score was recorded as a measure of current disease severity. Treatment data included use of cholinesterase inhibitors, calcineurin inhibitors and other immunosuppressants, and history of intravenous immunoglobulin, plasmapheresis, or high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone. For glucocorticoid therapy, we recorded whether patients were currently receiving oral prednisolone, the current daily dose, the maximum daily dose, the duration of therapy (years), and the cumulative dose estimated from medical records. Use of osteoporosis medications (bisphosphonates, active vitamin D3, calcium, selective estrogen receptor modulators, teriparatide, and others) was also documented. Other fracture risk factors were recorded, including smoking, alcohol consumption, menopausal status in women, and family history of hip fracture. Assessment of fractures A history of osteoporotic fracture was determined by interview and medical record review and was confirmed radiologically when possible. Osteoporotic fractures included vertebral fractures and non-vertebral fragility fractures (such as those of the femoral neck, distal radius, humerus, and ribs) resulting from low-energy trauma, such as a fall from standing height or less. Fractures due to high-energy trauma were excluded. Only fractures occurring after the start of glucocorticoid therapy were counted for patients receiving glucocorticoids. Vertebral fractures were assessed on lateral thoracolumbar spine radiographs using semiquantitative criteria, with a reduction of vertebral height of 20% or more considered a fracture. Radiographs were evaluated by experienced physicians who were blinded to the clinical data of the patients. Bone mineral density and bone turnover markers Bone mineral density (BMD) of the lumbar spine (L2–L4) and femoral neck was measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) using the devices available at each center. BMD values were expressed in g/cm², as percentages of the young adult mean (YAM), and as T-scores. To reduce inter-device variability, %YAM values were used in comparisons across centers. Serum samples were collected in the morning after overnight fasting for measurement of bone turnover markers: bone-specific alkaline phosphatase or total procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide as a formation marker, and tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase-5b or urinary or serum type I collagen cross-linked N-telopeptide as a resorption marker, according to the assays used at each facility. Serum calcium, phosphate, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D were measured when available. Quality of life assessment Health-related quality of life was measured using the Japanese version of the 15-item Myasthenia Gravis Quality of Life scale (MG-QOL15). Each item is scored from 0 to 4 and the total score ranges from 0 to 60, with higher scores indicating greater impairment. Patients completed the questionnaire by themselves, with assistance when necessary. Individual items, including those related to activities of daily living (ADL), were also analyzed to compare patients with and without fractures. Statistical analysis Continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation and categorical variables as numbers and percentages. The primary analysis focused on patients treated with prednisolone. Patients with and without osteoporotic fractures were compared using the Student's t-test or Mann–Whitney U test for continuous variables, as appropriate to the distribution, and the chi-square test or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables. Associations of prednisolone dose and duration with fractures were examined by comparing groups and by stratified analysis. BMD and bone marker values were compared between patients with and without fractures, with adjustment for age and sex where appropriate. Factors associated with osteoporotic fractures were first screened by univariate logistic regression. Variables with p < 0.10 in univariate analysis, together with clinically relevant covariates such as age, sex, and BMI, were entered into a multivariate logistic regression model. Because of the limited number of fracture events, the number of covariates was restricted to avoid overfitting, and collinearity among variables was checked. Odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. MG-QOL15 total and item scores were compared between patients with and without fractures using the Mann–Whitney U test. All tests were two-sided, and p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed with standard statistical software. Of the 363 patients with MG enrolled, 247 (68%) were female and the mean age was 57 ± 16 years. Mean disease duration was 12 ± 10 years. Glucocorticoids were administered to 283 patients (78%), and the remaining 80 patients (22%) did not receive glucocorticoids. Among those treated, the mean current prednisolone dose was 8.1 ± 6.4 mg/day, and the mean duration of glucocorticoid therapy was 10.3 ± 8.5 years. Other immunosuppressants were used in 112 patients (31%), most commonly tacrolimus and cyclosporine. Thymectomy had been performed in 148 patients (41%). Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies were positive in 297 patients (82%). Osteoporotic fractures in glucocorticoid-treated patients Eighteen of the 283 patients treated with prednisolone (6%) had a history of osteoporotic fractures. Vertebral fractures were the most frequent (n = 12), followed by femoral neck fractures (n = 3) and fractures at other sites (n = 3). Among the 80 patients not receiving glucocorticoids, two (3%) had a history of osteoporotic fracture; this difference was not statistically significant. Subsequent analyses were therefore focused on glucocorticoid-treated patients, comparing those with fractures (n = 18) and those without (n = 265). Patients with fractures were older than those without (66 ± 11 vs 56 ± 16 years, p = 0.01) and were more often female (89% vs 67%, p = 0.05). Disease duration did not differ significantly between groups. The proportion of patients with thymectomy and the frequency of antibody-positive status were also similar. Quantitative assessment of individual researchers underlies decisions on hiring, promotion, grant allocation, and institutional funding. Bibliometric indicators such as total citation counts, the h-index [1], and their many variants [2,3] have become routine instruments for this purpose, in part because they are cheap to compute and appear objective. Nearly all of them, however, were conceived for a setting in which a paper can be attributed to a single author. That setting has largely disappeared. Across virtually all disciplines the mean number of authors per paper has risen steadily over several decades [4,5], and in some fields, such as high-energy physics and genomics, papers with hundreds or thousands of authors are commonplace. The consequence is that a publication or citation record no longer reveals, by itself, how much of the recognized value of a work is attributable to any particular contributor. The credit assignment problem Several strategies have been proposed to apportion credit among coauthors. The simplest is full counting, in which every author receives the entire credit of a paper. This rewards participation in large collaborations and inflates the scores of prolific coauthors. Fractional counting divides the credit equally among the n authors, giving each 1/n [6]. It conserves total credit, but it assumes that all contributions are equal, which is rarely true. Positional schemes weight credit by byline order, for instance giving more to first and last authors, with arithmetic, geometric, or harmonic decay for intermediate positions [7,8]. These depend on disciplinary conventions: in some fields authors are listed alphabetically, in others by contribution, and in others the senior author appears last. Explicit contribution statements, as now required by some journals, offer more direct information [9], but they are self-reported, unavailable for the bulk of the existing literature, and hard to compare across venues. Network-based approaches, including those that adapt PageRank-type measures to coauthorship or citation graphs [10,11], capture structural position, yet they typically measure prestige or centrality rather than the individual contribution to a particular body of work. What these methods share is that the allocation rule is fixed a priori and applied identically to every paper. The rule is not tested against, or inferred from, the data. Because an author appears on many papers, and because the authors of each paper overlap with those of others, the coauthor network contains redundant information that could in principle be used to disentangle individual contributions. A researcher who appears in works of consistently high impact regardless of collaborators plausibly contributes more than one whose presence correlates with impact only when particular collaborators are present. Exploiting this redundancy requires a model. Approach of this paper We propose a simple statistical model built on the assumption that each author possesses an unvarying “author ability,” a latent quantity that contributes additively to the success of every work on which the author appears. Under this assumption, the measured impact of a paper, here quantified by its citation count, is modeled as a linear combination of the abilities of its authors plus noise. Each paper then provides one linear equation, and the collection of papers in a coauthor network forms a system of equations from which the abilities can be estimated by regression. The coefficients are thus determined by the data rather than imposed by convention, and the weights with which authors share credit within a paper emerge from the estimation. The approach is conceptually related to rating systems that infer latent strength from outcomes of team contests, and to additive-effects models used in econometrics and in the study of productivity, where individual effects are separated from group effects using overlapping membership [12,13]. The model is deliberately parsimonious. It does not describe the mechanisms of collaboration, the dynamics of careers, or differences in citation practices between fields, and the assumption that ability is constant over time is clearly an idealization. Its purpose is to provide a transparent baseline that is computable at scale, whose assumptions are explicit, and which can be compared directly with existing indicators. Identifiability is a central issue: authors who always publish together cannot be separated, and sparsely connected parts of the network yield poorly constrained estimates. We therefore discuss the structure of the coauthor network, the conditions under which the regression is well posed, and the use of regularization where it is not. Empirical test and contributions We apply the method to a coauthor network of somewhat more than five hundred authors extracted from the CiteSeerX digital library [14], and compare the resulting ranking with that obtained from total fractional citation counts. The latter serves as a natural benchmark, since it is the simplest credit-conserving measure and is widely used. The comparison shows how far the estimated abilities depart from equal sharing, and for which authors the differences are most pronounced. The contributions of this work are the following. First, we formulate author evaluation as a linear regression problem on the coauthor network, with explicit assumptions. Second, we describe an estimation procedure and discuss its identifiability and robustness. Third, we present an empirical comparison on real bibliographic data, quantifying the agreement and the discrepancies with fractional citation counting. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the model and the estimation procedure. Section 3 describes the data and its preprocessing. Section 4 presents results and the comparison with fractional counts. Section 5 discusses limitations and possible extensions, and Section 6 concludes. Data and coauthor network construction We use records from the CiteSeerX database [1], each comprising a list of authors and a citation count for the paper. Author names were disambiguated by matching normalized surnames and initials, followed by manual inspection of ambiguous cases. Papers with a single author or with missing citation data were retained only if they contributed information to the regression described below. We then extracted a connected subnetwork of authors linked by coauthorship, yielding N = 5xx authors and M papers. Following common practice [2], citation counts were taken as a proxy for the impact of a paper, and no field normalization beyond that described below was applied. Let the bipartite incidence matrix A ∈ {0,1}^{M×N} be defined by A{pi} = 1 if author i is listed on paper p and 0 otherwise. The coauthor network is the projection A^T A, in which two authors are linked if they share at least one paper. The connectedness of this network is necessary for the identifiability of the model below, since disconnected components would permit independent rescaling of ability within each component. Model of author ability We assume that each author i possesses a fixed, time-independent ability ai ≥ 0, and that the impact yp of paper p is determined by the abilities of its authors plus noise: yp = Σi w{pi} ai + εp, where w{pi} is the weight with which author i's ability contributes to paper p, and εp is a zero-mean error term with finite variance. In the simplest specification, adopted here, the contribution of an author is independent of the author's position in the byline and of the number of coauthors, so w{pi} = A{pi}. Thus the impact of a paper is the sum of its authors' abilities. An alternative specification, w{pi} = A{pi}/np with np the number of authors, corresponds to an average-ability model; we examine it as a sensitivity check. To reduce the heavy-tailed nature of citation distributions, we model the transformed response yp = log(1 + cp), where cp is the citation count of paper p. Because older papers accumulate more citations, we also divided cp by the mean citation count of papers published in the same year before transformation, which yields an approximate age normalization. Estimation In matrix form the model is y = W a + ε, with W the M×N weight matrix. The ability vector is estimated by regularized least squares: â = argmina ‖y − W a‖² + λ‖a‖², with solution â = (WᵀW + λI)⁻¹Wᵀy. The ridge penalty λ ≥ 0 is needed because many authors have few papers, making WᵀW ill-conditioned [3]. The penalty also shrinks the estimates of authors with little evidence toward zero, which is a desirable property for ranking. The parameter λ was selected by ten-fold cross-validation, minimizing the mean squared prediction error on held-out papers. When non-negativity of ability was imposed, we solved the equivalent non-negative least squares problem using an active-set algorithm [4]; the unconstrained and constrained solutions were compared. Uncertainty in the estimates was assessed by nonparametric bootstrap, resampling papers with replacement (B = 1000) and recomputing â. From the bootstrap distribution we derived standard errors and 95% percentile intervals for each author's ability and for each author's rank. Because the ranking depends on both point estimates and their precision, we report the rank intervals alongside point ranks. Identifiability and diagnostics The rank of W determines whether abilities are separately identifiable. For an author who appears only in papers coauthored with the same fixed set of collaborators, the columns of W may be collinear, and only sums of abilities can be estimated; ridge regularization resolves this by distributing credit equally. We computed the condition number of WᵀW and the effective degrees of freedom, tr[W(WᵀW + λI)⁻¹Wᵀ], to quantify this effect. Residuals were inspected for heteroscedasticity and for dependence on the number of authors, and the coefficient of determination R² was computed on held-out data. Comparison with fractional citation counts As the benchmark, we computed for each author i the total fractional citation count Fi = Σp A{pi} cp / np, in which each paper's citations are divided equally among its authors [5]. We compared the ranking by â with that by F using Spearman's rank correlation ρ and Kendall's τ, with confidence intervals obtained from the bootstrap. To characterize disagreements, we identified authors whose rank differs by more than a fixed percentile threshold (10% of N) between methods, and examined their publication profiles, specifically the number of papers, the average team size, and the abilities of their coauthors. The regression-based approach is expected to credit authors who collaborate with strong coauthors less than the fractional count does, since the coauthors' ability explains part of the paper's impact; this hypothesis was assessed by regressing the rank difference on the mean coauthor ability. Robustness checks We repeated the analysis (i) with raw rather than log-transformed citations, (ii) with the averaged weights w{pi} = A{pi}/np, (iii) with λ varied over two orders of magnitude around the cross-validated value, and (iv) after removing the most prolific 5% of authors. Stability was measured by the rank correlation of each variant's ranking with the baseline. All computations were implemented in Python using NumPy and SciPy [6], with a fixed random seed for reproducibility. Data and implementation summary. The coauthor network extracted from CiteSeerX comprised 512 authors connected through shared publications. For each paper, the citation count was treated as the response variable, and the author-incidence vector as the predictor. The model assumes that the citation count of paper p is approximately the sum of the abilities ai of its authors, cp ≈ Σ{i∈p} ai + εp. Abilities were estimated by ordinary least squares, with a small ridge penalty (λ = 0.1) to stabilize estimates in weakly connected components of the network. All reported results use this regularized estimator unless stated otherwise. Rankings were compared against the total fractional citation count (FCC), in which each paper's citations are divided equally among its authors [1,2]. Model fit and estimated abilities. The fitted model explained a moderate share of the variance in paper citation counts (R² ≈ 0.41). Residuals were right-skewed, reflecting the heavy-tailed distribution of citations noted in earlier bibliometric studies [3]. Applying a logarithmic transform, log(1 + cp), reduced this skewness and increased R² to approximately 0.48. The estimated abilities were also heavy-tailed. A small number of authors had large positive coefficients, while most were clustered near zero. A minority of authors received negative estimates. These were mostly authors with few papers, all of which were coauthored with high-ability collaborators and cited less than the model predicted. Such negative values should be interpreted

Stroke is a leading cause of death and long-term disability worldwide, and determining its etiology is central to both acute management and secondary prevention. The Trial of Org 10172 in Acute Stroke Treatment (TOAST) classification divides ischemic stroke into large artery atherosclerosis (LAA), cardioembolism, small vessel occlusion, stroke of other determined etiology, and stroke of undetermined etiology. Different subtypes carry different recurrence risks, prognoses, and therapeutic implications. Cardioembolic stroke, most often related to atrial fibrillation, accounts for roughly 15–30% of ischemic strokes and tends to be more severe and more disabling than other subtypes. Anticoagulation is highly effective for preventing recurrence in cardioembolic stroke, whereas antiplatelet therapy, statins, and management of the stenotic vessel are the mainstays for LAA. An accurate etiologic diagnosis is therefore of direct clinical consequence. Despite advances in imaging and extensive diagnostic work-up, including vascular imaging, echocardiography, and prolonged cardiac rhythm monitoring, the cause remains undetermined in about one fourth of all ischemic strokes. Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation may escape detection for weeks or months, and patients may have multiple competing potential sources, such as concurrent atherosclerosis and a cardiac source. In these circumstances, additional noninvasive markers that suggest an embolic mechanism could provide supportive evidence for classification and help guide earlier initiation of appropriate therapy. Several imaging features have been proposed to distinguish stroke mechanisms. Diffusion-weighted imaging patterns, such as multiple lesions in separate vascular territories, bilateral or cortical-subcortical involvement, and scattered small infarcts, are suggestive of embolism, whereas border-zone infarcts suggest hemodynamic compromise from large artery stenosis. Angiographic findings such as abrupt cutoff of a vessel, the susceptibility vessel sign on gradient-echo imaging, and clot burden have also been associated with cardioembolism. However, these features are neither sensitive nor specific, and their interpretation is often subjective. Moreover, many patients show overlapping patterns, limiting their usefulness in individual cases. An alternative approach is to consider the pathophysiologic differences between the two mechanisms. In LAA, stenosis or occlusion usually develops gradually, allowing the recruitment of collateral circulation through the circle of Willis, leptomeningeal anastomoses, and other channels. Such collaterals sustain perfusion in the ischemic territory and may produce a broad region of mild hypoperfusion surrounding a smaller area of severe hypoperfusion. In contrast, cardioembolic occlusion is typically abrupt, with little time for collateral development, and results in a sharply demarcated area of severe hypoperfusion with less surrounding mild hypoperfusion. Consequently, cardioembolic stroke is expected to show larger infarcts and more severe initial deficits, a pattern that has been reported in clinical series. Collateral status is also a well-established determinant of infarct growth, response to reperfusion therapy, and functional outcome. Perfusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers a means of quantifying these hemodynamic differences. Dynamic susceptibility contrast perfusion imaging can generate maps of time to maximum of the residual curve (Tmax), which reflects delay in arrival of contrast through the tissue. Tmax thresholds are widely used to define hypoperfused tissue; for example, Tmax greater than 6 s approximates the ischemic penumbra and critically hypoperfused tissue in trials such as DEFUSE and EPITHET, and Tmax greater than 10 s has been associated with severe hypoperfusion and poor collateral status. Different Tmax delay thresholds thus represent different degrees of hemodynamic compromise, and the relation among volumes at different thresholds may reflect the adequacy of collateral supply. A large volume of mildly delayed tissue relative to severely delayed tissue would suggest well-developed collaterals, as might be expected in LAA, while a small mildly delayed volume relative to the severely delayed volume would suggest poor collaterals, as in embolic occlusion. Ratios of Tmax volumes could therefore serve as quantitative markers of the underlying mechanism, independent of absolute lesion size. Although perfusion imaging has been widely studied for patient selection for reperfusion therapies, few studies have examined whether it can differentiate stroke etiologies. Prior work has focused mainly on infarct patterns, vessel imaging, and clinical features rather than on the quantitative perfusion profile. If perfusion MRI performed during routine acute stroke evaluation could help identify cardioembolism, it would offer an immediately available tool that does not depend on prolonged monitoring and could support etiologic classification in patients whose work-up is otherwise inconclusive. The aim of this prospective study was therefore to determine whether perfusion MRI performed within 24 hours of stroke onset can differentiate cardioembolic stroke from LAA stroke. We compared clinical characteristics, initial and final infarct volumes, and Tmax volumes at multiple delay thresholds between the two groups, and we evaluated the ratios of Tmax volumes at shorter lags to the volume at an 8-s lag as potential discriminators. We further assessed their diagnostic performance using receiver operating characteristic analysis and examined whether they remained predictive of cardioembolic stroke after adjustment for initial stroke severity. This prospective observational study was conducted at a single tertiary stroke center and approved by the institutional review board. Written informed consent was obtained from all patients or their legally authorized representatives. Patient Selection We consecutively screened adult patients admitted with acute ischemic stroke who underwent multimodal MRI within 24 hours of symptom onset or last known well. Inclusion criteria were: (1) age 18 years or older; (2) acute ischemic stroke in the anterior circulation with a visible diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) lesion; (3) a stroke mechanism classified as cardioembolism or large artery atherosclerosis (LAA) according to the Trial of Org 10172 in Acute Stroke Treatment (TOAST) criteria; and (4) perfusion MRI of sufficient quality for postprocessing. Exclusion criteria were: stroke of other determined or undetermined etiology (small vessel occlusion, other determined cause, or undetermined cause including multiple competing mechanisms); posterior circulation stroke; contraindications to MRI or gadolinium contrast; severe renal impairment; and prior disability with a modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score of 3 or higher. Clinical Data and Stroke Classification Demographic data, vascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, smoking, atrial fibrillation, coronary disease, prior stroke), laboratory results, and treatments, including intravenous thrombolysis and endovascular therapy, were recorded. Initial stroke severity was assessed on admission with the National Institute of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) by certified neurologists. All patients underwent a standardized etiologic work-up, including brain and vascular imaging (magnetic resonance angiography, computed tomography angiography, or carotid duplex ultrasonography), 12-lead electrocardiography, continuous telemetry monitoring for at least 48 hours, transthoracic echocardiography and, when indicated, transesophageal echocardiography or prolonged rhythm monitoring. Stroke subtype was determined by two stroke neurologists blinded to the perfusion results, according to TOAST criteria. Cardioembolic stroke required a major-risk cardiac source (e.g., atrial fibrillation, recent myocardial infarction, mechanical valve, left ventricular thrombus, or dilated cardiomyopathy). LAA stroke required ipsilateral stenosis of 50% or more, or occlusion of a relevant large artery, attributed to atherosclerosis, in the absence of a major cardioembolic source. Disagreements were resolved by consensus. MRI Acquisition Imaging was performed on a 3.0-T scanner with a standard head coil. The protocol included DWI (b = 0 and 1000 s/mm²) with apparent diffusion coefficient maps, fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), gradient-echo or susceptibility-weighted imaging, time-of-flight MR angiography, and dynamic susceptibility contrast perfusion-weighted imaging (PWI). For PWI, a gadolinium-based contrast agent (0.1 mmol/kg) was injected at 4 mL/s through an antecubital vein, followed by a 20-mL saline flush, with gradient-echo echo-planar images acquired over 40–60 dynamic time points covering the whole brain. A follow-up MRI (DWI and FLAIR) was obtained at 5–7 days after admission to determine final infarct volume. Image Postprocessing and Analysis Perfusion data were processed with automated software (RAPID) using singular value decomposition with delay-insensitive deconvolution. Maps of time to maximum of the residual curve (Tmax) were generated. Volumes of tissue with Tmax delays longer than 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 8 s were calculated automatically. Initial infarct volume was measured on the admission DWI as the region of restricted diffusion, and final infarct volume was measured on the follow-up DWI or FLAIR image, using semiautomated planimetric methods by an investigator blinded to clinical data. Volumes were obtained by multiplying lesion areas by slice thickness plus gap. To estimate the degree of collateral compensation, we calculated ratios of the Tmax volume at lower thresholds to the Tmax > 8 s volume (e.g., Tmax > 2 s/Tmax > 8 s, Tmax > 3 s/Tmax > 8 s, Tmax > 4 s/Tmax > 8 s, and Tmax > 5 s/Tmax > 8 s). A higher ratio indicates a large region of mild hypoperfusion relative to severe hypoperfusion, reflecting a more favorable collateral supply, whereas a lower ratio indicates a steeper perfusion gradient and poorer collaterals. Patients without any Tmax > 8 s volume were handled by [excluding the ratio calculation for that patient/assigning the ratio as undefined]. Outcome Measures The primary outcome was the ability of Tmax volume ratios to discriminate cardioembolic stroke from LAA stroke. Secondary measures included comparisons of initial NIHSS score, initial infarct volume, and final infarct volume between groups. Statistical Analysis Continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation or median (interquartile range), as appropriate, and categorical variables as numbers (percentages). Groups were compared with the Student t test or Mann–Whitney U test for continuous variables and the chi-square or Fisher exact test for categorical variables. Normality was assessed with the Shapiro–Wilk test. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to assess the discriminative performance of each Tmax volume ratio for cardioembolic stroke, with area under the curve (AUC) values and 95% confidence intervals computed. Optimal cutoff values were selected by maximizing the Youden index, and sensitivity and specificity were calculated at these thresholds. The dichotomized ratios were then entered into logistic regression models adjusted for initial NIHSS score, given the between-group difference in stroke severity, to obtain adjusted odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Because of the limited sample size, the number of covariates was restricted to avoid overfitting. Interrater reliability of infarct volume measurements was evaluated in a subset using intraclass correlation coefficients. All tests were two-tailed, and a p value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed with SPSS (IBM) and MedCalc statistical software. A total of 39 patients were included in the analysis: 17 with cardioembolic (CE) stroke and 22 with large artery atherosclerosis (LAA) stroke. All patients underwent perfusion MRI within 24 hours of symptom onset. Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics are summarized in Table 1. Age and sex did not differ significantly between the two groups. Atrial fibrillation was, as expected, more frequent in the CE group, whereas hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and dyslipidemia were more common, though not significantly so, in the LAA group. The interval from stroke onset to MRI was similar in both groups (CE: median 8.5 hours; LAA: median 9.0 hours; p=0.74). Clinical severity and infarct volumes Patients with CE stroke had significantly higher initial National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) scores than those with LAA stroke (median 14 vs. 5; p<0.001). Initial infarct volume on diffusion-weighted imaging was also larger in the CE group (median 22.4 mL vs. 4.1 mL; p=0.002), as was final infarct volume on follow-up imaging (median 58.7 mL vs. 9.3 mL; p=0.001). The volume of tissue with perfusion abnormality at all Tmax thresholds was larger in the CE group than in the LAA group. The differences were most pronounced for the more severe delay thresholds (Tmax >6 s and >8 s), which were roughly threefold to fivefold larger in CE patients (Table 2). Thus, CE strokes were characterized by more severe clinical presentation and larger ischemic lesions at both the acute and final stages.
