Sign languages are the primary means of communication for millions of deaf and hard-of-hearing people worldwide. Yet most hearing individuals do not know any sign language, and the scarcity of qualified interpreters creates persistent barriers in healthcare, education, employment, and everyday interaction [1]. Automatic sign language recognition (SLR) has therefore attracted sustained interest as a way to bridge this communication gap. A reliable system that translates signed gestures into text or speech could make services more accessible and allow deaf and hearing individuals to interact without a human intermediary. Research on SLR has followed two broad paths. Vision-based approaches use cameras to capture a signer and rely on image and video analysis to extract hand shape, motion, and facial cues [2, 3]. These methods are unobtrusive, but they are sensitive to lighting, background clutter, occlusion, and camera placement, and they often require substantial computation. Sensor-based approaches instead measure the signer's movements directly using instrumented gloves, inertial measurement units, or electromyography (EMG) devices [4, 5]. Commercial wearables such as the Myo armband, which combines EMG sensors with an inertial measurement unit, have made such data collection inexpensive and practical outside the laboratory. These devices produce multivariate time series describing hand position, hand orientation, and finger configuration, which are well suited to computational analysis. A sign can be viewed as a combination of gestures that unfold over time. Both the configuration of the hand at a given moment and the order and timing of configuration changes determine the meaning of a sign. Two signs may pass through similar hand postures yet differ in the trajectory or sequence by which they do so. Recognition is therefore naturally a temporal classification problem: given a variable-length sequence of sensor readings, assign it to one of a fixed set of sign classes. This setting introduces several challenges. Sequences of the same sign vary in duration and speed, both between signers and across repetitions by the same signer. Sensor noise, calibration differences, and signer-specific styles add further variability. Finally, the number of classes in a realistic vocabulary is large, while the number of labeled examples per class is typically small. In this work, we study sign recognition on a dataset collected by a group at the University of South Wales, which we refer to as the Australian Sign Language (Auslan) dataset [6]. It contains recordings of 95 distinct signs, each represented by a stream of parameters including hand position, hand rotation, and finger bend measured over time. The data were gathered from signers using instrumented devices and are available at two quality levels. The higher-quality recordings come from more precise equipment and exhibit lower noise, whereas the lower-quality recordings come from cheaper hardware that is closer to what consumer devices provide. This difference allows us to study how recognition methods degrade as data quality decreases, a question of direct practical importance for deployment on commodity sensors. Our goal is, for each input stream representing a sign, to predict the sign class to which the stream belongs. We begin with simple baselines: support vector machines (SVMs) [7] and logistic regression applied to fixed-length feature representations of the sequences. Such baselines are inexpensive to train, are easy to interpret, and establish a reference point against which more complex models can be judged. We find that they perform reasonably well on the high-quality data, suggesting that, when measurements are clean, summary statistics of a sequence may capture much of the information needed to discriminate between signs. On the lower-quality data, however, these models perform considerably worse. Noise obscures the summary features, and discarding temporal structure removes information that could help disambiguate similar signs. This observation motivates a more sophisticated treatment of time. We explore two families of temporal classification methods. The first is recurrent neural networks, in particular long short-term memory (LSTM) architectures [8]. LSTMs maintain an internal memory that can accumulate evidence across a sequence and mitigate the vanishing gradient problem of standard recurrent networks, and they have achieved strong results in speech recognition, handwriting recognition, and gesture classification [9, 10]. They can process sequences of varying length and learn temporal dependencies directly from raw measurements, without hand-designed features. The second family is sequential pattern mining [11], which discovers frequently occurring subsequences of discretized sensor states that characterize each class. Pattern-based methods offer a complementary, more interpretable view, because the mined patterns can be inspected as explicit descriptions of what distinguishes one sign from another, and they may be more robust to noise and to variations in timing. The contributions of this paper are as follows. First, we provide a systematic comparison of baseline classifiers and temporal models on a 95-class sign recognition task. Second, we examine how performance varies between high- and low-quality data, identifying the conditions under which simple models suffice and those under which temporal modeling becomes necessary. Third, we adapt LSTM and sequential pattern mining approaches to this problem and analyze their strengths and weaknesses, including their sensitivity to hyperparameters, sequence length, and the amount of training data. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on sign language recognition and temporal classification. Section 3 describes the dataset and preprocessing. Section 4 presents the models, Section 5 reports experimental results, and Section 6 concludes with a discussion of limitations and directions for future work. We used the Australian Sign Language (Auslan) dataset collected at the University of New South Wales, which contains recordings of 95 distinct signs [1]. Each sample is a multivariate time series recorded from instrumented gloves and position trackers. Every frame contains 22 continuous features: the x, y, and z position of each hand, the roll, pitch, and yaw of each hand, and the bend of four fingers on each hand, among others. Samples vary in length, with sequences ranging from roughly 45 to 140 frames. The dataset includes recordings from two signer groups: one using high-quality Flock of Birds trackers with Cyberglove-style sensors, and another using lower-cost Fifth Dimension Technologies gloves with a noisier signal. We treated these as "high quality" and "low quality" subsets and evaluated them separately to examine how model complexity interacts with data quality. Preprocessing Each feature was standardized to zero mean and unit variance using statistics computed from the training set only. For the baseline models, which require fixed-length inputs, we resampled each sequence to 50 time steps using linear interpolation and flattened the result into a single vector of 1,100 dimensions. We also computed a compact summary representation consisting of the mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, and final-minus-initial value of every channel. For the recurrent models, variable-length sequences were zero-padded to the maximum length within a batch and masked so that padded frames did not contribute to the loss. We held out 20% of samples as a test set, stratified by sign class and signer where possible, and used 5-fold cross-validation on the remaining data for hyperparameter selection. Baseline Models We first implemented multiclass logistic regression with L2 regularization and a soft-margin support vector machine (SVM) [2]. For logistic regression we used a softmax formulation optimized with L-BFGS. For the SVM we compared linear and radial basis function (RBF) kernels, using a one-versus-one scheme for multiclass prediction. The regularization strength C and the RBF bandwidth γ were selected by grid search over logarithmically spaced values from 10^-3 to 10^3. Both baselines were trained on the resampled-and-flattened representation and on the summary-statistic representation, allowing us to test how much temporal structure is retained by each. Long Short-Term Memory Networks To model temporal dependencies directly, we trained long short-term memory (LSTM) networks [3]. The input at each time step is the 22-dimensional feature vector. The architecture consists of one or two stacked LSTM layers with hidden sizes of 64 to 256 units, followed by dropout [4] and a fully connected softmax layer over the 95 classes. We compared two ways of producing a sequence-level prediction: using the hidden state at the final unmasked time step, and averaging hidden states across all time steps. We additionally evaluated bidirectional LSTMs [5], since a sign's identity may be disambiguated by both preceding and following movements. Networks were trained with the cross-entropy loss using the Adam optimizer [6], with an initial learning rate of 10^-3, a batch size of 32, and gradient clipping at a norm of 5 to mitigate exploding gradients. Early stopping on a validation split (10% of training data) with a patience of 15 epochs determined the stopping point. Because the low-quality data are noisy, we applied data augmentation during training, including additive Gaussian noise, random temporal scaling of up to ±15%, and small random offsets to the position channels. Hyperparameters (number of layers, hidden size, dropout rate between 0.2 and 0.6, and weight decay) were tuned using random search over 30 configurations. Sequential Pattern Mining As an alternative that explicitly represents each sign as a combination of gestures across time, we used a sequential pattern mining pipeline. First, continuous frames were discretized into symbols. We clustered all training frames with k-means (k in {20, 50, 100}) and replaced each frame with its cluster index, then collapsed consecutive repeats to obtain a compact symbol sequence. Second, we mined frequent subsequences from each class using a PrefixSpan-style algorithm [7], with a minimum support threshold set as a fraction of the class size (0.2 to 0.6) and a maximum pattern length of 6. Third, we selected discriminative patterns by ranking them according to their confidence for a given class and retaining the top patterns per class, removing those that were highly frequent across many classes. Each sample was then represented as a binary vector indicating which selected patterns occur as (not necessarily contiguous) subsequences of its symbol sequence. This representation was used to train a linear SVM and a random forest classifier [8]. We also evaluated a simple rule-based classifier that assigns the class whose patterns best match the sample, weighted by pattern confidence. Evaluation The primary metric was classification accuracy on the held-out test set. Because the dataset has 95 classes, we also report top-5 accuracy and macro-averaged F1 score. For every model, results were averaged over five random seeds or fold assignments, and we report means with standard deviations. Differences between models were assessed using paired comparisons over folds with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test at a significance level of 0.05. To understand failure modes, we inspected confusion matrices and identified sign pairs that were most frequently confused. We additionally measured the effect of training set size by training each model on 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% of the available training data. Implementation Baseline and pattern-mining classifiers were implemented using scikit-learn [9], and the LSTM models were implemented in TensorFlow [10]. Online convex optimization has become a central framework for sequential decision making, with applications ranging from data center capacity provisioning and energy generation scheduling to video streaming and portfolio management. In the standard formulation, a decision maker chooses an action at each time step after observing a convex cost function, and performance is measured against either the best fixed action in hindsight (regret) or the optimal dynamic sequence of actions (competitive ratio). A rich literature has produced algorithms with strong guarantees in these settings, yet most of it treats the future as entirely unknown, or at best as adversarial. In practice, this is overly pessimistic. Many systems have access to predictions of future inputs, such as workload forecasts in data centers, demand and price forecasts in energy markets, or weather forecasts in control applications. Despite the obvious value of such information, how to exploit predictions in online algorithms, and what guarantees can be provided, remains under-explored. This paper studies online convex optimization problems in which noisy predictions of future cost functions are available. We focus on problems with switching costs, where the cost of an action depends on the change from the previous action as well as on the current hitting cost. This structure, often called smoothed online convex optimization, captures many realistic problems in which changing the decision is expensive, for example turning servers on and off or ramping generators up and down. It also makes the use of predictions nontrivial: because current decisions affect future costs through the switching term, even a perfect forecast over a short window does not make the problem trivial, and the best way to use a limited window is unclear. Our first contribution is a general stochastic model of prediction errors. Existing work typically falls into two camps. The learning community often assumes adversarial inputs, possibly with a bounded lookahead window, while the stochastic control community often assumes specific, frequently independent, noise models. Neither captures key features of real forecasts. We propose a model in which the error in a prediction of a future cost is a weighted sum of noise terms that arrive over time. The model allows arbitrary correlation among prediction errors at different time horizons and captures the fact that predictions improve as the time of the event approaches. It generalizes prior models, including i.i.d. errors and the error structure arising from standard filtering and time series forecasts, and it is parameterized by a correlation function that governs how errors accumulate across the prediction horizon. Our second contribution is a pair of impossibility results in adversarial settings. We show that for algorithms that use a finite prediction window, achieving sublinear regret and a constant competitive ratio is not possible when predictions can be arbitrary. More precisely, we prove that attaining both sublinear regret and constant competitive ratio requires a prediction window that grows unboundedly with the problem horizon. This shows that the benefit of predictions cannot be captured by worst-case analysis with bounded windows, and it motivates the stochastic error model above. Our third contribution shows that the situation changes qualitatively under stochastic prediction errors. We analyze Averaging Fixed Horizon Control (AFHC), an algorithm that averages the decisions of several fixed horizon control policies whose planning phases are offset from one another. Fixed horizon control, which solves a finite-horizon problem using the available predictions and commits to the resulting actions, performs poorly at the boundaries of each planning period, where the lack of foresight about subsequent switching costs hurts. Averaging across staggered copies spreads this boundary penalty over time, and convexity ensures the averaged action is no worse than the average of the costs. We prove that, under our error model, AFHC simultaneously achieves sublinear expected regret and a constant expected competitive ratio using only a constant-sized prediction window. The required window depends on the correlation structure of the errors: the faster the correlation decays across the horizon, the smaller the window needed, and the resulting bounds make explicit how the quality of predictions translates into algorithmic performance. This stands in sharp contrast with the adversarial setting, where an unbounded window is unavoidable. Our final contribution concerns variability. Guarantees in expectation alone may be unsatisfying for systems that care about individual runs. We show that the cost of AFHC is tightly concentrated around its mean, with deviation probabilities that decay rapidly as the horizon grows. Thus the expected-case analysis is representative of the actual performance one would observe in a single execution rather than a statistical artifact. Taken together, these results give a more complete picture of the value of predictions in online optimization. They show that the worst-case barrier is a consequence of adversarial modeling rather than of the problem itself, and that a simple, practical algorithm can exploit modest amounts of imperfect forecast information to obtain strong guarantees. The analysis also gives practical guidance on how much lookahead is worth acquiring, since the bounds quantify the diminishing returns of longer prediction windows under a given error correlation structure. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We first formalize the problem and the prediction error model, and then present the lower bounds for adversarial settings. Next we describe the algorithms considered, including fixed horizon control and AFHC, and state our main results on expected regret, competitive ratio, and concentration. We conclude with a discussion of related work and directions for future research. We study online convex optimization with switching costs in which, at each time t, the decision maker chooses xt ∈ X ⊆ ℝ^n after observing the cost function ft (revealed only at time t) and pays ft(xt) + β‖xt − x{t−1}‖, where β > 0 weights the switching cost. The offline benchmark over horizon T is OPT = min{x} Σ{t=1}^T [ft(xt) + β‖xt − x{t−1}‖], with x0 fixed. We assume the ft are convex, and where required, Lipschitz or strongly convex. Online algorithms also have access to noisy predictions of future inputs within a window of w steps. Problem and Prediction Model We parametrize ft(x) = f(x; yt), where yt is an exogenous input (e.g., workload, price, or target trajectory) that is unknown until time t. At time τ the algorithm holds predictions y{t|τ} of yt for t > τ, with y{t|t} = yt. The prediction error is e{t|τ} = yt − y{t|τ}. We model the error as e{t|τ} = Σ{s=τ+1}^{t} R(t−s) e(s), where e(s) are zero-mean, uncorrelated innovations with covariance I, and R(·) is a deterministic matrix filter. Innovation e(s) is the new information arriving at time s, so predictions of yt improve as τ approaches t. The covariance of the error over a lookahead of k = t − τ steps is therefore Σ{s=0}^{k−1} R(s)R(s)ᵀ, which is nondecreasing in k. Define the cumulative error variance f(k) = trace(Σ{s=0}^{k−1} R(s)R(s)ᵀ). This model captures i.i.d. errors (R(s)=0 for s>0 after the first lag), and correlated errors such as those from ARMA or Wiener-type filters, and covers the error structures used in the learning and stochastic control literatures. We assume that f(k) is bounded for finite k, and that sub-Gaussian innovations are used when deriving concentration results. Performance Metrics For an algorithm ALG, we consider two metrics. Regret is the cost difference between ALG and the best fixed static decision sequence in hindsight, Regret(ALG) = E[cost(ALG)] − E[cost(STA)], and is sublinear if it is o(T). The competitive ratio is CR(ALG) = sup over inputs of E[cost(ALG)]/E[OPT]. We seek algorithms achieving both sublinear regret and constant competitive ratio, and we also study the distribution of cost(ALG) around its mean. Lower Bounds in the Adversarial Setting To show that a bounded window is insufficient in adversarial settings, we construct input sequences for which any deterministic online algorithm with window w incurs either linear regret or unbounded competitive ratio. The construction uses cost functions with oscillating minimizers, whose period exceeds w, so that the algorithm cannot distinguish a persistent change from a transient one inside its window. We choose the oscillation amplitude relative to β such that following the minimizers costs too much in switching, while staying put costs too much in hitting cost. Balancing these cases yields a bound growing with T/w, and thus requires w = Ω(T) to obtain both guarantees. Algorithms Fixed Horizon Control (FHC) with window w and offset ω ∈ {1,…,w}: at times t ≡ ω (mod w), the algorithm solves min{x{t},…,x{t+w−1}} Σ{s=t}^{t+w−1} [f(xs; y{s|t−1}) + β‖xs − x{s−1}‖] using the predictions available at t−1 and commits to the entire block. Because each block is planned from predictions made at the beginning of the block, errors accumulate over up to w steps. Let FHC^{(ω)} denote the resulting algorithm for offset ω. Averaging Fixed Horizon Control (AFHC) runs the w versions FHC^{(1)},…,FHC^{(w)} and plays the average xt = (1/w) Σ{ω} xt^{(ω)}. By convexity of ft and the norm, cost(AFHC) ≤ (1/w) Σω cost(FHC^{(ω)}). Averaging therefore preserves the guarantees of a typical FHC instance while smoothing the decisions and reducing the cost incurred at the block boundaries. Analysis Approach We decompose the expected cost of FHC^{(ω)} relative to the offline optimum. For each block, we compare the plan computed from predictions to the plan computed from true inputs, and bound the difference using the Lipschitz property of f in y and of the optimizer in the inputs. The expected excess cost per block is bounded by a function of the error variance at lookahead k, summed over k = 1,…,w, giving a per-step overhead of order (1/w)Σ{k=1}^{w} √f(k) or similar, plus the boundary switching cost of order β/w per step. Averaging over offsets bounds the AFHC cost by OPT plus these terms. For regret, we compare each block’s plan to the static optimum and use the fact that the total overhead grows as O(T·g(w)), where g(w) decreases when the error variance saturates. When errors decay sufficiently quickly with proximity (f(k) bounded in k), a constant w yields a overhead that is sublinear relative to the benchmark, and a constant competitive ratio follows by dividing by OPT, which we show is Ω(T) under nondegeneracy assumptions. Concentration To characterize the distribution of cost(AFHC), we view cost(AFHC) as a function of the independent innovations {e(s)}. We show that this function is Lipschitz in the innovations with a constant determined by R(·) and the cost Lipschitz constants, and apply a concentration inequality for Lipschitz functions of sub-Gaussian vectors (a bounded-differences/Azuma-type argument). This yields tail bounds of the form P(|cost − E cost| > ε) ≤ 2exp(−ε²/(2σ²T)), so the deviation is O(√T) with high probability, which is negligible relative to the linear mean cost. We study the online convex optimization problem in which, at each time t, the algorithm chooses xt to minimize a sum of hitting costs ct(xt) and switching costs β‖xt − x{t−1}‖, with access to noisy predictions of future cost functions within a window of length w. Performance is measured by regret against the best static offline solution and by the competitive ratio against the dynamic offline optimum. Our results fall into three groups: lower bounds for adversarial prediction models, guarantees for AFHC under stochastic prediction errors, and concentration of AFHC's cost. Adversarial lower bounds. We first ask whether a finite prediction window suffices when prediction errors are arbitrary. Our first result shows it does not. For any online algorithm that uses a prediction window of fixed size w, independent of the horizon T, there exist problem instances with bounded prediction errors for which regret grows linearly in T. Likewise, the competitive ratio of any such algorithm is bounded below by a constant strictly greater than one that depends on w and the switching cost, and it cannot be made to approach a fixed constant by a constant-sized window. The constructions exploit the fact that, without structure on the errors, an adversary can place a cost change just beyond the window, forcing the algorithm to pay either switching cost or hitting cost repeatedly in a way the offline optimum avoids. HbA1c is the principal biomarker for monitoring glycaemic control in diabetes and is used both to guide treatment and to estimate the risk of long-term complications. Landmark trials in type 1 and type 2 diabetes have shown that lowering mean glycaemia reduces the incidence of microvascular disease, and, with longer follow-up, possibly macrovascular disease [1–3]. However, HbA1c is not a perfect proxy for mean glucose exposure. Its relationship with mean blood glucose varies considerably between individuals, so that the same HbA1c may correspond to different average glucose concentrations in different people [4, 5]. Inter-individual variation in the glucose–HbA1c relationship Several biological mechanisms may explain this variation. These include differences in erythrocyte lifespan, in glucose transport across the erythrocyte membrane, in intracellular glucose concentrations, and in the rate of non-enzymatic glycation of haemoglobin, as well as genetic influences [6–8]. Because of these factors, some individuals consistently have higher or lower HbA1c than expected from their measured glycaemia. This phenomenon, first described as the "glycation gap" and later formalised as the haemoglobin glycation index (HGI), is quantified as the difference between observed HbA1c and the HbA1c predicted from glucose by linear regression in a reference population [9, 10]. Individuals can then be classified as high, moderate or low glycators. HGI is reproducible within individuals over time and has been shown to be partly heritable, supporting the notion that it reflects a relatively stable individual trait [10, 11]. HGI and clinical outcomes Whether HGI carries clinical information beyond HbA1c is uncertain. Observational and post hoc analyses have linked a higher HGI to a greater risk of microvascular complications, particularly nephropathy and retinopathy, in type 1 diabetes in the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial [12, 13]. In type 2 diabetes, higher HGI has been associated with retinopathy, nephropathy, cardiovascular disease and mortality in several cohorts [14–16]. One interpretation is that HbA1c overestimates mean glycaemia in high glycators, so that a given HbA1c target may lead to overtreatment in such individuals. Alternatively, a high HGI may reflect enhanced tissue glycation, with greater formation of advanced glycation end products and thus an intrinsic susceptibility to vascular damage independent of ambient glucose [17]. Findings have not been consistent. In the Action to Control Cardiovascular Risk in Diabetes (ACCORD) trial, a post hoc analysis suggested that participants with a low HGI had more hypoglycaemia and higher mortality with intensive therapy, while those with a high HGI appeared to benefit [18]. Other studies have found no association between HGI and outcomes after adjustment for HbA1c, or have found that the association disappeared with differing methods of calculating HGI [19, 20]. Methodological heterogeneity is considerable: HGI has been derived using fasting glucose, mean glucose from self-monitoring or continuous monitoring, or fructosamine, and the reference regression equation has been drawn from different populations. Moreover, because HGI is by construction correlated with HbA1c, it is difficult to determine whether it adds independent prognostic information. Few analyses have directly compared the predictive performance of HGI and HbA1c using identical covariate adjustment. HGI as a modifier of treatment effect A particularly attractive potential use of HGI is to identify individuals who are more or less likely to benefit from, or be harmed by, intensive glucose lowering. Intensive strategies targeting near-normal HbA1c have produced inconsistent results on cardiovascular events and mortality. ACCORD was stopped early because of increased mortality in the intensive arm [21], whereas the Action in Diabetes and Vascular Disease: Preterax and Diamicron Modified Release Controlled Evaluation (ADVANCE) trial and the Veterans Affairs Diabetes Trial showed no increase in mortality and no significant reduction in major cardiovascular events [22, 23]. ADVANCE did show a reduction in microvascular outcomes, mainly nephropathy, with intensive treatment [22]. Heterogeneity of treatment effect is plausible, and a simple biomarker able to identify subgroups with differing risk–benefit balance would be clinically valuable. Differences in the glucose–HbA1c relationship could cause some individuals to be treated to a lower true glycaemic exposure than intended, with consequent hypoglycaemia, a recognised mediator of adverse outcomes in intensive therapy [24, 25]. Whether HGI modifies the effect of intensive treatment has not been tested in a trial population other than ACCORD. Aims of the present study ADVANCE, with its large sample size, standardised measurement of HbA1c and fasting plasma glucose (FPG), randomisation to intensive or standard glucose control, and adjudicated macrovascular, microvascular and mortality outcomes, provides a suitable setting to address these questions. We therefore used baseline data from ADVANCE participants to calculate HGI from HbA1c and FPG. Our aims were: first, to determine whether HGI modifies the effect of intensive glucose control on mortality, cardiovascular and microvascular outcomes, and severe hypoglycaemia; second, to assess the association between HGI, analysed as categorical and continuous variables, and diabetes-related complications irrespective of treatment allocation; and third, to compare directly the predictive performance of HGI with that of HbA1c under identical adjustment. In doing so, we sought to establish whether HGI has any role in clinical practice in type 2 diabetes beyond that of HbA1c. Study population and design We used data from the Action in Diabetes and Vascular Disease: Preterax and Diamicron Modified Release Controlled Evaluation (ADVANCE) trial, whose design and principal results have been published [1, 2]. In brief, ADVANCE was a randomised factorial trial that enrolled 11,140 individuals with type 2 diabetes aged 55 years or older. Participants had a history of major macrovascular or microvascular disease, or at least one other vascular risk factor. They were recruited from 215 centres in 20 countries. Participants were randomised to a fixed combination of perindopril and indapamide or matching placebo, and to an intensive or standard glucose-control strategy. Intensive control was based on gliclazide modified release, with a target HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or lower. Standard control followed local guidelines. The trial was approved by ethics committees at all participating centres, and all participants gave written informed consent. Participants were followed for a median of 5 years. For the present analysis we included those with baseline HbA1c and fasting plasma glucose (FPG) measurements (n = 11,083). Laboratory measurements and calculation of HGI HbA1c and FPG were measured at baseline in the trial's central laboratory using standardised methods [2]. The haemoglobin glycation index (HGI) was calculated as the difference between observed HbA1c and the HbA1c predicted from FPG [3, 4]. The prediction came from a simple linear regression of HbA1c on FPG in the whole cohort: predicted HbA1c = a + b × FPG. HGI = observed HbA1c − predicted HbA1c. Participants were categorised into tertiles of HGI (low, medium, high) and, for comparison, tertiles of HbA1c. We also analysed HGI as a continuous variable, expressed per SD increase, to allow direct comparison of effect sizes with HbA1c per SD. Outcomes Outcomes were those prespecified in ADVANCE and adjudicated by an independent committee blinded to treatment allocation [2]. We examined all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, major macrovascular events (a composite of non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke or cardiovascular death), major microvascular events (a composite of new or worsening nephropathy or retinopathy), and their components. We also examined severe hypoglycaemia, defined as an episode requiring third-party assistance or medical assistance, as a potential adverse effect of intensive treatment. Participants were followed from randomisation until the first event of interest, death, or the end of follow-up. Statistical analysis Baseline characteristics were summarised by HGI tertile as mean (SD), median (interquartile range) or number (percentage), as appropriate, and compared using ANOVA, Kruskal–Wallis or χ² tests. Correlations between HGI, HbA1c and FPG were assessed with Pearson or Spearman coefficients. Treatment effect by HGI category. Cox proportional hazards models estimated the effect of intensive versus standard glucose control on each outcome within each HGI tertile, with HRs and 95% CIs. Models were stratified by region and adjusted for the randomised blood-pressure-lowering allocation. Heterogeneity of treatment effect across tertiles was assessed with a formal treatment-by-HGI interaction term, both for categorised and for continuous HGI. The same analyses were repeated using HbA1c tertiles to determine whether any differential effect was specific to HGI. Association between HGI and outcomes. We estimated the association of HGI, categorised and per SD, with each outcome using Cox models. Model 1 was adjusted for age, sex, and randomised treatment allocations. Model 2 additionally included duration of diabetes, BMI, systolic blood pressure, total and HDL-cholesterol, estimated GFR, urinary albumin/creatinine ratio, smoking status, history of macrovascular and microvascular disease, and use of glucose-lowering, lipid-lowering and antihypertensive medication at baseline. The proportional hazards assumption was checked using Schoenfeld residuals and log-minus-log plots. Linearity of the continuous associations was examined with restricted cubic splines. Analyses were conducted both overall and stratified by randomised glucose-control arm, and interaction between HGI and treatment arm was tested. Comparison of prediction by HGI and HbA1c. To compare the predictive value of HGI and HbA1c, we fitted Cox models that were identical in all covariates except for the exposure (HGI or HbA1c, each per SD) and compared HRs, Harrell's C-statistic, and Akaike information criterion. Differences in discrimination were assessed using bootstrapped confidence intervals for the difference in C-statistics. We also evaluated the incremental value of adding HGI to a model containing HbA1c, using likelihood-ratio tests, continuous net reclassification improvement and integrated discrimination improvement for five-year risk [5]. Because HGI is derived from HbA1c and FPG, we additionally fitted a model including both HbA1c and FPG to assess whether HGI offered information beyond its constituents. Sensitivity analyses. We repeated the analyses with HGI calculated separately within each randomised arm, and with exclusion of events in the first year of follow-up to limit reverse causation. We also repeated them with additional adjustment for baseline haemoglobin, as a marker of red-cell turnover that might influence glycation. All tests were two-sided, with p < 0.05 considered statistically significant. Given the exploratory nature of the subgroup and interaction analyses, no formal adjustment for multiple testing was made, and the findings are interpreted accordingly. Analyses were performed using SAS (version 9.4) and R (version 3.3). Study population and HGI distribution Of the 11,140 ADVANCE participants, 11,083 (99.5%) had baseline HbA1c and FPG measurements and were included. Linear regression of HbA1c on FPG gave the following equation: HbA1c (%) = 4.97 + 0.31 × FPG (mmol/l) (R² = 0.28). HGI was calculated for each participant as the observed minus the predicted HbA1c. By construction, the mean HGI was zero (SD 1.0 percentage points). Participants were classified into tertiles of HGI (low, moderate, high). Baseline characteristics by tertile are shown in Table 1. Compared with those in the low tertile, participants with high HGI were slightly younger, were more often women, and had a higher BMI, a longer diabetes duration, and higher HbA1c and lower FPG. They also had lower eGFR and a higher prevalence of insulin and metformin use. Participants in the high tertile were less often of Asian ethnicity. By design, HGI was uncorrelated with FPG (r = 0.00) and moderately correlated with HbA1c (r = 0.85). Allocation to intensive or standard glucose control was balanced across HGI tertiles (p = 0.71). Treatment effect of intensive glucose control by HGI category Over a median follow-up of 5.0 years, 1,031 participants died, 1,147 had a major macrovascular event and 1,319 had a major microvascular event. The effect of intensive treatment on the primary outcomes differed by HGI category for mortality (Table 2, Fig. 1). In the high HGI tertile, intensive glucose control reduced all-cause mortality (HR 0.74 [95% CI 0.61, 0.91]; p = 0.003), whereas no effect was seen in the moderate (HR 1.01 [0.82, 1.24]) or low (HR 1.05 [0.85, 1.30]) tertiles. The interaction between treatment and HGI tertile was significant (p for interaction = 0.02). A similar pattern, although less pronounced, was observed for cardiovascular death (HR 0.71 [0.54, 0.93] in the high tertile). For major macrovascular and microvascular events, the effects of intensive treatment did not differ significantly across HGI tertiles (p for interaction = 0.45 and 0.62, respectively). The medoid of a set of n points is the point that minimizes the sum of distances to all other points in the set. It is a natural notion of the "center" of a dataset and is closely related to the mean and the median. Unlike the mean, the medoid is always an element of the dataset, and it is defined for any distance function, not only the Euclidean one. This makes it useful when averaging is meaningless or undefined, such as with strings, graphs, or single-cell RNA-seq profiles under ℓ1 distance. The medoid is also more robust to outliers than the mean. It is the central subroutine in k-medoids clustering, and it appears in applications ranging from genomics to image summarization and social network analysis. Computing the medoid exactly requires evaluating all n(n−1)/2 pairwise distances, which costs O(n²) distance computations. For modern datasets with n in the hundreds of thousands or millions, this is prohibitive. This has motivated a long line of work on faster exact and approximate algorithms. Some methods use the triangle inequality to prune candidates (e.g., TOPRANK, trimed). These work well in low dimensions but degrade as the dimension grows. Other methods embed or sample to estimate the sums of distances. A recent line of work casts medoid identification as a multi-armed bandit problem. Each point is an "arm," and its unknown "mean reward" is its average distance to all other points. Pulling an arm corresponds to sampling a random reference point and computing its distance to the arm's point, which gives an unbiased estimate of that average distance. Finding the medoid is then a best-arm identification problem, which can be addressed with adaptive algorithms such as successive elimination or UCB-type methods. The RAND algorithm of Eppstein and Wang, and the Meddit algorithm of Bagaria et al., follow this idea. Meddit in particular reduces the number of distance computations from O(n²) to roughly O(n log n) under mild assumptions on the distribution of the average distances. This gives large practical savings over exact computation. However, a direct conversion to a standard bandit problem ignores structure specific to the computation. In a standard bandit, the rewards of different arms are independent: pulling arm i yields a sample that is unrelated to the sample obtained from arm j. In the medoid problem we have far more freedom. We control the randomness, and can therefore evaluate many arms against the same randomly chosen reference point. The estimates of the arms' averages are then correlated. What matters for identifying the best arm is not the accuracy of each individual estimate but the accuracy of the differences between estimates. When the distances from two points to a common reference are positively correlated, which is typical because nearby points see similar distances to any given reference, the variance of the difference is much smaller than that of independent samples. Correlated sampling therefore makes the arms easier to distinguish with fewer samples. In this work, we exploit this observation by introducing correlated sequential halving, an algorithm that combines correlated sampling with the sequential halving bandit algorithm of Karnin et al. The algorithm proceeds in rounds with a fixed total budget of distance computations. In each round, it draws a set of random reference points and, for every surviving candidate, computes the distance to each of these shared references. It then discards the half of the candidates with the largest estimated average distance. Because all candidates are evaluated against the same references, comparisons between them are far less noisy than under independent sampling. Sequential halving is a natural partner for this strategy: it makes decisions based on rankings within a round, which depend only on differences between estimates, and its fixed-budget structure is simple to implement and efficient in practice. In addition, the shared references allow efficient vectorized computation, which improves wall-clock time beyond what the count of distance computations alone suggests. Our contributions are as follows. 1. Algorithm. We propose correlated sequential halving for medoid identification, which modifies the traditional independent bandit sampling strategy to use shared reference points across arms, and pairs it with sequential halving. 2. Theory. We analyze the algorithm and bound its probability of error in terms of data-dependent parameters that capture the gaps between the average distances of points and the correlation between distances to a common reference. We show that the number of distance computations needed can be significantly smaller than for independent sampling, and we quantify the improvement. In particular, when the correlation structure is favorable, the guarantee is considerably stronger than that for Meddit-style algorithms. 3. Experiments. We evaluate the algorithm on real datasets, including single-cell RNA-seq data and image data, with various distance metrics. Compared with exact computation, we observe gains of four to five orders of magnitude in both the number of distance computations and the wall-clock time. The algorithm also outperforms previous bandit-based approaches at the same accuracy. The idea of exploiting problem structure to go beyond a black-box bandit reduction may apply more broadly to other computational problems that have been converted to bandit formulations, such as k-nearest neighbor graph construction and clustering. We discuss these directions at the end of the paper. Our code is publicly available online. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 formalizes the problem and reviews related work. Section 3 presents the algorithm. Section 4 gives the theoretical analysis. Section 5 reports experimental results, and Section 6 concludes. We consider n points x1,…,xn in a metric space with distance d. The medoid is x{i} with i = argmini θi, where θi = (1/(n−1)) Σ{j≠i} d(xi, xj). Computing every θi exactly requires O(n²) distance evaluations. We instead treat the problem as best-arm identification, but change how rewards are sampled so that the structure of the problem is exploited. Bandit formulation. Each point xi is an arm whose mean is θi. Pulling arm i once corresponds to drawing a reference index J uniformly from {1,…,n} (excluding i) and observing d(xi, xJ). This observation is an unbiased estimate of θi. Prior approaches (e.g., RAND, Meddit) draw an independent reference J for each arm and each pull, and use UCB-style adaptive allocation. Here we make two modifications: a different sampling strategy, and a different bandit algorithm. Correlated sampling. The goal is to identify the arm with the smallest mean, so what matters is the accuracy of the comparison between arms, not of each individual estimate. Consider two arms i and k with t reference points J1,…,Jt shared between them. The estimate of the gap is Δ̂{ik} = (1/t) Σ{s=1}^t [d(xi, x{Js}) − d(xk, x{Js})]. Its variance is governed by the variance of d(xi,xJ) − d(xk,xJ), not by the sum of the two individual variances. When arms are sampled with independent references, the variance of the difference is Var(d(xi,J)) + Var(d(xk,J)). With shared references it is this quantity minus 2Cov(d(xi,J), d(xk,J)). By the triangle inequality, |d(xi,xJ) − d(xk,xJ)| ≤ d(xi,xk), so the difference is bounded, and for nearby points the two distances are strongly positively correlated, so the covariance term removes much of the variance. Intuitively, a reference point that is far from the dataset center inflates the distances of all candidates, and this shift cancels in the comparison. We therefore use correlated sampling: at each round, a single batch of reference points is drawn and every surviving arm is evaluated against the same batch. A further practical benefit is that the same references are reused across arms, which gives regular computation patterns suitable for vectorization. Sequential halving. Because the correlated estimates of different arms are dependent, the confidence-bound arguments used by UCB-type methods, which rely on independent per-arm samples with arm-specific adaptive counts, do not apply cleanly. Sequential Halving fits the correlated scheme naturally, since all surviving arms receive the same number of pulls in each round. Given a budget T of distance computations, the algorithm proceeds as follows. 1. Initialize the set of surviving arms S0 = {1,…,n} and let R = ⌈log₂ n⌉ be the number of rounds. 2. In round r = 0,…,R−1, let tr = ⌊T / (|Sr| R)⌋ (capped at n, see below). Draw tr reference indices J1,…,J{tr} uniformly at random, shared by all arms. 3. For every i ∈ Sr compute θ̂i^{(r)} = (1/tr) Σs d(xi, x{Js}). 4. Retain the ⌈|Sr|/2⌉ arms with smallest θ̂i^{(r)} to form S{r+1}. 5. Output the single remaining arm. Estimates are computed fresh in each round; we do not pool samples across rounds, which simplifies the analysis. The total number of distance computations is at most Σr |Sr| tr ≤ T. Note that as |Sr| shrinks, tr grows geometrically, so the later rounds, where the surviving arms are close in mean and hard to distinguish, receive many more reference points per arm. Exact fallback. If tr ≥ n, the estimate for arm i could be computed exactly by evaluating all distances to the n points. In that case we compute θi exactly for the surviving arms and return the true minimizer among them. This guarantees that the algorithm never spends more than the cost of exact computation on the final candidates, and makes the procedure exact whenever the budget is large enough. Analysis outline. Let Δi = θi − θ{i}. In round r, the winner i is eliminated only if at least half of the surviving arms have estimates below that of i. Using Markov's inequality on the number of arms that beat i, together with a sub-Gaussian bound on the correlated gap estimates Δ̂{i i}, we bound the per-round error. For a pair (i, i) with shared references, the summands d(xJ, xi) − d(xJ, x{i}) lie in [−d(xi,x{i}), d(xi,x{i})], and are sub-Gaussian with a proxy variance σ{i}² that we define as the correlated variance parameter. Hoeffding-type inequalities then give P(Δ̂{i i} < 0) ≤ exp(−tr Δi² / (2σi²)). Combining over rounds yields an error probability of the form P(error) ≤ log₂ n · exp(−T / (c · log₂ n · max{i} (i σ{(i)}²/Δ{(i)}²))), where arms are sorted by gap and c is a constant. The relevant hardness is thus governed by the correlated parameters σi rather than the uncorrelated worst-case spread of distances. When σi is much smaller than the uncorrelated spread, as is typical for real datasets where distance to a common reference is highly correlated across nearby points, a much smaller budget T suffices for a given error probability. Implementation. Distances are computed in vectorized batches: for each round, the |Sr| × tr distance block is evaluated against the shared references. The budget is set to T = c₀ n for a small constant c₀ (tens to hundreds of distance computations per point), giving near-linear total cost. Randomness comes only from the reference draws, so repeated runs can be used to assess reliability. We evaluate Correlated Sequential Halving (corrSH) against exact computation, RAND, Meddit, and uniform-sampling Sequential Halving (SH) on real datasets. We report two metrics: the number of distance computations and wall-clock time. We also report the accuracy of each method, measured as the fraction of trials in which the true medoid is returned. Experimental setup. We use three datasets: RNA-Seq (single-cell gene expression profiles with ℓ1 distance, n ≈ 20,000 after subsampling), Netflix-prize ratings (cosine distance, n ≈ 100,000 users), and MNIST (ℓ2 distance, zero digit class, n ≈ 6,000). For each dataset we draw subsets of increasing size n and run each algorithm 100 times with independent randomness. Exact medoids are computed by brute force and used as ground truth. Meddit and RAND are tuned to achieve at least 90% accuracy, while corrSH and SH are run with a fixed budget of T = c·n distance computations, with c varied to trace accuracy-versus-budget tradeoffs. All experiments use the same hardware and implementations in the same language to make wall-clock comparisons fair. Number of distance computations. Primary Sjögren's syndrome (pSS) is a chronic systemic autoimmune disease characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of the exocrine glands, particularly the salivary and lacrimal glands, leading to the hallmark symptoms of dry mouth (xerostomia) and dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca). Beyond glandular involvement, pSS is frequently accompanied by fatigue, arthralgia, and a broad spectrum of extraglandular manifestations affecting the lungs, kidneys, skin, peripheral and central nervous system, and hematologic compartment. The disease predominantly affects women, with a female-to-male ratio of approximately 9:1, and typically presents in the fourth to fifth decades of life. Reported prevalence varies according to the classification criteria and population studied, but it is estimated at between 0.01% and 0.7% of the general population, making pSS one of the most common systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases. A particularly serious complication is the development of non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma, most often mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma, which occurs in roughly 5–10% of patients and is the main factor driving increased mortality. The pathogenesis of pSS is complex and incompletely understood. It is thought to arise from the interplay of genetic susceptibility, epigenetic modifications, environmental triggers such as viral infections, and hormonal factors. Epithelial cells of the salivary glands are considered active participants in the disease process rather than passive targets. Once activated, they express adhesion molecules, chemokines, and costimulatory molecules, and they present autoantigens, thereby promoting the recruitment and activation of T and B lymphocytes, dendritic cells, and macrophages. Dysregulated type I and type II interferon signatures, aberrant B-cell activation mediated by B-cell activating factor, and the production of autoantibodies such as anti-SSA/Ro and anti-SSB/La are central features. Persistent immune activation ultimately results in glandular destruction and secretory dysfunction, while systemic immune complex formation and cytokine release contribute to extraglandular disease. Despite these advances, the diagnosis of pSS remains challenging. The clinical presentation is heterogeneous, and early symptoms such as dryness and fatigue are nonspecific, overlapping with those of aging, medication effects, diabetes, other autoimmune diseases, and fibromyalgia. As a result, a considerable delay between symptom onset and diagnosis, often several years, is common. Current classification criteria, including the 2016 American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism criteria, rely on a combination of anti-SSA/Ro antibodies, focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with a focus score of at least 1 in minor salivary gland biopsy, ocular staining score, Schirmer's test, and unstimulated salivary flow rate. Although these tools are valuable, each has limitations. Anti-SSA/Ro antibodies are absent in a substantial proportion of patients and are not specific to pSS, being found also in systemic lupus erythematosus and other conditions. Minor salivary gland biopsy is invasive, depends on sampling and pathologist expertise, and may cause patient discomfort or complications. Functional tests of tear and saliva production are influenced by external factors and show limited reproducibility. Equally important is the difficulty of assessing disease activity and predicting prognosis. Clinical indices such as the EULAR Sjögren's Syndrome Disease Activity Index and the Patient Reported Index are useful in research and trials, but they require standardized assessment and may not capture subtle or early changes. Few laboratory parameters reliably reflect disease activity or identify patients at risk of systemic complications and lymphoma. Furthermore, therapeutic options remain largely symptomatic, with immunosuppressive and biologic agents showing inconsistent benefit in clinical trials. This inconsistency may partly reflect patient heterogeneity and the lack of sensitive biomarkers for stratifying patients and monitoring treatment response. Reliable biomarkers could therefore improve early diagnosis, define disease subtypes, predict outcomes, and serve as endpoints in therapeutic studies. In recent years, advances in genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics have led to the identification of numerous candidate biomarkers. These include autoantibodies beyond anti-SSA/SSB, cytokines and chemokines, soluble receptors, interferon-related proteins such as myxovirus-resistance protein A, growth factors and ligands such as Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3 ligand, and non-coding RNAs including microRNAs and long non-coding RNAs. Of particular interest are biomarkers obtainable through noninvasive methods. Saliva and tears are in direct contact with the affected glands and reflect local pathological processes; their collection is simple, painless, and repeatable, making them attractive for diagnosis and longitudinal monitoring. Salivary and tear proteomic and molecular signatures have shown promise in distinguishing patients with pSS from healthy individuals and from those with other causes of sicca symptoms. However, most candidate biomarkers have been evaluated in small, single-center studies, and results are frequently inconsistent because of differences in sample handling, analytical platforms, and patient selection. Few have been validated in independent cohorts or translated into clinical practice. A critical appraisal of the current evidence is therefore needed. This review summarizes recent progress in the identification of biomarkers for pSS, covering serological, salivary, tear, and molecular candidates, and discusses their potential value for diagnosis, assessment of disease activity, prediction of complications, and guidance of treatment decisions. This narrative review was designed to summarize recent advances in biomarkers for primary Sjögren's syndrome (pSS), with emphasis on markers that support diagnosis, reflect disease activity, and may guide treatment decisions. Because the literature on pSS biomarkers is heterogeneous in study design, biological material, and analytical platform, a narrative approach was chosen over a formal systematic review or meta-analysis. We nevertheless followed a structured and transparent process for literature identification, selection, and synthesis to reduce selection bias. Literature search strategy We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library for articles published from January 2010 to the most recent search date. The search combined controlled vocabulary (MeSH/Emtree terms) and free-text keywords related to the disease, to biomarkers, and to biological specimens. Disease terms included "Sjögren's syndrome," "Sjögren syndrome," "primary Sjögren's syndrome," and "pSS." Biomarker terms included "biomarker," "biological marker," "autoantibody," "cytokine," "chemokine," "interferon signature," "Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3 ligand," "FLT3L," "myxovirus-resistance protein A," "MxA," "non-coding RNA," "microRNA," "long non-coding RNA," "circular RNA," "proteomics," "metabolomics," and "extracellular vesicles." Specimen terms included "saliva," "tears," "serum," "plasma," "peripheral blood," "urine," and "salivary gland biopsy." Boolean operators combined the three groups of terms, and search strings were adapted to each database. The reference lists of relevant reviews and key original articles were also hand-searched to identify additional publications. Seminal earlier studies were included where necessary to provide context for the classification criteria and established serological markers. Eligibility criteria We included original research articles (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional, and longitudinal studies), clinical trials with biomarker analyses, meta-analyses, and high-quality reviews that evaluated biomarkers in patients with pSS. Eligible studies enrolled patients meeting recognized classification criteria, namely the American-European Consensus Group 2002 criteria or the ACR/EULAR 2016 criteria, and compared them with healthy controls, disease controls (for example, systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, or sicca symptoms without autoimmune disease), or across disease activity strata. Studies were required to report diagnostic performance (sensitivity, specificity, area under the curve), associations with disease activity indices (such as ESSDAI), glandular or extraglandular manifestations, lymphoma risk, or response to therapy. We also considered mechanistic studies when they identified candidate markers with clear translational relevance. We excluded articles that were not published in English, case reports, conference abstracts without full text, animal or in vitro studies lacking a human validation component, studies of secondary Sjögren's syndrome in which pSS could not be distinguished, and reports that did not provide sufficient information on the biomarker or the patient population. Study selection and data extraction Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, and then evaluated the full texts of potentially relevant articles. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or, when necessary, by consultation with a third reviewer. For each included study, we extracted the first author, year of publication, country, study design, sample size, classification criteria used, type of biological specimen, analytical method (for example, ELISA, multiplex immunoassay, flow cytometry, quantitative PCR, RNA sequencing, mass spectrometry), the biomarker(s) examined, and principal findings. Where available, we recorded diagnostic accuracy metrics, correlations with clinical and laboratory features, and information on validation in independent cohorts. Categorization of biomarkers Extracted data were organized according to the type of biomarker and the source of the specimen. Categories comprised (1) autoantibodies, including anti-SSA/Ro, anti-SSB/La, rheumatoid factor, anti-centromere antibodies, and novel autoantibodies such as anti-salivary gland protein 1, anti-parotid secretory protein, and anti-carbonic anhydrase VI; (2) cytokines, chemokines, and soluble mediators, including B-cell activating factor, β2-microglobulin, CXCL13, and FLT3L; (3) interferon-related markers, including the type I interferon signature and MxA; (4) non-coding RNAs, such as microRNAs, long non-coding RNAs, and circular RNAs; (5) proteomic and metabolomic signatures; and (6) cellular and histopathological markers. Within each category, we emphasized noninvasive biomarkers obtainable from saliva and tears, given their potential for repeated sampling and point-of-care use. Markers were further grouped by their intended clinical use: diagnosis, assessment of disease activity, prediction of complications such as lymphoma, and monitoring of treatment response. Quality considerations and synthesis Formal risk-of-bias scoring was not applied because of the narrative design and the diversity of study types. However, we qualitatively appraised the strength of evidence by considering sample size, use of appropriate control groups, adherence to standardized classification criteria, adjustment for confounders such as age, sex, medication, and disease duration, the presence of independent validation cohorts, and the reproducibility of findings across studies. Biomarkers supported by multiple independent studies or by validation in separate cohorts were regarded as having stronger evidence than those reported in single small studies. Limitations common to the literature, including variation in specimen collection and processing (for example, stimulated versus unstimulated saliva, Schirmer strip versus capillary tear collection), assay heterogeneity, and lack of standardized cutoffs, were noted during synthesis. Findings were synthesized descriptively. Because of heterogeneity in methods and outcome measures, quantitative pooling was not attempted. Instead, we compared the diagnostic and prognostic value of candidate markers, highlighted consistent findings, and identified gaps and inconsistencies. We then discussed the potential of the most promising biomarkers to be integrated into clinical practice for diagnosis, stratification, and treatment guidance, and outlined directions for future research. Our review of the recent literature identified candidate biomarkers for primary Sjögren's syndrome (pSS) in several categories: autoantibodies, cytokines and chemokines, interferon-related proteins, non-coding RNAs, and proteomic or metabolomic signatures in saliva and tears. These are summarized below according to their source and their potential diagnostic or disease-activity value. Autoantibodies Anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies remain the serological hallmarks of pSS and are included in current classification criteria. Anti-Ro/SSA is found in roughly 50–70% of patients and anti-La/SSB in 25–40%, but neither is specific, since both occur in systemic lupus erythematosus and other connective tissue diseases. Anti-Ro/SSA positivity is associated with younger age at onset, longer disease duration, greater glandular inflammation, and extraglandular manifestations. Several studies reported that anti-La/SSB is associated with higher focus scores and higher immunoglobulin levels. Additional autoantibodies have been proposed for seronegative patients, including anti-muscarinic type 3 receptor, anti-α-fodrin, anti-carbonic anhydrase VI, anti-salivary gland protein 1, and anti-parotid secretory protein antibodies. Reported sensitivities were variable, and anti-SP1, anti-CA6, and anti-PSP appeared in early or seronegative disease, although specificity and reproducibility across cohorts were limited. Anti-centromere antibodies identified a subset with prominent sicca features and Raynaud's phenomenon. Cryoglobulins, hypocomplementemia (low C4), and monoclonal gammopathy were consistently reported as predictors of lymphoma development. Cytokines, chemokines, and B-cell–related markers B-cell activation markers were the most consistently elevated serum markers of disease activity. Serum β2-microglobulin, free light chains, BAFF (B-cell activating factor), and CXCL13 were elevated in patients relative to controls and correlated with disease activity indices such as ESSDAI. CXCL13 also correlated with ectopic germinal center formation in the salivary glands and may help identify patients at higher risk of lymphoproliferative disease. BAFF levels were higher in anti-Ro-positive patients and correlated with autoantibody titers and hypergammaglobulinemia. Elevated IL-6, IL-17, IL-21, IL-22, and IL-23 reflected Th17 and follicular helper T-cell involvement. Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3 ligand (Flt3L) emerged as a promising candidate, being significantly elevated in the serum of pSS patients compared with healthy controls and patients with other autoimmune diseases in several studies. Flt3L levels correlated with disease activity and with the presence of anti-Ro/SSA, and appeared to distinguish pSS from non-Sjögren sicca in some cohorts, supporting a role in diagnosis and in monitoring dendritic cell–driven inflammation. Hybrid systems, which combine discrete computation with continuous evolution in physical time, are now pervasive in safety-critical applications such as automotive control, railway signalling, and medical devices. Their correctness is difficult to establish by testing alone, and a substantial body of work has therefore been devoted to formal verification. Deductive verification is one major approach. It offers a way to reason about systems with infinite or parameterised state spaces, and it can be made compositional, so that the proof for a system is assembled from proofs for its components. Hybrid CSP (HCSP) [1,2] extends Hoare's Communicating Sequential Processes with ordinary differential equations, interrupts triggered by continuous conditions or communications, and timed behaviour. It has been used to model and analyse industrial case studies, notably in Chinese high-speed train control systems and aerospace applications. A natural question is how to give HCSP a deductive proof system in the style of Hoare logic [3], where a triple {P} S {Q} relates a precondition and a postcondition of a program S. For hybrid systems this classical format is insufficient. The behaviour of interest is a trajectory over time rather than a pair of initial and final states, so assertions must refer to time. Parallel composition with communication also needs a treatment of interleaving, typically via assumptions about the environment. We have previously explored several ways to meet these demands. The first extended Hoare triples with differential invariants and with assertions over the final state, and was later generalised to parallel processes through assume/guarantee-style reasoning [4,5]. This was practical for safety properties, but had limited expressive power for properties of whole trajectories. A second approach used history formulas, written in an extension of first-order logic with time-indexed variables [6]. A third used the Duration Calculus (DC) [7,8], an interval temporal logic well suited for reasoning about durations of states, in which pre- and postconditions are replaced by temporal properties of the history. Each approach used its own assertion language, its own way of representing time, and its own proof notation. Each also had drawbacks: some were not compositional for parallel composition, some required auxiliary variables or an explicit encoding of communication traces, and some had proof rules that were hard to apply by hand or were complete only for restricted fragments of the language. In this paper we propose a new approach that combines the lessons from these earlier attempts. It rests on three principal ideas. First, we adopt weakly monotonic time as the semantic basis for interleaving. In many semantic models, the successive discrete steps of a process occur at strictly increasing times, or an artificial separation is imposed between discrete and continuous transitions. By permitting several consecutive discrete actions to occur at the same time point, while time never decreases, we obtain a model in which sequential composition is simple and in which the interleaving of parallel components can be described without additional machinery. Instantaneous communications and assignments are represented faithfully, and the semantics remains close to the operational intuition of HCSP. Second, we use DC with infinite intervals and general fixpoints as the assertion language. Allowing infinite intervals lets us describe non-terminating processes and the infinite behaviours that arise in reactive systems and in loops that run forever, whereas finite-interval DC [7] can only speak about terminating computations. General fixpoint operators, in the spirit of the modal µ-calculus [9] and of fixpoint extensions of interval logics [10], make the language expressive enough to characterise the behaviour of recursion and repetition directly, without recourse to invariants supplied by the user. They also allow strongest-postcondition-like formulas to be written within the logic itself, which is the key to a completeness result. Third, we give Hoare-like triples a new meaning that unifies assertions and temporal conditions. In the traditional reading, a precondition constrains the initial state and a postcondition the final state. In our reading, the first component of a triple describes the history up to the start of the process, and the second describes the extended history that includes the behaviour of the process, both expressed as DC formulas. A triple therefore states how a process transforms a history into a longer history. Because both parts live in the same logic, the same formula can express a state assertion, a bound on elapsed time, or a complex temporal property. The need for separate notations for assertions and for temporal conditions disappears, and the proof rules for sequential composition, choice, repetition, and continuous evolution become uniform. The main technical contribution is a proof system for triples in this form, together with a proof that it is complete relative to the validity of DC. That is, every valid triple is derivable provided that the valid formulas of DC may be used as axioms. Relative completeness of this kind is the standard yardstick for Hoare logics [3,11], and it separates the incompleteness inherent in the assertion logic from any weakness in the proof rules. Since DC itself is undecidable in general, relative completeness is the strongest result one can reasonably hope for. We also discuss compositionality: the rule for parallel composition combines the triples of the components without referring to their internal structure beyond the interface of communication events. The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 recalls HCSP and defines its semantics over weakly monotonic time. Section 3 presents DC with infinite intervals and fixpoints. Section 4 defines the new triples and their validity. Section 5 gives the proof system, and Section 6 proves its soundness and relative completeness. Section 7 discusses related work and concludes. Parallel components communicate only via channels and share no variables. 1. Semantic model. The behaviour of a process is a set of traces. Each trace is a function from a time domain, possibly an infinite interval [0,∞), to states, together with a record of communication events. In earlier work, interleaving was modelled by strictly monotonic time, in which discrete steps are separated by artificial delays, or by auxiliary timestamps [3,4]. We instead use weakly monotonic time: a trace is a sequence of segments, and several discrete actions may occur at the same real time instant, ordered by their position in the sequence. A state at time t is therefore a finite sequence of intermediate valuations, of which the observable value in the Duration Calculus is the last one. Sequential composition concatenates traces; parallel composition synchronises on common channels and interleaves the remaining discrete actions at equal time points. This removes the need for infinitesimal delays and makes the semantics of parallel composition compositional in the trace set. Divergence is represented by an infinite sequence of actions at one time instant, and non-terminating behaviour by traces on infinite intervals. 2. Logic language. Specifications are written in the Duration Calculus (DC) [5], an interval temporal logic whose formulas are evaluated over intervals [b,e]. We use the extension to infinite intervals [6], so that the end point e may be ∞, and we define a unary predicate on interval finiteness. Basic terms are state expressions over program variables and the interval length ℓ. Formulas are built from the chop operator ⌢ (concatenation of adjacent subintervals, including a finite prefix followed by an infinite suffix), Boolean connectives, first-order quantification over rigid variables, and general fixpoints μZ.φ(Z), with Z occurring positively. Fixpoints allow us to express iteration and recursion without separate induction rules, and they subsume the usual iteration operator φ and its infinite counterpart φ^ω. Standard abbreviations are ◇φ ≙ true⌢φ⌢true, □φ ≙ ¬◇¬φ, and ⌈S⌉ for “S holds throughout a non-point interval”. To describe left- and right-limit values at the boundaries of segments, we use initial and final value terms, written x⃖ and x⃗ respectively, which allows the same formula to talk about the start and end states of a computation. Communication is described by designated state variables recording the waiting status of each channel and by event predicates over the trace, in the style of [7]. Continuous evolution is characterised through its solution when available, or through differential invariants expressed as DC formulas over the state variables [8]. 3. Hoare-like triples. Classical triples {p} P {q} relate pre- and post-states, whereas the earlier HCSP proof systems used either a history formula with separate assertions [3], or duration-calculus-based triples with a pre-formula, a post-formula and a separate temporal condition [4]. We introduce a single form {φ} P {ψ}, in which both φ and ψ are DC formulas. Its meaning is: for every trace τ of P on an interval and every interval prefix decomposition in which the history preceding the execution of P satisfies φ, the history extended by τ satisfies ψ. Formally, if the history so far, on an interval [0,t], satisfies φ and τ is an execution of P starting at t, then the concatenation satisfies ψ, that is, the semantic condition is φ⌢τ ⊨ ψ in the sense of chop. Choosing φ to constrain only the final state recovers ordinary pre-/postconditions, while choosing ψ to constrain the whole interval yields temporal properties such as safety invariants or duration bounds. Assertions and temporal conditions are thereby unified in one formula language. Since divergence and infinite executions produce infinite intervals, ψ is required to hold for these as well, which yields a form of total correctness for infinite behaviours expressed by finiteness predicates. 4. Proof system. The proof system contains one axiom or rule for each construct. For example, assignment has the axiom {φ} x := e {φ ⌢ ⌈x⃗ = e⃖⌉-style point formula}, where the point interval records the update in the weakly monotonic setting; sequential composition is given by chaining {φ} P {χ} and {χ} Q {ψ}; and conditional and nondeterministic choice by case rules. Wait and continuous evolution rules generate a suitable non-point interval formula, with differential invariants for the latter. Interruptible evolution and communication use rules that introduce the respective event predicates. Repetition and recursion are treated by a fixpoint rule: if from {Z} P {...} one can derive the unfolding for the body then the triple holds for μX.P, with the least-fixpoint formula as the postcondition. For parallel composition we give a compositional rule that combines the triples of components through a synchronisation operator over formulas, together with side conditions on disjoint variables and channel alphabets. Auxiliary rules include consequence, disjunction, conjunction, and existential elimination of rigid variables. 5. Soundness and relative completeness. Soundness is established by induction on derivations, using the trace semantics and the semantic definition of chop. For completeness we follow the strategy of Cook [9]: we show that the logic is expressive, in that for every process P and DC formula φ the strongest postcondition sp(φ,P) is expressible, which is obtained by encoding the trace semantics via fixpoint formulas. We then prove that {φ} P {sp(φ,P)} is derivable by induction on P, and conclude by consequence that every valid triple is derivable, assuming an oracle for validity of DC formulas. Completeness is therefore relative to DC validity, which is itself undecidable in general [5,6]. We now present the main results of the paper: soundness and relative completeness of the proof system for the new triples, together with supporting lemmas and an illustrative case study.
