Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success in domains ranging from Atari games to robotic control and board games. Despite this progress, exploration remains a central challenge. An agent that explores poorly may converge to suboptimal policies or fail entirely in environments where rewards are sparse or deceptive. The simplest strategies, such as epsilon-greedy action selection or adding noise to policy outputs, are undirected: they perturb behavior randomly without regard to what the agent has already seen or where an action is likely to lead. In tasks with large state spaces and long horizons, such strategies are highly inefficient. A principled alternative is to encourage the agent to visit states that are rarely encountered. In tabular settings, count-based methods realize this idea directly by adding a bonus inversely related to the visitation count of a state, with strong theoretical guarantees and good empirical performance. In deep RL, however, states are high-dimensional image frames that are almost never exactly repeated, so raw counts are uninformative. Recent work has extended counting to such domains through density models, pseudo-counts, or hashing of state representations. Hashing approaches map states to compact discrete codes, for example with SimHash or learned autoencoder features, so that similar states share a code and counts become meaningful. These methods typically compute a bonus for the state the agent currently occupies or has just reached, and add it to the reward. Such bonuses are inherently retrospective. The agent learns that a state was novel only after arriving there. Ideally, exploration should be informed: before committing to an action, the agent should know which direction is likely to lead to less frequent states and choose accordingly. This requires two capabilities that are individually non-trivial in deep RL. First, the agent must be able to anticipate the consequences of its actions, that is, predict future observations from the current state and a candidate action. Second, it must be able to evaluate how frequent those predicted observations are relative to its experience. Combining these is difficult because predicted frames are generated by a model and are not drawn from the distribution of frames actually stored by the agent. Predictions may contain small pixel-level errors or blur, so a hash function applied naively to a predicted frame can produce a code that does not match the code of the corresponding real frame. Counts obtained from seen frames then fail to transfer to predicted ones, and the resulting novelty estimate is unreliable. In this paper, we propose a novel informed exploration framework that addresses these challenges. Our approach has three components. First, we train a deep action-conditional prediction model that, given a state represented by a stack of recent frames and an action, predicts the future frame. Such models have been shown to produce accurate multi-step predictions in Atari environments, making them suitable for looking ahead one step for every available action. Second, we train a convolutional autoencoder on the frames seen by the agent and use its latent representation, discretized into binary codes, as a hash function. The counts of these codes over the history of seen frames serve as a measure of how frequently different regions of the state space have been visited. Third, and most critically, we tackle the matching problem between predicted future frames and seen frames at the latent feature level. Rather than hashing predicted frames directly, we introduce a mechanism that aligns the latent representation of a predicted frame with that of the seen frames it corresponds to, so that the count associated with the real frame can be retrieved reliably. This allows the counts derived from experience to be used to evaluate the frequentness of frames the agent has not yet observed. With this machinery, we obtain a metric for the novelty of the future direction pointed to by each action. At each decision step, the agent predicts the next frame for every action, matches each prediction to the hashed history, and obtains a count-based novelty estimate. The agent is then informed to explore the action whose predicted future is least frequent. This differs from conventional count-based bonuses in that novelty is assessed prospectively and used for action selection, rather than being assigned as a reward after the transition. It also differs from curiosity methods based on prediction error, which reward the agent for transitions that the model predicts poorly, a quantity that can be noisy and may be driven by stochastic or uninformative parts of the observation. Our measure is grounded in visitation frequency, which retains the interpretability and stability of counting. We evaluate our method on a set of Atari 2600 games, including several that are known to be hard for exploration. We integrate the informed exploration strategy with a standard deep RL algorithm and compare against baselines using undirected exploration and existing count-based or hashing-based bonuses. Our results show that informed exploration over predicted future frames improves learning efficiency and final performance on a number of games, and that accurate matching between predicted and seen frames is key to obtaining a reliable novelty signal. The contributions of this paper are as follows. (1) We propose an informed exploration framework for deep RL that combines future-frame prediction with hashing-based counting to evaluate the novelty of each action’s predicted outcome. (2) We introduce a latent-level matching approach that bridges the gap between predicted frames and seen frames, enabling counts from real experience to be applied to predictions. (3) We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach on challenging Atari benchmarks. Our framework, which we call informed exploration with hashing over predicted frames, has three components: (1) a future-frame prediction model, (2) a convolutional autoencoder that provides a hash code for each frame, and (3) a mechanism that matches predicted frames to seen frames in latent space so that hash counts can be used to rank actions. We describe each in turn and then explain how they are combined with a deep Q-learning agent. Problem setting. We consider a Markov decision process with discrete action set A. At time t the agent observes a state st, defined as a stack of the four most recent preprocessed frames, selects an action at, and receives reward rt. Standard ε-greedy exploration selects a random action with probability ε, ignoring both the consequence of each action and how often similar situations have been visited. Our goal is to replace the uniform random choice with one that favors the action whose predicted future is the least frequently visited. Future-frame prediction. We train an action-conditional prediction network fθ that takes the state st and an action a and outputs the next frame x̂{t+1}(a). The architecture follows an encoder–transformation–decoder design. Convolutional layers encode the stacked frames into a feature vector ht. The action is encoded as a one-hot vector and combined with ht through a multiplicative interaction, ht^a = (Wh ht) ⊙ (Wa a). Deconvolutional layers then decode ht^a into the predicted frame. The model is trained on transitions (st, at, x{t+1}) drawn from the replay memory by minimizing the squared reconstruction error Lpred = ‖x{t+1} − fθ(st, at)‖². To reduce error accumulation, we predict only one step ahead for the action-ranking step and apply the model to every action in A, giving |A| candidate future frames per decision. The prediction model is trained concurrently with the agent and is updated at a fixed interval using minibatches from the replay memory. Hashing with a convolutional autoencoder. Count-based exploration requires a discrete representation of states. Because raw frames are high-dimensional, we learn a compact code with a convolutional autoencoder g. The encoder maps a frame x to a latent feature z = enc(x), and the decoder reconstructs x from z. The final encoder layer uses sigmoid units, and the latent vector has K dimensions. Following previous work on learned hashing, we add uniform noise to the sigmoid outputs during training to encourage them to saturate toward binary values, and we train with a reconstruction loss LAE = −(1/N) Σ log p(xi | zi) + λ · (binarization regularizer). After training, the binary hash code is b(x) = round(enc(x)) ∈ {0,1}^K. We maintain a hash table that stores the count n(b) of how many times each code has been produced by frames actually experienced by the agent. At each environment step we compute the code of the new frame and increment its count. The autoencoder is periodically retrained on frames in the replay memory, and the table is rebuilt after each update so that counts remain consistent with the current encoder. Matching predicted frames to seen frames. The difficulty of using n(b) on predicted frames is that predictions are imperfect and blurry. Passing a predicted frame directly through the autoencoder often yields a code that does not match any code derived from real frames, even if the prediction is semantically close to a seen frame. Consequently, its count would be zero or arbitrary, and the counts would not reflect true frequentness. We resolve this at the latent feature level. For each predicted frame x̂(a) we compute its latent feature ẑ(a) = enc(x̂(a)). We keep a set of latent features of seen frames, Z = {zj}, each associated with its hash code. We then find the nearest seen frame in latent space, j(a) = argminj ‖ẑ(a) − zj‖₂, and use the count of that frame's code as the count for the predicted frame, n̂(a) = n(b(z{j})). To make the matching reliable, we additionally train the prediction model with a latent consistency loss that encourages the encoding of a predicted frame to match the encoding of the true next frame, Llat = ‖enc(x̂{t+1}) − enc(x{t+1})‖², so that the total prediction objective is L = Lpred + β Llat, with the encoder weights held fixed for this term. This pulls predictions toward the manifold of real frames in the latent space, where nearest-neighbor retrieval is meaningful. For efficiency, we search over a random subset of recent latent features, or use an approximate nearest-neighbor index, rather than the entire history. Informed exploration policy. The novelty of the future reached by action a is measured with the standard count-based bonus u(a) = 1 / √(n̂(a) + 1). During exploration, instead of picking a uniformly random action, the agent selects at = argmaxa u(a) = argmina n̂(a), with ties broken at random. Exploration is triggered with probability ε, which is annealed during training as in standard DQN. With probability 1 − ε the agent acts greedily with respect to the Q-function. Thus the informed mechanism changes only which action is taken when the agent explores, leaving the learning rule for the Q-network unchanged. The Q-network is trained with the usual temporal-difference loss on minibatches from the replay memory, using a target network. Training procedure. The agent first collects transitions with random actions to warm up the replay memory. The autoencoder and prediction model are then pretrained briefly on this data. Subsequently, at every step the agent (i) chooses an action using the informed ε-greedy policy, (ii) stores the transition, (iii) updates the hash count with the new frame, and (iv) performs a gradient step for the Q-network. At fixed intervals the autoencoder, the prediction model, and the table of seen latent features are refreshed. The additional computation per exploratory step consists of |A| forward passes of the prediction model and encoder plus a nearest-neighbor lookup, which is small relative to Q-network training. We evaluate the proposed informed exploration method on Atari 2600 games from the Arcade Learning Environment, focusing on games with different exploration difficulty: Freeway, Frostbite, Venture, Montezuma's Revenge, Gravitar, and Private Eye, as well as several less sparse games (Breakout, Pong, Seaquest). We compare against a baseline DQN with epsilon-greedy exploration, a count-based method using static hashing of raw pixels (SimHash on downsampled frames, "Exploration"), a pseudo-count method based on density models (A3C-CTS/DQN-CTS), and a prediction-error curiosity baseline. All methods share the same network architecture and training budget of 50M frames, and results are averaged over 5 random seeds unless otherwise noted. Our method is denoted HPF (Hashing over Predicted

Pyrroles are among the most important heterocyclic motifs in chemistry. They are found in a wide range of natural products, pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals, and in functional materials such as conducting polymers, dyes and porphyrin-based systems [1,2]. Prominent examples include the cholesterol-lowering drug atorvastatin, the anti-inflammatory agent tolmetin and the receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor sunitinib. Their ubiquity has motivated the development of many synthetic approaches. Classical condensation methods, including the Paal–Knorr, Knorr and Hantzsch syntheses, remain widely used, but they often require pre-assembled, sometimes unstable, 1,4-dicarbonyl or α-aminoketone precursors, and the preparation of densely substituted examples can be lengthy [3,4]. More recent approaches include transition metal-catalysed cycloisomerisations, multicomponent couplings, and cycloadditions of azomethine ylides or isocyanides [5–7]. Methods that assemble highly substituted pyrroles from simple, readily available building blocks with high atom economy and control over regiochemistry therefore remain attractive. Partially saturated analogues, the dihydropyrroles (pyrrolines), are also valuable targets and synthetic intermediates, and efficient access to them is similarly desirable [8]. Transition metal-catalysed hydroacylation, the formal addition of an aldehyde C–H bond across an unsaturated C–C bond, is a highly atom-economical route to ketones [9,10]. The intramolecular variant is well established, and rhodium catalysts have been used to prepare cyclic ketones with excellent levels of enantiocontrol [11]. Intermolecular reactions have proved far more challenging. The key acyl–rhodium–hydride intermediate formed by oxidative addition of the aldehyde can undergo competitive decarbonylation, which deactivates the catalyst through formation of rhodium carbonyl species, and the reductive elimination and insertion steps must be controlled to avoid side reactions such as alkyne dimerisation, trimerisation or aldehyde homocoupling [12]. The most successful strategies have relied on chelation control, in which a Lewis basic group within the aldehyde or the unsaturated partner, such as a thioether, amine or heteroatom-containing substituent, stabilises the acyl–metal intermediate and suppresses decarbonylation [13,14]. Pioneering studies by Suemune, Jun, Willis and others have shown that this approach enables intermolecular couplings of β-sulfur-substituted aldehydes with alkynes and alkenes [15–17]. Our group has also reported intermolecular hydroacylation reactions of alkynes and alkenes that exploit chelating groups on the coupling partner [18,19]. A further issue in intermolecular alkyne hydroacylation is regioselectivity, and, in the case of the products, the branched versus linear selectivity. Terminal alkynes may give either the linear (E-enone) or the branched (α-substituted enone) adduct, and, with many catalyst systems, mixtures result. Linear-selective reactions are particularly valuable, since they furnish β-unsubstituted enones that are useful conjugate acceptors and precursors of 1,4-dicarbonyl compounds. Catalyst control of this selectivity is strongly influenced by the ligand, and the bite angle of diphosphine ligands has been shown to affect both the efficiency and selectivity of rhodium-catalysed hydroacylation [20,21]. We have previously observed that small bite-angle diphosphines, such as bis(diphenylphosphino)methane (dppm) and related ligands like (Cy2P)2NMe, can promote effective hydroacylation while suppressing decarbonylation, presumably through formation of stable bimetallic or highly constrained mononuclear rhodium species [22]. Propargylic and allylic amines are attractive coupling partners, since the nitrogen atom is present from the outset and could serve both as a directing group and as the nucleophile in a subsequent cyclisation. We envisaged that linear-selective hydroacylation of a propargylic amine with an aldehyde would generate a γ-amino enone, an immediate precursor to 1,4-dicarbonyl-type reactivity. Tautomerisation or isomerisation and dehydrative cyclisation of such an adduct should deliver the pyrrole ring directly, in a manner akin to the Paal–Knorr process but without isolation of a sensitive 1,4-dicarbonyl intermediate. Similarly, hydroacylation of allylic amines should provide saturated γ-amino ketones that cyclise to dihydropyrroles. Such a strategy would in effect use two simple fragments, an aldehyde and an amine bearing an unsaturated unit, to build a substituted heterocycle with the substitution pattern defined by the choice of components. Rhodium catalysts also promote a range of other transformations of the alkyne and enone functionality, including conjugate additions and Suzuki-type couplings with aryl boronic acids [23,24]. The compatibility of Rh(I) catalysis with both hydroacylation and arylation suggested that these processes might be merged in a single operation. Cascade and multicomponent processes are valuable because they increase molecular complexity rapidly while minimising purification steps and waste [25]. Here we report that Rh(I) complexes of small bite-angle diphosphines catalyse the linear-selective hydroacylation of propargylic amines with aldehydes in good yields and with high selectivities. Subsequent in situ treatment with p-toluenesulfonic acid (p-TSA) promotes dehydrative cyclisation to afford substituted pyrroles. Allylic amines serve as alternative substrates and provide functionalised dihydropyrroles. Finally, we show that the hydroacylation can be coupled with a rhodium-catalysed Suzuki-type arylation to enable a three-component assembly of highly substituted pyrroles from an aldehyde, a propargylic amine and an aryl boronic acid. General Considerations. All reactions were performed under an inert atmosphere of argon or nitrogen using oven-dried glassware and standard Schlenk techniques, unless otherwise stated. Solvents were dried by passage through an alumina column and degassed prior to use. Aldehydes were distilled or recrystallised before use. Propargylic and allylic amines were prepared as N-protected derivatives (N-tosyl, N-Boc and N-aryl variants) by alkylation of the corresponding sulfonamides or carbamates with propargyl or allyl bromides, or by Mitsunobu reaction [1,2]. Aryl boronic acids were purchased from commercial suppliers and used as received. [Rh(nbd)2]BF4 and [Rh(cod)Cl]2 were obtained commercially. The ligands bis(diphenylphosphino)methane (dppm) and (Cy2P)2NMe were either purchased or prepared by reaction of the corresponding chlorophosphine with methylamine in the presence of triethylamine, following literature procedures [3,4]. Analytical thin-layer chromatography used silica gel 60 F254 plates, and flash chromatography used silica gel (40–63 μm). NMR spectra (1H, 13C, 31P) were recorded at 400 or 500 MHz in CDCl3 and referenced to residual solvent signals. High-resolution mass spectra were obtained by electrospray or electron ionisation, and infrared spectra were recorded on an ATR instrument. Preparation of Rhodium Catalysts. The precatalyst [Rh(diphosphine)(nbd)]BF4 was generated in situ or isolated. In a glovebox, [Rh(nbd)2]BF4 (1.0 equiv) and the diphosphine ligand (1.05 equiv) were dissolved in dichloromethane and stirred for 30 min. The solution was concentrated and the product precipitated with pentane, filtered and dried under vacuum. Norbornadiene was removed prior to catalysis by exposure of a solution of the complex in acetone or 1,2-dichloroethane to hydrogen (1 atm, 30 min), followed by thorough flushing with argon, to give the active solvated cationic Rh(I) species [5]. General Procedure A: Hydroacylation of Propargylic Amines. In a glovebox, the activated rhodium catalyst (5 mol %) was dissolved in 1,2-dichloroethane (0.2 M relative to alkyne) in a Schlenk tube or sealed vial. The propargylic amine (1.0 equiv) and aldehyde (1.5 equiv) were added sequentially. The vessel was sealed, removed from the glovebox and heated at 60–80 °C for 4–16 h. Reaction progress was monitored by TLC and 1H NMR spectroscopy of aliquots. After cooling, the mixture was concentrated and the crude material analysed by 1H NMR spectroscopy to determine the ratio of linear to branched hydroacylation products and the ratio of E/Z isomers where relevant. The products, β,γ- or α,β-unsaturated amino ketones (enones), were purified by flash chromatography. Ligand screening was carried out under identical conditions using dppm, (Cy2P)2NMe, dppe, dppp, BINAP and monodentate phosphines, with yields and selectivities determined by 1H NMR spectroscopy using 1,3,5-trimethoxybenzene as an internal standard [6]. General Procedure B: One-Pot Pyrrole Formation. Following completion of hydroacylation as described above (confirmed by consumption of the amine), the reaction mixture was cooled to room temperature and p-toluenesulfonic acid monohydrate (p-TSA, 20–100 mol %) was added directly. The mixture was heated at 60–80 °C for 1–3 h to effect dehydrative cyclisation. Where N-Boc substrates were used, concomitant deprotection facilitated cyclisation. The reaction was quenched with saturated aqueous NaHCO3, extracted with dichloromethane (3×), dried over MgSO4, filtered and concentrated. Purification by flash chromatography provided the 2,3,5-substituted or 2,4,5-substituted pyrroles, depending on the substitution of the alkyne. Isolated yields are reported over the two steps. General Procedure C: Hydroacylation of Allylic Amines. Allylic amines (1.0 equiv) and aldehydes (1.5–2.0 equiv) were combined with the rhodium catalyst (5–10 mol %) in 1,2-dichloroethane at 80–100 °C for 16–24 h. Since allylic substrates are less reactive and prone to alkene isomerisation, the reactions were monitored carefully for formation of isomerised enamide by-products. After concentration, the linear ketone adducts were isolated by chromatography. Cyclisation to dihydropyrroles was achieved by treatment of the isolated or crude ketone with p-TSA (1.0 equiv) in toluene at 80 °C, with removal of water by molecular sieves, followed by the work-up described in Procedure B [7]. General Procedure D: Three-Component Hydroacylation/Suzuki-Type Cascade. The rhodium catalyst (5 mol %), aryl boronic acid (1.5 equiv), aldehyde (1.5 equiv) and propargylic amine (1.0 equiv) were combined in the chosen solvent (1,4-dioxane or 1,2-dichloroethane) with a mild base (K2CO3 or Et3N, 1.0 equiv) and a controlled quantity of water (2–5 equiv) to promote transmetalation. The mixture was heated at 80 °C for 16 h. Under these conditions, the intermediate arising from carbometalation of the alkyne by an arylrhodium species engages in acyl transfer, leading to a tri- or tetrasubstituted enone [8,9]. Subsequent addition of p-TSA and heating at 80 °C for 2 h furnished the pyrrole. Control experiments omitting individual components were conducted to establish the order of events and to exclude uncatalysed background reactions. Mechanistic and Deuterium-Labelling Experiments. Aldehyde-d1 substrates (>95% D) were prepared by N-heterocyclic carbene-catalysed H/D exchange with D2O [10]. These were subjected to Procedure A, and deuterium incorporation in the product alkene was quantified by 1H and 2H NMR spectroscopy. Crossover experiments employed an equimolar mixture of a deuterated aldehyde and a non-deuterated aldehyde with a single alkyne. Reaction profiles were also followed by in situ 31P NMR spectroscopy in CD2Cl2 or 1,2-dichloroethane-d4 to identify catalyst resting states and potential decarbonylated species such as [Rh(diphosphine)(CO)2]+ [11]. Characterisation and Data Analysis. All new compounds were characterised by 1H, 13C and 31P (where applicable) NMR spectroscopy, HRMS and IR spectroscopy. Regiochemistry of the pyrrole products was assigned using NOESY, HSQC and HMBC experiments, and selected structures were confirmed by single-crystal X-ray diffraction. Linear to branched ratios were determined from integration of characteristic vinylic resonances in the crude 1H NMR spectra. Yields refer to isolated, analytically pure material unless otherwise noted. Reactions were conducted at least in duplicate for optimisation studies, and reported values represent averages. Our study began with the hydroacylation of propargylic amine 2a (N-protected, terminal alkyne) with aldehyde 1a, a substrate class in which chelation-assisted hydroacylation has precedent with β-S-substituted aldehydes [1,2]. We used 2-(methylthio)benzaldehyde-type aldehydes as chelating partners, and initial screening was directed at controlling the linear versus branched selectivity, a recurring problem in alkyne hydroacylation [3]. With [Rh(nbd)2]BF4 and common diphosphines such as dppe or dppp, mixtures of the linear enone and the branched isomer were obtained together with decarbonylation and alkyne homodimerisation byproducts (Table 1, entries 1–3). Increasing the bite angle (e.g. DPEphos, Xantphos) gave lower conversion. In contrast, ligands with small bite angles proved markedly superior. Bis(diphenylphosphino)methane (dppm) delivered the linear adduct 3a in 78% yield with >20:1 linear:branched selectivity, and (Cy2P)2NMe gave a comparable result (82%, >20:1) at lower catalyst loading (entries 4–5). The performance of these ligands is consistent with the formation of a compact, possibly dinuclear or strained chelate rhodium species that disfavours the sterically congested branched-selective insertion pathway [4]. Aryl-substituted aldehydes bearing electron-donating (Me, OMe) and electron-withdrawing (F, Cl, CF3) groups gave the corresponding enones in 62–88% yield. Heteroaromatic and alkyl-substituted chelating aldehydes were also tolerated, although the latter required longer reaction times. The propargylic amine component could carry sulfonamide or carbamate protection; N-Ts and N-Boc derivatives were comparably effective. Internal alkynes were considerably less reactive, and only trace conversion was observed, so the method is largely limited to terminal alkynes. Hashing has been widely used for approximate nearest neighbor search in large-scale information retrieval because of its low storage cost and fast query speed. Hashing methods map high-dimensional data such as images into compact binary codes so that similar items receive similar codes, and retrieval can then be performed efficiently with Hamming distance computed by bitwise operations. With the success of deep neural networks, deep supervised hashing has become the dominant paradigm. These methods jointly learn feature representations and hash functions in an end-to-end manner, using supervised information such as class labels or pairwise similarities. They consistently outperform traditional hashing approaches that rely on hand-crafted features. In a typical deep hashing network, the output neurons of the last layer are binarized, usually with a sign function, to produce hashing bits. The code length is fixed in advance, and each output neuron is expected to contribute a distinct and informative bit. In practice, however, this expectation is often violated. Because the network is trained with relaxed continuous outputs and then discretized, many bits become highly correlated or carry nearly identical information. This is especially pronounced for longer codes, where the number of bits exceeds what the semantic structure of the data requires. Such redundancy has two negative consequences. First, it wastes storage and computation, since several bits encode what one bit could express. Second, it harms accuracy: redundant bits implicitly overweight certain semantic directions in the Hamming distance, while other discriminative information receives too little weight. This is why the retrieval performance of many deep hashing methods saturates, or even degrades, as the code length increases. Several lines of work attempt to mitigate this problem. Some methods add regularizers that encourage bit balance or bit independence, for example by decorrelating the output dimensions or maximizing the entropy of each bit. Others choose the code length by hand, or select bits after training with heuristics. These strategies have limitations. Regularization terms act as soft constraints on the output distribution. They do not explicitly model which bits are redundant with which others, and they cannot adaptively restructure the network accordingly. Post-hoc bit selection treats redundancy as an afterthought and ignores the interaction between the selection process and representation learning. A principled mechanism that identifies redundancy during training and reduces it within the network itself is still lacking. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective Neurons Merging Layer (NMLayer) for deep supervised hashing. The key idea is to represent the redundancy relationship between hashing bits with a graph, whose nodes are output neurons and whose edges indicate how redundant two neurons are. This graph is not fixed beforehand. It is learned dynamically and then used to guide the learning of the hashing network. According to the learned graph, the NMLayer merges redundant neurons so that groups of neurons that behave similarly are combined into a single unit. This balances the importance of each output neuron: a piece of semantic information is no longer represented several times and given excessive weight, and the remaining neurons can capture complementary information. To learn the redundancy graph, we design a novel mechanism built on two alternating phases, an active phase and a frozen phase. In the active phase, the graph is updated by observing the relationships among neurons as the network trains, so the estimated redundancy reflects the current state of the representation. In the frozen phase, the graph is fixed, and the network parameters are optimized under the merging structure it defines. Alternating between the two phases lets the redundancy estimate and the feature learning improve each other. It also avoids the instability that would result from changing the graph and the network parameters simultaneously. Moreover, a single merging step is often insufficient to compress a very long, highly redundant code into a compact one without losing information. We therefore stack multiple NMLayers and train them progressively. Starting from a long redundant code, each NMLayer merges a portion of the redundant neurons and reduces the code length step by step, so the network gradually learns a more compact code. This progressive reduction is gentler than directly training a short code, since the network can first exploit the capacity of a long code to learn rich semantics and then condense it. The result is a final hashing code that is shorter and more discriminative than one trained directly at the same length. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: - We propose the Neurons Merging Layer, which explicitly models redundancy between hashing bits with a graph and merges redundant output neurons, thereby balancing the importance of each neuron and improving both storage efficiency and retrieval accuracy. - We introduce a dynamic graph learning mechanism based on active and frozen phases, which estimates redundancy relationships during training while keeping optimization stable. - We develop a progressive training strategy with multiple NMLayers that compresses a long redundant code into a compact one in several stages. - We conduct extensive experiments on four datasets, showing that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art hashing methods, and we provide analyses that verify the effect of each component. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on deep supervised hashing and redundancy reduction. Section 3 describes the proposed NMLayer, the graph learning mechanism, and the progressive training scheme. Section 4 presents experimental results and analysis, and Section 5 concludes the paper. Our method augments a deep hashing network with one or more Neurons Merging Layers (NMLayers). Starting from a long, redundant hash code, each NMLayer progressively merges redundant output neurons according to a learned redundancy graph, producing a shorter and more compact code. Problem Setting and Backbone. Let X = {xi}, i = 1..N, be training images with labels Y = {yi}. Let S = {sij} be the pairwise similarity matrix, where sij = 1 if xi and xj share at least one label and sij = 0 otherwise. A backbone CNN f(·; θ) maps an image to a K-dimensional real-valued output ui = f(xi; θ) ∈ R^K, where K is deliberately larger than the target length. The binary code is bi = sign(ui) ∈ {−1, +1}^K. We use a pairwise likelihood loss on the inner products of the outputs, Ls = −Σ{sij∈S} ( sij Θij − log(1 + e^{Θij}) ), Θij = ½ uiᵀuj, and a quantization loss Lq = Σi ‖ui − sign(ui)‖² that reduces the discretization gap. The base objective is L = Ls + λLq. Redundancy Graph. Redundancy between hash bits is represented by an undirected weighted graph G = (V, E), whose K nodes are the output neurons. The edge weight wkl ∈ [0, 1] measures how redundant neurons k and l are. Two neurons are redundant if they carry similar information about the data, i.e. they produce nearly identical (or opposite) bits for most samples. Over a mini-batch, we compute the empirical correlation of the activations of neurons k and l, ckl = | Σi uik uil | / ( ‖u{·k}‖ ‖u{·l}‖ ), and use it as the instantaneous observation of redundancy. The absolute value is taken because a bit and its negation convey the same information. Rather than relying on a single noisy estimate, the graph is learned dynamically through two alternating phases. Active Phase. In the active phase, the network parameters and graph are both updated. The graph weights are accumulated with a momentum update, wkl ← η wkl + (1 − η) ckl, so the graph aggregates evidence over many mini-batches and tracks the changing representation as training proceeds. Meanwhile, the network is trained with the loss L, so that neurons become discriminative and their relationships grow more meaningful. The active phase lasts for a fixed number of iterations, after which the graph is considered to reflect the current redundancy structure. Frozen Phase. In the frozen phase, the graph is held fixed, and the merging operation derived from it is applied. Freezing prevents the merging structure from changing while the network adapts to it, which would otherwise make training unstable. Only the network weights are fine-tuned, allowing the remaining neurons to compensate for the information of merged ones. After this phase, the next active phase begins if further NMLayers are to be added. Neurons Merging Layer. Given the frozen graph, we group neurons by clustering. We apply a greedy procedure: the edge with the highest weight is selected, and its two endpoints are merged into one group provided the weight exceeds a threshold τ; this is repeated until the desired number K' < K of groups remains. Each group g contains a set of neurons Vg. The NMLayer is a linear layer with a fixed sparse merging matrix M ∈ R^{K'×K}, producing v = M u, Mgk = σk / |Vg| for k ∈ Vg, and 0 otherwise, where σk ∈ {−1, +1} aligns the sign of neuron k with a reference neuron in the group, determined by the sign of their correlation. Thus negatively correlated neurons are flipped before averaging, and averaging combines redundant neurons into a single output. This balances the importance of the outputs: a piece of information that was originally duplicated across several bits is now represented by only one bit, so it no longer dominates the Hamming distance. The merged output v ∈ R^{K'} is then fed into the loss in place of u, and the final code is b = sign(v). To let the merged neurons adjust their contributions, a learnable per-neuron scale can be applied on top of M while preserving its sparsity pattern. Progressive Training with Multiple NMLayers. Directly reducing a very long code to the target length in one step would discard much information at once. Instead, we stack several NMLayers and shrink the code progressively: K = K0 > K1 > … > KT. Training proceeds in stages. In stage t, we (1) run an active phase on the current network to learn the graph over K{t−1} neurons, (2) construct the NMLayer that merges them into Kt neurons and insert it after the current output, and (3) run a frozen phase to fine-tune the network with the new layer. The loss at each stage is computed on the output of the most recently added NMLayer. After T stages, the network produces a compact KT-bit code distilled from the long redundant code. Because earlier merging decisions are fixed, later stages operate on already-consolidated bits, and the graph learned at each stage reflects the residual redundancy. Optimization and Inference. The network is optimized with mini-batch stochastic gradient descent with backpropagation. The sign function is relaxed during training, with its gradient approximated as identity (or tanh smoothing), so that the quantization loss and the pairwise loss are differentiable. The merging matrices are not updated by gradients except for the optional scale parameters. Graph updates require only a K×K correlation computation per mini-batch, adding negligible cost. At test time, a query image is passed through the backbone and all NMLayers, binarized with sign, and compared to database codes by Hamming distance. Since the NMLayers are linear, they add no meaningful inference overhead, and the final code length is KT bits. We evaluate the proposed NMLayer on four widely used image retrieval benchmarks and compare it with state-of-the-art shallow and deep hashing methods. Retrieval quality is measured by mean average precision (mAP) at several code lengths, along with precision-recall curves and precision@top-k curves. Unless stated otherwise, all numbers are averaged over five runs with different random seeds. Comparison with state-of-the-art methods. Table 1 reports mAP for code lengths of 12, 24, 32, and 48 bits. Our method achieves the best mAP in nearly all settings across the four datasets. On CIFAR-10, NMLayer improves over the strongest competing deep hashing baseline by 1.8, 2.1, 2.4, and 2.2 points at 12, 24, 32, and 48 bits respectively. The gains are larger on the more challenging multi-label datasets such as NUS-WIDE and MS-COCO, where average improvements of 2–4 points are observed. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic, heterogeneous autoimmune disease characterized by the production of autoantibodies and immune-complex deposition, which can involve virtually any organ system. It predominantly affects women of childbearing age, and its incidence and prevalence vary substantially across ethnic groups and geographic regions [1,2]. Reported prevalence is higher in people of Asian, African, and Hispanic ancestry than in those of European ancestry, and disease in these populations is often more severe, with more frequent renal involvement and greater damage accrual [3,4]. In China, the estimated prevalence of SLE is among the highest in the world, at approximately 30 to 70 per 100,000 people, implying that more than one million Chinese people may be living with the disease [5,6]. SLE is associated with an increased risk of death compared with the general population. Standardized mortality ratios reported in cohorts from Europe, North America, and Asia typically range from 2 to 5, with the greatest excess observed in young patients and in those with renal disease [7,8]. Survival has improved markedly over the past six decades. Five-year survival was below 50% in the 1950s, rose to approximately 80–90% in the 1970s and 1980s, and exceeds 90% in many contemporary series [9,10]. This improvement is generally attributed to earlier diagnosis, including recognition of milder disease, more effective use of glucocorticoids and immunosuppressive agents, better management of lupus nephritis, improved dialysis and transplantation services, and advances in the prevention and treatment of infection and of comorbid conditions [10,11]. Nonetheless, several reports suggest that the gains in survival have plateaued since the 1990s, and that mortality in SLE remains clearly higher than expected [12,13]. The causes of death in SLE have also changed over time. A bimodal pattern of mortality was described in early studies, in which early deaths were attributed to active lupus and infection, and late deaths to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease [14]. In Western cohorts, cardiovascular disease, malignancy, and infection now account for a large proportion of deaths, whereas death from active disease, particularly renal failure, has declined [8,15]. Comparatively little is known about whether this pattern applies in Asian populations. Studies from Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand suggest that infection and active lupus remain leading causes of death, whereas cardiovascular death appears less common [16–18]. Differences in genetic background, disease phenotype, treatment practices, health care access, and the prevalence of infectious diseases such as tuberculosis may all contribute to such variation [4,19]. Despite the very large population of patients, long-term prognosis of SLE in China has not been well summarized. Systematic registries and national surveillance of SLE only began to develop in recent years, and most available information comes from single-center hospital cohorts of varying size, design, and period. Many of these reports were published in Chinese-language journals and are not easily accessible to international readers, and they are rarely captured by the search strategies of previous meta-analyses, which have focused on English-language literature [9,20]. Consequently, existing global estimates of SLE survival and mortality draw on limited data from mainland China, even though the Chinese population accounts for a substantial fraction of all patients with SLE worldwide. Individual Chinese studies report heterogeneous survival rates, in part because of differences in referral patterns, severity of disease at enrollment, calendar period, and duration of follow-up. Pooling these data can offer more precise and generalizable estimates. Likewise, data on the causes of death in Chinese patients with SLE are scattered across case series and cohort studies, many of which are small and use different classification schemes. Understanding the distribution of causes of death is of practical importance, because it can identify targets for intervention and guide the allocation of clinical resources. For example, if infection is the dominant cause of death, strategies such as vaccination, prophylaxis, judicious use of glucocorticoids and immunosuppressants, and early detection of opportunistic infection may be prioritized. If cardiovascular disease is relatively uncommon in this population, or is likely to become more important as survival lengthens, preventive strategies would need to be adapted accordingly [21]. Comparing the causes of death in China with those reported elsewhere may also shed light on the influence of ethnicity, environment, and treatment approach on lupus outcomes. Given these gaps, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies published in English and Chinese. Our first objective was to estimate the pooled 5-year and 10-year survival rates of Chinese patients with SLE from cohort studies, and to compare them with estimates from other Asia-Pacific and Western populations. Our second objective was to describe the distribution of causes of death among Chinese patients with SLE by synthesizing cohort studies and case series, and to explore how this distribution differs from that reported in other regions. We hope that these findings will provide a more complete picture of the contemporary prognosis of SLE in China and will inform clinical practice and future research. This systematic review was designed and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement [1] and the Meta-analysis of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (MOOSE) guidelines [2]. Because the analysis used only published data, ethical approval and informed consent were not required. Search strategy We searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), WANFANG, and SINOMED from database inception to December 2013. English and non-English (Chinese) articles were eligible. The principal search terms were "systemic lupus erythematosus" or "SLE", combined with "follow-up", "prognosis", "survival", "mortality", "death", and "China" or "Chinese". Medical Subject Headings and free-text terms were combined with Boolean operators, and the strategy was adapted to the indexing system of each database. Additional studies were identified by consulting clinical experts, screening the reference lists of selected papers and relevant reviews, and searching related Chinese textbooks of rheumatology and internal medicine. Eligibility criteria For the survival analysis, we included cohort studies that enrolled Chinese patients with SLE diagnosed according to the American College of Rheumatology classification criteria [3,4] or the Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics criteria [5], and that reported survival rates at 5 and/or 10 years, or provided data allowing their calculation (number of patients, number of deaths, and follow-up duration). Studies from mainland China, Hong Kong, and Taiwan were considered. For the death-cause analysis, both cohort studies and case series were eligible if they reported the number of deaths and the distribution of causes of death among Chinese patients with SLE. We excluded studies restricted to special subpopulations (e.g., pediatric-onset only, pregnancy-only, or single-organ involvement such as lupus nephritis alone) when these would bias survival estimates, case reports, reviews, conference abstracts without sufficient data, and studies with fewer than 10 deaths for cause analysis. When several publications reported on overlapping populations from the same center, the report with the largest sample or longest follow-up was retained. Study selection and data extraction Two authors independently screened titles and abstracts, then assessed full texts of potentially eligible articles. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or by consulting a third reviewer. Two authors independently extracted data using a predesigned chart covering: (1) study characteristics (first author, publication year, region, setting, design, recruitment period, and follow-up duration); (2) clinical data (sample size, sex ratio, age at onset, disease duration, diagnostic criteria, and treatment); (3) analytic data (number of deaths, 5- and 10-year survival rates and confidence intervals, standardized mortality ratios where available, and the numbers of deaths attributed to each cause); and (4) study quality indicators. Causes of death were harmonized into categories: infection, renal involvement, lupus encephalopathy (neuropsychiatric lupus), cardiovascular disease, pulmonary involvement (including pulmonary hemorrhage and pulmonary hypertension), hematologic involvement, gastrointestinal involvement, malignancy, and others. Where original authors used different labels, categories were assigned by consensus based on the descriptions provided. Quality assessment Methodological quality of cohort studies was assessed using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale [6], evaluating representativeness of the cohort, ascertainment of outcome, adequacy and completeness of follow-up, and comparability. For case series, we used items adapted from quality criteria for case series [7], including clear definition of the population, consecutive enrollment, explicit criteria for attributing cause of death, and the source of death information (medical records, death certificates, or autopsy). Quality scores were used descriptively and in sensitivity analyses rather than as exclusion criteria. Statistical analysis Survival rates at 5 and 10 years were pooled as proportions. Because proportions near 1 produce skewed distributions and unstable variance, rates were transformed using the Freeman–Tukey double arcsine transformation before pooling and back-transformed for presentation [8]. When studies reported survival only as a Kaplan–Meier curve, rates were read from the curve at the specified time points. Likewise, the proportion of deaths attributable to each cause was pooled from the number of deaths with that cause divided by the total number of observed deaths in each study. All pooled analyses were performed using both random-effects (DerSimonian–Laird) [9] and fixed-effects (inverse variance) models, and results from both are reported to allow assessment of robustness. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran's Q test and the I² statistic, with I² values above 50% considered substantial [10]. Sources of heterogeneity were explored by sensitivity analysis, in which each study was omitted in turn to evaluate its influence on the pooled estimates, and by restricting analyses to higher-quality studies. For the death-cause analysis, we additionally performed prespecified subgroup comparisons by region (mainland China versus Hong Kong/Taiwan) and by period of observation (before versus after 2000), where data permitted. Potential publication bias was examined by visual inspection of funnel plots and by Egger's regression test [11], with P < 0.10 indicating possible asymmetry. Given the small number of survival studies, these tests were interpreted cautiously. The pooled survival rates were qualitatively compared with those reported from other Asia-Pacific countries and from Western cohorts identified in prior publications. All tests were two-sided, with P < 0.05 considered statistically significant unless otherwise stated. Analyses were conducted using Stata (version 12.0; StataCorp, College Station, TX) and Review Manager (version 5.2; The Cochrane Collaboration). A total of 2,846 records were initially identified through database searching (MEDLINE, EMBASE, CNKI, WANFANG, and SINOMED), and an additional 37 records were obtained through expert consultation, reference lists, and textbooks. After removal of duplicates and screening of titles and abstracts, 214 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Five cohort studies met the criteria for survival analysis [1–5], and 36 studies (cohort studies and case series) were suitable for death-cause analysis [6–41]. The main reasons for exclusion were lack of survival data, insufficient follow-up information, overlapping patient populations, and absence of specified causes of death. Characteristics of included studies The five survival studies comprised 4,469 Chinese patients with SLE and 380 observed deaths. They were conducted in mainland China, Hong Kong, and Taiwan, and patient disease onset ranged from 1995 to 2013. Sample sizes ranged from several hundred to more than 1,500 patients. All studies were hospital-based or registry-based cohorts, and the majority of patients were women. Study quality assessment indicated generally adequate representativeness and outcome ascertainment, although loss to follow-up was incompletely reported in two cohorts. The 36 death-cause studies included 2,179 observed deaths derived from more than 20,000 patients with SLE. These were mostly single-center series published in Chinese-language journals, covering periods from the 1980s to the 2010s. Pooled survival rates The overall pooled 5-year survival rate after disease onset was 94% (95% CI, 92%–96%) under the random-effects model, and the fixed-effects estimate was similar. The pooled 10-year survival rate was 89% (95% CI, 85%–92%) under the random-effects model, with a comparable fixed-effects result. Heterogeneity was moderate for the 5-year estimate and more pronounced for the 10-year estimate, probably reflecting differences in region, period of recruitment, and care setting. Survival in the cohorts from more recent decades tended to be higher than in earlier cohorts, although the small number of studies precluded formal meta-regression. Publication bias and sensitivity analysis Funnel plots for the survival analyses were approximately symmetrical, and Egger regression tests did not suggest significant publication bias (P > 0.05 for both 5- and 10-year survival), although the small number of studies limited the power of these tests. Composite resins have become the material of choice for direct restorations in anterior and posterior teeth, owing to their esthetic properties, adhesive capability, and conservative cavity preparation requirements [1,2]. Despite continuous improvements in filler technology and monomer chemistry, the clinical longevity of resin-based restorations remains limited, with fracture, marginal degradation, and secondary caries identified as the principal causes of failure [3,4]. These failures are closely linked to the extent of polymerization achieved at placement and to the ability of the material to resist degradation in the oral environment over time. Polymerization, radiant exposure, and material properties Light-activated composite resins undergo free-radical polymerization initiated by photosensitizers, most commonly camphorquinone, in the presence of an amine co-initiator [5]. The degree of conversion (DC), defined as the percentage of aliphatic carbon–carbon double bonds converted into single bonds, is a key determinant of the physical, mechanical, and biological behavior of the polymer network. Incomplete conversion is associated with reduced stiffness and strength, greater water uptake, and increased elution of unreacted monomers, with potential consequences for biocompatibility and durability [6,7]. The energy delivered to the material, expressed as radiant exposure (J/cm²) and calculated as the product of irradiance and exposure time, is the principal clinical variable controlling the amount of photons available to activate the initiator system [8]. Although manufacturers typically recommend 20–40 s exposure at approximately 400–1000 mW/cm², the literature offers no consensus regarding the minimum radiant exposure required for adequate properties. Values ranging from approximately 6 to 24 J/cm² have been proposed, depending on the composite shade, translucency, filler content, increment thickness, and the property being evaluated [9–11]. Furthermore, the reciprocity between irradiance and exposure time is not absolute, since high irradiance with short exposure can alter network formation, increase polymerization stress, and yield a less homogeneous polymer [12]. The development of high-output light-curing units and of reduced-time protocols has made the question of minimum radiant exposure increasingly relevant to clinical practice. Filler technology Composite resins are commonly classified according to filler particle size and distribution. Micro-hybrid composites contain a blend of particles of different dimensions, generally in the range of 0.4–1 µm, providing high filler loading and good mechanical properties [13]. Nanofilled composites incorporate discrete nanometric particles and nanoclusters, improving polish retention and esthetics while maintaining acceptable strength [14]. These differences in filler size, load, and silane coupling influence light scattering and penetration, the mobility of the monomer, and the filler–matrix interface, and consequently may alter both the response to radiant exposure and the susceptibility to degradation [15]. Comparative information on how these two classes respond to different energy levels, particularly in the long term, remains scarce. Aging and hydrolytic degradation In the oral cavity, restorations are subjected to water, enzymes, temperature fluctuations, masticatory loading, and exposure to radiation from ambient and therapeutic sources. Water diffuses into the polymer network, causing plasticization, swelling, hydrolysis of ester bonds in the matrix, and degradation of the filler–matrix interface, along with leaching of unreacted components [16,17]. Water sorption (WS) and solubility (WL) are therefore widely used as indicators of network integrity and of the hydrolytic stability of composites [18]. Because these processes occur over years, laboratory studies rely on accelerated aging protocols such as thermocycling, prolonged water storage, and artificial weathering with ultraviolet (UV) light and condensation [19]. UV-accelerated aging combines photo-oxidative and hydrothermal stresses that may promote chain scission, additional crosslinking, surface cracking, and filler debonding, and it has been used to simulate long-term changes in color and mechanical behavior [20,21]. However, the effects of such aging on the physico-chemical and mechanical properties of composites cured with different radiant exposures have not been thoroughly investigated. Rationale and objective Most studies on radiant exposure examine properties immediately or shortly after polymerization, while aging studies usually employ a single curing protocol. As a consequence, it remains unclear whether a deficiency in initial energy delivery persists, is attenuated, or is exacerbated after prolonged aging, and whether initially superior properties obtained with higher radiant exposure are maintained over time. Additionally, it is uncertain whether the relation between radiant exposure and hydrolytic degradation differs between micro-hybrid and nanofilled materials. Clarifying these questions may help establish evidence-based curing recommendations that favor long-term clinical performance. Therefore, the objective of this study was to evaluate the effect of radiant exposure (3.75, 9, and 24 J/cm²) and UV-accelerated aging (0, 500, 1000, and 1500 h) on the degree of conversion, flexural strength, modulus, water sorption, and solubility of a micro-hybrid and a nanofilled composite resin. The null hypotheses tested were that neither radiant exposure nor accelerated aging time would significantly affect these properties, and that the response would not differ between the two composite resins. Experimental design Two commercial light-cured resin composites were investigated: a nanofilled composite (Filtek Supreme, shade A2B, 3M ESPE, St. Paul, MN, USA) and a micro-hybrid composite (Filtek Z250, shade A2, 3M ESPE). The study followed a 3 × 4 factorial design for each material, with radiant exposure (3.75, 9, and 24 J/cm²) and UV accelerated aging time (0, 500, 1000, and 1500 h) as the independent variables. The response variables were degree of conversion (DC), flexural strength (FS), flexural modulus (M), water sorption (WS), and solubility (WL). Specimens were randomly allocated to the experimental groups (n = 10 per group for FS and M, n = 5 for DC, and n = 10 for WS and WL). Sample size was based on previous studies using similar protocols [1,2]. Light-curing and radiant exposure A quartz-tungsten-halogen/LED unit (specify model) was used for photoactivation. Irradiance was measured before each specimen-preparation session using a calibrated radiometer and verified with a spectrometer-based power meter placed at the specimen surface distance. The irradiance was approximately 600 mW/cm². Radiant exposure (J/cm²) was calculated as the product of irradiance (W/cm²) and exposure time (s). The three radiant exposures were obtained by varying the exposure time: 6 s (3.75 J/cm²), 15 s (9 J/cm²), and 40 s (24 J/cm²). The tip of the light guide was positioned in contact with the Mylar strip covering the specimen. For bar-shaped specimens, the tip was applied in overlapping sections to cover the entire length, and each section received the nominal exposure [3]. Specimen preparation Bar-shaped specimens (25 × 2 × 2 mm) for FS and M were fabricated in a stainless-steel split mold in accordance with ISO 4049 [4]. The composite was inserted in a single increment, covered with a polyester strip and a glass slide to extrude excess material, and light-cured as described above. Disc-shaped specimens (6 mm diameter × 1 mm thickness) for WS, WL, and DC were prepared in a similar manner. After removal from the molds, specimens were examined and any with visible voids or flaws were discarded. All specimens were stored dry in light-proof containers at 37 °C for 24 h before aging or testing. UV accelerated aging Specimens were subjected to accelerated aging in a UV weathering chamber (e.g., QUV, Q-Lab) in accordance with ASTM G154 [5]. Cycles consisted of 8 h of UV exposure at 60 °C using UVB-313 lamps, followed by 4 h of condensation at 50 °C. Specimens were placed with the irradiated surface facing the lamps, and their positions were rotated periodically to ensure uniform exposure. Aging durations were 500, 1000, and 1500 h. Control specimens (0 h) were not exposed to the chamber and were stored dry at 37 °C. After aging, specimens were kept in dry conditions until testing, except for WS and WL analyses. Degree of conversion DC was determined by Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy with attenuated total reflectance (FTIR-ATR). Spectra of uncured material were obtained by placing a small amount of composite on the diamond crystal. Spectra of cured specimens were collected from the top surface of the discs at 32 scans and 4 cm⁻¹ resolution over 400–4000 cm⁻¹. DC was calculated from the ratio of the aliphatic C=C absorbance peak (1638 cm⁻¹) to the internal reference aromatic C=C peak (1608 cm⁻¹) in cured and uncured states [6]: DC (%) = [1 − (Rcured / Runcured)] × 100, where R is the ratio of the aliphatic to aromatic peak intensities. For aged groups, DC was measured after the corresponding aging period, as an index of the residual unsaturation and structural change of the aged network. Flexural strength and modulus Flexural strength and flexural modulus were assessed by a three-point bending test in a universal testing machine (e.g., EMIC DL 2000) with a 20 mm span and a crosshead speed of 0.5 mm/min until fracture. Specimen dimensions were measured with a digital caliper (0.01 mm accuracy). FS (MPa) was calculated as FS = 3Fl / 2bh², where F is the maximum load (N), l the span (mm), b the specimen width (mm), and h its height (mm). Flexural modulus (GPa) was calculated from the slope of the linear elastic portion of the load–displacement curve: M = F₁l³ / 4bh³d, where F₁ is the load at a point in the linear region and d the corresponding deflection [4]. Tests were performed at room temperature. Water sorption and solubility WS and WL were evaluated according to ISO 4049 [4]. Discs were placed in a desiccator containing silica gel at 37 °C and weighed daily on an analytical balance (0.0001 g precision) until a constant mass (m₁) was achieved. Diameter and thickness were measured to calculate volume (V). Specimens were then immersed in distilled water at 37 °C for 7 days, blotted dry, and weighed (m₂). They were then reconditioned in the desiccator until constant mass (m₃). WS and WL (µg/mm³) were calculated as: WS = (m₂ − m₃)/V; WL = (m₁ − m₃)/V. The test was conducted on specimens of each aging time and radiant exposure. Statistical analysis Data were checked for normality (Shapiro–Wilk) and homogeneity of variances (Levene). For each composite and each response variable, two-way ANOVA was used with radiant exposure and aging time as factors, including their interaction. Pairwise comparisons were conducted with Tukey's post hoc test. All analyses were performed at a significance level of α = 0.05 using standard statistical software. Degree of conversion Two-way ANOVA showed that radiant exposure, accelerated aging time, and their interaction significantly affected DC for both the micro-hybrid (Filtek Z250) and the nanofilled (Filtek Supreme) composite (p<0.05). In the non-aged groups (0 h), DC increased progressively with radiant exposure. Specimens cured at 3.75 J/cm² had significantly lower DC than those cured at 9 and 24 J/cm² (p<0.05) for both materials. For Z250, DC rose from approximately 52% at 3.75 J/cm² to approximately 60% at 24 J/cm². For Filtek Supreme, DC rose from approximately 48% to approximately 57% over the same range. The difference between 9 and 24 J/cm² was smaller and reached significance only for the nanofilled material. After UV aging (500, 1000, and 1500 h), the relationship between DC and radiant exposure was lost. Within each aging period, DC values did not differ consistently among radiant exposures (p>0.05). Aging produced a general increase in DC relative to the 0 h condition, which was most evident in specimens cured at the lowest radiant exposure. As a result, the initial differences among radiant exposure groups were reduced or eliminated. DC then remained stable or changed only slightly between 500 and 1500 h. Across aging periods, Filtek Supreme tended to show lower DC than Z250, although this difference was not significant in all conditions. Flexural strength FS was significantly influenced by radiant exposure, aging time, and their interaction for both composites (p<0.05). In the non-aged condition, FS was lowest at 3.75 J/cm² and increased at higher radiant exposures. Z250 showed values of roughly 110–140 MPa, and Filtek Supreme showed slightly lower values. Increases from 3.75 to 9 J/cm² were significant for both materials, whereas the further increase to 24 J/cm² was significant only for Z250. Aging had a marked effect on FS. After 500 h of UV aging, FS decreased significantly relative to baseline in most groups (p<0.05). Plants adjust their development to seasonal change, and the timing of flowering is among the most consequential of these adjustments. Flowering at an appropriate time maximizes reproductive success and, in crops, determines yield and geographic range. Day length (photoperiod) and temperature are the two principal seasonal cues, and their integration allows plants to distinguish, for example, a warm autumn from a spring of similar day length [1,2]. In the facultative long-day plant Arabidopsis thaliana, long photoperiods accelerate flowering through the transcriptional induction of FLOWERING LOCUS T (FT), which encodes the florigen produced in leaf vascular tissue and transported to the shoot apical meristem [3,4]. There, FT interacts with the bZIP transcription factor FD to activate floral identity genes such as SOC1 and APETALA1 [5,6]. The photoperiodic regulation of FT is mediated largely by CONSTANS (CO), a B-box zinc finger transcriptional activator [7,8]. CO transcription is controlled by the circadian clock through GIGANTEA (GI) and the FLAVIN-BINDING, KELCH REPEAT, F-BOX 1 (FKF1) protein, which together degrade CYCLING DOF FACTOR repressors in the afternoon [9,10]. Equally important is post-translational regulation. CO protein is destabilized in darkness by the E3 ubiquitin ligase CONSTITUTIVE PHOTOMORPHOGENIC 1 (COP1) in complex with SUPPRESSOR OF PHYA-105 (SPA) proteins, and is stabilized in light by photoreceptors, with blue light-sensing cryptochromes and FKF1 and far-red light-sensing phytochrome A (phyA) counteracting COP1 activity, while phytochrome B (phyB) promotes CO degradation in the morning [11–14]. This "external coincidence" mechanism restricts CO accumulation to the end of long days, when FT is induced at dusk [7,15]. Light quality also modulates flowering. Reduced red/far-red (R/FR) ratios, as occur in canopy shade, inactivate phyB and accelerate flowering, whereas phyA mediates FR-dependent promotion of flowering [16,17]. The evening component of the circadian clock, including EARLY FLOWERING 3 (ELF3), a component of the Evening Complex, represses FT directly and indirectly by controlling GI and PHYTOCHROME INTERACTING FACTOR 4 (PIF4) [18–20]. Temperature adds a further layer: warm ambient temperatures promote flowering through PIF4 and the florigen FT, and the Evening Complex acts as a temperature-responsive regulator of gene expression [21–23]. Prolonged cold, meanwhile, silences the floral repressor FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC) through vernalization, which ensures flowering after winter [24]. Much of this knowledge derives from laboratory experiments performed under highly simplified conditions: constant temperature, abrupt light-dark transitions, light provided by fluorescent or white LED sources with a high R/FR ratio, and photoperiods that are fixed rather than changing. Under such conditions, FT expression in long days typically shows a prominent peak at dusk, about 12–16 h after dawn, consistent with the external coincidence model [7,25]. Yet natural environments differ substantially. Light intensity and spectrum change gradually at dawn and dusk, with lowered R/FR ratios during twilight; temperatures fluctuate daily and seasonally; and plants experience combinations of cues that are rarely reproduced in growth chambers [26,27]. Studies in the field have shown that gene expression, including that of flowering genes, can differ strikingly from laboratory patterns, and that laboratory-derived models can fail to predict flowering time in nature [28–30]. For instance, FT expression in field-grown Arabidopsis and in rice has been reported to show profiles and levels that cannot be explained by laboratory responses to single environmental variables [29,31]. These observations highlight a gap between mechanistic understanding gained in controlled environments and the regulation operating in natural seasons. Closing this gap requires both characterizing molecular responses in natural environments and identifying which environmental parameters are sufficient to reproduce them under controlled conditions. Field experiments, although informative, are difficult to replicate and genetically dissect because many variables change simultaneously. If key parameters can be identified and incorporated into laboratory conditions, it would be possible to apply the full power of Arabidopsis genetics and molecular biology to seasonal responses [32]. Here we examined FT expression in Arabidopsis grown outdoors in natural long days in spring and found that FT peaks in the morning, in addition to a smaller dusk peak, a pattern distinct from that seen under standard laboratory long days. We then asked which environmental features account for this difference. We found that supplementing growth conditions with a R/FR ratio similar to that of open fields, together with a daily temperature oscillation, is sufficient to reproduce both the morning FT expression and the flowering time observed in nature. Using these adjusted conditions, we analyzed the contributions of light signaling components and show that phyA and ELF3 are important for morning FT induction. Finally, we show that these conditions stabilize CO protein in the morning, suggesting that morning CO accumulation is a critical mechanism underlying photoperiodic flowering in nature. Our results demonstrate that modest refinements of standard growth conditions can reveal regulatory mechanisms relevant to natural environments and provide a framework for studying seasonal responses in the laboratory. Plant materials and growth conditions Arabidopsis thaliana accession Columbia-0 (Col-0) was used as the wild type. The mutants and transgenic lines used were phyA-211, elf3-4, co-10, ft-10, and pFT::GUS, as well as lines expressing CO under its native promoter (pCO::HA-CO) in the co-10 background [1-4]. Seeds were surface sterilized, stratified at 4°C in the dark for 3 days, and sown on half-strength Murashige and Skoog medium containing 0.8% agar and 1% sucrose, or on soil as indicated. Plants were grown in controlled-environment chambers (Percival) under long days (16 h light/8 h dark). Standard laboratory conditions (LD) consisted of constant 22°C and white fluorescent light of approximately 100 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ with a red/far-red (R:FR) ratio of about 6-7. Adjusted conditions (termed "natural-like" long days, NLD) used white light supplemented with far-red LEDs to reduce the R:FR ratio to about 1.0-1.2, matching open-field measurements, and a daily temperature oscillation that tracked field measurements (minimum 12°C before dawn, maximum 22°C in the afternoon, with gradual ramping). Photon flux density was kept equal between conditions. Light spectra were measured with a spectroradiometer (Apogee SS-110) at plant height, and temperature was verified with data loggers placed at rosette level. Field sampling Plants of Col-0 were grown outdoors at the field site in spring (March-May) after germination in the greenhouse and transfer outdoors at the seedling stage. Aerial parts of 10-15 plants were pooled per sample and harvested every 4 h over 24 h on selected days with day lengths of approximately 12-15 h. Samples were immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen. Light intensity, R:FR ratio, and air temperature were recorded concurrently with a quantum sensor, spectroradiometer, and temperature logger. Three biological replicates were collected from independent days or independent plant pools. Flowering time measurement Flowering time was scored as the number of rosette leaves at bolting and as days to bolting (first visible inflorescence of 1 cm). At least 15 plants per genotype and condition were scored in each of three independent experiments. Plants were randomized within chambers and rotated weekly to minimize positional effects. Statistical differences were evaluated by one-way ANOVA with Tukey's post hoc test or Student's t-test as appropriate (P < 0.05). RNA extraction and quantitative RT-PCR Seedlings (10-day-old unless noted) were harvested at the indicated Zeitgeber times (ZT) and frozen in liquid nitrogen. Total RNA was extracted using a Plant RNeasy kit (Qiagen) with on-column DNase I treatment. One microgram of RNA was reverse transcribed with oligo(dT) and SuperScript III (Invitrogen). Quantitative PCR was performed using SYBR Green master mix on a CFX96 real-time system (Bio-Rad). Transcript levels of FT, CO, GI, PIF4, and clock genes were normalized to PROTEIN PHOSPHATASE 2A SUBUNIT A3 (PP2AA3) or ISOPENTENYL PYROPHOSPHATE:DIMETHYLALLYL PYROPHOSPHATE ISOMERASE 2 (IPP2) [5]. Relative expression was calculated by the 2^−ΔΔCt method. Primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 1. Each experiment included three biological replicates with technical triplicates. Histochemical GUS staining Seedlings carrying pFT::GUS were fixed in 90% acetone, washed, and incubated in X-Gluc solution (1 mM X-Gluc, 50 mM sodium phosphate pH 7.0, 0.5 mM potassium ferricyanide/ferrocyanide, 0.1% Triton X-100) at 37°C for a fixed duration, cleared in 70% ethanol, and imaged with a stereomicroscope. Protein extraction and immunoblot analysis Seedlings were harvested at the indicated time points and ground in liquid nitrogen. Total proteins were extracted in buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 0.1% Nonidet P-40, 1 mM PMSF, 50 µM MG132, and a protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche). Extracts were cleared by centrifugation at 14,000 g for 10 min at 4°C. Equal amounts of protein were separated by 8% SDS-PAGE, transferred to PVDF membranes, and probed with anti-HA-peroxidase (Roche, 3F10) for HA-CO.
