Deep learning has achieved remarkable success in image recognition, speech recognition, and natural language processing, largely because multilayered neural networks can acquire hierarchical representations of input patterns [1], [2]. Among these models, the Deep Belief Network (DBN) is a representative generative architecture in which Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) are stacked and pre-trained layer by layer in an unsupervised manner [3], [4]. The greedy layer-wise pre-training provides good initial parameters for subsequent supervised fine-tuning and alleviates difficulties such as vanishing gradients and poor local minima in deep networks [4], [5]. The RBM, a two-layer stochastic network with visible and hidden neurons, is trained efficiently with contrastive divergence (CD) [6], and DBNs built on it have shown strong performance on benchmarks such as MNIST and CIFAR-10 [3], [7]. Despite these advantages, the performance of RBMs and DBNs depends strongly on the network structure, namely the number of hidden neurons in each RBM and the number of layers in the DBN. These quantities are usually fixed in advance by trial and error, grid search, or the experience of the designer [8]. If the network is too small, it cannot represent the distribution of the input space; if it is too large, it suffers from overfitting, redundant neurons, and unnecessary computational cost. Because a conventional RBM or DBN cannot change its structure during learning, the designer must train many candidate models, which is expensive for large data sets. Methods such as random search and Bayesian optimization of hyperparameters [9], [10] reduce this burden, but they still treat the structure as an external setting rather than as something the model itself acquires from data. Adaptive structure learning has long been studied for neural networks. Constructive approaches such as cascade correlation [11] grow a network by adding units, whereas pruning approaches such as optimal brain damage [12] remove unimportant connections from a large network. For energy-based models, several works have proposed adding or removing hidden units of RBMs according to training progress [13], [14], and nonparametric formulations have been explored as well [15]. However, most of these studies address only a single RBM, and the determination of an appropriate depth for a DBN has received comparatively little attention. Since the representational power of a DBN is closely related to its depth, a mechanism that decides when a new layer is required is of considerable importance. In our previous research, we proposed an adaptive structural learning method of RBM, which we call Adaptive RBM [16]. This method monitors the energy-based learning state during training and automatically generates a new hidden neuron when the existing neurons are insufficient to represent the input patterns, detected through the fluctuation of the network parameters. Neurons that are found to be unnecessary are removed by a neuron annihilation procedure. As a result, the model can discover a suitable number of hidden neurons according to the complexity of the input space, without requiring prior knowledge. Experimental results indicated that the Adaptive RBM achieved higher generalization capability than a conventional RBM with a fixed number of hidden neurons on several benchmark data sets [16]. A further issue is the interpretability and sparseness of trained networks. Deep models are often regarded as black boxes, and extracting explicit knowledge from a trained network requires that its structure be compact and its connections sparse [17], [18]. Regularization approaches, including weight decay and L1 penalties, are common ways to encourage sparsity [19]. The Learning Forgetting method [20] is another approach, in which weights that make little contribution are gradually decayed so that only essential connections remain, thereby producing a skeletal structure suitable for rule extraction. We then developed a hybrid method that combines the Adaptive RBM with Learning Forgetting, which reduced redundant connections while maintaining the ability to represent the input data [21]. Nevertheless, this hybrid method was limited to a single RBM and did not address how multiple RBMs should be stacked into a deep architecture. In this paper, we propose an adaptive learning method of DBN that determines the optimal number of layers during learning by means of a layer generation algorithm. The proposed method first trains an Adaptive RBM on the input data. When the trained RBM cannot sufficiently represent the data, as judged by the remaining reconstruction error or the energy-based criterion on the hidden representation, a new RBM is generated and stacked on top of the current network, using the hidden activations of the lower layer as its input. Layer generation continues until no further improvement is obtained, so that the depth of the DBN is decided automatically from the data rather than predefined. Because each layer also adjusts its own number of hidden neurons and, with the Learning Forgetting method, its own sparse connections, the resulting DBN is expected to have a compact structure with moderate computational cost and good model stability. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows. First, we present a layer generation algorithm that extends the adaptive structural learning of RBM to a DBN with a self-organized depth. Second, we integrate the algorithm with the neuron generation and annihilation mechanism and the Learning Forgetting method, so that the numbers of neurons, weights, and layers are all determined adaptively. Third, we evaluate the proposed model on benchmark data sets and compare it with conventional DBNs having fixed structures, examining classification accuracy, network size, and the effect of the generated layers. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the RBM, the DBN, and the adaptive structural learning method with Learning Forgetting. Section 3 describes the proposed layer generation algorithm. Section 4 presents the experimental settings and results. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper and discusses future work. The proposed method builds on the adaptive structural learning of the Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) and extends it to the Deep Belief Network (DBN) by adding a layer generation mechanism. The method has three components: (1) adaptive RBM learning, which adjusts the number of hidden neurons during training; (2) the Learning Forgetting method, which sparsifies the trained weights; and (3) the layer generation algorithm, which stacks new RBMs on the existing network until no further improvement is obtained. 1. Restricted Boltzmann Machine An RBM is an undirected bipartite graphical model with a visible layer v ∈ {0,1}^I and a hidden layer h ∈ {0,1}^J. Its energy function is E(v,h) = −Σi bi vi − Σj cj hj − Σ{i,j} vi Wij hj, where bi and cj are the visible and hidden biases and Wij is the connection weight. The joint distribution is p(v,h) = exp(−E(v,h))/Z, where Z is the partition function. Because of the bipartite structure, the conditional distributions factorize: p(hj=1|v) = σ(cj + Σi Wij vi), p(vi=1|h) = σ(bi + Σj Wij hj), with σ the logistic sigmoid. Parameters are trained by approximately maximizing the log-likelihood with contrastive divergence (CD) [1]. For one training pattern, the updates are ΔWij = η(⟨vi hj⟩data − ⟨vi hj⟩recon), with analogous rules for the biases, where η is the learning rate. 2. Adaptive structural learning of RBM In a standard RBM, the number of hidden neurons is fixed beforehand. Our adaptive method monitors the training state and changes the number of hidden neurons during learning, following the neuron generation and annihilation scheme [2]. The monitored quantity is the variance of the weight-update magnitude, which indicates whether the current capacity is sufficient. Neuron generation. Let the training error be the mean squared reconstruction error, and let its change over a fixed window of epochs be tracked. If the error stops decreasing while it remains above a tolerance, the network is judged to have insufficient representational capacity. A new hidden neuron is then inserted. Its weights are initialized with small random values, and its bias is set to zero. Insertion is repeated at most once per monitoring window, so that the effect of each new neuron can be observed before another is added. Neuron annihilation. After the generation phase, the activation probability of each hidden neuron is averaged over the training set. Neurons whose average activation is persistently close to zero or close to one contribute little information, because their outputs are almost independent of the input. Such neurons are removed together with their connections. This step prevents overgrowth and keeps the computational cost low. The resulting procedure ends when the reconstruction error falls below a predefined threshold or the maximum number of epochs is reached. The number of hidden neurons is thus determined by the input space rather than set manually. 3. Learning Forgetting method The explicit extraction of knowledge from a trained network requires sparse connectivity. We therefore apply the Learning Forgetting method [3] to the trained RBM, as in our previous work. A penalty term that drives weights toward zero is added to the learning objective, which yields the update ΔWij = η(⟨vi hj⟩data − ⟨vi hj⟩recon) − κ·sgn(Wij), where κ is the forgetting coefficient. Weights that are not consistently supported by the data decay to zero, whereas weights carrying essential regularities are maintained. After this phase, weights with absolute value below a small threshold are pruned. Neurons left with no connections are removed. The result is a compact RBM whose remaining connections can be inspected as explicit features. 4. Deep Belief Network A DBN is constructed by stacking RBMs and training greedily layer by layer [4]. The first RBM is trained on the input data. The hidden activation probabilities of the trained RBM are then used as the visible data of the next RBM, and the procedure is repeated. After pre-training, the stack is used either as a feature extractor for a classifier or fine-tuned with supervised learning. In a traditional DBN the number of layers and the number of neurons in each layer must be specified in advance. 5. Layer generation algorithm The proposed algorithm determines the number of layers automatically. It operates as follows. 1. Train the first RBM with the adaptive structural learning method (Section 2), followed by the Learning Forgetting method (Section 3). 2. Evaluate the current top layer. The evaluation criterion is the reconstruction error of the RBM on the training data for the unsupervised case, and the classification error of a supervised output layer attached to the top hidden layer for the labeled case. 3. If the criterion exceeds the tolerance, and the previous layer addition improved it by more than a minimum margin δ, generate a new RBM. Its visible layer has as many neurons as the current top hidden layer, and its hidden layer starts with a small number of neurons. 4. Train the new RBM on the hidden activations of the layer below, again using adaptive structural learning and forgetting. 5. Repeat steps 2–4. Terminate when the criterion falls below the tolerance, or when adding a layer no longer yields an improvement of at least δ. The last added layer is then discarded if it degraded performance. By this process the depth of the network grows only as far as the data requires. Because each new RBM can itself add or remove hidden neurons, both the width of each layer and the overall depth adapt to the complexity of the input space. A theoretical motivation is that adding a layer to a DBN can increase a variational lower bound on the log-likelihood provided the new layer is properly initialized [4]; the stopping rule approximates the point at which this gain vanishes. 6. Experimental setting We evaluate the method on benchmark data sets, including MNIST [5] and CIFAR-10 [6], measuring classification accuracy, the final number of layers and neurons, and the sparsity of the trained weights. The proposed model is compared with a DBN with a fixed structure trained with CD, and with an adaptive RBM without layer generation. Hyperparameters, including the learning rate η, the forgetting coefficient κ, the monitoring window, and the threshold δ, are chosen on a validation subset. Hip fracture is among the most serious consequences of osteoporosis in the elderly and is associated with high mortality, long-term disability, loss of independence, and a considerable economic burden on health systems [1,2]. Because of population ageing, the global incidence of hip fracture is projected to rise substantially over the coming decades [3]. Roughly one fifth of patients die within a year of the fracture, and many survivors never regain their pre-fracture mobility [4]. Reliable, patient-specific identification of individuals at high risk is therefore essential, so that preventive pharmacological or lifestyle interventions can be targeted and the costs of surgical treatment and rehabilitation reduced. Clinical assessment of fracture risk Clinical assessment still relies largely on areal bone mineral density (aBMD) measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), usually expressed as a T-score at the proximal femur or lumbar spine [5]. Although low aBMD is a well-established risk factor, it explains only part of fracture risk. A large proportion of fragility fractures occur in patients whose T-scores lie above the osteoporotic threshold [6]. DXA is a two-dimensional projection technique. It cannot resolve the three-dimensional geometry, the cortical–trabecular distribution, or the spatial heterogeneity of density that govern the mechanical response of the femur. Tools such as FRAX improve prediction by adding clinical risk factors, but they do not account for the mechanical competence of an individual's bone or for the loading conditions that cause fracture [7]. Image-based finite element analysis Finite element analysis (FEA) based on quantitative computed tomography (QCT) has emerged as a promising alternative. In this approach, patient-specific geometry is reconstructed from CT data, and heterogeneous material properties are assigned to each element through empirical relationships between CT attenuation (Hounsfield units), apparent density, and elastic modulus [8,9]. Such models have been validated against ex vivo mechanical tests, where they predict femoral strength and fracture location with reasonable accuracy [10,11]. QCT-based FEA has also been shown to discriminate fractured from non-fractured subjects better than aBMD alone in prospective and retrospective cohorts [12,13]. Fracture risk indicators (FRI), usually defined as the ratio of the local stress or strain to the failure strength or strain of bone, provide a spatially resolved measure of the likelihood of failure and allow the probable site of fracture initiation to be identified [14]. Loading configurations and the femoral neck The femoral neck is the principal site of hip fracture because of its slender geometry, thin cortex, and high load transmission. The outcome of an analysis depends heavily on the loading configuration. The single-legged stance represents physiological loading during walking and standing, in which the joint reaction force produces compression and bending, with tensile stresses at the superior neck and compressive stresses at the inferior neck [15]. By contrast, a sideways fall onto the greater trochanter is the dominant cause of hip fracture in the elderly, and more than 90% of hip fractures are associated with falls [16]. The loading direction in a fall reverses the stress pattern in the neck and may induce high stress on the superior cortex, which is thin and fragile with age [17]. Several studies have simulated both configurations, and some have suggested that fracture risk may be underestimated if only stance loading is considered [18,19]. However, comparative evaluation of the FRI distribution for stance and fall configurations under identical load magnitudes has received limited attention, particularly in vivo. Bilateral variation and the choice of hip Another unresolved issue is the choice of hip to be examined. In clinical practice, DXA or QCT scanning is normally performed on a single hip, often selected arbitrarily or by convention, on the assumption that left and right femurs are sufficiently symmetrical to be interchangeable [20]. However, asymmetry in the proximal femur has been reported in geometry, density, and cortical thickness, and may result from limb dominance, habitual loading, pathology, or natural variation [21,22]. Bilateral differences in aBMD of several percent are common, and in some individuals they alter the diagnostic classification [23]. Given that FEA is highly sensitive to geometry and spatial density distribution, even modest asymmetries could produce meaningful differences in computed stress and FRI fields. Previous FE studies have mostly modelled a single femur per subject, or used small samples, so the extent to which bilateral differences influence predicted fracture risk, and whether they differ between men and women, is poorly understood. This question matters because women have lower peak bone mass, undergo accelerated postmenopausal bone loss, and suffer the majority of hip fractures [24]. Aim and scope of the present study The present work therefore examines the variation of fall-induced hip fracture risk between the right and left femurs using QCT-based FEA. Models of both femurs of thirty anonymous subjects were generated, and FRI was evaluated at the superior and inferior aspects of the femoral neck under single-legged stance and sideways fall configurations with equal load magnitude. The specific objectives were: (i) to compare FRI distributions between the two loading configurations and identify the likely site of fracture initiation; (ii) to quantify the left–right variability of FRI and test its statistical significance; and (iii) to compare the bilateral FRI of men and women. By clarifying the need for bilateral assessment, this preliminary study aims to contribute to more accurate, patient-specific hip fracture prediction and, consequently, to more effective preventive strategies for the geriatric population. Subject data and image acquisition Quantitative Computed Tomography (QCT) datasets of the proximal femora of thirty anonymous patients (both left and right sides) were retrieved retrospectively from a clinical image repository. The cohort included both men and women, and all personal identifiers were removed before analysis. Scans were acquired with a calibrated clinical CT scanner at a slice thickness of 1 mm and an in-plane resolution of approximately 0.8–1.0 mm. A calibration phantom was included in the field of view so that Hounsfield units (HU) could be converted to equivalent bone mineral density [1,2]. Patients with prior hip surgery, implants, or visible pathological lesions were excluded. Each dataset was handled with the same image-processing and modelling workflow so that any difference between sides could not be attributed to procedural variation. Geometry reconstruction and meshing The proximal femur was segmented in medical image-processing software using intensity thresholding followed by manual correction to separate the femoral head from the acetabulum and to remove soft tissue and the pelvis. Cortical and trabecular bone were not segmented separately, and the femur was treated as a single continuous domain with spatially varying material properties [3]. A triangulated surface was generated, smoothed to remove stair-step artefacts, and used to build a volumetric mesh of ten-node quadratic tetrahedral elements. A mesh convergence study on one representative femur showed that an average element edge length of about 2 mm kept the change in peak principal strain below 5%, and this size was adopted for all models [4]. Left and right femurs were meshed with identical parameters. Material property assignment The HU values were converted to equivalent K₂HPO₄ density and then to apparent density (ρapp) by linear calibration. Young's modulus was assigned to each element from empirical density–modulus relationships of the power-law form E = aρ^b, with separate coefficients for cortical and trabecular regimes [5,6]. Values were mapped element by element, with a limited number of discrete material bins to keep the computation tractable. Poisson's ratio was set to 0.3 throughout. Bone was modelled as isotropic and linear elastic, which is acceptable for estimating the onset of failure at physiological loads [7]. Ultimate stress and strain thresholds were defined as density-dependent, with distinct tensile and compressive limits to reflect the asymmetric strength of bone [8]. Loading and boundary conditions Two loading configurations were simulated for every femur, namely single-legged stance and sideways fall. Single-legged stance. The femur was oriented anatomically, with the shaft axis inclined at about 7° to the vertical in the frontal plane. A joint contact force was applied to the femoral head, and an abductor force was applied to the greater trochanter [9]. The distal end of the shaft was fully constrained. Sideways fall. The femur was rotated so that the shaft was inclined at about 30° to the horizontal and the neck was internally rotated by about 15°, following previous fall models [10,11]. The impact force was applied to the greater trochanter, and the femoral head was restrained by constraining its superior surface in the loading direction, with the distal end constrained to resist rigid-body motion. To ensure that any difference in the fracture risk indicator (FRI) came from the bone's geometry and density distribution and not from different loading, the same load magnitude was applied to every model and both configurations. The load was scaled to a value equivalent to a typical body weight multiple, and the same load direction relative to the femoral axis was used for the left and right sides. Where the left femur was mirrored for setup, mirroring was applied consistently. Finite element analysis and fracture risk indicator All simulations were run as static linear analyses in a commercial finite element solver. The FRI was defined at each node or element as the ratio of the computed local stress or strain to the corresponding density-dependent failure limit, with the tensile ratio used where the principal stress was tensile and the compressive ratio used where it was compressive [12]. FRI values of 1 or more indicate predicted local failure. Distributions were extracted over the femoral neck, which is the weakest region of the proximal femur. Nodal values were sampled on defined paths along the superior and inferior surfaces of the neck, from the head-neck junction to the intertrochanteric region, using the same anatomical landmarks in all femurs. Peak and mean FRI along each path were recorded, and the percentage difference between the configurations was calculated as |FRIfall − FRIstance|/FRIstance × 100 for each aspect. Left–right comparison and statistical analysis For each subject, the FRI distributions of the left and right femurs were compared under both loading configurations, with the difference expressed in absolute and percentage terms. Paired-sample t-tests were used to test whether the mean FRI differed between left and right femurs, with subjects serving as their own controls. The normality of paired differences was checked with the Shapiro–Wilk test. The significance threshold was set at p ≤ 0.05, and tests were two-tailed. Subjects were subsequently grouped by sex, and mean FRI values were compared between men and women for each side and load case. Because of the small subgroup sizes, these comparisons were treated as descriptive. Analyses were performed in standard statistical software. Assumptions and limitations of the modelling approach Isotropic linear elastic behaviour, a static load, and the omission of muscle forces other than the abductor were simplifying assumptions applied equally to all models [7,9]. The aim was a comparison between sides within the same subject, and not an absolute prediction of fracture load, so these assumptions affect both sides in the same way. Model characteristics and validation The finite element models of the 60 femora (30 left, 30 right) were generated from QCT datasets with a mean element count of approximately 2.1 × 10⁵ tetrahedral elements after the mesh convergence check. Density-based material mapping yielded a heterogeneous elastic modulus distribution in every model. The mean peak von Mises strain differed by less than 3% between the two finest mesh densities, so the selected mesh was considered adequate. The predicted strain patterns agreed qualitatively with those reported in earlier image-based studies [1,2]. Highest values were concentrated in the femoral neck in both loading configurations, and the load transfer paths matched the known trabecular architecture. Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is the most common muscular dystrophy of childhood, affecting approximately 1 in 5000 live male births. It is caused by mutations in the DMD gene that disrupt the open reading frame and abolish production of functional dystrophin in muscle. Absence of dystrophin leads to progressive muscle fibre damage, replacement of muscle by fibrotic and adipose tissue, and a relentless loss of motor function. Most affected boys lose independent ambulation in their early teens, and subsequent respiratory and cardiac complications reduce life expectancy. Corticosteroid treatment is currently the only pharmacological intervention that has been shown to slow the decline in motor function, prolong ambulation and delay the onset of respiratory and cardiac complications, and it has become part of standard care in many countries. Over the last decade, a number of experimental therapies aimed at the underlying molecular defect have entered clinical development. These include antisense oligonucleotides that induce exon skipping to restore the reading frame, compounds that promote read-through of premature stop codons, gene therapy approaches and agents that act on downstream pathways such as inflammation, fibrosis and muscle regeneration. Several of these have progressed to phase II and III trials, and some have reached regulatory review. The design of such trials depends critically on an accurate understanding of the natural history of the disease in the population being studied. Sample size calculations, the choice of primary outcome measure, the duration of follow-up, the age range for inclusion and the interpretation of any observed treatment effect all rely on knowing how patients are expected to change over time in the absence of treatment, and which factors modify that change. The assessment of motor function in ambulant boys with DMD has traditionally relied on timed tests, particularly the 6-minute walk test, which has been widely used as a primary outcome in recent trials. Although valuable, timed tests have limitations. They depend on the cooperation and motivation of the child, they are difficult to perform in younger boys, and they capture a limited aspect of function. The NorthStar Ambulatory Assessment (NSAA) was developed as a functional rating scale specifically for ambulant children with DMD. It comprises 17 items, including standing, rising from the floor, stepping, hopping and running, each scored 0, 1 or 2, giving a total score of 0 to 34. The scale has good reliability and validity, it can be used in children from about 3 years of age, and it reflects activities relevant to daily life. The NSAA has been implemented through the UK NorthStar clinical network, which since 2003 has collected standardised data prospectively from many specialist centres. This has created one of the largest longitudinal datasets of motor function in DMD. More recently, Rasch analysis has shown that the raw NSAA score is an ordinal measure and that it can be converted into a linear score from 0 to 100, with equal intervals that allow more appropriate parametric analysis and easier interpretation of change over time. Several factors are known or suspected to influence the progression of DMD, and these must be understood if they are to be accounted for in trial design. Glucocorticoid treatment is the most important. Most studies of steroids have been conducted in boys starting treatment at around 5 to 7 years of age, when motor function has already begun to plateau or decline. Clinical practice has progressively shifted towards earlier initiation, sometimes before any decline is evident, but evidence about the effect of starting steroids in younger boys on motor performance is limited. Moreover, regimens differ between centres, with daily and intermittent schedules and different molecules in use, and this may further complicate comparisons. Genotype is a second potential modifier. Although all out-of-frame mutations produce a severe phenotype, there is growing evidence that the location of the mutation may influence the rate of progression. Deletions that are amenable to skipping of particular exons, such as exons 44, 45, 51 and 53, are the targets of different exon-skipping compounds, and each of these subgroups represents a relatively small proportion of the DMD population. Trials in these genetically defined groups will therefore be small, and any differences in their natural history relative to the wider DMD population would have substantial implications for the interpretation of results, particularly when external or historical controls are considered. Previous reports of genotype-related differences in disease course have been limited by small numbers and by the use of outcome measures that were not designed for longitudinal comparison across the full ambulant age range. In this study we used the NorthStar database to describe the natural history of motor function in a large cohort of ambulant UK boys with DMD, using both raw and linearised NSAA scores. Our aims were to define the trajectory of change with age, the age at loss of ambulation and the level of function preceding it, and to assess the effects of early glucocorticoid initiation. To study the effect of genotype, particularly deletions amenable to skipping of specific exons, we also combined the UK data with those of an Italian cohort of boys assessed with the same scale, thereby increasing the numbers in each genetic subgroup. We hope that these findings will provide information useful for the design of future clinical trials. Data were collected through the NorthStar Network, a UK-wide collaboration of neuromuscular centres that uses standardised clinical assessments and a shared database for boys with DMD. Assessors at each centre were trained in the administration of the NorthStar Ambulatory Assessment (NSAA) and followed a common protocol. Data entered between 2004 and 2012 were analysed. Ethical approval and consent for data collection and use were obtained according to local and national requirements, and data were anonymised before analysis. Participants Inclusion criteria were a confirmed diagnosis of DMD (clinical phenotype with dystrophin gene mutation or absent dystrophin on muscle biopsy), ambulatory status at the time of assessment, and at least one NSAA recorded. Boys were excluded if their records lacked a date of birth or assessment date, or if they were participating in an interventional trial of a disease-modifying agent at the time of assessment. This yielded 513 ambulant UK boys. For the genotype analysis, we also included 172 boys with DMD from Italian centres who had been assessed with the NSAA using the same protocol, giving a combined genetic cohort. Clinical assessments The NSAA is a 17-item functional scale developed for ambulant boys with DMD. Items include standing, walking, rising from the floor, stair climbing, hopping, and running. Each item is scored 0 (unable), 1 (modified method, achieves goal without assistance), or 2 (normal), giving a total raw score from 0 to 34. Age at loss of ambulation (LOA) was defined as the age at which the boy could no longer walk independently, with a sustained inability to walk 10 metres, as recorded by the treating clinician. Boys still ambulant at last follow-up were treated as right-censored. Additional variables extracted were date of birth, date of assessment, genotype, glucocorticoid use (agent, regimen, start date, and stop date), and the centre of assessment. Linearisation of NSAA scores Because the raw NSAA is an ordinal scale with unequal intervals between total scores, raw scores were converted into linear (interval-level) scores. The conversion used the published Rasch-derived transformation of the NSAA, which maps the raw total (0–34) onto a 0–100 linear scale. Analyses were performed on the linearised score, and results were also expressed on the raw scale for clinical interpretation. Raw-scale equivalents were derived by applying the inverse conversion to the estimated linear values. Glucocorticoid exposure Glucocorticoid treatment was classified by age at initiation: not treated, started before 3 years, started between 3 and 5 years, and started after 5 years. Boys were classified as treated if they received daily or intermittent prednisolone or deflazacort for at least 6 months. The primary comparison was between boys starting glucocorticoids between 3 and 5 years and those starting later or never treated, with motor function change assessed up to age 7. Regimen (daily versus intermittent) was recorded and examined as a covariate where numbers allowed. Genotype classification Mutations were identified by multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification, array comparative genomic hybridisation, or sequencing, and were reviewed against the reading-frame rule. For the exon-skipping analysis, boys with deletions were grouped according to the exon-skipping strategy to which their deletion is amenable: exon 44, exon 45, exon 46, exon 51, exon 53, and other. Boys with deletions not amenable to a single exon skip, duplications, point mutations, and small rearrangements were categorised separately. The reference group comprised all other boys with DMD. Genotype comparisons used the combined UK and Italian data to maximise numbers in each subgroup. Statistical analysis Descriptive statistics summarised baseline characteristics, including age at first assessment, number of assessments per boy, glucocorticoid use, and genotype distribution. Continuous variables are reported as mean (SD) or median (range) as appropriate. Longitudinal NSAA trajectories were analysed using linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts and slopes for individuals to account for repeated measures and varying follow-up. Time was modelled as age, and piecewise linear terms were used to capture different slopes before and after age 7, a point at which the group-level trajectory changes from stability or gain to decline. Annual rates of change were estimated as the slope of the linearised score per year. Models were also adjusted for centre where appropriate. The effect of glucocorticoid initiation age was evaluated by including treatment group and its interaction with age in the model, restricting the primary analysis to the period up to age 7. Differences are reported as additional linearised units per year with 95% confidence intervals. For genotype, change in NSAA over 2 years was calculated for boys with assessments approximately 24 months apart (within a window of ±3 months). Two-year change was compared between each exon-skipping subgroup and the remaining boys using linear regression adjusted for baseline NSAA score, age at baseline, and glucocorticoid use. Results are expressed in linearised units with raw-scale equivalents, and p values are reported for each comparison. A p value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant; given the number of subgroup comparisons, results were interpreted with caution. Age at LOA was analysed using Kaplan–Meier methods, with median age and 95% confidence intervals reported. Boys who had not lost ambulation by last assessment were censored at that date. To describe the functional status preceding LOA, the NSAA score was modelled backwards from the date of LOA, and the mean linearised and raw scores 2 years before LOA were estimated using mixed models anchored on time to LOA. Missing data were not imputed; mixed models used all available observations under a missing-at-random assumption. Analyses were performed using Stata and R. A total of 513 ambulant boys with DMD from 15 UK NorthStar centres contributed 2,166 NSAA assessments between 2004 and 2012. For the genotype analysis, 172 Italian boys were added to the UK cohort. Mean age at first assessment was 7.3 years (range 3.0 to 16.2), and the median number of assessments per boy was 4 (range 1 to 12). Of the UK boys, 396 (77%) had received glucocorticoids at some point, and 117 (23%) were glucocorticoid naive at the time of analysis. Linearisation of the NSAA Raw NSAA scores (0 to 34) were converted to a linear scale (0 to 100) using the Rasch-derived conversion table. The linearised scores had a more even distribution across the range than the raw scores, which showed pronounced ceiling effects in younger boys. Items such as standing on one leg, hopping, and rising from the floor were the most discriminating between functional levels. Overall motor trajectory On the linearised scale, mean scores were stable or slightly increased until about age 6 to 7 years, with a peak around age 6. After age 7, scores declined by an average of 8 linearised units per year (95% CI 7.2 to 8.8), corresponding to about 4 raw NSAA points per year. Modern communication systems must deliver data that is both reliable and confidential. Traditionally these two goals are addressed separately: an error-correcting code protects the message against channel noise, and a cryptographic primitive protects it against eavesdroppers. This layered approach requires two processing stages at the transmitter and two at the receiver, which increases latency, hardware cost, and energy consumption. These costs matter most in resource-constrained settings such as wireless sensor networks, satellite links, RFID systems, and embedded devices. Joint encryption-encoding schemes address this by merging encryption and channel coding into a single operation, so that one algorithm provides both error correction and confidentiality. The idea has its roots in code-based cryptography. McEliece proposed in 1978 a public-key cryptosystem based on the hardness of decoding a general linear code, using a hidden binary Goppa code whose structure allows efficient decoding only for the legitimate receiver. Niederreiter later gave a dual formulation. These systems have withstood decades of cryptanalysis and are now regarded as leading candidates for post-quantum cryptography. However, their public keys, which are generator or parity-check matrices of large dimension, are very large, often hundreds of kilobytes to megabytes. This limits their use in constrained environments. Rao and Nam subsequently proposed a secret-key variant of the McEliece system, in which the code is shared by both parties. Such secret-key schemes can be viewed as joint encryption-encoding systems, since the same codeword both carries redundancy and conceals the plaintext. Several later proposals follow this line, but they still use classical linear codes, such as Goppa or generalized Reed–Solomon codes, whose key sizes remain considerable and which have faced structural attacks. Low Density Parity Check (LDPC) codes are a natural alternative. Their sparse parity-check matrices permit compact representation, and iterative decoding with belief propagation achieves performance close to the Shannon limit at moderate complexity. These properties suggest shorter keys and better error correction than classical codes. Nevertheless, the same sparsity that makes LDPC codes attractive also exposes them to attacks. In the McEliece setting, the low-weight rows of the parity-check matrix are dual codewords of minimum weight, and an adversary can search for them directly. Attempts to hide the sparse structure, such as those of Monico et al. and Baldi et al., use quasi-cyclic (QC) structure and matrix transformations to resist this attack. QC structure shrinks the key further, because a whole circulant block is described by a single row. Such designs must still be assessed carefully against both structural attacks and information-set decoding. Among the available LDPC constructions, codes based on finite geometries, namely Euclidean and projective geometries, have several useful features. They have well-defined algebraic structure, they can be made quasi-cyclic, and they have large minimum distance and good girth properties for their length. They also exist for many lengths and dimensions, giving a wide range of code rates. Their parity-check matrices are fully determined by the geometry and a few parameters, which allows very compact descriptions. These characteristics make them promising for a joint encryption-encoding scheme that needs small keys, flexible rates, and strong decoding performance. In this paper we propose a joint encryption-encoding scheme using QC-LDPC codes based on finite geometry. The secret key consists of a compact description of the code together with additional components that scramble and mask the codeword, and the sender intentionally adds a random error vector as part of encryption. The legitimate receiver, knowing the secret key, removes the transformation and decodes with an efficient LDPC decoder, whereas an attacker faces a general decoding problem for a code that does not reveal its sparse structure. We examine the scheme against the known attacks on code-based secret-key cryptosystems, including information-set decoding, known-plaintext and chosen-plaintext attacks, and attacks that attempt to recover sparse dual codewords. We show that appropriate parameter choices resist all of them. The main contributions of this work are as follows. First, we give a complete construction of a joint encryption-encoding scheme built on finite-geometry QC-LDPC codes. Second, we show that, owing to the quasi-cyclic structure and the algebraic description of the geometry, the key size is reduced to about one fifth of that of the best comparable scheme. Third, we show that a wide range of transmission rates can be achieved by selecting different geometries and parameters, so that the scheme can be adapted to different communication and cryptographic standards. Fourth, we provide a security analysis against known cryptanalyses and a complexity analysis showing that encryption and decryption have low computational cost. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the necessary background on LDPC codes, finite geometries, and quasi-cyclic codes, together with related joint encryption-encoding schemes. Section 3 describes the proposed scheme. Section 4 analyzes its security. Section 5 evaluates key size, transmission rate, and computational complexity and compares them with previous schemes. Section 6 concludes the paper. The proposed scheme is a symmetric (secret-key) joint encryption-encoding system in the McEliece/Rao-Nam family. It uses a QC-LDPC code built from finite geometry, so the secret key is compact and the code has a large minimum distance and strong error-correcting capability. 1. Code construction Let q = 2^s and consider the finite geometry (Euclidean or projective) over GF(q). The point-line incidence matrix of the chosen geometry is partitioned into circulant blocks. Cyclic classes of lines yield a parity-check matrix H of the form H = [H1 H2 … Hn0], where each Hi is a p×p circulant matrix with row weight wi. Each circulant is fully described by its first row, so H is stored with n0·p bits at most, and in practice only the positions of the nonzero entries are kept. Because of the finite-geometry structure, H has no 4-cycles in its Tanner graph. This gives good iterative decoding performance with sum-product or bit-flipping decoders. The code length is n = n0·p and the dimension is k = n − rank(H). Varying the geometry parameters (s, the dimension, the number of circulant blocks selected, and the column or row grouping) gives a family of codes with rates from low to high. This is the source of the scheme's range of transmission rates. A systematic generator matrix G = [I | Q] is derived from H by Gaussian elimination over circulant blocks. The blocks of Q are circulant, so G is also quasi-cyclic and can be stored compactly. 2. Key generation The secret key consists of: 1. The sparse parity-check matrix H (stored as circulant first rows). 2. A random non-singular scrambling matrix S of size k×k, built as a block-circulant matrix with circulant blocks of size p. Its invertibility is checked via the invertibility of the corresponding polynomial matrix in GF(2)[x]/(x^p+1). 3. A permutation (or sparse-circulant transformation) matrix P of size n×n, composed of p×p circulant permutation blocks. 4. A seed for a pseudo-random generator used to produce the intentional error vectors. The generator matrix actually used is G' = S·G·P. All components are quasi-cyclic, so the key size is on the order of (k·n)/p bits rather than k·n bits. The key is shared in advance between sender and receiver. 3. Encryption and encoding For a plaintext block m of k bits: 1. Compute the codeword c = m·G' (encoding and encryption in one step). 2. Generate an error vector e of length n and Hamming weight t. The weight t is at most the guaranteed correction capability of the LDPC decoder. The vector is drawn from the keyed pseudo-random generator, with a fresh value for each block. 3. Transmit y = m·G' + e. The error vector e plays two roles: it provides cryptographic randomization, and it is indistinguishable from channel noise. The receiver therefore treats the combined noise as errors. If the channel also introduces errors of weight tc, the intentional weight is chosen so that t + tc remains within the decoder's correction capability. This is how reliability and security are achieved in one step. 4. Decryption and decoding The receiver computes y·P⁻¹ = m·S·G + e·P⁻¹. Since P is a permutation (or sparse circulant structure), e·P⁻¹ has the same weight as e (or a bounded weight in the sparse case). The LDPC iterative decoder, using H, removes this error vector and recovers m·S·G, hence m·S from the systematic part. The message is then m = (m·S)·S⁻¹. Decoding uses sum-product or bit-flipping decoding, whose complexity is linear in n per iteration owing to the sparsity of H. 5. Security analysis methodology We evaluate the scheme against known attacks on code-based secret-key systems: - Information set decoding (ISD). The work factor is estimated for Prange, Lee-Brickell, Stern, and the more recent BJMM-style variants. Parameters (n, k, t) are chosen so that the minimum work factor exceeds 2^80 and 2^128 for the respective security levels. Quasi-cyclic structure is accounted for by applying the known speed-up factor of about √p. - Chosen-plaintext attacks (Rao-Nam type). Since the same G' is reused, an adversary choosing plaintexts could try to learn G' or to cancel the error vectors. Fresh pseudo-random errors for each block prevent these attacks. We also analyze the case of repeated or related plaintexts, and the difference-based attack on pairs of ciphertexts. - Dual-code and low-weight codeword attacks. Because H is sparse, the dual code contains low-weight words. G' is dense, however, and S and P hide the dual structure. We assess whether low-weight dual codewords of the public code can be found, and whether they reveal H. The scrambling by S and P gives no direct view of H, and the choice of weights prevents a successful search. - Structural and key-recovery attacks. We consider exhaustive search over S and P, and algebraic exploitation of the circulant structure. The number of possible keys is computed from the number of invertible circulant matrices and the number of circulant permutations. 6. Performance evaluation Key size is computed as the total number of stored bits for H, S, P, and the seed, and compared with earlier joint schemes based on classical codes (such as those using Goppa, GRS, and unstructured LDPC codes) at equivalent security levels. The transmission rate is k/n for each parameter set. Computational complexity is counted in binary operations for encryption (a sparse-circulant product), decryption (decoding plus multiplication by S⁻¹), and key generation. Error-correction performance is measured by Monte Carlo simulation over a binary symmetric channel and an AWGN channel, reporting bit and frame error rates against the number of decoder iterations. We evaluated the proposed scheme along four axes: key size, transmission rate, security against known attacks, and computational complexity. All comparisons are made against the best previously reported joint encryption-encoding schemes based on classical linear codes and on QC-LDPC codes built by non-geometric constructions. Code construction and parameters. We built QC-LDPC codes from finite geometries (Euclidean and projective), whose parity-check matrices consist of circulant blocks of size L with row weight and column weight determined by the geometry. For example, codes derived from the Euclidean geometry EG(2, 2^s) yield circulant permutation-sum blocks with no 4-cycles, which gives good minimum distance and strong iterative decoding performance. Using different geometries and different choices of circulant array dimensions, we obtained code rates ranging from approximately 0.4 to 0.9. Each secret key consists of the first rows of the circulant blocks of the secret matrices, so the key size scales with the number of circulants times L, not with the full k×n dimension of a generator matrix. Key size. Because the secret key is stored in compact quasi-cyclic form, only one row per circulant block is needed. For comparable security levels (an 80-bit work factor), the key of the best previously known scheme required several thousand bits, whereas our key required roughly one fifth of that. The reduction arises from two sources: (i) the circulant structure reduces storage from O(n²) to O(n) bits, and (ii) the sparsity and regularity of finite-geometry parity-check matrices allow the matrices to be described by the positions of a small number of nonzero entries. Plant cells build their walls under the guidance of cortical microtubules (CMTs), a dynamic polymer network anchored to the inner face of the plasma membrane during interphase. CMTs direct the trajectories of cellulose synthase complexes and thereby influence the orientation and structure of cellulose microfibrils, which in turn constrain cell expansion and determine organ and cell shape [1,2]. The arrangement of CMTs varies widely among cell types and developmental stages, from highly parallel arrays in elongating cells to mixed, netted arrays in cells such as the lobed pavement cells of the leaf epidermis [3,4]. Understanding how these patterns arise and are maintained is therefore central to understanding plant morphogenesis. Because plant cells lack a centrosome-like microtubule organizing center, CMT arrays self-organize. Microtubules are nucleated at the cortex, often from existing microtubules through branching nucleation mediated by the γ-tubulin complex and its associated proteins [5,6]. They are released and then show treadmilling behavior, with slow depolymerization at the minus end and dynamic growth at the plus end [7]. The plus end undergoes dynamic instability, switching stochastically between growth, pause, and shrinkage, with transitions to shrinkage (catastrophe) and to growth (rescue) [8]. Together with microtubule–microtubule interactions, these dynamics are sufficient to drive array organization [9,10]. Microtubule interactions and encounter-based catastrophe In the two-dimensional cortical environment, growing microtubules inevitably meet one another. The outcome of an encounter depends strongly on the angle of contact. At shallow angles, the growing plus end is typically deflected and continues along the existing microtubule, resulting in zippering and bundling. At steeper angles, the growing microtubule may cross over the obstacle, or it may undergo catastrophe and begin to depolymerize [11,12]. Computational and experimental studies have shown that the relative frequencies of zippering, crossover, and induced catastrophe, together with severing at crossover sites, can account for the transition from isotropic to aligned arrays [13–15]. Induced catastrophe has been considered a key selective mechanism: microtubules at steep angles are preferentially removed, while those that align with the prevailing direction persist [10,16]. Catastrophe is therefore not solely an intrinsic property of the microtubule tip, but also depends on the local environment. Catastrophes may be broadly separated into those that occur at encounters with another microtubule (encounter-based) and those that occur in free space (free catastrophes). Although the encounter-induced pathway has been documented and incorporated into models, its prevalence relative to free catastrophe in living cells, and the factors that modulate it, have been less thoroughly quantified. Several features of CMT behavior suggest that mechanical constraints may play a role. Microtubules are tethered to the plasma membrane, and the strength of this attachment may influence whether a growing tip can lift over or bend around an obstacle [17,18]. Growing ends under compressive load show pausing and increased catastrophe probability in vitro [19], suggesting that physical barriers could destabilize tips by impeding polymerization. Microtubule-associated proteins and membrane anchoring Numerous microtubule-associated proteins regulate CMT dynamics and interactions. Among them, CLASP (CLIP-associated protein) is a plus-end tracking and lattice-associated protein that stabilizes microtubules, promotes rescue and pause states, and suppresses catastrophe at cell-edge and cell-wall transitions [20,21]. In Arabidopsis, CLASP has been implicated in cortical array organization, in the behavior of microtubules at cell edges, and in the connection between microtubules and the plasma membrane [22,23]. The clasp-1 mutant displays altered microtubule dynamics and array patterning, and thus provides a useful genetic background for examining how differences in dynamics and membrane association affect microtubule behavior at encounters [24]. Feedback between array patterning and microtubule dynamics Most studies have treated array organization as an emergent consequence of individual microtubule dynamics and interactions. However, the converse question remains largely unaddressed: does array pattern in turn influence the behavior of individual microtubules? In a highly parallel array, most microtubules share similar orientations, and encounters are expected to occur at shallow angles that result in zippering. In disordered arrays, microtubules approach each other at a wide range of angles, so steep encounters, and hence induced catastrophes, should be more frequent. If so, array order would feed back on catastrophe rates, with consequences for how dynamic parameters are measured and interpreted. In particular, the widely used catastrophe frequency (Fcat), calculated as the number of catastrophes per unit time spent growing or pausing, is commonly treated as an intrinsic property of microtubules, yet it may in fact reflect the local organization of the array [25]. Aims of this study Here, we used live-cell imaging of microtubules in Arabidopsis cotyledon and leaf epidermal cells to quantify the contributions of encounter-based and free catastrophe in vivo. We compared ordered and disordered CMT arrays to test the hypothesis that disordered arrangements provide more opportunities for microtubule–microtubule interactions and thus increase encounter-based catastrophe. We also examined behavior preceding catastrophe, the influence of plasma membrane anchoring using the clasp-1 mutant, and the consequences of array order and anchoring for Fcat measurements. By linking array pattern to individual microtubule fate, this work addresses how CMT organization and dynamics reciprocally shape one another. Plant materials and growth conditions Arabidopsis thaliana (L.) Heynh. ecotype Columbia-0 (Col-0) was used as the wild type. The clasp-1 mutant (SALK120118) was used to test the effect of reduced MT-plasma membrane anchoring [1]. Both genotypes expressed the MT marker GFP-TUA6 (35S::GFP-TUA6) [2]; clasp-1 plants were obtained by crossing and confirmed by PCR genotyping in the F3 generation. Seeds were surface-sterilized in 70% ethanol followed by 20% bleach with 0.01% Triton X-100, rinsed five times in sterile water, and stratified for 3 days at 4 °C in darkness. Seeds were sown on half-strength Murashige and Skoog medium (pH 5.7) containing 1% sucrose and 0.8% agar. Plates were grown vertically at 22 °C under a 16 h light/8 h dark photoperiod. Cotyledons were imaged at 5–7 days after germination, and the first true leaves at 10–12 days. Live-cell imaging Whole seedlings were mounted in water under a 1.5 coverslip with the abaxial surface of the cotyledon or leaf facing the coverslip. Pavement cells of the epidermis were imaged on a spinning-disk confocal microscope (Yokogawa CSU-X1) mounted on an inverted stand, with a 100× oil-immersion objective (NA 1.45) and an EM-CCD camera. GFP was excited at 488 nm and emission was collected through a 525/50 nm filter. Single optical sections of the cortical cytoplasm were acquired every 2 s for 5 min, with exposure times of 200–300 ms. Laser power was kept low to minimize photobleaching and phototoxicity. Cells showing drift, cytoplasmic streaming artefacts, or loss of focus were discarded. Imaging was done on at least 10 seedlings per genotype from independent growth batches, and 3–5 cells were imaged per seedling. Classification of CMT array order Array order was quantified for each cell region analyzed. Using Fiji/ImageJ [3], the maximum projection of each time series was analyzed with the FibrilTool plugin [4] to calculate the anisotropy score of the array in 20 × 20 µm regions of interest. Arrays with anisotropy greater than 0.2 and a single dominant orientation were classified as ordered (parallel), whereas arrays with anisotropy of 0.2 or lower and multiple MT orientations were classified as disordered (mixed). Classification was confirmed independently by two investigators blinded to genotype. In addition, the distribution of MT angles relative to the mean orientation was calculated manually from individual tracked MTs and compared between categories. Measurement of MT dynamics and catastrophe classification Plus-end dynamics were measured by manually tracking individual MT plus ends through time series in Fiji using kymographs generated with the KymoResolution Combine tool [5] and the Manual Tracking plugin. Only MTs whose plus ends could be followed unambiguously for at least five frames were included. Growth, shrinkage, and pause phases were defined by velocity: growth was a displacement rate above 0.05 µm/min in the direction of the plus end, shrinkage a retraction above the same threshold, and pause an interval of at least two consecutive frames with net displacement below this threshold. Rescue and catastrophe frequencies were calculated by two methods. Fcat was calculated as the number of catastrophe events divided by the total time spent in growth and pause, and the alternative per-MT catastrophe rate as events per unit MT growth time [6]. Rescue frequency was the number of rescues divided by the total shrinkage time. Each catastrophe was assigned to one of two categories by inspecting the frames immediately preceding the transition from growth or pause to shrinkage. Encounter-based catastrophes were those in which the growing plus end contacted the lattice of another MT at an angle, failed to cross over or to bundle with it, and then began depolymerizing within 10 frames of contact. Free catastrophes were those in which no contact with another MT occurred before the transition. Events at bundling (zippering) encounters, where the MT changed direction to follow the encountered MT, were not scored as catastrophes. Whenever the classification was ambiguous because of axial overlap, the event was excluded. The proportion of encounter-based catastrophes was calculated for each cell and compared among array types. The number of catastrophes per unit MT length and per unit time was calculated in each region, and the number of MT-MT encounters was counted on the same kymographs to estimate encounter frequency. The duration of pause before catastrophe was measured as the time between first contact and the onset of shrinkage, and compared between encounter-based and free catastrophes. Assessment of MT-membrane anchoring Anchoring strength was inferred genetically and by behavior. clasp-1 was used as a weakly anchored background, since CLASP promotes MT-plasma membrane attachment [1,7]. In addition, we recorded detachment of MT plus ends (free-end lifting and swiveling) and the lateral wobbling of the end of each MT as a proxy for attachment, and compared catastrophe types between tightly attached (stable, straight plus ends) and weakly attached (wobbling or detaching) MTs. Statistical analysis Cells or seedlings were treated as the experimental unit to avoid pseudoreplication. Proportions were compared using Fisher’s exact test or a generalized linear mixed model with a binomial error structure, with seedling as a random effect. Continuous variables (velocities, pause duration, Fcat) were compared with the Mann–Whitney U test or Kruskal–Wallis test followed by Dunn’s post hoc correction, after assessing normality with the Shapiro–Wilk test. Differences were considered significant at P < 0.05. Data are presented as mean ± standard error unless otherwise stated. Analyses were performed in R (version 4.x) and GraphPad Prism, and sample sizes (n of MTs, cells, and seedlings) are provided in the figure legends. Encounter-based catastrophe is the predominant catastrophe mechanism in cortical microtubule arrays To quantify catastrophe mechanisms, we imaged GFP-TUA6-labeled CMTs in the abaxial pavement cells of Arabidopsis cotyledons and leaves using spinning-disk confocal microscopy at 2–5 s intervals. Individual plus-end trajectories were followed from growth through catastrophe. Each catastrophe was classified as encounter-based if the growing plus end contacted another CMT and failed to cross over or bundle before switching to shrinkage. It was classified as free if no contact with another CMT was apparent within the preceding several frames. Of 1,046 catastrophes scored across 62 cells, approximately 87% were encounter-based and 13% were free. Within encounter-based events, the majority occurred at steep encounter angles, consistent with the known angle dependence of zippering versus crossover or catastrophe [1,2]. Shallow-angle contacts typically led to zippering and continued growth. Array disorder increases the proportion and abundance of encounter-based catastrophe We next asked whether array organization affects these proportions. Cells were assigned to ordered (parallel, anisotropy above a threshold) or disordered (mixed orientation, low anisotropy) categories, based on the anisotropy of CMT orientations measured with FibrilTool [3]. Ordered arrays were most common in elongated, anisotropically growing cells, whereas disordered arrays were found in cells with isotropic expansion or in lobed pavement cells. Disordered arrays showed a significantly higher proportion of encounter-based catastrophes relative to free catastrophes than ordered arrays (P < 0.01, Fisher's exact test). In ordered arrays, free catastrophes made up a substantially larger share of events. The overall number of catastrophes per unit of CMT length and time was also higher in disordered arrays. Accommodation is the process by which the eye changes its optical power to focus on near objects. In the phakic eye, contraction of the ciliary muscle relaxes zonular tension, allowing the crystalline lens to become thicker and more curved, with a forward shift of its anterior surface and a modest backward shift of its posterior surface [1,2]. These changes have been characterized extensively with Scheimpflug photography, ultrasound biomicroscopy, magnetic resonance imaging, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) [3-6]. Together they give a coherent picture of anterior segment biometry during accommodation, but the response of the whole eye, including the posterior segment, is less well understood. Axial length changes during accommodation Several studies have reported small but measurable changes in axial length (AL) during accommodation. Drexler and colleagues used partial coherence interferometry and found a transient increase in AL during near focusing in young subjects [7]. Later work, using optical biometry and similar techniques, confirmed that AL increases by a few to several tens of micrometers, with the magnitude correlating with accommodative demand [8-10]. Proposed mechanisms include traction of the ciliary muscle on the choroid, which could pull the posterior pole forward and thin the choroid, as well as contraction of the extraocular muscles and changes in intraocular pressure [11,12]. Since the axial elongation is small and potentially confounded by choroidal thickness changes, the sources of the elongation remain debated. Interest in the phenomenon has grown because sustained near work and accommodative effort have been implicated in myopia development and progression [13,14]. Mechanical load transferred through the ciliary body and choroid during accommodation has been hypothesized to contribute to axial elongation over time [15]. Limitations of conventional measurements Most previous studies relied on devices that report AL as a single value, such as optical biometers based on partial coherence interferometry or low-coherence reflectometry. These instruments do not resolve the individual intraocular components in a single, simultaneously acquired image, and their reported values depend on assumed group refractive indices. Conventional OCT systems have limited imaging depth and typically scan the anterior segment or the retina separately, so whole-eye biometry requires multiple acquisitions, with associated registration errors and motion artifacts. Because accommodative changes in AL are on the order of tens of micrometers, measurement error and the compounding of separate scans can approach the size of the effect. Ultra-long scan depth OCT (UL-OCT) addresses these limitations by imaging from the anterior cornea to the retina in a single scan [16-18]. Such systems, based on swept-source or extended-depth spectral-domain designs, allow the central corneal thickness (CCT), anterior chamber depth (ACD), lens thickness, vitreous length (VL), and AL to be derived from the same image. This capability has been used to examine changes in ocular biometry and lens shape during accommodation in phakic eyes [19,20]. Pseudophakic eyes as a model Pseudophakic eyes offer a distinct opportunity for studying the contribution of structures other than the lens to accommodative biometric changes. A monofocal intraocular lens (IOL) has a fixed thickness and shape, so changes in its position can be attributed to ciliary body and capsular bag mechanics rather than to deformation of the lens itself. This removes the confounding effect of lens thickening on the measured ACD and VL. Moreover, because IOLs are well defined and highly reflective in OCT images, their boundaries can be segmented reliably. Studies of pseudophakic eyes have shown small, variable IOL movements during accommodation or pharmacological stimulation, with both forward and backward shifts reported depending on IOL design, haptic configuration, and capsular bag status [21-24]. Anterior displacement has been seen with some plate-haptic designs, whereas posterior or negligible displacement has been described for others, and the direction of the IOL shift may influence the apparent change in ACD and VL. Pilocarpine, a muscarinic agonist, is commonly used to induce ciliary muscle contraction and thus to simulate the accommodative response in eyes in which voluntary accommodation is absent or unreliable, such as older and pseudophakic subjects [25,26]. It also produces miosis, which facilitates imaging, and it avoids the variability in effort and fixation stability associated with visual stimuli. However, pilocarpine can induce a strong, sustained ciliary muscle contraction that may differ from physiological accommodation, and it can alter choroidal thickness and intraocular pressure [27]. The effects of such stimulation on whole-eye axial biometry in pseudophakic eyes have not been well documented. Purpose of the present study Whether the AL increases in pseudophakic eyes during ciliary muscle contraction, and how the individual intraocular distances contribute to any change, has not been determined with simultaneous whole-eye imaging. Establishing this would help distinguish the contribution of the lens from that of the ciliary-choroidal complex to accommodative axial elongation, and would aid in understanding IOL position stability under ciliary muscle activity. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to use a custom-built UL-OCT system to measure CCT, ACD, IOL thickness, VL, and AL in pseudophakic eyes before and after pilocarpine-induced accommodation, and to quantify the associated changes in these biometric parameters. Subjects Twenty-five healthy volunteers (age range 49 to 84 years) who had previously undergone uncomplicated cataract surgery with implantation of a monofocal posterior-chamber IOL in the capsular bag were recruited. Only the right eye of each participant was measured. Inclusion criteria were a well-centered IOL, a clear posterior capsule or a patent Nd:YAG capsulotomy that did not interfere with imaging, a best-corrected visual acuity of 20/40 or better, and an intraocular pressure below 21 mmHg. Exclusion criteria were a history of glaucoma, uveitis, retinal detachment, or macular disease; prior corneal or refractive surgery; zonular weakness or pseudoexfoliation; use of any medication known to affect accommodation or pupil size; and known hypersensitivity to pilocarpine. The study followed the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki, and the protocol was approved by the institutional ethics committee. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants after the nature of the study was explained. Ultra-long scan depth OCT system Whole-eye imaging was performed with a custom-built ultra-long scan depth optical coherence tomography (UL-OCT) system, based on the swept-source Fourier-domain design described previously [1,2]. In brief, the system used a wavelength-swept laser centered near 1050 nm and a high-speed balanced detector. A long coherence length of the source and a high-bandwidth digitizer provided an imaging depth in air greater than 30 mm, which allowed simultaneous visualization of the anterior cornea through the retina in a single B-scan. The axial resolution in tissue was approximately 20 µm, and the sampling interval was calibrated against a reference of known thickness. Each B-scan consisted of several hundred A-lines acquired along a horizontal meridian through the corneal vertex. Fixation was provided by an internal target, and alignment was verified in real time by the presence of the corneal vertex reflex and the foveal pit. The power at the cornea was below the limits of the ANSI Z136.1 safety standard. Image acquisition protocol Measurements were taken in a dimly lit room. Participants were seated with the head stabilized on a chinrest and were instructed to fixate on the target and blink just before acquisition. For each state, several consecutive B-scans were acquired, and at least three high-quality images with a visible corneal vertex, IOL surfaces, and retinal pigment epithelium were retained for analysis. Baseline (non-accommodative) images were first obtained without pharmacological intervention. Accommodation was then pharmacologically stimulated with two drops of 0.5% pilocarpine hydrochloride instilled in the imaged eye, separated by a 5-minute interval [3]. Pilocarpine acts as a muscarinic agonist, contracting the ciliary muscle and inducing a stimulus largely independent of visual effort. Following the same protocol as at baseline, images were acquired again 30 minutes after the first drop, when the pharmacological effect was expected to be established. Pupil constriction was noted, and participants were monitored for adverse effects. The same operator performed all acquisitions, and each eye was imaged twice in each state to evaluate repeatability. Image processing and biometric analysis Raw interferograms were processed by background subtraction, resampling to linear wavenumber, dispersion compensation, and Fourier transformation. Custom automated software written in MATLAB (MathWorks, Natick, MA) was used to segment the interfaces of interest. Anterior and posterior corneal surfaces, anterior and posterior IOL surfaces, and the retinal pigment layer were detected using edge detection and curve fitting, with manual verification of every segmentation by an experienced observer. Optical distances were converted to geometric distances by dividing by the group refractive index of the corresponding medium: 1.376 for the cornea, 1.336 for the aqueous and vitreous humors [4], and the manufacturer-specified group index for the IOL material. Because the lens materials differed among eyes, the index appropriate for each IOL was used. The following parameters were derived along the optical axis: central corneal thickness (CCT), the distance between the anterior and posterior corneal surfaces; anterior chamber depth (ACD), the distance from the posterior corneal surface to the anterior IOL surface; IOL thickness (IOLT), the distance between the anterior and posterior IOL surfaces; and vitreous length (VL), the distance from the posterior IOL surface to the retinal pigment epithelium. Axial length (AL) was calculated as the sum of CCT, ACD, IOLT, and VL. Because ACD here was measured from the posterior cornea, this sum corresponds to the distance from the anterior corneal surface to the retinal pigment epithelium. Changes with accommodation were obtained by subtracting the baseline value from the value after pilocarpine for each parameter. Because the IOL is a rigid, nonaccommodating element, IOL displacement was inferred from ACD changes, with a posterior shift corresponding to an increase in ACD. Repeatability Within-subject standard deviation and the coefficient of variation were computed from the repeated acquisitions in each state, and intraclass correlation coefficients were calculated for each parameter [5]. These values were used to confirm that the measured changes exceeded the measurement variability of the system. Statistical analysis Data are expressed as mean ± standard deviation. The normality of the distribution of each parameter and of the paired differences was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Differences between the non-accommodative and accommodative states for CCT, ACD, IOLT, VL, and AL were evaluated with the paired Student's t-test, or the Wilcoxon signed-rank test when normality was not satisfied. Associations between changes in AL and changes in ACD and VL, as well as with age and baseline AL, were examined with Pearson or Spearman correlation coefficients as appropriate. A two-tailed P value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed using SPSS (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY) and MATLAB. Subject characteristics and image quality Of the 25 pseudophakic subjects enrolled, all completed both imaging sessions, and every dataset was suitable for analysis. Mean age was 67.4 ± 8.6 years (range, 49–84 years). All eyes had a monofocal IOL positioned within the capsular bag, and the interval between cataract surgery and the study visit exceeded three months in every case. The UL-OCT system visualized all ocular interfaces from the anterior corneal surface to the retinal pigment epithelium in a single B-scan. The automated segmentation software identified the corneal surfaces, the anterior and posterior IOL surfaces, and the retinal boundary in all images without manual correction of boundary positions in more than 5% of frames. Because the optical path was referenced to the refractive index of each medium, the reported distances are geometric lengths. Repeatability of baseline measurements The two images acquired in each state were compared to determine measurement repeatability. The within-subject standard deviations were 2.1 µm for CCT, 9.4 µm for ACD, 7.8 µm for IOLT, 13.6 µm for VL, and 14.2 µm for AL. The corresponding intraclass correlation coefficients exceeded 0.98 for all parameters. These values are an order of magnitude smaller than the accommodative changes reported below, except for CCT and IOLT, for which no significant change was observed. Pilocarpine-induced changes in anterior segment parameters Table 1 summarizes the biometric parameters in the two states.
