Laryngoscopy and orotracheal intubation are among the most stimulating events in general anesthesia. Mechanical stimulation of the supraglottic and tracheal structures provokes a reflex sympathoadrenal discharge, with increased plasma catecholamine concentrations, tachycardia, and hypertension. These changes usually appear within seconds of laryngoscopy, peak at one to two minutes, and subside within five to ten minutes. In healthy patients the response is generally well tolerated. In patients with hypertension, coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, or intracranial pathology, however, it may precipitate myocardial ischemia, arrhythmia, acute heart failure, cerebral hemorrhage, or raised intracranial and intraocular pressure. Attenuating this response is therefore a recognized goal of anesthetic management, and many pharmacological and non-pharmacological strategies have been proposed. Among these are deepening anesthesia with volatile agents or propofol, topical or intravenous lidocaine, beta-blockers such as esmolol and labetalol, calcium channel blockers, vasodilators such as nitroglycerin and nitroprusside, magnesium sulfate, gabapentinoids, and opioids. Each has limitations. Beta-blockers may cause excessive bradycardia or hypotension and are contraindicated in some patients. Lidocaine has inconsistent efficacy. Vasodilators attenuate the pressor response but may cause reflex tachycardia. Opioids are the most widely used class, although their dose-related adverse effects, such as respiratory depression, chest wall rigidity, bradycardia, and hypotension, require care. Remifentanil is an ultra-short-acting synthetic μ-opioid agonist metabolized by nonspecific plasma and tissue esterases, which gives it a context-sensitive half-time of about three to four minutes regardless of the duration of infusion. Its rapid onset and predictable offset make it well suited to blunting brief, intense stimuli such as laryngoscopy. Several studies have shown that bolus or infusion doses of remifentanil effectively suppress the hemodynamic response to intubation. The same pharmacological profile has drawbacks: bolus administration can cause marked bradycardia, hypotension, and muscle rigidity, and rapid offset may leave patients with hyperalgesia or inadequate postoperative analgesia. Dexmedetomidine is a highly selective α2-adrenoceptor agonist with sedative, anxiolytic, analgesic, and sympatholytic properties. It has an α2:α1 selectivity ratio of about 1600:1, roughly eight times that of clonidine. Through its action on central α2 receptors, particularly in the locus coeruleus, it reduces central sympathetic outflow and circulating norepinephrine, which blunts stress responses while causing little respiratory depression. It also reduces the requirements for anesthetic and analgesic agents. Single preinduction doses of 0.5 to 1 µg/kg have been reported to attenuate the pressor response to intubation, although biphasic blood pressure effects, with transient hypertension from peripheral α2B-mediated vasoconstriction followed by hypotension and bradycardia, are well described, particularly with rapid injection. Several trials have compared dexmedetomidine with fentanyl, esmolol, lidocaine, or clonidine for controlling the intubation response, but comparisons with remifentanil are fewer and results are inconsistent. Some investigators found dexmedetomidine superior in controlling heart rate and blood pressure, whereas others found remifentanil equal or better, and differences in doses, timing of administration, induction agents, and patient populations make the findings difficult to reconcile. In addition, because the two drugs act through different receptor systems and have complementary hemodynamic profiles, combining them at reduced doses is an attractive option. In principle, a combination could provide additive or synergistic attenuation of sympathetic responses while limiting dose-dependent adverse effects of each agent, such as the bradycardia and hypotension seen with larger doses of either drug. Evidence about the combination given immediately before intubation is scarce. Evaluating the efficacy of these drugs is clinically relevant in everyday practice, particularly in settings where more invasive monitoring, or drugs such as esmolol, may not be available or may be costly. Both dexmedetomidine and remifentanil are increasingly available in Iranian hospitals, and local data comparing them would help guide practice. Moreover, the dose, timing, and combination strategies that provide hemodynamic stability without clinically important hypotension or bradycardia remain to be established. We therefore designed this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial to compare the efficacy of dexmedetomidine (1 µg/kg), remifentanil (1 µg/kg), and a mixture of the two (0.5 µg/kg each) with normal saline in blunting the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and orotracheal intubation in patients undergoing elective surgery under general anesthesia. The primary outcomes were changes in blood pressure and heart rate at defined intervals after intubation, and oxygen saturation was monitored as a safety measure. We hypothesized that all three active regimens would attenuate the response compared with saline, and that the combination might offer more effective hemodynamic control than either drug alone. This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial was conducted at Amirkabir Hospital, affiliated with Arak University of Medical Sciences, Arak, Iran. The study protocol was approved by the institutional ethics committee and registered in the Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials (IRCT2016092722254N1). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants before enrollment, and the study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Participants Adult patients of both sexes scheduled for elective surgery under general anesthesia with orotracheal intubation were screened. Inclusion criteria were age 18 to 60 years, American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status I or II, and an expected uncomplicated intubation (Mallampati class I or II). Exclusion criteria were: a history of hypertension, ischemic heart disease, arrhythmia, or heart block; treatment with beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, clonidine, or other drugs affecting hemodynamics; baseline bradycardia (heart rate below 50 beats/min); diabetes mellitus; significant renal, hepatic, or pulmonary disease; known allergy to the study drugs; pregnancy; obesity (body mass index above 35 kg/m²); anticipated difficult airway; and more than one intubation attempt or laryngoscopy longer than 30 seconds. Patients who needed additional drugs because of hemodynamic instability before the measurement points were also excluded. Sample size The sample size was calculated from previous reports of the hemodynamic response to intubation, assuming a type I error of 0.05, a power of 80%, and a clinically meaningful difference in mean arterial pressure of about 10 mmHg between groups. This yielded approximately 31 patients per group. A total of 124 patients were therefore enrolled. Randomization and blinding Patients were allocated equally to four groups (n = 31 each) using a computer-generated random number sequence with sealed, opaque, sequentially numbered envelopes. The groups were: DEX (dexmedetomidine 1 µg/kg), REM (remifentanil 1 µg/kg), DEX-REM (an equal mixture, 0.5 µg/kg of each drug), and NS (normal saline placebo). An anesthesia nurse not involved in patient care or data collection prepared all study solutions in identical 10 mL syringes diluted with normal saline to the same volume and labeled only with the patient number. The anesthesiologist administering the drugs, the observer recording the data, and the patients were all unaware of group allocation. The data analyst was also blinded to group identity until the analysis was complete. Anesthetic procedure Patients fasted for at least 8 hours before surgery, and no sedative premedication was given. On arrival in the operating room, standard monitoring was applied, including electrocardiography, noninvasive blood pressure, and pulse oximetry. A peripheral intravenous line was secured, and Ringer's lactate was infused. Baseline systolic, diastolic, and mean blood pressure (MBP), heart rate (HR), and arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2) were recorded. All patients were preoxygenated with 100% oxygen for 3 minutes. Anesthesia was induced with midazolam 0.02 mg/kg, fentanyl 1 µg/kg was not used in order to avoid interference with the study opioid, and thiopental sodium 5 mg/kg was administered. Atracurium 0.5 mg/kg was given to facilitate intubation, and ventilation was supported by mask. The study drug was infused intravenously over 1 minute, beginning 1 minute before laryngoscopy, so that laryngoscopy began after the infusion was complete. Laryngoscopy was performed with a Macintosh blade by an experienced anesthesiologist, and the trachea was intubated with an appropriately sized cuffed endotracheal tube. Laryngoscopy duration was kept below 30 seconds. Correct tube placement was confirmed by capnography and auscultation. Anesthesia was maintained with isoflurane in an oxygen-air mixture and additional atracurium as needed, with controlled ventilation to maintain end-tidal CO2 at 35 to 40 mmHg. Measurements Blood pressure, HR, and SaO2 were recorded at the following time points: on arrival in the operating room (baseline), 1 minute before laryngoscopy and intubation, immediately after intubation, and subsequently at 1, 3, and 5 minutes, then every 5 to 15 minutes during the procedure. MBP was calculated as diastolic pressure plus one third of the pulse pressure or taken directly from the monitor. Adverse events were also noted, including bradycardia (HR below 50 beats/min), hypotension (decrease in MBP of more than 20% from baseline or systolic pressure below 90 mmHg), desaturation (SaO2 below 90%), and muscle rigidity. Bradycardia was treated with atropine 0.5 mg intravenously, and hypotension was treated with intravenous fluid boluses and ephedrine 5 to 10 mg when required. Demographic variables (age, sex, weight, ASA class) were also recorded. Outcomes The primary outcome was the change in MBP and HR after laryngoscopy and intubation relative to baseline and pre-intubation values. Secondary outcomes were SaO2 and the incidence of adverse effects. Statistical analysis Data were analyzed using SPSS version 18.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). Continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation, and categorical variables as numbers and percentages. The normality of data distribution was assessed with the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. Baseline characteristics were compared among groups using one-way analysis of variance for continuous variables and the chi-square test for categorical variables. Hemodynamic variables at each time point were compared among the four groups with one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test for pairwise comparisons. Changes in MBP, HR, and SaO2 over time within and between groups were evaluated with repeated-measures ANOVA, with Greenhouse-Geisser correction applied when the assumption of sphericity was violated. A P value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant. A total of 124 patients were enrolled and randomized equally into four groups of 31 patients each: dexmedetomidine (DEX), remifentanil (REM), the DEX-REM mixture, and normal saline (NS). All patients completed the study and were included in the analysis, and no participant was excluded because of difficult intubation or protocol deviation. Baseline characteristics The four groups were comparable in age, sex distribution, and baseline hemodynamic variables recorded on arrival to the operating room. Baseline mean blood pressure (MBP) did not differ significantly among the groups (P = 0.157), nor did baseline heart rate (HR) (P = 0.105) or arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2) (P = 0.366). The groups were therefore considered homogeneous before the intervention. Hemodynamic changes before intubation One minute before laryngoscopy, after administration of the study drug, MBP and HR in the three intervention groups tended to be lower than their baseline values, whereas values in the NS group remained close to baseline. The mixture group showed the largest pre-intubation decline in MBP. No patient developed severe hypotension or bradycardia requiring pharmacologic treatment before intubation. Hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and intubation In the NS group, laryngoscopy and orotracheal intubation produced the expected pressor response, with clear increases in MBP and HR immediately after intubation relative to pre-intubation values. These elevations persisted at subsequent measurements and returned toward baseline only gradually. In contrast, none of the three active-treatment groups showed a significant rise in MBP or HR after intubation. Values in the DEX, REM, and DEX-REM groups remained at or below baseline at all measured time points. Post hoc comparisons (Tukey) showed that MBP and HR were significantly higher in the NS group than in each of the other three groups at every time point after laryngoscopy and intubation (P < 0.05). Differences among the DEX, REM, and DEX-REM groups were generally not statistically significant for either MBP or HR, indicating that single-agent DEX and single-agent REM were similarly effective in attenuating the response. Blood pressure The mixture group had numerically and descriptively the lowest MBP throughout the postintubation period, followed by the REM and DEX groups, whereas the NS group had the highest values. Compared with NS, MBP in the mixture group was lower at all postintubation measurements (P < 0.05). Between-group differences among the active drugs remained small and did not reach statistical significance in the post hoc analysis. Repeated-measures analysis demonstrated a decreasing trend in MBP over time after intubation in the three intervention groups. This trend reflected a gradual fall from the immediate postintubation values through the later measurements

Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is a major force in prokaryotic evolution. It allows bacteria to acquire adaptive traits such as antibiotic resistance, virulence factors, and new metabolic capabilities, and it shapes the structure of bacterial genomes and the diversity of populations. Among the three classical mechanisms of HGT, conjugation, transduction, and natural transformation, only natural transformation is entirely under the control of the recipient cell. Transformable bacteria express a specialized set of proteins during a physiological state called competence. These proteins bind extracellular DNA, translocate it into the cell, and, when sufficient sequence similarity exists, integrate it into the chromosome by homologous recombination. Natural transformation is widespread among bacteria, with over eighty species from diverse phyla shown to be competent, and its machinery is conserved, which suggests an ancient origin and strong selective maintenance. Despite its prevalence, the selective forces that maintain natural transformation remain debated. The most prominent hypothesis holds that transformation is a form of bacterial sex that generates genetic variation, breaks up unfavorable allelic associations, and facilitates the spread of beneficial mutations while purging deleterious ones. Theoretical work shows that such benefits depend on conditions such as population structure, the strength and form of selection, and the supply of DNA, and they accrue mainly at the population or lineage level. They are also delayed relative to the costs borne immediately by the transformed cell. Because competence is a trait of individual cells, it is important to ask whether immediate, cell-level benefits exist that could favor the evolution and maintenance of DNA uptake independently of the long-term advantages of recombination. Two such alternative hypotheses have been proposed. First, DNA is a rich source of carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus, and DNA taken up by competent cells could be degraded and used as a nutrient. Consistent with this, some species, such as Haemophilus influenzae, preferentially take up DNA containing specific uptake sequences, and in some species competence is induced by starvation. Second, taken-up DNA could serve as a template for repair of damaged chromosomal DNA. Competence is induced by DNA-damaging agents in several species, including Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila, which supports a link between transformation and the DNA damage response. Experimental evidence for a repair function has been mixed, however, and in several systems the induction of competence by genotoxic stress could reflect a general stress response rather than a repair benefit. Transformation may also carry direct costs. Incoming DNA can include harmful elements such as selfish genetic elements, and recombination can disrupt well-adapted genotypes. Competence systems can also impose physiological burdens, including the expression of costly machinery and, in some species, lysis of neighboring cells or growth arrest. Another possible cost lies in the processing of the incoming single-stranded DNA. Taken-up DNA is protected by the protein DprA and loaded with RecA to form a nucleoprotein filament that searches for homology. How this process interacts with host DNA repair and replication, and whether it generates chromosomal lesions, has received little attention. Quantifying immediate costs and benefits requires experiments that separate the effects of DNA uptake from those of recombination. Acinetobacter baylyi (strain ADP1) is well suited to this question. It is constitutively and highly competent, which removes confounding effects of competence regulation and stress-induced induction. It takes up DNA without strong sequence specificity, so both homologous and heterologous DNA can be tested. Its genetics are tractable, and mutants lacking the uptake machinery or the recombination mediators can be built readily. Mutants lacking the DNA uptake pore ComEC or the DNA-binding protein ComP cannot take up DNA, while mutants lacking DprA take up DNA but cannot recombine it efficiently. This lets us dissect uptake from recombination in head-to-head competition between isogenic strains. Here we investigate the immediate fitness effects of DNA uptake and recombination in A. baylyi under benign and genotoxic conditions. We use UV irradiation as a stressor because it produces lesions repaired by nucleotide excision repair, and because a repair benefit of taken-up DNA, if present, should be most evident under such stress. We compete uptake-proficient and uptake-deficient strains in the presence of homologous and heterologous DNA, and we test whether any advantage depends on recombination by using strains lacking DprA. We then ask how recombination with taken-up DNA affects survival of cells under increasing UV doses and whether it interferes with nucleotide excision repair. Finally, we examine the contribution of the RecBCD and RecFOR recombinational repair pathways to transformation, to test whether recombination with incoming DNA involves strand breaks that require these pathways for processing. Our results reveal a recombination-independent physiological benefit of DNA uptake, together with a cost of recombination arising from strand breaks. These findings provide a new perspective on the immediate trade-offs that shape the evolution of natural transformation. Bacterial strains and growth conditions. All strains were derived from Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 (BD413). Strains were grown in lysogeny broth (LB) at 30 °C with shaking at 200 rpm, or on LB agar. Where required, antibiotics were added at the following concentrations: kanamycin 20 µg/ml, gentamicin 10 µg/ml, rifampicin 100 µg/ml, streptomycin 50 µg/ml. Deletion mutants were constructed by replacing target genes (comEC, comA, dprA, recA, recBCD, recF, recO, recR, uvrA) with resistance cassettes using overlap-extension PCR products, which were transformed into the wild type and verified by PCR and sequencing. Strains used for competition carried chromosomally integrated, neutral markers: either a gentamicin resistance cassette or a streptomycin resistance (rpsL) allele, allowing discrimination of competitors by selective plating. Marker effects were tested by competing marked and unmarked strains and found to be neutral. Transformation assays. Overnight cultures were diluted 1:100 in fresh LB and grown to exponential phase, then diluted to approximately 10^7 CFU/ml. Aliquots of 100 µl were mixed with 100 ng of transforming DNA and incubated for 90 min at 30 °C with shaking. Transforming DNA was either a PCR product carrying a rifampicin resistance allele (rpoB) flanked by homologous sequence, or genomic DNA from a kanamycin-resistant donor carrying a cassette at a neutral locus. Reactions were stopped with DNase I (10 U, 10 min). Cells were diluted and plated on selective and non-selective agar. Transformation frequency was calculated as transformants per total CFU. Experiments were performed with at least three independent biological replicates. For recombination-deficient mutants, frequencies below the detection limit were reported as the limit. DNA preparations. Homologous DNA was purified from A. baylyi genomic preparations (Qiagen genomic tip). Heterologous DNA was obtained from Escherichia coli MG1655 and from salmon sperm, which share no appreciable sequence homology with A. baylyi sufficient for recombination. DNA concentrations were measured fluorometrically (Qubit). DNA was sheared by passage through a needle where fragment size was to be standardized, and fragment size was verified on agarose gels. To test nutritional use, DNA was also supplied in carbon-limited medium in some assays. Competition experiments. Competitions were performed between a DNA uptake-proficient strain (wild type) and an uptake-deficient strain (ΔcomEC or ΔcomA), each carrying a different marker. Strains were grown separately to exponential phase, mixed at a 1:1 ratio, and diluted into fresh medium with or without DNA (homologous, heterologous, or none; 1 µg/ml). To separate effects of DNA uptake from recombination, competitions were also performed with a recombination-deficient but uptake-proficient strain (ΔrecA, ΔdprA) against the uptake-deficient strain. Initial and final (after 90 min to 24 h, depending on experiment) densities were determined by plating on selective agar. Relative fitness was calculated as the ratio of Malthusian parameters, w = ln(Nf,A/Ni,A)/ln(Nf,B/Ni,B). Marker swaps were performed to control for marker effects. At least six replicates per condition were performed. UV treatment. Exponentially growing cultures were washed and resuspended in phosphate-buffered saline, spread as thin layers in open Petri dishes and exposed to UV-C (254 nm) at defined doses (0–60 J/m², measured with a radiometer) under dim light to prevent photoreactivation. Cells were then returned to LB, with or without DNA, and incubated in darkness. For competitions under UV stress, mixed cultures were irradiated before the competition phase. Survival was calculated as the ratio of CFU after treatment to CFU of untreated controls, comparing strains with and without DNA addition and with different DNA types. To test interaction with nucleotide excision repair, the same assays were performed in ΔuvrA backgrounds and in combinations with recombination-deficient mutants. Survival after transformation. Cells were incubated with DNA as for transformation assays, then exposed to UV at increasing doses and plated. Survival of wild-type cells exposed to homologous DNA, heterologous DNA, or no DNA was compared with that of uptake-deficient and recombination-deficient mutants to identify costs attributable to recombination as opposed to DNA uptake. Analysis of recombination pathways. The contribution of recombinational repair pathways to transformation was assessed by measuring transformation frequencies of deletion mutants lacking recBCD (RecBCD pathway), recF, recO or recR (RecFOR pathway), and double mutants, using both PCR-fragment and genomic DNA. Complemented strains, carrying the intact gene at a neutral chromosomal site, were used to confirm phenotypes. Growth rates of all mutants were measured in LB in microplate readers (OD600, 15-min intervals) to exclude general growth defects. Statistical analysis. Analyses were performed in R. Data on frequencies and survival were log10-transformed before analysis. Relative fitness values were compared to the neutral expectation of 1 using one-sample t-tests, and between treatments using Welch’s t-test or ANOVA with Tukey post hoc tests, as appropriate. Effects of UV dose and DNA treatment on survival were evaluated using linear models including interaction terms. Nonparametric tests were used when assumptions of normality were violated. P values below 0.05 were considered significant, with correction for multiple testing where applicable. Data are presented as means with standard errors from independent biological replicates. The two strains carried distinct, neutral antibiotic resistance markers, and we confirmed that the markers did not affect growth in monoculture or in control competitions (relative fitness not different from 1). Competitions were started at a 1:1 ratio, and relative fitness was calculated from the change in strain ratio over the incubation period. DNA uptake confers a fitness benefit independent of UV stress In the absence of added DNA, the uptake-proficient and uptake-deficient strains were equally fit. When homologous genomic DNA was added, the uptake-proficient strain outcompeted the uptake-deficient strain, indicating a significant fitness advantage of DNA uptake. A similar advantage was observed when UV-irradiated cells were competed, and the magnitude of the benefit did not increase with UV dose. We therefore found no evidence that taken-up DNA specifically serves as a template for repair of UV damage. The benefit was thus present under benign conditions and was not enhanced by genotoxic stress. The benefit applies to heterologous DNA and does not require recombination To test whether the benefit depended on sequence homology, we repeated the competitions with heterologous DNA (from Escherichia coli or salmon sperm) that cannot recombine into the A. baylyi chromosome. The uptake-proficient strain again showed a fitness advantage, of similar magnitude to that with homologous DNA. We next used a recombination-deficient background (ΔrecA, and ΔcomM and ΔdprA derivatives) to separate uptake from recombination. In competitions between uptake-proficient and uptake-deficient strains that were both recombination-deficient, the benefit of uptake remained. DprA is required to load RecA onto incoming single-stranded DNA, and ΔdprA cells still took up DNA and still benefited. Together these results show that the fitness benefit is not caused by integration of DNA and is consistent with a physiological, likely nutritional, effect of DNA uptake. Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death worldwide, and the burden is shifting toward low- and middle-income countries. South Asians are particularly affected. They develop coronary artery disease about a decade earlier than people in Western populations, and their rates of premature myocardial infarction are high even after accounting for conventional risk factors. In Pakistan, rapid urbanization, sedentary lifestyles, tobacco use, and changing food environments have coincided with a rising incidence of acute myocardial infarction (AMI) among adults younger than 45 years. Premature AMI has serious consequences for individuals, families, and health systems. It strikes people in their most economically productive years and carries a long period of disability and medical expenditure. Identifying modifiable determinants of AMI in young adults is therefore a public health priority. Diet is among the most important modifiable determinants of CVD. Earlier research focused on single nutrients or foods, such as saturated fat, cholesterol, salt, fiber, or fish. This approach has limits. Nutrients and foods are consumed in combination, their effects may be interactive or cumulative, and they are highly correlated, which makes it hard to separate individual effects. Single-nutrient analyses may also miss small effects that become apparent only when the whole diet is considered. Dietary pattern analysis has been proposed to address these problems. It examines the overall diet by using statistical methods such as factor analysis or principal component analysis to derive patterns from observed food intake. This approach reflects how people actually eat and gives results that are easier to translate into dietary guidance. Studies in Western and some Asian populations have repeatedly described a "prudent" pattern, rich in vegetables, fruits, legumes, whole grains, and fish or poultry, and a "Western" pattern, characterized by red and processed meat, refined grains, fried foods, and high-fat dairy. The prudent pattern is generally associated with lower risk of coronary heart disease, whereas the Western pattern is associated with higher risk. The INTERHEART study, which included South Asian participants, found that a prudent diet and regular fruit and vegetable intake were protective against AMI worldwide, while a diet high in fried foods and salty snacks increased risk. However, the foods that make up dietary patterns differ with local culture, availability, and cooking practices. Findings from Western countries cannot be assumed to apply to South Asians, whose diets feature wheat flatbreads, lentils and other legumes, ghee and vegetable oils, spiced meat curries, and tea with milk. Evidence on dietary patterns and AMI in Pakistan is very limited, and almost none concerns young adults. Other factors may also mediate or modify the link between diet and AMI. Dietary intake of folate and vitamin B12 influences plasma homocysteine, an amino acid whose elevation has been linked with atherothrombosis and which is notably common in South Asian populations. Iron status, reflected by ferritin, and exposure to lead, which can enter the food chain through contaminated soil, water, spices, and cookware, have been proposed as contributors to oxidative stress and vascular injury. Dietary composition also influences the lipid profile, including total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and triglycerides. Dyslipidemia with low HDL cholesterol and high triglycerides is especially prevalent among South Asians. Examining these biochemical markers alongside dietary patterns can help show whether any associations with AMI are consistent with plausible biological pathways or whether they may be explained by them. Karachi, the largest city in Pakistan, is a rapidly growing metropolis with a diverse population. Its residents are exposed to a nutrition transition marked by greater availability of fast food, processed and fried snacks, sweetened beverages, and energy-dense foods, alongside traditional dietary habits. This setting provides an opportunity to study how food choices relate to premature coronary disease in an urban South Asian population. Detailed dietary assessment tools such as long, validated food frequency questionnaires are costly and burdensome, and they are often impractical in hospital settings, particularly shortly after an acute event. A short food frequency questionnaire covering commonly consumed foods may offer a feasible alternative for identifying broad dietary patterns in such populations. In this context, we conducted a hospital-based case-control study in Karachi to investigate the association between major dietary patterns and the risk of first AMI in adults younger than 45 years. We used a simple 14-item food frequency questionnaire to assess usual intake in patients and in age- and gender-matched healthy controls, and we derived dietary patterns by factor analysis. We then estimated the association of each pattern with AMI using conditional logistic regression. We also measured homocysteine, folate, vitamin B12, blood lead, ferritin, and lipid parameters to characterize the biochemical profile of participants across dietary patterns. We hypothesized that a prudent dietary pattern would be associated with lower risk of premature AMI and that a Western-type pattern would be associated with higher risk. The findings are intended to inform culturally appropriate dietary recommendations and prevention strategies for young adults in Pakistan and similar populations. This case-control study was conducted at a tertiary care cardiac hospital in Karachi, Pakistan. Cases were enrolled consecutively over the study period from patients admitted with their first acute myocardial infarction (AMI). The study protocol was approved by the institutional ethics review committee, and written informed consent was obtained from all participants before enrollment. Study participants Cases were patients aged below 45 years who presented with a first episode of AMI. The diagnosis was based on standard criteria: typical ischemic chest pain lasting more than 20 minutes, characteristic electrocardiographic changes (ST-segment elevation or new pathological Q waves), and a rise in cardiac enzymes (creatine kinase-MB and/or troponin). Patients with a previous history of myocardial infarction, known coronary artery disease, chronic renal or hepatic disease, malignancy, or a history of dietary modification for medical reasons were excluded. In total, 203 patients (146 males and 57 females) were enrolled. Controls were 205 healthy adults without any history or clinical evidence of cardiovascular disease. They were recruited from among hospital staff, attendants of patients unrelated to the cases, and community volunteers from the same urban population. Each control was matched to a case on gender and age (within 3 years). Controls were screened by interview and a brief clinical examination, and individuals with a history of diabetes, hypertension, or other chronic illness requiring dietary change were not included. Data collection Trained interviewers administered a structured questionnaire to all participants to collect demographic information (age, gender, ethnicity, education, occupation, household income), lifestyle characteristics (smoking status, physical activity), personal medical history, and family history of coronary artery disease. Height and weight were measured, and body mass index was calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared. Blood pressure was measured with a mercury sphygmomanometer after at least five minutes of rest. For cases, dietary information was obtained after clinical stabilization, and participants were asked to report their usual intake before the onset of symptoms. Dietary assessment Habitual dietary intake was assessed using a simple 14-item food frequency questionnaire designed to capture foods commonly consumed in the local population. The items were: legumes (pulses), vegetables, wheat (bread/chapatti), chicken, fruits, eggs, fish, fruit juices, coffee, red meat (beef/mutton), tea with milk, rice, dairy products, and fried or snack foods. Participants reported how often they consumed each item using frequency categories (never or rarely, one to three times per month, once per week, several times per week, and daily). Responses were converted to a numerical scale of consumption frequency for analysis. The questionnaire was administered in the participants' preferred language (Urdu or English) and was pre-tested on a small group before use. Laboratory analyses Venous blood samples were collected after an overnight fast of 10 to 12 hours. For cases, samples were drawn within 24 hours of admission to limit the effect of the acute event on the analytes. Plasma or serum was separated by centrifugation and stored at −70°C until analysis. Total homocysteine was measured in plasma by high-performance liquid chromatography or immunoassay. Serum folate, vitamin B12, and ferritin were measured by chemiluminescence immunoassay. Blood lead (Pb) was determined in whole blood using atomic absorption spectrophotometry. Total cholesterol, HDL-cholesterol, and triglycerides were measured enzymatically on an automated analyzer, and LDL-cholesterol was calculated using the Friedewald equation when triglycerides were below 400 mg/dL. Internal quality control samples were run with each batch. Identification of dietary patterns Dietary patterns were derived by exploratory factor analysis (principal component extraction) of the frequency scores of the 14 food items. The suitability of the data for factor analysis was assessed with the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure of sampling adequacy and Bartlett's test of sphericity. The number of factors retained was determined by eigenvalues greater than 1, inspection of the scree plot, and interpretability. Factors were rotated orthogonally using the varimax method to improve interpretability. Foods with absolute factor loadings of 0.30 or greater were considered to contribute meaningfully to a pattern. Three patterns were retained and labeled according to their dominant food components: a prudent pattern, a combination pattern, and a western pattern. Factor scores were calculated for each participant for each pattern and categorized into tertiles (low, moderate, and high consumption) based on the distribution among controls. Statistical analysis Continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation and categorical variables as numbers and percentages. Differences between cases and controls were examined using the t-test or chi-square test as appropriate. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to compare the biochemical and demographic characteristics, including homocysteine, folate, vitamin B12, blood Pb, ferritin, and lipid levels, across tertiles of each dietary pattern, with post-hoc comparisons where significant. Associations between dietary patterns and the risk of AMI were estimated using conditional logistic regression to account for the matched design. Odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated for the moderate and high tertiles relative to the lowest tertile, which served as the reference. Models were first unadjusted and then adjusted for potential confounders, including body mass index, smoking, family history of coronary artery disease, hypertension, diabetes, education, and income. Additional models considered the biochemical variables (homocysteine, folate, vitamin B12, blood Pb, ferritin, and lipids). Tests for linear trend across tertiles were performed by entering the median value of each tertile as a continuous variable. All tests were two-sided, and a p-value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed using SPSS statistical software. A total of 203 cases (146 males, 57 females) with a first AMI and 205 age- and gender-matched controls were included in the analysis. The mean age of cases was 39.6 ± 4.5 years and that of controls was 39.2 ± 4.8 years, with no significant difference between the groups (p = 0.41). Males constituted 71.9% of cases and 71.2% of controls. Compared with controls, cases had a higher prevalence of smoking, hypertension, diabetes mellitus and a family history of premature coronary artery disease (all p < 0.05). Biochemical characteristics Cases had significantly higher mean concentrations of homocysteine, blood lead, total cholesterol, LDL-cholesterol and triglycerides than controls (all p < 0.01). HDL-cholesterol, folate and vitamin B12 were significantly lower in cases (p < 0.01). Ferritin concentrations were higher in cases, although the difference was modest (p = 0.04). These differences persisted after stratification by gender. Identification of dietary patterns Factor analysis of the 14 food items yielded three dietary patterns with eigenvalues greater than 1, which together explained 46.8% of the total variance in dietary intake. The first factor, labelled the prudent dietary pattern, was characterized by high loadings for legumes, vegetables, wheat, chicken and fruits, and explained 19.5% of the variance. The second factor, labelled the combination dietary pattern, loaded heavily on eggs, fish, fruits, juices and coffee and explained 15.1% of the variance. The third factor, the western dietary pattern, loaded on meat, fish and tea with milk and explained 12.2%. Factor loadings of 0.40 or above were considered to define each pattern. Decisions rarely occur in isolation. Organisms continuously adjust their behavior according to the consequences of earlier choices, and this capacity to learn from errors and successes is essential for adaptive behavior in a changing and uncertain environment [1,2]. In humans and other animals, one of the best-documented manifestations of such adjustment is post-error slowing, in which reaction times lengthen after a mistake, often accompanied by changes in accuracy [3,4]. Sequential effects of this kind show that the outcome of a decision is not merely a terminal event but also a signal that is retained and used to calibrate subsequent decision processes. Understanding how and where in the brain this information is represented is a central question in the neuroscience of decision making. A large body of work has described the neural correlates of perceptual decisions. In tasks in which monkeys discriminate sensory stimuli, activity in sensory areas reflects the physical properties of the stimulus, whereas activity in association and frontal regions reflects the accumulation of evidence and the formation of the choice [5–8]. Areas such as the lateral intraparietal area, the frontal eye fields, the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the premotor cortex have been shown to carry signals that covary with the upcoming decision and, in some cases, with its confidence or reliability [9–12]. Complementary work on performance monitoring has identified the medial frontal cortex, particularly the anterior cingulate cortex and the supplementary eye field, as a key structure signaling errors, conflict and reward prediction errors [13–15]. Dopaminergic and orbitofrontal circuits likewise contribute to evaluating outcomes and updating values [16,17]. Together, these findings suggest that the evaluation of decisions is distributed across several cortical and subcortical networks. The ventral premotor cortex (PMv) has traditionally been considered part of the circuitry for sensorimotor transformation, especially for grasping and for the control of hand and orofacial movements [18,19]. More recently, however, recordings in monkeys performing a vibrotactile discrimination task have shown that PMv neurons participate in several stages of perceptual decision making. In this task, animals compare the frequencies of two mechanical vibrations applied sequentially to the fingertip and report, with a push button, whether the second frequency was higher or lower than the first. During the task, PMv neurons were found to encode the memory of the first stimulus, the comparison between the two stimuli, and the motor choice, with dynamics consistent with the transformation of sensory evidence into a decision [20–22]. Strikingly, after the animal had reported its choice and the outcome was known, PMv neurons continued to carry information about the stimuli, the decision and the outcome, that is, all of the variables required to evaluate whether the decision had been correct [23]. These observations led us to propose that PMv is involved not only in forming decisions but also in assessing them, and that this assessment could be used to shape future behavior. If PMv indeed participates in the use of outcome information to guide subsequent choices, several predictions follow. First, behavior and neuronal activity in a given trial should depend on the outcome of the immediately preceding trial. Second, because the usefulness of outcome information declines with temporal distance, any such influence should be restricted to recent trials, and trials further in the past should have little or no effect. Third, the impact of the outcome should depend on the difficulty of the previous decision: errors in difficult trials are less informative about a failure of the observer’s strategy and are expected, whereas the outcomes of difficult trials may nevertheless carry greater uncertainty and therefore more potential for learning, so the magnitude of the neural and behavioral effects is expected to vary with difficulty [24,25]. Testing these predictions requires analyzing both performance and single-neuron activity as a function of the history of outcomes and the difficulty of previous trials. In the present study, we addressed these questions by reanalyzing behavioral data and PMv single-unit recordings obtained while monkeys performed the vibrotactile discrimination task. We sorted trials according to whether the preceding trial (n−1) was correct or incorrect and compared both behavioral performance and neuronal firing in the current trial (n). To determine the temporal extent of these effects, we repeated the analysis using the outcome of trial n−2. Finally, we separated previous trials by difficulty, defined by the similarity between the two stimulus frequencies, to test whether the consequences of an outcome depend on how demanding the decision was. We found that the outcome of trial n−1 significantly modified both the activity of individual PMv neurons and behavioral performance in trial n, whereas the outcome of trial n−2 had no detectable influence on either measure. Moreover, outcomes of difficult trials had a larger behavioral impact and engaged a greater number of PMv neurons than outcomes of easy trials. These results support the hypothesis that PMv evaluates the decision process and exploits this information to adjust future behavior, thereby extending the role of this area beyond sensorimotor transformation to include the use of experience for improving performance. Subjects and apparatus Two adult male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) were used (monkey 1, 8 kg; monkey 2, 10 kg). All procedures complied with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and the European Union directive on animal experimentation, and were approved by the institutional ethics committee. Animals sat in a primate chair facing a computer monitor, with the right hand free to operate a push button and the left hand restrained. Stimulus presentation, event timing and reward delivery were controlled by custom software, and behavioral events were recorded with millisecond resolution. Task Monkeys performed a vibrotactile frequency discrimination task, as previously described [1,2]. Each trial began when a probe indenter descended onto the glabrous skin of the distal segments of one digit of the restrained hand. The monkey responded by placing its free hand on a stationary key (pushbutton). After a variable prestimulus delay (500–1500 ms), a first mechanical vibration (f1) was delivered for 500 ms. A fixed delay of 3 s followed, after which a second vibration (f2) of 500 ms was applied. The monkey then released the key (PK) and pressed one of two buttons to indicate whether f2 was higher or lower in frequency than f1. Correct responses were rewarded with a drop of juice; incorrect responses were followed by no reward and a brief auditory cue. Stimulus amplitudes were adjusted to equate perceived intensity across frequencies, and stimulus pairs were presented in pseudorandom order. The stimulus set comprised 14 (f1, f2) pairs, with f1 ranging from 10 to 34 Hz and f2 differing from f1 by 6–8 Hz in either direction, with equal numbers of f1>f2 and f1<f2 trials. Pairs were balanced such that f1 alone could not predict the correct response. Trials were classified by difficulty according to the absolute frequency difference relative to the base frequency, and by the Weber-like ratio (f2−f1)/f1; trials with ratios in the lower range were defined as difficult and those in the higher range as easy [3]. Trial sequences were generated so that each pair followed every other pair with comparable probability, preventing outcome-dependent stimulus statistics. Neuronal recording Recordings were made with an array of seven independent, movable microelectrodes (tip impedance 1–1.5 MΩ) inserted through a stainless steel chamber implanted over the left hemisphere, contralateral to the stimulated hand. Electrodes were positioned with a manipulator to target the ventral premotor cortex (PMv), lateral to the arcuate sulcus and ventral to the spur, at sites previously identified [2,4]. Recording locations were verified by stereotaxic coordinates and structural magnetic resonance imaging. Neuronal signals were amplified, filtered and sorted online, and spike waveforms and times were stored for offline verification. Neurons were included if they were well isolated and recorded for at least 10 correct and 5 incorrect trials per condition analyzed. No preselection based on task-related responses was applied; neurons were recorded if they showed stable spiking during the task. Behavioral analysis Trials were sorted according to the outcome of the preceding trial (n−1): correct (C) or error (E). Analogous sorting was applied to trial n−2. Only trials that followed completed trials were included; aborted trials, such as those with premature key release, were excluded together with the subsequent trial. Performance was defined as the percentage of correct responses in trial n conditional on the previous outcome. Differences between conditions were tested with chi-square tests and with a binomial generalized linear model including previous outcome, difficulty and their interaction, with session as a random factor [5]. To assess the effect of the previous trial's difficulty, trials n−1 were divided into easy and difficult, separately for correct and error outcomes, and performance in trial n was compared across these categories. Reaction times and movement times were compared with Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. To exclude confounds, we verified that the distribution of (f1, f2) pairs in trial n did not differ across previous-outcome conditions (chi-square test, P>0.05). We also examined whether errors reflected shifts in response strategy, such as a bias toward one button, by computing the probability of repeating the previous motor response after correct and error trials. Neuronal analysis Firing rate was computed in successive windows (typically 250 ms, 50 ms steps) aligned to key events: f1 onset, f2 onset, and the PK. We focused on three periods: the prestimulus period (500 ms before f1), the interval after f1, and the postdecision period after the push button press. For each neuron and period, firing rates in trial n were compared between trials preceded by correct and by incorrect outcomes with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (P<0.05). To avoid sensitivity to differences in trial counts, comparisons were repeated on subsamples matched in number and in stimulus-pair composition. Neurons with significant differences were considered modulated by previous outcome. The proportion of modulated neurons was tested against the 5% false-positive rate with a binomial test, and permutation tests (1000 shuffles of previous-outcome labels) provided empirical null distributions [6]. A previous-outcome index was computed as (FRE − FRC)/(FRE + FRC), where FRE and FRC are mean firing rates in trial n after error and correct trials. Population values were evaluated with signed-rank tests. Analyses were repeated for outcome at trial n−2 and for easy versus difficult n−1 trials. To dissociate effects of previous outcome from those of the current choice, we additionally fit a multiple linear regression to firing rate with predictors of previous outcome, previous difficulty, current stimulus frequency, current choice and current outcome [7]; significance of coefficients was assessed by permutation. The proportions of neurons significantly modulated under difficult versus easy conditions were compared with chi-square tests. Statistics Unless stated otherwise, tests were two-tailed with α=0.05. Data are presented as mean ± SEM. Analyses were performed in MATLAB (MathWorks). Multiple comparisons were corrected using the Bonferroni or false discovery rate procedure [8]. Data from the two animals were first analyzed separately and pooled when results were consistent. We analyzed behavioral and neuronal data from two monkeys performing a vibrotactile frequency discrimination task, in which animals compared two mechanical vibrations (f1 and f2) applied to the fingertip and reported whether f2 was higher or lower than f1 by pressing one of two buttons. Correct responses were rewarded with a drop of juice, and errors were followed by no reward and a brief timeout. We recorded 312 PMv neurons across sessions, of which 241 had task-related activity during at least one trial period and were included in subsequent analyses. Trials were classified according to the outcome of the preceding trial (n−1) as post-correct or post-error, and, for the control analysis, by the outcome of trial n−2. Behavioral effects of the previous outcome Overall, animals performed at 87.4 ± 3.1% correct (mean ± SD). Performance in trial n depended significantly on the outcome of trial n−1. Accuracy was lower after an error than after a correct trial (82.1% vs. 88.6%; paired t-test across sessions, p < 0.001). Polar codes, introduced by Arıkan, are the first class of channel codes proven to achieve the capacity of binary-input memoryless symmetric channels under low-complexity successive cancellation (SC) decoding. Their construction is based on channel polarization: as the code length grows, the synthesized bit channels become either almost noiseless or almost useless. Information bits are placed on the reliable channels (unfrozen bits) and fixed bits on the unreliable ones (frozen bits). Despite their asymptotic optimality, the finite-length performance of polar codes under SC decoding is unsatisfactory, mainly because of the suboptimality of SC decoding itself. A well-known improvement is SC list (SCL) decoding, proposed by Tal and Vardy, which keeps L candidate paths in parallel. When combined with a cyclic redundancy check (CRC), the resulting CRC-aided SCL (CA-SCL) decoder can outperform LDPC and turbo codes at short and moderate lengths, and polar codes with CA-SCL decoding have been adopted for the control channel in 5G. The drawback is complexity: the time and memory requirements of SCL decoding grow roughly linearly with L, and the sorting and path-copying operations add further latency. This motivates decoders that approach CA-SCL performance at a complexity closer to that of SC decoding. The key weakness of SC decoding is error propagation. Bits are decoded sequentially, and each decision uses all previous hard decisions as if they were correct. Once an unfrozen bit is wrongly estimated, subsequent decoding is performed with a wrong partial-sum context, and further errors become very likely. Consequently, the block error is largely determined by the position of the first error. If this bit can be found and corrected, the remaining decoding is often successful. This observation underlies SC-flip (SCF) decoding, in which a failed CRC triggers a re-decoding attempt with one chosen bit flipped. Candidate bits are chosen according to the magnitude of their log-likelihood ratios (LLRs), and the process can be repeated for several trials. Later work generalized the idea to multiple flips, introduced dynamic flip sets, and used metrics that account for the probability that a bit is the first error. Yet existing approaches have limitations. Simple LLR-based ordering may need many trials to hit the first error, particularly at low SNR. Handling several errors requires searching over combinations of flip positions, whose number grows combinatorially with the number of errors, so that the gain over SC decoding comes at a large cost in complexity unless the candidate set is carefully limited. In this paper we address both problems. First, we construct a critical set S of unfrozen bits that contains, with high probability (typically above 99%), the position where the first error occurs. The construction exploits the structure of polar codes: whether an unfrozen bit is likely to be the first error depends on the reliability of its bit channel and on the frozen bits that precede it, and the set can be obtained offline for a given code and channel condition. Since the set is much smaller than the whole set of unfrozen bits, restricting flip attempts to S sharply reduces the search space without noticeably sacrificing the ability to correct the first error. Second, we develop a progressive multi-level bit-flipping decoding algorithm that handles multiple errors layer by layer. After the first error is located and corrected using the first-layer critical set, decoding proceeds, and a second error may occur later. Rather than treating all bits jointly, we construct a second-layer critical set using the remaining undecoded subtree associated with the previous layer, that is, the portion of the decoding tree that follows the first flipped bit. The procedure is repeated, giving multiple layers of critical sets. The level of the decoder is the number of such layers, and indicates the number of independent errors that can be corrected. Because each layer's set is built from the remaining subtree, the candidate flips at each layer are few, and the total number of trials grows far more slowly than in exhaustive multi-bit flipping. We evaluate the proposed decoder through simulations. As the level increases, the block error rate (BLER) approaches that of CA-SCL decoding; for example, a level-4 progressive bit-flipping decoder performs comparably with CA-SCL decoding with list size L = 32. We also analyze the average complexity. Since most received blocks are decoded correctly by the initial SC pass at medium to high SNR, additional flipping trials are rarely needed, and the average complexity is close to that of SC decoding and much lower than that of SCL decoding. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: - We propose a systematic construction of a critical set of unfrozen bits that contains the first error with probability above 99%. - We design a progressive multi-level bit-flipping algorithm in which layered critical sets are built from the remaining undecoded subtrees, enabling the correction of multiple independent errors with a limited number of trials. - We show by simulation that the proposed decoder with level 4 matches CA-SCL decoding with L = 32 in BLER, while its average complexity is similar to SC decoding at medium to high SNR. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews polar codes, SC decoding, SCL decoding and SCF decoding. Section III describes the construction of the critical set. Section IV presents the progressive multi-level bit-flipping decoding algorithm. Section V gives simulation results and complexity analysis, and Section VI concludes the paper. We consider a polar code of length N = 2^n with K information bits and a CRC of length r included among the unfrozen bits. Let A denote the unfrozen index set and A^c the frozen set. The codeword is transmitted over a BPSK-AWGN channel, and the decoder observes the channel LLR vector y. SC decoding produces estimates û1,…,ûN sequentially, with ûi = ui for i in A^c. 1. Critical set construction Let i denote the index of the first erroneous unfrozen bit in an SC decoding attempt. Because bits before i are correct, the SC decoder under a genie-aided assumption has the same LLR statistics as for the true codeword. We seek a set S ⊆ A of small cardinality such that P(i ∈ S) exceeds 0.99. For each unfrozen index i, we estimate the genie-aided error probability pi = P(ûi ≠ ui | u1^{i-1} correct) by Gaussian approximation (density evolution) at the design SNR. The probability that i is the first error is then qi = pi ∏{j∈A, j<i} (1 − pj). The critical set is formed by sorting the indices by qi in descending order and adding them until the cumulative sum Σ{i∈S} qi reaches a threshold (1−ε)·Σ{i∈A} qi, with ε = 0.01. Since the qi decay for large i because of the product term, and the pi of highly reliable bits are negligible, |S| is much smaller than K. Monte Carlo simulation confirms that the empirical coverage of i by S is typically above 99% across the SNR range of interest. We denote the elements of S in increasing order, s1<s2<…<s{|S|}. 2. Single-level bit flipping The level-1 decoder first runs standard SC decoding to obtain û. If the CRC passes, decoding stops. Otherwise, the decoder assumes that the first error lies in S and tries to correct it. For each candidate sk ∈ S, taken in order of a reliability metric, it re-runs SC decoding with û{sk} flipped. The metric is the absolute LLR |L{sk}| recorded in the first pass: the smaller it is, the more likely the decision was wrong. After flipping, SC decoding resumes from sk, reusing the stored partial sums and LLRs for all earlier nodes, so only the portion of the decoding tree after sk is recomputed. Candidates are tried up to a maximum number T1, and decoding terminates as soon as the CRC is satisfied. 3. Layered critical sets and progressive multi-level flipping A single flip can only fix one error. To correct multiple independent errors, we build a second critical set after the first flip. Suppose a flip at position s has been made. The remaining undecoded part of the code is described by the subtree of the SC decoding tree associated with the indices greater than s. We treat this remaining subtree as a shorter polar code with a modified channel (the LLRs conditioned on the decided prefix). A second-layer critical set S^{(2)}(s) ⊆ A ∩ {i > s} is constructed using the same procedure as in Section 1, but with the genie-aided error probabilities pi recomputed for the residual subtree and the first-error probabilities normalized over indices after s. Because the residual structure depends only on s, these sets can be precomputed offline. Repeating the construction yields layered sets S^{(ℓ)}(s1,…,s{ℓ−1}), where ℓ is the layer. A level-ω decoder corrects up to ω errors by flipping at most ω bits, one from each layer. The flips are called independent in that each flipped bit is the first error of the residual decoding problem after the previous correction; errors induced by propagation from an earlier error are not separately targeted, since they vanish once the earlier error is fixed. The algorithm proceeds progressively: 1. Run SC. If the CRC passes, output û. 2. For layer ℓ = 1,…,ω: for the current flip pattern F{ℓ−1} (initially empty), take the SC pass that follows F{ℓ−1}, rank the candidates in S^{(ℓ)} by |Li|, and attempt flips in that order (up to Tℓ candidates). Each attempt resumes SC from the flipped index. If the CRC passes, output the result. 3. Attempts that fail the CRC are kept in a queue ordered by a path metric, the sum of |L{s}| over flipped positions. The lowest-metric failed attempt is expanded next at layer ℓ+1 with its own critical set. 4. If all budgets are exhausted without a CRC pass, output the SC estimate (or the lowest-metric candidate). The total number of SC re-decodings is bounded by Σ{ℓ=1}^{ω} Tℓ-type products, controlled by choosing Tℓ small for deeper layers. Larger ω improves BLER by covering more error patterns, approaching CA-SCL with moderate list sizes (ω = 4 versus L = 32 in our experiments). 4. Complexity analysis SC decoding costs O(N log N). A flip at index s requires recomputation only of the nodes affected after s, whose cost is on average smaller than a full decoding. Let Pf(γ) denote the probability that the initial SC pass fails the CRC at SNR γ. The average complexity is approximately Cavg ≈ CSC + Pf(γ) · Cflip, where Cflip is the expected extra cost of the flipping phase, bounded by the number of attempts times the average partial re-decoding cost. At medium to high SNR, Pf is small, so Cavg approaches CSC, whereas SCL costs O(L N log N) regardless of SNR. At low SNR, the number of attempts approaches the maximum, and complexity is bounded by that cap. 5. Simulation setup We evaluate polar codes with CRC for several lengths and rates over AWGN. Critical sets are designed at a fixed SNR and used across the tested range. We compare BLER with SC, CA-SCL for L = 2,…,32, and report average numbers of SC-equivalent operations and critical set coverage rates. We evaluate the proposed progressive bit-flipping (PBF) decoder by Monte Carlo simulation over the binary-input AWGN channel with BPSK modulation. Unless otherwise stated, the polar codes have length N = 1024 and rate R = 1/2, constructed by Gaussian approximation at the design SNR, and a 16-bit CRC is appended for the CRC-aided decoders. Each point is simulated until at least 100 block errors are collected. The reference decoders are SC, CA-SCL with list sizes L = 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, and the dynamic SC-flip (DSCF) decoder with a comparable number of flipping attempts. Critical set accuracy. Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory skin disease that affects approximately 2–3% of the world population. Its most common form, psoriasis vulgaris or chronic plaque psoriasis, presents with sharply demarcated erythematous plaques covered by silvery scales, most often on the extensor surfaces, scalp and lumbosacral region. The disease is associated with considerable physical and psychosocial burden and with comorbidities such as psoriatic arthritis, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease and depression. These associations suggest that psoriasis is a systemic inflammatory disorder rather than a disease confined to the skin. The pathogenesis of psoriasis is complex and involves interactions between genetic susceptibility, environmental triggers, keratinocytes and cells of the innate and adaptive immune systems. The prevailing model emphasizes the IL-23/Th17 axis: activated dendritic cells produce IL-23 and IL-12, which drive differentiation and expansion of Th17 and Th1 cells. These cells release IL-17, IL-22, TNF-α and interferon-γ, which stimulate keratinocyte hyperproliferation, abnormal differentiation and production of chemokines and antimicrobial peptides, thereby sustaining a self-amplifying inflammatory loop. Although T cells have received most attention, there is growing recognition that neutrophils and other innate cells contribute significantly to lesion development and maintenance. The histological hallmarks of psoriasis include epidermal acanthosis, parakeratosis, loss of the granular layer, elongated rete ridges, dilated dermal capillaries and a mixed dermal infiltrate of lymphocytes and macrophages. Equally characteristic is the accumulation of neutrophils in the epidermis. Collections of neutrophils in the parakeratotic stratum corneum form Munro microabscesses, and collections within the spinous layer form spongiform pustules of Kogoj. Neutrophils are attracted to the epidermis by chemokines such as IL-8 (CXCL8), CXCL1 and CXCL5 and by IL-17, and their presence is so consistent that it is used as a diagnostic criterion. In pustular variants of psoriasis neutrophil infiltration is even more prominent. Circulating neutrophils from patients with psoriasis also show enhanced activation, increased adhesion and altered chemotaxis, and the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio has been proposed as a marker of disease activity and cardiovascular risk. Neutrophils are the most abundant circulating leukocytes and the first line of defense against invading microorganisms. When activated, they degranulate, produce reactive oxygen species through the NADPH oxidase system, and release neutrophil extracellular traps. Myeloperoxidase (MPO) is a heme-containing enzyme stored in large amounts in the azurophilic granules of neutrophils, where it accounts for about 5% of the cell’s dry weight. In the presence of hydrogen peroxide, MPO oxidizes chloride to hypochlorous acid, a potent microbicidal oxidant. Hypochlorous acid and other MPO-derived products, however, can also damage host tissue by oxidizing lipids, proteins and DNA, and they may amplify inflammation. MPO has been implicated in atherosclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease and neurodegenerative disorders. In addition, MPO consumes nitric oxide and generates nitrating species such as nitrogen dioxide, linking its activity to nitrogen-based oxidative stress. Nitric oxide (NO) is a short-lived free radical produced from L-arginine by nitric oxide synthases. The inducible isoform (iNOS, NOS2) is expressed in response to cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1 and interferon-γ and to bacterial products, and it generates large, sustained amounts of NO. In normal skin iNOS expression is minimal, but it is upregulated in keratinocytes, macrophages, endothelial cells and infiltrating leukocytes during inflammation. NO produced in psoriatic skin may cause vasodilation and erythema, promote keratinocyte proliferation and contribute to cytotoxic effects through formation of peroxynitrite. Increased iNOS expression has been reported in psoriatic lesions, and some studies have found elevated serum or tissue NO metabolites in patients, although findings across studies have been inconsistent. Moreover, a functional interaction between MPO and the NO pathway is plausible, because MPO products and neutrophil-derived oxidants can influence NO bioavailability and the signaling pathways that regulate iNOS transcription, including NF-κB. Despite these observations, relatively few studies have examined MPO and iNOS together in psoriasis, and fewer still have assessed both systemic levels and local tissue expression in the same patients. Serum measurements reflect systemic neutrophil activation and inflammatory burden, whereas immunohistochemistry of lesional and uninvolved skin shows whether the cells infiltrating the lesion are actively synthesizing these enzymes. Comparing these compartments could clarify whether neutrophil-derived MPO acts mainly as a systemic marker or as a local effector of tissue inflammation, and whether it is related to iNOS induction. Such information might also identify new therapeutic targets, since current treatments mainly target T-cell-derived cytokines and are not effective, safe or affordable for all patients. The aim of this study was therefore to investigate the contribution of neutrophils to the pathogenesis of psoriasis at the blood and tissue levels by measuring serum MPO and iNOS concentrations in patients with chronic plaque psoriasis and healthy controls, and by evaluating the immunohistochemical expression of MPO and iNOS in lesional and uninvolved skin biopsies from the same patients. This cross-sectional case-control study was carried out in the Department of Dermatology and Venereology in collaboration with the Departments of Pathology and Biochemistry. The study protocol was approved by the local ethics committee, and all procedures were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants before enrollment. Study population Fifty adult patients with chronic plaque-type psoriasis (psoriasis vulgaris) and 25 age- and sex-matched healthy volunteers were enrolled. The diagnosis of psoriasis was established clinically by dermatologists and confirmed histopathologically. Disease severity was assessed using the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI), and age, sex, disease duration, age at onset, body mass index, and smoking status were recorded. Inclusion criteria for patients were age of 18 years or older, a diagnosis of chronic plaque psoriasis, and a lesion suitable for biopsy. Exclusion criteria were other psoriasis subtypes (guttate, pustular, erythrodermic), systemic inflammatory, autoimmune, or infectious disease, diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular disease, malignancy, renal or hepatic disease, pregnancy or lactation, and any systemic anti-psoriatic therapy (including phototherapy, methotrexate, cyclosporine, acitretin, and biologic agents) within the previous 3 months or topical therapy within the previous 2 weeks. Healthy controls had no dermatological or systemic disease and no history of regular drug use. Individuals with acute infection at the time of sampling were excluded from both groups. Blood sampling and ELISA Venous blood samples (5 ml) were drawn from the antecubital vein after overnight fasting. Samples were allowed to clot at room temperature for 30 minutes and centrifuged at 3000 rpm for 10 minutes. Serum was separated, aliquoted, and stored at -80°C until analysis. Repeated freeze-thaw cycles were avoided. Serum MPO and iNOS concentrations were measured with commercially available human sandwich ELISA kits according to the manufacturers' instructions. Briefly, standards and samples were added in duplicate to microplate wells precoated with specific capture antibodies and incubated. After washing, biotin-conjugated detection antibody and then streptavidin-horseradish peroxidase were added, followed by substrate solution. The reaction was stopped with stop solution, and absorbance was read at 450 nm using a microplate reader. Concentrations were calculated from a standard curve generated for each plate. Results were expressed as ng/ml. Intra- and inter-assay coefficients of variation were within the limits provided by the manufacturer. All assays were performed by the same investigator, who was blinded to group allocation. Skin biopsies In each patient, two 4-mm punch biopsy specimens were obtained under local anesthesia with lidocaine: one from the center of an active plaque lesion and one from clinically uninvolved skin at least 5 cm away from any lesion. Biopsies were taken from comparable body regions where possible. Specimens were fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin, processed routinely, and embedded in paraffin. Sections 4 µm thick were stained with hematoxylin and eosin to confirm the diagnosis and to evaluate typical histological features, including parakeratosis, acanthosis, elongation of rete ridges, loss of the granular layer, neutrophil infiltration, and Munro microabscesses. Immunohistochemistry For immunohistochemistry, 4-µm sections were mounted on positively charged slides, deparaffinized in xylene, and rehydrated through graded alcohols. Antigen retrieval was performed by heating sections in citrate buffer (pH 6.0) in a microwave oven or water bath. Endogenous peroxidase activity was blocked with 3% hydrogen peroxide for 10 minutes, and nonspecific binding was blocked with protein block solution. Sections were incubated with primary antibodies against human MPO and iNOS at the manufacturer-recommended dilutions, followed by incubation with a biotinylated secondary antibody and streptavidin-peroxidase complex. Immunoreactivity was visualized with 3,3'-diaminobenzidine as chromogen, and sections were counterstained with Mayer's hematoxylin, dehydrated, and mounted. Human tonsil tissue served as a positive control, and negative controls were prepared by omitting the primary antibody. Staining was evaluated independently by two pathologists blinded to clinical data using a light microscope. MPO staining was assessed in infiltrating leukocytes (neutrophils) in the epidermis and dermis, and iNOS staining was assessed in epidermal keratinocytes and inflammatory cells. Staining intensity was graded semiquantitatively as 0 (none), 1 (weak), 2 (moderate), or 3 (intense), and the extent of positive cells was scored as 0 (<5%), 1 (5–25%), 2 (26–50%), 3 (51–75%), or 4 (>75%) in ten randomly selected high-power fields (×400). A combined score was obtained by multiplying intensity and extent scores. Discrepancies between observers were resolved by consensus at a multi-head microscope. Lesional and uninvolved skin from the same patient were compared. Statistical analysis Data were analyzed with SPSS software. The distribution of continuous variables was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test and histograms. Normally distributed variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation and compared between patients and controls using the independent samples t-test; non-normally distributed variables were expressed as median (interquartile range) and compared using the Mann-Whitney U test. Categorical variables were compared using the chi-square or Fisher's exact test. Immunohistochemical scores of lesional and uninvolved skin were compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Correlations between serum MPO and iNOS levels, tissue scores, and PASI were evaluated with Spearman's correlation coefficient. Interobserver agreement was assessed with the kappa statistic. A two-tailed p value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant. A total of 50 patients with chronic plaque psoriasis (28 men, 22 women; mean age 41.6 ± 12.3 years) and 25 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (14 men, 11 women; mean age 39.8 ± 11.5 years) were included. There were no significant differences between the groups in age (p = 0.52) or sex distribution (p = 0.91). The mean disease duration in the patient group was 11.2 ± 8.4 years, and the mean Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) score was 14.7 ± 8.9. Biopsies were obtained from both lesional and uninvolved skin in all 50 patients, and all specimens were adequate for histological and immunohistochemical evaluation. Serum myeloperoxidase levels Serum MPO levels were significantly higher in patients with psoriasis than in healthy controls. The mean serum MPO concentration was 38.4 ± 17.6 ng/ml in the patient group and 21.3 ± 9.8 ng/ml in the control group (p < 0.001). The distribution of values in the patient group was wider, and a subset of patients had levels well above the upper range of the controls. When patients were stratified by disease severity (PASI < 10 versus PASI ≥ 10), serum MPO tended to be higher in the more severe group (42.9 ± 18.4 versus 32.1 ± 14.2 ng/ml). A weak-to-moderate positive correlation was observed between serum MPO and PASI score (r = 0.36, p = 0.01). No significant correlation was found between serum MPO and disease duration, age, or sex. Serum iNOS levels In contrast to MPO, serum iNOS levels did not differ significantly between the groups. The mean serum iNOS level was 2.84 ± 1.35 ng/ml in patients and 2.61 ± 1.22 ng/ml in controls (p = 0.48). Serum iNOS did not correlate with PASI score (r = 0.11, p = 0.44) or with disease duration (r = 0.08, p = 0.58). There was also no significant correlation between serum iNOS and serum MPO levels in either the patient group (r = 0.17, p = 0.23) or the control group (r = 0.12, p = 0.57). Histopathological findings Lesional biopsies showed the typical features of psoriasis vulgaris, including regular epidermal hyperplasia with elongated rete ridges, parakeratosis, loss of the granular layer, suprapapillary thinning, dilated capillaries in the papillary dermis, and a mixed dermal inflammatory infiltrate.
