Oral cavity cancer is among the most common malignancies in South and Southeast Asia, and the oral tongue is the most frequent subsite in many series. In India, tobacco and areca nut use contribute to a particularly high burden of the disease. Squamous cell carcinoma accounts for the vast majority of these tumors. Oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma (OTSCC) is notable for its aggressive biological behavior, with a marked propensity for local invasion into the rich lingual musculature and for early lymphatic spread to cervical nodes. Despite advances in surgery, radiotherapy, and systemic therapy, regional nodal metastasis remains the single most important prognostic factor, roughly halving survival when present. Surgical resection is the mainstay of treatment for early OTSCC (T1 and T2 tumors). The primary lesion is addressed by wide local excision or partial glossectomy. The management of the clinically negative neck (cN0) has been debated for decades. Occult nodal metastasis is reported in approximately 20–40% of clinically node-negative early oral tongue cancers. Observation with close follow-up risks nodal relapse that is often detected late, requires more extensive treatment, and carries a worse outcome. Elective neck dissection, in contrast, exposes all patients to the morbidity of the procedure, including shoulder dysfunction, cosmetic deformity, and prolonged hospital stay, although most of them harbor no nodal disease. Randomized evidence, including the trial by D'Cruz and colleagues, has shown that elective neck dissection improves overall and disease-free survival compared with therapeutic dissection on nodal relapse in early oral cancer. Even so, the concern about overtreatment persists, especially in centers with reliable follow-up and in patients with very thin tumors, who have a low risk of nodal disease. A dependable method of identifying patients at low or high risk of occult metastasis before surgery would therefore be of considerable clinical value. Among the histopathological predictors of nodal metastasis, tumor thickness (TT) and depth of invasion (DOI) have emerged as the most consistent. Numerous studies have shown that the risk of cervical metastasis rises with increasing thickness, with proposed cutoffs ranging between 3 and 5 mm. The eighth edition of the American Joint Committee on Cancer staging system has incorporated DOI into the T category of oral cancer, underscoring its importance. Because pathological measurement is available only after resection, it cannot guide the extent of the initial operation. Decisions about whether to perform an elective neck dissection, which is often done in the same sitting as the primary resection, would be better informed by accurate preoperative assessment of thickness. Clinical palpation is a subjective and imprecise estimate of tumor thickness, particularly for deeper lesions or those with submucosal extension. Cross-sectional imaging, including magnetic resonance imaging and computed tomography, can estimate tumor dimensions, but each has limitations. These modalities are expensive and not universally available, and they are susceptible to motion and dental artifacts. In addition, the tumor may be difficult to distinguish from adjacent tissue, particularly when it is small. Their use for very small superficial lesions is therefore limited. High-resolution ultrasonography (USG) is an attractive alternative. It is inexpensive, widely available, noninvasive, radiation free, and can be performed rapidly in an outpatient setting. The superficial location of the tongue makes it readily accessible to intraoral transducers, and the contrast between the hypoechoic tumor and the surrounding echogenic musculature allows the tumor to be delineated with high spatial resolution. The same equipment can be used to evaluate cervical lymph nodes for size, shape, loss of the echogenic hilum, and vascular pattern, with or without fine-needle aspiration cytology. Intraoral ultrasound has therefore been investigated for measuring tumor thickness, and several studies have reported good agreement with histopathology. However, the existing literature comprises small series with variable methodology, differing definitions of thickness and depth, and inconsistent reporting of agreement beyond simple correlation. Few studies have specifically examined early, clinically node-negative tongue cancers managed by a uniform elective neck dissection policy, and fewer still have related ultrasonographic thickness to the pathological nodal status. An additional source of discrepancy is shrinkage of tissue during formalin fixation and processing, which can lead to underestimation of microscopic thickness relative to in vivo or fresh measurements. Comparison of ultrasonographic findings with both fresh-specimen and paraffin-section measurements may help clarify the extent of these differences. We therefore conducted a prospective study of patients with early (T1 and T2, clinically N0) OTSCC who were treated with primary resection and ipsilateral elective neck dissection (levels I–IV). The first objective was to assess the statistical correlation and agreement between tumor thickness measured by preoperative intraoral ultrasonography and that determined by histopathological examination. The second objective was to evaluate the ability of ultrasonographically measured thickness to predict occult cervical nodal metastasis, and to identify a thickness threshold that might help guide the decision for elective neck dissection in early oral tongue cancer. This prospective observational study was conducted in the Department of Head and Neck Surgical Oncology of a tertiary care referral center over a period of 2 years, from 2012 to 2013. The study was carried out after approval from the institutional ethics committee, and written informed consent was obtained from all participants before enrollment. Patient selection Consecutive patients presenting with biopsy-proven squamous cell carcinoma of the oral tongue were screened for eligibility. Inclusion criteria were: (1) clinically early-stage disease (T1 or T2 according to the AJCC staging system, with clinical tumor size of 4 cm or less) with no clinically or radiologically palpable cervical lymphadenopathy (cN0); (2) primary lesion involving the anterior two-thirds of the tongue; (3) no prior treatment, including surgery, radiotherapy, or chemotherapy; and (4) fitness for surgery under general anesthesia. Exclusion criteria were: (1) clinically node-positive neck; (2) lesions extending to the floor of the mouth, mandible, or base of tongue that precluded reliable ultrasound assessment; (3) recurrent tumors or second primary tumors; (4) patients who declined surgery or elective neck dissection; and (5) inability to tolerate intraoral ultrasound probe placement because of severe trismus or pain. Twenty-four patients satisfying these criteria were included in the final analysis. Clinical evaluation All patients underwent detailed history taking and complete head and neck examination, including inspection and bimanual palpation of the primary lesion and neck. Clinical T stage was assigned on the basis of the greatest dimension of the lesion. Incisional biopsy was performed to confirm the diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma before further workup. Ultrasonographic evaluation Preoperative ultrasonography was performed by a single experienced radiologist who was aware of the diagnosis but blinded to the final histopathological results. A high-frequency linear array transducer (7.5–12 MHz) was used. Intraoral ultrasound of the tongue was carried out with the patient in the supine position with the neck slightly extended. A water-based gel was applied, and the probe, covered with a sterile sheath, was placed directly on the dorsal or lateral surface of the tongue lesion. Where necessary, a transcutaneous submental approach was used as an adjunct to confirm depth. The tumor appeared as a hypoechoic area relative to the surrounding normal tongue musculature. Tumor thickness was measured in the plane perpendicular to the mucosal surface, from the surface of the tumor, or from the level of the adjacent normal mucosa in ulcerative lesions, to the deepest point of tumor invasion. Measurements were taken in both transverse and longitudinal planes, and the greatest value was recorded in millimeters. Ultrasonography of the neck was performed in the same session to evaluate cervical lymph nodes at levels I to V bilaterally. Nodes were assessed for size, shape (short-to-long axis ratio), loss of the echogenic hilum, cortical thickening, necrosis, and vascular pattern. Nodes were considered suspicious if they were rounded, lacked a fatty hilum, or showed necrosis or abnormal vascularity. Only patients with sonographically negative necks were retained as clinically N0 for the purpose of this study. Surgical treatment After histopathological confirmation, all patients underwent wide local excision of the primary tumor with a clinical margin of at least 1 cm, along with ipsilateral elective supraomohyoid neck dissection (levels I to IV), as per institutional protocol. The glossectomy specimen was oriented and sent fresh to the pathology laboratory. Intraoperative and pathological measurement of tumor thickness Immediately after resection, the fresh specimen was examined, and tumor thickness was measured by a surgeon using a sterile ruler or caliper, from the tumor surface to the deepest point of invasion on a cut section through the lesion. The specimen was then fixed in 10% buffered formalin and processed routinely. Sections were cut at the thickest portion of the tumor, embedded in paraffin, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin. Microscopic tumor thickness was measured by a pathologist, blinded to the ultrasound findings, using an ocular micrometer, from the surface of the tumor (or the reconstructed mucosal level in ulcerated lesions) to the deepest point of invasion, excluding keratin. Pathological T stage, depth of invasion, differentiation, perineural and lymphovascular invasion, and margin status were recorded. Neck dissection specimens were examined for the number of nodes retrieved, number of positive nodes, and extracapsular spread. Occult nodal metastasis was defined as histopathologically positive nodes in a clinically and sonographically negative neck. Outcome measures The primary outcome was the correlation and agreement between ultrasonographic tumor thickness and microscopic tumor thickness. The secondary outcome was the association of tumor thickness and pathological T stage with pathological nodal status, and the determination of a thickness threshold predictive of occult cervical metastasis. Differences between ultrasound and histopathological measurements were categorized as within 1 mm, within 2 mm, or greater than 2 mm. Statistical analysis Data were entered into a spreadsheet and analyzed using SPSS statistical software. Continuous variables were summarized as mean and range, and categorical variables as frequencies and percentages. The correlation between ultrasonographic and microscopic tumor thickness was assessed using Pearson's correlation coefficient, and the reliability of the two methods was evaluated using the intraclass correlation coefficient. Agreement was further assessed by Bland–Altman analysis, calculating the mean difference (bias) and 95% limits of agreement. The association of pathological T stage and tumor thickness (categorized using cutoffs such as <4 mm and ≥4 mm) with pathological nodal status was tested using the Chi-square test. A P value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. A total of 24 patients with early (T1 and T2, clinically N0) oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma were enrolled during the study period from 2012 to 2013. All patients underwent preoperative intraoral and neck ultrasonography, resection of the primary lesion, and ipsilateral elective neck dissection (levels I to IV). All 24 patients were included in the final analysis, and none were lost to follow-up or excluded because of inadequate imaging or specimen handling. Patient and tumor characteristics The cohort comprised patients with a predominance of lesions on the lateral border of the tongue. Histopathology confirmed squamous cell carcinoma in all cases. Most tumors were well or moderately differentiated. On final pathological staging, the distribution of pT1 and pT2 lesions was similar to the clinical staging, with a small number of cases upstaged because of thickness or size on microscopic examination. Ultrasonographic tumor thickness (TT) was obtained in every patient, and the lesion was clearly visualized as a hypoechoic area contrasting with the adjacent normal tongue musculature. Correlation between ultrasonographic and histopathological tumor thickness A significant statistical correlation was found between TT measured by ultrasonography and the microscopic measurement from paraffin sections. The Pearson correlation coefficient was r = 0.678 (P < 0.001), indicating a strong positive linear relationship. The intraclass correlation coefficient was 0.808, indicating good to excellent agreement between the two methods. The absolute difference between the two measurements was within 1 mm in 9 of 24 cases (37.5%) and within 2 mm in 7 cases (29.16%). Thus 16 of 24 cases (66.7%) had a discrepancy of 2 mm or less. In the remaining 8 cases (33.3%), the difference was greater than 2 mm. These larger discrepancies occurred in both directions, with ultrasonography overestimating thickness in some cases and underestimating it in others, without a consistent pattern. Bacterial biofilms are structured communities of cells embedded in a self-produced extracellular matrix of polysaccharides, proteins, lipids and extracellular DNA. They are now recognized as the predominant mode of bacterial life in both natural and clinical settings [1]. It is estimated that biofilms are involved in a large majority of chronic and recurrent infections, including those associated with implanted medical devices, chronic wounds, cystic fibrosis lung disease, osteomyelitis and endocarditis [2,3]. Biofilm-embedded bacteria tolerate antibiotic concentrations that are 10 to 1000 times higher than those that kill their planktonic counterparts, so standard therapy frequently fails and infections relapse [4]. This tolerance is multifactorial. The matrix limits antibiotic diffusion and can bind or inactivate drugs, steep nutrient and oxygen gradients create zones of slow-growing or dormant cells, and a subpopulation of metabolically inactive persister cells survives lethal exposure without carrying heritable resistance determinants [5,6]. Persisters are widely considered the main reservoir for relapse and a stepping stone toward genetic resistance [7]. The clinical problem is aggravated by the global spread of antimicrobial resistance, particularly among the ESKAPE pathogens, which include Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii and Pseudomonas aeruginosa [8]. Treating a biofilm infection therefore resembles sailing between Scylla and Charybdis. Increasing antibiotic doses to overcome biofilm tolerance leads to systemic toxicity, as with aminoglycosides and polymyxins, and promotes resistance selection. Using conventional doses, in contrast, leaves the biofilm intact. New antibiotics are few, and few of them have specific anti-biofilm activity [9]. Alternative strategies are therefore needed, and combination therapy with adjuvants that sensitize biofilms to existing drugs is among the most attractive. Proposed approaches include matrix-degrading enzymes, quorum-sensing inhibitors, chelators, and agents that revive persisters metabolically [10,11]. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are a natural source of such adjuvants. They are evolutionarily ancient effectors of innate immunity found in virtually all organisms, and they are typically cationic and amphipathic [12]. Many AMPs act on bacterial membranes, which are targets that are hard to modify by mutation, and some also interact with intracellular targets [13]. Importantly, several AMPs are active against slow-growing and dormant cells and can penetrate or disrupt biofilms, which distinguishes them from many classical antibiotics whose action depends on active cell growth [14,15]. Synergy between AMPs and conventional antibiotics has been reported repeatedly. Permeabilization of the outer or cytoplasmic membrane by the peptide may increase intracellular access of the small-molecule drug, while the antibiotic may in turn weaken the cell’s ability to repair peptide-induced damage [16,17]. Nevertheless, clinical development of individual AMPs has been hampered by toxicity, proteolytic instability, high production costs and the limited activity of single peptides in physiological conditions [18]. In nature, however, the host does not rely on a single peptide. Immune responses produce mixtures of AMPs of different structural classes that act together and often synergistically, which broadens the activity spectrum and reduces the chance of resistance emerging [19,20]. The resulting complexity cannot be reproduced by studying isolated peptides. Insects are a particularly rich source of such multicomponent systems, as their humoral immunity depends largely on inducible AMPs secreted into the hemolymph after infection [21]. The blowfly Calliphora vicina is notable in this respect. Its larvae live in highly contaminated necrotic substrates and have been used for centuries in maggot debridement therapy of chronic wounds, which is attributed in part to antimicrobial and anti-biofilm secretions [22,23]. Upon bacterial challenge, C. vicina produces a set of AMPs that includes defensins, cecropins, diptericins and proline-rich peptides, which differ in structure and mechanism of action [24,25]. Defensins and cecropins act mainly on membranes, whereas proline-rich peptides can enter the cell and inhibit protein synthesis and chaperone function [26]. A natural combination of these peptides could therefore attack bacterial cells at several levels at once. We previously isolated from the hemolymph of bacteria-challenged C. vicina larvae a complex of AMPs, designated FLIP7 (fly immunity peptides), and showed that it contains these four peptide classes [27]. Whether such a native host AMP complex can potentiate conventional antibiotics against biofilms, and by what mechanism, has not been systematically examined. Most synergy studies to date have used planktonic cultures, synthetic single peptides and a narrow range of antibiotics, and they rarely distinguish between effects on growing cells, persisters and the biofilm matrix [16,28]. In this study we hypothesized that the AMP complex of the host immune system can improve the anti-biofilm activity of antibiotics. We tested FLIP7 in combination with antibiotics of different classes, including β-lactams, aminoglycosides, glycopeptides, macrolides, lincosamides, phenicols, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones and polymyxins. Model biofilms and planktonic cultures of S. aureus, Escherichia coli, P. aeruginosa, K. pneumoniae and A. baumannii were used. Interactions were quantified by the checkerboard method with fractional inhibitory concentration indices, using a cell viability assay based on trimethyl tetrazolium chloride and a crystal violet biofilm eradication assay supplemented with microscopy. We also compared biofilm and planktonic interactions, analyzed dose–effect curves for signs of persister involvement, and evaluated whether the combinations allow the effective anti-biofilm antibiotic concentration to be lowered below clinically achievable levels. FLIP7 isolation. Third-instar larvae of the blowfly Calliphora vicina were reared at 25 °C and challenged by pricking with a needle dipped in a suspension of Escherichia coli and Micrococcus luteus to induce the immune response [1]. Hemolymph was collected 24 h after challenge, acidified with 1% acetic acid, and centrifuged at 14,000 g for 20 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was loaded onto Sep-Pak C18 cartridges (Waters) equilibrated with 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA). After washing with 5% acetonitrile, peptides were eluted with 60% acetonitrile in 0.1% TFA and lyophilized. The fraction was further purified by solid-phase extraction and reversed-phase HPLC on a Jupiter C18 column (Phenomenex) using a linear acetonitrile gradient in 0.1% TFA. Fractions containing the defensin, cecropin, diptericin and proline-rich peptide groups were pooled in native proportions to obtain the complex designated FLIP7. Peptide composition was verified by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry (Bruker Ultraflex) and compared with known masses of C. vicina AMPs [1,2]. Total peptide concentration was determined by the bicinchoninic acid assay and by absorbance at 280 nm, and stock solutions were stored at −20 °C. Bacterial strains and growth conditions. The study used Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 29213, Escherichia coli ATCC 25922, Pseudomonas aeruginosa ATCC 27853, Klebsiella pneumoniae ATCC 700603 and Acinetobacter baumannii ATCC 19606, as well as clinical isolates of each species from the departmental collection. Cultures were stored in 20% glycerol at −80 °C and grown on tryptic soy agar. For experiments, single colonies were grown overnight in cation-adjusted Mueller–Hinton broth (CAMHB) at 37 °C with shaking, diluted, and grown to mid-logarithmic phase. Suspensions were adjusted to 0.5 McFarland (~1.5×10^8 CFU/mL) and diluted as required. Antibiotics. Meropenem, amikacin, kanamycin, gentamicin, ampicillin, oxacillin, cefotaxime, vancomycin, clindamycin, erythromycin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline, ciprofloxacin and polymyxin B (Sigma-Aldrich) were dissolved according to the manufacturers’ instructions, filter-sterilized and prepared freshly or stored at −20 °C. Not all antibiotics were tested against all species; combinations were selected according to the clinical relevance and intrinsic activity of each drug. Minimal inhibitory concentrations. MICs for planktonic cultures were determined by broth microdilution in 96-well plates according to CLSI guidelines [3], with a final inoculum of 5×10^5 CFU/mL. Plates were incubated for 18–20 h at 37 °C. MIC was defined as the lowest concentration preventing visible growth. Minimal biofilm-inhibitory concentrations were determined as described below. Biofilm formation. Biofilms were grown in 96-well polystyrene flat-bottom plates. Overnight cultures were diluted to 10^6 CFU/mL in tryptic soy broth supplemented with 1% glucose (S. aureus) or 0.25% glucose (Gram-negative species), and 100 µL was added per well. Plates were incubated statically for 24 h at 37 °C. Planktonic cells were removed, and wells were washed twice with sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) to leave adherent biofilms. Fresh medium containing test agents was then added and plates were incubated for a further 24 h. Checkerboard assay. Interactions between FLIP7 and antibiotics were assessed by the checkerboard method [4] in two-dimensional serial twofold dilutions, with antibiotic along the rows and FLIP7 along the columns, in both planktonic and biofilm formats. Growth and sterility controls were included on each plate. Cell viability was measured by reduction of 2,3,5-triphenyl (trimethyl) tetrazolium chloride (TTC): after treatment, 0.1% TTC was added and plates were incubated for 2 h at 37 °C in the dark; formazan was dissolved in ethanol and absorbance measured at 490 nm. The concentration yielding ≥90% decrease in absorbance relative to untreated control was taken as the inhibitory endpoint. The fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) was calculated as FICI = MIC(A in combination)/MIC(A alone) + MIC(B in combination)/MIC(B alone), and the minimal FICI for each combination was used. Interactions were interpreted as high synergy (FICI <0.25), synergy (0.25–0.5), additivity (>0.5–1), indifference/no interaction (>1–4) and antagonism (>4) [5]. Each checkerboard was run in triplicate on at least three independent days. Dose–effect analysis. Dose–effect curves of antibiotics alone and with fixed sub-inhibitory FLIP7 concentrations were fitted with a four-parameter logistic model in GraphPad Prism. Biphasic profiles and plateau levels of residual viability were examined as indicators of a persister subpopulation tolerant to the antibiotic [6]. Changes in plateau height and in the half-effective concentration were compared between conditions. Crystal violet biofilm eradication assay. After 24 h treatment, wells were washed twice with PBS, fixed with methanol for 15 min, air-dried, and stained with 0.1% crystal violet for 15 min. Excess dye was removed by washing with water, and bound dye was solubilized in 30% acetic acid. Absorbance was read at 570 nm. The minimal biofilm eradication concentration was defined as the lowest concentration reducing biomass by ≥90% relative to untreated biofilm. Results were compared with peak serum concentrations achievable clinically, taken from published pharmacokinetic data [7]. Microscopy. Biofilms were grown on glass-bottom dishes or coverslips and treated with antibiotic, FLIP7, or their combination for 24 h. Samples were examined by phase-contrast microscopy and by confocal laser scanning microscopy after staining with the LIVE/DEAD BacLight kit (SYTO 9/propidium iodide; Thermo Fisher) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Additional samples were fixed with 2.5% glutaraldehyde, dehydrated through an ethanol series, sputter-coated and imaged by scanning electron microscopy to evaluate integrity of the biofilm matrix. At least five fields per sample were captured. Statistical analysis. All experiments were performed in at least three biological replicates with technical triplicates. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation. Differences between groups, including FICI values in planktonic versus biofilm cultures, were assessed by Student’s t-test or one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test, after testing for normality. P < 0.05 was considered significant. Analyses were carried out in GraphPad Prism 9. FLIP7 was obtained from the hemolymph of bacteria-challenged C. vicina larvae by solid-phase extraction followed by reversed-phase HPLC. The preparation contained the four major AMP families known for this species: defensins, cecropins, diptericins and proline-rich peptides, as confirmed by mass spectrometry [12,14]. Protein arginine methylation is a widespread post-translational modification that contributes to the regulation of chromatin structure, transcription, RNA processing, signal transduction, and DNA damage response [1,2]. The modification is catalyzed by the protein arginine methyltransferase (PRMT) family, whose nine mammalian members use S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) as the methyl donor to generate monomethylarginine, asymmetric dimethylarginine (ADMA), or symmetric dimethylarginine (SDMA). PRMTs are classified by product: type I enzymes (PRMT1, 2, 3, 4/CARM1, 6, and 8) generate ADMA, type II enzymes (PRMT5 and PRMT9) generate SDMA, and PRMT7 is a type III enzyme that catalyzes only monomethylation [3]. Dysregulation of several PRMTs has been linked to human disease, and PRMT5 and type I PRMT inhibitors have advanced into clinical evaluation in oncology, supporting the tractability of this enzyme class as a therapeutic target [4,5]. CARM1 biology Coactivator-associated arginine methyltransferase 1 (CARM1, also known as PRMT4) was first identified as a binding partner of the p160 steroid receptor coactivator GRIP1 and was shown to enhance nuclear receptor-dependent transcription [6]. CARM1 methylates histone H3 at arginine 17 and arginine 26 (H3R17me2a, H3R26me2a), marks associated with transcriptional activation [7]. In addition, CARM1 methylates a diverse set of non-histone substrates, including transcriptional coactivators such as p300/CBP and SRC-3, chromatin remodeling components such as BAF155, and RNA-binding and splicing factors such as PABP1, SmB, CA150, and HuR [8–10]. Through these substrates CARM1 has been implicated in transcriptional coactivation, pre-mRNA splicing, mRNA stability, cell cycle progression, autophagy, and differentiation of cell types including adipocytes, chondrocytes, and hematopoietic cells [11,12]. Germline Carm1 deletion in mice results in perinatal lethality, underscoring its importance in development, while conditional models have revealed context-specific roles in the hematopoietic and immune systems [13,14]. CARM1 in cancer CARM1 overexpression has been reported in breast, prostate, colorectal, and hepatocellular carcinomas, among others, and often correlates with poor prognosis [15–17]. In estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, CARM1 functions as a coactivator of ERα-dependent gene expression and promotes proliferation [18]. In prostate cancer, CARM1 is upregulated in castration-resistant disease and coactivates androgen receptor and E2F1 programs [16]. Methylation of BAF155 by CARM1 has been associated with enhanced metastatic potential in breast cancer [9]. More recently, CARM1 has been linked to hematologic malignancies, where it contributes to leukemic transformation driven by fusion oncoproteins such as AML1-ETO and MLL-associated alterations [19]. However, most of these conclusions derive from RNA interference, overexpression, or genetic knockout studies, which cannot readily distinguish catalytic from scaffolding functions and are poorly suited to pharmacologic validation in vivo. Limitations of existing CARM1 tool compounds Efforts to develop small-molecule CARM1 inhibitors have produced several chemotypes, including SAM-analogue and bisubstrate inhibitors, pan-PRMT inhibitors such as AMI-1, and compounds identified by screening, such as TBBD and related benzimidazoles [20–22]. Most of these suffer from limited potency, poor selectivity against other PRMTs and methyltransferases, low cell permeability, or unfavorable pharmacokinetic properties. More selective compounds, such as the substrate-competitive inhibitor SGC2085 and the peptidomimetic and bisubstrate series, show good biochemical potency but little or no cellular activity [23,24]. Consequently, no CARM1 inhibitor has been available that combines biochemical potency, selectivity across the methyltransferase family, cellular target engagement, and oral exposure sufficient for efficacy studies in animal models. This gap has hindered clarification of which cancer types depend on CARM1 catalytic activity and has limited assessment of CARM1 as a therapeutic target. Multiple myeloma as a potential CARM1-dependent malignancy Multiple myeloma (MM) is a malignancy of terminally differentiated plasma cells that remains largely incurable despite advances with proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulatory agents, and anti-CD38 antibodies, and relapsed or refractory disease continues to present a major clinical challenge [25]. Epigenetic dysregulation is a recognized feature of MM, and inhibition of chromatin-modifying enzymes such as EZH2 has shown preclinical activity [26,27]. Notably, public cell line dependency and expression datasets suggest that a subset of MM lines is sensitive to CARM1 depletion, and CARM1 substrates including PABP1 and SmB are highly expressed in plasma cell contexts characterized by intense transcriptional and secretory demands. These observations led us to hypothesize that CARM1 enzymatic activity supports MM cell proliferation and that selective pharmacologic inhibition could provide anti-tumor benefit. Present study Here we report the discovery and characterization of EZM2302 (GSK3359088), a potent, selective, and orally bioavailable small-molecule inhibitor of CARM1. We describe its biochemical potency and selectivity against a panel of histone methyltransferases, its effect on cellular methylation of the CARM1 substrates PABP1 and SmB, and its anti-proliferative activity across MM cell lines. We further demonstrate pharmacodynamic target inhibition and dose-dependent anti-tumor efficacy following oral administration in an MM xenograft model. Together, these data establish a role for CARM1 catalytic activity in MM models and provide the research community with a validated chemical probe for interrogating CARM1 biology in cancer and other diseases. Recommender systems have become an integral part of the online experience. They help users navigate large collections of products, media, and people, and they are deployed in domains as varied as entertainment, e-commerce, social networking, and employment [1, 2]. Their success rests on exploiting the collective behavior of users: by identifying patterns in past interactions, recommenders deliver highly targeted, personalized suggestions that would be impossible to produce through manual curation. Collaborative filtering, in particular, infers the preferences of a user from those of similar users, and it remains one of the most widely used families of recommendation algorithms [3, 4]. The same property that makes recommenders effective also makes them vulnerable. Because they learn from user behavior, they inherit whatever biases that behavior contains. Users may preferentially consume items of certain genres, interact more with content produced by particular demographic groups, or favor items with particular attributes. Such tendencies are reflected in the data and, in turn, in the models trained on them. The concern about bias in algorithmic decision making has grown considerably in recent years, with studies documenting discriminatory outcomes in areas such as advertising, hiring, and criminal justice [5, 6]. In recommendation, bias can affect both the users who receive recommendations and the providers or items that are recommended, with consequences for visibility, exposure, and economic opportunity [7, 8]. Reproducing the biases of the input is a concern in itself, but a more subtle problem arises when a recommender amplifies them. We refer to this phenomenon as bias disparity: the degree of bias in the recommendations differs from, and in particular exceeds, the degree of bias in the data from which the recommendations were produced. For instance, if users of a given group show a moderate preference for items of a given category, a recommender may respond by suggesting items of that category far more often than the input would justify. Bias disparity is distinct from the mere presence of bias. It captures the change introduced by the algorithm and therefore points to the recommender itself as a contributor to the problem. Related effects have been discussed under labels such as popularity bias, filter bubbles, and feedback loops [9, 10, 11], but these notions typically concern a single dimension, such as item popularity, or the narrowing of individual user experience. Bias disparity offers a more general lens for comparing preference distributions over arbitrary groups of users and categories of items before and after recommendation. Understanding when and why bias disparity occurs is important for several reasons. First, amplification can reinforce stereotypes, for example when recommendations steer different demographic groups toward different types of content or opportunities. Second, because recommendations influence what users subsequently consume, amplified bias may feed back into the data used for future training, creating a cycle in which the bias grows over time [12, 13]. Third, a practitioner who wishes to mitigate the problem needs to know which properties of the data and which algorithmic choices make amplification more likely. Studying these questions on real data is difficult, since the underlying distribution of preferences cannot be controlled and the long-term effects of recommendations cannot be observed without deploying the system. Synthetic data, in contrast, permit systematic variation of the input conditions and simulation of the feedback process. In this short paper, we present a preliminary experimental study of bias disparity based on synthetic data. We generate preference data in which we control the group structure of users and items, the strength of the bias within each group, and the relative sizes of the groups. We then apply standard collaborative filtering algorithms and measure how the bias in the recommendations compares with the bias in the input. This design allows us to identify the conditions under which a recommender exhibits bias disparity, and to examine how the effect depends on factors such as the initial level of bias and the representation of groups in the data. We further simulate the long-term effect of recommendations by iteratively adding recommended items to the user profiles and retraining, thereby observing how data bias evolves when users act on the recommendations they receive. Beyond characterizing the problem, we consider a simple mitigation strategy. Specifically, we study a re-ranking algorithm that post-processes the recommendation lists so that the bias in the output is brought closer to that of the input. Post-processing approaches are attractive because they are independent of the underlying recommendation model and can be applied to existing systems without retraining [14, 15]. We evaluate the extent to which re-ranking reduces bias disparity and the cost it incurs in recommendation quality. Finally, we complement the synthetic analysis with observations on real data, examining whether the patterns identified in controlled settings are visible in commonly used recommendation datasets. Our contributions can be summarized as follows. We formalize bias disparity as a measure of the change in preference bias between input and output of a recommender. We present an experimental study on synthetic data that reveals conditions leading to amplification and illustrates its long-term dynamics. We evaluate a simple re-ranking approach for reducing bias disparity. We also report preliminary observations on real data. Although preliminary, these results offer a first step toward a systematic understanding of how recommenders transform the biases present in user behavior. We study bias disparity in collaborative filtering recommenders through controlled experiments on synthetic data, followed by an analysis of real data. We first formalize the notion of bias and bias disparity, then describe the data generation process, the recommendation algorithms, the long-term feedback simulation, and the re-ranking procedure. Problem Formulation and Definitions Let U be a set of users and I a set of items. Users are partitioned into groups according to a categorical attribute (e.g., gender), denoted by G = {g1, ..., gk}, and items are partitioned into categories (e.g., genre), denoted by C = {c1, ..., cm}. In the experiments we consider two user groups (a majority and a minority, or two balanced groups) and two item categories, which allows for a clear interpretation of the results while retaining the essential dynamics. We define the preference ratio of a group g for a category c in a set of user-item interactions as the fraction of interactions of g that involve items of c. Bias is measured relative to the category's share in the catalog. Let P(c) be the fraction of items belonging to category c. The input bias of group g toward category c is Bin(g, c) = [ Σ{u∈g} Σ{i∈c} r(u,i) / Σ{u∈g} Σ{i∈I} r(u,i) ] / P(c), where r(u,i)=1 if u has interacted with i. A value above one indicates that the group over-consumes the category relative to its catalog presence. The output bias Bout(g, c) is computed identically but over the top-n recommendation lists produced by the recommender, so that r(u,i)=1 if i appears in u's list. Bias disparity is then the relative change BD(g, c) = (Bout(g, c) − Bin(g, c)) / Bin(g, c). A positive value indicates that the recommender amplifies the bias present in the input, and a negative value indicates attenuation. Synthetic Data Generation We generate a user-item interaction matrix with controllable group sizes, category sizes, and preference strengths. Each user is assigned to a group, and each item to a category. For each group-category pair, we specify a preference probability p(g, c) that controls the likelihood that a user in g interacts with a given item in c. Interactions are sampled as independent Bernoulli trials with these probabilities, scaled to obtain a target density. By varying p we create different levels of input bias, ranging from none (identical preferences across groups) to strong, in which one group strongly prefers one category. We examine several experimental dimensions: (i) the relative size of the groups, from balanced to highly skewed; (ii) the relative size of the categories in the catalog; (iii) the strength of the group preferences; and (iv) the matrix density. For each configuration we generate multiple random instances (ten in our setup) and report averages, which mitigates sampling variance. To avoid the trivial case in which all users are identical, we also add item popularity heterogeneity by drawing item-specific multipliers from a long-tailed distribution, reflecting the popularity skew typical of real systems [1]. Recommendation Algorithms We consider representative collaborative filtering approaches. The first is a user-based k-nearest-neighbor method [2], which scores items by the similarity-weighted interactions of the most similar users, using cosine similarity. The second is an item-based neighborhood method [3]. The third is a matrix factorization model optimized for implicit feedback, such as weighted regularized matrix factorization [4] or Bayesian personalized ranking [5]. As a non-personalized baseline, we use a most-popular recommender, which helps separate the effect of popularity from that of personalization. Hyperparameters (neighborhood size, number of latent factors, regularization) are fixed to reasonable defaults across configurations, since our aim is to compare conditions rather than to tune accuracy. For each user, the top-n unseen items (n=10 in our default setting) form the recommendation list, from which Bout is computed. Long-Term Effect of Recommendations To study how recommendations influence data bias over time, we simulate an iterative feedback loop, in the spirit of prior analyses of feedback effects in recommenders [6]. At each iteration, the recommender is trained on the current interaction matrix and produces top-n lists. Each user then "consumes" a recommended item with a probability determined by the underlying preference p(g, c) of the user's group for the item's category, so that users accept recommendations they would plausibly like and reject others. Accepted items are added to the interaction matrix, and the model is retrained. We repeat this process for a fixed number of iterations and record Bin and Bout at each step. This allows us to determine whether bias disparity compounds over time, converges to a stable level, or dissipates, and how this depends on the initial conditions. Bias Disparity Mitigation We evaluate a simple post-processing re-ranking algorithm, in the spirit of fairness-aware re-ranking approaches [7]. For each user, the recommender produces a candidate list of size larger than n (e.g., 2n–5n) with predicted scores. The re-ranker then selects n items from the candidates so as to keep the category distribution of the group's aggregate recommendations close to the input bias of that group. Concretely, it greedily replaces items from over-represented categories with the highest-scoring candidates from under-represented categories until the group-level output bias approaches Bin(g, c) within a tolerance. We assess the trade-off between bias disparity reduction and recommendation quality, measured by precision@n and recall@n on held-out interactions, with a random 80/20 split per user. Analysis on Real Data To complement the synthetic study, we examine real data, using the MovieLens dataset [8] with user gender as the group attribute and movie genre as the item category, and, where applicable, a second dataset with comparable attributes. We compute Bin from the observed ratings (treated as implicit interactions), train the same recommenders, and compute Bout and BD for each group-genre pair. Because the real data have uncontrolled characteristics, this analysis is descriptive: we report the pairs where bias is amplified or attenuated and compare the patterns with those seen in the synthetic experiments, without drawing causal conclusions. Evaluation Protocol All synthetic results are averages over repeated random draws, and we report variability across runs. Unless stated otherwise, we vary one factor at a time while holding the others at default values, enabling attribution of changes in bias disparity to specific data properties. We first examine synthetic data, where the input bias is controlled, and then turn to the effect of re-ranking and to observations on real data. Bias disparity is defined as the relative change between the bias of a group of users toward an item category in the input data and the bias of the corresponding recommendations. Positive values indicate amplification, and negative values indicate attenuation. All synthetic results are averaged over 10 runs with different random seeds, and variation across runs was small (standard deviation below 0.02 in all reported settings). Pursuit-evasion games have been studied for decades, motivated by applications such as search and rescue, surveillance, security, wildlife monitoring, and human-robot interaction. In the classical formulation, one or more pursuers attempt to capture an evader, while the evader tries to avoid capture indefinitely. The answer to whether capture is possible depends on the relative motion capabilities of the players, their sensing, and the geometry of the environment. Much of the literature assumes that both players are holonomic point or disk agents. Real mobile robots, however, are frequently subject to kinematic constraints that limit their maneuverability. In this paper we study how such a constraint affects the outcome of a pursuit-evasion game. We consider a differential drive robot (DDR) pursuing an omnidirectional evader in a bounded convex environment. Both players are unit disks with the same maximum speed. The evader can instantaneously change its velocity in any direction, whereas the DDR can change its heading only at a bounded angular rate. The DDR wins if it collides with the evader, and the evader wins if it avoids collision forever. At first glance the DDR appears to be at a severe disadvantage. With equal speeds and no turning limitation, a single pursuer in a convex region can capture the evader, but an evader that can instantly change direction can exploit a pursuer's turning delay, for instance by moving tangentially to the pursuer's turning circle. We show that, despite this limitation, the DDR can still guarantee capture. Related Work The study of pursuit-evasion originates in differential games [1], where the lion-and-man problem [2] and its variants established that capture depends delicately on the speed ratio, the environment, and the information available. In bounded convex domains, a single pursuer with speed at least that of the evader can capture it in finite time under mild conditions [3], while in unbounded or non-convex environments multiple pursuers may be needed [4]. Visibility-based pursuit-evasion [5], in which pursuers must detect an evader with a limited field of view, and graph-based variants such as cops and robbers [6] have produced a substantial body of complementary results. Cooperative strategies using multiple pursuers, including those based on Voronoi partitions [7] and sweeping or encirclement [8], have been extensively analyzed. Pursuit with nonholonomic constraints has received comparatively less attention. The classical homicidal chauffeur problem [1] considers a slower but agile evader against a faster pursuer with a minimum turning radius, and it characterizes the capture region through a barrier surface. Subsequent work analyzed Dubins-type pursuers and evaders [9], pursuit by car-like vehicles [10], and games between unicycles with different speed and turning bounds [11]. These studies typically rely on optimal control and Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs techniques, which produce capture conditions in terms of the state space but are difficult to scale or to extend to bounded environments with obstacles or boundaries. Moreover, the homicidal chauffeur assumes a speed advantage for the pursuer, whereas here the speeds are equal. Related work on differential drive robots has considered target tracking and visibility maintenance [12], and reactive strategies for pursuing mobile targets [13], though often without guarantees of capture against an adversarial evader. Another line of work concerns pursuers whose sensing or motion is constrained, such as bounded-curvature pursuers in polygonal environments [14] and pursuers with limited field of view [15]. Most of these results concern detection or tracking, not capture of an adversary that can react instantaneously. Challenges and Approach The principal difficulty is that the DDR cannot respond immediately to evader motion. When the evader is close and located to the side of the DDR, a heading change requires finite time, during which the evader may move away or circle around the pursuer. Strategies for holonomic pursuers, such as moving directly toward the evader or maintaining a fixed relative bearing, no longer apply directly, since the induced pursuer trajectory may violate the angular-rate bound. Furthermore, the equal-speed assumption removes any advantage that could compensate for the delay; any capture guarantee must therefore come from exploiting the geometry of the environment, in particular the convexity of the domain, which prevents the evader from escaping indefinitely and forces it eventually into regions where its freedom is restricted. Our approach is to design a pursuit strategy for the DDR and prove that it yields capture in finite time against any evader strategy. We analyze the evolution of relative geometry between the players, identify a configuration set from which the DDR can force a decrease of a suitable potential, and show that the evader cannot remain outside this set indefinitely. The analysis accounts for the turning-rate limit through reachable-set arguments for the DDR and the evader, and uses convexity to bound the region in which the evader can maneuver. Contributions The contributions of this paper are as follows. First, we formulate a pursuit-evasion game between a bounded-turning-rate DDR and an omnidirectional evader of equal speed in a convex environment, with finite-size players and capture defined as collision. Second, we present a pursuit strategy for the DDR and prove that it guarantees capture in finite time, showing that the angular-rate limitation does not, in itself, enable the evader to escape. Third, we provide supporting analysis characterizing the reachable sets and relative-motion geometry that underlie the proof, which may be useful for other pursuit problems involving nonholonomic agents. Organization Section II formalizes the problem and notation. Section III introduces the DDR model and the geometric preliminaries. Section IV presents the pursuit strategy, and Section V proves its correctness and establishes capture. Section VI discusses extensions and limitations, and Section VII concludes with directions for future work. Problem Formulation and Model. Let W ⊂ ℝ² be a compact convex polygonal environment. Two agents move in W: a differential drive robot (DDR) P and an omnidirectional evader E. Both are closed disks of radius r (unit disks after normalization), and the position of each is the center of its disk. The DDR state is qP = (xP, yP, θ) ∈ W × S¹, with kinematics ẋP = v cos θ, ẏP = v sin θ, θ̇ = ω, with |v| ≤ 1, |ω| ≤ ωmax. The evader has state xE ∈ W and single-integrator dynamics ẋE = u, ‖u‖ ≤ 1. Both players therefore share the same maximum linear speed, while only the DDR is subject to a bounded turning rate. Capture occurs at time tc if ‖xP(tc) − xE(tc)‖ ≤ 2, that is, if the disks touch. The evader wins if capture never occurs. We assume that both players have full information about the state of the other at all times, that the DDR can rotate in place (v = 0, |ω| = ωmax), and that the initial configuration is collision-free. Strategies are non-anticipative: each player selects its control at time t as a function of the history up to t, which prevents the evader from gaining an advantage from knowing the future DDR control. Overview of Approach. The speed-matched, omnidirectional pursuit–evasion problem in a convex region is known to be winnable by a pursuer with the same speed and no kinematic constraint, by shrinking the region available to the evader [1], [2]. A pursuer with a turning-rate bound does not generally have this ability, because the evader can exploit the pursuer's inability to change heading instantaneously. Our approach is to reduce the DDR game to a sequence of phases in which (i) the DDR reduces the problem to a configuration in which its heading is favorable relative to the evader, and (ii) the DDR then applies a geometric strategy that monotonically decreases a potential function while preserving a favorable heading. Relative Coordinates. Let d = xE − xP, ρ = ‖d‖, and let φ be the bearing of the evader in the DDR body frame, φ = arg(d) − θ ∈ (−π, π]. The relative dynamics are ρ̇ = u·d̂ − v cos φ, φ̇ = (1/ρ) u·d̂⊥ − v sin φ/ρ − ω. When φ = 0 and the DDR moves at v = 1, the closing rate satisfies ρ̇ ≤ 0 for every admissible u. A nonzero bearing lets the evader move perpendicular to d without opposition, causing rotation of the line of sight at rate up to 1/ρ. Because |ω| ≤ ωmax, the DDR can compensate for line-of-sight rotation only if ρ ≥ ρ := 1/ωmax (the minimum turning radius at unit speed). We therefore distinguish two regimes: the far regime ρ > ρ, in which the DDR can track the line of sight while advancing, and the near regime ρ ≤ ρ, in which the evader can potentially outmaneuver the DDR locally. Pursuit Strategy: Far Regime. In the far regime the DDR uses a pure-pursuit-like law with saturation: ω = sat{ωmax}(k φ) and v = max{0, cos φ} (or v = 1 when |φ| ≤ φ₀ for a threshold φ₀). We show using the Lyapunov function V = φ² that |φ| is driven below φ₀ in finite time whenever ρ > ρ, and remains below it as long as ρ is above a slightly larger threshold. Intuitively, the evader's contribution to φ̇ is bounded by 1/ρ < ωmax, so the DDR's turning authority dominates. Near Regime and Region Reduction. When ρ falls below ρ, the evader may circle the DDR. We handle this using a Voronoi-type decomposition. Let 𝒱(t) = {x ∈ W : ‖x − xP‖ ≤ ‖x − xE‖} be the set of points the DDR can reach no later than the evader, ignoring heading. The evader's safe region is W \ 𝒱, bounded by the bisector of xP and xE. For the holonomic pursuer, the bisector sweeps monotonically toward the evader [2]. For the DDR we define a heading-aware reachable set 𝒟(t), the set of points the DDR can reach before the evader, taking turning cost into account using Dubins-path arrival times [3]. Since the Dubins path length exceeds the Euclidean distance by at most a bounded additive term c(ωmax) = O(1/ωmax), the set 𝒟(t) contains the Voronoi cell 𝒱 shrunk by a margin of c(ωmax). This margin is the quantitative price of the turning constraint. Potential Function and Capture Argument. We define the potential Φ(t) = area of the evader's safe region 𝒮(t) = W \ 𝒟(t), with the convention that Φ = 0 implies capture. The key lemma states that, if the DDR is in a favorable configuration (|φ| ≤ φ₀ and ρ ≥ ρmin), then there exists a DDR control for which Φ is non-increasing against every evader control and strictly decreasing at a rate bounded away from zero whenever the evader is not at the boundary of W. When the evader is on the boundary, convexity of W guarantees that the DDR can trap the evader into a corner: the safe region is contained in a wedge and the DDR can progress along the wedge's bisector. The proof proceeds by (a) bounding the rate at which 𝒟 expands via Dubins reachability, (b) bounding the rate at which the evader can enlarge 𝒮 by moving, and (c) showing, via convexity, that the first rate dominates the second when the favorable configuration holds. Maintaining Favorable Configurations. The remaining difficulty is that the evader can attempt to force |φ| > φ₀. We show that such attempts require the evader to move laterally, which in turn reduces its distance to the boundary of 𝒮 and allows the DDR to reorient by rotating in place while the evader's progress decreases Φ. Combining this with the potential lemma yields a finite bound on the total time spent in unfavorable configurations, and hence on the capture time, T ≤ T(W, ωmax, xP(0), xE(0)). Termination. By the lemmas above, Φ is non-increasing, strictly decreasing during favorable intervals, and unfavorable intervals have bounded total duration. Hence Φ reaches zero in finite time, which implies capture. The same argument shows that the guarantee holds for any initial condition in W, completing the proof of the main result. Stock markets attract the attention of researchers and investors alike, since successful prediction of price movements can bring substantial financial gains. At the same time, stock prediction is notoriously difficult. Prices are shaped by a large number of interacting factors, including company performance, macroeconomic conditions, political events, investor sentiment and market microstructure, and the influence of each factor changes rapidly over time. The efficient market hypothesis even argues that prices already reflect all available information, so that consistent excess returns should not be possible. Nevertheless, a large body of empirical work suggests that markets are not perfectly efficient and that some predictable structure can be exploited, which motivates a continuing search for better prediction methods. Traditionally, two main approaches to stock analysis are distinguished. Fundamental analysis evaluates the intrinsic value of a company from financial statements, industry conditions and the broader economy. Technical analysis, in contrast, studies historical price and volume data to identify patterns that may indicate future movements. Technical analysts use a wide range of indicators, such as moving averages (MA), the moving average convergence divergence (MACD), the relative strength index and many others. These indicators are simple to compute and widely used in practice, and they often serve as benchmarks for more advanced models. Their drawback is that they are usually derived from a limited window of aggregated values and may react late to changes in trend, producing many false signals in volatile or sideways markets. Another long-established tool of technical analysis is the Japanese candlestick chart. Each candlestick summarizes the open, high, low and close (OHLC) prices of one trading period in a compact visual form. Its body shows the relation between opening and closing price, and its shadows show the extremes reached during the period. Traders have long described named formations of one or several consecutive candlesticks, such as the hammer, doji or engulfing patterns, and associate them with possible reversals or continuations of the trend. In this sense, candlesticks already behave like a visual alphabet, and sequences of candlesticks resemble words and sentences carrying information about market behavior. This analogy is the starting point of our work. In recent years, machine learning and deep learning have been applied extensively to stock prediction, using models such as support vector machines, random forests, recurrent neural networks, LSTM networks and convolutional networks. Most of these methods operate on numeric time series of prices and technical indicators, and many require extensive feature engineering, large datasets and careful tuning. In parallel, natural language processing (NLP) has made major progress with distributed word representations. Word2Vec, introduced by Mikolov and colleagues, learns dense vectors from large text corpora so that words appearing in similar contexts obtain similar representations. In finance, NLP has mostly been used to analyze textual sources such as news, social media and financial reports for sentiment. Much less attention has been paid to applying NLP techniques directly to price data after its transformation into a symbolic language. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to stock trend prediction that combines Japanese candlesticks with the Word2Vec model. First, we define a simple language of candlesticks: each candlestick in the OHLC data is converted into a word according to properties such as the size and direction of its body and the lengths of its shadows. A sequence of consecutive candlesticks then forms a sentence. These sentences are used to train the Word2Vec model, which learns vector representations of the candlestick words and their contexts. An important feature of our method is the labeling of the training data, which explicitly takes trading commissions into account. A sentence is therefore labeled as a buy or sell signal only if the subsequent price movement is large enough to cover transaction costs, which makes the learned model more realistic with respect to actual trading conditions. The trained model is finally used to predict trading actions on unseen data. We evaluate the approach by simulated trading and compare the achieved yield with three common benchmark strategies: Buy & Hold, MA and MACD. The evaluation proceeds in two stages. First, we test the method on three individual shares, Apple, Microsoft and Coca-Cola, chosen to represent different sectors and behaviors. Second, we test it on a broader set of stocks from the Russell Top 50 Index, using separate test and validation phases to assess how well the method generalizes to different market periods. This design allows us to examine both the performance on selected well-known stocks and the robustness across a larger and more diverse group. The main contributions of this paper are as follows. (1) We introduce a simple, interpretable language of Japanese candlesticks that converts OHLC data into sequences of words. (2) We show how the Word2Vec model can be applied to this language for trend prediction, with a classification scheme that incorporates trading commissions. (3) We provide an experimental comparison with Buy & Hold, MA and MACD on individual shares and on stocks from the Russell Top 50 Index, showing that the proposed method yields positive results in all scenarios and higher average yields than MA and MACD. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on technical analysis, machine learning in stock prediction and NLP in finance. Section 3 describes the proposed method, including the candlestick language, the training of the Word2Vec model and the labeling procedure. Section 4 presents the experimental setup and results. Section 5 discusses the findings, and Section 6 concludes with directions for future research. Data and Candlestick Language Daily OHLC (open, high, low, close) data were collected for the selected stocks. Two experimental scenarios were defined. In the first, Apple, Microsoft and Coca-Cola were used as individual case studies. In the second, a broader set of stocks from the Russell Top 50 Index was used to assess generalization. For each stock, the time series was split chronologically into a training, a test and a validation period, so that no future information was available during model construction. Each trading day was converted into a candlestick and then into a word. A candlestick is described by its body (the difference between close and open), its upper shadow (high minus the larger of open and close) and its lower shadow (the smaller of open and close minus low). These quantities were normalized by the opening price to make them comparable across stocks and price levels. Each component was discretized into a small number of categories using thresholds derived from the empirical distribution of the training data (quantile-based bins). The body was assigned a direction (bullish or bearish) and a size category (e.g., small, medium, large), while the shadows were assigned size categories (e.g., none, short, long). The concatenation of the category symbols forms a single word, so the vocabulary is finite and compact. Gaps between the previous close and the current open were optionally encoded as an additional symbol. The resulting sequence of words for a stock is a text in the "language" of candlesticks. Sentence Construction The word sequence was divided into sentences using a sliding window of fixed length n (consecutive trading days). Each sentence therefore represents the recent price history up to a given day. Window length was treated as a hyperparameter and selected on the test period. The sentence ending at day t is the input used to decide on the trading action for day t+1. Labeling with Trading Commissions To train a supervised classifier, each sentence needed a label describing the appropriate action. Labels were derived from the future price movement over a short horizon, taking trading commissions into account. For a sentence ending at day t, the relative change between the closing price at t and the closing price at t+h was computed. If the gain exceeded the round-trip commission cost plus a margin, the sentence was labeled Buy. If the price decline exceeded the same threshold, it was labeled Sell. Otherwise, it was labeled Hold, since a trade would not be profitable after fees. This labeling discourages the model from learning to trade on small fluctuations that would be erased by transaction costs. The commission rate was fixed across all experiments. Word2Vec Model Word2Vec was trained on the candlestick words of the training period to obtain dense vector embeddings for each word. We used the skip-gram architecture (with the continuous bag-of-words variant tested for comparison) with negative sampling. Embedding dimension, context window and number of epochs were tuned on the test period. Words that were very rare were still retained because the vocabulary is small. A sentence vector was computed by averaging the embeddings of its words. These sentence vectors were used as features for a classifier that predicts one of the three labels (Buy, Sell, Hold). A logistic regression classifier was used as a simple and robust choice, and class weights were applied to compensate for label imbalance. At prediction time, a new sentence was transformed into its vector, and the classifier produced the predicted action for the next period. Trading Simulation Predicted actions were evaluated through a simulated trading strategy. The simulated investor started with a fixed amount of capital and held either cash or a long position in a single stock; short selling was not allowed. A Buy signal while in cash led to buying with all available capital at the next opening price, a Sell signal while holding led to liquidation of the position, and a Hold signal left the position unchanged. Commission was deducted at each transaction. The performance measure was the yield, defined as the relative change of portfolio value between the start and end of the evaluated period. For the Russell Top 50 experiment, yields were averaged across stocks. Comparative Models Word2Vec was compared with three benchmark strategies: 1. Buy & Hold: the stock is purchased at the beginning of the period and held until the end, incurring a single round of commission. 2. Moving Average (MA): a Buy signal is generated when the short-term moving average crosses above the long-term moving average, and a Sell signal when it crosses below. Window lengths were optimized on the training data. 3. Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD): the difference between a fast and a slow exponential moving average forms the MACD line, and crossings of this line with its signal line generate Buy and Sell signals. Standard parameters (12, 26, 9) were used as a baseline, with optional tuning on the training data. All benchmark strategies were simulated under the same capital, commission and execution assumptions as the Word2Vec strategy. Experimental Protocol For each stock, models were trained on the training period. Hyperparameters (window length, labeling horizon and margin, embedding size, context size) were selected through grid search by maximizing the yield in the test phase. The selected configuration was then applied without modification to the validation phase, which served as an out-of-sample assessment. Because neural embedding training is stochastic, each configuration was run multiple times with different random seeds and the results were averaged. Yields in the test and validation phases were reported separately for all methods and compared across scenarios. We evaluated the proposed Word2Vec trading model in two experiments: (1) three individual shares (Apple, Microsoft, Coca-Cola), and (2) a broader set of stocks from the Russell Top 50 Index. In both experiments the data were split into a training period, a test phase used for model selection and parameter tuning, and a validation phase used for the final out-of-sample comparison. Performance is reported as the yield (percentage return on initial capital) after trading commissions, and the Word2Vec model is compared with Buy & Hold (B&H), the moving average crossover strategy (MA), and the MACD strategy.
