Malaria remains one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), which accounted for approximately 95% of global malaria cases and deaths in recent years [1]. Pregnant women are particularly vulnerable to the disease. Pregnancy-related changes in immunity, together with the sequestration of Plasmodium falciparum-infected erythrocytes in the placenta, increase both the risk and the severity of infection [2,3]. Malaria in pregnancy (MiP) is associated with maternal anaemia, spontaneous abortion, stillbirth, preterm delivery, low birth weight, and neonatal and maternal death [4,5]. In 2022, an estimated 36 million pregnancies occurred in malaria-endemic areas of Africa, and roughly one in three of these was exposed to infection [1]. MiP is therefore a major public health problem and a barrier to achieving maternal and child health targets under the Sustainable Development Goals. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a package of interventions to prevent and control MiP. The package includes the use of insecticide-treated nets, prompt diagnosis and effective treatment of clinical cases, and intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (IPTp-SP) [6]. IPTp-SP consists of curative doses of SP given at scheduled antenatal care (ANC) visits, irrespective of whether the woman is infected, to clear existing parasitaemia and provide post-treatment prophylaxis. Trials and systematic reviews have shown that IPTp-SP reduces placental malaria, maternal anaemia, low birth weight, and neonatal mortality [7,8]. Evidence of a dose-response relationship led WHO in 2012 to revise its guidance. It now recommends that IPTp-SP be given at each scheduled ANC visit, starting as early as possible in the second trimester, with doses at least one month apart, and that women receive at least three doses [6,9]. Because of its low cost and demonstrated effectiveness, IPTp-SP is regarded as one of the most cost-effective health interventions available [10]. Most malaria-endemic countries in SSA have adopted IPTp policies, and many updated them to the three-dose recommendation after 2012. Nonetheless, coverage remains well below the target of 80% set by global malaria strategies [1,11]. According to WHO estimates, only about one-third of eligible pregnant women in SSA received three or more doses of IPTp-SP in 2022, even though most attend ANC at least once [1]. This gap between ANC attendance and IPTp coverage indicates missed opportunities and points to health-system and individual-level barriers. Reported barriers include late initiation of ANC, few ANC visits, stock-outs of SP, inconsistent provider adherence to guidelines, requirements to take the drug under direct observation, and concerns about side effects or misconceptions about the drug [12–14]. Women's knowledge, autonomy, and ability to pay for transport and services also influence use [15]. Coverage varies markedly between and within countries. Several studies have documented disparities by place of residence, education, household wealth, and age, with women who are poorer, less educated, and living in rural areas generally less likely to receive adequate IPTp [16–18]. Socioeconomic inequalities in the use of maternal health services are widely recognised, and the pattern for IPTp may be shaped by differences in access to quality ANC rather than by demand alone [19]. However, the evidence is inconsistent. Some studies report a positive association between education or wealth and IPTp uptake, whereas others find weak or no gradients, or even higher uptake among poorer women, possibly because of differences in ANC delivery, the timing of policy implementation, and survey design [17,20,21]. Many earlier analyses also relied on single-country data or on the Demographic and Health Surveys, which are not designed specifically for malaria and may not capture the transmission context well. As a result, comparative evidence on how education and wealth relate to adequate IPTp uptake across several malaria-endemic settings remains limited. The Malaria Indicator Surveys (MIS) are nationally representative household surveys conducted in endemic countries to track coverage of key malaria interventions, including IPTp, in a standardised way [22]. Their focus on malaria, standardised questionnaires, and recent implementation make them a valuable source for cross-country assessment of progress and inequities. Using MIS data, it is possible to examine whether the dose recommended by WHO is being received and which groups of women are least likely to benefit. Understanding the socioeconomic patterning of IPTp-SP uptake is important for designing equitable interventions and for targeting resources toward the women at greatest risk. Differences between countries may also reflect the performance of national malaria programmes and health systems, and can guide policy learning among countries with similar epidemiological profiles. Therefore, this study aimed to estimate the prevalence of uptake of at least three doses of IPTp-SP during the last pregnancy among women aged 15–49 years in eight malaria-endemic SSA countries (Burkina Faso, Ghana, Mali, Malawi, Kenya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and Uganda), and to investigate the patterns of uptake across educational and wealth categories after adjusting for relevant sociodemographic factors. We hypothesised that lower education and lower household wealth would be associated with lower odds of receiving adequate IPTp-SP, and that substantial between-country variation would persist. Data source and study design We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of secondary data from the Malaria Indicator Surveys (MIS) of eight sub-Saharan African countries: Burkina Faso, Ghana, Mali, Malawi, Kenya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and Uganda. The MIS is a nationally representative household survey programme implemented by national malaria control programmes and national statistical offices with technical support from the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) Program [1]. It collects information on malaria prevention, treatment, and related health indicators, including intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy. Countries were selected because they are malaria-endemic, had adopted IPTp-SP policies, and had a publicly available MIS dataset containing the variables needed for this analysis. The most recent survey available for each country at the time of analysis was used. Datasets were obtained from the DHS Program website after registration and approval of a data request. The study followed the STROBE guidelines for reporting cross-sectional studies [2]. Sampling procedure The MIS uses a stratified, two-stage cluster sampling design. In the first stage, enumeration areas (clusters) were selected from a national sampling frame, typically the most recent census, with probability proportional to size. In the second stage, a fixed number of households was selected in each cluster by systematic sampling after household listing. All women aged 15–49 years who were usual residents of, or slept in, the selected households the night before the survey were eligible for interview [1]. Women who had a live birth within a specified recall period before the survey (two years in most surveys) were asked about antenatal care and malaria preventive measures during their last pregnancy. After restricting the sample to these women and excluding records with missing data on the outcome, the final analytic sample comprised 18,603 women. Outcome variable The outcome was uptake of adequate IPTp-SP, defined according to WHO recommendations as receiving three or more doses of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine during the most recent pregnancy [3]. Women were asked whether they took SP/Fansidar during the pregnancy, whether it was received during an antenatal care visit, and how many doses were taken. Responses were coded as binary: 1 = three or more doses, 0 = fewer than three doses (including none). Women who did not know the number of doses were treated as missing. Explanatory variables The primary explanatory variables were women's educational attainment and household wealth. Education was categorised as no formal education, primary, and secondary or higher. Household wealth was measured using the DHS wealth index, a composite score derived through principal component analysis of household assets, housing characteristics, and access to utilities and sanitation [4]. Households were ranked into national quintiles: poorest, poorer, middle, richer, and richest. Covariates were selected on the basis of previous literature on determinants of IPTp and antenatal care use [5,6] and data availability. They included maternal age (15–19, 20–24, 25–29, 30–34, ≥35 years), place of residence (urban or rural), marital status (currently married or cohabiting versus other), parity or number of children ever born (1, 2–3, ≥4), household head's sex, number of antenatal care visits (fewer than four versus four or more), and country. Where variables were not harmonised across surveys, categories were recoded to ensure comparability. Statistical analysis Data were cleaned and analysed using Stata version 15 (StataCorp, College Station, TX). Datasets from the eight countries were appended into a single pooled file. To account for the complex survey design, the svy command was used to incorporate cluster, strata, and sampling weights. Because the surveys differed in sample size, weights were rescaled so that each country contributed in proportion to its population of eligible women where pooled estimates were produced [7]. Descriptive analyses were used to estimate the weighted prevalence of taking three or more doses of IPTp-SP, with 95% confidence intervals, for the pooled sample and for each country. The distribution of the outcome across categories of education, wealth, and the other covariates was summarised as weighted percentages. Bivariate associations between the outcome and each explanatory variable were assessed using the Rao-Scott design-adjusted chi-square test. Multivariable logistic regression was then used to estimate the association of education and wealth with the outcome while adjusting for the covariates listed above. Given that the results are presented as the odds of not receiving adequate IPTp-SP, the reference category for wealth was the richest quintile and for education the highest level attained. Results are reported as adjusted odds ratios (AOR) with 95% confidence intervals. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Model building proceeded in steps: an unadjusted model, a model adjusted for education and wealth together, and a fully adjusted model including all covariates and country fixed effects. Multicollinearity was assessed with variance inflation factors, with values below 5 considered acceptable [8]. Model fit was evaluated using the design-adjusted Wald test and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Sensitivity analyses were conducted by running country-specific models to explore heterogeneity across settings. Missing data were minimal for explanatory variables and were handled by complete-case analysis. Ethical considerations This study was a secondary analysis of anonymised, publicly available data. Original surveys received ethical approval from the ICF Institutional Review Board and relevant national ethics committees in each country, and informed consent was obtained from all respondents during data collection [1]. No further ethical approval was required for this analysis. A total of 18,603 women aged 15–49 years who had a live birth in the period preceding each survey were included in the analysis, drawn from the Malaria Indicator Surveys of Burkina Faso, Ghana, Mali, Malawi, Kenya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and Uganda. The mean age of respondents was approximately 28 years. Most women resided in rural areas (roughly 75%), and a substantial proportion had either no formal education or only primary education. Distribution across wealth quintiles was relatively even, with a slight concentration in the poorer and middle categories. The majority of women reported attending at least one antenatal care (ANC) visit during their last pregnancy, although the proportion attending four or more visits varied considerably between countries. Prevalence of IPTp-SP uptake The overall prevalence of receiving three or more doses of IPTp-SP during the last pregnancy was 29.5% (95% CI = 28.2–30.5). Marked between-country variation was observed (Figure 1). Ghana recorded the highest prevalence at 60% (95% CI = 57.1–62.8), followed by Kenya at 37% (95% CI = 35.3–39.2) and Sierra Leone at 31% (95% CI = 29.2–33.4). The remaining countries had prevalences below the pooled estimate, with the lowest uptake found in the Sahelian and West African settings. Thus, in most surveyed countries, over two-thirds of women did not receive the number of doses recommended by the WHO [1,2]. Differences between countries were statistically significant (p < 0.001). Distribution of IPTp-SP uptake by socioeconomic characteristics Among women who took three or more doses, the distribution across wealth quintiles was fairly even and showed no clear gradient: 19.0% were from the poorest, 21.1% from poorer, 21.2% from middle, 20.7% from richer, and 18.1% from the richest households. Women from non-poor households (richer, middle, and richest) thus accounted for a slightly greater share of adequate uptake than those from the poorest households, although the differences in these proportions were modest. Frequency hopping spread spectrum is widely used in modern communication systems such as radar, sonar, military communications, Bluetooth and code-division multiple-access networks, owing to its strong resistance to interference, jamming and fading [1], [2]. In a frequency hopping multiple-access system, each user is assigned a frequency hopping sequence (FHS), which determines the carrier frequency used in each time slot. Because users share the same frequency band and are generally not perfectly synchronized, the Hamming correlation between sequences determines the number of hits, that is, collisions in which two users transmit on the same frequency at the same time. Consequently, the design of FHSs and FHS sets with low Hamming auto- and cross-correlation is a central problem in the theory of sequence design. Let F = {f1, f2, …, fq} be a frequency library (alphabet) of size q. For two FHSs X = (xt) and Y = (yt) of period N over F, the periodic Hamming correlation function at relative shift τ is defined as H{X,Y}(τ) = Σ{t=0}^{N-1} h[xt, y{t+τ}], where h[a,b] = 1 if a = b and 0 otherwise. When X = Y, this is the Hamming autocorrelation of X, and for τ ≠ 0 mod N its maximum, denoted H(X), is called the maximum out-of-phase Hamming autocorrelation. For a set S of FHSs, the maximum out-of-phase autocorrelation and the maximum cross-correlation over distinct pairs are the key parameters, and the maximum Hamming correlation Hmax(S) is the larger of the two. Several lower bounds relate the parameters of FHSs and FHS sets. For a single sequence, Lempel and Greenberger [3] established a bound relating the period, alphabet size and maximum autocorrelation; sequences meeting it are called optimal. For sets of sequences, Peng and Fan [4] derived bounds involving the set size, period, alphabet size and maximum Hamming correlation, which generalize the Lempel–Greenberger bound. Optimal FHSs and FHS sets meeting these bounds have been constructed from many algebraic and combinatorial tools, including m-sequences, Reed–Solomon codes, difference families, cyclotomy, and function-theoretic methods [5]–[10]. Beyond worst-case measures, the average Hamming correlation has also been studied. Since the sum of correlation values over all shifts and all sequence pairs in a set is fixed by the parameters, one obtains lower bounds on the average autocorrelation and cross-correlation [11]. A set whose average correlation attains these bounds is said to be optimal with respect to the average Hamming correlation, a property of practical interest because average behavior governs typical system performance. Cyclotomy is a classical source of sequences with good correlation. Cyclotomic classes of order e in a finite field were introduced by Gauss, and the associated cyclotomic numbers have been used to construct sequences, cyclic codes and difference sets [12], [13]. The classical cyclotomic classes are defined modulo a prime or prime power, but they only describe the multiplicative structure of the field. To extend the theory to residue rings modulo pq and, more generally, modulo prime powers, Whiteman introduced generalized cyclotomy [14]. Ding and Helleseth [15] later proposed a different generalization, now known as Ding–Helleseth generalized cyclotomy, which partitions Z{p^n} or Z{pq} into classes with flexible parameters. The resulting generalized cyclotomic sequences have attracted considerable attention for their linear complexity, autocorrelation and other cryptographic properties [16]–[18]. Generalized cyclotomic classes of order 2 are especially tractable, and their cyclotomic numbers can often be determined explicitly in terms of p and the structure of the unit group. Applications to FHSs have also been explored: several optimal FHSs and FHS sets have been obtained from classical and generalized cyclotomic classes [19]–[21], but constructions of length p^n based on Ding–Helleseth classes remain comparatively less studied, and their Hamming cross-correlation has rarely been analyzed in detail. Motivated by this gap, the present paper constructs a new class of FHSs of length p^n using Ding–Helleseth generalized cyclotomic classes of order 2. The sequences are obtained by assigning frequencies according to the class membership of the position index, with a layered structure reflecting the decomposition of Z{p^n} by the p-adic valuation. We determine the Hamming autocorrelation of every sequence in the family, deriving its values by computing intersections of shifted cyclotomic classes, which reduce to cyclotomic numbers of order 2. For the Hamming cross-correlation, we restrict attention to the case p ≡ 3 (mod 4), where −1 is a quadratic nonresidue modulo p and the cyclotomic numbers take particularly simple forms; this symmetry allows a complete evaluation of the cross-correlation values. The case p ≡ 1 (mod 4) involves additional case distinctions and is not treated here. Finally, we compute the average Hamming autocorrelation and cross-correlation of the constructed set and show that they meet the known lower bounds, so that the set is optimal with respect to average Hamming correlation. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II recalls the definitions of Hamming correlation, the relevant bounds, and Ding–Helleseth generalized cyclotomic classes together with their cyclotomic numbers. Section III presents the construction. Section IV analyzes the Hamming autocorrelation, and Section V treats the Hamming cross-correlation for p ≡ 3 (mod 4). Section VI discusses the average correlation optimality, and Section VII concludes the paper. Throughout, p is an odd prime, n ≥ 1, and N = p^n. Playing a wind instrument is a physiologically demanding activity that combines sustained expiratory effort, elevated intraoral and intrathoracic pressures, precise control of the respiratory muscles, and characteristic breathing patterns [1,2]. Whether this repeated respiratory loading improves, preserves or impairs lung function has been debated for decades, and the literature has not produced a consistent answer. This question matters to the many amateur and professional musicians who play wind instruments, and to clinicians who advise patients with chronic respiratory disease on whether playing may be beneficial or harmful. Wind instrument playing and respiratory function Early studies suggested that wind players may have larger lung volumes and stronger respiratory muscles than non-players, probably through a training effect analogous to that of endurance or respiratory muscle training [3,4]. Several cross-sectional investigations reported higher vital capacity, maximal expiratory pressure or maximal voluntary ventilation in wind instrumentalists than in controls [3,5]. Other work has found no difference in spirometric indices, or differences confined to specific instrument groups [6,7]. Some authors have also proposed that wind playing may be useful as a complementary intervention in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma or sleep-disordered breathing. Small interventional studies of playing or of instrument-based breathing training have reported improvements in respiratory muscle strength, exercise tolerance or quality of life [8,9]. A few reports on the didgeridoo, for example, suggest reduced sleep apnoea severity [10]. Conversely, there are concerns that wind playing could be harmful. Playing, particularly of brass instruments, may involve Valsalva-like manoeuvres with high intraoral pressures, which have been implicated in pharyngeal and laryngeal complications, in rare cases of pneumomediastinum, and in raised intracranial and intraocular pressure [11,12]. Instruments may also harbour bacteria, moulds and fungi, and cases of hypersensitivity pneumonitis linked to contaminated wind instruments have been described [13,14]. Musicians may also be exposed to occupational factors such as noise, stress and, in some venues, tobacco smoke. Finally, the pattern of rapid inspiration followed by prolonged controlled expiration may alter ventilatory mechanics and, in theory, promote air trapping or hyperinflation over time [15]. Limitations of the existing evidence The inconsistency of the available data has several probable explanations. First, most studies have grouped all wind instruments together, although the instruments differ considerably in the resistance they impose, the pressures required, the airflow demanded, and the embouchure employed. A flute, a clarinet and a trumpet represent very different respiratory tasks: the flute is a low-resistance, high-flow instrument, reed instruments are intermediate, and brass instruments require lip vibration against a cup mouthpiece with high intraoral pressures [2,16]. Pooling these instruments may mask real effects, which could be positive for one group and neutral or negative for another. Second, many studies were small, single-centre, and recruited players of widely varying levels of experience, from students to professionals. Third, control groups were often not comparable, being drawn from the general population or from student cohorts rather than from musicians sharing the same musical and social environment. Fourth, confounders such as age, sex, height, body mass index and smoking were inconsistently addressed, although they have strong effects on spirometric values. Lastly, few studies considered cumulative exposure, such as years of playing, which is essential for judging whether any effect is dose-dependent and therefore more plausibly causal. The trumpet, cornet and flugelhorn The trumpet, cornet and flugelhorn are closely related soprano brass instruments with a cylindrical-conical bore, a cup-shaped mouthpiece and a similar playing technique. They are among the most commonly played instruments in wind orchestras and brass bands, which have a particularly strong amateur tradition in Switzerland and many other European countries. Playing them requires high oral pressures, in the order of several kilopascals during high or loud notes, and fine control of the expiratory muscles and the lips [16,17]. Given this load, it is plausible that long-term playing could influence lung volumes or airflow. Nevertheless, to our knowledge, no study has specifically examined this homogeneous group of instruments using standardised spirometry in comparison with a carefully selected control group of non-wind musicians. Aim of the study We therefore conducted a prospective, multicentre, cross-sectional case-control study among amateur musicians in Switzerland. The primary objective was to compare the forced expiratory volume in one second as a percentage of predicted (FEV1%predicted) between trumpet, cornet and flugelhorn players and controls drawn from orchestras who had never played a wind instrument. Using musicians as controls was intended to reduce differences in social and cultural environment and in exposure to the musical setting. Secondary objectives were to compare forced vital capacity (FVC) and other spirometric indices, to assess the burden of respiratory symptoms by questionnaire, and to explore whether the cumulative duration of playing was associated with lung function after adjustment for relevant confounders. By restricting the exposure to a single group of closely related instruments, we aimed to provide more precise data on the respiratory effects of brass playing and to contribute to the evidence base used to counsel musicians and patients. Study design and setting We conducted a prospective, multicentre, cross-sectional, case-control study in Switzerland between [month/year] and [month/year]. Recruitment took place at rehearsals of wind orchestras, brass bands and symphony or amateur orchestras in several cantons, so that cases and controls came from comparable musical and social settings. The study was approved by the responsible ethics committee (Ethikkommission [region], reference [number]) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki [1]. All participants gave written informed consent; for participants younger than 18 years, consent was also obtained from a legal guardian. Reporting follows the STROBE recommendations for observational studies [2]. Participants Cases were trumpet, cornet or flugelhorn players. These instruments were grouped because they share a cylindrical-bore, cup-mouthpiece design and similar playing technique and respiratory demand [3]. Inclusion criteria for cases were age of 16 years or older and self-reported regular playing of one of these instruments for at least one year. Controls were members of an orchestra who had never played a wind instrument, including brass, woodwind and bagpipe-type instruments. Exclusion criteria for both groups were inability to perform spirometry, inability to understand the questionnaire in German, French or Italian, and acute respiratory infection within the previous four weeks. Players of other wind instruments were not eligible as cases. Participation was voluntary and no financial incentive was offered. Data collection Each participant attended a single study visit, during which a standardised questionnaire was completed, anthropometric data were measured, and spirometry was performed. Visits were carried out by trained study staff using the same protocol and equipment type at all sites. Questionnaire. Participants reported age, sex, smoking status (never, former, current) and pack-years, history of physician-diagnosed asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or other lung disease, and occupational exposures. For cases we recorded the main instrument, the number of years of playing, the average weekly practice time, and whether other wind instruments were played. Respiratory symptoms (cough, sputum, wheeze, dyspnoea, chest tightness) were assessed with a structured symptom questionnaire adapted from validated instruments [4,5], yielding a total score in which higher values indicate greater symptom burden. Anthropometry. Height was measured without shoes using a stadiometer, and weight was measured with a calibrated scale in light clothing. Body mass index (BMI) was calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared. Spirometry. Pre-bronchodilator spirometry was performed with portable spirometers calibrated daily with a 3-L syringe. Manoeuvres were performed seated, with a nose clip, according to the American Thoracic Society/European Respiratory Society standards [6]. At least three acceptable manoeuvres were required, with the two largest values of forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) and forced vital capacity (FVC) differing by less than 150 mL. The highest FEV1 and FVC values were recorded. Results were expressed as absolute values, as the FEV1/FVC ratio, and as percentage of predicted values using the Global Lung Function Initiative 2012 reference equations [7]. Participants were asked to refrain from vigorous exercise before testing, and cases were asked not to play their instrument for at least one hour beforehand to avoid acute effects of playing on airway calibre. Outcomes The primary end-point was the difference in FEV1 % predicted between trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn players and controls. Secondary end-points were the difference in FVC % predicted, the FEV1/FVC ratio, and the respiratory symptom score between groups. In an exploratory analysis restricted to cases, we examined the association between the number of years of playing and the spirometric parameters. Obstruction was defined as an FEV1/FVC ratio below the lower limit of normal (z-score < −1.645) [7]. Sample size The sample size was calculated for the primary end-point. Assuming a difference in FEV1 % predicted of 8 percentage points between groups, a standard deviation of 15 percentage points [8], a two-sided significance level of 0.05 and a power of 80%, approximately 56 participants per group were needed with equal allocation. Because cases were easier to recruit than controls, a 2:1 allocation ratio was targeted, which gave comparable power with a total of about 150 participants. Recruitment was stopped when this number was reached. Statistical analysis Continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation or median (interquartile range), depending on distribution assessed by visual inspection and the Shapiro–Wilk test. Categorical variables are presented as counts and percentages. Baseline characteristics were compared using Student's t-test or the Mann–Whitney U test for continuous variables and the chi-squared or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables. For the primary and secondary spirometric end-points, crude between-group differences were first estimated using t-tests. Multivariable linear regression models were then fitted with group (case vs control) as the main exposure. Because the groups differed in age, sex, smoking status and BMI, models were adjusted for these potential confounders. Since GLI predicted values already account for age, sex and height, age and height were not included in models of percent-predicted outcomes unless otherwise stated. Results are reported as regression coefficients with 95% confidence intervals. In the exploratory analysis among players, linear regression was used to relate years of playing to FEV1 % predicted and FVC % predicted, adjusting for smoking status, sex and height. Linearity was assessed with restricted cubic splines, and the assumptions of homoscedasticity and normality of residuals were checked graphically. Weekly practice time was explored as an additional covariate in sensitivity analyses. Symptom scores were compared with the Mann–Whitney U test. Missing data were infrequent and handled by complete-case analysis. A two-sided p-value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant, and no adjustment for multiplicity was made for secondary and exploratory analyses, which should therefore be interpreted cautiously. All analyses were performed using [software, version]. Study population Between the start of recruitment and study closure, 162 individuals were screened across participating wind orchestras, brass bands and symphony orchestras. Fifteen were excluded (six did not complete spirometry according to ATS/ERS acceptability criteria [12], four had played another wind instrument for more than one year, three were younger than 16 years, and two withdrew consent), leaving 147 participants for analysis: 99 trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn players and 48 controls. Recruitment was distributed over seven sites, with no site contributing more than 24% of participants. Baseline characteristics are summarised in Table 1. Controls were significantly younger than players (median 34 vs 43 years, p = 0.004), more frequently male (65% vs 47%, p = 0.041) and had a lower body mass index (22.9 ± 3.1 vs 24.8 ± 3.6 kg/m², p = 0.002). The proportion of current smokers was higher among controls (17% vs 6%, p = 0.038), whereas the proportion of never-smokers did not differ significantly between groups. Height was comparable. Among players, the median duration of playing was 22 years (interquartile range 10–35), and the median reported practice time was 4 hours per week (IQR 2–7). Most players (71%) played the trumpet, 21% the cornet and 8% the flugelhorn; 38% played in a brass band and 62% in a wind orchestra. Because of these baseline imbalances, adjusted analyses were prespecified. Lung function: crude comparisons Spirometric results are given in Table 2. Mean FEV1%predicted was 91.9% in controls and 94.2% in players (mean difference 2.3 percentage points, 95% CI −2.2 to 6.8; p = 0.316).

Shock is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in critically ill neonates and children, accounting for a substantial proportion of pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) admissions worldwide [1, 2]. It is defined as a state of acute circulatory failure in which oxygen delivery fails to meet metabolic tissue demands, and it may result from hypovolemic, distributive, cardiogenic, or obstructive mechanisms, frequently in combination. Sepsis and septic shock remain the most common etiologies, with reported pediatric mortality ranging from approximately 10% to more than 40%, depending on the population studied and the resources available [3, 4]. Early recognition and goal-directed management are therefore central to current pediatric resuscitation guidelines. Conventional management and the problem of refractory shock Contemporary guidelines recommend prompt fluid resuscitation, followed by vasoactive support with catecholamines such as dopamine, epinephrine, and norepinephrine, with inotropes such as dobutamine or milrinone added according to the hemodynamic phenotype [5, 6]. A proportion of children, however, remain hypotensive or hypoperfused despite adequate volume loading and escalating catecholamine doses. This condition, termed catecholamine-resistant or refractory shock, is associated with markedly higher mortality and with prolonged organ dysfunction [7]. The mechanisms of catecholamine resistance are multifactorial and include adrenergic receptor downregulation, receptor desensitization, acidosis-induced reduced receptor responsiveness, excessive nitric oxide production, and activation of ATP-sensitive potassium channels in vascular smooth muscle [8, 9]. In addition, high-dose catecholamines carry their own risks, including tachyarrhythmias, increased myocardial oxygen consumption, metabolic derangements, and peripheral or splanchnic hypoperfusion [10]. These limitations have prompted interest in non-catecholamine vasopressors acting through alternative pathways. Rationale for vasopressin and terlipressin Arginine vasopressin (AVP) is an endogenous neurohypophyseal hormone that mediates vasoconstriction through V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle, and water reabsorption through V2 receptors in the renal collecting duct. In vasodilatory shock, plasma AVP concentrations are inappropriately low after an initial surge, a state described as relative vasopressin deficiency, which has been documented in adults and children with septic shock and after cardiac surgery [11, 12]. Exogenous AVP restores vascular tone through catecholamine-independent mechanisms, potentiates the effects of catecholamines, and inhibits ATP-sensitive potassium channels and nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation [8]. Terlipressin (TP), a synthetic long-acting AVP analogue and prodrug of lysine-vasopressin, has greater V1 selectivity and a longer half-life, allowing bolus or intermittent administration [13]. Experience in adults has been informative but not definitive. The Vasopressin and Septic Shock Trial (VASST) found no overall mortality difference between low-dose AVP and norepinephrine, although a possible benefit was suggested in less severe shock [14]. Subsequent meta-analyses have suggested catecholamine-sparing effects and, in some analyses, modest mortality reductions, but have also reported an increased risk of digital and splanchnic ischemia [15, 16]. Consequently, the Surviving Sepsis Campaign suggests adding vasopressin to norepinephrine in adults with a weak recommendation [17]. Evidence in pediatric and neonatal populations Extrapolating adult data to children is problematic because of age-dependent differences in vascular physiology, receptor expression, endogenous hormone responses, and the distribution of underlying diseases. Neonates in particular exhibit distinct features, including pulmonary hypertension, ductal shunting, and immature adrenergic and vasopressin receptor systems [18]. Despite this, AVP and TP have been increasingly used as rescue therapy in pediatric refractory shock, based predominantly on case series, observational studies, and small before-and-after investigations that reported improved blood pressure and reduced catecholamine requirements [19–21]. Some of these reports, however, described adverse effects such as hyponatremia, digital necrosis, and mesenteric ischemia, and observed mortality remained high [22, 23]. The few randomized controlled trials available enrolled small numbers of patients, used heterogeneous dosing regimens, and focused on specific etiologies such as septic or vasodilatory shock after cardiac surgery [24–26]. Pediatric guidelines consequently provide no firm recommendation on the use of vasopressin analogues, and practice varies widely between centers [5, 6]. Rationale and objectives Previous syntheses of pediatric data have been limited by narrow inclusion criteria, restriction to single etiologies, or the absence of formal assessment of whether the accumulated evidence is sufficient to support firm conclusions. When trials are few and small, conventional meta-analysis is vulnerable to random error and repetitive testing, and may produce false-positive or false-negative conclusions. Trial sequential analysis (TSA) addresses this by estimating the required information size and applying adjusted monitoring boundaries, thereby indicating whether further trials are needed [27]. We therefore undertook a systematic review, meta-analysis, and TSA to evaluate the efficacy and safety of adjunctive AVP or TP, compared with conventional therapy consisting of fluid resuscitation and catecholamine vasopressor and inotropic support, in neonates and children with refractory shock of any cause. The primary outcomes were mortality and tissue ischemia. Secondary outcomes included PICU length of stay and other clinically relevant measures. By additionally describing all reports of AVP and TP use in the pediatric population, we sought to characterize the current evidence base and to define the need for future adequately powered trials. Protocol and registration This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [1] and is reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement [2]. The protocol was registered a priori in the PROSPERO international prospective register of systematic reviews (CRD42016035872). Eligibility criteria We considered studies enrolling neonates, infants, and children aged 0 to 18 years with refractory shock of any etiology (septic, cardiogenic, vasodilatory after cardiac surgery, or other distributive shock). Refractory shock was defined as persistent hypotension or hypoperfusion despite adequate fluid resuscitation and treatment with conventional vasopressor and inotropic agents (e.g., dopamine, dobutamine, epinephrine, norepinephrine), as defined by the individual study authors. The intervention of interest was the addition of arginine vasopressin (AVP) or terlipressin (TP), administered by any route, dose, or duration. The comparator was conventional therapy, consisting of fluid resuscitation and vasopressor and inotropic support without AVP/TP. For the systematic review, we included all reports of AVP/TP use in the pediatric population, including randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized comparative studies, "before-and-after" trials without a concurrent comparator, cohort studies, and case series. For quantitative synthesis, only clinical trials with a comparator group were pooled. Studies in adults, animal studies, reviews, editorials, and conference abstracts without sufficient data were excluded. Studies using AVP/TP for indications other than shock (e.g., variceal bleeding, diabetes insipidus, or cardiac arrest) were excluded. No language restrictions were applied. Outcomes The primary outcomes were all-cause mortality (at the longest follow-up reported, typically PICU or hospital discharge or 28 days) and the occurrence of tissue ischemia, defined as clinically evident peripheral, digital, mesenteric, or cutaneous ischemic events attributed to the study drug. Secondary outcomes were length of stay in the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU), duration of mechanical ventilation, changes in hemodynamic variables (mean arterial pressure, heart rate), vasoactive-inotropic requirements, urine output, serum lactate, serum sodium, and other reported adverse events. Search strategy We searched MEDLINE (via PubMed), EMBASE, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to February 2016. The strategy combined controlled vocabulary and free-text terms for vasopressin, terlipressin, and related synonyms (e.g., arginine vasopressin, antidiuretic hormone, Pitressin, glypressin) with terms for shock (septic shock, vasodilatory shock, cardiogenic shock, hypotension, vasoplegia) and with pediatric filters (neonate, newborn, infant, child, adolescent, pediatric). The full search strings are provided in the Additional file. The reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews were manually screened to identify additional reports, and experts were consulted regarding unpublished or ongoing trials. Study selection and data extraction Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, then assessed full texts of potentially eligible reports against the inclusion criteria. Disagreements were resolved by consensus or by consulting a third reviewer. Two reviewers independently extracted data using a standardized, piloted form, capturing study design, setting, population characteristics (age, shock etiology, illness severity), intervention details (agent, dose, timing, duration), comparator, outcomes, follow-up, and funding. Where necessary, corresponding authors were contacted for missing information. Data from neonatal and non-neonatal populations were extracted separately when reported. Risk of bias and quality assessment The risk of bias of RCTs was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool [3], covering sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants, personnel, and outcome assessors, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other bias. Non-randomized and uncontrolled studies were appraised using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale or the Institute of Health Economics checklist for case series, as appropriate [4]. The overall quality of evidence for each pooled outcome was evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach [5]. Assessments were performed independently by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved by discussion. Statistical analysis Dichotomous outcomes (mortality, tissue ischemia) were expressed as relative risks (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), and continuous outcomes (PICU length of stay) as mean differences (MD) with 95% CI. When studies reported medians and ranges or interquartile ranges, means and standard deviations were estimated using established methods [6]. Given anticipated clinical heterogeneity in populations, etiologies, and dosing regimens, pooled estimates were calculated using the DerSimonian–Laird random-effects model [7]. For trials with zero events in one arm, a continuity correction of 0.5 was applied. Statistical heterogeneity was quantified using the Cochran Q test and the I² statistic, with I² values of approximately 25%, 50%, and 75% interpreted as low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively [8]. Publication bias was to be explored with funnel plots and Egger's test if at least ten studies were available [9]. Pre-specified subgroup analyses were planned according to age group (neonates versus older children), agent (AVP versus TP), and shock etiology, subject to the number of available trials. Analyses were performed with Review Manager (RevMan) and Stata software; a two-sided P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Trial sequential analysis Because meta-analyses of small trials are susceptible to random error and repeated significance testing, we performed trial sequential analysis (TSA) for the primary outcomes [10, 11]. TSA estimates the required information size (RIS), the cumulative sample size needed to detect or reject a realistic intervention effect, and constructs adjusted trial sequential monitoring boundaries for benefit, harm, and futility. For mortality, the RIS was calculated with a two-sided type I error of 5%, a power of 80%, an anticipated relative risk reduction of 20–30%, a control-group event proportion derived from the pooled comparator arms, and heterogeneity-adjusted diversity (D²) from the random-effects model. The same framework was applied to tissue ischemia. The cumulative Z-curve was plotted against the monitoring boundaries; crossing a boundary was interpreted as conclusive evidence, whereas failure to cross indicated that the evidence was inconclusive and that further trials are required. TSA was conducted using TSA software (Copenhagen Trial Unit) [12]. Sensitivity analyses Sensitivity analyses were planned to test the robustness of the findings by restricting pooling to RCTs, excluding trials at high risk of bias, and applying a fixed-effect model. The before-and-after studies without comparators were synthesized narratively and were not included in the quantitative pooling. Study selection The initial search identified 1,247 records across MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov. After removal of duplicates, 986 titles and abstracts were screened, and 54 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Of these, 46 were excluded for the following reasons: case reports or small case series without extractable outcome data (n = 29), adult populations (n = 6), non-shock indications (n = 7), and duplicate or overlapping cohorts (n = 4). Eight studies were included in the qualitative synthesis: three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and five before-and-after studies without a comparator group [1–8]. Only the three RCTs contributed to the quantitative comparison of AVP/TP with conventional therapy. Agreement between reviewers on full-text selection was substantial (κ = 0.82). Characteristics of included studies The eight studies enrolled 224 neonates and children with refractory shock, of whom 152 received AVP or TP. Oral anticoagulation is one of the cornerstones of treatment in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) and venous thromboembolism (VTE). In non-valvular AF, anticoagulation reduces the risk of ischaemic stroke and systemic embolism by approximately two thirds, and in VTE it prevents both extension of existing thrombosis and recurrence. For decades, vitamin K antagonists (VKAs), of which warfarin is the most widely used, were the only oral agents available for these indications. Although non-vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants (NOACs) are now recommended in preference to VKAs in most patients with non-valvular AF and in many with VTE, warfarin remains highly relevant in clinical practice. It is still the drug of choice in patients with mechanical heart valves or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis, in those with severe renal impairment, in antiphospholipid syndrome, and wherever reimbursement policies, cost, or patient preference limit access to NOACs. A large proportion of patients worldwide therefore continue to receive warfarin, and optimising its use remains an important clinical goal. The main limitation of warfarin is its narrow therapeutic window and marked inter- and intra-individual variability in dose response. Its effect is monitored using the international normalised ratio (INR), with a target range of 2.0-3.0 for most indications. Values below this range expose the patient to thromboembolic events, whereas values above it increase the risk of bleeding, including intracranial haemorrhage. Warfarin pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics are influenced by genetic polymorphisms (CYP2C9, VKORC1), diet and vitamin K intake, alcohol consumption, acute illness, comorbidities, and numerous drug interactions. Consequently, even in carefully managed patients, INR values frequently fluctuate outside the therapeutic range. The quality of anticoagulation is most commonly expressed as the percentage of time spent in the therapeutic range (TTR), usually calculated by the Rosendaal linear interpolation method. TTR has been shown to correlate closely with clinical outcomes: higher TTR is associated with fewer thromboembolic and haemorrhagic complications and lower mortality. Observational and trial-based analyses have suggested that the benefit of warfarin over alternative strategies diminishes when TTR falls below roughly 60-70%. Current guidelines therefore recommend a TTR of at least 70%, and values above 80% are regarded as indicating particularly high-quality control. Moreover, a low TTR is one of the components of the HAS-BLED score, underlining its prognostic significance. In real-world practice, however, mean TTR is often well below these targets; in many registries and community-based studies it ranges between 50% and 65%, and a considerable proportion of patients remain persistently outside the therapeutic range. Identifying patients likely to have poor anticoagulation control is therefore of substantial practical value. Such patients could be offered more frequent monitoring, intensified education, self-monitoring or self-management, or an early switch to a NOAC where this is possible. Several clinical scores, such as SAMe-TT2R2, have been proposed to predict TTR using variables including sex, age, comorbidities, interacting medication, tobacco use, and ethnicity. Their discriminative ability, however, has been modest and inconsistent across populations and healthcare settings. Individual factors reported to be associated with worse control include older age, female sex, heart failure, diabetes, renal dysfunction, hypertension, hepatic disease, anaemia, polypharmacy, interacting drugs such as amiodarone, poor adherence, and low educational level. Data on the role of body weight and obesity are conflicting, as both dose requirements and variability may be altered by increased body mass. Much of the available evidence derives from large registries or clinical trials with differing monitoring arrangements, which may not reflect the situation in an individual centre with structured follow-up. The organisation of care is itself an important determinant of anticoagulation quality. Dedicated anticoagulation clinics, systematic patient education, regular contact with the treating team, and clear dosing algorithms have been shown to improve TTR compared with usual care. Less is known about how far good-quality care can offset patient-related risk factors, and which of those factors remain relevant when patients are trained and followed under standardised conditions. Data from Central and Eastern Europe, where NOAC use has long been limited by reimbursement constraints and where warfarin is still widely prescribed, are relatively scarce. Against this background, we undertook an analysis of anticoagulation control in patients treated with warfarin for non-valvular AF and/or VTE at a single cardiac centre, where each patient received structured education about the therapy and remained under continuous medical supervision. The aim of this study was to assess the quality of anticoagulant therapy, expressed as TTR, over an 18-month observation period, and to identify clinical factors associated with its deterioration. We hypothesised that, even under conditions of intensive education and monitoring, certain comorbidities and concomitant medications would independently predict a lower proportion of time in the therapeutic range. Identification of such factors could help clinicians to select patients who require closer supervision or alternative anticoagulant strategies. This was a retrospective, single-centre observational study conducted at a tertiary cardiology centre. The study protocol was consistent with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Because the analysis was based on anonymised data collected during routine clinical care, the requirement for individual informed consent was waived in accordance with local regulations. Study population We analysed consecutive adult patients who were treated with warfarin in the centre's outpatient anticoagulation clinic over an 18-month observation period. The indications for anticoagulation were non-valvular atrial fibrillation (AF) and/or venous thromboembolism (VTE), including deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. Patients were eligible if they had been receiving warfarin for at least 3 months before the beginning of the observation period, so that the initial dose-titration phase did not influence the results, and if they had at least four INR measurements during follow-up. The target INR range was 2.0–3.0 for all patients. Exclusion criteria were: mechanical heart valves or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis; other indications for anticoagulation, or a target INR range other than 2.0–3.0; treatment with another oral anticoagulant during the observation period; end-stage renal failure requiring dialysis; active malignancy under chemotherapy; severe hepatic impairment; pregnancy; and incomplete medical or laboratory records. After applying these criteria, 149 patients were included in the final analysis. Patient education and monitoring Each patient received structured education at the start of treatment, delivered by a physician and a trained nurse. The training covered the mechanism of action of warfarin, the importance of regular INR testing, the signs of bleeding and thromboembolic complications, the effects of diet (particularly foods rich in vitamin K), alcohol, and interactions with other drugs and herbal products, and the need to report any new medication or acute illness. Patients received written materials and a treatment booklet in which INR values and doses were recorded. Education was reinforced at follow-up visits. All patients remained under the constant care of the same anticoagulation clinic. INR was usually measured every 1–4 weeks depending on stability, and more frequently after dose changes, the introduction of interacting drugs, or intercurrent illness. Doses were adjusted by the physician according to a standard clinic protocol. Data collection Data were obtained from electronic and paper medical records. Collected variables included demographics (age, sex), body mass index (BMI), the indication for anticoagulation, duration of warfarin therapy, and comorbidities: arterial hypertension, diabetes mellitus, heart failure, coronary artery disease, previous stroke or transient ischaemic attack, chronic kidney disease, thyroid disease, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Obesity was defined as BMI ≥ 30 kg/m², and BMI was also analysed as a continuous variable. Concomitant pharmacotherapy was recorded, including amiodarone, beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers, diuretics, statins, antiplatelet drugs, and proton pump inhibitors. Laboratory data included serum creatinine with estimated glomerular filtration rate, haemoglobin, and liver enzymes. Hypertension was defined as a documented diagnosis or the use of antihypertensive therapy. A total of 2460 INR measurements were collected during the 18-month period. INR was measured in the clinic with a standardised laboratory method or a point-of-care coagulometer calibrated according to the manufacturer's instructions. Assessment of anticoagulation quality The quality of anticoagulation was assessed with the percentage of time in therapeutic range (TTR), calculated for each patient using the Rosendaal linear interpolation method. This method assumes a linear change in INR between two consecutive measurements and assigns an INR value to each day between them. TTR was expressed as the proportion of person-days with INR between 2.0 and 3.0 relative to all days of observation. Intervals between consecutive measurements longer than 56 days were not interpolated. The mean and median TTR of the entire cohort were calculated. Because the median TTR was 80%, we defined high-quality anticoagulation as TTR ≥ 80%. Patients were divided into a stable anticoagulation group (TTR ≥ 80%) and an unstable anticoagulation group (TTR < 80%). The characteristics of the two groups were compared, and factors associated with unstable anticoagulation were identified. Statistical analysis Categorical variables are presented as numbers and percentages, and continuous variables as mean ± standard deviation or median with interquartile range, depending on the distribution. Normality was assessed with the Shapiro–Wilk test. Continuous variables were compared between groups using Student's t-test or the Mann–Whitney U test, as appropriate. Categorical variables were compared using the χ² test or Fisher's exact test when expected counts were small. Univariate logistic regression was first used to evaluate the association of each candidate variable with unstable anticoagulation (TTR < 80%). Variables with p < 0.10 in the univariate analysis, together with clinically relevant variables, were entered into a multivariate logistic regression model with stepwise selection. Results are presented as odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Model fit was assessed with the Hosmer–Lemeshow test, and collinearity between variables was checked before inclusion in the model. Two-sided p values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. All analyses were performed using Statistica software (StatSoft) or an equivalent statistical package. A total of 149 patients (59% male) were included in the analysis. The mean age was 68.8 ± 12.6 years. The indication for anticoagulation was non-valvular atrial fibrillation in most patients, and the remainder had venous thromboembolism or both conditions. During the 18-month observation period, 2460 INR measurements were collected, which corresponds to a mean of approximately 16.5 measurements per patient. Quality of anticoagulation The mean TTR in the entire cohort was 76 ± 21%, and the median was 80%. The distribution of TTR was skewed toward higher values, with a substantial proportion of patients achieving excellent control. Using the median value as the threshold for high-quality anticoagulation, 75 patients (50.3%) had TTR ≥ 80% and were assigned to the stable anticoagulation group. The remaining 74 patients (49.7%) had TTR < 80% and constituted the unstable anticoagulation group. Comparison of clinical characteristics between groups The groups did not differ significantly in age or sex distribution. The mean age was 67.9 ± 12.8 years in the stable group and 69.7 ± 12.4 years in the unstable group (p = 0.39). Men accounted for 61% of the stable group and 57% of the unstable group (p = 0.64). The indication for anticoagulation (atrial fibrillation versus venous thromboembolism) was similarly distributed between groups. Arterial hypertension was more common in the unstable anticoagulation group than in the stable group (73% vs. 52%, p = 0.007). Obesity, expressed as a higher body mass index, was also more prevalent among patients with unstable anticoagulation; mean BMI was 29.6 ± 5.1 kg/m² in this group compared with 27.8 ± 4.4 kg/m² in the stable group (p = 0.03). Amiodarone therapy was more frequent in patients with TTR < 80% (23% vs. 8%, p = 0.01). Other comorbidities, including diabetes mellitus, heart failure, coronary artery disease, history of stroke or transient ischaemic attack, chronic kidney disease, and thyroid disorders, did not differ significantly between the groups. Similarly, the use of other concomitant drugs, such as beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, statins, and diuretics, was comparable in both groups. Mean daily warfarin dose, the number of INR measurements per patient, and the duration of therapy were not significantly different between groups, although patients with unstable anticoagulation tended to have more frequent INR controls, reflecting dose adjustments after out-of-range values. Predictors of unstable anticoagulation Variables with p < 0.10 in univariate analysis (arterial hypertension, obesity, amiodarone therapy) as well as clinically relevant parameters (age, sex, heart failure, diabetes, renal function)

The growth of data-intensive science has made parallel file systems a central component of modern high-performance computing (HPC) infrastructure. Lustre [1] is among the most widely deployed of these systems, powering a large share of the fastest supercomputers and many university and laboratory clusters. Lustre achieves high aggregate bandwidth by separating metadata management from data storage and by distributing file contents across multiple Object Storage Targets (OSTs). This distribution, known as striping, divides a file into fixed-size chunks that are placed round-robin on a configurable number of OSTs. Two parameters, the stripe count and the stripe width (or size), determine how a file is laid out and, consequently, how much parallelism is available to applications that read or write it. Choosing striping parameters is a well-known tuning problem. A large stripe count allows many OSTs to serve a single file concurrently and is generally advantageous for large files accessed sequentially or by many clients in parallel [2, 3]. However, high stripe counts increase the overhead of metadata operations, enlarge the number of servers and network connections involved in each access, and raise the probability that a file is affected by the failure or congestion of any one OST [4]. Conversely, a small stripe count minimizes this overhead and suits small files and workloads dominated by metadata operations, but it constrains throughput for large transfers. Stripe width interacts with these effects, since it determines how well application request sizes align with object boundaries and how much data is transferred per server request [5]. The best configuration therefore depends on the size of the file, the access pattern, and the load on the system. In current Lustre deployments, striping is normally fixed when a file is created. Users may set parameters explicitly per file or per directory, and administrators supply system-wide defaults that are typically conservative, such as a stripe count of one or a small constant. This static model works acceptably when the final file size and access pattern are known in advance, so that an expert can select suitable parameters. Many workloads do not satisfy this condition. Output sizes of simulations may depend on runtime convergence behavior, network monitoring tools produce logs whose volume depends on traffic, and bioinformatics pipelines generate intermediate files whose sizes vary with their inputs. In such cases a user must either guess, risking underutilized bandwidth for files that grow large or wasted resources and overhead for files that remain small, or restripe files after the fact, which requires copying the data and is disruptive. This paper investigates an alternative that we call dynamic striping: the ability to assign different striping characteristics to contiguous segments of a single file as the file grows. Under this model, the beginning of a file may reside on a single OST, as is appropriate for small files, while later segments are spread over progressively more OSTs, or are written with different stripe widths. The file system thus adapts the layout to the file’s actual size rather than to a prediction made at creation time. The idea relates to progressive file layouts, which have been discussed for Lustre [6], and to adaptive data placement techniques explored in other parallel file systems and middleware [7, 8]. Our contribution is not a new mechanism for placement but an empirical assessment of how such a policy behaves across representative workloads. We evaluate a simple watermark-based strategy. One or more size thresholds, or watermarks, are chosen in advance. When a file’s size exceeds a watermark, subsequent data are written using a larger stripe count or a different stripe width. This policy is easy to reason about, requires no knowledge of future behavior, and can be implemented with little state. It also allows us to explore the central trade-off of striping: small files avoid the overhead of wide striping, while large files gain the bandwidth of many OSTs once their size justifies it. To measure the effects of this strategy, we use three workloads with distinct characteristics. First, we employ a modified version of the IOR benchmark [9], which allows controlled variation of file size, transfer size, and access pattern and provides a baseline for sequential and random operations. Second, we use a netflow analysis workload, representative of processing large volumes of network traffic records, in which data files grow unpredictably and are subsequently scanned. Third, we run the blastn algorithm from NCBI BLAST [10], a widely used sequence alignment tool whose database searches combine large sequential reads with irregular access. Together these workloads span synthetic and real applications, and span both write-dominated file growth and read-dominated analysis. Our results indicate that dynamic striping is beneficial for tasks whose data file size is unpredictable and for those dominated by large sequential reads, where the additional parallelism of later segments improves throughput without penalizing small files. For workloads with significant random read phases, the outcome is less conclusive: the benefit of added parallelism is offset in some cases by the cost of contacting more servers for small, scattered requests, and the effect depends on where the accessed regions fall relative to the watermarks. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews background on Lustre striping and related work. Section 3 describes the design of the watermark strategy and its implementation. Section 4 presents the experimental methodology and workloads. Section 5 reports and discusses results, and Section 6 concludes with directions for future work. Experiments were conducted on a dedicated Lustre testbed consisting of one metadata server (MDS) with a single metadata target (MDT), four object storage servers (OSS) each exporting two object storage targets (OSTs), and sixteen client nodes. Servers and clients were connected via a 10 Gb/s Ethernet fabric. Each OST was backed by a RAID-6 array of commodity SATA disks. All nodes ran a Linux 2.6-series kernel with Lustre 2.x [1]. Client caches were dropped between runs, and no other jobs used the file system during measurements. Each configuration was repeated at least five times, and we report mean values with standard deviations. Dynamic Striping Strategy We define dynamic striping as assigning different striping parameters (stripe count and stripe size, or width) to contiguous segments of a single file as it grows. Our implementation follows a watermark-based strategy. A file is created with an initial layout, typically a stripe count of one. A set of watermarks, expressed as file offsets, is configured. When the file size crosses a watermark, the layout of all subsequently written data is changed to the parameters associated with that watermark. Data already written retains its original layout, so a file becomes a concatenation of segments, each with its own stripe count or width. This design avoids the cost of restriping existing data and does not require prior knowledge of the final file size. We evaluated two variants. In the first, the stripe count increases at each watermark (for example, 1, 2, 4, then 8 OSTs). In the second, the stripe width increases at each watermark while the count is held constant. We selected watermarks at geometric intervals (for example, 64 MB, 256 MB, and 1 GB) so that small files remain on few OSTs, limiting metadata and locking overhead, while large files progressively gain aggregate bandwidth [2]. Layout extension was implemented through a modified client I/O path that appends a new layout component to the file's metadata when a write crosses a watermark. Baselines were static layouts with fixed stripe counts of 1, 2, 4, and 8 and a fixed stripe size of 1 MB, which is the Lustre default. Synthetic Benchmark: Modified IOR We used a modified version of the IOR benchmark [3] to generate controlled workloads. IOR was extended so that it could write to files whose final size is not declared at creation, mimicking applications that cannot predict output size. The modified benchmark supported watermark layouts through the mechanism above. We ran IOR with the POSIX API in file-per-process and single-shared-file modes, with 1 to 16 client processes and a transfer size of 1 MB. Total file sizes ranged from 128 MB to 16 GB per process so that files would cross zero, one, two, or three watermarks. Test phases consisted of sequential write, sequential read, and random read. For random reads, offsets were drawn uniformly over the file with a fixed seed, so every configuration received an identical access sequence. We recorded aggregate throughput per phase, calculated from the slowest process's completion time. Netflow Analysis Workload To represent a data-intensive workload with unpredictable output sizes, we used a netflow analysis task. Network flow records were drawn from a collection of anonymized NetFlow v5 traces [4]. The task read the raw flow files sequentially, aggregated records by source and destination address and by port, and wrote intermediate and result files. Because the number of distinct flows depends on the data, the size of the output files cannot be known beforehand. This makes the workload a natural candidate for dynamic striping. We ran the analysis over input sets of several sizes, from a few gigabytes to over 100 GB, with the input stored under each layout policy in turn. The reported metrics were total wall-clock time and the time spent in I/O, obtained from instrumented timers around read and write calls. BLAST Workload For a bioinformatics workload, we used the blastn program from NCBI BLAST+ [5]. Queries were nucleotide sequences searched against a large nucleotide database (the NCBI nt collection [6]) formatted into volumes with makeblastdb. The database files are read largely in sequential scans during the initial loading and scoring stages, but access to sequence data after seeding shows significant random read behavior. We ran a fixed set of queries with 1 to 16 concurrent blastn processes on separate clients, each with a single search thread, so that file system behavior rather than computation was the dominant variable. Database files were copied into the file system under each layout policy before every experiment. The measured quantity was the total search time, with the I/O fraction determined by comparing against runs from a warm local RAM disk. Metrics and Instrumentation The primary metrics were aggregate and per-client throughput for IOR and elapsed time for the netflow and BLAST workloads. We also collected OST utilization and request distribution via Lustre server-side statistics (the obdfilter stats files) to verify whether load was spread evenly across OSTs. Metadata overhead was assessed by counting RPCs to the MDS using client-side llite statistics. To quantify imbalance we computed the coefficient of variation of bytes served per OST during each run. Differences between layouts were assessed with Welch's t-test at a significance level of 0.05. Experimental Controls To reduce confounding factors, the OST allocation order was randomized per file by the MDS's default round-robin allocator, and we verified after each run that the layouts reported by lfs getstripe matched the intended configuration. Server caches were flushed by remounting the OSTs between experiments. Network throughput was verified before each session with a point-to-point test to confirm that no link was degraded. Where files spanned multiple watermark segments, we confirmed that the segment boundaries fell at the configured offsets. Finally, the same data sets, query sets, and random seeds were used for every layout policy so that observed differences could be attributed to striping alone. We evaluated dynamic striping against three static configurations: a single stripe (default), a fixed stripe count of four, and a fixed stripe count spanning all available OSTs. The dynamic configuration used two watermarks, increasing the stripe count from one to four at 1 GB and from four to all OSTs at 16 GB. Each experiment was repeated ten times, and we report mean values with standard deviations. Unless noted otherwise, differences discussed below were significant under Welch's t-test (p < 0.05).
