Population ageing is one of the most significant demographic transformations of the twenty-first century. In Europe, the share of people aged 65 and over is steadily increasing, and projections indicate that by 2050 almost one in three Europeans will belong to this age group [1]. Longer life expectancy is a social achievement, but it is accompanied by a growing prevalence of chronic diseases, frailty, cognitive decline, and motor impairments, which place considerable pressure on healthcare systems, formal caregivers, and families [2]. Institutional care is costly and, importantly, is often at odds with the preferences of older adults, most of whom wish to remain in their own homes for as long as possible, a notion commonly referred to as "ageing in place" [3]. Technologies that make this option safe and sustainable are therefore a strategic priority. Ambient Assisted Living (AAL) addresses this need through the use of information and communication technologies to support autonomy, safety, and quality of life in the domestic environment [4]. Advances in low-cost sensing, wireless communication, embedded computing, and cloud platforms have made it feasible to instrument ordinary homes with unobtrusive devices that monitor activities, detect hazardous situations, and notify caregivers when intervention is required [5]. Typical applications include fall detection, monitoring of vital signs, detection of gas leaks, smoke, or flooding, tracking of daily routines, and remote control of household appliances [6], [7]. When properly designed, such systems can act as a "virtual caregiver" that reassures both the assisted person and their relatives, while reducing unnecessary hospitalisations and delaying institutionalisation [8]. Despite this potential, the diffusion of AAL solutions remains limited, and several obstacles persist. First, many commercial and research systems are built as vertical, proprietary solutions in which sensors, gateways, and applications from different vendors cannot easily cooperate, resulting in vendor lock-in and fragmented user experiences [9]. The lack of interoperability and of shared standards hinders scalability and increases installation and maintenance costs. Second, usability is frequently underestimated: interfaces that are not tailored to older users or to people with motor disabilities lead to low acceptance and abandonment [10]. Third, and critically, alarm systems based on a single sensor are prone to false positives and false negatives. Wearable fall detectors, for example, may be left unworn or may misinterpret abrupt but harmless movements, whereas ambient or vision-based solutions may be affected by occlusions, lighting, and privacy concerns [11], [12]. Frequent false alarms erode trust and overload caregivers, while missed events can have severe consequences. Reliable alarm generation therefore remains an open challenge. A promising direction to improve robustness is multi-sensor data fusion, in which complementary information coming from heterogeneous devices is combined to obtain more accurate and reliable inferences than any single source could provide [13]. Fusion approaches have been explored at the signal, feature, and decision levels for activity recognition and fall detection, generally showing improved performance with respect to single-modality methods [14], [15]. However, many of these studies are validated in laboratory conditions or on simulated data, and few are integrated into complete, interoperable architectures that have been tested in real homes with real users. Likewise, the Internet of Things (IoT) paradigm and cloud computing offer the means to connect Smart Objects (SOs), process their data at scale, and provide timely responses [16], but their combination with standardised communication and effective alarm confirmation strategies is rarely addressed in a unified manner. This paper presents the main results of HDOMO, an AAL project carried out by a consortium of 16 Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) and 2 research institutes. The project aimed to create an autonomous and automated domestic environment primarily intended for elderly people and people with physical and motor disabilities. The guiding principle is that a known and familiar environment should assist users in their daily activities and, when necessary, autonomously summon relief efforts, thereby simplifying the lives of people in need of support while preserving their independence in their private space. Technically, HDOMO relies on a set of heterogeneous SOs that communicate with one another, with a cloud-based infrastructure, and with both assisted users and caregivers. The design emphasises interoperability and standardisation of devices, usability of the interfaces, and effectiveness of the alarm system. While the state of the art includes projects that satisfy only a subset of these requirements [6], [9], HDOMO seeks to fulfil all of them within a single, coherent framework. The main contributions of this work are the following. First, we describe the architecture of the HDOMO platform, including the SOs, the communication layer, and the cloud services that enable real-time data extraction and processing. Second, we propose a novel technique to improve the accuracy of alarm detection based on a multi-SO approach, in which information from different interoperable devices is fused to confirm primary alarms and reduce erroneous notifications. Third, we report the results of experimental trials conducted in a real scenario, which assess the accuracy and efficiency of the system and its ability to respond promptly to user needs. The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on AAL systems, interoperability, and sensor fusion. Section 3 describes the HDOMO architecture and the smart objects employed. Section 4 details the proposed fusion method for alarm detection. Section 5 presents the experimental setup and results, and Section 6 discusses the findings and concludes with directions for future work. The HDOMO system was designed as a modular, cloud-based architecture in which heterogeneous Smart Objects (SOs) acquire data about the user and the domestic environment, exchange information through a shared platform, and generate alarms for caregivers. The methodology comprised four phases: requirements elicitation, system and SO design, development of a multi-SO information fusion technique for alarm detection, and experimental validation in a real scenario. Requirements Elicitation Requirements were collected through structured interviews and focus groups with elderly users, people with motor disabilities, formal and informal caregivers, and the 16 participating SMEs. Following user-centred design principles [1], the needs identified were grouped into safety (falls, domestic hazards, prolonged inactivity), health monitoring, comfort and home automation, and communication with caregivers. Non-functional requirements included interoperability, low intrusiveness, ease of use, data protection, and reliability of alarms, with particular attention to limiting false alarms, which are a known cause of abandonment of AAL technologies [2]. System Architecture The architecture comprises three layers. The perception layer consists of SOs installed in the home, including wearable devices (inertial and physiological sensors), environmental sensors (presence, door/window contacts, temperature, humidity, gas and smoke detectors, flood sensors), and actuators (smart plugs, lighting, shutters, valves). The communication layer uses a local gateway that collects data from SOs through their native protocols (e.g., Bluetooth Low Energy, Zigbee, Wi-Fi) and forwards them to the cloud using MQTT over TLS [3]. To ensure interoperability among devices from different manufacturers, each SO was described through a common data model, with standardized message formats and semantic annotations of device type, location, unit of measurement, and timestamp. The application layer, hosted in the cloud, includes a data storage and processing module, a rule and alarm engine, and user interfaces. These interfaces comprise a simplified touch and voice-based application for assisted users, and a web and mobile dashboard for caregivers and relief services. Time synchronization among SOs was achieved through gateway-level NTP alignment, so that events from different devices could be correlated within a common temporal reference. Personal data were pseudonymized, encrypted in transit and at rest, and managed in compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation [4]. Smart Objects and Single-Device Alarm Detection Each SO implemented local processing to extract features and produce a preliminary event. For wearable devices, tri-axial accelerometer data sampled at 50 Hz were segmented into sliding windows of 2 s with 50% overlap. Features such as signal magnitude vector, jerk, variance, and post-impact inactivity duration were computed, and a threshold-based algorithm combined with a lightweight classifier labelled windows as activity of daily living or potential fall [5]. Environmental SOs generated events by threshold crossing (e.g., gas concentration, water presence) or by state change (e.g., door opening). Presence sensors were used to derive occupancy and inactivity indicators for each room. Each preliminary event was transmitted with a confidence score in the interval [0,1] derived from the margin by which the decision threshold or classifier output was exceeded. Multi-SO Information Fusion To reduce false alarms and increase robustness, a decision-level fusion technique was developed in the alarm engine. Preliminary events from different SOs were collected in a temporal buffer and associated when they referred to the same user and occurred within a configurable time window Δt (set at 30 s for fall events and 5 min for inactivity-related events). For each alarm type a, the fused confidence was computed as a weighted combination of the confidences ci of the n contributing SOs: Ca = Σ wi ci / Σ wi, where weights wi reflect the reliability of each device for that alarm type, estimated from preliminary laboratory tests. An alarm was confirmed when Ca exceeded a threshold τa, or when a single-SO event of critical severity (e.g., gas leak) was received. Contextual rules, expressed as logical conditions, were added to exploit complementary information. For example, a wearable fall event was confirmed if followed by absence of movement detected by room presence sensors, or if the user did not respond to a vocal request for confirmation. Conversely, a fall event accompanied by normal movement patterns shortly afterwards was downgraded. Unconfirmed events were stored as warnings without notifying emergency contacts. Confirmed alarms followed an escalation procedure: notification to the user, then to designated caregivers via application and SMS, and finally to a relief centre if no acknowledgement was received within a predefined time. Experimental Trials Trials were conducted in real apartments equipped with the full set of SOs. Participants were elderly volunteers and people with motor disabilities who provided written informed consent; the protocol followed the Declaration of Helsinki [6]. Participants were monitored during normal daily life for several weeks. In addition, supervised scripted scenarios were performed to obtain labelled ground truth: simulated falls (forward, backward, lateral, from a seated position) executed with safety mats, activities that commonly cause false positives (sitting abruptly, lying down on a bed or sofa, picking up objects), prolonged inactivity, and simulated domestic hazards. Ground truth for daily-life data was obtained through participant diaries and caregiver reports. Evaluation Metrics and Analysis System performance was evaluated in terms of sensitivity, specificity, precision, and F1-score for alarm detection, comparing single-SO detection with the multi-SO fusion approach on the same dataset [7]. The false alarm rate per day of monitoring was also computed. Efficiency was assessed by measuring end-to-end latency, from event occurrence to caregiver notification, and data loss rate. Usability was assessed through the System Usability Scale [8] and semi-structured interviews with users and caregivers. Differences between detection approaches were tested with McNemar's test for paired classifications, with significance set at p < 0.05. Fusion weights and thresholds were tuned on a development subset, and results are reported on the remaining data to avoid optimistic bias. The HDOMO system was evaluated in a real-scenario trial over a period of eight weeks in 12 apartments occupied by elderly volunteers (age range 68–91 years, mean 79.4) living independently, some with mild motor impairments. The Internet of Things (IoT) envisions a world in which billions of everyday objects, equipped with sensing, actuation, computation, and communication capabilities, are interconnected and cooperate to deliver services to people, organizations, and other machines. Over the last decade, this vision has moved from a futuristic scenario to a concrete technological and economic reality, with applications spanning smart homes, smart cities, healthcare, industrial automation, logistics, agriculture, and environmental monitoring. Research and industrial efforts have produced a wealth of contributions: communication protocols for constrained devices, middleware platforms for data collection and integration, cloud and edge computing architectures, semantic models for interoperability, and a variety of frameworks and tools for programming specific classes of devices and applications. Despite this progress, the way IoT systems are conceived, designed, and built remains largely ad hoc. Most proposals address a specific problem or layer of the technology stack, such as device connectivity, data streaming, or security, and are typically validated in a particular application domain. Developers who wish to build a complete IoT system must therefore assemble heterogeneous technologies, reconcile different programming models, and make critical architectural decisions with little methodological guidance. The result is that IoT systems are often tightly coupled to specific platforms or deployments, hard to evolve, hard to reuse, and difficult to reason about in terms of correctness, scalability, and dependability. This situation closely resembles earlier phases in the history of other computing paradigms, such as object-oriented, distributed, and agent-based systems, where the maturation of the field required principled software engineering approaches that provided shared abstractions, modeling languages, development processes, and tool support. The IoT poses a distinctive set of challenges that make the adaptation of existing methodologies nontrivial. First, IoT systems are extremely heterogeneous: devices vary by orders of magnitude in computational power, energy availability, connectivity, and functionality, and they are produced by different vendors adopting different standards. Second, they are inherently distributed and open, with devices joining and leaving at runtime, often in unpredictable ways, and with ownership and control spread across multiple stakeholders. Third, they are deeply embedded in the physical world, so that software behavior is tied to the dynamics of the environment, to real-time constraints, and to the uncertainty of sensing and actuation. Fourth, they are expected to exhibit autonomy and adaptivity, reacting to context changes and coordinating with one another with little or no human intervention. Finally, they raise cross-cutting concerns, including security, privacy, trust, and sustainability, that cannot be treated as afterthoughts. These characteristics call for a methodology that can span multiple levels of abstraction, from the physical devices up to the application and social levels, and that can accommodate the continuous evolution of the system. Several existing lines of work provide valuable building blocks. Model-driven engineering approaches offer ways to describe IoT systems and generate code for heterogeneous platforms. Service-oriented and resource-oriented architectures, such as those based on web services and the Web of Things, help to address interoperability. Agent-oriented software engineering contributes abstractions for autonomy, interaction, and organization. Cyber-physical systems and embedded software engineering emphasize the integration of computation with physical processes. Yet each of these perspectives captures only part of the picture, and they rely on different, often incompatible, vocabularies. What is currently missing is a coherent conceptual framework that identifies the key abstractions of IoT systems and shows how they relate to one another throughout the development life cycle. In this paper, we take a step toward filling this gap. By synthesizing from the state of the art in the area, we attempt to frame the key concepts and abstractions that revolve around the design and development of IoT systems and applications. These include, among others, the notions of thing, the environment in which things are situated, the services and data they expose, the infrastructures that connect them, and the applications and goals that emerge from their cooperation. Starting from these abstractions, we draft a software engineering methodology that guides developers through the main phases of the development process, namely requirements analysis, design, implementation, deployment, and runtime evolution. The methodology is intended to be general, in the sense that it does not commit to a specific technology, platform, or application domain, while still being concrete enough to support the systematic production of IoT systems. The contribution of this work is therefore twofold. On the conceptual side, we provide a structured view of the abstractions emerging from the literature, clarifying their roles and mutual dependencies. On the methodological side, we outline a process that leverages such abstractions to drive analysis and design decisions, and we discuss how existing approaches and tools can be positioned within it. We do not claim to present a complete or definitive methodology; rather, we aim to provide a foundation and a research agenda that can stimulate discussion and further refinement by the community. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the state of the art and the main challenges in IoT development. Section 3 presents the key concepts and abstractions. Section 4 describes the proposed methodology. Section 5 discusses open issues and research directions, and Section 6 concludes. The methodology was developed through a three-step process: (i) a synthesis of the state of the art, (ii) the extraction of recurring concepts and abstractions, and (iii) the organization of those abstractions into a staged software engineering process. Literature synthesis. We surveyed work on IoT architectures, middleware, programming models, and agent-oriented and service-oriented engineering. Sources were drawn from major digital libraries (IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, SpringerLink, ScienceDirect) and from proceedings of venues in pervasive computing, distributed systems, multi-agent systems, and software engineering. Search terms combined "Internet of Things," "IoT," "smart objects," "cyber-physical systems," and "ubiquitous computing" with "methodology," "software engineering," "middleware," "programming model," and "architecture." We included works that proposed a concrete design or development approach, a reference model, or a platform with explicit abstractions. We excluded works addressing only hardware, communication protocols, or domain-specific signal processing, unless they bore directly on software design. Publications were screened by title and abstract, then by full text, and each retained work was annotated with the abstractions it used, the problem it addressed, and the development phase it supported. Extraction of abstractions. We coded the annotated works inductively to identify recurring concepts. Concepts were retained if they appeared across several independent proposals and were useful for reasoning about design rather than implementation. We merged synonyms (for example, "thing," "smart object," and "device") and separated terms that conflated distinct notions (for example, a physical entity versus its digital representation). This produced a conceptual framework in which the following abstractions are treated as first-class: physical entities and their digital counterparts; devices and resources that sense, actuate, or compute; services exposing capabilities; users and stakeholders; the environment and its context; and the interaction patterns (event-driven, request-response, publish-subscribe) that connect them. We also identified cross-cutting concerns, including heterogeneity, scale, dynamism and mobility, uncertainty of data, autonomy, security and privacy, and resource constraints. Layered organization. To relate the abstractions to one another, we arranged them along two dimensions. The first is a set of levels of abstraction: the physical level (entities, sensors, actuators), the virtualization level (digital twins and resource abstractions), the service and application level (composition and orchestration), and the user level (goals and requirements). The second is the distribution of computation across the device, edge, and cloud tiers. Each abstraction was placed according to where it is most naturally modeled and where it is most commonly deployed in the surveyed work. This allowed us to check that the framework covers the range of architectures found in the literature without privileging a single technology stack. Derivation of the process. The methodology was drafted by mapping the abstractions onto conventional software engineering phases, adapted to the specific features of IoT. We began from a generic iterative lifecycle and, for each phase, asked which IoT abstractions must be captured, which decisions must be taken, and which artifacts result. 1. Requirements analysis: identification of stakeholders, goals, and the physical phenomena and entities of interest, together with non-functional constraints such as latency, energy, and privacy. 2. Domain and system modeling: definition of entities, their digital representations, devices, resources, and context, and specification of the relations among them. 3. Architecture and design: allocation of functionality to device, edge, and cloud tiers; selection of interaction patterns; definition of services and their composition; and treatment of cross-cutting concerns. 4. Implementation: mapping of models to platforms, middleware, and programming abstractions, with attention to heterogeneity and portability. 5. Deployment and configuration: provisioning, discovery, and bootstrapping of devices and services, including support for mobility and changing topology. 6. Verification, validation, and operation: testing in simulated and real environments, runtime monitoring, and adaptation and evolution of the system after deployment. Because IoT systems are open and change after deployment, the process was designed to be iterative, with feedback from runtime monitoring returning to the modeling and design phases. Consistency checking. To assess whether the draft methodology was coherent and sufficiently general, we performed two checks. First, we conducted a coverage analysis: each surveyed proposal was mapped onto the methodology to verify that its main abstractions and phases could be represented, and gaps or ambiguities led to revision of the framework. Second, we traced a set of representative application scenarios, such as smart buildings, environmental monitoring, and logistics, through the phases to confirm that the abstractions could express their requirements and design choices. These checks are qualitative and intended to demonstrate the expressiveness and applicability of the approach rather than to provide empirical validation. Quantitative evaluation through case studies and controlled comparison with existing practice is left to future work. Scope and limitations. The methodology is intentionally technology-neutral. It prescribes concepts, phases, and artifacts rather than specific languages, protocols, or tools, so that it can be instantiated with different platforms. Because it is derived from a non-exhaustive synthesis of the literature, it reflects the proposals and terminology available at the time of writing, and the selection and coding of the sources involved interpretive judgment by the authors. The methodology emerging from our synthesis is organized around a small set of core abstractions, a layered process that operates on them, and a set of design guidelines derived from the surveyed literature. We report each in turn. Key abstractions. Analysis of the surveyed proposals, covering middleware, programming models, architectures, and agent-based and service-oriented approaches, showed that most can be described using five recurring abstractions. 1. Things: physical or virtual entities with sensing, actuating, computing, or communication capabilities. We distinguish passive things (e.g., tagged objects), which are only observable, from active things, which can autonomously sense, decide, and act. 2. Digital representations: software counterparts of things (proxies, digital twins, or agents) that expose a uniform interface and hide heterogeneity of protocols and hardware. 3. Services and capabilities: the functionalities offered by things, described independently of their implementation so that they can be discovered and composed. 4. Contexts and spaces: logical or physical scopes (a room, a building, a city district) that delimit interaction, naming, and access, and that provide situational information to applications. 5. Collectives and applications: dynamic aggregations of things and services that jointly achieve a goal, with behavior that is not reducible to any single member. These abstractions proved sufficient to map every proposal we examined onto at least one of them. Approaches differed mainly in which abstractions they treated as first-class. Middleware solutions emphasized digital representations and services, whereas programming models emphasized collectives and contexts. Few treated all five uniformly, which motivates a methodology that makes them explicit. Methodology phases. The methodology comprises five iterative phases, each producing artifacts expressed in terms of the abstractions above. Requirements analysis identifies stakeholders, goals, and constraints specific to IoT, namely energy budgets, latency, intermittent connectivity, privacy, and physical safety. Outputs are goal models and scenarios that state which things and contexts are involved. Domain modeling identifies the things, their capabilities, and the spaces in which they operate. Spasticity and dystonia are common and often disabling consequences of cerebral palsy (CP), the most prevalent cause of motor disability in childhood [1]. Increased tone impairs function, causes pain, contributes to contractures and hip displacement, and complicates positioning, hygiene, and caregiving. When oral agents, botulinum toxin injections, and physical therapy provide insufficient relief, or when systemic side effects such as sedation limit their use, continuous intrathecal delivery of baclofen has become an established option [2,3]. Baclofen, a gamma-aminobutyric acid type B receptor agonist, acts at the level of the spinal cord. Direct intrathecal administration achieves high cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) concentrations with a fraction of the oral dose, thereby limiting central adverse effects [4]. Randomized and observational studies have demonstrated reductions in spasticity and, in selected patients, improvements in comfort, ease of care, and in some cases function [5,6]. Despite these benefits, intrathecal baclofen (ITB) pump implantation in children carries a substantial burden of complications. Reported rates of surgical complications range widely but are frequently cited at 20% to 40% or higher, and include CSF leak and pseudomeningocele, wound dehiscence, infection, catheter malfunction, and the need for pump explantation or revision [7–9]. Children with CP are particularly vulnerable. They are often undernourished, have little subcutaneous tissue over which to cover a pump, and may have scoliosis or prior spinal instrumentation that complicates catheter placement. Infection rates in pediatric series are higher than in adult populations, and some reports show that infections and CSF-related wound problems account for a large proportion of unplanned returns to the operating room [8,10]. These events cause morbidity, prolong hospitalization, interrupt baclofen delivery, and may lead to abandonment of therapy. Efforts to reduce complications have therefore focused on surgical technique, such as subfascial pump placement, meticulous dural closure, and perioperative antibiotic protocols, as well as on patient selection and nutritional optimization [9,11]. One potential and underappreciated contributor to CSF-related complications is unrecognized elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) due to arrested or compensated hydrocephalus. Many children with CP have a history of conditions that predispose to disordered CSF dynamics, including prematurity with intraventricular hemorrhage, perinatal infection, and congenital brain malformations [12]. A subset of these patients receive CSF shunts in infancy, but others may have ventriculomegaly that stabilized without treatment and has been labeled "arrested" hydrocephalus. The concept of arrested hydrocephalus is controversial, since ventricular size correlates poorly with ICP, and some patients with apparently stable ventricles may in fact have a marginally compensated state in which CSF absorption remains impaired [13,14]. Creating a durable intrathecal puncture, placing a catheter, and then closing a wound over a pump pocket in the presence of elevated CSF pressure could plausibly promote persistent leakage along the catheter tract, pseudomeningocele formation, wound breakdown, and secondary infection. Recognizing elevated ICP clinically in this population is difficult. The usual signs of hydrocephalus, including headache, vomiting, irritability, lethargy, and declining school or motor performance, are nonspecific and hard to elicit in children who are nonverbal, have impaired cognition, or have chronic baseline neurological deficits and frequent gastrointestinal symptoms. Papilledema may be absent or difficult to assess. Neuroimaging may show ventriculomegaly, but this is common in CP owing to periventricular injury and white matter loss, and it does not reliably distinguish ex vacuo enlargement from pressure-related dilation [13]. Consequently, patients with clinically silent hydrocephalus may proceed to ITB implantation without any direct measurement of ICP. Case reports and small series describe patients with repeated CSF leaks after ITB placement who were later found to have hydrocephalus, with resolution of the problem after CSF diversion [15,16], supporting the plausibility of this mechanism, but systematic data are lacking. Lumbar puncture performed with manometry offers a direct, minimally invasive means of measuring CSF pressure. When done under general anesthesia, however, interpretation requires attention to confounders such as anesthetic agents, ventilation, positioning, and carbon dioxide levels, so standardization is important. A threshold opening pressure above approximately 20 to 25 cmH2O is generally regarded as elevated in children [17]. Incorporating such a measurement into the preoperative pathway could identify patients at risk before an implant is placed, and permit consideration of CSF diversion or alternative strategies for spasticity management. At our institution, concern about persistent CSF leaks and wound complications after ITB implantation prompted the development of a standardized protocol that included mandatory cranial imaging and lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement before pump implantation. Patients with elevated pressure were not implanted at that time; instead, they were counseled regarding neurosurgical options, including ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement followed by reconsideration of ITB therapy, or continued nonoperative spasticity management. In this report, we describe our experience with this algorithm in a consecutive series of pediatric candidates for ITB implantation, characterize the frequency of previously unrecognized elevated ICP, and review the subsequent management and outcomes of these patients. We aim to provide a practical framework for the evaluation of hydrocephalus in this population and to stimulate further study of the relationship between CSF dynamics and ITB-related complications. We conducted a retrospective case series of all pediatric patients evaluated for intrathecal baclofen (ITB) pump implantation at Seattle Children's Hospital between September 2012 and October 2014. The study was approved by the institutional review board, which waived the requirement for informed consent given the retrospective design and the use of de-identified data. Reporting followed published recommendations for case series [1]. Patient Population Patients were eligible if they were referred to the neurosurgery service for ITB pump implantation to treat medically refractory spasticity, dystonia, or both, in the setting of cerebral palsy or related static encephalopathy. Candidacy for ITB therapy was determined by a multidisciplinary spasticity team that included pediatric neurosurgeons, physiatrists, orthopedic surgeons, and neurologists. Standard indications were generalized or lower-extremity spasticity or dystonia that interfered with care, comfort, positioning, or function and that did not respond adequately to oral agents, botulinum toxin injections, or both [2,3]. Patients were excluded from analysis if they had an active systemic or local infection, a previously implanted ITB pump, or if the family declined further evaluation before any preoperative assessment was completed. Patients with an existing CSF diversion device were not considered for the protocol, as their ICP status was managed through shunt evaluation. Standardized Preimplantation Protocol Because of high complication rates in our early ITB experience, including CSF leak, pseudomeningocele, wound dehiscence, and infection, which are consistent with the published literature [4,5], a standardized preoperative protocol was adopted in September 2012. The rationale was that clinically unrecognized arrested or compensated hydrocephalus might be present in this population, in whom baseline neurological impairment, communication limitations, and chronic neurological deficits obscure the usual symptoms and signs of raised ICP [6]. The protocol had three components. First, all patients underwent cranial imaging, either magnetic resonance imaging or computed tomography, before the procedure. Images were reviewed by a pediatric neurosurgeon and a neuroradiologist for ventricular size, periventricular changes, evidence of prior hemorrhage or periventricular leukomalacia, and other structural abnormalities. Ventriculomegaly alone was not considered diagnostic of active hydrocephalus, since it commonly occurs from ex vacuo change in patients with cerebral palsy [7]. Second, all patients underwent a lumbar puncture (LP) for measurement of opening pressure under general anesthesia, as a separate preliminary step before pump implantation. Third, a predefined decision rule determined whether implantation proceeded. Lumbar Puncture and ICP Measurement LPs were performed in the operating room under general anesthesia with standard monitoring. Patients were positioned in the lateral decubitus position with the hips and knees flexed to the extent permitted by their tone and contractures. A spinal needle was inserted at the lower lumbar interspaces under sterile conditions, and a manometer was attached to measure opening pressure after the CSF level stabilized and showed respiratory variation. To reduce confounding from anesthetic effects on ICP, the anesthesia team maintained normocapnia (end-tidal CO2 of approximately 35–40 mmHg), avoided agents known to substantially elevate ICP where possible, and kept the head of the bed neutral. Opening pressure was recorded in cmH2O. When indicated, CSF was sent for cell count, protein, glucose, and culture to exclude occult infection before implantation of hardware. An opening pressure above 21 cmH2O was defined as elevated, based on pediatric reference values for lumbar opening pressure [8]. Patients with opening pressures of 21 cmH2O or lower were assigned to the "normal ICP" group, and those with higher values to the "elevated ICP" group. Management Algorithm Patients in the normal ICP group proceeded to ITB pump implantation, either in the same anesthetic session or at a later date, depending on scheduling and family preference. In the elevated ICP group, pump implantation was aborted, and the findings were discussed with the family. Alternative management options were presented, including observation, additional evaluation such as ophthalmologic examination for papilledema, repeat or continuous ICP monitoring, endoscopic third ventriculostomy, and ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt placement. Families who chose CSF diversion underwent the procedure by a pediatric neurosurgeon using standard techniques with programmable valves. Those patients were reconsidered for ITB pump implantation after recovery from shunt surgery, with a reasonable interval allowed for wound healing and clinical stabilization. Other families elected to forgo further intervention or to pursue non-ITB treatments for spasticity. ITB Pump Implantation Pump implantation followed a standard technique. Patients received perioperative intravenous antibiotics. Under general anesthesia, patients were placed in the lateral decubitus position. A catheter was placed through a paramedian needle into the lumbar intrathecal space and advanced to the desired spinal level under fluoroscopic guidance. The catheter was secured to the fascia, tunneled subcutaneously, and connected to a pump placed in a subcutaneous or subfascial abdominal pocket. Meticulous watertight fascial closure was performed. Patients received a screening bolus trial of baclofen before implantation when this was part of the team's practice. Pumps were programmed initially at a low dose, and doses were titrated in clinic. Data Collection and Outcomes Data were abstracted from electronic medical records and included age, sex, etiology of cerebral palsy, Gross Motor Function Classification System level, prior neurosurgical history, imaging findings, opening pressure, CSF studies, and subsequent management. The primary outcomes were the proportion of patients with elevated opening pressure and the proportion ultimately undergoing ITB pump implantation. The secondary outcome was postoperative complications, including CSF leak, pseudomeningocele, wound breakdown, infection, catheter malfunction, and need for reoperation, assessed through the most recent follow-up visit. Statistical Analysis Given the small sample, analysis was descriptive. Categorical variables were summarized as counts and percentages, and continuous variables as medians and ranges. Comparisons between the normal and elevated ICP groups were not powered for inferential testing. Eighteen patients were evaluated for ITB pump implantation at our institution during the study period (September 2012 to October 2014) and underwent lumbar puncture under general anesthesia according to the standardized protocol. The cohort comprised 10 male and 8 female patients with a mean age of 11.2 years (range 5–19 years) at the time of evaluation. All patients had a diagnosis of cerebral palsy with spasticity, dystonia, or a mixed movement disorder. Most were classified as Gross Motor Function Classification System level IV or V (15/18, 83.3%). Etiologies of cerebral palsy included prematurity with or without intraventricular hemorrhage (9 patients), hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (5), and other or unknown causes (4). Four patients had a documented history of neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage, and none had a previously placed CSF diversion device. Preoperative imaging All patients underwent cranial imaging (MRI in 14 patients, CT in 4) before lumbar puncture. Ventricular enlargement of varying degree was identified in 9 patients, while 9 had normal or ex vacuo–appearing ventricles. Imaging findings were not sufficiently discriminating to predict ICP. Of the 8 patients with elevated opening pressure, 6 had ventriculomegaly on imaging and 2 had ventricles of normal size. Conversely, 3 of the 10 patients with normal opening pressure had ventriculomegaly that was judged to be stable or secondary to volume loss. Before the procedure, none of the patients had clinical signs that would have prompted a diagnosis of hydrocephalus; caregivers did not report new headache, vomiting, or changes in alertness, although the baseline neurological function of this population limited the reliability of such assessments.

Ovarian cancer is the most lethal gynecologic malignancy and one of the leading causes of cancer death among women worldwide. Its high mortality reflects, in large part, late diagnosis: because early disease is usually asymptomatic or produces nonspecific symptoms, most patients present with advanced stage disease, when five-year survival falls below 30%. When the disease is detected at stage I, five-year survival exceeds 90%. Accurate preoperative evaluation of women with a pelvic mass is therefore central to improving outcomes. Pelvic masses are common, and the great majority are benign. The clinical challenge is to identify the minority that are malignant before surgery so that these patients can be referred to a gynecologic oncologist or a center with appropriate expertise. Evidence consistently shows that women with ovarian cancer who are operated on by gynecologic oncologists are more likely to be optimally staged and cytoreduced, and have better survival than those treated by general surgeons or non-specialist gynecologists. Conversely, overestimating risk leads to unnecessary referral, extensive surgery, and anxiety for women with benign disease, and strains limited specialist resources. This balance is particularly relevant in many Asian countries, where access to gynecologic oncology services may be unevenly distributed. Several tools have been proposed to triage pelvic masses. Transvaginal or transabdominal ultrasound is the first-line imaging modality, and morphologic features such as solid components, papillary projections, septations, bilaterality, ascites, and abnormal vascularity are associated with malignancy. However, ultrasound interpretation depends on operator experience, and the accuracy reported by expert examiners is often not reproduced in general practice. The serum biomarker cancer antigen 125 (CA-125) has long been used, but it has limited specificity, as it is elevated in many benign conditions including endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic inflammatory disease, and menstruation, and in premenopausal women in general. Its sensitivity is also limited in early stage disease and in certain histologic subtypes such as mucinous tumors. To improve discrimination, multivariable approaches have been developed. The risk of malignancy index (RMI) combines ultrasound score, menopausal status, and CA-125 level, and is widely used, particularly in the United Kingdom. Its performance varies across populations and depends on how ultrasound scoring is applied. Human epididymis protein 4 (HE4) is a more recently characterized biomarker that is overexpressed in epithelial ovarian carcinomas, particularly serous and endometrioid types, and is rarely elevated in common benign gynecologic conditions such as endometriosis. HE4 has been reported to show higher specificity than CA-125, especially in premenopausal women. The risk of ovarian malignancy algorithm (ROMA) combines HE4, CA-125, and menopausal status in a logistic regression equation to classify women as being at high or low risk of epithelial ovarian cancer, and has been cleared by regulatory authorities for use in women with a pelvic mass. Studies comparing ROMA with RMI have produced mixed results, with some showing superior sensitivity for ROMA and others showing comparable performance, and the findings differ by menopausal status, histologic type, and study population. Most validation studies of these tools were conducted in Western populations. Biomarker levels, the distribution of histologic subtypes, and the prevalence of benign conditions such as endometriosis may differ in Asian women, and HE4 levels are influenced by factors including age, renal function, and smoking. Data from prospective multicenter studies in Asia are comparatively limited, and it is uncertain whether algorithms developed elsewhere perform optimally in these populations. Notably, ROMA does not incorporate imaging findings, whereas RMI includes only a crude ultrasound score. Because ultrasound and serum markers capture different aspects of tumor biology, it is plausible that combining HE4 with ultrasound features and menopausal status would yield a more discriminating model than either approach alone. A model that integrates these readily available variables could be implemented in routine clinical settings without sophisticated additional testing. Furthermore, a score that stratifies women into several graded risk categories, rather than a single dichotomous cutoff, may better support clinical decisions, for instance by identifying women who can safely be managed locally and those who should be referred for specialist surgery. The purpose of this study was therefore to develop a risk prediction score for distinguishing benign from malignant pelvic masses using CA-125, HE4, ultrasound findings, and menopausal status in a prospective multicenter cohort of women from six Asian countries who were scheduled for surgery. We compared the performance of models containing CA-125 alone, CA-125 combined with HE4, and HE4 combined with menopausal status and ultrasound findings, applied bootstrap validation to assess the stability of the final model, and compared its diagnostic performance with that of ROMA and RMI. This prospective, multicenter observational study was conducted at six centers in six Asian countries. The study was approved by the institutional review board or ethics committee at each participating site and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice guidelines. All participants provided written informed consent before enrollment. Study population Women aged 18 years or older were eligible if they had a pelvic mass detected by imaging (ultrasound, computed tomography, or magnetic resonance imaging) and were scheduled to undergo surgery for the mass. Exclusion criteria were pregnancy, a prior diagnosis of malignancy within the preceding five years, current or previous chemotherapy, and inability to provide informed consent. Women with insufficient serum samples or without a final histopathological diagnosis were also excluded from analysis. Menopausal status was recorded at enrollment; women were classified as postmenopausal if they had experienced at least 12 months of amenorrhea not attributable to other causes, had undergone bilateral oophorectomy, or were older than 50 years after hysterectomy without oophorectomy. Sample collection and biomarker assays Blood samples were collected before surgery. Serum was separated by centrifugation, aliquoted, and stored at −70 °C to −80 °C until analysis. Freeze-thaw cycles were avoided. Serum CA-125 and HE4 concentrations were measured using automated chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassays (ARCHITECT, Abbott Diagnostics) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Assays were performed by laboratory personnel blinded to clinical, imaging, and pathological findings. Quality control materials were run at the beginning of each batch to ensure assay performance. Ultrasound evaluation Transabdominal or transvaginal ultrasound was performed before surgery by experienced examiners at each center according to local practice. The following findings were recorded using a standardized case report form: multilocular cyst, solid areas, bilateral lesions, presence of ascites, and intra-abdominal metastases. Each finding was scored as present (1) or absent (0). Following the approach used for the risk of malignancy index (RMI), the ultrasound score (U) was defined as 0 for no findings, 1 for one finding, and 3 for two or more findings. Patients without documented ultrasound findings were excluded from the models involving ultrasound but were retained for biomarker-only analyses. Reference standard The reference standard was the final histopathological diagnosis of the surgical specimen, established by the local pathologist at each center according to World Health Organization criteria. Tumors were classified as benign, borderline, or malignant. Epithelial ovarian cancer, including fallopian tube and primary peritoneal cancers, was grouped with other primary ovarian malignancies for the primary analysis. Pathologists were blinded to biomarker results. Comparator algorithms The RMI was calculated as U × M × CA-125 (U/mL), where M was 1 for premenopausal and 3 for postmenopausal women, and a cutoff of 200 was used. The risk of ovarian malignancy algorithm (ROMA) was calculated from HE4 and CA-125 using menopause-specific formulas. For premenopausal women, the predictive index (PI) was −12.0 + 2.38 × ln(HE4) + 0.0626 × ln(CA-125). For postmenopausal women, PI was −8.09 + 1.04 × ln(HE4) + 0.732 × ln(CA-125). ROMA (%) was calculated as exp(PI) / [1 + exp(PI)] × 100. Previously recommended cutoffs for high-risk classification were applied: 7.4% for premenopausal and 25.3% for postmenopausal women. Statistical analysis Descriptive statistics are presented as medians with ranges or interquartile ranges for continuous variables and as counts and percentages for categorical variables. Differences between benign and malignant groups were evaluated with the Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables and the chi-square or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables. CA-125 and HE4 values were log-transformed to approximate normality before modeling. Univariable logistic regression was first used to identify factors associated with malignancy. Variables with a P-value below 0.10 were entered into multivariable logistic regression models using stepwise selection. Three models were developed: (1) CA-125 alone, (2) CA-125 and HE4, and (3) HE4, menopausal status, and ultrasound findings. Model discrimination was assessed with the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) with 95% confidence intervals, and AUCs were compared using the DeLong method. Calibration was evaluated with the Hosmer-Lemeshow test. The regression coefficients of the final model were used to construct a risk prediction score. Predicted probabilities were categorized into risk groups (very low, low, medium-low, medium, and high) on the basis of the observed prevalence of malignancy in each stratum, with the aim of providing clinically interpretable categories. Statistical spoken dialogue systems have received considerable attention in recent years because they promise to reduce the manual effort of system design while improving robustness to speech recognition errors and other sources of uncertainty. Modelling dialogue as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) allows the system to maintain a belief over user goals and to optimize its behaviour through reinforcement learning (RL). In this framework the dialogue policy, which maps belief states to system actions, is learned from interaction with real or simulated users, guided by a reward signal. The reward function is therefore the central means by which the system designer specifies what constitutes good behaviour. In task-oriented dialogue, the reward typically combines several components. The most common are a large positive reward for dialogue success and a small penalty for each dialogue turn, which encourages short dialogues. Other components are possible, such as penalties for confirming too often, rewards for user satisfaction estimates, or costs for particular system actions. These components frequently conflict. A system that asks many confirmation questions is more likely to succeed but produces longer and more tedious dialogues, whereas a system that terminates quickly may be efficient but fail more often. How the components are weighted determines the trade-off the learned policy will make. In practice, the weights are usually set by hand and rarely questioned. A typical choice is a success reward of 20 and a turn penalty of -1, which has been adopted in many studies largely by convention. There is, however, no guarantee that this choice is appropriate for a given domain or application. Domains differ in complexity, in the number of slots and values, in the level of noise, and in what users tolerate. A weighting that works well for a small restaurant-search domain may be a poor choice for a larger domain in which reaching success requires more turns. Moreover, the designer may have preferences about the final system's performance, such as a minimum success rate, that are only indirectly related to the weights. Finding good weights thus becomes a search problem in its own right. A straightforward approach is to train a separate policy for each candidate weighting and compare the results. This is very expensive. Each policy requires thousands of training dialogues, and the number of candidate weightings grows quickly as components are added. When training involves human users, for example via crowdsourcing, this cost is prohibitive. Even with simulated users, the repeated training makes systematic exploration of reward weights unattractive. As a consequence, the reward weighting has remained one of the least examined design decisions in statistical dialogue systems. In this work we propose a structured method for finding a good balance between reward components. Our central idea is to treat dialogue policy learning as a multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) problem. Instead of collapsing the reward components into a single scalar before training, MORL maintains a vector-valued reward and learns a set of policies, or a value function that is a function of the weighting, that covers many possible trade-offs simultaneously. Once such a solution has been learned, the policy that is optimal for any particular weighting can be obtained without training from scratch. This allows us to evaluate many candidate weightings at a small fraction of the cost of independent training runs, and thus to search for the weighting that yields the most desirable system behaviour. We use this approach to reduce the number of training dialogues needed to explore the weight space significantly. Training is performed once, with the data efficiently shared across weightings, and the search over weights then proceeds by evaluating the resulting policies. The designer can specify an objective for the search, for instance maximizing the success rate subject to a constraint on dialogue length, or maximizing a combined quality measure, and the method returns the weighting that best satisfies it. This makes the choice of reward weights explicit, reproducible and tied to a measurable criterion rather than to convention. We apply the proposed method to six domains of differing size and complexity, and compare the optimized weights and the resulting policies against a default baseline weighting commonly used in the literature. This lets us investigate whether the default is adequate across domains and how much is gained by tuning. We also examine how the optimal weights vary with domain characteristics, which provides insight into how reward design depends on the task. The contributions of this paper are as follows. First, we formulate the selection of reward component weights for dialogue policy optimization as a search problem and propose a structured procedure for solving it. Second, we show how multi-objective reinforcement learning makes this search feasible by greatly reducing the number of required training dialogues. Third, we present an empirical study in six domains, comparing optimized weights to a default baseline and analysing how the best weighting differs among domains. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on reward design and multi-objective reinforcement learning. Section 3 introduces the background on POMDP-based dialogue management. Section 4 describes the proposed method, Section 5 presents the experiments and results, and Section 6 concludes. We consider dialogue policy optimization as a Markov decision process in which, at every turn t, the policy maps a belief state bt to a system action at. The turn-level reward is a vector rt = (rt^1, ..., rt^K) of K components. In this work we use two components: a success component, which gives 1 at the end of a dialogue if it was successful and 0 otherwise, and a length component, which gives −1 for each turn. The scalar reward used in conventional training is the weighted sum rt = w^T rt, with w = (w1, ..., wK). Because the success reward is defined only at the end of the dialogue, we fix its weight to 1 and vary only the turn penalty weight w2 = −λ, with λ ≥ 0. The default baseline corresponds to a success reward of 20 and a turn penalty of −1, i.e., λ = 1/20 after normalization. The goal is to find the λ that yields the best-balanced policy for a given domain. Reward-weight search A naive approach would train a separate policy for each candidate weight vector and evaluate each of them. This is expensive, since each policy requires thousands of dialogues. We therefore adopt multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL), which learns a set of policies covering many weightings in a single training run, so the training data is shared across candidate weights. Multi-objective policy learning We use a multi-objective variant of Q-learning in which the value function is vector-valued: Q(b, a) = E[Σt γ^t rt | b0 = b, a0 = a] ∈ R^K. For any fixed weight vector w, the scalarized value is Qw(b, a) = w^T Q(b, a). Following the idea of linear scalarization with a convex coverage set, we maintain the vector-valued function approximator and, at decision time, act greedily with respect to Qw, i.e., at = argmaxa w^T Q(bt, a). Thus one trained model yields a policy for any w without retraining. Because belief states are continuous, we use a Gaussian process (GP) approximation as in GP-SARSA. We model each reward component with its own GP sharing the same kernel over belief-action pairs. The kernel is the sum of a belief kernel (a Gaussian kernel) and a discrete-action kernel (delta). Using the linearity of the GP posterior, the posterior mean of the weighted return is the weighted sum of the component posterior means, which allows exact scalarization at action-selection time. For exploration during training, we sample a weight vector w from a distribution over the admissible range of λ at the start of each dialogue and follow an ε-greedy policy with respect to Qw. Because the return vector is observed regardless of the sampled w, every dialogue provides training information for all weightings. This is off-policy with respect to weights, and we correct for it by using the vector-valued update only with the greedy successor action under the same w within the dialogue, keeping w constant throughout the dialogue. Training continues for a fixed budget of dialogues. Evaluation of candidate weights After training, we extract a policy πλ for each λ in a grid, e.g., λ ∈ {0, 0.01, ..., 0.2}. Each policy is evaluated with a simulated user over N test dialogues, yielding its average success rate S(λ) and average dialogue length L(λ). These pairs trace an empirical Pareto front between success and length. The front shows the trade-off explicitly: low turn penalties produce longer, more successful dialogues, while high penalties produce short but less successful ones. To select a single weighting we need a criterion that is independent of the weighting used in training, since otherwise the evaluation would favor the policy trained for that specific weighting. We therefore define a target utility U(S, L) = S·R − L, with R being a fixed success reward, chosen to reflect the desired operating point of the system. In practice, we select the λ whose policy maximizes this utility on a held-out set of dialogues. Alternatively, a minimum success-rate constraint can be imposed (e.g., S ≥ 0.9), and the λ with the shortest average length is chosen among the feasible ones. We report results under the constraint-based criterion. Experimental setup We apply the method to six domains from a spoken dialogue system framework: information-seeking tasks for finding restaurants, hotels, laptops, TVs, and similar entities, which differ in the number of slots and database sizes and hence in complexity. For each domain we train one MORL model for 5,000 dialogues. The dialogue state tracker is a rule-based belief tracker, and the dialogue manager's action set comprises the standard summary actions (e.g., request, confirm, inform, select, bye). The user is an agenda-based simulator with a semantic error rate of 15%, producing noisy semantic inputs through an error model. A dialogue is successful if the system offers an entity matching the user's constraints and provides all requested information. As a comparison we train baseline policies with the default fixed weighting using standard GP-SARSA on the same number of dialogues and the same settings. To measure the savings in training data, we additionally train single-objective policies for each λ in the grid and compare them with the MORL-derived policies for the same weights at several training budgets. Each experiment is repeated for multiple random seeds, and we report mean success rate, mean length, and the utility together with 95% confidence intervals. Final policies are tested on 1,000 dialogues per seed and weighting. Differences between the optimized and baseline weights are assessed with a two-sided t-test. We first examine whether multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) can replace repeated single-objective training, and then report the optimized weights found for each domain and how they compare with the default baseline. Efficiency of the MORL-based search. We compared the proposed approach with a conventional grid search in which a separate policy is trained from scratch for every candidate weighting. Both approaches used the same simulated user and the same number of training dialogues per policy. With MORL, a single training run yields a policy set that covers the entire range of weightings, so each candidate weighting can be evaluated without retraining. In our experiments the MORL approach reached a stable estimate of the best weighting after roughly 4,000 training dialogues. The grid search needed several times more dialogues, because every point on the grid required its own training run. The policies retrieved from the MORL model for a given weighting performed close to policies trained directly for that weighting. The gap in average return was small, within the confidence intervals after about 3,000 dialogues, and it shrank further with more training data. This indicates that sharing experience across weightings does not noticeably degrade policy quality, while the number of required dialogues falls substantially. The rapid development of information and communication technologies has changed the conditions in which modern education operates. Universities and schools are expected to prepare graduates who can work with large volumes of information, collaborate in digital environments and keep learning throughout life. In this context, cloud technologies are among the most promising directions for modernizing the educational process. They give users access to software, storage and computing resources through the Internet, without installing programs on a local computer or maintaining expensive hardware. For education, this means that teaching materials, tools for creating and processing data, and platforms for communication and assessment can be reached from any device, at any time and from any place. Interest in cloud technologies in education is supported by national and international strategies for digitalizing society. Documents on the development of the information society, the modernization of higher education and the creation of a common European educational space all stress the need for open, flexible and accessible learning environments. Cloud services meet many of these requirements. They are usually inexpensive or free, they are updated automatically, they allow joint work on one document or project, and they scale easily as the number of users grows. They also support the shift from a reproductive model of teaching to one that stresses independent inquiry, project work and the development of students' digital competence. Geography is a particularly suitable subject for these technologies. It studies natural and social phenomena at different spatial scales, and it relies on maps, statistical data, satellite images, graphs, diagrams and other visual material. Students must learn to read and build spatial models, analyze the dynamics of demographic and economic processes, compare territories and see how global and local phenomena are connected. Traditional teaching tools such as printed atlases, wall maps and textbooks are often not enough to show the changing character of these processes or to let students work actively with data. Interactive maps, online visualization of statistics, augmented reality, electronic quizzes and graphic editors can fill this gap. They make abstract material concrete, increase motivation and allow students to move from passive reception of information to its active investigation. Researchers have studied the use of cloud technologies in education from several angles. Work on cloud-oriented learning environments has covered their architecture, the models of their deployment and the ways they change the roles of teacher and student. Other studies concern general-purpose office and communication suites, learning management systems and services for collaborative work. Geography education has its own literature on geographic information systems, virtual globes and web mapping. However, specialized online services that address concrete tasks of geographical education remain much less systematized. Teachers often learn about such services by chance, lack information on their capabilities and limitations, and have few methodological recommendations for including them in the curriculum. As a result, many useful tools are used rarely or without a clear didactic purpose. The problem is made sharper by the diversity of available products. Services differ in functionality, language support, cost, technical requirements, the quality of their content and the degree of control the teacher has over the learning process. Some, such as Gapminder and the statistical resources of the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (DESA), provide data and visualizations for analyzing global development. Others, such as Settera Online and Click-that-hood, serve to learn and test knowledge of political and physical maps or of urban territory. Some tools, such as HP Reveal, add augmented reality to learning materials, while MOZAIK education offers interactive three-dimensional content. Graphic editors such as Canva and Paint Instant help students and teachers to create infographics, posters and illustrations. Choosing among them requires a clear understanding of their advantages and disadvantages from economic, technical, technological and didactic points of view. The aim of this article is to substantiate the feasibility of using cloud technologies in teaching geography to students of higher school and to present a selection of online services that can contribute to the effective acquisition of geographical knowledge. To reach this aim, we address the following tasks: to clarify the essence and educational potential of cloud technologies; to describe the functional capabilities of the selected services; to generalize their advantages and disadvantages according to economic, technical, technological and didactic criteria; and to illustrate, with visual examples, how they can be applied in learning activities. The novelty of the study lies in the systematic review of a group of specialized, mostly freely available services within a single framework of analysis oriented to the needs of geographical education. The practical value lies in the possibility of using the results when planning lectures, practical classes and independent work, and when developing electronic courses. In the longer term, the services considered may become part of virtual information and educational environments that are linked first into a common national and then a global educational space, which would widen access to quality geographical education and support the integration of educational systems. The study was designed as an analytical and descriptive review of cloud-based services that can support geography teaching in higher education. It combined a theoretical analysis of the pedagogical literature with a practical evaluation of selected online tools. The work proceeded in four stages: identification of candidate services, formulation of evaluation criteria, hands-on testing, and generalization of the results. Selection of services. At the first stage, we searched for cloud technologies applicable to teaching geography. We used academic databases (Google Scholar, Scopus, Web of Science, and national electronic libraries), the catalogues of educational applications, and the professional recommendations of geography teachers and university lecturers. Search terms included "cloud technologies in education," "online services for geography teaching," "interactive maps for learning," "data visualization in education," and "augmented reality in education," together with their equivalents in the national language. We included services that met the following conditions: (1) they run in a web browser or as a mobile application, without complex local installation; (2) a free version or a free educational plan is available; (3) their functions relate directly to the content of geographical disciplines, such as statistical analysis, cartography, toponymy, regional studies, and visualization; (4) they were stable and regularly updated at the time of the study. Services that required costly licenses, or that were designed exclusively for professional GIS work, were excluded. Ten services were selected: Gapminder, DESA (the United Nations statistical resources), two further online resources for working with maps and geographic data, HP Reveal, MOZAIK education, Settera Online, Click-that-hood, Canva, and Paint Instant. Evaluation criteria. At the second stage, we developed a set of criteria grouped into four categories. 1. Economic: cost of use, availability of a free version, and absence of hidden expenses for the institution or the student. 2. Technical: hardware and software requirements, platform independence, need for registration, interface language, stability under limited internet bandwidth, and compatibility with mobile devices. 3. Technological: the ability to create, store, and export content, collaboration and sharing options, integration with other platforms and learning management systems, and the possibility of embedding results into presentations or websites. 4. Didactic: correspondence to the curriculum content, the potential for visualization and interactivity, support for independent and group work, opportunities for self-assessment and knowledge control, and the capacity to develop spatial thinking, analytical skills, and digital competence. Each service was described according to these categories, and its advantages and limitations were recorded in a comparative table. Practical testing. At the third stage, each service was tested by the authors in the role of both instructor and student. Testing was conducted on desktop computers and on mobile devices running different operating systems, using several popular browsers. For each tool, we modelled typical learning tasks: - analyzing demographic and socio-economic indicators over time and comparing countries with Gapminder and the DESA databases; - working with thematic maps and geographic data using the corresponding online map resources; - creating augmented-reality content for a lecture, a field trip, or a laboratory class with HP Reveal; - using MOZAIK education for interactive multimedia learning materials; - memorizing toponyms and the political map through Settera Online and Click-that-hood; - designing infographics, posters, and presentations with Canva; - producing simple sketches, schemes, and map annotations with Paint Instant. During testing we documented the sequence of operations, the time required to master the tool, difficulties encountered, and the quality of the final product. Screenshots were captured to provide visual examples of application and are included in the article as illustrations. Analytical methods. The theoretical part of the research used analysis and synthesis of scientific sources on the implementation of cloud computing in education, comparison of the characteristics of the services, classification of the tools by their predominant didactic function (data visualization, cartographic training, augmented reality, content creation, and knowledge testing), and generalization of the results to formulate conclusions. A systematic approach was applied to consider the services as elements of a potential virtual information and educational environment. Qualitative content analysis was used to interpret the functionality and user documentation of each service. Because the study was exploratory and based on expert evaluation, no statistical hypothesis testing was undertaken, and the assessments were formulated descriptively rather than as numerical scores. Generalization and validation. At the final stage, the results of the individual evaluations were compared and discussed by the authors to reduce subjectivity. Discrepancies were resolved by repeated testing of the problematic functions. The conclusions on advantages and disadvantages were then summarized by criterion category, and recommendations were made for use of the services in lectures, practical classes, independent work, and distance learning. The prospects for combining these tools into integrated virtual educational environments, which could be linked at national and later global levels, were considered on the basis of their interoperability and the openness of their formats. Limitations. The evaluation reflects the state of the services at the time of the study. Cloud products change quickly in features, pricing policy, and availability, so some characteristics may become outdated. The assessment was carried out by the authors and has not yet been supported by a large-scale pedagogical experiment with students, which is planned as a subsequent stage of research. The analysis of cloud services for teaching geography showed that the selected tools can be grouped by their dominant didactic function: data visualization and statistical analysis (Gapminder, DESA), augmented reality and interactive content (HP Reveal, MOZAIK education), knowledge testing and consolidation (Settera Online, Click-that-hood), and creation of graphic and presentation materials (Canva, Paint Instant). The two services whose names are given as URLs in the abstract were also assessed, as mapping and content-creation resources. Below we present the findings for each group. Data visualization and statistical analysis. Gapminder proved to be the most useful service for studying the socio-economic geography of the world. It allows students to build dynamic bubble charts that show changes in indicators such as life expectancy, income per capita, fertility, and CO2 emissions across countries over more than two centuries. In practical classes, students were able to identify regional disparities, trace demographic transitions, and formulate hypotheses about the causes of differences in development. The main didactic advantages are clarity, the ability to compare many countries simultaneously, and the presence of ready-made teaching presentations. Its limitations include the English-language interface, a restricted set of indicators, and the fact that the most recent data for some countries may be missing. The statistical databases of the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (DESA) offer more extensive and authoritative data on population, migration, urbanization, and sustainable development. They are well suited to independent research assignments, such as calculating population growth rates or comparing urbanization levels in different regions. However, working with them requires developed skills in handling tables and interpreting indicators, so first-year students often needed additional guidance from the instructor. Augmented reality and interactive content. HP Reveal (formerly Aurasma) makes it possible to attach multimedia objects (video, 3D models, animations) to printed maps, textbook illustrations, or posters.
