Mammalian oocyte developmental competence is acquired progressively during folliculogenesis and the final stages of growth, and it depends on coordinated nuclear and cytoplasmic maturation [1,2]. Cytoplasmic maturation includes the accumulation and storage of maternal RNAs, proteins and organelles. These are needed to sustain meiotic progression, fertilization, and the first embryonic divisions, which occur before embryonic genome activation (EGA) takes over [3]. Because transcription in the fully grown oocyte is largely silent, early development relies almost entirely on maternal factors. Defects in their storage, stability or timely utilization can therefore have consequences long after the oocyte itself has completed meiosis. Chromatin configuration and developmental competence In the mouse, fully grown antral oocytes can be separated into two classes according to the organization of their chromatin. Oocytes with a ring of condensed chromatin around the nucleolus are termed SN (Surrounded Nucleolus). Those lacking such a ring are termed NSN (Not Surrounded Nucleolus) [4,5]. SN oocytes are transcriptionally quiescent and can complete meiotic maturation, be fertilized, and develop to term. NSN oocytes are still transcriptionally active. They can resume meiosis and be fertilized, but the resulting embryos arrest at the 2-cell stage [5,6]. Because this arrest coincides with minor EGA, it has been attributed to defects in maternal programs required for genome activation, chromatin remodelling and epigenetic reprogramming [7,8]. Nuclear transfer experiments, in which the NSN germinal vesicle was placed in SN cytoplasm and vice versa, indicated that the cytoplasm is a major determinant of the block, which points to a cytoplasmic deficiency in NSN oocytes [9]. However, the cytoplasmic factors responsible have not been identified conclusively. Cytoplasmic lattices Cytoplasmic lattices (CPLs) are fibrillar, filamentous structures first described by electron microscopy in oocytes and preimplantation embryos of several mammalian species, including mouse, hamster, rhesus monkey and human [10,11]. Their abundance in oocytes and early embryos, and their disappearance as development proceeds, long suggested a storage function. Evidence for this was provided by the identification of components of the subcortical maternal complex (SCMC), notably PADI6, as essential constituents of CPLs. Female mice lacking Padi6 are infertile because their embryos arrest at the 2-cell stage, and CPLs are absent from their oocytes [12,13]. Mutations in human SCMC genes and in PADI6 are associated with embryonic arrest, recurrent molar pregnancy and imprinting disorders [14,15]. More recent work has shown that CPLs store ribosomes, which are made available to the oocyte and early embryo in a regulated fashion, and are thus a platform for translational competence [16]. They also contain proteins involved in other processes, including regulators of microtubule dynamics and spindle assembly, and metabolic and epigenetic factors [16,17]. Taken together, these observations indicate that CPLs are multifunctional assemblies that support oocyte maturation and the oocyte-to-embryo transition. CPLs are also dynamic. In the mouse, they undergo marked reorganization at key stages of oocyte maturation, and the transition from the germinal vesicle to the metaphase II stage is accompanied by changes in their distribution and abundance [18]. Ultrastructural analysis of SN and NSN oocytes showed that CPLs are abundant in the cytoplasm of SN oocytes but scarce in NSN oocytes [19]. This difference was interpreted as a possible explanation for the NSN 2-cell arrest, by analogy with the Padi6-null phenotype, in which an absence of CPLs coincides with arrest at the same stage. The resulting hypothesis is that insufficient CPLs in NSN oocytes limit the supply of ribosomes and other maternal factors, and thereby compromise development beyond the 2-cell stage. Rationale and aims This hypothesis rests on observations made in oocytes, whereas the arrest becomes manifest in the embryo. CPLs are not static, and their abundance in the oocyte does not necessarily predict their presence in the embryo. NSN oocytes may assemble or remodel CPLs after meiotic resumption, activation or fertilization. In addition, the sperm contributes factors that could influence cytoplasmic organization, so the mode of embryo production could be a confounding variable. No ultrastructural data have been reported on CPLs in 2-cell embryos derived from SN and NSN oocytes. Thus, whether a CPL deficit actually persists in the arrested embryos, and so could account for the block, remains untested. We therefore examined CPLs by transmission electron microscopy in 2-cell mouse embryos derived from SN and NSN oocytes. To separate effects of the oocyte from those of the sperm, embryos were generated by two independent approaches, intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) and parthenogenetic activation. Comparing the presence, abundance and distribution of CPLs between embryos of different origin allowed us to determine whether CPL depletion is a plausible cause of 2-cell arrest in NSN-derived embryos. Our results bear on the relationship between CPLs and developmental competence, and on the search for the factors responsible for the NSN phenotype. They may also inform the use of oocyte morphological and ultrastructural features as indicators of developmental potential in assisted reproduction. Animals and ethics Female B6C3F1 mice (6–8 weeks old) were used as oocyte donors, and male mice of the same strain (10–12 weeks old) as sperm donors. Animals were housed under controlled temperature (22 ± 2 °C), a 12 h light/dark cycle, and had ad libitum access to food and water. All procedures were carried out in accordance with national and institutional guidelines for animal welfare and were approved by the relevant ethics committee. Oocyte collection and classification Mice were primed with 5 IU pregnant mare serum gonadotropin (PMSG), and ovaries were collected 46–48 h later. Fully grown germinal vesicle (GV) oocytes were released from antral follicles by puncturing with a needle in M2 medium (Sigma-Aldrich) supplemented with 0.2 mM 3-isobutyl-1-methylxanthine (IBMX) to prevent meiotic resumption. Cumulus cells were removed by repeated gentle pipetting through a narrow-bore glass pipette. Denuded oocytes were stained with Hoechst 33342 (1 µg/ml, 10 min) and classified under epifluorescence according to chromatin configuration [1,2]. Oocytes with a ring of condensed chromatin around the nucleolus were classified as SN (Surrounded Nucleolus), and those with decondensed chromatin not enclosing the nucleolus as NSN (Not Surrounded Nucleolus). Oocytes were exposed to UV light for the minimum time necessary, and only oocytes with an intact zona pellucida and homogeneous cytoplasm were retained. SN and NSN oocytes were handled separately throughout. In vitro maturation Classified oocytes were washed free of IBMX and cultured in groups of 20–30 in 50 µl drops of MEM-alpha supplemented with 5% fetal bovine serum, under mineral oil, at 37 °C in 5% CO₂ in air. After 16–17 h, oocytes were examined for extrusion of the first polar body, and only metaphase II (MII) oocytes were used for subsequent procedures. Maturation rates were recorded for each group. Production of 2-cell embryos Intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI). Spermatozoa were collected from the cauda epididymis, allowed to disperse in HEPES-buffered medium containing 10% polyvinylpyrrolidone, and the heads separated from tails by applying piezo pulses. ICSI was performed on MII oocytes in M2 medium at room temperature using a piezo-driven micromanipulator (Prime Tech) mounted on an inverted microscope. Injected oocytes were left for 10 min at room temperature, then washed and cultured in KSOM medium (37 °C, 5% CO₂). Fertilization was assessed by the presence of two pronuclei 6–8 h post-injection. Parthenogenetic activation. MII oocytes were activated in Ca²⁺-free CZB medium containing 10 mM SrCl₂ and 5 µg/ml cytochalasin B for 2.5 h, to prevent extrusion of the second polar body. Oocytes were then washed and cultured in KSOM. Activation was verified by pronucleus formation. Embryos were cultured to the 2-cell stage (approximately 24 h after ICSI or activation) and scored for cleavage. Only morphologically normal 2-cell embryos with two evenly sized blastomeres were collected for ultrastructural analysis. A subset of embryos from each group was left in culture for up to 96 h to confirm developmental arrest at the 2-cell stage in NSN-derived embryos and progression in SN-derived embryos. Transmission electron microscopy Embryos were fixed in 2.5% glutaraldehyde in 0.1 M cacodylate buffer (pH 7.3) for at least 2 h at 4 °C and stored in the same buffer until processing. Samples were post-fixed in 1% osmium tetroxide in the same buffer for 1 h, rinsed, and embedded in a small drop of 2% agar to facilitate handling. They were dehydrated through a graded ethanol series, passed through propylene oxide, and embedded in epoxy resin (Epon-Araldite), which was polymerized at 60 °C for 48 h. Semi-thin sections (1 µm) were stained with toluidine blue to locate the embryos. Ultrathin sections (60–70 nm) were cut with a diamond knife on an ultramicrotome, collected on copper grids, and contrasted with uranyl acetate and lead citrate. Sections were examined with a transmission electron microscope operated at 80 kV, and images were acquired with a digital camera at magnifications from 3,000× to 40,000×. Identification and quantification of cytoplasmic lattices Cytoplasmic lattices were identified by their established ultrastructural appearance: dense, fibrillar, interconnected arrays associated with ribosomes and frequently with mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum [3,4]. For each embryo, sections were taken at several levels, separated by at least 5 µm, to avoid sampling the same structure twice. Both blastomeres were examined whenever possible. Micrographs were taken of randomly selected cytoplasmic areas, excluding the nuclear region. Lattice abundance was evaluated as the number of lattice profiles per unit of cytoplasmic area (measured in ImageJ) and as the percentage of cytoplasmic area occupied by lattices. In addition, the presence or absence of lattices was recorded for each embryo. Analyses were performed by two independent observers blinded to the origin of the samples (SN or NSN; ICSI or parthenogenesis). Other organelles (mitochondria, vesicles, endoplasmic reticulum) were examined to evaluate general ultrastructural integrity. Experimental design and statistical analysis At least three independent experiments were performed for each experimental group (SN-ICSI, NSN-ICSI, SN-parthenotes, NSN-parthenotes), with a minimum of several embryos per group processed for TEM. The embryo was considered the experimental unit. Developmental rates were compared with the chi-square or Fisher's exact test. Quantitative lattice data were tested for normality (Shapiro–Wilk) and compared between groups with the Student's t-test or the Mann–Whitney U test, as appropriate, or by two-way ANOVA with oocyte type and production method as factors. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were carried out with GraphPad Prism. Ultrastructural identification of cytoplasmic lattices in 2-cell embryos Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) of 2-cell embryos showed that cytoplasmic lattices (CPLs) can be reliably identified by their established features [1,2]. These were bundles of parallel, fibrous filaments of electron-dense material, often cut longitudinally or in cross-section, forming a regular mesh-like pattern. They were frequently associated with ribosome-like particles and lay in close proximity to mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum cisternae and lipid droplets. Their characteristic morphology made them easy to distinguish from the surrounding granular cytoplasm, from microtubules, and from other fibrillar structures. In total, 2-cell embryos derived from SN and NSN oocytes were examined, with at least two blastomeres per embryo sectioned wherever possible, and CPLs were scored by morphology and localization. CPLs are present in 2-cell embryos derived from SN oocytes In embryos derived from SN oocytes and produced by intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI), CPLs were consistently detected in the cytoplasm of both blastomeres. They occurred as individual bundles or small clusters scattered throughout the cytoplasm, with no obvious polarization relative to the nucleus or the cell cortex. Compared with the abundance reported in mature SN oocytes [1,3], the lattices appeared less extensive, consistent with a progressive reduction of these structures after fertilization and during early cleavage [2,4]. Their ultrastructure, however, was indistinguishable from that described in oocytes. Similarly, parthenogenetically activated SN-derived embryos contained CPLs of comparable morphology and distribution, indicating that the presence of lattices at this stage does not depend on sperm entry or on the paternal genome. CPLs are also present in 2-cell embryos derived from NSN oocytes Contrary to the expectation that the paucity of CPLs in NSN oocytes [3] would persist after activation, lattices were clearly detected in 2-cell embryos derived from NSN oocytes. Babesia spp. are tick-borne apicomplexan protozoa that infect the erythrocytes of a wide range of vertebrate hosts. They are considered the second most common blood-borne parasites of mammals after trypanosomes [1, 2]. Babesiosis is of major veterinary importance because infection can cause fever, hemolytic anemia, hemoglobinuria, and death, and chronically infected animals suffer reduced productivity. Economic losses in cattle alone are estimated in the billions of US dollars annually, and the burden falls especially on tropical and subtropical regions where tick vectors are abundant [3, 4]. Some species also infect humans, notably B. microti, B. divergens, B. duncani, and B. venatorum, so the genus has public health relevance as well [5]. Diversity and host associations of Babesia The genus comprises more than 100 described species, and new lineages continue to be identified. Traditionally, species were distinguished by morphology, host range, and vector specificity. These criteria are now known to be unreliable: the small and large forms of piroplasms overlap in size, many species are morphologically indistinguishable, and host specificity is not absolute [6]. Molecular phylogenetics based on the 18S rRNA gene has resolved Babesia into several clades, including Babesia sensu stricto, the Babesia microti group, and the Theileria/Cytauxzoon groups, and has demonstrated that some taxa historically assigned to Babesia are phylogenetically distinct [7, 8]. In livestock, the principal agents are B. bovis, B. bigemina, and B. divergens in cattle, B. ovis and B. motasi in small ruminants, and B. caballi (together with the related Theileria equi) in equids. In dogs, B. canis, B. vogeli, B. rossi, and B. gibsoni are the most important [9]. Increasing evidence indicates that animals may harbor species typically associated with other hosts, as well as previously uncharacterized species, but such findings are seldom documented because most diagnostic assays are designed to detect specific pathogens in specific hosts [10]. Limitations of current diagnostics Microscopic examination of Giemsa-stained blood smears remains widely used, but sensitivity is poor in carrier animals with low parasitemia, and species identification is difficult. Serological assays, such as indirect fluorescent antibody tests and ELISA, detect exposure rather than active infection and are limited by cross-reactivity among species and by variable antibody persistence [11]. PCR-based methods offer markedly higher sensitivity and specificity. Many conventional and real-time PCR assays have been described, but the majority are species-specific [12]. Surveying for several pathogens therefore requires multiple reactions, which increases cost, sample consumption, and the chance that unexpected species will be missed. Pan-genus or broad-range assays amplifying conserved regions of the 18S rRNA gene, followed by sequencing or melting-curve analysis, can overcome this limitation. Conventional broad-range PCRs are used frequently, but they require post-amplification handling and are less suited to high-throughput work. Real-time formats using fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) hybridization probes combine the sensitivity of quantitative PCR with the specificity afforded by probe melting temperature, which can discriminate sequence variants within an amplicon [13]. A well-designed FRET-qPCR targeting conserved regions of Babesia could therefore detect diverse species in a single closed-tube reaction while providing preliminary species-level information, and it could flag unusual samples for sequencing. A key challenge is avoiding amplification of closely related apicomplexans that commonly co-occur in the same hosts, such as Theileria, Hepatozoon, and Toxoplasma. Babesiosis in the Caribbean The Caribbean region provides climatic conditions favorable to tick vectors, including Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus, R. annulatus, Dermacentor nitens, and Amblyomma variegatum, which has been established on several islands [14]. Livestock production is important to local economies and food security, yet animals are often kept under extensive systems with limited tick control, and movement of animals among islands is common. Earlier investigations of babesiosis in the region were few, were generally restricted to a single island or a small number of animals, and relied mostly on serology or microscopy [15, 16]. These studies indicated that B. bovis, B. bigemina, and B. caballi are widespread, but the true prevalence and diversity of Babesia in Caribbean livestock remain poorly defined. Little is known regarding infection in small ruminants and donkeys, or the extent to which species typical of other hosts, including canine Babesia, infect livestock in an environment where domestic animals, ticks, and wildlife are in close contact. Objectives The aims of this study were therefore twofold. First, we sought to develop and evaluate a pan-Babesia FRET-qPCR, designed from alignments of 18S rRNA gene sequences of multiple Babesia species, that detects a broad range of Babesia species in a single reaction while excluding closely related protozoa. Second, we applied the assay to DNA extracted from whole blood of cattle, sheep, goats, donkeys, and horses sampled on five Caribbean islands, in order to determine the occurrence of Babesia infections, identify the species present, and detect unexpected or novel species. The resulting data are intended to improve understanding of the epidemiology of babesiosis in the region and to provide a tool for broader surveillance. Primer and probe design Complete and partial 18S rRNA gene sequences of 22 Babesia species were retrieved from GenBank and aligned with the Clustal Multiple Alignment program implemented in BioEdit [1,2]. Sequences of related apicomplexans (Theileria, Hepatozoon, Toxoplasma, Cytauxzoon) and of host species (Bos taurus, Ovis aries, Capra hircus, Equus spp., Canis lupus familiaris) were included to identify regions that were conserved across Babesia but divergent in non-target organisms. Candidate forward and reverse primers and two adjacent hybridization probes for fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) were selected from conserved regions flanking a variable region. Primer properties (melting temperature, secondary structure, primer-dimer formation) were assessed with OligoAnalyzer, and specificity was checked in silico using BLASTn against the GenBank nucleotide database [3]. One probe was labeled at the 3' end with fluorescein and the other at the 5' end with LC Red 640 (or equivalent acceptor dye). Reference DNA and analytical evaluation Reference DNA from B. gibsoni, B. canis, B. vogeli, B. microti, B. bovis and B. divergens was used to assess analytical performance. Non-target DNA from Hepatozoon americanum, Theileria equi, Toxoplasma gondii and uninfected host blood was used to evaluate cross-reactivity. DNA was quantified spectrophotometrically. Analytical sensitivity was estimated from ten-fold serial dilutions of reference DNA tested in triplicate, with the limit of detection defined as the lowest dilution at which all replicates were positive. Repeatability was assessed by testing the same dilutions in replicate within and between runs. Study area and sample collection Whole-blood samples were collected from 752 cattle, sheep, goats, donkeys and horses on five Caribbean islands. Animals were sampled opportunistically on farms and smallholdings, with the permission of owners and in accordance with local veterinary authority regulations. Blood was drawn by jugular or coccygeal venipuncture into EDTA tubes. The species, sex, approximate age and location of each animal were recorded. Samples were kept cooled during transport and stored at −20 °C until DNA extraction. Sampling protocols were reviewed and approved by the relevant institutional animal care committee. DNA extraction Genomic DNA was extracted from 200 µl of whole blood using a commercial spin-column kit (e.g., QIAamp DNA Blood Mini Kit, Qiagen) according to the manufacturer's instructions and eluted in 100 µl of elution buffer. Extraction controls (nuclease-free water) were included in each batch to monitor contamination. DNA was stored at −20 °C. Pan-Babesia FRET-qPCR Amplification was performed in a 20 µl reaction volume containing 2 µl of template DNA, 1× commercial hybridization-probe master mix, 0.5 µM of each primer, 0.2 µM of each FRET probe, and MgCl2 adjusted to a final concentration of 3–4 mM. Reactions were run on a LightCycler real-time instrument (Roche) with an initial denaturation at 95 °C for 10 min, followed by 45 cycles of 95 °C for 10 s, annealing at the optimized temperature for 10 s, and 72 °C for 15 s, with fluorescence acquired in the acceptor channel at the end of each annealing step. A melting-curve analysis followed (95 °C for 30 s, 40 °C for 30 s, then a gradual increase to 85 °C at 0.1 °C/s with continuous acquisition). Because the probes hybridize to species-specific sequences with differing numbers of mismatches, melting temperature (Tm) peaks were used to provide preliminary discrimination among Babesia species. Each run included positive controls (B. bovis or B. gibsoni DNA) and no-template controls. Samples were considered positive if they showed an exponential amplification curve and a melting peak within the range observed for reference species. Samples with atypical Tm values were flagged for sequencing. Conventional PCR and sequencing To confirm species identity, a subset of positive samples, including all with melting peaks that differed from those of reference species, was amplified with the pan-Babesia primers in conventional format, or with established genus-level 18S rRNA primers [4] when longer fragments were needed. Amplicons were separated on 1.5–2% agarose gels stained with ethidium bromide or a safe alternative, and purified with a commercial kit. Purified products were sequenced in both directions by Sanger sequencing using the amplification primers. Chromatograms were inspected, and forward and reverse reads were assembled and edited manually. Consensus sequences were compared with GenBank entries using BLASTn [3]. Species assignment required ≥99% identity to a reference sequence; sequences with lower identity were designated as unknown Babesia spp. and aligned with reference sequences. Phylogenetic relationships were inferred by neighbor-joining or maximum-likelihood analysis in MEGA [5], with 1,000 bootstrap replicates. Data analysis Prevalence was calculated for each host species and island as the proportion of positive animals, with 95% exact binomial (Clopper–Pearson) confidence intervals. Differences in prevalence among host species, islands, sexes and age classes were evaluated with the chi-square or Fisher's exact test as appropriate. Associations between Babesia positivity and host or location variables were further explored by multivariable logistic regression, with results expressed as odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. Analyses were performed in R [6] or equivalent statistical software. Contamination control Pre-PCR and post-PCR procedures were performed in physically separate areas using dedicated pipettes and filter tips. Negative extraction and no-template controls were included in every run, and all were negative. Design and analytical performance of the pan-Babesia FRET-qPCR Alignment of 18S rRNA gene sequences from 22 Babesia species revealed conserved regions flanking a variable segment suitable for genus-level amplification. Primers were placed in the conserved flanks, and two adjacent hybridization probes (donor fluorescein and acceptor LC-Red) were positioned within the intervening region to allow melting curve analysis. Under controlled conditions, the assay amplified DNA of B. gibsoni, B. canis, B. vogeli, B. microti, B. bovis and B. divergens. No amplification or specific melting peaks were obtained from DNA of Hepatozoon americanum, Theileria equi or Toxoplasma gondii, or from uninfected host DNA. Melting temperatures (Tm) differed among species, ranging between approximately 55 °C and 66 °C. Species with identical probe-binding regions could not be distinguished by Tm alone. Tm values were reproducible between runs (standard deviation <0.5 °C), so Tm profiles were used for preliminary grouping of positive samples. Sequencing was then used to assign species identity. Prevalence of Babesia in livestock A total of 752 animals were tested: cattle, sheep, goats, donkeys and horses from five Caribbean islands. Overall, 525 (70%) tested positive. Prevalence varied by host species and island. It was highest in cattle, followed by small ruminants and equids, although positivity was substantial in all host groups. Differences among islands were evident, and on some islands nearly all sampled animals of a given species were positive. Amplification products from a subset of positive samples from each host species and island were sequenced to confirm species identity. Babesia species in cattle The expected bovine parasites B. bovis and B. bigemina accounted for most infections in cattle. Both species were found on several islands, and mixed infections were detected, shown by composite melting curves and confirmed by sequencing of cloned amplicons. In addition, sequences from cattle matched B. vogeli and B. gibsoni, species normally associated with dogs. These were not isolated findings, and several animals on different islands carried them. Sequence identity with the reference sequences was high (≥99% for most amplicons). Some cattle sequences could not be assigned to a described species and are discussed

Artificial neural networks (ANNs) have become the dominant approach to a wide range of cognitive tasks, including image classification, speech recognition, and natural language processing [1,2]. Their success relies on large-scale training and inference workloads that are executed almost exclusively on conventional digital hardware, such as CPUs, GPUs, and dedicated accelerators. These platforms suffer from the von Neumann bottleneck, in which the continual transfer of data between memory and processing units dominates both latency and energy consumption [3]. The problem is compounded by the slowdown of CMOS scaling, which no longer delivers the exponential efficiency gains that sustained earlier generations of computing [4]. As models grow in size and are increasingly deployed at the edge, where power budgets are severely constrained, there is strong motivation to explore alternative hardware that implements neural functions natively and compactly. Neuromorphic hardware and emerging nanodevices A broad research effort has therefore emerged around neuromorphic computing, in which the physical dynamics of devices are used to emulate the building blocks of neural networks [5,6]. Much of this work has focused on synapses, where memristive and resistive memories arranged in crossbar arrays perform multiply-accumulate operations in place, directly exploiting Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws [7,8]. Comparatively less attention has been paid to the compact and efficient realization of neurons, which in most proposals still rely on analog or digital CMOS circuits that occupy substantial area and can offset the gains obtained at the synaptic level [9]. Emerging nanodevices, including spintronic, memristive, and phase-change elements, offer nonlinear and dynamical behaviors that could be harnessed to implement neurons directly in the physical substrate [10,11]. Nano-oscillators as computing elements Among these candidates, nanoscale oscillators, notably spin-torque and spin-Hall nano-oscillators, as well as oscillators based on metal–insulator transitions, are particularly attractive [12,13]. They are compact, with lateral dimensions of tens of nanometers, operate in the gigahertz range, are compatible with CMOS integration, and exhibit strong nonlinearity. Their frequency can be tuned over wide ranges by applied currents or voltages, and they can be synchronized to one another or to external signals through electrical or magnetic coupling [14,15]. These properties have motivated proposals in which information is encoded in the frequency, phase, or amplitude of oscillating signals. Coupled oscillators have been used for associative memory, vowel recognition, and pattern matching, and networks of spin-torque oscillators have demonstrated reservoir computing and spoken digit recognition [16–19]. Oscillatory computing paradigms have also been considered for combinatorial optimization and for convolution-like filtering operations [20,21]. Most of these demonstrations, however, exploit either the temporal dynamics of fixed, randomly coupled oscillator ensembles or the relaxation of the system toward a low-energy state. Fewer works have addressed feedforward, layered networks trained with standard gradient-based methods, which currently constitute the reference for accuracy on classification tasks. Bridging the two perspectives requires a neuron whose input–output relation is well defined, controllable, and compatible with established training procedures, while still being based on the intrinsic physics of oscillators. Synchronization as a neuronal nonlinearity The synchronization of an oscillator to an external signal is a threshold-like phenomenon: when the frequency mismatch lies within a locking range, whose width depends on the coupling strength, the oscillator adopts the frequency of the drive, whereas outside this range it evolves independently [22]. Combined with the frequency tunability of nano-oscillators, this behavior provides a natural source of nonlinearity. In this work, we exploit it by building a neuron from a pair of oscillators whose relative frequencies are set by the weighted sum of the neuron inputs, and whose degree of synchronization determines the output. As we show, this construction yields a response curve that differs qualitatively from the monotonic sigmoid or rectified-linear activation functions commonly employed in ANNs. Notably, the response is non-monotonic, a feature that has practical consequences: a single neuron with such an activation can separate classes that are not linearly separable, so that functions such as XOR, which require at least two layers of conventional neurons, can be realized with a single compact unit [23]. Contributions and organization The objective of this paper is to establish the viability of a neural network built from synchronized pairs of nano-oscillators, from the single-neuron level to the network level, and to assess its robustness to a fundamental non-ideality. Our main contributions are the following. First, we introduce the oscillator-pair neuron and characterize its response curve using a model of coupled oscillators. Second, we show that this neuron naturally implements generic Boolean logic gates, including XOR, without requiring additional hidden layers. Third, we incorporate the measured or modeled response into simulated multilayer networks, train them, and evaluate their performance on two reference classification benchmarks, showing accuracy comparable to that of standard networks with conventional activation functions. Fourth, we examine the influence of oscillator phase noise, which is intrinsic to nanoscale oscillators owing to thermal fluctuations and is known to broaden linewidths and perturb synchronization [24,25], and we quantify how it degrades classification accuracy. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II describes the oscillator model, the neuron design, and its response curve. Section III demonstrates logic-gate operation. Section IV presents the network architecture, training methodology, and classification results. Section V analyzes the impact of phase noise. Finally, Section VI discusses implications for hardware implementation and concludes. Oscillator model and synchronization dynamics Each nano-oscillator is described by the Thiele-like auto-oscillator model of a spin-torque nano-oscillator (STNO) [1,2], reduced to its amplitude and phase degrees of freedom. The complex amplitude c = √p e^{iφ} obeys dc/dt + iω(p)c + Γ₊(p)c − Γ₋(p)c = −ωinj-term, where ω(p) = ω₀ + Np is the power-dependent frequency, Γ₊ and Γ₋ are the positive damping and negative (spin-torque) damping, and N is the nonlinear frequency shift [2]. The oscillator is driven by a current Idc that sets its free-running frequency ffree(Idc) through the experimentally observed tunability [3]. Coupling between oscillators is modeled as a common-signal interaction: the ac current generated by one oscillator through magnetoresistance is injected into the other, producing a coupling term of the form εe^{iφext}. In the phase-reduced limit, the relative phase ψ = φ₁ − φ₂ follows an Adler-type equation, dψ/dt = 2π(f₁ − f₂) − 2πΔlock sin ψ, with f₁ and f₂ the free-running frequencies and Δlock the locking range determined by coupling strength. When |f₁ − f₂| < Δlock the pair synchronizes and ψ is fixed, otherwise it drifts. Parameters were taken from experimentally realistic magnetic tunnel junction oscillators [3,4]: free frequencies of a few GHz, tuning slopes of tens of MHz/mA, and locking ranges of tens of MHz. Neuron design A neuron consists of two oscillators. Oscillator A is driven by a current proportional to the weighted sum of inputs, IA = Σj wj xj + b, so its frequency encodes the neuron's pre-activation. Oscillator B is held at a fixed reference current and frequency fref. The neuron output is a scalar read from the pair, namely the time-averaged rectified power of the combined signal (equivalently, the amplitude of the beat or of the synchronized mode). When the frequencies are within the locking range, the combined output is large and approximately constant; outside it, the phase drift averages the output down to a lower value. The output as a function of IA therefore displays a non-monotonic, bell-like (resonant) response centered on fref, in contrast with sigmoid or ReLU functions. Response curves were computed by numerically integrating the coupled equations over durations of at least 1 µs after discarding a transient, using a fourth-order Runge–Kutta scheme with a time step of 1/50 of the oscillation period. The resulting curves were also fitted by a Lorentzian-like analytical function to allow fast simulation of large networks and gradient computation. Logic gate implementation Two-input gates were realized by a single neuron with inputs x₁, x₂ ∈ {0,1}, weights w₁, w₂, and bias b. Because the response is non-monotonic, XOR can be realized by placing the input sums 0 and 2 (both inputs equal) outside the resonance window and the sum 1 within it. AND, OR, NAND, and NOR were obtained by positioning thresholds on either flank of the response. For each gate, weights and bias were determined by grid search over the experimentally accessible current range, and the output was binarized with a threshold at half the maximum output. A gate was considered correct if all four input combinations were classified correctly with a margin exceeding the numerical noise floor. Network architecture and training Networks were fully connected feed-forward architectures with one hidden layer of oscillator-pair neurons and an output layer. Two benchmark classification tasks were considered: the Iris dataset (4 features, 3 classes, 150 samples) [5] and the MNIST handwritten digit dataset (28×28 images, 10 classes, 60,000 training and 10,000 test images) [6]. Iris used a 70/30 train/test split with features normalized to zero mean and unit variance; MNIST pixel values were scaled to [0,1]. Hidden-layer sizes were 10 for Iris and 100 for MNIST unless stated otherwise. Training was performed offline on a conventional computer using backpropagation with the analytical oscillator response function as the activation, since its derivative is available in closed form. Optimization used Adam [7] with a learning rate of 10⁻³, mini-batches of 32 (Iris) or 128 (MNIST), and cross-entropy loss with a softmax at the output, which is computed digitally. Weights were initialized following Glorot [8], and the input to each neuron was scaled so that the pre-activation fell into the oscillator's accessible current range. Early stopping on a validation subset prevented overfitting. Trained weights were then transferred to the oscillator-level simulation, where each hidden neuron was simulated with the full coupled-oscillator model to verify that inference accuracy matched that of the analytical network. As a baseline, networks of identical topology with sigmoid and ReLU activations were trained with the same procedure and hyperparameters. Each configuration was repeated with ten random seeds, and mean accuracies and standard deviations are reported. Phase noise analysis Phase noise was incorporated by adding stochastic terms to the oscillator equations, representing thermal fluctuations [9]. A white Gaussian noise term ξ(t) with ⟨ξ(t)ξ(t′)⟩ = 2Dδ(t − t′) was added to the phase equation, where D sets the intrinsic linewidth Δf = D/π of the oscillator. Linewidths from 0.1 MHz to 100 MHz were explored, spanning values reported for single and coupled STNOs [3,10]. Integration used the Euler–Maruyama method with a time step of 1/50 period. Noise affects the neuron response by smoothing the locking transition and reducing the output contrast. For each noise level, the neuron output was averaged over a finite measurement window Tmeas (10–1000 ns) to quantify the trade-off between computation time and accuracy. Network accuracy was evaluated on the full test sets with noisy oscillators in the inference stage, using weights trained either without noise or with noise injected in the activation during training, to assess noise-aware training. Accuracy was recorded as a function of linewidth and Tmeas, averaged over 20 noise realizations. Performance metrics Classification accuracy on the test sets was the primary metric. For logic gates, the metrics were correctness and the output contrast between logical states. Statistical variation was reported as standard deviation across seeds and noise realizations. All simulations were implemented in Python with NumPy and PyTorch [11]. Response of a synchronized oscillator-pair neuron We first characterized the neuron, which consists of two nano-oscillators whose frequencies are tuned by input currents. In the model, each oscillator is described by a standard auto-oscillator equation with nonlinear damping and frequency shift, and the two are coupled with strength κ [12,14]. One oscillator is driven at a frequency set by the weighted sum of the neuron inputs, and the other is held at a reference frequency. The neuron output is the amplitude of the coupled signal, as measured by a rectifying readout. When the detuning Δf between the oscillators lies within the locking range, the oscillators synchronize and the output is high. Distributed source coding studies how correlated sources observed at separate terminals can be compressed efficiently. The Slepian-Wolf theorem showed that two correlated sources can be reconstructed losslessly at a common decoder with a sum rate equal to their joint entropy, even though the encoders do not cooperate. Two closely related problems, the Wyner-Ahlswede-Körner (WAK) network and the Gray-Wyner (GW) network, address variations in which the decoder needs only partial information, or in which a single encoder produces several descriptions for several decoders. In this paper we relate these two networks through a code-reduction argument and use the relation to obtain a converse bound for the WAK network from a converse bound for the GW network. In the WAK network, two correlated sources X and Y are encoded separately. The decoder has to reconstruct X losslessly, while Y serves only as side information that the decoder obtains through a rate-limited link. The optimal rate region was determined independently by Wyner and by Ahlswede and Körner. It is characterized by an auxiliary random variable U satisfying the Markov chain U – Y – X, and the region consists of rate pairs (RX, RY) with RX ≥ H(X|U) and RY ≥ I(Y;U). The WAK problem is a basic example of a coding problem with a single-letter characterization, and it is also tied to many further topics such as the information bottleneck, common information, and hypothesis testing under communication constraints. The converse part of the WAK theorem has two versions. The weak converse requires that every code with vanishing error probability have rates in the region in the limit. The strong converse is more demanding: it says that rates outside the region force the error probability to tend to one, not merely to be bounded away from zero. Ahlswede, Gács and Körner proved the strong converse for the WAK network with the blowing-up lemma, which is a measure-concentration tool. Their approach is powerful but yields rather coarse bounds, and it is tied to a specific proof technique. Later work gave alternative proofs through other tools, including the information spectrum method, hypercontractivity, and reverse hypercontractivity. These alternatives have refined the understanding of the problem, but each requires machinery that is particular to the WAK setting. The GW network is a different multiterminal problem. A single encoder observes a pair (X, Y) and sends a common message to two decoders, together with a private message to each. One decoder must reconstruct X and the other must reconstruct Y. The rate region, determined by Gray and Wyner, is expressed by an auxiliary random variable W, with rate triples satisfying R0 ≥ I(X,Y;W), R1 ≥ H(X|W), and R2 ≥ H(Y|W). The region has a natural geometric structure and is linked to Wyner's common information, which is the minimum common rate at which the sum of rates equals the joint entropy. Strong converse results for the GW network are also available, and methods developed for it have recently led to refined bounds, for example by means of the information-theoretic properties of the lossless case and via the so-called one-shot or non-asymptotic analyses. The idea of this paper is that a WAK code can be converted into a GW code. In the WAK network the encoder for Y produces a message that, together with the message of the X-encoder, lets the decoder recover X. Given such a code, we construct a GW code in which the common message is the output of the Y-encoder and the private messages are built so that the two GW decoders recover the sources with controlled error. The central difficulty is that the WAK code only guarantees that X is recovered; it says nothing about recovering Y. We therefore need a construction in which the private message for Y compensates for what the WAK code does not provide, at a cost that vanishes in rate, or is otherwise controlled, so that the rate relation of the GW code is a direct consequence of the rates of the original WAK code. The reduction is explicit and does not rely on the structure of the optimal region. Once the reduction is available, any converse bound on the GW network translates into a converse bound on the WAK network. Applying a known strong converse bound for the GW network, we obtain a bound on the success probability of WAK codes whose rates lie outside the optimal region. The bound decays exponentially in the blocklength when the rate pair is outside the region, and so it gives the strong converse theorem for the WAK network. Our proof is thus an alternative to the earlier approaches. It does not use the blowing-up lemma directly, and it makes explicit a structural link between two classical networks which have usually been studied separately. Besides giving a new proof, the reduction illustrates a useful general principle: converse results for a network with a richer interaction structure can be transferred to a network with a simpler one by a coding argument, with no need to repeat the converse analysis. We expect this viewpoint to be useful for other pairs of problems. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II fixes notation and defines the WAK and GW networks and their rate regions. Section III presents the reduction from WAK codes to GW codes. Section IV derives the converse bound for the WAK network and deduces the strong converse. Section V concludes with a discussion. We consider a pair of correlated discrete memoryless sources (X,Y) with joint distribution P{XY} on a finite alphabet X×Y. Throughout, X^n and Y^n denote n i.i.d. copies. Network models. WAK network. An (n, M1, M2, ε) WAK code consists of encoders φ1: X^n → {1,…,M1} and φ2: Y^n → {1,…,M2}, and a decoder ψ: {1,…,M1}×{1,…,M2} → X^n, such that Pr[ψ(φ1(X^n), φ2(Y^n)) ≠ X^n] ≤ ε. Here Y^n serves as rate-limited side information for reconstructing X^n. The achievable region consists of pairs (R1,R2) with R1 ≥ H(X|U), R2 ≥ I(Y;U) for some U with U–Y–X a Markov chain. GW network. An (n, M0, M1, M2, δ1, δ2) GW code has a single encoder f: X^n×Y^n → {1,…,M0}×{1,…,M1}×{1,…,M2}, with outputs (W0,W1,W2), and two decoders g1(W0,W1) = \hat X^n and g2(W0,W2) = \hat Y^n. The error requirements are Pr[\hat X^n ≠ X^n] ≤ δ1 and Pr[\hat Y^n ≠ Y^n] ≤ δ2 (or the corresponding distortion-based variants). The rate region is the set of (R0,R1,R2) satisfying R0 ≥ I(X,Y;W), R1 ≥ H(X|W), R2 ≥ H(Y|W) for some auxiliary W. We use a converse bound for the GW network that holds for finite blocklength with nonvanishing error, expressed through the entropy-type quantities of the code. Reduction from WAK codes to GW codes. The key step is a construction that turns a WAK code into a GW code with controlled rates and error probabilities. Let (φ1, φ2, ψ) be a WAK code with error probability ε. Define the GW encoder as follows. Given (x^n, y^n), compute W0 = φ2(y^n), W1 = φ1(x^n), and let the common message be W0 together with nothing else, while the private message to decoder 1 is W1. Decoder 1 receives (W0, W1) and outputs ψ(W1, W0), which equals x^n except with probability at most ε. Thus the first decoder inherits the WAK error probability: δ1 = ε. Decoder 2 must reconstruct Y^n from (W0, W2). Since W0 = φ2(Y^n) is only a compressed description of Y^n, the private message W2 must carry the residual information. We let W2 be a description of Y^n that, given W0, identifies Y^n exactly. Its alphabet size is bounded by the largest cardinality of a preimage of φ2, M2' ≤ max{j} |φ2^{-1}(j)|. To control this, we restrict to a subset of Y^n composed of sequences of a single type class and thereby bound the rate of W2. Concretely, we partition the sequences by type, and by a standard argument pick a type class T{Q} whose contribution is not negligible (polynomially many types, so the loss is O(log n) in rate). Within this class, the preimage of each index of φ2 is bounded in size by |TQ| minus the information carried by φ2, giving log M2' ≲ n H(Q) − log(number of effectively distinguishable indices) up to a vanishing term. The resulting GW code has rates (1/n) log M0 = (1/n) log M2, (1/n) log M1 = (1/n) log M1^{WAK}, (1/n) log M2' ≈ H(Y) − I(Y;W) terms, so the GW rate triple is determined by the WAK rate pair and the marginal entropy of Y. Because the GW decoder 2 must be exact only on a high-probability subset, we allow δ2 to be a constant strictly below one by discarding the atypical sequences; this loses only a vanishing additional probability. The reduction therefore maps an (n, M1, M2, ε) WAK code into a GW code with (δ1, δ2) = (ε, ε') for ε' arbitrarily small, with rates given above. Converse bound. Apply the GW converse to the constructed code. Let W = (W0) be the common message and define auxiliary variables Ui = (W0, Y^{i-1}) in the usual single-letterization manner, with time-sharing variable T uniform on {1,…,n} independent of everything. The GW converse yields, for the code with error probability ε, (1/n) log M0 ≥ I(X^n,Y^n; W0)/n − small terms, (1/n) log M1 ≥ H(X^n|W0)/n − (ε-dependent Fano term). Using Fano's inequality for decoder 1 with error probability ε, H(X^n | W0, W1) ≤ 1 + ε n log|X|. Since W0 is a function of Y^n, I(X^n,Y^n;W0)=I(Y^n;W0) and the Markov chain W0–Y^n–X^n holds. Single-letterization with U = (W0, X^{T-1}, Y{T+1}^n)-type auxiliaries preserves the Markov chain U–Y–X and gives R2 ≥ I(Y;U) − o(1), R1 ≥ H(X|U) − ε log|X| − o(1). To obtain a bound valid for ε not tending to zero, we avoid Fano and instead keep the converse in a form that retains a dependence on ε through a change of the measure on the set of correctly decoded pairs: restrict (X^n,Y^n) to the success event 𝒢 with probability at least 1−ε, and evaluate the entropic quantities under the conditional distribution P{X^nY^n|𝒢}. The bound's slack ηn depends on ε only through log(1/(1−ε))/n and type-counting terms of order (log n)/n. Hence for every fixed ε<1, rate pairs outside the WAK region cannot be achieved with error ε, because the right-hand sides remain within ηn→0 of the region boundary. In the GW network, a single encoder observes (X^n,Y^n) and sends a common message at rate R0 and two private messages at rates R1 and R2, and decoders 1 and 2 reconstruct X^n and Y^n respectively. Micro aerial vehicles (MAVs) have become attractive platforms for inspection, search and rescue, surveillance, and mapping, largely because of their agility, low cost, and ability to access cluttered or hazardous spaces [1], [2]. Their small size, however, strongly limits payload, power, and onboard computation. As a result, many MAV deployments cannot rely on heavy sensors such as scanning lidar, and they often operate where satellite positioning is degraded or unavailable, such as indoors, under canopy, or in urban canyons [3]. Lightweight cameras are an appealing alternative: they are inexpensive, passive, and information-rich, and they support both state estimation and scene understanding [4]. Reliable six degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) pose estimation from a monocular camera is therefore a central enabling capability for autonomous MAV flight. Deploying several MAVs as a swarm further increases coverage, redundancy, and task throughput [5]. It also creates an opportunity: vehicles that observe overlapping parts of the environment, or each other, can share information to improve localization beyond what any single vehicle could achieve. This idea, known as collaborative localization, has been studied extensively for ground robots and, more recently, for aerial teams. This paper develops a monocular vision based collaborative localization framework for MAV swarms and evaluates it in a high-fidelity simulation environment. Related Work Monocular visual localization. Visual odometry and visual simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) have matured considerably. Feature-based systems such as PTAM [6] and ORB-SLAM [7] estimate camera motion by tracking salient points and optimizing over keyframes, while direct methods such as LSD-SLAM [8] and DSO [9] operate on image intensities. Visual-inertial approaches [10], [11] resolve the metric scale ambiguity inherent to monocular sensing and improve robustness during aggressive motion. Despite these advances, a single MAV running such a pipeline accumulates drift, can fail under rapid rotation, textureless regions, or motion blur, and has a limited field of view that restricts the amount of environment that can be observed at once. Multi-robot and collaborative SLAM. Cooperative mapping and localization have been explored with centralized and decentralized architectures. Centralized systems offload computation to a ground station that fuses data from all agents, as in collaborative structure-from-motion for MAVs [12] and CCM-SLAM [13]. Such designs can yield consistent global maps but create a single point of failure and demand substantial communication bandwidth. Distributed approaches instead let each agent maintain its own estimate and exchange compact information with neighbors [14], [15]. Classical cooperative localization methods based on filtering [16] rely on relative range or bearing measurements between robots, and careful treatment of cross-correlations is required to avoid overconfident estimates. In vision-based settings, inter-robot loop closure through place recognition and feature matching is commonly used to align the trajectories and maps of different agents [17]. Relative pose estimation from two views, using epipolar geometry and the essential matrix [18], offers a complementary route in which relative measurements between vehicles constrain their poses without requiring a shared prior map. Simulation for aerial autonomy. Evaluating multi-vehicle algorithms on physical hardware is costly and risky. Simulators such as Gazebo [19] and Microsoft AirSim [20] provide photorealistic rendering, physics-based vehicle dynamics, and simulated sensors, enabling repeatable experiments with several vehicles and ground-truth poses for quantitative assessment. Motivation and Challenges Several issues remain open for monocular collaborative localization on MAV swarms. First, a monocular camera cannot recover depth from a single image, so a group must bootstrap a shared map through cross-vehicle feature correspondence and multiple-view geometry before individual tracking is possible. Second, once a map exists, each vehicle must estimate its pose from tracked features in the presence of outliers caused by mismatches, moving objects, and repetitive texture, which calls for robust estimation such as RANSAC-based schemes [21]. Third, relative measurements between vehicles are informative but sporadic, since they depend on overlapping views, so they must be fused opportunistically with individual estimates. Finally, the algorithm should be distributed to scale with swarm size and limit dependence on communication links and central computation. Contributions This paper addresses these challenges with a framework that combines individual and relative pose estimation within a distributed architecture. The main contributions are as follows: 1. A map initialization procedure in which MAVs detect and match features across vehicles to produce a sparse reconstruction of the observed environment, which serves as a common global reference. 2. An individual localization module that tracks features against this map and employs robust outlier rejection to estimate each vehicle's 6-DoF pose. 3. A relative localization module that uses feature matching between vehicles and multiple-view geometry to compute relative poses, which are intermittently fused with individual estimates to reduce drift and improve accuracy. 4. An implementation and evaluation using MAVs and environments simulated in Microsoft AirSim, together with an analysis of the benefits and limitations of collaboration relative to single-vehicle localization. Organization The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II formulates the problem and describes the system architecture. Section III details map initialization, individual pose estimation, and relative pose computation and fusion. Section IV presents the simulation setup and experimental results, and Section V discusses their implications. Section VI concludes and outlines directions for future work. 1. System Overview We consider a swarm of N micro aerial vehicles (MAVs), each carrying a forward-facing monocular camera with known intrinsic matrix K and an onboard processor. The vehicles exchange messages over a communication channel with limited bandwidth. Each vehicle i maintains an estimate of its pose Ti^W ∈ SE(3) in a common world frame W. The framework has three stages: (i) collaborative map initialization, (ii) individual pose estimation against the shared map, and (iii) occasional relative-measurement fusion. The algorithm is distributed. Each MAV runs the same pipeline and transmits only compact data (keyframe descriptors, 3D landmarks, and pose estimates), not raw images. 2. Collaborative Map Initialization Monocular vision gives no metric scale and no initial depth, so the swarm first builds a sparse global map. Each MAV i extracts ORB features [1] from its image Ii and computes binary descriptors. Descriptors are broadcast to neighbors and matched by Hamming distance with a ratio test (threshold 0.75) and a mutual-consistency check. For a pair (i, j) with enough putative matches, we estimate the essential matrix E with a five-point solver [2] inside a RANSAC loop [3]. The relative rotation Rij and a unit-norm translation direction tij come from decomposing E, and the cheirality condition selects the correct solution among the four candidates. Inlier correspondences are triangulated linearly and refined by minimizing reprojection error. The initial map is M = {pk ∈ ℝ³, dk}, where pk is a landmark position and dk its descriptor. The world frame is anchored to the first vehicle, and the scale is fixed by the known baseline between the two vehicles at initialization, obtained from an initial inter-vehicle range measurement. With more than two vehicles, pairwise reconstructions are merged by aligning shared landmarks with a similarity transform [4], followed by a local bundle adjustment over all poses and landmarks. 3. Individual Pose Estimation Once M is available, each MAV localizes independently. Feature tracking. Landmarks projected into the current frame, using the predicted pose, are tracked with a pyramidal Kanade–Lucas–Tomasi tracker [5]. New features are detected when the number of tracked landmarks falls below a threshold. Tracking gives 2D–3D correspondences (uk, pk). Pose computation with outlier rejection. The pose of vehicle i at time t is estimated by solving the Perspective-n-Point (PnP) problem. We use an EPnP minimal-sample hypothesis within RANSAC [6]: (R, t) = argmin Σk ρ(‖uk − π(K(R pk + t))‖²), where π is the perspective projection and ρ is a robust Huber kernel. A correspondence is an inlier if its reprojection error is below 2 px. The best hypothesis is refined with Levenberg–Marquardt on the inlier set. If fewer than 20 inliers remain, the estimate is rejected and the vehicle propagates its previous pose using a constant-velocity model until tracking recovers. Map growth. When a vehicle observes new features in two keyframes with sufficient parallax, it triangulates them and adds them to its local copy of the map. The new landmarks are broadcast to the swarm and merged with the global map. Duplicates are detected by descriptor similarity and 3D proximity. 4. Relative Pose Estimation and Fusion Individual estimates drift because of accumulated tracking error and the weak geometry of monocular vision. To limit this drift, vehicles occasionally exchange relative measurements. Relative measurement. When vehicles i and j have overlapping fields of view, they match features between their current images, as in Section 2. Multiple-view geometry then gives the relative rotation Rij and a translation direction tij. Because tij has no scale, the baseline length is recovered by triangulating matched points that are also in the global map and comparing the result with the map's metric scale. The relative pose measurement is zij = (Rij, s·tij), with covariance Σij, obtained by propagating the image-noise covariance through the Jacobian of the pose solver. Fusion. Each vehicle keeps a pose estimate xi with covariance Pi from the individual PnP refinement, using the inverse of the Gauss–Newton Hessian. When a relative measurement arrives, vehicle i predicts its pose from that of vehicle j, x̂i = xj ⊕ zij^{-1}, and fuses it with its own estimate. Because the cross-correlation between xi and xj is unknown in a distributed setting, we use covariance intersection [7]: Pf^{-1} = ω Pi^{-1} + (1−ω) P̂i^{-1}, xf = Pf(ω Pi^{-1} xi + (1−ω) P̂i^{-1} x̂i), with ω chosen to minimize trace(Pf). This avoids overconfident estimates caused by double counting information. For SE(3), the update is performed on the tangent space around the current estimate. A fusion is accepted only if the Mahalanobis distance between xi and x̂i is below a χ² gate at 95% confidence, which rejects erroneous matches. 5. Distributed Implementation Each MAV runs three asynchronous threads: tracking and pose estimation at frame rate, map management at a lower rate, and communication. Messages carry keyframe poses, new landmarks with descriptors, and relative measurements. Time-stamped messages are buffered, and relative measurements are applied to the pose history at the corresponding timestamp and then propagated forward. The cost of communication grows with the number of new landmarks, not with the image size. 6. Simulation Setup We implemented the framework in Microsoft AirSim [8], which provides photorealistic environments built on Unreal Engine and multirotor dynamics. Each simulated MAV carries a forward-facing RGB camera (640×480, 90° field of view) with additive Gaussian noise. Ground-truth poses from the simulator are used only for evaluation. The vehicles fly predefined trajectories in the simulated environments. We evaluate absolute trajectory error [9] after similarity alignment, compared across three configurations: individual localization only, collaborative map initialization with individual tracking, and the full framework with relative-measurement fusion. Experiments were conducted in Microsoft AirSim using three simulated quadrotor MAVs, each equipped with a forward-facing monocular camera (640×480 pixels, 90° horizontal field of view) that streamed images at 30 Hz. Ground-truth poses from the simulator were used only for evaluation. Two environments were used: a structured urban block with buildings, vehicles and vegetation, and a less structured outdoor scene with sparse texture and repetitive elements. In each environment the MAVs flew predefined trajectories of 150–250 m with speeds of 1–4 m/s, with partially overlapping fields of view. Feature detection used ORB [1] with 1000 features per frame, and matching used Hamming-distance nearest neighbors with a ratio test. Relative pose was computed from essential matrix estimation within a RANSAC loop [2], and individual pose was estimated with PnP against the map [3]. Results are averaged over ten runs with different random seeds for the RANSAC and the simulated sensor noise. Map Initialization The initial sparse map was built from inter-vehicle feature matches. Wireless networks face a steady growth in demand for multimedia content, much of which is requested repeatedly and is predictable in nature. Caching exploits this predictability by prefetching popular content into storage at the network edge or in user devices during off-peak hours, thereby reducing peak-time load. Conventional caching delivers only a local caching gain, which depends on the fraction of the library that each user can store. In their seminal work, Maddah-Ali and Niesen showed that a much larger global caching gain is attainable when cache placement and delivery are designed jointly [1]. In their coded caching scheme, users store carefully chosen fragments of every file, and the server transmits coded messages that are simultaneously useful to several users. The resulting gain grows with the aggregate cache size and is, in principle, unbounded as the number of users increases. The original scheme was designed for a single shared link. Wireless systems with multiple antennas offer an additional resource: spatial multiplexing. Several works have studied the combination of coded caching with multi-antenna transmission [2]-[4]. It was shown in [2] and [3] that the spatial multiplexing gain and the coded caching gain are additive, so that the degrees of freedom of a system with L antennas, K users and normalized cache size γ can reach L + Kγ. Practical approaches based on multicast beamforming, in which coded data chunks are sent to selected user groups and each group is served with a precoded multicast signal, were proposed in [5]-[7]. These schemes use the cache contents to cancel interference and to decode the desired file at each user, and they have been shown to improve the achievable symmetric rate under realistic channel models, including the finite signal-to-noise ratio regime. Despite these advantages, a major obstacle to practical deployment is subpacketization, the number of packets into which each file must be split. In the original scheme, the subpacketization level equals the binomial coefficient C(K, Kγ), which grows exponentially with the number of users for a fixed cache fraction. Each file must be large enough to be divided into this many packets, and the header overhead, the signaling and the computational complexity of encoding and decoding increase accordingly. Lahtonen et al. and Shangguan et al. have shown that, for a fixed finite file size, the coded caching gain cannot be sustained as the number of users grows [8], [9]. Therefore, the practical value of coded caching depends critically on reducing subpacketization. Several approaches to this problem have been proposed in the single-antenna setting. Placement delivery arrays were introduced in [10] as a unified framework for describing placement and delivery, and constructions with subpacketization growing only linearly or sub-exponentially in K were obtained, at the expense of a lower coded caching gain. Combinatorial designs, such as resolvable designs and Ruzsa-Szemerédi graphs, were used in [11] and [12] for the same purpose. Grouping-based schemes divide users into groups and apply the original scheme within each group, which reduces subpacketization but also reduces the multicast gain [13]. These designs are all tied to the single-link model, and their extension to multi-antenna systems is not straightforward, because the delivery phase must additionally account for the beamforming structure and the number of users that can be served simultaneously. In the multi-antenna case, subpacketization has been addressed only to a limited extent. The authors of [14] showed that the presence of multiple antennas can itself relax the subpacketization requirement, since spatial multiplexing can substitute for part of the multicast gain. Others have proposed schemes in which the transmitter serves users in groups with a reduced packet count [15]. However, existing proposals typically offer a single operating point, or a small number of them, determined by the system parameters. A system designer cannot choose the subpacketization to match the storage, computational and power resources available, and the effect of such a choice on the achievable rate is not well understood. In this paper, we present a new multi-antenna coded caching scheme in which the subpacketization level can be selected from a set of predefined values determined by basic network parameters, namely the number of transmit antennas and the number of users. The smallest value in this set corresponds to a highly reduced packet count, while the largest corresponds to the full subpacketization of existing high-performance schemes. The scheme uses multicast beamforming for delivery, and the placement is designed so that each transmission serves a controllable number of users with common coded content. We also introduce a simple efficiency index, which relates the achievable gain to the subpacketization level, as a means to compare schemes and operating points on a common scale. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: - We propose a coded caching scheme for multi-antenna communications that supports multiple subpacketization levels and recovers existing schemes as special cases. - We define an efficiency index that serves as a performance indicator across different subpacketization levels. - We provide numerical examples showing that larger subpacketization generally yields a better efficiency index and a higher symmetric rate, whereas smaller subpacketization leads to a significant rate loss, thereby characterizing the trade-off between complexity and performance. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II describes the system model. Section III presents the proposed scheme. Section IV introduces the efficiency index and analyzes the achievable rate. Section V reports numerical results, and Section VI concludes the paper. We consider a downlink network in which a server with L transmit antennas serves K single-antenna users over a shared wireless channel. The server holds a library of N files, each of size F bits. Each user has a cache that stores a fraction γ = M/N of the library, where M is the cache size in files. The system operates in two phases, placement and delivery, following the standard coded caching framework [1], [2]. Placement Phase Each file is split into Fs equal packets, where Fs is the subpacketization level. In the baseline multi-antenna scheme of [3], users are partitioned by all subsets of size t = Kγ, so that Fs = C(K,t). Each packet is labeled by one such subset and stored in the caches of the t users in that subset. This placement is uncoded and symmetric across files. To make subpacketization a design parameter, we instead group users. Let the K users be partitioned into G groups of size K/G, assuming for simplicity that G divides K. Users in the same group receive identical cache content. Placement is then applied at the group level with parameter tg = Gγ. The file is split into Fs = C(G,tg) packets, each stored by all users of the tg groups in its label. The admissible values of G, which divide K, define the predefined set of subpacketization levels. Setting G = K recovers the baseline, and smaller G gives exponentially fewer packets. The cache constraint is met because each user stores a fraction tg/G = γ of every file. Because users in a group have identical caches, they need not be served differently by the cache content. Their requested files may still differ, so the transmission must separate their demands in the spatial domain. This is the source of the rate loss at low subpacketization, which we quantify below. Delivery Phase Each user k requests file W{dk}. The delivery consists of a sequence of transmissions, each serving a set S of tg + α groups, where α is the number of additional groups served per transmission. In the multi-antenna setting, the spatial degrees of freedom allow α to be as large as L [3]. A transmission to a set S carries, for each user k in S, a packet that is cached by all other groups in a (tg)-subset of S∖{group of k}, so that interference is removed either by the cache or by beamforming. Specifically, for a transmitted vector xS, we write xS = Σ{k∈S} wk s{k}, where sk is the coded symbol intended for user k and wk is its beamforming vector. Each wk is chosen to null sk at the L−1 users whose caches do not contain the required side information, namely the users that must be suppressed spatially. The remaining users in S either have the interfering content cached or lie in the null space of wk. The received signal at user k is yk = hkᴴ wk sk + Σ{j∈S, j≠k} hkᴴ wj sj + nk, where hk is the channel vector and nk is Gaussian noise. After cancelling cached terms, only the desired symbol and noise remain. Each user then recovers its missing packets over successive transmissions, and the file is reconstructed by combining these with cached packets. Since each transmission is a multicast to a group of users, the rate is limited by the worst user in S. For a unit-power constraint the multicast beamformer is obtained as the solution of max{w} min{k∈S} |hkᴴ w|² subject to ‖w‖² ≤ P, which is approximated by standard semidefinite relaxation with randomization [4]. We use the resulting per-transmission rate rS = log₂(1 + SINRS), where SINRS is the minimum over users in the multicast set. Efficiency Index To evaluate the effect of subpacketization without full channel simulation, we define a simple efficiency index. Let D be the number of users served per transmission, counting the spatial and coded multicast gains, which equals the sum degrees of freedom. The efficiency index is η = D / Dmax, where Dmax = Kγ + L is the maximum attainable value under unconstrained subpacketization [3]. For a given grouping G, the number of simultaneously served users is reduced because group members with different demands must be separated spatially, which uses transmit dimensions. Consequently D(G) ≤ Dmax, and η ∈ (0,1]. The index equals one in the baseline G = K and decreases as G decreases. It is inexpensive to compute because it depends only on K, L, γ and G, and it gives a first-order indication of the loss incurred by a given subpacketization level. Subpacketization Selection The scheme exposes the set 𝒢 = {G : G divides K, G ≥ max(L, tg+1)} of feasible group counts. For each G ∈ 𝒢, the subpacketization is Fs(G) = C(G, Gγ) and the number of transmissions is C(G, tg+α)·(tg+α)/(…) according to the chosen α. A system designer can thereby trade computational cost, which grows with Fs through the number of beamformers computed and signalling overhead, against the achievable rate. Given a limit Fmax on the packet count, the chosen configuration is the largest G satisfying Fs(G) ≤ Fmax. Performance Evaluation Setup We evaluate the schemes numerically for the symmetric rate, defined as the common rate achievable by all users when each requests distinct files. Channels are drawn i.i.d. from a complex Gaussian distribution with unit variance, and results are averaged over independent realizations. The total transmit power and noise variance are fixed so that the nominal SNR is the same across schemes. The symmetric rate is computed as Rsym = F / T, where T is the total time required to deliver all requested files, obtained by summing the inverse per-transmission rates over all transmissions. We compare the proposed scheme at several values of G with the baseline of [3] and with an uncoded unicast scheme using zero-forcing beamforming without caching gain. Parameters K, L and γ are varied to illustrate the dependence of η and Rsym on subpacketization. The beamformer optimization uses 100 Gaussian randomizations per multicast set. We evaluate the proposed scheme in a downlink setting with a base station equipped with L antennas serving K single-antenna users, each with a cache of fractional size γ = t/K.
