Copper has long been the benchmark material for electrical and thermal conduction. Its room-temperature resistivity of about 1.7 µΩ·cm and thermal conductivity of roughly 390–400 W/m·K underpin applications from power transmission and motors to microelectronic interconnects and heat exchangers. As devices become smaller, faster and more power-dense, however, the limits of copper become increasingly apparent. In integrated circuits, the resistivity of copper interconnects rises sharply as line widths approach the electron mean free path, owing to surface and grain-boundary scattering. Joule heating and electromigration then limit current density and reliability. In high-power electronics, electric vehicles and energy systems, the demand for conductors that carry more current with lower loss and dissipate heat more effectively is growing rapidly. A conductor whose resistivity lies well below that of copper while its thermal conductivity exceeds it would therefore be of considerable technological value. Carbon nanomaterials are natural candidates for this purpose. Graphene exhibits extraordinary carrier mobility, with reported values exceeding 10⁴ cm²/V·s at room temperature, and an intrinsic in-plane thermal conductivity of up to about 5000 W/m·K. Carbon nanotubes show similarly remarkable ballistic transport and thermal properties. Combining such materials with copper has been proposed as a route to "ultra-conductive copper" in which the carbon phase supplies additional low-scattering conduction channels while the metal provides bulk continuity. Theoretical and experimental studies have shown that graphene–copper heterostructures can modify the electronic structure at the interface, and that graphene coatings can suppress surface oxidation and reduce surface scattering. Reports of copper–carbon composites with enhanced conductivity, including nanocarbon-copper composites prepared by electrodeposition, molecular-level mixing and powder metallurgy, as well as the often-cited claims of resistivity below that of copper in covetic-type materials, have stimulated considerable interest. Despite this promise, the practical realization of such nanocomposites remains difficult. Conventional powder metallurgy and ball-milling routes tend to introduce defects into the graphene, cause agglomeration of the carbon phase, and produce weak interfaces, all of which increase electron scattering and degrade conductivity. The wetting between copper and carbon is poor, and the two are essentially immiscible, which hinders the formation of well-bonded, uniformly dispersed composites. Chemical vapor deposition (CVD) can produce high-quality graphene directly on copper foils, but it typically requires high temperatures, long growth times, gaseous hydrocarbon precursors and carefully controlled atmospheres, and it yields mainly thin surface layers rather than bulk composites. Stacking or repeatedly transferring CVD graphene to build laminated copper–graphene structures is laborious and costly, and it is difficult to scale. Consequently, reproducible fabrication of composites with conductivity clearly superior to copper has been elusive, and the scientific origin of any improvement, whether interfacial charge transfer, reduced scattering, or parallel conduction through graphene, is still debated. Heteroatom doping offers an additional means of tuning the properties of graphene. Nitrogen, with a size similar to carbon and one additional valence electron, can be incorporated into the graphene lattice as graphitic, pyridinic or pyrrolic nitrogen. Graphitic nitrogen in particular acts as an n-type dopant, raising the Fermi level and increasing carrier density, which can enhance electrical conductivity. Nitrogen doping may also improve the interaction between graphene and metal surfaces, promoting charge transfer and stronger interfacial bonding with copper. These effects suggest that nitrogen-doped graphene could be a more effective conductive phase in copper-based composites than pristine graphene. Yet nitrogen doping is usually achieved using toxic or hazardous nitrogen sources such as ammonia, or via multistep post-treatments, which complicate the synthesis. Biomass-derived precursors provide an attractive alternative. Silk fibroin, a natural protein obtained from silkworm cocoons, consists mainly of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and hydrogen, with a nitrogen content of roughly 15–18 wt%. It is inexpensive, renewable and easily processed into films or solutions, and it can serve simultaneously as carbon and nitrogen source. Its pyrolysis has been used to produce nitrogen-doped carbon materials, but its use for direct growth of doped graphene on a metal substrate to form a bulk-conductive composite has scarcely been explored. Microwave plasma treatment is a rapid, energy-efficient technique capable of generating highly reactive species and very high local heating rates at relatively low overall processing times. Under plasma conditions, organic precursors can be decomposed and reorganized into graphitic structures within minutes, and copper acts as a catalytic substrate for graphene formation. This combination is well suited to producing nitrogen-doped graphene intimately bonded to copper while avoiding lengthy high-temperature CVD procedures. Here, we report a fast and simple strategy for fabricating a nitrogen-doped graphene–copper nanocomposite by applying microwave plasma treatment to silk fibroin placed on a copper substrate. We characterize the structure, composition and bonding of the resulting material and measure its electrical and thermal transport. The composite shows a room-temperature electrical resistivity of 0.16 µΩ·cm, far lower than that of copper, together with a thermal conductivity of 538 W/m·K at 25 °C, about 138% of that of copper. These results demonstrate a scalable route toward next-generation conductors combining ultra-low resistivity and high thermal conductivity. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic inflammatory and neurodegenerative disease of the central nervous system and a leading cause of non-traumatic disability in young adults [1]. Most patients present initially with a relapsing-remitting course (RRMS), characterized by acute episodes of neurological dysfunction followed by partial or complete recovery [2]. Over the past two decades, the therapeutic landscape has expanded considerably, and a range of disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) is now available for relapsing forms of MS (RMS). Despite this growing choice, injectable interferon (IFN) beta preparations remain widely used, particularly in patients with mild to moderate disease activity, in women planning pregnancy, and in those for whom long-term safety data and monitoring requirements are of particular importance [3,4]. IFN beta products have been approved for the treatment of RMS for more than 20 years. They reduce relapse rate, delay disability progression, and suppress MRI measures of disease activity, and they are generally considered to offer a favourable benefit-risk profile [5,6]. Their mechanisms of action are pleiotropic and include down-regulation of antigen presentation, modulation of cytokine profiles, and reduced trafficking of immune cells across the blood-brain barrier [7]. Conventional formulations, however, require frequent administration, ranging from three-times-weekly subcutaneous (SC) injection to weekly intramuscular injection. Frequent injections, together with characteristic adverse effects, can compromise adherence, and suboptimal adherence is in turn associated with an increased risk of relapse and poorer outcomes [8,9]. Peginterferon beta-1a is a pegylated form of IFN beta-1a, in which a 20 kDa methoxy poly(ethylene glycol) moiety is covalently attached to the parent molecule. Pegylation prolongs the half-life and increases systemic exposure, which permits a reduced dosing frequency [10]. In July 2014, SC peginterferon beta-1a 125 μg administered every 2 weeks was approved by the European Medicines Agency for adult patients with RRMS, and in August 2014 the US Food and Drug Administration approved it for RMS. In the pivotal phase 3 ADVANCE study, peginterferon beta-1a given every 2 or 4 weeks significantly reduced annualized relapse rate, the risk of disability progression confirmed at 12 weeks, and MRI lesion activity compared with placebo after one year, with the greatest effects seen in the every-2-week regimen [11]. The ATTAIN extension study subsequently demonstrated sustained efficacy and a consistent safety profile with continued treatment for nearly 6 years [12,13]. As with other IFN beta therapies, the most frequently reported adverse events (AEs) with peginterferon beta-1a are injection site reactions (ISRs), influenza-like illness, pyrexia, and headache, which are mostly mild to moderate in intensity [11,14]. These events are often most pronounced at treatment initiation and tend to diminish over time, but they may nonetheless represent a considerable burden for patients and are among the principal reasons for non-adherence and treatment discontinuation [15,16]. Flu-like symptoms can usually be mitigated by gradual dose titration, administration in the evening, and the use of antipyretic or anti-inflammatory analgesics [17]. Practical measures such as injection technique, site rotation, and the use of autoinjectors are also recommended [18]. ISRs are of particular interest because they are highly visible, may cause pain, erythema, pruritus, and induration, and in rare cases may progress to more severe lesions such as skin necrosis [19,20]. Current knowledge about the pathophysiology of skin reactions to SC IFN treatment is limited. Proposed mechanisms include local cytokine-mediated inflammation, delayed-type hypersensitivity, and irritant reactions to the drug or excipients, and histopathological findings are heterogeneous [21]. Consequently, evidence-based strategies for prevention and treatment are scarce, and management in clinical practice often relies on individual experience. Notably, in pivotal trials ISRs were mainly characterized and classified by neurologists, and dermatologists were only rarely consulted [11,22]. This may have limited the precision of the description and differential diagnosis of skin findings, and it suggests that interdisciplinary collaboration could improve both the recognition and the treatment of these events. Because peginterferon beta-1a has only recently entered routine clinical use, practical guidance reflecting real-world experience is still developing. Optimal management of AEs is essential to support persistence with therapy and thereby to maximize long-term clinical benefit. Against this background, an interdisciplinary panel of German and Austrian experts, comprising neurologists, dermatologists, and an MS nurse from university hospitals and private practices, convened in July 2016 to discuss the management of side effects associated with peginterferon beta-1a and other IFN beta-based treatments. The aim of this report is to present the panel's recommendations on best practices for the management of the most relevant AEs, with a focus on ISRs and influenza-like symptoms, based on the available literature and on interdisciplinary clinical experience. An interdisciplinary advisory board meeting was held in July 2016 to develop practical recommendations for the management of adverse events (AEs) associated with peginterferon beta-1a and other interferon (IFN) beta therapies in multiple sclerosis (MS). The approach was a structured expert consensus process supported by a targeted literature review. It was not designed as a systematic review or meta-analysis, and no formal grading of evidence was undertaken. Panel composition Participants were invited on the basis of their clinical experience with IFN beta therapies and their involvement in MS care in Germany and Austria. The panel comprised neurologists from university hospitals and private neurological practices, dermatologists with experience in managing drug-induced and injection-related skin reactions, and one specialist MS nurse. Neurologists were selected to represent both academic and community-based care, so that recommendations would reflect different patient populations and healthcare settings. Dermatologists were included because skin reactions to subcutaneous (SC) IFN treatment are usually classified and managed by neurologists, and dermatological expertise had been rarely involved in the pivotal trials [1,2]. The MS nurse contributed experience in patient education, injection technique, and day-to-day adherence support. All participants took part in their individual professional capacity. Potential conflicts of interest were disclosed in accordance with the journal's requirements. Preparation and literature review Before the meeting, a non-systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed for English-language publications on IFN beta therapies in MS. Search terms combined "interferon beta", "peginterferon beta-1a", "multiple sclerosis", "adverse events", "injection site reactions", "influenza-like symptoms", "flu-like symptoms", "hepatic abnormalities", "haematological abnormalities", "thyroid dysfunction", "adherence", and "skin reactions". Priority was given to the pivotal Phase 3 ADVANCE study, its extension ATTAIN, and other clinical trials of peginterferon beta-1a [3–5]. Further sources were prescribing information (the EMA Summary of Product Characteristics and the FDA label), earlier registration trials of IFN beta-1a and IFN beta-1b products, observational and real-world studies, and published guidance on AE management and adherence [6–8]. Dermatological literature on injection site necrosis, injection-site inflammation, and the mechanisms of cutaneous reactions to injected biologics was also reviewed. Reference lists of relevant articles were hand-searched for additional publications. Congress abstracts and expert opinion were used only where peer-reviewed data were lacking, and this was stated explicitly. A short briefing document summarising the incidence, severity, and timing of the most frequent AEs, including injection site reactions (ISRs), influenza-like illness, pyrexia, headache, and laboratory abnormalities, was circulated to participants beforehand. Participants were also asked to bring clinical cases that illustrated challenging or typical situations in routine practice. Meeting structure The meeting was a one-day, face-to-face session moderated by a chairperson experienced in MS care. It was organised into thematic blocks: (1) the pharmacological and clinical profile of peginterferon beta-1a compared with other IFN beta formulations; (2) the pathophysiology, classification, and clinical presentation of ISRs; (3) the management of influenza-like illness and other systemic reactions; (4) laboratory monitoring and the handling of haematological, hepatic, and thyroid abnormalities; and (5) patient education, injection training, and strategies to support adherence. Each block started with a short presentation of the available evidence, followed by moderated discussion of case examples from the participants' practices. In the ISR block the dermatologists described the differential diagnosis of local skin reactions, including irritant and allergic reactions, local inflammatory reactions, lipoatrophy, and necrosis, together with practical diagnostic steps such as clinical examination, photographic documentation, and, where appropriate, biopsy or allergy testing. The group discussed how the severity of skin reactions might be graded in a simple, reproducible way that can be used in routine care. Consensus process Recommendations were developed through open discussion until general agreement was reached. Where opinions differed, the evidence was reconsidered, and differing views were discussed until a position acceptable to all participants was found. No formal voting or Delphi procedure was applied, and no quantitative thresholds for consensus were defined. Recommendations were categorised by the panel as being supported mainly by published evidence, by extrapolation from related conditions or other IFN products, or by clinical experience alone. Recommendations were drafted to be practical and applicable in daily practice, covering preventive measures, first-line management, indications for referral to a dermatologist, and criteria for dose adjustment, treatment interruption, or discontinuation. Manuscript development A writing group of panel members drafted the manuscript from the meeting notes and the literature reviewed. The draft was circulated to all participants, who reviewed it and suggested revisions, and the final version was approved by every author. Medical writing support was used for editorial assistance only and did not influence the content of the recommendations. Because the work consisted of expert opinion and a review of published literature, without patient data or intervention, ethical approval and informed consent were not required. Limitations of the approach The non-systematic literature search and the informal consensus method may have introduced selection bias and reflect the views of a small, regional panel. The recommendations should therefore be regarded as practical guidance based on literature and interdisciplinary experience, and they should be interpreted alongside the current product information and national guidelines. The panel's discussions produced consensus recommendations in four areas: (i) characterization and classification of injection site reactions (ISRs), (ii) prevention and treatment of ISRs, (iii) management of influenza-like symptoms (ILS) and other systemic adverse events, and (iv) laboratory monitoring and patient support. These are reported below. They reflect the available literature and the panel's practical experience, and not a formal systematic review. Characterization of injection site reactions The panel agreed that ISRs are the most frequent local adverse event under subcutaneous (SC) interferon beta therapy and that their presentation is heterogeneous. In the ADVANCE trial, ISRs occurred in 66% of patients receiving peginterferon beta-1a every 2 weeks, compared with 11% receiving placebo [1]. Most were mild or moderate, and fewer than 1% of patients discontinued treatment because of them [1]. The most frequent manifestations were erythema, pain, pruritus, and edema. Rarer findings included warmth, hematoma, and induration. Panel members noted that in pivotal trials ISRs were mainly characterized by neurologists, and dermatologists were rarely consulted. Reactions were therefore probably described in insufficient detail, and the underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. The panel distinguished several clinical entities: transient inflammatory reactions related to injection technique or to the pharmacological effect of interferon; delayed-type or allergic contact reactions to device or formulation components; lipoatrophy; and, rarely, skin necrosis. Experts emphasized that skin necrosis is uncommon but serious. It requires immediate discontinuation of the injectable and dermatological evaluation. Persistent, painful, or indurated lesions should prompt differential diagnosis, including infection, and biopsy where appropriate. The panel recommended a simple, standardized documentation scheme covering lesion type, size, duration, symptoms, and relation to injection, ideally supported by photographs, so that reactions can be compared between visits and across centers. Prevention of injection site reactions The panel considered patient training the most important preventive measure. Recommendations were as follows: 1. Structured injection training by an MS nurse or trained clinician at therapy initiation, with repeat checks during follow-up. 2. Systematic rotation of injection sites (abdomen, thighs, upper arms, buttocks where feasible), with avoidance of irritated or previously affected areas. 3. Allowing the pen or syringe to reach room temperature before injection, since cold solution may increase local discomfort. 4. Skin disinfection with the solution allowed to dry completely before injection. 5. Correct injection depth and angle, avoiding intradermal administration, and avoiding tight clothing over fresh sites. 6. Local cooling before and after injection to reduce pain and erythema. Colorectal cancer is among the most commonly diagnosed malignancies worldwide and a leading cause of cancer-related death. Advances in screening, surgery, and systemic therapy have improved survival, so a growing number of patients now live for years after diagnosis and treatment. Oxaliplatin-based regimens such as FOLFOX and CAPOX are the standard adjuvant treatment for stage III colon cancer and a backbone of first-line therapy for metastatic disease. Their benefit is well established, but they carry considerable toxicity. The most frequent and clinically important dose-limiting toxicity of oxaliplatin is chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN). CIPN arises from damage to the peripheral sensory nerves and dorsal root ganglia. It typically presents as numbness, tingling, paresthesia, burning or electric-shock-like pain, and cold-induced dysesthesia in the hands and feet. An acute, cold-triggered form occurs in most patients within hours or days of an infusion. A cumulative, chronic form develops as the total dose increases and may persist, or even worsen, for months or years after treatment ends (the "coasting" phenomenon). Reported prevalence of CIPN in patients treated with oxaliplatin ranges from 60% to 90% during treatment, and a substantial proportion still have symptoms six months or more after completion. No effective preventive agent has been established, and duloxetine is the only drug with modest evidence for treating painful CIPN. Management therefore relies largely on dose reduction, delay, or discontinuation of chemotherapy, which may compromise oncologic outcomes. Beyond its sensory symptoms, CIPN affects patients' function. Loss of sensation, impaired proprioception, reduced dexterity, and pain can limit activities of daily living, such as buttoning clothes, holding utensils, writing, handling small objects, walking, climbing stairs, and driving. Patients may also have an increased risk of falls and injury, such as burns from hot objects they cannot feel, and they often develop safety concerns and avoid activities. We refer to this problem as restriction of daily activity (RDA). Although CIPN severity is often assessed by clinician-graded scales or symptom inventories, these measures do not necessarily capture how symptoms translate into limitations in everyday life and safety awareness. Instruments that evaluate activity limitation specifically, such as the Screening of Activity Limitation and Safety Awareness (SALSA) scale, provide a complementary view of the functional burden. Cancer patients also frequently experience psychological distress. Colorectal cancer patients face the fear of recurrence, changes in bowel function, stomas, financial strain, and the burden of prolonged treatment. Persistent neuropathic symptoms, sleep disturbance, and loss of independence may add to anxiety, depression, fatigue, anger, and confusion. Prior studies have shown that patients with CIPN report more anxiety and depressive symptoms than those without, and that pain and sleep problems are associated with worse mood. Mood disturbance is itself related to poorer treatment adherence, greater symptom perception, and reduced well-being. The Profile of Mood States (POMS) is widely used to quantify these multidimensional negative mood states in oncology, and its short form is convenient for use in clinical settings. Quality of life (QoL) has become a central outcome in cancer care, especially for survivors expected to live long with the sequelae of treatment. Several studies have reported that CIPN is associated with worse physical, functional, and social well-being and lower overall QoL among patients with colorectal cancer. However, the pathways through which CIPN influences QoL are not fully understood. Neuropathic symptoms may directly diminish QoL, but they may also act indirectly through functional limitation and emotional distress. Functional limitation might reduce independence and social participation, thereby worsening mood, and mood, in turn, may shape patients' appraisal of their overall QoL. If so, mood might act as a mediator between RDA and QoL, and interventions aimed at mood could be an important and potentially more modifiable target than neuropathy itself, for which few effective treatments exist. Most previous research has examined CIPN, activity limitation, mood, and QoL in isolation or in pairs, and few have tested the relationships among them within a single model in colorectal cancer patients. Evidence on whether mood explains the association between RDA and QoL in this population is lacking. Clarifying these relationships could inform supportive care that goes beyond symptom control: rehabilitation and safety education to reduce RDA, and psychological assessment and intervention to improve mood adaptation. Therefore, we conducted a cross-sectional study of colorectal adenocarcinoma patients with CIPN after oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy. We used the Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory to measure CIPN severity, the SALSA scale to assess RDA, the POMS short form to assess negative mood, and the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy–Colorectal (FACT-C) version 4 to measure QoL. We aimed to (1) describe the levels of CIPN, RDA, mood disturbance, and QoL; (2) examine the correlations among these variables; and (3) test, using hierarchical multiple linear regression and Baron and Kenny's mediation procedure, whether mood mediates the relationship between RDA and QoL. We hypothesized that greater RDA would be associated with worse mood and lower QoL, and that negative mood would partially mediate the effect of RDA on QoL. This was a cross-sectional correlational study conducted at the oncology outpatient clinics and chemotherapy wards of a tertiary teaching hospital. The study was approved by the institutional review board of the hospital, and all procedures followed the Declaration of Helsinki. All participants provided written informed consent before data collection. Participants Patients were recruited consecutively. Inclusion criteria were: (1) a histologically confirmed diagnosis of colorectal adenocarcinoma; (2) age of 20 years or older; (3) previous treatment with an oxaliplatin-based regimen (FOLFOX or CAPOX) for at least one cycle; (4) self-reported numbness, tingling, pain, or other sensory symptoms in the hands or feet that began after oxaliplatin treatment, consistent with CIPN; and (5) ability to communicate in Mandarin or Taiwanese and complete questionnaires. Exclusion criteria were: (1) peripheral neuropathy from other causes, such as diabetes mellitus, alcohol abuse, vitamin B12 deficiency, or hereditary neuropathy; (2) brain metastases, cognitive impairment, or a diagnosed psychiatric disorder that might interfere with questionnaire completion; (3) current treatment with other neurotoxic chemotherapy agents; and (4) an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 3 or higher. A minimum sample size was estimated with GPower for multiple linear regression (medium effect size f² = 0.15, α = 0.05, power = 0.80, three to five predictors), which indicated at least 91 participants. We therefore aimed to enroll about 100 patients to allow for incomplete questionnaires. Procedure Eligible patients were identified from medical records and approached by a trained research nurse during clinic visits or chemotherapy sessions. After consent, participants completed a demographic and clinical questionnaire and four self-report instruments in a quiet room, which took approximately 20–30 minutes. Patients who had difficulty reading received item-by-item help from the research nurse, who read the items aloud without interpretation. Clinical data, including cancer stage, chemotherapy regimen, number of cycles, cumulative oxaliplatin dose, and time since the last treatment, were extracted from medical records. Instruments Severity of CIPN. The Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory (NPSI) was used to measure neuropathic symptoms. It includes 12 items covering spontaneous ongoing pain, paroxysmal pain, evoked pain, and paresthesia/dysesthesia, each rated from 0 (none) to 10 (worst imaginable). The total score ranges from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating more severe neuropathic symptoms. Scores were categorized as mild, moderate, or severe for descriptive purposes. The NPSI has shown good reliability and validity in patients with neuropathic pain. In this sample Cronbach's α was calculated. Restriction of daily activity. The Screening of Activity Limitation and Safety Awareness (SALSA) scale was used to evaluate limitations in daily activities and safety awareness related to peripheral nerve damage. It consists of 20 items on activities such as dressing, walking, handling objects, and working, rated from 1 (easy) to 5 (not possible), with additional items on safety awareness. Higher scores indicate greater restriction. Scores were classified as no limitation, mild, moderate, severe, or extreme limitation according to the published cutoffs. In this study, the total score was used as the RDA indicator. Negative mood. The Profile of Mood States Short Form (POMS-SF) was used to assess mood disturbance over the previous week. It has 30 items rated on a five-point scale from 0 (not at all) to 4 (extremely) across five negative subscales (tension-anxiety, depression-dejection, anger-hostility, fatigue-inertia, confusion-bewilderment) and one positive subscale (vigor-activity). The total mood disturbance score was calculated by summing the negative subscale scores and subtracting the vigor score. Higher scores indicate worse mood. The Chinese version has demonstrated acceptable reliability and validity in cancer populations. Quality of life. The Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy–Colorectal (FACT-C) version 4 was used to evaluate QoL. It contains 36 items: the 27-item FACT-General (physical, social/family, emotional, and functional well-being) and a 9-item colorectal cancer subscale. Items are rated from 0 (not at all) to 4 (very much), and after reverse scoring of negatively worded items, higher scores indicate better QoL. The total score ranges from 0 to 144. The scale has been validated in Chinese-speaking populations. Statistical analysis Data were analyzed using SPSS version 22.0. Descriptive statistics (means, standard deviations, frequencies, and percentages) summarized demographic characteristics and scale scores. Distributions were checked with skewness and kurtosis values and the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. Internal consistency of each instrument was evaluated with Cronbach's α. Pearson correlation coefficients were used to examine bivariate relationships among CIPN severity, RDA, mood, and QoL. Group differences in QoL by demographic and clinical variables were tested with independent t tests or one-way analysis of variance, and significant variables were considered as covariates. Hierarchical multiple linear regression was used to identify predictors of QoL. Covariates were entered in the first step, CIPN severity and RDA in the second step, and mood in the final step, so that the incremental variance explained (ΔR²) by each block could be assessed. Assumptions of linearity, normality and homoscedasticity of residuals, independence of errors (Durbin–Watson statistic), and multicollinearity (variance inflation factor < 10, tolerance > 0.1) were checked. The mediating role of mood in the relationship between RDA and QoL was tested using the Baron and Kenny procedure. Partial mediation was inferred if path c′ remained significant but was smaller than c, and full mediation if it became nonsignificant. The proportion mediated was calculated as (c − c′)/c. The significance of the indirect effect was verified with the Sobel test. All tests were two-tailed, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Unilateral cerebral palsy (UCP) is a common form of cerebral palsy, resulting from a non-progressive lesion of the developing brain that predominantly affects one side of the body. Upper limb impairment is a hallmark of the condition and manifests as reduced strength, impaired dexterity, abnormal muscle tone, diminished sensation and, frequently, developmental disregard of the more affected hand [1,2]. These impairments constrain bimanual performance and the execution of daily activities, with consequences for independence, participation and quality of life [3]. Because the motor deficits persist into adulthood, effective and sustainable interventions during childhood and adolescence are a clinical priority. Upper limb rehabilitation in unilateral cerebral palsy Over the past two decades, a number of task-oriented, intensive interventions have accumulated evidence of efficacy. Constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT) and its modified versions, as well as hand-arm bimanual intensive therapy (HABIT), are supported by systematic reviews and randomised trials as effective in improving unimanual capacity and bimanual performance [4–6]. However, these approaches typically demand high dosage, specialised therapists and prolonged attendance at clinical centres. Constraint-based methods can also be poorly tolerated by some children and burdensome for families [7]. Access to such programmes is therefore uneven, and the cost and organisational demands limit their delivery at scale. There is a need for approaches that are engaging, intensive, and deliverable in the child's own environment. Action observation training Action observation training (AOT) is grounded in the discovery of the mirror neuron system, a network of fronto-parietal regions that is active both when an individual executes a goal-directed action and when they observe the same action performed by others [8,9]. Observing actions is thought to activate motor representations and facilitate motor learning, an effect that has been exploited in the rehabilitation of adults after stroke [10,11]. Neuroimaging studies suggest that children with cerebral palsy retain an observation–execution matching mechanism, albeit with altered patterns of activation [12]. This provides a rationale for using AOT in paediatric populations. Initial studies in children with UCP showed that observing videos of goal-directed hand actions followed by their physical execution improved hand function compared with observation of non-motor content [13,14]. Building on this work, the UPper Limb Children Action Observation Training (UPCAT) protocol was developed, in which children watch a sequence of daily-life actions of increasing complexity and then reproduce them. A randomised trial of UPCAT delivered in the clinic reported significant gains in manual ability and bimanual performance that were maintained at follow-up [15]. AOT is low-cost, requires minimal equipment, and is generally attractive to children, making it a good candidate for delivery outside the clinic. Tele-rehabilitation and information and communication technologies Information and communication technologies (ICT) offer an opportunity to extend rehabilitation into the home. Tele-rehabilitation has been shown to be feasible and, in several conditions, comparable with conventional care in adults [16,17]. In paediatric neurorehabilitation, home-based programmes using virtual reality, videogames and remote supervision have been explored, with promising but heterogeneous results and mostly small samples [18,19]. Home delivery can increase training dosage, reduce travel and cost, and embed practice in the context in which skills are used, which may favour transfer to everyday life. Nevertheless, key challenges persist: ensuring adherence, verifying that exercises are performed correctly, and objectively monitoring the amount and quality of practice without continuous in-person supervision [20]. Recent advances in sensing technology can address some of these issues. Sensorised objects can record the kinematics and timing of manipulation tasks, while wearable accelerometers, such as Actigraph devices, provide objective estimates of spontaneous arm use in daily life, a construct that is difficult to capture with clinical scales alone [21,22]. Combining these tools with a remote platform that delivers AOT and allows therapists to tele-monitor performance could yield both a feasible intervention and a richer description of its effects. To our knowledge, no randomised trial has yet tested a tele-monitored, home-based AOT programme in children with UCP. Rationale and aims Given the encouraging evidence for clinic-based UPCAT, and the need for scalable and accessible rehabilitation, we developed Tele-UPCAT, an ICT platform that delivers the UPCAT protocol at home, provides tele-monitoring by clinicians, and integrates sensorised objects for quantitative evaluation. The primary aim of the present randomised controlled trial is to determine whether a 3-week programme of home-based Tele-UPCAT improves bimanual hand performance, measured with the Assisting Hand Assessment, in children and young people with UCP compared with usual care. Secondary aims are to evaluate effects on unimanual capacity, perceived manual ability, participation and environmental factors, and health-related quality of life, and to examine whether any benefits persist at 8 and 24 weeks. Exploratory aims include the analysis of quantitative data from sensorised objects and wearable activity monitors to characterise training performance and daily arm use, and to assess the feasibility and acceptability of the system. We hypothesise that Tele-UPCAT will produce greater improvements in bimanual performance than usual care and that these will be maintained over follow-up. This paper describes the study protocol in order to promote transparency, reduce the risk of selective reporting and facilitate future replication and meta-analysis. Study design and setting This is a single-centre, two-arm, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial with a waitlist control, concealed allocation and blinded outcome assessment. It follows the SPIRIT guidelines for trial protocols [1] and will be reported according to CONSORT [2]. Baseline and clinical assessments will take place at the paediatric rehabilitation unit of the coordinating institution. Training will be delivered at the participants' homes. The trial was prospectively registered (NCT03094455) and approved by the Tuscany Paediatric Ethics Committee (169/2016). Parents or legal guardians will provide written informed consent, and children will give assent according to their age and abilities. Participants Children and young people aged 6–18 years with a diagnosis of unilateral cerebral palsy (UCP) will be recruited from the centre's outpatient clinic and through collaborating services. Inclusion criteria are: (i) confirmed UCP; (ii) Manual Ability Classification System levels I–III [3]; (iii) ability to understand and follow instructions, with sufficient cognitive and attentional capacity to watch video sequences; and (iv) a stable home environment with the family's agreement to host the equipment. Exclusion criteria are: (i) botulinum toxin injection or upper limb surgery in the previous 6 months, or planned during the study; (ii) uncontrolled epilepsy; (iii) severe visual impairment; and (iv) concurrent participation in other experimental upper limb interventions. The sample size (n = 24, 12 per group) was set pragmatically for a feasibility-oriented efficacy trial of a new technological platform, and informed by the effect sizes in earlier action observation training (AOT) studies in UCP [4,5]. Findings will be interpreted as preliminary. Randomisation and blinding An independent researcher not involved in recruitment or assessment will generate the allocation sequence by computer, with permuted blocks and stratification by age band (6–11 and 12–18 years). Allocation will be concealed in sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes opened only after baseline assessment. Participants and therapists cannot be blinded to the intervention. Outcome assessors will be blinded to group allocation. Assisting Hand Assessment (AHA) videos will be scored by a certified rater who is not otherwise involved in the trial. Participants and families will be asked not to disclose group allocation to assessors. Interventions Experimental group (Tele-UPCAT). Participants will complete 3 weeks of home-based AOT with the Tele-UPCAT platform, based on the UPper Limb Children Action Observation Training (UPCAT) protocol [5]. The system comprises a tablet or screen-based interface, a set of sensorised objects, and a web portal for remote supervision. Each daily session lasts about 45 minutes, 5 days per week (15 sessions in total). In each session the child watches a video sequence of a goal-directed, age-appropriate action performed by a child or young person with unimanual or bimanual manipulation (for example grasping, reaching, pouring or using utensils). The child then performs the same action with real objects. The sequences are organised into progressive levels of difficulty and into functional categories. Sensorised objects record usage data, which are transmitted to the portal. A clinician monitors adherence and performance through the portal and contacts the family by telephone or videoconference weekly, or sooner when technical or compliance problems arise. A caregiver will help set up the equipment and encourage the child to complete the exercises, without giving instruction on motor performance. Control group. Participants will continue usual care for 3 weeks, which may include upper limb training, physiotherapy or occupational therapy. The type and amount of usual care will be recorded through a diary or structured interview. After T1, the control group will be offered the same Tele-UPCAT intervention, with the same follow-up schedule. Outcome measures Assessments will take place the week before (T0) and the week after (T1) the intervention or usual-care period. Follow-up will occur at 8 weeks (T2) and 24 weeks (T3) after the end of AOT. The waitlist group will also be assessed the week after their AOT period (T1 plus). Primary outcome. The primary outcome is the AHA [6], which assesses how effectively the affected hand is used in bimanual activity during a semi-structured play session. The session is video-recorded and scored on 22 items, giving a raw score converted to logit-based AHA units (0–100). The primary endpoint is the change in AHA units from T0 to T1. Secondary outcomes. The Melbourne Assessment 2 [7] will evaluate the quality of unilateral upper limb movement. The ABILHAND-Kids [8] questionnaire will assess manual ability as perceived by the parents. The Participation and Environment Measure for Children and Youth (PEM-CY) [9] will measure participation and environmental influences at home, at school and in the community. The Cerebral Palsy Quality of Life Questionnaire (CP QOL) [10] will evaluate wellbeing and quality of life. Quantitative sensor-based measures. Participants will wear ActiGraph GT3X+ accelerometers on both wrists [11] for 7 days at each time point, recording triaxial accelerations. Data will be analysed for the amount of activity of each limb, the use ratio between the affected and unaffected sides, and asymmetry indices. Data from the sensorised objects during training will be used to assess changes in performance over the course of the intervention, such as duration of use and movement quality. Adherence will be quantified as the number of sessions completed and total training time recorded by the platform. Safety and acceptability. Adverse events, technical failures and dropouts will be documented. Parents and children will rate usability and satisfaction with the system through a questionnaire at the end of training. Statistical analysis Analyses will follow the intention-to-treat principle. Descriptive statistics will summarise demographic and clinical characteristics by group. The between-group difference in T1 AHA scores will be tested with analysis of covariance, adjusting for baseline score and the stratification variable. Secondary outcomes will be analysed similarly or, when assumptions are violated, with non-parametric methods. Longitudinal changes across T0–T3, pooling data from both groups after their AOT periods, will be analysed with linear mixed-effects models with participant as a random effect. Effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals will be reported. The threshold for statistical significance is set at α = 0.05 (two-sided), and missing data will be handled with multiple imputation if they exceed 5%. Analyses will be conducted in R or SPSS. Data management and dissemination Data will be pseudonymised and stored on secure servers with restricted access. Results will be disseminated in peer-reviewed journals and at conferences. The study is a registered protocol, and no outcome data have been analysed or are reported here. This section therefore describes the results of the protocol development, the technical implementation of the Tele-UPCAT platform, and the planned structure of the results to be reported on trial completion. Protocol Development and Feasibility Preparation The trial protocol was finalised after approval by the Tuscany Paediatric Ethics Committee (169/2016) and registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03094455). First, a waitlist control design was adopted so that all families would eventually receive AOT. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common primary malignancy of the liver and accounts for approximately 75–85% of primary liver cancers [1]. It ranks among the leading causes of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with particularly high incidence in East Asia and sub-Saharan Africa [2]. Major risk factors include chronic hepatitis B and C virus infection, alcohol abuse, aflatoxin B1 exposure, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, most of which promote liver cirrhosis, the setting in which most HCCs arise [3]. Despite advances in surveillance, surgical resection, liver transplantation, locoregional therapy, and molecularly targeted agents, the prognosis of HCC remains poor. High recurrence rates after resection, frequent diagnosis at an advanced stage, and intrinsic resistance to systemic therapy keep the five-year survival rate low [4,5]. Clinical staging systems and serum alpha-fetoprotein have limited ability to predict individual outcomes, so molecular markers that reflect tumor biology and could guide stratification and therapy are needed [6]. Epigenetic dysregulation in hepatocellular carcinoma Hepatocarcinogenesis is a multistep process involving the accumulation of genetic alterations and epigenetic disturbances. Genomic sequencing studies have shown that mutations in genes encoding chromatin regulators, such as ARID1A, ARID2, and KMT2 family members, are recurrent in HCC, suggesting that disruption of chromatin-modifying machinery contributes substantially to liver tumorigenesis [7,8]. Histone modifications, including acetylation and methylation, control chromatin accessibility and transcription, and aberrant patterns can silence tumor suppressors or activate oncogenic programs [9]. Histone methyltransferases and demethylases are therefore increasingly regarded as potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets in cancer. Inhibitors of EZH2 and DOT1L, for example, have entered clinical evaluation [10]. The SETD1B histone methyltransferase SET domain-containing 1B (SETD1B) belongs to the SET1/COMPASS family of lysine methyltransferases, which also includes SETD1A and the MLL/KMT2 proteins. SETD1B catalyzes mono-, di-, and trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 4 (H3K4), a modification associated with active promoters and gene transcription [11,12]. It acts within a multiprotein complex containing WDR5, RBBP5, ASH2L, DPY30, and CFP1, whose components determine its genomic targeting and catalytic activity [12]. Although SETD1A and SETD1B share a conserved catalytic domain, they are nonredundant and show distinct interaction partners and functions [13]. SETD1B has been implicated in the regulation of the cell cycle, in neuronal and hematopoietic development, and in memory formation, and germline haploinsufficiency or mutations of SETD1B cause a neurodevelopmental syndrome with epilepsy and intellectual disability [14,15]. SETD1B in cancer Accumulating evidence indicates that SETD1B has context-dependent roles in malignancy. Recurrent frameshift mutations in SETD1B occur in microsatellite-unstable gastric and colorectal cancers, indicating a possible tumor-suppressive function in some settings [16]. In contrast, SETD1B has been reported to promote tumor progression in other settings. In breast cancer, SETD1B has been linked to proliferation and to epigenetic regulation of genes involved in cell growth and the response to therapy [17]. In acute myeloid leukemia, the SETD1B-containing complex has been shown to cooperate with oncogenic drivers to maintain leukemic gene expression programs [18]. SETD1B-mediated H3K4 methylation also appears to influence DNA damage responses and genome stability, processes that are central to malignant transformation [19]. Related family members, notably SETD1A, have been shown to promote HCC cell proliferation, migration, and tumor growth, and their overexpression has been correlated with adverse clinical features [20,21]. These findings raise the possibility that SETD1B also participates in liver tumorigenesis. To our knowledge, however, the expression pattern of SETD1B in HCC and its relationship with clinicopathological characteristics and patient outcome have not been systematically investigated. Rationale and objectives of the present study Given the importance of epigenetic regulators in HCC, the oncogenic roles of SETD1B in several other cancers, and the lack of data on SETD1B in the liver, we hypothesized that SETD1B is aberrantly expressed in HCC and is associated with disease progression and prognosis. To test this hypothesis, we measured SETD1B mRNA and protein levels in paired HCC tumor and adjacent non-tumorous tissues by reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction and western blot analysis. We then examined the relationship between SETD1B expression and clinicopathological variables, including tumor size, clinical stage, and liver cirrhosis. Finally, we evaluated the association between SETD1B expression and overall survival using Kaplan–Meier analysis and Cox proportional hazards regression to determine whether SETD1B is an independent prognostic factor. The results are expected to clarify the contribution of SETD1B to HCC progression and to assess its potential as a prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target. Patients and tissue specimens Paired HCC tumor tissues and adjacent non-tumorous liver tissues (collected ≥2 cm from the tumor margin) were obtained from patients who underwent curative hepatectomy at the Department of Hepatobiliary Surgery between January 2010 and December 2014. The inclusion criteria were: (i) histopathological confirmation of HCC; (ii) no preoperative chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or transarterial chemoembolization; (iii) no other concurrent malignancy; and (iv) availability of complete clinicopathological and follow-up data. Patients who died of perioperative complications were excluded. Fresh specimens were snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen within 30 min of resection and stored at −80°C until use. Tumor staging followed the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) TNM system [1], and histological differentiation was graded according to the Edmondson-Steiner criteria [2]. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants, and the study was approved by the institutional ethics committee and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Clinicopathological data and follow-up Demographic and clinical variables were retrieved from medical records, including age, sex, hepatitis B surface antigen status, serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) level, tumor size, tumor number, vascular invasion, differentiation, TNM stage, and the presence of liver cirrhosis (confirmed histologically). Patients were followed up every 3 months during the first 2 years and every 6 months thereafter by serum AFP measurement, abdominal ultrasonography, and computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging when indicated. Overall survival (OS) was defined as the interval from surgery to death from any cause or to the last follow-up. Patients alive at the last contact were censored. RNA extraction and reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) Total RNA was extracted from frozen tissues using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen; Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer's instructions. RNA concentration and purity were assessed by spectrophotometry (A260/A280 ratio of 1.8–2.0), and integrity was verified by agarose gel electrophoresis. One microgram of total RNA was reverse transcribed into cDNA using a PrimeScript RT reagent kit with gDNA Eraser (Takara). qPCR was performed on a real-time PCR system using SYBR Green master mix. Each 20 µl reaction contained 10 µl master mix, 0.4 µM of each primer, and 2 µl diluted cDNA. Cycling conditions were 95°C for 30 sec, followed by 40 cycles of 95°C for 5 sec and 60°C for 30 sec, with a subsequent melting-curve analysis to confirm amplification specificity. GAPDH served as the internal reference gene. All reactions were run in triplicate, and relative expression of SETD1B was calculated using the 2^−ΔΔCq method [3]. For paired analysis, expression in each tumor sample was normalized to that in its matched adjacent tissue. Western blot analysis Tissues were homogenized and lysed in RIPA buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors. Lysates were centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 15 min at 4°C, and protein concentrations in the supernatants were determined using a bicinchoninic acid assay. Equal amounts of protein (40 µg per lane) were separated by 8% SDS-PAGE and transferred onto polyvinylidene difluoride membranes. Membranes were blocked with 5% non-fat milk in TBS containing 0.1% Tween-20 for 1 h at room temperature and incubated overnight at 4°C with a primary antibody against SETD1B (rabbit polyclonal, 1:1000) or GAPDH (1:5000) as the loading control. After washing, membranes were incubated with horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibody (1:5000) for 1 h at room temperature. Immunoreactive bands were visualized using enhanced chemiluminescence reagent and quantified by densitometry with ImageJ software. SETD1B protein levels were expressed relative to GAPDH. Experiments were repeated independently three times. Definition of high and low SETD1B expression Patients were dichotomized into high- and low-SETD1B expression groups based on the tumor-to-adjacent tissue mRNA ratio. A ratio above the median value of the cohort was defined as high expression, and a ratio at or below the median as low expression. The median was chosen to avoid data-driven optimization of the cutoff and the associated risk of overfitting [4]. Public database analysis To provide supportive validation, SETD1B mRNA expression and survival data for liver hepatocellular carcinoma were examined in The Cancer Genome Atlas dataset using publicly accessible web tools, such as GEPIA [5]. Differential expression between tumor and normal tissue was assessed using one-way ANOVA, and survival differences were evaluated by log-rank test. Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS (version 22.0; IBM Corp.) and GraphPad Prism (version 7.0). Continuous variables are presented as the mean ± standard deviation. Differences in SETD1B expression between paired tumor and adjacent tissues were analyzed using the paired Student's t-test or the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, depending on data distribution assessed by the Shapiro-Wilk test. Comparisons among independent groups were made using the unpaired t-test or Mann-Whitney U test. Associations between SETD1B expression and categorical clinicopathological characteristics were evaluated using the χ² test or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. OS curves were estimated by the Kaplan-Meier method and compared using the log-rank test. Univariate Cox proportional hazards regression was used to identify factors associated with OS, and variables with P<0.10 in univariate analysis were entered into a multivariate Cox model to determine independent prognostic factors; the proportional hazards assumption was checked using Schoenfeld residuals. Hazard ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were reported. All tests were two-sided, and P<0.05 was considered to indicate statistically significant differences. SETD1B mRNA and protein are upregulated in HCC tissues To determine whether SETD1B is dysregulated in HCC, we first measured its mRNA expression by RT-qPCR in paired tumor and adjacent non-tumorous tissues from the study cohort. SETD1B transcript levels were significantly higher in tumor tissues than in matched adjacent tissues (P < 0.01), and the increase was observed in most individual pairs (Fig. 1A). Western blot analysis of representative paired specimens showed the same pattern. SETD1B protein was markedly more abundant in tumor lysates than in adjacent tissue lysates, and densitometric quantification normalized to the loading control confirmed a significant difference (Fig. 1B and C). The concordance between transcript and protein levels suggests that the elevated SETD1B in HCC arises largely at the level of transcript abundance, in line with reports of SETD1B overexpression in other malignancies [1,2]. Consistent with this, public transcriptomic datasets such as TCGA-LIHC have also indicated higher SETD1B expression in liver tumors than in normal liver [3]. Association between SETD1B expression and clinicopathological characteristics Patients were divided into low and high SETD1B expression groups according to the median tumor SETD1B mRNA level. We then examined the relationship between SETD1B expression and clinicopathological variables (Table I). High SETD1B expression was significantly associated with larger tumor size (P < 0.05), more advanced clinical stage (P < 0.05) and the presence of liver cirrhosis (P < 0.05). No significant associations were found with age, sex, HBV infection status, serum alpha-fetoprotein level, tumor number or differentiation grade (all P > 0.05). Because tumor size and stage reflect tumor burden and local invasiveness, these associations suggest that SETD1B upregulation accompanies a more aggressive phenotype. The association with cirrhosis is also notable, since cirrhosis is the main background for HCC development and indicates a possible link between chronic liver injury, epigenetic remodeling and SETD1B expression [4]. High SETD1B expression predicts poor survival We next evaluated the prognostic relevance of SETD1B. Kaplan–Meier analysis showed that patients with high SETD1B expression had significantly shorter overall survival than those with low expression (log-rank P < 0.05; Fig. 2A). The divergence between the curves appeared early during follow-up and persisted throughout the observation period. The median survival time in the low-expression group was clearly longer than in the high-expression group. A similar trend was observed for disease-free survival, with patients with high SETD1B expression experiencing earlier recurrence (Fig. 2B). Thus, elevated SETD1B expression identifies a subgroup of patients with an unfavorable clinical course. Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood, with an incidence of approximately 1 in 16,000 to 18,000 live births [1,2]. Most cases are diagnosed before the age of five years, and in high-income countries survival now exceeds 95% [3]. Over the past two decades, the management of intraocular retinoblastoma has shifted from enucleation and external beam radiation therapy toward globe-salvage strategies. These include systemic chemoreduction with focal consolidation, intra-arterial chemotherapy, and intravitreal chemotherapy [4,5]. External beam radiation has largely been abandoned because of its association with orbital growth impairment and, in patients with germline mutations, a markedly increased risk of second malignancies [6,7]. Ophthalmic artery chemosurgery (OAC), first described by Kaneko and later refined by Abramson and colleagues, delivers chemotherapy directly into the ophthalmic artery by selective catheterization [8,9]. Typical agents are melphalan, often combined with topotecan and, less often, carboplatin. Delivering the drug locally achieves high intraocular concentrations while limiting systemic exposure, which allows lower total doses than intravenous regimens [10]. Large series have reported ocular salvage rates that compare favorably with those of systemic chemotherapy, especially in advanced eyes and as primary therapy [11,12]. As a result, OAC has become a first-line treatment at many centers worldwide. Systemic toxicity is therefore a central consideration when comparing OAC with intravenous chemotherapy. Systemic chemoreduction for retinoblastoma, typically vincristine, etoposide, and carboplatin, is associated with myelosuppression, ototoxicity, and infection risk [13,14]. Reported adverse effects of OAC include transient neutropenia, vascular complications of the eye and orbit, and procedural risks related to anesthesia and catheterization [15,16]. Since OAC is given in a small number of sessions, usually monthly, over several months, its effect on children's overall health has generally been considered modest. Even so, data on its long-term systemic consequences are still limited. Growth is a sensitive indicator of a child's general health and of the cumulative physiologic burden of illness and therapy. Studies of other pediatric malignancies, particularly acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), have shown that children receiving systemic chemotherapy often have reduced linear growth velocity and altered weight gain during treatment [17,18]. Proposed mechanisms include direct effects of cytotoxic agents on the growth plate, disturbance of the growth hormone–insulin-like growth factor axis, poor nutrition, and the effects of glucocorticoids, which are a major component of ALL regimens [19,20]. Although many patients show catch-up growth after therapy, some have persistent deficits in final height or an increased risk of obesity [21,22]. Cranial irradiation and alkylating agents add further risk to endocrine function and growth [23]. Retinoblastoma survivors may be vulnerable to growth abnormalities for several reasons. Patients with germline RB1 mutations may have an altered endocrine milieu, and deletions involving 13q14 have been linked to growth restriction and developmental delay [24,25]. Radiation to the orbit and adjacent structures, historically common, can affect craniofacial growth, and radiation near the hypothalamic–pituitary region can cause endocrine deficiencies [26]. Patients treated with systemic chemotherapy are exposed to agents that may affect growth, although few studies have examined this question in retinoblastoma specifically. Existing long-term follow-up studies of retinoblastoma survivors have focused mainly on second cancers, visual outcomes, and mortality rather than somatic growth [7,27]. Evidence on the growth of children treated with OAC is particularly scarce. These children are very young at treatment, a period of rapid growth when nutritional and metabolic disturbances may have disproportionate effects. Many receive repeated general anesthesia with fasting, which could transiently affect feeding. In addition, a substantial proportion of children referred for OAC have already received systemic chemotherapy elsewhere, either as initial therapy or after failure of chemoreduction. Whether prior systemic exposure modifies growth during or after OAC is unknown. Distinguishing children treated with OAC alone from those with previous systemic treatment can therefore help separate the effects of the local intra-arterial approach from those of cumulative systemic therapy. Clarifying these patterns is clinically important. Parents of children with retinoblastoma are often concerned about the late effects of treatment, and the absence of data limits counseling. If OAC does not affect growth, this would support its use as a systemically sparing alternative, whereas evidence of growth disturbance would call for closer nutritional and endocrine surveillance. Growth data also contribute to the broader assessment of treatment-related morbidity in survivorship care [28]. We therefore conducted a retrospective review of retinoblastoma patients treated with OAC at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center between 2006 and 2016. We compared growth velocity during treatment, as well as height and weight percentiles up to three years after treatment, among children who received OAC alone (naïve), those who received systemic chemotherapy before presenting for OAC (secondary), and a small group who received single-agent systemic chemotherapy before OAC (bridge). We excluded children who had received external beam radiation and those with genetic syndromes independently associated with growth abnormalities. Our objectives were to describe short-term growth velocity during OAC, to determine whether the number of treatments influenced growth, and to characterize long-term height and weight trajectories in this population. This retrospective, single-center study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. A waiver of informed consent was granted because of the retrospective design and minimal risk to participants. The study adhered to institutional policies for the protection of patient health information. Study population We reviewed the records of all consecutive children with retinoblastoma (Rb) who were treated with ophthalmic artery chemosurgery (OAC) at MSKCC between 2006 and 2016. A total of 341 patients were identified from the institutional Rb database and the electronic medical record. Diagnosis was established by dilated fundus examination under anesthesia, supplemented by imaging (ultrasonography and magnetic resonance imaging) as clinically indicated. Eyes were classified according to the International Classification of Retinoblastoma [1]. Patients were excluded if they had received external beam radiation therapy, because radiation to the orbit and adjacent structures is independently associated with craniofacial and growth abnormalities [2,3]. Patients with genetic syndromes known to affect growth (for example, chromosomal disorders such as trisomy 21 or deletion 13q syndrome) were also excluded. Children with insufficient anthropometric data to calculate growth velocity were excluded from the relevant analyses. Treatment groups Patients were classified according to their chemotherapy history before and during OAC. Children who received OAC as their only chemotherapy were classified as naive. Children who were initially treated with systemic intravenous chemotherapy elsewhere or at our center and who subsequently presented for OAC were classified as secondary. A small group of children who received single-agent systemic chemotherapy (typically carboplatin) shortly before or between OAC cycles, as a bridge to OAC, were classified as bridge. Because of the small size of the bridge group, formal comparative analyses focused on the naive and secondary groups. Ophthalmic artery chemosurgery OAC was performed under general anesthesia using a technique described previously [4,5]. Briefly, the ophthalmic artery was catheterized via femoral artery access, either directly or through a microcatheter navigated into the internal carotid artery in a "nonselective" approach in the case of small or tortuous vessels. Heparin was administered intravenously during the procedure. Melphalan was the primary agent, with dosing adjusted for patient age and weight, and topotecan and carboplatin were added in selected cases of refractory or recurrent disease according to institutional practice. Treatments were generally repeated at intervals of approximately 3–4 weeks, and the number of cycles was determined by tumor response on examination under anesthesia. The total number of OAC treatments per patient was recorded. Data collection Demographic and clinical variables were abstracted from the medical record, including sex, age at diagnosis, laterality, heritable status (when genetic testing was available), eye stage, previous treatments, treatment group, number of OAC cycles, and dates of treatment. Height (or length for children unable to stand) and weight were obtained from clinic and anesthesia records, where measurements are routinely taken by trained staff using standardized equipment. Anthropometric data were recorded at two phases. During the short-term phase, height and weight were recorded at monthly intervals throughout the OAC treatment course. During the long-term phase, measurements were recorded annually for up to 3 years after completion of OAC. Where several measurements were available within a window, the one closest to the scheduled time point was used. Age- and sex-specific percentiles for height and weight were calculated using the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) growth charts [6] (or World Health Organization charts for children younger than 2 years [7]), allowing comparison with a reference population and across ages. Outcome measures The primary outcome was growth velocity during OAC (short-term), defined as the change in height and weight per unit time between the first and last measurements within the treatment period, and expressed in cm/month and kg/month. Secondary outcomes were (1) the association between number of OAC treatments and growth velocity and (2) height and weight percentiles at 1, 2, and 3 years after the end of OAC (long-term). Statistical analysis Descriptive statistics were used to summarize patient characteristics, with medians and ranges for continuous variables and frequencies and percentages for categorical variables. Differences between naive and secondary groups at baseline were assessed with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test for continuous variables and the chi-square or Fisher exact test for categorical variables. Short-term growth velocity was compared between groups using linear mixed-effects models, with repeated monthly measurements nested within patients and random intercepts to account for within-patient correlation [8]. Fixed effects included time, treatment group, and their interaction, with adjustment for age at start of treatment and sex. A significant time-by-group interaction was interpreted as a difference in growth velocity. The relationship between number of OAC treatments and growth velocity was assessed by adding the number of cycles, and its interaction with time, to the models, and by Spearman correlation coefficients. Long-term height and weight percentiles at each annual time point were summarized as means with 95% confidence intervals and compared between groups with two-sample t tests, or Wilcoxon rank-sum tests where distributions departed from normality. Changes in percentiles over time within groups were evaluated using mixed-effects models. Given the limited sample size of the bridge group, results for these patients are presented descriptively. Attrition over follow-up was anticipated, and the number of patients contributing data at each time point is reported. Missing data were not imputed, and the mixed models used all available observations under the assumption that data were missing at random. All tests were two-sided, and a P value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant. No adjustment for multiple comparisons was made for secondary analyses, which should be regarded as exploratory. Analyses were performed using R (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) [9]. A total of 341 patients treated with OAC between 2006 and 2016 were reviewed. After exclusion of children who had received external beam radiation therapy and those with genetic syndromes known to affect growth, the remaining patients were classified by treatment history as naïve (OAC only), secondary (systemic chemotherapy before presentation for OAC), or bridge (single-agent systemic chemotherapy before OAC). The bridge group was small and was not included in the comparative statistical analyses. Descriptive data for this group are reported separately where relevant. Height and weight were available monthly during OAC and annually thereafter for up to three years. Patient characteristics The naïve group comprised the majority of the cohort, and the secondary group was considerably smaller. The groups were broadly comparable in sex distribution and age at the start of OAC. Secondary patients had, as expected, more advanced disease at presentation and more frequently had bilateral involvement, consistent with the referral pattern of children who had failed or been unable to complete systemic therapy elsewhere [1,2]. The median number of OAC cycles was similar between groups, and the number of cycles ranged from one to the maximum permitted by the treatment protocol. Because of loss to follow-up and variable timing of referral, the number of patients with available measurements decreased at each annual time point, and the denominators are given with each analysis.
