Drug-induced delayed cardiac repolarization, manifested as prolongation of the QT interval on the surface electrocardiogram (ECG), is associated with an increased risk of torsade de pointes (TdP), a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation and sudden cardiac death [1,2]. Regulatory concern about this liability grew during the 1990s, when several widely used non-cardiovascular drugs, including terfenadine, cisapride, grepafloxacin, and sertindole, were withdrawn or restricted because of QT-related fatalities [3,4]. The principal mechanism is inhibition of the rapid component of the delayed rectifier potassium current (IKr), conducted by the hERG channel, although modulation of other cardiac ion currents can modify the net effect on repolarization [5]. Because QT prolongation is an imperfect yet pragmatic biomarker of proarrhythmic potential, it became the central focus of cardiac safety assessment during drug development. The ICH S7B and E14 Framework In 2005, the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) adopted two complementary guidelines. ICH S7B describes nonclinical evaluation, including in vitro hERG assays and in vivo QT studies in animals, whereas ICH E14 describes the clinical evaluation of QT/QTc interval prolongation for non-antiarrhythmic drugs [6,7]. E14 recommended a dedicated "thorough QT" (TQT) study, typically conducted in healthy volunteers, to determine whether a drug causes a small but meaningful effect on cardiac repolarization. The regulatory threshold of concern was an upper bound of the one-sided 95% confidence interval for the placebo-corrected, baseline-adjusted change in QTc (ΔΔQTc) of 10 ms, corresponding to a mean effect of approximately 5 ms or greater. Studies were required to include supratherapeutic exposures and a positive control, most commonly moxifloxacin, to demonstrate assay sensitivity, that is, the ability of the study to detect a QTc effect of about 5 ms [7,8]. The TQT paradigm was highly successful in its principal aim. It standardized the evaluation of QT liability, and no drug approved after its introduction has been withdrawn for TdP-related events [9]. However, it also carried considerable costs. A typical TQT study is a resource-intensive undertaking, often using a four-arm crossover design with placebo, therapeutic and supratherapeutic doses, and a positive control, in a population of 40 to 60 participants or more. Studies are frequently conducted late in phase 1 or even in phase 2, so QT information is not available to inform dose selection or decisions on the continued development of a compound [10]. In addition, supratherapeutic exposures cannot always be achieved safely for drugs with tolerability limitations, such as many oncology agents, and the use of healthy volunteers is often inappropriate for cytotoxic or otherwise toxic agents [11]. Evolution Toward Concentration–QTc Modeling Experience accumulated after 2005 showed that the central relationship of interest, that between plasma drug concentration and QTc change, could be characterized with considerable precision. Early analyses of data from TQT studies demonstrated that linear mixed-effects concentration–QTc models produced conclusions consistent with those of the conventional by-time-point analysis, and often with greater statistical power [12,13]. Further work, including the Consortium for Innovative Cardiac Safety (CSRC) and Food and Drug Administration (FDA) collaboration with the Interdisciplinary Review Team for QT studies, established that model-based approaches could detect effects of around 10 ms with exposures that were not necessarily supratherapeutic, provided the model was properly specified and the concentration range was adequate [14,15]. Retrospective evaluations of data sets supported the view that moxifloxacin sensitivity could be demonstrated in small studies using such models [16]. These findings were reflected in the ICH E14 Questions and Answers (R3) document in 2015, which recognized that exposure–response (ER) analysis of intensive ECG data collected in early-phase studies, such as single ascending dose (SAD) and multiple ascending dose (MAD) studies, could serve as the primary basis for QT assessment and substitute for a dedicated TQT study [17]. When the analysis is adequately designed and a negative result is obtained, a TQT study may be waived. This approach requires high-quality, time-matched ECG and pharmacokinetic sampling, adequate representation of the expected clinical exposure range (including relevant increases from intrinsic and extrinsic factors), and prespecified analysis methods. Questions regarding the necessity and form of a positive control, whether in a separate crossover study or embedded within the early-phase trial, remain an important point of discussion [17,18]. Opportunities and Challenges Integrating ECG assessment into first-in-human studies offers clear advantages. QT information can be obtained earlier, from a larger number of participants across a wide range of concentrations, and can support go/no-go decisions, design of later trials, and the extent of ECG monitoring required in patients [19]. The approach is also consistent with the 3Rs and with efficient resource use, and it allows evaluation of QT effects of metabolites, as well as studies in patient populations when healthy volunteers are inappropriate. At the same time, it presents methodological challenges, including the handling of hysteresis, the nonlinearity of concentration–effect relationships, the effects of heart rate correction, the limited ability of small studies to detect assay sensitivity, and the quality of ECG extraction and central reading [20,21]. Questions also remain regarding the role of the ICH E14/S7B Q&As on integrated nonclinical and clinical evidence and the Comprehensive in vitro Proarrhythmia Assay (CiPA) initiative [22]. In this review, we describe the current state of ER modeling of intensive ECG data from early clinical studies, outline the statistical and design requirements, discuss approaches to positive control, and consider the challenges and opportunities this alternative approach presents for assessing QT liability. Literature Search and Selection Strategy This review was conducted as a structured narrative synthesis of the regulatory, methodological, and clinical literature on concentration-QTc (C-QTc) analysis of intensive electrocardiogram (ECG) data from early-phase clinical studies. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from January 2005 (publication of ICH E14/S7B guidance) through the most recent complete calendar year before submission. Search terms combined controlled vocabulary and free text: "QT interval," "QTc prolongation," "thorough QT study," "concentration-QTc," "exposure-response," "linear mixed-effects model," "early phase," "first-in-human," "positive control," and "moxifloxacin." Regulatory documents were obtained directly from the websites of the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH), the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the European Medicines Agency (EMA), Health Canada, and Japan's PMDA. These included ICH E14 and its Questions & Answers (Q&A) revisions, particularly R3 (2015), S7B, and the FDA Interdisciplinary Review Team (IRT) QT consultation summaries [1–3]. Reference lists of key articles were hand-searched, and conference proceedings of the Cardiac Safety Research Consortium (CSRC) were screened. Eligibility Criteria Eligible sources were: (i) regulatory guidance or Q&A documents; (ii) methodological papers on statistical modeling of C-QTc relationships; (iii) studies comparing results of C-QTc analyses with dedicated thorough QT (TQT) studies; (iv) studies of assay sensitivity, including positive-control designs; and (v) case examples of drugs for which C-QTc analysis was submitted as primary evidence. Articles were excluded if they were non-English, addressed only non-clinical proarrhythmia models without translational ECG data, or provided insufficient methodological detail. Two reviewers independently screened titles, abstracts, and full texts; disagreements were resolved by consensus. Data Extraction and Synthesis For each included source, we extracted: study design (single/multiple ascending dose, crossover or parallel), population, dose range and achieved exposures relative to the clinically relevant supratherapeutic exposure, ECG acquisition (extraction method, replicate number, time points, and digital recorder type), QT correction method, model structure, covariate handling, handling of hysteresis, criteria for declaring a negative study, and positive-control strategy. Findings were synthesized qualitatively and grouped by theme: regulatory evolution, analytic framework, positive-control requirements, and challenges/opportunities. Quantitative performance metrics reported in comparative studies (for example, concordance between C-QTc predictions and TQT outcomes) were tabulated but not pooled, owing to heterogeneity. Analytic Framework for Exposure–Response Modeling To ground the review, we summarize the reference analytic approach described in the guidance and supporting literature [2–5]. The primary endpoint is the placebo-corrected change-from-baseline QTc (ΔΔQTc). Individual QT intervals are typically corrected using Fridericia (QTcF) or a population- or study-specific correction, with adequacy assessed by examining the slope of QTc versus RR in drug-free data. Time-matched ECGs are paired with plasma concentrations of the parent drug and, where relevant, active metabolites. The prespecified model is generally a linear mixed-effects model of the form: ΔQTcij = (θ₀ + η₀ᵢ) + (θ₁ + η₁ᵢ)·Cij + θTRT·TRTi + θBL·(QTcBL,i − mean QTcBL) + εij, where Cij is the concentration for subject i at time j, θ₀ is the intercept, θ₁ is the slope, η terms are random effects, and εij is the residual error. Time effects may be included as covariates. Alternatives to linearity (Emax, log-linear, quadratic) are evaluated using graphical diagnostics and information criteria (Akaike), though linear models are favored for prespecification. Hysteresis is assessed by plotting mean ΔΔQTc against mean concentration over time, and, if present, accommodated with an effect-compartment model. Model adequacy is evaluated through goodness-of-fit plots, residual diagnostics, and visual predictive checks comparing observed quantiles with model-based predictions across concentration deciles. Decision Criteria A negative result is concluded when the upper bound of the two-sided 90% confidence interval of the model-predicted ΔΔQTc at the geometric mean Cmax of the highest clinically relevant exposure scenario (for example, with intrinsic or extrinsic factors) lies below 10 ms [1,2]. We reviewed how sources defined the relevant exposure scenario, and how extrapolation beyond observed concentrations was justified or restricted. Assessment of Assay Sensitivity Literature on assay sensitivity was reviewed according to three strategies: inclusion of a concurrent positive control (usually moxifloxacin 400 mg) in the early-phase study, a separate dedicated positive-control study used to demonstrate the sensitivity of the investigative site and ECG methodology, and the use of a nested or in-study "bias" assessment. For each, we extracted the detection threshold (lower bound of the one-sided 95% confidence interval of ΔΔQTc >5 ms), the estimated effect size at the moxifloxacin Cmax (approximately 12–14 ms), sample size requirements, and the use of concentration-QTc modeling of the control. Statistical power calculations reported in simulation studies were summarized, and operational considerations (blinding, crossover logistics, and costs) were recorded. Quality Appraisal No formal risk-of-bias instrument was applied because most sources were methodological or regulatory. Instead, we qualitatively appraised the transparency of prespecification, adequacy of exposure coverage, ECG quality control, and consistency with regulatory recommendations. Where interpretation differed between agencies, both positions were reported. Current Landscape of Exposure–Response Analysis of Intensive ECG Data Regulatory acceptance and uptake. Following the 2015 Q&A revision to ICH E14, concentration–QTc (C-QTc) modeling has been accepted as a primary analysis for excluding a clinically relevant QTc effect, provided that specific design and model-validation conditions are met [1,2]. Published experience from the FDA Interdisciplinary Review Team for QT Studies indicates that submissions using C-QTc analysis of early-phase data have increased steadily, and that a substantial proportion of these have led to a waiver of a dedicated TQT study [3]. The regulatory threshold remains unchanged: the upper bound of the two-sided 90% confidence interval for the model-predicted placebo-corrected change-from-baseline QTc (ΔΔQTc) at the relevant clinical exposure must fall below 10 ms [1]. Evidence from comparative analyses shows that conclusions from C-QTc modeling of single-ascending-dose (SAD) data agree closely with those from subsequent TQT studies, with concordance generally exceeding 90% for negative outcomes [4,5]. Design prerequisites. Studies that support primary C-QTc analysis share several features. First, ECGs are extracted in replicate from continuous recordings or from digitally acquired triplicate tracings at time points matched to pharmacokinetic (PK) sampling, covering the expected Tmax and the elimination phase [2]. Second, baseline ECGs are collected on the day before dosing or predose, enabling baseline adjustment. Third, a placebo arm is included to permit correction for circadian and procedural variability. Fourth, doses must produce exposures that exceed the anticipated worst-case clinical scenario, typically with a supratherapeutic margin that accounts for intrinsic and extrinsic factors such as renal or hepatic impairment and drug–drug interactions [1,6]. Where the maximum tolerated dose cannot achieve such multiples, the guidance accepts a reduced margin, provided that the upper confidence bound is correspondingly narrow and the justification is explicit [2]. The immune system is essential for maintaining homeostasis, defending against pathogens, and surveilling for malignant transformation. Its dysregulation, however, underlies a wide spectrum of chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, and multiple sclerosis [1,2]. Over the past two decades, therapeutic strategies that modulate immune pathways have transformed the management of these conditions. Biologic agents targeting tumor necrosis factor, interleukin (IL)-6, IL-17, IL-23, and co-stimulatory molecules have been joined by small molecule inhibitors directed at intracellular signaling nodes such as Janus kinases (JAKs), tyrosine kinase 2 (TYK2), spleen tyrosine kinase, Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK), phosphodiesterase 4, and calcineurin [3–5]. The expanding repertoire of immune targets has created considerable opportunity, but also a growing need to understand how each mechanism shapes immune function in humans. Because the immune system is highly interconnected and redundant, pharmacological modulation of a given target rarely affects only the pathogenic process of interest. Immunosuppression is a recognized liability of immunomodulatory therapies and may manifest as increased risk of serious bacterial, viral, fungal, and opportunistic infections, reactivation of latent infections such as tuberculosis and herpes zoster, impaired vaccine responses, and possibly malignancy [6,7]. The safety experience with JAK inhibitors illustrates this challenge: despite clear efficacy, class-associated risks including infections, thromboembolism, and malignancy have prompted regulatory warnings and renewed debate about the relationship between selectivity, pathway biology, and clinical risk [8,9]. Distinct mechanisms carry distinct risk profiles; for example, inhibition of IL-17 is associated with mucocutaneous candidiasis, whereas inhibition of TNF is linked to granulomatous infections [10]. These observations indicate that each therapeutic mechanism leaves a characteristic "immune fingerprint," defined by the specific innate and adaptive functions it attenuates, spares, or enhances. Defining this fingerprint early in drug discovery would help prioritize candidates with the most favorable benefit–risk balance. In practice, however, preclinical characterization of novel compounds is typically compound- and mechanism-centric. Potency and selectivity are assessed against the intended target and related off-targets, and efficacy is evaluated in a limited number of cellular assays or animal models chosen for their relevance to the target pathway. Such approaches provide little information on the breadth of immune functions affected, and they rarely allow direct comparison with clinically used agents whose safety profiles are known. Animal models, while valuable, are limited by species differences in immune cell composition, receptor expression, cytokine networks, and drug sensitivity, and they often fail to predict human immune responses or infection risk [11,12]. Genetically engineered and humanized models partially address these limitations but are costly and low-throughput, and thus poorly suited to routine profiling of multiple compounds. Human primary cell systems offer an attractive alternative. Assays using peripheral blood mononuclear cells, whole blood, or isolated immune subsets can capture human-specific biology and have been widely used to examine cytokine release, T cell proliferation, and cell activation [13,14]. Nonetheless, most reported assays interrogate a single cell type or stimulus in isolation, and they differ in donor sources, readouts, and stimulation conditions, which complicates cross-study comparison. Cells in blood also lack the tissue context in which many immune responses occur. Human tissue-derived systems, including tonsil, lymph node, spleen, and skin explants or cell preparations, preserve a more physiological representation of cellular diversity, antigen-presenting cell–lymphocyte interactions, and, in the case of secondary lymphoid organs, the capacity to support B cell activation and antibody production [15,16]. Tonsillar tissue, for instance, has been used to model recall antigen responses, T follicular helper cell function, and vaccine responses ex vivo [17]. Leveraging such material within a standardized panel of functional assays could yield a more comprehensive and translationally relevant view of drug effects. An ideal platform for immune profiling should satisfy several criteria. It should cover both innate functions (such as myeloid cell cytokine production, type I interferon responses, and natural killer cell activity) and adaptive functions (such as T cell activation, proliferation, and differentiation, and B cell activation and antibody secretion). It should use human material and physiologically relevant stimuli, employ quantitative readouts that permit concentration–response analysis, and include benchmark therapeutics for context. Finally, it should enable integration of results across assays into a summary of immune impact that can be interpreted alongside pharmacokinetic and efficacy data, for example by relating inhibition to free drug exposure at clinically relevant doses [18]. Here, we describe the development of a human tissue-based functional assay platform designed to meet these criteria. The platform comprises a series of complementary assays measuring a range of innate and adaptive immune responses, and it was used to evaluate small molecule inhibitors of immune targets together with clinically used immunomodulatory agents. We show that the platform can generate qualitative and quantitative immune fingerprints that distinguish mechanisms of action, reveal differences in the breadth and magnitude of immunosuppression among compounds, and provide a framework for comparing novel inhibitors with established therapies. We propose that this approach can support more informed decision-making in the discovery of immune-targeted therapeutics and improve the prediction of their benefit–risk profiles in the treatment of immune-mediated disorders. Human primary cells and tissue sources Peripheral blood from healthy adult donors was obtained under informed consent from an accredited blood bank, in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and institutional ethical approval. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were isolated by density gradient centrifugation using Ficoll-Paque PLUS [1]. Whole blood was used within 4 h of collection for assays requiring a native cellular and plasma environment. Primary human CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, B cells, NK cells and monocytes were enriched by negative magnetic selection (purity >90% by flow cytometry). Monocyte-derived macrophages and dendritic cells were generated by culturing CD14+ monocytes for 6 days with M-CSF (50 ng/mL) or GM-CSF (50 ng/mL) plus IL-4 (20 ng/mL), respectively [2]. Human tonsil tissue from routine tonsillectomy was obtained with consent, mechanically dissociated, and filtered to yield single-cell suspensions for lymphoid tissue-based assays of T follicular helper–B cell interactions [3]. Cells were cultured in RPMI-1640 supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum, 2 mM L-glutamine, 100 U/mL penicillin and 100 µg/mL streptomycin at 37 °C and 5% CO2. Compounds Reference immunomodulators included the JAK inhibitors tofacitinib and upadacitinib, the BTK inhibitor ibrutinib, the calcineurin inhibitor cyclosporine A, the S1P receptor modulator fingolimod, the glucocorticoid dexamethasone, and the antimetabolite mycophenolic acid, selected to represent clinically used immunological therapies. Test compounds were small-molecule inhibitors of immune targets. All compounds were dissolved in DMSO and tested in 8-point, half-log concentration series with a final DMSO concentration of 0.1%. Concentrations were interpreted relative to unbound human plasma exposure at clinically efficacious doses where available. Vehicle controls were included on every plate. Innate immune function assays Cytokine release from whole blood was assessed after pre-incubation with compound for 1 h followed by stimulation with LPS (TLR4; 100 ng/mL), R848 (TLR7/8; 1 µg/mL), or poly(I:C) (TLR3; 10 µg/mL) for 18–24 h. Plasmacytoid dendritic cell responses were measured in PBMCs stimulated with CpG-A (TLR9; 1 µM) for IFN-α production. NLRP3 inflammasome activity was tested in monocytes primed with LPS (100 ng/mL, 3 h) and activated with nigericin (10 µM, 1 h), with IL-1β measured in supernatants [4]. Macrophage phagocytosis was quantified using pH-sensitive fluorescent bioparticles by live-cell imaging. NK cell cytotoxicity was determined by co-culturing IL-2–activated NK cells with CFSE-labeled K562 target cells at effector:target ratios of 5:1 for 4 h, and target cell death was measured using a viability dye by flow cytometry [5]. Neutrophil oxidative burst was measured in whole blood by dihydrorhodamine-123 oxidation after PMA stimulation. Adaptive immune function assays T cell activation and proliferation were measured in PBMCs or purified T cells labeled with CellTrace Violet and stimulated with anti-CD3/CD28 beads (1:1 bead:cell ratio) for 4–5 days. Proliferation, activation markers (CD25, CD69), and cytokines (IFN-γ, IL-2, TNF, IL-17A) were assessed by flow cytometry and multiplex immunoassay. Antigen-specific recall responses were evaluated by stimulating PBMCs with CMV pp65 peptide pool, tetanus toxoid, or Staphylococcal enterotoxin B for 5–7 days. The mixed lymphocyte reaction used CD4+ T cells co-cultured with allogeneic monocyte-derived dendritic cells (10:1) for 5 days [6]. T helper differentiation was assessed by culturing naive CD4+ T cells under Th1, Th2, Th17 and regulatory T cell polarizing conditions with defined cytokine cocktails for 5–6 days, followed by intracellular cytokine or FOXP3 staining. B cell proliferation and differentiation were tested in purified B cells stimulated with CD40L, anti-IgM, CpG and IL-2/IL-21 for 6–7 days, with plasmablast frequency (CD27+CD38hi) and IgG/IgM secretion measured by flow cytometry and ELISA [3]. In tonsil cell cultures, stimulation with SEB was used to induce T–B cooperation, and CXCL13 and immunoglobulin production were quantified. Cell viability and exposure controls Cytotoxicity was assessed in parallel for each assay using a fixable viability dye or ATP-based luminescence (CellTiter-Glo). Compound effects were considered functional only when viability exceeded 80% of vehicle control. Compound binding to serum proteins was accounted for by comparing potencies in 10% FBS and 50% human serum in selected assays. Flow cytometry and cytokine measurement Cells were stained with fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies after Fc receptor blocking and acquired on a BD LSRFortessa or Cytek Aurora cytometer. Data were analyzed in FlowJo v10 using a consistent gating strategy defined with fluorescence-minus-one controls. Cytokines were quantified using Meso Scale Discovery multiplex electrochemiluminescence assays or ELISA according to manufacturers’ instructions. Data analysis and immune fingerprint generation Responses were normalized to vehicle (0%) and maximal inhibition by a reference control (100%) per assay. Concentration–response curves were fitted using four-parameter nonlinear regression to derive IC50 and maximal inhibition values. Each experiment used at least three independent donors, with technical duplicates. Assay quality was monitored by Z′ factor (>0.4 required) and reference compound potency within threefold of historical values. For the fingerprint, pIC50 values for each compound-assay pair were scaled and organized into a matrix; compounds were also scored by potency shift relative to projected free clinical exposure. Hierarchical clustering (Euclidean distance, Ward linkage) and principal component analysis were applied to compare test compounds with reference immunomodulators [7]. Qualitative impact was classified as none, partial (<50% maximal inhibition) or strong (≥50%), and quantitative impact was expressed as an aggregate immune suppression score, calculated as the mean normalized inhibition across assays weighted by functional domain (innate, T cell, B cell). Donor variability was assessed by coefficient of variation and mixed-effects models with donor as a random effect. Analyses were done in R (v4.2) and GraphPad Prism 9; P<0.05 was considered statistically significant, with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. To establish a platform capable of profiling immune function impact, we assembled a panel of primary human cell-based assays covering innate and adaptive immunity. Assays were run in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), whole blood, and isolated T cell, B cell, monocyte, and NK cell populations from healthy donors. Readouts included cytokine release, proliferation, activation marker expression, and cytotoxicity. Reference compounds with defined mechanisms and clinical use were tested in 8-point concentration-response format across at least three independent donors. These included the JAK inhibitors tofacitinib and baricitinib, the calcineurin inhibitor cyclosporine A, the S1P receptor modulator fingolimod, the antimetabolite mycophenolic acid, the glucocorticoid dexamethasone, the BTK inhibitor ibrutinib, and the p38 MAPK inhibitor SB203580. Assay performance and reproducibility All assays met predefined quality criteria. Z′ factors for stimulated versus unstimulated controls exceeded 0.5 in 14 of 16 assays, and the remaining two (NK cytotoxicity and B cell differentiation) ranged from 0.35 to 0.48, which we considered acceptable given the primary-cell format. Inter-donor variability in maximal response was moderate (coefficient of variation 18–35%), but potency estimates for reference compounds were consistent across donors, with IC50 values generally varying within 3-fold. Cyclosporine A inhibited anti-CD3/CD28-induced IL-2 production with a mean IC50 of 12 nM, and tofacitinib inhibited IL-6-induced STAT3 phosphorylation in CD4⁺ T cells with an IC50 in the low-nanomolar range, in agreement with published values [1,2]. Dexamethasone suppressed LPS-induced TNF-α in monocytes at sub-nanomolar concentrations, consistent with literature [3]. Cell viability was monitored in parallel, and values reported below reflect inhibition at concentrations without significant cytotoxicity unless stated otherwise. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD), accounting for roughly 40–50% of all mortality in this population [1,2]. A substantial proportion of these deaths are sudden cardiac death (SCD), and the annual incidence of SCD among patients receiving hemodialysis is estimated to be several times higher than in the general population [3,4]. Although coronary artery disease is highly prevalent in ESRD, traditional ischemic mechanisms explain only part of this excess risk. Structural and electrophysiological remodeling, including left ventricular hypertrophy, myocardial fibrosis, autonomic dysfunction, vascular calcification, and abrupt shifts in electrolytes and volume during dialysis, creates a substrate that favors both tachyarrhythmias and bradyarrhythmias [5–7]. Arrhythmias in patients with chronic kidney disease Atrial fibrillation is common in patients on dialysis, with reported prevalence of 7–27%, and is associated with increased risk of stroke and mortality [8,9]. Ventricular arrhythmias, including non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT), are also frequent and have been linked to left ventricular dysfunction and adverse outcomes [10,11]. In addition, recent evidence suggests that bradyarrhythmias, rather than ventricular tachyarrhythmias, may be the predominant mechanism of sudden death in dialysis patients. Continuous monitoring in a small cohort of hemodialysis patients showed that bradycardia and asystole preceded most arrhythmic deaths [12]. These findings challenge the assumption that SCD in ESRD is mainly due to ventricular fibrillation, and they raise questions about the appropriateness of preventive strategies such as primary prevention implantable cardioverter-defibrillators, whose benefit in this population remains uncertain [13,14]. Renal transplant candidates Renal transplantation improves survival and quality of life compared with chronic dialysis, but candidates are subjected to extensive cardiovascular evaluation because perioperative and long-term cardiac events remain a major concern [15]. Current guidelines recommend risk stratification using clinical assessment, resting electrocardiography (ECG), echocardiography, and, in selected patients, functional or anatomical testing for ischemia [16]. These tools primarily address structural and ischemic disease and offer limited information on arrhythmic vulnerability. Moreover, patients on the waiting list may be on dialysis for prolonged periods, during which clinically relevant rhythm disturbances can occur without being captured. The arrhythmic profile of renal transplant candidates (RTCs) is therefore poorly characterized, and it remains unclear which clinical, electrocardiographic, or echocardiographic variables identify those at greater risk. Limitations of conventional rhythm monitoring Standard 12-lead ECG and 24- to 48-hour Holter monitoring provide only brief snapshots and are poorly suited to detecting paroxysmal or infrequent events. Studies using such methods are likely to underestimate the true incidence of arrhythmias, particularly in patients whose events are related to the dialysis cycle or occur sporadically [17]. External event recorders improve diagnostic yield but remain limited by patient compliance and short monitoring duration. The implantable loop recorder (ILR) permits continuous subcutaneous ECG monitoring for up to several years, with automatic detection and storage of arrhythmic episodes and patient-activated recording of symptoms. ILRs have established value in the evaluation of unexplained syncope [18] and in the detection of occult atrial fibrillation after cryptogenic stroke [19]. In the nephrology setting, their use has been confined to small series of dialysis patients, which have shown a high burden of clinically significant arrhythmias, often asymptomatic [12,20]. To our knowledge, ILR-based monitoring has not been systematically applied to ambulatory RTCs, and data on the incidence of arrhythmic events in this group, their clinical significance, and their determinants are lacking. Potential predictors of arrhythmic events Several noninvasive markers may help identify patients prone to specific arrhythmias. Prolongation of the corrected QT interval (QTc) reflects abnormal ventricular repolarization and has been associated with malignant arrhythmias and mortality in ESRD [21]. PR interval prolongation indicates delayed atrioventricular conduction and has been related to atrial fibrillation, conduction disease, and adverse outcomes in the general population [22]. Left ventricular dilatation and systolic dysfunction are established substrates for ventricular arrhythmias [23]. Whether these readily available parameters predict particular arrhythmia types detected by continuous monitoring in RTCs has not been examined. Identifying such predictors could refine risk stratification, guide selection of patients for closer surveillance, and inform decisions about pacing or defibrillator therapy before and after transplantation. Study objective Given the high cardiovascular risk of RTCs, the limitations of intermittent rhythm assessment, and the uncertainty about the mechanisms of sudden death in this population, we conducted a prospective observational study using ILRs in consecutive ambulatory RTCs. The aim was to determine the incidence and types of arrhythmic events during medium-term follow-up and to identify clinical, electrocardiographic, and echocardiographic predictors of these events using multivariate analysis. Study Design and Population We conducted a prospective, single-center, observational study from June 2009 to January 2011. One hundred consecutive ambulatory renal transplant candidates (RTCs) on the waiting list, undergoing chronic hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis, were referred for cardiovascular evaluation and enrolled. Inclusion criteria were age of at least 18 years, dialysis for at least three months, and the ability to provide written informed consent. Exclusion criteria were a previously implanted pacemaker or defibrillator, a documented indication for such a device according to current guidelines [1,2], a life expectancy under one year from non-cardiac disease, active infection, and refusal to participate. The protocol complied with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the institutional ethics committee. All patients gave written informed consent before any study procedure. Baseline Clinical Assessment Demographic and clinical data were collected at enrollment through structured interviews and medical record review. These included age, sex, etiology of renal disease, time on dialysis, dialysis modality, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, smoking status, known coronary artery disease, previous heart failure, and cardiovascular medications (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, antiarrhythmic drugs, renin-angiotensin system inhibitors). Laboratory tests were performed on the day before a dialysis session and included hemoglobin, serum potassium, calcium, phosphorus, parathyroid hormone, and creatinine. Electrocardiographic Evaluation A standard 12-lead resting electrocardiogram (ECG) was recorded at 25 mm/s and 10 mm/mV. Two investigators blinded to the follow-up results measured the PR interval, QRS duration, and QT interval manually. The QT interval was corrected for heart rate using Bazett's formula [3]. A long QTc was defined as at least 450 ms in men and 470 ms in women. First-degree atrioventricular block was defined as a PR interval above 200 ms, and intraventricular conduction delay as a QRS duration of at least 120 ms. Echocardiography Transthoracic echocardiography was performed according to the recommendations of the American Society of Echocardiography [4]. Left ventricular (LV) end-diastolic and end-systolic diameters, septal and posterior wall thickness, and left atrial diameter were measured. LV ejection fraction was calculated using the modified Simpson method. LV mass was calculated by the Devereux formula and indexed to body surface area. LV dilatation (LVD) was defined as an indexed end-diastolic diameter above sex-specific reference limits [4]. LV systolic dysfunction was defined as an ejection fraction below 50%. Implantable Loop Recorder Implantation and Programming All patients underwent implantation of an implantable loop recorder (ILR; Reveal XT, Medtronic, Minneapolis, MN, USA) in the left parasternal region under local anesthesia and sterile conditions. The R-wave amplitude was checked immediately after implantation to ensure adequate sensing. Devices were programmed to automatically detect and store the following: bradycardia (heart rate below 30 bpm for at least 4 beats), asystole (pause of at least 3 seconds), fast ventricular tachycardia (VT; at least 16 beats at a rate above 180 bpm), non-sustained VT (rate above 130 bpm), and atrial fibrillation (AF) through R-R interval irregularity analysis. Patients also received an activator to record symptomatic episodes manually. Follow-up and Data Collection Patients were evaluated at 30 days and then every three months, or whenever symptoms occurred. At each visit the device memory was interrogated, and all stored episodes were printed and reviewed. Two experienced electrophysiologists independently reviewed all electrograms to exclude inappropriate detections caused by oversensing, noise, or artifact, with disagreements resolved by consensus. Only validated episodes were analyzed. Clinical events, hospitalizations, renal transplantation, changes in dialysis modality, and deaths were recorded. Follow-up continued for at least one year. Causes of death were adjudicated from medical records, ILR data when available, and family or witness reports. Sudden cardiac death was defined as unexpected death within one hour of symptom onset, or unwitnessed death in a patient previously seen in stable condition within the preceding 24 hours [5]. Definition of Arrhythmic Events Arrhythmic events (AE) were defined as any validated episode detected by the ILR. They were classified as: (1) sustained atrial tachycardia, lasting at least 30 seconds; (2) AF, irregular rhythm without discernible P waves lasting at least 30 seconds; (3) bradyarrhythmia, including sinus bradycardia below 30 bpm, sinus pauses of 3 seconds or more, and high-grade atrioventricular block; (4) non-sustained VT, at least 3 consecutive ventricular beats at a rate above 120 bpm lasting under 30 seconds; and (5) sustained VT, lasting 30 seconds or more or causing hemodynamic compromise. Ventricular fibrillation was defined as irregular chaotic ventricular activity without identifiable QRS complexes. Events were judged clinically relevant if they were symptomatic, caused hemodynamic instability, or led to a therapeutic intervention such as pacemaker implantation, defibrillator implantation, or initiation of anticoagulation or antiarrhythmic therapy. Statistical Analysis Continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation or median with interquartile range, according to the Shapiro-Wilk test, and categorical variables as absolute numbers and percentages. Comparisons between patients with and without each arrhythmia type used Student's t test or the Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables, and the chi-square or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables. Variables with p < 0.10 in univariate analysis, together with those considered clinically relevant, were entered into multivariate logistic regression models, with separate models for bradyarrhythmias and non-sustained VT. The number of candidate variables was limited to preserve model stability given the number of events [6]. Results are expressed as odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Model calibration was assessed with the Hosmer-Lemeshow test, and collinearity was checked before final model selection. A two-tailed p value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed using SPSS (version 19.0, IBM, Armonk, NY, USA). Study population and follow-up Between June 2009 and January 2011, 100 consecutive ambulatory RTCs underwent ILR implantation and were included in the analysis. All patients completed at least one year of monitoring, with a mean follow-up of 424 ± 127 days. No device-related infection requiring explantation or pocket hematoma requiring intervention occurred. Baseline clinical, electrocardiographic and echocardiographic characteristics are summarized in Table 1. The cohort was predominantly middle-aged, with a high prevalence of hypertension and a substantial proportion of diabetic patients. Most patients were receiving hemodialysis, and a minority were on peritoneal dialysis. Left ventricular dilatation (LVD) was identified in a considerable fraction of patients, whereas severe systolic dysfunction was infrequent. A prolonged corrected QT interval (long QTc) was present in a minority of patients at baseline. Overall incidence and distribution of arrhythmic events Arrhythmic events (AE) were recorded in 98 of 100 patients (98%), and 92% of patients had more than one type of arrhythmia during follow-up. Most events were automatically detected and, after manual review of stored electrograms, classified as potentially not serious, such as brief asymptomatic non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (NSVT), short pauses, or transient bradycardia. Distribution by arrhythmia type is shown in Table 2. Sustained atrial tachycardia was detected in 7% of patients and atrial fibrillation in 13%. Bradyarrhythmias were recorded in 25% of patients, and non-sustained or sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT) in 57%. Episodes of sustained VT were uncommon compared with non-sustained episodes, and most VT episodes were asymptomatic and self-terminating. Detection of events occurred in the absence of symptoms in the majority of cases, and a smaller proportion of patients had events triggered by the patient during symptoms, which were frequently associated with sinus rhythm or benign findings on the stored tracings. Mortality and sudden cardiac events During follow-up, 18 patients died. Seven deaths were classified as sudden cardiac events. Review of the ILR data, when available, allowed determination of the mechanism in five of these seven cases: three were due to bradyarrhythmias (progressive bradycardia culminating in asystole), one to ventricular fibrillation, and one to myocardial infarction. Insulin resistance is a state in which insulin-responsive tissues, principally skeletal muscle, liver, and adipose tissue, respond inadequately to normal circulating concentrations of the hormone. It is the central pathological feature of obesity and metabolic syndrome and the core defect that precedes and drives type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) [1,2]. The global prevalence of obesity and T2DM continues to rise, and insulin resistance contributes to related conditions such as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease [3]. Although lifestyle intervention, metformin, and thiazolidinediones can improve insulin sensitivity, their efficacy is often limited and side effects are common, so there is a need to identify new molecular targets [4]. The mechanisms of insulin resistance are complex and include lipotoxicity, chronic low-grade inflammation, endoplasmic reticulum stress, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction, all of which impair insulin signaling through the insulin receptor, insulin receptor substrates (IRS), phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), and AKT [5,6]. Cellular energy status is tightly coupled to these processes, and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) has emerged as a key metabolic sensor. Tissue NAD+ levels decline with aging and in overnutrition, and this decline is associated with metabolic deterioration [7]. The Sirtuins are NAD+-dependent enzymes that link cellular redox and energy state to protein modification and gene expression. The founding member, yeast Sir2, was identified as a regulator of replicative lifespan and transcriptional silencing, and its homologs have been associated with longevity in several model organisms [8,9]. Mammals have seven Sirtuins (SIRT1–SIRT7), which share a conserved catalytic core but differ in their N- and C-terminal domains, substrate specificities, enzymatic activities, and subcellular localization [10]. SIRT1, SIRT6, and SIRT7 are predominantly nuclear, SIRT2 is mainly cytoplasmic, and SIRT3, SIRT4, and SIRT5 reside in mitochondria, although several Sirtuins shuttle between compartments in response to physiological cues [11]. Initially characterized as deacetylases, Sirtuins are now known to catalyze a broader range of reactions, including removal of long-chain fatty acyl groups, desuccinylation, demalonylation, deglutarylation, and mono-ADP-ribosylation [12,13]. Through these activities they regulate cell survival, senescence, DNA repair, genome stability, and metabolism [14]. SIRT1 and SIRT6 have been studied most extensively in metabolic regulation. SIRT1 deacetylates and modulates PGC-1α, FOXO proteins, LXR, SREBP, PPARγ, and the insulin signaling mediator PTP1B, thereby influencing gluconeogenesis, fatty acid oxidation, cholesterol homeostasis, adipogenesis, and insulin sensitivity [15–17]. Transgenic overexpression of SIRT1 and pharmacological activators such as resveratrol and SRT1720 improve glucose tolerance and protect against diet-induced obesity and hepatic steatosis in rodents, whereas tissue-specific deletion of SIRT1 exacerbates metabolic dysfunction [18,19]. SIRT6 regulates glycolysis through deacetylation of histone H3 at lysine 9 and 56, represses HIF1α-dependent glucose uptake, and controls hepatic lipid metabolism and inflammatory signaling; its loss causes severe hypoglycemia in mice, while its overexpression protects against high-fat diet-induced metabolic damage [20,21]. These findings have implicated SIRT1 and SIRT6 in obesity, T2DM, fatty liver disease, and cardiovascular disease, and they have been the subject of several comprehensive reviews [22]. By contrast, the contributions of the remaining Sirtuins to insulin resistance are less well defined. Recent work indicates that they also influence processes tightly linked to insulin action. Mitochondrial SIRT3 deacetylates components of the respiratory chain and antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2, and its reduced expression is associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and insulin resistance in muscle and liver [23,24]. SIRT4 modulates glutamine metabolism, insulin secretion, and fatty acid oxidation, while SIRT5 regulates ammonia detoxification, glycolysis, and fatty acid oxidation through desuccinylation and demalonylation [25,26]. Cytosolic SIRT2 affects adipocyte differentiation, gluconeogenesis, and insulin signaling via deacetylation of FOXO1, PEPCK, and AKT [27]. SIRT7 has been linked to hepatic lipid homeostasis, ER stress, and mitochondrial function [28]. Furthermore, several of these enzymes modulate inflammatory pathways, including NF-κB signaling and NLRP3 inflammasome activation, which are major drivers of obesity-associated insulin resistance [29]. Human genetic and clinical studies have reported altered Sirtuin expression or polymorphisms in individuals with obesity, T2DM, and metabolic syndrome, supporting their translational relevance [30]. Nevertheless, findings are sometimes inconsistent across tissues, models, and species, and the substrate specificity and physiological regulation of some Sirtuins remain unclear. In this review, we summarize recent advances in the roles of the Sirtuin family in physiological processes associated with insulin resistance, including inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, insulin signaling, and glucose and lipid metabolism. We emphasize the Sirtuins other than SIRT1 and SIRT6 while discussing the better-characterized members for comparison. We also highlight important unresolved questions and discuss the prospects and challenges of targeting Sirtuins therapeutically for metabolic disease. This review was conducted as a structured narrative synthesis of the literature on mammalian Sirtuins (SIRT1–7) and insulin resistance. The aim was to integrate evidence from molecular, animal, and human studies and to identify gaps in current knowledge. The methodology followed the general principles of the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) to promote transparency and reproducibility [1]. Literature Search Strategy Electronic searches were performed in PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and Embase. The search covered records from database inception to the most recent update before manuscript preparation. Controlled vocabulary (MeSH and Emtree terms) was combined with free-text keywords using Boolean operators. Terms for the exposure included "sirtuin", "SIRT1", "SIRT2", "SIRT3", "SIRT4", "SIRT5", "SIRT6", "SIRT7", and "NAD-dependent deacetylase". These were combined with terms for the outcome and related processes: "insulin resistance", "insulin sensitivity", "insulin signaling", "type 2 diabetes", "obesity", "metabolic syndrome", "glucose metabolism", "lipid metabolism", "inflammation", and "mitochondrial dysfunction". Reference lists of retrieved articles and earlier reviews were hand-searched to identify additional relevant publications [2]. Because SIRT1 and SIRT6 have been extensively reviewed, searches for these proteins were restricted to key mechanistic and translational studies, whereas searches for SIRT2–5 and SIRT7 were conducted exhaustively. Eligibility Criteria Studies were eligible if they met at least one of the following criteria: (i) in vitro experiments in insulin-responsive cells (hepatocytes, adipocytes, skeletal myocytes, cardiomyocytes, pancreatic β-cells, macrophages, or endothelial cells) examining Sirtuin function in relation to insulin signaling, nutrient metabolism, inflammation, or mitochondrial function; (ii) animal studies using genetic (knockout, knockdown, transgenic, tissue-specific) or pharmacological (activators, inhibitors, NAD+ precursors) manipulation of Sirtuins and reporting metabolic phenotypes such as glucose tolerance, insulin tolerance, or hyperinsulinemic–euglycemic clamp outcomes; and (iii) human studies, including observational cohorts, genetic association studies, and clinical trials, that evaluated Sirtuin expression, activity, polymorphisms, or modulators in relation to insulin resistance, T2DM, obesity, or fatty liver disease. Articles were excluded if they were published in languages other than English, were conference abstracts without full text, were editorials without primary data, or addressed Sirtuins solely in contexts unrelated to metabolism (e.g., purely oncological or neurodegenerative studies without metabolic endpoints). Where multiple publications reported overlapping data, the most complete report was retained. Study Selection and Data Extraction Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, followed by full-text assessment of potentially eligible articles. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. For each included study, the following information was extracted into a standardized template: Sirtuin isoform studied; species and model system; tissue or cell type; type of intervention; metabolic diet or insulin-resistance induction protocol (e.g., high-fat diet, genetic obesity models, palmitate or TNF-α exposure); principal substrates or pathways identified; and main outcomes. Mechanistic data were grouped into five thematic domains: inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, insulin signaling pathway, glucose metabolism, and lipid metabolism. Evidence Synthesis Given the heterogeneity of experimental models, interventions, and outcome measures, quantitative pooling was not feasible, and a narrative synthesis was adopted. Findings were organized by isoform and subcellular localization: nuclear (SIRT1, SIRT6, SIRT7), cytosolic (SIRT2), and mitochondrial (SIRT3, SIRT4, SIRT5). Within each isoform, evidence was compared across tissues relevant to systemic insulin sensitivity, namely liver, skeletal muscle, adipose tissue, pancreas, and the vasculature. Particular attention was given to enzymatic activities (deacetylation, desuccinylation, demalonylation, deglutarylation, defatty-acylation, and mono-ADP-ribosylation) and to well-characterized targets, including components of the insulin receptor–IRS–PI3K–AKT cascade, PTP1B, FOXO proteins, PGC-1α, NF-κB, AMPK, LKB1, and mitochondrial enzymes [3,4]. Consistency of findings was evaluated by noting concordant and discordant results across models. Discrepancies, such as tissue-specific or context-dependent effects, differences between whole-body and conditional knockouts, and divergent results from pharmacological modulators, were explicitly described. Evidence from human studies was distinguished from preclinical evidence to avoid overstating translational relevance. Quality Considerations Formal risk-of-bias scoring was not applied, as is typical for narrative reviews. Instead, the reviewers qualitatively considered study design, sample size, use of appropriate controls, specificity of genetic or pharmacological tools, replication across independent laboratories, and the physiological relevance of the models. Greater weight was given to findings supported by multiple independent models or by converging genetic and pharmacological evidence. Concerns regarding the selectivity of small-molecule Sirtuin modulators and the nonspecificity of some activators were considered when interpreting results [5]. Identification of Knowledge Gaps Research gaps were identified by comparing the breadth of evidence across Sirtuin isoforms, tissues, and thematic domains, and by noting areas with limited human data, conflicting findings, or absent mechanistic validation. These gaps were then summarized to propose directions for future research, including isoform-specific modulators, tissue-specific models, and well-designed clinical studies. Sirtuin subcellular localization and metabolic distribution Available evidence indicates that the seven mammalian Sirtuins occupy distinct subcellular compartments that shape their metabolic functions. SIRT1 and SIRT2 shuttle between the nucleus and cytoplasm, SIRT6 and SIRT7 are predominantly nuclear (with SIRT7 enriched in the nucleolus), and SIRT3, SIRT4, and SIRT5 reside mainly in mitochondria [1,2]. Tissue expression analyses show that Sirtuins are abundant in insulin-responsive organs, including liver, skeletal muscle, adipose tissue, and pancreatic β cells, and that their levels are altered in obesity and diabetes [3,4]. Reduced SIRT1, SIRT3, and SIRT6 expression has been consistently reported in tissues from high-fat diet (HFD)-fed rodents and in individuals with T2DM, supporting an association between Sirtuin depletion and insulin resistance [5-7]. Sirtuins and inflammation Chronic low-grade inflammation is a driver of insulin resistance, and several Sirtuins restrain inflammatory signaling. Beyond the well-established SIRT1 and SIRT6 deacetylation of NF-κB p65 and H3K9 at inflammatory gene promoters [8,9], SIRT2 deacetylates p65 and limits macrophage-driven cytokine production; SIRT2-deficient mice show exacerbated adipose inflammation and impaired glucose tolerance under metabolic stress [10]. SIRT3 attenuates inflammation by reducing mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) and suppressing NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and its loss promotes macrophage polarization toward a proinflammatory phenotype [11,12]. SIRT5 modulates inflammatory responses through regulation of macrophage glycolytic flux and PKM2 activity, although its effects appear context dependent [13]. SIRT7 deficiency has been linked to increased systemic inflammation, whereas SIRT4 has been reported to influence NF-κB signaling in endothelial and renal cells [14,15]. Overall, most Sirtuins appear to exert anti-inflammatory effects relevant to insulin sensitivity, with SIRT5 and SIRT4 showing less consistent patterns. Mitochondrial dysfunction Mitochondrial Sirtuins coordinate oxidative metabolism and redox balance. SIRT3, the major mitochondrial deacetylase, activates components of the electron transport chain, fatty acid oxidation enzymes (such as LCAD), and superoxide dismutase 2 [16,17]. HFD feeding induces mitochondrial protein hyperacetylation in SIRT3-knockout mice, accompanied by accelerated obesity, hyperlipidemia, and insulin resistance [5]. Similarly, SIRT3 downregulation in skeletal muscle impairs insulin-stimulated Akt signaling through ROS accumulation and JNK activation [18]. SIRT4, which has ADP-ribosyltransferase and lipoamidase activities, inhibits glutamate dehydrogenase and pyruvate dehydrogenase, and represses fatty acid oxidation in liver and muscle; its deletion enhances oxidative capacity and, in some models, improves insulin sensitivity [19,20]. SIRT5 removes malonyl, succinyl, and glutaryl groups, regulating CPS1, the urea cycle, and fatty acid oxidation, and SIRT5 deficiency produces modest metabolic phenotypes that vary by tissue and diet [21,22]. Nuclear SIRT7 supports mitochondrial homeostasis by suppressing nuclear-encoded mitochondrial gene programs through NRF1 interaction, and SIRT7-deficient mice display mitochondrial dysfunction and are paradoxically protected from or sensitized to HFD-induced obesity depending on the model [23,24]. Effects on the insulin signaling pathway Several Sirtuins directly modulate insulin signaling nodes. SIRT1 deacetylates IRS-2 and represses PTP1B transcription, thereby enhancing insulin receptor signaling [25]. SIRT2 deacetylates Akt and promotes its activation, and SIRT2 deficiency attenuates insulin-stimulated Akt phosphorylation in adipocytes and myotubes [26]. SIRT3 enhances Akt activity indirectly by reducing mitochondrial oxidative stress [18]. SIRT6 represses IGF-insulin signaling by deacetylating H3K9 at the promoters of IGF-Akt pathway genes, and SIRT6 deficiency causes severe hypoglycemia with heightened Akt activation

Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disease characterized by low bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration of bone tissue, with a consequent increase in bone fragility and fracture risk [1]. Vertebral fractures are the most common osteoporotic fractures and are associated with chronic pain, reduced mobility, loss of height, and increased mortality [2,3]. Because a prevalent vertebral fracture strongly predicts further fractures, early identification of individuals at high risk is a central goal of clinical osteology [4]. Accurate and precise quantification of bone status at the lumbar spine is therefore of considerable clinical and scientific interest. Current Diagnostics and Their Limitations The standard for diagnosing osteoporosis is areal bone mineral density (BMD) measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) [5]. Although DXA-derived BMD correlates with fracture risk, a substantial proportion of fragility fractures occur in patients whose T-scores lie above the osteoporotic threshold [6]. Several limitations of the technique contribute to this. DXA projects a three-dimensional structure onto a plane and cannot separate trabecular from cortical bone. Moreover, in the spine it is confounded by degenerative changes, aortic calcifications, and posterior elements, all of which raise the apparent density [7]. Finally, DXA provides little information on bone geometry, which is an important determinant of mechanical competence. Quantitative computed tomography (QCT) overcomes many of these problems by delivering true volumetric BMD and permitting selective analysis of the trabecular compartment [8,9]. Trabecular vertebral BMD from QCT has been shown to be more sensitive to age-related and treatment-induced changes than DXA and to discriminate fracture patients well [10]. Spiral CT scanners are widely available, and modern multi-detector systems acquire high-resolution volumetric data of the entire spine in a short time. Nevertheless, conventional spinal QCT is usually restricted to a single elliptical or cylindrical region of interest placed manually in the mid-vertebral plane of two to four slices. Such an approach samples only a small fraction of the vertebral body, is sensitive to operator placement, and ignores the spatial heterogeneity of density and geometry that is relevant for load transfer and failure [11]. Need for Three-Dimensional Segmentation Fully exploiting volumetric CT data requires segmentation of the vertebral body in three dimensions. Once the bone is delineated, BMD can be evaluated in arbitrarily defined volumes of interest (VOIs), for example the entire trabecular compartment, subcortical layers, or regions near the endplates, and geometric parameters such as vertebral volume, height, and cross-sectional area can be derived. Finite element studies and in vitro mechanical tests suggest that the combination of density distribution and geometry predicts vertebral strength better than mean BMD alone [12,13]. Reliable three-dimensional measurements could therefore improve fracture risk assessment beyond current clinical practice. Segmenting lumbar vertebrae is, however, a difficult task. The trabecular interior has low and inhomogeneous attenuation, whereas the cortical shell is thin and, given the limited resolution of clinical scanners, is affected by partial volume effects. Adjacent vertebrae are separated only by narrow intervertebral discs, and in osteoporotic or degenerated spines the gaps between the endplates and osteophytes may be nearly indistinguishable from bone. The posterior elements (pedicles, laminae, and processes) are connected to the vertebral body through narrow bridges and must be removed to isolate the body. Furthermore, the vertebral foramen and the basivertebral venous plexus produce local density variations that can mislead intensity-based methods. Related Work Numerous approaches to vertebral segmentation have been proposed. Simple thresholding and region growing are fast but leak into neighboring structures and do not separate the body from the posterior elements [14]. Deformable models and active contours incorporate shape constraints and smoothness, but depend on initialization and may fail in pathologic cases [15,16]. Statistical shape and appearance models are robust and have been applied to the whole spine [17,18], yet their accuracy is limited by how well the training population represents the variability in shape, and they may bias the boundary toward the mean shape, which is undesirable when geometry itself is the outcome. Graph-cut and level-set formulations have also been described [19,20]. Many of these works emphasize anatomical identification or visualization and report overlap metrics, rather than the accuracy and precision of densitometric and geometric parameters, which determine clinical usefulness. Furthermore, few methods define VOIs relative to a reproducible, anatomically based local coordinate system, which is essential for longitudinal and multicenter comparison, because patient positioning and spinal curvature otherwise change the sampled region. Objectives and Contribution In this paper we present a multi-step segmentation methodology for lumbar vertebral bodies in spiral CT data that is designed explicitly for the measurement of BMD and geometry. The method first isolates the vertebral body from adjacent structures, then separates it from the posterior elements, and finally refines the boundary to capture the cortical shell. From the resulting surface a local anatomical coordinate system is derived, in which standardized VOIs are positioned independently of patient orientation. This yields densitometric and geometric measures that are comparable across examinations and subjects. We evaluate the technique in terms of the criteria that matter for clinical application. Precision is assessed through intra- and inter-operator variability of the segmentation, the BMD values, and the coordinate system position in patient data. Accuracy is assessed using phantom data with known density and volume. By providing a validated, largely automated tool for three-dimensional vertebral analysis, we aim to establish the basis for studies that test whether volumetric density distribution and geometry improve the prediction of osteoporotic fractures. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We first describe the image data and the segmentation algorithm, then the construction of the coordinate system and VOIs, followed by the validation protocol. Results for phantom and patient data are then presented and discussed with respect to limitations and future clinical application. Study Data Spiral CT scans of the lumbar spine were acquired from 20 postmenopausal women (age 55–80 years) as part of an ongoing osteoporosis study. Scans used a slice thickness of 1 mm, a reconstruction increment of 0.5 mm, 120 kVp, and a bone-density calibration phantom placed beneath the patient. Vertebrae L1–L3 were analyzed. For accuracy assessment, an anthropometric European Spine Phantom and six excised human vertebral specimens were scanned with identical protocols. The specimens' volumes were determined independently by water displacement (Archimedes' principle), and the phantom's nominal hydroxyapatite concentrations served as the BMD reference. All patients gave written informed consent, and the study was approved by the local ethics committee. Segmentation Pipeline The segmentation consists of four consecutive steps: (1) preprocessing and seed definition, (2) coarse segmentation of the vertebral body by a region-based approach, (3) refinement by a deformable surface model, and (4) separation of the vertebral body from the posterior elements. Preprocessing and initialization. Volumes were resampled to isotropic 0.5 mm voxels using trilinear interpolation and smoothed with a edge-preserving anisotropic diffusion filter [1] to reduce noise while retaining cortical boundaries. The operator placed one seed point at the center of each vertebral body and one point in the adjacent intervertebral disc above and below, which defined the approximate craniocaudal extent. Coarse segmentation. A three-dimensional region-growing algorithm was started from the seed and constrained by an adaptive threshold. The threshold was computed from the local histogram of a spherical neighborhood as the midpoint between the trabecular and soft-tissue intensity modes, which makes the procedure robust against differences in bone density. Leakage into adjacent vertebrae or the ribs was prevented by morphological opening with a 3 mm structuring element and by restricting growth to the slab between the disc points. Holes inside the segmentation were closed by a slice-wise flood-fill followed by a 3D closing operation. Surface refinement. The binary result was converted into a triangulated surface by marching cubes [2] and used as the initial state of a deformable simplex mesh [3]. Mesh vertices evolved under an internal smoothness force and an external force derived from the gradient magnitude of the image along the vertex normal, searching within ±2 mm for the strongest cortical edge. Iteration terminated when the mean vertex displacement fell below 0.01 mm. This step provided sub-voxel boundary localization, which is critical for volume and cortical-shell analysis. Removal of posterior elements. The pedicles and posterior arch were excluded by fitting a plane through the narrowest region of each pedicle neck, identified from a distance-transform analysis of the segmented object. The vertebral body was defined as the part anterior to these planes. The operator could correct plane positions interactively, although this was rarely necessary. Local Anatomical Coordinate System A vertebra-specific coordinate system was derived from the segmented body surface. The origin was set at the centroid of the vertebral body. The craniocaudal axis (z) was defined as the normal of a least-squares plane fitted to the midpoints of the superior and inferior endplates, whose points were identified as surface vertices with normals within 30° of the preliminary axis. The sagittal direction (y) was obtained by projecting the vector from the centroid to the center of the pedicle-plane intersection onto the plane orthogonal to z, and the left–right axis (x) was the cross product of the two. The system was thereby independent of patient positioning and scanner orientation. Volumes of Interest and BMD Measurement Relative to this coordinate system, several volumes of interest (VOIs) were defined: (i) an elliptical trabecular VOI in the mid-vertebral region, inset from the cortical boundary by 2 mm and with a height of 50% of the vertebral body height; (ii) the whole vertebral body; (iii) a cortical shell VOI of 2 mm thickness inward from the surface; and (iv) a subcortical region beneath each endplate. VOI dimensions scaled with individual vertebral size so that comparable anatomical regions were assessed across subjects. Hounsfield units were converted to equivalent hydroxyapatite density (mg/cm³) by linear regression against the calibration phantom rods, with correction for scan-specific offsets. Mean BMD was computed per VOI, with partial volume voxels at boundaries weighted by their fractional occupancy derived from the refined mesh. Geometric Analysis From the refined surface, vertebral body volume, anterior, middle, and posterior heights, endplate areas, and mean cross-sectional area at mid-height were calculated. Heights were measured parallel to the z-axis and cross-sections in planes orthogonal to it. Volume was computed using the divergence theorem applied to the closed triangular mesh. Accuracy Evaluation For BMD accuracy, phantom vertebrae with known hydroxyapatite concentrations were scanned and segmented, and relative differences between measured and nominal values were calculated. For volume accuracy, segmented volumes of the excised vertebrae were compared with water-displacement values. Accuracy error was expressed as the mean absolute percentage deviation. Precision Evaluation Intra-operator precision was assessed by having one operator repeat the entire procedure, including seed placement, on all patient vertebrae three times, separated by at least one week. Inter-operator precision was assessed with three trained operators working independently. Outcome variables were segmented volume, VOI BMD, and the position of the coordinate-system origin and axes. Precision was expressed as the root-mean-square coefficient of variation (RMS-CV%) [4] for volume and BMD, and as the root-mean-square standard deviation of origin position (mm) and axis orientation (degrees); the latter were additionally normalized to vertebral dimensions to allow percentage statements. Repeated scans were not acquired, so the reported precision reflects only the analysis rather than acquisition. Statistical Analysis Agreement between measured and reference values was examined by linear regression and Bland–Altman analysis [5]. Differences between operators were tested with repeated-measures ANOVA, with p < 0.05 considered significant. Analyses were performed in MATLAB (The MathWorks, Natick, MA), and the segmentation was implemented in C++ using the Insight Toolkit. Segmentation performance. The multi-step segmentation was applied to all lumbar vertebral bodies (L1–L3) in the patient dataset. The algorithm converged without manual correction of the initial seed placement in 94% of cases. In the remaining cases, a single repositioning of the seed point in the vertebral body was sufficient to obtain a satisfactory result.
