Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progressive and life-threatening disease characterized by sustained elevation of pulmonary arterial pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance, which ultimately leads to right ventricular hypertrophy, right heart failure, and death [1,2]. The pathological hallmarks of PAH include endothelial dysfunction, proliferation and apoptosis resistance of smooth muscle cells, medial hypertrophy, perivascular inflammation, and fibrosis of small pulmonary arteries [3]. Although current therapies targeting the prostacyclin, endothelin, and nitric oxide pathways improve symptoms and exercise capacity, they only modestly alter the underlying vascular remodeling, and long-term survival remains poor [4]. New therapeutic strategies that target additional pathogenic mechanisms are therefore needed. The renin-angiotensin system (RAS) has been implicated in the pathogenesis of pulmonary hypertension. The classical axis, composed of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), angiotensin II (Ang II), and the Ang II type 1 receptor (AT1R), promotes vasoconstriction, cell proliferation, inflammation, and fibrosis [5]. Increased ACE activity and Ang II levels have been reported in patients with PAH and in experimental models, and AT1R blockade or ACE inhibition attenuates pulmonary vascular remodeling in some animal studies [6,7]. In contrast, the counter-regulatory axis, centered on ACE2, has attracted attention as a protective pathway. ACE2 converts Ang II to Ang-(1-7), which acts mainly through the Mas receptor to induce vasodilation and exert anti-proliferative and anti-inflammatory effects [8]. Reduced pulmonary ACE2 expression has been observed in PAH, and ACE2 overexpression, ACE2 activators, or Ang-(1-7) administration ameliorate pulmonary hypertension in rodents [9–11]. ACE2 also converts Ang I to Ang-(1-9) by removing the C-terminal leucine residue [12]. Ang-(1-9) was long regarded as an inactive intermediate, serving mainly as a precursor of Ang-(1-7) through ACE-mediated cleavage. However, recent studies have shown that Ang-(1-9) has biological activity of its own. In rodent models of cardiovascular disease, Ang-(1-9) reduced cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis after myocardial infarction and in hypertensive rats, improved endothelial function, and attenuated vascular remodeling, independently of its conversion to Ang-(1-7) [13–15]. Ang-(1-9) has also been shown to reduce oxidative stress, to limit cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, and to prevent neointimal formation and inflammation in injured vessels [16,17]. Notably, these effects were generally abolished by the Ang II type 2 receptor (AT2R) antagonist PD123319 rather than by the Mas receptor antagonist A779, suggesting that Ang-(1-9) acts as a functional ligand of AT2R [13,15]. AT2R signaling is typically associated with vasodilation, anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic actions, and modulation of apoptosis, and it has been proposed as a promising target in cardiovascular and lung diseases [18,19]. Activation of AT2R by selective agonists such as compound 21 has been reported to attenuate pulmonary hypertension and fibrosis in experimental models [20,21]. Despite this evidence, the effect of Ang-(1-9) on pulmonary hypertension has not been examined. Because the pulmonary circulation expresses high levels of ACE and ACE2 and is exposed to substantial amounts of circulating angiotensin peptides, Ang-(1-9) may play a relevant role in regulating pulmonary vascular homeostasis. Furthermore, inflammation and apoptosis of endothelial cells are central to the initiation and progression of PAH. Endothelial injury and the release of inflammatory mediators, including tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), and interleukin-6 (IL-6), promote vascular remodeling and perivascular inflammatory cell infiltration [22,23]. Altered expression of apoptosis-related proteins, such as Bax, Bcl-2, and caspases, has been described in the lungs of animals with experimental pulmonary hypertension [24]. Whether Ang-(1-9) can modulate these processes in the pulmonary vasculature is unknown. The monocrotaline (MCT) model is a widely used and well-characterized model of PAH. A single subcutaneous injection of MCT in rats is metabolized in the liver to the reactive pyrrole derivative, which causes pulmonary endothelial injury, followed by inflammation, medial hypertrophy of pulmonary arterioles, interstitial fibrosis, increased pulmonary arterial pressure, and right ventricular hypertrophy [25,26]. Because the model reproduces endothelial damage and inflammatory features that are important in human disease, it is suitable for evaluating candidate agents that target these mechanisms. In the present study, we therefore hypothesized that Ang-(1-9) protects against the development of MCT-induced pulmonary hypertension through AT2R. We examined the effects of continuous Ang-(1-9) infusion on right ventricular systolic pressure, right ventricular hypertrophy, pulmonary arteriolar remodeling, endothelial damage, and pulmonary fibrosis in MCT-treated rats. To determine the receptor mechanism, we assessed whether the effects of Ang-(1-9) were blocked by an AT2R antagonist or a Mas receptor antagonist. In addition, we measured plasma lactate dehydrogenase and inflammatory cytokines, and evaluated the expression of apoptosis-related proteins in lung tissue, to clarify the potential contributions of anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic actions to the effects of Ang-(1-9). Animals and ethics Male Sprague-Dawley rats (6 weeks old, 180–200 g) were housed under controlled conditions (22 ± 2 °C, 55 ± 5% humidity, 12-h light/dark cycle) with free access to standard chow and water. Animals were acclimated for one week before experimentation. All procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and conformed to the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals published by the US National Institutes of Health [1]. Experimental design Rats were randomly assigned to groups (n = 8–10 per group): (1) control (saline pump plus vehicle injection); (2) Ang-(1-9) alone; (3) MCT plus saline; (4) MCT plus Ang-(1-9); (5) MCT plus Ang-(1-9) plus the AT2R antagonist PD123319; and (6) MCT plus Ang-(1-9) plus the Mas receptor antagonist A779. Ang-(1-9) (576 µg/kg/day) or saline was delivered via osmotic mini-pumps (Alzet model 2ML4) implanted subcutaneously in the dorsal region under isoflurane anesthesia and continued for 3 weeks. This dose was selected based on previous studies of cardiac and vascular remodeling [2,3]. Three days after pump implantation, rats received a single subcutaneous injection of MCT (50 mg/kg) dissolved in 1 N HCl, neutralized with NaOH to pH 7.4, or an equal volume of vehicle [4]. PD123319 (36 mg/kg/day) and A779 (100 µg/kg/day) were co-infused through separate mini-pumps beginning at the same time as Ang-(1-9) [5]. Body weight and general condition were monitored throughout. Experiments were terminated 3 weeks after pump implantation. Hemodynamic measurements and right ventricular hypertrophy Rats were anesthetized with an intraperitoneal injection of pentobarbital (50 mg/kg). A polyethylene catheter filled with heparinized saline was inserted via the right jugular vein into the right ventricle under pressure-waveform guidance, and right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) was recorded using a pressure transducer and a data acquisition system (PowerLab, ADInstruments). After hemodynamic recording, blood was collected from the abdominal aorta into EDTA tubes and centrifuged (3,000 × g, 15 min, 4 °C); plasma was stored at −80 °C. The heart was excised, and the right ventricle (RV) was dissected from the left ventricle plus septum (LV+S). Right ventricular hypertrophy was expressed as the Fulton index, RV/(LV+S), and as RV weight normalized to body weight. Histology and morphometry The left lung was perfused with saline, fixed in 10% neutral-buffered formalin at constant pressure, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned at 4 µm. Sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin and Masson’s trichrome. For medial hypertrophy, pulmonary arterioles (external diameter 50–100 µm) were examined in at least 10 vessels per animal by an observer blinded to group allocation. Medial wall thickness was calculated as percentage: [(external diameter − internal diameter)/external diameter] × 100 [6]. Pulmonary fibrosis was assessed by the proportion of collagen-positive (blue) area in Masson-stained sections using ImageJ software (NIH), averaged across ten random fields per animal at 200× magnification. Endothelial damage was evaluated by immunohistochemistry for von Willebrand factor (vWF) and endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS). Deparaffinized sections underwent antigen retrieval in citrate buffer, blocked for endogenous peroxidase and nonspecific binding, and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies, followed by HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies and diaminobenzidine development. Positive staining in the vascular endothelium was quantified by densitometry. Measurement of plasma LDH and cytokines Plasma lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) activity was determined using a commercial colorimetric assay kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Plasma concentrations of TNF-α, MCP-1, IL-1β, and IL-6 were measured by rat-specific enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits. All samples were assayed in duplicate, and concentrations were calculated from standard curves. Western blot analysis Right lung tissue was snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and homogenized in RIPA buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors. Lysates were centrifuged (12,000 × g, 20 min, 4 °C), and protein concentrations in the supernatants were measured by the BCA method. Equal amounts of protein (30 µg) were separated by SDS-PAGE (10–12%) and transferred to PVDF membranes. After blocking in 5% nonfat milk for 1 h, membranes were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies against Bax, Bcl-2, cleaved caspase-3, cleaved caspase-9, and β-actin (loading control). Membranes were then incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. Bands were visualized by enhanced chemiluminescence and quantified by densitometry with ImageJ. Protein levels were normalized to β-actin and expressed relative to the control group. TUNEL assay Apoptotic cells in lung sections were detected using a terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) kit following the manufacturer’s protocol [7]. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI. The apoptotic index was calculated as the percentage of TUNEL-positive nuclei among total nuclei in ten randomly selected fields per animal. Drugs and reagents Ang-(1-9), PD123319, A779, and MCT were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich or equivalent suppliers. Antibodies and ELISA kits were obtained from commercial vendors and used at the recommended dilutions. All other chemicals were of analytical grade. Statistical analysis Data are expressed as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Normality of distribution was assessed with the Shapiro–Wilk test and homogeneity of variance with Levene’s test. Differences among multiple groups were analyzed by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test; Kruskal–Wallis testing with Dunn’s correction was used when assumptions were not met. Analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism (version 8.0). A P value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Investigators performing histological and biochemical analyses were blinded to group assignment. Ang-(1-9) attenuates MCT-induced right ventricular hypertrophy and pulmonary hypertension Three weeks after MCT injection, rats showed marked pulmonary hypertension. Right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) was significantly higher in the MCT group than in the control group (p<0.01). The ratio of right ventricular weight to left ventricular plus septal weight (Fulton index, RV/[LV+S]) and the ratio of right ventricular weight to body weight were also increased. Co-administration of Ang-(1-9) significantly reduced RVSP and both indices of right ventricular hypertrophy compared with MCT alone (p<0.05). Ang-(1-9) alone did not alter these parameters in control rats. Body weight gain was reduced in MCT-treated rats, and this was partly prevented by Ang-(1-9). Systemic arterial pressure and heart rate did not differ among groups, indicating that the hemodynamic benefit was not attributable to systemic blood pressure changes. Ang-(1-9) improves pulmonary vascular remodeling and fibrosis Histological examination of lung sections showed thickening of the pulmonary arteriolar wall and narrowing of the lumen in MCT rats. Quantitative analysis showed that the percentage of medial wall thickness was significantly increased by MCT (p<0.01) and was significantly lower in rats co-treated with Ang-(1-9) (p<0.05). The proportion of muscularized small pulmonary arterioles was similarly increased by MCT and reduced by Ang-(1-9). Immunostaining for von Willebrand factor showed loss of endothelial staining in the pulmonary arterioles of MCT rats, indicating endothelial damage. This loss was attenuated by Ang-(1-9). Masson's trichrome staining showed increased collagen deposition in perivascular and interstitial areas of the lungs of MCT rats, and the fibrotic area was significantly reduced by Ang-(1-9) treatment (p<0.05). Thus, Ang-(1-9) improved endothelial damage, medial hypertrophy and fibrosis in the lungs of MCT-treated rats. Effects of AT2R and Mas receptor blockade To identify the receptor responsible for the effects of Ang-(1-9), the AT2R antagonist PD123319 or the Mas receptor antagonist A779 was co-administered with Ang-(1-9) in MCT rats. PD123319 abolished the beneficial effects of Ang-(1-9) on RVSP and right ventricular hypertrophy, so that values were similar to those in the MCT group (p<0.05 vs. MCT+Ang-(1-9)). PD123319 likewise abrogated the improvement in medial wall thickness, endothelial staining and fibrosis. In contrast, A779 did not significantly modify the reductions in RVSP, right ventricular hypertrophy, vascular remodeling or fibrosis produced by Ang-(1-9).
