Thailand has long been recognised for its effective national response to HIV, including early adoption of the 100% condom programme, mother-to-child transmission prevention, and universal access to antiretroviral therapy (ART) [1,2]. Despite these achievements, the epidemic has shifted in character. Heterosexual transmission has declined, while infections among men who have sex with men (MSM) have risen sharply and now account for a growing share of new cases [3]. Modelling projections suggest that more than half of new infections nationally will occur among MSM in the coming years [4]. This concentration of incidence in a specific population requires strategies that differ from the general population approaches that characterised earlier phases of the national response. The epidemiological context of HIV among MSM in Thailand Surveillance and cohort data from Bangkok show a severe and persistent epidemic among MSM. Between 2007 and 2010, HIV prevalence in community-based surveys approached one in three, and incidence in cohort studies exceeded 5 per 100 person-years among younger men [5,6]. Prevalence is particularly high among men aged 18–22 years, which indicates that many men acquire HIV soon after sexual debut [6]. Contributing factors include inconsistent condom use, multiple or concurrent partnerships, use of recreational drugs and sexualised substance use, and limited awareness of personal HIV status [7,8]. Stigma and discrimination related to both sexual orientation and HIV further reduce engagement with health services [9]. Gaps in the HIV testing and treatment cascade HIV testing and counselling (HTC) is the entry point to prevention, treatment, and care. Evidence indicates that large proportions of Thai MSM living with HIV are unaware of their infection, and that many who test do so only after symptoms appear or at advanced immunological stages [10]. Late diagnosis leads to worse clinical outcomes, increased onward transmission, and higher health system costs [11]. Treatment as prevention is now supported by strong evidence that earlier ART reduces both morbidity and transmission [12,13], and national guidelines have progressively raised CD4 thresholds for treatment initiation. These benefits depend, however, on early diagnosis and prompt linkage to care. Barriers to HTC among MSM include fear of a positive result, perceived low risk, concerns about confidentiality, discomfort with health providers who may be judgemental, and inconvenient clinic hours or locations [9,10]. Conventional outreach and clinic-based services, largely delivered through hospitals and a few community organisations, have not reached sufficient numbers of MSM at risk, particularly younger men and those who do not identify with established gay communities. Communications technologies and online engagement Internet and mobile technologies offer an opportunity to address these gaps. Thailand has high rates of internet and social media use, and MSM are among the most active internet-using groups in the country. Many seek sexual partners, social networks, and health information online [14]. Globally, online interventions have been used to deliver HIV prevention messages, promote testing, and recruit hard-to-reach populations, with promising results in settings such as the United States, China, and Europe [15–17]. The anonymity and accessibility of digital platforms may lower barriers related to stigma and enable tailored, peer-style communication. Online counselling can address misconceptions, assess risk, and offer personalised referral. Nevertheless, the evidence base for such approaches in low- and middle-income settings remains limited. Few programmes have described how online engagement can be systematically connected to physical services, an approach often termed “online-to-offline”, and fewer still have reported outcomes across the full pathway from online contact to testing, diagnosis, and linkage to treatment. In Thailand, existing online HIV content for MSM has largely been informational, was not integrated with service delivery, and rarely used incentives or marketing techniques that are standard in commercial settings. Moreover, MSM-friendly service providers, including private clinics and hospitals, were not well connected to online outreach efforts, which limited the capacity to refer men to services that they found acceptable and convenient [10]. The Adam's Love programme To address these gaps, the Thai Red Cross AIDS Research Centre, a long-standing leader in HIV research, clinical care, and community services in Thailand, developed Adam's Love in 2011. The strategy combines a dedicated website with social media and web message boards for online counselling and appointment making. It also includes a membership club offering non-financial incentives for HTC, targeted marketing and promotion, and collaboration with MSM-friendly clinics to widen access to services. The programme draws on principles of social marketing, peer-based counselling, and health communication theory, and is intended to build trust and normalise regular testing among MSM [18]. Objectives This paper describes the design, implementation, and outcomes of Adam's Love from its launch in September 2011 through January 2015. We describe the components of the strategy, report indicators of online reach and engagement, and document the number of MSM counselled online and referred to HTC, sexually transmitted infection (STI) testing, and HIV treatment services. We also examine the uptake and HIV diagnoses among men recruited online who joined the club membership programme. By documenting these experiences, we aim to assess the feasibility of online-to-offline models for increasing early HIV testing and linkage to care among Thai MSM, and to offer lessons applicable to similar settings in the region where epidemics among MSM are expanding. Programme setting and design This programme description and evaluation was conducted by the Thai Red Cross AIDS Research Centre (TRCARC) in Bangkok, Thailand. Adam's Love was designed as an online-to-offline (O2O) demand-creation and linkage strategy. Its aim was to reach gay men and other MSM who had never tested for HIV or had not tested recently, and to link them to HIV testing and counselling (HTC), sexually transmitted infection (STI) services and treatment. The intervention was developed using a participatory approach. Community-based organisations, MSM peer educators, clinicians and communications specialists took part in formative discussions, and the design drew on social marketing principles [1,2] and earlier experience with web-based outreach to MSM in Asia [3]. We analysed routinely collected programme data from the launch in September 2011 to January 2015. No experimental comparison group was used. Intervention components Dedicated website. A Thai-language website was developed with content on HIV prevention, risk assessment, HTC procedures, post-exposure prophylaxis, STI information, antiretroviral therapy (ART) and service locations. Content was written in language and imagery acceptable to MSM, was non-stigmatising and was reviewed by clinicians for accuracy. The site was updated regularly with news, personal stories and service promotions. Integrated social media and web message boards. The website was linked to a Facebook page, other social networking platforms, and message-board functions. Trained online counsellors, who were peer educators and nurses, staffed these channels. They answered queries, conducted brief risk assessments, encouraged HTC and made appointments. Counsellors followed standard operating procedures covering confidentiality, motivational counselling techniques, referral pathways and escalation of urgent concerns. Clients who reported being HIV positive were advised about CD4 testing, ART initiation and available treatment services. Counsellors received initial training and regular supervision and case review. Club membership programme. MSM recruited online were invited to join a membership club that offered non-financial incentives. These included priority appointments, reminders for repeat testing, access to members-only events and promotional items, and discounts at partner venues. Eligibility required being male, aged 18 years or older, reporting sex with men and providing informed consent for registration and follow-up. At enrolment members completed a short questionnaire covering demographics, sexual behaviour and previous testing. Members were encouraged to take an HIV test at least every six months, or every three months if they were at higher risk. Targeted marketing and promotion. Online banners, search-engine optimisation, social media advertisements and collaborations with popular MSM websites and mobile applications raised awareness of the site. Promotional campaigns were timed to coincide with key events such as World AIDS Day and Pride festivals, and offered themed messages. Promotional material was refined over time based on website analytics and audience feedback. Service network and accessibility. TRCARC collaborated with MSM-friendly clinics, community-based organisations and private hospitals to widen the range of HTC sites, extend opening hours (including evenings and weekends) and reduce travel and waiting times. Partner sites agreed to follow national HTC guidelines [4], which include pre-test information, rapid or laboratory-based testing, post-test counselling and same-day results where possible. Clients could choose a preferred site when they made an appointment. Those diagnosed with HIV were referred for CD4 testing and ART, with counsellors providing follow-up reminders. Data sources and indicators Data came from three sources. 1. Website analytics. We used web analytics software to record unique viewers, page views, session duration and traffic sources. 2. Online counselling records. Counsellors recorded each counselling contact in a standardised log. The log captured the topic of the query, the advice given and referrals made to HTC, STI testing or HIV treatment services. Because a single individual might make more than one contact, the number of individuals counselled was estimated by removing duplicate contacts using usernames, email addresses and session information where available. 3. Club membership database. Enrolment records included demographic and behavioural data as well as HIV test results from affiliated services. Test results were entered by clinic staff using a unique member identifier, and the data were kept separate from personal identifiers. The main programme indicators were: (i) reach, measured as unique viewers and page views; (ii) estimated number receiving online counselling; (iii) number of referrals to HTC, STI testing and HIV treatment services; (iv) number of members enrolled in the club; and (v) HIV positivity among members who took an HIV test. HIV positivity was defined as the proportion of members tested who received a confirmed HIV-positive result according to national testing algorithms [4]. Laboratory procedures Participating sites performed HIV testing using nationally approved rapid or enzyme immunoassay screening followed by confirmatory testing in line with Thai Ministry of Public Health guidelines [4]. Reactive results were confirmed using a second and, where required, a third assay. Results were delivered by trained counsellors with post-test counselling, and those with positive results were offered immediate linkage to care. Data analysis We analysed data descriptively, with counts and proportions used to summarise programme reach, referrals and membership. Trends in website traffic and counselling contacts were examined by calendar period. Characteristics of club members were summarised with medians and interquartile ranges for continuous variables and frequencies for categorical variables. HIV positivity was calculated with exact 95% confidence intervals. Chi-square or Fisher's exact tests were used to compare positivity across demographic and behavioural subgroups, where numbers allowed. Analyses were performed using standard statistical software, and a two-sided p value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Because referral figures reflect counsellor records rather than confirmed attendance, they were interpreted as indicators of intent and activity rather than of completed service uptake. Ethical considerations Programme activities and the use of routinely collected, de-identified data for evaluation were approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Faculty of Medicine, Chulalongkorn University. Online users were informed that their communications were confidential and that information would be used for programme improvement. Club members provided written or electronic informed consent at enrolment. Identifiable information was stored on password-protected servers accessible only to authorised staff, and results were reported only in aggregate form. Website reach and engagement From its launch in September 2011 to January 2015, the Adam's Love website recorded 1.69 million unique viewers and more than 8 million page views, an average of about 4.7 page views per viewer. Traffic rose steadily over the period, with the sharpest increases following targeted promotions and the integration of social media channels. Peaks in visits also coincided with World AIDS Day activities and with campaigns on popular MSM web boards and social networking applications. Most visitors accessed the site through search engines or links from partner platforms. Smaller proportions arrived through direct entry or social media referrals. Mobile devices accounted for a growing share of sessions in each successive year, which reflects wider smartphone use in the target population. Online counselling and referral During the study period, an estimated 11,120 gay men and other MSM received online counselling through the web message boards, social media messaging and live chat. The fifth generation (5G) of wireless networks is expected to support enhanced mobile broadband, ultra-reliable low-latency communications, and massive connectivity within a single architecture [1], [2]. To meet these requirements, 5G combines the wide coverage and robust propagation of sub-6 GHz bands with the multi-gigahertz bandwidths available in the millimeter wave (mmWave) range [3]. At the same time, cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) has emerged as a promising network paradigm in which a large number of geographically distributed access points (APs), coordinated by a central processing unit (CPU), jointly serve all user equipments (UEs) without cell boundaries [4], [5]. This architecture offers macro-diversity and uniform quality of service, and it is therefore a natural candidate for deploying mixed sub-6 GHz/mmWave networks. Motivation and Problem Statement Despite these benefits, mmWave links are highly sensitive to blockage. Human bodies, vehicles, and buildings can cause attenuation of tens of decibels and rapid transitions between line-of-sight (LOS) and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions [6], [7]. In a cell-free network, a UE may thus see markedly different channel qualities toward different APs and frequency bands. Moreover, the downlink (DL) and uplink (UL) are not equally affected. The transmit power asymmetry between APs and UEs, the different array gains, and the distinct interference patterns create a propagation imbalance, so that the best DL serving node or band is not necessarily the best one for the UL [8]. Conventional systems that couple UL and DL to the same AP and carrier are therefore suboptimal in blockage-prone environments. UL/DL decoupling (DUDe) addresses this issue by allowing a UE to associate with different APs, and possibly different frequency bands, in the two directions [9], [10]. Earlier studies on heterogeneous networks showed that decoupling improves UL throughput, load balancing, and energy efficiency [9]–[11]. More recently, it has been extended to mixed sub-6 GHz/mmWave scenarios, where the lower band can act as a robust fallback for the UL while the mmWave band delivers high DL rates [12]. However, practical decoupling needs fast and reliable radio resource management. The usual approach relies on continuous measurement of the DL reference signal receive power (RSRP) on every candidate band and AP. For mmWave, such measurements require beam sweeping and frequent reporting, which increase latency, signaling overhead, and UE energy consumption [13]. Hence, there is a tension between reliability, which demands accurate knowledge of both bands, and latency, which demands few measurements. Related Work Machine learning (ML) has been widely investigated to reduce this measurement burden. Supervised learning has been applied to beam prediction, handover management, and blockage prediction in mmWave systems [14]–[16]. Several works exploit sub-6 GHz channel information to infer mmWave channel characteristics, relying on the partial correlation of the two bands' spatial structure [17], [18]. Deep neural networks have been proposed to predict mmWave beams and blockage from sub-6 GHz channels, but they commonly require large datasets and long training phases [17]. Other studies use LOS/NLOS identification based on the Rician $K$-factor, which characterizes the ratio between the dominant specular component and the scattered power, and thus provides a compact indicator of link state [19], [20]. For user association in cell-free networks, existing methods are largely based on large-scale fading or optimization frameworks that assume full knowledge of all links [5], [21]. To the best of our knowledge, a learning-based decoupling scheme that eventually dispenses with mmWave measurements has not been addressed. Proposed Approach and Contributions In this paper, we introduce a semi-blind UL/DL decoupling framework for mixed sub-6 GHz/mmWave cell-free massive MIMO networks. The term "semi-blind" reflects the two-stage operation. In an initial phase, after activation of the scheme, the CPU collects measurements of the Rician $K$-factor and the DL RSRP at both 2.6 GHz and 28 GHz, and labels each sample with the frequency and AP that are best for the UL and for the DL. These labeled data train a non-linear support vector machine (SVM), chosen for its good generalization with limited training data, its robustness to overfitting in moderate-dimensional feature spaces, and its low inference complexity through kernel methods [22], [23]. In the second phase, the CPU permanently stops the mmWave measurements and feeds only sub-6 GHz features to the trained classifier, which blindly predicts the target frequencies and APs for the UL and DL. The main contributions are as follows: - We formulate UL/DL decoupling in mixed sub-6 GHz/mmWave cell-free massive MIMO as a multi-class classification problem, with features derived from the Rician $K$-factor and RSRP, and labels given by the best UL and DL frequency/AP pairs under blockage. - We design a semi-blind protocol that limits mmWave measurements to a finite training period, thereby reducing signaling overhead, UE energy consumption, and decision latency in steady-state operation. - We develop a non-linear SVM classifier and study kernel selection, feature choice, and training set size. We compare it with other standard classifiers to justify the selection. - Through simulations with realistic channel models that include LOS/NLOS transitions, we show that the proposed classifier reaches an accuracy of $95\%$ with few training samples, and we assess the resulting UL and DL performance relative to coupled association. Organization of the Paper The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II describes the system model, the channel and blockage models, and the UL and DL signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio expressions. Section III formulates the decoupling problem and details the measurement features. Section IV presents the SVM-based classification algorithms and the semi-blind procedure. Section V reports numerical results and discusses complexity. Section VI concludes the paper and outlines future directions. A. System Model and Channel Characterization We consider a cell-free massive MIMO network in which L access points (APs), each equipped with both a sub-6 GHz (2.6 GHz) and a mmWave (28 GHz) radio unit, jointly serve K single-antenna user equipments (UEs) under the coordination of a central processing unit (CPU) [1], [2]. Time-division duplexing is assumed at both carriers, so that channel reciprocity holds within each coherence block. The channel between AP l and UE k at carrier f ∈ {2.6, 28} GHz is modeled as a Rician fading vector, h{lk}^{(f)} = sqrt(β{lk}^{(f)}) ( sqrt(K{lk}^{(f)}/(K{lk}^{(f)}+1)) h̄{lk}^{(f)} + sqrt(1/(K{lk}^{(f)}+1)) h̃{lk}^{(f)} ), where β is the large-scale fading coefficient, K is the Rician K-factor, h̄ is the deterministic LOS component of unit-modulus entries, and h̃ ~ CN(0, I) is the non-line-of-sight (NLOS) component. Path loss, LOS probability, and blockage follow the 3GPP urban-micro model [3], with an additional blockage penalty applied at 28 GHz to reproduce the propagation imbalance between the two bands. The K-factor is a compact indicator of the LOS condition: large values correspond to unobstructed links, while values close to zero indicate blockage or heavy scattering. B. Measurement Phase and Feature Construction After the decoupling procedure is activated, the CPU enters a training phase of N measurement instants. For each UE–AP pair (k,l) and each carrier f, it collects (i) the downlink reference signal received power (RSRP), RSRP{lk}^{(f)} = Pl^{(f)} β{lk}^{(f)} G^{(f)} , averaged over the reference-signal resource elements, and (ii) an estimate of the Rician K-factor. The K-factor is estimated from pilot observations through the moment-based estimator [4], K̂ = sqrt(1 − γ) / (1 − sqrt(1 − γ)), γ = Var(|y|²)/E²(|y|²), where y denotes the received pilot samples over a sliding window. The moment-based estimator avoids iterative maximum-likelihood fitting and is therefore suitable for low-latency operation at the CPU. For every UE–AP pair, the feature vector is x = [RSRP^{(2.6)}, K̂^{(2.6)}, RSRP^{(28)}, K̂^{(28)}]ᵀ (in dB scale for the RSRP and K-factor), standardized to zero mean and unit variance using training statistics. Once training is finished, the CPU discards the mmWave measurements permanently, and the operational feature vector reduces to xs = [RSRP^{(2.6)}, K̂^{(2.6)}]ᵀ. This reduction is what makes the scheme semi-blind: mmWave quantities are required only to build the labels and train the classifier, not to take decoupling decisions. C. Labeling of Target Frequencies and Access Points Decoupling means that the uplink and downlink may be served by different carriers and different APs. During training, the full measurement set is used to define ground-truth labels. For the downlink, the target is (fDL, lDL) = argmax{f,l} RSRP{lk}^{(f)}, and for the uplink, accounting for the lower transmit power of UEs and the carrier-dependent path loss, the target is (fUL, lUL) = argmin{f,l} PL{lk}^{(f)} , with PL derived from the RSRP and the known AP transmit power and antenna gains [5]. Each distinct pair (f,l) is associated with a class index, so that UL and DL decisions are two separate multiclass problems, and the cases where they differ define the decoupled regime. In practice, the number of candidate APs per UE is limited to the M strongest ones to keep the number of classes tractable. D. Non-Linear SVM Classifier Given the training set {(xi, yi)}{i=1}^{N}, with yi the class label, a soft-margin SVM with kernel mapping φ(·) solves [6] min{w,b,ξ} ½‖w‖² + C Σi ξi s.t. yi(wᵀφ(xi)+b) ≥ 1 − ξi, ξi ≥ 0. The dual problem depends only on the kernel κ(xi,xj)=φ(xi)ᵀφ(xj). We adopt the Gaussian radial basis function kernel, κ(xi,xj) = exp(−g‖xi − xj‖²), since the boundary separating LOS-dominated from blocked regions in the (RSRP, K) plane is non-linear. Multiclass classification is performed with a one-versus-one scheme and majority voting. During training the classifier is learned on the four-dimensional features, to reveal how the mmWave information is encoded in the labels; it is then retrained, or equivalently fit directly, on the two-dimensional sub-6 GHz features paired with the same labels, so that inference needs only 2.6 GHz data. The hyperparameters C and g are selected through grid search with k-fold cross-validation over logarithmically spaced values. Because the number of training samples is intentionally small, class weights inversely proportional to class frequency are used to compensate for imbalance. E. Simulation Setup and Performance Metrics UEs and APs are dropped uniformly in a square area with wrap-around to avoid boundary effects, and independent shadowing and blockage realizations are drawn for each drop. The dataset is split into training and test subsets; the training size N is varied to assess sample efficiency. Performance is evaluated through the accuracy score, Acc = (1/Nt) Σ{j=1}^{Nt} 1{ŷj = yj}, computed separately for the UL and DL decisions, together with per-class precision and recall and the confusion matrix. Results are averaged over multiple Monte Carlo drops. As benchmarks we consider a linear SVM, k-nearest neighbors, and a rule-based strategy that selects the carrier with the highest 2.6 GHz RSRP, thereby quantifying the gain of the non-linear classifier and the information contributed by the K-factor. F. Complexity and Signaling Considerations Training an SVM scales between O(N²) and O(N³) in the number of samples, which remains manageable at the CPU owing to the small N. At inference, the cost is O(Nsv d) per decision, where Nsv is the number of support vectors and d the feature dimension. Stopping mmWave measurements after training eliminates the associated reference-signal overhead, beam-sweeping latency, and UE energy consumption, while the decoupling decisions are updated using only sub-6 GHz measurements. Simulation Setup We consider a cell-free massive MIMO network in a 1 km² urban area, where L = 30 APs, each co-located at sub-6 GHz (2.6 GHz) and mmWave (28 GHz), serve K = 40 randomly distributed UEs. Large-scale fading follows the 3GPP urban microcell model [3], with distance-dependent LOS probability and blockage. The Rician K-factor is computed per UE-AP link from the LOS component and the scattered power. The DL RSRP is computed at both bands, and log-normal shadowing is added. Noise power, transmit powers and antenna gains follow standard 5G NR values [4]. The ground-truth label of each UE specifies the best DL and UL AP/frequency pair, obtained from the maximum RSRP in DL and the minimum path loss under the UE power constraint in UL. The features are the K-factor and RSRP at 2.6 GHz and 28 GHz during the training phase, and only the 2.6 GHz features thereafter. All features are standardized. An SVM with a Gaussian radial basis function (RBF) kernel is trained, with the regularization parameter C and kernel width

Cholera is an acute diarrhoeal disease caused by ingestion of food or water contaminated with toxigenic Vibrio cholerae serogroups O1 and O139. Infection is often asymptomatic or mild, but approximately 5–10% of infected individuals develop severe watery diarrhoea and vomiting that can lead to profound dehydration, hypovolaemic shock, and death within hours if untreated [1,2]. Global burden estimates suggest that 1.3 to 4.0 million cases and 21,000 to 143,000 deaths occur annually, with the greatest burden in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia [3]. Cholera is a marker of inequity: it persists where access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) is inadequate, and it emerges explosively where conflict, displacement, or disasters disrupt these services [4,5]. Transmission and established risk factors The classical transmission pathway is faecal–oral, through contaminated drinking water or food. Epidemiological investigations in diverse settings have identified a recurring set of risk factors. These include consumption of untreated surface or shared water sources, storage of water in open or unclean containers, inadequate handwashing, consumption of food from street vendors or at social gatherings, contact with a cholera patient in the household, and attendance at funerals of cholera victims [6–9]. Protective factors include household water treatment, use of soap, and oral cholera vaccination [10,11]. However, the relative importance of these determinants varies with local ecology, culture, and infrastructure. Locally specific dietary practices, such as the consumption of raw produce or particular foods, may constitute additional, context-dependent vehicles of transmission that are not captured by generic prevention guidance [12]. Case-control studies conducted during outbreaks therefore remain essential for informing targeted interventions. The cholera epidemic in Yemen Yemen has experienced cholera intermittently, but the current epidemic is unprecedented in scale. Following the escalation of armed conflict in 2015, the country's health, water, and sanitation systems deteriorated markedly. Cholera cases were reported from October 2016, and after a first wave, a much larger second wave began in April 2017 [13,14]. By 2018, more than 1.4 million suspected cases and several thousand associated deaths had been reported, making this the largest documented cholera outbreak in modern history [15]. Genomic analyses indicate that the outbreak strain belongs to the seventh pandemic El Tor lineage, closely related to isolates circulating in East Africa, suggesting introduction from outside the country followed by sustained local transmission [16]. The drivers of this epidemic are complex. Fighting has damaged water treatment plants, pumping stations, and sewage networks; fuel shortages limit water pumping and waste disposal; and unpaid public-sector workers, including health and sanitation staff, have curtailed services [14,17]. Millions of people have been displaced, often into crowded settings with limited WASH facilities. Malnutrition, which is highly prevalent among Yemeni children, further increases susceptibility to severe disease [17]. Under these conditions, households rely on alternative water sources such as water trucks, shared tanks, and unprotected wells, which are vulnerable to contamination. Health authorities and humanitarian partners have responded with case management through diarrhoea treatment centres and oral rehydration points, chlorination of water, hygiene promotion, and, from 2018, targeted oral cholera vaccination in selected districts [15,18]. Nevertheless, the epidemic has continued in successive waves. Rationale for the present study Effective prevention requires an understanding of how transmission occurs in the specific circumstances of Yemen. Several features of Yemeni society could shape exposure. Khat (Catha edulis), a leafy stimulant chewed daily by a large proportion of the adult population, is typically consumed fresh and unprocessed, often in social gatherings, and is grown with irrigation water of uncertain quality and handled by multiple intermediaries before sale. Whether khat, like other raw produce, can act as a vehicle for faecal–oral pathogens has received little attention, and washing practices before chewing are variable. In addition, population movement within and between governorates, and visits by relatives from affected areas, may facilitate introduction of infection into communities. Despite the magnitude of the epidemic, published analytical epidemiological evidence from Yemen is scarce. Most available information derives from surveillance reports describing the distribution of suspected cases by time, place, and age, which cannot quantify the contribution of specific exposures [13,15]. Security constraints, limited access, and the overburdened health system have made field investigations difficult. Aden, the temporary capital and a major port city that has received large numbers of displaced persons and has experienced repeated epidemic waves, provides an important setting in which to examine risk factors. Its urban environment, with a mixture of piped and non-piped water supplies, is also representative of many conflict-affected cities. Identifying modifiable behavioural and environmental determinants of cholera in this setting is a prerequisite for evidence-based public health messaging and for prioritising limited resources, such as water chlorination, distribution of soap and household water treatment products, and community hygiene education. We therefore conducted a case-control study in Aden in 2018 to identify risk factors associated with cholera infection during the ongoing outbreak, considering demographic characteristics, travel and contact history, food and water exposures, and household hygiene practices. The findings are intended to guide control measures in Yemen and to inform preparedness in other fragile settings where cholera threatens populations affected by conflict. Study design and setting We conducted an unmatched case-control study in Aden Governorate, southern Yemen, between [month] and [month] 2018, during the ongoing cholera epidemic that began in late 2016. Aden is a port city divided into eight districts, with a population of roughly one million. It hosts a large number of internally displaced persons, and its water, sanitation and health infrastructure has been severely damaged by conflict [1,2]. Cholera cases are treated at diarrhoea treatment centres (DTCs) and cholera treatment units run by the Ministry of Public Health and Population and supported by humanitarian partners. The study was nested within routine surveillance and was designed in accordance with World Health Organization (WHO) and Global Task Force on Cholera Control guidance on case-control investigations of cholera [3]. Reporting followed the STROBE guidelines for observational studies [4]. Case definition and selection Cases were identified from the three largest DTCs in Aden. A suspected case was defined using the WHO definition: a person aged two years or older who developed acute watery diarrhoea, with or without vomiting, during the study period [3]. To improve specificity, we included only patients with a positive rapid diagnostic test (Crystal VC-O1 dipstick) or, when available, culture-confirmed Vibrio cholerae O1 from a stool or rectal swab. Patients were eligible if they had resided in Aden for at least the preceding two weeks, had onset of symptoms within the previous 72 hours, and gave consent (or consent was given by a guardian). Patients who were severely ill and unable to respond, or who had no available proxy respondent, were excluded. Consecutive eligible patients were enrolled until the target sample size was reached. Control selection Two community controls were selected per case. A control was defined as a person living in the same district as the case, aged two years or older, who had not had acute diarrhoea in the preceding four weeks. Controls were recruited from the neighbourhood of each case using a modified random-walk procedure: from the case's household, the interviewer chose a random direction, selected every third household, and enrolled one eligible resident. If no eligible person was present, the next household was visited. Where more than one eligible person lived in a household, one was selected by lottery. Controls were frequency-matched to cases by age group (<15 and ≥15 years) to keep the age distribution comparable, and persons from the same household as a case were not eligible. Sample size Sample size was calculated for a two-sided significance level of 5% and 80% power, assuming a control-to-case ratio of 2:1, an expected exposure prevalence of 30% among controls to a major risk factor (e.g. use of unsafe water), and a detectable odds ratio of 3.0 [5]. This yielded a minimum of approximately 55 cases and 110 controls. We enrolled 59 cases and 118 controls to allow for incomplete data. Data collection A structured questionnaire in Arabic was developed from published cholera case-control studies and WHO tools [3,6,7]. It was pre-tested on a small group of patients and community members outside the study sample, and adjusted for clarity and cultural appropriateness. Trained interviewers, who were health workers with experience in epidemiological surveillance, administered the questionnaire face to face at the DTC (cases) or at the home (controls). Interviewers were not blinded to case status. For children, the primary caregiver answered the questions. The questionnaire covered: (i) sociodemographic characteristics (age, sex, education, household size, income, displacement status); (ii) exposure history in the three days before symptom onset for cases, and in the three days before interview for controls; (iii) travel outside Aden Province and visitors from outside the province in the preceding two weeks; (iv) contact with a person with diarrhoea; (v) food history, including meals eaten outside the home, consumption of raw vegetables, fruit, seafood, and khat (Catha edulis), and whether these were washed before consumption; (vi) water source (piped network, public tap, water trucking, protected or unprotected well, or bottled water), storage, and treatment; common-source water was defined as water obtained from a shared point used by multiple households; (vii) household hygiene and sanitation, including latrine type, handwashing practices, soap availability, and use of chlorine for water or surface disinfection; and (viii) receipt of oral cholera vaccine, although vaccination campaigns had not been conducted in Aden at that time. Variables and definitions The outcome was cholera case status. Exposures were coded as binary variables, with the least risky category taken as reference. Continuous variables such as age and household size were categorised using clinically or programmatically meaningful cut-offs. Handwashing and soap use were self-reported, and soap presence was verified by observation where permitted. Data management and statistical analysis Data were double-entered into EpiData 3.1 and analysed with Stata version 15 (StataCorp, College Station, TX) [8]. Descriptive statistics were used to summarise participant characteristics. Differences between cases and controls were assessed using the chi-square or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables and the Student t-test or Mann–Whitney U test for continuous variables, as appropriate. In bivariate analysis, crude odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using unconditional logistic regression. Variables with p<0.20 in bivariate analysis, together with those considered biologically relevant a priori, were considered for the multivariable model. We used backward stepwise elimination based on likelihood ratio tests, retaining variables with p<0.05, and adjusted for age group and sex regardless of significance. Collinearity was checked using variance inflation factors and correlation among exposures; where two variables were highly correlated (e.g. soap use and chlorine use), the one with greater plausibility was retained. Model fit was assessed using the Hosmer–Lemeshow test, and discrimination using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Adjusted ORs (aORs) with 95% CIs are reported. All tests were two-sided, with a significance level of 0.05. Missing data were minimal (<5% for any variable) and a complete-case analysis was performed. Ethical considerations The study was approved by the ethics committee of [institution] and by the Aden Governorate Health Office. Written informed consent was obtained from all adult participants and from parents or guardians of minors, with assent obtained from children aged 12 years and older. Participation was voluntary, and confidentiality was maintained through anonymised coding. Treatment of cases was not affected by participation, and controls reporting symptoms were referred to health services. Interviewers received training on infection prevention and used personal protective equipment during household visits. Study population and participant characteristics A total of 59 cholera cases and 118 community controls were enrolled, giving a case-to-control ratio of 1:2. The analysis of high-dimensional data is a central task in machine learning (ML) and knowledge discovery (KD). It is also notoriously difficult. Many algorithms degrade as the number of features grows: nearest-neighbor search loses its discriminative power, distance-based clustering becomes unstable, and the sample size needed for reliable estimation increases dramatically. These phenomena are collectively known as the curse of dimensionality. Their practical importance has led to a large body of literature that investigates their origins and consequences, using tools from statistics, computer science, and mathematics. A recurring observation is that the nominal dimension of a data set, meaning the number of coordinates used to represent each point, is often a poor predictor of how hard the data are to analyze. Data may lie close to a low-dimensional manifold, may be strongly clustered, or may have rapidly decaying variance along most directions. Conversely, data in a low-dimensional ambient space can exhibit behavior typical of high dimension. This motivates the notion of intrinsic dimension: a quantity meant to capture the effective complexity of the data, independent of the particular representation. Numerous estimators have been proposed, among them PCA-based approaches, fractal and correlation dimensions, and nearest-neighbor-based maximum likelihood estimators. They are often useful in practice, but they rest on different assumptions and are usually justified heuristically. They may give inconsistent answers on the same data, and it is rarely clear which properties a reasonable notion of dimension should satisfy. From a mathematical perspective, a particularly illuminating explanation of the dimension curse is the concentration of measure phenomenon. In high-dimensional spaces such as spheres, cubes, or Gaussian spaces, every sufficiently regular function is almost constant on a set of nearly full measure. As a consequence, distances between random points concentrate around a typical value, and the contrast on which many ML algorithms rely vanishes. This link was recognized in the ML/KD literature, and it suggests that intrinsic dimension should be tied to concentration properties. Pestov developed this idea into an axiomatic approach: a dimension function for metric spaces with measure should, among other requirements, assign the expected dimension to standard objects, behave monotonically under suitable maps, and reflect the concentration phenomenon through a suitable observable diameter. Gromov's metric measure geometry supplies the framework for this, providing the notions of observable diameter, concentration function, and the distance between metric measure spaces. Pestov's approach was developed for idealized objects, namely metric spaces with probability measures, whereas data sets are finite, may carry additional structure, and are analyzed by algorithms that use only certain features of that structure. The present work aims to bridge this gap. We introduce a model of a geometric data set that combines a metric measure space, which describes the geometry and distribution of the data, with a family of functions, or features, which describes what a given ML/KD algorithm can observe. This second ingredient makes the model adaptable: different algorithms, for instance those using only linear functionals, Lipschitz functions, or the outputs of a given class of classifiers, correspond to different feature classes and therefore to different notions of intrinsic dimension. We define isomorphism of geometric data sets and study the set of isomorphism classes. Our first main contribution is structural. We introduce a metric on the set of isomorphism classes, inspired by the Gromov–Wasserstein and box distances, which makes it possible to quantify how close two data sets are, including a finite sample and the underlying distribution from which it is drawn. We also define a partial order, a form of domination, which expresses that one data set is a simplification of another, obtained through feature-preserving maps. We investigate the topological and order-theoretic properties of these objects, including compatibility between the order and the metric. Our second main contribution is an axiomatic treatment of intrinsic dimension for geometric data sets. Building on Pestov's axioms, we formulate requirements for a dimension function: monotonicity with respect to the partial order, continuity or stability with respect to the metric, normalization on reference examples, and consistency with measure concentration. We show that these requirements are mutually compatible by constructing a concrete dimension function that satisfies them. The function is defined through the concentration behavior of the feature class, via a notion of separation or observable diameter, and we prove its basic properties, including its behavior under products and its relation to the classical notion of dimension on model spaces. Third, we address computational feasibility. A definition that cannot be evaluated on real data would be of limited value to the ML/KD community. We show that our dimension function can be estimated from finite samples and we describe algorithms for doing so. Experiments on synthetic and real data sets illustrate that the resulting values reflect known intrinsic structure, that they respond sensibly to the choice of feature class, and that they correlate with the performance of specific algorithms, such as nearest-neighbor classification, on the data. The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the necessary background from metric measure geometry and Pestov's axioms. Section 3 defines geometric data sets, their isomorphism classes, and the metric and partial order. Section 4 presents the axioms and the dimension function and proves its properties. Section 5 discusses estimation and computation, and Section 6 reports experiments. We conclude with a discussion of limitations and directions for future work. We work in the framework of metric measure geometry and adapt it to finite data sets equipped with a family of functions that model the "observables" of a learning algorithm. Geometric data sets. A geometric data set is a triple X = (X, dX, μX), where (X, dX) is a finite (or more generally compact) metric space and μX is a Borel probability measure on X, together with a class FX of real-valued functions on X, typically the 1-Lipschitz functions or a subclass determined by the ML/KD task, for example the functions realizable by a given hypothesis class. Two geometric data sets are isomorphic if there is a measure-preserving isometry between the supports of their measures that maps FX onto FY. We denote by 𝒢 the set of isomorphism classes. For a finite sample x1,…,xn, we take μ to be the empirical measure, optionally weighted, and d to be the Euclidean metric or another task-appropriate metric. Metric on 𝒢. To compare data sets of different size and ambient space, we use a Gromov-type approach based on the Prokhorov and box distances. Let X and Y be geometric data sets. A parametrization of X is a Borel map φ: [0,1] → X with φλ = μX, where λ is Lebesgue measure. We define the observable distance dconc(X,Y) = inf over parametrizations φ, ψ of dH(φ^FX, ψ^FY), where dH is the Hausdorff distance between the pulled-back function classes, measured in the Ky Fan metric on measurable functions on [0,1]. This is a concentration-type distance: it vanishes in the limit for Lévy families, and it is sensitive to the concentration behavior of the functions in F. We show that dconc is a metric on 𝒢 and that sequences of finite samples of a fixed compact geometric data set converge to it in this metric when the empirical measures converge weakly. The proof uses the standard compactness of parametrizations and the stability of the Ky Fan metric under weak convergence. Partial order. We say X dominates Y, written Y ≺ X, if there is a 1-Lipschitz, measure-preserving map π: X → Y with FY ∘ π ⊆ FX. This relation is reflexive and transitive, and antisymmetric on 𝒢 by an argument based on the rigidity of measure-preserving isometric embeddings of compact spaces. We prove that ≺ is closed with respect to dconc, which is needed for the compatibility of the dimension function with limits. Intuitively, Y ≺ X means that Y is a "compression" of X that loses no more concentration than the data itself carries. Axioms for intrinsic dimension. Following Pestov, an intrinsic dimension function is a map dim: 𝒢 → [0,∞) satisfying: 1. Monotonicity: Y ≺ X implies dim(Y) ≤ dim(X). 2. Continuity: dim is continuous with respect to dconc, or at least lower semicontinuous. 3. Normalization: dim of the standard Euclidean sphere or cube of dimension k, with the uniform measure and Lipschitz functions, equals k, up to a universal constant. 4. Concentration (curse of dimensionality): for any Lévy family (Xn), dim(Xn) → ∞. 5. Product behavior: dim(X × Y) ≤ dim(X) + dim(Y) for the ℓ₂-product, with equality up to constants for products of identical factors. We establish which subsets of these axioms are consistent and show they are jointly satisfiable by the function constructed below. Dimension function. Our construction is based on the observable diameter. For κ > 0, the κ-observable diameter of X is ObsDiamκ(X) = sup over f ∈ FX of diam(fμX; 1−κ), where diam(ν; 1−κ) is the smallest length of an interval carrying ν-mass at least 1−κ. For high-dimensional spheres or cubes this quantity decays as the dimension grows, reflecting measure concentration. We define the dimension via the inverse relationship with the observable diameter normalized by a reference scale: dim(X) = sup over κ in a fixed range (0, κ₀] of c(κ) · (DX / ObsDiamκ(X))², where DX is the metric (or L²-) diameter scale of X and c(κ) is a normalization constant chosen so that the unit sphere S^k receives value k. Using Lévy's isoperimetric inequality we show that ObsDiamκ(S^k) ≍ √(log(1/κ)/k), which yields the normalization and the concentration axiom. Monotonicity follows because 1-Lipschitz measure-preserving maps cannot increase observable diameter. Continuity follows from Lipschitz-type estimates of ObsDiamκ in dconc, with a shift in κ. Computation. For a finite sample of size n, we approximate FX by a finite family of functions, in practice (a) distance functions to randomly chosen anchor points, (b) coordinate projections and random linear projections, and (c) functions derived from the algorithm under study, such as the classifier score of a k-nearest-neighbor model or the output of a trained network. For each f, we compute the empirical push-forward measure and its shortest (1−κ)-interval in O(n log n) time by sorting. The overall cost is O(mn log n) for m functions, plus the cost of evaluating them. We estimate DX by the empirical standard deviation of pairwise distances computed on a subsample. We average over repeated subsamples and report standard deviations to quantify the sampling variability. By the convergence result above, the estimates are consistent as n and m increase. Experimental protocol. We evaluate the dimension function on synthetic data (spheres, cubes, Gaussian mixtures, and linear and nonlinear manifolds embedded in higher-dimensional spaces) to check agreement with known dimension, and on real image and tabular data sets. For algorithm adaptation, we vary FX to the function class of a given method and compare the resulting dimension with the observed performance degradation of that method as dimension increases. We also compare against standard estimators (PCA-based, maximum likelihood, correlation dimension) using the same samples. We first summarize the structural results on geometric data sets, then the axiomatic dimension theory, and finally the experimental findings. Geometric data sets and their comparison. We define a geometric data set as a triple (X, d, μ) consisting of a finite set X, a metric d, and a probability measure μ, together with a finite family of real-valued feature functions F that encode the geometry relevant to a given learning task. Two such data sets are isomorphic if there is a measure-preserving isometry that also carries the feature families onto one another. On the set of isomorphism classes we introduced a metric, denoted dG, which combines a Gromov–Prokhorov-type (box) distance on the underlying metric measure spaces with a term comparing the feature families. We proved that dG is a genuine metric, that it is complete on the class of data sets with bounded diameter, and that finite data sets sampled with increasing size from a fixed distribution converge to the underlying space in dG with high probability. Convergence rates depend on the covering properties of the support but not on the ambient dimension. We also introduced a partial order ≺

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, accounting for nearly one third of all deaths each year [1]. Epidemiological studies have consistently shown that premenopausal women have a lower incidence of coronary heart disease, hypertension, and heart failure than age-matched men, and that this relative protection diminishes after menopause [2,3]. The incidence of cardiovascular events in women rises sharply in the decade following the cessation of ovarian function, eventually approaching that of men [4]. These observations have led to the long-standing hypothesis that endogenous ovarian hormones, particularly 17β-estradiol (E2), confer protection against cardiac injury and adverse remodeling. E2 is the most abundant and biologically potent estrogen in premenopausal women. Beyond its classical roles in reproductive physiology, E2 exerts pleiotropic effects on the cardiovascular system, including vasodilation, modulation of lipid metabolism, attenuation of inflammation, and inhibition of vascular smooth muscle proliferation [5,6]. In the myocardium, experimental studies indicate that E2 reduces cardiomyocyte apoptosis, limits infarct size after ischemia-reperfusion injury, attenuates pathological hypertrophy, and preserves mitochondrial function [7-9]. Ovariectomy in animal models aggravates cardiac dysfunction after pressure overload or myocardial infarction, and these deleterious effects are largely reversed by E2 supplementation [10,11]. Collectively, these findings underscore the importance of E2 in maintaining cardiac homeostasis in women of reproductive age. The biological actions of E2 are mediated primarily through estrogen receptors (ERs). Three ER subtypes have been identified in cardiomyocytes: the classical nuclear receptors ERα and ERβ, and the membrane-associated G protein-coupled estrogen receptor GPR30 (also known as GPER) [12,13]. ERα and ERβ are ligand-activated transcription factors encoded by separate genes, and they share a conserved structure comprising a DNA-binding domain and a ligand-binding domain. Upon E2 binding, they dimerize and translocate to the nucleus, where they regulate the transcription of target genes by binding to estrogen response elements or by interacting with other transcription factors such as AP-1 and Sp1 (the genomic pathway) [14]. In addition, a subpopulation of ERα and ERβ localizes at the plasma membrane and in caveolae, where it rapidly activates kinase cascades, including PI3K/Akt, MAPK/ERK, and endothelial nitric oxide synthase signaling, within seconds to minutes (the nongenomic pathway) [15,16]. GPR30 further contributes to rapid estrogen signaling through the activation of adenylyl cyclase, transactivation of the epidermal growth factor receptor, and mobilization of intracellular calcium [17]. The relative contribution of each receptor subtype to cardioprotection is context dependent, and accumulating evidence suggests that the receptors may act cooperatively or in a compensatory manner depending on the type of cardiac insult [18,19]. Given the apparent cardioprotective effects of E2, hormone replacement therapy (HRT) was initially promoted as a strategy for preventing CVD in postmenopausal women. Early observational studies supported this notion, reporting significant reductions in coronary events among HRT users [20]. However, large randomized controlled trials, notably the Heart and Estrogen/Progestin Replacement Study and the Women's Health Initiative, failed to demonstrate cardiovascular benefit and instead reported increased risks of thromboembolism, stroke, breast cancer, and endometrial cancer [21,22]. Subsequent analyses have proposed the "timing hypothesis," which suggests that the cardiovascular effects of estrogen depend on the age of the patient and the time elapsed since menopause, with benefit observed when therapy is initiated early [23]. Nevertheless, safety concerns, particularly regarding hormone-dependent malignancies, have substantially limited the clinical use of conventional estrogen therapy and stimulated the search for safer alternatives. Phytoestrogens are plant-derived polyphenolic compounds whose structures resemble that of E2 and which can bind to ERs, with a generally higher affinity for ERβ than for ERα [24]. The major classes include isoflavones (genistein, daidzein), lignans, coumestans, and stilbenes such as resveratrol, which are abundant in soybeans, flaxseed, legumes, and grapes [25]. Populations consuming diets rich in these compounds, such as those in East Asia, display a lower incidence of CVD and fewer menopausal symptoms than Western populations [26]. Experimental studies have shown that phytoestrogens can reduce oxidative stress, improve endothelial function, inhibit cardiomyocyte apoptosis, and attenuate cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis, in part through ER-dependent activation of PI3K/Akt and related survival pathways [27-29]. Because of their selective receptor binding and weaker estrogenic activity, phytoestrogens may behave as natural selective estrogen receptor modulators, potentially providing cardiovascular benefit with a reduced risk of adverse effects on the breast and uterus [30]. Clinical findings, however, remain inconsistent, reflecting variability in compounds, doses, study populations, and individual metabolism, such as the gut microbial conversion of daidzein to equol [31]. A better understanding of ER-mediated signaling in cardiomyocytes is therefore essential for the rational development of phytoestrogen-based therapies. In this review, we summarize current knowledge of estrogen and ER-mediated genomic and nongenomic pathways that underlie cardioprotection against diverse stresses. We further discuss the clinical implications of ERs and phytoestrogens and provide insights into the potential of phytoestrogens as alternatives in estrogen replacement therapy. This review was conducted as a narrative literature review following the general principles of the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) to promote transparency in literature identification, selection, and synthesis [1]. Because the topic spans basic molecular biology, preclinical models, and clinical studies, a narrative approach was chosen over a formal systematic review or meta-analysis, as heterogeneity in experimental designs, phytoestrogen preparations, doses, and outcome measures precluded quantitative pooling [2]. Literature search strategy Relevant publications were identified through searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and Embase from database inception to the most recent search date. Searches combined controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH terms) and free-text keywords using Boolean operators. Terms were grouped into four conceptual domains: (i) estrogen and receptors ("17β-estradiol", "estrogen receptor alpha", "estrogen receptor beta", "ERα", "ERβ", "GPR30", "GPER"); (ii) cardiac tissue and cell types ("cardiomyocyte", "heart", "myocardium", "cardiac"); (iii) cardiovascular conditions and stresses ("cardioprotection", "ischemia/reperfusion", "myocardial infarction", "hypertrophy", "heart failure", "apoptosis", "oxidative stress", "doxorubicin"); and (iv) phytoestrogens and therapy ("phytoestrogen", "isoflavone", "genistein", "daidzein", "equol", "resveratrol", "coumestrol", "lignan", "flavonoid", "hormone replacement therapy", "estrogen replacement"). Reference lists of key articles and previous reviews were hand-searched to identify additional studies not captured electronically [3]. Clinical trial registries were consulted to identify relevant completed trials on phytoestrogen supplementation and cardiovascular endpoints. Eligibility criteria Studies were included if they: (1) investigated the role of E2 or its receptors (ERα, ERβ, GPR30) in cardiomyocytes or cardiac tissue, including genomic and nongenomic signaling; (2) examined cardioprotective effects of phytoestrogens or related compounds with demonstrated ER binding or ER-dependent activity; (3) reported clinical or epidemiological data on estrogen replacement therapy, ER polymorphisms, or phytoestrogen intake in relation to cardiovascular outcomes; or (4) were original research articles, clinical trials, meta-analyses, or high-quality reviews published in English. Priority was given to studies using ER-selective agonists or antagonists, receptor knockout or knockdown models, or ovariectomized animals, as these provide mechanistic evidence for receptor involvement [4]. Exclusion criteria were: studies focusing solely on non-cardiac tissues (e.g., breast, bone, or uterus) without relevance to cardiac signaling; reports on phytoestrogens lacking evidence of ER-related mechanisms; conference abstracts, editorials, and non-peer-reviewed material; and articles lacking sufficient methodological detail to interpret findings. Studies of vascular endothelium and smooth muscle were included selectively when they offered mechanistic insight applicable to cardiomyocyte signaling or helped contextualize clinical outcomes. Study selection and data extraction Titles and abstracts were screened for relevance, and full texts of potentially eligible articles were then evaluated against the criteria above. Disagreements regarding inclusion were resolved through discussion among the authors. For each included study, information was extracted on the experimental model (cell line, primary cardiomyocytes, isolated heart, animal species, or human population), the estrogenic compound and dose, the receptor subtype implicated, the cardiac insult applied, the signaling pathways assessed, and the principal outcomes. For clinical studies, details on population characteristics (age, menopausal status), intervention duration, and cardiovascular endpoints were recorded [5]. Thematic organization and synthesis Extracted evidence was organized into thematic categories reflecting the structure of the review. The first category addressed the biosynthesis, physiology, and cardiac actions of E2, including receptor expression patterns in cardiomyocytes. The second covered receptor-specific signaling: genomic pathways involving ligand-dependent nuclear translocation of ERα and ERβ and transcriptional regulation via estrogen response elements, and nongenomic pathways involving membrane-associated ERs and GPR30, with activation of PI3K/Akt, MAPK/ERK, nitric oxide synthase, and calcium-handling cascades [6,7]. The third examined protective effects against specific insults, including ischemia/reperfusion injury, pressure-overload hypertrophy, oxidative stress, apoptosis, and chemotherapy-induced cardiotoxicity. The fourth critically appraised clinical evidence on estrogen replacement therapy, including the divergent findings of large randomized trials and observational studies and the "timing hypothesis" [8]. The fifth evaluated phytoestrogens, grouped by chemical class (isoflavones, stilbenes, lignans, coumestans), with attention to relative ER affinity, receptor subtype selectivity, metabolism (e.g., equol production by gut microbiota), and bioavailability [9]. Findings were synthesized qualitatively. Concordant and discordant results across models were compared, and differences were considered in light of species, sex, hormonal status, dose, and treatment timing. Where available, evidence from receptor-selective pharmacological tools and genetic models was weighted more heavily than correlative observations when inferring receptor-specific mechanisms. Quality considerations and limitations Formal risk-of-bias scoring was not applied given the narrative design; nevertheless, methodological strengths and weaknesses, such as sample size, presence of appropriate controls, use of physiological versus supraphysiological concentrations, and confounding in observational research, were considered when interpreting findings [10]. Limitations of this approach include potential selection bias, restriction to English-language publications, and possible underrepresentation of negative or null results due to publication bias. Mechanistic insights derived from in vitro or rodent models may not fully translate to humans, and this caveat is explicitly noted where relevant. Chemical structures and receptor nomenclature follow current IUPHAR recommendations. Estrogen receptor subtypes and their cardiomyocyte distribution Literature analysis showed that the three ER subtypes, ERα, ERβ and GPR30 (GPER), are all expressed in cardiomyocytes, although their relative abundance varies with species, sex, developmental stage and disease state [1,2]. ERα and ERβ localize to the nucleus, plasma membrane caveolae and mitochondria, whereas GPR30 resides mainly at the endoplasmic reticulum and plasma membrane [3,4]. Expression of ERβ was reported to increase in hypertrophied and failing myocardium, while ERα expression was frequently reduced after ischemic injury, suggesting that subtype balance shifts under stress [5,6]. Genomic signaling mediated by ERα and ERβ Across the reviewed studies, E2 binding to ERα or ERβ induced receptor dimerization and binding to estrogen response elements in target gene promoters. In cardiomyocytes, this regulated genes involved in antioxidant defense (superoxide dismutase, glutathione peroxidase), anti-apoptotic control (Bcl-2, Bcl-xL), calcium handling (SERCA2a) and energy metabolism (PGC-1α, NRF-1) [7–9]. Estrogen treatment also suppressed pro-hypertrophic transcriptional programs, including calcineurin/NFAT and GATA4 activity, and attenuated expression of fibrotic mediators such as TGF-β1 and collagen I [10,11]. ERα was most consistently linked to reduced infarct size and preserved contractile function after ischemia-reperfusion, whereas ERβ was more strongly associated with anti-hypertrophic and anti-fibrotic effects under pressure overload [6,12]. Ovariectomized animals displayed greater hypertrophy, mitochondrial dysfunction and apoptosis, and these changes were largely reversed by E2 replacement [13]. Nongenomic signaling pathways Rapid E2 actions, occurring within seconds to minutes, were attributed to membrane-associated ERα, ERβ and GPR30. The most frequently reported cascade was activation of PI3K/Akt, which phosphorylated eNOS, GSK-3β and Bad, thereby promoting nitric oxide production, inhibiting mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening and limiting apoptosis [14,15]. MAPK/ERK1/2 activation was also observed and was linked to survival signaling in cardiomyocytes exposed to hypoxia/reoxygenation [16]. Activation of GPR30 by E2 or the selective agonist G-1 stimulated adenylyl cyclase, EGFR transactivation and downstream PI3K/Akt and ERK pathways, reducing infarct size in isolated perfused hearts and improving postischemic functional recovery [17,18]. Conversely, the GPR30 antagonist G-15 abolished these protective effects [18]. In addition, E2 modulated L-type calcium channel activity and intracellular calcium transients, limiting calcium overload during stress [19]. Cardioprotection against specific insults Ischemia-reperfusion. E2, ERα-selective agonist PPT, ERβ-selective agonist DPN and G-1 all improved recovery of left ventricular developed pressure and reduced lactate dehydrogenase release, with effects attributed to Akt activation, reduced reactive oxygen species and preservation of mitochondrial membrane potential [12,17,20]. Pressure overload and hypertrophy.
