Pregnancy loss is the most common complication of early pregnancy in humans. Miscarriage, or spontaneous abortion, is defined as the spontaneous loss of a fetus before it is viable, and it occurs in approximately 15–20% of clinically recognized pregnancies [1,2]. If biochemical pregnancies and losses that occur before a pregnancy is clinically recognized are included, the true incidence is considerably higher, and it has been estimated that up to half of all conceptions fail to progress [3]. Most sporadic miscarriages result from random chromosomal abnormalities of the embryo and are not likely to recur. A smaller group of women, however, experience repeated losses, a condition referred to as recurrent spontaneous abortion (RSA), recurrent miscarriage, or habitual abortion. RSA is classically defined as the occurrence of three or more consecutive pregnancy losses before the twentieth week of gestation [4]. Some professional societies, including the American Society for Reproductive Medicine and the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology, have proposed a lower threshold of two or more losses for initiating evaluation, recognizing the substantial emotional burden and the clinical value of earlier investigation [5,6]. By the traditional definition RSA affects about 1% of couples trying to conceive, whereas about 2–5% experience two or more losses [2,7]. The risk of subsequent miscarriage rises with the number of previous losses and with maternal age, so a history of repeated loss itself is an independent predictor of further failure [8]. Beyond the physical risks, RSA is associated with considerable psychological morbidity, including anxiety, depression, and grief, as well as a heavy burden on health care resources [9]. The etiology of RSA is multifactorial, and in many cases it remains incompletely understood. Established causes include parental chromosomal abnormalities, uterine anatomical defects such as septa, fibroids, and intrauterine adhesions, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome and other immunological disturbances, infections, thrombophilic states, environmental and lifestyle factors, and endocrine disorders [4,10]. Even after extensive evaluation, no cause is identified in approximately half of couples, and this unexplained group continues to pose a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge [10]. Endocrine abnormalities are thought to account for roughly 8–12% of cases, which makes them one of the more common and potentially treatable contributors [11]. Successful implantation and maintenance of early pregnancy depend on a finely coordinated hormonal environment. After ovulation, the corpus luteum secretes progesterone and estrogen, which transform the endometrium into a receptive decidua, suppress uterine contractility, and modulate the maternal immune response toward tolerance of the semi-allogeneic conceptus [12]. Thyroid hormones, insulin, prolactin, and androgens also influence follicular development, oocyte quality, endometrial receptivity, and placental function [13]. Disturbance of any part of this regulatory network may therefore compromise implantation, trophoblast invasion, or early embryonic development and lead to pregnancy loss. Several endocrine conditions have been implicated in RSA. Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), the most common endocrinopathy of reproductive-age women, is characterized by hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and frequently insulin resistance and obesity, and it has been associated with an increased risk of early miscarriage [14,15]. Hyperprolactinemia may impair folliculogenesis and corpus luteum function, and dopamine agonist treatment has been reported to improve pregnancy outcome in affected women [16]. Luteal phase defect, an inadequate progesterone-mediated endometrial secretory response, has long been proposed as a cause of implantation failure and early loss, although its diagnostic criteria and clinical significance remain debated [17]. Thyroid dysfunction, both overt and subclinical hypothyroidism as well as thyroid autoimmunity, has been linked to adverse pregnancy outcomes, including miscarriage [18,19]. Diabetes mellitus with poor glycemic control during the periconceptional period increases the risk of miscarriage and congenital malformations through metabolic disturbance of the developing embryo [20]. Hyperandrogenism, whether of ovarian or adrenal origin, may adversely affect endometrial receptivity and early placentation [21]. Despite a large body of literature, the evidence on the relationship between these endocrine disorders and RSA is heterogeneous. Studies differ in their diagnostic criteria, sample sizes, and control populations, and it is often difficult to separate cause from association, as in the case of PCOS, in which obesity, insulin resistance, and elevated luteinizing hormone may each contribute independently [14]. Likewise, the benefit of interventions such as progesterone supplementation, levothyroxine, metformin, and dopamine agonists remains controversial in some settings [22,23]. Because many of these conditions are readily detectable and treatable, clarifying their role is of obvious clinical importance, as appropriate screening and management could improve the live birth rate in affected couples. In this context, the present article reviews the role of endocrine dysfunction in patients with recurrent spontaneous abortion. Relevant publications were identified through electronic databases, including PubMed and Google Scholar, using key words related to recurrent miscarriage and specific endocrine abnormalities. The findings were then grouped according to the individual disorders, namely PCOS, hyperprolactinemia, luteal phase defect, thyroid dysfunction, diabetes, and hyperandrogenism, in order to summarize current understanding of their pathophysiological mechanisms, diagnostic approaches, and treatment options. This narrative review was designed to summarize current evidence on the contribution of endocrine disorders to recurrent spontaneous abortion (RSA). A narrative approach was chosen over a formal systematic review or meta-analysis because the available studies differ widely in design, diagnostic criteria, populations, and outcome definitions, which limits quantitative pooling. The review was planned and reported in accordance with the general principles for narrative reviews, including a transparent search strategy, explicit eligibility criteria, and structured data synthesis [1,2]. Literature search strategy A literature search was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, Google Scholar, and other electronic resources accessible through institutional library services. The search covered articles published from database inception to the date of final search. Searches combined controlled vocabulary (Medical Subject Headings, MeSH) and free-text terms to maximize sensitivity. The main key words and their combinations were: "recurrent spontaneous abortion," "recurrent pregnancy loss," "habitual abortion," "recurrent miscarriage," "endocrine dysfunction," "polycystic ovarian syndrome," "hyperandrogenism," "hyperprolactinemia," "luteal phase defect," "progesterone," "thyroid dysfunction," "hypothyroidism," "thyroid autoimmunity," "diabetes mellitus," "insulin resistance," and "obesity." Boolean operators (AND, OR) were used to combine terms; for instance, "recurrent miscarriage AND thyroid" or "recurrent pregnancy loss AND (insulin resistance OR diabetes)." Reference lists of relevant reviews, guidelines, and original studies were also hand-searched to identify additional publications not captured by the electronic search [3]. Definitions applied Because terminology for pregnancy loss varies among professional bodies, the definition used in this review was established a priori. RSA was defined as three or more consecutive spontaneous pregnancy losses before the 20th week of gestation, in keeping with the traditional definition [4]. Studies using the more recent definition of two or more losses, as recommended by some societies [5,6], were included provided that the criteria were clearly stated and the findings were interpreted with that distinction in mind. Miscarriage was defined as spontaneous loss of a fetus before viability. Eligibility criteria Articles were included if they (i) were original research (case–control, cohort, cross-sectional, or randomized controlled studies), meta-analyses, systematic reviews, or clinical practice guidelines; (ii) examined the relationship between an endocrine abnormality and RSA or recurrent pregnancy loss, or evaluated diagnostic or therapeutic interventions for such abnormalities in women with RSA; (iii) involved human participants; and (iv) were published in English. The endocrine conditions considered were polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), hyperandrogenism, hyperprolactinemia, luteal phase defect, thyroid dysfunction (including overt and subclinical hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, and thyroid autoimmunity), and diabetes mellitus together with related disturbances of glucose metabolism. Articles were excluded if they (i) focused exclusively on anatomical, genetic, infectious, or immunological causes of RSA without an endocrine component; (ii) were case reports, editorials, conference abstracts without full text, or letters lacking original data; (iii) concerned sporadic single miscarriage, induced abortion, or stillbirth beyond 20 weeks only; (iv) were animal or in vitro studies, unless they provided essential mechanistic background; or (v) were duplicate publications. Where overlapping datasets were identified, the most complete or most recent report was retained. Study selection Titles and abstracts retrieved from the searches were screened for relevance. Full texts of potentially eligible articles were then obtained and assessed against the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Disagreements regarding eligibility were resolved by discussion among the authors until consensus was reached. Priority was given to recent publications, large well-designed studies, randomized trials, and meta-analyses, while older landmark studies were retained when they provided foundational evidence or when more recent data were scarce. Data extraction and organization For each included publication, information was extracted on the first author and year, country, study design, sample size, characteristics of the study population, diagnostic criteria for the endocrine disorder, main findings (such as prevalence in women with RSA, odds ratios or relative risks for pregnancy loss, and hormonal parameters), and reported effects of treatment on pregnancy outcome. The results of the separate searches were then combined and grouped according to the specific endocrine abnormality, namely PCOS and hyperandrogenism, hyperprolactinemia, luteal phase defect, thyroid dysfunction, and diabetes mellitus. Within each group, evidence was organized to address epidemiology, proposed pathophysiological mechanisms, diagnostic evaluation, and management strategies [7]. Quality considerations and synthesis A formal quality scoring tool was not applied, consistent with the narrative design. Nonetheless, the strength of evidence was considered qualitatively by taking into account study design, sample size, adequacy of control groups, clarity of diagnostic definitions, and adjustment for confounders such as maternal age, body mass index, and number of previous losses. Discrepancies among studies, such as differences in reference ranges for thyrotropin or in the definition of luteal phase defect, were noted and discussed as potential sources of heterogeneity. Findings were synthesized descriptively, and areas of controversy or insufficient evidence were explicitly identified to guide recommendations for future research [8]. Ethical considerations As this review used only previously published data and involved no direct contact with human participants, ethical approval and informed consent were not required. Review of the literature identified endocrine abnormalities as contributing to a substantial proportion of recurrent spontaneous abortion (RSA) cases. Studies were grouped according to the principal endocrine disorder examined: polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), hyperprolactinemia, luteal phase defect (LPD), thyroid dysfunction, diabetes mellitus, and hyperandrogenism. Findings for each group are summarized below. Polycystic ovarian syndrome PCOS was consistently reported as being more prevalent among women with RSA than in the general population. Prevalence estimates in women with recurrent pregnancy loss ranged from approximately 8% to 40%, depending on diagnostic criteria and the population studied [1,2]. Several mechanisms were proposed. Hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance, frequently present in PCOS independent of body mass index, were associated with elevated plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 levels, reduced fibrinolytic activity, and impaired endometrial receptivity [3]. Elevated luteinizing hormone (LH) concentrations in the follicular phase were associated with premature oocyte maturation and poorer oocyte quality, although later trials did not confirm that LH suppression improves outcomes [4]. Obesity, which often accompanies PCOS, was independently associated with increased miscarriage risk [5]. Reduced glycodelin and insulin-like growth factor binding protein-1 in the endometrium were also reported. Evidence on metformin was inconsistent: some observational studies suggested a reduced first-trimester loss rate, whereas randomized trials showed no clear benefit in live birth rates [6,7]. Hyperprolactinemia Elevated prolactin was found in a minority of women with RSA, and both excessively high and abnormally low levels were linked to adverse outcomes. Hyperprolactinemia was thought to impair folliculogenesis and corpus luteum function, thereby reducing progesterone production and compromising endometrial development [8]. Prolactin also appears to have immunomodulatory and decidual effects, so that disturbed levels may affect implantation. In a small randomized study, women with RSA and hyperprolactinemia treated with bromocriptine had a significantly higher live birth rate than untreated controls (86% versus 52%) [9]. Cabergoline was likewise reported to reduce pregnancy loss, with a favorable tolerability profile [10]. However, the number of controlled studies remains limited. Luteal phase defect LPD, characterized by inadequate progesterone secretion or insufficient endometrial response to progesterone, was reported in approximately 8–12% of women with RSA in older series [11]. Diagnosis remains problematic: endometrial dating by biopsy showed poor reproducibility, and a single midluteal serum progesterone value has limited predictive value because of pulsatile secretion [12]. Human pose estimation, the task of localizing the body joints of a person in an image or video, is a fundamental problem in computer vision with applications in action recognition, human-computer interaction, surveillance, and animation. Over the past few years, deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have dramatically advanced the accuracy of pose estimation on static images. Among the most successful designs are multi-stage architectures, such as Convolutional Pose Machines and stacked hourglass networks, in which a sequence of CNN stages progressively refines the joint confidence maps predicted by the preceding stage. Each stage takes the image evidence together with the previous belief maps and produces a more accurate estimate, so that long-range dependencies among joints are implicitly captured through large effective receptive fields. Despite this success on still images, applying these models to videos remains unsatisfactory. The most direct approach is to run a single-image model independently on every frame. This has three main drawbacks. First, it is computationally expensive: a multi-stage network must be fully evaluated for each frame, and the cost grows linearly with the number of stages. Second, frame-wise prediction ignores the temporal structure of video. Adjacent frames show nearly the same pose, yet independent predictions are not constrained to agree, which produces jittering outputs and visible flicker. Third, video frames frequently suffer from motion blur, defocus, self-occlusion, and unusual viewpoints. A model that sees only one frame has no means of recovering from such degradation, whereas a human observer easily infers the hidden or blurred joint position from preceding frames. Together, these problems cause performance degeneration and make the predictions inconsistent over time. Previous attempts to address video pose estimation usually add post-processing or explicit temporal modeling on top of single-frame networks. Examples include optical flow to propagate predictions between frames, graphical models or tracking-by-detection frameworks that enforce smoothness, and spatio-temporal convolutions over stacked frames. These approaches typically require additional components, such as flow estimators, which are expensive and prone to error under exactly the conditions (blur, occlusion) where help is most needed. They also treat temporal reasoning as separate from the pose network itself, which complicates training and inference. In this paper, we propose a different view. We observe that if the weights of the stages in a multi-stage CNN are shared, the network becomes equivalent to a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) unrolled over stages: each stage applies the same transformation to the previous belief maps and the image features. Under this view, stage-wise refinement is simply a recurrent computation. This observation has two important consequences. First, it decouples the stages from one another. Rather than running every stage on every frame, the recurrence can be unrolled along the time axis of the video, so that each new frame needs only one pass through the shared module, with the refinement carried over from earlier frames. This yields a significant speedup when processing video. Second, the recurrent formulation allows us to insert Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) units naturally, so that the refinement is performed across video frames instead of across redundant stages of a single frame. We call the resulting model the LSTM Pose Machine. It consists of a fully convolutional feature extractor, an initial prediction module, and a recurrent refinement module with convolutional LSTM units whose parameters are shared across all frames. At each time step, the network receives the current frame, and the LSTM combines the current image evidence with its memory of earlier frames and earlier predictions to output the joint confidence maps. The memory cells thus accumulate information about the pose and motion of the person over time. This imposes geometric consistency across frames, because the prediction at one time step is conditioned on the state summarizing the past, and it improves robustness to degraded inputs, since information from clean frames can compensate for blurred or occluded ones. The whole system is trained end to end with supervision on every frame, without optical flow or any other external motion model. We evaluate our approach on two large-scale video pose estimation benchmarks and show that it significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in accuracy while also being considerably faster than repeatedly invoking a multi-stage CNN on each frame. Qualitative results demonstrate that our predictions are visibly more stable and remain accurate under motion blur and occlusion. Beyond reporting performance, we also look inside the network and analyze the memory cells of the LSTM. Our analysis shows that different cells specialize in encoding information such as the motion direction of particular body parts and the spatial configuration of the joints, providing insight into why such a memory mechanism benefits pose estimation in video. The contributions of this work are summarized as follows. (1) We show that a multi-stage CNN with shared weights can be rewritten as an RNN, and exploit this to decouple the stages and greatly reduce the computation for video. (2) We introduce LSTM units between frames, yielding a model that enforces temporal and geometric consistency and handles quality degradation. (3) We achieve state-of-the-art results on two large-scale video benchmarks. (4) We analyze the learned memory cells to explain the behavior of the model. Our approach builds on the Convolutional Pose Machine (CPM), a multi-stage CNN for single-image pose estimation, and converts it into a recurrent architecture that operates over video frames. We first review the CPM, then show how weight sharing yields an equivalent RNN, and finally describe the LSTM Pose Machine, which adds memory across frames. Multi-stage pose machines. Given an image x, the goal is to predict confidence maps for P body parts plus background. A CPM consists of T stages. The first stage applies a fully convolutional network to the image and produces belief maps b1. Each later stage t ≥ 2 takes as input the image features and the belief maps from the previous stage, and outputs refined belief maps: bt = gt(φ(x), b{t-1}), where φ(x) denotes convolutional features computed from the image and gt is a stage-specific convolutional module. Each stage is supervised by an L2 loss between predicted and ground-truth Gaussian-shaped belief maps, which mitigates vanishing gradients through intermediate supervision. In the standard CPM, each gt has its own parameters. Applied to video, this design requires running all T stages for each frame, which is computationally heavy, and it treats frames independently. Weight sharing converts the CPM into an RNN. If the stage modules for t ≥ 2 share parameters, gt = g, the refinement becomes bt = g(φ(x), b{t-1}), which is a recurrence in which the belief maps act as the hidden state and the stage index acts as time. We therefore rewrite the multi-stage network as an RNN unrolled over stages. Weight sharing also reduces the parameter count. We keep a separate initial module for stage 1, since its input differs, as it receives no previous belief maps. In training, the shared module is supervised at every iteration, as in the original CPM. The important consequence arises for video. Because the recurrence is now a model of the iteration itself, we can reinterpret the recurrent axis as the frame axis rather than the stage axis. Each frame is processed by one pass of the shared module, using the state from the previous frame, rather than by T independent stages. Refinement then happens across time, with information from preceding frames playing the role that earlier stages played within one image. This decouples the stages from one another and reduces the per-frame cost to a single initial module plus one recurrent step. LSTM Pose Machine. A plain recurrence over belief maps carries only low-dimensional, explicit predictions. To retain richer temporal information, we replace the recurrent module with a convolutional LSTM. For frame k, let the input be the image feature φ(xk) together with the previous belief maps. The LSTM maintains a memory cell ck and hidden state hk, updated as: ik = σ(Wi [Fk, h{k-1}] + bi) fk = σ(Wf [Fk, h{k-1}] + bf) ok = σ(Wo [Fk, h{k-1}] + bo) gk = tanh(Wg [Fk, h{k-1}] + bg) ck = fk ⊙ c{k-1} + ik ⊙ gk hk = ok ⊙ tanh(ck) where is convolution, ⊙ is element-wise multiplication, and Fk is the feature input for frame k. Using convolutions in the gates preserves spatial structure, so the memory cell is a spatial feature map aligned with the image. The belief maps for frame k are obtained by applying convolutional layers to hk. The input gate controls how much new evidence is written, the forget gate controls how long previous information persists, and the output gate controls what is exposed to the prediction layers. The full network has three parts. (1) A feature extractor, shared across frames, computes φ(xk). (2) An initial module produces first-pass belief maps from φ(xk). (3) The LSTM module takes the first-pass belief maps, the image features, and, via its recurrent connections, the memory from earlier frames, and outputs refined belief maps. Because the same parameters are applied at every frame, the model can handle sequences of arbitrary length. The memory cell lets the model enforce geometric consistency: when a joint is blurred or occluded in the current frame, the memory supplies evidence from earlier frames about its likely location and appearance, and stabilizes outputs against frame-to-frame flicker. Training. We train on video clips of fixed length by backpropagation through time. Each frame has ground-truth belief maps, generated by placing a Gaussian at each annotated joint location. The loss is the sum over frames and parts of the squared difference between predicted and ground-truth maps: L = Σk Σp Σu ||bk^p(u) − b^p(u)||². We supervise both the initial module and the LSTM output, so the early prediction receives a direct gradient signal. Training proceeds in two phases. First, the feature extractor and initial module are pretrained on single-image pose data, which provides a strong initialization. Second, the LSTM module is trained jointly on video clips with the rest of the network, with a smaller learning rate for pretrained layers. The hidden and cell states are initialized to zero at the start of each sequence. Data augmentation consists of random scaling, rotation, and cropping, applied consistently across all frames in a clip so that motion remains coherent. Inference. At test time, frames are processed sequentially. The memory and hidden states are carried forward, and each frame requires one forward pass through the feature extractor, initial module, and LSTM module. Joint locations are taken as the maxima of the final belief maps. Since no multi-stage cascade is repeated per frame, inference is considerably faster than running a full CPM on each frame, and it is naturally suited to online operation because it uses only past frames. We evaluate LSTM Pose Machines on two large-scale video pose estimation benchmarks, the Penn Action dataset and the Sub-JHMDB dataset. We report the Percentage of Correct Keypoints (PCK), where a prediction is correct if it lies within α·max(h, w) of the ground truth, with h and w the height and width of the person bounding box. Unless noted otherwise, α = 0.2. We compare against the single-image multi-stage CNN baseline (Convolutional Pose Machines), and against published video-based methods. Penn Action. Penn Action contains 2,326 video sequences of 15 actions, with 13 annotated joints per person. We follow the standard split of 1,258 training and 1,068 testing sequences. Table 1 reports PCK per joint. The LSTM Pose Machine reaches a mean PCK of 97.7% at α = 0.2, compared with 94.5% for the strongest published video-based method and 95.6% for the frame-by-frame multi-stage CNN baseline. Gains are largest on the joints that are hardest to localize, namely wrists and ankles, where our model improves over the baseline by 3.1 and 2.4 points, respectively. These extremities move quickly and are often blurred or occluded, so they benefit most from temporal information. Gains on head and shoulders are smaller (under 1 point) because the baseline is already near saturation there. Sub-JHMDB. Dementia is a progressive neurodegenerative syndrome characterized by decline in memory, reasoning, language, and the capacity for independent living. Alzheimer's disease (AD) accounts for the majority of cases, and the number of affected individuals is rising rapidly as populations age. Despite decades of research, available therapies remain largely symptomatic. Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibitors such as donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine, together with the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonist memantine, temporarily alleviate symptoms but do not halt disease progression, and their use is often limited by gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, and other adverse effects. There is therefore considerable interest in safer, food-derived materials that can help prevent or delay cognitive decline. The cholinergic system plays a central role in learning and memory, and cholinergic deficits in the hippocampus and cortex are an early feature of AD. Scopolamine, a muscarinic receptor antagonist, disrupts cholinergic transmission and induces transient amnesia in rodents and humans. It also increases oxidative stress in the brain by elevating lipid peroxidation and reducing the activity of endogenous antioxidant enzymes. For these reasons, the scopolamine-induced amnesia model is widely used to screen compounds with potential cognitive-enhancing effects. Behavioral tests such as the Morris water maze, which evaluates spatial learning and memory, and the passive avoidance test, which evaluates associative fear memory, are commonly used to assess memory function in this model. At the molecular level, memory formation depends on signaling cascades in the hippocampus. Activation of extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) leads to phosphorylation of the cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB), a transcription factor that promotes expression of genes involved in synaptic plasticity and neuronal survival. One of its major targets is brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), which supports neuronal growth, differentiation, and long-term potentiation. Reduced levels of p-ERK, p-CREB, and BDNF have been reported in AD brains and in scopolamine-treated animals, and oxidative stress is known to impair this pathway. Antioxidants that reduce oxidative damage may therefore preserve ERK–CREB–BDNF signaling and protect cognitive function. Spirulina (Arthrospira) is a filamentous cyanobacterium that has long been consumed as a food and dietary supplement. Spirulina maxima is rich in protein, essential fatty acids, vitamins, minerals, and pigments, including phycocyanin, chlorophyll, and carotenoids. Extracts of Spirulina have been reported to exert antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, and neuroprotective effects. Among its constituents, β-carotene is one of the most abundant and best-characterized antioxidants. Epidemiological and experimental studies suggest that carotenoids may be associated with reduced cognitive decline, owing to their ability to quench singlet oxygen and scavenge free radicals. However, direct evidence that β-carotene improves memory in animal models of dementia remains scarce, and its contribution to the bioactivity of Spirulina has not been clarified. Fermentation with lactic acid bacteria is a traditional and safe bioprocess that can enhance the functional properties of food materials. During fermentation, microbial enzymes can degrade cell walls and macromolecules, release bound phenolics and pigments, produce new metabolites such as peptides and organic acids, and thereby increase bioavailability and bioactivity. Fermented plant and algal materials have been shown to exhibit stronger antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective activities than their unfermented counterparts. Spirulina has a rigid cell wall composition and a strong characteristic odor that limit its use in foods, and fermentation could improve both its sensory qualities and its functional value. Lactobacillus plantarum strains are widely used for such purposes because of their robust growth, generally recognized as safe status, and beneficial metabolic capacity. Some L. plantarum strains have themselves been reported to influence brain function through the gut–brain axis, suggesting that fermentation with these organisms may offer additional benefits. Nevertheless, to our knowledge, the effect of fermented S. maxima extract on memory impairment has not been investigated. In a previous screening, we found that S. maxima extract fermented with L. plantarum HY-08 showed enhanced antioxidant properties and an increased content of bioactive components compared with the unfermented extract. These observations led us to hypothesize that the fermented extract could mitigate cognitive deficits by reducing oxidative stress and activating neurotrophic signaling in the hippocampus. Because practical application of a functional food ingredient depends on dose efficiency as well as efficacy, determining a dose that provides substantial benefit at reasonable cost is also important. The objectives of this study were therefore to (i) evaluate the cognitive-enhancing effect of the fermented S. maxima extract in scopolamine-treated mice using the Morris water maze and passive avoidance tests, with donepezil as a positive control; (ii) compare the effects of different doses to identify an economically feasible dose; (iii) examine whether β-carotene, a major bioactive component of S. maxima, has memory-enhancing activity; and (iv) clarify the underlying mechanism by analyzing oxidative stress markers and the expression of p-ERK, p-CREB, and BDNF in the hippocampus. The findings may support the development of fermented Spirulina as a functional food material for the prevention of memory impairment and dementia. Spirulina maxima powder was suspended in distilled water (5%, w/v) and sterilized at 121 °C for 15 min. Lactobacillus plantarum HY-08 was pre-cultured in MRS broth at 37 °C for 24 h, inoculated into the Spirulina suspension at 1% (v/v, approximately 10^6 CFU/mL), and fermented at 37 °C for 48 h. A non-fermented control was prepared identically without inoculation. Fermentation was monitored by pH and viable cell counts on MRS agar. The fermented and non-fermented suspensions were extracted with 70% ethanol (1:10, w/v) at 60 °C for 3 h, filtered through Whatman No. 2 paper, concentrated under reduced pressure, and freeze-dried. Extracts were stored at -20 °C and dissolved in saline before use. Chemical analysis β-Carotene was quantified by HPLC. Extracts were dissolved in acetone, filtered (0.45 μm), and injected onto a C18 column (250 × 4.6 mm, 5 μm) maintained at 30 °C. The mobile phase was acetonitrile:methanol:dichloromethane (70:20:10, v/v/v) at 1.0 mL/min with detection at 450 nm. Quantification used a standard curve of authentic β-carotene. Total phenolic content was determined by the Folin-Ciocalteu method with gallic acid as the standard. Antioxidant capacity was assessed by DPPH and ABTS radical scavenging assays, with results expressed as the percentage of radical scavenged and as IC50 values. Animals Male ICR mice (6 weeks old, 28–30 g) were housed at 22 ± 2 °C and 55 ± 5% humidity under a 12 h light/dark cycle with free access to standard chow and water. After one week of acclimatization, mice were randomly assigned to groups (n = 10 per group): (1) normal control (vehicle, saline); (2) scopolamine control (scopolamine plus vehicle); (3) positive control (donepezil, 5 mg/kg); (4) non-fermented extract (400 mg/kg); (5) fermented extract, low dose (200 mg/kg); (6) fermented extract, high dose (400 mg/kg); and (7) β-carotene (dose matched to the amount present in the 400 mg/kg fermented extract). Test substances were administered orally once daily for 14 days. From the start of behavioral testing, scopolamine (1 mg/kg, intraperitoneal) was injected 30 min after the final oral administration and 30 min before each test; the normal control received saline. All procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and complied with national guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals. Morris water maze The test was performed in a circular pool (diameter 90 cm, height 40 cm) filled with water (22 ± 1 °C) made opaque with non-toxic white ink. The pool was divided into four quadrants, and a hidden platform (diameter 8 cm) was submerged 1 cm below the surface in one quadrant. Visual cues were fixed around the pool. During four consecutive training days, each mouse received four trials per day from different starting positions and was allowed 90 s to find the platform; mice failing to do so were guided to it and left there for 15 s. On the test day, the escape latency, defined as the time to reach the platform, was recorded using a video-tracking system. Longer escape latencies indicate poorer spatial memory. Passive avoidance test The apparatus consisted of a light compartment and a dark compartment separated by a guillotine door, the dark compartment having a grid floor. In the acquisition trial, each mouse was placed in the light compartment; upon entering the dark compartment, the door was closed and a foot shock (0.5 mA, 3 s) was delivered. Twenty-four hours later, in the retention trial, the mouse was again placed in the light compartment and the latency to enter the dark compartment was measured, with a cutoff of 300 s. Scopolamine was given 30 min before acquisition. Longer step-through latency indicates better memory retention. Tissue preparation After behavioral testing, mice were anesthetized and euthanized. Brains were rapidly removed on ice and the hippocampi dissected, snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at -80 °C. For protein extraction, hippocampi were homogenized in ice-cold RIPA buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors, centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 20 min at 4 °C, and the supernatants collected. Protein concentration was measured by the BCA assay. Western blot analysis Equal amounts of protein (30 μg) were separated by SDS-PAGE (10–12% gels) and transferred to PVDF membranes. Membranes were blocked with 5% skim milk or BSA in TBST for 1 h and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies against p-ERK, ERK, p-CREB, CREB, BDNF, and β-actin. After washing, membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. Bands were visualized by enhanced chemiluminescence and quantified by densitometry. Phosphorylated proteins were normalized to their total forms, and BDNF to β-actin. Oxidative stress markers Hippocampal lipid peroxidation was measured as malondialdehyde (MDA) content using the thiobarbituric acid reactive substances assay. Superoxide dismutase activity and glutathione levels were measured using commercial kits according to the manufacturers' instructions, and values were normalized to protein content. Statistical analysis Data are expressed as mean ± standard error of the mean. Differences among groups were analyzed by one-way analysis of variance followed by Duncan's multiple range test, and p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed using SPSS software. All in vitro assays were performed in triplicate. Fermentation of S. maxima extract with L. planetarium HY-08 Fermentation of the S. maxima extract with L. planetarium HY-08 was carried out and the resulting fermented extract (FSM) was compared with the unfermented extract (SM). The fermented extract showed higher radical-scavenging activity than the unfermented extract in DPPH and ABTS assays, and its β-carotene content was also higher. Under the same conditions, β-carotene was the major carotenoid detected by HPLC in both samples, which supported its selection as a candidate active compound for the behavioral and mechanistic experiments. Morris water maze test In the Morris water maze, mice in the normal control group found the hidden platform quickly during the training period, and their escape latency decreased progressively over consecutive days. In contrast, the scopolamine-treated control group showed significantly longer escape latencies throughout the training period, which confirmed that scopolamine induced spatial learning and memory impairment (p<0.05). Administration of FSM reduced this impairment in a dose-dependent manner. On the final test day, the escape latency of the scopolamine group was markedly prolonged compared with that of the normal group. Mice receiving 400 mg/kg FSM showed an escape latency of 88.5 sec by the measure used in the study, a value comparable to that of the donepezil-treated group (81.3 sec). The 200 mg/kg FSM group also showed a significant improvement over the scopolamine group, and the difference between the 200 and 400 mg/kg groups was small. The unfermented extract at the same doses was less effective than FSM, and its effects were generally intermediate between those of the scopolamine group and the FSM groups. Mice given β-carotene alone also had significantly shorter escape latencies than the scopolamine group, indicating that β-carotene itself has memory-enhancing activity. However, its effect was smaller than that of FSM at the corresponding dose. In the probe trial, the scopolamine group spent less time in the target quadrant and crossed the former platform position fewer times than the normal group. FSM and donepezil significantly reversed these changes. Swimming speed did not differ among groups, so the differences in latency were not attributable to motor impairment. Cannabis sativa has been used for centuries for medicinal, recreational, and ritual purposes. Its therapeutic potential was recognized in ancient medicine, where preparations were employed to relieve pain, inflammation, and nausea. The scientific era of cannabinoid research began in the 1960s with the isolation and structural characterization of Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the principal psychoactive constituent of the plant. Subsequent work identified more than one hundred related phytocannabinoids, among them cannabidiol (CBD), cannabigerol, and cannabinol, which differ considerably in their pharmacological profiles and their affinity for cannabinoid receptors. The discovery of specific binding sites for THC in the brain and the cloning of the first cannabinoid receptor in 1990 led to the recognition that mammals possess an endogenous signaling network that responds to these compounds. This network is now known as the endocannabinoid system (ECS). The ECS comprises cannabinoid receptors (CBs), their endogenous lipid ligands, and the enzymes responsible for the synthesis, transport, and degradation of these ligands. Two classical receptors have been characterized, CB1 and CB2, both belonging to the family of G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). CB1 is abundantly expressed in the central nervous system, where it modulates neurotransmitter release, but is also present in peripheral tissues. CB2 is found predominantly in cells of the immune system and hematopoietic lineage, although its expression has also been detected in neurons and other cell types under certain conditions. In addition, the orphan receptor GPR55 has been proposed as a third putative cannabinoid receptor, and several other targets, including transient receptor potential vanilloid channels (TRPV1, TRPV2), peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), and GPR119, are modulated by cannabinoids and endocannabinoid-like compounds. The best-studied endocannabinoids are N-arachidonoylethanolamine (anandamide, AEA) and 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG). In contrast to classical neurotransmitters, they are not stored in vesicles but are synthesized on demand from membrane phospholipid precursors, by enzymes such as N-acyl phosphatidylethanolamine-specific phospholipase D (NAPE-PLD) and diacylglycerol lipase (DAGL). Their action is terminated by cellular uptake and enzymatic hydrolysis, mainly by fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH) for AEA and monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL) for 2-AG. Through these components the ECS regulates a wide range of physiological processes, including appetite, pain perception, memory, immune responses, energy metabolism, reproduction, and the balance between cell survival and death. Because of this involvement in cell fate decisions, the ECS has attracted considerable attention in oncology. The first indication that cannabinoids may have anticancer properties came from studies in the 1970s showing that THC and other cannabinoids inhibited the growth of Lewis lung adenocarcinoma cells in mice. Since then, numerous in vitro and in vivo studies have demonstrated that natural, synthetic, and endogenous cannabinoids can reduce the proliferation of cancer cells, induce apoptosis and autophagy-associated cell death, and impair tumor angiogenesis, invasion, and metastasis in models of glioma, breast, prostate, colorectal, lung, pancreatic, and hematological malignancies. Importantly, these effects often occur at concentrations that spare, or even protect, non-transformed cells. Cannabinoids are already used in clinical practice as palliative agents to alleviate chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, cancer-related pain, and cachexia, which has encouraged investigation of their direct antitumor potential in patients. Alterations of the ECS have been observed in many types of cancer. Expression of CB1, CB2, GPR55, and enzymes involved in endocannabinoid metabolism is frequently changed in tumor tissue compared with normal tissue, and in a number of malignancies these changes correlate with tumor grade, disease progression, and patient survival. Endocannabinoid levels may also be altered in tumors, suggesting that the ECS can function as an endogenous regulator of tumor growth, or alternatively be hijacked by transformed cells. The consequences of ECS activation are not uniform: depending on the cancer type, receptor expression level, ligand, concentration, and experimental conditions, cannabinoids may elicit antitumor effects or, in some settings, promote proliferation and survival. This apparent duality complicates interpretation of the literature and underscores the need for a systematic understanding of the underlying mechanisms. Antitumor actions of cannabinoids are mediated by a complex network of signaling pathways. Although many effects result from stimulation of classical CBs, cannabinoids also interact with other molecular targets and influence both prosurvival and proapoptotic signaling cascades, such as the PI3K/Akt/mTOR, MAPK/ERK, and p38 pathways, endoplasmic reticulum stress responses, ceramide synthesis, and the regulation of reactive oxygen species. It should also be emphasized that exogenous cannabinoids, particularly plant-derived and synthetic compounds, differ significantly in their mode of action from endocannabinoids, which are rapidly metabolized and act locally. Consequently, results obtained with one class of compounds, or in vitro versus in vivo, cannot be easily compared or extrapolated. In this review, we summarize the main signaling pathways involved in the antitumor activity of cannabinoids and the influence of their activation on cancer cell biology, including proliferation, cell death, angiogenesis, and invasion. We further discuss changes in the expression pattern of ECS components in various cancer types and their impact on disease progression and patient survival. Finally, we consider the experimental evidence supporting the possible exploitation of cannabinoids in cancer therapy. This review was prepared as a narrative synthesis of the preclinical and clinical literature on the endocannabinoid system (ECS) in cancer. We aimed to describe the signaling pathways through which (endo)cannabinoids influence tumor cell biology and to summarize how alterations in ECS component expression relate to disease progression and patient outcome. Because the evidence base is heterogeneous in design, models, compounds, and endpoints, a narrative rather than a systematic or meta-analytic approach was chosen. The review was not registered, and no formal risk-of-bias scoring was performed. Literature search strategy We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science for articles published from the earliest available records to the date of manuscript preparation. Search terms were combined with Boolean operators and included: "endocannabinoid system," "cannabinoid receptor," "CB1," "CB2," "GPR55," "TRPV1," "anandamide," "2-arachidonoylglycerol," "FAAH," "MAGL," "NAPE-PLD," "DAGL," "cannabinoid," "cannabidiol," "THC," "synthetic cannabinoid," each combined with "cancer," "tumor," "carcinoma," "apoptosis," "autophagy," "proliferation," "angiogenesis," "invasion," "metastasis," "prognosis," and "survival." Reference lists of relevant original articles and earlier reviews were hand-searched to identify additional publications. Clinical trial registries (ClinicalTrials.gov) were consulted to identify studies of cannabinoids in oncology. Eligibility criteria We included English-language original research articles and reviews that met at least one of the following criteria: (i) investigated the effect of endogenous, phytogenic, or synthetic cannabinoids on cancer cells in vitro or in animal models, with mechanistic information on signaling; (ii) measured the expression of cannabinoid receptors, endocannabinoid ligands, or metabolic/transport enzymes in human tumor tissue, biological fluids, or cell lines; (iii) analyzed associations between ECS component expression and clinicopathological parameters, progression, or survival; or (iv) reported clinical or case-based data on cannabinoids as antitumor agents. Studies were excluded if they focused solely on palliative or symptomatic effects (e.g., nausea, pain, appetite) without relevance to tumor biology, if they were conference abstracts without full text, or if methodological details were insufficient to interpret the results. Study selection and data extraction Titles and abstracts were screened for relevance, and full texts of potentially eligible articles were then assessed. Disagreements regarding inclusion were resolved by discussion among the authors. From the selected publications, we extracted the following information where available: cancer type; model system (cell line, primary culture, xenograft, syngeneic or genetic animal model, human specimens); cannabinoid compound, dose, and exposure time; receptor or target involvement as determined by pharmacological antagonists, receptor knockdown, or knockout; downstream signaling events; cellular outcomes (proliferation, cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, autophagy, migration, invasion, angiogenesis, immune modulation); method of ECS expression analysis (immunohistochemistry, qPCR, western blotting, transcriptomic datasets); and associations with prognosis or clinical variables such as tumor grade, stage, and overall or disease-free survival. Organization and synthesis of evidence Extracted data were grouped thematically. First, we described the components of the ECS, including the classical receptors CB1 and CB2, the putative third cannabinoid receptor GPR55, other targets such as TRPV1 and PPARs, endogenous ligands, and the enzymes responsible for their synthesis, transport, and degradation. Second, we compared the pharmacology of endogenous ligands with that of exogenous plant-derived and synthetic cannabinoids, paying particular attention to differences in receptor affinity, efficacy, metabolic stability, receptor-independent actions, and experimental concentrations, since these differences limit direct comparison between studies. Third, we summarized signaling pathways implicated in antitumor activity, including modulation of cAMP/PKA, PI3K/Akt/mTOR, MAPK/ERK, p38 and JNK, ceramide synthesis and endoplasmic reticulum stress, the p8/TRIB3 axis, and regulators of apoptosis and autophagy, as well as pathways relevant to angiogenesis (e.g., VEGF) and invasion (e.g., MMPs, TIMP-1). Fourth, we reviewed cancer-type-specific ECS expression patterns and their prognostic value, organizing the data by tumor site. Where studies reported conflicting results, such as tumor-promoting versus tumor-suppressive effects depending on concentration, receptor context, or cell type, these were presented together with the potential explanations offered by the authors. Evaluation of evidence We did not pool quantitative data. Instead, the strength of evidence was considered qualitatively, taking into account the model used (in vivo evidence and use of human samples were weighted more heavily than single cell-line experiments), use of receptor-specific tools to confirm mechanisms, cohort size and statistical analysis in expression and survival studies, and reproducibility across independent groups. Findings derived from supraphysiological concentrations or from compounds with known off-target effects were interpreted cautiously. Limitations of the available literature, including publication bias toward positive findings, variability in antibody specificity for cannabinoid receptors, and the scarcity of controlled clinical trials, are discussed in the relevant sections. The literature search identified consistent evidence that components of the ECS are dysregulated across a broad range of malignancies, and that this dysregulation is frequently associated with clinical behavior. The findings are organized below by receptor expression, signaling pathways, cellular effects, and clinical correlates. Expression of ECS components in tumors CB1 and CB2 were found to be overexpressed in many tumor tissues relative to matched healthy tissue, although the pattern varied by tumor type. In prostate, breast, and hepatocellular carcinoma, CB1 and CB2 levels were elevated compared with normal epithelium. In gliomas, CB2 expression correlated positively with tumor grade, being highest in glioblastoma and low or absent in normal brain parenchyma. In colorectal cancer, by contrast, CB1 expression was frequently reduced in tumors, often through promoter hypermethylation, whereas CB2 expression was variable. GPR55 was upregulated in several tumor types, including glioblastoma, pancreatic, breast, and ovarian cancers, and its expression tracked with aggressive phenotypes. Enzymes controlling endocannabinoid tone were also altered. Fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH) and monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL), which degrade anandamide (AEA) and 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) respectively, were increased in aggressive tumors such as prostate, ovarian, and melanoma. Elevated MAGL was linked to a pro-tumorigenic lipid network in which released arachidonic acid fed prostaglandin synthesis and other signaling lipids. Levels of AEA and 2-AG were increased in some tumors (e.g., colon, prostate, glioblastoma) compared with normal tissue, suggesting a compensatory, and possibly protective, endogenous response. Signaling pathways mediating antitumor activity Activation of CB1 and CB2 by endogenous and synthetic agonists engaged several convergent pathways. Receptor coupling to Gi/o proteins inhibited adenylyl cyclase, reducing cAMP and protein kinase A activity. A major mechanism was inhibition of the PI3K/Akt/mTOR axis, which decreased survival signaling and promoted autophagy-associated cell death. In glioma, melanoma, and pancreatic models, cannabinoids increased de novo synthesis of ceramide, which induced endoplasmic reticulum stress through upregulation of the stress protein p8 (NUPR1), ATF4, and CHOP, and led to TRIB3-dependent inhibition of Akt. Sustained activation of ERK and p38 MAPK, and in some cases JNK, contributed to cell cycle arrest and apoptosis, whereas transient ERK activation was associated with survival. Cannabinoids also regulated apoptotic effectors directly. Treatment decreased anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 and survivin, increased Bax and caspase-3 activation, and promoted mitochondrial cytochrome c release. Receptor-independent mechanisms were documented as well, including interaction with TRPV1, TRPV2, and PPARγ, as well as lipid raft–dependent effects. Activation of TRPV1 by AEA produced calcium influx and cell death in some cell lines. Cannabidiol, which has low affinity for classical CBs, acted through TRPV2, increased reactive oxygen species, and sensitized glioma cells to chemotherapeutics. Signaling via GPR55, in contrast, generally promoted proliferation through RhoA, ERK, and NFAT, and its antagonism reduced tumor growth in preclinical models. Differences between exogenous and endogenous ligands were evident. Synthetic and plant-derived cannabinoids

Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in women worldwide and a leading cause of cancer mortality. A family history of the disease is among the strongest established risk factors: first-degree relatives of affected women have approximately a two-fold increased risk. Twin and family studies indicate that inherited factors account for a substantial proportion of this excess risk. Rare, high-penetrance mutations in genes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2, and moderate-penetrance variants in genes such as CHEK2, ATM and PALB2, explain roughly a fifth of the familial risk. The remainder is likely to be due, at least in part, to the combined effects of many common variants, each conferring a small increase or decrease in risk. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have been the principal tool for identifying such variants. Since the first breast cancer GWAS were reported in 2007, successive analyses of progressively larger sample sizes, together with large-scale replication efforts including those using the custom iCOGS array, have identified common susceptibility variants in 79 loci. Together these variants explain approximately 14% of the familial relative risk of breast cancer, and polygenic risk scores based on them can stratify women into groups with meaningfully different absolute risks. Such scores are of growing interest for risk-adapted screening and prevention. However, the identified loci account for only a fraction of the heritability attributable to common variation. Estimates based on genome-wide data suggest that many additional variants of small effect remain undiscovered, and that increasing sample size should continue to yield new associations. Beyond risk prediction, the identification of susceptibility loci offers a route to understanding the biology of breast cancer. Most associated variants lie in non-coding regions and are thought to act by modulating the regulation of nearby genes. Pinpointing the causal variants and their target genes is therefore challenging, but integrating association data with functional genomic annotations can help. Resources such as ChIP-Seq data for transcription factors and histone modifications in mammary cell lines, and chromatin interaction maps generated by methods such as ChIA-PET in the ENCODE project, allow candidate regulatory elements to be identified and linked to the promoters of putative target genes. Previous studies have shown that breast cancer risk variants are enriched in regulatory elements active in mammary epithelial cells and in binding sites for factors such as ER, FOXA1 and GATA3, supporting this approach. Occasionally, associations are instead driven by coding variants that alter protein function, which can provide more direct insight into mechanism. Imputation based on the 1000 Genomes Project reference panel has greatly expanded the set of variants that can be tested in GWAS. Compared with earlier HapMap-based imputation, it captures a much larger number of SNPs, including many with lower allele frequencies and short insertions and deletions, and improves the resolution at which association signals can be localised. Earlier large analyses of breast cancer were largely based on HapMap-imputed or directly genotyped data, so a systematic analysis of denser imputed data in large datasets offers the potential to detect both new loci and new signals at known ones. The Breast Cancer Association Consortium (BCAC) has assembled data from a large number of case-control studies, many of which were genotyped using the iCOGS array, a custom array designed to follow up promising signals from earlier GWAS and to fine-map known loci. In addition, a number of GWAS have been conducted in populations of European ancestry, some of which have been analysed only in part or only in earlier, smaller combinations. Combining the iCOGS data with these GWAS provides an opportunity to increase statistical power substantially, since the iCOGS array covers a limited fraction of the genome but in very large samples, while the GWAS cover the genome more comprehensively. Meta-analysis of the two data sources after imputation to a common dense reference panel allows the full set of samples to contribute to the evaluation of each variant genome-wide. Here, we report a meta-analysis of 11 GWAS, comprising 15,748 cases and 18,084 controls, together with 46,785 cases and 42,892 controls from 41 studies genotyped on the iCOGS array, giving a total of more than 120,000 women of European ancestry. Genotypes for over 11 million SNPs were imputed using the 1000 Genomes Project reference panel. We identify 15 previously unreported loci associated with breast cancer risk at genome-wide significance (P<5×10⁻⁸). To interpret these findings, we integrated the association results with ChIP-Seq data from mammary cell lines and with ChIA-PET chromatin interaction data from ENCODE. This analysis points to likely target genes at two of the new regions: SETBP1 at 18q12.3, and RNF115 and PDZK1 at 1q21.1. We also show that one association, in the DNA repair gene EXO1, appears to be driven by an amino-acid substitution, suggesting a direct effect on protein function. These results extend the catalogue of common breast cancer susceptibility loci and provide new leads for understanding the genes and pathways underlying inherited susceptibility to the disease. Study populations. We performed a meta-analysis of 11 breast cancer genome-wide association studies (GWAS) comprising 15,748 cases and 18,084 controls, together with data from 41 studies of the Breast Cancer Association Consortium (BCAC) genotyped on the iCOGS custom array (46,785 cases and 42,892 controls). All participants were women of European ancestry. Cases were women with invasive breast cancer or carcinoma in situ, ascertained through population-based, hospital-based, or screening-based studies. Controls were women without breast cancer at recruitment. All participants provided written informed consent, and each study was approved by its local ethics committee. Information on age, estrogen receptor (ER) status, tumor grade, and other clinical features was collected where available. Genotyping and quality control. GWAS samples were genotyped on Illumina or Affymetrix genome-wide arrays, as described for the individual studies. iCOGS samples were genotyped on an Illumina custom array of ~211,155 SNPs, designed to follow up GWAS signals and to fine-map known loci. Standard quality control was applied within each study. We excluded samples with call rate <95%, abnormal heterozygosity (extreme outliers in the distribution of the study), discordant sex, or unexpected duplication. For related pairs, identified by identity-by-descent estimates, one individual was removed. SNPs were excluded if the call rate was <95% (or <99% for SNPs with minor allele frequency <5%), if they deviated from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium in controls (P<10^-5), or if cluster plots were poor. Population structure was assessed with principal components analysis using a set of uncorrelated markers and HapMap reference populations. Individuals with <80% estimated European ancestry were excluded. The principal components were used as covariates in association analyses to control for stratification. Genomic inflation factors were calculated for each dataset, and for the iCOGS data they were adjusted using a subset of null SNPs. Imputation. Genotypes for more than 11 million variants were imputed for each dataset using the 1000 Genomes Project Phase I (v3, March 2012) cross-ethnic reference panel. Haplotypes were first pre-phased with SHAPEIT, and imputation was then carried out with IMPUTE2 in chunks of approximately 5 Mb. SNPs with an imputation quality (info) score <0.3 or minor allele frequency <0.01 were excluded from the analysis. For the iCOGS data, imputation was performed separately in batches to account for differences in array composition and cohort structure. Imputation accuracy was assessed by comparing imputed to directly genotyped data in selected regions. Statistical analysis. Within each dataset, we estimated per-allele log odds ratios and standard errors using logistic regression under an additive model, with imputed dosages (or genotype probabilities via SNPTEST) to account for imputation uncertainty. Analyses were adjusted for principal components; in the iCOGS analysis, the first principal components and country of origin were included as covariates. Results from the GWAS and iCOGS were combined by fixed-effects inverse-variance weighted meta-analysis implemented in METAL. Heterogeneity between studies was evaluated with Cochran's Q and I² statistics. Genome-wide significance was defined as P<5×10^-8. We considered a locus novel if the lead SNP was located >500 kb from, and not correlated (r²<0.1) with, any previously reported breast cancer susceptibility variant. Regional association plots were produced with LocusZoom. To identify independent signals within loci, we performed conditional analyses by adding the lead SNP as a covariate and testing the remaining variants in a ±500 kb window. Subtype analyses. Associations were assessed separately for ER-positive and ER-negative disease, where tumor pathology was available, using case-only and case-control analyses. Differences between subtypes were evaluated using a case-only test of heterogeneity. Associations with tumor grade and other characteristics were similarly explored with case-only logistic regression. Functional annotation. To prioritize candidate causal variants and target genes, we defined credible sets of variants for each locus as those with P within two orders of magnitude of the lead SNP, or as those correlated with it (r²>0.4) in 1000 Genomes European samples. We overlaid these variants on ChIP-Seq data for histone modifications (H3K4me1, H3K4me3, H3K27ac), transcription factors (including ER-alpha, FOXA1, and CTCF), and DNase hypersensitivity from mammary cell lines (MCF-7, T-47D, HMEC, and others) obtained from ENCODE and published sources. Chromatin interactions were assessed using ChIA-PET data from ENCODE (RNA polymerase II and ER-alpha in MCF-7 cells) to link regulatory elements containing candidate variants to the promoters of putative target genes. Genes were considered likely targets if a credible variant lay in a regulatory element that physically interacted with the gene promoter. Variants were annotated for coding consequences using the Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor, and for predicted functional impact of missense variants using SIFT and PolyPhen-2. Expression analysis. We evaluated expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) associations between lead SNPs and nearby genes using data from breast tumor and normal breast tissue (The Cancer Genome Atlas and the Molecular Taxonomy of Breast Cancer International Consortium), as well as publicly available datasets of normal tissue. Associations were tested by linear regression of normalized expression on genotype dosage, with correction for multiple testing within each locus. Software. Analyses used PLINK, SNPTEST, IMPUTE2, SHAPEIT, METAL, and R. Linkage disequilibrium was calculated from 1000 Genomes European samples. We performed a meta-analysis combining data from 11 breast cancer GWAS (15,748 cases and 18,084 controls) and 41 studies genotyped on the iCOGS array (46,785 cases and 42,892 controls), all of European ancestry. After quality control, genotypes for more than 11 million SNPs were imputed using the 1000 Genomes Project (Phase I, version 3) reference panel. Association was assessed within each dataset using logistic regression adjusted for principal components of ancestry, and results were combined using fixed-effects inverse-variance meta-analysis. The genomic inflation factor for the combined analysis was 1.11 (λ1000 = 1.01), consistent with the large sample size and polygenic architecture rather than substantial population stratification. Novel susceptibility loci We identified 15 previously unreported loci associated with overall breast cancer risk at P<5×10−8, each more than 500 kb from, and independent of, the 79 known susceptibility variants. Lead variants had minor allele frequencies ranging from 0.02 to 0.49, and per-allele odds ratios ranged from 1.04 to 1.20. Most were common variants with modest effects (OR 1.04–1.08), whereas the two strongest associations involved lower-frequency variants. Odds ratios were consistent between the GWAS and iCOGS datasets for all 15 loci, with no significant heterogeneity (P>0.01 after correction for multiple testing). The new loci lie on chromosomes 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 16, 18 and 19, and several contain plausible candidate genes involved in cell-cycle control, DNA repair, transcriptional regulation and mammary development. We then examined associations by tumour subtype. Most loci showed stronger associations with estrogen receptor (ER)-positive disease, consistent with the greater number of ER-positive cases, though a few showed similar or stronger effects for ER-negative disease. Several variants showed evidence of heterogeneity by ER status, tumour grade or other pathological features, suggesting that some loci influence subtype-specific tumour development.
