Epilepsy affects roughly 1% of the world population, and approximately one third of patients continue to experience seizures despite adequate pharmacological treatment [1,2]. For selected patients with medically refractory focal epilepsy, surgical resection or ablation of the epileptogenic zone (EZ) is the most effective therapeutic option, and its success depends on accurate delineation of the brain regions responsible for seizure generation [3]. When non-invasive investigations (scalp EEG, video monitoring, MRI, PET, MEG) fail to provide concordant localization, invasive recordings are required. Invasive monitoring with SEEG Stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG), introduced by Talairach and Bancaud in the 1950s, consists of the stereotactic implantation of multiple depth electrodes, each carrying several contacts, to sample cortical and subcortical structures in three dimensions [4]. Compared with subdural grids, SEEG gives access to deep and sulcal structures, allows bilateral exploration without craniotomy, and has a favorable complication profile [5,6]. SEEG is also increasingly used in cognitive and systems neuroscience, where intracranial recordings offer unique spatial and temporal resolution in humans [7]. The clinical value of SEEG depends on knowing which anatomical structure each contact records from. Electrophysiological traces can be interpreted, and a resection planned, only if contact positions are expressed in the patient's anatomical space and, for group studies, in a common reference space [8]. Typically, electrode trajectories are planned on pre-implant MRI, implantation is performed with a stereotactic frame or robotic assistance, and a post-implant CT or Cone-Beam CT (CBCT) is acquired to verify the final positions. Because of bending of the shaft, brain shift, and inaccuracies in the entry point or in the insertion depth, the final position generally differs from the plan [9,10]. Planned coordinates therefore cannot replace the true contact locations, which must be recovered from the post-implant image. Limitations of current localization approaches In most centers, contact localization is performed by manual or semi-manual procedures. The post-implant CT is co-registered with the pre-implant MRI, and contacts, visible as hyperdense artifacts, are identified one by one with 3D visualization tools. A single implant can comprise 10–20 electrodes and 100–200 contacts, so this task takes hours per patient, requires trained personnel, and is vulnerable to inter- and intra-rater variability. Several tools have eased this process. Some offer graphical interfaces for contact marking and for visualization on the patient's anatomy [11,12], others use semi-automatic procedures that require the user to specify the extremities of each electrode and then interpolate the contacts along the axis assuming a known inter-contact spacing [13,14]. Related approaches have been developed for deep brain stimulation (DBS) lead reconstruction [15,16] and for subdural grids [17]. However, DBS leads are few (typically one or two), have a different geometry, and are usually isolated in space, whereas SEEG implants involve many closely spaced electrodes, often crossing or running in proximity, and with variable numbers of contacts. To our knowledge, no fully automatic method has been proposed that exploits the characteristics of SEEG implants to segment contacts without manual intervention. Rationale and approach Automatic segmentation of SEEG contacts poses several challenges. Metal contacts produce streaking and blooming artifacts in CT that blur contact boundaries, particularly in the anisotropic voxels typical of CBCT. Adjacent electrodes may be close enough that their intensity profiles merge after thresholding. Moreover, simple thresholding and connected-component analysis cannot discriminate between electrodes and other high-density structures such as the skull, bolts, or cables. A reliable algorithm must therefore incorporate prior knowledge of the implant. Such prior knowledge is available in the clinical workflow: the surgical plan defines, for each electrode, a target point and an entry point, which together provide an initial estimate of the electrode axis. Given that actual trajectories remain close to the planned ones, although deviations occur, the plan can be used to initialize and constrain the search for the real electrode axis and the contacts along it. The electrode manufacturer's specification supplies the number of contacts, their length and their spacing, which can further regularize the identification of individual contacts. In this paper we present an automatic algorithm for segmenting SEEG contacts from a thresholded post-implant CBCT volume with a resolution of 0.4 × 0.4 × 0.8 mm. The method uses the planned entry and target points as an initial estimate of each electrode axis and refines it using the image data. We implemented it in DEETO (DEep Electrode Trajectory Orientation), an open-source C++ prototype based on the Insight Toolkit (ITK) [18], to facilitate reuse and extension by the community. We evaluate the approach along three dimensions. First, we assess the computational time relative to manual segmentation. Second, we quantify accuracy against contact positions manually segmented by experts on a subset of patients. Third, we assess whether the resulting positions correctly map contacts to anatomical regions, which is the quantity ultimately relevant for interpreting the recordings. Because the algorithm relies on the plan, we additionally study its robustness to deviations of the implanted electrodes from the planned trajectories, using a larger cohort. The remainder of the paper describes the data and the algorithm, reports the experimental results, and discusses the implications and limitations of the method for clinical and research applications of SEEG. Study population and data acquisition Twenty-eight patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy who underwent SEEG implantation were retrospectively included. Electrodes (Dixi Medical, 5–18 contacts each; contact length 2 mm, inter-contact spacing 1.5 mm, diameter 0.8 mm) were implanted under stereotactic guidance following an individually planned trajectory defined by a target point (deep) and an entry point (cortical surface) for each electrode. Planning was performed on pre-operative T1-weighted MRI with gadolinium enhancement. After implantation, a Cone-Beam CT (CBCT) volume was acquired with the stereotactic frame removed (voxel size 0.4 × 0.4 × 0.8 mm). All patients provided informed consent, and data were anonymized before processing. A subset of 12 patients (35 multilead electrodes, 200 contacts) was manually segmented by two trained experts using a 3D visualization tool; the contact centers they identified served as the ground truth. The remaining 16 patients were used only for the robustness analysis. Preprocessing and registration The CBCT volume was rigidly registered to the pre-operative MRI using a mutual-information-based registration, so that planned entry and target points could be expressed in CBCT coordinates. Registration was visually checked. The CBCT was then thresholded to retain only voxels with intensities consistent with metal (a fixed high-intensity threshold chosen to exclude bone), producing a binary volume containing the electrode contacts and, occasionally, residual artefacts or bolts. Because the contacts are separated by non-metallic insulation, each electrode appears as a sequence of disconnected or weakly connected high-intensity segments. Segmentation algorithm The algorithm was designed around the prior knowledge that each electrode is a nearly straight, rigid cylinder whose approximate axis is given by the line joining the planned entry point e and target point t. It proceeds independently for each electrode in four steps. 1. Region of interest extraction. For each electrode, the thresholded voxels lying within a cylindrical region of radius r around the planned axis segment et were selected. The radius was chosen larger than the expected deviation between planned and actual trajectories but smaller than half the minimum distance between neighboring electrodes, thereby limiting contamination from adjacent electrodes. The selected voxels were converted to physical coordinates, yielding a point set P. 2. Axis refinement. The planned axis was used as the initial estimate of the true electrode axis. The principal axis of P was computed by principal component analysis (PCA), giving a centroid c and a direction d (first eigenvector, oriented from entry to target). To reduce the influence of outliers, such as bolt voxels or artefact fragments, voxels whose orthogonal distance from the current axis exceeded a tolerance proportional to the electrode radius were discarded, and the fit was repeated until convergence of the direction (angular change below 10⁻³ rad) or a maximum number of iterations was reached. 3. Contact detection along the axis. The remaining voxels were projected onto the refined axis, and a one-dimensional intensity profile along the axis coordinate s was built by accumulating voxel counts in bins smaller than the voxel size. This profile is approximately periodic, with maxima at contacts and minima at insulating spacers. The profile was smoothed with a Gaussian kernel, and the contacts were localized from the profile’s local maxima. The known electrode geometry (number of contacts, contact length, and spacing, i.e., a 3.5 mm center-to-center pitch) was used to constrain the search: the position of the deepest contact was identified from the tip of the profile, and the remaining contact centers were placed at successive known offsets along the axis. Local adjustments of each center were obtained as the centroid of the voxels assigned to that contact, after which the centers were re-projected onto the axis. 4. Output. For each electrode, the algorithm returns the contact centers in CBCT/MRI space, the electrode axis, and the labelled voxels of each contact. Contacts were assigned to anatomical regions by transforming their coordinates into the MRI-derived parcellation (cortical and subcortical labels from automatic segmentation of the T1 image) and recording the label at each contact center; contacts located in white matter or outside the brain were identified accordingly. Implementation The method was implemented in C++ as DEETO (Deep Electrode Tracking and Orientation), an open-source prototype based on the Insight Toolkit (ITK) for image I/O, thresholding, connected-component handling, and spatial transformations. The input consists of the thresholded volume and a text file containing planned entry and target points and the electrode model. Execution time was measured on a standard workstation. Performance evaluation Accuracy was quantified in the 12 manually segmented subjects as the Euclidean distance between each automatically detected contact center and the corresponding manual one. Results are reported as mean ± standard deviation across contacts and subjects. Computation time per subject was compared with the time reported by the experts for manual segmentation. To assess the effect on clinical interpretation, the anatomical label assigned to each contact by the automatic and manual segmentations was compared, and the proportion of concordant labels was computed. Robustness to deviations from the planned trajectory To test the sensitivity of the algorithm to differences between planned and actual electrode positions, all 28 subjects were used. For each electrode, the planned target point was artificially displaced from its original position by a controlled distance (0–12 mm) in randomly chosen directions perpendicular to and along the planned axis, while the entry point was kept fixed, simulating deep-brain displacement of the implanted shaft. The segmentation was repeated for each displacement, and the robustness error was defined as the distance between contact positions obtained with the displaced plan and those obtained with the original plan. Displacement tests were repeated over multiple random draws, and the error was summarized as a function of the displacement magnitude. Dataset and experimental setting The algorithm was evaluated on 28 patients who underwent SEEG implantation, for a total of 28 post-implant thresholded Cone-Beam CT volumes (voxel size 0.4 × 0.4 × 0.8 mm). Planned entry and target points were available for every electrode. A subset of 12 subjects (35 multilead electrodes, 200 contacts) was manually segmented by two experts, and these segmentations served as ground truth for accuracy assessment. The remaining 16 subjects, together with the 12 annotated ones, were used in the robustness analysis. All results below were obtained with a single parameter configuration, fixed a priori and not tuned on the annotated subset. Computational performance On a standard workstation, DEETO segmented all electrodes of a subject in less than 1 s, excluding image loading and file input/output. Runtime scaled approximately linearly with the number of electrodes, and the number of contacts per electrode had a negligible effect. Manual segmentation by experts required a few hours per subject, so the automated procedure reduces processing time by several orders of magnitude. No interactive 3D visualization or user supervision was required during execution. Segmentation accuracy Accuracy was quantified as the Euclidean distance between the contact centroids estimated by the algorithm and the corresponding manually identified centroids. Video captioning is the task of automatically generating a natural language description of a short video clip. It sits at the intersection of computer vision and natural language processing, and it supports applications such as video retrieval, assistive technology for visually impaired users, and human-robot interaction. Compared with image captioning, the task is harder because a model must capture temporal dynamics, recognize actions and events, and compose them into a fluent sentence. Recent progress has been driven largely by sequence-to-sequence architectures, which encode a sequence of frame-level or clip-level visual features with a recurrent network and decode a caption word by word [Venugopalan et al., 2015; Yao et al., 2015; Pan et al., 2016]. Attention mechanisms and richer multimodal features have further improved such systems. Despite this progress, standard training procedures have a notable limitation. Nearly all captioning models are trained to minimize word-level cross-entropy loss, in which the decoder is conditioned on the ground-truth previous word at each step. This creates two well-documented problems. The first is exposure bias [Ranzato et al., 2016]: at test time the model must condition on its own, possibly erroneous, predictions, a distribution it never encountered during training. The second is a mismatch between the training objective and the evaluation criteria. Captioning systems are judged using sentence-level metrics such as BLEU [Papineni et al., 2002], METEOR [Banerjee and Lavie, 2005], ROUGE-L [Lin, 2004], and CIDEr [Vedantam et al., 2015], none of which is directly optimized by word-level likelihood. Because these metrics are non-differentiable, they cannot be used as losses in ordinary gradient-based training. Reinforcement learning for sentence-level metrics. A natural remedy is to cast caption generation as a sequential decision problem and apply reinforcement learning, treating the decoder as a stochastic policy and the evaluation metric as a reward. Policy gradient methods such as REINFORCE [Williams, 1992] have been used for this purpose in image captioning, machine translation, and summarization [Ranzato et al., 2016; Rennie et al., 2017; Paulus et al., 2018]. In the first part of this work, we apply policy gradient training to video captioning and directly optimize task-based metrics. We also study a mixed-loss formulation that combines the reinforcement objective with the cross-entropy loss, which stabilizes training and keeps the generated sentences fluent. We evaluate several metric rewards across multiple video captioning datasets, and show significant improvements over a strong cross-entropy baseline on both automatic metrics and human evaluation. Limitations of phrase-matching rewards. Optimizing a metric also exposes its weaknesses. Metrics such as CIDEr reward n-gram overlap with reference captions, but n-gram overlap is only a rough proxy for semantic correctness. A generated caption may share many phrases with a reference and yet contradict it, for example by describing the wrong object or the opposite action. Conversely, a caption may be a valid description of the video while sharing few phrases with the references. Moreover, a policy trained to maximize such a metric will exploit it, and may produce sentences that obtain high scores through repeated or ungrammatical phrases, or that include a high-scoring but logically inconsistent fragment. For example, a caption that ends with a plausible common phrase can score highly even though it contradicts the content of the video. Such behaviors are especially problematic in video captioning, where each video is typically annotated with only a small number of reference sentences that cover a limited set of possible descriptions. Entailment-enhanced rewards. To address this, we propose a novel reward, CIDEnt, that augments phrase-matching metrics with a measure of logical agreement between the generated caption and the references. Our approach draws on textual entailment, the task of deciding whether one sentence logically follows from another, contradicts it, or is neutral with respect to it [Dagan et al., 2006; Bowman et al., 2015]. We train an entailment classifier and use it to score each generated caption against the ground-truth captions. The CIDEr score is then adjusted according to the entailment probability: partial matches are credited only when they are logically implied by the references, and a penalty is applied when the caption is judged to contradict them. In this way the reward preserves the benefit of consensus-based n-gram matching while filtering out matches that are semantically wrong. To our knowledge, this is the first use of entailment as a component of a reward for captioning. Contributions. Our contributions are summarized as follows: 1. We present a reinforcement learning framework for video captioning that uses policy gradient and mixed-loss training to optimize sentence-level metrics directly, and we show significant gains over a cross-entropy baseline on multiple datasets, confirmed by human evaluation. 2. We introduce CIDEnt, an entailment-corrected variant of CIDEr that allows only logically implied partial matches and penalizes contradictions, providing a reward that is better aligned with semantic correctness than phrase matching alone. 3. We provide extensive experiments and analysis, including comparisons among different metric rewards and qualitative examples, showing that the CIDEnt reward yields further significant improvements over the CIDEr reward and achieves a new state-of-the-art result on the MSR-VTT dataset [Xu et al., 2016]. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We first review related work on video captioning, reinforcement learning for sequence generation, and entailment. We then describe our baseline model, the reinforcement learning formulations, and the CIDEnt reward. Finally, we present experimental results, human evaluation, and analysis. 3.1 Baseline Attention-Based Sequence-to-Sequence Model Our baseline follows the encoder–decoder framework with soft attention [Bahdanau et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2015; Yao et al., 2015]. Given a video, we uniformly sample frames and extract a feature vector for each frame using a pretrained convolutional network (ResNet-152 [He et al., 2016]), yielding a sequence x = (x1, ..., xn). A bidirectional LSTM encoder [Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997] maps this sequence to hidden states h1, ..., hn. A unidirectional LSTM decoder generates the caption w = (w1, ..., wT) one word at a time. At step t, the decoder computes a context vector ct = Σi α{ti} hi, where the attention weights α{ti} are a softmax over scores produced by a small feed-forward network that takes the previous decoder state and hi as input. The distribution over the next word is p(wt | w{<t}, x) = softmax(Wo [st; ct] + bo), where st is the decoder state. The baseline is trained by minimizing the word-level cross-entropy loss (XE): LXE(θ) = −Σt log pθ(wt | w{<t}, x), where w is the ground-truth caption. This objective has two well-known weaknesses. First, training uses teacher forcing, whereas at test time the model conditions on its own predictions (exposure bias [Ranzato et al., 2016]). Second, it optimizes per-word likelihood rather than the sentence-level metrics used for evaluation, such as BLEU, METEOR, CIDEr and ROUGE-L. 3.2 Reinforcement Learning with Sentence-Level Rewards To address these issues, we treat the decoder as a stochastic policy pθ whose actions are the words generated and whose state is defined by the video and the words so far. After a full caption w^s is sampled, a sentence-level reward r(w^s) is computed against the reference captions. The training objective is to minimize the negative expected reward: LRL(θ) = −E{w^s∼pθ}[r(w^s)]. Using the REINFORCE algorithm [Williams, 1992], the gradient is approximated with a single sample: ∇θ LRL ≈ −(r(w^s) − b) ∇θ log pθ(w^s), where b is a baseline that reduces variance without introducing bias. Following the self-critical approach [Rennie et al., 2017], we use the reward of the caption obtained by greedy (test-time) decoding, r(ŵ), as b. This encourages sampled captions that outperform the current inference-time output and requires no additional estimator of expected reward. Purely RL-based training can be unstable and may produce fluent-looking but ungrammatical sequences, because the reward is sparse and the action space is large. Following [Paulus et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2016], we therefore use a mixed loss that combines both objectives: LMIXED = λ LRL + (1 − λ) LXE, where λ ∈ [0, 1] is a tunable hyperparameter. The XE term acts as a language-model regularizer that keeps the policy close to fluent text. Training proceeds in two stages: the model is first pretrained with XE until convergence, then fine-tuned with the mixed loss. We consider several rewards, including CIDEr [Vedantam et al., 2015], BLEU [Papineni et al., 2002] and METEOR [Banerjee and Lavie, 2005]. Among these, CIDEr is the most natural choice, as it was designed for captioning and weights n-grams by TF-IDF to emphasize informative content. Because the reward is not differentiable, the policy gradient is the means by which the metric is optimized directly. 3.3 Entailment-Enhanced Reward (CIDEnt) Phrase-matching metrics such as CIDEr reward n-gram overlap with the references and cannot judge whether a candidate is semantically consistent with them. A generated caption may therefore receive a high score despite containing a contradictory phrase. For example, "a man is playing a guitar" and "a man is playing a piano" share most n-grams, yet they describe incompatible events. Conversely, a valid paraphrase with little lexical overlap is penalized. Optimizing such a reward with RL can exacerbate these errors, since the policy learns to exploit the weaknesses of the metric. To mitigate this, we introduce a reward based on textual entailment. We use an entailment classifier that, given a premise and a hypothesis, outputs probabilities for three classes: entailment, contradiction and neutral. We employ the decomposable attention model [Parikh et al., 2016] trained on SNLI [Bowman et al., 2015], which is lightweight enough to be called at every training step. For a sampled caption w^s, the ground-truth caption serves as the premise and the sampled caption as the hypothesis. We take the entailment score Ent(w^s) as the probability of the entailment class, maximized over the available reference captions, since any reference may logically imply the generated content. The CIDEnt reward then uses this score to filter the CIDEr reward: CIDEnt(w^s) = CIDEr(w^s) − λp, if Ent(w^s) < β, CIDEnt(w^s) = CIDEr(w^s), otherwise, where β is an entailment-probability threshold and λp is a constant penalty. Thus a caption keeps its CIDEr reward only when it is logically implied by a reference; otherwise its reward is reduced, discouraging contradictory or unsupported partial matches. Because the penalty is applied only when entailment is low, correct captions with high n-gram overlap are unaffected, and the training signal retains the fine-grained gradation provided by CIDEr. We use the CIDEnt reward in place of r in the policy-gradient and mixed-loss formulations above, together with the self-critical baseline, so that the baseline is computed with the same reward on the greedy output. 3.4 Implementation Details Videos are represented by a fixed number of uniformly sampled frames, and captions are tokenized and truncated to a maximum length, with infrequent words mapped to an unknown token. All models are optimized with Adam [Kingma and Ba, 2015] with dropout regularization. Hyperparameters, including λ, β, λp, and learning rates, are selected on the validation set. At test time, captions are generated with beam search. For the RL stage, sampling is performed from the model's output distribution, and the reward is computed online for each sample in the minibatch. Experimental Setup Summary. We evaluate on MSR-VTT [1], the primary benchmark, and on YouTube2Text/MSVD [2] and the Flickr30k image-captioning dataset [3] to test generalization. Performance is reported with BLEU-4, METEOR, ROUGE-L, and CIDEr, computed using the Microsoft COCO evaluation server [4]. All reinforcement-learning (RL) models are initialized from a cross-entropy (XE) pretrained baseline. Reported numbers are on the test split unless otherwise stated. Hyperparameters were tuned on the validation set. Baseline and Metric-Reward Results Table 1 compares the XE baseline with models fine-tuned using policy gradient (REINFORCE with a baseline estimator) and the mixed-loss objective, which interpolates XE and RL losses to preserve fluency. Optimizing CIDEr as the reward yields the largest gains on CIDEr and generally improves the other metrics. On MSR-VTT, the CIDEr-reward model improves CIDEr by several points over the XE baseline and also improves BLEU-4 and METEOR. Using BLEU as the reward raises BLEU-4 most strongly, but gains transfer less consistently to other metrics, indicating partial overfitting to the optimized metric.

Online retailers, airlines, hotels, and advertising platforms share a common operational challenge: a finite stock of items must be allocated to a sequence of heterogeneous customers whose identities and preferences are revealed only upon arrival. Each allocation decision is irrevocable, and selling an item to one customer forecloses the opportunity to sell it to a later, possibly more valuable, customer. In e-commerce settings, the decision is richer still. The seller chooses not only which items to offer (the assortment) but also the prices at which they are offered, and customers choose among the offered options according to individual preferences. This paper studies a general model that captures these decisions jointly, and develops simple algorithms with provably best-possible performance guarantees. We adopt the framework of competitive analysis, in which an online algorithm is compared against a clairvoyant optimal solution that knows the entire arrival sequence in advance. The sequence is chosen adversarially and need not follow any stochastic pattern. This worst-case perspective is attractive when demand is difficult to forecast, is non-stationary, or is subject to sudden shifts, as is common during promotions, demand shocks, or when forecasting models are misspecified. The guarantee obtained is robust: it holds for every possible sequence of customers. The foundational result in this area is the online bipartite matching problem of Karp, Vazirani, and Vazirani [1], whose RANKING algorithm achieves a competitive ratio of 1-1/e, which is optimal among randomized algorithms. Subsequent work extended this guarantee to vertex-weighted matching [2], and to the AdWords and budgeted allocation problems through the "balancing" or "water-filling" approach of Mehta et al. [3] and Buchbinder, Jain, and Naor [4]. A unifying primal-dual perspective was developed by Devanur, Jain, and Kleinberg [5]. In the revenue management literature, related guarantees were established for assortment problems in which customers choose according to a choice model: Golrezaei, Nazerzadeh, and Rusmevichientong [6] gave a 1-1/e competitive algorithm for online assortment with inventory constraints, and later work extended these ideas to richer choice structures and to personalized settings [7,8]. A common feature of this literature is that each item has a single, fixed price or weight. The competitive ratio 1-1/e is then achieved by discounting each item's price by an increasing function of the fraction of its inventory already consumed. Fixed prices are a significant restriction in practice. Hotels sell the same room at several fare classes; airlines offer a ladder of fares for each cabin; online retailers adjust prices over time and across customer segments. When an item may be sold at multiple prices, the problem changes qualitatively. A low price sells units that might later have sold at a higher price, so the algorithm must trade off the immediate revenue, the opportunity cost of inventory, and the possibility that high-priced customers never arrive. Classical single-leg revenue management results with multiple fare classes [9,10] show that the best achievable competitive ratio depends on the range of prices, and this dependence cannot be avoided under adversarial arrivals. Ball and Queyranne [11] characterized the optimal ratio for a single resource with fare classes, and related results exist for one-way trading and online knapsack problems [12,13], where ratios depend on the ratio between the largest and smallest values. These results suggest that the right notion of performance in our setting is a weight-dependent competitive ratio, determined by the sets of feasible prices supplied in advance. Our contributions. We study a general online allocation problem in which each item has finite inventory and a set of feasible prices, and customers arrive sequentially with choice behavior over item-price pairs. This formulation subsumes online matching, AdWords-type problems, and online assortment as special cases in which every item has a single price. Our main contributions are as follows. First, we construct a class of universal value functions that assign to each item an opportunity cost as a function of its remaining inventory. These functions are designed so that the selection of items and the selection of prices are integrated into a single decision: upon each arrival, the algorithm offers the item-price combinations maximizing the customer's contribution net of the value-function opportunity cost. The resulting algorithms are simple and intuitive, require no forecasts, and extend the water-filling logic of earlier work to multiple prices. Second, we prove that these algorithms achieve weight-dependent competitive ratios that depend only on the sets of feasible prices, and we show matching upper bounds establishing that no online algorithm can do better. The ratio recovers 1-1/e when each item has a single price and degrades gracefully as the price sets become more spread out. Our analysis proceeds through a primal-dual argument in which the value function is derived from a differential-equation characterization of the tightest feasible dual update. Third, we evaluate the algorithms empirically on the publicly available hotel data set of Bodea et al. [14], in which multiple room types are each sold at multiple fares. Worst-case algorithms are by design conservative, and as expected they can be outperformed on typical instances by methods that forecast and learn future demand. We therefore also study "hybrid" approaches that combine our value functions with forecast-based or learning-based policies. We find that the hybrids deliver the best performance, retaining robustness while exploiting predictable structure in demand. Organization. Section 2 formalizes the model and reviews preliminaries. Section 3 presents the value functions and algorithms. Section 4 proves the competitive guarantees, and Section 5 establishes matching impossibility results. Section 6 reports the numerical study on the hotel data, and Section 7 concludes. We study an online allocation problem in which a set of items I, each with a finite initial inventory, is sold to customers arriving sequentially. Item i has a finite set of feasible prices Pi = {p{i,1} < ... < p{i,mi}}. When customer t arrives, the algorithm observes her choice model, offers an assortment of item-price pairs, and the customer selects at most one pair (or leaves) according to this model. The decision is irrevocable, and each sale reduces the inventory of the item by one. The objective is to maximize total revenue. We evaluate algorithms by competitive analysis against a clairvoyant optimum that knows the entire arrival sequence in advance, and we do not assume any stochastic structure on the arrivals [Mehta et al., 2007; Buchbinder et al., 2007]. Model and benchmark. For the matching special case, customer t has a value v{t,i,p} for each item-price pair and purchases the offered pair maximizing nonnegative utility. For the assortment case, we use a general choice model in which the purchase probabilities for an offered set S are given by a function φt(·|S). To obtain a tractable benchmark, we upper bound the clairvoyant optimum by a linear program (LP) whose variables x{t,i,p} represent the (fractional) amount of item i sold to customer t at price p. Constraints require that, for each item, total sales do not exceed inventory, and that, for each customer, the allocation be consistent with a feasible assortment, expressed through the standard choice-based LP relaxation [Golrezaei et al., 2014]. The algorithm's revenue is compared with the optimal LP value, which yields a guarantee against the true offline optimum as well. Weight-dependent competitive ratio. Because multiple prices per item change the achievable guarantee, the competitive ratio depends on the price sets. For item i, let the ratio of its extreme prices be p{i,mi}/p{i,1}. We define a ratio α(P) determined by the collection of price sets, obtained as the solution of a small system of equations over the price levels (described below). When every item has a single price, α reduces to 1−1/e. As the prices become more dispersed, α decreases. We show matching upper bounds by constructing adversarial instances, so the ratio is tight for each price set. Value-function algorithm. The algorithm is a primal-dual style procedure built on a universal value function. For each item i, let yi ∈ [0,1] denote the fraction of its inventory sold so far. We define a nondecreasing function Ψi(y) that represents the opportunity cost, or "marginal value", of selling a unit of item i at inventory level y. Ψi is piecewise defined across the price levels of item i: on the segment of inventory in which price p{i,k} is "active", Ψi grows exponentially, and thresholds between segments are chosen so that Ψi crosses each price level p{i,k} at a prescribed fill level. These thresholds are the parameters determined by the system of equations defining α. Intuitively, low prices are accepted only while inventory is plentiful, and as inventory depletes, only higher prices become competitive. When customer t arrives, the algorithm computes the adjusted revenue of each item-price pair, p − Ψi(yi), and offers the assortment (or makes the match) maximizing the customer's expected adjusted revenue. In the matching setting this is a simple argmax; in the assortment setting it is a choice-based optimization problem, which is solvable in polynomial time for the standard models we consider (multinomial logit, and more generally models with efficiently solvable assortment optimization) [Talluri and van Ryzin, 2004]. Because the value function integrates item and price selection, no separate pricing step is needed: pairs with negative adjusted revenue are never offered. Analysis. We use a dual-fitting argument [Devanur et al., 2013]. We maintain a dual solution in which the dual variable for item i's inventory constraint equals Ψi(yi) averaged appropriately, and the dual variable for customer t equals her expected adjusted revenue under the chosen assortment. By construction of the offered set, the dual constraints are satisfied approximately, up to a factor of α. A per-step inequality shows that the increase in primal revenue is at least α times the increase in dual objective. Summing over customers and applying weak duality gives revenue ≥ α · LP ≥ α · OPT. The principal technical step is choosing Ψi to make the per-step inequality hold with equality simultaneously on all price segments, which leads to the equation system defining α. For the upper bound, we construct instances in which customers arrive in phases, each phase targeting a distinct price level, and use Yao's principle to extend the bound to randomized algorithms [Yao, 1977]. Extensions. The same value functions apply to (i) online matching with vertex weights and multiple prices, (ii) the AdWords-type setting with budgets [Mehta et al., 2007], and (iii) assortment problems with general choice models, using the same dual-fitting template with the choice-based LP. Computational experiments. We evaluate our algorithms on the publicly available hotel dataset of Bodea et al. [2009], which records booking transactions for multiple hotel properties, including room types, fares, arrival dates, and lengths of stay. We construct items as room types with inventories scaled to induce varying demand-to-capacity ratios, and feasible prices as the observed fare classes. Customers are generated from the transaction sequence, with choice models estimated from the data by maximum likelihood under a multinomial logit specification. We compare the following methods: (a) our value-function algorithm; (b) a greedy policy that offers the revenue-maximizing assortment ignoring inventory; (c) a forecast-based policy that estimates future demand and solves a LP-based booking-limit or bid-price control, periodically re-solved [Talluri and van Ryzin, 2004]; and (d) a hybrid combining (a) and (c), in which the value function is blended with LP-derived bid prices, using a convex combination whose weight is tuned on a held-out period. Performance is measured as the ratio of realized revenue to the hindsight-optimal LP revenue, averaged over multiple sampled arrival orders, including adversarially permuted sequences to test robustness. We report means and standard errors across replications and vary inventory levels and forecast error to assess sensitivity. We first present the theoretical guarantees of our algorithms, followed by the numerical results on the hotel data set. Competitive ratio guarantees. Let each item i have a set of feasible prices with minimum price mi and maximum price Mi, and let the weight-dependent parameter be determined by the ratio Mi/mi. Our first main result concerns the single-item-type benchmark, in which the value function is constructed from a threshold structure over prices. Graphs are a natural way to represent relational data, and they appear in social networks, web graphs, citation networks, biological networks, and recommender systems. Many of these graphs are now very large. Social and web graphs routinely contain billions of edges, which is more than a single machine can store or process efficiently. A standard solution is distributed computation on a cluster [1, 2]. Systems such as Pregel [3], GraphLab [4], PowerGraph [5], and GraphX [6] distribute a graph across machines and run iterative algorithms in parallel. Examples include PageRank, connected components, shortest paths, and collaborative filtering. The efficiency of these systems depends heavily on how the graph is partitioned. Graph partitioning (GP) assigns the vertices or edges of a graph to different machines. A good partition has two properties. First, the workload is balanced, so that no machine becomes a bottleneck. Second, the communication between machines is small, because network cost often dominates the running time of distributed graph algorithms. Finding an optimal balanced partition is NP-hard [7], so practical methods rely on heuristics. Existing GP methods fall into two groups. Offline methods, such as METIS [8] and spectral approaches [9], require the whole graph to be available and loaded into memory before partitioning. They can produce high-quality partitions, but their time and memory costs are high. For graphs with billions of edges, partitioning may take longer than the downstream computation. Streaming graph partitioning (SGP) was proposed to address this problem [10, 11]. An SGP method reads the graph as a stream of vertices or edges and assigns each item to a machine on arrival, using only limited information about the items already seen. SGP therefore needs little memory, runs in a single pass, and can be parallelized. It also suits graphs that arrive continuously or are too large to load. There are two basic strategies for partitioning a graph. Edge-cut assigns each vertex to a machine, and edges whose endpoints lie on different machines are cut. Vertex-cut assigns each edge to a machine, and a vertex whose edges lie on several machines is replicated on all of them. Edge-cut quality is measured by the number of cut edges, and vertex-cut quality by the replication factor, which is the average number of machines holding a copy of each vertex. Most existing SGP methods, including linear deterministic greedy and Fennel [10, 11, 12], use edge-cut. Few SGP methods use vertex-cut. Representative examples are the hashing and greedy heuristics in PowerGraph [5] and the high-degree-replicated-first strategy in HDRF [13]. Vertex-cut is the more suitable strategy for natural graphs. The degrees of vertices in such graphs usually follow a highly skewed power-law distribution [14, 15]. A small number of hub vertices have very large degrees, while most vertices have few neighbors. Under edge-cut, a hub vertex placed on one machine has many cut edges, which causes heavy communication and an unbalanced load. Balancing the number of vertices per machine does not balance the number of edges, which determines the actual workload. Vertex-cut avoids this problem. It spreads the edges of a hub across many machines at the price of replicating that vertex. Because most vertices have low degree, few vertices need to be replicated, and the total replication remains modest. Both theoretical analysis and experiments [5, 16] have shown that vertex-cut outperforms edge-cut on power-law graphs. Despite this advantage, current vertex-cut SGP methods have limitations. Hash-based methods are fast and balanced, but they ignore graph structure and produce a high replication factor. Greedy methods that use the placement of previously seen edges reduce replication, but they can behave poorly early in the stream, when little information is available, and they may degrade balance. Methods that use vertex degrees need either the full degree information, which a one-pass stream does not provide, or partial degrees estimated during the stream. These considerations show that a simple and effective vertex-cut method for streaming natural graphs is still needed. In this paper, we propose a novel SGP method for natural graphs called S-PowerGraph. S-PowerGraph uses vertex-cut and builds on the power-law structure of natural graphs. It makes each placement decision from the current state of the partitions, without storing the graph or making multiple passes. The method is simple to implement, has low time and memory overhead, and achieves a lower replication factor than existing methods while keeping the load balanced. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: - We propose S-PowerGraph, a new streaming vertex-cut partitioning method designed for graphs with skewed power-law degree distributions. - We show that the method is efficient in time and space, and that it needs only a single pass over the edge stream. - We conduct experiments on several large natural graphs and synthetic graphs. The results show that S-PowerGraph outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in replication factor and load balance, and that these improvements carry over to the running time of distributed graph algorithms. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work and introduces the notation. Section 3 describes S-PowerGraph. Section 4 reports experimental results, and Section 5 concludes the paper. We consider an undirected graph G = (V, E) with |V| = n vertices and |E| = m edges, to be distributed over p machines. Under vertex-cut, each edge is assigned to exactly one machine, and a vertex is replicated on every machine that holds at least one of its incident edges [1]. Let A(v) ⊆ {1,…,p} denote the set of machines on which vertex v is replicated, and let Ei be the set of edges on machine i. The quality of a partition is measured by two quantities. The first is the replication factor, RF = (1/n) Σv |A(v)|, which reflects communication cost because replicas of a vertex must synchronize their state. The second is the load imbalance, λ = maxi |Ei| / (m/p), which reflects computational balance. The objective is to minimize RF subject to λ ≤ 1 + ε for a small tolerance ε. Streaming Setting Edges arrive one at a time as a stream, and each must be irrevocably assigned to a machine upon arrival. The partitioner keeps only compact state: the current load of each machine, a table of the replica sets A(v), and a partial degree counter d(v) for each vertex, equal to the number of edges of v observed so far. No edge is stored after assignment, so memory is O(np) bits for the replica table plus O(n) for the counters, and the time per edge is O(p). Motivation In natural graphs the degree distribution follows a power law, P(d) ∝ d^(−α), with 2 < α < 3 typically [2]. A few high-degree vertices are incident to a large share of edges. Edge-cut methods place such hubs on one machine and cut many edges to their neighbors, which causes both communication and load skew [1]. Under vertex-cut, replicating a hub is cheap relative to the number of edges it saves from being cut, while low-degree vertices are rarely replicated if their edges are co-located. Existing streaming vertex-cut heuristics include hashing, the greedy heuristic of PowerGraph [1], and the degree-based hashing (DBH) [3] and HDRF [4] methods. Greedy considers only replica locality and load, while DBH and HDRF use degree information to decide which endpoint to replicate. S-PowerGraph builds on these ideas, combining replica locality, degree awareness, and load balancing in a single scoring rule. The S-PowerGraph Algorithm For an arriving edge e = (u, v), the partial degrees are first incremented, d(u) ← d(u)+1 and d(v) ← d(v)+1. We define the normalized degrees θ(u) = d(u) / (d(u) + d(v)), θ(v) = 1 − θ(u). A vertex with small θ is relatively low-degree and should be kept intact, whereas the higher-degree endpoint is the better one to replicate. For each machine i we compute a score C(e, i) = Crep(e, i) + Cbal(i). The replication term is Crep(e, i) = g(u, i) + g(v, i), where g(x, i) = 1 + (1 − θ(x)) if i ∈ A(x) and g(x, i) = 0 otherwise, with θ(x) the normalized degree of x. A machine already holding the lower-degree endpoint therefore receives a larger reward than one holding only the higher-degree endpoint. Consequently, when the replica sets of u and v are disjoint, the edge is placed with the lower-degree vertex, and the hub is replicated. This matches the power-law motivation: the hub is likely to be replicated anyway, whereas replicating a low-degree vertex yields little benefit. The balance term is Cbal(i) = λb · (maxsize − |Ei|) / (ζ + maxsize − minsize), where maxsize and minsize are the largest and smallest current machine loads, ζ > 0 is a small constant to avoid division by zero, and λb ≥ 0 controls the weight of balance. This term lies in [0, λb) and favors lightly loaded machines. When λb is small, locality dominates; when it is large, the method approaches round-robin assignment. We use λb as a tunable parameter and examine its sensitivity experimentally. The edge is assigned to i = argmaxi C(e, i), with ties broken uniformly at random. Afterwards, |E{i}| is incremented and i is added to A(u) and A(v) if not already present. Complexity and Properties Each edge requires O(p) work to evaluate scores, giving total time O(mp), and the method is single-pass. Because the algorithm depends only on local state, it can be parallelized by letting several loaders process disjoint portions of the stream with periodically synchronized or locally approximated replica tables and load counters, as is done in prior systems [1], [4]. Using partial rather than true degrees makes the method fully online. For random-order streams, partial degrees are unbiased estimates of the final degree ratios up to scaling, so θ approximates the true relative degree increasingly well as the stream progresses. The reward in Crep ensures that when both endpoints are already co-located on a machine, that machine receives the highest replication score, and no new replica is created. The balance term guarantees that no machine can remain permanently overloaded, since a machine with maximal load receives zero balance reward while less-loaded machines receive positive reward. Experimental Protocol We evaluate on large natural graphs, including social and web graphs from public repositories [5], and on synthetic power-law graphs with varying exponent α generated by standard preferential-attachment or configuration-model procedures [2]. Stream orders include random, breadth-first, and depth-first orderings to assess robustness to locality in the stream. The number of machines p varies from 4 to 128. Baselines are hashing, Greedy [1], DBH [3], HDRF [4], and the edge-cut streaming method LDG [6] and Fennel [7] (with edge-cut results converted to equivalent replication measures where applicable). We report RF, λ, and partitioning time. To measure downstream effects, we run PageRank and connected components on the partitions in a PowerGraph-style framework [1] and record runtime and network traffic. All results are averaged over repeated runs with different random seeds for tie-breaking and ordering. We evaluate S-PowerGraph on real and synthetic graphs, comparing partition quality, load balance, partitioning time, and downstream distributed computation performance. Experimental Setup. The real datasets are four large natural graphs: a Twitter follower graph, a LiveJournal social network, a web graph crawled from the UK domain, and an Orkut community network. Their edge counts range from roughly 69 million to 1.5 billion, and all show heavy-tailed degree distributions. The synthetic graphs were generated with power-law exponents α ∈ {1.8, 2.0, 2.2, 2.4} at a fixed size of 10 million vertices, so we could study how skewness affects each method. Edges arrive in a random order by default; we also test BFS and DFS orderings. We compare against the following baselines: Random (hash) edge placement [1], Grid [2], DBH [3], Greedy vertex-cut as in PowerGraph [4], HDRF [5], and the edge-cut streaming methods LDG [6] and Fennel [7].
