Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, systemic inflammatory disease that primarily affects the joints and, if inadequately controlled, leads to progressive structural damage, functional disability, reduced quality of life and increased mortality. The prevalence of RA in Germany is estimated at roughly 0.5–1% of the adult population, and the disease causes substantial direct and indirect costs for the health care system and society. Over the past two decades, the treatment of RA has changed considerably. Early and aggressive treatment with conventional synthetic disease modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (csDMARDs), most notably methotrexate, is the cornerstone of therapy. Patients who do not reach the treatment target with csDMARDs, or who do not tolerate them, are candidates for biological DMARDs (bDMARDs). Current European guidelines recommend a treat-to-target strategy aiming at remission or at least low disease activity. Tumour necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors were the first class of bDMARDs introduced and are still the most frequently used first-line biologicals in clinical practice. Since then, bDMARDs with other modes of action have become available, including the T-cell co-stimulation modulator abatacept, the interleukin-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab and the B-cell depleting antibody rituximab. These agents have demonstrated efficacy in clinical trials and have markedly improved outcomes for many patients with RA. Despite these advances, a considerable proportion of patients do not achieve or maintain an adequate response to their first bDMARD. Primary non-response, secondary loss of efficacy, for example through development of anti-drug antibodies, and adverse events or patient preference lead to treatment discontinuation. Observational studies and registry data consistently show that persistence with a first anti-TNF therapy is far from ideal, with a substantial share of patients stopping treatment within the first year. As a consequence, many patients receive a second and, in some cases, a third bDMARD during the course of their disease. The question of how to proceed after failure of a first anti-TNF is clinically important. Guidelines recommend that patients with an inadequate response to a first bDMARD should receive another bDMARD, but they do not clearly prefer one strategy over another. Treatment options include cycling to a second anti-TNF or switching to a biological with a different mode of action. Evidence from randomised trials, registries and some observational studies suggests that switching to a non-anti-TNF agent such as rituximab may be associated with better clinical outcomes than cycling to another anti-TNF, whereas other studies have found comparable effectiveness. Overall, the evidence base is heterogeneous, and the comparison is complicated by differences in patient populations, reasons for discontinuing the first agent, outcome definitions and follow-up. Drug survival, or treatment persistence, is a widely used measure in observational research. It reflects the time a patient remains on a given therapy and integrates aspects of effectiveness, safety, tolerability and patient and physician satisfaction. It is therefore considered a pragmatic proxy for overall treatment success in real-world settings. While drug survival of first-line bDMARDs has been described in numerous studies, considerably less is known about the persistence of second-line bDMARD therapy. In particular, it is not well established whether the mode of action of the second bDMARD is associated with different persistence rates. Moreover, many existing studies are based on selected registry populations or specialist centres, and they often do not distinguish between permanent discontinuation, temporary interruption followed by re-initiation, and switching to a further bDMARD. This distinction matters, because a treatment gap followed by re-start has different clinical implications than definitive cessation or a switch to a third agent. Claims data from statutory health insurance funds offer an opportunity to study treatment patterns in an unselected, real-world population over time. They capture all reimbursed prescriptions regardless of the prescriber, include a broad range of patients treated in routine care, and allow assessment of comorbidity and co-medication before and during treatment. Their limitations, notably the lack of clinical information such as disease activity and reasons for discontinuation, must be considered in interpretation, but they allow robust analyses of persistence and treatment sequences. Against this background, we aimed to assess, in a large German claims database, the proportions of RA patients who discontinued, re-initiated or continued a second bDMARD, as well as the proportion who switched to a third bDMARD within 12 months after starting the second agent. We focused on patients whose first bDMARD was an anti-TNF and compared those who received a second anti-TNF with those who received a bDMARD with a different mode of action. In addition, we estimated drug survival of the second bDMARD and explored patient characteristics, including age, sex, comorbidity and prior medication, that were associated with earlier discontinuation or switching. We hypothesised that persistence would be higher in patients who changed to a non-anti-TNF mode of action than in those who cycled to another anti-TNF. Study design and data source We conducted a retrospective, non-interventional cohort study using German claims data from a statutory health insurance fund. The database covers inpatient and outpatient diagnoses (ICD-10-GM codes), outpatient prescriptions dispensed in pharmacies (coded by Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical [ATC] classification and Central Pharmaceutical Number), inpatient procedures, and demographic information (age, sex, date of death). The observation period ran from January 2010 to December 2013. The data were anonymized before analysis in accordance with German data protection regulations, so informed consent and ethics approval were not required for this secondary data analysis. Study population Patients were eligible if they had at least one inpatient or confirmed outpatient diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis (ICD-10-GM M05.– or M06.–, excluding M06.1 and M06.3) and continuous insurance coverage during the observation period. Biological DMARDs (bDMARDs) were identified by ATC code. Anti-TNF agents comprised adalimumab, certolizumab pegol, etanercept, golimumab and infliximab. Non-anti-TNF bDMARDs comprised abatacept, rituximab and tocilizumab. Patients were included in the analysis if they had at least one prescription of an anti-TNF agent (first bDMARD) and at least one subsequent prescription of a second bDMARD that differed from the first anti-TNF agent. The second bDMARD could therefore be another anti-TNF (anti-TNF cycling) or a bDMARD with a different mode of action (non-anti-TNF). To ensure that the second bDMARD was a true second-line therapy, patients with bDMARD prescriptions before the first anti-TNF in a pre-observation period were excluded. Patients with a follow-up shorter than the required period, other than due to death, were excluded. Index date and follow-up The index date was the date of the first prescription of the second bDMARD. Follow-up started at the index date and lasted 12 months or until death, whichever came first. The pre-index period of up to 12 months before the index date was used to describe baseline characteristics. Treatment episodes and outcome definitions Treatment episodes were constructed from prescription dates and the defined daily dose or the labelled dosing interval of each substance. A grace period (permissible gap) of 60 days between the theoretical end of supply of one prescription and the next prescription was allowed to account for stockpiling and irregular dispensing; longer gaps were regarded as discontinuation. The following mutually exclusive outcomes were defined for the 12-month follow-up: 1. Continuation: continued prescriptions of the second bDMARD without a gap exceeding the grace period and without prescription of another bDMARD. 2. Switch: prescription of a third bDMARD different from the second bDMARD during follow-up. Switching was assigned to the date of the first prescription of the third agent. 3. Discontinuation without re-start: no further prescription of the second bDMARD after a gap exceeding the grace period, and no other bDMARD prescribed until the end of follow-up. 4. Discontinuation with re-start: a gap exceeding the grace period followed by a new prescription of the same second bDMARD within follow-up. Drug survival was defined as time from the index date to discontinuation (gap exceeding the grace period, with or without re-start) or switch to a third bDMARD, whichever came first. Patients who were still on treatment at the end of follow-up or who died were censored. Covariates Covariates were assessed in the 12 months before the index date. They comprised age, sex, and comorbidity measured by the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) adapted for claims data. We also assessed concomitant and previous medication: conventional synthetic DMARDs (e.g., methotrexate, leflunomide, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine), glucocorticoids, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and painkillers (non-opioid and opioid analgesics). Further variables were the specific first anti-TNF agent, the specific second bDMARD, the time between the first anti-TNF and the second bDMARD, and selected comorbidities such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes and depression. Statistical analysis Patient characteristics were described with means and standard deviations for continuous variables and absolute and relative frequencies for categorical variables. Patients receiving an anti-TNF as second bDMARD were compared with those receiving a non-anti-TNF bDMARD. Differences were tested using t-tests or Mann–Whitney U tests for continuous variables, depending on distribution, and chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests for categorical variables. Proportions of patients continuing, discontinuing, re-starting or switching were compared between groups with chi-square tests. Drug survival was estimated with the Kaplan–Meier method and groups were compared with the log-rank test. Mean drug survival time within the 12-month window was reported in days. Cox proportional hazards regression was used to identify factors independently associated with discontinuation (including re-start) or switch. The model included the mode of action of the second bDMARD (anti-TNF vs. non-anti-TNF), age, sex, CCI, and the medication variables listed above. Results are reported as hazard ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals. The proportional hazards assumption was checked using log-minus-log plots and Schoenfeld residuals. A two-sided p-value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant. No adjustment for multiple testing was made because the analyses were exploratory. All analyses were performed with SAS or SPSS statistical software. Because claims data record dispensed prescriptions rather than actual intake, and contain no clinical measures of disease activity, the reasons for discontinuation or switching could not be determined; these limitations were considered in interpreting the results. A total of 2667 patients with RA and at least one anti-TNF prescription were identified in the claims database between 2010 and 2013. Of these, 451 patients (16.9%) received a second bDMARD that differed from the first anti-TNF and had at least one follow-up prescription of that drug, and they formed the study population. Of these, 340 patients (75.4%) received a second anti-TNF and 111 patients (24.6%) received a non-anti-TNF bDMARD as second-line therapy. Patient characteristics Patients in the anti-TNF group were younger than those in the non-anti-TNF group (mean age 52.6 vs. 55.9 years). The groups were otherwise broadly comparable with respect to sex distribution and the use of concomitant conventional synthetic DMARDs and glucocorticoids. Comorbidity, measured by the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), was similar between groups, although a higher CCI was associated with poorer persistence in the multivariable analysis (see below). Previous painkiller medication was common in both groups. Baseline characteristics of both groups are shown in Table 1. Treatment outcomes during 12 months of follow-up Treatment pathways during the 12-month follow-up are summarized in Table 2. Overall, 56.8% of patients continued their second bDMARD for the full follow-up period, and 60% were on treatment if patients who re-started therapy after a gap were included. Switching to a third bDMARD was significantly more frequent in the second anti-TNF group than in the non-anti-TNF group (28.8% vs. 11.7%, p < 0.001). Discontinuation without re-start occurred in 14.1% of patients in the anti-TNF group and 19.8% in the non-anti-TNF group, a difference that was not statistically significant (p = 0.179). Re-start after a treatment interruption was observed in 3.8% of anti-TNF patients and 1.8% of non-anti-TNF patients (p = 0.387). Continuation of the second bDMARD without discontinuation or switch was more common among non-anti-TNF patients than among anti-TNF patients (66.7% vs. 53.5%, p < 0.050). Thus, the higher rate of switching in the anti-TNF group was the main driver of the difference in persistence, while simple discontinuation without further bDMARD therapy was numerically, but not significantly, more common in the non-anti-TNF group. Drug survival Drug survival differed between the two groups. The mean drug survival time of the second bDMARD was longer in patients receiving a non-anti-TNF (295 days) than in patients receiving a second anti-TNF

The Antarctic ice sheet holds enough ice to raise global mean sea level by about 58 m, most of it in the East Antarctic Ice Sheet (EAIS). Although the EAIS has long been considered stable relative to the West Antarctic Ice Sheet, parts of it rest on bedrock well below sea level and drain through outlet glaciers that are sensitive to ocean forcing. The Wilkes Subglacial Basin and the Aurora Subglacial Basin together hold a marine-based ice volume equivalent to several metres of sea level. Whether these basins are vulnerable to atmospheric and oceanic warming is a central question for projections of future sea-level rise, and it can be addressed only by examining how the ice sheet responded in past warm climates. The Pliocene epoch (5.3–2.6 Myr ago) is a particularly useful target. Atmospheric CO2 concentrations during the mid-Pliocene warm period (about 3.3–3.0 Myr ago) were approximately 350–450 ppm, comparable to present-day and near-future values, and global mean temperatures were roughly 2–3 °C above pre-industrial levels. Continental configurations and topography were similar to today, although the details of subglacial topography remain uncertain. Reconstructions of Pliocene sea level nevertheless vary widely, from a few metres to more than 25 m above present, depending on the proxy, the correction for glacial isostatic adjustment and dynamic topography, and the assumptions made about ice sheet sources. Such high estimates imply substantial loss of Greenland, West Antarctic and possibly East Antarctic ice. In contrast, the most recent assessment of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (AR5) concluded that Pliocene sea level on Milankovitch timescales likely did not exceed +20 m, and that the Antarctic contribution was constrained mainly by indirect evidence. Geological evidence from the East Antarctic margin and interior gives a seemingly contradictory picture. Marine sediment cores from Wilkes Land and Prydz Bay, and from the Ross Sea, record episodes of reduced sea ice, elevated productivity and ice-margin retreat during the Pliocene, and have been interpreted as showing that marine-based sectors of the EAIS retreated inland. Isotopic and provenance data from offshore sediments point in the same direction. Terrestrial records, on the other hand, such as high-elevation geomorphology of the Transantarctic Mountains, the persistence of ancient surfaces and buried ice in the Dry Valleys, and the survival of sparse tundra-like deposits at elevation, have been used to argue either for a persistently cold, stable interior or for substantial thinning and warm episodes. The two lines of evidence need not conflict if marginal retreat occurred together with interior thickening, a pattern predicted by some models because a warmer atmosphere and reduced sea ice carry more moisture to the continent, increasing snowfall over the high plateau. Testing this prediction requires direct constraints on past ice surface elevations. Cosmogenic nuclide exposure dating of bedrock and glacial erratics provides such constraints. Nuclides such as 10Be, 26Al and 21Ne accumulate in rock surfaces exposed above the ice, and so record when mountain summits and nunataks were last uncovered. In Antarctica, where erosion rates are among the lowest on Earth, nuclide concentrations can preserve information over millions of years, and paired nuclides allow burial and complex exposure histories to be identified. Elevation transects of exposure ages along outlet glaciers can document ice thickness changes through time. A considerable dataset has now been assembled for the Transantarctic Mountains, Dronning Maud Land and the Lambert–Amery system. However, the interpretation of exposure ages is not straightforward. Cold-based ice can cover surfaces without eroding them, producing inherited nuclides. Ages are therefore minimum or ambiguous constraints, and individual sites are strongly influenced by local glaciological conditions. Synthesis across regions, together with a physical framework to interpret regional trends, is therefore needed. Ice sheet models offer such a framework but are themselves sensitive to uncertain boundary conditions, including bedrock topography, climate forcing, basal sliding and ocean melt. Simulations of Pliocene Antarctica have produced a wide range of ice volumes, and some show a major retreat in the Wilkes and Aurora basins while others retain a nearly modern ice sheet. Comparing model output with geological data at specific sites narrows these uncertainties and clarifies whether the geological records are mutually consistent. In this study we combine new cosmogenic nuclide exposure ages from East Antarctica with previously published data to reconstruct Plio-Pleistocene changes in ice thickness along the EAIS margin and interior. We then use a three-dimensional thermomechanical ice sheet model driven with mid-Pliocene boundary conditions to test whether the exposure record can be explained by interior thickening accompanied by retreat in the major subglacial basins. We evaluate the implied net EAIS contribution to sea level in the context of West Antarctic and Greenland contributions and the AR5 estimate. Finally, we consider the role of the climatic transition around 3 Myr ago, when cooling, expanded sea ice and reduced moisture transport are expected to have reduced snow accumulation and thinned the ice sheet, at least in coastal areas. Cosmogenic nuclide exposure ages were compiled from nunataks and moraine sequences in the Transantarctic Mountains, Dronning Maud Land and the Prince Charles Mountains, and combined with new measurements from the Aurora Basin sector. Ice sheet simulations were then used to place the exposure data in the context of continental-scale ice volume. Field sampling. Samples of bedrock and glacial erratics were collected from elevation transects at sites bordering the present ice margin. Sampling targeted flat, stable surfaces showing no evidence of recent toppling, burial by till or snow, or significant surface erosion. We recorded sample location by handheld GPS and elevation by barometric altimetry calibrated against differential GPS benchmarks. Topographic shielding was measured with a clinometer and compass. Sample thickness was measured directly. Only the uppermost few centimetres of each rock were taken, using a hammer and chisel or a rock saw. Laboratory procedures. Samples were crushed and sieved to 250–500 µm. Quartz was isolated by magnetic separation, froth flotation and repeated leaching in dilute HF/HNO₃, until purity was verified by ICP-OES measurement of aluminium (<150 ppm). Beryllium and aluminium were extracted following standard ion-exchange chromatography after dissolution in concentrated HF, with a ⁹Be carrier added. For samples with low concentrations, a few grains were additionally processed for ²¹Ne by stepwise heating and noble-gas mass spectrometry. Be and Al were precipitated as hydroxides, oxidised to BeO and Al₂O₃, and mixed with niobium or silver powder before pressing into cathodes. ¹⁰Be/⁹Be and ²⁶Al/²⁷Al ratios were measured by accelerator mass spectrometry, normalised to the standards KN-5-2 and ICN01-5-1 (¹⁰Be) and ZAL94 (²⁶Al). Procedural blanks were processed with each batch of samples, and their ratios were subtracted with uncertainties propagated in quadrature. Exposure age calculation. Ages were calculated using the CRONUS-Earth online calculator framework with an Antarctic sea-level high-latitude production rate and time-dependent Lal/Stone scaling. Atmospheric pressure was derived from the ERA reanalysis pressure–elevation relationship appropriate for Antarctica instead of the standard atmosphere, which overestimates pressure. Sample density was set to 2.65 g cm⁻³. We report minimum exposure ages assuming zero erosion and also ages for erosion rates of 0.1–1 m Myr⁻¹, constrained where nuclides were close to saturation. Samples with ²⁶Al/¹⁰Be ratios falling below the constant-exposure field were interpreted as having complex histories involving burial by ice, and were treated as indicating at least one episode of cover. In these cases, the ages are minimum estimates of total history rather than the timing of final deglaciation. Previously published ages were recalculated with the same production-rate scheme to ensure internal consistency. Reconstructing ice thickness change. Exposure age–elevation relationships were used to infer the timing and rate of ice surface lowering. Where a transect exhibited an age increase with elevation, we fitted linear regressions with uncertainty weighting. Sites with older ages at the highest elevations were used to infer when the ice surface last stood above the sample. Inheritance from earlier exposure was evaluated through nuclide pair relationships and by comparing neighbouring samples. Outliers were identified using reduced chi-squared and removed only when statistically justified and geomorphologically explainable. To compare sites, ice-surface elevation changes were corrected for glacio-isostatic adjustment using a simple Earth model, and for changes in the geoid where relevant. Ice sheet model. We used the thermomechanical ice sheet model PISM (Parallel Ice Sheet Model) run on a 10 km grid across the Antarctic continent, using a hybrid of the shallow-ice and shallow-shelf approximations. Present-day bed topography was taken from Bedmap2, and geothermal heat flux from a published geophysical estimate. Basal sliding followed a pseudo-plastic power law with till friction angle dependent on bed elevation. Surface mass balance was calculated with a positive-degree-day scheme (melt factors for snow and ice of 3 and 8 mm w.e. K⁻¹ d⁻¹). Ice shelf calving was handled with a combination of eigencalving and a thickness threshold, and sub-shelf melt was parameterised as a function of ocean temperature. Bedrock response used an elastic lithosphere–relaxing asthenosphere model. Mid-Pliocene boundary conditions. Mid-Pliocene atmospheric and oceanic forcing was derived from PlioMIP climate model output, expressed as anomalies relative to the pre-industrial simulation and added to present-day observational climatologies (precipitation scaled exponentially with temperature change, ~5% per K). Atmospheric CO₂ was set at 400 ppm. Initial topography used the PRISM4 reconstruction, with reduced ice volume and the Wilkes and Aurora subglacial basins assumed to be isostatically adjusted. Ocean warming was applied to sub-shelf melt rates, and we tested sensitivity to the magnitude by varying ocean temperature anomalies between 0 and +3 °C. Experiment design. Simulations were spun up for 100 kyr from present-day ice and then run for 500 kyr under constant mid-Pliocene forcing, allowing equilibrium to be approached. Orbital variability was explored by modulating the forcing between cold and warm orbital extremes with a glacial index. We carried out an ensemble varying key uncertain parameters: positive-degree-day factors, basal sliding exponent, calving threshold, ocean melt coefficient, and precipitation scaling. Ensemble members were scored against the present-day ice thickness and extent, and against the exposure age constraints. Model outputs for ice-thickness change at the sample locations were interpolated and compared directly with the exposure data. Sea-level contribution. Ice volume changes were converted to sea-level equivalent above floatation, taking into account the density contrast and the area of the ocean. Contributions from West Antarctica and Greenland were taken from published simulations and combined with the East Antarctic results, and compared against the IPCC AR5 assessment. Exposure ages from the Transantarctic Mountains and the East Antarctic coast and margin nunataks record a coherent pattern of surface lowering since the Pliocene. We compiled 214 new and previously published 10Be, 26Al and 21Ne exposure ages from 17 sites, and report here both the compiled data and the ice sheet model experiments. Exposure ages and elevation transects. Samples from the highest elevations at interior sites (more than 150 m above the present ice surface) yield minimum exposure ages of 2.5 to 5.1 Myr, with the oldest ages in the Dry Valleys region and the Sør Rondane and Prince Charles Mountains. Cosmogenic nuclide concentrations in these samples approach the values expected for steady-state erosion, and erosion rates calculated from 10Be alone are 0.1 to 0.6 m Myr⁻¹. Paired 26Al/10Be ratios in 38 samples fall below the constant-exposure line, indicating burial or intermittent cover by ice. For these samples, simple burial histories imply that the high-elevation surfaces were covered by ice for cumulative periods of 0.4 to 1.9 Myr after initial exposure. At interior sites, the pattern is of older exposure ages at higher elevations. Ages at 50 to 150 m above the modern ice decrease systematically to 0.1 to 1.2 Myr, consistent with progressive thinning. In contrast, the coastal and outlet glacier sites show a different pattern. Near the coast, exposure ages above 100 m rarely exceed 1 Myr, and the oldest surfaces at these locations have been shaped by repeated Pleistocene glaciations. Cosmogenic inheritance is common in the youngest coastal samples (about 20% of samples show ages inconsistent with deglaciation chronologies), but it does not change the regional pattern. Taken together, the data imply that interior ice surfaces were higher than at present at times in the Pliocene by tens to about 150 m, depending on the site,

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common primary malignancy of the liver and a leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide. Its incidence continues to rise, particularly in East Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, where chronic hepatitis B infection is endemic, and in Western countries, where hepatitis C, alcohol-related liver disease, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease are major contributors. Because HCC usually arises in the setting of chronic liver disease and cirrhosis, treatment decisions must balance tumor burden against underlying hepatic function. Curative options, including resection, liver transplantation, and local ablation, are available only to patients diagnosed at an early stage. Unfortunately, a large proportion of patients are diagnosed at an intermediate or advanced stage, when curative treatment is no longer feasible. For patients with intermediate-stage disease, namely those with multinodular, unresectable HCC, preserved liver function, and no vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread, transcatheter hepatic arterial chemoembolization (TACE) is the recommended first-line therapy in major clinical guidelines, including the Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer staging system. TACE exploits the fact that HCC receives its blood supply predominantly from the hepatic artery, whereas normal hepatic parenchyma is supplied mainly by the portal vein. Selective delivery of a chemotherapeutic agent, followed by embolization of the tumor-feeding arteries, produces both a high local drug concentration and ischemic necrosis. Randomized trials and meta-analyses have shown that TACE improves survival in carefully selected patients compared with conservative management. Nevertheless, TACE has important limitations. Complete tumor necrosis is achieved in a minority of patients, and recurrence and progression are common. Moreover, embolization induces hypoxia in residual viable tumor, which upregulates hypoxia-inducible factor-1α and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and other pro-angiogenic factors. This response may promote neovascularization, tumor revascularization, and metastasis, thereby undermining the benefit of the procedure. Repeated TACE sessions may also worsen liver function. These observations provided the rationale for combining TACE with systemic antiangiogenic therapy. Sorafenib, an oral multikinase inhibitor, targets Raf kinase, VEGF receptors, and platelet-derived growth factor receptor-β, thereby exerting both antiproliferative and antiangiogenic effects. In the SHARP and Asia-Pacific trials, sorafenib significantly prolonged overall survival and time to progression in patients with advanced HCC compared with placebo, establishing it as the first effective systemic agent for this disease. It was therefore hypothesized that sorafenib could counteract the surge in angiogenic signaling following TACE, delay tumor progression, and ultimately improve survival. Preclinical data and early-phase studies supported the feasibility and apparent safety of the combination, and several retrospective and non-randomized studies, particularly from Asia, reported encouraging outcomes. However, results from prospective randomized trials have been less consistent. The SPACE trial, a phase II study of drug-eluting bead TACE with sorafenib or placebo, showed a trend toward improved time to progression but no significant survival benefit. The post-TACE trial conducted in Japan and Korea found no improvement in time to progression with sorafenib after TACE. The TACE 2 trial in the United Kingdom, as well as a trial from China, also investigated the combination in double-blind, placebo-controlled designs, with variable findings. Differences among these studies in patient populations, etiologies of liver disease, TACE techniques (conventional versus drug-eluting beads), timing of sorafenib initiation, treatment duration, and dose intensity may have contributed to heterogeneous results. In addition, the small sample sizes of some trials limited their statistical power to detect differences in survival. Open-label studies and retrospective analyses are further susceptible to bias, which complicates interpretation of the overall evidence. Safety is another important consideration. Sorafenib is associated with characteristic adverse events, including hand and foot skin reaction (HFSR), rash, diarrhea, fatigue, hypertension, and anorexia, which frequently necessitate dose reduction or interruption. When sorafenib is added to TACE, which itself causes post-embolization syndrome and may transiently impair liver function, the tolerability of combined treatment may be reduced, and reduced adherence may in turn diminish efficacy. Quantitative assessment of the incremental toxicity of the combination relative to TACE alone is therefore essential for balanced clinical decision-making. Several previous meta-analyses have evaluated TACE plus sorafenib, but many pooled randomized and non-randomized studies, including retrospective cohorts and open-label trials, which introduces substantial heterogeneity and risk of bias. To provide a more reliable estimate of the effect of the combination, it is preferable to restrict the analysis to double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trials, in which performance and detection biases are minimized, particularly for subjective outcomes such as radiological progression and adverse event reporting. Therefore, we conducted a meta-analysis of double-blind randomized controlled trials comparing TACE combined with sorafenib with TACE plus placebo in patients with HCC. We aimed to evaluate the effects of the combination on time to progression and overall survival, and to quantify the risks of sorafenib-related adverse events, including HFSR, rash, fatigue, diarrhea, and nausea. We also sought to explore sources of heterogeneity through subgroup analysis, so as to clarify the benefit–risk profile of this combination strategy. This meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. The protocol defined the research question, eligibility criteria, outcomes, and analytic approach before data extraction. Search strategy We searched PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, and ClinicalTrials.gov from database inception to the date of the final search. The search combined controlled vocabulary and free-text terms related to the intervention and disease: "hepatocellular carcinoma," "liver cancer," "HCC," "transcatheter arterial chemoembolization," "transarterial chemoembolization," "TACE," "sorafenib," "Nexavar," "randomized," "double-blind," and "placebo." No language restrictions were applied initially. We also manually screened the reference lists of included trials, previous meta-analyses, and relevant reviews, as well as abstracts from major oncology and hepatology meetings, to identify additional eligible studies. Eligibility criteria Studies were included if they met the following criteria: (1) randomized controlled trial with a double-blind, placebo-controlled design; (2) participants were adults with HCC diagnosed by histology or by accepted noninvasive imaging criteria; (3) the experimental arm received TACE (conventional or drug-eluting bead) combined with sorafenib, and the control arm received TACE combined with placebo; and (4) the study reported at least one outcome of interest, namely time to progression (TTP), overall survival (OS), or sorafenib-related adverse events. Exclusion criteria were non-randomized or open-label designs, studies comparing sorafenib with other systemic agents, studies in which sorafenib was given after TACE failure as a salvage therapy without a placebo control, duplicate publications, conference abstracts without sufficient data, and animal or in vitro studies. When multiple reports described the same trial, the most complete or most recent dataset was used. Study selection and data extraction Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, then assessed the full texts of potentially eligible records. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or by consultation with a third reviewer. Data were extracted independently by two reviewers using a standardized form. Extracted items included first author, year of publication, trial name, countries of enrollment, sample size per arm, patient characteristics (age, sex, etiology of liver disease, Child-Pugh class, ECOG performance status, tumor stage), TACE regimen and schedule, sorafenib dose and timing relative to TACE, duration of follow-up, hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for TTP and OS, and the number of patients experiencing each adverse event. Adverse events of interest were hand and foot skin reaction (HFSR), rash, fatigue, diarrhea, and nausea; where available, we extracted any-grade events, and otherwise used the grading reported by the trial. When HRs were not reported directly, they were estimated from Kaplan-Meier curves or other published statistics using established methods. Risk of bias assessment Methodological quality was assessed independently by two reviewers with the Cochrane Collaboration risk of bias tool, which evaluates random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other sources of bias. Each domain was rated as low, unclear, or high risk. We additionally recorded whether analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle. Disagreements were resolved by consensus. Outcomes The primary efficacy outcomes were TTP, defined as the interval from randomization to radiologic tumor progression, and OS, defined as the interval from randomization to death from any cause. The safety outcomes were the incidence of sorafenib-related adverse events, namely HFSR, rash, fatigue, diarrhea, and nausea. Statistical analysis For time-to-event outcomes, log HRs and their standard errors were pooled using the inverse-variance method, and results are presented as HRs with 95% CIs. An HR below 1 favored the experimental (TACE plus sorafenib) group. For adverse events, risk ratios (RRs) with 95% CIs were calculated and pooled using the Mantel-Haenszel method. An RR above 1 indicated a greater risk in the experimental group. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran's Q test and quantified with the I² statistic, with I² values above 50% or a p value below 0.10 for the Q test considered to indicate substantial heterogeneity. A fixed-effect model was used when heterogeneity was low, and a random-effects model (DerSimonian-Laird) was used when substantial heterogeneity was present. Because of anticipated clinical differences among trials, such as geographic region, TACE technique, and timing of sorafenib initiation, we examined the robustness of results using both models where appropriate. To explore sources of heterogeneity, particularly for HFSR, we conducted sensitivity analyses by sequentially omitting each study (leave-one-out analysis) and performed a subgroup analysis restricted to studies without significant heterogeneity in the HFSR data. Potential publication bias was to be evaluated by visual inspection of funnel plots and Egger's test; however, given the small number of included trials (fewer than 10), these tests were interpreted with caution and considered of limited power. All tests were two-sided, and a p value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed using Review Manager (RevMan, version 5.3; Cochrane Collaboration) and Stata software (StataCorp). The quality of evidence for each outcome was interpreted in light of risk of bias, heterogeneity, imprecision, and the number of available trials. A total of 312 records were identified through database searches (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science). After removal of duplicates and screening of titles and abstracts, 14 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Ten were excluded because they were non-randomized, open-label, lacked a placebo control, or did not report TTP, OS, or adverse event data. Four double-blind, placebo-controlled RCTs met the inclusion criteria and were included in the quantitative synthesis. The trials enrolled a total of 877 patients with HCC from 14 countries, including China and the USA; 439 were allocated to TACE plus sorafenib (experimental groups) and 438 to TACE plus placebo (control groups). Baseline characteristics, including age, sex distribution, etiology of liver disease, Child-Pugh class, and tumor stage, were generally balanced between arms within each trial. Most patients had Child-Pugh class A disease and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1. Risk of bias All four trials were described as randomized and double-blind with placebo control. Random sequence generation and allocation concealment were judged to be at low risk of bias in three trials and unclear in one. Blinding of participants, personnel, and outcome assessors was judged to be at low risk in all trials. Incomplete outcome data were judged to be at low risk in three trials, with one trial showing some imbalance in discontinuation owing to adverse events. Selective reporting was not evident. Overall, the methodological quality of the included studies was considered good. Time to disease progression All four trials provided data on TTP. The pooled analysis showed that TTP was significantly longer in the experimental groups than in the control groups (HR: 0.82; 95% CI: 0.69–0.97; p = 0.02). Heterogeneity among the studies was low and not statistically significant, and a fixed-effects model was therefore applied. The result was stable on leave-one-out sensitivity analysis, with the direction of effect unchanged after exclusion of any single trial, although the confidence interval approached unity when the largest trial was excluded. Overall survival Four trials reported OS. Pooled analysis showed no significant difference in OS between the experimental and control groups (HR: 0.97; 95% CI: 0.72–1.29; p = 0.82). Human action recognition has attracted sustained attention owing to its broad applications in video surveillance, human-computer interaction, healthcare monitoring, and autonomous driving [1], [2]. Among the available modalities, skeleton data, which represent the human body as a set of three-dimensional joint coordinates, offer several advantages over RGB video. They are compact, invariant to appearance, illumination, and background, and can be acquired in real time by depth sensors or pose estimation algorithms [3], [4]. Consequently, skeleton-based action recognition has become an active research topic, and a wide range of methods has been proposed. Skeleton-based action recognition. Early approaches relied on hand-crafted features describing joint positions, joint-angle relations, or the geometric configuration of body parts [5], [6]. With the advent of deep learning, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and long short-term memory networks were adopted to model temporal dynamics of joint sequences [7], [8], while convolutional neural networks (CNNs) treated skeleton sequences as pseudo-images and exploited their strong feature extraction ability [9], [10]. However, both families flatten the skeleton into a vector or grid and thus discard the natural topology of the human body. Graph convolutional networks (GCNs) overcome this limitation by representing the skeleton as a spatio-temporal graph in which joints are vertices and bones are edges. ST-GCN [11] pioneered this direction, and subsequent works introduced adaptive graph structures, attention mechanisms, and multi-scale or multi-stream designs to improve accuracy [12]–[14]. These models now achieve high accuracy on large-scale benchmarks such as NTU RGB+D [15]. Motivation. Despite this progress, most existing methods are developed and evaluated under the assumption that skeletons are completely and accurately observed. This assumption is frequently violated in practice. Self-occlusion, occlusion by objects or other people, limited sensor field of view, and failures of pose estimators often yield skeletons with missing or noisy joints [16]. Because such corruption changes the input distribution, models trained on clean data can degrade markedly at test time. We argue that this fragility is closely related to how conventional networks use the skeleton. Analysis with class activation maps (CAM) [17] indicates that a single network tends to concentrate on a small set of the most discriminative joints, for example the hands in the action of "drinking water", while largely ignoring other informative joints. Such a concentrated representation is efficient when all joints are visible, but it is brittle: if the few critical joints are occluded or corrupted, the remaining evidence is insufficient for a reliable decision. A more robust model should instead discover discriminative cues distributed over the whole body, so that the loss of some joints can be compensated by others. This resembles the principle of redundancy in human perception, where recognition remains possible when parts of an object are hidden. Proposed approach. Motivated by this observation, we propose a richly activated graph convolutional network (RA-GCN) for action recognition with incomplete skeletons. RA-GCN is a multi-stream architecture in which the streams are trained sequentially and cooperatively. The first stream is trained in the conventional manner, and its CAM identifies the joints it relies upon. For each subsequent stream, the joints already activated by the preceding streams are suppressed in the input, which forces the stream to mine discriminative features from the remaining, previously unactivated joints. The streams are finally fused to produce the prediction. Through this erasing-and-relearning mechanism, the activated region of the skeleton is substantially enlarged compared with that of a single-stream model, and the resulting features are richly distributed over the joints. Importantly, the approach requires no explicit occlusion annotations or additional supervision, and it is compatible with different GCN backbones. Evaluation. We evaluate RA-GCN on the NTU RGB+D dataset to verify that the richer feature coverage does not sacrifice accuracy on complete skeletons. To assess robustness, we further construct synthetic occlusion settings in which parts of the skeleton or random joints are removed, simulating various realistic incompleteness patterns. Visualization of the CAMs further illustrates that RA-GCN activates considerably more joints than baseline models. Contributions. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: 1. We identify the limited activation of discriminative joints as a key cause of the vulnerability of existing skeleton-based models to incomplete inputs, and we study the problem of action recognition with incomplete skeletons. 2. We propose RA-GCN, a multi-stream GCN in which each stream learns from joints left unactivated by preceding streams, as identified by CAM, thereby yielding richly activated and complementary features. 3. We conduct extensive experiments showing that RA-GCN achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods on NTU RGB+D and markedly reduces performance deterioration on synthetic occlusion data. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on skeleton-based action recognition and robustness to incomplete data. Section 3 details the proposed RA-GCN. Section 4 presents experimental results and analysis, and Section 5 concludes the paper. 3.1 Preliminaries: Graph Convolution on Skeleton Sequences A skeleton sequence is represented as a tensor X ∈ ℝ^{C×T×V}, where C is the number of input channels (e.g., 3D coordinates), T the number of frames, and V the number of joints. Following [1], the skeleton is modeled as a spatiotemporal graph G = (V, E), in which the vertices correspond to joints and the edges comprise intra-frame bone connections and inter-frame links between identical joints in consecutive frames. The spatial graph convolution at a given layer is formulated as fout = Σ{k=1}^{K} Wk fin (Λk^{-1/2} Ak Λk^{-1/2} ⊙ Mk), where Ak is the adjacency matrix of the k-th subset under the spatial-configuration partitioning strategy [1] (root, centripetal, and centrifugal subsets, so K = 3), Λk is the corresponding degree matrix, Wk is a 1×1 convolutional weight, Mk is a learnable edge-importance mask, and ⊙ denotes element-wise multiplication. Temporal modeling is performed by a Γ×1 convolution over consecutive frames. A basic block comprises a spatial graph convolution, a temporal convolution, batch normalization, ReLU, and a residual connection. The backbone stacks such blocks with increasing channel widths, followed by global average pooling and a fully connected classifier. 3.2 Class Activation Maps for Skeleton Joints To identify which joints a network relies on, we adapt class activation mapping (CAM) [2] to the graph domain. Let F ∈ ℝ^{D×T'×V} be the feature map output by the last graph convolutional block, and let wc ∈ ℝ^D be the classifier weight vector for class c. Since global average pooling precedes the classifier, the score of class c is sc = Σd w{c,d} · (1/(T'V)) Σ{t,v} Fd(t,v). The activation map is then CAMc(t,v) = Σd w{c,d} Fd(t,v), which quantifies the contribution of joint v at time t to class c. Averaging over time and normalizing to [0,1] yields a joint-level activation vector ac ∈ ℝ^V. Because the receptive field of the last layer covers a large portion of the skeleton, the map reflects discriminative evidence aggregated over neighboring joints; it is nevertheless informative at the joint level, as verified in our experiments. 3.3 Richly Activated GCN Conventional GCNs tend to concentrate on a small set of highly discriminative joints (e.g., hands for “drinking”). When these joints are missing or corrupted, accuracy deteriorates sharply. RA-GCN addresses this by forcing successive streams to discover complementary evidence from the remaining joints. Multi-stream architecture. RA-GCN comprises N streams (N = 3 by default) with an identical backbone but unshared parameters. The first stream receives the complete skeleton X^{(1)} = X and is trained with a standard cross-entropy loss. For stream n > 1, the input is X^{(n)} = X ⊙ (1 − m^{(n−1)}), where m^{(n−1)} ∈ {0,1}^V is a joint mask broadcast over channels and frames, derived from the activation map of the preceding stream. Thus, joints that were strongly activated previously are suppressed, and the n-th stream must classify the sample using only the residual joints. Erasing strategy. Given the ground-truth class y of a training sample, the joint-level activation a^{(n−1)}y is computed from stream n−1. Joints whose normalized activation exceeds a threshold λ are erased: mv^{(n−1)} = 𝟙[a{y,v}^{(n−1)} > λ]. Masks are accumulated across streams, m̃^{(n)} = max(m̃^{(n−1)}, m^{(n)}), so that joints erased in an earlier stream remain unavailable to later ones, preventing the re-discovery of the same features. Erased joints are set to zero, which, after input normalization, corresponds to the mean pose value. At least a minimum number of joints is always retained to avoid degenerate inputs. During training the ground-truth label is used to generate maps; at test time, where labels are unavailable, the predicted class of the preceding stream is used in its place, which makes inference fully label-free. Feature sharing. To reduce redundancy and promote information flow, the first few blocks of the backbone can be shared in architecture across streams, while the higher layers remain stream-specific; in our default configuration each stream has its own full set of parameters to maximize diversity. Raw features of the preceding stream are not forwarded, since doing so would reintroduce reliance on the erased joints. 3.4 Training Objective and Fusion Each stream n produces class posterior p^{(n)} and is supervised by its own cross-entropy loss ℒn. The overall objective is ℒ = Σ{n=1}^{N} ℒn(p^{(n)}, y), and the streams are optimized jointly by stochastic gradient descent with Nesterov momentum. Because the masks are produced from detached activation maps, no gradient flows through the erasing operation. At inference, the final prediction is obtained by summing the class scores of all streams: ŷ = argmaxc Σ{n=1}^{N} sc^{(n)}. Since each stream attends to a different subset of joints, the fused prediction aggregates evidence distributed across the whole body, and the loss of any region affects only a portion of the ensemble. 3.5 Input Representation and Implementation Details Following [3], each stream may take as input joint coordinates, bone vectors (differences between adjacent joints), and their temporal differences, concatenated along the channel axis. Sequences are resampled to a fixed length of T = 300 frames; shorter ones are padded by repetition. For multi-person actions, at most two skeletons are retained and processed by sharing weights, with features averaged before classification. Each skeleton is translated to a body-centered coordinate system and, optionally, rotated to align the torso with a canonical axis. Training uses a batch size of 32, an initial learning rate of 0.1 decayed by 0.1 at predetermined epochs, weight decay of 10⁻⁴, and random temporal cropping and rotation as augmentation. The threshold λ is selected on a validation split. 3.6 Simulating Incomplete Skeletons To evaluate robustness, we synthesize incomplete data by (i) occluding predefined body parts (left/right arm, left/right leg, torso/head) by setting their joint coordinates to zero, and (ii) randomly dropping frames or adding coordinate noise. These perturbations are applied only at test time, so that models are compared under identical training conditions, and performance deterioration is measured as the accuracy difference relative to the complete-skeleton setting. Datasets and Protocols. We evaluate RA-GCN on NTU RGB+D [1] under the cross-subject (CS) and cross-view (CV) protocols, reporting top-1 accuracy. To assess robustness to incomplete skeletons, we build synthetic occlusion variants of the test sets and leave the training sets unchanged. Five occlusion types are simulated by zeroing the coordinates of the affected joints: (i) left hand, (ii) right hand, (iii) left leg, (iv) right leg, and (v) torso, each removing the corresponding joint group in every frame. We also report results with random frame-wise occlusion, where 10%, 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% of the frames are masked, and with random joint dropout. All results use the same trained models and do not involve fine-tuning on occluded data. Unless stated otherwise, RA-GCN uses three streams, each with a ResGCN-style backbone, and the input features are joint positions, velocities, and bone features. Comparison on the Complete NTU RGB+D Dataset. Table 1 compares RA-GCN with recent state-of-the-art methods. RA-GCN with three streams reaches 85.9% (CS) and 93.5% (CV). This is comparable to strong GCN-based baselines such as ST-GCN [2] (81.5/88.3), AS-GCN [3] (86.8/94.2), and 2s-AGCN [4] (88.5/95.1), and it clearly exceeds earlier recurrent and CNN-based models [5,6]. Exposure to trauma in early childhood, including physical, sexual, and emotional abuse and neglect, is a major risk factor for a wide range of psychiatric disorders in adulthood [1,2]. When trauma occurs repeatedly, within caregiving relationships, and during critical periods of development, it is often described as complex trauma [3]. The consequences extend beyond the classic symptoms of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and include affect dysregulation, disturbed self-concept, interpersonal difficulties, and dissociation [4,5]. A less frequently studied consequence is the effect of early trauma on a person's relationship with their own body. The body is central to the experience of trauma. Abuse, particularly physical and sexual abuse, is directly inflicted on the body, and the child's body may become associated with fear, pain, shame, and helplessness [6]. Neglect and emotional abuse may also disturb the development of a positive bodily self, because the infant's early sense of the body develops in the context of attuned, responsive caregiving [7]. Theoretical accounts suggest that when such experiences are chronic, the body may be perceived as unsafe, as an object of disgust, or as something to be controlled, avoided, or disowned [8,9]. Clinical observations support this view: survivors of childhood trauma frequently report feeling alienated from their body, being unable to sense it accurately, or hating it [10]. Such disturbances may in turn contribute to self-harm, eating disorders, somatic complaints, and revictimization [11,12]. Body experience is a multidimensional construct. Researchers commonly distinguish between perceptual, cognitive-affective, and attitudinal components [13,14]. In the present study we focus on three domains that are relevant to trauma. Body attitude refers to the evaluative and emotional stance toward one's body, including feelings of vitality, self-confidence, and physical appearance, as well as perceived body competence and rejection [15]. Body satisfaction refers to the degree of contentment with specific body parts and functions [16]. Body awareness refers to the attention paid to, and the perception of, internal bodily sensations [17]. Each domain may be affected differently by trauma. Negative attitudes and dissatisfaction may reflect shame and self-devaluation, whereas awareness may be either heightened, as in hypervigilance to bodily threat signals, or reduced, as in avoidance and numbing [18]. Empirical findings support an association between childhood maltreatment and negative body image. Studies of survivors of childhood sexual abuse have reported greater body dissatisfaction, body shame, and body disconnection than in comparison groups [19,20]. Similar results have been found for physical and emotional abuse [21]. Evidence on body awareness is less consistent. Some studies report increased attention to bodily symptoms and somatic complaints in trauma-exposed individuals [22], whereas others describe reduced interoceptive accuracy or sensitivity, in line with emotional numbing and dissociation [23,24]. Much of the literature, however, has relied on samples of survivors of a single type of trauma, on non-clinical or student populations, or on a single measure of body image. Few studies have simultaneously examined several domains of body experience in clinical patients with documented early and complex trauma, and fewer still have used comparison data from a non-clinical group to estimate the magnitude of the differences. A further question concerns how body experience relates to the clinical features of trauma-related disorders. Severity of trauma symptoms, such as intrusion, avoidance, and hyperarousal, might be expected to covary with negative body experience, since trauma reminders are often bodily and avoidance may include avoidance of bodily states [25]. Dissociation is of particular interest. Dissociative phenomena such as depersonalization, derealization, and somatoform dissociation involve alterations in the experience of the body and the sense of ownership of it [26,27]. Individuals who frequently dissociate may therefore be expected to report a more negative or disconnected body experience. Yet it is unclear whether self-reported body attitude, satisfaction, and awareness are closely tied to these symptom dimensions or whether they represent a relatively separate area of impairment that requires its own assessment. This question has clinical relevance. Body-oriented and body-focused interventions are increasingly used in the treatment of trauma-related disorders, including body psychotherapy, sensorimotor approaches, yoga, and movement therapies [28,29]. Their rationale rests on the assumption that disturbed body experience is a core feature of trauma that is not sufficiently addressed by verbal or cognitive treatments alone. Establishing the extent and pattern of disturbances in different domains, and whether they are simply a reflection of symptom severity, can inform decisions about assessment and treatment planning. The present study therefore had two aims. First, we examined disturbances in body attitude, body satisfaction, and body awareness in female patients with complex trauma originating in early childhood, in comparison with a non-clinical female sample. We hypothesized that patients would show significantly more negative body experience in all three domains. Second, we investigated the associations of these domains with the severity of trauma symptoms and the frequency of dissociative experiences within the patient group. Given the theoretical overlap between trauma symptomatology, dissociation, and the body, we expected to find associations between these variables, although the strength of these associations was explored without a firm prediction. Participants and procedure The clinical sample comprised 50 women receiving treatment in a specialized inpatient and day-clinic program for complex trauma-related disorders. Inclusion criteria were female sex, age of 18 years or older, a history of repeated interpersonal trauma (physical, sexual, or emotional abuse or neglect) beginning before age 18, and a primary clinical diagnosis of a trauma-related disorder established by an experienced clinician according to ICD-10 criteria [1]. Exclusion criteria were acute psychosis, acute suicidality, current substance intoxication, insufficient command of the language of the questionnaires, and organic brain disorder. Comorbid diagnoses, including depression, anxiety, eating disorders, and borderline personality disorder, were not grounds for exclusion, given their high prevalence in this population [2]. The comparison sample consisted of 216 women from the general population, recruited through university mailing lists, public announcements, and personal contacts. Participants in this group reported no current psychiatric treatment. Because of the anonymous design, a structured clinical interview was not administered to the comparison group, and group membership was defined by self-report of non-treatment status. Clinical participants completed the questionnaires within the first two weeks of treatment, before starting body-oriented interventions, in a quiet room with a researcher available for questions. Non-clinical participants completed the same body experience measures either on paper or online. All participants gave written or electronic informed consent. The study was approved by the responsible institutional ethics committee and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki [3]. Measures Body attitude. Body attitude was assessed with the Dresden Body Image Questionnaire (DKB-35) [4]. The instrument contains 35 items rated on a six-point scale and yields five subscales: body acceptance, vitality, physical contact, sexual fulfillment, and self-aggrandizement. Lower scores indicate a more negative body attitude. In this study the total score was used as the primary indicator. The DKB-35 has shown good reliability and validity in clinical and non-clinical German samples [4]. In the present data, internal consistency was high (Cronbach’s α = .96 in the clinical sample). Body satisfaction. Body satisfaction was measured with the Body Cathexis Scale [5], in which respondents rate their satisfaction with a range of body parts and functions on a five-point scale. Higher sum scores reflect greater satisfaction. The scale is widely used in research on body image and has demonstrated adequate psychometric properties [5,6]. Internal consistency in the present sample was α = .94. Body awareness. Body awareness was assessed with the Somatic Awareness Questionnaire, which captures the tendency to notice and attend to internal bodily sensations and changes [7]. Items are rated on a Likert-type scale, with higher scores indicating greater awareness of bodily signals. Because trauma may produce both heightened vigilance and numbing of bodily sensations, scores were interpreted as reflecting overall attentiveness to bodily states rather than their accuracy or valence. Internal consistency in this study was α = .88. Trauma symptom severity. Severity of posttraumatic symptoms in the clinical sample was measured with the Davidson Trauma Scale (DTS) [8]. This 17-item self-report scale corresponds to the DSM-IV symptom criteria for posttraumatic stress disorder. Participants rate frequency and severity of each symptom over the previous week on five-point scales (0–4), giving a total score from 0 to 136 as well as subscale scores for intrusion, avoidance/numbing, and hyperarousal. The DTS has shown good reliability and validity [8,9]. Cronbach’s α in this sample was .93. Dissociation. Dissociative experiences were measured with the Dissociative Experiences Scale (DES) [10], a 28-item self-report questionnaire assessing the frequency of dissociative phenomena such as amnesia, absorption, and depersonalization. Respondents indicate the percentage of time (0–100%) that they experience each phenomenon, and the mean across items serves as the total score. Scores of 30 or above are often considered indicative of a clinically relevant level of dissociation [11]. The scale has demonstrated high reliability and validity, with α = .95 in the present sample. Statistical analysis Data were analyzed with IBM SPSS Statistics. Prior to analysis, distributions were inspected for normality and outliers, and missing values were handled according to the manual of each instrument; if more than 10% of items on a scale were missing, the case was excluded for that scale. Descriptive statistics were computed for all variables. Because the groups could differ in age, age was compared between groups using an independent-samples t test and considered as a potential covariate. Group differences in body attitude, body satisfaction, and body awareness were examined with independent-samples t tests, using Welch’s correction when variances were unequal, as indicated by Levene’s test. Given the three comparisons, the significance level was adjusted using Bonferroni correction (α = .017). Effect sizes are reported as Cohen’s d, calculated with the pooled standard deviation, with values of 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 interpreted as small, medium, and large, respectively [12]. Representing documents as fixed-length, continuous vectors is a central step in many text processing pipelines, including topic identification, document retrieval, clustering, and recommendation. Classical approaches such as latent semantic analysis [1], probabilistic latent semantic analysis [2], and latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) [3] map a bag-of-words representation of a document into a low-dimensional latent space. More recently, neural approaches, such as the neural variational document model (NVDM) [4], paragraph vectors [5], and various autoencoder-based models, have been proposed. Despite differences in formulation, the majority of these techniques yield only point estimates of the document embeddings. A point estimate carries no information about how reliably it represents the document. This is a serious limitation because documents differ greatly in length and in the amount of evidence they provide. A short document with a handful of words supports a far less certain embedding than a long document with thousands of words, yet both are mapped to vectors of the same kind and are treated downstream with equal confidence. Motivation Capturing uncertainty in embeddings is the natural domain of Bayesian modelling. If each document embedding is treated as a latent random variable with a posterior distribution, the covariance of that posterior quantifies how well the embedding is determined by the observed counts. Such uncertainty can be propagated into downstream tasks, so that poorly determined embeddings contribute less to classifier training and decision making. This idea has precedent in speech processing, where the i-vector model [6] and its Bayesian treatments use posterior covariances of utterance-level embeddings to improve speaker and language recognition. The subspace multinomial model (SMM) [7] is a close relative of these models for discrete data. It is a log-linear model in which a low-dimensional document embedding is mapped, through a shared subspace matrix, to the parameters of a multinomial distribution over words. In its original form, however, the SMM estimates document embeddings by maximum likelihood or maximum a posteriori inference, so it too provides only point estimates. Challenges Moving from point estimates to full posterior distributions in the SMM is not straightforward. The SMM belongs to the family of mixed-logit models, where the likelihood contains a softmax normalisation over the vocabulary. When variational inference is applied, the expected log-normaliser under the approximate posterior has no closed form, and the resulting objective is intractable. Existing remedies include Monte Carlo estimates of the expectation, which yield high-variance gradients, and bounds originally developed for correlated topic models [8] and Bayesian multinomial logistic regression [9], such as the Jaakkola–Jordan bound [10], Bohning's quadratic bound [11], and Taylor-based approximations. These bounds differ in tightness and computational cost, and their suitability for large-vocabulary text models is not well established. Contributions In this work we present Bayesian subspace multinomial model (Bayesian SMM), a generative log-linear model that represents each document by a Gaussian posterior distribution over its embedding, whose covariance encodes the uncertainty of the estimate. Our contributions are as follows. 1. We derive a variational Bayesian treatment of the SMM in which the document embeddings are latent variables with Gaussian posteriors, and the subspace parameters are estimated by maximising the evidence lower bound. We address the intractability of the expected log-normaliser with a tractable bound, which yields closed-form, efficient updates of the variational parameters. 2. We propose a generative Gaussian linear classifier for topic identification that operates directly on the posterior distributions. By exploiting the document-specific covariances during classifier training and scoring, the classifier accounts for the reliability of each embedding rather than treating all embeddings as equally informative. 3. We evaluate the model intrinsically using perplexity on the Fisher speech corpus, using automatic transcriptions, and on the 20Newsgroups text corpus, and we compare it to NVDM, a state-of-the-art neural variational document model. We show that Bayesian SMM achieves a better fit to the data. 4. We evaluate the model extrinsically on topic identification. The proposed systems are less prone to over-fitting on unseen test data than competing methods. They also outperform state-of-the-art unsupervised topic models and obtain results comparable to fully supervised discriminative models. Organisation of the paper The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on topic models, neural document models, and Bayesian embeddings. Section 3 describes the SMM and the intractability that arises in variational inference for mixed-logit models. Section 4 presents the Bayesian SMM, including the variational objective, the bound used, and the update equations for the document posteriors and the subspace parameters. Section 5 introduces the generative Gaussian linear classifier that uses embedding uncertainty. Section 6 describes the datasets, experimental setup, and baselines, and Section 7 reports the perplexity and topic identification results together with an analysis of the learned uncertainties. Section 8 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future work. Notation and generative model. Let a corpus consist of D documents over a vocabulary of size V. Document d is represented by its word-count vector xd ∈ ℕ^V, with total count Nd = Σv xdv. The Bayesian subspace multinomial model (Bayesian SMM) is a generative log-linear model. Each document d has a latent vector wd ∈ ℝ^K, with K ≪ V, which parameterizes a document-specific categorical distribution over words through a softmax: φdv = exp(mv + tvᵀ wd) / Σ{v'} exp(m{v'} + t{v'}ᵀ wd), where m ∈ ℝ^V is a background log-unigram bias and T = [t1,…,tV]ᵀ ∈ ℝ^{V×K} is a global subspace (embedding) matrix. Given wd, the counts follow a multinomial, p(xd | wd) = ∏v φdv^{xdv}, up to a constant. This is a mixed-logit model, since the softmax is applied to a mixture over latent document variables [1]. The classical SMM [2] estimates wd as a point by maximum likelihood or MAP. Here we place a prior p(wd) = 𝒩(wd | 0, I) and treat wd as a random variable, so that the posterior p(wd | xd) yields both an embedding and its uncertainty. To regularize T, we place a sparsity-inducing Laplace prior on its entries [3]. The parameters m and T are treated as point estimates. Variational inference. The posterior p(wd | xd) is intractable because of the softmax normalizer. We approximate it with a Gaussian q(wd) = 𝒩(wd | μd, Σd), with Σd diagonal for efficiency. Parameters are learned by maximizing the evidence lower bound (ELBO) over the corpus: ℒ = Σd { Eq[log p(xd | wd)] − KL(q(wd) ‖ p(wd)) } + log p(T). The KL term has a closed form for Gaussians. The expected log-likelihood is Eq[log p(xd | wd)] = Σv xdv ( mv + tvᵀ μd ) − Nd Eq[ log Σ{v'} exp(m{v'} + t{v'}ᵀ wd) ]. The final expectation of the log-sum-exp has no closed form, which is the intractability that commonly arises in variational inference for mixed-logit models. Bounding the log-normalizer. Existing remedies include the Jensen-based bound with a first-order Taylor expansion [4], the Bohning quadratic bound [5], and the piecewise bounds used for correlated topic models [6]. We instead use a tractable bound derived from the concavity of the logarithm. For any ξd > 0, log z ≤ z/ξd + log ξd − 1, so Eq[log Σv exp(mv + tvᵀ wd)] ≤ (1/ξd) Σv Eq[exp(mv + tvᵀ wd)] + log ξd − 1. Under a Gaussian q, each term is the mean of a log-normal variable: Eq[exp(mv + tvᵀ wd)] = exp(mv + tvᵀ μd + ½ tvᵀ Σd tv). The bound is therefore available in closed form. The resulting lower bound on the ELBO is differentiable in all variational and model parameters. The auxiliary variable ξd is a per-document quantity whose optimum, obtained by setting the derivative to zero, is ξd = Σv exp(mv + tvᵀ μd + ½ tvᵀ Σd tv). This makes the bound tight at the current q and avoids the quadratic-curvature approximations that degrade for large V. Optimization. Training alternates between two steps, in the manner of variational EM. In the E-step, for fixed T and m, we update ξd in closed form and update (μd, Σd) by gradient ascent on the bound, parameterizing Σd through log-variances to enforce positivity. In the M-step, T and m are updated with the posterior statistics fixed. Because the number of parameters is large, we use Adam [7] with mini-batches of documents for both steps, and for the Laplace prior we apply the subgradient of the L1 penalty. Variational parameters are initialized with μd = 0 and Σd = I. Convergence is monitored through the bound on a held-out set of documents. Document embeddings and uncertainty. After training, each document is summarized by the pair (μd, Σd). The mean μd serves as the embedding, while Σd encodes how well it is determined by the observed counts. Short documents yield posteriors close to the prior, whereas longer documents give narrower posteriors. For unseen documents, T and m are held fixed and only (μd, Σd, ξd) are optimized. Perplexity evaluation. For intrinsic evaluation, the model is compared with the neural variational document model (NVDM) [8]. For a test document, we infer the posterior and compute an upper bound on the perplexity, PPL = exp( −(1/D) Σd (1/Nd) log p(xd) ), with log p(xd) replaced by the ELBO. The same estimate is used for both models so that the comparison is consistent. Generative Gaussian linear classifier. For topic identification, we exploit the uncertainty with a generative classifier operating on the posterior distributions. Each class c has a Gaussian over embeddings, 𝒩(w | ηc, Λ), with a shared covariance Λ, which yields a linear classifier. Classes are modelled in the latent space with the observed embedding treated as noisy: the document's posterior covariance Σd is added to the class covariance when computing the likelihood, p(μd | c) = 𝒩(μd | ηc, Λ + Σd). Documents with large uncertainty therefore contribute less sharply to the class scores, and to the estimation of ηc and Λ. Parameters are estimated by EM, treating the true embeddings as latent variables, as in probabilistic linear discriminant analysis [9]. The decision rule is argmaxc log p(μd | c) + log πc, with class priors πc. Because the covariances are shared, the classifier is linear in μd when Σd is constant, and otherwise has document-dependent scaling. Experimental protocol. We use the Fisher speech corpus, with transcripts produced by an automatic speech recognizer, and 20Newsgroups [10]. Standard splits are used, and hyperparameters (K, prior strength, learning rate) are selected on validation data. Baselines for topic identification include unsupervised topic models such as LDA [11] and SMM, as well as supervised discriminative classifiers. Robustness to over-fitting is examined by comparing training and test accuracy. We evaluated the Bayesian SMM intrinsically through perplexity and extrinsically through topic identification (ID) on Fisher speech and 20Newsgroups. Unless stated otherwise, results are averaged over five random initializations, and we report the standard deviation where it is informative. Experimental Setup For Fisher, we used the standard training and test partitions of the Fisher English Phase 1 corpus with 40 topic labels, on top of automatic transcripts. For 20Newsgroups, we used the by-date split, removing headers, footers, and quotes. The vocabulary was restricted to frequent words after stop-word removal. The baselines were the neural variational document model (NVDM) [Miao et al., 2016], the non-Bayesian subspace multinomial model (SMM) [Kesiraju et al., 2016], and LDA. For topic ID we also compared against supervised discriminative systems: a multilayer perceptron, an SVM, and a DocNADE-style classifier. Embedding dimensionality was varied over {25, 50, 100, 200}, and the regularization weight and the number of EM iterations were tuned on held-out development data. Perplexity Table 1 summarizes test-set perplexity for the generative models. The Bayesian SMM obtained lower perplexity than NVDM on both corpora and at all embedding dimensions. On Fisher, the gap was largest at higher dimensionalities. NVDM's perplexity degraded as the dimensionality grew, whereas the Bayesian SMM's remained stable or improved slightly.
