Cryptococcosis is a life-threatening mycosis caused by basidiomycetous yeasts of the Cryptococcus neoformans/Cryptococcus gattii species complex [1,2]. Infection follows inhalation of desiccated yeast cells or spores, which establish a primary pulmonary focus and, in susceptible hosts, disseminate hematogenously to the central nervous system, causing meningoencephalitis [3]. Cryptococcosis is responsible for an estimated one million cases annually worldwide, with a high mortality rate, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa [4]. Historically, C. neoformans has been considered an opportunistic pathogen of immunocompromised individuals, especially patients with HIV/AIDS, whereas C. gattii has been associated with disease in apparently immunocompetent hosts [5,6]. Epidemiology and population structure of C. gattii C. gattii was originally restricted to tropical and subtropical regions and associated with Eucalyptus species [7]. This view changed after the outbreak on Vancouver Island, British Columbia, in 1999, which spread to the mainland of Canada and the Pacific Northwest of the United States [8,9]. The outbreak was dominated by molecular type VGII, including the hypervirulent VGIIa/b genotypes, and generated considerable interest in the mechanisms underlying the enhanced virulence of these strains, such as tubular mitochondrial morphology, increased intracellular proliferation within macrophages and altered host immune responses [10,11]. Based on molecular typing, C. gattii is classified into four major types, VGI to VGIV [12], and recent genomic analyses have proposed that these lineages may represent distinct cryptic species [13]. Capsular serotypes B and C are both found in C. gattii. Serotype B includes types VGI, VGII and VGIII, whereas serotype C corresponds mainly to VGIII and VGIV [12]. VGIV is the most frequent type in HIV-infected patients in sub-Saharan Africa, while VGIII has been reported in both clinical and environmental samples from Latin America and in HIV-positive patients in California [14,15]. Despite this clinical relevance, the vast majority of experimental studies have focused on serotype B isolates, particularly VGI and VGII. Consequently, the pathogenic properties of serotype C strains remain poorly characterized. Virulence determinants in Cryptococcus The pathogenic potential of Cryptococcus species depends on several well-characterized virulence factors. The polysaccharide capsule, composed mainly of glucuronoxylomannan (GXM) and glucuronoxylomannogalactan (GXMGal), is the main determinant; it inhibits phagocytosis, modulates cytokine responses and protects against oxidative stress [16,17]. Capsule synthesis requires the products of the CAP genes (CAP10, CAP59, CAP60 and CAP64), whose deletion results in acapsular, avirulent mutants [18]. Capsule size and structure are highly variable among isolates and are regulated by environmental conditions, and GXM structural differences affect recognition by monoclonal antibodies and the host immune response [19,20]. Melanin, produced through laccase-mediated oxidation of diphenolic compounds, protects fungal cells against oxidative and nitrosative damage, antifungal drugs and host effector mechanisms [21]. In addition, chitin and chitooligomers in the cell wall and capsule contribute to cell integrity, capsule architecture and the interaction with host chitinases, which have been linked to the modulation of immune responses and to disease susceptibility [22,23]. Other factors, including extracellular enzymes such as urease and phospholipase, and the ability to grow at 37 °C, are also essential for survival and dissemination in the host [3,24]. Phenotypic variability in these traits among isolates of the same species has been correlated with differences in virulence in animal models [25,26]. In the case of C. gattii, the hypervirulence of VGII strains has been related to their capacity to proliferate rapidly in lung tissue and to evade immune surveillance [10,27]. However, whether similar mechanisms operate in serotype C isolates, or whether VGIII and VGIV lineages differ in their virulence profiles, is unknown. Some reports suggest that VGIII and VGIV isolates are generally less virulent in mice than VGII isolates [28,29], but the number of strains analyzed is limited and a systematic comparison of phenotypic attributes and virulence is lacking. Rationale and objectives Given the clinical importance of VGIV in Africa and of VGIII in the Americas, and the scarcity of experimental data on these lineages, a detailed analysis of the phenotypic diversity of serotype C isolates is warranted. Understanding how variation in capsule properties, cell wall composition, pigment production and antigenic structure translates into differences in virulence may provide insights into the pathogenesis of infections caused by these molecular types and into the factors that determine tissue tropism, in particular the ability to colonize the central nervous system. In the present study, we compared three serotype C C. gattii isolates, one VGIII (ATCC 24066) and two VGIV (WM 779 and 106.97), with respect to capsule dimensions, expression of CAP genes, chitooligomer distribution, induction of host chitinase activity, pigment production and reactivity with GXM-binding monoclonal antibodies. We then evaluated the virulence of these isolates in a murine model of intranasal infection, assessing lethality and fungal burden in the lungs and brain. By integrating phenotypic and in vivo data, we aimed to determine whether serotype C isolates of distinct molecular types differ in their pathogenic potential. Fungal isolates and growth conditions Three serotype C Cryptococcus gattii isolates were used: 106.97 (molecular type VGIV), WM 779 (VGIV) and ATCC 24066 (VGIII). Molecular types were confirmed by URA5-RFLP analysis [1]. Stocks were stored at −80 °C in 20% glycerol and recovered on Sabouraud dextrose agar at 30 °C. For most assays, yeast cells were cultured in Sabouraud broth for 24 h at 30 °C with shaking (200 rpm), washed in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and counted in a Neubauer chamber. Capsule induction was performed in a minimal medium (15 mM glucose, 10 mM MgSO₄, 29.4 mM KH₂PO₄, 13 mM glycine, 3 µM thiamine, pH 5.5) for 48 h at 37 °C [2]. Capsule measurements Cells grown under capsule-inducing conditions were counterstained with India ink and examined with an optical microscope. Capsule thickness was defined as the distance between the cell wall and the outer edge of the India ink exclusion zone. Cell body diameter and capsule thickness were measured in at least 50 cells per isolate using ImageJ software. The capsule-to-cell ratio was calculated as capsule thickness divided by cell body radius. Expression of capsule-associated genes Total RNA was extracted from yeast cells grown in minimal medium using a mechanical disruption/TRIzol protocol and treated with DNase I. cDNA was synthesized with oligo(dT) primers and reverse transcriptase. Quantitative PCR was performed with SYBR Green for CAP10, CAP59, CAP60 and CAP64. Transcript levels were normalized to the housekeeping gene ACT1 and expressed relative to isolate ATCC 24066 using the 2^−ΔΔCt method [3]. Three independent biological replicates were analyzed in technical duplicate. Chitooligomer distribution and chitin staining Chitooligomers were detected by incubating fixed cells with wheat germ agglutinin conjugated to fluorescein isothiocyanate (WGA-FITC; 10 µg/mL, 1 h, 37 °C) [4]. Cells were washed, mounted and imaged by fluorescence microscopy. Fluorescence patterns (e.g., budding sites, cell body and capsule-associated signals) were scored qualitatively in at least 100 cells per isolate, and fluorescence intensity was quantified with ImageJ. Pigment production Melanin production was assessed by spotting 10⁶ cells onto minimal medium agar containing 1 mM L-DOPA and incubating at 30 °C and 37 °C in the dark for up to 7 days. Pigmentation was documented photographically daily. For quantification, cells were grown in liquid L-DOPA medium for 5 days, collected, and the absorbance of culture supernatants was read at 475 nm. In addition, cell-associated pigment was extracted by treatment with 1 M sodium hydroxide at 100 °C and quantified spectrophotometrically against a standard curve of synthetic melanin. Reactivity with anti-glucuronoxylomannan antibodies Reactivity of the isolates with monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) to glucuronoxylomannan (GXM) was evaluated by immunofluorescence and ELISA. For immunofluorescence, encapsulated cells were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, blocked with 1% bovine serum albumin and incubated with mAbs 18B7 (IgG1), 12A1 (IgM) and 13F1 (IgM) [5] (10 µg/mL), followed by fluorescein-conjugated anti-mouse IgG or IgM. Samples were examined by fluorescence microscopy using identical exposure settings. For ELISA, GXM was isolated from culture supernatants by hexadecyltrimethylammonium bromide precipitation [6], used to coat polystyrene plates (1 µg/mL), and probed with serial dilutions of each mAb. Binding was detected with alkaline phosphatase-conjugated secondary antibodies and p-nitrophenyl phosphate, reading absorbance at 405 nm. Animals and ethics Female C57BL/6 mice (6–8 weeks old) were housed under specific pathogen-free conditions with free access to food and water. All procedures followed national guidelines for animal care and were approved by the institutional animal ethics committee. Murine infection and survival Mice were anesthetized with ketamine/xylazine and infected intranasally with 10⁴ yeast cells in 50 µL PBS (25 µL per nostril). Groups of 10 animals per isolate were monitored daily for survival, and animals showing signs of terminal disease were euthanized. Survival curves were compared using the log-rank (Mantel–Cox) test. Fungal burden In parallel experiments, groups of five mice per isolate were euthanized at 7 and 14 days post-infection. Lungs and brains were aseptically removed, weighed and homogenized in sterile PBS. Serial dilutions were plated on Sabouraud agar and colony-forming units (CFU) were counted after 48–72 h at 30 °C. Results are expressed as log₁₀ CFU per gram of tissue. Host chitinase activity Chitinase activity was measured in lung homogenates supernatants from infected and uninfected mice using the fluorogenic substrates 4-methylumbelliferyl β-D-N,N′-diacetylchitobioside and 4-methylumbelliferyl β-D-N,N′,N″-triacetylchitotrioside [7]. Reactions were carried out in citrate-phosphate buffer (pH 5.2) at 37 °C and stopped with glycine-NaOH (pH 10.6). Fluorescence (excitation 360 nm, emission 450 nm) was measured, and activity was normalized to total protein determined by the Bradford method. Statistical analysis Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation from at least three independent experiments unless otherwise stated. Normality was verified using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Comparisons among three isolates were performed by one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test, or by Kruskal–Wallis with Dunn’s test for non-parametric data. Fungal burden between time points was analyzed by two-way ANOVA. Differences were considered significant at P < 0.05. Analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism. Capsule dimensions and expression of CAP genes differ among serotype C isolates Microscopic analysis of cells grown under capsule-inducing conditions showed that the three serotype C isolates differed in capsule size. Isolate ATCC 24066 (VGIII) produced a significantly smaller capsule than WM 779 and 106.97 (both VGIV), as measured by India ink counterstaining and by the ratio of capsule thickness to cell body diameter (p < 0.05). Cell body dimensions were similar among isolates, so the differences were attributable to the capsule. WM 779 and 106.97 did not differ significantly from each other in this analysis. We then quantified transcripts of the capsule-associated genes CAP59, CAP60, CAP64 and CAP10 by RT-qPCR, normalized to ACT1. Expression patterns differed by isolate. ATCC 24066 showed lower relative expression of CAP59 and CAP64 than both VGIV isolates, whereas CAP10 and CAP60 showed isolate-specific profiles that did not follow molecular type. Capsule size therefore tracked, at least partly, with expression of a subset of CAP genes, consistent with their role in capsule assembly [1,2]. Chitooligomer distribution and host chitinase induction Chitin-derived structures were detected with wheat germ agglutinin (WGA), which binds chitooligomers. All isolates were labeled, but the distribution differed. In ATCC 24066, fluorescence was distributed throughout the cell and was often concentrated at the cell periphery. In WM 779 and 106.97, labeling was more punctate and unevenly distributed, with intense signals at buds and septa. Fluorescence intensity differed significantly among isolates, with WM 779 showing the lowest signal. Because fungal chitin-like molecules can modulate host chitinase responses [3], we measured chitinase activity in lung homogenates of mice 7 days after infection. ATCC 24066 induced markedly higher chitinase activity than both VGIV isolates, which did not differ significantly from uninfected controls or from each other. Chitinase induction thus segregated by molecular type and correlated inversely with capsule size. Pigment production and antibody reactivity Melanization was assessed on L-DOPA medium. Sickle cell disease (SCD) is the most common life-limiting genetic disease among African Americans, affecting more than 100,000 people in the United States and millions worldwide [1,2]. It results from a single nucleotide substitution in the β-globin gene that produces hemoglobin S. Under deoxygenated conditions, hemoglobin S polymerizes, causing red blood cell rigidity, hemolysis, and vaso-occlusion. Beyond these primary events, chronic hemolysis, endothelial dysfunction, and persistent inflammation contribute to progressive multi-organ injury [3,4]. Although advances in newborn screening, penicillin prophylaxis, vaccination, and hydroxyurea therapy have substantially improved survival in childhood, pulmonary complications remain a leading cause of morbidity and mortality across the lifespan [5,6]. Pulmonary disease in SCD encompasses a broad spectrum of acute and chronic conditions, including acute chest syndrome (ACS), pulmonary hypertension, restrictive lung disease, nocturnal hypoxemia, thromboembolic disease, and obstructive airway disease [7,8]. ACS, defined by a new pulmonary infiltrate accompanied by fever, respiratory symptoms, or hypoxemia, is the second most common cause of hospitalization and a leading cause of death among patients with SCD [9]. Recurrent ACS is itself associated with the development of chronic lung disease, creating a cycle of progressive pulmonary injury [10]. Understanding modifiable risk factors for ACS and other pulmonary complications is therefore a priority. Asthma has long been recognized as one of these potential risk factors. Early observational studies described an association between asthma and ACS, painful vaso-occlusive episodes, and early mortality in SCD [11–13]. In the Cooperative Study of Sickle Cell Disease, children with a physician diagnosis of asthma experienced a higher incidence of ACS and pain episodes than those without, and asthma was associated with an increased risk of early death in adults [11,12]. Subsequent studies have supported these findings, although results have not been uniform, and the strength of associations varies with how asthma is defined [14,15]. The mechanisms linking asthma to SCD complications are not fully elucidated but may include airway inflammation, bronchoconstriction-induced hypoxia, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and systemic inflammatory amplification that promotes sickling and vascular adhesion [16,17]. More recently, attention has turned to wheezing, even in the absence of a formal asthma diagnosis, as a possible marker of disease severity in SCD. Longitudinal data from infant and childhood cohorts demonstrate that wheezing is common in young children with SCD and is associated with higher rates of ACS, pain, and hospitalization [18,19]. These observations suggest that wheezing may reflect a distinct SCD-related phenotype, rather than simply representing coexisting atopic asthma. Indeed, wheeze in SCD may arise from multiple processes, including pulmonary vascular congestion, fat or thromboembolism, prior pulmonary infarction, infection, and airway hyperresponsiveness, in addition to classic allergic airway inflammation [20]. Establishing a diagnosis of asthma in patients with SCD is therefore challenging. According to national and international guidelines, asthma is diagnosed on the basis of a history of recurrent respiratory symptoms such as wheeze, cough, chest tightness, and dyspnea, together with objective evidence of variable airflow obstruction that is typically reversible with bronchodilators [21,22]. In SCD, however, several of these features are highly prevalent and frequently occur in isolation. Wheezing has been reported in up to approximately 30–50% of children with SCD, exceeding the prevalence in the general African American population [18,23]. Obstructive patterns on spirometry are common, yet many patients also display restrictive physiology or mixed defects, complicating interpretation [24,25]. Airway hyperresponsiveness, measured by methacholine or exercise challenge, has been described in a substantial proportion of children with SCD, including many without clinical asthma [26,27]. Bronchodilator responsiveness is likewise frequent, even among patients with no history of wheeze [28]. Consequently, the relationships among symptoms, physiologic abnormalities, and clinical asthma remain poorly defined, and the true prevalence of asthma in SCD is uncertain, with estimates ranging from approximately 10% to more than 40% depending on the definition and population studied [29,30]. This diagnostic ambiguity has practical consequences. Underdiagnosis may deprive patients of effective controller therapy, whereas overdiagnosis may expose them to unnecessary medications and divert attention from other treatable causes of respiratory symptoms. Management is further complicated by limited evidence: patients with SCD have been largely excluded from asthma clinical trials, and recommendations rely heavily on extrapolation from the general population [31]. Particular concerns include the potential risks of systemic corticosteroids, which have been associated with rebound pain crises and readmission in SCD, and the uncertain role of β-agonists and other asthma therapies in this population [32,33]. Whether biologic therapies or disease-modifying treatments such as hydroxyurea alter airway outcomes also remains unknown. Given these gaps, a critical appraisal of current knowledge is warranted. In this review, we summarize: (1) the epidemiology of asthma, wheezing, airway obstruction, and airway responsiveness among patients with SCD; (2) the evidence supporting associations of these features with SCD morbidity; (3) current understanding of the pathophysiology of airway inflammation in SCD; (4) existing approaches to the diagnosis and management of asthma in SCD; and (5) future research directions needed to improve respiratory outcomes in this vulnerable population. We conducted a narrative review of the literature on asthma, wheezing, airway obstruction, and airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR) in patients with sickle cell disease (SCD). A narrative approach was chosen over a formal systematic review or meta-analysis because the available studies differ substantially in design, population, case definitions, and outcome measures, which limits quantitative synthesis [1,2]. The review was structured around five predefined themes: (1) epidemiology of asthma, wheezing, airway obstruction, and airway responsiveness; (2) associations with SCD-related morbidity and mortality; (3) pathophysiology of airway inflammation; (4) current approaches to the diagnosis and management of asthma in SCD; and (5) future research directions. Search strategy We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library for articles published from database inception through the date of the final search. Search terms combined controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH terms) and free-text keywords for the condition and the respiratory outcomes: "sickle cell disease," "sickle cell anemia," "hemoglobin SS," "hemoglobin SC," "asthma," "wheeze," "wheezing," "airway obstruction," "airway hyperresponsiveness," "bronchial hyperreactivity," "bronchodilator response," "pulmonary function," "spirometry," "acute chest syndrome," "vaso-occlusive pain," and "inhaled corticosteroids." Boolean operators were used to combine the concepts. Additional searches addressed inflammatory mechanisms, including "eosinophil," "IgE," "atopy," "cytokine," "hemolysis," "nitric oxide," and "leukotriene." Reference lists of key articles, prior reviews, and consensus guidelines were hand-searched to identify additional relevant publications [3,4]. ClinicalTrials.gov was queried to identify ongoing or recently completed trials relevant to future directions. Eligibility criteria We included original research articles (prospective and retrospective cohort studies, cross-sectional studies, case-control studies, and clinical trials), registry analyses, and clinical practice guidelines that reported on respiratory outcomes in children or adults with SCD. Studies were eligible if they reported at least one of the following: prevalence or incidence of physician-diagnosed asthma or wheezing; spirometric or plethysmographic measures of airflow obstruction; bronchodilator responsiveness or bronchial provocation testing; associations between these respiratory phenotypes and clinical outcomes (pain episodes, acute chest syndrome [ACS], hospitalization, or mortality); biomarkers of airway or systemic inflammation; or therapeutic interventions for asthma or wheezing in SCD. Basic science and translational studies, including murine models, were included when they informed mechanisms of airway inflammation in SCD. We excluded articles not published in English, conference abstracts without full-text data, case reports, and studies focusing exclusively on pulmonary hypertension, restrictive lung disease, or sleep-disordered breathing without relevant airway outcomes. General population asthma guidelines were reviewed to provide diagnostic and therapeutic context [5,6]. Study selection and data extraction Titles and abstracts were screened for relevance, and full texts of potentially eligible articles were reviewed. Disagreements regarding inclusion were resolved by discussion among the authors. For each included study, we extracted the following information where available: study design, setting, sample size, age group, SCD genotype, definitions used for asthma, wheeze, airway obstruction, and AHR, methods of pulmonary function testing, comparison groups, principal findings, and adjustment for confounders. Because definitions of asthma vary across studies (e.g., parental report, physician diagnosis, medication use, or administrative codes), we recorded the definition used in each study and considered this when interpreting prevalence estimates [7]. Similarly, we noted whether airway obstruction was defined by the forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity ratio relative to the lower limit of normal or by fixed thresholds, and which reference equations were used, given the known impact of race-specific equations on interpretation [8]. Synthesis and appraisal Findings were synthesized qualitatively within each thematic domain. For epidemiologic data, we compared prevalence estimates across studies and with those of the general African American population, taking into account age, geography, and case definition. For studies of morbidity, we emphasized those that used longitudinal designs and adjusted for relevant covariates such as age, genotype, hydroxyurea use, and hemoglobin level, and we highlighted where evidence derived from single-center or retrospective studies might be subject to selection and ascertainment bias. For mechanistic evidence, we distinguished human studies from animal and in vitro studies. We did not perform a formal risk-of-bias assessment or pooled quantitative analysis; instead, we considered study size, design, and consistency of findings across cohorts when weighing the strength of evidence [2]. For the diagnosis and management section, we compared recommendations from national asthma guidelines and SCD-specific expert panel recommendations, and we identified areas in which evidence specific to SCD was lacking and recommendations were extrapolated from the general population [5,6,9]. Particular attention was given to the role of spirometry, bronchodilator reversibility testing, and methacholine challenge in distinguishing asthma from isolated wheeze or AHR in SCD, as well as to the safety and efficacy of corticosteroids, given reports of rebound pain and ACS after systemic steroid exposure [10]. Gaps in knowledge identified across the preceding sections were used to generate the proposed future directions, including prospective phenotyping, biomarker development, and clinical trials of asthma therapies in SCD. Because this review synthesizes published literature, the findings are organized by the five themes outlined above. Citations refer to the studies identified in the literature search. Epidemiology of asthma, wheezing, airway obstruction, and airway hyperresponsiveness Reported asthma prevalence in children with SCD ranges from approximately 10% to 48%, depending on case definition and study design [1–3]. Studies relying on physician diagnosis typically report prevalence of 20–30%, which exceeds the 8–13% observed in African American children without SCD [2,4]. Prospective cohorts using standardized criteria, such as the Cooperative Study of Sickle Cell Disease and the Sleep and Asthma Cohort, found that fewer children met full diagnostic criteria than were initially labeled as asthmatic [3,5]. Parent-reported wheezing was considerably more common than asthma, occurring in up to 50–70% of children in some cohorts, and frequently occurred without a physician diagnosis, atopy, or family history of asthma [5,6]. Airway obstruction on spirometry was observed in a minority of patients, with reductions in the FEV1/FVC ratio in 10–25% of children [7,8]. By contrast, restrictive patterns became more prevalent with advancing age and were reported in up to 20–74% of adults [8,9]. Bronchodilator responsiveness was seen in 25–50% of children with SCD, including many without a clinical asthma diagnosis or baseline obstruction [7,10]. Airway hyperresponsiveness, assessed by methacholine challenge, was documented in roughly 50–70% of children with SCD, a proportion that did not differ consistently between those with and without wheeze or asthma [10,11]. These physiologic features frequently appeared in isolation: in several cohorts, fewer than half of children with bronchodilator responsiveness or airway hyperresponsiveness had a clinical asthma diagnosis [10,11]. Associations with SCD morbidity Asthma has been repeatedly associated with higher rates of acute chest syndrome (ACS). In a Cooperative Study analysis, children with asthma had approximately 2.4 times the incidence of ACS and more frequent pain episodes than those without asthma [1]. Subsequent single-center and registry studies confirmed increased ACS recurrence and hospitalization among children with asthma, and asthma-associated ACS episodes were more often accompanied by wheezing and respiratory failure [12,13]. Asthma was also linked to earlier mortality; in the Cooperative Study, adults with asthma had increased risk of death compared with those without [14]. Wheezing independent of asthma diagnosis was likewise associated with morbidity. Children with SCD and recurrent wheezing had higher rates of ACS and vaso-occlusive pain than non-wheezing peers, and these associations persisted after adjustment for asthma diagnosis

Large-scale data collection from individuals underpins personalized services, public-health surveillance, and the training of modern machine learning models. At the same time, the data that users contribute are frequently sensitive, and centralized collection exposes them to breaches, misuse, and untrusted curators. Differential privacy (DP) [1] offers a rigorous guarantee that the output of an analysis is insensitive to any single individual's record, but its standard formulation presumes a trusted aggregator. Local differential privacy (LDP) [2], [3] removes this assumption: each user perturbs her data on her own device before transmission, so the aggregator never observes raw values. Because of this strong threat model, LDP has been deployed in industrial systems such as Google's RAPPOR [4], Apple's iOS and macOS telemetry [5], and Microsoft's telemetry collection [6]. Most of the LDP literature considers simple data types. Substantial progress has been made on categorical frequency estimation [4], [7], [8], heavy-hitter identification [9], and mean estimation for numerical attributes [10], [11]. Real-world data, however, are often richer. In particular, key-value data, the basic data model of NoSQL stores, appear in user-profile databases, e-commerce logs, and smart-device records. A key-value pair couples a categorical key (e.g., a product or an app) with a numerical value (e.g., a rating or usage time). Such data arise naturally in applications such as estimating how many users own a certain item and what average rating they give it. Challenges of Key-Value Data under LDP Key-value data cannot be handled by applying existing mechanisms independently to keys and values. First, the key and value are correlated: a value is meaningful only if its key is present, and perturbing them separately wastes the privacy budget and yields biased estimates. Second, a user typically holds many keys, so the data are high-dimensional and sparse, and the privacy budget must be split across potentially many coordinates, degrading utility. Third, the value domain is continuous or ordinal, requiring perturbation that preserves unbiased aggregates. PrivKV [12] was the first work to formalize LDP for key-value data, perturbing each pair by a sequence of value and key randomization steps and supporting frequency and mean estimation. Subsequent refinements, such as interactive variants, reduce estimation error [12], [13]. Nevertheless, existing mechanisms still suffer from considerable variance when the privacy budget is small or the key domain is large, and the correlation between key and value perturbation is not fully exploited. A further limitation is that current methods deliver only marginal statistics: the frequency of each key and the mean of the values of each key. Many downstream tasks require conditional information. Naive Bayes classification, decision-tree induction, association-rule mining, and recommendation systems all depend on conditional probabilities or conditional means, such as the probability that a user holds key B given that she holds key A, or the mean value of key B among users holding key A [14], [15]. Estimating such quantities under LDP is challenging because the conditioning event itself is observed only through noisy reports, and errors in the condition compound errors in the target statistic. Our Contributions In this paper, we address these gaps by designing new perturbation mechanisms for key-value data and by building conditional analysis on top of them. Our main contributions are as follows. 1. New key-value perturbation mechanisms. We propose a family of LDP mechanisms that jointly perturb the key and value of a pair while satisfying ε-LDP under a unified privacy budget. The mechanisms are designed so that unbiased estimators of key frequency and value mean can be derived in closed form, and we analyze their estimation variance, showing improved accuracy over existing approaches. 2. Conditional frequency estimation. We introduce a method for estimating the conditional frequency of one key given another from perturbed reports, enabling the recovery of conditional probabilities and marginal statistics for key analysis. We prove the estimator's unbiasedness and bound its error. 3. Conditional mean estimation. We develop an estimator of the mean of the values associated with one key, conditioned on the presence of another key, supporting richer value analysis than marginal means. 4. Support for learning tasks. We show how the released conditional statistics can be used directly in downstream learning tasks, and illustrate this with classification based on conditional probabilities. 5. Extensive evaluation. We conduct experiments on synthetic datasets with varied distributions and on real-world rating datasets. The results show that our mechanisms achieve lower error in frequency and mean estimation than state-of-the-art competitors across a wide range of privacy budgets and key-domain sizes, and that conditional estimates remain accurate enough to be useful. Organization The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on LDP and key-value data. Section III presents preliminaries, including the formal definition of LDP and the problem statement. Section IV describes the proposed perturbation mechanisms and their theoretical analysis. Section V develops conditional frequency and conditional mean estimation. Section VI reports experimental results, and Section VII concludes the paper. Problem Setting and Preliminaries Consider a population of n users, each holding a key-value pair ⟨k, v⟩, where k ∈ K = {1,…,d} is a discrete key and v ∈ [−1,1] is a numerical value. (Users holding multiple pairs are handled by sampling one pair uniformly, which is standard in prior work [1].) An untrusted aggregator wishes to estimate (i) the key frequency fk, (ii) the mean value mk of each key, (iii) the conditional frequency f{k|c} = Pr[key k | condition c], and (iv) the conditional mean m{k|c} = E[v | key k, condition c], where c is a predicate on a second key or attribute held by the same user. Each user perturbs the pair locally with a randomized mechanism M satisfying ε-LDP [2]: for all inputs x, x′ and outputs y, Pr[M(x)=y] ≤ e^ε Pr[M(x′)=y]. By sequential composition [3], when a user's report is split into components with budgets ε₁ and ε₂, the overall guarantee is (ε₁+ε₂)-LDP. We build on randomized response (RR) [4] for categorical data and on stochastic rounding for numerical data [5]. A value v is discretized to v ∈ {−1,1} with Pr[v=1] = (1+v)/2, which is unbiased, and v is then flipped by RR with keep probability e^{ε₂}/(e^{ε₂}+1). The prior key-value mechanism PrivKV [1] perturbs the value first and then the key-presence bit, which couples the two estimates and induces bias in the mean when the key is absent. Our design aims to remove this coupling. Key-Value Perturbation Mechanism Each user encodes its input as a d-dimensional vector in which a held key k carries the discretized value v ∈ {−1,1} and every other entry is 0. A report is generated by sampling one coordinate j and perturbing only that coordinate, so the output domain is {−1,0,1}. The sampling step is analogous to the one in [6], and the estimator is rescaled by d to correct for it. For the sampled coordinate with true entry x ∈ {−1,0,1}, the mechanism outputs y with probability Pr[y | x] = p if y = x, and q = (1−p)/2 otherwise, with p = e^ε/(e^ε+2). The ratio p/q = 2e^ε/(1−p)… more precisely, p/q = 2e^ε/2 = e^ε after normalization, so the mechanism satisfies ε-LDP, since any two inputs differ only by the ratio p/q. Using a three-way mechanism over the joint key-value domain spends the whole budget once rather than splitting it between key and value, which gives lower variance than sequential perturbation at equal ε. Unbiased Estimators Let ny(j) be the number of reports that sample coordinate j and output y ∈ {−1,0,1}, and let Nj be the number of reports sampling j. Defining the debiased counts ĉ₊ = (n₊ − qNj)/(p−q), ĉ₋ = (n₋ − qNj)/(p−q), where n₊ and n₋ denote the counts of outputs +1 and −1 on coordinate j, we have E[ĉ₊] = c₊ and E[ĉ₋] = c₋, the true counts of users holding key j with discretized value +1 and −1 respectively. The key frequency estimator is f̂j = (ĉ₊ + ĉ₋)/Nj, and the mean estimator is m̂j = (ĉ₊ − ĉ₋)/(ĉ₊ + ĉ₋). The frequency estimator is unbiased because the sampling is uniform and the debiasing is linear. The mean estimator is a ratio of unbiased quantities and is therefore asymptotically unbiased; a second-order Taylor expansion shows the bias is O(1/(n fj)). Because estimates may fall outside [−1,1] or be negative, we apply a post-processing projection (clipping and normalization), which preserves LDP by the post-processing property [3] and does not increase the expected error. The variance of ĉ₊ is of order d·q(1−q)/(p−q)² per user, so the mean squared error scales as O(d e^ε/(n(e^ε−1)²)). Iterative Refinement To reduce error on sparse keys, we optionally run a two-round protocol. In round one, a fraction of users reports under the mechanism above, producing preliminary estimates m̂j. These estimates are broadcast, and in round two the remaining users apply the same mechanism but the aggregator calibrates the estimate by replacing the uninformative prior used in debiasing with m̂j. This is analogous to the iterative scheme in [1] but is applied to the aggregated statistics, so no user is queried twice and the privacy guarantee remains ε. Conditional Frequency and Conditional Mean Estimation Let a user additionally hold a categorical attribute a ∈ A (or a predicate c(·) thereof). Conditional statistics require joint information on (a, k, v). We consider two strategies. Joint encoding. The user forms the composite key (a, k), so the domain has size |A|·d, and applies the mechanism above. The aggregator obtains f̂{(a,k)} and m̂{(a,k)} directly and computes f̂{k|a} = f̂{(a,k)} / Σ{k′} f̂{(a,k′)}, m̂{k|a} = m̂{(a,k)}. This is simple and asymptotically unbiased, but the variance grows with |A|d. Split-budget encoding. The user spends εa on a (using generalized RR [7]) and εk = ε − εa on the key-value pair. For a pair of reports (ã, ỹ), the joint distribution is related to the true one through the Kronecker product of the two perturbation matrices, P = Pa ⊗ Pkv. The aggregator estimates the joint distribution by inverting this matrix: π̂ = (Pa⁻¹ ⊗ Pkv⁻¹) r, where r is the empirical distribution of reports. Because the inverse of a Kronecker product factorizes, the computation costs O(|A|² + d²) rather than O(|A|²d²). Conditional frequency is then f̂{k|a} = π̂(a,k)/Σ{k′} π̂(a,k′), and the conditional mean follows by applying the mean estimator to the signed components of π̂. The budget split εa is chosen by minimizing the approximate variance expression derived above, which we do by one-dimensional numerical search. For a general condition c defined on a subset Ac ⊆ A, we aggregate π̂(a,k) over a ∈ Ac before normalization. As with the marginal estimators, we project π̂ onto the probability simplex [8] before forming ratios, which stabilizes the conditional estimates when the denominators are small. Privacy and Utility Analysis Each user's report is produced by a single invocation of an ε-LDP mechanism (joint encoding) or by composition of two mechanisms whose budgets sum to ε (split encoding), so both protocols satisfy ε-LDP. Utility guarantees follow by applying Hoeffding-type concentration to the debiased counts, giving, with probability at least 1−δ, a maximum error of O(√(d log(d/δ)·e^ε/n)/(e^ε−1)) over all keys for frequency, with corresponding bounds for conditional estimates that scale with the inverse of the conditioning mass. Experimental Setup. We evaluate the proposed mechanisms on synthetic and real-world key-value datasets. The synthetic data contain 10⁵ users and 100 keys. Key frequencies follow either a uniform or a Zipf distribution, and values are drawn from a truncated Gaussian on [−1, 1]. The real-world datasets are a movie-rating dataset (MovieLens [1]) and an e-commerce rating dataset, with ratings rescaled to [−1, 1]. We compare our mechanisms with PrivKV [2] and its iterative variants PrivKVM and PrivKVM+, as well as with the naive baseline that applies randomized response to keys and a Duchi-style mechanism [3] to values with the budget split evenly. The privacy budget ε ranges from 0.5 to 5 and is split between key and value perturbation. Accuracy is measured by mean squared error (MSE) for frequency estimation and mean estimation, and by mean absolute error for conditional

Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) is an extracorporeal blood purification technique that removes large molecular weight substances from the circulation, such as autoantibodies, immune complexes, paraproteins, and toxins, and replaces the removed plasma with albumin solutions or fresh frozen plasma. It is established as first-line or adjunctive therapy in a wide range of neurological, hematological, renal, and immune-mediated diseases, including thrombotic microangiopathies, Guillain-Barré syndrome, myasthenic crises, anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, ANCA-associated vasculitis, and humoral rejection after transplantation. Plasma can be separated either by centrifugation or by membrane filtration. In membrane-based TPE, blood is pumped through a highly permeable plasmafilter, and the separated plasma is discarded and replaced. Any extracorporeal circuit exposes blood to artificial surfaces and thereby activates the coagulation cascade and platelets, with a risk of clotting of the filter and lines. Clotting reduces the efficacy of the procedure, causes blood loss, and increases costs and workload. Anticoagulation is therefore needed. Unfractionated heparin is the most widely used agent in membrane-based TPE, but its use is limited by the risk of bleeding, which is particularly relevant in patients with thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, recent surgery or biopsy, uremic platelet dysfunction, or active vasculitis with hemorrhagic lesions. Heparin may also induce heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, and its effect is variable and difficult to predict. Moreover, TPE itself removes coagulation factors and may alter the response to heparin. Low molecular weight heparins and other agents such as argatroban or nafamostat have been used, but they share a systemic effect and are costly or not universally available. Regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) was developed to confine the anticoagulant effect to the extracorporeal circuit. Citrate chelates ionized calcium, a cofactor essential for several steps of the coagulation cascade, so that infusing citrate at the beginning of the circuit decreases ionized calcium and prevents clotting. Part of the citrate-calcium complex is removed in the effluent, and the remainder returns to the patient, where it is rapidly metabolized by the liver, skeletal muscle, and kidney cortex to bicarbonate, releasing calcium. RCA has become the preferred anticoagulation strategy in continuous renal replacement therapy, as recommended by the KDIGO guidelines, with lower bleeding rates and longer filter life compared with heparin. Its use has also been described in intermittent hemodialysis, hemodiafiltration, and in apheresis procedures. However, RCA is not free of risk. Excessive citrate delivery can cause systemic hypocalcemia, with paresthesia, cramps, arrhythmias, and hypotension, as well as metabolic alkalosis due to bicarbonate generation. Conversely, citrate accumulation, particularly in patients with impaired hepatic metabolism or poor tissue perfusion, can lead to metabolic acidosis with an elevated anion gap and a high total to ionized calcium ratio. Insufficient citrate yields inadequate reduction of ionized calcium in the circuit, and thus filter clotting. Safe and effective RCA requires a balance between these limits, and it depends on the target concentration of ionized calcium in the extracorporeal blood, generally considered to lie between 0.25 and 0.35 mmol/l. Protocols for RCA in continuous techniques are well standardized, usually using a fixed ratio of citrate infusion to blood flow, with adaptation based on post-filter ionized calcium measurements and systemic calcium replacement. TPE differs importantly from these techniques. Blood flow rates are higher, sessions are shorter, and the plasma removed contains most of the citrate-calcium complexes, so that the amount of citrate returned to the patient depends on the plasma fraction removed and replacement fluids. In addition, replacement with fresh frozen plasma brings additional citrate, since plasma units are themselves anticoagulated with citrate, whereas albumin solutions contain little calcium. The volume of distribution of calcium and citrate and the proportion of calcium bound to albumin vary with the patient's hematocrit and plasma composition. Since the plasma is separated from blood cells, the hematocrit determines the plasma flow and therefore the amount of citrate needed per unit of blood to reach a given plasma citrate concentration. Despite these particularities, the literature on RCA in TPE is limited to small series and empirical protocols using fixed citrate infusion rates relative to blood flow, often with calcium infusion adapted from clinical experience. To our knowledge, no individualized prescription has been proposed that takes into account patient characteristics and the physicochemical determinants of calcium chelation. Such a model would help clinicians to start treatment at the appropriate citrate dose, avoid early clotting of the circuit, limit exposure to excess citrate, and reduce the need for repeated measurements. The objective of this study was therefore to identify the determinants of the blood citrate concentration needed to achieve effective regional anticoagulation during membrane-based TPE, and to develop, using a mathematical approach, an individualized prescription algorithm for citrate and calcium supplementation. We also evaluated the efficacy of the resulting protocol in terms of circuit patency, as well as its safety in terms of systemic ionized calcium and acid–base balance. This was a prospective observational study conducted in the intensive care and nephrology units of a university hospital. The protocol was approved by the local ethics committee, and all patients provided informed consent, or consent was obtained from a relative when the patient was unable to give it. Adult patients scheduled for TPE for standard clinical indications were eligible. Patients were excluded if they had severe hepatic failure (given the risk of citrate accumulation), if they were pregnant, or if they had a known allergy to the materials used in the circuit. Study population and treatment procedures Fourteen patients underwent a total of 47 TPE sessions. TPE was performed by membrane plasma separation using a hollow-fiber plasmafilter, with blood flow, plasma removal rate and session duration prescribed by the treating physician according to the patient's plasma volume. Vascular access was obtained through a double-lumen dialysis catheter. The replacement fluid was 4% albumin or fresh frozen plasma, according to the clinical indication, and was infused post-plasmafilter. No systemic anticoagulation was given. Sessions in which the circuit clotted were recorded, as were any premature terminations. Citrate anticoagulation Trisodium citrate was infused continuously into the arterial line pre-plasmafilter using a dedicated volumetric pump. Calcium chloride was infused through a separate line into the patient's venous return, using a central venous route distinct from the dialysis catheter, to compensate for citrate-bound calcium loss in the removed plasma and for the citrate returned to the patient. The aim of anticoagulation was to lower the ionized calcium concentration in the blood entering the plasmafilter to a level that prevents clotting, without exposing the patient to excess citrate. Sampling and measurements Blood samples were drawn at standardized time points: before the start of the session, at fixed intervals during treatment, and at the end of the session. At each time point, samples were collected from the post-plasmafilter port, representing circuit ionized calcium, and from the patient (systemic). Ionized calcium, pH, bicarbonate, base excess, sodium and lactate were measured on a blood gas analyzer with ion-selective electrodes. Hematocrit, total calcium, magnesium, albumin and coagulation parameters were obtained before treatment from routine laboratory analysis. Hypocalcemia was defined as a systemic ionized calcium below a prespecified threshold (<0.9 mmol/l), and was considered significant when it required intervention beyond the protocol adjustments or was symptomatic. Acid–base disturbances were defined by deviations in pH and bicarbonate from normal ranges. Calcium supplementation algorithm A calcium supplementation algorithm was defined a priori. The calcium infusion rate was started in proportion to the citrate infusion rate and then adjusted according to systemic ionized calcium measured at each time point. The infusion was increased when systemic ionized calcium fell below the target range and decreased when it rose above it. The aim was to maintain systemic ionized calcium within the physiological range throughout and at the end of the session. Discovery phase In the discovery phase, citrate was infused at a fixed starting rate relative to blood flow. The rate was then adapted according to the post-plasmafilter ionized calcium obtained at the first measurement, with the target range for the post-filter value defined from the literature on regional citrate anticoagulation in continuous renal replacement therapy. Citrate was increased if post-plasmafilter ionized calcium exceeded the target and decreased if it was below. The final citrate infusion rate required to reach the target, together with the corresponding pre-filter ionized calcium concentration, was recorded for each session. The relation between circuit clotting and pre-filter ionized calcium was examined to define the concentration range that prevented coagulation of the extracorporeal circuit. Mathematical modeling and development of the prescription equation The determinants of the required blood citrate concentration were explored by considering the patient and treatment variables available before the session: hematocrit, pre-treatment systemic plasma ionized calcium, total calcium, albumin, blood flow, plasma flow, and replacement fluid type. Because citrate chelates calcium in the plasma phase, the plasma flow entering the filter was calculated from blood flow and hematocrit. The citrate dose needed to bring plasma ionized calcium from its baseline to the target level was then modeled mathematically, using the chelation relationship between citrate and ionized calcium observed in the discovery data. Variables were retained in the model if they significantly improved the fit. The resulting equation allowed calculation of the citrate infusion rate needed for a given blood flow, hematocrit and baseline ionized calcium, to achieve a prefilter ionized calcium within the target range. Validation phase The equation was then applied prospectively in subsequent sessions to prescribe the initial citrate infusion rate individually. Post-plasmafilter ionized calcium was measured to verify that the target was reached, and the agreement between predicted and observed values was assessed. Occurrence of circuit clotting, systemic hypocalcemia and acid–base disturbances was recorded. Statistical analysis Continuous variables are expressed as mean ± standard deviation or median and interquartile range, according to distribution. Because multiple sessions were obtained in the same patient, repeated measures were accounted for by mixed-effects models. Associations between variables and the required citrate rate were tested using linear regression, first univariate and then multivariate. Agreement between predicted and measured values was evaluated with Bland–Altman analysis. Categorical variables are presented as counts and percentages. A two-sided p value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed with standard statistical software. Patient and treatment characteristics Fourteen patients underwent a total of 47 TPE sessions, 29 of which were performed in the discovery phase and 18 in the validation phase using the individualized protocol. The indications for TPE were neurological autoimmune disease, antibody-mediated rejection or ABO-incompatible transplantation, thrombotic microangiopathy, and vasculitis. Median blood flow was 100 ml/min (range 80–150) and median plasma removal rate was 25% of blood flow. Median session duration was 120 minutes, and a median of 1.2 plasma volumes was exchanged per session. Pre-treatment hematocrit ranged from 23% to 44%, and pre-treatment systemic ionized calcium from 1.00 to 1.31 mmol/l. Discovery phase: citrate dose and post-filter ionized calcium During the discovery phase citrate was infused pre-plasmafilter at a fixed starting rate and subsequently adapted according to the post-plasmafilter ionized calcium measurements. With the fixed starting rate, post-plasmafilter ionized calcium varied widely between sessions (from 0.12 to 0.52 mmol/l), indicating that a single rate could not provide uniform anticoagulation. Sessions with low hematocrit tended to overshoot, with post-filter ionized calcium below the target, whereas sessions with high hematocrit and high baseline ionized calcium were under-anticoagulated. Rates had to be modified in most sessions within the first 15 minutes. Determinants of the required citrate rate In univariate analysis, the citrate rate required to reach the target post-filter ionized calcium correlated positively with pre-treatment plasma ionized calcium (r = 0.61, p < 0.001) and negatively with pre-treatment hematocrit (r = −0.58, p < 0.001). Blood flow was by design a determinant of the absolute infusion rate, and the required citrate dose was therefore expressed per liter of blood treated. Plasma flow rate, patient weight, sex, and plasma exchange volume were not independently associated with the requirement. In multivariable regression, hematocrit and baseline ionized calcium remained the only significant determinants and together explained about 70% of the variability of the required citrate concentration in blood. Dictionary learning, the problem of finding a set of atoms in which a collection of signals admits sparse representations, is a cornerstone of modern signal processing and machine learning [1], [2]. When the atoms are constrained to be shift-invariant filters, the model is called convolutional dictionary learning (CDL) [3], [4]. Each signal is then expressed as a sum of a small number of translated filters. This model is well suited to data in which a small number of recurring motifs occur at unknown times and with unknown amplitudes, as in audio, seismic recordings, natural images, and neural electrophysiology. Learning the filters from data is thus a form of blind source separation: given only the number of sources and the assumption that few of them overlap at any moment, one seeks to recover the sources and their activation times. Classical CDL algorithms alternate between two steps: a sparse-coding step, which solves an ℓ1-regularized convolutional least-squares problem (convolutional LASSO) with the dictionary fixed, and a dictionary-update step, which refines the filters with the codes fixed [5]–[7]. These methods are interpretable and come with a growing body of theory [8], [9], but they face practical obstacles. Each iteration requires solving a sparse-coding problem over all training signals, which becomes costly for large datasets. The methods are also difficult to parallelize across data and to run on streaming data, and their performance depends on hand-tuned parameters. In parallel, deep learning has produced powerful architectures, yet they are often opaque, require large labeled datasets, and offer few guarantees. A promising bridge is algorithm unrolling [10], which began with the Learned ISTA (LISTA) of Gregor and LeCun [11]. Here the iterations of an optimization algorithm are interpreted as the layers of a recurrent or deep network, whose parameters are then trained by back-propagation. Unrolled architectures have been developed for sparse coding [11], [12], image restoration [13], and dictionary learning [14], and they often reach a given accuracy with far fewer iterations than their classical counterparts. However, most such approaches treat the parameters of the encoder as free variables, decoupled from those of the decoder, and are typically trained in a supervised manner or for fast approximation of a fixed model. Consequently, the learned weights lose their interpretation as a dictionary, and the guarantees of the underlying optimization problem no longer apply. Contributions In this paper we propose the constrained recurrent sparse auto-encoder (CRsAE), an auto-encoder whose structure is dictated by the alternating-minimization approach to CDL. The encoder unrolls a fixed number of FISTA iterations [15] to compute a sparse code from an input signal and a current dictionary estimate. The decoder applies the same dictionary to the code to reconstruct the signal. The encoder's filters are the transpose (flipped version) of the decoder's filters, so a single set of weights parameterizes the whole network. This constraint is the key design element. It ensures that training the network amounts to learning a dictionary, so that the weights remain interpretable, the number of parameters is minimal, and the network directly mirrors the optimization problem it is meant to solve. To our knowledge, this tying of encoder and decoder parameters through the unrolled recurrence has not previously been enforced in this setting. Our main contributions are as follows. 1. We introduce CRsAE and show that its forward pass corresponds to the sparse-coding step, and a gradient step on the reconstruction loss with respect to the shared weights corresponds to the dictionary-update step of alternating minimization. 2. We derive the back-propagation algorithm for CRsAE, accounting for the fact that the dictionary appears in both the encoder and the decoder and at every unrolled iteration. This yields exact gradients, which differ from those obtained by treating the encoder and decoder weights as independent. 3. We show that, because training proceeds in mini-batches with GPU-friendly convolutional operations, CRsAE scales to large datasets and long signals where conventional CDL solvers are impractical. It is also trained without labels, and the regularization parameter is the only quantity requiring tuning. 4. We apply CRsAE to spike sorting, a source separation problem in computational neuroscience in which extracellular voltage recordings contain action potentials from several neurons, each with a characteristic waveform, corrupted by noise [16], [17]. Neurons are the sources, their waveforms are the dictionary elements, and spike times are the sparse codes. Overlapping spikes are a well-known difficulty for traditional pipelines based on thresholding, feature extraction, and clustering, whereas the convolutional model handles superposition naturally [18]. 5. We evaluate the ability of CRsAE to recover the underlying dictionary on synthetic and real data, and characterize its sensitivity as a function of signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Related Work CRsAE relates to several lines of work. Beyond the CDL solvers cited above, online and stochastic variants reduce memory and per-iteration cost [19], but still require an explicit sparse-coding solve for each sample. Unrolled networks such as LISTA and its convolutional extensions [12], [14] accelerate sparse coding but generally decouple the encoder and decoder parameters. Sparse auto-encoders [20] and their convolutional versions [21] encourage sparsity through penalties or thresholds without an explicit optimization-based encoder, so their filters need not correspond to a generative dictionary. Finally, existing spike-sorting methods that exploit the convolutional model [18], [22] rely on greedy or iterative solvers that do not readily scale. Section IV details the training procedure and implementation. Section V presents experiments on simulated and real spike-sorting data, including a study of sensitivity to SNR. Section VI concludes and discusses future directions. Problem formulation. Let y ∈ ℝ^N denote an observed signal, modeled as a sparse superposition of shifted copies of C filters. The model is y = Σc Hc xc + n, where xc ∈ ℝ^K are sparse codes and n is noise. The decoder reconstructs ŷ = H xT = Σc hc ∗ x{T,c}. In generic auto-encoders the encoder and decoder weights are independent, or tied only through transposition. Because gradients propagate only through the support of the codes, the backward pass inherits the sparsity of the forward pass. Initialization and hyperparameters. Filters are initialized as random Gaussian vectors normalized to unit norm. The number of unrolled iterations T is chosen so that FISTA approximately converges (T of order 10²) [4], the filter length M is set from the expected duration of the sources, and C is the assumed number of sources. Training signals are segmented into windows of length N, with convolutions applied with zero padding so that code length K matches the signal length. Source separation and spike sorting. After training, the dictionary elements are interpreted as the sources' waveforms, and the sparse codes as their activation times and amplitudes. Diabetic retinopathy and diabetic macular edema (DME) remain leading causes of visual impairment among working-age adults worldwide, and the global prevalence of diabetes continues to rise [1,2]. Because diabetes accelerates lens opacification and is associated with earlier and more frequent cataract formation, a substantial proportion of patients with DME will require cataract extraction during the course of their disease [3]. Phacoemulsification is now a highly refined and safe procedure in the general population. In diabetic eyes, however, the visual outcomes are less predictable, largely because of the risk of postoperative progression of retinopathy and worsening of macular edema [4,5]. The pathogenesis of macular edema after cataract surgery in diabetic patients is multifactorial. Surgical trauma induces the release of inflammatory mediators, including prostaglandins and cytokines, which disrupt the blood-retinal barrier [6]. In eyes with a preexisting compromised barrier and chronic upregulation of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), this additional inflammatory stimulus can exacerbate vascular leakage and lead to clinically significant macular edema [7]. Previous studies have shown that central macular thickness increases after uncomplicated phacoemulsification in diabetic patients, even in those without retinopathy, and that the increase is considerably greater in eyes with preexisting DME [8,9]. Moreover, pre-existing DME at the time of surgery is one of the strongest predictors of poor postoperative visual recovery [10]. Optimal management of macular edema before, during, and after cataract surgery therefore remains a clinical challenge. Various strategies have been proposed to reduce the risk of macular edema exacerbation after cataract surgery, including topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, periocular and intravitreal corticosteroids, macular laser photocoagulation, and anti-VEGF agents [11,12]. Intravitreal corticosteroids, such as triamcinolone acetonide and dexamethasone implants, effectively reduce both inflammation and vascular permeability, but their use is limited by the risk of elevated intraocular pressure and accelerated cataract progression [13]. Anti-VEGF therapy has emerged as the first-line treatment for center-involving DME, based on landmark trials demonstrating that monthly or as-needed ranibizumab produces significant gains in visual acuity and reductions in retinal thickness [14,15]. Ranibizumab, a recombinant humanized antibody fragment that binds all isoforms of VEGF-A, has also been shown to be effective in reducing macular edema in the setting of cataract surgery [16]. Several investigators have evaluated the use of intravitreal anti-VEGF agents in combination with phacoemulsification in diabetic patients. Studies using bevacizumab and ranibizumab have reported reduced central macular thickness and improved visual outcomes when injections were administered before or at the time of surgery compared with surgery alone [17,18]. Other studies, however, have found only a transient benefit, with macular thickness returning toward baseline values as the pharmacologic effect waned [19]. A randomized trial from the Diabetic Retinopathy Clinical Research Network reported that, in eyes with center-involved DME undergoing cataract surgery, perioperative intravitreal treatment with either ranibizumab or triamcinolone together with prompt or deferred laser produced favorable visual results, although the outcomes depended on the agent used and the timing of treatment [20]. Furthermore, the optimal timing of the injection relative to surgery remains undetermined. Preoperative injection may stabilize the blood-retinal barrier before the inflammatory insult of surgery, but the effect may diminish by the time the postoperative inflammatory peak occurs. Intraoperative injection offers the convenience of a single procedure and may cover the early postoperative period, yet it requires injection in an eye with an opened anterior segment and carries theoretical concerns about drug washout and endophthalmitis. Postoperative injection allows treatment to be tailored to the actual development of edema but may delay therapy during a critical period [21]. Because the existing literature compares heterogeneous regimens, different anti-VEGF agents, and different follow-up intervals, direct evidence on the relative efficacy of different injection timings with the same agent is scarce. Moreover, the duration of the effect of a single ranibizumab injection relative to the course of postoperative inflammation has not been clearly defined. Understanding whether a single injection given preoperatively, intraoperatively, or postoperatively provides a superior anatomic and functional outcome would help clinicians plan the sequence of care for diabetic patients with cataract and DME, and would inform decisions regarding the need for additional injections after surgery. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to compare the efficacy of intravitreal ranibizumab injections administered 2 weeks before, during, or 2 weeks after uncomplicated phacoemulsification on visual acuity and foveal thickness in patients with advanced cataract and DME, with follow-up at 1 week and at 1 and 3 months postoperatively. This retrospective, comparative, interventional case series was conducted at the Department of Ophthalmology and followed the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki [1]. Approval was obtained from the institutional ethics committee, and written informed consent was obtained from all patients before cataract surgery and intravitreal injection. Records of consecutive patients treated between the study period start and end dates were reviewed. Patients Fifty-nine eyes of 59 patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus were included. Eligible patients were adults with advanced cataract (nuclear sclerosis grade 3 or higher according to the Lens Opacities Classification System III [2]) and clinically significant DME. DME was confirmed by optical coherence tomography (OCT) and defined as central foveal thickness (FT) above 300 µm with intraretinal or subretinal fluid, in line with the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study criteria [3]. Only one eye per patient was included; when both eyes were eligible, the eye operated on first was analyzed. Exclusion criteria were: previous intravitreal injection of anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents or corticosteroids within the preceding 6 months; previous macular laser photocoagulation or panretinal photocoagulation within 6 months; vitreoretinal surgery; proliferative diabetic retinopathy with active neovascularization or vitreous hemorrhage; vitreomacular traction or epiretinal membrane; other macular pathologies (age-related macular degeneration, retinal vein occlusion, uveitis); glaucoma; history of ocular trauma; uncontrolled hypertension; glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c) above 10%; history of thromboembolic events within the previous 3 months; and renal failure. Eyes that developed intraoperative complications (posterior capsule rupture, vitreous loss, zonular dialysis) were excluded to ensure that only uneventful surgeries were analyzed. Cataract density precluding adequate OCT imaging was not an exclusion criterion if a scan of signal strength sufficient for analysis could be obtained. Study Groups Patients were allocated into three groups according to the timing of a single intravitreal injection of 0.5 mg/0.05 mL ranibizumab (Lucentis, Novartis, Basel, Switzerland) relative to phacoemulsification: - Group 1 (preoperative): injection 2 weeks before surgery. - Group 2 (intraoperative): injection at the end of surgery, during the same session. - Group 3 (postoperative): injection 2 weeks after surgery. The timing was chosen by the treating surgeon according to scheduling and the clinical presentation, and groups were compared for baseline characteristics to assess comparability. Injection Procedure All injections were performed under sterile conditions in the operating theatre. After topical anesthesia with proparacaine hydrochloride 0.5%, the periocular skin and conjunctival sac were disinfected with 10% and 5% povidone-iodine, respectively, and a sterile lid speculum was placed. Ranibizumab was injected through the pars plana 3.5–4.0 mm posterior to the limbus (depending on lens status) using a 30-gauge needle. Optic nerve perfusion was verified by indirect ophthalmoscopy, and topical antibiotic drops were prescribed for 5 days. In group 2, the injection was administered after completion of surgery and wound closure, once the intraocular pressure had been confirmed to be normal. Surgical Technique All operations were performed by the same experienced surgeon under topical anesthesia. A 2.2 mm clear corneal incision was created, followed by a continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis of approximately 5.5 mm, hydrodissection, and phacoemulsification using a stop-and-chop technique. A foldable hydrophobic acrylic intraocular lens was implanted in the capsular bag. Incisions were hydrated and checked for watertightness. Postoperatively, all patients received topical moxifloxacin 0.5% four times daily for 1 week and topical prednisolone acetate 1% four times daily, tapered over 4 weeks. No topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs were used, to avoid confounding effects on macular thickness [4]. No additional laser or intravitreal therapy was administered during the 3-month follow-up unless the study protocol was discontinued for safety reasons. Examinations and Outcome Measures A complete ophthalmologic examination was performed at baseline and included best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) measured with a Snellen chart, slit-lamp biomicroscopy, Goldmann applanation tonometry, and dilated fundus examination. Fluorescein angiography was used where media clarity allowed to grade retinopathy severity. BCVA was converted to the logarithm of the minimum angle of resolution (logMAR) for statistical analysis [5]. Macular imaging was performed with spectral-domain OCT (Spectralis, Heidelberg Engineering, Heidelberg, Germany) after pupil dilation. The primary morphological outcome was FT, defined as the mean retinal thickness in the central 1 mm diameter subfield of the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study grid. Scans were reviewed for segmentation errors, which were corrected manually when needed. All measurements were obtained by the same experienced technician, who was unaware of group allocation. Follow-up visits took place at 1 week and at 1 and 3 months after cataract surgery. BCVA, FT, and intraocular pressure were recorded at each visit. Primary outcomes were change in BCVA and FT from baseline to month 3 and differences between groups. Secondary outcomes were the occurrence of ocular and systemic adverse events, including endophthalmitis, retinal detachment, intraocular inflammation, elevated intraocular pressure (>21 mmHg), and thromboembolic events. Systemic data, including diabetes duration, HbA1c, and blood pressure, were obtained from patient records. Statistical Analysis Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS software (version 20.0, IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation, and categorical variables as frequencies and percentages. The distribution of data was assessed with the Shapiro–Wilk test. Within-group changes across time points were analyzed using the Friedman test, with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Bonferroni correction for post hoc comparisons against baseline. Between-group comparisons of continuous variables were performed using the Kruskal–Wallis test, or one-way analysis of variance when normality was satisfied, and categorical variables were compared with the chi-square test. A p value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant, except where Bonferroni adjustment was applied. The sample size was determined by the number of eligible patients, and a post hoc power analysis was considered for the interpretation of nonsignificant results [6]. A total of 59 eyes of 59 patients with advanced cataract and DME were included in the analysis. Group 1 (ranibizumab 2 weeks preoperatively) comprised 20 eyes, group 2 (intraoperative injection) comprised 19 eyes, and group 3 (ranibizumab 2 weeks postoperatively) comprised 20 eyes. All patients completed the 3-month follow-up, and no eyes were excluded because of intraoperative complications. Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics, including age, sex distribution, diabetes duration, HbA1c level, baseline best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), and foveal thickness (FT), did not differ significantly between the groups (all p > 0.05), indicating that the groups were comparable at enrollment (Table 1). Mean age of the entire cohort was in the sixth to seventh decade, consistent with previous series of diabetic patients undergoing cataract surgery [1,2]. Visual acuity outcomes Visual acuity, expressed as logMAR, improved in all three groups after surgery. In group 1, mean BCVA improved from baseline to 1 week and continued to be significantly better than baseline at 1 month (p < 0.05). In group 2, a similar significant improvement over baseline was observed at 1 month (p < 0.05). In group 3, the improvement in BCVA at 1 month was also statistically significant compared with baseline (p < 0.05). At 3 months, visual acuity remained better than baseline in all groups, with values that were stable or slightly improved relative to month 1, although the magnitude of the additional gain between months 1 and 3 was small and not statistically significant in any group. The proportion of eyes gaining at least two lines of visual acuity at 3 months was numerically highest in group 2, but this difference did not reach statistical significance. Between-group comparison of BCVA at each time point (1 week, 1 month, and 3 months) revealed no significant differences (p > 0.05 for all comparisons), and the change in BCVA from baseline was likewise similar across groups (Table 2).
