Parkinson's Disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder after Alzheimer's Disease, affecting millions of people worldwide and roughly one million in the United States alone. It is characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, which leads to motor symptoms such as tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia, as well as a wide range of non-motor symptoms including cognitive impairment, sleep disturbance, and depression. PD is highly heterogeneous: patients differ substantially in age of onset, symptom profile, and rate of progression. This heterogeneity, together with the absence of a definitive diagnostic test during life, makes early and accurate identification of PD a persistent clinical challenge. Diagnosis currently relies largely on clinical examination, and misdiagnosis rates, especially in early disease, remain considerable. Objective, data-driven markers that can distinguish PD patients from healthy controls are therefore of high value, both for clinical care and for the design of trials of disease-modifying therapies. In recent years, a growing body of work has applied machine learning to predictive and progression modeling of PD using clinical assessments, genetic data, and fluid biomarkers. Large observational cohorts such as the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) have made such studies possible by collecting longitudinal clinical, biospecimen, and imaging data from carefully characterized participants. Among these sources, neuroimaging holds particular promise. Structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), and functional or molecular imaging each capture different aspects of brain organization and pathology, such as regional atrophy, white matter integrity, and connectivity changes. Because PD affects distributed brain circuits rather than isolated regions, analyses that consider the brain as a network are especially appealing. Despite this promise, effective use of neuroimaging data presents several difficulties. First, imaging data are high-dimensional while the number of subjects is relatively small, which invites overfitting. Second, different modalities provide complementary but heterogeneous views of the same subjects, and how to combine them is not obvious. Simple strategies, such as concatenating features from all modalities or reducing each modality independently with techniques like principal component analysis (PCA), ignore the relational structure among subjects and across views. Such approaches treat each subject as an independent sample and cannot exploit the similarity patterns that often carry diagnostic information. Third, the signal that separates PD from controls in imaging is often subtle, and linear dimensionality reduction methods that are not guided by the prediction task may discard it. Graph-based learning offers a natural way to address these issues. When subjects are represented as nodes and their pairwise similarities as edges, the cohort becomes a graph on which information can propagate between similar individuals. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) generalize convolution to graph-structured data and have achieved strong results in semi-supervised node classification, link prediction, and related tasks. In the medical domain, GCNs have been used for disease prediction on population graphs, brain network classification, and analysis of molecular structures. However, most existing GCN formulations assume a single graph, whereas multimodal neuroimaging naturally yields multiple graphs, one per modality or feature type, each encoding a different notion of similarity between subjects. Collapsing these into a single graph before learning risks losing view-specific information, while treating them separately forgoes the benefit of their complementarity. In this paper, we propose a Multi-View Graph Convolutional Network (MVGCN) for fusing multiple modalities of brain images. Each imaging modality is used to construct a view-specific graph over subjects, and graph convolutional layers learn view-specific embeddings that incorporate neighborhood information. These embeddings are then integrated through a fusion mechanism so that the final representation reflects the complementary content of all views. We formulate the task as relationship prediction: given the learned representations, the model predicts whether pairs of subjects share the same status, which supports distinguishing PD cases from controls. The whole architecture is trained end to end, so that representation learning and fusion are directly guided by the prediction objective rather than by an unsupervised criterion such as variance preservation. We evaluate the proposed method on the PPMI cohort using multiple neuroimaging modalities. Our approach achieves an AUC of 0.9537 ± 0.0587, compared with 0.6443 ± 0.0223 for traditional approaches such as PCA-based feature reduction followed by standard classifiers. This large margin suggests that modeling inter-subject relationships and learning multi-view representations jointly captures information that conventional pipelines miss. The main contributions of this work are as follows: - We introduce a multi-view graph convolutional framework that fuses heterogeneous neuroimaging modalities by building and learning on view-specific subject graphs. - We cast PD versus control discrimination as a relationship prediction problem, enabling the model to exploit pairwise structure in the data. - We conduct extensive experiments on the PPMI dataset, showing substantial improvements over traditional dimensionality reduction baselines. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We first review related work on PD modeling and graph neural networks, then describe the proposed method, present experimental settings and results, and finally discuss implications and directions for future research. We propose a multi-view graph convolutional network (MVGCN) that fuses several neuroimaging modalities to predict relationships between subjects, which are then used to separate PD patients from healthy controls. Data and preprocessing. We used data from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI). Each subject has multiple imaging modalities: T1-weighted structural MRI and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI). Structural images were skull-stripped, bias-corrected, and parcellated into N brain regions using a standard atlas. For each region we extracted features such as cortical thickness, volume, and surface area. DWI data were processed with eddy-current and motion correction, followed by deterministic tractography, producing a region-by-region connectivity matrix of streamline counts. Features were z-normalized within each modality. Each modality is treated as one "view" of the subject. Problem formulation. Let there be M subjects and V views. For view v, subject i has a feature vector xi^(v) ∈ R^{dv}. We construct for each view a subject graph G^(v) = (𝒱, E^(v)) whose nodes are subjects and whose adjacency matrix A^(v) encodes similarity between subjects in that view. A^(v) is built by a k-nearest-neighbor rule on Pearson correlation between feature vectors, with Gaussian-kernel weights, then symmetrized. Some subjects have known diagnostic labels (PD or control). Rather than classifying nodes directly, we predict pairwise relationships: for a pair (i, j), the target yij = 1 if both subjects share the same diagnostic label and 0 otherwise. A pair-level predictor of this kind can be used to assign a test subject to the class with which it is most often predicted to be related to labeled subjects. View-specific graph convolution. For each view, we apply a graph convolutional encoder. With Â^(v) = D̃^{-1/2}(A^(v)+I)D̃^{-1/2}, the layer-l propagation is H^(v,l+1) = σ(Â^(v) H^(v,l) W^(v,l)), where H^(v,0) = X^(v), W^(v,l) are learnable weights, and σ is ReLU. We stack two layers per view, yielding embeddings Z^(v) ∈ R^{M×h}. This allows each subject's representation to incorporate information from subjects who are similar in that modality, while view-specific weights retain modality-specific characteristics. Multi-view fusion. We combine view embeddings via a learned attention-weighted sum: Z = Σv αv Z^(v), αv = softmaxv(q^T tanh(Wa z̄^(v) + b)), where z̄^(v) is the mean embedding of view v, and q, Wa, b are learnable. We also evaluated concatenation and simple averaging as alternatives. To encourage agreement between views, we add a consistency regularizer that penalizes the distance between normalized embeddings of different views: Lcon = Σ{u<v} ||Ẑ^(u) Ẑ^(u)T − Ẑ^(v) Ẑ^(v)T||F², where Ẑ are row-normalized embeddings. Relationship prediction. For a subject pair (i, j) the predicted relationship probability is ŷij = sigmoid( MLP([zi ⊙ zj ; |zi − zj|]) ), which is symmetric in i and j. The primary loss is binary cross-entropy over a sampled set of labeled training pairs, with positive and negative pairs balanced by sampling. The total objective is L = LBCE + λ Lcon + γ ||Θ||², where λ and γ are hyperparameters. Inference. For a test subject t, we compute ŷtj for all labeled training subjects j and define a PD score as the average of ŷtj over PD training subjects minus the average over control training subjects (equivalently, a relationship-weighted vote). This score is used to compute AUC. Test subjects are included in the graphs during training (transductive setting) but their labels are never used. Baselines. We compared against traditional pipelines in which features from all modalities are concatenated and reduced by principal component analysis (PCA), followed by logistic regression or a support vector machine. The number of components was selected by cross-validation. We also compared with single-view GCNs and with a multi-view model without the consistency regularizer, to quantify the contributions of fusion and regularization. Implementation and training. The model was implemented in PyTorch. Hidden dimension was 64 for the first graph layer and 32 for the second; the pair MLP had one hidden layer of 32 units. We trained with Adam (learning rate 0.01, weight decay 5e-4), dropout of 0.5, and up to 300 epochs with early stopping on a validation split. The neighbor count k, λ, and γ were chosen by grid search on validation data. In each epoch, we sampled 10,000 balanced labeled pairs from the training subjects. Evaluation. We used stratified 10-fold cross-validation, with each fold's test subjects held out from labels and pair sampling; a further 10% of the training subjects served as validation. Performance was measured by area under the ROC curve (AUC), reported as mean ± standard deviation across folds. All methods used identical splits. Features used for PCA baselines were fit on training subjects only to avoid leakage. Paired comparisons across folds were used to assess whether differences between methods were consistent. We evaluated the proposed multi-view graph convolutional network (MVGCN) on the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) cohort, comparing PD patients with healthy controls. All results are reported as mean ± standard deviation over repeated cross-validation runs with different random splits, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) is the primary metric. Overall performance. MVGCN achieved an AUC of 0.9537 ± 0.0587 for relationship prediction used to distinguish PD cases from controls. In contrast, the traditional pipeline that reduced the concatenated imaging features with principal component analysis (PCA) and then applied a standard classifier reached only 0.6443 ± 0.0223 AUC. This is an absolute improvement of about 0.31 AUC. High-throughput RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) has become the dominant technology for profiling transcriptomes, largely replacing microarrays because of its higher resolution, wider dynamic range, and lower background noise [1,2]. A central task in RNA-seq studies is differential expression (DE) analysis, which aims to identify genes whose expression levels differ systematically across biological conditions. The results of such analyses guide downstream investigations including pathway enrichment, biomarker discovery, and functional validation [3]. RNA-seq data are typically summarized as read counts, the number of reads mapped to each gene in each sample. Because counts are discrete, non-negative, and over-dispersed relative to the Poisson distribution, most statistical methods model them with the negative binomial distribution. Representative methods include edgeR [4], DESeq [5], and DESeq2 [6], which differ mainly in how they estimate the dispersion parameters and how they stabilize gene-wise estimates by borrowing information across genes. Other approaches include Poisson-based models [7], transformation-based methods such as voom combined with linear models in limma [8], and nonparametric procedures such as SAMseq [9]. Comparative studies have shown that no single approach is uniformly best, although the negative binomial based methods remain among the most widely used [10,11]. Most of these methods were originally developed and evaluated for the two-condition comparison, such as treatment versus control or tumor versus normal tissue. Experimental designs in practice are becoming more complex. Studies may involve several drug doses, multiple time points, different developmental stages, or several disease subtypes, so that the number of conditions can be three or more. In this setting, the question of interest is often whether a gene is differentially expressed in any of the conditions, that is, whether its expression is not constant across all conditions. The generalized linear model (GLM) framework adopted by edgeR and DESeq2 accommodates multiple conditions through a likelihood ratio test or a Wald-type test on several coefficients simultaneously. For K conditions, this omnibus test has K−1 degrees of freedom. Although this test is valid, its power can be limited when K is large, because the number of tested parameters grows with K while the true signal may be concentrated in a low-dimensional pattern, for example a monotone trend across doses or time. An alternative is to perform all pairwise comparisons and combine the results, which requires multiple testing adjustment and does not make efficient use of shared structure among conditions. Methods designed for time-course data, such as those based on splines [12], or for ordered alternatives [13], exploit specific structure but require prior knowledge of the ordering or the temporal form, and thus do not apply to unordered conditions. The problem of testing an interaction effect with many degrees of freedom has a long history in the statistical literature on two-way tables. In a log-linear model with two factors, the interaction between row and column effects can be decomposed in a low-rank form, as in the association models of Goodman [14] and the multiplicative interaction models of Tukey [15] and Mandel [16]. Such decompositions represent the interaction by a small number of multiplicative terms and reduce the number of free parameters. In the first-order form, the interaction is expressed as the product of a gene-specific parameter and a condition-specific parameter. Under the null hypothesis of no differential expression, the gene-specific parameter is zero, and the test of that single parameter has one degree of freedom regardless of the number of conditions. This construction suggests a route to substantially higher power for DE detection with multiple conditions, particularly when the condition-specific pattern is shared across many genes. Related ideas of low-dimensional structure have been used in the analysis of gene expression through reduced-rank regression and factor models [17], but they have not been systematically exploited for count-based DE testing. In this paper, we propose multiDE, a dimension reduced model based method for DE analysis of RNA-seq count data with multiple treatment conditions. The read count is assumed to follow a log-linear model with condition and gene as the two factors, where the gene-by-condition interaction quantifies differential expression. Through a first-order decomposition of the interaction, the number of degrees of freedom of the DE test is reduced to one. The condition-specific parameters are shared across genes and therefore can be estimated with considerable precision from the whole dataset, while the gene-specific parameters are tested individually. We develop an estimation procedure and a test statistic for this model, and we implement them in an R package. We evaluate multiDE by simulation under a range of scenarios, including settings in which the first-order decomposition is severely misspecified, and compare it with edgeR and DESeq2. We also apply the method to two real RNA-seq datasets with multiple conditions and assess the biological relevance of the genes it identifies. The results show that multiDE performs comparably to the benchmark methods when there are two conditions and increasingly outperforms them as the number of conditions grows. Model. Let yijk denote the read count for gene i (i = 1,…,G) in sample k of condition j (j = 1,…,J). We assume yijk follows a negative binomial distribution with mean μijk and dispersion φi, a standard choice for overdispersed RNA-seq counts [1,2]. The mean is modeled by the log-linear model log μijk = log sjk + αi + βj + γij, where sjk is a sample-specific size factor that accounts for sequencing depth and is estimated by the median-of-ratios or TMM normalization [2,3]. The term αi is the gene effect, βj is the condition effect, and γij is the gene-by-condition interaction. For identifiability we impose the constraints Σi αi = 0, Σj βj = 0, Σi γij = 0 and Σj γij = 0. Gene i is differentially expressed (DE) if γij ≠ 0 for at least one j. The corresponding null hypothesis is H0: γi1 = … = γiJ = 0. A conventional test of this hypothesis, as in the likelihood-ratio or Wald tests of edgeR and DESeq2 [2,4], uses J − 1 degrees of freedom. Power therefore declines as J grows. Dimension reduction of the interaction. To reduce the degrees of freedom, we apply a first-order decomposition to the interaction matrix Γ = (γij), as in the Tukey one-degree-of-freedom model for non-additivity and the related bilinear (AMMI) models [5,6]: γij = λ θi δj, where δ = (δ1,…,δJ) is a condition-specific vector with Σj δj = 0 and Σj δj² = 1, θi is a gene-specific coefficient, and λ is a scale constant absorbed into θi. The model becomes log μijk = log sjk + αi + βj + θi δj. The vector δ is shared across genes and describes the overall pattern of condition-specific expression changes. The scalar θi measures the magnitude of the DE of gene i along that pattern. The null hypothesis reduces to H0: θi = 0, which has one degree of freedom regardless of J. When Γ is truly of rank one, the decomposition is exact. Otherwise it is the best rank-one approximation, which captures the dominant direction of DE. A single test statistic along this direction can retain power even when the model is misspecified, because most DE signals share a common direction across the many genes used to estimate δ. Parameter estimation. Because δ is common to all genes, it can be estimated stably using information from the whole transcriptome. Estimation proceeds by iterating the following steps. 1. Initialization. Size factors sjk are computed from the raw counts. Gene-wise dispersions φi are estimated by Cox–Reid adjusted profile likelihood [7] and shrunk toward a fitted mean–dispersion trend by empirical Bayes moderation [2,4]. An initial δ is obtained from the leading right singular vector of the doubly centered matrix of log normalized mean counts, which is the least-squares solution of the bilinear model. 2. Update of (αi, βj, θi) given δ. With δ fixed, the model is a generalized linear model (GLM) with the covariate δj. Parameters are estimated by iteratively reweighted least squares for each gene. 3. Update of δ given (αi, θi, βj). With θi fixed, the model is a GLM in δj with gene-specific offsets and covariates θi. The likelihood is summed over all genes to estimate δ, which is then centered and rescaled to unit norm. 4. Iteration. Steps 2 and 3 are alternated until the relative change in the total log-likelihood falls below 10⁻⁶ or a maximum number of iterations is reached. Hypothesis testing. For each gene, H0: θi = 0 is tested using a likelihood-ratio statistic comparing the full model with the reduced model without the interaction. With δ estimated from all genes, the statistic is referred to a χ² distribution with one degree of freedom. Because δ is estimated from a very large number of genes, the contribution of any single gene to δ is negligible, and the effect of estimating δ on the null distribution is minor. We checked this through simulations under the global null, in which the p-values were approximately uniform. P-values are adjusted for multiple testing by the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure [8], and genes with an adjusted p-value below 0.05 are declared DE. Simulation studies. We generated count data from negative binomial distributions with gene-specific dispersions drawn from a distribution fitted to real data. The number of genes was 10,000, of which 10% were DE. The number of conditions was J = 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, with 3 replicates per condition. Baseline expression levels were sampled from the empirical distribution of a real dataset. We considered three scenarios for the interaction. In scenario 1 the interaction was exactly rank one, with γij = θi δj. In scenario 2 the interaction matrix had rank greater than one, with condition effects varying independently across genes, which is a severe misspecification. In scenario 3 only a subset of conditions had nonzero effects for each DE gene. Performance was evaluated by the area under the ROC curve, power at a fixed false discovery rate of 5%, and the observed false discovery rate. Each setting was replicated 100 times. We compared multiDE with edgeR (quasi-likelihood F-test and likelihood-ratio test) [2,9] and DESeq2 (likelihood-ratio test across all conditions) [4], using default settings. Real data analysis. We applied multiDE and the benchmark methods to two public RNA-seq datasets with more than two conditions. Raw counts were filtered to remove genes with fewer than 10 total reads. For each method, DE genes were identified at an adjusted p-value below 0.05. The biological relevance of the DE genes was assessed by Gene Ontology and KEGG pathway enrichment analysis using hypergeometric tests [10], with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. We compared the number of significant terms and the specificity of enrichment to the biological context of each experiment among the methods. Implementation. multiDE is implemented in R, using GLM routines for the iterative fitting steps and the edgeR and DESeq2 infrastructure for normalization and dispersion estimation. The package is freely available at http://homepage.fudan.edu.cn/zhangh/softwares/multiDE. We evaluated multiDE against edgeR and DESeq2 using simulated data and two real RNA-seq datasets. For multiple conditions, edgeR and DESeq2 were applied using their likelihood ratio tests across all conditions, which have degrees of freedom equal to the number of conditions minus one. multiDE tests a single-degree-of-freedom interaction term. Simulation design Read counts were generated from negative binomial distributions with gene-specific dispersions drawn from an empirical distribution estimated from real data [1,2]. We varied the number of conditions (K = 2, 3, 4, 6), the number of replicates per condition (3 and 5), and the proportion of DE genes (10% and 20%). Library sizes varied across samples. To assess robustness, we considered three scenarios for the condition effects of DE genes. In scenario I, the effects followed the rank-one structure assumed by multiDE, so the model was correctly specified. In scenario II, effects were generated with moderate departures from the rank-one structure, adding independent noise to the condition-specific log fold changes. In scenario III, the model was severely misspecified: each DE gene had a randomly chosen subset of conditions with nonzero effects, and the signs and magnitudes were unrelated across genes. Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) is the most severe form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis and remains a major cause of death and disability worldwide. The World Health Organization estimates that around 10 million people develop tuberculosis each year, and central nervous system involvement accounts for roughly 1% to 5% of cases. The true burden of TBM is uncertain because diagnosis is difficult and notification is incomplete. Even with treatment, mortality is approximately 20% to 25% in HIV-uninfected adults and may exceed 50% in those co-infected with HIV. Up to half of survivors are left with neurological sequelae, including cognitive impairment, cranial nerve palsies, motor deficits and epilepsy. Delayed diagnosis, advanced disease at presentation, drug resistance and HIV co-infection are all associated with poor outcome. Despite these figures, TBM has received far less research investment than pulmonary tuberculosis, and many management decisions still rest on extrapolation from pulmonary disease, small observational series or expert opinion. The pathogenesis of TBM helps explain why treatment is so challenging. Following haematogenous dissemination from a primary focus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis seeds the brain and meninges, forming subpial or subependymal granulomas (Rich foci). Rupture of these foci into the subarachnoid space triggers an intense inflammatory response, producing a thick basal exudate. This exudate underlies the principal complications of the disease: hydrocephalus from obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid flow or impaired absorption, vasculitis and infarction affecting small and medium-sized vessels, cranial neuropathies, and tuberculomas. Clinical deterioration therefore results not only from bacillary replication but also from a dysregulated host immune response. Effective management consequently requires three components: antimicrobial therapy that achieves bactericidal concentrations at the site of infection, modulation of harmful inflammation, and supportive care to manage raised intracranial pressure, hydrocephalus, hyponatraemia, seizures and other complications. Current antimicrobial regimens for TBM are largely derived from those developed for pulmonary tuberculosis. Guidelines generally recommend an intensive phase of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for two months, followed by isoniazid and rifampicin for a further 7 to 10 months. This approach does not take into account the differing ability of these drugs to cross the blood-brain barrier. Isoniazid and pyrazinamide penetrate the cerebrospinal fluid well, whereas rifampicin, which is the most potent sterilizing agent in the regimen, achieves relatively low concentrations because of its high protein binding and its status as a substrate for efflux transporters. Ethambutol penetrates poorly, and streptomycin does so only in the presence of inflamed meninges. These pharmacokinetic limitations have prompted interest in higher doses of rifampicin, in fluoroquinolones, and in newer agents such as linezolid, which have more favourable central nervous system penetration. At the same time, the emergence of isoniazid- and multidrug-resistant tuberculosis complicates treatment, as the evidence for second-line regimens in TBM is very limited and the toxicity of prolonged therapy is considerable. Adjunctive therapies are equally important. Corticosteroids, principally dexamethasone, have been shown to reduce mortality in HIV-uninfected patients and are standard of care, although their effect on disabling neurological outcome is less certain and their role in HIV-associated TBM has not been established. The recognition that inflammation and thrombosis drive much of the morbidity has stimulated interest in other host-directed therapies, including aspirin, thalidomide, anti-tumour necrosis factor agents and other immunomodulators. Variation in host genetic factors, such as polymorphisms in the LTA4H gene that influence the balance of pro- and anti-inflammatory eicosanoids, may determine which patients benefit from particular immunomodulatory strategies, raising the possibility of individualized treatment. Increasing understanding of innate immune pathways in the central nervous system may also reveal novel therapeutic targets. Supportive management, in particular of hydrocephalus, remains a neglected area. Hydrocephalus occurs in a large proportion of patients and is a strong predictor of death and disability. Options include medical therapy with acetazolamide and furosemide, repeated lumbar puncture, and neurosurgical diversion by ventriculoperitoneal shunt or external ventricular drain. However, the evidence for each is sparse, the selection and timing of intervention are poorly defined, and data for patients with HIV co-infection, who often present with advanced immunosuppression and a different pattern of disease, are almost absent. Resource constraints in many high-burden settings further limit access to neurosurgical care and intensive monitoring. Several recent and ongoing clinical trials have begun to address these gaps, with mixed results. Phase 2 studies suggested that intensified rifampicin may improve survival, yet the most recent larger trial using 15 mg/kg/day did not demonstrate a mortality benefit, leaving uncertainty about the optimal dose and the role of other drugs. In this review, we systematically evaluate the evidence for current and emerging antimicrobial agents, host-directed therapies and supportive measures in the treatment of TBM in adults. We summarize pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic considerations, appraise clinical trial data, and highlight priorities for future research, with particular attention to high-dose rifampicin, newer antimicrobials with improved central nervous system penetration, immunomodulation, and the management of hydrocephalus in people living with HIV. We conducted a systematic review of the literature on the treatment of tuberculous meningitis (TBM) and its complications in adults. The review was designed to evaluate evidence for current and emerging antimicrobial agents, host-directed therapies, and supportive management, including the treatment of hydrocephalus. It was planned and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, adapted to a narrative synthesis because of the heterogeneity of the available studies. The review protocol was not registered prospectively. Search strategy We searched MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Web of Science for articles published from database inception to the date of the final search. We also searched ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform for ongoing or unpublished trials. The search combined controlled vocabulary terms and free-text keywords for three concepts: disease (tuberculous meningitis, central nervous system tuberculosis, tuberculoma, tuberculous hydrocephalus), intervention (rifampicin, rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, streptomycin, fluoroquinolones, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, linezolid, corticosteroids, dexamethasone, aspirin, thalidomide, infliximab, immunomodulation, host-directed therapy, ventriculoperitoneal shunt, external ventricular drain, endoscopic third ventriculostomy, lumbar puncture), and outcome (mortality, survival, disability, neurological outcome, pharmacokinetics, cerebrospinal fluid penetration, adverse events). We additionally searched for studies of genetic polymorphisms (for example LTA4H, TLR2, and related innate immune pathway genes) and mediators of the innate immune response in relation to treatment response. Reference lists of retrieved articles, previous systematic reviews, and international guidelines were hand-searched to identify further relevant publications. Searches were limited to English-language publications. Eligibility criteria We included randomized controlled trials, non-randomized comparative studies, prospective and retrospective cohort studies, pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies, case series with more than five participants, and systematic reviews or meta-analyses addressing treatment of TBM in adults (aged 15 years or older, or studies in which adults formed the majority of participants). Studies in both HIV-infected and HIV-uninfected populations were eligible, and those reporting data on drug-resistant TBM were included. Preclinical and mechanistic studies (in vitro, animal, or immunological) were considered where they informed the rationale for emerging antimicrobials or host-directed therapies, or where clinical data were absent. We excluded studies focused exclusively on children, studies of extrapulmonary tuberculosis that did not report central nervous system outcomes separately, single case reports, conference abstracts without full data, and articles addressing only diagnosis or prevention. Study selection Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts for relevance, followed by full-text assessment of potentially eligible articles. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or, when necessary, by consultation with a third reviewer. Where multiple publications reported on the same trial or cohort, the most complete or most recent report was used, with secondary publications consulted for additional data such as long-term follow-up or sub-studies. Data extraction Using a standardized form, two reviewers independently extracted the following: study design, setting, years of enrolment, sample size, participant characteristics (age, HIV status, disease severity by modified British Medical Research Council grade, drug-resistance status), intervention and comparator (agent, dose, route, duration), and outcomes. Primary outcomes of interest were all-cause mortality and survival, with disability or neurological outcome (for example modified Rankin Scale) as secondary outcomes. Additional outcomes included the incidence of stroke or other complications, time to cerebrospinal fluid sterilization or bacterial clearance, drug concentrations in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid, adverse events (particularly hepatotoxicity and bleeding), and, for hydrocephalus, shunt function, complications, and post-procedural outcomes. For pharmacokinetic studies, we recorded the ratio of cerebrospinal fluid to plasma exposure and, where available, the protein binding and lipophilicity of the drug. Quality assessment The risk of bias in randomized trials was assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool, and observational studies were appraised with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Pharmacokinetic and small studies were assessed qualitatively for sample size, sampling methodology, and assay validity. The overall certainty of evidence for key interventions was graded narratively as high, moderate, low, or very low, informed by the GRADE approach, considering risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. Data synthesis Because of substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity in populations, dosing regimens, comparators, and outcome definitions, meta-analysis was not undertaken. Findings were synthesized narratively and organized by therapeutic category: first-line antimicrobials and optimization of dose, second-line and repurposed antimicrobials, adjunctive corticosteroids, other host-directed and anti-inflammatory therapies, pharmacogenetic and immunological targets, and supportive management of complications including hydrocephalus. Within each category, we contrasted evidence from HIV-infected and HIV-uninfected populations and highlighted where evidence was lacking. Results from randomized trials were prioritized over observational and mechanistic data, and the strength and limitations of the evidence base were summarized to identify priorities for future research. Antimicrobial therapy Current regimens are based largely on those for pulmonary tuberculosis, with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol given for an intensive phase of two months, followed by isoniazid and rifampicin for a total of 9–12 months. These regimens were not designed around penetration of the blood-brain barrier. Isoniazid and pyrazinamide penetrate the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) well, with CSF concentrations approaching those in plasma. Rifampicin penetrates poorly because it is highly protein-bound and a substrate for efflux transporters, with CSF concentrations of roughly 10–20% of plasma levels. Ethambutol has minimal CSF penetration, and streptomycin penetrates only in the presence of inflamed meninges. Higher-dose rifampicin was assessed in several phase II studies. Intravenous and oral doses of 13–35 mg/kg/day produced higher plasma and CSF exposures, and in some studies were associated with improved survival, particularly early in treatment. Pharmacokinetic data showed approximately dose-proportional increases in CSF exposure. However, the most recent large randomized trial, using 15 mg/kg/day, did not demonstrate a survival benefit over standard dosing. Dose-finding studies suggest that doses up to 35 mg/kg/day are safe, with no excess hepatotoxicity, although adverse events such as raised transaminases and hyperbilirubinemia should be monitored. Trials testing these higher doses are ongoing. Fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) have good CSF penetration and bactericidal activity. They are recommended as important second-line agents in drug-resistant TBM. As first-line agents, trials of added levofloxacin or moxifloxacin have not shown a clear survival benefit. Some studies suggested a trend toward reduced early mortality, but results were inconsistent and underpowered. Moxifloxacin exposure is also reduced by high-dose rifampicin through induction of metabolism, complicating combination regimens. Linezolid has good CNS penetration, with CSF-to-plasma ratios approaching one. Early studies, including in drug-resistant disease, suggest it is promising and that it may be tolerated in the short term. Long-term use is limited by myelosuppression, peripheral and optic neuropathy, and serotonergic interactions. Other agents under evaluation include high-dose isoniazid (particularly for patients with rapid acetylator status or inhA mutations), bedaquiline, delamanid and carbapenems, though CNS data are limited. Host-directed therapies Corticosteroids. Dexamethasone reduces mortality in HIV-uninfected adults with TBM, and meta-analyses of earlier trials support a survival benefit of about 25%. The benefit appears greatest in those with less severe disease at presentation, and the effect on disabling neurological sequelae is less clear. In HIV co-infection, evidence is lacking. A trial in Vietnam of HIV-infected adults was underpowered to show a significant mortality reduction, and the effect on survival was uncertain, although there was no evidence of excess serious adverse events. Ongoing studies are addressing this question. Aspirin. Aspirin has anti-inflammatory and anti-thrombotic effects, inhibiting thromboxane A2 and modulating prostaglandin pathways. Mycotoxins are toxic secondary metabolites produced by filamentous fungi that contaminate a wide range of agricultural commodities and processed foods. The Food and Agriculture Organization has estimated that a considerable proportion of the world's food crops is affected by mycotoxins each year, causing substantial economic losses and public health concerns [1,2]. Among them, ochratoxin A (OTA) is one of the most important and frequently detected mycotoxins. It is produced mainly by Aspergillus and Penicillium species, notably Aspergillus ochraceus, Aspergillus carbonarius, Aspergillus niger, and Penicillium verrucosum [3]. OTA has been found in cereals, coffee, cocoa, dried fruits, spices, grape juice, beer, and wine, and consequently it enters the human diet through numerous routes [4,5]. Structurally, OTA consists of a dihydroisocoumarin moiety linked through an amide bond to L-β-phenylalanine. It is chemically stable and resists most conventional food processing, including heating, so contamination of raw materials is likely to persist into final products [6]. Toxicologically, OTA is nephrotoxic, hepatotoxic, teratogenic, and immunosuppressive, and the International Agency for Research on Cancer has classified it as a possible human carcinogen (Group 2B) [7]. It has been implicated in Balkan endemic nephropathy and in urinary tract tumors, and it has a long half-life in human blood because of its strong binding to serum albumin [8]. Regulatory authorities have therefore established maximum permitted levels in foodstuffs; the European Union, for example, has set a limit of 2.0 μg/kg for wine and grape juice, and 3.0 μg/kg for processed cereal products [9]. Wine is regarded as the second major source of OTA exposure after cereals in European populations, and red wine is generally more contaminated than white or rosé wine, probably because of the longer maceration of grape skins and the susceptibility of grapes to black aspergilli in warm climates [10,11]. Preventive measures, such as good agricultural and manufacturing practice, are the primary means of controlling OTA, but they cannot completely prevent contamination. Therefore, effective decontamination strategies are needed. Physical and chemical approaches, including adsorption by activated carbon, fining agents, and treatment with ammonia or ozone, have been investigated. However, they may be limited by incomplete efficacy, loss of nutritional and sensory quality, and safety concerns about residues [12,13]. Particularly for beverages like wine, the removal of toxin without affecting color, aroma, and phenolic composition is a major challenge. Biological detoxification, using microorganisms or their enzymes to remove or degrade mycotoxins, has attracted growing attention as an environmentally friendly and specific alternative. Several microorganisms have been reported to reduce OTA, including yeasts, lactic acid bacteria, filamentous fungi, and bacteria of the genera Bacillus, Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas, and Phenylobacterium [14–16]. Two main mechanisms are generally recognized: enzymatic degradation, in which the amide bond of OTA is hydrolyzed by carboxypeptidases or amidases to the far less toxic ochratoxin α and phenylalanine, and physical binding or adsorption to components of the cell wall [17,18]. Distinguishing between these mechanisms is important for practical application because adsorption by dead cells can be applied in a manner similar to a fining agent, whereas enzymatic degradation requires active metabolism or purified enzymes. The genus Bacillus is of particular interest for this purpose. Bacillus species are widely used in the food and feed industries, and many strains have Generally Recognized as Safe or Qualified Presumption of Safety status. They produce spores that are robust under processing and storage conditions, secrete numerous enzymes and antimicrobial compounds, and can inhibit fungal growth and mycotoxin production [19]. Bacillus subtilis strains have been shown to degrade or remove aflatoxin B1, zearalenone, and OTA, and the OTA-degrading activity of B. subtilis CW14 and of other Bacillus strains has been attributed to extracellular enzymes or to cell-associated components [20,21]. Reports are not consistent, however, on whether the activity resides in viable cells, cell-free supernatants, or intracellular fractions, and the effect of heat treatment on cells is not well understood. Traditional fermented foods are a rich source of microorganisms with useful functional properties. Kimchi, a traditional Korean fermented vegetable dish, harbors a diverse microbiota dominated by lactic acid bacteria, although Bacillus species are also present and contribute to fermentation and flavor development [22,23]. The ingredients of Kimchi, such as red pepper powder, garlic, and ginger, may be contaminated by toxigenic fungi, so microorganisms from this environment may have adapted to the presence of mycotoxins and might possess the ability to reduce them. Despite this potential, few studies have screened Kimchi isolates for OTA-reducing activity. Accordingly, the present study aimed to isolate and identify a new Bacillus strain from Kimchi and to evaluate its ability to reduce OTA in culture medium. We characterized the strain by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, followed its growth kinetics in relation to OTA reduction, and compared the activity of viable cells, heat-killed cells, and intracellular and extracellular extracts to clarify the probable mode of action. Finally, we assessed the potential application of the heat-treated cells for removing OTA from artificially contaminated red wine. Isolation and identification of the bacterial strain Kimchi samples were collected from local markets in Seoul, Republic of Korea. Ten grams of each sample were homogenized in 90 mL of sterile 0.85% saline and serially diluted. Aliquots (100 µL) were spread onto nutrient agar and incubated at 37 °C for 24–48 h. Colonies with distinct morphologies were purified by repeated streaking. Isolates were screened for OTA-reducing activity, and the most effective isolate, designated KU-153, was selected for further study. Genomic DNA was extracted with a commercial bacterial genomic DNA kit following the manufacturer's instructions. The 16S rRNA gene was amplified using the universal primers 27F (5′-AGAGTTTGATCMTGGCTCAG-3′) and 1492R (5′-GGTTACCTTGTTACGACTT-3′) [1]. PCR products were purified and sequenced commercially. Sequences were compared with entries in the GenBank database using BLAST, and a phylogenetic tree was constructed by the neighbor-joining method in MEGA X with 1000 bootstrap replicates [2,3]. Gram staining and catalase tests were performed as supporting phenotypic characterization. Chemicals and reagents OTA standard (from Aspergillus ochraceus) was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. A stock solution (1 mg/mL) was prepared in methanol and stored at −20 °C in the dark. HPLC-grade acetonitrile, methanol, and acetic acid were used for chromatographic analysis. Nutrient broth (NB) and all other media were obtained from commercial suppliers. Working OTA solutions were prepared by diluting the stock in the relevant medium so that the final methanol content did not exceed 1% (v/v). Growth kinetics and OTA reduction in culture medium A single colony of B. subtilis KU-153 was inoculated into NB and grown at 37 °C with shaking at 150 rpm for 18 h. The culture was adjusted to approximately 10^8 CFU/mL and inoculated (1%, v/v) into fresh NB containing OTA at 2 µg/mL. Cultures were incubated at 37 °C with shaking, and samples were withdrawn at 0, 6, 12, 24, 36, and 48 h. Bacterial growth was monitored by measuring optical density at 600 nm and by viable plate counts. At each time point, cells were removed by centrifugation (10,000 × g, 10 min, 4 °C), and residual OTA in the supernatant was quantified by HPLC. Uninoculated NB containing OTA served as the control. The OTA reduction rate was calculated as: reduction (%) = [(C₀ − Cₜ)/C₀] × 100, where C₀ is the OTA concentration in the control and Cₜ is that in the treated sample. Preparation of cell fractions and extracts To determine the OTA-reducing component, B. subtilis KU-153 cells were grown for 24 h in NB and separated into several fractions. Extracellular extract was obtained by centrifuging the culture (10,000 × g, 10 min) and filtering the supernatant through a 0.22 µm membrane. For the intracellular extract, the cell pellet was washed twice with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH 7.4), resuspended in PBS, and disrupted by sonication on ice (10 cycles of 30 s pulses with 30 s intervals). The lysate was centrifuged (12,000 × g, 15 min, 4 °C) and the supernatant filtered as above [4]. Viable cells were washed twice in PBS and resuspended to approximately 10^9 CFU/mL. Heat-killed cells were prepared by autoclaving the washed cell suspension at 121 °C for 15 min, and loss of viability was confirmed by absence of growth on nutrient agar. Each fraction (extracellular extract, intracellular extract, viable cells, and heat-killed cells) was mixed with OTA (2 µg/mL final concentration) and incubated at 37 °C for 24 h. Controls consisted of OTA in the corresponding buffer or medium without bacterial material. After incubation, samples were centrifuged and the supernatants analyzed for residual OTA. To assess whether reduction resulted from binding rather than degradation, pellets from heat-killed cell treatments were washed with PBS and extracted with methanol, and the recovered OTA was quantified. OTA reduction in artificially contaminated red wine Commercial red wine with no detectable OTA was purchased from a local retailer. Wine was spiked with OTA to a final concentration of 2 µg/mL and the pH was recorded (approximately 3.5). Heat-killed B. subtilis KU-153 cells (approximately 10^9 cells/mL) were added to the spiked wine and incubated at 25 °C for 24 h with gentle agitation. Spiked wine without cells served as control. Samples were then centrifuged (10,000 × g, 10 min) and filtered (0.22 µm) before HPLC analysis. All treatments were performed in triplicate. HPLC analysis of OTA OTA was quantified using an HPLC system equipped with a fluorescence detector (excitation 333 nm, emission 460 nm) [5]. Separation was achieved on a C18 reversed-phase column (250 × 4.6 mm, 5 µm) at 30 °C. The mobile phase consisted of acetonitrile:water:acetic acid (99:99:2, v/v/v) at a flow rate of 1.0 mL/min, and the injection volume was 20 µL. Wine and medium samples were diluted with mobile phase where necessary and filtered through 0.22 µm filters before injection. OTA was identified by comparing retention times with the standard and quantified using a calibration curve prepared from standard solutions (0.01–5 µg/mL; R² > 0.99). The limits of detection and quantification were calculated from signal-to-noise ratios of 3 and 10, respectively. Recovery was evaluated by spiking blank matrices at three levels and was within acceptable limits (85–105%). Statistical analysis All experiments were conducted in triplicate and repeated independently at least twice. Data are expressed as mean ± standard deviation. Differences among treatments were analyzed by one-way analysis of variance followed by Duncan's multiple range test using SPSS software, and differences were considered significant at p < 0.05. Identification of the isolate Strain KU-153 was isolated from Kimchi and selected for further study on the basis of its growth in the presence of OTA. Cells were Gram-positive, rod-shaped and endospore-forming, and colonies were opaque with irregular margins on nutrient agar. Analysis of the 16S rRNA gene sequence (approximately 1,450 bp) showed more than 99% similarity to reference sequences of Bacillus subtilis in the GenBank database. In the phylogenetic tree constructed by the neighbor-joining method, KU-153 clustered with B. subtilis type strains and was clearly separated from the closely related species B. amyloliquefaciens and B. licheniformis, supported by high bootstrap values. The isolate was therefore designated B. subtilis KU-153. This result agrees with earlier reports that B. subtilis is a frequent member of the microbiota of Korean fermented foods [1,2]. Growth kinetics and OTA reduction in culture medium The growth of B. subtilis KU-153 and the OTA content of the medium were monitored over 72 h in medium supplemented with OTA. The strain entered the exponential phase after a short lag of about 4 h and reached the stationary phase at approximately 24 h, with a maximum viable count of about 9 log CFU/mL. No OTA reduction was seen in the uninoculated control throughout the incubation, which showed that OTA was stable under the test conditions. In inoculated cultures the OTA concentration fell progressively, and the decrease was most rapid during the exponential and early stationary phases. By the end of the experiment viable cells had lowered the OTA concentration by about 22% relative to the control. Because the decrease coincided with bacterial growth, it was necessary to determine whether it was due to metabolic activity, such as enzymatic degradation, or to physical binding to the cells. Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) encompasses a broad spectrum of anomalies, from mild acetabular dysplasia and subluxation to complete, high-riding dislocation of the femoral head. Its reported incidence varies widely with geographic region, ethnic background, and diagnostic criteria, ranging from about 1 per 1,000 live births for dislocation to more than 10 per 1,000 when milder instability and radiographic dysplasia are included [1,2]. When the condition is recognized early, in the neonatal period or the first months of life, conservative treatment with a harness or abduction splint is successful in most cases [3]. In many settings, however, screening is incomplete, and children present late, after walking age, with established dislocation or residual dysplasia. Residual acetabular dysplasia may also persist despite initially successful reduction [4,5]. Untreated or inadequately treated DDH has well-documented consequences. Persistent acetabular insufficiency leads to abnormal load distribution across the joint, labral damage, and early osteoarthritis, and dysplasia is considered one of the most important causes of secondary hip arthrosis in young adults [6,7]. The spontaneous remodeling potential of the acetabulum declines with age, and beyond roughly 18 to 24 months, it is generally considered unreliable [8]. In children older than 2 years, closed reduction becomes increasingly unlikely to succeed, and open reduction, often combined with femoral shortening and a pelvic osteotomy, is usually required to obtain a stable concentric joint [9,10]. Several pelvic osteotomies have been proposed to correct acetabular deficiency in children. They are broadly divided into redirectional procedures, such as the Salter, Steel, Tönnis, and Ganz osteotomies, which rotate the acetabulum as a unit, and reshaping procedures, such as the Pemberton and Dega osteotomies, which hinge the acetabular roof through the iliac cortices and alter its volume and configuration [11–13]. Salter's innominate osteotomy provides anterior and lateral cover but requires a stable, concentric reduction and may increase intra-articular pressure through medialization and lengthening of the limb [14]. The Pemberton osteotomy is a pericapsular procedure that reduces acetabular volume, and it depends on a flexible triradiate cartilage [12]. Each technique has specific indications and limitations, and no single procedure has been shown to be superior across all patterns of dysplasia. The osteotomy described by Dega in 1953 is an incomplete transiliac osteotomy that runs from the outer cortex of the ilium toward the triradiate cartilage, leaving the inner cortex intact at the hinge [15]. The acetabular roof is then levered downward and held with a bone graft. Depending on the site of the deficiency, the osteotomy can be modified to increase anterior, lateral, or posterior coverage, which makes it attractive for the heterogeneous acetabular deformities seen in DDH, including those associated with neuromuscular disease [16,17]. Since its original description, the procedure has been refined by several authors, and it has gained renewed interest because of its versatility, relatively low morbidity, and the avoidance of internal fixation in many cases [18,19]. Nevertheless, most published reports on the Dega osteotomy are short or medium term, involve small or mixed series, or combine different etiologies, and the English-language literature on its long-term outcome in idiopathic DDH remains limited [20,21]. Long-term data are particularly important in DDH, since the ultimate goal of treatment is not only radiographic normalization in childhood but also preservation of a painless, functional hip into adulthood. Radiographic indices such as the acetabular index, center-edge angle, and Sharp angle may look satisfactory at skeletal maturity, yet degenerative changes may emerge decades later [22]. Avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head is the most feared complication of treatment, especially after open reduction, and it is a major determinant of poor outcome [23,24]. Other factors suggested to influence prognosis include age at surgery, degree of preoperative dislocation, the need for femoral osteotomy, residual acetabular dysplasia, and the quality of the reduction [9,25]. However, the relative weight of these predictors for the long-term survival of the hip after a Dega osteotomy has not been clearly established. Assessment of acetabular morphology and femoral head coverage has also evolved. Plain radiographs may be difficult to interpret in the young child because of variable ossification and projection, and computed tomography has been used to define the three-dimensional pattern of acetabular deficiency and to verify reduction [26]. Whether such imaging adds prognostic or operative value in children undergoing Dega osteotomy is uncertain. The purpose of this multicenter study was therefore to report the long-term clinical and radiographic results of the Dega osteotomy in children younger than 8 years with DDH, treated between 1988 and 2000 and followed for at least 13 years. We combined prospectively and retrospectively collected cases to analyze outcomes, complications, and the need for secondary surgery. We paid particular attention to the factors predictive of hip arthrosis and to the survival of the hip after the procedure, with the aim of clarifying the indications and expected long-term results of the Dega osteotomy in this population. This multicenter study was conducted at three tertiary pediatric orthopedic centers. It was approved by the institutional review board at each center, and informed consent was obtained from the parents or legal guardians of all prospectively enrolled patients. For retrospective cases, consent for the use of anonymized data was obtained in accordance with local regulations. The study adhered to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Patients All children younger than 8 years who underwent a Dega osteotomy for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) between January 1988 and October 2000 were considered eligible. Seventeen hips were identified retrospectively from hospital records and radiographic archives. Forty-one hips were enrolled prospectively after a standardized protocol was introduced. Inclusion criteria were: (1) a diagnosis of DDH, including acetabular dysplasia, subluxation, and complete dislocation; (2) age at surgery between 2 and 8 years; (3) a Dega osteotomy performed as part of the index procedure; and (4) a minimum follow-up of 13 years. Exclusion criteria were teratologic or neuromuscular dislocations, syndromic conditions (e.g., arthrogryposis, myelomeningocele), previous surgery on the affected hip, and incomplete clinical or radiographic records. Fifty-eight hips in 48 children (ten bilateral cases) met these criteria. Demographic data, laterality, age at diagnosis, previous treatment (such as Pavlik harness, closed reduction, or traction), and age at surgery were recorded. Dislocations were graded according to the Tönnis classification [1]. Surgical technique All procedures were performed or supervised by experienced pediatric orthopedic surgeons using the technique originally described by Dega [2] and modified by later authors [3]. Under general anesthesia, the hip was approached through an anterior iliofemoral (Smith-Petersen) incision. The iliac apophysis was split and the lateral wall of the ilium subperiosteally exposed down to the capsule. A curved incomplete osteotomy was made through the lateral cortex from just above the anterior inferior iliac spine toward the posterior limb of the triradiate cartilage, preserving the medial cortex and the continuity of the sciatic buttress. The acetabular roof was then levered downward and outward with a curved osteotome to redirect the acetabulum, and the osteotomy was held open with a wedge-shaped bone graft. The graft was taken from the iliac wing or, in some cases, was a bank allograft. Kirschner wires were used for fixation at the surgeon's discretion. Open reduction was performed through the same incision when the femoral head was dislocated, with capsulotomy, resection of the ligamentum teres and pulvinar, release of the transverse acetabular ligament, and capsulorrhaphy. Adductor tenotomy and psoas release were performed as needed. Femoral shortening, with or without derotation or varization, was added when the reduction was under tension or when excessive anteversion was present [4]. Postoperatively, the children were immobilized in a hip spica cast for 4–6 weeks in cases of open reduction or femoral osteotomy; others were mobilized according to surgeon preference. Weight bearing was progressively restored after radiographic evidence of union. Radiographic evaluation Standardized anteroposterior pelvic radiographs were obtained with the patient supine and the lower limbs in neutral rotation. Radiographs were taken preoperatively, immediately postoperatively, at 6 weeks or at cast removal, at 6-month intervals (and/or as clinically indicated) for 3 years, and then annually until the last follow-up. The following parameters were measured: acetabular index [5], center–edge angle of Wiberg [6], femoral head coverage, Sharp angle, and Shenton's line continuity. Hip congruency and joint space were assessed. Proximal femoral growth disturbance and avascular necrosis (AVN) were graded according to the Kalamchi and MacEwen classification [7]. Osteoarthritic changes at final follow-up were graded according to the Tönnis grading system [1], and the final radiographic result was classified using the criteria of Severin [8]. A single-cut computed tomographic (CT) scan through the acetabular roof was obtained in all prospectively enrolled patients to assess acetabular version, acetabular anteversion angle, and the position of the femoral head in relation to the acetabulum [9]. CT was used preoperatively and at the first postoperative follow-up to confirm concentric reduction and graft position. To reduce radiation exposure, a single low-dose axial slice at the level of the femoral heads was used. All radiographic measurements were made independently by two observers not involved in the surgery. Disagreements were resolved by consensus. Interobserver reliability was assessed with the intraclass correlation coefficient. Clinical evaluation Clinical examination was performed at each visit and at the final follow-up. Parameters included pain, gait (presence of limp and Trendelenburg sign), range of motion, limb length discrepancy, and activity level. Functional outcome was graded using the modified McKay criteria [10]. The final clinical outcome was dichotomized as favorable (excellent or good) or unfavorable (fair or poor). Hips were deemed to have failed if they had persistent pain, required a secondary surgical procedure (acetabuloplasty, arthroplasty, or other), or both. Complications, including redislocation, residual subluxation, infection, graft displacement, loss of correction, and AVN, were recorded. Outcome measures and predictive factors The primary outcome was hip survival, defined as the absence of a secondary operation (acetabuloplasty or arthroplasty) during follow-up, together with a favorable clinical result. Secondary outcomes included radiographic indices at final follow-up and the incidence of complications. Potential predictors of hip arthrosis and failure were analyzed: age at surgery, Tönnis grade, previous treatment, laterality, concomitant femoral osteotomy, preoperative and postoperative acetabular index, the correction achieved, postoperative center–edge angle, presence of AVN, and CT-derived acetabular version. Statistical analysis Continuous variables are presented as means with standard deviations and ranges, and categorical variables as frequencies and percentages. Comparisons between groups used Student's t test or the Mann–Whitney U test for continuous variables, and the chi-square or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables, as appropriate. Associations between potential predictors and hip arthrosis were evaluated with univariate analysis, and significant variables were entered into a multivariate logistic regression model. Hip survival was estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, with secondary surgery or pain as the endpoint, and groups were compared using the log-rank test [11]. Receiver operating characteristic curves were used to determine cut-off values for radiographic predictors. Because bilateral cases contribute correlated observations, sensitivity analyses were performed with one randomly selected hip per patient. A p value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed with SPSS software. A total of 58 hips in 48 children (38 girls, 10 boys) were included; 41 hips were assessed prospectively and 17 retrospectively. Ten patients underwent bilateral surgery. The mean age at operation was 4.6 years (range 2.0–7.9 years), and the mean follow-up was 17.8 years (range 13–25 years). All patients had reached skeletal maturity at the final evaluation, and none were lost to follow-up. Twenty-three hips were classified as dislocated, 21 as subluxated, and 14 as dysplastic with a centered femoral head. Eighteen hips had undergone previous treatment (closed reduction, bracing, or both) before the index procedure. Concomitant femoral shortening and derotation osteotomy was performed in 27 hips, and open reduction was performed in 24 hips. Radiographic outcomes The mean acetabular index improved from 35.2° (range 24–52°) preoperatively to 19.4° (range 8–31°) immediately postoperatively, a mean correction of 15.8° (p < 0.001). At the last follow-up the mean acetabular index was 8.1° in skeletally mature hips, based on the sourcil angle, and the mean center-edge angle was 27.3° (range 4–42°).
