Infectious illnesses such as influenza, common cold and diarrhea are among the most frequent causes of illness-related absenteeism among school children. In Denmark, as in many other high-income countries, children spend a large part of their waking hours in school, where they are in close daily contact with many peers in shared classrooms, canteens and toilet facilities. These settings facilitate the transmission of pathogens through direct contact, contaminated surfaces and the fecal-oral route. Infections acquired at school are rarely confined to the child: they spread to families and the wider community, causing parental absence from work, health care use and, in some cases, serious complications. Illness-related absenteeism may also affect children's learning, social participation and well-being, and repeated absence has been associated with poorer academic achievement and school drop-out. Hand hygiene is widely regarded as one of the most effective and least costly measures to prevent the spread of infectious diseases. Systematic reviews have concluded that hand washing with soap reduces the incidence of diarrhea and respiratory infections, and that school-based hand hygiene programs can reduce infection-related absenteeism. However, the evidence base has important limitations. Many studies have been conducted in low-income settings, where sanitation conditions, baseline infection burden and the feasibility of interventions differ substantially from those in Northern Europe. Studies from high-income countries are fewer, often small, and frequently based on a few classes or schools. Most have not been randomized, and those that were have often had short follow-up, limited statistical power, or lacked adjustment for clustering. Outcome measurement has also been a challenge, as many studies rely on school registers of absenteeism, which seldom distinguish illness from other causes, or on retrospective questionnaires, which are vulnerable to recall bias. Hand hygiene behavior in schools is shaped by more than knowledge. School toilets are frequently reported by children as unpleasant, dirty, lacking soap or paper, or offering little privacy, and many children avoid using them during the school day. Poor toilet conditions may lead to withholding of urine and stool, with possible consequences for children's comfort, concentration and health, and may reduce hand washing after toilet use. Moreover, hand washing before meals is typically not organized in Danish schools, and children seldom have routines for washing hands at times when it matters. Interventions that combine education with changes in the physical and organizational environment may therefore be more effective than education alone, because they address both motivation and opportunity. Despite this, to our knowledge no previous trials have included education about healthy and appropriate toilet behavior as part of the curriculum, and none have tested the effect of supplementary cleaning of school toilets during the school day. Another gap concerns the scale and methods of data collection. Large trials of infectious illness require frequent, valid and low-burden measurement of symptoms and absence. Traditional diaries and repeated questionnaires are costly and often suffer from low response and incomplete data. Short message service (SMS, text message) is widely used in Denmark and offers a possible way to collect repeated information directly from parents at short intervals, reducing recall problems. Yet the feasibility, response patterns and validity of SMS data collection in large school populations have rarely been examined. Against this background, the Hi Five study was designed to develop, implement and evaluate a multi-component school-based intervention aimed at improving hand hygiene and well-being and reducing infectious illness among Danish school children aged 6–15 years. The name reflects the five elements that guided the work: hygiene, infection, health, hand washing and well-being. The intervention consisted of three components: a curriculum component on hand hygiene, infection and toilet behavior; mandatory daily hand washing before lunch; and extra cleaning of school toilets during the school day. The intervention was developed in collaboration with teachers, school leaders, cleaning staff and children, and was informed by existing evidence and by principles for health promotion in school settings. The study was conducted as a cluster-randomized controlled trial in a national random sample of schools, with two intervention arms and a control arm, to allow assessment of the effect of the intervention package and of its components in a real-life school context. The primary aim was to reduce the prevalence of infections among children in intervention schools by 20% compared with control schools. Secondary aims were to assess effects on illness-related absenteeism, hand hygiene behavior, toilet behavior and well-being, and to evaluate the implementation process, including fidelity, dose and acceptability to pupils and staff. The purpose of this paper is to describe the development of the Hi Five intervention and the design of its effect and process evaluations. Publishing the design in detail promotes transparency, allows readers to distinguish between pre-specified and post hoc analyses, and offers guidance for researchers planning similar trials. The paper also describes the use of SMS text messages to collect data on infectious illness and absenteeism in a large study population, thereby providing a basis for future evaluation of this method. The Hi Five study was designed as a three-arm cluster-randomized controlled trial with schools as the unit of randomization. The study was conducted in Danish public schools and included pupils from preschool class to ninth grade (6–15 years). The intervention was developed in 2011–2012 and implemented from August 2012 to June 2013. Setting and recruitment A national random sample of schools was drawn from the Danish Ministry of Education register of public schools. Schools were eligible if they had at least two classes per grade level in the relevant grades, and special-needs schools were excluded. Selected schools were invited by letter and telephone to participate. Headmasters gave consent on behalf of the school, and parents or guardians received written information and could decline participation for their child. Forty-four schools agreed to participate. A total of 8,438 pupils were enrolled. Randomization After baseline data collection, schools were randomized by an independent statistician using computer-generated random numbers. Randomization was stratified by school size and geographical region. Schools were allocated to one of two intervention groups (n = 29 in total) or to a control group (n = 15). Because of the nature of the intervention, schools and teachers could not be blinded. Data analysts were blinded to allocation where possible. Intervention The intervention was developed through literature review, consultation with experts in hygiene, microbiology, health promotion and pedagogy, and pilot testing with teachers and pupils. It consisted of three components: 1. Curriculum component. Teaching materials covered hand hygiene, respiratory hygiene, and healthy and appropriate toilet behavior. Materials were tailored to three age groups (preschool to 3rd grade, 4th–6th grade, and 7th–9th grade) and comprised lesson plans, practical exercises, experiments and discussions. Teachers received written instructions and an introductory seminar. The materials were intended to be taught during three to four lessons per semester and integrated into subjects such as science and health education. 2. Mandatory hand washing. Pupils washed their hands with soap and water under teacher supervision before lunch each school day. Schools were supplied with soap and paper towels as needed. Teachers were instructed in the hand-washing procedure and in how to organize the routine in their class. 3. Extra toilet cleaning. Schools were provided with additional cleaning of pupil toilets during the school day, in addition to the standard daily cleaning. Cleaning was performed by school cleaning staff or contracted cleaners according to a written procedure. The two intervention arms differed in the components they received (curriculum plus hand washing, and curriculum plus hand washing plus extra toilet cleaning). Control schools continued usual practice and received no intervention materials during the study period, but were offered the materials after the trial ended. Data collection Baseline data were collected from December 2011 to April 2012, and follow-up data from December 2012 to April 2013. Questionnaires. Pupils completed web-based questionnaires at baseline and follow-up, with younger children assisted by teachers or parents. Questionnaires covered hand-washing behavior, toilet habits, school toilet satisfaction, and well-being, using validated instruments where available. Parents of the youngest pupils answered proxy questionnaires. Teachers and school leaders provided information on school characteristics, hygiene facilities and routines. Infectious illness and absenteeism. Data were collected through short message service (SMS, text message). Parents received a text message every other week during the data collection periods asking about their child’s illness and absence in the preceding period. Questions included whether the child had had diarrhea, vomiting, influenza-like illness or other infection, and the number of days absent due to illness. Non-responders received one reminder. Parents could also respond through a web-based form. Response rates were monitored to evaluate the usability of SMS for large-scale data collection. Hygiene facilities. Trained staff recorded the condition of school toilets and hand-washing facilities (e.g., availability of soap, paper towels, toilet paper, and cleanliness) using a standardized checklist. Process evaluation. Process data assessed reach, dose delivered, fidelity, and acceptability. Teachers completed logbooks and questionnaires on how many lessons were taught, how often hand washing was carried out, and barriers and facilitators. Selected schools were visited for observations and interviews with teachers, pupils, school leaders and cleaning staff. Soap and paper towel consumption was recorded. Outcomes The primary outcome was the proportion of pupils with infectious illness (diarrhea, vomiting or influenza-like illness) reported by SMS during follow-up. Secondary outcomes were illness-related absenteeism, self-reported hand-washing behavior, toilet behavior and satisfaction with school toilets, and well-being, including school satisfaction. Sample size The study aimed to detect a 20% relative reduction in the prevalence of infections in intervention schools compared with control schools. Sample size calculations accounted for clustering at school level, with an assumed intracluster correlation coefficient based on previous school studies, a significance level of 5% and a power of 80%. The number of schools and pupils enrolled was sufficient under these assumptions. Statistical analysis Analyses will follow the intention-to-treat principle, comparing each intervention arm and the combined intervention group with the control group. Multilevel regression models (logistic, Poisson or negative binomial, and linear, depending on the outcome) with random effects for school and class will be used to account for clustering, adjusting for baseline values, age, sex, and the stratification variables. Repeated SMS responses will be analyzed with generalized estimating equations or mixed models. Subgroup analyses will explore effects by age group, sex and baseline hygiene. Missing data will be handled using multiple imputation, with sensitivity analyses. Process data will be analyzed descriptively and used in dose–response analyses. Ethics According to Danish legislation, questionnaire-based studies do not require ethical committee approval. The study was approved by the Danish Data Protection Agency and registered in the ISRCTN registry (ISRCTN19287682). This is a design paper, so the results presented here describe the outcomes of the development, recruitment, randomization and baseline data collection phases. Effect estimates are not reported. Recruitment and randomization A national random sample of Danish schools was drawn from the register of public schools. Schools were invited by letter and telephone, and 44 schools agreed to participate. After stratification by school size and geographic region, schools were randomized by an independent statistician. Twenty-nine schools were allocated to one of two intervention groups and 15 to the control group. Intervention group 1 (n = 14 schools) received the curriculum component and the mandatory hand washing component. Intervention group 2 (n = 15 schools) received these two components plus extra cleaning of the school toilets during the school day. No schools withdrew between randomization and the start of the intervention. Study population In total, 8,438 children in grades 0 to 9 (ages 6 to 15 years) were enrolled across the 44 schools. This corresponded to 4,000 to 4,500 children in the two intervention groups combined and about 2,000 in the control group. Class sizes were comparable across the three arms, as were the proportions of girls and boys. The median school size was approximately 500 pupils (range 120 to 900). The distribution of schools across regions reflected the national distribution of the school population, and both urban and rural schools were represented. The proliferation of multi-homed devices, such as smartphones equipped with both WiFi and cellular interfaces and servers connected to several networks, has created an opportunity to use multiple network paths simultaneously. Traditional TCP binds a connection to a single pair of IP addresses and therefore a single path, leaving additional connectivity idle and offering no resilience when the active path degrades. Multipath TCP (MPTCP) [1], standardized by the IETF in RFC 6824 and later revised in RFC 8684, addresses this limitation. It extends TCP so that a single transport connection can be split into several subflows, each traversing a different path, while remaining transparent to applications. By aggregating the capacity of the available paths, MPTCP can improve throughput, increase robustness against link failures, and support seamless handover between access networks [2], [3]. Despite these benefits, MPTCP must still provide the same service guarantee as TCP: a reliable, in-order byte stream delivered to the application. Data are assigned a connection-level sequence number at the sender, transmitted over different subflows, and reordered at the receiver in a connection-level buffer before delivery. When paths differ in delay and bandwidth, as is typical for heterogeneous combinations such as WiFi and LTE, packets sent later on a fast path may arrive before packets sent earlier on a slow path. The receiver must then hold the early arrivals until the missing data come in. This out-of-order (OFO) arrival problem inflates the receive buffer occupancy, increases application-level delay and jitter, and can cause head-of-line blocking [4]. When the receive window is exhausted by buffered out-of-order data, the sender is stalled and the aggregate throughput may fall below that of the best single path [5], [6]. The problem is therefore not only a latency concern but also a fundamental obstacle to realizing the potential gains of multipath transport. The packet scheduler, which decides on which subflow each packet is transmitted, plays a central role in mitigating this problem. The default scheduler in the Linux MPTCP implementation, minRTT, selects the available subflow with the smallest smoothed round-trip time that has space in its congestion window [7]. Although simple, it ignores the bandwidth and delay differences that determine when a packet will actually arrive, and it performs poorly under path heterogeneity. Round-robin scheduling is even less informed, since it distributes packets evenly regardless of path quality. Numerous alternatives have been proposed. Some, such as DAPS [8], plan the allocation of packets to paths in advance, using delay and window information so that packets arrive in order. Others, such as BLEST [9], estimate whether using a slow subflow will block the connection-level send window and skip that subflow when blocking is likely. ECF [10] considers the completion time of the remaining data on fast and slow paths and may wait for the fast path rather than use a slow one. Other approaches reinject or retransmit packets on faster paths [11], or use learning-based techniques to adapt scheduling decisions [12]. While these schemes yield improvements in particular scenarios, many rely on round-trip time as a proxy for path delay. The use of RTT is problematic for in-order delivery. What determines the order of arrival at the receiver is the one-way, forward delay of each path, not the round-trip delay. RTT includes the reverse path delay, which may differ substantially from the forward delay owing to asymmetric routing, asymmetric link capacities, and different queueing on acknowledgments' return path. In cellular and WiFi networks, uplink and downlink characteristics are often markedly different, and ACK compression or delay can further distort RTT samples. A scheduler guided by RTT may thus mispredict arrival times and dispatch packets in an order that causes reordering. Moreover, delay alone is insufficient: the time a packet spends in the network also depends on the transmission time governed by path throughput and on queueing behind packets already sent on the same path. An effective scheduler must account jointly for forward delay and throughput differences. Motivated by these observations, we propose the forward-delay-based packet scheduling (FDPS) algorithm for MPTCP. FDPS estimates the forward delay of each subflow and combines it with an estimate of subflow throughput to predict the arrival time of a packet if it were sent on each path. The sender then dispatches packets so that those with earlier sequence numbers are expected to arrive earlier, and so that the arrival sequence at the receiver closely follows the transmission sequence. By making scheduling decisions on the basis of the forward path characteristics, FDPS reduces the dependence on potentially misleading round-trip measurements and limits the buffering needed for reordering. The main contributions of this paper are as follows. First, we analyze why RTT-based and delay-agnostic scheduling lead to out-of-order arrivals in heterogeneous multipath environments. Second, we design FDPS, which uses estimated forward delay and throughput differences among paths to schedule packets. Third, we evaluate FDPS through simulations under a variety of network conditions, varying bandwidth, delay, and asymmetry, and compare it with several existing schedulers. The results show that FDPS substantially improves in-order arrival at the receiver, reducing the reordering burden relative to the baselines. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on MPTCP scheduling. Section III describes the design of FDPS. Section IV presents the simulation setup and results. Section V concludes the paper and outlines future work. FDPS operates at the sender of an MPTCP connection. It estimates the forward delay and throughput of each subflow and uses these estimates to decide which subflow carries each packet, so that packets reach the receiver in the order of their data sequence numbers. The subsections below cover the system model, forward delay estimation, the scheduling rule, and the simulation setup. System Model We consider an MPTCP connection with N subflows, indexed i = 1,…,N, between a sender and a receiver, following the architecture in RFC 6824 [1]. Each subflow i has its own congestion window cwndi, smoothed round-trip time srtti, and subflow-level sequence space. A connection-level data sequence number (DSN) orders the byte stream across subflows. The scheduler assigns each DSN-mapped segment to a subflow that has available congestion window space. The receiver reorders segments in a shared receive buffer before delivering them to the application. A segment arriving with a DSN greater than the next expected one is out of order and must wait in the buffer. This causes head-of-line blocking and, when the buffer is limited, throttles throughput [2], [3]. For subflow i, the one-way forward delay Di is the time from transmission at the sender to arrival at the receiver. It consists of propagation delay pi, transmission delay s/Bi for a segment of size s on a path of bandwidth Bi, and queueing delay qi: Di = pi + s/Bi + qi. Using srtti/2 as a proxy for Di is common [4], but it fails on asymmetric paths and when reverse-path congestion inflates ACK delays. FDPS therefore estimates the forward component directly. Forward Delay Estimation The receiver stamps each arriving segment with its local clock and returns the stamp in a TCP option carried on the ACK, in the manner of the TCP timestamp option [5]. The sender records the send time Ts of each segment. Clocks are not assumed to be synchronized. Instead, the sender computes a relative forward delay, di(k) = Tr(k) − Ts(k), which equals Di(k) plus an unknown constant clock offset δ. For subflow i, the sender keeps the minimum observed value di^min, which approximates pi + s/Bi + δ when queues are empty. The offset δ is the same for all subflows because it is a property of the host pair. Differences between subflows are therefore unaffected by δ. The queueing-inclusive delay of the k-th sample is then D̂i(k) = di(k) − dmin, where dmin = minj dj^min. The result is a delay estimate of each path relative to the fastest one. The estimate is smoothed with an exponentially weighted moving average, D̄i ← (1 − α) D̄i + α D̂i(k), with α = 1/8, following the srtt convention [6]. Samples from retransmitted segments are discarded to avoid ambiguity. Throughput is estimated per subflow as the ratio cwndi/srtti, which gives the sending rate Ri the congestion controller currently permits. This is smoothed over a window of the most recent ACKs to dampen short-term oscillation. Scheduling Rule Suppose the scheduler is about to send a segment of size s on subflow i at time t. Its expected arrival time is Ai = t + D̄i + Qi/Ri, where Qi is the amount of data already queued or in flight on subflow i beyond what has been acknowledged, and Qi/Ri is the expected additional wait. The scheduler seeks to give consecutive DSNs arrival times that are monotonically non-decreasing. FDPS maintains Alast, the largest expected arrival time among segments already scheduled. For the next segment, it builds the candidate set C = { i : cwndi − inflighti ≥ s }. It then selects the subflow whose expected arrival time is closest to, but not earlier than, Alast: i = argmin{i∈C, Ai ≥ Alast} (Ai − Alast). This choice keeps the segment from overtaking earlier ones. If no subflow satisfies the constraint, because all candidates would deliver earlier than Alast, the scheduler selects the subflow with the largest Ai, which minimizes the reordering. If C is empty, transmission waits until an ACK opens a window. After the assignment, Alast is updated to A{i} and Q{i} is increased by s. Because a fast subflow may often be blocked by its window while a slow subflow is idle, FDPS also uses the throughput estimates. A slow subflow is assigned a segment only if its expected arrival is no later than that of a faster subflow after it becomes available. This means that, when delay differences are large, the slow path is used only for segments whose DSNs are far enough ahead of those on the fast path. In practice, the slow subflow receives earlier DSNs than the fast subflow in proportion to the delay gap D̄slow − D̄fast multiplied by Rfast. This is the same principle used by delay-aware schedulers such as DAPS [7], but here it is driven by measured forward delays instead of RTT ratios. Retransmissions are sent on the subflow with the smallest Ai, and opportunistic retransmission and penalization [3] are retained when the receive window blocks progress. Simulation Setup We implemented FDPS in the ns-3 simulator using the MPTCP module [8]. The topology contains one sender and one receiver connected by two to four disjoint paths. Each path has its own bottleneck link. Bandwidth is varied from 1 to 50 Mbps and one-way propagation delay from 10 to 200 ms, to create both homogeneous and heterogeneous conditions. Bottleneck queue sizes equal the bandwidth-delay product, and random loss rates range from 0 to 2%. Background TCP cross traffic is added in selected scenarios to create dynamic queueing delay. Each subflow uses the coupled congestion control algorithm LIA [9]. The application is a bulk transfer lasting 100 s, and the receive buffer is set to 64 KB–2 MB. We compare FDPS with the default minimum-RTT scheduler [10], round-robin, and DAPS [7]. The performance metrics are: 1. the number of out-of-order packets at the receiver, measured as the fraction of segments arriving with DSN greater than expected; 2. the reordering delay, i.e. the time a segment waits in the receive buffer before delivery; 3. the maximum receive buffer occupancy; 4. the aggregate goodput. Each scenario is repeated 20 times with different random seeds, and we report means with 95% confidence intervals. We evaluated FDPS through simulations in the ns-2 network simulator with the MPTCP module. The topology consisted of one multihomed sender and one multihomed receiver connected by two disjoint paths, with a shared 1 Mbps bottleneck for each path where background traffic was introduced. We compared FDPS with three schedulers: the default round-robin (RR) scheduler, the lowest-RTT-first (minRTT) scheduler used in the Linux MPTCP implementation [1], and a delay-aware scheduler based on round-trip estimates (DAPS) [2]. Forensic entomology uses insects associated with decomposing remains to answer questions of medico-legal importance, most commonly to estimate the time elapsed since death, or post-mortem interval (PMI) [1,2]. Because insects colonize a corpse soon after death, the age of the oldest insects found on the remains can provide a minimum estimate of PMI, and this approach is particularly valuable once the usefulness of medical methods has declined, typically after the first two or three days post mortem [3]. Age estimation relies on the strong dependence of insect development on temperature. Developmental data obtained under controlled conditions are used to build models, such as isomorphen diagrams, isomegalen diagrams, or thermal summation models, which are then applied to specimens sampled at a crime scene together with temperature records from the site [4,5]. The accuracy of such estimates is limited by several sources of error. These include differences between the temperature at the scene and that recorded at the nearest weather station, the effects of larval aggregations and heat generation, geographic variation among populations, and the variability of development inherent to the species [6,7]. Even under constant laboratory conditions, individuals of the same cohort differ markedly in the time required to complete development, and this variation is carried into the confidence limits of age estimates, which may be broad enough to reduce their usefulness in casework [8]. Methods that explain part of this variation, and thereby narrow the prediction error, are therefore of considerable interest. One potential source of information is body size. In insects, size at emergence reflects the growth history of an individual, and is affected by temperature, food quality and quantity, and larval density [9,10]. Body size is often correlated with development time, although the direction and strength of the relationship vary among species and conditions. In many insects, individuals that develop slowly attain larger sizes, whereas in others rapid development under favourable conditions yields large individuals [11,12]. If size is consistently related to the thermal requirements of development, then it might serve as a proxy for physiological age. Size-based corrections are not unknown in forensic entomology, as the length and mass of larvae are routinely used to estimate age, but they have rarely been applied to adults. Adult size is a stable and easily measured trait, remains constant after sclerotization, and can be recorded from specimens preserved in the field, which suggests that it could improve age predictions for insects that colonize remains late in decomposition. Beetles are a major component of the fauna of decomposing remains and are especially useful when remains are at advanced stages of decay and fly evidence is absent or ambiguous [13,14]. However, the development of forensically relevant beetles has received much less attention than that of blow flies, and models for beetle age estimation are comparatively few [15]. Among them, the rove beetle Creophilus maxillosus (Linnaeus, 1758) (Staphylinidae) is a large, widely distributed predatory species, occurring across the Holarctic and introduced to other regions [16]. Adults and larvae are frequently recorded on carcasses and human cadavers, where they feed mainly on fly eggs and larvae and on other small invertebrates, and they arrive during the bloated and decay stages [17,18]. Its regular occurrence in forensic cases, and its record of use in PMI estimation, make it a good candidate for improving developmental models [19]. Previous studies have described its development at constant temperatures and provided thermal requirements, but they did not evaluate how variation among individuals could be reduced [20,21]. The thermal summation approach expresses development as a constant amount of accumulated degree-days (K) above a lower developmental threshold (t0) required to complete a stage [22]. Under this model, K is assumed to be the same for all individuals, and age is estimated by dividing the accumulated thermal units by the temperature excess over the threshold. If K in fact varies with body size, using a single mean value will introduce error that could be removed by using size-specific values. Because sexual size dimorphism and sex-specific growth patterns are common in beetles, it is also possible that the relationship between size and K differs between males and females, and that sex-specific models might further increase accuracy [23]. Sex can be determined easily in adult C. maxillosus, so such models would be feasible in practice. Here we test the concept that size at emergence can be used to predict the physiological age of adult C. maxillosus and thereby improve the accuracy of age estimates. We first determined, using a laboratory rearing experiment, the relationship between thermal summation value needed for emergence and beetle size, expressed as body length. We then built general, sex-specific, and size-based models and compared their predictive performance in an independent validation study, by testing whether K estimated from beetle size was closer to the true value than K from the general thermal summation model. We hypothesized that larger beetles would have lower K values and that the best predictions would be obtained from sex-specific models using body length as the predictor. Beetles used in the experiments originated from a laboratory colony established from adults of C. maxillosus collected with baited pitfall traps in a mixed forest near Poznań, western Poland. Adults were kept in plastic containers (20 × 15 × 10 cm) filled with moist peat, at 22 °C and a 16:8 h light:dark photoperiod. They were fed minced pork and live blowfly larvae (Lucilia sericata), which also served as oviposition and larval food substrates [1,2]. Eggs were collected daily and transferred to separate containers to obtain cohorts of known age. Individuals from the second laboratory generation were used in all experiments to reduce the influence of field-derived maternal effects. Development study (model building) Newly hatched larvae were randomly assigned to one of four constant temperatures (15, 18, 21 and 24 °C ± 0.5 °C) in incubators with a 16:8 h light:dark photoperiod. At each temperature, larvae were reared individually in 250 ml containers with a 5 cm layer of moist peat and fed ad libitum with minced pork and fly larvae, replaced every two days to avoid decay and mold. Sample size at each temperature was 60 individuals at the start of the experiment. Containers were inspected twice daily (08:00 and 20:00), and the dates of moulting, wandering, pupation and adult emergence were recorded. Development time to emergence was calculated from egg hatching to the first appearance of the adult beetle, expressed in hours and converted to days. Newly emerged adults were left for 24 h to allow cuticle hardening and were then killed by freezing at −20 °C. Body length was measured as the distance from the anterior margin of the head to the tip of the abdomen, with the abdomen in a natural, non-extended position, using a stereomicroscope equipped with a calibrated digital camera and image analysis software (accuracy 0.01 mm). Pronotum width was also measured as a secondary size index. Each beetle was measured twice and the mean was used; measurement repeatability, assessed with the intraclass correlation coefficient, exceeded 0.95. Sex was determined by examining the terminal abdominal sternites [3]. Dry body mass was not used because it requires destructive drying that would be unsuitable for a forensic protocol. Thermal summation The thermal summation value (K, in degree-days, °D) required for emergence was calculated for each individual using the linear degree-day model [4]: K = D(T − T₀), where D is development time in days, T is rearing temperature and T₀ is the lower developmental threshold. T₀ was estimated by linear regression of development rate (1/D) against temperature, as the x-intercept, using mean development rates of all individuals at each temperature [4,5]. Individual K values were then computed using this T₀. Effects of temperature on development time and survival were tested with ANOVA and chi-square tests, respectively. Relationship between K and beetle size The relationship between K and beetle length was analysed with linear regression. Models were fitted for (i) all individuals pooled, (ii) males and (iii) females separately. Sex, length and their interaction were tested with analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) to determine whether slopes and intercepts differed between sexes. Temperature was included as a covariate to verify that the K–size relationship was not an artefact of rearing temperature. Residuals were inspected for normality (Shapiro–Wilk test) and homoscedasticity, and the Box–Cox transformation was applied when assumptions were violated. Alternative models using pronotum width as a predictor were compared with length-based models using Akaike's information criterion (AIC). Validation study An independent group of beetles was reared to test the accuracy of age estimates. Larvae from different parental pairs than those used for model building were reared at three constant temperatures (16, 19 and 23 °C) and at one fluctuating regime (mean 19 °C, range 14–24 °C, changing in a sinusoidal pattern), with 40 individuals per treatment and the same rearing protocol. Development time, sex and body length at emergence were recorded as before. For each validation individual, the true K was calculated from its known development time and temperature history; under fluctuating temperatures, K was obtained by summing hourly degree-hours above T₀ and dividing by 24. Age at emergence was then estimated in a forensic-like manner using four approaches: (1) the general model, in which the mean K of the model-building dataset was used for all beetles; (2) a model regressing K on length for pooled sexes; (3) a sex-specific model regressing K on length; and (4) a model using pronotum width. Estimated K was converted to estimated development time by dividing by the mean temperature above T₀. Accuracy was expressed as the absolute error between estimated and true K (|Kest − Ktrue|) and as the relative error (percentage of true K). Statistical analysis Absolute errors of the different approaches were compared with the Friedman test followed by Wilcoxon signed-rank post hoc tests with Bonferroni correction, because errors were not normally distributed and observations were paired within individuals. Differences among temperature treatments were assessed using Kruskal–Wallis tests. Mean error and the proportion of estimates within 10% of the true value were also reported. All tests were two-tailed with α = 0.05. Analyses were performed in R version 4.2 [6], with the packages car, MASS and ggplot2. Values are given as mean ± SD unless otherwise stated. Development time and thermal requirements Beetles completed development from egg to adult emergence at all tested temperatures, although survival varied among treatments. Total development time decreased markedly with rising temperature, from a mean of approximately 60 days at the lowest temperature to roughly 21 days at the highest. The relationship between development rate and temperature was linear within the intermediate range, and the general thermal summation model, fitted to pooled data for both sexes, yielded a lower developmental threshold (t0) of 9.4 ± 0.8 °C and a mean thermal constant (K) of 262 ± 11 degree-days (DD) [see Ikemoto and Takai, 2000, for the fitting method]. Despite this clear temperature dependence, individual variation in development time within each temperature was considerable. The coefficient of variation in K ranged from 8% to 17%, and the range of individual K values within a single temperature often exceeded 60 DD. Applying the general model to estimate age of emerging adults would therefore produce relatively large errors, especially for individuals at the extremes of the distribution. Body size at emergence Beetle length at emergence varied from 11.2 to 19.6 mm (mean 15.4 ± 1.8 mm). Females were on average slightly larger than males (15.8 vs. 15.0 mm; t-test, P < 0.01), although the size ranges overlapped almost completely. Temperature had a significant effect on size: beetles reared at intermediate temperatures tended to be larger than those from the extremes (ANOVA, P < 0.001), though temperature explained only a small part of the total variance in length. Sex and temperature did not significantly interact in their effect on body length (P > 0.05). Relationship between thermal summation value and size Thermal summation value required for emergence was negatively correlated with beetle length (Pearson r = −0.62, P < 0.001, n = 214). Crowdsourcing has become a standard tool for tasks that are difficult to automate, such as labeling images, transcribing audio, and judging relevance [1, 2]. Its success rests largely on decomposing work into short, well-defined microtasks that anonymous workers can complete quickly and independently. Many problems of interest, however, are complex and open-ended, and they do not decompose naturally. Asking a worker to "build a map of what causes what" or "describe the structure of a domain" typically yields low-quality, redundant, or abandoned contributions, because workers favor brief, repetitive tasks over sustained, creative effort [3, 4]. Designing mechanisms that elicit high-quality structured knowledge from many independent workers, while keeping each contribution small, remains a central challenge. We study one important instance of this challenge: using the crowd to explore large networks whose topology is not known in advance and can only be revealed through human judgment. Networks of this type arise in many settings, including social ties, hyperlinked information, concept hierarchies, and knowledge graphs [5, 6]. Exhaustive querying is infeasible, since the number of candidate node pairs grows quadratically with the number of nodes, and the underlying networks are typically sparse. Efficient exploration therefore requires directing limited worker effort toward the parts of the network most likely to contain meaningful edges, without relying on workers coordinating with each other or sustaining long sessions. We focus on the network of causal attributions, in which a directed edge from one concept to another indicates that the first is perceived as a cause of the second. Causal knowledge underlies explanation, prediction, planning, and decision making [7, 8], and a large-scale map of causal beliefs would be valuable for several reasons. It could support automated reasoning and question answering, supply background knowledge for causal inference from observational data [9], and allow study of how people perceive and organize causes and effects. Existing resources are limited. Curated knowledge bases cover few causal relations, and automatic extraction from text suffers from the implicit, ambiguous, and context-dependent ways causality is expressed in language [10, 11]. Causal relationships are also more subjective than taxonomic ones: people disagree about strength, directness, and even direction, which makes the crowd both an appealing and a demanding source of data. Our contributions are threefold. First, we run experiments on Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) examining how workers propose and validate individual causal relationships. We compare alternative question formats and assess how reliably workers generate plausible causes and effects of a given concept and how consistently other workers confirm them. These experiments establish which microtasks yield trustworthy edges and inform the design of the larger system. Second, we introduce a method that allows independent crowd workers to explore large networks. The core of the method, which we call Iterative Pathway Refinement, builds on a simple idea: each worker receives a pathway, a chain of concepts linked by previously collected causal edges, and performs a small modification such as inserting, replacing, or extending a step. The refined pathway is then passed to subsequent workers. Because every worker sees the accumulated work of predecessors, the process concentrates effort on promising regions of the network and gradually discovers longer and more intricate causal chains, yet each task remains a short microtask requiring no direct communication. This design is related to iterative and sequential crowd workflows [12, 13] but is tailored to graph exploration, and we provide a theoretical analysis showing that it explores the network efficiently under a natural model of worker behavior. We also evaluate the method on synthetic networks with known structure, where discovered edges can be compared against ground truth and against baselines such as random and breadth-first querying. Third, we deploy the method on AMT to extract a large-scale causal attribution network and analyze it from several perspectives. We examine its structural properties, including degree distributions, connectivity, hubs, and the prevalence of cycles and feedback, and compare them with those of other real-world networks [14]. We also study the workers who built it, characterizing their activity patterns, the distribution of effort across participants, the quality and novelty of their contributions, and the efficiency of the process in terms of edges discovered per unit of cost. These analyses show how workers navigate the space of concepts and reveal characteristics of causal perception, such as which kinds of concepts act as common causes or common effects and how causal chains tend to be organized around abstract versus concrete events. The resulting data bear on both crowdsourcing and the study of causality. For crowdsourcing, our results show that a carefully structured sequence of independent microtasks can accomplish exploration that would otherwise require sustained, coordinated effort. For research on causality, the network offers an empirical window on lay causal beliefs, which may complement formal causal discovery methods and help prioritize hypotheses for testing [9, 15]. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We first review related work on crowdsourcing complex tasks, network exploration, and causal knowledge acquisition. We then describe the worker experiments, present Iterative Pathway Refinement with its theoretical analysis and synthetic evaluation, and report the deployment on AMT together with the analysis of the resulting network and worker behavior. We conclude with limitations and directions for future work. We conducted all experiments on Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT). Workers were restricted to those with an approval rate above 95% and at least 500 completed tasks, and were paid at rates calibrated to approximately the U.S. federal minimum wage. Workers could complete any number of tasks, but each task was independent and no worker saw the global network. Microtask Design We studied two elementary microtasks. In the proposal task, a worker is shown a focal event or phenomenon (e.g., "obesity") and asked to type, in free text, a direct cause (backward direction) or a direct effect (forward direction). In the validation task, a worker is shown a candidate pair (A, B) and asked whether A directly causes B, with response options of yes, no, or unsure. Each pair was presented in random order and direction to control for position effects. Instructions defined "direct" causation as the absence of an intermediate step the worker would consider necessary to mention, and included worked examples and a brief qualification quiz. To test how proposal and validation behave, we ran a pilot with 50 seed concepts drawn from news headlines and encyclopedic health, economic, and environmental topics. Each seed received 10 proposals per direction. Free-text responses were normalized by lowercasing, removing stop words, and lemmatizing, then merged when their embedding cosine similarity exceeded 0.85 [1] and a manual audit confirmed equivalence. Each proposed relationship was validated by five independent workers, and we measured agreement using Fleiss' kappa [2]. We compared proposal framing (open-ended versus suggestion-assisted) and validation framing (binary versus three-option) in between-subject conditions, assigning workers randomly. Iterative Pathway Refinement Exploring a large network by asking workers to enumerate it is infeasible, as no worker can hold the whole structure and effort concentrates on popular nodes. Iterative Pathway Refinement (IPR) instead builds the network through independent microtasks that each extend or refine a pathway. The procedure maintains a pool of pathways, each a sequence of nodes v₀ → v₁ → … → vk linked by validated causal edges. At each step: 1. Selection. A pathway is sampled from the pool with probability proportional to a priority score that favors short pathways and nodes with few observed neighbors, balancing exploration and exploitation. 2. Extension. A worker is shown the terminal node and asked to propose a direct effect (or, for backward exploration, a cause). The proposal is appended to the pathway. 3. Refinement. A different worker is shown the pathway endpoints and asked whether intermediate steps are missing; if so, they insert a node between two adjacent nodes, which splits one edge into two. 4. Validation. Each new edge is validated by independent workers, and is added to the network only if a majority endorses it. Rejected edges are recorded and not re-queried. Because each task depends only on the current pathway state, workers need not coordinate. Refinement permits discovery of mediating structure that single-step proposals would miss, and the pool grows adaptively toward under-explored regions. We analyzed IPR as an exploration process on a hidden graph G with an edge oracle subject to noise. Under the assumptions that worker proposals sample neighbors of the queried node with probabilities bounded below by pmin and validation errors are independent with rate ε < 0.5, we derived bounds on the expected number of queries needed to recover all nodes within distance d of a seed, and showed that majority voting over m validators drives the false-edge probability down exponentially in m [3]. The priority rule ensures that each node's neighborhood is sampled at a rate bounded away from zero, which yields coverage guarantees comparable to coupon-collector arguments [4]. Synthetic Evaluation We evaluated IPR on synthetic networks of 1,000 to 100,000 nodes generated from Erdős–Rényi, Barabási–Albert [5], and stochastic block models, with directed edges. Simulated workers proposed a neighbor drawn from the true neighborhood with a probability of success s (0.6–0.95) and otherwise proposed a random node, and validated edges with accuracy 1−ε (ε ∈ {0.05, 0.1, 0.2}). We compared IPR with (a) random-edge querying, (b) breadth-first expansion, and (c) a single-step proposal baseline without refinement. Metrics were edge recall, precision, and the number of queries needed to reach 80% recall. Each configuration was repeated 50 times, and we report means with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Large-Scale Deployment We deployed IPR on AMT starting from 100 seed concepts spanning health, environment, economics, politics, and technology. The deployment ran for several weeks and collected proposals, refinements, and validations. Each candidate edge received at least three validations, with a fourth and fifth added when the first three disagreed. We retained edges with majority endorsement. Attention checks, consisting of known true and known false causal pairs, were interleaved at a rate of 5%, and workers failing more than 30% were excluded and their responses discarded. Network and Worker Analyses We characterized the resulting network using degree distributions (fit with maximum-likelihood power-law estimation [6]), weakly and strongly connected components, clustering, path lengths, and cycle frequency. Community structure was identified with the Louvain algorithm [7]. To study causal perception, we examined reciprocal edges, transitivity of causal judgments (whether A→B and B→C implies endorsement of A→C), and the relationship between node abstraction and degree. For worker behavior, we computed tasks per worker, session length, time per task, agreement with the majority, and the yield of new nodes and edges per unit of payment. We used Mann–Whitney U tests and Spearman correlations, with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons. Efficiency was defined as validated edges per dollar and compared across task types and exploration depths. Ethics The study involved no personally identifiable information beyond anonymized AMT worker IDs, which were hashed before analysis. Participation was voluntary and workers could abandon tasks at any time. We first report results from the experiments on individual causal relationships, then evaluate Iterative Pathway Refinement (IPR) on synthetic networks, and finally describe the causal attribution network obtained from AMT and the behavior of the workers who built it. Proposing and validating individual causal relations. In the proposal experiment, 300 workers each provided causes or effects for a set of seed concepts. Workers produced valid, interpretable responses in 91% of cases, and responses were highly skewed toward a small set of common concepts: the ten most frequent responses accounted for 18% of all proposals. Proposals of effects were generated more quickly than proposals of causes (median 14 s versus 19 s; Mann-Whitney U, p < 0.01), suggesting that forward reasoning is cognitively easier than backward reasoning, consistent with prior work on causal perception [1,2]. In the validation experiment, each proposed relation was rated by five independent workers. Agreement among raters was moderate (Fleiss' κ = 0.52), and majority-vote validation retained 74% of proposed edges. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, systemic autoimmune disease characterized by inflammation of the synovial joints, progressive destruction of articular cartilage and bone, and substantial disability if inadequately treated [1]. The autoimmune nature of RA is reflected in the production of a broad spectrum of autoantibodies, including rheumatoid factor directed against the Fc portion of IgG and, more specifically, anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA) [2,3]. ACPA are detectable in sera and synovial fluids of approximately 60–70% of RA patients, may appear years before clinical onset, and are associated with a more severe, erosive disease course. ACPA seropositivity is therefore incorporated into the current classification criteria for RA [4,5]. Citrullination and ACPA in RA Citrullination is a post-translational modification in which peptidylarginine residues are converted to peptidylcitrulline by calcium-dependent peptidylarginine deiminases (PADs). This conversion removes a positive charge, alters the hydrogen-bonding capacity and isoelectric point of the protein, and can promote unfolding, enhanced proteolytic susceptibility, and the generation of neoepitopes that escape immunological tolerance [6,7]. Citrullination occurs physiologically during apoptosis, differentiation, and inflammation, and is therefore not unique to RA. However, in the genetically susceptible host, particularly carriers of HLA-DRB1 shared-epitope alleles, citrullinated peptides are presented with higher affinity to CD4+ T cells, which supports B cell activation and ACPA production [8,9]. Smoking and other mucosal insults, as well as periodontal infection, have been proposed as triggers of citrullination that precede joint involvement [10]. A growing number of citrullinated autoantigens have been identified in the rheumatoid joint, including fibrin(ogen), vimentin, α-enolase, and type II collagen [11–14]. Citrullinated proteins and PAD enzymes are abundant in the inflamed synovium, and ACPA can form immune complexes with these antigens, activating complement and Fc receptor-bearing cells and thereby amplifying inflammation [15]. ACPA reactive with cartilage-derived citrullinated epitopes have also been reported to induce or enhance arthritis in experimental models, suggesting that antigens within the cartilage itself may be pathogenically relevant targets [16]. Aggrecan as an autoantigen in arthritis The large aggregating proteoglycan (PG) aggrecan is one of the most abundant macromolecules of articular cartilage, where it provides compressive resistance through its highly charged glycosaminoglycan chains. Aggrecan comprises three globular domains (G1, G2, and G3) and an extended interglobular and glycosaminoglycan-attachment region. The N-terminal G1 domain binds hyaluronan and link protein, anchoring the molecule within the extracellular matrix [17]. Aggrecan has long been recognized as an arthritogenic autoantigen. Immunization of BALB/c mice with human cartilage PG induces a progressive, erosive polyarthritis (proteoglycan-induced arthritis, PGIA) that resembles human RA, with autoantibody production and T cell-dependent disease [18,19]. In addition, T cell responses to human PG, and in particular to peptides from the G1 domain, have been detected in RA patients [20,21]. Importantly, more recent studies demonstrated that T cells from RA patients respond to citrullinated aggrecan peptides, and that citrullinated epitopes within the G1 domain bind with high affinity to shared-epitope-containing HLA-DR molecules [22,23]. Citrullinated PG epitopes can also be recognized by T cells in the SKG and PGIA mouse models [24]. These findings suggest that citrullinated aggrecan may serve as a joint-specific target of both T and B cell responses. This could help explain the localization of the autoimmune attack to the joints, despite the systemic distribution of ACPA and of citrullinating enzymes. Knowledge gap and aims Despite this evidence, a fundamental question remains unanswered: whether the aggrecan molecule is actually citrullinated in vivo in human cartilage. Most studies have employed synthetic citrullinated peptides or in vitro modified proteins, which establish the immunological potential of citrullinated aggrecan but do not demonstrate the presence of the modified protein in the tissue. Cartilage is avascular and has low cellular density, and its matrix proteins turn over slowly, which could favor the accumulation of post-translational modifications. Moreover, it is unknown whether citrullinated PG (CitPG) occurs in normal cartilage or only in diseased tissue, which fragments of the molecule carry the modification, and whether its distribution differs between osteoarthritis (OA) and RA. Clarifying these points is essential for judging whether CitPG can serve as a target for ACPA, form local immune complexes, and contribute to the initiation or perpetuation of joint inflammation. In the present study, we therefore sought to determine whether citrullinated aggrecan is present in human articular cartilage and to characterize its molecular features. We used sera from ACPA-positive RA patients to probe PG purified from normal cartilage and cartilage extracts from OA and RA patients, and we identified the PG fragments, particularly those containing the G1 and G3 domains, that carry citrulline-containing epitopes. We confirmed the citrullination status of an in vitro citrullinated recombinant human G1 domain (rhG1) using both antibody-based and chemical detection, and used molecular modeling to explore the potential sites of citrullination within this domain. Finally, we quantified CitPG-specific serum autoantibodies by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay and compared the immunohistochemical localization of CitPG in OA and RA cartilage. Together, these approaches aim to establish CitPG as a bona fide in vivo cartilage autoantigen and to define its potential relevance to ACPA-mediated autoimmunity in RA. Human cartilage specimens and sera Human articular cartilage was obtained with institutional review board approval and written informed consent. Normal cartilage came from tissue donors with no history of joint disease. OA cartilage came from patients undergoing total knee replacement, and RA cartilage came from patients undergoing joint replacement surgery. Specimens were kept at −80 °C until use. Serum samples were collected from RA patients who fulfilled the 2010 ACR/EULAR classification criteria [1]. Anti-citrullinated protein antibody (ACPA) status was determined with a commercial anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP2) ELISA, using the manufacturer's cut-off. Samples were classified as ACPA+ or ACPA−. Sera from ACPA− healthy individuals or OA patients served as controls. All sera were aliquoted and stored at −80 °C, and repeated freeze-thaw cycles were avoided. Extraction and purification of proteoglycan Cartilage was pulverized in liquid nitrogen and extracted with 4 M guanidine hydrochloride in 50 mM sodium acetate buffer (pH 5.8) containing a protease inhibitor cocktail, for 48 h at 4 °C [2]. The extracts were dialyzed against distilled water and then against buffer. Proteoglycan (PG) was purified by CsCl density-gradient ultracentrifugation (starting density 1.5 g/mL; 40,000 rpm, 48 h, 15 °C), and the high-density (A1) fraction was collected [2]. Aliquots were deglycosylated with chondroitinase ABC, keratanase and endo-β-galactosidase (0.01–0.1 U/mg PG, 37 °C, 6 h) to expose the core protein and its fragments. Protein concentration was measured by the BCA assay. Recombinant human G1 domain and in vitro citrullination The recombinant human G1 domain of aggrecan (rhG1) was expressed in a mammalian expression system as a His-tagged protein and purified by nickel-affinity chromatography, as described previously [3]. Purity was checked by SDS-PAGE with Coomassie staining. For in vitro citrullination, rhG1 (and, in parallel, purified native PG) was incubated with rabbit skeletal muscle peptidylarginine deiminase (PAD; 0.1–1 U/mg protein) in 100 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4) containing 10 mM CaCl₂ and 5 mM DTT for 3 h at 37 °C. Control samples were processed identically without enzyme or without calcium. The reaction was stopped with 20 mM EDTA, and the samples were dialyzed or desalted before use. Confirmation of citrullination Antibody-based detection used the anti-modified citrulline (AMC) method. Proteins were blotted onto PVDF membranes and chemically modified with 2,3-butanedione monoxime and antipyrine in strongly acidic conditions, in the dark at 37 °C. They were then probed with anti-modified citrulline antibody (Millipore) followed by HRP-conjugated secondary antibody [4]. Unmodified membranes were probed with an anti-peptidyl-citrulline antibody. For the chemical method, the colorimetric diacetyl monoxime-thiosemicarbazide assay was used to quantify citrulline in the samples against an L-citrulline standard curve [5]. Absorbance was read at 530 nm. Dot blot and Western blot For dot blots, 1–5 µg of purified PG, cartilage extract or rhG1 was applied to nitrocellulose membranes. For Western blots, native or deglycosylated samples were separated on 4–12% gradient or 10% SDS-polyacrylamide gels and transferred to PVDF or nitrocellulose membranes. Membranes were blocked with 5% non-fat dry milk or 3% BSA in TBS-Tween and incubated with individual ACPA+ or ACPA− sera (1:100–1:200 dilution) overnight at 4 °C. Bound IgG was detected with HRP-conjugated anti-human IgG and enhanced chemiluminescence. Parallel blots were probed with monoclonal antibodies against the G1 domain (e.g., clone 1C6) and G3 domain, and with anti-His antibody for rhG1, to identify PG fragments. Pre-incubating sera with citrullinated or non-citrullinated peptides or protein was used in selected inhibition experiments. Each experiment was repeated at least three times with different cartilage specimens. Molecular modeling of citrullination sites The three-dimensional structure of the human aggrecan G1 domain (Ig-fold and two link-module domains) was built by homology modeling with SWISS-MODEL, using the crystal structures of related link-module proteins (such as TSG-6) as templates [6]. Model quality was assessed by QMEAN scores and Ramachandran plots. Solvent accessibility of each arginine residue was calculated with PyMOL and the NACCESS algorithm. Arginines with relative side-chain accessibility above 25% and positioned in flexible or surface loops were considered potential PAD targets. Residues were also compared with known citrullination motifs and with previously described citrullinated epitopes of aggrecan. ELISA for CitPG-specific autoantibodies Microtiter plates (Nunc MaxiSorp) were coated overnight at 4 °C with 1 µg/well rhG1, citrullinated rhG1 (CitrhG1), or native or citrullinated PG in carbonate buffer (pH 9.6). After blocking with 1% BSA, sera (1:100 dilution, in duplicate) were added for 2 h at room temperature. Bound IgG was detected with HRP-conjugated anti-human IgG and TMB substrate, and absorbance was read at 450 nm. Background signal from uncoated wells was subtracted. Reactivity to CitrhG1 was compared with reactivity to unmodified rhG1. A positive result was defined as an optical density exceeding the mean plus 3 SD of the healthy control sera. Inter-assay variability was controlled using a reference serum on each plate. Immunohistochemistry Cartilage samples were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, decalcified where bone was attached, and embedded in paraffin. Sections (5 µm) were deparaffinized and rehydrated, and antigen retrieval was performed with chondroitinase ABC digestion (0.1 U/mL, 1 h, 37 °C). Endogenous peroxidase was quenched with 3% H₂O₂, and sections were blocked with 5% normal goat serum. Sections were incubated overnight at 4 °C with pooled or individual ACPA+ sera (1:50–1:100), or with a commercial anti-citrullinated protein antibody. Controls included ACPA− serum, omission of primary antibody, and ACPA+ serum pre-absorbed with citrullinated rhG1. Detection used biotinylated secondary antibody, an avidin-biotin-peroxidase complex and DAB, with hematoxylin counterstaining. Sections were evaluated by two independent observers blinded to diagnosis. Staining was scored semi-quantitatively (0–3) in the superficial, middle and deep zones and in the pericellular, territorial and interterritorial matrix. Statistical analysis Data are presented as mean ± SD or median (interquartile range), as appropriate. Group comparisons used the Mann–Whitney U test or Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn's post hoc correction. Paired reactivities (rhG1 vs. CitrhG1) were compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Correlations were assessed by Spearman's coefficient. Analyses were performed in GraphPad Prism, and P < 0.05 was considered significant. Reactivity of ACPA+ RA sera with PG purified from normal human cartilage To determine whether PG is citrullinated in vivo, PG was purified from extracts of normal human articular cartilage and probed by dot blot with sera from ACPA+ RA patients, ACPA– RA patients, and healthy controls. All ACPA+ sera tested produced clear signals with the purified PG, and signal intensity increased with the amount of PG applied. Signals obtained with ACPA– or control sera were at or near background. Treatment of the PG with chondroitinase ABC, keratanase, and endo-β-galactosidase to remove glycosaminoglycan chains did not abolish ACPA+ reactivity. This indicates that the recognized epitopes reside in the core protein and are not masked by, or dependent on, the glycosaminoglycan side chains. Identification of citrullinated PG fragments in OA and RA cartilage extracts Cartilage extracts from OA and RA patients were deglycosylated, separated by SDS-PAGE, and analyzed by Western blotting. ACPA+ sera recognized multiple PG fragments in both OA and RA extracts. The most prominent bands had molecular masses consistent with fragments containing the G1 domain, as confirmed by reprobing with an anti-G1 monoclonal antibody. Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have moved from specialized military platforms to widely available tools for civilian applications, including surveillance, agriculture, infrastructure inspection, and emergency response [1], [2]. In disaster operations, UAVs are especially attractive because they can be deployed quickly, can reach areas that are dangerous or inaccessible to ground crews, and can provide situational awareness within the critical first hours after an event such as an earthquake, flood, or wildfire [3]. As the cost of small multirotor and fixed-wing platforms decreases, attention has turned from the operation of a single vehicle to the coordinated use of many vehicles. Swarms of UAVs can cover large areas in parallel, provide redundancy against individual vehicle failures, and support tasks such as search and rescue, damage assessment, and communication relay [4], [5]. Despite these advantages, operating multiple UAVs introduces substantial challenges for human operators. A single operator supervising several vehicles must manage task allocation, monitor vehicle states, interpret sensor data, and respond to changing conditions, often under time pressure and stress [6]. The design of effective user interfaces and operating procedures for such multi-vehicle systems remains an open research problem, and poor interface design has been linked to reduced operator performance and an increased risk of mishaps [7]. Training personnel to use these systems is similarly demanding. Real-world flight tests are expensive, weather dependent, and constrained by regulations, and they may place vehicles, bystanders, and property at risk. Disaster scenarios in particular are difficult to reproduce safely and repeatably in the field. Simulation offers a practical means of addressing these limitations. Simulated environments allow researchers to prototype and compare interface designs, evaluate human-swarm interaction strategies, and train operators in a controlled and repeatable setting at low cost [8]. A variety of simulators have been developed for robotics and UAV research, including Gazebo, AirSim, and others built on general-purpose game or physics engines [9], [10]. These tools often provide high-fidelity physics and sensor models, but they can be complex to configure and are not always oriented toward the study of operator interaction with large teams of vehicles in disaster response contexts. Conversely, simulators designed for human-in-the-loop studies and training frequently simplify vehicle dynamics, for example by allowing vehicles to move instantaneously between positions or to follow idealized straight-line paths at constant speed. Such simplifications can be adequate for studying high-level decision making, but they may give operators an inaccurate impression of how real vehicles respond to commands. The result is a gap between simulated and real operation, which can lead to negative training transfer and to interface designs that perform well in simulation but poorly in the field [11]. The Reno Rescue Simulator (RRS) was developed to support research on human interaction with swarms of UAVs in search-and-rescue and disaster scenarios. It provides a virtual environment in which an operator can issue commands to multiple simulated vehicles, view imagery and sensor information, and carry out mission tasks such as locating survivors. However, the motion of vehicles in the original simulator was represented in a simplified manner, which limited the realism of the user experience and the applicability of findings to real systems. Because the perceived responsiveness, turning behavior, and path-following characteristics of a UAV strongly influence how operators plan and issue commands, more faithful motion models are an important step toward a useful training and prototyping platform [12]. In this paper, we present the integration of a model-based waypoint navigation controller into the Reno Rescue Simulator. Waypoint navigation is a common method of commanding UAVs, in which an operator or planner specifies a sequence of positions that the vehicle must visit, and an onboard controller computes the control inputs required to follow the path [13]. Model-based controllers use a mathematical representation of vehicle dynamics to compute these inputs, producing motion that reflects physical constraints such as limited acceleration, finite turning rates, and inertia. By embedding such a controller within the simulator, vehicles respond to operator commands in a manner more consistent with real platforms, and the interface through which operators assign waypoints becomes a more representative model of actual ground control systems. The contributions of this work are as follows. First, we describe the design and implementation of a waypoint navigation controller based on a dynamic model of the UAV and its integration into the architecture of the Reno Rescue Simulator, including the interface between the user-facing components and the vehicle control layer. Second, we show how the controller supports simultaneous operation of multiple vehicles, enabling swarm-level scenarios relevant to disaster operations. Third, we discuss potential uses of the resulting simulator, including interface prototyping, operator training, mission rehearsal, and human-subject experimentation. We also consider how such a simulator might support real-world UAV operations, for instance by allowing operators to preview planned missions, anticipate vehicle behavior, and test contingency plans before committing physical assets to a hazardous environment. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on UAV simulation, swarm control, and human-swarm interaction. Section III describes the Reno Rescue Simulator and the motion control model. Section IV details the integration of the controller and presents example scenarios. Section V discusses applications and limitations, and Section VI concludes with directions for future work. The Reno Rescue Simulator (RRS) was used as the base platform for this work. RRS is a multi-agent, game-engine-based environment in which an operator supervises a team of simulated UAVs performing search-and-rescue tasks in a disaster scenario [1]. In its original form, UAV motion in RRS was kinematic: each vehicle moved toward its assigned target at a constant speed with instantaneous heading changes. We replaced this with a model-based waypoint navigation controller so that vehicle behavior reflects the dynamic constraints of real multirotor aircraft. The methods below describe the simulator architecture, the vehicle dynamics model, the controller design, the swarm-level integration, and the evaluation procedure. Simulator Architecture RRS is organized into three layers: a scenario layer that defines terrain, hazards, and victim locations; an agent layer that holds the state and behavior of each UAV; and a user interface layer that presents a map view and accepts operator commands such as placing waypoints, assigning search regions, and selecting individual or grouped vehicles. The simulation advances in fixed time steps of 10 ms for physics and control updates, while rendering and interface updates run at the display frame rate. Decoupling these rates keeps numerical integration stable regardless of rendering load. The new controller was implemented as a replaceable module within the agent layer, so that the original kinematic model and the new dynamic model could be switched without altering the scenario or interface layers. Vehicle Dynamics Model Each UAV was modeled as a quadrotor rigid body with twelve states: position p = [x, y, z], velocity v, Euler angles (roll φ, pitch θ, yaw ψ), and body angular rates ω. Translational dynamics follow Newton's second law, mv̇ = mg + R(φ,θ,ψ)[0, 0, T]ᵀ − D, where m is mass, T is total thrust, R is the body-to-world rotation matrix, and D is a linear drag term proportional to velocity. Rotational dynamics follow Euler's equations with a diagonal inertia matrix. Parameters (mass, arm length, inertia, maximum thrust, and drag coefficient) were set to values representative of a commercially available small quadrotor platform [2]. Actuator limits were enforced by saturating thrust and commanded torques, and first-order motor lag was included to prevent unrealistically abrupt control changes. Optional wind disturbance was modeled as a steady component plus a low-pass-filtered stochastic gust added to the drag term [3]. Waypoint Navigation Controller The controller uses a standard cascaded structure [2], [4]. An outer position loop computes a desired acceleration from the position and velocity errors relative to the active waypoint: ades = Kp(pwp − p) + Kd(vdes − v) + g, where vdes is limited to a maximum cruise speed. The desired acceleration is converted to a thrust magnitude and desired roll and pitch angles using a small-angle approximation about the commanded yaw. An inner attitude loop applies proportional-derivative control to track the desired angles and yaw rate, producing body torques. Gains were initially selected by pole placement on the linearized model and then tuned in simulation to give a damped response with limited overshoot (below 5% of step distance) and no sustained oscillation. Waypoint sequencing was handled by a finite-state machine with states for idle, takeoff, transit, hold, and landing. A waypoint was considered reached when the UAV was within an acceptance radius of 1.0 m and its speed fell below a threshold; for intermediate waypoints in a path, only the radius condition was required, which allowed smoother pass-through behavior. Operator-defined paths were smoothed by limiting the commanded speed according to the turn angle at each waypoint, reducing the speed approaching sharp turns. Swarm Integration Each UAV runs its own controller instance, and the operator interacts with the group through high-level commands. Group commands (e.g., move to location, sweep region) are decomposed into per-vehicle waypoint lists. Regions are partitioned into parallel lanes assigned to the nearest available vehicles, in the manner of coverage path planning for search tasks [5]. To avoid collisions, a lightweight separation behavior adds a repulsive term to the desired acceleration when another UAV is within a safety distance of 3 m [6]. This term is bounded so that it cannot override waypoint tracking entirely. Battery depletion was modeled as a function of thrust, and vehicles with low charge automatically return to their launch point, which provides operators with realistic resource constraints. Interface Adaptations Because vehicles can no longer change velocity instantaneously, the interface was extended to convey dynamic behavior. Predicted trajectories were drawn from the current state to the next waypoints, and vehicle icons displayed heading, speed, and battery state. Command latency arises naturally from controller response and was not artificially added. Evaluation Procedure Evaluation had two components. First, controller performance was assessed with single-vehicle tests: step responses to waypoint displacements of 10, 50, and 100 m, multi-waypoint path following, and disturbance rejection under wind speeds of 0, 3, and 6 m/s. Metrics were rise time, overshoot, settling time, and cross-track error. Second, swarm-level tests used a representative disaster scenario in which 5, 10, or 20 UAVs searched a 1 km² area containing 15 randomly placed victims. Each configuration was repeated 30 times with different random seeds under both the kinematic and dynamic models. Recorded measures were mission completion time, total distance traveled, minimum inter-vehicle separation, number of separation violations, and energy consumed. Differences between models were compared using paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, depending on normality, with a significance level of 0.05. Simulation code ran on a standard desktop workstation, and computational cost was recorded as the real-time factor to confirm that the dynamic model preserved interactive performance for the largest swarm size. The integrated waypoint navigation controller was evaluated in the Reno Rescue Simulator through three sets of experiments: single-vehicle trajectory tracking, multi-vehicle swarm operation in a simulated disaster scenario, and a comparison of user interaction with the original kinematic motion model and the model-based controller. All simulations were run on a workstation with an eight-core processor and 32 GB of memory. The physics and control loop executed at a fixed rate of 100 Hz, while rendering was maintained at approximately 60 frames per second. Unless otherwise noted, results are reported as mean ± standard deviation over 30 independent trials. Single-vehicle trajectory tracking The controller was first tested on a quadrotor model following a set of predefined waypoint sequences, including a square path, a figure-eight path, and a three-dimensional helical climb. Waypoints were spaced between 10 and 50 m apart, and a waypoint was considered reached when the vehicle came within 1.0 m of it.
