Explosions are the leading cause of injury in modern armed conflict, accounting for roughly 79% of combat-related injuries. Improvised explosive devices and other munitions also pose a growing threat to civilians, through terrorist attacks and accidental detonations. Blast exposure rarely produces a single, isolated injury. Instead, the blast wave, penetrating fragments, and acceleration or deceleration of the body combine to cause polytrauma affecting several organ systems at once. Gas-filled organs such as the lungs and bowel are especially vulnerable to the primary blast wave, and primary blast lung is a major cause of early mortality. The brain is also susceptible. Blast-induced traumatic brain injury (bTBI) has been called the signature injury of recent conflicts, and many service members who survive their initial injuries go on to develop persistent cognitive, emotional, and behavioral problems. Internal hemorrhage is a central, and largely untreated, consequence of blast polytrauma. Bleeding from the lungs, liver, spleen, and other organs is difficult to detect and cannot be controlled with tourniquets or compression, which work for external wounds. In the field, the only options are fluid resuscitation, which can dilute clotting factors and raise blood pressure enough to dislodge nascent clots, and rapid transport to surgical care. Delays in evacuation make non-compressible hemorrhage a leading cause of preventable death in combat. A therapy that could be given at the point of injury, by a medic or first responder, to promote clotting at sites of internal bleeding would address a critical gap in trauma care. Therapeutic options for TBI are also limited. Current management is mainly supportive and aims to control intracranial pressure and maintain cerebral perfusion. Despite many clinical trials, no drug has been approved that directly interrupts the secondary injury cascade. This cascade includes blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and apoptosis, and it unfolds over hours to days after the initial insult. Blast exposure triggers these processes with particular force, and microvascular damage and BBB breakdown appear to be early events that can feed later neurodegeneration. Because secondary injury starts quickly, the timing of intervention may strongly influence long-term outcomes. Delivering treatment immediately, before secondary mechanisms become established, may therefore offer the greatest chance of preventing lasting deficits. Corticosteroids such as dexamethasone have strong anti-inflammatory and vascular-stabilizing effects and have been tested in neurotrauma. However, high systemic doses carry notable side effects, and large clinical trials of corticosteroids in TBI have shown no benefit or even harm. These results suggest that how a drug is delivered, including its timing, location, and dose, may matter as much as the drug itself. Targeted delivery that concentrates an anti-inflammatory agent at injury sites while limiting systemic exposure could revive the therapeutic potential of such compounds. Nanoparticle platforms offer a route to this kind of targeting. We have previously developed hemostatic nanoparticles (hNPs) made from poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA), a biocompatible, biodegradable polymer, decorated with a peptide that binds activated platelets. The peptide, a glycine-arginine-glycine-aspartic acid-serine (GRGDS) sequence, targets the integrin GPIIb/IIIa on activated platelets. When administered intravenously, these particles accumulate at bleeding sites and enhance platelet aggregation, reducing bleeding time and blood loss in models of liver injury, extremity trauma, and blast-associated polytrauma. Because the particles are guided to sites of active injury by platelet activation, they can also serve as carriers for therapeutic cargo. Encapsulating dexamethasone within the PLGA core allows its sustained release at injured tissue, giving a single agent that both promotes hemostasis and delivers local anti-inflammatory therapy. We reasoned that this dual action would be particularly useful after blast, where hemorrhage and inflammation occur together and each worsens the other. Anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress, and other emotional disturbances are among the most common and disabling sequelae of blast exposure. They are frequently linked to dysfunction in limbic structures, especially the amygdala, which regulates fear and emotional responses and is sensitive to vascular injury, inflammation, and apoptosis. Rodent models of blast injury reproduce anxiety-like behavior, and such outcomes provide a functional readout that goes beyond survival alone. Few preclinical studies, however, have tested whether an immediate post-injury intervention can both improve survival and prevent long-term behavioral and neuropathological consequences in a clinically relevant blast polytrauma model. Here, we used an Advanced Blast Simulator to expose rats to a single blast wave that produced primary blast lung injury and bTBI, reproducing key features of human blast polytrauma. We tested the hypothesis that immediate administration of hemostatic nanoparticles encapsulating dexamethasone (hDNPs) would improve survival and mitigate long-term sequelae. We compared hDNPs with appropriate controls and sham animals, and assessed survival, anxiety-related behavior, and histological markers of apoptosis and BBB disruption in the amygdala. Our results indicate that early, targeted intervention after blast can improve survival and limit the neuropathological and emotional consequences of injury. Animals. All procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and followed national guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals. Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats (250–300 g) were housed in pairs on a 12 h light/dark cycle with food and water ad libitum and acclimated for one week before experiments. Animals were randomly assigned to four groups: sham (anesthesia without blast), blast plus saline (vehicle control), blast plus hemostatic nanoparticles without drug (hNPs), and blast plus hemostatic nanoparticles encapsulating dexamethasone (hDNPs). Investigators performing behavioral scoring and histological analysis were blinded to group allocation. Nanoparticle fabrication. Poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid)-poly(L-lysine)-poly(ethylene glycol) (PLGA-PLL-PEG) block copolymers were synthesized by carbodiimide chemistry as previously described. The hemostatic targeting peptide GRGDS was conjugated to the PEG terminus via a maleimide-thiol reaction. Nanoparticles were prepared by single-emulsion solvent evaporation. PLGA-PLL-PEG-GRGDS, together with dexamethasone for the hDNPs formulation, was dissolved in dichloromethane and added dropwise to an aqueous polyvinyl alcohol solution under probe sonication on ice. The emulsion was stirred for 3 h to evaporate solvent, and particles were collected by centrifugation, washed three times in deionized water, resuspended in sucrose cryoprotectant, lyophilized, and stored at −20 °C. Hydrodynamic diameter, polydispersity and zeta potential were measured by dynamic light scattering, and morphology was confirmed by scanning electron microscopy. Dexamethasone loading and encapsulation efficiency were determined by dissolving particles in acetonitrile and quantifying drug by high-performance liquid chromatography against a standard curve. Release kinetics were assessed by incubating particles in phosphate-buffered saline at 37 °C with agitation and sampling the supernatant at defined intervals. Before injection, particles were resuspended in sterile saline at 25 mg/mL and briefly sonicated. Blast exposure. Rats were anesthetized with isoflurane (3–4% induction, 2% maintenance) and placed in a prone position, secured in a holder inside the test section of an Advanced Blast Simulator, with the right side or head-on orientation facing the oncoming wave as determined by the shock tube configuration. A single blast wave was generated by rupturing calibrated membranes with compressed helium. Peak incident overpressure was recorded by pressure transducers mounted at the specimen location, and the overpressure-time profile was verified to confirm a Friedman waveform. The thorax and abdomen were not shielded, so that animals sustained primary blast lung injury together with blast-induced traumatic brain injury; the head was free to move to reproduce a polytraumatic exposure. Sham animals underwent identical anesthesia and handling without blast. Animals were removed immediately after exposure. Treatment. Within five minutes after blast, animals received 0.5 mL of saline, hNPs, or hDNPs through the jugular or tail vein under continued anesthesia, with the dose of hDNPs delivering a defined amount of dexamethasone per kilogram. Animals were then recovered on a warming pad and monitored continuously. Buprenorphine was given for analgesia in all groups according to protocol. Survival and physiological assessment. Survival was recorded at 1 h, 24 h and daily thereafter to the study endpoint. Animals found dead or euthanized for humane endpoints were necropsied to confirm lung hemorrhage and to document other internal bleeding. Lungs of animals surviving to the endpoint were examined and scored for hemorrhage grossly and histologically. Behavioral testing. Beginning 7 days after injury, surviving animals were tested for anxiety-like behavior. Testing took place during the light phase in a quiet, dimly lit room after 30 min habituation. In the elevated plus maze, each rat was placed in the center facing an open arm and recorded for 5 min; time spent in open arms, number of open-arm entries, and total arm entries were scored with automated tracking software. In the open field test, rats explored a square arena for 10 min and time in the center zone, distance traveled and rearing were quantified. Apparatus was cleaned with 70% ethanol between animals. Anxiety indices were computed as the ratio of open-arm to total exposure time. Tissue collection and histology. At the endpoint, animals were deeply anesthetized and transcardially perfused with cold saline followed by 4% paraformaldehyde. Brains were post-fixed, cryoprotected in sucrose, and sectioned coronally at 20 µm on a cryostat. Sections containing the amygdala were identified using a rat brain atlas. Apoptosis was assessed by terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) using a commercial kit and by immunostaining for cleaved caspase-3, with DAPI counterstain. Blood-brain barrier disruption was evaluated by immunofluorescence for extravasated immunoglobulin G (IgG) and by staining for the tight junction protein claudin-5 and endothelial marker lectin. Sections were blocked, incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies, washed, and incubated with fluorophore-conjugated secondary antibodies. Images were obtained with a fluorescence microscope using identical exposure settings across groups. In each animal, at least three sections and three non-overlapping fields in the basolateral and central amygdala were analyzed. TUNEL-positive cells were counted and expressed as a percentage of DAPI-positive nuclei; IgG immunoreactivity was quantified as mean fluorescence intensity after background subtraction using ImageJ. Statistical analysis. Data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean. Survival was analyzed with Kaplan-Meier curves and compared with the log-rank test. Behavioral and histological data were tested for normality with the Shapiro-Wilk test and compared among groups by one-way ANOVA with Tukey post hoc tests, or by Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's test when assumptions were not met. Sample sizes were chosen from prior blast studies and pilot data. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05, and analyses were performed in GraphPad Prism. Characterization of hemostatic dexamethasone nanoparticles hDNPs were fabricated by nanoprecipitation of PLGA-PLL-PEG-GRGDS conjugates with encapsulated dexamethasone. Dynamic light scattering showed a mean hydrodynamic diameter of approximately 150 nm with a polydispersity index below 0.2 and a slightly negative zeta potential. Dexamethasone loading was approximately 5% by weight, with an encapsulation efficiency of about 60%. In vitro release showed an initial burst over the first several hours followed by sustained release over 72 hours. Nanoparticle batches were consistent across preparations, and the characteristics were stable after lyophilization and resuspension. Blast exposure produced reproducible primary blast lung and bTBI Rats exposed to the Advanced Blast Simulator received a single blast wave with a mean peak overpressure of approximately 130 kPa. Pressure traces were similar across injured groups, with no significant differences in peak overpressure, positive-phase duration, or impulse among animals assigned to the hDNP, saline, or control nanoparticle groups (p > 0.05). Immediately after blast, injured animals showed transient apnea, a righting-reflex delay, and labored breathing. Necropsy of animals that died early revealed extensive pulmonary hemorrhage and contusion, confirming primary blast lung injury, and in some cases subdural and subarachnoid blood. Sham animals underwent identical anesthesia and handling without blast exposure and showed no signs of injury. hDNP treatment increased survival Animals received an intravenous injection of hDNPs, saline vehicle, or control nanoparticles shortly after blast. Most deaths in the injured groups occurred within the first hour after injury, and few occurred after the first 24 hours. Survival at the end of the acute period was 100% in the sham group. Among blast-exposed animals, survival was significantly higher in the hDNP group than in the control groups (Kaplan–Meier with log-rank test, p < 0.05). Gross examination of animals that died showed that pulmonary hemorrhage was the predominant finding, with fewer signs of bleeding in the abdomen. Cancer is a heterogeneous group of diseases driven by the accumulation of genomic alterations that confer selective advantages to cells, including sustained proliferation, evasion of cell death and the capacity to invade and colonize distant tissues. Over the last decade, large-scale sequencing initiatives such as The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC) have profiled thousands of tumors across dozens of cancer types. These efforts have produced extensive catalogues of somatic mutations, copy number alterations, gene fusions and expression changes, and have enabled the identification of hundreds of cancer driver genes using methods that search for signals of positive selection, such as recurrence, functional impact bias or clustering of mutations in protein sequence and structure. Such cohort-level analyses have been invaluable for understanding the landscape of cancer genomics. However, they describe the properties of populations of tumors, and their conclusions do not translate directly to the individual patient. A typical tumor carries from tens to thousands of somatic coding mutations, and only a handful of them, sometimes just one or none, affect known driver genes. The remaining alterations are usually considered passengers, although some may be rare drivers, may modulate the effect of the main drivers, or may represent unexplored therapeutic opportunities. Moreover, tumors of the same histological type frequently differ in their molecular makeup, and the same gene can play different roles, as oncogene or tumor suppressor, depending on the tissue. Interpreting the alterations found in a single patient therefore requires placing them in the context of the tumor type, the available knowledge on driver genes, and the functional and structural consequences of each variant. Precision oncology aims precisely at this goal: matching each patient with the therapy most likely to be effective on the basis of the molecular characteristics of the tumor. Clinical sequencing, from targeted gene panels to whole exomes and genomes, is becoming increasingly common, and molecular tumor boards are being established in many hospitals. Nevertheless, translating a list of variants into clinically meaningful information remains a major bottleneck. Several resources address parts of this problem. Databases such as COSMIC, cBioPortal and the ICGC Data Portal provide access to mutation data and cohort-level exploration; OncoKB, CIViC, the Cancer Genome Interpreter and My Cancer Genome curate evidence on the oncogenic effect and clinical actionability of variants and on drug responses; and tools such as IntOGen compile cancer driver genes derived from large cohorts. Yet these resources typically differ in scope, in the nomenclature and annotations they use, and in whether they emphasize the cohort or the individual. Clinicians and researchers must often consult several of them and integrate the results manually, which is time-consuming and prone to inconsistency. A further limitation is that most interpretation strategies treat genes as isolated entities. Proteins function within complex networks of physical interactions, and the consequences of a mutation depend on its cellular environment. A mutation may disrupt a protein-protein interface and rewire specific interactions, affect a catalytic or ligand-binding site, or destabilize the fold. Network-based approaches have shown that cancer genes tend to occupy particular positions in the interactome and that mutations in different genes can converge on the same pathways or complexes. Likewise, three-dimensional structural information, whether experimental or derived from homology modelling, allows mutations to be mapped onto functional regions, pockets and interfaces, providing mechanistic hypotheses about their impact and, potentially, about druggability. Incorporating these layers into the interpretation of personal cancer genomes remains uncommon in accessible tools. Another challenge is the need for a coherent view that combines complementary perspectives. A cohort-centric view answers questions such as how frequently a gene is mutated in a tumor type, whether it is a recognized driver, and what the typical patterns of co-occurrence and mutual exclusivity are. A patient-centric view asks which of the mutations in a given tumor are likely to be functionally relevant, how they relate to each other in terms of pathways and interactions, and whether there is evidence of clinical actionability. Bridging both views allows an individual profile to be compared with relevant cohorts, helping to distinguish expected from unusual alterations and to prioritize variants for follow-up. Here we present Cancer PanorOmics, a web-based resource designed to provide a comprehensive, multi-layered view of personal cancer genomes. The platform integrates data and annotations for 26 tumor types, including cancer driver predictions, mutation frequencies and patterns, and clinical and scientific evidence on variants, genes and therapies. Users can explore cohort-level information for each tumor type and, in parallel, submit or select the variants of an individual tumor to obtain a patient-centric report. In addition, the resource maps mutations onto the human interactome to reveal their cellular context, and onto protein structures, with quasi-atomic detail whenever available, to highlight potential functional consequences. By combining these perspectives in a single, accessible interface, Cancer PanorOmics aims to facilitate the interpretation of individual tumors and, together with appropriate genetic counselling and medical advice, to contribute to the identification of actionable alterations that can guide clinical decision-making. Data sources and cohort definition Somatic mutation, copy number and clinical data for 26 tumor types were collected from public cohorts, mainly The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC), and were retrieved through cBioPortal and the corresponding data portals. Tumor types were defined by the cohort's primary site and histology. Variants were mapped to the GRCh37/hg19 reference genome, and coordinates were lifted over where necessary. Only point mutations and short insertions/deletions in coding regions were considered for the cohort-level analyses. Synonymous variants were retained for background mutation rate estimation but excluded from driver identification. Identification of cancer driver genes Tumor type specific driver genes were identified by combining the outputs of complementary methods that detect signals of positive selection. These included methods based on mutational clustering within the protein sequence (OncodriveCLUST), functional impact bias (OncodriveFM), and recurrence relative to a gene-specific background mutation rate (MutSigCV and dNdScv-like approaches). Each method was run separately for every tumor type. P values were corrected for multiple testing with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, and genes with q < 0.05 were considered significant. Results from individual methods were integrated by a rank-based combination, and genes were assigned a confidence tier according to the number of methods supporting them. Genes were also cross-referenced with the Cancer Gene Census and with curated lists of known drivers to flag previously described cancer genes. Drivers were further classified as oncogenes or tumor suppressors on the basis of the distribution of missense and truncating mutations. Annotation of variants Variants from a personal genome, supplied as VCF or MAF files or as a list of gene/protein changes, were annotated with the Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor. Annotations included the consequence type, affected transcript and protein position. Functional impact was estimated with SIFT, PolyPhen-2 and the Mutation Assessor score, and the scores were combined into a consensus categorization (high, medium, low or neutral impact). Population frequencies from the 1000 Genomes Project and gnomAD were used to filter likely germline polymorphisms. Variants with allele frequency above 1% were labeled as common polymorphisms. For each variant, we also queried its recurrence in the tumor cohorts and in COSMIC. Patient-centric and cohort-centric views In the cohort-centric view, users select a tumor type and explore its driver genes, mutation frequencies, mutual exclusivity and co-occurrence patterns, and the distribution of mutations along protein domains. Mutual exclusivity and co-occurrence between gene pairs were assessed with a one-sided Fisher's exact test, with multiple testing correction. In the patient-centric view, each mutated gene in the submitted genome is placed in the context of the selected tumor type. The system reports whether the gene is a driver in that tumor type, whether the exact variant or the same residue is recurrently mutated, and the predicted impact. Genes and variants are ranked by a score combining driver status, recurrence, functional impact and presence in clinical evidence databases, so that putative drivers are prioritized over passenger events. Clinical and scientific evidence Information on the clinical relevance of alterations was obtained from the Cancer Genome Interpreter catalog of validated oncogenic mutations, CIViC, OncoKB-compatible public resources, and DGIdb. Evidence was classified by level (approved therapies, clinical trials, case reports and preclinical data) and by the nature of the association (sensitivity, resistance or prognosis). Alterations were matched to evidence at the level of the exact variant, the gene or the mutation type, and matches were annotated by tumor type, distinguishing evidence from the same tumor type from evidence extrapolated from other tumors. Relevant literature was linked through PubMed identifiers. Drug-target relationships were retrieved from ChEMBL and DrugBank. Interactome mapping To explore the cellular environment of mutations, we built a human protein-protein interaction network by integrating curated experimental interactions from BioGRID, IntAct, HPRD and Reactome. Only interactions supported by direct experimental evidence were retained. Mutated genes from a patient were mapped onto this network, and their first-order neighbors, shared interactors and connected components were computed using NetworkX. The network was annotated with driver status, mutation frequency in the tumor type and drug targets. Over-represented pathways among the mutated genes and their neighbors were identified with a hypergeometric test using KEGG and Reactome annotations, with FDR correction. Structural annotation Protein structural information was obtained from the Protein Data Bank and from homology models in ModBase and SWISS-MODEL. Protein residues were mapped to structures with SIFTS and, for models, to UniProt positions. Mutated residues were classified as being located in the protein core, on the surface or at an interface, according to relative solvent accessibility computed with DSSP. Interface residues were identified from structures of complexes, defined as residues whose accessible surface area changes upon complex formation. Residues within 4 Å of a bound ligand, small molecule or nucleic acid were labeled as binding site positions. Structures were displayed with an embedded NGL viewer, highlighting the mutated residues and their neighbors. Implementation The back end was implemented in Python with a relational database storing cohort data, annotations and evidence. Precomputed results for each tumor type are served through a RESTful API. The front end uses HTML5, JavaScript and D3.js for interactive visualizations, including lollipop plots, oncoprints and network diagrams. Uploaded patient data are processed in memory, are not shared, and are deleted after the session. The resource is freely available without registration. Limitations and intended use The results are intended for research and to support interpretation by clinical experts. They do not replace genetic counselling or medical advice, and all findings require validation with appropriate clinical-grade assays. Cancer PanorOmics is organized around two complementary entry points: a cohort-centric view, in which the user explores the alterations and driver genes of a given tumor type, and a patient-centric view, in which the user uploads the variants of an individual tumor and obtains a contextualized report. Both views rely on the same underlying integrated database, which covers 26 tumor types and combines somatic mutation data from large sequencing consortia, curated catalogues of driver genes, clinical annotations of variant actionability, protein interaction networks and structural information. Cohort-centric view: the landscape of each tumor type For each of the 26 tumor types, the resource reports the set of genes identified as cancer drivers by complementary computational methods, together with their mutation frequencies and the type of alterations observed (missense, truncating, in-frame indels, copy number changes). Users can query a gene and immediately see in which tumor types it is recurrently altered, whether it acts predominantly as an oncogene or a tumor suppressor based on its mutational pattern, and how its alterations are distributed along the protein sequence. Mutation hotspots and domain-level enrichment are displayed in lollipop-style plots, allowing the user to assess whether a mutation falls in a recurrently mutated position or in a functionally annotated region. We also provide a summary of co-occurrence and mutual exclusivity between driver alterations within each cohort. These patterns help place a gene in a pathway context: mutually exclusive alterations frequently affect the same pathway, whereas co-occurring alterations may point to cooperating events. The cohort view therefore serves as a reference frame against which individual tumors

Knitting is among the oldest and most widely practiced methods of producing textiles, and knitted fabric is ubiquitous in apparel, sportswear, medical products, and technical textiles. Industrial knitting machines can produce entire garments automatically with little or no sewing, which makes them attractive for on-demand and customized manufacturing [McCann et al. 2016; Narayanan et al. 2018]. Yet the potential for personalization remains largely untapped. Programming a knitting machine requires low-level control over individual stitches, needle movements, and yarn carriers, and the proprietary software that ships with commercial machines is aimed at trained technicians rather than casual designers. As a result, the people who wear knitted garments are rarely able to shape them. Recent research has begun to close this gap. Several systems let users generate knitting instructions from three-dimensional surface meshes, either by converting a mesh into a stitch mesh [Yuksel et al. 2012; Wu et al. 2019] or by tracing a surface with courses of stitches that are then scheduled for machine execution [Narayanan et al. 2018; Popescu et al. 2018]. Other work provides domain-specific languages and compilers that expose machine capabilities to expert programmers [Ikeda et al. 2020; Lin et al. 2018]. Interactive tools for hand knitting and for pattern design have also been proposed [Kaspar et al. 2019; Igarashi et al. 2008]. While powerful, these approaches generally sit at one of two extremes. Mesh-based methods give broad geometric freedom but offer little intuitive control over the garment's structure, such as the placement of sleeves, hems, and necklines, and they can yield instructions that are hard to edit once generated. Low-level languages and stitch-level editors, in contrast, give precise control but demand substantial knitting expertise and effort for even modest garments. Garment design in practice rarely starts from an arbitrary surface or from individual stitches. Designers typically begin from familiar components such as bodies, sleeves, and collars, and adapt them by changing measurements, then add surface decoration such as colorwork, textures, and lace. Computer-aided design (CAD) software for sewn clothing reflects this workflow through parametric panels and templates, and image editing software provides layers that can be composited and reused. Knitting, however, has distinctive constraints that complicate the direct application of these ideas. Fabric is constructed row by row, so shape changes are expressed as increases and decreases that must follow valid machine operations. Stitch patterns interact with shaping, because cables, ribs, and lace alter the local width and height of the fabric, and a pattern designed for one size must be adapted when the garment is resized. Finally, the connectivity between pieces determines how the garment can be scheduled and knitted. In this paper we present Knitting Skeletons, an interactive design system that combines concepts from CAD and image editing for the composition of machine-knitted garments. Our central idea is to represent a garment as an assembly of parametric knitted primitives, each of which is a simple, regular shape with a well-defined stitch layout, such as a tube, a cone, or a flat panel. These primitives are connected through a skeletal structure that specifies how they join and how their parameters, including length, circumference, and taper, may vary. Because every primitive has a regular structure, the system can automatically lay out stitches, determine the shaping operations needed to join and transition between pieces, and produce a valid knitting program without user intervention at the level of individual needles. On top of this geometric representation, we introduce stitch pattern layers inspired by raster image editors. Users paint or place patterns, such as colorwork motifs and textured stitches, on layers that are mapped onto the surface of the garment. Each layer is assigned a resampling behavior that defines how it responds when the underlying shape changes. For instance, a motif may be preserved at constant scale and tiled, stretched to fit new dimensions, or cropped, while a texture may be repeated to fill additional area. Since the primitives are regular, this resampling can be evaluated quickly, which allows the system to give real-time visual feedback as the user manipulates both shape and pattern. The system serves two groups of users. Casual users can select from existing templates, adjust a few high-level parameters, and apply patterns to obtain a customized garment without knowing how the machine operates. More advanced users can author new templates by composing primitives and defining parameters and constraints, then share them with others. Because shape and pattern are described parametrically and separately, customizations can be transferred between users and between bodies: a pattern designed for one person's garment can be reapplied to another's garment of different dimensions, and a tailored fit can be reused with new surface designs. Our contributions are as follows: - A parametric representation of knitted garments built from composable primitives with automated stitch layout and shaping. - A layered stitch pattern model with distinct resampling behaviors that adapt patterns to changes in garment shape. - An interactive interface that offers real-time feedback and supports both casual customization and template authoring for advanced users. - A demonstration of the system on a variety of garments and patterns, including the transfer of shape and pattern customizations between users, with several designs fabricated on an industrial knitting machine. By raising the level of abstraction from stitches and meshes to primitives and layers, our approach aims to make the customization of machine-knitted garments accessible, while retaining the structure needed to generate reliable machine instructions. Our system represents a garment as a composition of parametric knitted primitives, called skeletons, onto which stitch pattern layers are applied. We first describe the primitive representation, then composition and automated layout, then the patterning layers and their resampling behaviours, and finally the compilation to machine instructions. Knitting Skeletons as Parametric Primitives A skeleton is a low-dimensional description of a knitted piece that captures its topology and the way its stitch grid deforms. Each skeleton is a tube or sheet defined by a small set of parameters (e.g., width, length, and taper angles) and a set of boundary edges, called ports, where it can connect to other skeletons. The stitch grid is generated procedurally from these parameters. Following prior work on stitch meshes [1] and on knit-aware shaping [2], we model the fabric as a quad-dominant grid of stitches in which each row corresponds to a knitting pass. Shaping is expressed through increases and decreases, whose positions are determined by the skeleton's parameters so that the target width profile is achieved at every row. Because each primitive is regular, row and column counts are closed-form functions of its parameters and of the user's gauge, measured as stitches and rows per unit length from a swatch of the target yarn and machine [3]. Changing a parameter therefore requires only re-evaluating these functions, not re-meshing or re-optimizing. We provide primitives for common garment components, including rectangular panels, tapered tubes for sleeves and torsos, and shaped caps for shoulders and necklines. Advanced users may define new templates by specifying a parameterization, a set of ports, and a shaping function that maps row index to stitch count. Templates are stored in a serializable format so they can be shared. Composition and Automated Layout Garments are built by connecting ports of different skeletons in a graph. Each edge of the graph specifies a join, either a seam, a continuous knit-through transfer, or a held-stitch connection, in the manner of machine-knitting scheduling frameworks [4]. When two ports are joined, their stitch counts must be compatible. Rather than demanding exact matches from the user, the system resolves mismatches automatically. We treat the constraint as a small linear system over the parameters of the connected skeletons: each join contributes an equation equating port widths measured in stitches, while user-pinned parameters are held fixed. Unpinned parameters are solved in the least-squares sense and rounded to integers, with a local adjustment of shaping rows to absorb rounding error. If the system is over-constrained, the interface highlights the conflicting joins. After parameters are resolved, the layout stage positions each skeleton in a common two-dimensional knitting coordinate frame and determines the knitting order. Pieces joined by continuous transfer are placed on the same needle bed segment, whereas seamed pieces are scheduled independently. Because primitives are regular, layout reduces to a traversal of the composition graph and does not require a global search, which keeps it fast enough to run on every edit. Stitch Pattern Layers Surface patterning follows an image-editing metaphor. A pattern layer is a two-dimensional array of stitch operations (knit, purl, tuck, miss, and cable or lace operations) defined in a layer-local coordinate system. Layers are stacked and combined by blend modes, with a mask controlling where each layer is visible. Each layer is mapped onto a skeleton through that skeleton's parameterization, so that pattern coordinates follow the garment's shaping instead of the raw needle grid. Since the garment's stitch count changes with the user's measurements and gauge, a layer must be resampled to fit. We offer three behaviours, each suited to different pattern types. (1) Tiling repeats the pattern unit and truncates at borders, preserving stitch-level appearance for textures such as ribs and seed stitch. (2) Stretching resamples the layer by nearest-neighbour lookup in the pattern's coordinate frame, preserving the global motif, such as a colorwork image, at the expense of stitch-level fidelity [5]. (3) Anchored placement fixes the pattern to a chosen reference, such as a seam or the center line, at its native size, and fills the remainder with a background layer, which suits motifs like cables or logos that should not be distorted. Because operations such as cables change stitch counts locally, we validate each resampled layer and replace operations that would violate local constraints with the nearest valid operation, for instance by substituting plain knit for a cable crossing that straddles a boundary. Layers are evaluated at the stitch level, with cost proportional to the number of stitches, so the preview can update in real time. The preview renders the stitch grid with a yarn-like shading model, offering immediate feedback on both shape and pattern. Compilation to Machine Instructions Once layout and patterning are complete, the stitch grid is converted to a sequence of machine operations. We target a V-bed knitting machine, and use an intermediate representation of stitch operations with loop dependencies [6]. Increases and decreases are realized by racking and transfers, and each pass is assigned to a bed and direction to respect carriage constraints. The resulting program is verified with a simulator for needle conflicts and loop-ordering errors before being exported. Transferring Customizations Since shape and pattern are stored as parameters and layers rather than as fixed stitch grids, a customization can be transferred between users. A shared garment records its composition graph, pinned and free parameters, and layers with their resampling behaviours. When applied to a new user, the system substitutes that user's measurements and gauge, re-solves the free parameters, and re-resamples the layers, so the original design intent is preserved at a new size. Implementation The system is implemented as an interactive desktop application. We evaluate its output by knitting garments on an industrial flat-bed machine and by assessing the responsiveness of layout and preview across a range of garment sizes. We evaluated Knitting Skeletons along four axes: the range of garments and patterns the system can express, the fidelity of the interactive preview to the knitted result, system performance, and the usability of the tool for casual and advanced users. All garments were fabricated on a industrial V-bed knitting machine (Shima Seiki SWG091N2, 15 gauge) using a mid-weight acrylic yarn, and compiled to machine instructions through our back end, which follows the scheduling approach of prior knitting compilers [1, 2]. Garment Gallery. Figure 1 shows a set of garments composed entirely within our tool: a raglan sweater, a drop-shoulder pullover, a hooded vest, a pair of mittens, a tube scarf with a pocket, and a child's hat. Each was assembled from between three and nine primitives (e.g., tube, cone, sleeve, and hem segments) joined along skeleton edges. Composition required no manual

Bone defects resulting from trauma, tumor resection, congenital malformation, or degenerative disease remain a major clinical challenge. Autologous bone grafting is still considered the gold standard for reconstruction, but it is limited by donor-site morbidity, restricted tissue availability, and unpredictable resorption. Allografts and xenografts avoid some of these problems but carry risks of immune rejection and disease transmission. Bone tissue engineering, which combines a scaffold, responsive cells, and bioactive signals, has therefore emerged as an attractive alternative for regenerating functional bone. Synthetic polymers such as poly-lactic-co-glycolic acid (PLGA) are widely used as scaffolds because they are biodegradable, have been approved by regulatory agencies for several clinical applications, and offer tunable mechanical properties and degradation rates. However, most synthetic polymers lack specific biological recognition motifs. Their surfaces are typically hydrophobic and chemically inert, which limits protein adsorption, cell attachment, and spreading, and gives rise to poor integration with host tissue and compromised osteogenic activity. Surface modification to provide cell-instructive cues is therefore needed to make these materials truly osteoinductive. One common approach is to supplement scaffolds with soluble growth factors, particularly bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs). BMP-2 and BMP-7 are potent inducers of osteogenic differentiation and have been used clinically. Nevertheless, recombinant proteins have important drawbacks. They have short half-lives in vivo, are susceptible to proteolytic degradation and denaturation, and often must be delivered at supraphysiological doses, which has been associated with ectopic bone formation, inflammation, and high cost. Short bioactive peptides derived from native growth factors represent an appealing alternative, since they are more stable, cheaper to synthesize, less immunogenic, and easier to chemically manipulate and immobilize than full-length proteins. Bone forming peptide-1 (BFP-1) is a peptide derived from the immature (pro-) region of BMP-7. Unlike the mature BMP-7 domain, this truncated sequence has been reported to display higher osteogenic activity than full-length mature BMP-7, and it has been found to induce osteogenic differentiation of several cell types. Its short sequence makes it well suited for incorporation into biomaterials. Despite these properties, the osteoinductive effect of BFP-1 on human adipose-derived stem cells has not been well characterized, and strategies for presenting BFP-1 on polymeric scaffold surfaces remain underexplored. The choice of cell source is equally important. Bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells have been the most extensively studied for bone engineering, but their harvest is invasive and painful, and the yield and differentiation capacity decline with donor age. Human adipose-derived stem cells (hASCs) offer a practical alternative. Adipose tissue is abundant and can be obtained in large quantities with minimal morbidity, for example from liposuction aspirates, and hASCs can be expanded readily in culture. They are multipotent and can differentiate along osteogenic, chondrogenic, and adipogenic lineages. These characteristics make hASCs a promising cell source for bone tissue engineering and a suitable platform for testing osteogenic peptides and materials. Immobilization of bioactive molecules on a scaffold surface can prolong their local presence and stabilize their activity, which may allow more sustained stimulation of cells than soluble delivery. Conventional immobilization methods often require multistep chemistry, harsh conditions, or substrate-specific reactions that can damage the material or the biomolecule. Inspired by the adhesive proteins of marine mussels, which are rich in 3,4-dihydroxy-L-phenylalanine (DOPA) and lysine, dopamine has been shown to self-polymerize under mildly alkaline conditions and form a thin, adherent polydopamine (pDA) layer on virtually any material surface. The polydopamine coating contains catechol and quinone groups that react with nucleophiles such as amines and thiols through Michael addition or Schiff base formation, allowing simple one-step covalent attachment of peptides and proteins under mild aqueous conditions. In addition, polydopamine coating improves surface hydrophilicity and has itself been reported to enhance cell adhesion and osteogenic differentiation. This method has been used to immobilize various biomolecules on polymeric materials, but its use with BFP-1 on PLGA has not been reported. In this study, we therefore sought to evaluate the osteoinductive potential of BFP-1 on hASCs, both as a soluble factor and as an immobilized signal on a biomaterial surface. We first examined the effects of free BFP-1 on the osteogenic differentiation of hASCs under osteoinductive conditions, assessing expression of the osteogenic markers alkaline phosphatase (ALP), osteocalcin (OC), and the transcription factor RUNX2. We then used polydopamine-mediated immobilization to functionalize PLGA substrates with BFP-1, generating pDA-BFP-1-PLGA, and compared the osteogenic response of hASCs on this material with that on control surfaces. Finally, we implanted hASCs seeded on pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds into nude mice to determine whether the material could promote bone formation in vivo. We hypothesized that BFP-1 would enhance osteogenic differentiation of hASCs and that its stable presentation on PLGA through a mussel-inspired coating would produce a biomaterial with improved bioactivity. Our findings provide a simple and effective strategy for creating peptide-functionalized scaffolds that may be valuable for bone tissue engineering. Cell isolation and culture. Human adipose tissue was obtained from healthy donors undergoing elective liposuction after written informed consent, under a protocol approved by the institutional review board. Lipoaspirates were washed extensively with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and digested with 0.1% type I collagenase at 37°C for 60 min with gentle agitation. The digest was neutralized with complete medium and centrifuged at 1200 × g for 5 min. The stromal vascular pellet was resuspended, filtered through a 100-μm strainer, and plated in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM) containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin at 37°C in 5% CO2. Non-adherent cells were removed after 24 h, and adherent hASCs were expanded to 80% confluence and passaged with trypsin-EDTA. Cells at passages 3–5 were used for all experiments. Surface phenotype was confirmed by flow cytometry (positive for CD73, CD90, CD105; negative for CD34 and CD45). Peptides. Bone forming peptide-1 (BFP-1; sequence derived from the immature BMP-7 prodomain) and a scrambled control peptide were synthesized by solid-phase synthesis, purified to >95% by HPLC, and verified by mass spectrometry. Peptides were dissolved in sterile water and stored at −20°C. Osteogenic induction with soluble BFP-1. hASCs were seeded in 24-well plates at 2 × 10^4 cells/cm². At confluence, medium was changed to osteogenic medium (OM; DMEM, 10% FBS, 10 mM β-glycerophosphate, 50 μg/mL ascorbic acid, 100 nM dexamethasone) supplemented with BFP-1 at 0, 10, 50, or 100 μg/mL or with the scrambled peptide. Growth medium served as the negative control, and OM with recombinant human BMP-7 (100 ng/mL) served as the positive control. Medium was replaced every 3 days. Preparation of PLGA substrates and dopamine-assisted immobilization. PLGA (75:25) was dissolved in dichloromethane and cast into films (for in vitro experiments) or fabricated into porous scaffolds by solvent casting/particulate leaching using sieved sodium chloride particles (250–425 μm) (for in vivo experiments). Films and scaffolds were washed and sterilized with 75% ethanol and UV irradiation. Substrates were immersed in dopamine hydrochloride solution (2 mg/mL in 10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.5) and shaken at room temperature for 12 h in the dark to form a polydopamine (pDA) layer, then rinsed with deionized water and dried. pDA-coated PLGA was subsequently incubated in BFP-1 solution (100 μg/mL in 10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.5) for 24 h at room temperature, allowing covalent coupling through Michael addition/Schiff base reactions, followed by thorough washing with PBS to remove unbound peptide. Control groups were uncoated PLGA, pDA-PLGA, and pDA-PLGA treated with scrambled peptide. Peptide immobilization was quantified indirectly by measuring the peptide concentration of the solution before and after coating using a micro-BCA assay. Surface characterization. Surface morphology was examined by scanning electron microscopy after gold sputtering. Water contact angles were measured on a goniometer using 5-μL droplets (n = 5). Surface chemistry was analyzed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, with attention to the N 1s signal as an indicator of pDA and peptide deposition. Cell adhesion and proliferation. hASCs were seeded onto films at 1 × 10^4 cells/cm² in OM. Adhesion was assessed at 4 h by counting DAPI-stained nuclei in five random fields per sample. Proliferation at days 1, 3, 5, and 7 was determined with the CCK-8 assay by measuring absorbance at 450 nm. Alkaline phosphatase activity and staining. At day 7, cells were lysed in 0.1% Triton X-100. ALP activity was measured by the conversion of p-nitrophenyl phosphate to p-nitrophenol (absorbance at 405 nm) and normalized to total protein (BCA assay). For staining, cells were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde and stained with BCIP/NBT. Mineralization. At day 21, cells were fixed and stained with 2% Alizarin Red S (pH 4.2) for 20 min. For quantification, stain was extracted with 10% cetylpyridinium chloride and absorbance read at 562 nm. Quantitative real-time PCR. Total RNA was extracted with TRIzol at day 7 and 14, and 1 μg was reverse transcribed. qPCR was performed with SYBR Green master mix for ALP, osteocalcin (OC), RUNX2, and GAPDH as the reference gene. Relative expression was calculated by the 2^−ΔΔCt method. Experiments were performed in triplicate with cells from at least three donors. Western blotting and immunofluorescence. Proteins were extracted in RIPA buffer, separated by SDS-PAGE, transferred to PVDF membranes, and probed with antibodies against RUNX2, OC, and β-actin, followed by HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies and chemiluminescent detection. Band intensities were quantified with ImageJ. For immunofluorescence, fixed cells were permeabilized, blocked with 5% BSA, incubated with anti-OC antibody and fluorescent secondary antibody, and counterstained with DAPI. In vivo implantation. All animal procedures were approved by the institutional animal care and use committee. hASCs (5 × 10^6 cells per scaffold) were seeded onto PLGA, pDA-PLGA, or pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds and pre-cultured in OM for 3 days. Six-week-old female athymic nude mice were anesthetized, and scaffolds were implanted subcutaneously in dorsal pockets (n = 6 per group). After 8 weeks, mice were euthanized and implants harvested. Samples were scanned by micro-computed tomography to determine bone volume/total volume. Samples were then fixed, decalcified, paraffin-embedded, sectioned at 5 μm, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin and Masson's trichrome; OC immunohistochemistry was also performed. New bone area was quantified from five sections per sample using ImageJ. Statistical analysis. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation. Ameloblastoma is a benign but locally aggressive odontogenic neoplasm that arises from the epithelium of the tooth-forming apparatus. It is the most common clinically significant odontogenic tumor, accounting for roughly 1% of all tumors of the jaws [1,2]. Although the tumor lacks the capacity for significant metastasis in most cases, it is characterized by slow, infiltrative growth, a propensity for local recurrence, and the potential to cause marked facial deformity, functional impairment, and, rarely, death through extension to the skull base or through distant spread [3]. The great majority of cases occur in the mandible, particularly the posterior body and ramus, with a smaller proportion arising in the posterior maxilla [2]. Patients typically present in the third to fifth decades of life, with no marked sex predilection, although some variation in demographic patterns has been reported across geographic regions [4]. The current World Health Organization classification recognizes several clinicopathologic variants of ameloblastoma, including conventional (solid/multicystic), unicystic, peripheral, and metastasizing forms [5]. Conventional ameloblastoma is histologically defined by islands and strands of odontogenic epithelium showing peripheral palisading of columnar cells with reverse polarity and a central region resembling stellate reticulum. Follicular and plexiform growth patterns are the most common, and acanthomatous, granular cell, desmoplastic, and basal cell patterns are less frequent [1,5]. Unicystic ameloblastoma, in contrast, presents as a cystic lesion lined by ameloblastomatic epithelium and usually affects younger patients, often in association with an impacted tooth [6]. These subtypes differ in their clinical behavior and, as is now apparent, in their underlying molecular alterations. Management of ameloblastoma has historically been surgical. Because tumor cells infiltrate the surrounding cancellous bone well beyond the radiographic margin, conservative approaches such as enucleation and curettage are associated with high recurrence rates, reported at 50% to 90% for conventional tumors [7]. Wide local resection with a margin of normal bone reduces recurrence substantially but often necessitates extensive reconstruction, with attendant morbidity that is particularly burdensome in young patients [7,8]. Moreover, recurrences may appear many years after initial treatment, mandating long-term follow-up. The difficulty of balancing complete eradication against preservation of form and function has long motivated a search for biologically informed, less mutilating therapies. Such efforts, however, were for decades hindered by a lack of understanding of the tumor’s molecular drivers. Early investigations of ameloblastoma pathogenesis relied on candidate-gene approaches and immunohistochemical studies. These reported altered expression of molecules involved in developmental signaling, cell cycle control, and apoptosis, including components of the WNT/β-catenin, Notch, and sonic hedgehog (SHH) pathways, as well as TP53, BCL2, and cyclins [9–11]. Although these studies suggested that ameloblastoma recapitulates aspects of odontogenic epithelial signaling, they could not distinguish driver events from secondary or incidental changes, and no consistent genetic lesion emerged. Cytogenetic and comparative genomic hybridization studies likewise revealed heterogeneous and nonspecific chromosomal alterations [12]. As a result, ameloblastoma remained poorly understood at the molecular level and was widely regarded as a tumor without a defined genetic basis. This situation changed in 2014, when next-generation sequencing identified recurrent activating mutations in BRAF, most commonly the c.1799T>A (p.V600E) substitution, in a substantial proportion of ameloblastomas [13,14]. Shortly thereafter, independent groups reported mutations in SMO, encoding the transmembrane activator of the hedgehog pathway, and in FGFR2, RAS family genes, and other components of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascade [15–17]. Together, these findings indicated that mutations activating MAPK signaling are present in the large majority of cases and that ameloblastoma is, in molecular terms, a tumor driven by a limited set of recurrent oncogenic events. Subsequent studies have shown that the mutational spectrum varies with anatomic site, histologic subtype, and patient population: BRAF V600E predominates in mandibular tumors, whereas maxillary tumors more frequently harbor SMO, RAS, or FGFR2 alterations [15,17,18]. Differences between populations, notably higher rates of RAS and FGFR2 mutations in some African cohorts, have also been described [19]. These discoveries have not resolved all questions. The significance of SMO mutations remains debated: some investigators regard them as an alternative initiating mechanism that activates hedgehog signaling, whereas others have found them to be subclonal or co-occurring with MAPK pathway mutations and therefore consider them secondary events [15,17,20]. The relationship between genotype and clinical behavior, the cell of origin, the cooperating events that permit progression to malignant forms, and the mechanisms by which MAPK activation maintains the odontogenic phenotype are likewise incompletely understood. The identification of BRAF V600E mutations has immediate translational relevance, because targeted inhibitors developed for melanoma and other cancers are available. Case reports and small series describing dramatic responses of BRAF-mutant ameloblastomas to vemurafenib and dabrafenib, alone or with MEK inhibitors, have generated considerable enthusiasm for neoadjuvant or definitive medical therapy [21,22]. Mutation-specific immunohistochemistry and molecular testing may also aid diagnosis and risk stratification. In this review, we summarize the recent advances in the molecular pathogenesis of ameloblastoma, examine the evidence and controversy surrounding MAPK and SHH pathway alterations, and discuss their diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic implications. This review was designed as a narrative review with a structured search strategy to identify and synthesize studies describing the molecular pathogenesis of ameloblastoma and the diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic implications of these findings. The review was conducted in accordance with the general principles of the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) [1], and elements of the PRISMA framework were adopted where applicable to improve transparency of study identification and selection [2]. Because the field of ameloblastoma genomics is recent and the available literature is heterogeneous in design, a formal systematic review with meta-analysis was not considered appropriate. Literature Search Strategy A literature search was performed in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science from database inception through the date of the final search. The search combined controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH and Emtree terms) with free-text keywords. Core terms included "ameloblastoma," "odontogenic tumor," "BRAF," "BRAF V600E," "FGFR2," "RAS," "KRAS," "HRAS," "NRAS," "MAPK," "mitogen-activated protein kinase," "Smoothened," "SMO," "sonic hedgehog," "PTCH1," "mutation," "next-generation sequencing," "targeted therapy," and "BRAF inhibitor." Boolean operators were used to combine concepts (e.g., "ameloblastoma" AND ["BRAF" OR "MAPK" OR "SMO" OR "hedgehog"]). Reference lists of included articles and previous reviews were manually screened to identify additional relevant publications [3]. Preprints and conference abstracts were reviewed for context but were not used as primary evidence unless subsequently published in peer-reviewed form. Eligibility Criteria Studies were included if they (i) were published in English; (ii) examined human ameloblastoma or ameloblastoma-derived cells, or used experimental models directly relevant to ameloblastoma pathogenesis; and (iii) reported original data on somatic or germline genetic alterations, pathway activation, genotype–phenotype correlations, or treatment responses linked to molecular findings. Study types considered included genomic and targeted sequencing studies, immunohistochemical and functional investigations, case reports and case series of molecularly targeted therapy, and clinical studies evaluating prognostic or diagnostic utility of mutation testing. Review articles were not treated as primary evidence but were consulted for background and to identify additional sources. Studies were excluded if they focused exclusively on other odontogenic tumors or cysts without separate ameloblastoma data, lacked sufficient molecular detail, or were non-human studies without relevance to the pathways under review. Where duplicate reports of overlapping cohorts were identified, the most comprehensive or most recent report was prioritized. Study Selection Titles and abstracts retrieved from the searches were screened for relevance by two independent reviewers. Full texts of potentially eligible articles were then assessed against the eligibility criteria. Disagreements were resolved by discussion and, when necessary, consultation with a third reviewer. Given the narrative design, a formal PRISMA flow diagram was not required, though the numbers of records identified and retained were tracked internally. Data Extraction For each included study, the following information was extracted using a standardized form: authors, year of publication, study design, sample size, tumor type and anatomical site (mandibular or maxillary), histologic subtype (e.g., conventional/solid-multicystic, unicystic, desmoplastic, peripheral, or metastasizing), and patient demographics. Molecular data comprised the genes analyzed, sequencing platform or detection method (e.g., whole-exome sequencing, targeted next-generation sequencing, Sanger sequencing, allele-specific PCR, or VE1 immunohistochemistry for BRAF V600E), the specific variants identified, and their reported frequencies. Where available, we also extracted information on variant allele fractions, co-occurrence or mutual exclusivity of mutations, and the source of tissue (fresh-frozen versus formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded specimens), because these factors influence assay sensitivity [4,5]. Clinical and outcome data were collected where reported, including recurrence, response to therapy, and follow-up duration. For studies of targeted therapy, we recorded the agents used (e.g., BRAF inhibitors such as vemurafenib or dabrafenib, alone or with MEK inhibitors such as trametinib), dosing, duration of treatment, radiographic or clinical response, adverse events, and evidence of resistance or relapse after discontinuation. Synthesis of Evidence Findings were synthesized qualitatively and organized thematically into: (i) mutations affecting MAPK pathway components (BRAF, FGFR2, and RAS isoforms); (ii) alterations in the sonic hedgehog pathway, with particular attention to SMO; (iii) associations between genotype and anatomical site, histologic subtype, and clinical behavior; and (iv) diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic implications. Mutation frequencies were compared across studies, and differences were considered in light of cohort composition, geographic and ethnic variation, and detection methodology, which are known to influence reported prevalence [4–6]. Frequencies were not statistically pooled because of heterogeneity in methods and sample selection. The controversy regarding SMO and hedgehog pathway mutations was addressed by comparing reports in terms of variant allele fractions, tumor subsets analyzed, co-occurrence with MAPK pathway alterations, and functional evidence of pathway activation. This approach allowed assessment of whether such mutations are more consistent with an alternative initiating mechanism or with secondary, subclonal events [7]. Quality Appraisal Methodological quality was appraised qualitatively. Considerations included the adequacy of sample size, clarity of case definition according to the contemporary World Health Organization classification of head and neck tumors [8], the sensitivity and validation of mutation detection methods, the possibility of contamination by non-neoplastic stromal tissue, and the reporting of follow-up in clinical studies. Case reports and small series were interpreted cautiously, recognizing the risk of publication bias favoring positive therapeutic responses. Limitations of the Approach As a narrative review, this work is subject to selection bias inherent in non-exhaustive searching, and restriction to English-language publications may have omitted relevant studies. The rapid evolution of the field means that additional data may have appeared after the final search date. Mutational Landscape of Ameloblastoma Early candidate-gene and targeted sequencing studies, followed by whole-exome and next-generation sequencing of formalin-fixed and fresh-frozen tumors, identified recurrent somatic mutations in a limited set of genes in the majority of conventional ameloblastomas [1,2]. The most frequent alteration is the BRAF p.V600E (c.1799T>A) substitution, reported in approximately 46–82% of cases across cohorts, with a notably higher prevalence in mandibular than maxillary tumors [2–4]. Mutations in RAS family members (HRAS, KRAS, NRAS), most commonly affecting codons 12, 13, and 61, were detected in roughly 5–15% of tumors and were largely mutually exclusive with BRAF mutations [3,5]. Activating FGFR2 mutations, including p.C382R and p.S252W, were identified in a further 5–10% of tumors, again predominantly in a mutually exclusive pattern [1,5]. Collectively, these MAPK pathway alterations are present in up to 90% of ameloblastomas when comprehensive sequencing approaches are used [5,6]. Geographic and Anatomic Variation Mutation frequencies show substantial variation by population and anatomic site. BRAF V600E predominates in cohorts from Europe, North America, and Asia, whereas studies from African populations report lower BRAF frequencies and a relatively greater proportion of RAS and FGFR2 mutations [6,7]. Mandibular ameloblastomas are enriched for BRAF V600E, while maxillary tumors more often harbor SMO, RAS, or FGFR2 alterations [4,8]. These differences suggest that anatomic and possibly germline or environmental factors influence the spectrum of driver events, although sample sizes for maxillary tumors remain small. Centrosomes are the primary microtubule-organizing centers of animal cells, and their duplication must be tightly controlled, since errors in centrosome number contribute to aneuploidy, genome instability, and disease. Centrosome duplication occurs once per cell cycle and is accomplished by assembly of a new centrosome adjacent to the existing one. Although many centrosome components have been identified, how they assemble into a functional organelle in a defined temporal order remains poorly understood. The budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae offers a powerful system to address this question. Its centrosome equivalent, the spindle pole body (SPB), is a compact, multilayered cylindrical structure embedded in the nuclear envelope (NE) throughout the cell cycle, and it is built from a relatively small set of well-characterized proteins. The SPB comprises 18 core components that form distinct layers. The outer plaque, facing the cytoplasm, anchors cytoplasmic microtubules and contains Cnm67 and Spc72. The central plaque, which spans the NE, contains Spc42, Spc110 and Cmd1 and the proteins Spc29 and Cnm67. The inner plaque, within the nucleoplasm, nucleates nuclear microtubules through the γ-tubulin complex (Tub4, Spc97, Spc98) bound to Spc110. Adjacent to the central plaque lies the half-bridge, a NE-associated extension containing Sfi1, Cdc31, Mps3 and Kar1, which is the site of new SPB assembly. Finally, a group of integral membrane proteins, Mps2, Bbp1, Ndc1 and Nbp1, anchors the SPB in the NE and is thought to mediate insertion of the new SPB into the NE through a poorly understood process akin to assembly of nuclear pore complexes. Duplication has been described as a series of discrete morphological steps, largely derived from electron microscopy of synchronized cells and of mutants arrested at specific stages. In G1, the half-bridge elongates through Sfi1 association with Cdc31, and a darkly staining structure called the satellite or duplication plaque forms at the distal tip of the bridge. The duplication plaque then expands and is inserted into the NE, and the bridge separates, yielding two side-by-side SPBs that each can organize a spindle. Genetic and biochemical work has defined requirements for many components, and the kinase Mps1 and cell cycle kinases such as Cdk1 have been implicated in regulating early steps. Sfi1 molecules are arranged in an antiparallel manner with their N termini at the distal end of the bridge, and a model proposes that new Sfi1 is added with its C terminus anchored to the old SPB-bound Sfi1 N terminus, so that the bridge doubles at mitotic exit. However, the order in which components arrive at the new SPB, their relative quantities, and the dependencies that link them have been difficult to establish. The main obstacle is resolution. The SPB is roughly 150 nm in diameter, and the newly forming SPB lies within a few hundred nanometers of the mother, which is below the diffraction limit of conventional fluorescence microscopy. Thus, standard light microscopy cannot separate old from new SPB or reveal the substructure of the half-bridge. Electron microscopy provides the resolution but is low throughput, offers limited ability to identify specific proteins, and gives little quantitative information. Super-resolution approaches such as photoactivated localization microscopy and stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy require special labeling and are difficult to apply to many endogenously tagged proteins in living or lightly fixed yeast. Structured illumination microscopy (SIM) doubles resolution relative to widefield imaging while remaining compatible with standard fluorescent protein fusions, making it attractive for a systematic survey. Yet a single SIM image of an individual SPB has limited signal-to-noise and is susceptible to reconstruction artifacts. Because every SPB is built to the same specification, the structure is well suited to single-particle averaging, in which many aligned images are combined to improve signal and reveal the consistent underlying organization. Here we combine two-color SIM with single-particle averaging (SPA-SIM) to localize and quantify all 18 SPB components during duplication. By pairing each protein, tagged with a fluorescent protein at its endogenous locus, with a reference marker, we could align large numbers of SPBs and derive averaged images that report both position relative to the SPB and intensity, providing a measure of protein abundance at the old and new SPB. Using synchronized cells and a series of mutants, we then analyzed the order and dependencies of assembly. Our results refine the standard model of SPB duplication. We find that duplication begins at mitotic exit with formation of an asymmetric Sfi1 filament, rather than with assembly of a symmetric bridge, followed by Mps1-dependent recruitment of a complex containing Spc29 and Spc42 at its distal tip. Unexpectedly, membrane proteins implicated in NE insertion, including Mps2, Bbp1 and Ndc1, accumulate at the new SPB early, at the time the Spc29–Spc42 complex assembles, rather than only after the structure is complete. This suggests that SPB assembly and NE insertion are coupled in wild-type cells. These findings illustrate the value of SPA-SIM for dissecting assembly of reproducible macromolecular structures in vivo and provide a framework for understanding centrosome duplication more broadly.
