Drug-eluting stents (DES) have greatly reduced the incidence of restenosis after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), yet late adverse events such as in-stent restenosis, late stent thrombosis, and recurrent ischemic symptoms remain clinically important. These events are increasingly attributed not only to stent-related mechanical factors but also to the quality of the vascular healing response, particularly the nature of the neointimal tissue that covers the stent struts. Neointimal hyperplasia is a physiological response to vessel injury and is necessary for strut coverage, but its composition varies considerably between patients and lesions. Neointima may be stable, homogeneous, and fibrous, or it may be immature, lipid-laden, or inflamed, and the latter types are thought to be more prone to complications. In addition, neoatherosclerosis, defined as the accumulation of lipid-laden foamy macrophages within the neointima with or without necrotic core formation and calcification, has emerged as a key substrate for very late stent failure. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is an intravascular imaging modality with an axial resolution of 10–15 μm, roughly ten times that of intravascular ultrasound. This resolution permits detailed in vivo assessment of stent strut coverage, neointimal thickness, and tissue characteristics that cannot be resolved by other clinical imaging techniques. Several OCT-based patterns of neointimal tissue have been described, including homogeneous, heterogeneous, and layered patterns, as well as neointima with signal-rich or signal-poor regions. Lipid-rich neointima and neoatherosclerosis appear as diffusely bordered, signal-poor regions with marked signal attenuation, whereas fibrous neointima appears as a homogeneous, high-intensity signal band. The peri-strut low-intensity area (PLIA) is a characteristic OCT finding, defined as a low-intensity region surrounding stent struts within the neointima. It was initially described in the setting of bare-metal stents and first-generation DES, and has been interpreted in different ways. Histological correlations suggest that such areas may represent fibrin deposition, proteoglycan-rich extracellular matrix, edema, inflammatory cell infiltration, or early lipid accumulation around struts, reflecting delayed or incomplete vascular healing. Because these processes are associated with persistent inflammation and hypersensitivity to polymer or drug, PLIA could theoretically indicate a neointima that is unstable and vulnerable to later clinical events. Previous reports have linked PLIA to the use of DES, particularly first-generation sirolimus-eluting stents, and to longer follow-up intervals, but the results are inconsistent, and the relation of PLIA to patient characteristics has not been well established. Understanding the determinants of PLIA is relevant for several reasons. First, if specific clinical features, such as dyslipidemia, diabetes, the initial presentation with acute coronary syndrome (ACS), or comorbid atherosclerotic disease in other vascular beds, predispose to PLIA formation, then patients at risk of abnormal vascular healing might be identified early and managed with more intensive lipid-lowering and antiplatelet strategies, or with closer follow-up. Second, the timing of PLIA appearance after stent implantation is unclear. It is uncertain whether it is a transient phenomenon of the early healing phase that resolves with maturation of the neointima or a persistent marker of chronic dysfunction of the stented segment. Third, and most importantly, the prognostic significance of PLIA is largely unknown. Most existing studies of OCT neointimal patterns are cross-sectional, have short clinical follow-up, or focus on surrogate imaging endpoints rather than on clinical outcomes. Whether PLIA predicts major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), or particular manifestations such as unstable angina (UA), has not been systematically examined. The clinical presentation after stent implantation can be heterogeneous. Late events include not only target lesion revascularization due to restenosis but also UA, which may arise from progression of neoatherosclerosis, neointimal rupture, thrombosis, or disease progression in non-stented segments. Because UA is common and affects patients’ quality of life and health-care use, identifying imaging markers associated with its development could add value to routine follow-up evaluations. If PLIA reflects an unstable neointimal phenotype, it may be associated with UA even in the absence of overt restenosis or hard cardiovascular events. Given these gaps, we conducted a prospective study of patients who underwent OCT reexamination after PCI and had documented neointimal hyperplasia. We classified peri-strut intensity into low-intensity and high-intensity patterns and investigated the clinical, angiographic, and laboratory factors associated with the PLIA pattern. We then followed patients who did not undergo revascularization at the time of OCT reexamination for a median of more than 3.8 years to determine whether PLIA was associated with MACEs and with UA. We hypothesized that PLIA would be associated with adverse metabolic profiles and ACS presentation and would identify patients at higher risk of subsequent UA. The findings may help clarify the genesis of PLIA and its potential role as an imaging marker for risk stratification after stent implantation. Study population This was a single-center, prospective observational study. Patients who underwent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with stent implantation and subsequently underwent OCT reexamination at follow-up angiography between 2009 and 2011 were consecutively screened. Inclusion criteria were: (1) age ≥18 years; (2) previous implantation of at least one drug-eluting or bare-metal stent; (3) neointimal hyperplasia within the stent documented by OCT at reexamination; and (4) adequate OCT image quality for analysis. Exclusion criteria were: (1) left main disease; (2) in-stent lesions with severe calcification or tortuosity precluding OCT pullback; (3) hemodynamic instability, cardiogenic shock, or severe heart failure; (4) renal insufficiency precluding contrast use; (5) poor image quality caused by residual blood, artifacts, or incomplete pullback; and (6) lack of informed consent. The study was approved by the institutional ethics committee and complied with the Declaration of Helsinki. All patients provided written informed consent. Data collection Baseline demographic and clinical data were collected from medical records, including age, sex, body mass index, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, smoking, history of myocardial infarction, history of cerebrovascular disease, and initial clinical presentation (stable angina vs. acute coronary syndrome [ACS], comprising unstable angina, non-ST-elevation and ST-elevation myocardial infarction). Procedural details were recorded: target vessel, stent type, number, length and diameter, and the interval between stent implantation and OCT reexamination (stent implantation time). Fasting blood samples were obtained at the time of OCT reexamination, and total cholesterol, triglycerides, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, glucose, creatinine, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein were measured by standard laboratory methods. OCT image acquisition OCT imaging was performed with a frequency-domain OCT system (ILUMIEN or C7-XR, St. Jude Medical) using a 2.7-F imaging catheter. After intracoronary nitroglycerin administration, the catheter was advanced distal to the stented segment over a guidewire. Blood was cleared by continuous contrast or low-molecular-weight dextran flush through the guiding catheter, and automated pullback was performed at 20 mm/s (or 10 mm/s depending on the system). Images were digitally stored for offline analysis. OCT image analysis Images were analyzed offline by two experienced independent observers blinded to clinical data, using dedicated software. Cross-sections were analyzed at 1-mm intervals within the stented segment. Lumen, stent, and neointimal areas were measured, and neointimal thickness was measured over each strut as the distance from the strut's endoluminal surface to the lumen border. Struts were classified as covered or uncovered, and malapposed if the distance between the strut and vessel wall exceeded the strut thickness plus polymer thickness. Neointimal tissue characteristics were evaluated according to signal intensity. PLIA was defined as a region of low signal intensity with a diffuse border located around stent struts, within the neointima and distinct from the strut shadow, in contrast to the homogeneous high-intensity signal of typical neointima. Patients were classified into two patterns: the low-intensity pattern, when PLIA was present in at least one cross-section, and the high-intensity pattern, when neointima showed homogeneous high signal without PLIA. Other neointimal patterns such as layered or heterogeneous tissue and neoatherosclerosis (lipid-laden neointima with signal-poor regions and diffuse borders, with or without calcification) were recorded. Disagreements between the two observers were resolved by consensus with a third investigator. Interobserver and intraobserver variability were assessed by the kappa statistic in a randomly selected subset of cases. Follow-up and clinical outcomes Patients who did not undergo revascularization at the time of OCT reexamination were followed after the procedure through outpatient visits, telephone interviews, or medical record review. Median follow-up exceeded 3.8 years. Patients who underwent revascularization at reexamination were excluded from the prognostic analysis. The primary outcome was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), a composite of cardiac death, myocardial infarction, and target lesion revascularization. The secondary outcome was unstable angina (UA) requiring hospitalization, defined as new-onset or worsening angina at rest or with minimal exertion, with or without transient ST-T changes and without elevation of cardiac biomarkers. Events were adjudicated by clinicians blinded to OCT findings, based on medical records and, when necessary, coronary angiography. Statistical analysis Continuous variables were tested for normality with the Shapiro–Wilk test and are presented as mean ± standard deviation or median (interquartile range); they were compared between groups using the Student t test or Mann–Whitney U test. Categorical variables are expressed as counts and percentages and were compared with the chi-square or Fisher exact test. To identify factors associated with PLIA, variables with P < 0.10 in univariate analysis, together with clinically relevant variables, were entered into a multivariable logistic regression model, and odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. Because of the limited number of PLIA cases, the number of covariates was restricted and model fit was assessed with the Hosmer–Lemeshow test. Event-free survival curves were estimated by the Kaplan–Meier method and compared using the log-rank test. The association between PLIA and clinical outcomes was assessed with Cox proportional hazards regression, and hazard ratios (HR) with 95% CI were reported; the proportional hazards assumption was checked with Schoenfeld residuals. Interobserver agreement was evaluated using Cohen's kappa. A two-sided P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed using SPSS software (version 22.0, IBM Corp.) or R. A total of 128 patients who underwent OCT reexamination after stent implantation were included in the analysis. Peri-strut low-intensity area (PLIA) was detected in 22 patients (17.2%), and the remaining 106 patients (82.8%) showed a high-intensity pattern. The OCT reexamination was performed at a median of 11.2 months after the index procedure (interquartile range, 8.5–14.0 months) in the overall cohort. Baseline clinical characteristics Baseline characteristics are summarized in Table 1. The mean age was similar between the PLIA and high-intensity groups, as were the proportions of male patients, current smokers, and patients with hypertension or diabetes mellitus. Patients with PLIA had higher levels of serum triglyceride and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) than those with high-intensity neointima. A history of cerebrovascular disease was more frequent in the PLIA group (n = 4, 18.2%) than in the high-intensity group (n = 2, 1.9%; P = 0.008). Initial presentation with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) was also more common among patients with PLIA (72.7% vs. 41.5%, P = 0.010). Stent implantation time, defined as the interval between stent implantation and OCT reexamination, was shorter in the PLIA group. The proportions of patients receiving statins, antiplatelet agents, β-blockers, and renin-angiotensin system inhibitors at follow-up did not differ significantly between groups. Stent type (drug-eluting vs. bare-metal), stent length, and stent diameter were comparable between groups. Predictors of PLIA In the multivariable logistic regression analysis, several variables were independently associated with the presence of PLIA (Table 2). Higher serum triglyceride (OR: 2.11, 95% CI: 1.14–3.90, P = 0.017) and higher LDL-C (OR: 2.61, 95% CI: 1.22–5.66, P = 0.015) were positively correlated with PLIA. A history of cerebrovascular disease showed a strong positive association (OR: 101.11, 95% CI: 6.54–1562.13, P < 0.001), although the wide confidence interval reflects the small number of patients with this history. Initial clinical presentation of ACS was likewise an independent predictor (OR: 18.77, 95% CI: 2.73–128.83, P = 0.003). In contrast, stent implantation time was negatively correlated with PLIA (OR: 0.57, 95% CI: 0.33–0.98, P = 0.043), indicating that PLIA was more often observed at earlier time points after implantation and less often at later time points. Age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, smoking, and stent type were not independently associated with PLIA. Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) establish a direct communication pathway between the brain and external devices, and they have been applied in rehabilitation, communication, entertainment, and information retrieval [1], [2]. Among the various BCI paradigms, those based on event-related potentials (ERPs) are widely used because of their stable signal characteristics and minimal user training requirements. The P300 component is a positive deflection that occurs approximately 300 ms after a rare or task-relevant stimulus is presented, and it has been exploited in spellers, control systems, and lie detection [3], [4]. Rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) is a paradigm in which images are shown sequentially at the same spatial location at high rates, typically 5-20 images per second [5]. When a participant searches for target images embedded in a stream of non-target distractors, targets elicit a P300 response, whereas non-targets do not. Because the human visual system can recognize meaningful content within a few hundred milliseconds, an RSVP-based BCI can screen images much faster than manual inspection. This property has led to applications including aerial image analysis, medical image screening, object detection in remote sensing, and image retrieval [6]-[8]. In such systems, the EEG signals evoked by each image are classified to decide whether the image is a target, and the images flagged as targets are then passed on for further analysis. The practical value of an RSVP-based system depends on the accuracy of single-trial P300 detection. However, single-trial EEG has a low signal-to-noise ratio, because the P300 is small in amplitude relative to spontaneous background activity, ocular and muscle artifacts, and environmental noise [9]. In addition, the high presentation rates of RSVP cause temporal overlap between consecutive responses, and phenomena such as the attentional blink can degrade target-related responses [10]. Consequently, single-trial detection performance is considerably lower than that obtained by averaging or combining multiple trials, as in P300 spellers where repeated stimulus presentations are commonly used to improve accuracy [11]. Considerable effort has therefore been devoted to improving single-trial classification. Traditional approaches include linear discriminant analysis, support vector machines, and spatial filtering methods such as xDAWN and common spatial patterns, often combined with hierarchical discriminant component analysis [12]-[14]. More recently, deep learning models, including convolutional neural networks such as EEGNet and its variants, have been proposed to learn spatiotemporal features directly from raw or minimally processed EEG [15], [16]. Although these methods have achieved notable gains, performance remains limited by the intrinsic variability of single-trial signals, inter-subject differences, and the scarcity of labeled data. Improvements in algorithms alone are thus unlikely to fully close the gap to multitrial performance. An alternative is to modify the paradigm so that multitrial information can be exploited. In conventional RSVP, each image is typically displayed once, so there is no repeated evidence for a given image. Repeating the whole sequence would increase the number of trials per image but would multiply the total search time and reduce the efficiency advantage of RSVP. Some studies have examined repeated presentation within RSVP and showed that combining responses across repetitions improves accuracy, at the cost of speed [17]. A paradigm that supplies multiple observations of a target without proportionally increasing presentation time would be highly desirable. Motivated by this, we previously proposed a triple-RSVP paradigm in which three images are presented simultaneously at different spatial positions, and the sequence is arranged so that each image appears three times, once at each position, within different triplets [18]. In this way, a target image elicits three P300 responses within a single pass through the image set, and the total presentation time is comparable to that of a standard RSVP with the same number of images and a similar rate. The three responses can be jointly analyzed by multitrial P300 classification methods, which is expected to boost detection accuracy compared with single-trial approaches. Such a design draws on the idea of combining evidence across repeated stimuli while preserving the high throughput characteristic of RSVP. In the present study, we extend and validate this mechanism and generalize it to a multi-RSVP framework in which the number of simultaneously presented images and the number of repetitions can vary. We examine the characteristics of this framework, including how the ERP responses to simultaneously presented images behave, how the spatial arrangement of the images affects the evoked responses, and how detection accuracy relates to the number of combined trials and the presentation speed. To demonstrate that the scheme is not tied to a specific classifier, we employ two different P300 detection algorithms within the multi-RSVP paradigm and compare their performance with that obtained under the standard RSVP paradigm. The main contributions of this work are as follows. First, we present a multi-RSVP paradigm that provides multitrial P300 evidence for each image without increasing total presentation time. Second, we describe a detection pipeline that integrates responses from repeated presentations of the same image. Third, we show experimentally, with two distinct detection algorithms, that the multi-RSVP paradigm achieves higher detection accuracy than the standard RSVP paradigm, indicating that the approach is universally applicable. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II describes the experimental paradigm, data acquisition, and detection algorithms. Section III presents the results. Section IV discusses the findings and limitations, and Section V concludes the paper. Participants Twelve healthy volunteers (seven males, five females; age 21–28 years, mean 23.9) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision took part in the experiment. None had a history of neurological disorders. All participants gave written informed consent, and the protocol was approved by the local institutional ethics committee. Stimuli and Experimental Paradigm Stimuli were natural images drawn from a public image database, divided into target (aircraft) and non-target (landscapes, buildings, vehicles other than aircraft) categories. Images were resized to 400 × 400 pixels and shown on a 24-inch LCD monitor with a 60 Hz refresh rate at a viewing distance of approximately 70 cm. Two paradigms were compared. In the standard RSVP paradigm, images were presented one at a time at the screen center at a rate of 5 Hz (200 ms per image, no inter-stimulus interval). Targets occurred with a probability of 5%. Participants were instructed to silently count target images and report the count at the end of each block. In the multi-RSVP paradigm, several images were shown simultaneously at distinct screen positions, and each target image was repeated across positions in successive frames. For the triple-RSVP, three images were displayed in a row in each frame, and the sequence was arranged so that every image appeared three times, occupying the left, middle, and right positions in three consecutive frames in a cyclic-shift (Latin-square) manner. Consequently, a target image elicited three P300 responses within a short interval (600 ms), whereas a non-target image elicited three non-target responses. Frame duration was 200 ms, so the total number of frames equaled the number of images plus two. To limit the effect of spatial attention, participants were asked to fixate on the central position and to attend to all three positions. A dual-RSVP variant (two images per frame, each image shown twice) was also included to examine how the number of simultaneous streams affects performance. The number of distinct images and the target probability were identical across paradigms. Each paradigm comprised 10 blocks of 100 distinct images (5 targets per block), with block order counterbalanced across participants and rest periods between blocks. Data Acquisition EEG was recorded using a 64-channel active electrode cap positioned according to the international 10–20 system, with the reference at the right mastoid and the ground at AFz. Signals were amplified, sampled at 1000 Hz, and band-pass filtered between 0.1 and 100 Hz with a 50 Hz notch filter. Electrode impedances were kept below 10 kΩ. Stimulus onset triggers were sent from the presentation software (Psychtoolbox in MATLAB) and verified with a photodiode to remove presentation latency. Preprocessing Offline, data were re-referenced to the average of both mastoids, band-pass filtered at 0.5–30 Hz using a zero-phase fourth-order Butterworth filter, and downsampled to 100 Hz. Ocular artifacts were attenuated using independent component analysis [1]. Epochs from 0 to 800 ms relative to image onset (for multi-RSVP, relative to frame onset) were extracted and baseline-corrected using the 200 ms prestimulus interval. Epochs with amplitudes exceeding ±100 μV were rejected. For the multi-RSVP paradigm, the three epochs corresponding to the three presentations of the same image were grouped into one multitrial sample, with each epoch aligned to its own frame onset. P300 Detection Algorithms To demonstrate that the framework is independent of the specific classifier, two widely used P300 detection algorithms were implemented. 1) Hierarchical discriminant component analysis (HDCA) [2]. Spatial weights were learned by Fisher linear discriminant analysis within consecutive 100 ms windows, yielding one discriminant component per window. A second-level logistic regression combined the window outputs into a single score for each trial. 2) xDAWN with Bayesian linear discriminant analysis (BLDA) [3], [4]. xDAWN spatial filters enhanced the signal-to-noise ratio of the evoked response, and the first several filtered components were concatenated into feature vectors, which were classified by BLDA. For the standard RSVP, a single-trial score was produced per image. For multi-RSVP, the classifier was trained on single-epoch data, and the scores of the three epochs of an image were averaged, which is equivalent to log-likelihood fusion under a conditional-independence assumption [5]. The fused score was compared against a decision threshold to label the image as target or non-target. Additionally, the data of the three presentations were also averaged at the signal level prior to classification, and the two fusion strategies were compared. Evaluation Procedure Performance was assessed using tenfold cross-validation within each participant, ensuring that epochs of the same image were never split between training and test sets. Because of the strong class imbalance, the training set was balanced by oversampling target samples, whereas test sets retained the natural class ratio. Metrics included area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), balanced accuracy, true positive rate, and false positive rate. The information transfer rate was also computed to account for the different image throughputs of the paradigms. Target-detection accuracy at the image level was defined as the proportion of correctly classified images. Characteristics of the Multi-RSVP Framework To explore the framework further, we analyzed (i) grand-average event-related potentials at Fz, Cz, and Pz and their topographies at the P300 peak for each stream position, in order to assess spatial effects; (ii) the influence of the number of simultaneous images (one, two, three) on classification; (iii) the effect of training-set size, by progressively reducing the number of training blocks; and (iv) the contribution of each repetition to the fused decision. Statistical Analysis Normality was checked using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Differences among paradigms were assessed using repeated-measures ANOVA with paradigm and algorithm as factors, followed by paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction for post hoc comparisons. Greenhouse–Geisser correction was applied when sphericity was violated. The significance level was set at p < 0.05. The experiments were conducted with 14 participants, and the data were analyzed offline. Two P300 detection algorithms, hierarchical discriminant component analysis (HDCA) [1] and a spatial-temporal feature-based support vector machine (SVM) classifier [2], were applied to both the standard RSVP and the multi-RSVP paradigms. Performance was assessed with ten-fold cross-validation using accuracy, recall, precision, F1 score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction were used for comparisons between conditions unless otherwise stated. ERP Characteristics Grand-average ERPs at electrode Pz showed a clear difference between target and nontarget stimuli in both paradigms. In the standard RSVP condition, target stimuli elicited a positive deflection peaking at approximately 380 ms after stimulus onset, with a mean amplitude of 5.8 μV, whereas nontarget stimuli elicited a flat response of about 0.9 μV. This is consistent with the classical P300 component reported in earlier RSVP studies [3]. In the triple-RSVP condition, the P300 peak occurred slightly later (approximately 410 ms) and had a somewhat lower amplitude (5.1 μV), which may reflect the higher perceptual load of monitoring three simultaneous images. A matching in a graph is a set of pairwise disjoint edges, and it is maximal if it is not properly contained in any other matching. A graph is called equimatchable if all of its maximal matchings have the same cardinality; equivalently, every maximal matching is maximum. The notion was introduced independently in the 1970s by Grünbaum [1], Lesk, Plummer and Pulleyblank [2], and Meng [3], and it has since attracted considerable attention in the study of matching theory. Equimatchable graphs are closely related to the better-known class of randomly matchable graphs, in which every maximal matching is perfect, and which were characterized by Sumner [4]. They also relate to well-covered graphs: a graph is equimatchable exactly when its line graph is well-covered, that is, when all maximal independent sets of the line graph have the same size [5]. Despite this connection, the structure of equimatchable graphs is not well understood in general. Recognition is known to be in co-NP, since a certificate of non-equimatchability is simply a pair of maximal matchings of different sizes. A polynomial-time recognition algorithm for the general case is not known, and the problem is not known to be co-NP-complete either. This situation contrasts with that of well-covered graphs, whose recognition is co-NP-complete [6,7]. Because the line graph of an equimatchable graph is well-covered but the converse class of line graphs is restricted, hardness results for well-covered graphs do not transfer directly. Consequently, much work has been devoted to characterizing equimatchable graphs within restricted classes, where structural properties can be exploited. A fundamental tool is the Gallai–Edmonds structure theorem. Using it, Lesk et al. [2] showed that the study of equimatchable graphs can be reduced to the case of factor-critical graphs and of graphs with a perfect matching, together with a description of how the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition of an equimatchable graph must look. This reduction led to characterizations for several classes. Equimatchable graphs with a perfect matching are well studied: Favaron [8] and others investigated those that are 2-connected and factor-critical, and Eiben and Kotrbčík [9] gave bounds on the size of factor-critical equimatchable graphs in terms of connectivity-type parameters. Characterizations have been obtained for bipartite graphs [10,11], for chordal graphs [12], for graphs of girth at least five [13], for planar graphs with additional restrictions, and for cubic graphs and some other regular classes [14]. Further results address equimatchable graphs of low genus and of bounded maximum degree. Each of these results exploits a specific structural restriction, and in several cases yields polynomial-time recognition. In this paper we study equimatchable graphs within the class of claw-free graphs, that is, graphs with no induced K{1,3}. Claw-free graphs form a rich and widely studied class that contains line graphs, complements of triangle-free graphs, and unit interval graphs, among others. Their structure has been described in depth by Chudnovsky and Seymour [15], and matching problems on them behave well: for instance, a maximum matching can be found efficiently in general graphs, and claw-free graphs of sufficient connectivity possess strong matching-extension properties. Notably, every connected claw-free graph of even order has a perfect matching [16,17], and the analogous statement for odd order is that connected claw-free graphs of odd order are close to factor-critical in many cases. These properties make the claw-free setting a natural one in which to seek a complete characterization of equimatchability. The main contribution of this paper is, to the best of our knowledge, the first characterization of connected equimatchable claw-free graphs. We show that every such graph belongs to one of a small number of explicitly described families, and, conversely, that every graph in these families is equimatchable. Some of these families are infinite and are defined by structural conditions on the neighborhoods of vertices and on the arrangement of cliques; others consist of sporadic graphs of bounded size. Our proof proceeds by separating the cases according to whether the graph has a perfect matching or is factor-critical, and, using the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition, by showing that no other configuration is compatible with both equimatchability and claw-freeness. In the perfect matching case we analyze the local structure around matching edges and show that the absence of claws severely restricts which pairs of matching edges may have augmenting paths of length three after the removal of suitable vertices. In the factor-critical case we use the fact that equimatchability forces strong conditions on the graph obtained after deleting the endpoints of any edge. An important consequence of the characterization is an efficient recognition algorithm. Since membership in each family can be tested by verifying simple structural conditions, we obtain a polynomial-time procedure for deciding whether a given claw-free graph is equimatchable. Thus, on the class of claw-free graphs, recognition of equimatchability is tractable. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces notation and preliminary results, including the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition and basic properties of equimatchable graphs. Section 3 treats claw-free graphs with a perfect matching. Section 4 treats the remaining cases. Section 5 states the full characterization and the recognition algorithm, and Section 6 concludes with open problems. We consider finite, simple, undirected graphs. For a graph G, V(G) and E(G) denote its vertex and edge sets, N(v) the open neighbourhood of v, and N[v] = N(v) ∪ {v}. A matching is maximal if it is not properly contained in another matching. G is equimatchable if all maximal matchings have equal cardinality. A claw is the complete bipartite graph K{1,3}. Our approach combines structural graph theory with the known matching-theoretic properties of equimatchable graphs, and proceeds in four stages: (i) reduction to connected graphs and to a canonical class of building blocks, (ii) a local analysis of claw-free neighbourhoods, (iii) a classification by the existence of a perfect or near-perfect matching, and (iv) an algorithmic derivation of the recognition procedure. Preliminaries and tools A graph is factor-critical if G−v has a perfect matching for every vertex v. By the Gallai–Edmonds structure theorem [1,2], every graph G has a canonical partition D(G), A(G), C(G), where D(G) is the set of vertices missed by some maximum matching, A(G) is the set of neighbours of D(G) outside D(G), and C(G) is the remainder. We use the following standard facts. Every maximum matching matches A(G) into distinct components of G[D(G)], each component of G[D(G)] is factor-critical, and G[C(G)] has a perfect matching. Equimatchability is closely related to the notion of randomly matchable graphs, in which every maximal matching is perfect; these were characterized by Sumner and by Lesk, Plummer and Pulleyblank [3,4]: a connected randomly matchable graph of even order is either K{2n} or K{n,n}. A connected equimatchable graph without a perfect matching is factor-critical when it is 2-connected [5]. A further key ingredient is the structure theorem of Lesk et al. [4] and its refinement by Eiben and Kotrbčík [6], which bounds the structure of equimatchable graphs with respect to the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition: in a connected equimatchable graph, every component of G[D(G)] is itself equimatchable and factor-critical, and the matched structure between A(G) and D(G) is rigid. We also use the observation that equimatchability is preserved under no simple vertex deletion, but that for a vertex v, if M is a maximal matching of G−N[v], then M extended by an edge at v (when available) remains maximal. This "extension principle" underlies the local arguments below. Reduction and local analysis Since a graph is equimatchable if and only if each of its components is, and since a disconnected graph has all components equimatchable with at most one non-trivial arrangement of isolated vertices, we restrict to connected graphs. Let G be connected, claw-free and equimatchable. Step 1: Forbidden configurations. We establish a catalogue of small graphs that cannot appear as induced subgraphs, or as subgraphs with prescribed attachment, in an equimatchable graph. The typical argument takes two maximal matchings of different sizes arising from the extension principle: given an induced subgraph H and a maximal matching M of G−V(H), we compute the sizes of maximal extensions of M inside H and show they differ unless the neighbourhood of H is constrained. For example, if an induced path or cycle admits maximal matchings of different sizes that extend to maximal matchings of G, G is not equimatchable. Combined with claw-freeness, this restricts the neighbourhood of each vertex: N(v) is covered by at most two cliques, and so degrees and clique structure are tightly controlled [7]. Step 2: Cut vertices and 2-connectivity. We separate the case where G has a cut vertex. Using the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition, we show that claw-freeness forces any cut vertex to lie in A(G) or to be incident to a pendant structure, and that the number of components of G−v is at most two. This yields a small number of families with cut vertices, typically obtained by joining factor-critical cliquelike pieces through a bridge or a single vertex. The remaining case is 2-connected graphs. Step 3: 2-connected graphs. For 2-connected equimatchable graphs, G either has a perfect matching or is factor-critical [5]. In each case we use the known bound that equimatchable graphs with a perfect matching are either randomly matchable or have a restricted structure with respect to their 2-factors, and that a 2-connected equimatchable graph with a perfect matching has bounded "matching-tight" structure [6]. We combine this with the local clique-cover structure of claw-free graphs. A claw-free graph with a perfect matching has a line-graph-like or clique-path-like structure along maximal cliques; we use the classification of connected claw-free graphs with independence number at least four or with local structure of quasi-line graphs [8] to organize the case analysis. Graphs with independence number at most two are handled directly, since every maximal matching leaves an unmatched set that is a clique, and hence of size at most one or two vertices. Step 4: Case verification. For each candidate family obtained, we prove sufficiency: we show directly that every maximal matching has the same size, typically by exhibiting a partition of the vertex set into cliques or factor-critical pieces such that any maximal matching must leave a prescribed number of vertices uncovered. Necessity is established by exhaustive argument in the preceding steps. Where the number of cases is finite and small, we confirm the results computationally by enumerating all connected claw-free graphs up to a modest order and testing equimatchability by brute force, which serves as an independent check on the case analysis. Algorithmic consequences Given the characterization, recognition proceeds by (a) testing claw-freeness in O(n·m) time or faster via matrix techniques [9]; (b) computing a maximum matching and the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition in O(m√n) time [10]; (c) identifying the family membership by checking the clique-cover and attachment conditions, each of which is verifiable in polynomial time. The overall running time is dominated by steps (a) and (b), and thus the procedure is polynomial. This contrasts with the general case, where recognition is in co-NP and its complexity remains open in general [6]. Throughout, a graph is assumed connected, since a disconnected graph is equimatchable only if at most one component has an edge and that component is equimatchable. We write ν(G) for the matching number and say a graph is factor-critical if G−v has a perfect matching for every vertex v. Preliminary facts. We rely on the following known results. A connected equimatchable graph either has a perfect matching or is factor-critical when it is 2-connected [1,2]. Moreover, every maximal matching of an equimatchable graph with a perfect matching is itself perfect, so such a graph is randomly matchable. Randomly matchable graphs are characterized as K{2n} and K{n,n} [3]. For equimatchable graphs without a perfect matching, the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition has a rigid structure [4]: the set D of vertices missed by some maximum matching induces factor-critical components, and every maximal matching must match A(G) into distinct components of D. Voltage-gated sodium channels (VGSCs) are essential for the initiation and propagation of action potentials in neurons, cardiac myocytes, and skeletal muscle. Their rapid activation and inactivation, occurring within milliseconds of membrane depolarization, underlie the electrical excitability of these tissues. The importance of precise sodium channel function is underscored by the large number of inherited and acquired diseases linked to channel dysfunction. Mutations in the genes encoding sodium channel α-subunits cause epilepsy, chronic pain syndromes, cardiac arrhythmias such as Brugada and long QT syndromes, myotonias, and periodic paralyses. Despite decades of study, many aspects of how these channels are assembled, regulated, and coordinated remain incompletely understood. The pore-forming α-subunit of mammalian VGSCs is a single polypeptide of about 2,000 amino acids organized into four homologous domains (DI–DIV), each containing six transmembrane segments (S1–S6). Segments S1–S4 of each domain form the voltage-sensing module, whereas S5 and S6 from the four domains come together to form the central ion-conducting pore. This pseudotetrameric architecture is thought to have arisen through two rounds of gene duplication from an ancestral single-domain channel resembling bacterial sodium channels and modern potassium channels. Whereas potassium channels and bacterial sodium channels assemble as homo- or heterotetramers of individual subunits, eukaryotic sodium channels are widely believed to be functional as monomers, with a single α-subunit sufficing to form a complete pore. This view has been reinforced by recent cryo-electron microscopy structures of sodium channels, which typically show a single α-subunit associated with auxiliary β-subunits and regulatory proteins. However, several lines of evidence are difficult to reconcile with a strictly monomeric model. Co-expression of wild-type and mutant sodium channels has in some cases produced dominant-negative effects or altered gating that are hard to explain if each channel acts independently. In the heart, mutations in SCN5A, which encodes Nav1.5, can exert dominant-negative effects on co-expressed wild-type channels, and this has been linked to Brugada syndrome. Biochemical studies have indicated that sodium channel α-subunits can be co-immunoprecipitated from native tissues and heterologous systems, and that β-subunits can promote or stabilize such associations. Additionally, functional studies have reported that the gating of neighboring channels can be coordinated, with cooperative openings producing unusual current kinetics and apparent non-independence of single-channel events. Together, these observations suggest that sodium channels may interact physically and functionally, yet no mechanistic framework has established whether such interactions reflect true assembly of higher-order complexes or incidental clustering. Regulatory partner proteins are plausible candidates for mediating such interactions. Among them, the 14-3-3 family of proteins is notable. These small acidic proteins exist as obligate dimers, with each monomer able to bind phosphorylated motifs on target proteins. By virtue of their dimeric structure, 14-3-3 proteins can bridge two separate client proteins or two sites on the same protein, thereby acting as molecular scaffolds. They regulate numerous ion channels, including potassium and calcium channels, affecting trafficking, localization, and gating. For sodium channels, 14-3-3 has been reported to interact with the DIII–DIV linker region and the C-terminal domain of Nav1.5, and to modulate inactivation properties. The C-terminal region is also a hub for calmodulin and fibroblast growth factor homologous factors, which fine-tune channel gating. Whether 14-3-3 could serve as a physical and functional linker between two α-subunits has not been tested. Understanding whether sodium channels function as dimers has substantial implications. If two α-subunits gate in a coupled manner, then the effect of a single mutation could be transmitted to a partner channel, offering a mechanistic explanation for dominant-negative behavior and for the variable phenotypes seen in heterozygous patients. Coupled gating would also complicate pharmacology, since drug binding to one subunit could allosterically influence the other. Furthermore, interfering with the dimerization interface or the 14-3-3-mediated coupling might provide a new route to modulate channel activity without directly blocking the pore, an approach that could improve selectivity compared with existing sodium channel blockers. In this study, we sought to determine whether sodium channel α-subunits assemble and function as dimers. Using Nav1.5 as a primary model, we combined biochemical, biophysical, and electrophysiological approaches to test for direct physical interaction between α-subunits and to examine whether their gating is coupled. We mapped the region of the channel that mediates dimerization and tested the role of 14-3-3 in coordinating the behavior of the two subunits. By expressing channels with differing properties, including pharmacologically or mutationally altered subunits, we asked whether modifying one subunit influences the gating of its partner. Finally, because sodium channel isoforms share considerable sequence similarity in the relevant regions, we examined whether dimerization and coupled gating are conserved across other mammalian sodium channels. Our results show that sodium channel α-subunits associate as dimers, that a defined cytoplasmic region mediates this interaction, and that 14-3-3 is required for coupled gating of the two pores. These findings challenge the prevailing monomeric paradigm and provide a framework for reinterpreting sodium channel structure, function, and disease mechanisms, while suggesting new therapeutic targets for sodium channelopathies. Nursing is a profession grounded in ethical commitments, and the quality of nursing care depends largely on the values that guide nurses' judgments and actions. Professional values are defined as standards of action accepted by those in a profession, and they provide a framework for evaluating beliefs and attitudes that influence behavior [1, 2]. They serve as the foundation of nurses' practice, guide interactions with patients, colleagues and other members of the healthcare team, and shape the resolution of ethical dilemmas [3]. Professional codes of ethics, such as those of the American Nurses Association and the International Council of Nurses, articulate these values explicitly, including altruism, autonomy, human dignity, integrity and social justice [4, 5]. Healthcare systems worldwide are changing rapidly. Technological advances, rising patient expectations, resource constraints, increasing workloads and growing cultural diversity have created complex ethical challenges for nurses [6]. In this context, nurses are required to have knowledge and awareness of professional values as standards for providing safe, high-quality and ethical care. Evidence suggests that when nurses internalize professional values, they show greater job satisfaction, stronger professional commitment, and a lower tendency to leave the profession [7, 8]. Conversely, conflicts between personal and professional values, or a lack of clarity about the latter, may lead to moral distress, burnout and compromised patient care [9]. Nurses' perspectives on professional values affect their decision-making and the care they deliver. Values operate as a lens through which nurses interpret clinical situations, prioritize patient needs and decide on a course of action [10]. Accordingly, understanding how nurses rank the importance of different values can reveal the strengths and gaps in professional socialization and can inform strategies to reinforce ethical practice. Professional values are not innate; they are acquired through a process that begins in nursing education, continues through clinical experience and is shaped by organizational culture, role models and personal characteristics [11]. Therefore, demographic and professional variables such as age, work experience, education level and participation in ethics training may influence how nurses perceive these values [12, 13]. Several instruments have been developed to measure professional values in nursing. One of the most widely used is the Nursing Professional Values Scale, developed by Weis and Schank on the basis of the American Nurses Association Code for Nurses and later revised (NPVS-R) to reflect updated versions of the code [14, 15]. The scale has been used with students and practicing nurses in many countries, and studies using it have reported varying results. Some report high overall scores, with patient-centered values such as confidentiality, privacy and accountability ranked highest [16, 17]. Others have found that values related to professional development, participation in professional associations, research and health policy are rated lower [18, 19]. Such discrepancies imply that cultural, religious, organizational and educational contexts shape how professional values are perceived and prioritized [20]. In Iran, nursing has developed substantially over recent decades, with the expansion of university-based education, graduate programs and efforts to define professional standards. Nevertheless, Iranian nurses work in settings characterized by nursing shortages, heavy workloads, limited autonomy and sometimes inadequate institutional support, all of which may hinder the application of professional values in practice [21, 22]. Moreover, the Iranian cultural and Islamic context places strong emphasis on values such as respect for human dignity, confidentiality and compassion, which may influence nurses' value priorities differently from those in Western countries where most value research has been conducted [23]. Although some Iranian studies have examined professional values among nursing students and nurses, findings are inconsistent, and few have been conducted in the southeastern region of the country, including Kerman [24, 25]. Regional differences in educational resources, workforce composition and cultural characteristics make local evidence valuable for planning appropriate interventions. Furthermore, the continuing emergence of ethical challenges in clinical settings, such as end-of-life decisions, patient rights, resource allocation and the protection of patient privacy in the era of electronic records, makes it essential for nursing managers and educators to know which values nurses regard as important and which are undervalued [6, 26]. If values such as participation in research, involvement in professional associations and contribution to health policy are given low priority, this may impede the advancement of the profession, evidence-based practice and nurses' influence on healthcare decision-making [18]. Identifying such gaps can guide the design of in-service training, ethics education and organizational policies that foster a supportive ethical climate. Despite the recognized importance of professional values, there is limited information on how clinical nurses in hospitals affiliated with Kerman University of Medical Sciences perceive them and which personal and professional characteristics are associated with their perceptions. Therefore, the present study aimed to investigate the importance of professional values from the perspective of clinical nurses working in educational hospitals of Kerman University of Medical Sciences, Iran, using the Persian version of the NPVS-R, and to examine the relationship between nurses' perceptions and their demographic and professional characteristics. This cross-sectional descriptive study was conducted from April to September 2016 in four educational hospitals affiliated with Kerman University of Medical Sciences, southeastern Iran. These hospitals are the main referral and teaching centers in the province and offer a wide range of medical and surgical services. The study followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines for cross-sectional studies [1]. Study population and sampling The target population was all clinical nurses working in the participating hospitals. Inclusion criteria were a bachelor's degree or higher in nursing, at least six months of clinical experience, direct involvement in patient care, and willingness to participate. Nurses in management positions without direct patient care responsibilities and those who did not complete the questionnaire were excluded. The sample size was calculated from the standard deviation of professional values scores reported in a comparable study [2]. With a 95% confidence level, a precision of 1.5 points, and an anticipated standard deviation of approximately 12, the minimum sample was about 245 nurses. To allow for possible attrition, 280 questionnaires were distributed, and 250 were completed and entered into the analysis (response rate 89%). Stratified random sampling was used. Each hospital was treated as a stratum, and the number of nurses selected from each was proportional to its total nursing workforce. Within each hospital, a list of eligible nurses was obtained from the nursing office, and participants were chosen by simple random sampling with a computer-generated random number table. Data collection instruments Data were collected with a two-part questionnaire. The first part gathered demographic and professional characteristics: age, gender, marital status, educational level, work experience, employment type, ward of employment, and participation in professional ethics training courses, including workshops and in-service programs. The second part was the Nursing Professional Values Scale-Revised (NPVS-R), developed by Weis and Schank [3,4]. The instrument was derived from the American Nurses Association Code of Ethics for Nurses and measures the importance nurses assign to professional values. The revised version has 26 items rated on a five-point Likert scale from 1 (not important) to 5 (most important). Total scores range from 26 to 130, and higher scores indicate greater perceived importance of professional values. The items cluster into three factors: caring, activism, and professionalism [4]. For interpretation, scores were categorized into low, moderate, and high levels based on tertiles of the possible range. The Persian version of the NPVS-R was used. It had been translated using the forward-backward procedure, and its validity and reliability had been established in Iranian samples [5]. In the present study, content validity was reviewed again by ten faculty members of the School of Nursing and Midwifery, who judged the items clear and appropriate for the clinical context. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach's alpha in a pilot of 20 nurses who were not included in the main sample, and the alpha coefficient was 0.92, indicating excellent reliability. Cronbach's alpha in the main sample was similar. Data collection procedure After approval was obtained and permission was granted by the hospital authorities, the researcher visited the wards on different shifts to reach nurses working in rotating schedules. Selected nurses received an explanation of the study aims and procedures and were assured that participation was voluntary. Written informed consent was then obtained. The questionnaires were self-administered, anonymous, and completed in about 10 to 15 minutes. They were collected the same day or within two days in sealed envelopes to preserve confidentiality and reduce social desirability bias. Completed questionnaires were checked for missing data, and those with more than 10% unanswered items were excluded. Statistical analysis Data were analyzed with SPSS version 22 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). The normality of the distribution of the total score was assessed with the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and by inspecting histograms and Q-Q plots. Descriptive statistics, including frequencies, percentages, means, and standard deviations, were used to summarize demographic characteristics and the NPVS-R item and total scores. Items were ranked by mean score to identify the values considered most and least important. Relationships between the total score and demographic variables were examined using inferential tests. Independent-samples t-tests and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with post hoc Tukey tests compared mean scores across categorical variables such as gender, marital status, educational level, ward, and participation in ethics training. Pearson's correlation coefficient was used to examine associations between the total score and continuous variables such as age and work experience. Variables with a P value below 0.2 in the univariate analyses were entered into a multiple linear regression model to identify independent predictors, and the assumptions of linearity, independence of residuals, homoscedasticity, and absence of multicollinearity were checked. A P value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Ethical considerations The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Kerman University of Medical Sciences. The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki [6]. Participants gave written informed consent after being told the objectives and the voluntary nature of participation, their right to withdraw at any time without any consequence for their employment, and the confidentiality of their information. No names or identifying details were recorded, and the data were used for research purposes only. Permission to use the Persian version of the NPVS-R was obtained from the authors of the translated instrument. A total of 250 clinical nurses from four educational hospitals affiliated with Kerman University of Medical Sciences participated in the study, and all returned questionnaires were complete enough for analysis. The mean age of participants was 33.4 ± 6.8 years, and the mean work experience was 9.1 ± 6.3 years. Most participants were female (n = 187, 74.8%), married (n = 183, 73.2%), and held a bachelor's degree in nursing (n = 228, 91.2%). Approximately half of the nurses (n = 129, 51.6%) reported having participated in a professional ethics training course or workshop. The distribution of participants across hospitals was proportional to the number of nurses employed in each setting, in accordance with the stratified sampling design. When expressed as an item mean, the score was approximately 3.95 of 5, and no participant obtained a total score in the lowest quartile of the possible range. The scores were approximately normally distributed (skewness = −0.62; kurtosis = 0.41), which supported the use of parametric tests. The internal consistency of the Persian version in the present sample was satisfactory (Cronbach's alpha = 0.93), a value comparable to those reported in earlier validation studies of the instrument [1,2]. Colonization of freshwater habitats by marine organisms is among the most significant ecological transitions in vertebrate evolution. Freshwater and seawater impose opposite osmoregulatory challenges: fish in hyperosmotic environments lose water and gain ions, whereas fish in hypoosmotic environments gain water and lose ions [1,2]. Teleosts maintain internal osmolality at roughly one third of seawater through coordinated activity of the gills, intestine, kidney and skin, which regulate ion uptake and secretion [3]. Although only about 2.5% of teleost species are diadromous, these species must cope with both extremes within a single lifetime, and they provide valuable models for understanding the physiological flexibility that may precede, or facilitate, permanent habitat shifts [4,5]. The central molecular machinery of fish osmoregulation involves membrane transporters and the ATPases that energize them. Na+/K+-ATPase (NKA) generates the electrochemical gradients that drive secondary ion transport, and its gill activity typically increases in seawater, where it supports salt secretion by ionocytes, and in some species also in freshwater [6,7]. Vacuolar-type H+-ATPase (HA) is implicated in freshwater ion uptake, where it hyperpolarizes the apical membrane and allows Na+ entry through channels [8,9]. The intestine also contributes substantially, by absorbing water and monovalent ions in seawater-acclimated fish and by participating in ion uptake in freshwater [10]. Changes in the activity or expression of these enzymes therefore are commonly used as indicators of osmoregulatory acclimation and adaptation [11]. Landlocking, the permanent isolation of diadromous populations in freshwater, offers natural experiments on the evolution of osmoregulation. In several lineages, such as alewife (Alosa pseudoharengus), threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) and sockeye salmon (Oncorhynchus nerka), freshwater-resident populations have differentiated from their migratory ancestors in salinity tolerance, ionocyte function and ATPase regulation, sometimes within a few hundred generations [12-15]. Such studies reveal that loss of the marine phase may relax selection on seawater performance and may drive evolution of traits favoring freshwater life, although the tempo and the physiological targets of this divergence vary among taxa [16]. Whether divergence also modifies tolerance to low salinity, and which physiological processes underlie it, remains poorly understood. Galaxias maculatus (Jenyns, 1848), the common galaxias or puyen, is one of the most widely distributed freshwater fishes of the Southern Hemisphere, occurring in Australia, New Zealand, South America and various islands [17]. Most populations are amphidromous: adults spawn in the upper estuary or lower river during high tides, larvae are carried to the sea, where they develop for several months, and juveniles return to rivers to grow and mature [18]. However, numerous landlocked populations complete the full life cycle in freshwater lakes, in which larvae do not migrate to the sea [19]. In Patagonia, a number of such populations inhabit lakes formed or modified after the retreat of ice sheets at the end of the last glaciation, roughly 10,000 to 15,000 years ago [20,21]. Phylogeographic studies have shown that these populations are genetically structured and that landlocking has occurred repeatedly and independently across the species’ range [22,23]. Landlocked G. maculatus differ from their diadromous counterparts in life history and morphology, including body size, growth, reproductive timing and larval development [24,25]. Some work has also suggested differences in physiological responses to salinity, since juveniles and adults of this species show considerable euryhalinity [26,27]. Nevertheless, it is unclear whether the shift to a permanently freshwater life has been accompanied by a loss of salinity tolerance, as might be expected from relaxed selection, or by some other form of divergence. Moreover, the demographic context in which this divergence occurred is rarely documented, even though it is essential for interpreting adaptive change. Founder events and subsequent expansion may generate genetic differentiation through drift alone, and so physiological differences must be considered against a background of population history [28]. Mitochondrial DNA is well suited to reconstructing recent colonization scenarios, because of its high mutation rate, haploid inheritance and small effective population size, which allow fast detection of bottlenecks, founder effects and demographic expansions [29,30]. Combining analysis of haplotype genealogies and diversity indices with physiological experiments enables direct comparison of historical and functional divergence within the same pair of populations. Such an integrative approach is particularly informative when the time of isolation is short, as it allows evolutionary changes to be linked to specific ecological events [31]. In the present study, we examined an amphidromous population and a landlocked lake population of G. maculatus from the Andean region of Patagonia. First, we used mtDNA sequences to assess genetic diversity and differentiation and to infer the colonization history of the lake, testing the hypothesis of a recent founder event from the diadromous stock followed by population expansion. Second, we compared the osmoregulatory performance of both populations by measuring survival over eight days across salinities from 0 to 30 ppt, after progressive acclimation. Third, we quantified the activity of NKA, HA and other ATPases in gills and intestine to determine whether differences in tolerance are mirrored by differences in these enzymatic systems. We predicted that landlocked fish would show reduced tolerance to high salinity, as a consequence of relaxed selection in freshwater. Our results show instead that divergence has been unexpectedly pronounced at low salinities, indicating rapid adaptive modification of the osmoregulatory system within a few thousand years of isolation. Sampling and study populations Adult Galaxias maculatus were collected in the Valdivia River estuary (diadromous population; Chile, ~39°S) and in Lake Pirihueico (landlocked population; Andean region, ~39°S), a lake formed after the last deglaciation. Fish were captured with beach seine nets and minnow traps under permits issued by the national fisheries authority. For genetic analyses, a fin clip was taken from each fish and preserved in 95% ethanol at −20 °C. For physiological experiments, live fish were transported in aerated containers to the laboratory and held for four weeks in dechlorinated fresh water (0 ppt) at 12 ± 1 °C under a natural photoperiod, and fed daily with commercial pellets. Fish of similar size were used in both populations to reduce size-related variation in osmoregulatory capacity [1,2]. A fragment of the mitochondrial control region (D-loop) was amplified by PCR with primers previously used in galaxiids [4]. Reactions (25 µL) contained 50 ng DNA, 1× buffer, 2 mM MgCl2, 0.2 mM of each dNTP, 0.4 µM of each primer and 1 U Taq polymerase. Cycling consisted of an initial denaturation at 94 °C for 3 min; 35 cycles of 94 °C for 45 s, 55 °C for 45 s and 72 °C for 60 s; and a final extension at 72 °C for 7 min. Products were checked on 1.5% agarose gels, purified and sequenced in both directions on an automated sequencer. Sequences were edited and aligned using Clustal W [5] with manual verification, and deposited in GenBank. Population genetic analyses Haplotype diversity (H), the average number of nucleotide differences (Π), nucleotide diversity and the number of polymorphic sites were estimated for each population in Arlequin [6] and DnaSP [7]. Genetic differentiation was evaluated using pairwise GST (based on haplotype frequencies) and NST (which also incorporates sequence divergence), and the significance of NST > GST was assessed by permutation tests [8]. Significance was determined with 10,000 permutations. The genealogical relationships among haplotypes were reconstructed using a median-joining network [9]. To evaluate demographic history, Tajima's D [10] and Fu's Fs [11] were calculated, and mismatch distributions were compared with expectations under a sudden expansion model, with the sum of squared deviations and raggedness index used as goodness-of-fit statistics [12]. The time since expansion was estimated from the mismatch parameter τ using τ = 2μt, where μ is the mutation rate per sequence per generation, applying a range of mutation rates reported for teleost control regions [13] and a generation time of one year [14]. Colonization of the lake was interpreted by comparing the position and frequency of lake haplotypes relative to those of the diadromous stock in the network. Salinity challenge Fish from each population were randomly assigned to experimental salinities of 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 ppt (n = 10 fish per salinity per population, in duplicate tanks of 5 fish each). Experimental water was prepared by mixing dechlorinated fresh water with artificial sea salt, and salinity was verified with a calibrated refractometer. To avoid osmotic shock, fish were acclimated progressively by raising salinity by 5 ppt per day until the target value was reached, after which they were maintained for 8 days. Control fish remained at 0 ppt. Tanks (50 L) were aerated, kept at 12 ± 1 °C, and one third of the water was renewed every second day with water of the corresponding salinity. Fish were not fed during the final 24 h before sampling. Mortality was recorded daily, and survival at the end of the experiment was calculated for each salinity and population. Survivors were anaesthetized with benzocaine (50 mg L⁻¹) and euthanized by spinal transection, in accordance with institutional guidelines for animal care [15]. Gills and the whole intestine were dissected on ice, rinsed in cold saline, frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until analysis. ATPase activity assays Tissues were homogenized in ice-cold buffer (250 mM sucrose, 30 mM Tris, 10 mM EDTA, 0.1% sodium deoxycholate, pH 7.4) and centrifuged at 5,000 × g for 10 min at 4 °C; the supernatant was used for assays. Protein concentration was determined by the Bradford method using bovine serum albumin as standard [16]. ATPase activity was measured as the release of inorganic phosphate from ATP [17]. Total ATPase activity was determined in the presence of Mg²⁺, Na⁺ and K⁺. Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (NKA) activity was defined as the ouabain-sensitive fraction (1 mM ouabain), and H⁺-ATPase (HA) activity as the fraction sensitive to N-ethylmaleimide (NEM, 1 mM) or bafilomycin A1 [18]. The remaining activity, insensitive to both inhibitors, was recorded as other ATPases. Samples were assayed in triplicate at 30 °C for 30 min, and reactions were stopped with trichloroacetic acid. Activities were expressed as µmol Pi mg protein⁻¹ h⁻¹. Statistical analysis Survival between populations at each salinity was compared with Fisher's exact test, and survival curves over the 8-day period were compared with Kaplan–Meier analysis and log-rank tests [19]. Enzyme activities were checked for normality (Shapiro–Wilk) and homogeneity of variances (Levene), and log-transformed when necessary. The effects of population, salinity and their interaction on the activity of each ATPase type in each tissue were assessed using two-way ANOVA, followed by Tukey's post hoc tests for multiple comparisons. When assumptions were not met, non-parametric Kruskal–Wallis tests were applied. Pairwise population differences within each salinity were evaluated with t-tests or Mann–Whitney tests, with Bonferroni correction. All analyses were conducted in R [20], and differences were considered significant at P < 0.05. Cancer remains one of the leading causes of death worldwide, and its burden continues to grow with population aging and changing lifestyles [1]. Surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy are the principal treatment modalities, but the clinical utility of many chemotherapeutic agents is limited by dose-dependent toxicity to normal tissues, acquired multidrug resistance and tumor recurrence [2,3]. The search for new antitumor agents with novel structures, distinct mechanisms of action and improved selectivity therefore remains a priority in drug discovery. Natural products as a source of antitumor agents Natural products and their derivatives have historically contributed a substantial proportion of approved anticancer drugs, including paclitaxel, vincristine, doxorubicin and mitomycin C [4,5]. Microorganisms are especially valuable producers because they can be cultured and scaled up by fermentation, avoiding the supply problems associated with plant and animal sources. However, repeated screening of microorganisms from conventional terrestrial habitats has led to high rediscovery rates of known compounds [6]. Attention has consequently shifted to underexplored environments, notably the oceans, where microbial diversity is vast and where unusual physicochemical conditions drive distinctive secondary metabolism [7]. Several marine-derived compounds, such as cytarabine, trabectedin, eribulin and brentuximab vedotin, have reached clinical use, which underscores the potential of this resource [8]. Antarctic microorganisms as a resource for bioactive substances The Antarctic is among the most extreme environments on Earth, characterized by persistently low temperatures, strong ultraviolet radiation, seasonal light variation, desiccation, high salinity in some habitats and scarce nutrients [9]. Microorganisms inhabiting these environments have evolved physiological and biochemical adaptations, including cold-active enzymes, cryoprotectants, membrane modifications and unique secondary metabolic pathways [10,11]. Such adaptations are thought to give rise to metabolites with novel scaffolds and bioactivities. Antarctic bacteria, actinomycetes and fungi have been reported to produce antibacterial, antifungal, antioxidant and cytotoxic compounds [12–14]. For example, new cytotoxic polyketides, alkaloids and peptides have been obtained from Antarctic sediment- and sponge-associated microorganisms [15,16]. Nevertheless, compared with other regions, Antarctic microbial resources remain poorly explored, largely because of the difficulty of sampling and the specialized conditions required for cultivation. Most studies have concentrated on sediments, soils and host-associated organisms, whereas microorganisms from surface seawater and meltwater have received considerably less attention, despite being exposed to strong environmental fluctuations that may stimulate the production of protective metabolites [17]. Bacillus species and antitumor activity The genus Bacillus comprises a metabolically versatile group of spore-forming bacteria that are widely distributed in terrestrial and marine habitats, including polar regions [18]. Members of this genus produce a remarkable range of bioactive substances, such as lipopeptides (surfactin, iturin and fengycin), polyketides, bacteriocins, enzymes such as L-asparaginase, and exopolysaccharides [19,20]. Several of these have been shown to inhibit tumor cell proliferation and to induce apoptosis, cell cycle arrest or membrane disruption in cancer cell lines, often with limited toxicity to normal cells [21,22]. In addition, because many Bacillus strains are regarded as safe and are readily fermented at industrial scale, they are attractive candidates for the development of antitumor agents or functional products for cancer prevention [23]. Cold-adapted Bacillus strains from the Antarctic may produce metabolites that differ from those of their mesophilic counterparts, but cytotoxic products from such strains have been little characterized. Activity-guided screening strategies Efficient discovery from large numbers of isolates requires a screening approach that rapidly identifies strains producing cytotoxic metabolites. The 3-(4,5-dimethyl-2-thiazolyl)-2,5-diphenyl-2H-tetrazolium bromide (MTT) assay is a well-established colorimetric method for assessing cell viability and is suitable for medium- to high-throughput evaluation of crude fermentation products [24]. Used in a cytotoxicity-tracking strategy, it allows active strains to be prioritized at an early stage, and subsequent fractionation, for example by molecular weight cut-off ultrafiltration, can then narrow down the nature of the active components. Evaluating selectivity against a panel of tumor cell lines and a normal cell line, together with stability toward pH and temperature, provides essential information about the therapeutic potential and processing feasibility of the active products [25]. Aim of the present study In view of the large untapped potential of Antarctic microorganisms and the limited information on those from surface water, we isolated microorganisms from surface water samples collected at different Antarctic sites and screened them for cytotoxicity using an MTT-based tracking approach. A strain with potent activity, designated N11-8, was identified by morphological and 16S rRNA gene phylogenetic analyses. The molecular weight distribution of its active fermentation products was then examined, and their inhibitory effects on several human cancer cell lines and on normal human lung fibroblasts were compared. The morphological effects on BEL-7402 cells were observed microscopically alongside mitomycin C, and the pH and thermal stability of the active products were assessed. This work aims to broaden knowledge of Antarctic microbial resources and to provide a basis for developing antitumor agents from polar Bacillus. Sample collection and microbial isolation Surface seawater samples (0–1 m depth) were collected at several sampling stations in the Antarctic during an expedition, using sterile containers. Samples were stored at 4 °C during transport and processed within 24 h. Aliquots (100 µL) of serial dilutions (10⁻¹–10⁻³) prepared in sterile artificial seawater were spread on Zobell 2216E agar and incubated at 4 °C and 15 °C for 7–14 days to recover psychrophilic and psychrotolerant strains [1,2]. Colonies with distinct morphology were picked and purified by repeated streaking until axenic. Pure isolates were preserved in 2216E broth containing 20% (v/v) glycerol at −80 °C.
