Cultures were centrifuged (10,000 × g, 15 min, 4 °C) to separate cells from supernatant. The supernatant was filtered (0.22 µm) and used as the extracellular fermented product. Cell pellets were washed with PBS, disrupted by ultrasonication on ice, and clarified by centrifugation to obtain intracellular fractions. All preparations were stored at −20 °C until bioassay. Cell lines and culture conditions Human hepatocellular carcinoma BEL-7402, glioma U251, colon carcinoma RKO, lung carcinoma A549, breast carcinoma MCF-7, and normal human fetal lung fibroblast HFL1 cells were obtained from a cell bank. Cells were maintained in DMEM or RPMI-1640 supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum, 100 U/mL penicillin and 100 µg/mL streptomycin at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO₂. Cells in the logarithmic growth phase were used for all experiments. Cytotoxicity screening by MTT assay Cytotoxicity was evaluated using the MTT assay [3]. Cells were seeded in 96-well plates (5 × 10³ cells/well) and allowed to adhere for 24 h. Medium was replaced with fresh medium containing fermentation products (10% v/v for primary screening). Mitomycin C served as positive control, uninoculated 2216E medium as negative control, and wells without cells as blanks. After 48 h, 20 µL MTT solution (5 mg/mL) was added to each well and plates were incubated for 4 h. The formazan crystals were dissolved in 150 µL dimethyl sulfoxide, and absorbance was read at 490 nm (or 570 nm) on a microplate reader. The inhibition rate was calculated as (1 − (Asample − Ablank)/(Acontrol − Ablank)) × 100%. Each treatment was performed in triplicate in at least three independent experiments. Strains giving inhibition above a predefined threshold (50%) were considered active and selected for further study. Identification of the active strain N11-8 Morphological characteristics were examined by Gram staining and light microscopy, and colony features were recorded on 2216E agar. Genomic DNA was extracted using a bacterial genomic DNA kit. The 16S rRNA gene was amplified with universal primers 27F (5′-AGAGTTTGATCCTGGCTCAG-3′) and 1492R (5′-GGTTACCTTGTTACGACTT-3′) under the following conditions: 95 °C for 5 min; 30 cycles of 94 °C for 30 s, 55 °C for 30 s and 72 °C for 90 s; and a final extension at 72 °C for 10 min. Related sequences were aligned with CLUSTAL W, and a neighbor-joining phylogenetic tree was constructed in MEGA with the Kimura two-parameter model and 1000 bootstrap replicates [5,6]. The cell-free supernatant was concentrated and sequentially fractionated by ultrafiltration through membranes with molecular weight cut-offs of 1, 10 and 30 kDa, yielding fractions of <1 kDa, 1–10 kDa, 10–30 kDa and >30 kDa. Fractions were sterilized by filtration and tested for cytotoxicity at different concentrations against all six cell lines by MTT assay as described above. Half-maximal inhibitory concentrations (IC₅₀) were calculated by nonlinear regression of dose–response curves. Selectivity was assessed by comparing inhibition of tumor cells with that of HFL1 cells. Morphological changes, including cell shrinkage, rounding, detachment and reduced density, were observed and photographed under an inverted phase-contrast microscope. Representative fields were captured from at least three wells per treatment. Stability of the fermented active products For pH stability, the active fraction was adjusted to pH 2–12 with HCl or NaOH, incubated at 25 °C for 2 h, and neutralized to pH 7.0 before testing. For thermal stability, samples were heated at 40, 60, 80, 100 °C for 30 min (and 121 °C for 20 min for autoclaving), then cooled on ice. Residual cytotoxicity against BEL-7402 cells was determined by MTT assay and expressed relative to untreated samples (100%). Statistical analysis Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) of at least three independent experiments. Differences among groups were analyzed by one-way analysis of variance followed by Tukey's or Dunnett's post hoc test using SPSS or GraphPad Prism. Differences with p < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. Isolation and preliminary screening of Antarctic microorganisms A total of 129 microbial strains were isolated from surface water samples collected at different Antarctic sites. Colonies differed in morphology, pigmentation, and growth rate on the isolation media. Most isolates grew at 4–15 °C, which is consistent with a psychrotolerant or psychrophilic ecology [1,2]. Crude fermentation extracts of all 129 isolates were tested against BEL-7402 cells in an MTT assay at a single concentration. Twelve strains (9.3%) reduced cell viability by more than 50% relative to untreated controls, and these were classed as potently cytotoxic. Inhibition rates ranged from 52.4% to 89.7%. Strain N11-8 gave one of the highest and most reproducible inhibition values across three independent screening rounds, so it was selected for further study. Morphological characterization and phylogenetic identification of strain N11-8 On solid medium, N11-8 formed opaque, cream-white, slightly raised colonies with irregular margins after 48 h at 15 °C. Light microscopy showed rod-shaped cells that stained Gram-negative in our hands. Because the genus Bacillus is typically Gram-positive, this result was unexpected. Members of the genus can stain variably in older cultures or when the cell wall is damaged [3], and we therefore interpret the staining result with caution. The nearly complete 16S rRNA gene sequence of N11-8 was amplified and compared with sequences in the GenBank and EzBioCloud databases. The strain showed more than 99% similarity to several Bacillus species. In the neighbor-joining tree, N11-8 clustered within the genus Bacillus, supported by a high bootstrap value, and was separated from the nearest type strains by short branch lengths. The strain was designated Bacillus sp. N11-8. Its position within the genus is clear, but 16S rRNA analysis alone could not resolve it to species level. This is a known limitation within closely related Bacillus lineages [4]. Sister chromatid cohesion, the physical association of replicated chromatids from S phase until anaphase, is essential for accurate chromosome segregation, DNA repair, and the regulation of gene expression [1,2]. Cohesion is mediated by cohesin, a member of the structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC) family of ATPases. Cohesin is built around a heterodimer of Smc1 and Smc3, whose long antiparallel coiled coils fold at a central hinge and terminate in ATP-binding cassette-like head domains. The heads are bridged by the kleisin subunit Scc1/Mcd1/Rad21, which in turn recruits the HEAT-repeat proteins Scc3/SA and Pds5 and the regulator Wapl [3,4]. Together, these subunits form a tripartite ring of roughly 35–50 nm in diameter, and the ring architecture is central to most models of cohesin function [5]. Models of cohesin–DNA association Cohesin loading onto chromosomes depends on the Scc2–Scc4 loader and on ATP hydrolysis by the Smc1/Smc3 heads, and the establishment of stable cohesion requires acetylation of Smc3 during DNA replication by Eco1/Esco proteins [6–8]. Cohesin release is promoted by Wapl–Pds5 and, at anaphase, by proteolytic cleavage of the kleisin by separase [9,10]. Biochemical and genetic evidence indicates that cohesin can entrap DNA topologically within its ring, and that cohesion depends on this entrapment [11,12]. This observation led to the "embrace" or single-ring model, in which one ring encircles both sister chromatids [5]. In its simplest form, the model predicts that a single cohesin complex is both necessary and sufficient to tether two sister DNAs. Alternative models invoke cooperation between multiple complexes. In the "handcuff" model, two rings, each encircling one sister, are joined to one another [13]. Other proposals suggest that cohesin oligomers or clusters form through interactions between subunits, and several studies have reported intermolecular associations between cohesin complexes, including self-interaction of Scc1 and Smc3 in vivo, oligomeric forms detected in vitro, and cohesin clusters observed by super-resolution microscopy [14–17]. Yet other work has indicated that such associations are artifacts of overexpression or crosslinking, and that individual rings are monomeric [18]. Stoichiometric estimates of cohesin at chromosomal sites are also difficult to reconcile with a single, simple topology [19]. Thus whether cohesin functions as a monomeric ring or through higher-order assemblies remains unresolved. Cohesin beyond cohesion Resolving this question matters beyond cohesion itself. Cohesin, like its relatives condensin and Smc5/6, organizes chromosome structure. It participates in chromosome condensation, in the formation of chromatin loops through loop extrusion, and in the establishment of topologically associating domains [20–22]. Loop extrusion models differ on whether one or several complexes act together, with some proposing dimeric or "handcuffed" extruders [23] and others favoring a single-complex mechanism [24]. Evidence for functional cooperation between cohesin complexes would therefore inform the mechanisms of both cohesion and chromosome compaction. Interallelic complementation as a test of cooperation Genetic approaches can address this problem directly. Interallelic (intragenic) complementation occurs when two different mutant alleles of a gene, each defective on its own, partially restore function when combined in the same cell [25]. Classically, this phenomenon is interpreted as evidence that the gene product functions as a multimer, within which a defect in one subunit is compensated by the functional domain of another. For a protein that acts as a single, discrete unit, interallelic complementation is not expected, because each complex would carry only one allele's product and would remain defective. Observing complementation between cohesin mutant alleles would therefore provide functional evidence that cohesin complexes interact, and could reveal which domains or activities are shared in trans. Although many cohesin mutants have been isolated in budding yeast, their potential for complementation has not been systematically examined. Mutations affect distinct activities, including ATP binding and hydrolysis, head engagement, kleisin binding, DNA entrapment, and interaction with regulators [26–28]. If cohesin complexes cooperate on DNA, combining alleles that affect different activities might restore function through intermolecular compensation. Approach and scope of this study Here we used diploid and haploid yeast strains expressing pairs of mutant cohesin subunits to screen for interallelic complementation. We identified three examples involving distinct subunits and asked whether complementation restores cohesion, condensation, or both, whether it requires DNA association, and whether it depends on the catalytic activities of the complexes. We further examined whether complementing complexes physically associate, and how the alleles' biochemical defects are reconciled in the heteromeric assembly. Our results indicate that two different mutant cohesin complexes can cooperate to restore function, which is difficult to reconcile with a strictly single-ring mechanism. Instead, they support a model in which multiple cohesin complexes interact on DNA to mediate both sister chromatid cohesion and chromosome condensation. Delineating research topics, fields, and specialties in the scientific literature is a long-standing problem in bibliometrics and the sociology of science. Maps of science, field-normalized indicators, research evaluation, and science policy all depend on some partition of the literature into thematic units. Over the past decades, a wide range of methods has been proposed for this task, based on bibliographic coupling, co-citation, direct citation, text similarity, or hybrids of these. Modularity optimization, the Infomap algorithm, and various hierarchical and agglomerative procedures are now routinely applied to large citation networks. Yet despite this progress, we still do not know to what extent any of these algorithms reconstruct a "ground truth", that is, the thematic structures that scientists themselves produce and recognize. Evaluations usually compare one algorithm's output with another's, or with expert judgments or classification schemes that are themselves imperfect proxies. Without an agreed ground truth, the question of which method is best remains open. In this paper we take a different route. Instead of choosing a general-purpose community detection algorithm and testing afterwards whether its output resembles topics, we start from properties that thematic structures can be expected to have, on theoretical and empirical grounds, and design an algorithm to match them. Three such properties guide our approach. First, topics overlap pervasively. Publications often contribute to more than one topic, and topics share methods, data, and concepts. Partitioning approaches that assign each paper to exactly one cluster ignore this and force artificial boundaries. Second, topics are locally defined. A research community is recognizable from the dense relations among its members and the comparatively sparse relations to its surroundings, and does not require knowledge of the global network. Methods that rely on global objective functions suffer from resolution limits and from the dependence of each cluster on the structure of the rest of the network. Third, the heterogeneity of topics, which vary widely in size, age, and cohesion, suggests that no single scale or resolution parameter suffices. These considerations motivate three design choices. We cluster citation links rather than publication nodes. A single citation usually reflects one specific intellectual relation between two papers, whereas a paper can be involved in several relations of different kinds. Link communities therefore allow nodes to belong to several topics naturally, because a node inherits the memberships of its links. Next, we use predominantly local information. We evaluate a set of links with a new cost function that depends on the set and its immediate neighbourhood, not on the entire network. Finally, we search for communities starting from seed subgraphs and expanding or modifying them, rather than dividing the whole network. The cost function is intended such that local minima in the cost landscape correspond to link communities. This is a strong assumption, but a plausible one: a set of links that cannot be improved by adding or removing individual links is, in a sense, self-consistent. The difficulty is that the landscape contains very many local minima, many of which are minor variations of one another or small fragments of larger structures. We therefore define a valid community as the community with the lowest minimum within a certain range, that is, the best solution among sufficiently similar candidates. This definition removes the need for a global resolution parameter and shifts the problem to identifying the set of such locally optimal solutions. Finding all valid communities exhaustively is infeasible for networks of realistic size. We therefore designed a memetic algorithm, which combines population-based probabilistic evolutionary strategies with deterministic local searches. The evolutionary component explores the space of link sets broadly through recombination and mutation of candidate communities, while the local search brings each candidate down to the nearest local minimum of the cost function. This hybrid is well suited to rugged landscapes, as the evolutionary operators allow escape from poor basins while the local search ensures that the candidates we compare are genuine minima. Maintaining a population additionally lets us compare candidates within a range and retain only the best of each neighbourhood. We apply the approach to two data sets from Astronomy & Astrophysics, a field with good literature coverage and a well-developed citation culture. The first is a network of about 15,000 papers published in 2010 together with their cited sources. The second is a network of about 100,000 papers published between 2003 and 2010 which are linked through direct citations. The two data sets differ in size and construction, which lets us examine how the method behaves on both a modest, source-enriched network and a larger, purely direct-citation network. The contribution of the paper is primarily methodological. We offer a theoretically motivated way of delineating overlapping thematic structures, a cost function for link sets, a definition of valid communities that avoids a global resolution parameter, and a memetic algorithm to approximate them in large networks. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We first review related work on topic delineation and overlapping community detection, then describe the cost function and the definition of valid communities, present the memetic algorithm, and report results for the two data sets, before discussing limitations and implications for the validation of topic detection methods. We represent the literature as an undirected citation network G = (V, E), where nodes are publications and edges are direct citation links. Rather than partitioning nodes, we search for communities of edges. A publication then belongs to every topic in which at least one of its links participates, so overlaps between topics arise naturally and can be pervasive. Link communities and local cost function A candidate community is a set of links C ⊆ E. Let V(C) be the nodes incident to C. For each node i in V(C), we count the links of C incident to i (ki^C) and compare this with its total degree ki. We define the cost of C as F(C) = (Σ{i∈V(C)} (ki − ki^C)^α) / (Σ{i∈V(C)} ki^C)^β, with α = 1 and β = 1 unless noted otherwise. The numerator measures how much of the neighbourhood of the community's nodes lies outside it, and the denominator rewards internal cohesion and size. The function is evaluated using only the links of C and the immediate neighbourhoods of its nodes, so no global network quantity such as the total number of links enters the computation. This locality makes the cost independent of network size and allows communities to be evaluated in isolation. We assume that local minima of F under addition and removal of single links correspond to link communities. Valid communities The cost landscape has many local minima, many of them trivial variants of one another. We call two sets of links neighbours if one can be reached from the other by at most d link additions or removals, where d is the range parameter. A local minimum C is a valid community if no set within this range has a lower cost. Valid communities are therefore the lowest minima within their neighbourhood, which removes minor variants while retaining distinct, possibly overlapping, topics. The set of valid communities does not depend on the order of the search. Enumerating all of them is infeasible for large networks because the number of candidate sets grows combinatorially, so we use a heuristic search. Memetic algorithm The algorithm combines a population-based evolutionary strategy (global exploration) with deterministic local search (exploitation of the cost landscape). Seeds. Initial individuals are small connected subgraphs: a randomly chosen link together with a random subset of links adjacent to it, up to a fixed size s (s = 3 to 5 in our runs). Seeds are drawn so that links not yet covered by any accepted community are favoured, which steers the search towards unexplored regions. Local search. Each individual is refined deterministically. In every iteration we evaluate F for all single-link additions (links adjacent to V(C)) and all single-link removals, and apply the move giving the largest cost decrease. The procedure stops when no move lowers the cost, which yields a local minimum. Link additions are restricted to the boundary, so only a small set of candidates must be evaluated, and cost changes are updated incrementally from the affected nodes. Evolutionary operators. Each generation, individuals undergo (i) mutation, in which a random fraction of links is removed and a random set of boundary links is added, and (ii) recombination, in which two overlapping individuals are merged by union or intersection. Every offspring is then refined by local search. Selection is probabilistic and favours low cost while preserving diversity: an offspring replaces its parent if its cost is lower, and it is retained as a new individual if it differs from all existing individuals by more than the range d. Validity check. After local search, each minimum is compared with all stored minima within range d. If a stored minimum has lower cost, the new one is discarded. If the new one has lower cost, it replaces all stored minima within its range. This maintains a growing archive of valid communities. The search ends when a fixed number of generations passes without new valid communities, or when a chosen share of links is covered. Post-processing Valid communities with fewer than a minimum number of links are discarded. For each community, publications are assigned to the topic if they are incident to its links. Each publication is assigned a membership weight equal to the fraction of its links belonging to the community, which allows us to distinguish core from peripheral members. Links not covered by any community are left unassigned and reported. Data We use two data sets from the Web of Science. The first contains about 15,000 Astronomy & Astrophysics papers published in 2010 together with their cited sources, linked through citations from the 2010 papers to those sources. The second contains about 100,000 Astronomy & Astrophysics papers published 2003–2010, linked through direct citations among them. Citation links are treated as undirected and unweighted, duplicates and self-citations are removed, and isolated nodes are dropped. The smaller network is used to tune parameters and inspect results in detail, and the larger network tests scalability. Evaluation We assess the solutions by (i) the distribution of community sizes, (ii) the extent of overlap, measured as the number of communities per publication and the share of links shared between communities, (iii) stability across independent runs with different random seeds, quantified by the share of communities in one run that have a counterpart in another with high Jaccard similarity of their link sets, and (iv) the coherence of communities, judged by the most frequent title terms and keywords of their publications. Sensitivity to the range d, seed size s and minimum community size is examined by varying one parameter at a time. Uterine fibroids, or leiomyomas, are the most common benign tumours of the female reproductive tract, affecting up to 70–80% of women by the age of 50. Although many are asymptomatic, a substantial proportion cause heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic pain, urinary symptoms, and reduced fertility, with a considerable impact on quality of life and healthcare costs. Hysterectomy and myomectomy remain the definitive surgical options, but there is growing demand for less invasive, uterus-preserving alternatives. These include uterine artery embolisation, radiofrequency ablation, and image-guided thermal ablation with high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU). HIFU is a non-invasive technique in which an extracorporeal transducer focuses ultrasound energy into a small target volume, raising the tissue temperature rapidly to levels causing coagulative necrosis while sparing the intervening tissues. Treatment is guided by either magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or ultrasound imaging. The technique has been shown to be safe and effective for symptom relief in uterine fibroids, with low complication rates and short recovery times. The principal measure of technical treatment success is the non-perfused volume (NPV) ratio, the proportion of the fibroid volume that is devascularised after treatment, as visualised on contrast-enhanced MRI. Higher NPV ratios have been associated with better symptom relief and lower rates of re-intervention, and an NPV ratio above 80% is commonly regarded as a favourable outcome. However, the NPV ratio achieved varies widely between patients and between individual fibroids. Several factors have been proposed to influence this variability, including fibroid size, location, and distance from the skin, the thickness of the subcutaneous fat and abdominal wall, T2-weighted signal intensity, and perfusion characteristics of the fibroid. The Funaki classification, which grades fibroids by their signal intensity on T2-weighted MRI relative to skeletal muscle and myometrium, has been widely used to reflect fibroid cellularity and water content, with hyperintense fibroids generally being harder to ablate. Other patient characteristics, such as parity, gravidity, age, and symptoms, may also be associated with outcomes, but their relative importance is less well understood. Because many of these variables are correlated and their individual effects are modest, it is difficult to determine from conventional statistical analyses which ones carry the most predictive information. Predicting treatment outcome before HIFU would be clinically valuable. It would help in selecting suitable candidates, in counselling patients about the likelihood of complete ablation, and in planning treatment strategy, for example the need for additional sessions, bowel or bladder preparation, or adjunct measures to improve acoustic access. Machine learning offers a means to combine multiple clinical and imaging variables into predictive models. Previous studies have applied regression models and machine learning approaches, including those based on radiomic features from pre-treatment MRI, to predict NPV ratio or ablation success. Many of these studies, however, relied on a single feature selection technique, often chosen without justification, or on models trained on small datasets with many candidate variables. In such circumstances the risk of overfitting is high, and the resulting feature sets may be unstable and poorly generalisable. Feature selection is therefore a critical step in building prediction models from clinical data. By removing irrelevant and redundant variables, it can improve classification performance, reduce computational cost, and improve the interpretability of the model. Feature selection methods are commonly divided into filter, wrapper, and embedded approaches. Filter methods rank features according to statistical or information-theoretic criteria independent of any classifier, making them computationally efficient and less prone to overfitting than wrapper methods. Among them, information-theoretic methods such as Mutual Information Maximisation (MIM), Joint Mutual Information (JMI), and minimum redundancy maximum relevance (mRMR) differ in how they balance the relevance of a feature to the target against its redundancy with other selected features. Different filters can yield different rankings for the same data, and their performance depends on the dataset and the classifier. A comparison of multiple methods, rather than reliance on one, may therefore provide more robust insight into which features are consistently informative. To our knowledge, a comprehensive comparison of several feature selection methods for HIFU treatment outcome classification in uterine fibroids has not been reported. In particular, it remains unclear which clinical and anatomical parameters are most informative and how sensitive classification performance is to the choice of feature selection method and the number of features selected. The aim of this study was therefore to apply multiple feature selection methods to retrospective clinical data from patients treated with HIFU for uterine fibroids, in order to identify the most important parameters for predicting treatment outcome. Fourteen filter-based methods were used to rank 39 features extracted from patient data, and the selected feature subsets were evaluated using a support vector classification model. Treatment outcome was categorised into three classes according to NPV ratio (<30%, 30–80%, and >80%). We further aimed to assess how classification performance varies with the feature selection method and the size of the feature set, and to derive a consensus ranking of the most informative features across methods. This retrospective study used data from patients with symptomatic uterine fibroids treated with magnetic resonance-guided high-intensity focused ultrasound (MR-HIFU). The institutional review board approved the study and the requirement for informed consent was waived because the data were analysed retrospectively and anonymised. Data from 66 HIFU treatments comprising 89 uterine fibroids were included. Each fibroid was treated as a separate sample. Treatment and outcome definition All treatments were performed under MRI guidance with a clinical MR-HIFU system. Patients were positioned prone, and treatment planning was done on T2-weighted images. Sonication cells were placed within the fibroid with a safety margin to the serosa, endometrium and bowel, and the energy was adjusted according to patient feedback and thermometry. Immediately after treatment, contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images were acquired. The non-perfused volume (NPV) was segmented by an experienced radiologist, and the fibroid volume was segmented on the same images. The NPV ratio was defined as NPV divided by fibroid volume. For classification, the NPV ratio was divided into three classes: <30% (low), 30–80% (medium) and >80% (high). Feature extraction A total of 39 features were extracted from the clinical records, the pretreatment MRI and the treatment reports. They fell into four groups: (i) patient demographics and history, including age, body mass index, gravidity, parity, previous abdominal surgery and the presence of urinary symptoms; (ii) anatomical features of the abdominal wall, such as subcutaneous fat thickness and fibroid distance from the skin; (iii) fibroid characteristics, including diameter, volume, location (for example fundus, anterior, posterior), submucosal type, and Funaki classification (types I, II and III) based on T2-weighted signal intensity relative to skeletal muscle and myometrium; and (iv) other symptom and imaging descriptors. Diameter was the longest axis measured on MRI, and volume was calculated from segmentation. Distance was measured from the skin to the anterior fibroid surface. Categorical variables were one-hot encoded, resulting in binary features for each category (for example Funaki type I and Funaki type III were separate features). Continuous features were standardised to zero mean and unit variance. Missing values (<5% of entries) were imputed using the median for continuous and the mode for categorical variables. Imputation and scaling were fitted on training data only within each cross-validation fold to avoid information leakage. Feature selection Fourteen filter-based feature selection methods were applied to rank the features independently of the classifier. The methods were drawn from the information-theoretic, statistical and similarity-based families. They included Mutual Information Maximisation (MIM), Joint Mutual Information (JMI), Conditional Mutual Information Maximisation (CMIM), Minimum Redundancy Maximum Relevance (mRMR), Interaction Capping (ICAP), Double Input Symmetrical Relevance (DISR), Conditional Infomax Feature Extraction (CIFE), Fisher score, Chi-squared, ANOVA F-test, ReliefF, Gini index, Laplacian score and Pearson correlation. Continuous features were discretised into equal-frequency bins for the mutual-information methods. Each method produced a ranked list of all 39 features. To obtain an overall ranking, the ranks of each feature were aggregated across methods and across cross-validation folds by averaging, giving the ordered list of the most important features. For each method, subsets consisting of the top k features (k = 1 to 39) were generated. Classification model The selected feature subsets were evaluated using a support vector classifier (SVC) with a radial basis function kernel. Multiclass classification used a one-versus-one scheme. Class weights were balanced to account for unequal class frequencies. The regularisation parameter C and kernel coefficient gamma were tuned by grid search (C from 10⁻² to 10³, gamma from 10⁻⁴ to 10¹ on a logarithmic scale) using an inner cross-validation loop. Validation and performance metrics Performance was assessed with stratified repeated k-fold cross-validation (5 folds, 10 repeats). Because several fibroids could belong to the same patient, folds were grouped by patient so that fibroids from one patient did not appear in both training and test sets. Within each outer training fold, feature ranking was performed and the SVC hyperparameters were tuned, and the resulting model was evaluated on the held-out fold. Performance was summarised with the F1-micro score, which pools true positives, false positives and false negatives over all classes, and is equivalent to accuracy in single-label multiclass problems. Macro-averaged F1 and per-class F1 scores were also calculated to examine class imbalance. Results are reported as mean and standard deviation across folds and repeats. For each feature selection method, the F1-micro score was calculated as a function of the number of features, and the performance of the top ten features was compared across methods. A baseline using all 39 features and a dummy classifier predicting the majority class were used as references. Implementation All analysis was performed in Python using scikit-learn for preprocessing, SVC and cross-validation, and scikit-feature together with in-house code for the filter methods. Random seeds were fixed for reproducibility. A total of 66 HIFU treatments involving 89 uterine fibroids were included in the analysis. After the NPV ratio was calculated for each fibroid, 27 fibroids (30%) were assigned to the <30% class, 34 (38%) to the 30–80% class and 28 (31%) to the >80% class. The classes were therefore reasonably balanced. Of the 39 extracted features, 23 were continuous or ordinal and 16 were binary or categorical (including Funaki type, fibroid location and submucosal type). Feature ranking The 14 filter-based methods produced different rankings, but several features were consistently placed near the top. Aggregating the ranks across all methods gave the following ten most highly ranked features, in order: fibroid diameter, subcutaneous fat thickness, fibroid volume, fibroid distance (from skin), Funaki type I, fundus location, gravidity, Funaki type III, submucosal fibroid type and urinary symptoms. Fibroid diameter and fibroid volume were ranked in the top five by most methods. This was expected given their strong correlation (Spearman ρ = 0.93). Subcutaneous fat thickness and fibroid distance were also moderately correlated (ρ = 0.58). Methods that explicitly penalise redundancy, such as JMI, mRMR and CMIM, tended to rank only one of the correlated size features highly and promoted less correlated features, such as gravidity and urinary symptoms, to higher positions. Univariate methods such as MIM, chi-squared and the Fisher score placed both diameter and volume among the top features. Features that were consistently ranked in the lower half across methods included patient age, body mass index, fibroid number, uterine position and most of the remaining clinical history variables. Rankings were most similar between MIM and JMI, and between the Fisher score and the t-score. Rankings from the Relief-based methods differed most from the information-theoretic methods, and some of them placed Funaki type II and posterior location higher. Classification performance The F1-micro scores obtained with the SVC model varied with both the feature selection method and the number of selected features. With very small feature sets (one to three features), scores ranged from approximately 0.40 to 0.52 across methods. In general, performance increased as features were added and reached a maximum between six and twelve features for most methods. After this point it plateaued or declined slightly, which suggests that the additional lower-ranked features contributed noise rather than useful information. Traumatic dental injuries are a common public health problem, particularly among children and adolescents, with an estimated one in five individuals sustaining a dental injury during their lifetime [1,2]. Avulsion, the complete displacement of a tooth from its alveolar socket, accounts for roughly 0.5–16% of traumatic injuries to the permanent dentition [3]. Immediate replantation is the treatment of choice, and prognosis depends primarily on the viability of periodontal ligament (PDL) cells remaining on the root surface [4]. When replantation is delayed and the tooth is stored dry, PDL cells become necrotic within approximately 60 minutes, and the long-term outcome is compromised [5,6]. Consequences of Delayed Replantation In teeth with a dry extra-alveolar time exceeding 60 minutes, the necrotic PDL cannot support regeneration of the attachment apparatus. The root surface is instead colonized by osteoblast-lineage cells from the adjacent alveolar bone, resulting in replacement resorption (ankylosis), in which the root is gradually remodeled and replaced by bone [7]. This process is progressive, particularly in growing patients, and frequently leads to infraocclusion, esthetic and functional impairment, and eventual tooth loss [8]. Current guidelines of the International Association of Dental Traumatology acknowledge that the prognosis of such teeth is poor, and that replantation primarily serves to preserve alveolar ridge dimensions and delay the need for prosthetic rehabilitation [9]. Various root surface treatments, including fluoride, bisphosphonates, enamel matrix derivative, and anti-inflammatory agents, have been proposed to slow resorption, but none reliably restores a functional periodontal attachment [10,11]. There is therefore a clear need for biologically based strategies that regenerate the periodontium on the denuded root surface. Mesenchymal Stem Cells in Periodontal Regeneration Tissue engineering offers an alternative approach, combining progenitor cells, scaffolds, and bioactive signals to reconstitute lost tissues [12]. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are particularly attractive because of their self-renewal capacity, multilineage differentiation potential, and immunomodulatory properties [13]. Human bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMMSCs), defined by plastic adherence, expression of CD73, CD90, and CD105, absence of hematopoietic markers, and the capacity to differentiate into osteogenic, adipogenic, and chondrogenic lineages, are the most extensively characterized MSC population [14]. Preclinical studies have shown that BMMSCs can contribute to the regeneration of cementum, PDL, and alveolar bone in periodontal defects and can reduce root resorption after replantation [15–17]. Nevertheless, effective use of these cells depends on a delivery system that retains them at the defect site, maintains their viability, and supports their proliferation and function. Direct injection of cell suspensions is limited by rapid cell dispersion and poor survival, underscoring the importance of an appropriate carrier [18]. Platelet-rich Fibrin as a Cell Carrier Platelet-rich fibrin (PRF), a second-generation autologous platelet concentrate introduced by Choukroun and colleagues, is prepared by centrifugation of peripheral blood without anticoagulants or other additives [19]. The resulting product is a three-dimensional fibrin matrix that entraps platelets, leukocytes, and circulating cells. Unlike first-generation platelet-rich plasma, PRF requires no bovine thrombin, and its dense fibrin architecture permits slow, sustained release of growth factors such as platelet-derived growth factor, transforming growth factor-β, vascular endothelial growth factor, and insulin-like growth factor over a period of one to two weeks [20,21]. These factors promote cell migration, proliferation, angiogenesis, and matrix synthesis [22]. PRF is autologous, inexpensive, easily prepared chairside, and biodegradable, and it has been used successfully in periodontal intrabony defects, sinus augmentation, extraction socket preservation, and regenerative endodontics [23–25]. Its mechanical properties allow it to be handled, cut, and shaped, making it a plausible scaffold for application to root surfaces. Several reports indicate that PRF supports the attachment and proliferation of dental pulp stem cells, PDL cells, and bone marrow-derived cells in vitro [26,27]. However, data on the behavior of human BMMSCs when seeded on PRF scaffolds, particularly with regard to a construct designed for the treatment of avulsed teeth, remain limited. Rationale and Aim of the Study Combining BMMSCs with PRF is hypothesized to yield a construct in which the fibrin matrix provides a biomimetic, growth factor-enriched microenvironment for cell adhesion, survival, and proliferation, while the stem cells supply the regenerative potential lacking in the necrotic PDL of dried replanted teeth. Such a construct might ultimately be wrapped around or applied to the root surface before replantation, promoting regeneration of periodontal tissues and limiting ankylosis. Before any in vivo or clinical evaluation, however, the feasibility of fabricating a stable cell–scaffold composite and its cytocompatibility must be established. Accordingly, the present study aimed to design and fabricate a PRF scaffold and to evaluate the viability, proliferation, and adhesion of human BMMSCs cultured on it. Human BMMSCs were first isolated and characterized by surface marker expression and osteogenic and adipogenic differentiation potential. The effects of PRF on BMMSC proliferation were then assessed over seven days using the MTT assay, and cell attachment and morphology on the fibrin matrix were examined by scanning electron microscopy. The findings are intended to provide a foundation for the development of a novel cell delivery system for periodontal regeneration after dental trauma. Study design and ethical approval This in-vitro study was conducted in three stages: (i) isolation and characterization of human bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMMSCs); (ii) fabrication of a platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) scaffold; and (iii) evaluation of BMMSC viability, proliferation, and adhesion on the scaffold. The protocol was approved by the institutional ethics committee, and written informed consent was obtained from all donors before sample collection. All procedures followed the Declaration of Helsinki [1]. Isolation and culture of human BMMSCs Bone marrow aspirates (2–3 mL) were obtained from the iliac crest of healthy adult volunteers under local anesthesia and collected in heparinized tubes. The aspirates were diluted 1:1 with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and layered over Ficoll-Paque density gradient medium (1.077 g/mL). After centrifugation at 400 × g for 30 min at room temperature, the mononuclear cell layer was collected, washed twice with PBS, and resuspended in low-glucose Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 µg/mL streptomycin [2]. Cells were seeded in T25 flasks and incubated at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere of 5% CO2. Non-adherent cells were removed after 72 h, and the medium was changed every 3 days. At 80% confluence, cells were detached with 0.25% trypsin-EDTA and subcultured. Cells at passages 3–4 were used in all experiments. Characterization of BMMSCs Immunophenotyping. Cells were characterized according to the minimal criteria of the International Society for Cellular Therapy [3]. Approximately 5 × 10⁵ cells per tube were incubated for 30 min at 4 °C in the dark with fluorochrome-conjugated monoclonal antibodies against CD73, CD90, CD105 (positive markers), and CD34, CD45, and HLA-DR (negative markers). Isotype-matched antibodies served as controls. After washing, samples were analyzed by flow cytometry, acquiring at least 10,000 events per sample, and data were processed using FlowJo software. Osteogenic differentiation. Cells were seeded at 3 × 10⁴ cells/well in 12-well plates and cultured to confluence. The medium was then replaced with osteogenic induction medium (DMEM, 10% FBS, 100 nM dexamethasone, 10 mM β-glycerophosphate, and 50 µg/mL ascorbic acid-2-phosphate) for 21 days, with medium changes twice weekly. Cells were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde and stained with 2% Alizarin Red S (pH 4.2) to detect calcium deposits. Adipogenic differentiation. Confluent cells were cultured in adipogenic induction medium (DMEM, 10% FBS, 1 µM dexamethasone, 0.5 mM isobutylmethylxanthine, 10 µg/mL insulin, and 100 µM indomethacin) for 21 days. Intracellular lipid droplets were visualized by Oil Red O staining and examined under an inverted light microscope. Undifferentiated cells maintained in standard medium served as negative controls. Preparation of the PRF scaffold Peripheral venous blood (10 mL) was drawn from healthy, non-smoking volunteers who had taken no medication affecting coagulation or platelet function for at least two weeks. Following Choukroun's protocol [4], blood was collected in plain glass-coated tubes without anticoagulant and immediately centrifuged at 400 × g (approximately 2700 rpm) for 12 min. Three layers formed: acellular plasma at the top, the PRF clot in the middle, and red blood cells at the bottom. The PRF clot was removed with sterile forceps, and the attached red blood cell fraction was carefully trimmed off with scissors under sterile conditions. The clot was gently compressed between two sterile gauze pieces to form a membrane of uniform thickness (about 1 mm) and cut into 5 × 5 mm pieces using a sterile surgical blade. Scaffolds were placed in 24-well plates and rinsed with culture medium before cell seeding. Seeding of BMMSCs onto PRF scaffolds Passage 3–4 BMMSCs were resuspended at 1 × 10⁵ cells in 50 µL of complete medium and dropped onto each PRF scaffold. After 2 h of incubation at 37 °C to allow initial attachment, 1 mL of complete medium was added to each well. Medium was changed every 2 days. Cells cultured on tissue-culture plastic without PRF served as the control group. Cell proliferation assay (MTT) Cell viability and proliferation were evaluated on days 1, 3, 5, and 7 using the 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) assay [5]. At each time point, the medium was replaced with 0.5 mg/mL MTT solution in serum-free medium and incubated for 4 h at 37 °C. The resulting formazan crystals were dissolved in 500 µL dimethyl sulfoxide with gentle shaking for 15 min. Aliquots (100 µL) were transferred to 96-well plates, and absorbance was measured at 570 nm with a reference wavelength of 630 nm using a microplate reader. PRF scaffolds without cells were processed identically to provide blank values, which were subtracted from experimental readings. Each condition was tested in triplicate wells, and experiments were repeated independently with cells from three donors. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) To assess cell attachment and morphology, BMMSC/PRF constructs were harvested at 4 h, 24 h, and 72 h after seeding. Samples were rinsed with PBS and fixed in 2.5% glutaraldehyde in 0.1 M cacodylate buffer for 2 h at 4 °C. They were then dehydrated through a graded ethanol series (30%, 50%, 70%, 90%, and 100%), chemically dried with hexamethyldisilazane, mounted on aluminum stubs, and sputter-coated with gold. Specimens were examined using a scanning electron microscope at an accelerating voltage of 15–20 kV. Cell-free PRF scaffolds were imaged to document baseline fibrin architecture. Statistical analysis Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation. Normality of distribution was verified using the Shapiro–Wilk test. MTT absorbance values between the PRF and control groups at each time point were compared using two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA; factors: group and time) followed by Tukey's post hoc test. Analyses were performed using SPSS software (version 22; IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA), and a P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Isolation and Characterization of Human BMMSCs Primary cultures of human bone marrow aspirates yielded adherent, plastic-adherent cells within 3–4 days of plating. By passage 3, the cells showed a homogeneous, spindle-shaped, fibroblast-like morphology and formed colonies, consistent with the typical mesenchymal stem cell phenotype [1,2]. Flow cytometric analysis showed that the cells were strongly positive for the mesenchymal markers CD90, CD105, and CD73 (>95% of the population for each). They were largely negative for the hematopoietic and endothelial markers CD34, CD45, and HLA-DR (<2%). This profile meets the minimal criteria for defining multipotent mesenchymal stromal cells proposed by the International Society for Cellular Therapy [3]. Multilineage potential was confirmed by induction assays. After 21 days in osteogenic medium, cultures showed extensive extracellular calcium deposits stained by Alizarin Red S, whereas control cultures in basal medium showed no mineralization. After 21 days in adipogenic medium, cells accumulated intracellular lipid droplets that stained with Oil Red O, and these were absent in controls. Together, these results show that the isolated cells were bona fide BMMSCs with osteogenic and adipogenic capacity. Participation in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields is widely regarded as essential to national economic competitiveness, innovation, and individual economic mobility. For decades, policymakers, employers, and educators have called for growth in the number of college graduates prepared to enter STEM careers. Yet the pipeline into those careers leaks substantially at the transition to postsecondary education and during the first years of college. Studies of national cohorts have found that roughly half of students who begin college intending to major in a STEM field either leave the field or leave college without a degree within six years, and attrition is especially pronounced among students from groups historically underrepresented in STEM, including Black, Latino/a, and Native American students, first-generation college students, students from low-income families, and, in some fields, women. Gateway courses in calculus, chemistry, and physics often serve as points at which students who are capable of succeeding lose confidence, struggle academically, or conclude that they do not belong. Many factors contribute to this attrition. Students arrive with unequal access to advanced high school coursework, laboratory experiences, and well-prepared teachers. Differences in academic preparation, particularly in mathematics, constrain the courses that students can take in their first semester and the pace at which they can progress through prerequisite sequences. Beyond academic preparation, students may lack knowledge about how colleges operate, struggle to build relationships with faculty and peers, encounter unwelcoming climates, or experience stereotype threat and impostor feelings. Financial pressures and competing family obligations compound these challenges. Persistence models in higher education emphasize that academic and social integration, a sense of belonging, self-efficacy, and identification with a scientific community all shape whether students remain in their chosen fields. Colleges and universities have responded with a range of interventions, among which summer bridge programs are one of the most common. Typically offered in the weeks before the first fall term, bridge programs bring incoming students to campus for an intensive experience that may include coursework, math and science review, study skills instruction, research experiences, advising, mentoring, community building, and introductions to campus resources. The underlying logic is straightforward: by providing early exposure to college-level expectations and supports, programs may help students strengthen their academic foundations, form peer and faculty connections, and develop the confidence and strategies needed to succeed. Bridge programs are also attractive because they can be adapted to local contexts, are often funded by federal agencies, state initiatives, or private foundations, and are frequently aimed specifically at students who might otherwise be at risk of leaving STEM. Despite their popularity, it is not clear what the accumulated evidence says about the effectiveness of STEM bridge programs. Individual reports describe programs that differ greatly in length, from a single week to ten weeks or more; in residential or commuter format; in target population; in the mix of academic and social components; and in the outcomes they examine. Some programs are designed primarily to remediate gaps in mathematics preparation, whereas others focus on research engagement, community building, or recruitment to particular majors. Outcomes of interest include course grades, grade point average, retention in college, retention in STEM majors, graduation, and psychosocial measures such as self-efficacy and sense of belonging. Evaluation designs range from simple descriptive reports of participant satisfaction to comparisons with matched or statistically adjusted groups. Because participation is usually voluntary or based on selection criteria, differences between participants and nonparticipants may reflect motivation or prior preparation rather than the effect of the program, complicating causal interpretation. Previous reviews of bridge and transition programs have tended to address them broadly, often without focusing on STEM, or have concentrated on a particular type of program or institution. A focused synthesis that describes how STEM bridge programs are structured, what goals they set for themselves, and whether they report achieving those goals would be valuable to program designers, evaluators, and funders. Such a synthesis can also identify gaps in the literature, such as limited attention to long-term outcomes, community college students, or the specific program components responsible for any benefits. This article addresses that need by reviewing 46 reports describing 30 unique STEM summer bridge programs published over the past 25 years. We examine the characteristics of each program, including its institutional context, target population, duration, components, and funding, along with the goals the program articulated and the evidence offered regarding whether those goals were met. Treating the program, rather than the report, as the unit of analysis allows us to avoid overcounting programs described in multiple publications while still drawing on the full range of available documentation. We then synthesize patterns across programs and use them to develop a set of recommendations for the design, implementation, and evaluation of STEM bridge programs. Our aim is to help practitioners and researchers build stronger bridges into college for the students who stand to benefit most from them, and to contribute to a more rigorous and cumulative body of knowledge about what works, for whom, and under what conditions. We conducted a systematic review of the literature on STEM summer bridge programs following the general principles of the PRISMA guidelines for systematic reviews. The review aimed to identify the characteristics and goals of STEM bridge programs and to determine whether programs reported meeting those goals. Definition and Scope For this review, a summer bridge program was defined as an intervention offered between high school completion and the start of the first postsecondary year (or, in a small number of cases, between the first and second years) intended to ease students' transition into college. To be considered a STEM bridge program, it needed to explicitly target students entering or intending to enter a STEM major or STEM-focused institution, or to be housed within a STEM college, school, or department. Programs could be residential or commuter, and of any duration, provided they occurred principally during the summer. Search Strategy We searched ERIC, Web of Science, Education Source, PsycINFO, Scopus, and Google Scholar for reports published between January 1995 and December 2019. Search strings combined terms for the intervention (e.g., "summer bridge," "bridge program," "pre-college program," "transition program," "summer transition") with terms for the discipline (e.g., "STEM," "science," "technology," "engineering," "mathematics," "computer science"). We also searched the proceedings of engineering education and STEM education conferences, including the American Society for Engineering Education annual conference, because many program evaluations are disseminated there. To limit publication bias, we included peer-reviewed articles, conference papers, dissertations, and technical or institutional reports. Finally, we hand-searched the reference lists of included reports and of earlier reviews of bridge and developmental programs, and we examined the websites of funding agencies that support such programs for associated reports. Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria Reports were included if they (a) described a summer bridge program meeting the definition above; (b) targeted STEM students; (c) were published in English between 1995 and 2019; (d) described the program's structure or activities; and (e) reported at least one outcome or evaluative finding, whether quantitative, qualitative, or mixed. Reports were excluded if they described programs for middle or high school students not yet admitted to college, programs serving only current upperclass undergraduates or graduate students, year-long or academic-year-only programs without a summer component, or programs that were purely proposals or plans without any outcome data. Opinion pieces and reports that offered no description of the program were also excluded. Screening Process The initial searches yielded 1,137 records. After removal of duplicates, two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts against the inclusion criteria. Records either reviewer judged potentially relevant moved to full-text review. Two reviewers then independently read each full text and decided on inclusion. Disagreements were resolved through discussion, with a third reviewer consulted when consensus could not be reached. Agreement between reviewers at the full-text stage was high (Cohen's kappa = 0.84). The process resulted in 46 reports describing 30 unique programs. Multiple reports about the same program (for example, an initial description followed by later outcome studies) were grouped together and treated as a single program for purposes of synthesis, with each report retained as a source of information. Data Extraction We developed a coding form through iterative piloting on a subset of eight reports. For each program, we extracted: institution type and location; years of operation; funding source; target population (e.g., underrepresented minority students, first-generation students, women, students with low placement scores); selection criteria; number of participants; program length; residential status; cost to students; and program components such as academic coursework, math or science preparation, research experiences, peer or faculty mentoring, study-skills instruction, advising, community building, and family involvement. We also coded each program's stated goals (e.g., improving retention, grade point average, persistence in STEM, academic preparation, sense of belonging, self-efficacy, and graduation), the outcomes measured, the research design, the comparison group used if any, and the reported results. Two coders independently coded each report, and discrepancies were reconciled through discussion. Assessment of Program Success Because the programs differed widely in goals and measures, we did not conduct a meta-analysis. Instead, for each program we compared the stated goals with the reported outcomes and classified each goal as met, partially met, not met, or not assessed. A goal was considered met when the authors reported a statistically significant positive difference relative to a comparison group or baseline, or, for descriptive studies lacking inferential statistics, when the reported outcomes clearly met a stated target. Goals were considered partially met when results were mixed across measures, subgroups, or time points. We also recorded the strength of the evidence by classifying designs as experimental or quasi-experimental with a comparison group, pre-post without comparison, descriptive or correlational, or qualitative only. We noted threats to validity such as self-selection into programs, absence of controls for prior achievement, small samples, and short follow-up periods. Synthesis We used a narrative synthesis approach. We first summarized program characteristics descriptively using frequencies and ranges. We then examined patterns across programs by goal type and by program feature, exploring whether features such as duration, residential format, inclusion of a research component, or mentoring were more common in programs that met their goals. Qualitative findings were analyzed through inductive thematic coding, and themes were compared with quantitative results to identify convergent and divergent conclusions. Recommendations were derived from features that recurred in programs reporting success, from issues in the evidence base (such as inconsistent outcome measurement and limited long-term tracking), and from the themes that students and staff identified as important. Of the 46 reports reviewed, 30 unique bridge programs were identified. Reports were published between 1995 and 2020, with more than half appearing after 2010. Most programs were located at four-year public institutions in the United States (n = 24), and several were housed at minority-serving institutions or historically Black colleges and universities (n = 7). Reports were primarily journal articles (n = 31), followed by conference proceedings (n = 11) and institutional or grant reports (n = 4). Program Characteristics Program length ranged from one week to ten weeks, with a median of five weeks. Eleven programs lasted four weeks or fewer, 13 lasted five to seven weeks, and six lasted eight weeks or longer. Most were residential (n = 19), while seven were commuter-based and four offered both options. Cohort size varied widely, from 12 to more than 300 students, though most programs served fewer than 100 students. Programs most often targeted students from groups underrepresented in STEM, including racial and ethnic minorities (n = 22), first-generation students (n = 17), and low-income students (n = 14). Nine programs targeted women, and six served students identified as academically underprepared based on placement test scores or high school grades. Selection was typically by application (n = 18); others enrolled students by placement results or automatic invitation (n = 12). Participation was usually free or subsidized; 21 programs provided stipends, housing, or tuition waivers. Programs shared several common components. Protein glycosylation is an essential modification in eukaryotes that influences folding, stability, localization and function of secretory and cell surface proteins. In fungi, O-mannosylation of serine and threonine residues is initiated in the endoplasmic reticulum by the protein O-mannosyltransferases (Pmts), which transfer mannose from dolichyl-phosphate-mannose to nascent polypeptides. The Pmt family is conserved from yeasts to humans and is divided into three subfamilies, PMT1, PMT2 and PMT4, whose members act as heteromeric complexes (Pmt1/Pmt2) or homomeric complexes (Pmt4). In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, there are seven PMT genes (PMT1 to PMT7), whereas the human fungal pathogen Candida albicans has five (PMT1, PMT2, PMT4, PMT5 and PMT6). O-mannosylation is critical for cell wall integrity, morphogenesis, and host-pathogen interactions. In C. albicans, deletion of PMT1 or PMT2 causes severe defects, including altered cell wall composition, hypersensitivity to cell wall perturbing agents, impaired hyphal growth and strongly attenuated virulence. Pmt isoforms are therefore of interest both as determinants of fungal cell biology and as potential antifungal targets. Because O-mannosylation is so important for cell wall homeostasis, its regulation must be tightly integrated with cellular physiology. Defects in protein N- or O-glycosylation cause glycostress, which in C. albicans and other fungi triggers compensatory responses, including upregulated transcription of PMT genes and cell wall remodeling through the cell wall integrity and unfolded protein response pathways. Much less is known about regulation of Pmt levels at the translational level, and about the factors that might couple the translational machinery to the demands of glycosylation. Dom34, known in higher eukaryotes as Pelota, is a conserved protein related to the translation termination factor eRF1. Together with the GTPase Hbs1 (and the ATPase Rli1/ABCE1), Dom34 recognizes ribosomes stalled on mRNAs, for example at the 3′ end of truncated transcripts lacking stop codons or within translation-blocking structures, and promotes subunit dissociation and recycling of the ribosome. In this way, Dom34 functions in no-go decay, non-stop decay and nonsense-mediated decay pathways, and in ribosome-associated quality control. Dom34 also contributes to the release of ribosomes from the 3′-UTR after termination, and to the recycling of empty 80S ribosomes under conditions of stress or nutrient limitation. By dissociating inactive 80S couples, Dom34 maintains a pool of free, activatable 40S and 60S subunits, and thereby upregulates translation. Accordingly, loss of Dom34 in yeast reduces polysomes, produces 80S accumulation and results in growth defects, particularly at low temperatures. Dom34 is also required for meiosis, differentiation and development in several organisms, and Pelota deficiency is embryonically lethal in mice, indicating important roles beyond quality control. These established activities act at the level of ribosomes rather than of specific transcripts, and Dom34 has largely been considered a general factor. However, there are hints that it may have more selective effects. Ribosome profiling studies have shown that loss of Dom34 alters ribosome distribution on particular mRNAs, and Dom34 and Pelota have been reported to bind RNA. Whether Dom34 can act as an RNA binding protein regulating translation of specific transcripts through their 5′-UTRs has not been explored. We became interested in Dom34 in the context of protein O-mannosylation through a genetic interaction between DOM34 and PMT1. In both S. cerevisiae and C. albicans, we found that lack of Dom34 aggravates phenotypes associated with defective Pmt1, suggesting that the two proteins participate in a common process. This prompted us to examine whether Dom34 influences Pmt1 production. In C. albicans, we show that overproduction of Dom34 ameliorates defects of pmt1 mutants and increases Pmt1 protein levels without increasing PMT1 transcript, pointing to a posttranscriptional mechanism. We demonstrate that this effect depends on the 5′-UTR of the PMT1 mRNA, which binds recombinant Dom34 directly at a CA/AC-rich sequence and which regulates translation in vitro. To determine how broadly Dom34 acts, we used polysomal profiling to compare translation in wild-type and dom34 mutant cells. Dom34 stimulated global translation only moderately, but was particularly important for the translation of transcripts encoding Pmt isoforms 1, 4 and 6. These findings suggest that Dom34 specifically upregulates the translation of PMT transcripts. Since defects in N- or O-glycosylation induce PMT transcription, Dom34-dependent translational enhancement may allow the cell to convert increased PMT mRNA levels efficiently into functional protein, thus optimizing the response to glycostress. Our results reveal a function of Dom34 as a 5′-UTR binding regulator of specific transcripts, complementing its known role in ribosome release at the 3′ end of mRNAs, and link translational control to protein O-mannosylation.
