Phylogenetic inference increasingly relies on large, multigene data sets assembled from public repositories, targeted sequencing, and genome-scale projects. Such data sets are rarely complete. Genes are sequenced unevenly across taxa, and the resulting matrices contain substantial missing data, often organized in block-like patterns determined by which loci were available for which species [1,2]. The consequences of missing data for phylogenetic accuracy have been debated for decades. Simulation and empirical studies suggest that incomplete taxa can often be placed accurately if enough informative characters are present [3,4], whereas other work shows that the distribution of missing data, rather than its amount, may be what undermines inference [5,6]. A less appreciated consequence of such patterns is that they can create ambiguity in the tree search itself, through a phenomenon known as phylogenetic terraces [7]. A terrace is a set of distinct trees that have identical optimality scores because of the pattern of data presence and absence in the matrix [7,8]. Terraces arise when the optimality criterion is decomposable across subsets of the data, so that the score of a tree is the sum of scores of the subtrees induced by each locus. This holds for maximum parsimony and for maximum likelihood under partitioned models in which branch lengths are unlinked (edge-unlinked) among partitions [7,9]. If two trees induce the same subtrees on every locus-specific taxon subset, then regardless of the sequence data they will have the same score, because each locus "sees" only its own subtree. These trees may differ in the placement of taxa that are never jointly sampled in any gene. Trees on a terrace are therefore equally optimal, and a search algorithm that arrives at one of them cannot distinguish it from others, even if the terrace contains thousands or millions of topologies [8,10]. Terraces matter for several reasons. First, a single reported tree may be an arbitrary representative of a very large set of equally optimal alternatives, and conventional tree-search software typically reports only one. Second, summary measures such as consensus trees and branch supports calculated from a limited sample of the optimal trees may misrepresent the true uncertainty [7,11]. Third, the problem can propagate to resampling procedures. If bootstrap replicate data sets give rise to terraces, the replicate trees may be arbitrarily chosen among many equally good topologies, and support for clades may be lowered or artifactually distorted [12]. Software has been developed to detect terraces and to calculate their sizes and consensus relationships [13,14], which makes surveys of empirical data feasible. Theory provides a foundation for anticipating when terraces occur. Sanderson and colleagues showed that a terrace is guaranteed to be of size one only when the data pattern satisfies particular conditions, and that a pattern in which at least one taxon is sampled in a manner that leaves some quartets unconstrained will produce multiple trees [7,8]. A simple sufficient condition exists in the form of a "terrace-free" structure, such as a taxon-by-locus matrix with a row-complete locus or a set of loci whose subsets of taxa overlap sufficiently to constrain all relationships [15]. Theory also predicts that terrace size can be enormous in data sets with low coverage, and that increasing the number of genes sampled per taxon may reduce terrace size, with a minimum gene sampling depth required to guarantee a single-tree terrace [8,15]. These predictions are mostly derived from simulations or from limited case studies, however, and it is unknown how often contemporary data sets assembled for large-scale phylogenies approach these thresholds. Empirical systematics has moved in two directions that make this question pressing. On one hand, supermatrix studies in plants, animals, and fungi routinely include hundreds or thousands of taxa with only a handful of loci, producing sparse matrices with low taxon coverage density [16,17]. On the other hand, transcriptomic and genomic data sets can include thousands of loci with relatively high coverage, which may effectively eliminate terraces [18]. Meanwhile, partitioned analyses with unlinked branch lengths have been used and recommended in some contexts, despite their effect on terrace formation, whereas edge-linked models (for example, proportional branch lengths) do not give rise to terraces [9,19]. Without a survey of real data, the practical importance of terraces remains uncertain. Here we present such a survey. We selected 26 recently published phylogenetic data sets and their trees, spanning a range of taxonomic groups, sizes, and data types, and analyzed each under a common set of assumptions in which terraces can form. For each, we identified the terrace to which the published tree belongs and measured its size. We then asked how terrace size relates to sampling properties of the data sets, namely taxon coverage density, defined as the proportion of taxon-by-gene cells containing data, and a measure of gene sampling sufficiency that compares the number of genes available with the theoretical minimum needed to reduce a terrace to a single tree. Finally, we examined terraces among bootstrap replicate trees to evaluate how terraces affect measures of statistical support. Our aims are to describe the prevalence and magnitude of terraces in current practice, to identify data characteristics that predict them, and to clarify the circumstances under which they should concern phylogenetic analysts. We surveyed 26 published phylogenetic data sets and their associated trees, and for each we characterized the phylogenetic terrace to which the published tree would belong under a common set of inference assumptions. Data set selection. We searched the recent literature and public repositories (TreeBASE, Dryad, and journal supplementary archives) for multigene data sets with accompanying tree topologies. Candidate studies had to provide (i) a concatenated or partitioned sequence alignment, (ii) a partition scheme or gene boundaries, and (iii) a published tree with taxon labels matching the alignment. We aimed for variation in taxonomic group (animals, plants, fungi, and others), number of taxa, number of genes, and data type (a small number of Sanger-sequenced loci through transcriptomic and genomic data). Where a study presented several trees, we used the principal tree reported by the authors. Taxon names were reconciled between alignments and trees, and taxa absent from either were pruned. Presence–absence matrices and coverage metrics. For each data set we constructed a binary matrix of taxa by genes (partitions), in which an entry was 1 if the taxon had any sequence data for that gene and 0 otherwise. A gene was scored as present if the taxon had at least one non-gap, non-ambiguous character in the partition. From this matrix we calculated taxon coverage density, the proportion of taxon-by-gene cells with data. We also calculated a gene sampling sufficiency measure based on the theoretical result that terrace size can be reduced to a single tree if the data contain a sufficient number of genes with an appropriate pattern of overlap [1,2]. Specifically, for a tree with a given number of taxa, we compared the number of genes in the data set to the theoretical minimum number needed to guarantee a unique tree. Sufficiency was expressed as the ratio of the observed gene number to this minimum; values ≥ 1 indicate that the sampling depth meets the theoretical guarantee. Terrace identification and size. Under parsimony, and under partitioned maximum likelihood with edge-unlinked branch lengths, trees that have identical induced partition subtrees for every gene have identical scores [1,3]. These trees therefore form a terrace. We assumed an unlinked model for all data sets, regardless of the model used in the original study, so as to apply a common assumption. For each published tree and presence–absence matrix, we determined whether the tree lay on a terrace and calculated its size, the number of distinct trees sharing the same set of induced subtrees. Analyses used the terrace-detection and enumeration algorithms implemented in Terraphy [4] and the phylogenetic software package IQ-TREE [5], which can detect terraces and report the number of trees on them. For very large terraces, exhaustive enumeration was infeasible, so we used the counting algorithms based on the terrace-structure representation of the presence–absence matrix and induced partition subtrees, which yield the size without listing every tree [4]. Terrace sizes were log10 transformed for analysis because they spanned many orders of magnitude. Relationships with sampling properties. We evaluated terrace size as a function of taxon coverage density and gene sampling sufficiency. Because the data were not expected to be normally distributed, we used Spearman rank correlations and, where appropriate, regression of log-transformed terrace size on each predictor. We also compared each data set's gene number to the theoretical minimum sampling depth and recorded the number of data sets meeting it. Data sets were grouped by coverage density (< 0.90, ≥ 0.94) and by data type (Sanger multilocus versus transcriptomic or genomic) to describe differences in terrace occurrence. Bootstrap analyses. To examine the effect of terraces on measures of support, we performed nonparametric bootstrap analyses [6] for each data set. We generated 100 bootstrap pseudoreplicate alignments by resampling sites within partitions with replacement, thereby preserving the presence–absence pattern of the original data. For each pseudoreplicate we inferred a maximum likelihood tree under a partitioned, edge-unlinked model with the best-fitting substitution model selected per partition by the Bayesian information criterion [7]. Each replicate tree was then assessed for terrace membership and size using the methods above. We recorded the proportion of replicate trees that lay on terraces and their sizes. To quantify the effect on support, we compared two summaries. The first was the conventional bootstrap proportion for each clade in the original tree, calculated using the single tree returned by the search for each replicate. The second was a terrace-aware summary in which, for each replicate that lay on a terrace, the tree set was considered and a clade was counted in proportion to the fraction of trees on the terrace that contained it, so that clades not present in all equally optimal trees contributed fractionally. Where a terrace was too large to enumerate, we estimated this fraction from a random sample of 1,000 trees drawn from the terrace. We compared mean support across clades between the two summaries and examined whether reductions were larger for data sets with larger terraces. Software and reproducibility. Alignments were handled with standard scripts in R and Python, and tree manipulation used the ape package [8]. Analyses were run with default settings unless noted. Input matrices, partition definitions, trees, and scripts are available from the authors on request. Assumptions and limitations. Our results describe terraces under unlinked inference assumptions. Terraces do not arise under edge-linked models, which several of the original studies used; we therefore interpret our results as potential rather than realized effects of those studies' analyses. Missing data were defined by complete absence of data for a gene in a taxon, and we did not account for partial sequence coverage within genes. We analyzed 26 empirical data sets spanning plants, animals, fungi, and other groups. They ranged from 19 to more than 700 taxa and from 2 to more than 1,000 loci. Taxon coverage density (the proportion of taxon-by-gene cells containing any data) ranged from 0.17 to 1.00. For each data set we took the published tree and determined the size of the terrace to which it would belong, assuming parsimony or partitioned, edge-unlinked likelihood scoring. Occurrence of terraces. Terraces were detected in 21 of the 26 data sets. Every data set with a taxon coverage density below 0.90 had a terrace of more than one tree. The exceptions were the high-coverage transcriptomic and genomic data sets (coverage density ≥ 0.94), in which the published tree occupied a terrace of size one. Thus, terraces were common in the multigene data sets typical of recent phylogenetic studies, and absent only where data were nearly complete. Data sets with intermediate coverage (0.90–0.94) were few, and results there were mixed: some had small terraces of a few trees, and others had none. Terrace size. Terrace size varied enormously among data sets. Herpes zoster (HZ), commonly known as shingles, results from reactivation of latent varicella zoster virus (VZV) residing in the dorsal root or cranial nerve ganglia after primary infection manifesting as chickenpox. Reactivation occurs when VZV-specific cell-mediated immunity declines, as happens with advancing age, immunosuppression, malignancy, chronic illness, or psychological stress. The virus then travels along the sensory nerve to the skin, producing a unilateral, painful, vesicular eruption confined to one or a few adjacent dermatomes. The lifetime risk of HZ is estimated at 20-30%, and it rises sharply after the fifth decade of life, reaching about 50% in those who live to 85 years. With ageing populations and increasing numbers of immunocompromised individuals, the burden of the disease is expected to grow. Although the rash is the most visible feature, pain is the symptom that most often brings patients to medical attention and is the major cause of morbidity. Pain frequently begins as a prodrome, days before the eruption appears, and may be burning, stabbing, throbbing, or shooting in character. It may be accompanied by allodynia and hyperalgesia. In many patients the pain persists after the skin lesions have healed. Pain is conventionally classified by its timing: acute herpetic neuralgia is pain present within 30 days of rash onset, subacute herpetic neuralgia lasts between 30 and 90 days, and postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) is pain persisting beyond 90 days. Acute pain can severely impair sleep, mood, daily activities, and quality of life, and its intensity is one of the strongest predictors of subsequent PHN, along with older age, severe prodromal pain, extensive rash, and ophthalmic involvement. The pathogenesis of zoster pain is complex. Viral replication in the ganglion causes inflammation, hemorrhagic necrosis, and neuronal destruction. This leads to peripheral sensitization, with ectopic discharges from damaged nociceptors, and to central sensitization in the dorsal horn, with loss of inhibitory interneurons. Effective management of acute pain may therefore require interventions that act at different points: suppressing viral replication, reducing neural inflammation, and modulating neuronal hyperexcitability. Prevention of central sensitization during the acute phase is thought to reduce the risk of chronic pain, which has made aggressive early treatment of acute herpetic neuralgia an attractive strategy. Antiviral therapy is the cornerstone of treatment. Acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir, started within 72 hours of rash onset, shorten the duration of viral shedding, accelerate healing, and reduce the severity and duration of acute pain. Valacyclovir, the prodrug of acyclovir, has superior bioavailability and a more convenient dosing schedule, and has been shown to resolve zoster-associated pain faster than acyclovir. However, antivirals alone do not reliably relieve pain, and their effect on preventing PHN is modest and inconsistent. Many patients continue to experience considerable pain despite adequate antiviral therapy, so adjuvant analgesic treatment is commonly needed. Among the adjuvants, the gabapentinoids, gabapentin and pregabalin, are widely used for neuropathic pain. They bind to the α2δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, reduce the release of excitatory neurotransmitters such as glutamate and substance P, and thereby dampen central sensitization. Pregabalin has more predictable linear pharmacokinetics, more rapid onset, and a simpler dosing schedule than gabapentin. Its efficacy in PHN is well documented, but evidence for its use in the acute phase, and specifically for its ability to prevent PHN, is limited and conflicting. Common adverse effects include dizziness, somnolence, and peripheral edema, which are especially relevant in elderly patients. Corticosteroids are another option, on the rationale that they suppress inflammation in the affected ganglion and nerve and thus limit neural damage and pain. Early trials suggested that prednisolone, added to acyclovir, improved acute pain relief, quality of life, and return to normal activity, though it did not clearly reduce long-term PHN. Concerns about dissemination of infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, hyperglycemia, hypertension, and other adverse effects have limited their use, particularly in older and diabetic patients, and guidelines remain divided on their role. Methylprednisolone has strong anti-inflammatory activity with minimal mineralocorticoid effect, but few studies have examined it in zoster. Most published studies have evaluated antivirals, gabapentinoids, or corticosteroids singly, or have focused on PHN rather than on acute pain. Prospective comparisons of combination regimens that target viral replication, inflammation, and neuropathic mechanisms simultaneously are scarce, especially in the Indian population. It is unclear whether adding pregabalin, with or without a short course of methylprednisolone, to valacyclovir provides additional benefit over antiviral therapy alone, and at what cost in adverse effects. We therefore conducted this pilot, randomized, single-blind, parallel-group study to compare the efficacy and safety of three systemic regimens for acute herpes zoster pain in patients presenting within 72 hours of onset: valacyclovir alone, valacyclovir with pregabalin, and valacyclovir with pregabalin and methylprednisolone. Pain was assessed with a verbal rating scale at baseline and during follow-up at 1, 4, and 6 weeks, and the incidence of PHN and adverse effects was recorded. This randomized, single-blind, parallel-group pilot study was conducted in the Department of Dermatology, Venereology and Leprosy of a tertiary care teaching hospital over a period of one year. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee, and written informed consent was obtained from all participants before enrolment. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Study population Patients of either sex presenting to the outpatient department with a clinical diagnosis of herpes zoster within 72 hours of onset of rash were screened for eligibility. The diagnosis was made clinically on the basis of unilateral, dermatomal, grouped vesicles on an erythematous base accompanied by pain. Inclusion criteria were: age 18 years or older; duration of rash of 72 hours or less; presence of pain at presentation with a verbal rating scale (VRS) score of at least mild severity; and willingness to provide informed consent and attend all follow-up visits. Exclusion criteria were: immunocompromised state, including HIV infection, malignancy, or use of immunosuppressive drugs; pregnancy and lactation; known hypersensitivity to valacyclovir, pregabalin, or methylprednisolone; renal impairment (raised serum creatinine or reduced creatinine clearance); hepatic dysfunction; uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, hypertension, peptic ulcer disease, tuberculosis, or other conditions in which systemic corticosteroids are contraindicated; disseminated or ophthalmic zoster, or zoster with motor involvement or central nervous system complications; use of antivirals, gabapentinoids, corticosteroids, or other analgesics for neuropathic pain in the preceding month; and a history of previous herpes zoster or of psychiatric illness or substance abuse. Sample size and allocation As this was a pilot study, no formal sample size calculation was performed. Forty-five eligible patients were enrolled and allocated in sequence to one of three groups of 15 patients each (Groups A, B, and C). Patients were allotted sequentially in the order of enrolment. The study was single-blind, with patients unaware of the group to which they were assigned and the comparative nature of the treatment regimens. Interventions All patients received oral valacyclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days as standard antiviral therapy. - Group A (control): valacyclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days alone. - Group B: valacyclovir as above plus pregabalin capsules 75 mg twice daily for 1 month. - Group C: valacyclovir and pregabalin as in Group B, plus oral methylprednisolone at 0.64 mg/kg body weight per day in two divided doses for 7 days. Paracetamol was permitted as rescue analgesia in all groups, and its use was recorded. Patients were advised on skin care, and topical antiseptic or soothing preparations were used for the skin lesions as required, uniformly across groups. Compliance was assessed through patient counselling, pill counts, and direct questioning at each visit. Baseline assessment A detailed history was taken, including age, sex, duration of rash and pain, site of involvement, and comorbidities. General physical, systemic, and dermatological examinations were performed. Baseline investigations included complete blood count, fasting and postprandial blood glucose, renal and liver function tests, and HIV serology, to confirm eligibility and for safety monitoring. The dermatome involved and the morphology of lesions were recorded. Outcome measures Pain severity was the primary outcome and was assessed using a verbal rating scale (VRS). Patients rated their pain as none (0), mild (1), moderate (2), or severe (3), according to the descriptors at the time of assessment. Pain was recorded at baseline and at follow-up visits at 1, 4, and 6 weeks. The primary efficacy endpoint was complete resolution of acute pain (VRS score of 0) at each time point. Acute herpetic neuralgia was defined as pain during the first 30 days after onset of herpes zoster, and persistence of pain beyond this period (assessed at 6 weeks) was considered postherpetic neuralgia (PHN). The proportion of patients with persistent pain at 6 weeks in each group, and the occurrence of PHN, were secondary outcomes. Safety was assessed by recording adverse events reported spontaneously or elicited by questioning at each visit, including nausea, vomiting, somnolence, dizziness, edema, weight gain, gastric symptoms, mood changes, and elevations in blood pressure or blood glucose. Patients were instructed to report any untoward symptoms between scheduled visits. Severity of side-effects and any need to discontinue the medication were noted. Follow-up Patients were followed at 1, 4, and 6 weeks after enrolment. At each visit, pain was graded using the VRS, the skin lesions were examined for healing, and adverse effects and rescue analgesic use were documented. Patients who did not attend follow-up were contacted by telephone and encouraged to return. Statistical analysis Data were entered into a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet and analyzed using standard statistical software. Categorical variables were expressed as frequencies and percentages, and continuous variables as mean ± standard deviation. Within-group changes in VRS pain scores from baseline to follow-up were analyzed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and comparisons of ordinal pain scores between groups were performed using the Kruskal–Wallis test. Proportions of patients with persistent pain, PHN, and adverse events were compared between groups using the Chi-square test or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. A P value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. A total of 45 patients with herpes zoster presenting within 72 hours of rash onset were enrolled and allocated sequentially to three groups of 15 each: Group A (valacyclovir alone), Group B (valacyclovir plus pregabalin), and Group C (valacyclovir, pregabalin, and methylprednisolone). All 45 patients completed follow-up at 1, 4, and 6 weeks, and none were lost to follow-up or withdrew because of adverse effects. Baseline characteristics The three groups were comparable at baseline with respect to age, sex distribution, site of involvement, and duration of symptoms before presentation. The mean age of the study population was in the sixth decade of life, with a slight male predominance. The thoracic dermatome was the most commonly affected site in all groups, followed by the cervical, trigeminal, and lumbosacral dermatomes. No statistically significant differences were found between the groups for any of these variables (P > 0.05). Baseline pain severity on the verbal rating scale (VRS) was also similar across groups, with most patients reporting moderate to severe pain at enrollment. Pain severity at follow-up In all three groups, pain scores declined progressively from baseline. At the end of the first week, a reduction in VRS scores was seen in all groups, with the greatest proportion of patients reporting improvement in Group C. Fewer patients in Group A had a reduction to mild pain or no pain than in Groups B and C. Between-group differences at 1 week favored the combination regimens, with Group C showing the most pronounced early relief. At the end of 4 weeks, the reduction in pain compared with baseline was statistically significant in each group individually (P < 0.05). The proportion of patients with complete resolution of pain was highest in Group C, followed by Group B and then Group A. Most patients in Group C had no pain or only mild pain at this point, while a considerable number of patients in Group A continued to report moderate pain. Optical fiber communication systems carry the vast majority of global data traffic, and the demand for higher capacity continues to grow at a steady pace. Since the deployment of coherent detection and digital signal processing, spectral efficiency has been increased mainly through higher-order modulation formats, polarization multiplexing, and advanced forward error correction (FEC). Most commercial systems still rely on conventional square quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM), in which constellation points are placed on a uniform rectangular grid with equal probability. While this choice is attractive for its simple implementation, symbol demapping, and compatibility with existing hardware, it is known to be suboptimal on the additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel. The gap between the capacity of the AWGN channel and the achievable rate of uniform QAM at high spectral efficiencies approaches 1.53 dB, the so-called ultimate shaping gain. Closing a portion of this gap is of considerable practical interest, since even a fraction of a decibel of signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) gain translates into increased reach or rate. Constellation shaping is the general term for techniques that reduce this gap. Two main approaches exist: probabilistic shaping (PS) and geometric shaping (GS). In PS, the constellation points remain on a regular grid, but they are transmitted with non-uniform probabilities, typically following a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, so that low-energy points are used more often than high-energy ones. PS has been shown to approach capacity closely and offers fine rate adaptivity, and it has been demonstrated in a number of experiments. However, it requires a distribution matcher, which adds complexity, introduces latency, and may incur rate loss at finite blocklengths. In GS, by contrast, all points are transmitted equiprobably, and the gain is obtained by optimizing the positions of the points in the signal space. GS avoids the distribution matching stage and therefore keeps the transmitter architecture simple. It is also naturally compatible with conventional bit-interleaved coded modulation (BICM) receivers. These properties motivate the continued study of GS, particularly for high-order formats. The design of a geometrically shaped constellation requires a performance metric to be optimized. Early work on GS often minimized the symbol error rate or maximized the minimum Euclidean distance subject to an average power constraint, which leads to sphere-packing-like arrangements. Although such criteria are meaningful at low SNR or for uncoded transmission, they do not directly reflect performance in modern systems that employ powerful soft-decision FEC codes. In such systems, the relevant quantities are information-theoretic: the mutual information (MI), which is the achievable rate for symbol-wise decoding, and the generalized mutual information (GMI), which is the achievable rate for BICM with bitwise decoding. Optimizing a constellation for these metrics ensures that the design is matched to the actual operating regime of coded systems. Moreover, the GMI depends on the binary labeling of the constellation, so both the point positions and the bit mapping must be considered jointly in the design. Optimizing constellations with respect to achievable information rates is a challenging task, especially for large constellation sizes. The number of free parameters grows linearly with the number of points, the objective is non-convex, and its evaluation requires numerical integration or Monte Carlo estimation. Consequently, many previous works have been restricted to small or moderate constellation sizes, such as 16 or 64 points, or have imposed structural constraints such as ring-based or symmetric layouts to reduce dimensionality. Recent approaches based on gradient descent and machine-learning tools, including autoencoders trained end to end, have made it possible to optimize larger constellations and to handle differentiable approximations of the rate metrics. Nevertheless, for constellations with 256 points, which are relevant for high-capacity short-reach and metro links as well as for microwave and wireless backhaul, reported gains over QAM have typically been modest or have been obtained under particular assumptions on the channel or the receiver. In this work, we design geometrically shaped constellations by directly maximizing achievable information rates, considering both MI and GMI as optimization targets. We employ a gradient-based optimization that updates all point coordinates under an average power constraint, and we initialize it appropriately to avoid poor local optima. For GMI, the binary labeling is also selected to be compatible with the shaped layout, so that the gain in MI is preserved under bitwise decoding. We focus on a 256-ary constellation and evaluate it on the AWGN channel over a wide range of SNRs, comparing against standard 256QAM and against other published shaped formats where applicable. The main contributions of this paper are as follows. First, we present a systematic procedure for optimizing large-scale constellations with respect to information-theoretic metrics rather than distance-based criteria. Second, we show that the resulting 256-ary constellation yields SNR gains of up to 1.18 dB over conventional 256QAM at a fixed achievable information rate, thereby recovering a large part of the available shaping gain without probabilistic shaping. Third, we discuss the structure of the optimized constellation and the effect of the choice of metric and labeling on the obtained gains. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the system model and defines the MI and GMI metrics. Section III describes the optimization procedure. Section IV presents numerical results and comparisons, and Section V concludes the paper. We consider transmission over a memoryless additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel, Y = X + N, where X is a complex-valued symbol drawn from a constellation C = {c1, ..., cM} with M = 256 and N is circularly symmetric complex Gaussian noise with variance σ² per complex dimension. The average signal power is constrained to E[|X|²] = P, and the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is defined as P/σ². Symbols are assumed equiprobable unless otherwise stated, so that all shaping gain arises from the constellation geometry rather than from probabilistic shaping. Achievable information rates Two achievable rates are used as design metrics. The first is the mutual information (MI), which for equiprobable symbols is I(X;Y) = log2 M − (1/M) Σi EN[ log2 Σj exp(−(|ci − cj + N|² − |N|²)/σ²) ], and which is the achievable rate for symbol-wise decoding with an optimal soft-decision decoder. The second is the generalized mutual information (GMI), which is the achievable rate for bit-interleaved coded modulation (BICM) with a binary labeling. With m = log2 M bits per symbol, bit labels b = (b1, ..., bm) assigned to each point, and a bit-metric decoder, the GMI is GMI = Σ{k=1}^{m} [ 1 − (1/M) Σ{i} EN[ log2 ( Σ{j} exp(−|ci − cj + N|²/σ²) / Σ{j∈S(k, bk(i))} exp(−|ci − cj + N|²/σ²) ) ] ], where S(k,b) is the subset of constellation points whose k-th label bit equals b. The expectations were evaluated by Gauss–Hermite quadrature in two dimensions, with Monte Carlo verification using 10⁵ noise samples per point. MI serves as an upper bound that is independent of labeling, while GMI captures the penalty of the binary labeling and the practical BICM receiver. We optimize both metrics separately, yielding constellations suited to coded modulation with multilevel/nonbinary codes (MI) and BICM (GMI). Constellation parameterization The constellation is described by 2M real parameters, the in-phase and quadrature coordinates of each point. To reduce the search space and enforce a symmetric structure, we impose four-fold rotational symmetry (invariance under multiplication by j). Only M/4 = 64 points are free, and the remaining points follow by rotation, giving 128 real degrees of freedom. A variant with additional mirror symmetry about the real axis was also tested to further reduce the dimensionality. After each update, the constellation is re-normalized to satisfy the average power constraint and recentered to have zero mean. Optimization procedure The objective is to maximize the chosen rate (MI or GMI) at a fixed target SNR, with the constellation as the variable. As the objective is smooth in the point coordinates, we use gradient-based optimization. Gradients were obtained by automatic differentiation through the quadrature-evaluated rate expression. We used the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 10⁻² decayed to 10⁻⁴, and batches of noise samples were redrawn at each iteration when stochastic estimates were used. Because the landscape is non-convex with many local optima, we used multiple initializations: square 256-QAM, a hexagonal-like arrangement, concentric-ring (amplitude-phase shift keying) layouts, and random perturbations of these. The best result among all runs was retained. Optimization was carried out for target SNRs spanning the region in which the 256-QAM rate lies between 5 and 7.5 bit/symbol, and the constellation optimized at one SNR was used as the starting point for the neighboring SNR to promote continuity (warm starting). For GMI optimization the labeling must also be chosen. Given a geometry, we initialized with binary reflected Gray labeling extended to the two-dimensional layout and then applied the binary switching algorithm, which iteratively swaps labels of pairs of points to minimize a bit-error-oriented cost. Geometry and labeling were optimized in alternation: several gradient steps on the coordinates with fixed labels, followed by a labeling refinement, until the GMI improvement fell below 10⁻⁴ bit/symbol. Performance evaluation Performance is quantified by the SNR gain at a fixed rate. For a given target rate R, we find the SNR at which each constellation achieves R, by bisection on the rate curve, and report the difference between the SNR required by the reference format, 256-QAM, and that required by the shaped constellation. We also report the rate gain at fixed SNR. The Shannon capacity log2(1+SNR) and the unconstrained Gaussian-input limit are used as references to determine the remaining gap, and the ultimate shaping gain limit of 1.53 dB provides context for the attainable improvement. Comparisons additionally include other 256-point formats from the literature, such as star-QAM and ring-based constellations, evaluated under identical conditions. Validation To confirm that the optimized constellations are robust, we evaluated their rates at SNR values different from the design SNR and verified that the gain degrades gracefully. We also simulated BICM transmission with an LDPC code of rate adapted to the GMI, using soft demapping, to verify that the computed GMI gains translate into lower post-FEC error rates. All computations used double precision, and the quadrature order was increased until the rate estimates changed by less than 10⁻⁵ bit/symbol. We evaluated the proposed constellations by numerical simulation over the additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel, using the mutual information (MI) and generalized mutual information (GMI) as achievable information rate (AIR) metrics. MI is the relevant metric for ideal coded modulation with soft-decision decoding of symbol metrics, whereas GMI is the relevant metric for bit-interleaved coded modulation (BICM) with a binary labeling. All constellations were normalized to unit average power, and the SNR is defined as the ratio of signal power to noise power per two real dimensions. Reference formats were conventional 256-ary quadrature amplitude modulation (256QAM) and, where noted, the Gaussian capacity limit log2(1+SNR). Optimized constellations. The 256-ary constellation was obtained by maximizing the AIR at a fixed target SNR, with the point positions as free parameters, using gradient-based optimization with several random and structured initializations (including the square QAM grid and hexagonal-like layouts). The optimization was repeated for target SNRs spanning 10 to 24 dB. The resulting constellations are not regular grids. Points are arranged in quasi-circular rings with a denser concentration near the origin and sparser spacing toward the outer region, approximating a discretized Gaussian-like distribution while retaining uniform symbol probabilities. At low SNR, the optimized points form an approximately hexagonal packing with a roughly circular boundary, reflecting the granular (packing) gain. At high SNR, the structure approaches a square-like arrangement with softened corners, since the available shaping gain saturates and the AIR gap to capacity becomes small. MI performance. For MI, the geometrically shaped (GS) 256-ary constellation outperforms 256QAM across the whole considered SNR range. The gain is most evident in the intermediate regime, where 256QAM departs from capacity. To quantify the improvement, we measured the SNR gain at a fixed AIR, that is, the horizontal distance between the AIR curves. Electronic mail remains one of the most widely used communication technologies in the world, carrying personal correspondence, financial records, medical information, legal documents, and corporate secrets. Yet the protocols that underpin email were designed in an era of small, trusted networks, and they offer no inherent guarantees of confidentiality. Messages traverse multiple servers in plaintext, are routinely stored unencrypted by providers, and can be intercepted, scanned, or altered at several points along their path [1]. Revelations of large-scale surveillance, together with a steady stream of data breaches at email providers, have made clear that transport-level protections such as STARTTLS are insufficient: they protect individual hops, are often negotiated opportunistically, and can be stripped by an active adversary [2]. Confidentiality that survives compromise of intermediate infrastructure requires end-to-end encryption, in which only the sender and intended recipient hold the keys needed to read a message. Technologies for end-to-end email encryption have existed for over three decades. Pretty Good Privacy (PGP), introduced in 1991 and later standardized as OpenPGP [3], and S/MIME [4] both provide message confidentiality, integrity, and sender authentication using public-key cryptography. Despite their maturity and strong security properties, neither has achieved broad adoption among ordinary users. Studies of usability have shown that even technically capable participants struggle to complete basic tasks such as generating keys, obtaining a correspondent's public key, and distinguishing between signing and encrypting [5], [6]. The seminal analysis of PGP 5.0 concluded that the interface and conceptual model of the software, rather than the cryptography, were the principal barriers to its effective use [5]. Subsequent work on modern tools has found that many of these difficulties persist [7]. Several interrelated obstacles explain this persistent gap. The first is usability: users must understand concepts such as public and private keys, key fingerprints, trust models, and revocation, none of which correspond to their everyday mental models of email. Errors in this domain are costly, since an accidentally disclosed private key or a message sent unencrypted defeats the purpose of the system. The second is key management. Distributing and verifying public keys, whether through key servers, a web of trust, or certificate authorities, imposes a burden that most users are unwilling or unable to bear [8]. The third is compatibility and integration. Many existing solutions are implemented as plugins for specific desktop clients, are unavailable on mobile platforms, or are incompatible with webmail interfaces, thereby forcing users to alter established habits or abandon their preferred email service. The fourth is the network effect: encryption is useful only when correspondents also use it, so individuals have little incentive to adopt a tool that few of their contacts support, and those contacts in turn have little incentive to adopt it themselves [9]. Alternative approaches have attempted to address some of these problems. Secure messaging applications such as Signal have demonstrated that strong end-to-end encryption can be delivered with minimal user effort by automating key exchange and hiding cryptographic details [10]. However, these applications operate in closed ecosystems and do not interoperate with email, which remains the dominant medium for formal and cross-organizational communication. Provider-based secure email services offer simplified encryption but typically require users to migrate to a new address or trust the provider with key material, which weakens the end-to-end guarantee and reintroduces a central point of compromise. Gateway-based enterprise products automate encryption at the organizational boundary but generally place keys under the control of the organization rather than the individual user. In this paper we present the Mobile Encryption Gateway (MEG), a system designed to bring practical, end-to-end email encryption to ordinary users by addressing these obstacles together rather than in isolation. MEG automatically encrypts outgoing messages and decrypts incoming messages using PGP, so that users need not understand the underlying cryptographic operations. Key generation, storage, and exchange are handled by the application. Because MEG acts as a gateway between the user and the email service rather than as an extension of any particular client, it is email-client-agnostic: users may continue to use virtually any email provider or client to send and receive messages. All cryptographic operations are performed on the user's mobile device, so private keys and plaintext content never leave the user's control and are never exposed to the email provider or to any MEG-operated server. To mitigate the network effect, MEG includes a mechanism for inviting non-users to join, allowing the community of encrypted correspondents to grow organically from existing communication relationships. The contributions of this work are as follows. First, we analyze the principal technical and social barriers to adoption of email encryption and derive design requirements from them. Second, we describe the architecture of MEG, including its approach to automated key management, message processing, and client independence. Third, we discuss the security properties of the system under a defined threat model, showing that confidentiality is preserved against compromised mail servers and network observers. Finally, we consider usability and deployment implications, including the invitation mechanism for addressing the network effect. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 presents the threat model and design goals. Section 4 describes the system architecture and implementation. Section 5 evaluates security and usability, and Section 6 concludes with directions for future work. The Mobile Encryption Gateway (MEG) was designed, implemented, and evaluated in three phases: requirements analysis, system development, and usability and security evaluation. The design goal was to provide automatic OpenPGP-based encryption and decryption of email while remaining independent of any specific email client or provider. System Architecture MEG is implemented as a mobile application that acts as a local gateway between the user's email client and the mail server. The architecture comprises four components: (i) a proxy module, (ii) a cryptographic engine, (iii) a key management module, and (iv) an invitation module. The proxy module exposes local SMTP and IMAP endpoints on the device loopback interface. The user's email client is configured to connect to these endpoints rather than directly to the provider's servers. The proxy then relays traffic to the actual provider over TLS [1]. This approach, similar to that employed by other bridge-style tools, allows MEG to intercept messages without requiring plug-ins for individual clients, which enables client-agnostic operation. For outgoing messages, the proxy parses the MIME structure [2], determines whether a public key is available for each recipient, and passes the message body and attachments to the cryptographic engine. The encrypted result is encoded as PGP/MIME as specified in RFC 3156 [3] and forwarded through the provider's SMTP server. For incoming messages, the proxy detects PGP/MIME and inline PGP content, decrypts it locally, verifies signatures, and presents the plaintext message to the email client through the local IMAP endpoint. Because decryption occurs on the device, the provider only ever handles ciphertext, which provides end-to-end confidentiality. Cryptographic Implementation The cryptographic engine follows the OpenPGP standard [4] and relies on an established open-source library rather than custom primitives, consistent with accepted practice for minimizing implementation errors [5]. Each message is encrypted with a randomly generated symmetric session key using AES-256, and the session key is encrypted with each recipient's public key. Default asymmetric keys were 3072-bit RSA or, where supported, Curve25519 keys. Messages are signed by default using the sender's private key to provide authenticity and integrity. Subject lines and other headers remain unencrypted under the standard PGP/MIME format, a limitation we document in the threat model below. Key Management Key pairs are generated on first launch on the user's device. Private keys are stored in the platform's hardware-backed secure storage (Android Keystore or iOS Secure Enclave and Keychain) and are protected by device biometrics or a passcode. Private keys never leave the device, and no key escrow is performed. An encrypted backup option, protected by a user-selected passphrase processed with a memory-hard key derivation function [6], allows recovery after device loss. Public key discovery uses three mechanisms in order: (a) a local keyring of previously exchanged keys, (b) lookup on public key servers and Web Key Directory [7], and (c) in-band exchange via attached public keys and the Autocrypt header [8]. Keys received through in-band exchange are treated using a trust-on-first-use model, with a fingerprint-comparison option (including QR-code scanning for in-person verification) for users who require stronger assurance. Key changes trigger a visible warning. Network Effect Mitigation When a recipient's public key cannot be located, MEG offers the user the option to send an invitation. The invitation is sent as an ordinary unencrypted email containing a brief explanation, a download link for MEG, and the sender's public key. The original message is withheld until the user chooses to send it unencrypted or until the recipient registers a key. Once the recipient installs MEG and generates a key pair, the key is returned automatically via an Autocrypt-style reply, and subsequent communication is encrypted without further action. Threat Model We assumed an adversary able to observe and modify network traffic and to compromise the email provider's servers, but unable to compromise the user's device or break the underlying cryptographic primitives. Under this model, MEG aims to protect message body and attachment confidentiality, integrity, and sender authenticity. Metadata (sender, recipient, timestamps, and subject) is explicitly out of scope, as is endpoint compromise, a limitation common to PGP-based systems [9]. Active attacks involving key substitution during first contact were considered and are addressed only through the optional fingerprint verification. Evaluation Functional testing was carried out against five widely used email services and six email clients on Android and iOS, verifying successful sending, receiving, attachment handling, and signature verification. Test messages included plain text, HTML, multipart messages, and attachments of up to 20 MB. Performance was measured as the added latency of encryption and decryption relative to unmodified delivery, averaged over 100 trials per message size on mid-range devices. Security analysis consisted of a review of the implementation against the threat model, packet capture to confirm that only ciphertext left the device, and static analysis of the code base for common vulnerabilities [10]. Usability was assessed in a study with 24 participants without prior encryption experience. Participants completed standardized tasks: installing MEG, sending an encrypted message, receiving and reading an encrypted message, and inviting a non-user. We recorded task completion rates and time on task, and participants completed the System Usability Scale questionnaire [11]. Participants gave informed consent, and no personally identifying data were retained. Descriptive statistics are reported, and differences between tasks were assessed using non-parametric tests given the small sample size. We evaluated MEG along four dimensions: functional correctness of the encryption and decryption pipeline, performance on mobile hardware, usability for non-expert users, and the effectiveness of the invitation mechanism in addressing network effects. Unless otherwise stated, values are reported as mean ± standard deviation. Functional Correctness and Interoperability MEG was tested against a corpus of 1,200 messages covering plain text, HTML, multipart messages, inline images, and attachments up to 20 MB. All messages were encrypted on the sender's device, transmitted through a mail provider, and decrypted on the recipient's device. Round-trip integrity was verified by comparing SHA-256 digests of the original and recovered content. All 1,200 messages (100%) were recovered without alteration. Signature verification succeeded for all signed messages, and tampered ciphertexts, produced by flipping random bytes in 100 test messages, were rejected in every case. Interoperability was assessed with five providers (Gmail, Outlook.com, Yahoo Mail, ProtonMail via bridge, and a self-hosted Postfix/Dovecot server). MEG exchanged messages successfully with all five using standard IMAP and SMTP, with no provider-specific modification. Messages encrypted by MEG were also decrypted correctly by GnuPG 2.4 and Thunderbird, and messages produced by these clients were decrypted by MEG, confirming compatibility with the OpenPGP standard [1]. Two difficulties arose. Gmail's web interface displayed the ASCII-armored ciphertext rather than a readable message, as expected for a non-participating client, and two providers occasionally rewrapped long lines in the body. Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) and related randomised search heuristics have been applied successfully to a wide range of optimisation problems in engineering, logistics, machine learning and design [1,2]. Their performance on real-world problems is, however, frequently complicated by uncertainty. Measurements may be corrupted by sensor error, simulations may be stochastic, and human evaluators may be inconsistent. In such settings the fitness function returns a noisy observation of the true objective value, and an algorithm that treats this observation as exact may accept inferior solutions, discard superior ones, and ultimately fail to converge [3,4]. Optimisation under noise has therefore become an established research area within evolutionary computation [5,6]. Coping with noise A variety of strategies have been proposed for noisy optimisation. These include population-based averaging, in which a large population implicitly smooths the noise [7]; modified selection schemes and thresholding [8]; and explicit resampling, in which each candidate solution is evaluated several times and the mean is used as the fitness estimate [9,10]. Resampling is perhaps the most widely used approach because it is simple, applicable to any algorithm, and reduces the variance of the estimate by a factor equal to the number of samples. Its cost is equally clear: each resample consumes part of a finite evaluation budget, so the designer must trade accuracy of individual estimates against the number of search steps that can be performed. Determining how many resamples to use, and whether the number should be static or adaptive, has motivated a substantial body of both empirical and theoretical work [11,12]. Runtime analysis and First Hitting Time The theoretical study of such trade-offs is largely carried out through runtime analysis, which derives bounds on the expected number of fitness evaluations required by an algorithm to solve a given problem [13,14]. In the noiseless setting, runtime is almost universally defined as the First Hitting Time (FHT): the number of evaluations until the optimum is first sampled. This definition is natural and mathematically convenient, and it has underpinned many results for simple algorithms such as the (1+1) EA on benchmark functions like OneMax and LeadingOnes [13]. It has also been carried over to noisy domains, where analyses have characterised the noise levels under which algorithms such as the (1+1) EA, ant colony optimisers and population-based EAs retain polynomial runtime, and how resampling alters those thresholds [15–18]. Under noise, however, the FHT is problematic. An algorithm is deemed to have succeeded the moment the optimum is evaluated, even if the algorithm cannot recognise that it has done so. Because the fitness observations are corrupted, the algorithm may immediately reject the optimum, and then wander away from it indefinitely. The FHT criterion ignores this behaviour. More fundamentally, the criterion presupposes knowledge that is unavailable in practice. In a real application the optimal solution and its objective value are unknown; if they were known, no search would be needed. A practitioner cannot halt the algorithm upon encountering the optimum, but must instead choose a stopping rule, typically a fixed budget, and accept whatever solution the algorithm returns at that point. The quality of that returned solution, rather than the moment at which an optimal solution happened to be sampled, is what matters operationally. Final solution quality This paper argues that the evaluation of noisy optimisation algorithms should instead focus on final solution quality: the true fitness (or the gap to the optimum) of the solution returned after a fixed evaluation budget. This measure aligns with how algorithms are deployed, accounts for the algorithm's ability to retain and recognise good solutions under noise, and naturally incorporates the cost of strategies such as resampling, since the budget is shared between sampling and search. It is also consistent with established practice in the empirical benchmarking of optimisers, where fixed-budget and anytime performance views are advocated [19,20], and with fixed-budget perspectives developed in runtime analysis [21]. Despite this, the FHT remains the dominant measure in noisy runtime analysis, and the consequences of this choice have not been examined systematically. Contributions and structure The contributions of this paper are as follows. First, we articulate why FHT is an inappropriate performance criterion for noisy optimisation, identifying the specific mechanisms by which it can overestimate the quality of an algorithm. Second, we propose and formalise final solution quality under a fixed evaluation budget as an alternative. Third, we present cases, both analytical and empirical, in which the two criteria yield markedly different conclusions about the relative merits of noisy optimisation algorithms and of resampling strategies; in particular, we show that an algorithm or parameter setting ranked favourably by FHT can perform poorly in terms of the solution it returns, and vice versa. We do not claim that FHT results are mathematically incorrect, but that their practical interpretation as indicators of real-world algorithm quality is unreliable. The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews noise models, resampling strategies and existing runtime results. Section 3 formalises the FHT and final-quality measures. Section 4 presents the comparative case studies. Section 5 discusses implications for the design and analysis of noisy optimisers, and Section 6 concludes. We compare two ways of evaluating noisy optimisation algorithms: First Hitting Time (FHT) and final solution quality after a fixed evaluation budget. The comparison uses a controlled benchmark in which the optimum is known to us as experimenters but is hidden from the algorithms. Problem Setting We consider pseudo-Boolean maximisation over bit strings x ∈ {0,1}^n, with the benchmark functions OneMax, f(x) = Σ xi, and LeadingOnes, f(x) = Σ{i=1}^n Π{j=1}^i xj. Both are standard in runtime analysis of noisy evolutionary algorithms [1,2]. We use n ∈ {20, 50, 100}. The true fitness f(x) is never available to the algorithm. Each evaluation returns a noisy value f̃(x). Two noise models are used: 1. Additive Gaussian noise: f̃(x) = f(x) + ε, with ε ~ N(0, σ²) and σ² ∈ {1, 4, 16}. 2. One-bit prior noise: with probability p ∈ {0.2, 0.5, 0.8}, one uniformly chosen bit of x is flipped before f is evaluated, as in [2,3]. Noise is drawn independently for each evaluation. Every call to the noisy fitness function counts as one unit of the evaluation budget, including repeated calls made by resampling. Algorithms We study three algorithms that are common in the noisy runtime-analysis literature. (1+1) EA with resampling. At each generation, the offspring y is created by flipping each bit of the parent x independently with probability 1/n. Both x and y are evaluated k times, and y replaces x if its mean noisy fitness is at least that of x. We test k ∈ {1, 5, 20, 100}, and also a variant where k grows with the generation counter. (μ+λ) EA. The population uses μ = λ ∈ {5, 10}. Each individual is evaluated k times per generation, and truncation selection is applied to the sample means. The (μ+λ) EA is used because populations are known to give some robustness to noise without resampling [4]. Compact Genetic Algorithm (cGA). A probability vector is maintained with hypothetical population size K ∈ {20, 50, 100}, and borders are set at [1/n, 1−1/n]. Two samples are drawn per iteration, each evaluated k times. The cGA has been shown to be robust to noise in theory [5]. Each configuration is run on every problem and noise setting. Performance Measures The two measures compare the same runs of the same algorithms. First Hitting Time. FHT is the number of fitness evaluations used until some evaluated or sampled solution x satisfies f(x) = n. The run stops at that moment, so FHT uses oracle knowledge of the optimum, as in much runtime analysis [1,6]. If the optimum has not been reached by the maximum budget B, the run is censored at B. We report the mean, median, and success rate. Where censoring occurs, we use the restricted mean and the expected running time estimate (total evaluations across all runs divided by the number of successes) [7]. Final solution quality. The algorithm runs for the full budget B and returns one solution under a recommendation rule that does not use f. For the (1+1) EA, the rule returns the current parent. For the (μ+λ) EA, it returns the individual with the highest sample mean in the final population. For the cGA, it returns the solution obtained by rounding the probability vector, setting xi = 1 if pi ≥ 0.5. After the run, we compute the true fitness f(xreturned) in a separate noise-free evaluation. We report: - the mean and median normalised true fitness f(x)/n; - the proportion of runs in which the returned solution is optimal; - the mean Hamming distance to the optimum. This corresponds to the simple-regret notion used in noisy optimisation [8]. The distinction matters for a specific reason. An algorithm that visits the optimum but then accepts a worse solution because of noise would stop with FHT but would return a poor solution under the final-quality measure. By recording both, we can quantify how often this occurs. For each run we also record the number of generations in which the optimum was held as the incumbent, and whether it was held at the end of the budget. Experimental Protocol The budget is B = 200·n² evaluations for OneMax and 400·n² for LeadingOnes, which is large enough for the noise-free algorithms to find the optimum. Each configuration is repeated 100 times with independent random seeds, and the same seeds are used across measures. Because both measures are computed from the same runs, differences in conclusions cannot be attributed to sampling variation between experiments. To compare algorithms, we rank the configurations of each algorithm under each measure and compute Kendall's τ between the rankings produced by FHT and final quality. We also record every pairwise comparison where the two measures disagree on which algorithm is better. Statistical significance of pairwise differences is assessed using two-sided Mann–Whitney U tests at α = 0.05 with Holm correction for multiple comparisons [9], and effect sizes are reported as Vargha–Delaney A12 [10]. Implementation All algorithms were implemented in Python with NumPy, and random number generators were seeded explicitly. The code and raw results will be made publicly available to support reproducibility. Experimental Setup We compare the two evaluation methods on noisy OneMax and LeadingOnes with n = 100 bits under additive Gaussian noise, N(0, σ²), with σ ∈ {0, 1, 2, 5}. Three algorithms are considered: a (1+1) EA with no resampling, a (1+1) EA with fixed resampling (m = 10 and m = 50 evaluations per solution), and a population-based (µ+λ) EA with µ = λ = 10 and no resampling. Each configuration was run 100 times independently. The budget was 10⁶ fitness evaluations, with each resample counted as one evaluation. Two metrics were recorded. For First Hitting Time (FHT), we recorded the number of evaluations until the true optimum was first sampled, regardless of whether the algorithm recognised it. For Final Solution Quality (FSQ), we recorded the true (noise-free) fitness of the solution the algorithm returned at budget exhaustion, which is the incumbent for the (1+1) EAs and the best-ranked individual by noisy fitness for the population-based algorithm. Differences between algorithms were assessed with Mann–Whitney U tests at α = 0.01, with Bonferroni correction, and effect sizes were reported as Vargha–Delaney A₁₂. Noise-Free Baseline At σ = 0 the two metrics agree. All algorithms reached the optimum in every run, and the algorithm ranking by FHT matches the ranking by FSQ (the (1+1) EA without resampling is the fastest, and resampling only adds overhead). Let K be a field and f ∈ K(t) a non-constant rational function. A decomposition of f is a representation f = g ∘ h with g, h ∈ K(t). It is non-trivial if both g and h have degree greater than one, and complete if neither g nor h can be decomposed further. Functional decomposition has applications in many areas, including computer algebra, the study of dynamical systems, cryptography, and the simplification of expressions. It is also closely tied to questions on algebraic curves, such as parametrizations, and to the construction of function fields with prescribed properties. The problem has a long history. For polynomials, Ritt showed in the 1920s that complete decompositions need not be unique, but that any two of them have the same length and are related by a sequence of elementary transformations. Ritt's theory was later extended by Fried and MacRae, Schinzel, and others. On the algorithmic side, Barton and Zippel gave the first polynomial-time algorithm for polynomials over fields of characteristic zero. Kozen and Landau improved this and gave algorithms using only arithmetic in K. Von zur Gathen then gave fast algorithms for the case where the characteristic does not divide the degree of f, and Gutierrez and Kozen, among others, studied the "wild" case. For rational functions, Zippel gave an algorithm based on the same ideas, and Alonso, Gutierrez and Recio gave an approach through the lattice of subfields. Further work by Gutierrez and Sevilla used the equivalence between decompositions and intermediate fields, and showed how to compute all non-equivalent complete decompositions. The key observation underlying much of this work is Lüroth's theorem. Every field L with K ⊊ L ⊆ K(t) is of the form K(h) for some h ∈ K(t) that is unique up to composition with a Möbius transformation on the left. Therefore, decompositions f = g ∘ h, up to equivalence, correspond to intermediate fields K(f) ⊆ K(h) ⊆ K(t). Since K(t)/K(f) is a finite extension of degree deg f, finding all decompositions amounts to computing the lattice of intermediate fields of this extension. When the extension is separable, the lattice is finite, and when it is not, there may be infinitely many intermediate fields, though the lattice of decompositions up to equivalence is still the object of interest in the algorithms. In this paper we revisit the subfield-lattice approach and make it efficient. Our main tool is the notion of a principal subfield. For a rational function a ∈ K(t), we consider the smallest subfield of K(t) containing K(f) and having a as a "generator-related" element, which is K(f, a) or an analogous construction defined through the minimal data needed to determine it. Principal subfields can be computed quickly, using Lüroth-type computations, and every subfield of K(t)/K(f) is an intersection of principal subfields. Hence the whole lattice can be derived from the principal subfields by intersecting them. This idea was introduced for subfields of finite field extensions and adapted here to the rational function setting. The second ingredient is a fast method for computing the intersection of two subfields. Naively, one intersects subfields by linear algebra over K, which is costly in the degree n = deg f. We instead represent subfields by suitable generators and use techniques that exploit the structure of K(t) as a function field, reducing intersection to operations on univariate polynomials, namely resultants, gcds, and fast arithmetic with truncated power series. These avoid expensive multivariate computations and yield a lower asymptotic cost in terms of field operations. Our main contributions are as follows. 1. We define principal subfields for the extension K(t)/K(f(t)) and show that they generate the full subfield lattice under intersection. 2. We give a fast algorithm for computing the intersection of subfields, and analyze its cost. 3. Combining these, we obtain a Las Vegas algorithm that computes the lattice of subfields, and thereby all non-equivalent complete decompositions of f. The randomness is used for choices of evaluation points and projections, and the output is always correct, with only the running time being probabilistic. The expected complexity improves on that of previous methods. 4. We implemented the algorithm and compare it with existing implementations. The experiments show better run times on a range of examples, including functions with many decompositions and functions over finite fields. The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we recall the correspondence between decompositions and subfields, and collect needed facts about Lüroth's theorem and degrees of rational functions. Section 3 introduces principal subfields and their basic properties. Section 4 presents the intersection algorithm. Section 5 assembles the decomposition algorithm and analyzes its correctness and complexity. Finally, Section 6 reports on timings and discusses open questions, in particular concerning the case where the characteristic of K divides the degree of f.
