Cell differentiation is the process by which a cell with broad potential acquires a specialized identity and function. Waddington's epigenetic landscape, in which a cell is a marble rolling down a branching valley system toward distinct fates, has long served as a metaphor for this process [1]. Advances in dynamical systems theory and systems biology have since given the metaphor a more quantitative interpretation. Cell states are described as attractors, or stable states, in a high-dimensional state space defined by gene expression and other molecular variables, and differentiation is described as a transition between attractors [2,3]. In this view, the landscape is not fixed. Signals that induce differentiation can reshape it, destabilizing the attractor of the undifferentiated state and allowing the system to move toward a new one [4,5]. Experimental evidence for this picture has accumulated mainly from single-cell measurements. Single-cell RNA sequencing and related techniques have shown that cells in nominally homogeneous populations fluctuate in their expression profiles, and that heterogeneity can increase during lineage commitment [6,7]. Studies of hematopoietic progenitors and embryonic stem cells have reported that transcriptional noise and fluctuations in key regulators are linked to the stochastic selection of fate [8,9]. Theoretical work predicts that near a transition between attractors, the stability of the existing state decreases and fluctuations increase, a signature that has been proposed as an early indicator of critical transitions [10,11]. Dynamical models of cell fate have also described how landscapes with a single attractor can flatten and then re-form with a different minimum as cells commit to a lineage [12,13]. However, directly visualizing how an attractor disappears and reappears during differentiation remains difficult. Most current approaches require cell lysis or fixation and labeling, are limited to a preselected set of molecules, or are affected by technical noise and dropout, which complicates the interpretation of cell-to-cell variability [14]. Raman spectroscopy offers a complementary, label-free route to characterizing cell state. Raman scattering arises from inelastic interaction between incident light and molecular vibrations, so a Raman spectrum reflects the overall composition of proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and other biomolecules within the illuminated volume [15,16]. When combined with confocal microscopy and scanning, Raman spectral imaging provides spatially resolved spectra within single cells and allows signals from specific compartments, such as the nucleus or cytoplasm, to be examined separately [17]. Raman measurements have been applied to distinguish cell types, to monitor the differentiation of embryonic and mesenchymal stem cells, and to detect cancer and other pathological states [18–21]. For example, changes in nucleic acid and lipid bands have been used to discriminate undifferentiated from differentiated pluripotent stem cells [19,22], and measurements of cardiomyocytes and neural cells derived from stem cells have identified marker bands for lineage identity [20,23]. Because the spectrum integrates many cellular components, it can be regarded as a high-dimensional readout of the cell state, in a way analogous to a transcriptome but obtained noninvasively and without labels. Multivariate analyses, in particular principal component analysis (PCA), are widely used to reduce the dimensionality of Raman data and to extract the spectral features that best explain variation among cells [24]. Because PCA yields a small number of continuous axes, it is naturally suited to constructing a low-dimensional state space in which the distribution of cells can be mapped. If many single cells are sampled along a differentiation time course, the density of cells in this space can be converted into a pseudo-potential, using the relation between the probability distribution and the potential in a stationary stochastic system [25,26]. Such a hypothetical potential landscape would allow the number, position, and depth of attractors to be assessed at each stage of differentiation. To our knowledge, this approach has not been applied to Raman data to follow a differentiation process. The nucleus is a particularly informative target for such analysis. It contains the genome and the regulatory machinery that define cell identity, and its chromatin organization, nucleic acid content, and protein composition change as cells differentiate [27,28]. Nuclear Raman spectra can therefore capture aspects of the cell state that are tightly connected to gene regulation. In addition, restricting the analysis to the nucleus reduces the contribution of cytoplasmic components, such as lipid droplets and cell-type-specific cytoskeletal proteins, which vary strongly with culture conditions and cell shape. In this study, we used Raman spectral imaging of cell nuclei, combined with PCA, to visualize cell state transitions during differentiation. We examined two well-established models. The first was the mouse myoblast line C2C12, which differentiates into multinucleated myotubes upon serum reduction [29,30]. The second was mouse embryonic stem cells, which exit pluripotency and differentiate when self-renewal signals are withdrawn [31,32]. In both systems, we asked whether cells that appear homogeneous before differentiation become heterogeneous in the early phase, and whether they converge again to a homogeneous population in the late phase. We then constructed hypothetical potential landscapes from the distributions of cells in the PCA-defined state space. Our results indicate that the attractor of the undifferentiated state disappears early in differentiation, when cells fluctuate stochastically among states, and that a new attractor appears at later stages. These findings demonstrate that Raman spectral imaging is a useful tool for experimentally depicting the dynamics of attractors in differentiation landscapes. Cell culture and differentiation C2C12 mouse myoblasts were maintained in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and penicillin–streptomycin at 37 °C in 5% CO2. For myogenic differentiation, cells were seeded on CaF2 substrates (Raman-grade, low background) coated with gelatin at a density of 1×10^4 cells/cm^2. When cells reached confluence, the growth medium was replaced with differentiation medium (DMEM containing 2% horse serum), and this time point was defined as day 0 [1]. Cells were analyzed at days 0, 1, 2, 3, and 5 of differentiation. The medium was replaced every 48 h. Mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs; E14 line) were cultured on gelatin-coated dishes in the presence of leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF) in medium containing 15% knockout serum replacement, nonessential amino acids, 2-mercaptoethanol, and L-glutamine [2]. Differentiation was induced by withdrawing LIF and adding retinoic acid (1 µM) to the medium. Cells were plated on CaF2 substrates coated with laminin and analyzed at 0, 1, 2, 4, and 6 days after induction. Differentiation was independently confirmed by immunostaining for myosin heavy chain (C2C12) and by reverse transcription quantitative PCR for Nanog, Oct4, and Nestin (mESCs). Sample preparation for Raman measurements Cells were washed twice with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 15 min at room temperature. After fixation, samples were washed with PBS and kept in PBS during measurement to avoid drying artifacts. Fixation was chosen to allow measurement of many cells at defined time points without temporal changes during acquisition [3]. Cell nuclei were identified by brief staining with Hoechst 33342 in parallel samples and by bright-field morphology in measured samples. Raman spectral imaging Raman imaging was performed using a custom-built line-scanning confocal Raman microscope equipped with a 532 nm continuous-wave laser, a water-immersion objective (60×, numerical aperture 1.2), and a spectrograph with a cooled charge-coupled device detector. Laser power at the sample was approximately 10 mW distributed along the illumination line. Spectra were collected in the range of 600–3050 cm^-1 with a spectral resolution of about 3 cm^-1. Exposure time was 1 s per line, and the pixel size was approximately 0.5 µm. For each time point, 30–50 nuclei were measured from at least three independent cultures. Wavenumber calibration was performed using the spectrum of toluene, and intensity was corrected using a standard halogen lamp. Preprocessing of spectral data Cosmic-ray spikes were removed by median filtering. Spectra were denoised by singular value decomposition, retaining components with significant singular values. The background contribution from the substrate and PBS was subtracted by fitting spectra from cell-free regions, and the baseline was corrected by polynomial fitting. Each spectrum was normalized to the intensity of the 1450 cm^-1 CH2 deformation band or, alternatively, to the total area under the fingerprint region, and the results were confirmed to be insensitive to the choice [4]. Nuclear regions were segmented by applying k-means clustering to the spectra of each image, using the intensity of the 1095 cm^-1 phosphodiester band and the 2930 cm^-1 CH stretching band as discriminative features. Pixels assigned to the nucleus were averaged for each cell to yield a single mean nuclear spectrum, which represented the state of that cell. In addition, pixel-level spectra within the nucleus were retained for analysis of intranuclear heterogeneity. Principal component analysis and state space construction Mean nuclear spectra from all cells and time points of each cell type were assembled into a matrix and subjected to principal component analysis (PCA) after mean-centering. Principal components (PCs) were interpreted from their loading spectra, in which bands were assigned to nucleic acids (785, 1095, 1578 cm^-1), proteins (1003, 1250–1300, 1665 cm^-1), and lipids (1300, 1440, 1740, 2850 cm^-1) according to published assignments [5]. The first two or three PCs, which together explained most of the variance, were used as axes of a low-dimensional state space in which each cell was plotted as a point. To assess robustness, PCA was repeated with bootstrap resampling of cells and with leave-one-culture-out validation. Estimation of hypothetical potential landscapes Assuming that the cellular state fluctuates stochastically and that the observed distribution approximates a quasi-steady state at each time point, the probability density p(x) of cells in the state space was estimated by Gaussian kernel density estimation, with bandwidth determined by Scott's rule. A hypothetical potential was then defined as U(x) = −ln p(x), following the relation between the Boltzmann distribution and landscape representations of cell fate [6,7]. Local minima of U were regarded as attractors. The number of attractors was determined by counting minima that persisted when the bandwidth was varied by ±30%. Landscapes were calculated separately for each time point and displayed as contour plots or surface plots along the principal axis of change. Quantification of heterogeneity Cell-to-cell heterogeneity at each time point was quantified as the mean Euclidean distance of cells from the population centroid in PC space and as the determinant of the covariance matrix. Differences between time points were evaluated by a permutation test (10,000 permutations) with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Multimodality was tested with Hartigan's dip test along the first PC and by comparing Gaussian mixture models with one to four components using the Bayesian information criterion. Statistical analysis and software Data processing was performed in Python using NumPy, SciPy, and scikit-learn, and in MATLAB. Unless otherwise stated, data are presented as mean ± standard deviation, and P < 0.05 was considered significant. Group comparisons used the Mann–Whitney U test or Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn's post hoc test. Raman spectral imaging of C2C12 nuclei during myogenic differentiation C2C12 myoblasts were induced to differentiate by serum reduction, and cells were fixed and imaged at day 0 (undifferentiated), day 1, day 2, and day 4. Raman spectral images were acquired from the nuclei, identified by DNA-specific band intensity at 784 cm⁻¹ and 1095 cm⁻¹ (phosphodiester backbone), and cytoplasmic regions were excluded. The average nuclear spectra showed prominent bands attributable to nucleic acids (784, 1095, 1578 cm⁻¹), proteins (1003 cm⁻¹ phenylalanine, 1450 cm⁻¹ CH₂ deformation, 1660 cm⁻¹ amide I), and lipids (1300 and 1440 cm⁻¹) [1,2]. Differences between days were modest in the mean spectra, with changes in the relative intensities of protein and lipid bands, indicating that subtle, distributed spectral changes accompany differentiation and that multivariate analysis was needed to resolve them. Principal component analysis defines a state space for cell states To describe cell states quantitatively, the nuclear mean spectrum of each cell was subjected to principal component analysis (PCA) across all time points. The first three principal components accounted for most of the variance (PC1, 41%; PC2, 17%; PC3, 9%). Loading plots showed that PC1 was dominated by bands from proteins and lipids, whereas PC2 was weighted toward nucleic acid bands, suggesting that the axes reflect biologically interpretable changes in nuclear composition. Psychiatric diagnosis is central to the organisation of mental health care. Diagnostic categories determine access to services and treatments, guide clinical decision-making, shape research and underpin statistics on the burden of disease. The International Classification of Diseases (ICD), maintained by the World Health Organization (WHO), is the principal classification used in the National Health Service (NHS) in England and in most countries worldwide. The chapter on mental and behavioural disorders is therefore one of the most influential documents in mental health practice. The 11th revision (ICD-11) was developed over a number of years and has been designed to improve on its predecessor in clinical utility, global applicability and scientific validity. A stated priority of the revision is that the classification should be useful to the front-line clinicians who use it in routine practice. Despite its widespread use, the validity and utility of psychiatric classification have been questioned for decades. Critics have pointed to high rates of comorbidity between categories, substantial heterogeneity within them, unclear boundaries between disorder and normal variation, and limited evidence that categories map onto discrete underlying biological or psychological entities. Clinicians report that diagnostic systems are often complex, do not fit the presentations seen in everyday practice, and are applied inconsistently. Primary care practitioners, who manage the majority of common mental health problems, have been particularly vocal that existing criteria are not designed for the settings in which they work. Field studies conducted by WHO have sought clinicians' views, but these have generally relied on structured case-vignette or ratings-based methods that offer limited opportunity for in-depth feedback. Service users have also raised concerns. Diagnosis can be experienced as helpful: it may provide an explanation for distress, validation, relief, access to support and a sense of community. Equally, it can be experienced as stigmatising, disempowering or reductive, and may be perceived as failing to capture the personal, social and cultural context of distress. Evidence suggests that receiving a diagnosis can influence a person's identity, their relationships with services and professionals, their expectations of recovery, and ultimately their outcomes. These effects appear to vary between diagnoses. Personality disorder, for example, is widely reported to carry heavy stigma and to be associated with exclusion from services, whereas diagnoses such as schizophrenia are associated with pessimistic assumptions about prognosis and public fears of dangerousness. Terminology, the wording of criteria and the way diagnoses are communicated may all contribute to such consequences. Since classification systems are intended to benefit those who use services, it is difficult to justify their development without systematic input from those who live with the diagnoses they describe. Involving service users in research and service development is now a firm expectation in UK health policy and research funding. Co-production, in which people with lived experience participate as equal partners in designing, conducting and interpreting research, is increasingly seen as a means of improving relevance, quality and impact. However, service user involvement in the development of diagnostic classifications has been limited. Previous revisions of the ICD and the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders were largely shaped by expert committees of professionals, with consultation mechanisms such as public comment periods that tend to favour those with existing access to the process. Few studies have explored in depth how service users and clinicians respond to the specific content of proposed diagnostic criteria, and the voices of people with lived experience have rarely been integrated with those of clinicians in a structured way. The timing of ICD-11 offers a valuable opportunity. The proposed diagnostic descriptions and guidelines have been drafted but are still open to refinement, and WHO has indicated openness to feedback from national groups. Several of the proposed changes are substantial. These include a reconceptualised approach to personality disorder based on severity with trait domain qualifiers, changes to the description of bipolar and depressive disorders, a revised conceptualisation of schizophrenia and other primary psychotic disorders that removes the traditional subtypes, and altered criteria for generalised anxiety disorder. How such changes are understood and experienced by those who will use or be given these diagnoses is not known. Anticipating unintended negative consequences before implementation is far preferable to addressing them afterwards. This paper describes the protocol for the INternational CLassification of Diseases (11th revision); Using lived experience to improve mental health Diagnosis in NHS England (INCLUDE) study. The study was developed in dialogue with WHO and takes a qualitative, co-produced approach, with people with lived experience involved in every stage from design to dissemination. Its aim is to elicit the views of service users and clinicians on the proposed ICD-11 criteria for five diagnoses selected for their prevalence, clinical significance and relevance to the concerns outlined above: personality disorder, bipolar I disorder, schizophrenia, depressive disorder and generalised anxiety disorder. Focus groups with service users and with clinicians (psychiatrists, general practitioners and clinical psychologists) will be analysed thematically, and the findings will form the basis of co-produced recommendations for the refinement of ICD-11. The specific objectives are to explore how service users and clinicians perceive the validity, clarity, acceptability and usefulness of the proposed criteria; to identify potential unintended consequences for identity, service use and outcomes; and to generate practical recommendations for improvement. Because the ICD is an international tool, a further aim is to develop a methodology that can be replicated by other groups in other settings. Publishing the protocol promotes transparency and allows the approach to be scrutinised and adopted. This qualitative study uses focus groups with service users and clinicians to gather feedback on the proposed ICD-11 diagnostic criteria for selected mental disorders. It was developed in dialogue with the WHO. The study is co-produced throughout, and service users, clinicians and researchers contribute to design, conduct, analysis and interpretation. Reporting will follow the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ). Co-production and governance A study steering group was established, comprising academic researchers, clinicians and people with lived experience of mental health diagnoses and of using NHS services. Service user co-researchers contributed to development of the topic guides, recruitment materials and information sheets. They will help facilitate focus groups, take part in coding and theme development, and help draft the recommendations. Co-researchers will receive training in qualitative methods and focus group facilitation, together with payment and supervision in line with INVOLVE guidance. Each focus group will be facilitated by a researcher and a co-researcher where possible. Setting and participants Participants will be recruited in NHS England through secondary care mental health services, primary care, voluntary sector organisations and service user networks. Service users. Adults (≥18 years) who have received a diagnosis of one of five conditions from a clinician will be eligible: personality disorder, bipolar I disorder, schizophrenia, depressive disorder or generalised anxiety disorder. They must be able to give informed consent and to participate in English. People will be excluded if they are acutely unwell or lack capacity to consent, as judged by their clinical team or the research team. Two focus groups will be held for each diagnosis, giving ten service user groups. Clinicians. Psychiatrists, general practitioners and clinical psychologists who use diagnostic classification in practice will be eligible. Four clinician focus groups will be conducted, with professional groups mixed or separate depending on feasibility and the need to encourage open discussion. Sample size Each group is planned to include approximately six to eight participants, a size that allows interaction while giving everyone the opportunity to speak. The total target is about 60–80 service users and 24–32 clinicians. Because of the fixed number of groups, sampling will be purposive, aiming for diversity in age, gender, ethnicity, duration of diagnosis and service setting. The adequacy of the sample will be reviewed during analysis in terms of information power and thematic saturation. Additional groups will be considered if new themes continue to emerge. Recruitment and consent Clinical teams and partner organisations will identify potential participants and distribute invitation packs containing an information sheet. Interested individuals will contact the research team directly. A researcher will check eligibility and answer questions. Written informed consent will be obtained before each focus group, with consent to audio recording. Participants may withdraw at any point, and data already collected may be retained unless a participant requests otherwise before analysis. Expenses will be reimbursed, and participants will receive a voucher in recognition of their time. Data collection Focus groups will last approximately 90 minutes and will be held in accessible, neutral community or NHS venues. Before each group, participants will receive a plain-language summary of the proposed ICD-11 criteria for the relevant diagnosis, including changes from ICD-10. A semi-structured topic guide, developed with co-researchers and reviewed by the steering group, will explore: understanding of and reactions to the proposed criteria; whether the descriptions reflect lived or clinical experience; terminology and language, including potential stigma; the clarity, usability and clinical utility of the criteria; perceived effects of diagnosis on identity, access to services and outcomes; and suggested changes. Clinician groups will additionally focus on application in routine practice, ease of use and diagnostic boundaries. The guide will remain flexible so participants can raise further issues. Facilitators will take field notes and a brief debrief will follow each session. Participants will also complete a short demographic questionnaire. A distress protocol will be in place, with a named clinician available for support and signposting if participants become distressed. Data management Audio recordings will be transcribed verbatim by an approved transcription service under a confidentiality agreement, then checked for accuracy and anonymised. Identifiable information will be removed and participants will be assigned codes. Data will be held on secure, password-protected university servers, with consent forms stored separately, in accordance with the Data Protection Act and Good Clinical Practice. NVivo will be used to manage the data. Data analysis Transcripts will be analysed using inductive thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke’s six phases: familiarisation, generation of initial codes, searching for themes, reviewing themes, defining and naming themes, and reporting. Researchers and co-researchers will independently code an initial subset of transcripts, then meet to compare interpretations, agree a coding framework and resolve discrepancies. The framework will be applied to the remaining transcripts and refined iteratively. Analysis will be conducted within each diagnostic group and then compared across diagnoses and between service users and clinicians to identify shared and divergent themes. Reflexivity will be supported by a reflexive journal and by discussion of how the team’s own backgrounds and experiences shape interpretation. Credibility will be enhanced through multiple coders, input from co-researchers, an audit trail and, where feasible, feedback of preliminary themes to participants. Development of recommendations Themes will form the basis of draft recommendations for the ICD-11 criteria and associated guidance. These will be refined in co-production workshops involving service users, clinicians and researchers and reviewed by the steering group. The final recommendations will be presented to the WHO in dialogue with those responsible for ICD-11 development, to inform revisions and clinical descriptions. Ethics The study has been approved by the Coventry and Warwickshire HRA Research Ethics Committee (16/WM/0479) and is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03131505). Confidentiality will be maintained, except where a participant discloses information indicating a risk of serious harm, in which case the risk protocol will be followed. Dissemination Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, conferences, service user and clinician networks, and summaries for participants. The methodology will be documented to enable replication internationally. This is a protocol paper, so no empirical findings have yet been generated. The results presented here describe the outputs of protocol development, the anticipated structure of the data, and the planned reporting of findings, rather than outcomes of the focus groups. Status of the study At the time of writing, ethical approval had been granted by the Coventry and Warwickshire HRA Research Ethics Committee (16/WM/0479), and the study had been registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03131505). Recruitment and data collection had not been completed, and no analysis of focus group data had been undertaken. Accordingly, no thematic findings are reported. Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin best known for its role in blood coagulation, where it serves as an essential cofactor for the post-translational conversion of specific glutamate residues to γ-carboxyglutamate (GLA) [1,2]. This reaction is catalyzed by gamma-glutamyl carboxylase (GGCX) in the endoplasmic reticulum and is coupled to oxidation of the reduced form of vitamin K (hydroquinone) to vitamin K epoxide. The epoxide is recycled by the vitamin K epoxide reductases VKORC1 and VKORC1L1, the target enzymes of the anticoagulant warfarin, to regenerate the hydroquinone [3,4]. γ-Carboxylation confers calcium-binding capacity on GLA-containing proteins, which is required for their conformation and function. The best characterized substrates include coagulation factors II, VII, IX and X, as well as proteins involved in bone and vascular homeostasis such as osteocalcin and matrix GLA protein [5,6]. Additional vitamin K-dependent proteins, including growth arrest-specific 6 (GAS6) and protein S, signal through TAM receptor tyrosine kinases (TYRO3, AXL and MER), which regulate cell survival, proliferation, migration and immune responses [7,8]. Vitamin K exists in two principal natural forms. Phylloquinone (K1) is synthesized by plants and is the predominant dietary form, found mainly in green leafy vegetables and plant oils. Menaquinones (K2, MK-n) are produced by bacteria and are present in fermented foods and animal products; they differ from K1 in having an unsaturated isoprenoid side chain of variable length [9]. Although both K1 and K2 support GGCX-mediated carboxylation, they differ in their absorption, tissue distribution, half-life and bioactivity. K1 is primarily delivered to the liver, whereas longer-chain menaquinones are redistributed to extrahepatic tissues [10,11]. Menaquinone-4 (MK-4), moreover, can be generated from K1 in tissues by the enzyme UBIAD1, and has been proposed to exert functions independent of carboxylation, including activation of the steroid and xenobiotic receptor (SXR/PXR) and modulation of transcription [12,13]. Interest in vitamin K in oncology has grown from observations that K vitamins influence cell proliferation, differentiation and survival. A substantial body of in vitro work has reported that K2, and to a lesser extent synthetic K3 (menadione), inhibits growth and induces apoptosis, cell cycle arrest or differentiation in leukemia, hepatocellular carcinoma, prostate, colon, lung, ovarian and breast cancer cells [14–18]. In contrast, K1 has typically been reported to have little or no effect on cancer cell proliferation at comparable concentrations [15,19]. Epidemiological studies have yielded mixed results. Higher dietary intake of K2, but not K1, has been associated with reduced risk of prostate cancer and lower cancer mortality in some cohorts [20,21], whereas associations with breast cancer risk have been inconsistent [22]. Furthermore, clinical studies of K2 in hepatocellular carcinoma recurrence have shown variable outcomes [23]. These disparate observations suggest that the biological actions of vitamin K in cancer are context dependent and may differ by vitamer, tumor type and the expression of the vitamin K cycle machinery. Breast cancer is a heterogeneous disease, and triple negative breast cancer (TNBC), defined by the absence of estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor and HER2 amplification, accounts for approximately 15–20% of cases [24]. TNBC is characterized by aggressive behavior, early recurrence, metastasis to visceral sites and a lack of targeted therapies, so that cytotoxic chemotherapy remains the standard of care [25]. A subpopulation of cells with stem-like properties is thought to contribute to therapeutic resistance and relapse in TNBC, and pathways that regulate stemness are therefore of considerable interest as therapeutic targets [26,27]. Notably, AXL signaling, which depends on γ-carboxylated ligands such as GAS6, has been implicated in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, stemness and drug resistance in TNBC [28,29]. This raises the possibility that the vitamin K cycle, by enabling γ-carboxylation, could influence TNBC progression. Despite these links, little is known about whether breast cancer cells express a functional vitamin K cycle or whether K1 and K2 exert distinct effects in this setting. Most studies of vitamin K in cancer cells have examined antiproliferative effects of K2 without assessing expression of GGCX and VKOR enzymes or the presence of GLA-modified proteins, and K1 has often been used only as a negative control. Consequently, it remains unclear whether the effects attributed to K2 are related to γ-carboxylation or occur through alternative mechanisms, and whether K1 is truly inert in cancer cells or may have its own effects. In this study, we therefore examined expression of GGCX, VKORC1 and VKORC1L1 across breast cancer cell lines and in clinical breast tumor datasets, and found highest expression in TNBC lines and in advanced-stage disease. We then compared the effects of K1 and K2 on growth, stemness and expression of GLA-modified proteins in TNBC cell lines Hs578T, MDA-MB-231 and SUM159PT, using warfarin to probe the role of VKOR activity. Our findings indicate that TNBC cells possess a functional vitamin K pathway and that K1 and K2 elicit divergent phenotypic effects, providing a basis for further mechanistic investigation of this pathway as a therapeutic target. Cell lines and culture conditions Human breast cancer cell lines Hs578T, MDA-MB-231, SUM159PT, MCF-7, T47D, and the non-tumorigenic mammary epithelial line MCF10A were obtained from ATCC or Asterand and authenticated by short tandem repeat profiling. Hs578T and MDA-MB-231 cells were maintained in DMEM with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), SUM159PT cells in Ham's F-12 with 5% FBS, insulin (5 µg/mL) and hydrocortisone (1 µg/mL), and MCF-7 and T47D cells in RPMI-1640 with 10% FBS [1]. MCF10A cells were grown in DMEM/F-12 supplemented with horse serum, EGF, insulin, hydrocortisone, and cholera toxin [2]. All cultures were kept at 37°C in 5% CO2 and tested negative for Mycoplasma monthly. Because standard FBS contains vitamin K, experiments used medium supplemented with charcoal-stripped or vitamin K-depleted serum where indicated. Phylloquinone (K1), menaquinone-4 (K2, MK-4), and warfarin (Sigma-Aldrich) were dissolved in ethanol or DMSO and protected from light. Cells were treated with K1 or K2 at 1–10 µM, or warfarin at 10 µM, with vehicle-matched controls (final solvent ≤0.1%). Media and treatments were replaced every 48 h. Gene expression analysis Total RNA was isolated with TRIzol (Invitrogen) and purified using column-based kits, with DNase treatment. RNA (1 µg) was reverse transcribed using random hexamers and M-MLV reverse transcriptase. Quantitative PCR was performed with SYBR Green master mix on a real-time thermocycler using primers specific for GGCX, VKORC1, VKORC1L1, and the stemness markers CD44, CD24, ALDH1A1, SOX2, and NANOG. Reactions were run in triplicate, and relative expression was calculated by the 2^-ΔΔCt method [3] normalized to GAPDH or ACTB. Melt-curve analysis confirmed single products. To assess expression across disease stage, publicly available datasets (TCGA breast invasive carcinoma and METABRIC) were queried through cBioPortal and UALCAN [4,5]. Tumors were grouped by pathological stage and PAM50/receptor subtype, and expression differences were evaluated by ANOVA with post hoc testing. Proliferation and viability assays Cells were seeded at 2–5 × 10³ cells/well in 96-well plates, allowed to attach overnight, and treated with vehicle, K1, K2, or warfarin for 24–120 h. Growth was measured by direct cell counting with trypan blue exclusion, by MTT or CellTiter-Glo assays according to manufacturer instructions, and by real-time confluence imaging (IncuCyte). Growth curves were normalized to vehicle controls. Apoptosis was assessed by Annexin V/propidium iodide staining and flow cytometry, and by immunoblotting for cleaved PARP and caspase-3. Cell cycle distribution was assessed by propidium iodide staining of ethanol-fixed cells followed by flow cytometry. Detection of γ-carboxyglutamate-modified proteins Cells were treated for 72 h, washed in PBS, and lysed in RIPA buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors. Protein concentration was determined by BCA assay. Equal amounts of protein (30–50 µg) were separated by SDS-PAGE, transferred to PVDF membranes, and blocked in 5% BSA in TBST. Membranes were probed with a monoclonal antibody specific for GLA residues (anti-γ-carboxyglutamyl; Sigma/BioMedica Diagnostics), which recognizes GLA-modified proteins independent of protein context [6]. Additional antibodies targeted GGCX, VKORC1, VKORC1L1, β-actin, and GAPDH. Bands were visualized with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies and enhanced chemiluminescence and quantified by densitometry in ImageJ. Recombinant or bovine prothrombin-containing samples and lysates from vitamin K-depleted cells served as positive and negative controls, respectively. Tumorsphere and stemness assays Stem-like properties were evaluated by mammosphere formation [7]. Single-cell suspensions were plated at 500–1,000 cells/well in ultra-low attachment 24-well plates in serum-free DMEM/F-12 supplemented with B27, EGF (20 ng/mL), bFGF (20 ng/mL), and heparin, with vehicle, K1, or K2. After 7–10 days, spheres larger than 50 µm were counted and sphere-forming efficiency calculated as spheres formed divided by cells seeded. Spheres were dissociated and replated to assess self-renewal in secondary passages. In parallel, the CD44+/CD24- subpopulation was quantified by flow cytometry using fluorophore-conjugated antibodies, and ALDH activity was measured with the ALDEFLUOR assay, using the inhibitor DEAB to define gating [8]. Colony formation Cells (500 per well) were seeded in six-well plates and treated for 10–14 days. Colonies were fixed with methanol, stained with 0.5% crystal violet, and colonies of more than 50 cells were counted. Statistical analysis All experiments were performed in at least three independent biological replicates, each with technical replicates. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation or standard error of the mean, as indicated. Comparisons between two groups used unpaired two-tailed Student's t tests; comparisons among multiple groups used one-way or two-way ANOVA with Tukey's or Dunnett's post hoc correction. Growth curves were analyzed by repeated-measures two-way ANOVA. Analyses were performed in GraphPad Prism, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. References [1] Neve RM, et al. Expression of vitamin K pathway genes in breast cancer cell lines and tumors We first measured transcript levels of GGCX, VKORC1, and VKORC1L1 by qPCR in a panel of breast cell lines representing non-malignant, luminal, and triple negative subtypes. All three genes were detected in every line, but expression varied significantly by subtype. The TNBC lines Hs578T, MDA-MB-231, and SUM159PT had the highest expression of GGCX, VKORC1, and VKORC1L1, whereas luminal lines (e.g., MCF-7, T47D) and the non-malignant line MCF10A had lower levels. GGCX expression was approximately 3- to 6-fold higher in TNBC lines than in luminal lines (p < 0.05). VKORC1 showed the broadest range, and VKORC1L1 was highest in Hs578T and SUM159PT. Analysis of publicly available tumor datasets [1,2] showed the same trend: expression of all three genes was higher in advanced-stage (stage III–IV) than in early-stage (stage I–II) disease, and was highest in basal-like tumors. These data indicate that the enzymatic machinery required for γ-carboxylation is present in TNBC cells and is enriched in more aggressive disease. K1 and K2 differentially affect TNBC cell growth To test whether the forms of vitamin K have different phenotypic effects, Hs578T, MDA-MB-231, and SUM159PT cells were cultured in medium supplemented with vehicle, K1 (phylloquinone), or K2 (menaquinone-4) at physiologically relevant to supraphysiologic concentrations. K1 increased cell growth in all three lines in a dose- and time-dependent manner. After 72 h, K1 increased cell number by roughly 20–40% relative to vehicle (p < 0.05), and the effect was reproducible in proliferation (MTS) and direct cell counting assays. In contrast, K2 reduced cell growth in a dose-dependent manner. At higher concentrations, K2 reduced cell number by more than 50% compared with vehicle in each cell line. The anti-proliferative effect of K2 was accompanied by increased markers of apoptosis, including cleaved PARP and elevated annexin V staining, consistent with previous reports of pro-apoptotic K2 activity in other cancer types [3,4]. The opposing effects were evident at equimolar concentrations, indicating that they were not attributable to differences in dosing or vehicle exposure. Fisheries are among the most pervasive human activities in the marine environment, and their expansion over the past century has altered food webs, habitats and the demography of many non-target species [1,2]. Industrial fishing now covers more than half of the ocean surface, and a large and growing proportion of this effort occurs in areas beyond national jurisdiction [3,4]. International waters account for over 60% of the world's oceans, yet they remain the least monitored and least regulated of marine areas. Management relies on regional fisheries management organisations, whose capacity to enforce regulations is limited by the vast scale of the area and by incomplete reporting of catch, effort and bycatch [5,6]. Consequently, how fisheries in these regions shape ecosystem processes is surprisingly poorly understood. Monitoring of fishing activity at sea has traditionally depended on logbooks, onboard observers and, more recently, vessel monitoring systems (VMS) and the Automatic Identification System (AIS). These approaches have transformed our view of global fishing effort [3,7], but each has limitations. Observer coverage is generally low and biased toward certain fleets, and VMS data are often not publicly accessible. AIS transmissions can be switched off or spoofed, and vessels engaged in illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing have a strong incentive to avoid detection [8,9]. Satellite-based radar and optical imagery can detect non-broadcasting vessels, but coverage is intermittent, limited by cloud and resolution, and costly to apply across ocean basins [10]. There is therefore a clear need for complementary methods that can detect vessels irrespective of whether they transmit their position. Seabirds are among the taxa most affected by fisheries. Many species are attracted to vessels, where they exploit discards, offal and baited hooks, and this behavior brings them into contact with fishing gear [11,12]. Incidental mortality in longline and trawl fisheries is considered the primary threat to albatrosses and large petrels, and it has contributed to the fact that albatrosses are now among the most threatened groups of birds, with most species listed as threatened or near-threatened [13,14]. At the same time, access to fishery waste may provide a food subsidy that influences foraging behavior, diet, breeding success and population dynamics [15,16]. Quantifying the interaction between seabirds and fisheries is therefore essential both for assessing bycatch risk and for understanding the wider ecological consequences of fishing. Most assessments of this interaction have been based on the spatial overlap between the distributions of tracked birds and the distributions of fishing effort, derived from VMS or AIS data [17,18]. Such estimates of overlap are indirect: they indicate where birds and vessels could encounter each other but not whether encounters actually occurred. Overlap analyses are also constrained by the resolution and completeness of the fisheries data, and they are likely to underestimate exposure in international waters where vessel data are sparse or absent [19]. Furthermore, spatial coincidence at coarse scales provides little information on the behavior of birds in relation to vessels, such as the duration of attendance or the frequency with which individuals follow ships. Direct observations of seabird–vessel interactions are needed to resolve these uncertainties. Recent advances in biologging provide such an opportunity. Small devices that detect the radar emissions of vessels, in combination with GPS loggers, allow the detection of ships by the birds themselves [20]. Because the marine radars carried by most vessels operate continuously, particularly at night and in poor visibility, such devices can record encounters between birds and vessels, including those from vessels that do not transmit AIS, and can thus reveal the true extent of overlap. Initial deployments on albatrosses and other seabirds in restricted regions have shown that this approach can detect IUU activity and quantify encounter rates [20,21]. Wide-ranging seabirds that cover immense areas may thereby serve as ocean sentinels, sampling the distribution of vessels over scales that are impractical for conventional surveys [22]. The wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans) is an ideal model for this approach. It is a wide-ranging, long-lived species that exploits the winds of the Southern Ocean to travel thousands of kilometers during foraging trips, and individuals are known to be attracted to fishing vessels [23,24]. Populations of wandering albatrosses have declined at several sites, partly as a result of bycatch in longline fisheries [13,25]. The Crozet Islands in the southern Indian Ocean hold one of the largest populations of the species, and birds breeding there forage across areas that include both national exclusive economic zones and international waters, where regulatory oversight is weak [24,26]. Despite decades of tracking, how often these birds actually encounter vessels, and where, remains unknown. Here, we used loggers combining GPS and radar detection, deployed on wandering albatrosses breeding at the Crozet Islands, to measure the true extent of overlap between albatrosses and fishing vessels. Our objectives were to (i) quantify the area patrolled by breeding albatrosses and the distances reached from the colony; (ii) determine the proportion of birds that detected vessels and the frequency of detections; (iii) compare detections with the distribution of vessels broadcasting AIS to estimate the proportion of non-broadcasting vessels; and (iv) generate estimates of the intensity of fishing and the distribution of vessels in international waters. We predicted that encounter rates would be higher than expected from overlap analyses based on AIS and VMS, particularly in areas beyond national jurisdiction. By doing so, we evaluate the potential of seabirds equipped with radar detectors as monitors of vessel presence, with implications for bycatch assessment, fisheries management and the detection of illegal fishing. Fieldwork was conducted at Possession Island, Crozet Archipelago (46°25′S, 51°45′E), southern Indian Ocean, during the incubation and brooding periods of wandering albatrosses (Diomedea exulans) in 2018–2019. The colony is monitored annually, and the identity, sex, age and breeding status of individuals are known from long-term ringing and nest surveys [1]. Adults were captured by hand on their nests, and all handling was kept to a minimum and carried out under permits issued by the Terres Australes et Antarctiques Françaises and the ethics committee of the Institut Polaire Français Paul-Émile Victor. Devices and deployment Each bird was equipped with a combined GPS and radar-detector logger (Sextant, Cefas/Toulouse design; mass approx. 60 g, <2% of body mass, below the 3% threshold generally recommended for flying seabirds [2]). The unit has a GPS receiver and a radar detector sensitive to X-band (9.4 GHz) emissions, the frequency used by the marine navigation radars carried by most fishing vessels [3]. The detector records a radar pulse whenever a vessel's radar beam is received, which is possible within approximately 5 km of the bird, depending on sea state and radar power. Detection events were logged with a time stamp and the bird's concurrent GPS position. GPS fixes were taken every 2 min, and radar detection was sampled continuously, with the number of pulses summarised in 1-min bins. Loggers were taped to the dorsal contour feathers with waterproof tape (Tesa) and secured with cyanoacrylate glue [4]. Birds were released at their nests within 15 min of capture. Devices were recovered after one or more foraging trips by recapturing birds at their nests, and the total deployment lasted between 5 and 40 days. Data processing All analyses were performed in R v4.0 [5]. GPS tracks were examined for errors and resampled at regular 10-min intervals using linear interpolation (package adehabitatLT [6]). Foraging trips were defined as continuous periods at sea beginning when a bird left the island and ending upon return, and trips of less than 1 h were discarded. Behavioural state was assigned from ground speed and sinuosity using a hidden Markov model (package moveHMM [7]) with three states: resting on the water, foraging (area-restricted search) and travelling. Maximum distance from the colony and total path length were calculated for each trip. Utilisation distributions were estimated by kernel density (package adehabitatHR [6]), and the 50% and 95% contours were taken as core and general ranges. The area patrolled was calculated from the cumulative 95% utilisation distribution of all birds, projected onto a Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection. Radar detections were treated as presence of a vessel. Consecutive detections separated by less than 30 min were grouped into a single encounter event, in line with previous work on albatross–vessel interactions [3]. For each encounter we extracted the position, time, duration and the bird's behavioural state before, during and after detection. Detections within 20 km of the colony were excluded because of the research station's radar and local supply and patrol vessels. Overlap with fisheries To place detections in the context of known fishing activity, we compared radar detections with Automatic Identification System (AIS) data from Global Fishing Watch [8], which provide vessel positions and apparent fishing effort at 0.1° resolution. Each radar encounter was classified as "matched" if an AIS-broadcasting fishing vessel was recorded within 10 km and ±1 h of the bird's position, and "unmatched" otherwise. Unmatched encounters could represent vessels that do not broadcast AIS, either because they are not required to or because transponders were switched off, and were considered potential non-reported or illegal activity [9]. They could also represent non-fishing vessels, so we also compared encounter locations with exclusive economic zone boundaries [10] and regional fisheries management organisation areas. Overlap with legal fisheries was quantified as the proportion of albatross locations within 50 km of AIS-registered fishing effort in the same month. Estimating vessel distribution and fishing intensity To map vessel distribution, the study area was divided into 1° × 1° grid cells. For each cell, we calculated the proportion of bird GPS fixes with a radar detection, adjusting for variation in bird use (time spent in the cell) by dividing the number of detections by the number of bird-hours. Cells with fewer than 10 bird-hours or fewer than three individuals were excluded to limit pseudoreplication. The resulting index of encounter rate was taken as a proxy for vessel density. We tested its relationship to AIS fishing effort per cell using generalised additive models with a negative binomial error and the log of bird-hours as an offset (package mgcv [11]). Statistical analysis The proportion of individuals that detected at least one vessel was computed per sex and breeding stage. Differences in encounter rate among sexes and foraging stages were tested with generalised linear mixed models with a Poisson error structure, with individual as a random intercept and log trip duration as an offset (package lme4 [12]). Differences in behaviour before and during encounters were tested with mixed models of speed and sinuosity, again with individual as a random effect. Model selection was based on Akaike's information criterion, and model fit was assessed through residual diagnostics (package DHARMa [13]). Spatial autocorrelation was checked using Moran's I on residuals. Means are reported ± SD, and significance was accepted at α = 0.05. A total of 169 wandering albatrosses from the Crozet Islands were equipped with combined GPS and radar detector loggers during the breeding season, yielding tracks from both incubation and chick-rearing. Loggers recorded for a mean of 17.4 ± 6.2 days per deployment, and 142 devices (84%) were recovered with complete data. Together, these tracks covered an area of more than 10 million km² of the southern Indian Ocean, extending from subantarctic waters north of the colony to the Antarctic shelf margin and east toward Kerguelen and Australian longitudes. Movement and spatial extent Birds ranged up to 2500 km from the colony (maximum 2512 km), with the greatest distances reached by incubating individuals and by males and females during long foraging trips. Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) is an active microwave imaging system that operates day and night and under nearly all weather conditions, and it has become an indispensable tool for Earth observation, disaster monitoring, marine surveillance, and military reconnaissance [1,2]. Spaceborne SAR systems are particularly valuable because they offer global access and repeatable coverage. As applications have matured, demand has grown for imagery that combines fine azimuth resolution with a wide observation area. Conventional stripmap mode ties the achievable azimuth resolution to the physical antenna length, and ScanSAR trades resolution for swath width by burst-wise beam switching in elevation [3]. Neither mode can deliver high resolution and wide swath (HRWS) at the same time. Spotlight and sliding spotlight modes Spotlight SAR extends the synthetic aperture time by steering the antenna beam to keep it on a fixed scene center, so the azimuth resolution is no longer limited by the antenna length [4]. The price is lost azimuth coverage, since only a single scene of limited extent is imaged per pass. Sliding spotlight mode relaxes this constraint. The beam is steered about a virtual rotation point located farther from the sensor than the scene, so the footprint moves along the ground at a velocity lower than that of the platform. This yields an intermediate resolution between stripmap and spotlight, together with continuous, longer azimuth coverage [5,6]. Sliding spotlight has therefore been adopted by many spaceborne systems, including TerraSAR-X, COSMO-SkyMed, and TanDEM-X [7,8]. Gaofen-3 (GF-3) is China's first civilian C-band multi-polarization SAR satellite with multiple imaging modes. It offers spatial resolutions from 1 m to 500 m and swaths from 10 km to 650 km, and it includes spotlight, stripmap, ScanSAR, and sliding spotlight modes [9]. Producing well focused sliding spotlight imagery from GF-3 data is both a practical necessity and a useful test of processing methods under real orbital and attitude conditions. Challenges in sliding spotlight processing Beam steering in sliding spotlight mode enlarges the total Doppler bandwidth of the received signal well beyond the pulse repetition frequency (PRF), which is chosen to match only the instantaneous Doppler bandwidth of each target. The raw data are therefore azimuth-undersampled, and the spectrum is folded or aliased. Because the time-frequency relation is also ambiguous, standard frequency-domain algorithms such as the range-Doppler, chirp scaling, and omega-K algorithms cannot be applied directly [10]. Several approaches have been proposed to address this problem. Subaperture methods split the data into pieces whose bandwidths fit within the PRF, but they complicate processing and require subaperture recombination [11]. The chirp scaling and extended chirp scaling variants have been adapted to the steered-beam geometry [12]. Time-domain back projection is accurate but computationally heavy for large scenes [13]. Another class of methods increases the effective sampling rate through zero padding, which raises the memory and computational load. The two-step processing approach of Lanari et al. offers a more efficient alternative [14]. In the first step, a deramping operation in the azimuth time domain, performed by multiplication with a linear frequency-modulated function, reduces the Doppler bandwidth of the signal to within the PRF. This removes the spectral folding, after which conventional stripmap algorithms can focus the data. In the second step, a further azimuth-scaling or deramping operation restores the correct time-frequency relation and resamples the data onto a proper azimuth grid. Applying this approach to actual spaceborne data requires careful treatment of the curved orbit, the earth rotation, and the range-dependent rotation center, as well as the appropriate choice of deramping reference parameters [15]. A second challenge is the accuracy of the Doppler parameters. Focusing quality depends strongly on the Doppler centroid and the Doppler frequency-rate. Errors in the centroid cause azimuth ambiguity and a loss of signal-to-noise ratio, and errors in the frequency rate degrade azimuth resolution and increase sidelobe levels [16]. In sliding spotlight mode the Doppler centroid varies with azimuth time because of the beam steering, and the effective frequency rate differs from that of stripmap mode, so the standard estimators such as the correlation Doppler estimator and the map-drift or autofocus method cannot be applied without modification [17,18]. Spectral folding adds a further difficulty, since the centroid estimate may be ambiguous by an integer multiple of the PRF. Estimation methods suited to the deramped data are thus required for an automatic, operational processor. Contributions and organization This paper presents an integrated imaging scheme for GF-3 sliding spotlight data that combines the two-step approach with Doppler parameter estimation. The main contributions are as follows. First, the signal model and Doppler characteristics of the GF-3 sliding spotlight mode are analyzed, and the origin of the azimuth spectral folding is clarified. Second, the two-step approach is incorporated into a complete spaceborne processing chain that removes the folding without oversampling the data. Third, Doppler centroid and frequency-rate estimation algorithms are developed for the sliding spotlight geometry and validated on real GF-3 data. The results are evaluated by image quality and by estimation accuracy. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the geometry and signal model of the sliding spotlight mode and analyzes its spectral characteristics. Section 3 presents the imaging scheme, including the two-step processing and the Doppler parameter estimation algorithms. Section 4 reports the experimental results from GF-3 data and discusses the accuracy and efficiency of the method. Section 5 concludes the paper. Signal Model and Imaging Geometry In the sliding spotlight mode, the antenna beam is steered in azimuth so that the beam footprint moves on the ground at a velocity lower than that of the sensor. The beam rotates about a virtual point located at a distance Rrot from the flight track, which lies below the scene center in the sliding spotlight configuration. The ratio of the footprint velocity to the platform velocity is defined by the scaling factor A = (Rrot − R0)/Rrot, where R0 is the closest slant range of the target. The azimuth bandwidth of the received signal is thereby extended beyond that of the stripmap mode, and the total Doppler bandwidth is the sum of the target bandwidth and the bandwidth produced by beam steering [1], [2]. When this bandwidth exceeds the pulse repetition frequency (PRF), the azimuth spectrum of the raw data is folded. The PRF is chosen to exceed only the instantaneous Doppler bandwidth, so that the unambiguous processing of the full-aperture signal requires special treatment. After range demodulation, the baseband echo of a point target is expressed as the product of a range envelope, an azimuth envelope determined by the steered antenna pattern, and a phase term determined by the instantaneous slant range R(η; R0). The slant range is described by a hyperbolic model with an effective velocity Vr, which accounts for the curved orbit and Earth rotation [3]. The Doppler centroid fdc and the Doppler frequency rate fr are the two parameters that govern focusing accuracy and are estimated from the data. Two-Step Processing Approach To overcome the azimuth spectral folding, a two-step approach combining azimuth deramping and conventional frequency-domain focusing is employed [4], [5]. The procedure is as follows. Step 1: Linear-FM deramping and spectrum unfolding. The raw data are multiplied in the range-Doppler domain or the time domain by a chirp function whose rate is determined by the reference range of the beam rotation center. This convolution-free operation removes the Doppler component caused by beam steering, and the signal bandwidth becomes smaller than the PRF. The data are then represented without aliasing in the azimuth frequency domain. Because the deramping function is applied in the azimuth time domain, the azimuth time axis is subsequently modified, and the azimuth signal is transformed into a frequency-domain representation that is a scaled copy of the target's time-domain envelope. Step 2: Range cell migration correction and focusing. After unfolding, range compression and range cell migration correction (RCMC) are performed using an extended chirp scaling algorithm (CSA) or an omega-K approach with a modified azimuth frequency-rate. The processed signal is multiplied by an azimuth matched filter in the two-dimensional frequency domain. The frequency-rate used in this filter is adapted to the sliding spotlight geometry through the scaling factor A, giving an effective rate fr' = fr/A... Following the compensation, an inverse deramping operation is performed. A phase function of opposite sign is multiplied in the azimuth time domain to eliminate the residual quadratic phase generated by the first step, and an azimuth inverse FFT yields the focused image [5], [6]. Step 3: Azimuth resampling and geometric correction. The azimuth sampling interval of the focused image is inconsistent across the extended bandwidth, and the azimuth time axis is corrected via an interpolation or a chirp-z transform so that a uniform pixel spacing is obtained. Residual phase errors in range-varying parameters are corrected using a sub-aperture phase compensation. Doppler Parameter Estimation Accurate Doppler parameters are essential because the sliding spotlight beam steering induces a time-varying Doppler centroid and the focusing is highly sensitive to errors in fr. Doppler centroid estimation. The fractional part of the Doppler centroid is estimated from the deramped data using the average cross-correlation coefficient (ACCC) method [7], in which the phase angle of the correlation between adjacent azimuth samples is computed and averaged over range. The ambiguity number is determined by the multi-look cross-correlation or the wavelength diversity algorithm [8]. Alternatively, the geometric Doppler centroid derived from the satellite attitude and ephemeris is used to resolve ambiguities and is compared with the data-based estimate for consistency. Because the antenna is steered, the centroid is defined in the deramped domain as the sum of a constant and a time-varying component, and only the constant is estimated from data. Doppler frequency rate estimation. The Doppler frequency rate is estimated by an autofocus technique based on map-drift (MD) or on the sub-aperture correlation [9]. The deramped data are split into two sub-apertures in the azimuth frequency domain, and each is compressed to form a look image. The relative shift between the looks is measured by cross-correlation, and the error in fr is calculated from the shift as Δfr = (Δx · fr)/(kT), where T is the sub-aperture time spacing and k is a geometry-dependent constant. The estimation is performed in several range blocks, and a low-order polynomial is fitted along the range to obtain the range-dependent effective velocity Vr. The process is iterated until the residual shift is smaller than a threshold of 0.1 pixel. Estimation accuracy is evaluated by comparing estimates with those from the orbit-based prediction and by examining the point-target impulse response width and the peak sidelobe ratio. Integrated Processing Flow The complete scheme integrates the above steps. The raw data are first subjected to range pulse compression and a coarse Doppler centroid estimate from the geometric parameters. The two-step approach is then run, where deramping unfolds the spectrum, the refined Doppler parameters are estimated from the unfolded data, and the CSA-based focusing, inverse deramping and azimuth resampling are applied. Finally, radiometric calibration is performed using the antenna pattern and the range spreading loss. The efficiency of the scheme derives from the exclusive use of FFTs, complex multiplications and one interpolation step, so that the computational load is on the order of N log N for N samples, comparable to that of stripmap processing. Experimental Data and Processing Configuration The proposed scheme was evaluated using raw sliding spotlight data acquired by the GF-3 SAR sensor in C-band. The scene covers a coastal area containing urban blocks, port facilities, and open water, which provides both strong point-like scatterers and homogeneous distributed regions. The data were acquired at a nominal incidence angle of approximately 40° with a transmitted bandwidth of 240 MHz, giving a slant-range resolution of about 0.6 m. The azimuth beam steering rate yields a steering-induced Doppler bandwidth that exceeds the pulse repetition frequency (PRF), so the unprocessed data exhibit azimuth spectral aliasing, as observed in the Doppler spectrum before preprocessing. Processing followed the integrated scheme: Doppler parameter estimation, the two-step azimuth preprocessing, and range-Doppler-domain focusing with residual phase compensation. The unicellular red alga Cyanidioschyzon merolae has emerged as a model organism for studying the complex interplay between cellular physiology and environmental responses in photosynthetic organisms [1]. One of the key phytohormones involved in this interplay is abscisic acid (ABA), which is synthesized in response to abiotic stresses such as drought, high salinity, and extreme temperatures [2]. ABA has been shown to induce a wide range of physiological responses in plants and algae, including stomatal closure, antioxidant production, and modulation of gene expression [3]. In Cyanidioschyzon merolae, ABA has been found to play a crucial role in regulating cell-cycle initiation, with exogenous application of ABA preventing cell-cycle progression [4]. Heme, a tetrapyrrole molecule, has been implicated in the regulation of cell-cycle initiation in Cyanidioschyzon merolae [5]. Unbound heme has been shown to act as a positive signaling molecule, promoting cell-cycle progression [6]. However, the application of ABA has been found to induce the accumulation of heme, while also preventing cell-cycle initiation [7]. This apparent paradox has been resolved by the discovery that ABA induces the expression of a heme scavenging protein, tryptophan-rich sensory protein-related protein O, which titrates the unbound heme and prevents its signaling function [8]. The mechanism by which ABA induces heme accumulation, however, remains unclear. Tetrapyrrole biosynthesis is a complex, multi-step process that involves the coordinated action of several enzymes [9]. The biosynthetic pathway begins with the synthesis of delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) from glutamate, followed by the formation of porphobilinogen, and ultimately the production of protoporphyrin IX [10]. The final steps of the pathway involve the insertion of iron or magnesium into the protoporphyrin IX ring, yielding heme or magnesium-protoporphyrin IX, respectively [11]. The regulation of tetrapyrrole biosynthesis is critical for maintaining cellular homeostasis, as imbalances in the pathway can lead to the accumulation of toxic intermediates [12]. The transcriptional regulation of tetrapyrrole biosynthetic genes is a key mechanism by which cells control the flow of metabolites through the pathway [13]. In plants and algae, the expression of these genes is often regulated by environmental cues, such as light intensity and quality [14]. For example, the expression of the gene encoding the enzyme ferrochelatase, which is responsible for the insertion of iron into protoporphyrin IX, has been shown to be regulated by light intensity in Arabidopsis thaliana [15]. Similarly, the expression of the gene encoding the magnesium-chelatase subunit, which is responsible for the insertion of magnesium into protoporphyrin IX, has been shown to be regulated by light quality in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii [16]. In Cyanidioschyzon merolae, the transcriptional regulation of tetrapyrrole biosynthetic genes has been found to play a critical role in responding to environmental stresses [17]. For example, the expression of the gene encoding the enzyme ALA synthase, which is responsible for the synthesis of ALA, has been shown to be upregulated in response to high salinity [18]. Similarly, the expression of the gene encoding the enzyme protoporphyrinogen oxidase, which is responsible for the conversion of protoporphyrinogen IX to protoporphyrin IX, has been shown to be downregulated in response to high temperature [19]. The objective of this study was to investigate the transcriptional regulation of tetrapyrrole biosynthetic genes in response to ABA treatment in Cyanidioschyzon merolae. We analyzed the accumulation of transcripts of key genes in the tetrapyrrole biosynthetic pathway, including ferrochelatase and magnesium-chelatase subunit, in response to ABA treatment. We also measured the contents of heme, magnesium-protoporphyrin IX, and protoporphyrin IX in response to ABA treatment, in order to determine the impact of ABA on the tetrapyrrole biosynthetic pathway. Our results provide new insights into the mechanisms by which ABA regulates tetrapyrrole biosynthesis in Cyanidioschyzon merolae, and have important implications for our understanding of the complex interplay between cellular physiology and environmental responses in photosynthetic organisms. The experimental approach used in this study involved the application of ABA to cultures of Cyanidioschyzon merolae, followed by the analysis of transcript accumulation and tetrapyrrole contents [20]. The results of this study are presented in the following sections, which describe the experimental design, results, and discussion of the findings. The implications of these findings for our understanding of tetrapyrrole biosynthesis and its regulation in Cyanidioschyzon merolae are also discussed. The study of tetrapyrrole biosynthesis in Cyanidioschyzon merolae has been facilitated by the availability of a fully sequenced genome [21]. The genome sequence has enabled the identification of genes involved in the tetrapyrrole biosynthetic pathway, and has provided a framework for understanding the regulation of these genes [22]. The use of bioinformatic tools has also enabled the prediction of regulatory elements and transcription factor binding sites in the promoters of tetrapyrrole biosynthetic genes [23]. These predictions have been validated by experimental studies, which have demonstrated the importance of specific transcription factors in regulating the expression of tetrapyrrole biosynthetic genes [24]. In conclusion, the study of tetrapyrrole biosynthesis in Cyanidioschyzon merolae is an active area of research, with important implications for our understanding of cellular physiology and environmental responses in photosynthetic organisms. The regulation of tetrapyrrole biosynthetic genes by ABA is a key aspect of this research, and is the focus of the present study. The results of this study provide new insights into the mechanisms by which ABA regulates tetrapyrrole biosynthesis, and have important implications for our understanding of the complex interplay between cellular physiology and environmental responses in Cyanidioschyzon merolae. Cyanidioschyzon merolae strain 10D [1] was obtained from the Microbial Culture Collection at the National Institute for Environmental Studies (Tsukuba, Japan) and cultured in Allen's medium [2] at 42°C under continuous light (40 μmol/m²/s) with shaking at 150 rpm. For the experiments, cells in the exponential growth phase were harvested by centrifugation at 1,500 × g for 5 minutes and resuspended in fresh medium to a density of 5 × 10⁶ cells/mL. Abscisic acid (ABA) was added to the medium at a final concentration of 10 μM, and the cells were further incubated for 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, or 12 hours. Total RNA was extracted from the cells using the RNeasy Plant Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) according to the manufacturer's instructions [3]. The quality and quantity of the extracted RNA were assessed using a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). First-strand cDNA synthesis was performed using the SuperScript III First-Strand Synthesis System (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) with oligo(dT) primers [4]. The resulting cDNA was diluted 10-fold with nuclease-free water and used as a template for quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis. qRT-PCR was performed using a StepOnePlus Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA) with the Power SYBR Green PCR Master Mix (Applied Biosystems) [5]. The primers used for qRT-PCR are listed in Table 1. The amplification conditions consisted of an initial denaturation at 95°C for 10 minutes, followed by 40 cycles of denaturation at 95°C for 15 seconds, and annealing and extension at 60°C for 1 minute. Melting curve analysis was performed to verify the specificity of the amplified products [6]. The relative expression levels of the target genes were calculated using the 2^(-ΔΔCt) method [7], with the actin gene (CmACT) serving as an internal control. For the analysis of tetrapyrrole contents, cells were harvested by centrifugation and extracted with methanol containing 0.1 N HCl [8]. The extracts were then analyzed using a high-performance liquid chromatograph (HPLC) equipped with a photodiode array detector (Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan) [9]. The HPLC conditions consisted of a reversed-phase column (Inertsil ODS-3, 4.6 × 250 mm, GL Sciences, Tokyo, Japan) with a linear gradient of 20-80% methanol in 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid over 30 minutes at a flow rate of 1 mL/min. The detection wavelengths were set at 400 nm for protoporphyrin IX, 420 nm for magnesium-protoporphyrin IX, and 400 nm for heme. To investigate the effect of ABA on the transcriptional regulation of tetrapyrrole biosynthetic genes, we performed a time-course analysis of gene expression using qRT-PCR. The genes examined included ferrochelatase (CmFC), magnesium-chelatase subunit (CmCHLH), protoporphyrinogen oxidase (CmPPO), and coproporphyrinogen oxidase (CmCPO) [10]. The results showed that the transcripts of CmFC and CmCHLH increased significantly after ABA treatment, while those of CmPPO and CmCPO decreased. These changes in gene expression were accompanied by an increase in heme and magnesium-protoporphyrin IX contents, and a decrease in protoporphyrin IX content. In addition to the analysis of tetrapyrrole contents, we also examined the expression of tryptophan-rich sensory protein-related protein O (CmTSPO), which is involved in the regulation of unbound heme [11]. The results showed that the transcript level of CmTSPO increased significantly after ABA treatment, suggesting that ABA-induced heme accumulation may be regulated by the transcriptional control of CmTSPO. To further investigate the relationship between ABA and heme accumulation, we performed a bioinformatics analysis of the promoter regions of the tetrapyrrole biosynthetic genes [12]. The results revealed that the promoter regions of CmFC and CmCHLH contain putative ABA-responsive elements, suggesting that ABA may directly regulate the transcription of these genes. Overall, our results suggest that ABA regulates the intracellular heme and other tetrapyrrole contents through the transcriptional regulation of biosynthetic genes in Cyanidioschyzon merolae. The increase in heme content after ABA treatment may be attributed to the upregulation of CmFC and CmCHLH, while the decrease in protoporphyrin IX content may be due to the downregulation of CmPPO and CmCPO. The transcriptional control of CmTSPO may also play a role in regulating unbound heme levels in response to ABA treatment. Further studies are needed to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying the ABA-induced transcriptional regulation of tetrapyrrole biosynthetic genes in Cyanidioschyzon merolae.
