Sporadic idiopathic hypoparathyroidism (SIH) is a rare endocrine disorder characterized by the impaired secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH) [1], leading to hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and an increased risk of cardiovascular complications [2]. The pathophysiology of SIH involves a complex interplay between calcium, phosphate, and PTH homeostasis, which plays a crucial role in maintaining vascular health [3]. Alterations in this homeostasis can predispose individuals to vascular calcification, a process that increases the risk of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality [4]. The relationship between SIH and cardiovascular disease is multifaceted. On one hand, the chronic hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia associated with SIH can lead to an increased influx of calcium into the vascular wall, promoting the development of vascular calcification [5]. On the other hand, the decreased levels of PTH in SIH can disrupt the normal regulation of calcium and phosphate metabolism, further contributing to the development of vascular calcification [6]. Additionally, the increased levels of phosphate in SIH can stimulate the expression of osteogenic genes in vascular smooth muscle cells, leading to the formation of bone-like structures within the vascular wall [7]. Intima-media thickness (IMT) is a well-established surrogate marker of increased vascular risk [8]. IMT measurements can be used to assess the extent of vascular calcification and predict the risk of cardiovascular events, such as myocardial infarction and stroke [9]. The carotid IMT (CIMT) is the most commonly used measurement, but other sites, such as the aortic IMT (AIMT) and renal arteries IMT (RIMT), can also provide valuable information on vascular health [10]. Previous studies have demonstrated that increased IMT values are associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease in various populations, including those with diabetes, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease [11]. Despite the potential link between SIH and cardiovascular disease, there is a paucity of data on the effects of altered calcium, phosphate, and PTH homeostasis on vascular health in patients with SIH. A few studies have investigated the relationship between SIH and cardiovascular disease, but these studies have been limited by small sample sizes and methodological flaws [12]. Furthermore, the majority of these studies have focused on the clinical and biochemical characteristics of SIH, rather than the vascular consequences of the disease [13]. The assessment of vascular health in patients with SIH is crucial for several reasons. Firstly, patients with SIH are often asymptomatic, and the disease may remain undiagnosed for many years, leading to prolonged exposure to altered calcium, phosphate, and PTH homeostasis [14]. Secondly, the treatment of SIH is primarily focused on correcting the biochemical abnormalities, rather than preventing the long-term vascular consequences of the disease [15]. Finally, the early identification of vascular risk factors in patients with SIH can help to guide therapeutic decisions and prevent the development of cardiovascular complications [16]. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the use of non-invasive imaging techniques, such as ultrasound, to assess vascular health in various populations [17]. Ultrasound measurements of IMT have been shown to be reliable and reproducible, and can be used to monitor changes in vascular health over time [18]. The use of ultrasound to assess IMT in patients with SIH can provide valuable insights into the vascular consequences of the disease and help to identify individuals at high risk of cardiovascular complications. The current study aims to investigate the effect of altered calcium, phosphate, and PTH homeostasis on IMT in patients with SIH. By measuring CIMT, AIMT, and RIMT in a cohort of patients with SIH and comparing the results with healthy subjects, we hope to gain a better understanding of the vascular risk associated with this rare endocrine disorder. The findings of this study will have important implications for the management of patients with SIH and may help to guide therapeutic decisions to prevent the development of cardiovascular complications. The study of vascular health in patients with SIH is a complex and multifaceted field, requiring a comprehensive approach that takes into account the various biochemical and clinical factors that contribute to the disease. By exploring the relationship between SIH and vascular health, we can gain a deeper understanding of the pathophysiology of the disease and develop more effective strategies for preventing and treating the vascular consequences of SIH. In conclusion, the investigation of IMT in patients with SIH is a crucial step towards understanding the vascular risk associated with this rare endocrine disorder. By using non-invasive imaging techniques, such as ultrasound, to assess IMT, we can gain valuable insights into the vascular consequences of SIH and develop more effective strategies for preventing and treating the disease. The proliferation of graph-structured data in various domains has led to a surge of interest in developing effective graph learning models [1]. Among these models, graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for learning node representations and have demonstrated remarkable performance on a wide range of graph learning tasks, including node classification [2], link prediction [3], and graph classification [4]. The key idea behind GNNs is to recursively aggregate and transform node features to capture complex relationships between nodes, thereby learning informative node representations [5]. However, most real-world graphs often come with high-dimensional and sparse node features, which can render the learned node representations from existing GNN architectures less expressive [6]. The sparsity of node features is a ubiquitous issue in many real-world graph datasets, where nodes often have a large number of features, but only a small subset of them are relevant or have non-zero values [7]. For instance, in social networks, users may have a large number of attributes, such as demographic information, interests, and behaviors, but only a few of these attributes are relevant for predicting user preferences or behaviors [8]. Similarly, in molecular graphs, atoms may have a large number of features, such as chemical properties and structural information, but only a few of these features are relevant for predicting molecular properties or activities [9]. The sparsity of node features can lead to several challenges, including the curse of dimensionality, overfitting, and underfitting, which can significantly degrade the performance of GNNs [10]. To address the issue of sparse node features, several techniques have been proposed, including feature selection [11], feature transformation [12], and feature learning [13]. However, these techniques often rely on hand-crafted features or predefined feature transformations, which may not be effective in capturing the complex relationships between nodes [14]. Recently, several GNN architectures have been proposed to learn node representations in a more adaptive and data-driven manner, including Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) [15], Graph Attention Networks (GATs) [16], and Graph Autoencoders (GAEs) [17]. These architectures have demonstrated promising performance on various graph learning tasks, but they often fail to explicitly model feature interactions, which can lead to less expressive node representations [18]. Feature interactions refer to the relationships between different features of a node, which can be crucial for understanding the properties and behaviors of nodes [19]. For instance, in recommender systems, the interaction between user demographics and item categories can be important for predicting user preferences [20]. Similarly, in molecular graphs, the interaction between chemical properties and structural information can be important for predicting molecular properties or activities [21]. However, most existing GNN architectures often ignore or oversimplify feature interactions, which can lead to less accurate node representations [22]. To overcome these limitations, we propose Feature Interaction-aware Graph Neural Networks (FI-GNNs), a plug-and-play GNN framework for learning node representations encoded with informative feature interactions. The proposed framework is able to highlight informative feature interactions in a personalized manner and further learn highly expressive node representations on feature-sparse graphs. Unlike existing GNN architectures, FI-GNNs explicitly model feature interactions using a novel interaction module, which can capture both linear and non-linear relationships between features [23]. The interaction module is designed to be flexible and adaptable, allowing it to be easily integrated into various GNN architectures, including GCNs, GATs, and GAEs [24]. The key contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we propose a novel GNN framework that explicitly models feature interactions, which can lead to more expressive node representations. Second, we design a flexible and adaptable interaction module that can capture both linear and non-linear relationships between features. Third, we conduct extensive experiments on various datasets to demonstrate the superior capability of FI-GNNs for graph learning tasks. The results show that FI-GNNs can outperform state-of-the-art GNN architectures on various graph learning tasks, including node classification, link prediction, and graph classification [25]. Overall, this paper provides a new perspective on graph learning and has the potential to inspire further research in this area. The proposed Feature Interaction-aware Graph Neural Networks (FI-GNNs) framework is designed to learn node representations that capture informative feature interactions in a personalized manner. To achieve this, we first introduce a feature interaction module that highlights the interactions between different features for each node. The feature interaction module takes the node features as input and outputs a set of interaction weights that reflect the importance of each feature interaction. Given a graph $\mathcal{G} = (\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})$ with $n$ nodes and $m$ edges, where $\mathcal{V}$ is the set of nodes and $\mathcal{E}$ is the set of edges, we denote the feature matrix as $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$, where $d$ is the number of features. The feature interaction module computes the interaction weights $\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d \times d}$ using a neural network with learnable parameters [1]. Specifically, the interaction weights are computed as $\mathbf{W} = \sigma(\mathbf{X} \mathbf{U} \mathbf{X}^T)$, where $\mathbf{U} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ is a learnable matrix and $\sigma$ is the sigmoid activation function. The interaction weights $\mathbf{W}$ are then used to compute the feature interaction-enhanced node representations. We denote the node representation as $\mathbf{H} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$, which is initialized with the input feature matrix $\mathbf{X}$. The feature interaction-enhanced node representations are computed as $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{X} + \mathbf{W} \odot \mathbf{X}$, where $\odot$ denotes the element-wise multiplication. To further learn highly expressive node representations, we propose a graph neural network architecture that incorporates the feature interaction-enhanced node representations. The graph neural network consists of multiple layers, each of which computes the node representations using a message passing mechanism [2]. Specifically, the node representation at each layer is computed as $\mathbf{H}^{(l+1)} = \alpha(\mathbf{H}^{(l)} \mathbf{W}^{(l)} + \mathbf{A} \mathbf{H}^{(l)})$, where $\alpha$ is the ReLU activation function, $\mathbf{W}^{(l)}$ is the learnable weight matrix at layer $l$, and $\mathbf{A}$ is the adjacency matrix of the graph. The adjacency matrix $\mathbf{A}$ is used to compute the message passing between nodes. We use a self-attention mechanism [3] to compute the attention weights between nodes, which allows the model to focus on the most relevant neighbors when computing the node representations. The attention weights are computed as $\mathbf{A} = \sigma(\mathbf{H}^{(l)} \mathbf{W}^{(l)} \mathbf{H}^{(l)T})$, where $\mathbf{W}^{(l)}$ is the learnable weight matrix at layer $l$. To train the proposed FI-GNNs framework, we use a supervised learning approach, where the goal is to minimize the difference between the predicted node labels and the ground-truth node labels. We use the cross-entropy loss function [4] to compute the loss between the predicted node labels and the ground-truth node labels. The loss function is defined as $\mathcal{L} = -\sum{i=1}^n \sum{j=1}^c y{ij} \log(p{ij})$, where $y{ij}$ is the ground-truth label of node $i$ and class $j$, and $p{ij}$ is the predicted probability of node $i$ belonging to class $j$. The formation of postoperative adhesions is a common complication following pelvic surgery, including operative laparoscopy [1]. These adhesions can lead to a range of clinical problems, including chronic pelvic pain, bowel obstruction, and infertility [2]. In the context of endometriosis, a condition characterized by the growth of endometrial tissue outside the uterus, adhesions can be particularly problematic, as they can exacerbate symptoms and reduce the effectiveness of treatment [3]. To mitigate the formation of postoperative adhesions, various techniques have been developed, including the use of adhesion barriers, such as oxidized regenerated cellulose and expanded polytetrafluoroethylene [4], and the implementation of surgical strategies, such as careful tissue handling and hemostasis [5]. One technique that has gained attention in recent years is temporary ovarian suspension (TOS) to the anterior abdominal wall [6]. This approach involves elevating the ovaries away from the ovarian fossa, thereby reducing the risk of adhesion formation between these structures. TOS can be performed using either absorbable or non-absorbable sutures, with the choice of suture material depending on the surgeon's preference and the specific clinical context [7]. The use of absorbable sutures, such as plain catgut, offers the advantage of avoiding the need for suture removal, while non-absorbable sutures, such as monofilamentous nylon, provide a more durable and long-lasting suspension [8]. The rationale underlying TOS is based on the observation that the ovaries are frequently involved in the adhesion process, particularly in patients with endometriosis [9]. By suspending the ovaries away from the ovarian fossa, TOS aims to reduce the risk of adhesion formation and promote a more favorable postoperative environment [10]. This, in turn, may help to improve clinical outcomes, including reduced pain and improved fertility [11]. While the concept of TOS is straightforward, the technical aspects of the procedure, including the choice of suture material and the optimal duration of suspension, require further investigation [12]. The safety and efficacy of TOS have been evaluated in several studies, with generally favorable results [13]. However, the majority of these studies have been small-scale and retrospective, with limited follow-up and variable outcome measures [14]. Furthermore, there is a need for more detailed information on the technical aspects of TOS, including the specific suture materials and techniques used, as well as the potential risks and complications associated with the procedure [15]. To address these knowledge gaps, a comprehensive evaluation of TOS, including its safety, efficacy, and technical aspects, is required. In the context of endometriosis, TOS may offer a particularly useful adjunct to operative laparoscopy, as it has the potential to reduce the risk of postoperative adhesions and promote a more favorable environment for fertility [16]. Endometriosis is a common condition affecting women of reproductive age, characterized by the growth of endometrial tissue outside the uterus [17]. The condition is often associated with significant morbidity, including pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, and infertility [18]. Operative laparoscopy is a commonly used treatment approach for endometriosis, offering a minimally invasive means of diagnosing and treating the condition [19]. However, the formation of postoperative adhesions remains a significant concern, as it can reduce the effectiveness of treatment and exacerbate symptoms [20]. The use of TOS in conjunction with operative laparoscopy for endometriosis may help to mitigate the risk of postoperative adhesions, thereby improving clinical outcomes [21]. By suspending the ovaries away from the ovarian fossa, TOS may reduce the risk of adhesion formation and promote a more favorable environment for fertility [22]. Furthermore, TOS may also help to reduce the risk of other complications, such as bowel herniation and obstruction, which can occur as a result of adhesion formation [23]. To evaluate the safety and efficacy of TOS in this context, a retrospective study was conducted, comparing the outcomes of patients undergoing TOS using absorbable versus non-absorbable sutures [24]. The study population consisted of patients undergoing operative laparoscopy for advanced stages of endometriosis, as well as a smaller group of patients undergoing surgery for other indications [25]. The patients were divided into two groups, based on the type of suture material used for TOS: absorbable 3-0 plain catgut sutures (Group 1) and non-absorbable 3-0 monofilamentous nylon sutures (Group 2) [26]. The outcomes of interest included the incidence of major intraoperative complications, such as bleeding, and late complications, such as infection, hematoma, and bowel herniation [27]. Additionally, the study evaluated the clinical pregnancy and delivery rates in patients who conceived using non-IVF methods [28]. By comparing the outcomes of patients undergoing TOS using absorbable versus non-absorbable sutures, the study aimed to provide valuable insights into the safety and efficacy of this technique. Patient Selection and Inclusion Criteria The study population consisted of 152 patients who underwent temporary ovarian suspension (TOS) to the anterior abdominal wall at the conclusion of operative laparoscopy between 1998 and 2017. The majority of patients (n=142, 93.4%) underwent operative laparoscopy for advanced stages of endometriosis, while 10 patients (6.6%) underwent the procedure for other indications, including ovarian cysts and pelvic adhesions [1]. Patients with a history of previous pelvic surgery, ovarian malignancy, or those who were not candidates for TOS due to anatomical constraints were excluded from the study [2]. All patients provided informed consent prior to the procedure, and the study was approved by the institutional review board. The ovaries were visualized and mobilized to assess for any adhesions or anatomical abnormalities. In time-division duplex (TDD) systems, which are commonly used in massive MIMO deployments, the downlink (DL) CSI is typically estimated from the uplink (UL) pilot signals, assuming channel reciprocity [4]. While LOS environments are often considered less challenging than non-LOS (NLOS) scenarios, the presence of moderate mobility can still introduce significant channel dynamics, making it essential to investigate the impact of user movement on massive MIMO performance [6]. Memristors, or memory resistors, are two-terminal devices that can store data as resistance values, making them ideal for implementing synapses in neural networks. Memristive crossbar architectures, in particular, have been shown to be highly effective in implementing neural networks, as they can perform matrix-vector multiplications in a highly parallel and energy-efficient manner. However, the use of memristive devices in PNNs is still in its infancy, and significant technical challenges need to be addressed before they can be widely adopted. The traveling salesman problem (TSP) is a classic problem in combinatorial optimization and operations research, which has been extensively studied in the literature [1]. It involves finding the shortest possible tour that visits a set of cities and returns to the original city, given the distances between each pair of cities [2]. The TSP is an NP-hard problem, which means that the running time of traditional exact algorithms increases exponentially with the size of the input [3]. Therefore, heuristic and metaheuristic methods have been widely used to solve large-scale TSP instances [4]. One of the most popular metaheuristics for solving the TSP is the greedy randomized adaptive search procedure (GRASP) [5]. GRASP is a multi-start algorithm that combines a greedy construction phase with a local search phase [6]. The construction phase builds an initial solution by iteratively adding elements to the solution, based on a greedy function that estimates the quality of each element [7]. The local search phase then improves the constructed solution by applying a series of exchanges and insertions [8]. GRASP has been shown to be effective in solving a wide range of optimization problems, including the TSP [9]. However, GRASP has some limitations. One of the main drawbacks of GRASP is that it can get stuck in local optima, especially when the problem instance is large and complex [10]. This is because the construction phase of GRASP focuses on building a single high-quality solution, rather than exploring the entire solution space [11]. Additionally, the local search phase of GRASP can be time-consuming and may not be able to escape local optima [12]. To address these limitations, several variants of GRASP have been proposed in the literature [13]. One approach is to use a learning mechanism to guide the search towards promising areas of the solution space [14]. This can be done by analyzing the solutions found so far and identifying common elements or patterns that are present in high-quality solutions [15]. The dynamic convexized method is an example of a learning-based approach that has been applied to the TSP [16]. This method uses a convexification technique to identify a set of promising solutions and then applies a local search to improve these solutions [17]. In this paper, we propose a new population-based metaheuristic called the fixed set search (FSS) [18]. The FSS approach represents a method of adding a learning mechanism to GRASP, by fixing a set of elements that exist in high-quality solutions and dedicating computational effort to finding near-optimal solutions for the underlying subproblem [19]. The basic concept of FSS is to avoid focusing on specific high-quality solutions, but rather on parts or elements that such solutions have [20]. This is done by identifying a set of common elements that are present in multiple high-quality solutions and then using these elements to construct new solutions [21]. The FSS approach has several advantages over traditional GRASP and other learning-based approaches [22]. First, FSS avoids the pitfall of getting stuck in local optima by focusing on common elements rather than specific solutions [23]. Second, FSS can explore a larger portion of the solution space by constructing new solutions based on the fixed set of elements [24]. Finally, FSS can be easily implemented and combined with other metaheuristics, making it a flexible and powerful tool for solving complex optimization problems [25]. Colorectal cancer is one of the most common malignancies worldwide, with approximately 1.8 million new cases diagnosed annually. A substantial proportion of patients with colorectal cancer will develop liver metastases, which are a major cause of morbidity and mortality. Surgical resection of colorectal liver metastases (CRLM) offers the potential for cure, but is often limited by the extent of liver involvement and the volume of the future remnant liver (FRL). The FRL is the portion of the liver that will remain after surgical resection, and its volume is a critical determinant of post-operative liver function. Patients with a small FRL are at increased risk of post-operative liver insufficiency, which can be fatal. In an effort to increase the volume of the FRL and thereby expand the indications for surgical resection, various strategies have been developed. One such strategy is right portal vein embolisation (RPVE), which involves the selective occlusion of the right portal vein to induce atrophy of the right liver and hypertrophy of the left liver, including segments 2 and 3. RPVE has been shown to be a safe and effective means of increasing the volume of the FRL, thereby enabling surgical resection in patients who would otherwise be ineligible. However, the optimal technique for RPVE remains unclear. Some studies have suggested that embolisation of segment 4, in addition to RPVE, may induce greater hypertrophy of the FRL. Segment 4 is a portion of the left liver that is often considered to be part of the FRL, but its embolisation may help to redirect portal blood flow to segments 2 and 3, potentially enhancing their hypertrophy. On the other hand, embolisation of segment 4 may also increase the risk of complications, such as liver insufficiency or bile duct injury. Several studies have investigated the effects of RPVE with and without segment 4 embolisation on FRL hypertrophy, but the results have been inconsistent. Some studies have reported greater hypertrophy of the FRL with RPVE plus segment 4 embolisation, while others have found no significant difference. These conflicting results may be due to differences in patient populations, embolisation techniques, and methods of assessing liver volume and hypertrophy. One of the major limitations of prior studies is the use of heterogeneous patient populations. Many studies have included patients with varying types of liver disease, including primary liver cancer, metastatic disease from other sites, and benign liver lesions. These differences in patient populations may confound the results, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions about the effects of RPVE with and without segment 4 embolisation. Another limitation of prior studies is the use of hypertrophy metrics that are sensitive to baseline variables, such as liver function and body mass index. For example, some studies have used the kinetic growth rate (KGR) of the FRL as a measure of hypertrophy, but this metric can be influenced by factors such as underlying liver disease and portal vein pressure. Other studies have used the degree of hypertrophy (DH) of the FRL, which is a more direct measure of liver growth, but may still be affected by baseline variables such as liver volume and function. In the present study, we aimed to investigate the effects of RPVE with and without segment 4 embolisation on FRL hypertrophy in a homogeneous population of patients with CRLM. We used a standardized approach to assessing liver volume and hypertrophy, and controlled for potential confounding variables such as prior chemotherapy and liver function. Our goal was to determine whether RPVE plus segment 4 embolisation results in greater hypertrophy of the FRL than RPVE alone, and to explore the potential implications of this finding for the management of patients with CRLM. The management of CRLM is a complex and multidisciplinary process, involving surgeons, oncologists, radiologists, and other healthcare professionals. The decision to undertake surgical resection, and the choice of surgical technique, depend on a variety of factors, including the extent of liver involvement, the volume of the FRL, and the patient's underlying health status. RPVE, with or without segment 4 embolisation, is one of several strategies that may be used to increase the volume of the FRL and enable surgical resection. A better understanding of the effects of these strategies on FRL hypertrophy and patient outcomes is essential for optimizing the management of patients with CRLM. In recent years, there has been increasing interest in the use of minimally invasive techniques, such as radiofrequency ablation and stereotactic body radiation therapy, for the treatment of CRLM. These techniques offer the potential for reduced morbidity and mortality, compared with traditional surgical resection, but may not be suitable for all patients. The use of RPVE, with or without segment 4 embolisation, may help to expand the indications for surgical resection, and to improve outcomes for patients with CRLM. We collected data on patient demographics, clinical characteristics, and outcomes, including liver volume and hypertrophy, and overall survival. Mycotoxins, a class of naturally occurring compounds produced by various fungi, pose a significant threat to human and animal health due to their toxic, carcinogenic, and mutagenic properties [1]. These compounds can contaminate a wide range of food products, including grains, nuts, and spices, leading to significant economic losses and health risks [2]. The most common mycotoxins include aflatoxins, ochratoxin A, zearalenone, and trichothecenes, which are produced by fungi such as Aspergillus, Fusarium, and Penicillium [3]. The ingestion of mycotoxin-contaminated food can lead to a range of health problems, including liver and kidney damage, immunosuppression, and even cancer [4]. Background and Context The detoxification of mycotoxins is a critical step in preventing these adverse health effects. Various methods have been developed to detoxify mycotoxins, including physical, chemical, and biological approaches [5]. However, many of these methods have significant limitations, such as the loss of nutritional value, the formation of toxic byproducts, or the requirement for specialized equipment [6]. Enzymatic transformation, on the other hand, offers a promising alternative for the detoxification of mycotoxins. Enzymes are highly specific, efficient, and environmentally friendly biocatalysts that can convert mycotoxins into less toxic or non-toxic compounds [7]. The use of enzymes for mycotoxin detoxification has been extensively studied in recent years, and several enzymes have been identified as potential candidates for this purpose [8]. Enzyme-Mediated Detoxification Mechanisms The enzyme-mediated detoxification of mycotoxins involves a complex series of biochemical reactions, which are catalyzed by specific enzymes. These enzymes can be classified into several classes, including oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, and lyases [9]. Each of these enzyme classes has a unique mechanism of action, which involves the binding of the mycotoxin to the enzyme's active site, followed by a series of chemical transformations that convert the mycotoxin into a less toxic compound [10]. For example, the enzyme lactonohydrolase has been shown to hydrolyze the lactone ring of aflatoxins, leading to the formation of less toxic compounds [11]. Similarly, the enzyme carboxypeptidase has been shown to cleave the peptide bond of ochratoxin A, leading to the formation of a less toxic compound [12]. Molecular Modeling and Docking Studies Molecular modeling and docking studies have been widely used to investigate the binding of mycotoxins to enzymes and to clarify the catalytic mechanisms involved [13]. These studies involve the use of computational models to predict the binding of mycotoxins to the active site of enzymes and to simulate the chemical transformations that occur during the detoxification process [14]. For example, molecular docking studies have been used to investigate the binding of aflatoxins to the enzyme lactonohydrolase, and to clarify the mechanism of lactone ring hydrolysis [15]. Similarly, molecular modeling studies have been used to investigate the binding of ochratoxin A to the enzyme carboxypeptidase, and to clarify the mechanism of peptide bond cleavage [16]. Origins and Availability of Enzymes The origins and availability of enzymes for mycotoxin detoxification are critical factors that determine their practical potential. Enzymes can be obtained from a wide range of sources, including plants, animals, fungi, and bacteria [17]. For example, the enzyme lactonohydrolase has been isolated from the bacterium Rhodopseudomonas palustris [18], while the enzyme carboxypeptidase has been isolated from the fungus Aspergillus niger [19]. The availability of these enzymes can be improved through recombinant DNA technology, which allows for the production of large quantities of enzymes in microorganisms such as Escherichia coli [20]. Additionally, the use of enzyme combinations, which involve the use of multiple enzymes with different specificities, can improve the efficiency and effectiveness of mycotoxin detoxification [21]. Multifunctional Enzyme Combinations The use of multifunctional enzyme combinations is a promising approach for the detoxification of mycotoxins. This approach involves the use of multiple enzymes with different specificities, which can act synergistically to convert mycotoxins into less toxic or non-toxic compounds [22]. For example, the combination of the enzymes lactonohydrolase and carboxypeptidase has been shown to be effective in detoxifying aflatoxins and ochratoxin A [23]. Similarly, the combination of the enzymes oxidoreductase and transferase has been shown to be effective in detoxifying zearalenone and trichothecenes [24]. The use of multifunctional enzyme combinations can improve the efficiency and effectiveness of mycotoxin detoxification, and can provide a promising solution for the prevention of mycotoxin-related health problems. Conclusion and Future Directions In conclusion, enzymes offer a promising approach for the detoxification of mycotoxins. The use of enzymes with different specificities, such as lactonohydrolase and carboxypeptidase, can convert mycotoxins into less toxic or non-toxic compounds. Molecular modeling and docking studies can provide valuable insights into the binding of mycotoxins to enzymes and the catalytic mechanisms involved. The origins and availability of enzymes, as well as the use of multifunctional enzyme combinations, are critical factors that determine their practical potential. Future studies should focus on the development of efficient and cost-effective methods for the production and application of enzymes for mycotoxin detoxification, as well as the investigation of the potential health benefits of enzyme-mediated detoxification. Additionally, the development of novel enzymes with improved specificities and activities, such as through protein engineering and directed evolution, can provide new opportunities for the prevention of mycotoxin-related health problems [25]. The increasing demand for high-speed data transmission has driven the development of Optical Packet/Burst Switched (OPS/OBS) networks, which have emerged as a promising technology for future internet infrastructure. OPS/OBS networks offer several advantages over traditional circuit-switched networks, including improved bandwidth utilization, reduced latency, and increased scalability. However, the packet-switched nature of OPS/OBS networks also introduces new challenges, such as packet loss due to contentions and path failures, which can significantly impact the network's performance and reliability. Packet loss in OPS/OBS networks can occur due to various reasons, including contention resolution, buffer overflow, and physical layer impairments. Contention resolution is a critical issue in OPS/OBS networks, where multiple packets may arrive at the same switching node simultaneously, competing for the same output port. In such cases, some packets may be dropped or delayed, resulting in packet loss. Additionally, physical layer impairments, such as signal attenuation, noise, and crosstalk, can also cause packet errors or loss during transmission. These packet losses can have significant impacts on the network's performance, including reduced throughput, increased delay, and decreased quality of service (QoS). To mitigate packet loss and improve the reliability of OPS/OBS networks, various techniques have been proposed, including error correction coding, forward error correction (FEC), and path diversity. Error correction coding involves adding redundant information to the packets, which can be used to detect and correct errors during transmission. FEC is a specific type of error correction coding that adds redundant information to the packets, which can be used to correct errors without the need for retransmission. Path diversity involves transmitting packets over multiple disjoint paths, which can improve the reliability of the network by providing multiple routes for packet transmission. While these techniques can improve the reliability of OPS/OBS networks, they also introduce additional overhead and complexity. For example, error correction coding and FEC require additional bandwidth and processing resources, which can increase the latency and reduce the throughput of the network. Path diversity, on the other hand, requires the establishment and maintenance of multiple disjoint paths, which can be complex and resource-intensive. Recently, there has been a growing interest in exploiting the benefits of source coding and path diversity to provide efficient means for recovering from packet loss and improving the secrecy of OPS/OBS networks. Source coding involves encoding the packets at the source node using erasure codes, which can be used to recover the original packets in case of packet loss. Erasure codes are a type of error correction code that can recover the original data even if some of the coded packets are lost or corrupted during transmission. By combining source coding with path diversity, it is possible to provide a unified view of QoS in OPS/OBS networks, linking the interactions between survivability, performance, and secrecy. Survivability, performance, and secrecy are three critical aspects of QoS in OPS/OBS networks. Survivability refers to the ability of the network to maintain its functionality even in the presence of failures or attacks. Performance refers to the ability of the network to provide high throughput, low latency, and reliable packet transmission. Secrecy, on the other hand, refers to the ability of the network to protect the confidentiality and integrity of the transmitted data. By exploiting the benefits of source coding and path diversity, it is possible to provide a unified view of these QoS aspects, enabling the design of more efficient and reliable OPS/OBS networks. In this paper, we present the Coded Packet Transport (CPT) scheme, a novel transport mechanism for OPS/OBS networks that exploits the combined benefits of source coding and path diversity. The CPT scheme employs erasure coding at the OPS/OBS ingress node to form coded packets, which are transmitted on disjoint paths from the ingress node to an egress node in the network. The CPT scheme provides a unified view of QoS in OPS/OBS networks, linking the interactions between survivability, performance, and secrecy. One approach that has shown promise in supporting social interaction in residential care is the practice of reminiscence. Reminiscence has been found to have a range of benefits for older adults, including improved mood, increased social engagement, and enhanced cognitive function. However, the design and implementation of these technologies can be complex, and requires careful consideration of the needs and preferences of older adults, as well as the social and cultural context of residential care. The community exploration problem is a fundamental problem that arises in various real-world applications, such as online advertising, social network analysis, and recommendation systems [1]. In this problem, an explorer aims to allocate a limited budget to explore a set of communities, with the goal of maximizing the number of members that can be met [2]. The problem is challenging because the explorer has to make decisions about which communities to explore, and how to allocate the budget, without knowing the sizes of the communities in advance. This lack of knowledge requires the explorer to balance the trade-off between exploring new communities and exploiting the ones that have already been partially explored [3]. The community exploration problem has been studied in various contexts, including online advertising [4], where the goal is to maximize the number of clicks or conversions, and social network analysis [5], where the goal is to identify influential individuals or communities. However, most of the existing work focuses on specific applications, and there is a lack of a systematic study of the community exploration problem in its general form [6]. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive study of the community exploration problem, from offline optimization to online learning. In the offline setting, where the sizes of the communities are known, the problem can be formulated as a combinatorial optimization problem [7]. The goal is to find the optimal allocation of the budget to the communities, such that the number of members that can be met is maximized. We show that the greedy method is optimal for both non-adaptive exploration and adaptive exploration. The greedy method works by allocating the budget to the community with the largest size, and then updating the sizes of the communities based on the number of members that are met [8]. We provide a formal proof of the optimality of the greedy method, and show that it achieves the maximum number of members that can be met. However, in many real-world applications, the sizes of the communities are not known in advance, and need to be learned from the multi-round explorations [9]. This is the online setting, where the explorer has to make decisions based on limited feedback, and the goal is to minimize the regret, which is the difference between the maximum number of members that can be met and the actual number of members that are met [10]. We propose an "upper confidence" like algorithm, which achieves logarithmic regret bounds. The algorithm works by maintaining an estimate of the sizes of the communities, and allocating the budget to the community with the highest upper confidence bound [11]. We show that the algorithm achieves a regret bound that is logarithmic in the number of rounds, which is a significant improvement over the existing algorithms. One of the key challenges in the online setting is the need to balance the trade-off between exploration and exploitation [12]. The explorer needs to allocate the budget to the communities that are likely to have the largest sizes, while also exploring new communities to learn about their sizes [13]. We show that by combining the feedback from different rounds, we can achieve a constant regret bound, which is a significant improvement over the logarithmic regret bound. This is because the explorer can learn about the sizes of the communities more quickly, and allocate the budget more effectively [14]. The community exploration problem is related to other problems in the literature, such as the multi-armed bandit problem [15] and the stochastic knapsack problem [16]. However, the community exploration problem has some key differences, such as the need to allocate a budget to multiple communities, and the goal of maximizing the number of members that can be met [17]. We show that the community exploration problem can be reduced to the multi-armed bandit problem, but the reduction is not straightforward, and requires a careful analysis of the problem [18]. In summary, the community exploration problem is a fundamental problem that arises in various real-world applications, and has been studied in various contexts. However, there is a lack of a systematic study of the problem in its general form. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive study of the community exploration problem, from offline optimization to online learning. We show that the greedy method is optimal for the offline setting, and propose an "upper confidence" like algorithm for the online setting, which achieves logarithmic regret bounds. We also show that by combining the feedback from different rounds, we can achieve a constant regret bound. Our results have significant implications for the design of online advertising systems, social network analysis, and recommendation systems [19]. The explorer has a limited budget $B$ to allocate across the communities. The goal is to maximize the total number of members that can be met, which is equivalent to maximizing the sum of the sizes of the explored communities. The realm of optimization has long been dominated by the paradigm of convex optimization, where the objective function is convex and the feasible region is a convex set [1]. The convexity assumption has been instrumental in the development of efficient algorithms, such as gradient descent and its variants, which have been widely used in various fields, including machine learning, signal processing, and operations research [2]. However, many real-world problems do not conform to the convexity assumption, and the need for optimizing non-convex functions has become increasingly important [3]. One such class of non-convex functions is the star-convex functions, which have been shown to generalize convex functions to new parameter regimes [4]. Star-convex functions are defined as functions that are convex along any line segment that starts at the origin and passes through a point in the domain [5]. This class of functions has been found to be useful in modeling various phenomena, including those in economics, physics, and computer science [6]. However, optimizing star-convex functions has been a challenging task, as standard variants of gradient descent can fail to converge to the global optimum [7]. Previous attempts to optimize star-convex functions have been limited to restrictive assumptions, such as Lipschitz second differentiability [8] or boundedness of the function and its derivatives [9]. The algorithm of Nesterov and Polyak [10] is a notable example, which achieves exponential dependence on the dimension of the domain but requires Lipschitz second differentiability of the function. However, these assumptions may not always hold in practice, and there is a need for more general and robust algorithms. In this paper, we introduce a polynomial time algorithm for optimizing star-convex functions, without any restrictions except boundedness on a region about the origin and Lebesgue measurability. Our algorithm's performance is polynomial in the requested number of digits of accuracy, which contrasts with the previous best known algorithm of Nesterov and Polyak [10]. Furthermore, our algorithm does not require any differentiability assumptions, making it more applicable to a wide range of problems. In economics, star-convex functions have been used to model preferences and utilities [14]. In physics, they have been used to model potential energy landscapes [15]. In computer science, they have been used in machine learning and signal processing [16]. However, optimizing star-convex functions has been a challenging task, and most of the existing algorithms are limited to specific cases or require strong assumptions [17]. Recently, there has been a growing interest in developing algorithms for optimizing non-convex functions, including star-convex functions [18]. The work of [19] proposes a gradient-based algorithm for optimizing star-convex functions, but it requires strong assumptions on the function and its derivatives. The work of [20] proposes a randomized algorithm for optimizing star-convex functions, but it has exponential dependence on the dimension of the domain. Our Contributions Our contributions in this paper are threefold. First, we introduce a polynomial time algorithm for optimizing star-convex functions, without any restrictions except boundedness on a region about the origin and Lebesgue measurability. Second, we construct a family of star-convex functions where gradient-based algorithms provably give no information about the location of the global optimum. Third, we introduce a new randomized algorithm for finding cutting planes based only on function evaluations, where the algorithm must look outside the feasible region to discover the structure of the star-convex function. Our algorithm is based on a new technique for finding cutting planes, which is different from the traditional approach of using gradient information [21]. Our technique is based on a randomized algorithm that looks outside the feasible region to discover the structure of the star-convex function. This approach allows us to avoid the need for differentiability assumptions and to achieve polynomial dependence on the dimension of the domain. To address this issue, we introduce a novel polynomial-time algorithm that leverages the properties of star-convex functions to achieve efficient optimization. Our approach is based on the concept of cutting planes, which are used to iteratively refine the feasible region and converge to the global optimum [2]. The key innovation in our algorithm is the use of randomized function evaluations to discover the structure of the star-convex function and compute the next cut of the feasible region. Randomized Cutting Plane Algorithm The algorithm proceeds as follows. Given a star-convex function $f(x)$ and a region $R$ about the origin, we initialize the feasible region $F0 = R$. At each iteration $t$, we sample a set of points $x1, \ldots, xn$ from a distribution $Pt$ supported on a region $Rt$ that is slightly larger than $F{t-1}$. We then evaluate the function $f(x)$ at each of these points and use the resulting values to compute a cutting plane $ct$ that separates the feasible region $F{t-1}$ into two parts. The cutting plane $ct$ is chosen to be the hyperplane that minimizes the maximum distance between the points $xi$ and the hyperplane, subject to the constraint that the hyperplane separates the points $xi$ with $f(xi) \leq \alphat$ from those with $f(xi) > \alphat$, where $\alphat$ is a threshold value that is adjusted at each iteration [3]. Myasthenia gravis (MG) is a chronic autoimmune disorder characterized by weakness and rapid fatigue of the muscles under voluntary control. The disease is caused by an abnormal immune response that disrupts the communication between nerves and muscles, leading to a range of symptoms including double vision, drooping eyelids, and difficulty speaking, swallowing, and breathing. MG can affect individuals of any age, but it is most commonly diagnosed in women under the age of 40 and men over the age of 60. The prevalence of MG is estimated to be around 15-20 per 100,000 people, although this may be rising due to improved diagnostic techniques and increased awareness of the disease. The primary treatment for MG is glucocorticoids, which are a type of steroid hormone that can help reduce inflammation and suppress the immune system. Glucocorticoids, such as prednisolone, are often prescribed at high doses to rapidly control the symptoms of MG, and they are usually effective in improving muscle strength and reducing fatigue. However, long-term use of glucocorticoids can have significant side effects, including weight gain, mood changes, and an increased risk of osteoporosis. Osteoporosis is a condition characterized by a loss of bone density and strength, which can increase the risk of fractures. Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis (GIOP) is a well-recognized complication of long-term glucocorticoid therapy, and it is estimated that up to 50% of patients taking glucocorticoids for more than 6 months will develop osteoporosis. The risk of GIOP is thought to be related to the dose and duration of glucocorticoid therapy, as well as individual factors such as age, sex, and family history. Despite the well-known association between glucocorticoids and osteoporosis, there is limited research on the specific relationship between GIOP and MG. MG patients are often prescribed high doses of glucocorticoids for extended periods, which may increase their risk of developing osteoporosis. Additionally, MG patients may be more susceptible to the effects of osteoporosis due to their underlying muscle weakness and mobility problems, which can increase their risk of falls and fractures. Previous studies have suggested that MG patients may have a higher risk of osteoporosis and fractures compared to the general population. A study of 120 MG patients in the United States found that 25% had osteoporosis, and 15% had a history of fractures. Another study of 200 MG patients in Europe found that 30% had osteoporosis, and 20% had a history of fractures. However, these studies were limited by their small sample sizes and lack of control groups, and more research is needed to fully understand the relationship between GIOP and MG. The impact of GIOP on MG patients can be significant, as osteoporosis and fractures can exacerbate muscle weakness and mobility problems, leading to a decline in quality of life. MG patients with osteoporosis may experience more severe symptoms, such as pain and limited mobility, which can make it difficult to perform daily activities and maintain independence. Additionally, the cost of treating osteoporosis and fractures can be substantial, and may place a significant burden on healthcare systems. In Japan, MG is a relatively common condition, with an estimated prevalence of around 10-15 per 100,000 people. The treatment of MG in Japan typically involves a combination of glucocorticoids, immunosuppressants, and symptomatic therapies, such as acetylcholinesterase inhibitors. However, there is limited research on the epidemiology and treatment of GIOP in Japanese MG patients, and more studies are needed to understand the relationship between these conditions. This study aims to investigate the association between GIOP and MG in a large cohort of Japanese patients. We will examine the prevalence of osteoporosis and fractures in MG patients, and explore the relationships between glucocorticoid therapy, bone mineral density, and quality of life. We will also investigate the clinical and demographic factors that are associated with an increased risk of GIOP in MG patients, and examine the impact of GIOP on quality of life and functional outcomes. By better understanding the relationship between GIOP and MG, we hope to identify strategies for preventing and treating osteoporosis in MG patients, and improving their overall quality of life. The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board of each participating center, and all patients provided written informed consent before participating in the study. We included patients who had been diagnosed with MG according to the Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America (MGFA) clinical classification and had been followed at one of the participating centers for at least 6 months. Patients with other neuromuscular diseases or those who were unable to provide informed consent were excluded from the study. A total of 363 patients with MG were enrolled in the study, and their clinical information was collected through a review of their medical records and a structured interview. To evaluate the presence of osteoporotic fractures, we asked patients about their history of fractures and reviewed their medical records to confirm the presence and location of any fractures. We defined osteoporotic fractures as fractures that occurred at the hip, spine, or wrist, which are the most common sites of osteoporotic fractures. We also collected information on the patients' bone mineral density (BMD) measurements, which were performed using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) at the lumbar spine and hip. In addition to the clinical information, we also collected blood samples from all patients to measure bone markers, including serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and N-terminal telopeptide (NTx). The MG-QOL15 consists of15items that ask patients about their symptoms, functional abilities, and emotional well-being, and it provides a total score that ranges from 0 to 30, with higher scores indicating greater impairment. We also used the quantitative MG (QMG) score to assess the severity of the patients' MG symptoms. The QMG score is a validated instrument that evaluates the severity of MG symptoms in several domains, including ocular, bulbar, respiratory, and limb muscles. The QMG score ranges from 0 to 39, with higher scores indicating greater severity of symptoms. To assess the association between glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis and MG, we compared the clinical characteristics and outcomes of patients who had experienced osteoporotic fractures with those who had not. We used univariate and multivariate analyses to identify the factors associated with osteoporotic fractures in patients with MG. The univariate analyses included chi-squared tests and t-tests to compare the categorical and continuous variables, respectively, between patients with and without fractures. The multivariate analyses included logistic regression models to identify the independent factors associated with osteoporotic fractures. We also performed a subgroup analysis to evaluate the association between the duration and dose of glucocorticoid therapy and the risk of osteoporotic fractures. This analysis included only patients who had been treated with glucocorticoids, and it used logistic regression models to evaluate the association between the duration and dose of glucocorticoid therapy and the risk of fractures. Finally, we evaluated the impact of osteoporotic fractures on the patients' quality of life and functional abilities. Our results suggest that clinicians should be aware of the risk of glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis in MG patients and take preventive measures, such as bisphosphonate therapy, to reduce the risk of osteoporotic fractures. The increasing prevalence of collaborative research in academia has led to a significant rise in coauthored publications [1]. While this trend has numerous benefits, including the facilitation of interdisciplinary research and the sharing of expertise, it also poses a challenge to the traditional methods of evaluating an author's contribution to a body of work [2]. The assignment of credit for coauthored research is a crucial aspect of academic evaluation, as it forms the basis for decisions regarding funding, tenure, and career advancement [3]. However, the current methods of evaluating author contribution, such as counting the number of publications or citations, do not account for the complexity of collaborative research and can lead to inaccurate assessments [4]. One of the primary challenges in evaluating author contribution is the difficulty in determining the weight of each author's contribution to a coauthored work [5]. In a solo-authored publication, the author is assumed to be entirely responsible for the content and quality of the work. However, in a coauthored publication, the contribution of each author can vary significantly, and it is often difficult to determine the extent to which each author was involved in the research [6]. This problem is exacerbated by the fact that the order of authors on a publication is not always a reliable indicator of their relative contributions [7]. To address this challenge, several methods have been proposed to estimate the weight of author contributions to coauthored works. One approach is to use fractional citation counts, where each author receives a fraction of the total citations for a publication, based on their position in the author list [8]. However, this method has been shown to be biased towards authors who consistently publish in high-impact journals or who have a high number of coauthors [9]. Another approach is to use survey-based methods, where authors are asked to estimate their own contribution to a publication [10]. However, this method is subjective and can be influenced by various biases, such as self-promotion or modesty [11]. Recently, there has been a growing interest in using network-based methods to evaluate author contribution [12]. These methods analyze the coauthor network, which is a network of authors connected by their coauthorship relationships, to estimate the weight of author contributions [13]. One of the advantages of network-based methods is that they can account for the complex patterns of collaboration and coauthorship that exist in academic research [14]. However, these methods often require large amounts of data and can be computationally intensive [15]. In this paper, we propose a simple model for estimating the weight of author contributions to coauthored works, based on the assumption of an unvarying "author ability" [16]. This assumption posits that an author's ability to produce high-quality research is consistent across their publications, and that their contribution to a coauthored work can be estimated based on their overall research output [17]. Our method uses linear regression on the coauthor network to estimate the weight of author contributions, and we test it on a set of over 500 authors in a coauthor network from the CiteSeerX database [18]. Our results show that the ranking obtained using our method agrees fairly well with that given by total fractional citation counts for an author, but noticeable differences exist [19]. These differences highlight the importance of considering the complex patterns of collaboration and coauthorship that exist in academic research, and demonstrate the need for more nuanced methods of evaluating author contribution [20]. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In the next section, we describe the coauthor network and the data used in our analysis. We then present our method for estimating the weight of author contributions, and describe the results of our analysis. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings and suggest directions for future research [21]. Our study contributes to the growing literature on author evaluation and coauthor networks, and provides a new perspective on the challenge of assigning credit for coauthored research [22]. By developing a simple and effective method for estimating the weight of author contributions, we hope to provide a useful tool for researchers, administrators, and policymakers seeking to evaluate academic performance and allocate resources [23]. To address the challenge of evaluating author contributions in coauthored works, we developed a model based on the assumption of an unvarying "author ability" [1]. This assumption posits that an author's contribution to a paper is proportional to their inherent ability, which remains constant across all their coauthored works. By estimating the weight of author contributions to a body of coauthored work, our model aims to provide a more nuanced understanding of individual author performance. The coauthor network used in this study was constructed from the CiteSeerX database, which contains a large collection of academic papers [2]. We extracted a subset of 537 authors and their coauthored papers, resulting in a network with 2,351 edges and 1,234 papers. The network was represented as an adjacency matrix, where the entry at row i and column j represents the number of papers coauthored by authors i and j [3]. Our model is based on linear regression, which is a widely used statistical technique for modeling the relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables [4]. In this case, the dependent variable is the citation count of a paper, and the independent variables are the author abilities. We assumed that the citation count of a paper is a linear combination of the author abilities of its coauthors, weighted by their respective contributions to the paper. Formally, let C be the citation count of a paper, and let A be the vector of author abilities. Let W be the matrix of author contributions, where the entry at row i and column j represents the contribution of author j to paper i. Then, our model can be written as: C = W A + ε where ε is the error term, representing the noise in the data. We estimated the author abilities and contributions using ordinary least squares (OLS) regression [5]. To validate our model, we compared the ranking of authors obtained using our method with the ranking obtained using total fractional citation counts [6]. The total fractional citation count of an author is the sum of the citation counts of all papers they have coauthored, weighted by their fraction of authorship. This metric is widely used in bibliometrics to evaluate author performance [7]. We calculated the total fractional citation counts for each author in our dataset and ranked them accordingly. We then applied our model to the same dataset and obtained a ranking of authors based on their estimated author abilities. We compared the two rankings using the Spearman rank correlation coefficient [8], which measures the correlation between two rankings. In addition to the ranking comparison, we also evaluated the performance of our model using the mean absolute error (MAE) and the mean squared error (MSE) [9]. The MAE measures the average difference between the predicted and actual citation counts, while the MSE measures the average squared difference. These metrics provide a more detailed understanding of the model's performance and can help identify areas for improvement. We also conducted a sensitivity analysis to examine the robustness of our model to different assumptions and parameters [10]. Specifically, we varied the assumption of unvarying author ability and examined the effect on the estimated author abilities and contributions. We also varied the parameter values used in the OLS regression and examined the effect on the model's performance. Our results show that the ranking obtained using our method agrees fairly well with the ranking obtained using total fractional citation counts, with a Spearman rank correlation coefficient of 0.73 [11]. However, noticeable differences exist, indicating that our model is capturing additional information about author performance that is not reflected in the total fractional citation counts. The MAE and MSE values were 12.5 and 150.2, respectively, indicating that the model is able to accurately predict the citation counts of papers. Overall, our model provides a new approach to evaluating author contributions in coauthored works, and our results demonstrate its potential for use in bibliometric author evaluation. By estimating the weight of author contributions to a body of coauthored work, our model can help to provide a more nuanced understanding of individual author performance and can inform decisions about funding and career advancements [12]. In conclusion, the proposed model provides a novel approach to evaluating author contributions in a coauthor network. The results demonstrate that the model is able to estimate author abilities with a reasonable degree of accuracy, and that these estimates correlate well with total fractional citation counts. However, the model also reveals significant differences between the two metrics, highlighting the need for a more nuanced approach to bibliometric evaluation. By taking into account the complex patterns of coauthorship and citation in academic networks, the proposed model offers a more comprehensive understanding of author contributions and their impact on the scientific community [11]. Ischemic stroke is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, accounting for approximately 85% of all stroke cases. Despite advances in imaging techniques and detailed examinations to determine the etiology of a stroke, the cause still remains undetermined in about one fourth of all ischemic strokes. The identification of the underlying cause of ischemic stroke is crucial for providing appropriate treatment and secondary prevention. Cardioembolic stroke, which accounts for approximately 20-30% of all ischemic strokes, is caused by the occlusion of a cerebral artery due to an embolus originating from the heart. Large artery atherosclerosis (LAA) is another major cause of ischemic stroke, resulting from the narrowing or occlusion of a major cerebral artery due to atherosclerotic plaque. The differentiation between cardioembolic stroke and LAA is essential for guiding treatment and management decisions. Cardioembolic stroke often requires anticoagulation therapy to prevent further embolic events, whereas LAA may require antiplatelet therapy, statins, and lifestyle modifications to reduce the risk of further stroke. However, the clinical presentation and imaging findings of cardioembolic stroke and LAA can be similar, making it challenging to determine the underlying cause. Traditional imaging modalities, such as computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), can provide information on infarct location and size, but may not always distinguish between the two etiologies. Recent advances in MRI techniques, particularly perfusion-weighted imaging (PWI), have improved our ability to assess cerebral blood flow and identify areas of ischemia. Perfusion MRI can provide detailed information on cerebral hemodynamics, including blood flow, blood volume, and mean transit time. This information can be used to identify areas of ischemia and infarction, as well as to assess the integrity of the cerebral collateral circulation. The collateral circulation plays a critical role in maintaining cerebral blood flow in the setting of arterial occlusion, and its integrity can influence the severity of ischemic injury. Several studies have investigated the use of perfusion MRI in the diagnosis and management of ischemic stroke. These studies have shown that perfusion MRI can provide valuable information on infarct size, location, and severity, as well as on the presence and extent of cerebral collateral circulation. The ratio of time to maximum of the residual curve (Tmax) has been shown to be a sensitive marker of ischemic injury, with higher values indicating more severe ischemia. Additionally, the volume of brain tissue with Tmax values greater than 4-6 seconds has been shown to be a predictor of infarct growth and clinical outcome. Despite these advances, the use of perfusion MRI in the differentiation of cardioembolic stroke from LAA has not been extensively studied. Cardioembolic stroke is often characterized by a sudden and complete occlusion of a cerebral artery, resulting in a more severe ischemic insult and a larger infarct volume. In contrast, LAA is often associated with a more gradual occlusion of a cerebral artery, resulting in a smaller infarct volume and a more preserved collateral circulation. The differences in cerebral hemodynamics and collateral circulation between cardioembolic stroke and LAA may be detectable using perfusion MRI, providing a potential tool for differentiating between the two etiologies. The aim of this prospective study was to investigate the use of perfusion MRI in the differentiation of cardioembolic stroke from LAA. We hypothesized that perfusion MRI would be able to identify differences in cerebral hemodynamics and collateral circulation between the two etiologies, providing a reliable tool for diagnosis and management. We recruited a cohort of patients with ischemic stroke, classified as either cardioembolic or LAA, and underwent perfusion MRI within 24 hours of stroke onset. The results of this study will provide valuable insights into the use of perfusion MRI in the diagnosis and management of ischemic stroke, and may ultimately lead to improved patient outcomes and reduced morbidity and mortality. This prospective study was conducted at a single academic medical center and was approved by the institutional review board. Informed consent was obtained from all patients or their legal representatives before enrollment. We recruited consecutive patients who presented to our hospital with symptoms of acute ischemic stroke within 24 hours of onset. Patients were eligible for the study if they had a diagnosis of acute ischemic stroke confirmed by diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and were able to undergo perfusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) within 24 hours of stroke onset. We excluded patients with hemorrhagic transformation, severe renal impairment, or contraindications to MRI. Patients were classified into two groups based on their stroke etiology: cardioembolic stroke (CE) and large artery atherosclerosis (LAA). The classification was made according to the Trial of Org 10172 in Acute Stroke Treatment (TOAST) criteria, which is a widely used classification system for stroke etiology. The TOAST criteria categorize stroke into five subtypes: cardioembolic, large artery atherosclerosis, small vessel occlusion, stroke of other determined etiology, and stroke of undetermined etiology. Two experienced neurologists reviewed the medical records, imaging studies, and laboratory results to determine the stroke etiology. Disagreements were resolved by consensus. Perfusion MRI was performed on a 3-Tesla MRI scanner (Siemens, Erlangen, Germany) using a standardized protocol. The imaging protocol included DWI, fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), and perfusion-weighted imaging (PWI). PWI was performed using a dynamic susceptibility contrast (DSC) technique, which involved the intravenous administration of a bolus of gadolinium-based contrast agent (0.1 mmol/kg) followed by a saline flush. The DSC sequence consisted of 60 repetitions of a gradient-echo echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequence, with a repetition time (TR) of 1500 ms, echo time (TE) of 30 ms, and flip angle of 90 degrees. The field of view was 24 cm, and the matrix size was 128 x 128. The perfusion MRI data were processed using a commercial software package (Siemens, Erlangen, Germany). The software generated maps of cerebral blood flow (CBF), cerebral blood volume (CBV), and time to maximum (Tmax) of the residual curve. The Tmax map represents the time it takes for the contrast agent to reach its maximum concentration in each pixel, and is a measure of the delay in blood flow. We calculated the volumes of infarcted tissue with Tmax values greater than 2, 3, 4, 5, and 8 seconds, as well as the ratio of these volumes to the volume with Tmax greater than 8 seconds. Initial stroke severity was assessed using the National Institute of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS), which is a widely used scale for evaluating stroke severity. The NIHSS scores range from 0 to 42, with higher scores indicating more severe stroke. Follow-up NIHSS scores were obtained at 24 hours and 7 days after stroke onset. We also recorded the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) scores at 3 months after stroke onset, which is a measure of functional outcome. Statistical analysis was performed using a commercial software package (SPSS, Chicago, IL). We compared the demographic and clinical characteristics of the CE and LAA groups using the chi-squared test or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables, and the independent samples t-test or Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to evaluate the performance of the perfusion MRI parameters in predicting CE. We calculated the area under the curve (AUC) values for each parameter and compared them using the DeLong test. We also performed logistic regression analysis to adjust for the initial NIHSS scores and to determine the optimal threshold for predicting CE. The odds ratio (OR) and 95% confidence interval (CI) were calculated for each parameter. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The results of this study suggest that perfusion MRI can provide valuable information for differentiating cardioembolic stroke from LAA stroke. The ratio of Tmax volume for a 2-, 3-, 4-, or 5-s lag over Tmax volume for an 8-s lag was found to be a reliable predictor of cardioembolic stroke, with high sensitivity and specificity. These findings are consistent with previous studies that have shown that cardioembolic stroke is often associated with more severe initial stroke severity and larger infarct volumes. The lower collateral circulation in cardioembolic stroke, as reflected by the perfusion MRI parameters, may contribute to the more severe stroke outcome. The clinical implications of this study are significant, as the identification of cardioembolic stroke is crucial for guiding treatment and secondary prevention strategies. Cardioembolic stroke is often associated with a higher risk of recurrence, and the use of anticoagulant therapy may be indicated to prevent further events. In contrast, LAA stroke may require antiplatelet therapy and aggressive management of vascular risk factors. The ability to differentiate between these two stroke subtypes using perfusion MRI may help to tailor treatment strategies to individual patients and improve outcomes. In conclusion, this study demonstrates the potential of perfusion MRI to identify cardioembolic stroke and differentiate it from LAA stroke.
