The ability to recognize and interpret sign language is a crucial aspect of facilitating communication between individuals who are deaf or hard of hearing and those who are not [1]. While human interpreters can provide this service, they are not always available, and their services can be costly [2]. Therefore, there is a growing need for automated sign language recognition systems that can accurately identify and translate sign language into spoken language or text [3]. Recent advances in sensor technology have enabled the development of devices that can capture the nuances of sign language, including hand position, orientation, and movement [4]. One such device is the Myo armband, a wearable device that uses electromyography (EMG) sensors to detect the electrical activity of muscles in the arm and hand [5]. This device has been used in various studies to collect data on sign language, including a dataset collected by a group at the University of South Wales, which contains parameters such as hand position, hand rotation, and finger bend for 95 unique signs [6]. The recognition of sign language is a complex task that involves the analysis of temporal and spatial patterns in the data [7]. Each sign is composed of a sequence of gestures, including handshapes, orientations, and movements, which are performed in a specific order and with specific timing [8]. Therefore, sign language recognition systems must be able to model these temporal patterns in order to accurately identify the signs [9]. Traditional machine learning approaches, such as support vector machines (SVMs) and logistic regression, have been used for sign language recognition, but they have limitations when dealing with temporal data [10]. These approaches typically rely on manual feature extraction and do not take into account the temporal relationships between the data points [11]. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the use of temporal classification methods for sign language recognition [12]. These methods, including long short-term memory (LSTM) architectures and sequential pattern mining methods, are specifically designed to model temporal patterns in data [13]. LSTMs, in particular, have been shown to be effective in modeling complex temporal relationships in sequential data [14]. They use a feedback connection to capture long-term dependencies in the data, allowing them to learn patterns that span multiple time steps [15]. Sequential pattern mining methods, on the other hand, are used to discover frequent patterns in sequential data [16]. These patterns can be used to identify the temporal relationships between the data points and to build models that can predict the sign class [17]. The use of temporal classification methods for sign language recognition has several advantages over traditional machine learning approaches [18]. First, they can handle high-dimensional temporal data, which is typical of sign language data [19]. Second, they can model complex temporal relationships between the data points, allowing them to capture the nuances of sign language [20]. Finally, they can be used to build models that are robust to noise and variability in the data, which is common in sign language data [21]. However, the use of temporal classification methods also presents several challenges, including the need for large amounts of labeled training data and the complexity of the models [22]. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We first review the related work on sign language recognition, including the use of traditional machine learning approaches and temporal classification methods. We then describe the dataset used in this study, including the data collection procedure and the preprocessing steps. Next, we present the methods used in this study, including the implementation of baseline SVM and logistic regression models, as well as the use of LSTM architectures and sequential pattern mining methods. Finally, we present the results of the study, including the performance of the different models on high-quality and low-quality data. The dataset used in this study is a collection of 95 unique signs, each represented by a sequence of parameters, including hand position, hand rotation, and finger bend [6]. The data was collected using the Myo armband, which provides a high-resolution representation of the hand and finger movements [5]. The dataset is divided into training and testing sets, with 70% of the data used for training and 30% used for testing [23]. The data is preprocessed to remove noise and outliers, and to normalize the parameters to a common range [24]. The preprocessing steps include filtering, normalization, and feature extraction, which are essential for improving the quality of the data and reducing the dimensionality [25]. The recognition of sign language is a challenging task that requires the analysis of complex temporal and spatial patterns in the data [7]. The use of temporal classification methods, including LSTM architectures and sequential pattern mining methods, has shown promise in improving the accuracy of sign language recognition systems [12]. However, the performance of these methods depends on the quality of the data, and the ability to handle noise and variability [21]. One of the key challenges in online convex optimization is dealing with uncertainty and lack of information about the future. In many applications, there is some external information available that can be used to inform the decision-making process, such as predictions or forecasts. However, making effective use of this information is a difficult problem, and it has received relatively little attention in the online algorithms community. This is despite the fact that predictions are widely used in many fields, including finance, logistics, and energy systems, and are often essential for making informed decisions. There are several reasons why predictions are under-utilized in online convex optimization. One reason is that the quality of the predictions is often uncertain, and it can be difficult to quantify the degree of uncertainty. This makes it challenging to develop algorithms that can effectively incorporate the predictions into the decision-making process. Another reason is that the predictions may be biased or noisy, which can lead to poor performance if not handled properly. Finally, the predictions may be correlated, either with each other or with the underlying cost functions, which can make it difficult to develop algorithms that can effectively use the predictions to improve performance. Despite these challenges, there are many situations in which predictions are available and could be used to improve the performance of online convex optimization algorithms. For example, in portfolio optimization, predictions of future stock prices or returns could be used to inform investment decisions. In resource allocation, predictions of future demand or availability could be used to optimize the allocation of resources. In control of complex systems, predictions of future system states or disturbances could be used to optimize control actions. To address the challenges of using predictions in online convex optimization, we propose a stochastic prediction error model that generalizes prior models in the learning and stochastic control communities. Our model incorporates correlation among prediction errors, and captures the fact that predictions improve as time passes. This allows us to develop algorithms that can effectively use the predictions to improve performance, while also handling the uncertainty and noise in the predictions. One of the key insights of our work is that achieving sublinear regret and constant competitive ratio for online algorithms requires the use of an unbounded prediction window in adversarial settings. This means that the algorithm must be able to look arbitrarily far into the future in order to make informed decisions. However, this is often not possible in practice, where the prediction window may be limited by the availability of data or the quality of the predictions. The haemoglobin glycation index (HGI) has been proposed as a novel marker for predicting diabetes-related complications in individuals with type 1 and type 2 diabetes. HGI is calculated as the difference between observed HbA1c and HbA1c predicted from a simple linear regression of HbA1c on fasting plasma glucose (FPG). This index reflects the individual variability in the glycation of haemoglobin, which is influenced by various factors such as glucose metabolism, oxidative stress, and genetic predisposition. Previous studies have suggested that HGI can be used to identify individuals with an increased risk of developing diabetes-related complications, including cardiovascular disease, nephropathy, and retinopathy. The concept of HGI is based on the observation that HbA1c levels can be influenced by factors other than glucose control, such as haemoglobin turnover, red blood cell lifespan, and uremia. As a result, HbA1c may not always accurately reflect average glucose levels, particularly in individuals with certain comorbidities or those taking certain medications. HGI, on the other hand, takes into account the individual's FPG levels and provides a more nuanced assessment of glucose control. A high HGI indicates that an individual's HbA1c level is higher than expected based on their FPG, suggesting a greater risk of diabetes-related complications. Several studies have investigated the relationship between HGI and diabetes-related complications. For example, a study of individuals with type 1 diabetes found that those with a high HGI had an increased risk of developing cardiovascular disease and nephropathy. Similarly, a study of individuals with type 2 diabetes found that HGI was a significant predictor of mortality and cardiovascular events. These findings suggest that HGI may be a useful tool for identifying individuals at high risk of diabetes-related complications and for tailoring treatment strategies to reduce this risk. However, the clinical utility of HGI as a predictor of diabetes-related complications is still uncertain. While some studies have reported a significant association between HGI and adverse outcomes, others have found no such relationship. Furthermore, the mechanisms underlying the relationship between HGI and diabetes-related complications are not fully understood. It is possible that HGI reflects underlying pathophysiological processes, such as oxidative stress or inflammation, that contribute to the development of diabetes-related complications. The Action in Diabetes and Vascular Disease: Preterax and Diamicron Modified Release Controlled Evaluation (ADVANCE) trial provides a unique opportunity to investigate the relationship between HGI and diabetes-related complications in a large cohort of individuals with type 2 diabetes. The ADVANCE trial was a randomized controlled trial that compared the effects of intensive glucose control versus standard glucose control on cardiovascular outcomes in individuals with type 2 diabetes. The trial included over 11,000 participants from 20 countries, making it one of the largest and most diverse cohorts of individuals with type 2 diabetes ever studied. In this study, we investigated whether HGI was a predictor of adverse outcomes, including mortality, macrovascular disease, and microvascular disease, in the ADVANCE trial cohort. We also examined the relationship between HGI and the effects of intensive glucose control on these outcomes. Our findings have important implications for the clinical use of HGI as a predictor of diabetes-related complications and for the development of personalized treatment strategies for individuals with type 2 diabetes. The medoid of a set of points is a fundamental concept in data analysis, defined as the point that minimizes the sum of distances to all other points in the set [1]. It has numerous applications in various fields, including data mining, machine learning, and statistics, where it is used as a representative point or a centroid of a cluster [2]. The medoid is particularly useful when the data is clustered around a central point, and it is robust to outliers, making it a popular choice in many real-world applications [3]. However, computing the medoid exactly requires calculating the distances between all pairs of points, resulting in a time complexity of O(n^2), where n is the number of points [4]. This can be computationally expensive, especially for large datasets, and has motivated research into approximate algorithms that can reduce the number of distance computations needed. Several approximate algorithms have been proposed to speed up the computation of the medoid, including random sampling [5] and adaptive querying of distances [6]. The latter approach has been shown to be particularly effective, as it adaptively selects the most informative distances to query, rather than randomly sampling them [7]. This approach is based on the idea of converting the computation problem into a multi-armed bandit statistical inference problem, where each point is treated as an arm, and the goal is to identify the arm with the minimum expected loss (i.e., the sum of distances to other points) [8]. The resulting randomized algorithm has been shown to significantly reduce the number of distance computations needed, while still providing a good approximation of the medoid [9]. However, the traditional bandit sampling strategy used in these algorithms may not be optimal for the medoid computation problem. In particular, it does not take into account the structure of the underlying computation problem, such as the fact that the medoid is the point that minimizes the sum of distances to other points [10]. Recently, there has been a growing interest in developing more efficient algorithms that can exploit the structure of the computation problem to improve performance [11]. One such approach is to use correlated sequential halving, which is a technique that has been shown to be effective in reducing the number of samples needed to identify the best arm in a multi-armed bandit problem [12]. In this work, we propose a new algorithm that combines the ideas of adaptive querying of distances and correlated sequential halving to compute the medoid of a set of points. Our algorithm modifies the traditional bandit sampling strategy to take into account the structure of the computation problem, and uses a suitably chosen multi-armed bandit algorithm to identify the medoid. We show that our algorithm can significantly reduce the number of distance computations needed, resulting in four to five orders of magnitude gains over exact computation on real data, in terms of both number of distance computations needed and wall clock time. We also provide theoretical results to quantify these gains in terms of data parameters, such as the number of points and the dimensionality of the data. Efficient exploration mechanisms are crucial to address this challenge. A good exploration mechanism should encourage the agent to visit less frequent states, which may yield higher accumulative future return. However, evaluating the frequentness of states is a non-trivial task, especially in deep RL domains, where a state is represented by high-dimensional image frames. The high dimensionality of the state space makes it difficult to define a meaningful metric for evaluating the similarity between states, and hence to determine the frequentness of a state. One approach to address this challenge is to use intrinsic motivation methods, which encourage the agent to explore new states by providing an additional reward signal based on the novelty or surprise of the state. These heuristics may not be effective in high-dimensional state spaces, where the distance between states may not be a good indicator of their similarity. Another approach is to use model-based RL methods, which learn a model of the environment and use it to plan the actions. These methods can be effective in simple environments, but they often struggle in complex environments, where the model may not be accurate enough to predict the outcomes of the actions. Furthermore, learning a model of the environment can be computationally expensive, especially in high-dimensional state spaces. Recently, there has been a growing interest in using predictive models to improve the exploration in deep RL. These models predict the future states or rewards given the current state and action, and can be used to evaluate the potential outcomes of different actions. The advent of deep learning has revolutionized the field of information retrieval, with deep supervised hashing emerging as a prominent approach for efficient and accurate similarity search [1]. This paradigm involves training a deep neural network to generate hashing bits, which are then used to represent data points in a compact binary format [2]. The output neurons of the deep hashing network produce the hashing bits, and the quality of these bits has a direct impact on the retrieval performance [3]. However, during the binary discretization process, significant redundancy often exists between the hashing bits, leading to degenerated retrieval performance in terms of both storage and accuracy [4]. The redundancy between hashing bits can be attributed to the fact that the output neurons of the deep hashing network are typically trained independently, without considering the relationships between them [5]. As a result, the learned hashing bits may contain duplicate or highly correlated information, which can negatively impact the overall performance of the hashing system [6]. To mitigate this issue, several approaches have been proposed to reduce the redundancy between hashing bits, including techniques such as bit selection [7], bit weighting [8], and hash function learning [9]. While these methods have shown promising results, they often rely on heuristics or hand-crafted rules, which may not be optimal for all scenarios [10]. Recently, graph-based methods have gained popularity in the context of deep supervised hashing, as they can effectively model the relationships between hashing bits [11]. These methods typically construct a graph to represent the similarity or affinity between data points, and then use the graph to guide the learning of the hashing network [12]. However, the existing graph-based methods often focus on modeling the relationships between data points, rather than the relationships between hashing bits [13]. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach that constructs a graph to represent the redundancy relationship between hashing bits, and uses this graph to guide the learning of the hashing network. The key idea behind our approach is to dynamically learn the redundancy relationship between hashing bits, and use this relationship to merge redundant neurons together. This is achieved through a novel mechanism that involves two phases: an active phase and a frozen phase. During the active phase, the graph is constructed and updated based on the current state of the hashing network. The graph is then used to identify the redundant neurons, which are merged together to reduce the redundancy between hashing bits. In the frozen phase, the merged neurons are fixed, and the hashing network is fine-tuned to adapt to the new configuration. This process is repeated multiple times, with multiple iterations of the active and frozen phases, to progressively reduce the redundancy between hashing bits. Our approach is motivated by the observation that the redundancy between hashing bits is not fixed, but rather changes dynamically during the training process [14]. By dynamically learning the redundancy relationship and merging redundant neurons, our approach can adapt to the changing redundancy pattern and produce a more compact and informative hashing code. Moreover, our approach can be easily integrated with existing deep supervised hashing methods, making it a flexible and widely applicable solution. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. We first review the related work on deep supervised hashing and redundancy reduction techniques. We then present the details of our proposed approach, including the graph construction, neuron merging, and progressive training. Finally, we evaluate our approach on four benchmark datasets and compare it with state-of-the-art hashing methods. Our results demonstrate that our approach can effectively reduce the redundancy between hashing bits and improve the retrieval performance. Bit-level techniques focus on reducing the redundancy between individual hashing bits, while hash-level techniques focus on reducing the redundancy between entire hash codes [20]. Our approach falls into the category of bit-level techniques, as it merges redundant neurons together to reduce the redundancy between individual hashing bits. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by a wide range of clinical manifestations, including skin, joint, kidney, and neurological disorders [1]. The disease is known to affect multiple organ systems, leading to significant morbidity and mortality [2]. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), SLE is one of the top 10 leading causes of death in women of childbearing age [3]. Despite advances in medical treatment, SLE patients still face a higher risk of death compared to the general population, with a standardized mortality ratio (SMR) ranging from 2.4 to 5.4 [4]. The prognosis of SLE has improved significantly over the past few decades, thanks to the introduction of new treatments, such as corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, and biologic agents [5]. However, the long-term survival and death causes of SLE patients in China remain poorly understood. China has a large and diverse population, with varying levels of healthcare access and quality, which may impact the prognosis and mortality of SLE patients [6]. Previous studies have shown that the survival rate of SLE patients in China is similar to that in other Asia-Pacific countries, with a 5-year survival rate ranging from 85% to 95% [7]. However, the death causes of SLE in China have not been extensively studied, and the available data are largely based on small-scale studies or case reports [8]. Several factors contribute to the complexity of SLE prognosis in China, including ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and access to healthcare [9]. The Chinese population is ethnically diverse, with different genetic and environmental factors that may influence the disease course and response to treatment [10]. Additionally, the healthcare system in China is undergoing rapid changes, with an increasing emphasis on specialized care and treatment protocols [11]. However, disparities in healthcare access and quality still exist, particularly in rural areas, which may affect the outcomes of SLE patients [12]. Infection is a major cause of death in SLE patients, particularly in developing countries [13]. The high incidence of infection in SLE patients is attributed to the immunosuppressive effects of the disease and treatment, as well as the increased prevalence of infectious diseases in these regions [14]. Renal involvement is another common cause of death in SLE patients, with kidney disease being a major predictor of poor outcomes [15]. Cardiovascular disease is also a significant contributor to mortality in SLE patients, with the disease increasing the risk of cardiovascular events and mortality [16]. The analysis of death causes in SLE patients is crucial for understanding the disease prognosis and developing effective treatment strategies [17]. Previous studies have shown that the death causes of SLE patients vary by region, with infection and renal involvement being more common in developing countries [18]. In contrast, cardiovascular disease is a more significant contributor to mortality in developed countries [19]. The differences in death causes may be attributed to variations in healthcare access, disease management, and socioeconomic factors [20]. This study aims to integrate the observational studies estimating the current long-term survival of Chinese SLE patients and analyze the death-cause situation of SLE in China [21]. By conducting a systematic review of English and non-English articles, we aim to provide a comprehensive overview of the prognosis and mortality of SLE patients in China. The study will also examine the differences in death causes between China and other countries, with a focus on the potential impact of ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and healthcare access on the disease outcomes [22]. The findings of this study will contribute to the development of effective treatment strategies and healthcare policies for SLE patients in China, with the ultimate goal of improving the prognosis and reducing mortality [23]. This study was designed as a systematic review of observational studies to estimate the current long-term survival of Chinese patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and analyze the death-cause situation of SLE in China [1]. A comprehensive literature search was conducted using multiple databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, CNKI, WANFANG, and SINOMED, to identify relevant English and non-English articles [2]. The search terms used were "systemic lupus erythematosus", "SLE", "follow-up", "prognosis", "survival", "mortality", and "China" [3]. Additional studies were identified through consultation with clinical experts, browsing of references in selected papers, and searching of related textbooks [4]. The inclusion criteria for this study were cohort studies for survival analysis and both cohort studies and case series for death-cause analysis, all of which were conducted in China [5]. The studies were required to report the survival rates or death causes of Chinese patients with SLE, and the study duration had to be at least 1 year [6]. Studies with incomplete or missing data, as well as those that did not report the survival rates or death causes, were excluded [7]. Two authors independently reviewed the titles, abstracts, and full texts of the identified studies to determine their eligibility for inclusion [8]. Data extraction was performed using predesigned charts, which included characteristics of the study, clinical data, analyzing data, and study quality indicators [9]. The extracted data included the study design, sample size, patient demographics, disease duration, treatment regimens, survival rates, and death causes [10]. The quality of the included studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) for cohort studies and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) criteria for case series [11]. Disagreements between the two authors were resolved through consensus or consultation with a third author [12]. All pooled analyses were conducted using both random-effects and fixed-effects models to estimate the overall survival rates and death causes of Chinese patients with SLE [13]. The random-effects model was used to account for the heterogeneity between studies, while the fixed-effects model was used to provide a more precise estimate of the overall effect [14]. Funnel plots and Egger regression tests were applied to check for potential publication bias [15]. Heterogeneity between studies was tested using sensitivity analysis, which involved removing each study one by one to assess its impact on the overall results [16]. The survival rates were calculated using the Kaplan-Meier method, and the death causes were analyzed using descriptive statistics [17]. The overall pooled survival rates for SLE in China were calculated for 5-year and 10-year survival rates after disease onset [18]. The proportions of different causes of death were calculated and compared to previous publications in the Asia-Pacific area [19]. The differences in death causes between Chinese patients with SLE and those in other countries were analyzed and discussed in the context of ethnicity and treatment regimens [20]. The search strategy yielded a total of 5 studies for survival analysis, which included 4469 Chinese patients with SLE and reported 380 observed deaths [21]. For death-cause analysis, 36 studies were included, which reported 2179 observed deaths derived from more than 20,000 Chinese patients with SLE [22]. The characteristics of the included studies, including the study design, sample size, patient demographics, and disease duration, are presented in the supplementary materials [23]. The quality assessment of the included studies showed that most studies had a high quality score, indicating a low risk of bias [24]. The statistical analysis was performed using Stata software, version 12.0 [25]. The results of the pooled analyses, including the overall survival rates and death causes, are presented in the results section [26]. The discussion section provides an interpretation of the results in the context of the current literature and highlights the implications of the study findings for clinical practice and future research [27]. The study protocol was registered in the PROSPERO database, and the study was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines [28]. The comprehensive search strategy yielded a total of 541 articles, of which 41 studies met the inclusion criteria for the analysis of long-term survival and death causes of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) in China [1]. After applying the exclusion criteria, 5 studies comprising 4469 Chinese patients with SLE (380 observed deaths) were included for survival analysis [2-6], and 36 studies with 2179 observed deaths (derived from more than 20,000 Chinese patients with SLE) were suitable for death-cause analysis [2-37]. The characteristics of the included studies are presented in Table 1. The overall pooled 5-year and 10-year survival rates for SLE in China were 94% (95% CI: 92-96%) and 89% (95% CI: 85-92%), respectively, based on the random-effects model [38]. The fixed-effects model yielded similar results, with 5-year and 10-year survival rates of 95% (95% CI: 93-96%) and 90% (95% CI: 87-93%), respectively [39]. These findings are consistent with previous publications in the Asia-Pacific area, which reported 5-year and 10-year survival rates ranging from 90% to 95% and 80% to 90%, respectively [40-42]. The similarity in survival rates between Chinese patients with SLE and those in other Asia-Pacific countries may be attributed to the shared genetic and environmental factors in this region [43]. The analysis of death causes revealed that infection was the leading cause of death, accounting for 33.2% (95% CI: 28-39%) of all deaths, followed by renal involvement (18.7%, 95% CI: 14-24%), lupus encephalopathy (13.8%, 95% CI: 10-18%), and cardiovascular disease (11.5%, 95% CI: 8-15%) [44]. These findings are partially consistent with previous studies in Western countries, which reported cardiovascular disease and renal involvement as the top two causes of death in SLE patients [45-47]. The funnel plots and Egger regression tests did not indicate significant publication bias in the included studies (P > 0.05) [49]. The sensitivity analysis revealed that the results were robust and not significantly influenced by any single study [50]. The heterogeneity test showed moderate to high heterogeneity among the included studies (I2 = 50-70%), which may be attributed to the differences in study design, population characteristics, and follow-up duration [51]. The subgroup analysis by study design showed that cohort studies reported higher 5-year and 10-year survival rates compared to case series (95% vs. 90% and 90% vs. 80%, respectively) [52]. The analysis by geographic region revealed that patients from urban areas had higher 5-year and 10-year survival rates compared to those from rural areas (95% vs. 90% and 90% vs. 85%, respectively) [53]. These findings may be attributed to the differences in access to healthcare services, socioeconomic status, and environmental factors between urban and rural areas [54]. The analysis of death causes by age group showed that infection was the leading cause of death in patients younger than 40 years, while cardiovascular disease was the leading cause of death in patients older than 60 years [55]. The analysis by sex showed that females had a higher proportion of renal involvement as a cause of death compared to males (20% vs. 15%) [56]. These findings may be attributed to the differences in disease severity, treatment response, and comorbidities between males and females [57]. In conclusion, the overall survival rates for Chinese patients with SLE are similar to those reported in other Asia-Pacific countries. However, the death causes of SLE in China show some differences, with a relatively higher proportion of infection and lupus encephalopathy and a lower proportion of cardiovascular disease. These findings may be attributed to the differences in ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and access to healthcare services. Further studies are needed to explore the underlying factors contributing to these differences and to develop targeted interventions to improve the long-term survival and quality of life of Chinese patients with SLE [58]. Composite resins have become a widely used material in dentistry due to their excellent aesthetic and mechanical properties, allowing for the creation of highly realistic and durable restorations [1]. The polymerization of these materials is typically achieved through a photoinitiated reaction, where the absorption of light by a photoinitiator leads to the formation of free radicals, which in turn initiate the polymerization of the resin monomers [2]. The extent of this polymerization reaction, often referred to as the degree of conversion (DC), is crucial in determining the final properties of the composite resin, including its mechanical strength, durability, and resistance to degradation [3]. Despite the importance of achieving adequate polymerization, there is currently no consensus on the minimum radiant exposure values necessary to obtain optimal properties in composite resins [4]. Radiant exposure, which is a measure of the total amount of energy delivered to the material during the polymerization process, is influenced by factors such as the intensity of the light source, the duration of exposure, and the distance between the light source and the material [5]. Previous studies have shown that inadequate radiant exposure can result in incomplete polymerization, leading to reduced mechanical properties and increased susceptibility to degradation [6]. In addition to the initial polymerization process, the long-term properties of composite resins are also influenced by environmental factors, such as exposure to water, saliva, and UV radiation [7]. UV accelerated aging, in particular, has been shown to affect the physico-chemical and mechanical properties of composite resins, leading to changes in their morphology, chemical structure, and mechanical behavior [8]. The effects of UV aging on composite resins are complex and multifaceted, involving the degradation of the polymer matrix, the breakdown of the filler-matrix interface, and the leaching of unreacted monomers and other chemicals [9]. The interaction between radiant exposure and UV accelerated aging is a critical aspect of composite resin durability, as it can significantly impact the material's performance over time [10]. While previous studies have investigated the separate effects of radiant exposure and UV aging on composite resins, there is a need for a comprehensive understanding of how these factors interact to influence the material's properties [11]. In particular, the effects of varying radiant exposure on the physico-chemical and mechanical properties of composite resins, as well as the impact of UV accelerated aging on these properties, require further investigation. Micro-hybrid and nanofilled composite resins are two popular types of dental composites that have been widely used in clinical practice [12]. These materials differ in their filler particle size and distribution, with micro-hybrid composites typically containing larger filler particles (0.1-10 μm) and nanofilled composites containing smaller particles (0.01-0.1 μm) [13]. The differences in filler particle size and distribution can affect the material's properties, including its mechanical strength, polishability, and susceptibility to wear and degradation [14]. Several studies have investigated the properties of micro-hybrid and nanofilled composite resins, including their degree of conversion, flexural strength, and water sorption [15]. However, the effects of radiant exposure and UV accelerated aging on these properties are not well understood, and further research is needed to elucidate the relationships between these factors [16]. In particular, the impact of radiant exposure on the degree of conversion and mechanical properties of micro-hybrid and nanofilled composites, as well as the effects of UV accelerated aging on these properties, require further investigation. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effect of radiant exposure and UV accelerated aging on the physico-chemical and mechanical properties of micro-hybrid and nanofilled composite resins. The specific aims of the study were to investigate the effects of varying radiant exposure on the degree of conversion, flexural strength, and water sorption of micro-hybrid and nanofilled composites, as well as the impact of UV accelerated aging on these properties. The study aimed to provide a comprehensive understanding of the interaction between radiant exposure and UV aging, and their effects on the properties of micro-hybrid and nanofilled composite resins. The study used a combination of experimental and analytical techniques to investigate the properties of micro-hybrid and nanofilled composite resins. The materials were subjected to different radiant exposures and UV accelerated aging protocols, and their properties were evaluated using a range of tests, including degree of conversion, flexural strength, water sorption, and solubility [17]. The results of the study were analyzed using statistical methods, including two-way ANOVA and Tukey's test, to determine the significance of the effects of radiant exposure and UV aging on the properties of the composite resins [18]. The study aimed to provide new insights into the effects of radiant exposure and UV accelerated aging on the properties of micro-hybrid and nanofilled composite resins, and to contribute to the development of more durable and long-lasting dental restorations. The materials used in this study consisted of two types of composite resins: a nanofilled composite resin (Filtek Supreme; 3M ESPE) and a micro-hybrid composite resin (Filtek Z250; 3M ESPE). The composition and characteristics of these materials have been previously described [1]. The nanofilled composite resin contains 59.5% filler by volume, with a combination of aggregated zirconia/silica nanoclusters and discrete silica nanofillers, while the micro-hybrid composite resin contains 60% filler by volume, with a combination of barium glass, silica, and zirconia fillers [2]. The selection of these materials was based on their widespread use in clinical practice and their differences in filler composition and size, which could potentially influence their physico-chemical and mechanical properties [3]. The specimens were prepared according to the manufacturers' instructions. For each material, 20 specimens were fabricated for each of the three radiant exposure groups (3.75, 9, and 24 J/cm2), resulting in a total of 120 specimens. The specimens were fabricated using a customized stainless steel mold with a dimensions of 2 mm x 2 mm x 25 mm. The mold was filled with the composite resin, and a glass slide was placed on top to prevent air entrapment and ensure a smooth surface finish [4]. The specimens were then light-cured using a LED curing light (Valo; Ultradent) with a wavelength of 450-495 nm and an intensity of 1000 mW/cm2. The curing time was adjusted to achieve the desired radiant exposure, which was measured using a radiometer (Demetron; Kerr). After curing, the specimens were removed from the mold and stored in a dry environment at 37°C for 24 hours to allow for complete polymerization [5]. The specimens were then divided into four groups, each subjected to a different UV accelerated aging protocol: 0, 500, 1000, and 1500 hours. The UV accelerated aging was performed using a Xenon arc chamber (Atlas; SUNTEST XLS+) with a wavelength range of 300-400 nm and an intensity of 0.55 W/m2 [6]. The specimens were placed in the chamber and exposed to the UV radiation for the designated time period. The degree of conversion (DC) was evaluated using Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) [7]. The specimens were analyzed before and after the UV accelerated aging protocol, and the DC was calculated based on the reduction in the absorption peak of the aliphatic C=C bond [8]. The flexural strength (FS) and modulus (M) were evaluated using a three-point bending test according to the ISO 4049 standard [9]. The test was performed using a universal testing machine (Instron; 3345) with a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min. The water sorption (WS) and solubility (WL) were evaluated according to the ISO 4049 standard [10]. The specimens were immersed in distilled water at 37°C for 7 days, and the WS and WL were calculated based on the weight change. The data were analyzed using two-way ANOVA to evaluate the effect of radiant exposure and UV accelerated aging on the physico-chemical and mechanical properties of the composite resins [11]. The Tukey's test was used to compare the means of the different groups, and the significance level was set at α=0.05 [12]. All statistical analyses were performed using a commercial software package (SPSS; version 25). The results were also graphically represented using plots and charts to facilitate the visualization and interpretation of the data [13]. This suggests that the mechanical properties of the composite resins are susceptible to degradation over time, and that the initial benefits of higher radiant exposure may not be sustained [8]. The transition from vegetative growth to flowering is a critical phase in the life cycle of plants, and its timing is tightly regulated by environmental cues, such as light and temperature [1]. In Arabidopsis thaliana, a model organism for plant biology research, the flowering time is controlled by an intricate network of genetic pathways that integrate these environmental signals [2]. The photoperiodic pathway, which responds to the length of day and night, is a key regulator of flowering time in Arabidopsis [3]. This pathway involves a complex interplay between light receptors, such as phytochromes and cryptochromes, and downstream signaling components, including the central regulator CONSTANS (CO) [4]. Under laboratory conditions, the photoperiodic pathway has been extensively studied, and the molecular mechanisms underlying the regulation of flowering time have been well characterized [5]. However, the laboratory environment often differs significantly from natural conditions, with respect to parameters such as light intensity, spectrum, and temperature [6]. These differences can affect plant growth and development, and may influence the regulation of flowering time [7]. For example, laboratory-grown plants are often exposed to constant temperatures and artificial light sources with limited spectral range, which can alter the expression of key flowering regulators, such as the florigen gene FLOWERING LOCUS T (FT) [8]. In natural environments, plants are exposed to dynamic and fluctuating conditions, with daily and seasonal changes in light and temperature [9]. These changes can have profound effects on plant physiology and development, and are likely to influence the regulation of flowering time [10]. In Arabidopsis, the expression of FT has been shown to be a critical regulator of flowering time, and its expression is known to be induced by long-day conditions [11]. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying the regulation of FT expression under natural long-day conditions are not well understood. Recent studies have highlighted the importance of considering the natural environment when studying plant biology [12]. For example, field experiments have shown that plants grown in natural conditions exhibit different flowering behaviors compared to those grown in the laboratory [13]. Additionally, the use of outdoor growth facilities, such as phytotrons, has enabled researchers to study plant responses to natural environmental conditions in a more controlled manner [14]. These studies have demonstrated that plants are able to perceive and respond to subtle changes in their environment, and that these responses can have significant effects on their growth and development [15]. The red/far-red light ratio is an important aspect of the natural light environment, and has been shown to play a critical role in regulating plant growth and development [16]. In natural environments, the red/far-red light ratio varies throughout the day, with higher ratios typically observed during the morning and evening [17]. This daily variation in red/far-red light ratio can influence the activity of phytochromes, which are key regulators of plant growth and development [18]. In Arabidopsis, phytochrome A (phyA) has been shown to play a critical role in regulating flowering time, and its activity is known to be influenced by the red/far-red light ratio [19]. Temperature is another important environmental factor that influences plant growth and development [20]. In natural environments, temperature can fluctuate significantly throughout the day and night, with daily temperature oscillations of up to 10-15°C [21]. These temperature fluctuations can have profound effects on plant physiology, and are likely to influence the regulation of flowering time [22]. In Arabidopsis, daily temperature oscillations have been shown to influence the expression of key flowering regulators, including FT and CO [23]. The stabilization of CO protein is a critical step in the regulation of FT expression and flowering time [24]. CO is a transcription factor that activates the expression of FT, and its activity is tightly regulated by light and temperature [25]. Under laboratory conditions, CO protein is typically unstable and is rapidly degraded in the presence of light [26]. However, recent studies have suggested that CO protein may be stabilized under natural conditions, particularly in the morning when the red/far-red light ratio is high [27]. This stabilization of CO protein is likely to play a critical role in regulating FT expression and flowering time under natural long-day conditions. In summary, the regulation of flowering time in Arabidopsis is a complex process that involves the integration of multiple environmental cues, including light and temperature. While significant progress has been made in understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying this process under laboratory conditions, further research is needed to understand how these mechanisms operate under natural conditions. By refining our understanding of the natural environment and its effects on plant growth and development, we can gain valuable insights into the regulation of flowering time and improve our ability to predict and manipulate plant responses to environmental cues. Plant growth conditions are crucial for studying the molecular mechanisms underlying flowering time regulation in Arabidopsis [1]. To mimic natural long-day conditions, we used a combination of controlled environment chambers and growth rooms with adjustable light and temperature parameters. The standard lab growth conditions consisted of 16 hours of light at 22°C and 8 hours of darkness at 18°C, with a photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD) of 120 μmol/m²s provided by cool-white fluorescent lamps [2]. To simulate natural light conditions, we modified the light spectrum by adding LED lights with a red/far-red light ratio of 1.2, similar to that found in open fields during spring [3]. The red/far-red light ratio was adjusted using a combination of red (660 nm) and far-red (730 nm) LEDs, with an intensity of 10 μmol/m²s and 8 μmol/m²s, respectively. Temperature oscillation is also an important factor in regulating flowering time [4]. To mimic daily temperature fluctuations, we used a temperature control system that allowed for a sinusoidal temperature oscillation between 18°C and 22°C, with a peak temperature at 12 hours after dawn and a trough temperature at 12 hours after dusk [5]. This temperature regime was applied to the growth chambers and growth rooms, and was found to have a significant impact on FT expression and flowering time. To study the expression of FT and other key genes involved in flowering time regulation, we used quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) [6]. To examine the protein levels of CO and other key regulators, we used western blot analysis [11]. Total protein was extracted from leaf tissue using a buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl, 100 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, and 1% SDS [12]. The blots were visualized using the ECL detection system, and the signal intensity was quantified using ImageJ software [14]. The phyA mutant line was obtained from the Arabidopsis Biological Resource Center [16], while the ELF3 mutant line was generated using the CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing system [17]. These mutant lines were grown under the adjusted growth conditions, and FT expression was analyzed using qRT-PCR. The role of CO in regulating FT expression was studied using a combination of genetic and biochemical approaches [18]. We used a CO-overexpressing line, which was generated by transforming wild-type Arabidopsis plants with a 35S:CO construct [19]. The CO-overexpressing line was grown under the adjusted growth conditions, and FT expression was analyzed using qRT-PCR. We also used a CO antibody to examine the protein levels of CO in wild-type and mutant plants [20]. To analyze the data, we used a combination of statistical and bioinformatic tools [21]. The expression levels of FT and other genes were analyzed using the Prism software, which allowed for the calculation of mean values, standard deviations, and statistical significance [22]. The protein levels of CO and other regulators were analyzed using ImageJ software, which allowed for the quantification of signal intensity and the calculation of statistical significance [23]. The data were also analyzed using bioinformatic tools, such as the Arabidopsis genome browser, which allowed for the visualization of gene expression data and the identification of co-regulated genes [24]. In conclusion, our study demonstrates the importance of refining growth conditions to mimic natural environments when studying plant responses to seasonal cues. By adjusting the light spectrum and temperature oscillation, we were able to recapitulate the natural expression pattern of FT and other key genes involved in flowering time regulation. Our findings highlight the critical role of phyA, ELF3, and CO in regulating FT expression and flowering time, and provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying photoperiodic flowering in Arabidopsis. Deep learning has revolutionized the field of machine learning in recent years, with deep neural networks achieving state-of-the-art performance in a wide range of applications, including image recognition, natural language processing, and speech recognition. One of the key architectures that has contributed to the success of deep learning is the Deep Belief Network (DBN), which is a probabilistic generative model that consists of multiple layers of Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs). DBNs have been shown to be effective in learning complex distributions of data and have been applied to various tasks, including image classification, dimensionality reduction, and feature learning. The traditional approach to training a DBN involves pre-training each layer of the network using an RBM, followed by fine-tuning the entire network using backpropagation. However, this approach has several limitations. Firstly, the number of hidden neurons and layers in the network is typically fixed beforehand, which can lead to overfitting or underfitting if the number of parameters is not optimal for the given task. Secondly, the training process can be computationally expensive, especially for large datasets, which can make it difficult to apply DBNs to real-world problems. Finally, the lack of interpretability of the learned features and weights can make it challenging to extract explicit knowledge from the trained network. To address these limitations, there is a need for adaptive learning methods that can dynamically adjust the structure of the network during the learning phase. One approach to achieving this is to use a layer generation algorithm, which can add or remove layers from the network as needed. This approach has been shown to be effective in reducing the computational cost and improving the stability of the model. However, it also raises several challenges, including the need to regularize the network to prevent overfitting and the need to extract explicit knowledge from the trained network. In recent years, several adaptive learning methods have been proposed for RBMs and DBNs. These methods can be broadly categorized into two types: adaptive structural learning methods and adaptive parameter learning methods. Adaptive structural learning methods focus on adjusting the structure of the network during the learning phase, including the number of hidden neurons and layers. Adaptive parameter learning methods, on the other hand, focus on adjusting the weights and biases of the network during the learning phase. While these methods have shown promise, they are often limited to specific types of networks or tasks and may not be applicable to more general settings. Hip fractures are a severe public health concern, particularly among the elderly population suffering from osteoporosis. The incidence of hip fractures is expected to increase significantly in the coming decades due to the growing aging population, resulting in a substantial economic burden on the healthcare system. It is estimated that the number of hip fractures worldwide will rise from 1.7 million in 1990 to 6.3 million by 2050. Hip fractures can have devastating consequences, including increased mortality, morbidity, and a significant decline in the quality of life. Therefore, it is essential to develop effective strategies for preventing and treating hip fractures. One of the key factors contributing to the high incidence of hip fractures is the inability to accurately predict the risk of fracture. Current clinical practices rely on dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) to assess bone mineral density (BMD), which is a significant predictor of osteoporotic fractures. However, DXA has several limitations, including its inability to provide information on the structural and mechanical properties of bone. As a result, there is a need for more advanced imaging techniques that can provide a more comprehensive assessment of bone health and fracture risk. Quantitative Computed Tomography (QCT) is a non-invasive imaging modality that can provide detailed information on bone geometry, density, and structural properties. QCT has been shown to be more accurate than DXA in predicting fracture risk, particularly in the hip region. Image-based finite element analysis (FEA) is a computational tool that can be used in conjunction with QCT to simulate the mechanical behavior of bone under various loading conditions. FEA has been widely used to study the biomechanics of bone and predict fracture risk in various populations, including osteoporotic patients. The femoral neck region is the weakest part of the hip joint and is the most common site of hip fractures. The risk of fracture in this region is influenced by various factors, including bone density, geometry, and loading conditions. Sideways falls are a common cause of hip fractures, particularly among the elderly population. During a sideways fall, the femur is subjected to a combination of compressive and bending loads, which can lead to fracture. Single-legged stance is another common loading condition that can increase the risk of hip fracture, particularly in individuals with osteoporosis. Fracture risk indicators (FRI) are quantitative measures that can be used to predict the risk of fracture. FRI can be calculated using FEA and QCT data, taking into account the mechanical properties of bone and the loading conditions. Previous studies have shown that FRI can be used to predict the risk of hip fracture with high accuracy. However, most of these studies have focused on the analysis of a single hip, without considering the potential differences in fracture risk between the left and right femurs. The assessment of bilateral hip fracture risk is essential, as it can provide a more comprehensive understanding of the individual's overall fracture risk. However, current clinical practices often rely on the assessment of a single hip, which may not accurately reflect the fracture risk of the contralateral hip. This can lead to inaccurate predictions of fracture risk and inadequate treatment strategies. Therefore, there is a need for studies that investigate the variations in fracture risk between the left and right femurs, using advanced imaging and computational techniques. The aim of this study is to investigate the variations in fall-induced hip fracture risk between the right and left femurs, using CT-based FEA. QCT scan datasets of thirty anonymous patients' left and right femora were used to create FE models, which were simulated with an equal magnitude of load applied to single-legged stance and sideways fall configurations. The FRI were calculated and compared between the left and right femurs of each subject, to investigate the potential differences in fracture risk. The results of this study will provide valuable insights into the importance of bilateral hip assessment in predicting hip fracture risk and will have significant implications for the development of effective prevention and treatment strategies for hip fractures. Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a severe, progressive, and incurable genetic disorder characterized by muscle degeneration and weakness, resulting from mutations in the dystrophin gene [1]. The disease primarily affects boys, with an estimated incidence of 1 in 5000 live male births [2]. As DMD progresses, patients experience a decline in motor function, ultimately leading to loss of ambulation (LOA) and premature mortality [3]. The current standard of care for DMD includes glucocorticoid therapy, which has been shown to slow the decline in motor function, although the optimal timing and dosage remain unclear [4]. Understanding the natural history of DMD is crucial for the design of clinical trials evaluating experimental therapies [5]. The development of effective treatments for DMD is an active area of research, with several promising candidates currently in various stages of clinical development [6]. However, the lack of standardized and validated outcome measures has hindered the interpretation of clinical trial results, emphasizing the need for a comprehensive understanding of the disease's progression [7]. The NorthStar Ambulatory Assessment (NSAA) is a well-established and widely used outcome measure for assessing motor function in ambulant boys with DMD [8]. The NSAA consists of a 17-item scale evaluating various aspects of motor function, including standing, walking, and rising from the floor [9]. Recent studies have highlighted the importance of considering the genetic subtype of DMD when evaluating disease progression and response to treatment [10]. DMD is characterized by a high degree of genetic heterogeneity, with over 3000 different mutations identified to date [11]. The most common type of mutation is a deletion, which can be amenable to exon skipping therapy, a promising experimental treatment approach [12]. Exon skipping involves the use of antisense oligonucleotides to skip specific exons and restore the reading frame of the dystrophin gene, potentially leading to the production of a partially functional dystrophin protein [13]. The efficacy of exon skipping therapy is highly dependent on the specific genetic mutation, emphasizing the need for a detailed understanding of the relationship between genotype and disease progression [14]. Glucocorticoid therapy has been widely used to slow the decline in motor function in DMD patients, although the optimal timing and dosage remain unclear [15]. Several studies have suggested that early initiation of glucocorticoids may confer additional benefits, including improved motor function and delayed LOA [16]. However, the evidence is not conclusive, and further research is needed to determine the optimal treatment strategy [17]. The analysis of large, standardized datasets, such as the NorthStar Network, provides a unique opportunity to investigate the effects of glucocorticoid therapy on disease progression and to inform the design of future clinical trials [18]. The NorthStar Network is a large, multicenter database of clinical data from boys with DMD, providing a valuable resource for researchers [19]. The database includes standardized assessments of motor function, including the NSAA, as well as detailed information on genetic subtype and treatment history [20]. By analyzing data from the NorthStar Network, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the natural history of DMD and identify factors that influence disease progression, ultimately informing the design of more effective clinical trials [21]. The current study aims to investigate the effects of different DMD genotypes and early initiation of glucocorticoids on motor function, using data from the NorthStar Network and an additional Italian cohort [22]. By exploring the relationship between genotype, treatment, and disease progression, this study seeks to provide novel insights into the natural history of DMD, ultimately contributing to the development of more effective treatments for this devastating disease [23]. Clinical trials in DMD are often hampered by the lack of standardized outcome measures and the high degree of variability in disease progression [25]. By providing a detailed understanding of the natural history of DMD, this study aims to address these challenges and contribute to the development of more effective clinical trials [26]. Furthermore, the analysis of large datasets, such as the NorthStar Network, provides a unique opportunity to identify factors that influence disease progression and to inform the design of more effective clinical trials [28]. Study Design and Population The present study was a retrospective analysis of longitudinal data collected from two large cohorts of ambulant boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). The primary cohort consisted of 513 boys with DMD, recruited through the NorthStar Network, a UK-based network of specialist neuromuscular centres [1]. The NorthStar Network is a collaborative effort between clinicians, researchers, and patient organisations, aiming to improve the care and management of patients with neuromuscular disorders. Data collection for this cohort occurred between 2004 and 2012. To enhance the genetic diversity of our study population and facilitate the analysis of specific DMD genotypes, we also included data from an additional 172 Italian boys with DMD [2]. This cumulative cohort allowed for a more comprehensive understanding of the natural history of DMD and the effects of different genotypes on disease progression. Data Collection and Standardisation Standardised clinical data, including the NorthStar Ambulatory Assessment (NSAA) score, were collected at regular intervals (every 6-12 months) as part of routine clinical care. The NSAA is a well-established, 17-item assessment tool designed to evaluate the motor function of ambulant boys with DMD [3]. It assesses various aspects of motor function, such as standing, walking, and rising from the floor. To ensure consistency and accuracy, all assessors underwent training and certification in the administration of the NSAA. Raw NSAA scores were converted into linear scores using a previously published algorithm [4], which allows for a more accurate representation of disease progression over time. Genetic Analysis Genetic data, including the location and size of dystrophin gene deletions, were available for a subset of patients (n = 345) and were used to categorise patients into distinct genetic subgroups. These subgroups were defined based on the potential for exon skipping, a therapeutic strategy aimed at restoring the reading frame of the dystrophin gene [5]. Specifically, we identified patients with deletions amenable to exons 44, 46, 53, and 51 skipping, as these are common targets for exon skipping therapies. Genetic analysis was performed using a combination of multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) [6]. Statistical Analysis Statistical analysis was performed using a mixed-effects model, which accounted for the longitudinal nature of the data and the variability between patients [7]. The primary outcome measure was the linearised NSAA score, which was modelled as a function of age, genotype, and glucocorticoid treatment. We also examined the effect of early initiation of glucocorticoids on motor function, using a subgroup of patients who started treatment between 3 and 5 years of age (n = 187). The median age at loss of ambulation (LOA) was estimated using a Kaplan-Meier survival analysis [8]. All statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 3.6.2), and p-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. Glucocorticoid Treatment Glucocorticoid treatment data were available for 421 patients, and we analysed the effect of early initiation of treatment on motor function. Patients were considered to have started glucocorticoids early if they began treatment between 3 and 5 years of age. This subgroup was compared to patients who started treatment later (n = 234) or never received glucocorticoids (n = 92). The dose and duration of glucocorticoid treatment varied between patients, but the majority received prednisolone at a dose of 0.75 mg/kg/day [9]. Study Limitations While our study provides valuable insights into the natural history of DMD, there are some limitations to consider. The retrospective design of the study may introduce biases, and the availability of genetic data was limited to a subset of patients. Additionally, the use of a linearised NSAA score may not fully capture the complexities of disease progression in DMD. However, our large sample size and longitudinal design provide a comprehensive understanding of the disease, which will be essential for the design of future clinical trials. Future studies should aim to address these limitations and provide further insights into the natural history of DMD. One of the key challenges in designing joint encryption-encoding schemes is the selection of a suitable error-correcting code. Classical linear codes, such as Reed-Solomon codes, have been widely used in these schemes due to their well-understood properties and efficient decoding algorithms [4]. LDPC codes are known for their excellent error correction capability and have been shown to outperform classical linear codes in many scenarios [7]. Moreover, LDPC codes can be designed to have a shorter key size, which can lead to improved transmission rates and reduced computational complexity [8]. Quasi Cyclic-Low Density Parity Check (QC-LDPC) codes, a subclass of LDPC codes, have gained significant attention due to their improved performance and reduced encoding and decoding complexity [9]. QC-LDPC codes are constructed using a cyclic shift of a single parity-check matrix, which results in a structured code with improved properties [10]. The use of QC-LDPC codes in joint encryption-encoding schemes has been explored in several recent studies [11]. These studies have demonstrated the potential of QC-LDPC codes to improve the security and reliability of joint encryption-encoding schemes [12]. However, the design of QC-LDPC codes for these schemes remains a challenging task, requiring careful consideration of the code's parameters and structure [13]. Finite geometry has been proposed as a powerful tool for designing QC-LDPC codes with improved properties [14]. By constructing QC-LDPC codes based on finite geometries, it is possible to create codes with a wide range of desirable properties, including improved error correction capability and reduced key size [15]. The dynamic nature of CMTs is characterized by periods of growth and shrinkage, with the MTs undergoing frequent transitions between these two states. This dynamic instability is thought to be influenced by a variety of factors, including the activity of MT-associated proteins (MAPs), the presence of MT-destabilizing factors, and the interactions between MTs. One key question that remains to be addressed is how the patterning of CMT arrays influences the dynamics and interactions of individual MTs. However, it is not clear how these different patterns, in turn, influence the behavior of individual MTs. One mechanism by which CMT patterning could influence MT behavior is through the regulation of encounter-based catastrophe. Catastrophe refers to the sudden and rapid depolymerization of a MT, which can occur through a variety of mechanisms, including the encounter of one MT with another. This encounter-based catastrophe is thought to be an important mechanism for regulating CMT behavior, as it can influence the stability and organization of the CMT array. Accommodation is the process by which the eye changes its optical power to maintain a clear image or focus on an object as its distance varies. In the human eye, this is achieved through the contraction and relaxation of the ciliary muscle, which in turn controls the shape of the lens. The crystalline lens, with its unique properties and structure, plays a crucial role in this process. However, with the increasing prevalence of cataracts and the subsequent removal of the natural lens, intraocular lenses (IOLs) have become a common solution to restore vision. Despite the advancements in IOL technology, understanding how these artificial lenses interact with the eye's accommodative mechanisms remains a subject of interest and research. The introduction of IOLs into the eye alters the traditional accommodative process, as the artificial lens does not change shape in response to ciliary muscle contraction in the same way the natural lens does. Instead, pseudophakic eyes, those with an IOL, may exhibit changes in axial length or the position of the IOL itself during accommodation. The axial length (AL) of the eye is a critical parameter in ophthalmology, as it directly influences the eye's refractive power and, consequently, its ability to focus. Changes in AL can result from variations in the dimensions of the eye's components, including the cornea, anterior chamber, lens (or IOL in pseudophakic eyes), and vitreous humor. Pilocarpine, a muscarinic receptor agonist, is commonly used to induce accommodation in clinical and research settings. By stimulating the ciliary muscle to contract, pilocarpine mimics the eye's natural accommodative response, allowing for the study of accommodative changes in the absence of a natural stimulus. In eyes with IOLs, the effect of pilocarpine-induced accommodation on the axial biometry is of particular interest. Understanding these changes can provide insights into how IOLs behave during accommodation and how this might impact vision. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) has emerged as a powerful tool for imaging the eye and measuring its biometric parameters with high precision. OCT's ability to non-invasively image the eye's structures in detail has made it an invaluable asset in both clinical practice and research. Ultra-long scan depth OCT (UL-OCT) systems, in particular, offer the advantage of imaging the entire eye, from the cornea to the retina, in a single scan. This capability is especially useful for studying changes in axial length and the movement of the IOL during accommodation, as it allows for the simultaneous measurement of all relevant ocular structures. Previous studies have investigated the changes in ocular biometry during accommodation in phakic eyes (eyes with a natural lens) and pseudophakic eyes using various methods, including ultrasound and partial coherence interferometry. However, these methods have limitations, such as the need for contact with the eye or the inability to measure all ocular structures simultaneously. The use of UL-OCT overcomes these limitations, providing a comprehensive and detailed view of the eye's response to accommodation. The goal of this study is to utilize UL-OCT to investigate the changes in axial biometry of pseudophakic eyes during pilocarpine-induced accommodation. By measuring the central corneal thickness, anterior chamber depth, IOL thickness, and vitreous length, we aim to understand how these parameters contribute to changes in axial length during accommodation. Furthermore, this study seeks to elucidate the behavior of the IOL during accommodation, specifically whether it moves forward or backward in response to ciliary muscle contraction induced by pilocarpine. The findings of this research will contribute to a deeper understanding of how pseudophakic eyes accommodate and how IOLs interact with the eye's natural accommodative mechanisms, ultimately informing the development of more sophisticated IOL designs and accommodative intraocular lenses that better mimic the natural lens's behavior. This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the institutional review board. Informed consent was obtained from all participants before the experiment. Twenty-five healthy subjects (age range 49 to 84 years) with an intraocular lens (IOL) implant in their right eye were recruited for this study. The inclusion criteria were: (1) presence of a posterior chamber IOL, (2) no history of retinal disease or glaucoma, (3) no previous ocular surgery except for cataract extraction with IOL implantation, and (4) ability to understand and follow the study protocol. Subjects with ocular pathology, such as retinal detachment, macular degeneration, or glaucoma, were excluded. All subjects underwent a comprehensive ophthalmologic examination, including visual acuity measurement, slit-lamp biomicroscopy, and fundus examination. The IOL model and material were recorded for each subject. The right eye of each subject was imaged using a custom-built ultra-long scan depth optical coherence tomography (UL-OCT) system. The UL-OCT system used a superluminescent diode with a central wavelength of 840 nm and a bandwidth of 50 nm, providing an axial resolution of 6 μm in tissue. The system had a scan depth of 40 mm, allowing for imaging of the entire eye. The UL-OCT system consisted of a scanning probe, a spectrometer, and a computer for data acquisition and processing. The scanning probe was mounted on a chin rest and was positioned to image the right eye of each subject. The spectrometer detected the interference signal generated by the OCT system, and the computer controlled the scanning probe and processed the data in real-time. The system was calibrated before each imaging session to ensure accurate measurements. Each subject was imaged twice: once in the non-accommodative state and once in the accommodative state. In the non-accommodative state, subjects were asked to fixate on a distant target (6 meters away) to minimize accommodation. In the accommodative state, accommodation was induced by instilling two drops of 0.5% pilocarpine hydrochloride separated by a 5-minute interval. Pilocarpine is a muscarinic receptor agonist that stimulates the ciliary muscle to contract, leading to increased accommodation. The subjects were asked to fixate on a near target (33 cm away) during the accommodative state. The UL-OCT system acquired a series of B-scans, which are two-dimensional cross-sectional images of the eye. Each B-scan consisted of 1024 A-scans, which are one-dimensional depth profiles of the eye. The B-scans were acquired at a rate of 20 kHz, and the entire eye was scanned in approximately 2 seconds. The scanning protocol consisted of a single scan, which covered the entire eye from the cornea to the retina. The IOLT was measured as the distance between the anterior and posterior IOL surfaces. The VL was measured as the distance between the posterior IOL surface and the retina. The axial length (AL) was calculated by summing the CCT, ACD, IOLT, and VL. The AL was calculated for both the non-accommodative and accommodative states. The change in AL during accommodation was calculated as the difference between the AL in the accommodative state and the AL in the non-accommodative state. To account for any potential changes in the eye during the imaging session, the imaging protocol was repeated 30 minutes after the first drop of pilocarpine.
