Laryngoscopy and orotracheal intubation are essential procedures in the administration of general anesthesia, allowing for the secure management of a patient's airway during surgical operations. However, these procedures can stimulate the sympathetic nervous system, leading to significant increases in blood pressure, heart rate, and cardiac output. This hemodynamic response can be detrimental to patients with pre-existing cardiovascular disease, as it may increase the risk of myocardial ischemia, arrhythmias, and even cardiac arrest. Furthermore, the stress response associated with laryngoscopy and intubation can also lead to increased intracranial pressure, intraocular pressure, and intrathoracic pressure, which can be problematic in patients with certain medical conditions, such as glaucoma, intracranial hypertension, or respiratory disease. To mitigate these adverse effects, anesthesiologists often employ pharmacological strategies to blunt the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and intubation. Various medications have been investigated for this purpose, including opioids, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, and alpha-2 adrenergic agonists. Among these, dexmedetomidine (DEX) and remifentanil (REM) have gained significant attention in recent years due to their unique pharmacological properties. Dexmedetomidine is a highly selective alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that produces sedation, anxiolysis, and analgesia without significant respiratory depression. It also has a sympatholytic effect, which can help to reduce the hemodynamic response to stressful stimuli. Remifentanil, on the other hand, is a potent opioid analgesic with a rapid onset and short duration of action, making it an ideal agent for blunting the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and intubation. The efficacy of DEX and REM in attenuating the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and intubation has been evaluated in several studies. These investigations have demonstrated that both medications can effectively reduce the increases in blood pressure and heart rate associated with these procedures. However, the relative efficacy of DEX and REM in this context is not well established, and there is limited information on the potential benefits of combining these medications. A few studies have suggested that the co-administration of DEX and REM may provide a more effective attenuation of the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and intubation compared to the use of either medication alone. This is potentially due to the synergistic effects of these medications on the sympathetic nervous system and the stress response. The present study aims to compare the efficacy of DEX and REM in blunting the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and orotracheal intubation in patients undergoing elective surgery under general anesthesia. We also sought to investigate the potential benefits of combining these medications, as well as the effects of DEX and REM on arterial oxygen saturation and other hemodynamic variables. To achieve this, we conducted a randomized, double-blind clinical trial in which patients were assigned to receive either DEX, REM, a combination of both medications, or normal saline prior to laryngoscopy and intubation. The primary outcome measures were the changes in blood pressure and heart rate during the peri-intubation period, while secondary outcomes included the effects on arterial oxygen saturation and the incidence of adverse events. The selection of the medications and dosages used in this study was based on the available literature and the pharmacological properties of DEX and REM. Dexmedetomidine was administered at a dose of 1 µg/kg, which is consistent with the recommended dosage for sedation and analgesia in the perioperative period. Remifentanil was also administered at a dose of 1 µg/kg, which is a commonly used dosage for blunting the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and intubation. The combination of DEX and REM was administered at a dose of 0.5 µg/kg each, which is based on the principle of using lower doses of each medication when they are combined to minimize the risk of adverse effects. The study was conducted at Amirkabir Hospital in Arak, Iran, and was approved by the institutional review board and the Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials. The study protocol was designed to ensure the safety and well-being of the patients, and all participants provided informed consent prior to enrollment. The results of this study will provide valuable information on the efficacy and safety of DEX and REM in blunting the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and orotracheal intubation, as well as the potential benefits of combining these medications. This information can be used to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes in the perioperative period. This randomized, double-blind clinical trial was conducted at Amirkabir Hospital, Arak, Iran, and was registered in the Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials with the registration number IRCT2016092722254N1. The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the hospital, and written informed consent was obtained from all participants before enrollment. Patients undergoing elective surgery under general anesthesia were eligible for inclusion in the study. The exclusion criteria included patients with a history of cardiovascular disease, hypertension, or respiratory disease, as well as those with a known allergy to dexmedetomidine or remifentanil. A total of 124 patients were enrolled in the study and were randomly assigned to one of four groups: dexmedetomidine (DEX), remifentanil (REM), a combination of dexmedetomidine and remifentanil (DEX-REM), or normal saline (NS). The randomization was performed using a computer-generated random number table, and the group assignments were kept confidential until the end of the study. Each group consisted of 31 patients. On the day of surgery, patients were transferred to the operating room and were monitored using standard anesthesia monitoring equipment, including electrocardiography, non-invasive blood pressure monitoring, and pulse oximetry. Baseline measurements of blood pressure, heart rate, and arterial oxygen saturation were recorded on arrival to the operating room. Patients were then premedicated with 1 mg of midazolam and 50 μg of fentanyl, and were subsequently induced with 2-3 mg/kg of propofol and 0.5 mg/kg of atracurium. One minute before laryngoscopy and tracheal intubation, patients in the DEX group received 1 μg/kg of dexmedetomidine, patients in the REM group received 1 μg/kg of remifentanil, patients in the DEX-REM group received a mixture of 0.5 μg/kg of dexmedetomidine and 0.5 μg/kg of remifentanil, and patients in the NS group received an equal volume of normal saline. The medications were administered intravenously over a period of 1 minute, and the syringes were prepared by an anesthesiologist who was not involved in the patient's care. Laryngoscopy and tracheal intubation were performed by an experienced anesthesiologist, and the duration of laryngoscopy was recorded. Hemodynamic measurements, including blood pressure, heart rate, and arterial oxygen saturation, were recorded at 1 minute before laryngoscopy, immediately after intubation, and every 5-15 minutes thereafter for a total of 30 minutes. The measurements were recorded by an anesthesiologist who was blinded to the group assignments. The primary outcome measures were the changes in blood pressure and heart rate in response to laryngoscopy and tracheal intubation. The secondary outcome measures included the incidence of hypotension, hypertension, and bradycardia, as well as the need for vasopressor or inotropic support. The data were analyzed using SPSS 18.0, and the results are presented as mean ± standard deviation. The groups were compared using analysis of variance (ANOVA) and the Tukey post-hoc test, and a p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. To ensure the quality of the data, the study was monitored by an independent data monitoring committee, and the data were verified by an independent auditor. The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki, and the rights and welfare of the patients were protected at all times. The results of the study are intended to provide valuable information on the efficacy of dexmedetomidine and remifentanil in blunting the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and tracheal intubation, and to guide clinical practice in the field of anesthesiology. Natural transformation is a fundamental process in prokaryotes that enables the acquisition of exogenous genetic material, driving genome evolution and facilitating the adaptation to changing environments [1]. This process, also known as competence, allows bacteria to take up free DNA molecules from their surroundings, which can then be integrated into the host genome through homologous recombination [2]. The ability to undergo natural transformation is widespread among bacteria, with many species exhibiting this trait, including the model organism Acinetobacter baylyi [3]. The evolutionary benefits of natural transformation are thought to be numerous, including the acquisition of new traits, such as antibiotic resistance or virulence factors, and the repair of damaged DNA [4]. Despite its importance, the selective forces driving the evolution and maintenance of natural transformation remain poorly understood [5]. One hypothesis is that taken-up DNA provides a source of nutrients, such as nucleotides, that can be used by the cell for various metabolic processes [6]. Alternatively, exogenous DNA may serve as a template for DNA repair, allowing cells to maintain genome integrity in the face of damage [7]. However, the relationship between DNA uptake and recombination is complex, and it is unclear whether the benefits of natural transformation are primarily derived from the acquisition of new genetic material or from the use of exogenous DNA as a nutrient source [8]. Acinetobacter baylyi is a naturally competent bacterium that has been extensively studied as a model organism for natural transformation [9]. This species is particularly well-suited for investigating the costs and benefits of natural transformation, as it is able to take up DNA efficiently and integrate it into its genome through homologous recombination [10]. Previous studies have shown that A. baylyi is able to acquire new traits through natural transformation, including antibiotic resistance and virulence factors [11]. However, the immediate effects of DNA uptake and recombination on the fitness of A. baylyi cells are not well understood, particularly in the context of environmental stressors such as UV radiation [12]. UV radiation is a potent inducer of DNA damage, causing the formation of cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and other lesions that can be lethal if not repaired [13]. Bacteria have evolved a range of mechanisms to repair DNA damage, including nucleotide excision repair (NER) and recombinational DNA repair pathways such as RecBCD and RecFOR [14]. However, the interaction between these repair pathways and the process of natural transformation is not well understood, and it is unclear whether the uptake and recombination of exogenous DNA can influence the ability of cells to repair DNA damage [15]. In this study, we investigated the immediate effects of DNA uptake and recombination on the fitness of A. baylyi cells in both benign and genotoxic conditions. We used a combination of head-to-head competition experiments and survival assays to examine the costs and benefits of natural transformation in A. baylyi, and to determine whether the uptake and recombination of exogenous DNA can influence the ability of cells to repair DNA damage. Our results show that DNA uptake provides a fitness benefit to A. baylyi cells independent of UV stress, and that this benefit is unrelated to recombination. In contrast, recombination with taken-up DNA reduces the survival of transformed cells with increasing levels of UV stress, suggesting that this process can interfere with NER and other DNA repair pathways [16]. Overall, our findings provide new insights into the costs and benefits of natural transformation in A. baylyi, and highlight the complex interactions between DNA uptake, recombination, and DNA repair in this model organism. The process of natural transformation is complex and involves multiple steps, including the uptake of exogenous DNA, the processing of this DNA, and its integration into the host genome [17]. The uptake of DNA is mediated by a set of proteins known as the DNA uptake machinery, which recognizes and binds to exogenous DNA molecules [18]. Once bound, the DNA is then transported into the cell through a process known as DNA translocation [19]. The processing of exogenous DNA involves the degradation of any non-homologous regions, as well as the preparation of the DNA for integration into the host genome [20]. The integration of exogenous DNA into the host genome is mediated by the homologous recombination pathway, which involves the formation of a joint molecule between the exogenous DNA and the host genome [21]. The costs and benefits of natural transformation have been the subject of much debate, with some studies suggesting that the process provides a significant fitness benefit to bacteria [22]. However, other studies have suggested that the costs of natural transformation, including the energy required for DNA uptake and integration, may outweigh any potential benefits [23]. The relationship between natural transformation and DNA repair is also complex, with some studies suggesting that exogenous DNA may serve as a template for DNA repair, while others have suggested that the process of natural transformation may actually interfere with DNA repair pathways [24]. In order to fully understand the costs and benefits of natural transformation, it is necessary to investigate the process in a range of different contexts, including in the presence of environmental stressors such as UV radiation [25]. UV radiation is a potent inducer of DNA damage, and bacteria have evolved a range of mechanisms to repair this damage [26]. The interaction between natural transformation and DNA repair is likely to be complex, and further studies are needed to fully understand the relationship between these two processes [27]. The use of A. baylyi as a model organism for natural transformation provides a number of advantages, including the ability to easily manipulate the genome and the presence of a well-characterized DNA uptake machinery [28]. The DNA uptake machinery of A. baylyi is composed of a set of proteins known as the Com system, which recognizes and binds to exogenous DNA molecules [29]. The Com system is highly conserved among bacteria, and is thought to play a key role in the uptake of exogenous DNA [30]. The processing and integration of exogenous DNA in A. baylyi is mediated by a range of enzymes, including the RecA protein, which plays a key role in the homologous recombination pathway [31]. The RecA protein is a key enzyme involved in the homologous recombination pathway, and is responsible for the formation of a joint molecule between the exogenous DNA and the host genome [32]. The RecA protein is highly conserved among bacteria, and is thought to play a key role in the integration of exogenous DNA into the host genome [33]. The interaction between the RecA protein and the DNA uptake machinery is complex, and further studies are needed to fully understand the relationship between these two processes [34]. Overall, the study of natural transformation in A. baylyi provides a unique opportunity to investigate the costs and benefits of this process, and to examine the complex interactions between DNA uptake, recombination, and DNA repair. The use of A. baylyi as a model organism allows for the easy manipulation of the genome, and the presence of a well-characterized DNA uptake machinery provides a number of advantages for the study of natural transformation [35]. Further studies are needed to fully understand the relationship between natural transformation and DNA repair, and to examine the costs and benefits of this process in a range of different contexts [36]. Bacterial strains and growth conditions: All experiments were performed with Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 [1] and its derivatives. Strains were grown in Luria-Bertani (LB) medium or on LB agar plates at 30°C. When required, antibiotics were added at the following concentrations: kanamycin, 50 μg/ml; gentamicin, 10 μg/ml [2]. To investigate the effects of DNA uptake and recombination, we constructed a series of strains with mutations in key genes involved in natural transformation and DNA repair. These included a DNA uptake-deficient strain (ΔcomEA) [3], a recombination-deficient strain (ΔrecA) [4], and strains lacking the RecBCD (ΔrecB, ΔrecC, ΔrecD) and RecFOR (ΔrecF, ΔrecO, ΔrecR) recombinational DNA repair pathways [5, 6]. DNA preparation: Plasmid DNA was isolated using a commercial kit (Qiagen) according to the manufacturer's instructions [7]. Genomic DNA was extracted from A. baylyi using a protocol described previously [8]. DNA concentrations were determined using a spectrophotometer (NanoDrop) and adjusted to 1 μg/μl. For competition experiments, we used a mixture of homologous and heterologous DNA, including plasmid pWH1266 [9] and genomic DNA from Escherichia coli MG1655 [10]. The DNA was added to the bacterial cultures at a final concentration of 1 μg/ml. Competition experiments: To investigate the fitness benefit of DNA uptake, we performed head-to-head competition experiments between DNA uptake-proficient and -deficient strains. Overnight cultures of the two strains were mixed in a 1:1 ratio and incubated in LB medium at 30°C for 24 hours. The cultures were then diluted 1:100 in fresh LB medium and grown for an additional 24 hours. The ratio of the two strains was determined by plating serial dilutions on LB agar plates with and without kanamycin. The fitness benefit of DNA uptake was calculated as the ratio of the DNA uptake-proficient strain to the DNA uptake-deficient strain [11]. UV stress experiments: To examine the effects of UV stress on natural transformation, we exposed bacterial cultures to increasing doses of UV radiation using a UV crosslinker (Stratagene) [12]. The cultures were then incubated in LB medium at 30°C for 30 minutes to allow for DNA repair. The survival of transformed cells was determined by plating serial dilutions on LB agar plates with and without kanamycin. The frequency of transformation was calculated as the number of transformants per total viable cells [13]. Recombination assays: To investigate the effects of recombination on cell survival, we used a recombination assay based on the repair of a UV-induced lesion in the lacZ gene [14]. The assay measures the ability of cells to repair a DNA strand break and restore lacZ function. The frequency of recombination was calculated as the number of lacZ+ colonies per total viable cells [15]. Biochemical assays: To examine the role of RecBCD and RecFOR in natural transformation, we performed biochemical assays to measure the activity of these enzymes. Cell extracts were prepared from A. baylyi using a protocol described previously [16]. The extracts were then incubated with DNA substrates and the products were analyzed by gel electrophoresis [17]. The activity of RecBCD and RecFOR was measured as the amount of DNA substrate converted to product [18]. Statistical analysis: All experiments were performed in triplicate and the results were analyzed using statistical software (R) [19]. The data were tested for significance using a two-tailed t-test or analysis of variance (ANOVA) as appropriate. A p-value of <0.05 was considered significant [20]. The results are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) or standard error (SE) as indicated. Supplementary experiments: Additional experiments were performed to confirm the results and explore the mechanisms underlying the observed phenomena. These included experiments to examine the effects of DNA uptake and recombination on gene expression, protein production, and cellular physiology [21, 22]. The results of these experiments are presented in the supplementary material. To investigate the immediate effects of DNA uptake and recombination on the naturally competent bacterium Acinetobacter baylyi, we conducted a series of experiments in both benign and genotoxic conditions. First, we assessed the fitness benefit of DNA uptake in the absence of external stressors. We competed DNA uptake-proficient (wild-type) and -deficient (ΔcomEA) strains of A. baylyi in a head-to-head competition experiment, where both strains were grown together in the same medium [1]. The results showed that the wild-type strain outcompeted the ΔcomEA strain, indicating a fitness benefit of DNA uptake (Figure 1A). This benefit was observed with both homologous and heterologous DNA, suggesting that the advantage is not limited to the acquisition of specific genetic traits [2]. To determine whether recombination is required for the observed fitness benefit, we repeated the competition experiment using a strain deficient in the RecA protein (ΔrecA), which is essential for homologous recombination [3]. The ΔrecA strain still outcompeted the ΔcomEA strain, indicating that recombination is not necessary for the fitness benefit of DNA uptake

Acute myocardial infarction (AMI), commonly known as a heart attack, is a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, accounting for significant healthcare expenditures and loss of productivity. The burden of AMI is particularly pronounced in low- and middle-income countries, where the epidemiological transition is leading to an increasing prevalence of cardiovascular diseases. In Pakistan, a developing country with a large and growing population, the incidence of AMI is rising alarmingly, with a significant proportion of cases occurring in young individuals. This trend is concerning, as premature AMI can have devastating consequences on the quality of life, productivity, and economic stability of affected individuals and their families. The pathogenesis of AMI is complex and multifactorial, involving the interplay of genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors. While genetic predisposition and family history play a significant role, modifiable risk factors such as diet, physical activity, smoking, and stress are increasingly recognized as critical determinants of AMI risk. Among these, dietary patterns have emerged as a key factor, with certain diets shown to exert protective effects against AMI, while others may increase the risk. The relationship between diet and AMI is complex, with various dietary components, including nutrients, foods, and dietary patterns, influencing the risk of developing cardiovascular disease. In recent years, there has been a shift in focus from individual nutrients to overall dietary patterns, which are thought to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship between diet and disease. Dietary patterns are defined as the habitual consumption of foods and drinks, and they can be characterized using various methods, including factor analysis, cluster analysis, and principal component analysis. These methods allow researchers to identify patterns of dietary intake that are associated with specific health outcomes, including AMI. Several studies have investigated the relationship between dietary patterns and AMI risk in different populations. The most well-known dietary patterns associated with reduced AMI risk are the Mediterranean diet, characterized by high consumption of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and healthy fats, and the DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet, which emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy products. In contrast, the Western diet, characterized by high intake of red meat, processed foods, and refined carbohydrates, has been associated with increased AMI risk. In the context of Pakistan, the relationship between dietary patterns and AMI risk is not well understood. The Pakistani diet is unique, with a mix of traditional and modern foods, and is influenced by cultural, socioeconomic, and regional factors. The country has undergone significant economic and nutritional transitions in recent decades, leading to changes in dietary patterns and an increasing prevalence of obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. However, there is a lack of research on the relationship between dietary patterns and AMI risk in the Pakistani population, particularly in young individuals. Young individuals, defined as those under the age of 45, are an important group to study, as they are more likely to be affected by premature AMI, which can have significant consequences on their quality of life and productivity. The risk factors for AMI in young individuals may differ from those in older individuals, with a greater emphasis on lifestyle factors, such as diet and physical activity. Furthermore, identifying dietary patterns associated with reduced AMI risk in young individuals can inform the development of targeted prevention strategies, which can help to reduce the burden of cardiovascular disease in this population. This study aims to investigate the relationship between major dietary patterns and the risk of AMI in a young, urban Pakistani population. Using a case-control design, we will examine the dietary patterns of individuals who have experienced AMI and compare them with those of healthy controls. We will use a simple food frequency questionnaire to assess dietary intake and factor analysis to identify major dietary patterns. We will also measure a range of biochemical markers, including homocysteine, folate, vitamin B12, blood lead, ferritin, cholesterol, LDL-cholesterol, HDL-cholesterol, and triglycerides, to examine their relationship with dietary patterns and AMI risk. The findings of this study will provide valuable insights into the relationship between dietary patterns and AMI risk in a young, urban Pakistani population and will inform the development of targeted prevention strategies to reduce the burden of cardiovascular disease in this population. This case-control study was conducted at the Aga Khan University Hospital, Karachi, Pakistan, from January 2015 to December 2017. The study population consisted of 203 consecutive patients (146 males and 57 females) with their first acute myocardial infarction (AMI) and age below 45 years. Patients were enrolled within 24 hours of admission to the hospital with informed consent. The diagnosis of AMI was confirmed by the presence of at least two of the following three criteria: typical chest pain, elevated cardiac biomarkers (troponin T or creatine kinase-MB), and electrocardiographic changes (ST-segment elevation or depression, Q-waves, or T-wave inversion). Patients with a history of previous AMI, coronary artery bypass grafting, or percutaneous coronary intervention were excluded from the study. Similarly, 205 healthy adults (143 males and 62 females) were included as controls. Controls were selected from the community and were matched with cases for age (within 3 years) and gender. Controls were free from any known cardiovascular disease, as confirmed by a detailed medical history and physical examination. Informed consent was obtained from all controls before enrollment. Dietary intake of both cases and controls was assessed using a simple 14-item food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) developed and validated for the Pakistani population. The FFQ included questions on the consumption of common food items, such as fruits, vegetables, legumes, whole grains, meat, fish, eggs, dairy products, and beverages. Participants were asked to report their average consumption of each food item over the past year, using a serving size chart to help estimate portion sizes. The FFQ was administered by trained interviewers, and responses were recorded on a standardized form. To identify major dietary patterns, factor analysis was performed on the FFQ data. Principal component analysis (PCA) was used to extract factors, and the number of factors to retain was determined by the scree plot and eigenvalues greater than 1. Factors were rotated using varimax rotation to simplify the factor structure and improve interpretability. Factor scores were calculated for each participant, and the resulting dietary patterns were labeled based on the food items that loaded heavily on each factor. Fasting plasma/serum samples were collected from both cases and controls and analyzed for various biochemical markers. Homocysteine, folate, and vitamin B12 levels were measured using automated immunoassays (Abbott Laboratories, USA). Blood lead (Pb) levels were measured using atomic absorption spectroscopy (PerkinElmer, USA). Ferritin, cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, and triglycerides were measured using automated clinical chemistry analyzers (Roche Diagnostics, Germany). Data were analyzed using SPSS version 23 (IBM, USA). Descriptive statistics, such as means and standard deviations, were calculated for continuous variables, and frequencies and percentages were calculated for categorical variables. Differences in demographic and biochemical characteristics between cases and controls were compared using independent samples t-tests and chi-square tests, respectively. To predict the association of dietary patterns with AMI, conditional logistic regression analysis was performed. The dependent variable was AMI (yes/no), and the independent variables were the factor scores for each dietary pattern. Potential confounding variables, such as age, gender, smoking, physical activity, and family history of cardiovascular disease, were also included in the model. Odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated to estimate the strength and direction of associations. A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. The study protocol was approved by the Ethical Review Committee of the Aga Khan University, Karachi, Pakistan. Informed consent was obtained from all participants before enrollment, and confidentiality of participant data was maintained throughout the study. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and the International Conference on Harmonisation (ICH) Good Clinical Practice (GCP) guidelines. The dietary patterns of the study population were identified using factor analysis, which revealed three major patterns: prudent dietary pattern, combination dietary pattern, and western dietary pattern. The prudent dietary pattern was characterized by high consumption of legumes, vegetables, wheat, chicken, and fruits, and explained 23.1% of the variance in dietary intake. The combination dietary pattern, which explained 18.5% of the variance, was characterized by high intake of eggs, fish, fruits, juices, and coffee. The western dietary pattern, which explained 14.2% of the variance, was characterized by high intake of meat, fish, and tea with milk. The distribution of the study population according to the tertiles of the dietary patterns is shown in Table 1. The majority of the cases (63.1%) were in the lowest tertile of the prudent dietary pattern, while the majority of the controls (61.5%) were in the highest tertile. In contrast, the majority of the cases (55.2%) were in the highest tertile of the western dietary pattern, while the majority of the controls (53.2%) were in the lowest tertile. The association between the dietary patterns and the risk of acute myocardial infarction (AMI) was assessed using conditional logistic regression. After adjusting for age, sex, and other potential confounders, the results showed that consumption of a prudent dietary pattern was significantly associated with a decreased risk of AMI. The odds ratio (OR) for the highest tertile of the prudent dietary pattern was 0.43 (95% CI: 0.24-0.77) compared to the lowest tertile. This association was dose-dependent, with a significant trend of decreasing risk with increasing consumption of the prudent dietary pattern (p for trend = 0.001). Moderate to high consumption of the combination dietary pattern was also associated with a decreased risk of AMI. The OR for the middle tertile of the combination dietary pattern was 0.63 (95% CI: 0.39-1.02) compared to the lowest tertile, while the OR for the highest tertile was 0.56 (95% CI: 0.33-0.95). However, the association between the combination dietary pattern and AMI risk was not dose-dependent, and the trend was not significant (p for trend = 0.12). In contrast, no significant association was observed between the western dietary pattern and the risk of AMI. The OR for the highest tertile of the western dietary pattern was 1.13 (95% CI: 0.67-1.91) compared to the lowest tertile, and the trend was not significant (p for trend = 0.63). The results of the conditional logistic regression analysis are shown in Table 2. The models were adjusted for age, sex, smoking status, physical activity level, family history of cardiovascular disease, and socioeconomic status. The results showed that the association between the prudent dietary pattern and AMI risk was independent of these potential confounders. The association between the combination dietary pattern and AMI risk was also independent of these confounders, although the OR was slightly attenuated after adjustment. The biochemical markers of the study population are shown in Table 3. The cases had significantly higher levels of homocysteine, blood lead, and triglycerides, and lower levels of folate, vitamin B12, and HDL-cholesterol compared to the controls. The prudent dietary pattern was significantly associated with lower levels of homocysteine and blood lead, and higher levels of folate and vitamin B12. The combination dietary pattern was significantly associated with lower levels of triglycerides and higher levels of HDL-cholesterol. The results of this study suggest that consumption of a prudent dietary pattern, characterized by high intake of legumes, vegetables, wheat, chicken, and fruits, is protective against the risk of premature AMI in a Pakistani population. The study also suggests that moderate to high consumption of a combination dietary pattern, characterized by high intake of eggs, fish, fruits, juices, and coffee, may also be protective against AMI risk. However, the study found no significant association between the western dietary pattern, characterized by high intake of meat, fish, and tea with milk, and AMI risk. These findings are consistent with previous studies that have shown that a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains can reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. The study's findings have important implications for the prevention of premature AMI in Pakistan, where the disease is a major public health problem. The ability to learn from experience and adapt to changing environments is a fundamental aspect of intelligent behavior. This process, often referred to as learning from feedback, allows individuals to refine their decisions and improve their performance over time. In order to understand the neural mechanisms underlying this process, researchers have focused on the neural correlates of decision-making and the ways in which the brain evaluates the outcome of past choices. One brain region that has been implicated in this process is the ventral premotor cortex (PMv), a area known to be involved in a range of cognitive and motor functions, including perceptual decision-making. Previous studies have shown that neurons in the PMv represent several elements of perceptual decisions, including the sensory evidence, the chosen action, and the expected outcome. However, one of the most striking findings to emerge from this research is that, after the outcome of the choice is known, neurons in the PMv encode all the information necessary for evaluating the decision process. This includes information about the accuracy of the decision, the level of confidence in the choice, and the magnitude of the reward or penalty associated with the outcome. These results suggest that the PMv may play a critical role in evaluating the decision process and using this information to guide future behavior. The idea that the PMv is involved in evaluating the decision process and shaping future behavior is consistent with a number of other lines of evidence. For example, studies have shown that the PMv is active not only during the execution of a decision, but also during the period following the outcome, when the individual is evaluating the consequences of their choice. For example, the PMv receives input from the prefrontal cortex, which is involved in working memory and executive control, and sends output to the basal ganglia, which is involved in motor control and habit formation. In particular, it is unclear how the PMv uses information about past outcomes to guide future decisions, and how this process is reflected in the activity of individual neurons. Polar codes have emerged as a promising class of error-correcting codes, which can achieve the capacity of a binary-input discrete memoryless channel with efficient encoding and decoding algorithms. The successive cancellation (SC) decoding algorithm, proposed by Arıkan in his seminal paper, is a low-complexity decoding method that can be used to decode polar codes. However, the SC decoding algorithm has a major drawback: an incorrect estimate of any prior unfrozen bit can lead to severe error propagation in the following decoding process. This error propagation can significantly degrade the performance of the SC decoding algorithm, especially at high signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs). To mitigate the error propagation problem, several improved decoding algorithms have been proposed, including the successive cancellation list (SCL) decoding algorithm and the cyclic redundancy check (CRC) aided SCL (CA-SCL) decoding algorithm. The SCL decoding algorithm improves upon the SC decoding algorithm by maintaining a list of candidate decoding paths, rather than just a single path. This allows the SCL decoding algorithm to correct some errors that would have caused the SC decoding algorithm to fail. The CA-SCL decoding algorithm further improves upon the SCL decoding algorithm by using a CRC to aid in the selection of the correct decoding path from the list of candidates. While the SCL and CA-SCL decoding algorithms can significantly improve upon the performance of the SC decoding algorithm, they come at a cost. The SCL decoding algorithm has a higher computational complexity than the SC decoding algorithm, especially for large list sizes. The CA-SCL decoding algorithm also has a higher computational complexity than the SC decoding algorithm, due to the need to compute the CRC for each candidate decoding path. Furthermore, the CA-SCL decoding algorithm requires the use of a CRC, which can add overhead to the communication system. Recently, a new class of decoding algorithms, known as bit-flipping decoding algorithms, has been proposed for polar codes. Bit-flipping decoding algorithms work by identifying and correcting errors in the decoding process, rather than trying to avoid errors altogether. The basic idea behind bit-flipping decoding algorithms is to construct a critical set of unfrozen bits, which with high probability includes the bit where the first error occurs. The decoder then flips the bits in the critical set, one at a time, and checks if the resulting decoding path is valid. If a valid decoding path is found, the decoder outputs the corresponding codeword. Otherwise, the decoder continues to flip bits until a valid decoding path is found or a maximum number of iterations is reached. Bit-flipping decoding algorithms have been shown to have a number of advantages over traditional decoding algorithms, including low computational complexity and high performance. However, existing bit-flipping decoding algorithms have a number of limitations. For example, most existing bit-flipping decoding algorithms are only able to correct a single error, which can limit their performance in noisy channels. Furthermore, existing bit-flipping decoding algorithms often require the use of a complex critical set construction algorithm, which can add overhead to the decoder. In this paper, we propose a progressive multi-level bit-flipping decoding algorithm for polar codes, which can correct multiple errors over multiple-layer critical sets. The proposed algorithm works by constructing a critical set of unfrozen bits, which with high probability includes the bit where the first error occurs. The decoder then flips the bits in the critical set, one at a time, and checks if the resulting decoding path is valid. If a valid decoding path is found, the decoder outputs the corresponding codeword. Otherwise, the decoder continues to flip bits until a valid decoding path is found or a maximum number of iterations is reached. The key innovation of the proposed algorithm is the use of multiple-layer critical sets, which allows the decoder to correct multiple errors in a progressive manner. The proposed algorithm has a number of advantages over existing decoding algorithms. For example, the proposed algorithm has a low computational complexity, similar to that of the SC decoding algorithm, making it suitable for use in resource-constrained communication systems. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm can correct multiple errors, which can significantly improve its performance in noisy channels. The proposed algorithm also does not require the use of a CRC, which can reduce overhead in the communication system. Finally, the proposed algorithm can be easily parallelized, which can further improve its performance in practice. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In the next section, we review the basics of polar codes and the SC decoding algorithm. We then describe the proposed progressive multi-level bit-flipping decoding algorithm in detail, including the critical set construction algorithm and the bit-flipping decoding process. We also provide simulation results, which demonstrate the performance of the proposed algorithm in a variety of scenarios. Finally, we conclude the paper with a discussion of the advantages and limitations of the proposed algorithm, as well as directions for future research. To construct the critical set $S$ of unfrozen bits, we start by analyzing the error propagation behavior in SC polar decoding. Given a polar code of length $N$ and dimension $K$, the decoding process can be represented as a binary tree with $N$ leaves, each corresponding to a received symbol. The unfrozen bits are located at the leaf nodes, and the frozen bits are located at the internal nodes. When an error occurs in the decoding of an unfrozen bit, it can propagate to the subsequent bits, leading to a large number of errors. To identify the critical set $S$, we consider the following two factors: (1) the error probability of each unfrozen bit, and (2) the number of subsequent bits that can be affected by an error in each unfrozen bit. We define the error probability of each unfrozen bit as the probability that the bit is decoded incorrectly, given that all previous bits have been decoded correctly. This probability can be estimated using the Bhattacharyya parameter, which is a measure of the reliability of each bit. The Bhattacharyya parameter $Z(W)$ of a binary symmetric channel $W$ is defined as $Z(W) = \sum{y} \sqrt{W(y|0)W(y|1)}$. For a polar code, the Bhattacharyya parameter of each bit channel can be calculated recursively using the formula $Z(Wi) = 2^{1-2i}Z(W{2i-1})Z(W{2i})$, where $Wi$ is the bit channel corresponding to the $i$-th unfrozen bit. To calculate the number of subsequent bits that can be affected by an error in each unfrozen bit, we consider the decoding tree of the polar code. For each unfrozen bit, we count the number of leaf nodes that are descended from the node corresponding to the bit. This count represents the number of subsequent bits that can be affected by an error in the bit. By combining the error probability and the count of affected bits, we can identify the critical set $S$ of unfrozen bits that are most likely to cause error propagation. The critical set $S$ is constructed by selecting the top $|S|$ unfrozen bits with the highest error probability and the largest number of affected bits. The size of the critical set $|S|$ is a design parameter that can be chosen based on the desired trade-off between error correction capability and computational complexity. In our simulations, we choose $|S|$ to be around $10\%$ of the number of unfrozen bits, which provides a good balance between error correction capability and complexity. Once the critical set $S$ is constructed, we develop a progressive multi-level bit-flipping decoding algorithm to correct multiple errors over the multiple-layer critical sets. The basic idea of the algorithm is to iteratively flip the bits in the critical set $S$ and re-decode the polar code to check if the error can be corrected. If the error is corrected, the algorithm moves on to the next layer of critical sets. If the error cannot be corrected, the algorithm backtracks and tries a different bit-flipping combination. The progressive bit-flipping decoding algorithm consists of the following steps: (1) initialization: initialize the critical set $S$ and the number of layers $L$; (2) layer construction: construct the multiple-layer critical sets $S1, S2, ..., SL$ using the remaining undecoded subtree associated with the previous layer; (3) bit-flipping: for each layer $l$, flip each bit in the critical set $Sl$ and re-decode the polar code; (4) error checking: check if the error is corrected after each bit-flipping operation; (5) backtracking: if the error cannot be corrected, backtrack and try a different bit-flipping combination; (6) termination: terminate the algorithm when the maximum number of layers $L$ is reached or when the error is corrected. The level of the progressive bit-flipping decoder indicates the number of independent errors that can be corrected. For example, a level 4 progressive bit-flipping decoder can correct up to 4 independent errors. Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales, affecting approximately 2-3% of the global population [1]. The pathogenesis of psoriasis involves a complex interplay between immune cells, keratinocytes, and environmental factors, leading to an abnormal immune response and subsequent epidermal hyperplasia [2]. Histological changes of psoriasis include invasion of neutrophils into the epidermis and formation of Munro abscesses in the epidermis, which are collections of neutrophils in the stratum corneum [3]. Neutrophils are the predominant white blood cells in circulation when stimulated; they discharge the abundant myeloperoxidase (MPO) enzyme that uses hydrogen peroxide to oxidize chloride for killing ingested bacteria [4]. MPO is a key component of the neutrophil's arsenal against microbial invasion, and its release can lead to the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which can cause tissue damage and contribute to the development of inflammatory diseases [5]. The role of neutrophils in psoriasis has been extensively studied, and it is now well established that these cells play a crucial role in the initiation and maintenance of the disease [6]. Neutrophils are recruited to the skin through the action of various chemokines and cytokines, including interleukin-8 (IL-8) and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) [7]. Once in the skin, neutrophils release a range of pro-inflammatory mediators, including MPO, which can contribute to the development of psoriatic lesions [8]. MPO has been shown to be elevated in the serum and skin of patients with psoriasis, and its levels have been correlated with disease severity [9]. Furthermore, MPO has been implicated in the degradation of the skin's extracellular matrix, leading to the formation of psoriatic lesions [10]. In addition to MPO, inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) has also been implicated in the pathogenesis of psoriasis [11]. iNOS is an enzyme that catalyzes the production of nitric oxide (NO) from the amino acid L-arginine [12]. NO is a potent vasodilator and has been shown to play a role in the regulation of inflammation and immune responses [13]. In psoriasis, iNOS is overexpressed in lesional skin, leading to an increase in NO production [14]. This can contribute to the development of psoriatic lesions through the promotion of angiogenesis, the enhancement of immune cell recruitment, and the modulation of keratinocyte proliferation [15]. Furthermore, NO has been shown to stimulate the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including TNF-α and IL-1β, which can further exacerbate the disease [16]. The relationship between MPO and iNOS in psoriasis is complex and not fully understood. However, it is thought that the release of MPO from neutrophils can stimulate the production of iNOS, leading to an increase in NO production [17]. This can create a vicious cycle of inflammation and oxidative stress, contributing to the development and maintenance of psoriatic lesions [18]. Therefore, understanding the contribution of MPO and iNOS to the pathogenesis of psoriasis is crucial for the development of effective therapeutic strategies. This study aims to investigate the contribution of neutrophils to the pathogenesis of psoriasis at the blood and tissue levels through MPO and iNOS. By examining the levels of MPO and iNOS in the serum and skin of patients with psoriasis, we hope to gain a better understanding of the role of these enzymes in the disease and identify potential targets for therapy. The diagnosis of psoriasis is typically based on clinical presentation, with characteristic features including well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales [19]. However, the disease can be heterogeneous, and various subtypes have been identified, including plaque psoriasis, guttate psoriasis, and pustular psoriasis [20]. The chronic plaque form of psoriasis is the most common subtype, accounting for approximately 90% of cases [21]. This subtype is characterized by the presence of well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales, typically affecting the elbows, knees, and scalp [22]. The pathogenesis of chronic plaque psoriasis is complex and involves a range of immune cells, including T cells, dendritic cells, and neutrophils [23]. The disease is thought to be triggered by a combination of genetic and environmental factors, including stress, infection, and trauma [24]. In recent years, a range of therapeutic options has become available for the treatment of psoriasis, including topical corticosteroids, vitamin D analogs, and biologic agents [25]. These therapies can be effective in reducing disease severity and improving quality of life; however, they are often associated with significant side effects and can be costly [26]. Therefore, there is a need for the development of new therapeutic strategies that can effectively target the underlying mechanisms of the disease. By understanding the contribution of MPO and iNOS to the pathogenesis of psoriasis, we hope to identify potential targets for therapy and contribute to the development of more effective treatments for this debilitating disease. This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the institutional review board [1]. A total of 50 adult patients with a chronic plaque form of psoriasis and 25 healthy controls were enrolled in this study. The diagnosis of psoriasis was based on clinical and histological findings [2]. Patients with a history of psoriatic arthritis, other autoimmune diseases, or those who had received systemic treatment for psoriasis within the past 3 months were excluded from the study [3]. The control group consisted of healthy individuals with no history of psoriasis or other skin diseases. Blood samples were collected from all participants and serum was separated and stored at -80°C until analysis [4]. Serum myeloperoxidase (MPO) and inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) levels were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits (R&D Systems, Minneapolis, MN, USA) according to the manufacturer's instructions [5]. The sensitivity of the MPO ELISA kit was 0.15 ng/mL and the intra-assay and inter-assay coefficients of variation were 4.5% and 6.2%, respectively. The sensitivity of the iNOS ELISA kit was 0.31 ng/mL and the intra-assay and inter-assay coefficients of variation were 5.1% and 7.5%, respectively. Two biopsy specimens were taken from each patient, one from the center of the lesion and one from uninvolved skin, using a 4-mm punch biopsy needle [6]. The biopsy specimens were fixed in 10% formalin and embedded in paraffin wax. Sections of 4-μm thickness were cut and mounted on glass slides. Immunohistochemistry was performed using a streptavidin-biotin-peroxidase complex method [7]. The primary antibodies used were mouse monoclonal anti-MPO (Dako, Glostrup, Denmark) and rabbit polyclonal anti-iNOS (Abcam, Cambridge, UK) [8]. The secondary antibodies used were biotinylated goat anti-mouse and goat anti-rabbit (Vector Laboratories, Burlingame, CA, USA) [9]. The chromogen used was 3,3'-diaminobenzidine (DAB) and the sections were counterstained with hematoxylin [10]. The immunohistochemical staining was evaluated by two independent observers using a semi-quantitative scoring system [11]. The intensity of staining was scored as 0 (no staining), 1 (weak staining), 2 (moderate staining), and 3 (strong staining). The percentage of positively stained cells was also estimated and scored as 0 (0-10%), 1 (11-25%), 2 (26-50%), and 3 (51-100%) [12]. The scores for intensity and percentage of positively stained cells were multiplied to give a final score ranging from 0 to 9. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS software (version 22.0, IBM, Armonk, NY, USA) [13]. The serum MPO and iNOS levels were compared between patients with psoriasis and healthy controls using the Mann-Whitney U test [14]. The immunohistochemical staining scores were compared between lesional and non-lesional skin using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test [15]. The study was also powered to detect a significant difference in immunohistochemical staining scores between lesional and non-lesional skin, assuming a mean difference of 2 scores and a standard deviation of 1 score [19]. Immunohistochemistry was performed on both normal and psoriasis vulgaris biopsies using specific antibodies against MPO and iNOS [3]. The results showed intense staining of leukocytes with MPO in psoriatic skin, particularly in the epidermis and dermis, whereas minimal staining was observed in uninvolved skin (p < 0.01) [4]. A significant positive correlation was found between serum MPO levels and PASI score (r = 0.63, p < 0.01), indicating that higher MPO levels are associated with more severe disease [9]. In contrast, no significant correlation was found between serum iNOS levels and PASI score (r = 0.23, p = 0.12). The expression of MPO and iNOS in psoriatic skin was also compared with clinical parameters, such as age, sex, and disease duration [10]. The results showed that MPO expression was significantly higher in patients with longer disease duration (p < 0.05), whereas iNOS expression was not significantly associated with any clinical parameter [11]. These findings suggest that MPO may play a more significant role in the chronic inflammation and tissue damage observed in psoriasis. Overall, the results of this study demonstrate that neutrophils in psoriasis lesions are actively producing MPO, which may contribute to the pathogenesis of the disease [12]. The significant correlation between MPO and iNOS expression in psoriatic skin suggests that targeting MPO or its synthesis may be a potential therapeutic strategy for the treatment of psoriasis [13]. Early detection and accurate staging of oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma (OTSCC) are crucial for determining the optimal treatment approach and improving patient outcomes [2]. Tumor thickness (TT) is a significant prognostic factor in OTSCC, as it has been shown to correlate with the risk of lymph node metastasis and local recurrence [3]. The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) staging system for OTSCC is primarily based on the size of the primary tumor (T stage) and the presence of lymph node metastasis (N stage) [4]. However, the current AJCC staging system does not take into account the thickness of the tumor, which can be a critical factor in determining the extent of surgical resection and the need for adjuvant therapy. Several studies have demonstrated that preoperative assessment of TT can help identify patients with early OTSCC who are at high risk of occult nodal metastasis, thereby guiding the decision for elective neck dissection [5, 6]. Traditionally, TT has been measured intraoperatively or postoperatively from the resected specimen, which limits its utility in preoperative planning [7]. In recent years, ultrasonography (USG) has emerged as a non-invasive and cost-effective imaging modality for evaluating TT in patients with OTSCC [8]. USG has been shown to provide accurate measurements of TT, which correlate well with histopathological measurements [9]. Moreover, USG can be performed in the outpatient setting, making it a convenient tool for preoperative assessment. The use of USG for TT evaluation has several advantages over other imaging modalities, such as computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) [10]. USG is a rapid and relatively inexpensive procedure that does not expose patients to ionizing radiation [11]. Additionally, USG can provide real-time imaging, allowing for accurate measurement of TT and assessment of the relationship between the tumor and surrounding tissues [12]. However, the accuracy of USG for TT measurement can be affected by several factors, including the skill of the operator, the quality of the equipment, and the presence of artifacts [13]. Despite the potential benefits of USG for TT evaluation, there is limited evidence on its predictive capacity in detecting nodal metastasis in patients with early OTSCC [14]. Several studies have suggested that a TT of 4 mm or greater is associated with an increased risk of occult nodal metastasis [15, 16]. However, the optimal cutoff value for TT that predicts nodal metastasis remains unclear, and further research is needed to establish a reliable threshold. Furthermore, the relationship between TT and other prognostic factors, such as tumor grade and lymphovascular invasion, requires further investigation [17]. In the present study, we aimed to assess the statistical correlation between TT measured by USG and microscopic measurement in patients with early OTSCC. We also sought to evaluate the predictive capacity of TT by USG in detecting nodal metastasis and to identify the optimal cutoff value for TT that predicts nodal metastasis. Our study provides new insights into the role of USG in the preoperative evaluation of OTSCC and has implications for the management of patients with this disease. The findings of our study contribute to the growing body of evidence on the use of USG for TT evaluation and highlight the importance of accurate preoperative assessment in determining the optimal treatment approach for patients with OTSCC. The management of OTSCC involves a multidisciplinary approach, including surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy [18]. Accurate preoperative staging is essential for determining the extent of surgical resection and the need for adjuvant therapy [19]. Elective neck dissection is often performed in patients with early OTSCC to prevent regional recurrence and improve survival [20]. However, the decision to perform elective neck dissection is based on various factors, including the size and thickness of the primary tumor, the presence of lymph node metastasis, and the overall health of the patient [21]. The use of USG for TT evaluation can provide valuable information for guiding the decision for elective neck dissection and can help identify patients who are at high risk of occult nodal metastasis. In conclusion, the preoperative evaluation of TT by USG is a promising approach for guiding the management of patients with early OTSCC. This prospective study was conducted over a period of two years, from 2012 to 2013, and included 24 patients diagnosed with early oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma (OTSCC) [1]. The inclusion criteria were patients with a confirmed diagnosis of OTSCC, clinically staged as T1 or T2, and N0, with no evidence of distant metastasis [2]. Patients with a history of previous head and neck cancer, or those who had received prior treatment for OTSCC, were excluded from the study. Patient Selection and Preparation All patients underwent a thorough clinical examination, including a complete head and neck examination, and a biopsy to confirm the diagnosis of OTSCC. The biopsy samples were reviewed by a experienced pathologist to confirm the diagnosis and grade the tumor [3]. The patients were then scheduled for preoperative ultrasonography (USG) to evaluate the tumor thickness (TT) and nodal status. The USG examination was performed by a single experienced radiologist, using a high-frequency linear probe (12-15 MHz) [4]. The patients were positioned in a supine position, with the tongue protruded, and the USG probe was placed on the surface of the tongue to obtain the images. Ultrasonography Protocol The USG examination protocol included the evaluation of the primary tumor, as well as the cervical lymph nodes. The primary tumor was evaluated in both the longitudinal and transverse planes, and the TT was measured from the surface of the tongue to the deepest point of the tumor [5]. The TT was measured in millimeters, and the measurements were recorded and stored for further analysis. The cervical lymph nodes were evaluated in the transverse plane, and the presence or absence of nodal metastasis was noted [6]. Surgical Procedure After the preoperative USG examination, all patients underwent resection of the primary tumor, and an ipsilateral elective neck dissection (Level I-IV) [7]. The surgical procedure was performed by a single experienced surgeon, and the resected specimen was sent for histopathological examination. The TT was measured intraoperatively from the fresh glossectomy specimen, and postoperatively from the histopathological paraffin section examination [8]. Histopathological Examination The resected specimen was examined by a experienced pathologist, who measured the TT from the surface of the tongue to the deepest point of the tumor [9]. The TT was measured in millimeters, and the measurements were recorded and stored for further analysis. The presence or absence of nodal metastasis was also noted, and the nodal status was correlated with the preoperative USG findings [10]. Data Analysis The statistical correlation between the TT measured by USG and histopathology was assessed using Pearson's correlation coefficient [11]. The chi-square test was used to find the association between the pathological T stage, TT, and nodal status [12]. The interclass correlation coefficient (ICC) was calculated to assess the agreement between the USG and histopathological measurements [13]. The average difference between the microscopic and USG thickness (bias) was calculated, and the limits of agreement were determined [14]. The rate of occult nodal metastasis was calculated, and the predictive capacity of TT by USG in detecting nodal metastasis was assessed [15]. Statistical Software The statistical analysis was performed using the Statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS) version 20.0 [16]. The level of significance was set at p < 0.05, and the confidence interval was set at 95% [17]. The study was approved by the institutional review board, and informed consent was obtained from all patients prior to the study [18]. The study population consisted of 24 patients with early oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma (OTSCC) who underwent preoperative ultrasonography for tumor thickness evaluation. The mean age of the patients was 45.6 years (range, 25-65 years), with a male-to-female ratio of 1.5:1. The clinical characteristics of the patients are summarized in Table 1. All patients had a confirmed diagnosis of OTSCC based on histopathological examination of incisional biopsy specimens. Tumor thickness measurements were obtained using ultrasonography (USG) and compared with microscopic measurements. The mean tumor thickness measured by USG was 4.23 mm (range, 1.5-8.2 mm), while the mean microscopic measurement was 4.51 mm (range, 1.8-9.1 mm). A significant statistical correlation was observed between the two measurements, with a Pearson's correlation coefficient (r) of 0.678 (P < 0.001) [1]. The interclass correlation coefficient (ICC) was 0.808, indicating excellent agreement between the two measurements [2]. The average difference between microscopic and USG thickness (bias) was -0.14637, with 95% limits of agreement ranging from -4.863 to 4.717. The difference between USG and microscopic measurements was within 1 mm in 37.5% (9/24) of cases, within 2 mm in 29.16% (7/24), and greater than 2 mm in 8 cases. The maximum difference observed was 3.5 mm, which was seen in two cases. The Bland-Altman plot (Figure 1) shows the distribution of differences between USG and microscopic measurements, with the majority of points clustering around the mean difference [3]. These results suggest that USG is a reliable tool for measuring tumor thickness in patients with early OTSCC. The relationship between tumor thickness and nodal metastasis was also evaluated. The rate of occult nodal metastasis was 16.6% (4/24), with all cases having a tumor thickness greater than 4 mm. None of the patients with a tumor thickness less than 4 mm had nodal metastasis. The association between pathological T stage, tumor thickness, and nodal status is shown in Table 2. A significant association was observed between tumor thickness and nodal status, with thicker tumors more likely to have nodal metastasis (P = 0.012) [4]. The chi-square test revealed a significant association between pathological T stage and nodal status (P = 0.025), but not between tumor thickness and pathological T stage (P = 0.067). The predictive capacity of tumor thickness in detecting nodal metastasis was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. The area under the ROC curve (AUC) was 0.833, indicating good predictive accuracy [5]. A tumor thickness cutoff of 4 mm was found to have a sensitivity of 100% and specificity of 80% in predicting nodal metastasis. These results suggest that tumor thickness measured by USG can be used as a predictor of nodal metastasis in patients with early OTSCC. The results of this study are consistent with previous reports on the use of USG in measuring tumor thickness in head and neck cancers [6, 7]. The high correlation between USG and microscopic measurements observed in this study suggests that USG is a reliable tool for evaluating tumor thickness in patients with early OTSCC. The ability to predict nodal metastasis based on tumor thickness measured by USG can help guide management decisions, such as the need for elective neck dissection. In conclusion, the results of this study demonstrate the reliability and predictive accuracy of USG in measuring tumor thickness and detecting nodal metastasis in patients with early OTSCC. The use of USG as a non-invasive and cost-effective tool can aid in the preoperative evaluation and management of patients with early OTSCC. Further studies are needed to validate these findings and establish the role of USG in the routine management of head and neck cancers.
