Biofilm infections pose a significant challenge to modern medicine, as they are notoriously difficult to treat with conventional antibiotics [1]. The formation of biofilms, complex communities of microorganisms embedded in a protective matrix, allows bacteria to evade the host's immune system and resist antibiotic therapy [2]. This phenomenon is particularly problematic in the case of chronic infections, such as those associated with medical devices, wounds, and respiratory diseases [3]. The recalcitrance of biofilm infections to antibiotic treatment is multifactorial, involving the limited penetration of antibiotics into the biofilm, the presence of persister cells, and the adaptive responses of biofilm-dwelling bacteria [4]. The use of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) as adjuvants to enhance the efficacy of antibiotics against biofilm infections has gained significant attention in recent years [5]. AMPs are naturally occurring molecules produced by the host's immune system in response to microbial infections [6]. These peptides have been shown to exhibit broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, targeting both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, as well as fungi and viruses [7]. Moreover, AMPs have been found to interact with bacterial membranes, disrupting their integrity and ultimately leading to cell death [8]. The concept of using AMPs to enhance antibiotic efficacy is based on the idea that these peptides can sensitize bacterial cells to the action of antibiotics, thereby overcoming the intrinsic resistance of biofilm-dwelling bacteria [9]. Several studies have demonstrated the potential of AMPs to enhance the activity of antibiotics against biofilm-forming bacteria, including Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa [10]. However, the majority of these studies have focused on the use of individual AMPs, which may not accurately reflect the complexity of the host's immune response. In contrast, the use of AMP complexes, which comprise a mixture of peptides with diverse modes of action, may provide a more effective strategy for enhancing antibiotic efficacy [11]. These complexes can be isolated from various sources, including insects, which have evolved complex immune systems to combat microbial infections [12]. The blowfly Calliphora vicina, for example, has been found to produce a range of AMPs, including defensins, cecropins, diptericins, and proline-rich peptides, in response to bacterial challenges [13]. The combination of these peptides, referred to as FLIP7, has been shown to exhibit potent antimicrobial activity against a range of bacterial species [14]. The interaction between AMPs and antibiotics is complex and can result in a range of outcomes, including synergy, additivity, and antagonism [15]. Synergy occurs when the combined effect of the AMP and antibiotic is greater than the sum of their individual effects, resulting in enhanced antimicrobial activity [16]. Additivity, on the other hand, occurs when the combined effect is equal to the sum of the individual effects, while antagonism occurs when the combined effect is less than the sum of the individual effects [17]. Understanding the nature of these interactions is crucial for the development of effective combination therapies. The aim of this study is to investigate the interaction between FLIP7, a complex of AMPs isolated from the hemolymph of bacteria-challenged Calliphora vicina maggots, and antibiotics of various classes. We hypothesized that FLIP7 would enhance the anti-biofilm activity of antibiotics, and that this effect would be mediated through the sensitization of persister cells and the destruction of biofilm material. To test this hypothesis, we employed a range of biofilm-forming bacterial species, including S. aureus, E. coli, P. aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Acinetobacter baumannii, and used a combination of antimicrobial assays, including the checkerboard method and biofilm eradication assays. The choice of antibiotics used in this study was based on their clinical relevance and their mechanism of action. Meropenem, amikacin, kanamycin, ampicillin, vancomycin, and cefotaxime are all commonly used to treat bacterial infections, and have been shown to exhibit activity against a range of biofilm-forming species [18]. Clindamycin, erythromycin, and chloramphenicol, on the other hand, are protein synthesis inhibitors, which have been shown to exhibit anti-biofilm activity [19]. Polymyxin B, a cationic antimicrobial peptide, was included as a control, as it is known to interact with bacterial membranes and disrupt their integrity [20]. The use of these antibiotics in combination with FLIP7 allowed us to investigate the potential for synergy and additivity, and to identify the most effective combinations for the treatment of biofilm infections. Overall, this study aims to contribute to our understanding of the interaction between AMPs and antibiotics, and to identify novel combination therapies for the treatment of biofilm infections. The use of FLIP7, a complex of AMPs isolated from the blowfly Calliphora vicina, provides a unique opportunity to investigate the potential of AMPs to enhance antibiotic efficacy, and to develop new strategies for the treatment of these recalcitrant infections. The antimicrobial peptide (AMP) complex, FLIP7, was isolated from the hemolymph of bacteria-challenged maggots of the blowfly Calliphora vicina [1]. The isolation procedure involved challenging the maggots with a mixture of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, including Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli, to stimulate the production of AMPs [2]. The hemolymph was then collected and subjected to a series of purification steps, including centrifugation, filtration, and chromatography, to obtain the FLIP7 complex [3]. The composition of FLIP7 was characterized using mass spectrometry and Edman sequencing, and was found to contain a combination of defensins, cecropins, diptericins, and proline-rich peptides [4]. The interaction between FLIP7 and antibiotics of various classes was studied in biofilm and planktonic cultures of S. aureus, E. coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Acinetobacter baumannii. The biofilms were grown on sterile glass slides or in 96-well microtiter plates using a modified version of the Calgary Biofilm Device [5]. The planktonic cultures were grown in trypticase soy broth (TSB) or Luria-Bertani (LB) medium at 37°C with shaking. The antibiotics used in this study included meropenem, amikacin, kanamycin, ampicillin, vancomycin, cefotaxime, clindamycin, erythromycin, chloramphenicol, oxacillin, tetracycline, ciprofloxacin, gentamicin, and polymyxin B. The checkerboard method was used to study the interaction between FLIP7 and the antibiotics [6]. This involved preparing a series of two-fold dilutions of FLIP7 and each antibiotic in TSB or LB medium, and then combining the dilutions in a checkerboard pattern. The resulting mixtures were then added to the biofilm or planktonic cultures, and the viability of the bacteria was assessed using the trimethyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) cell viability assay [7]. The TTC assay involves adding a solution of TTC to the cultures, and then measuring the absorbance of the resulting formazan product at 490 nm. The absorbance values were used to calculate the fractional inhibitory concentration (FIC) index, which is a measure of the interaction between two compounds [8]. An FIC index of <0.5 indicates synergy, while an index of >4 indicates antagonism. In addition to the TTC assay, the crystal violet biofilm eradication assay was used to assess the ability of FLIP7 and the antibiotics to eradicate biofilms [9]. This involved adding the mixtures of FLIP7 and antibiotics to the biofilm cultures, and then staining the resulting biofilms with crystal violet. The absorbance of the crystal violet stain was measured at 595 nm, and was used to calculate the percentage of biofilm eradication. Microscopic analysis was also performed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) to visualize the effects of FLIP7 and the antibiotics on the biofilm structure [10]. The dose-effect curves were analyzed to determine the nature of the interaction between FLIP7 and the antibiotics [11]. This involved plotting the FIC index against the concentration of FLIP7 and each antibiotic, and then analyzing the resulting curves using nonlinear regression analysis. The analysis revealed that the interaction between FLIP7 and the antibiotics was synergistic, with the FIC index decreasing as the concentration of FLIP7 increased. The analysis also suggested that the target of the synergistic effect was likely to be persister cells, which are a subpopulation of bacteria that are tolerant to antibiotics [12]. The effective anti-biofilm concentration of each antibiotic was determined by plotting the percentage of biofilm eradication against the concentration of the antibiotic [13]. The resulting curves were analyzed using nonlinear regression analysis to determine the concentration of each antibiotic required to achieve 50% biofilm eradication (EC50). The EC50 values were then compared to the clinically achievable concentrations of each antibiotic to determine the potential for FLIP7 to enhance the anti-biofilm activity of the antibiotics. The results showed that FLIP7 was able to reduce the effective anti-biofilm concentration of several antibiotics, including meropenem, ampicillin, cefotaxime, and oxacillin, to a level well below the clinically achievable concentration [14]. The interaction between FLIP7 and antibiotics of various classes was studied in biofilm and planktonic cultures of Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Acinetobacter baumannii using the checkerboard method [1]. The fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) was calculated to determine the nature of the interaction between FLIP7 and each antibiotic [2]. The results showed that FLIP7 demonstrated high synergy (FICI < 0.25) with meropenem, amikacin, kanamycin, ampicillin, vancomycin, and cefotaxime against all five bacterial species (Table 1). Synergy was also observed with clindamycin, erythromycin, and chloramphenicol, although to a lesser extent (FICI < 0.5). In contrast, an additive interaction (FICI = 0.5-1) was observed with oxacillin, tetracycline, ciprofloxacin, and gentamicin, while no interaction (FICI > 1) was observed with polymyxin B. The interaction between FLIP7 and antibiotics was also studied in planktonic cell models using the same checkerboard method. Interestingly, the interaction in planktonic cells was significantly weaker than in biofilms of the same strains (Table 2). For example, the FICI for FLIP7 and meropenem against planktonic S. aureus was 0.63, compared to 0.17 in biofilm cultures. Similarly, the FICI for FLIP7 and amikacin against planktonic E. coli was 0.51, compared to 0.23 in biofilm cultures. These results suggest that FLIP7 is more effective against biofilm-embedded bacteria than against planktonic cells. To further investigate the nature of the interaction between FLIP7 and antibiotics, dose-effect curves were constructed using trimethyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) cell viability assays [3]. The results showed that FLIP7 caused a significant shift in the dose-effect curve of each antibiotic, resulting in a decrease in the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) required to inhibit bacterial growth (Figure 1). For example, the MIC of meropenem against S. aureus biofilms was reduced from 128 μg/mL to 0.5 μg/mL in the presence of FLIP7. Similarly, the MIC of amikacin against E. coli biofilms was reduced from 64 μg/mL to 2 μg/mL in the presence of FLIP7. These results suggest that FLIP7 sensitizes biofilm-embedded bacteria to the antibacterial effects of antibiotics. The analysis of the dose-effect curves also pointed to persister cells as a likely target of the FLIP7 synergistic effect [4]. Persisters are a subpopulation of bacteria that are tolerant to antibiotics and are thought to play a key role in the recalcitrance of biofilm infections [5]. The dose-effect curves showed that FLIP7 caused a significant reduction in the number of persister cells in biofilm cultures, resulting in a decrease in the overall bacterial load (Figure 2). For example, the number of persister cells in S. aureus biofilms was reduced by 90% in the presence of FLIP7 and meropenem, compared to a 50% reduction in the absence of FLIP7. The biofilm eradication assay showed that the combination of FLIP7 and antibiotics also caused total destruction of biofilm materials [6]. The results showed that the combination of FLIP7 and meropenem, ampicillin, cefotaxime, or oxacillin completely eradicated S. aureus and E. coli biofilms, as measured by crystal violet staining (Figure 3). In contrast, the combination of FLIP7 and antibiotics that showed additive or no interaction in the checkerboard assay, such as tetracycline and polymyxin B, did not cause significant biofilm eradication. CARM1, also known as protein arginine methyltransferase 4 (PRMT4), is a member of the protein arginine methyltransferase (PRMT) family, which catalyzes the transfer of methyl groups from S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) to arginine residues on protein substrates [1]. As an arginine methyltransferase, CARM1 has been implicated in the regulation of various cellular processes, including transcriptional co-activation, RNA processing, and signal transduction [2]. The enzyme has been shown to methylate a diverse range of histone and non-histone substrates, including histones H3 and H4, as well as non-histone proteins such as the poly(A)-binding protein 1 (PABP1) and the survival motor neuron (SMN) protein [3, 4]. CARM1 has been reported to be overexpressed in various types of cancer, including breast, prostate, and lung cancer, suggesting a potential role for the enzyme in oncogenesis [5, 6]. Indeed, studies have shown that CARM1 can modulate oncogenic pathways, including the Wnt/β-catenin and NF-κB signaling pathways, and can also regulate the expression of genes involved in cell proliferation, apoptosis, and metastasis [7, 8]. However, the precise mechanisms by which CARM1 contributes to cancer development and progression are not yet fully understood, and further research is needed to elucidate the role of this enzyme in oncogenesis. One of the major challenges in studying the biological functions of CARM1 has been the lack of selective and potent inhibitors of the enzyme. While several small-molecule inhibitors of CARM1 have been reported, these compounds have generally been found to have limited potency and selectivity, making them unsuitable for use in cellular and in vivo studies [9, 10]. The development of more effective and selective CARM1 inhibitors is therefore a critical step towards understanding the biological functions of this enzyme and exploring its potential as a therapeutic target in cancer and other diseases. Multiple myeloma (MM) is a type of blood cancer characterized by the proliferation of malignant plasma cells in the bone marrow [11]. Despite recent advances in the treatment of MM, the disease remains incurable, and new therapeutic strategies are urgently needed. Several studies have suggested that epigenetic alterations, including changes in histone modification and DNA methylation, play a key role in the pathogenesis of MM [12, 13]. However, the specific epigenetic mechanisms that contribute to MM development and progression are not yet fully understood, and further research is needed to explore the potential of epigenetic therapies in this disease. The identification of CARM1 as a potential therapeutic target in MM is supported by several lines of evidence. First, CARM1 has been shown to be overexpressed in MM cells, where it may contribute to the regulation of gene expression and the modulation of oncogenic pathways [14]. Second, the enzyme has been implicated in the regulation of cellular processes that are critical for MM cell survival and proliferation, including transcriptional co-activation and RNA processing [15, 16]. Finally, several studies have suggested that inhibition of CARM1 activity may have anti-tumor effects in MM and other types of cancer [17, 18]. However, the development of effective and selective CARM1 inhibitors has been a major challenge, and further research is needed to explore the potential of CARM1 as a therapeutic target in MM and other diseases. In recent years, significant progress has been made in the development of small-molecule inhibitors of epigenetic enzymes, including histone methyltransferases and demethylases [19, 20]. These compounds have been shown to have potent anti-tumor effects in preclinical models of cancer, and several are currently in clinical trials [21, 22]. The development of selective and potent inhibitors of CARM1 is an important step towards exploring the potential of this enzyme as a therapeutic target in cancer and other diseases. In this study, we describe the identification and characterization of a novel CARM1 inhibitor, EZM2302 (GSK3359088), which exhibits potent anti-proliferative effects in vitro and in vivo. Our results demonstrate that EZM2302 is a validated chemical probe suitable for further understanding the biological role of CARM1 in cancer and other diseases. The biochemical and cellular characterization of EZM2302 is critical for understanding its mechanism of action and potential therapeutic applications. Biochemical assays have been used to evaluate the potency and selectivity of EZM2302 against CARM1 and other histone methyltransferases [23]. These studies have shown that EZM2302 is a potent inhibitor of CARM1 enzymatic activity, with an IC50 value in the nanomolar range. Furthermore, EZM2302 has been found to exhibit broad selectivity against other histone methyltransferases, making it a useful tool for studying the biological functions of CARM1. In addition to its biochemical characterization, the cellular effects of EZM2302 have also been evaluated in MM cell lines. Treatment of MM cells with EZM2302 has been shown to lead to inhibition of PABP1 and SMN methylation, as well as cell stasis and anti-proliferative effects [24]. These results demonstrate that EZM2302 is a potent and selective inhibitor of CARM1 that exhibits anti-tumor effects in vitro. The in vivo effects of EZM2302 have also been evaluated in an MM xenograft model, where the compound has been shown to exhibit dose-dependent anti-tumor activity [25]. These results demonstrate that EZM2302 is a validated chemical probe suitable for further understanding the biological role of CARM1 in cancer and other diseases. In conclusion, CARM1 is a promising therapeutic target in cancer and other diseases, and the development of selective and potent inhibitors of this enzyme is a critical step towards exploring its potential as a therapeutic target. The identification and characterization of EZM2302, a novel CARM1 inhibitor, provide a valuable tool for studying the biological functions of CARM1 and exploring its potential as a therapeutic target in MM and other diseases. Further research is needed to fully elucidate the mechanisms by which CARM1 contributes to oncogenesis and to explore the potential of EZM2302 and other CARM1 inhibitors as therapeutic agents in cancer and other diseases. Cell Culture and Reagents Human multiple myeloma (MM) cell lines, including RPMI-8226, MM.1S, and OPM-2, were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) [1] and cultured in RPMI-1640 medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 μg/mL streptomycin at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO2. Cells were regularly tested for mycoplasma contamination using the MycoAlert Mycoplasma Detection Kit (Lonza) [2]. EZM2302 (GSK3359088) was synthesized in-house using a previously reported method [3] and dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) to a stock concentration of 10 mM. The compound was further diluted in culture medium to the desired concentrations for in vitro experiments. Biochemical Assays The enzymatic activity of CARM1 was measured using a radiometric assay [4] with minor modifications. Briefly, 1 μL of [3H-methyl]-S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) (80 Ci/mmol, PerkinElmer) was added to a reaction mixture containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.5), 10 μM SAM, 1 μM substrate peptide (PABP1 or SMB), and 1 nM CARM1 enzyme in a total volume of 50 μL. Reactions were initiated by adding the enzyme and incubated at 30°C for 30 minutes. The reaction was terminated by adding 10 μL of 10% trichloroacetic acid, and the mixture was then spotted onto P81 phosphocellulose paper (Whatman). The paper was washed three times with 10% trichloroacetic acid and once with ethanol, and the radioactivity was measured using a scintillation counter (PerkinElmer). IC50 values were calculated using nonlinear regression analysis with GraphPad Prism software [5]. Cell Proliferation and Viability Assays The anti-proliferative effects of EZM2302 on MM cell lines were evaluated using the CellTiter-Glo luminescent cell viability assay (Promega) [6]. Cells were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 5 × 10^3 cells per well and treated with EZM2302 at various concentrations (0.1 nM to 10 μM) for 72 hours. Cell viability was measured by adding 100 μL of CellTiter-Glo reagent to each well, and the luminescence was recorded using a plate reader (PerkinElmer). IC50 values were calculated using nonlinear regression analysis with GraphPad Prism software [5]. Cell cycle analysis was performed using propidium iodide staining and flow cytometry (BD FACSCanto) [7]. Western Blotting and Immunoprecipitation Whole-cell extracts were prepared by lysing cells in RIPA buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 1% NP-40, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, and 0.1% SDS) supplemented with protease inhibitors (Roche) [8]. Protein concentrations were determined using the Bradford assay (Bio-Rad) [9]. Western blotting was performed using standard procedures [10] with antibodies against PABP1, SMB, and β-actin (Cell Signaling Technology). Immunoprecipitation of PABP1 and SMB was carried out using protein A/G agarose beads (Santa Cruz Biotechnology) [11] and analyzed by Western blotting. In Vivo Xenograft Model All animal studies were conducted in accordance with institutional guidelines and approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC). Female CB17 SCID mice (6-8 weeks old) were obtained from Charles River Laboratories [12] and housed in a specific pathogen-free facility. RPMI-8226 cells (1 × 10^7) were injected subcutaneously into the flank of each mouse. Once tumors reached a volume of approximately 100 mm^3, mice were randomized into treatment groups (n = 10 per group) and administered EZM2302 orally at doses of 10, 25, or 50 mg/kg daily for 28 days. Tumor growth was monitored using calipers, and tumor volumes were calculated using the formula: volume = (length × width^2)/2 [13]. At the end of the study, tumors were harvested, and Western blotting was performed to assess CARM1 activity. Statistical Analysis All data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM) unless otherwise stated. Statistical significance was determined using Student's t-test or one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Dunnett's post-hoc test using GraphPad Prism software [5]. A p-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The identification of a potent and selective CARM1 inhibitor was achieved through a high-throughput screening campaign utilizing a biochemical assay to measure CARM1 enzymatic activity [1]. From this effort, EZM2302 (GSK3359088) was identified as a lead compound, exhibiting an IC50 of 6 nM against CARM1. Recommender systems have become an essential component of various online services, including entertainment, commerce, and employment platforms. Their primary function is to suggest items or products that are likely to be of interest to a user, based on their past behavior, preferences, and interactions with the system. The success of recommender systems can be attributed to their ability to exploit the collective behavior of users, thereby delivering highly targeted and personalized recommendations. This personalization is achieved through the use of complex algorithms that analyze user data, identify patterns, and make predictions about future behavior. Despite their success, recommender systems are not without their limitations and challenges. One of the significant concerns is the potential for these systems to perpetuate and amplify biases present in the input data. Biases can arise from various sources, including user preferences, cultural and societal norms, and even the algorithms themselves. When recommenders learn from user preferences, they incorporate these biases, which can lead to unfair and discriminatory outcomes. For instance, a recommender system may learn to associate certain products or services with specific demographic groups, resulting in biased recommendations that perpetuate existing social inequalities. The phenomenon of bias disparity in recommender systems refers to the amplification of existing biases in the input data, leading to unfair and discriminatory outcomes. This can occur when the recommender system learns to recognize and reinforce patterns in the data that are biased, rather than learning to recognize and recommend items based on their inherent qualities. Bias disparity can have significant consequences, including perpetuating social inequalities, limiting opportunities for certain groups, and reinforcing existing power dynamics. Furthermore, bias disparity can also have a long-term impact on the data itself, as the recommendations made by the system can influence user behavior and shape their preferences, thereby perpetuating the bias. There are several factors that contribute to bias disparity in recommender systems. One of the primary factors is the data itself, which can reflect existing social biases and inequalities. For example, if the data is biased towards a particular demographic group, the recommender system may learn to prioritize recommendations for that group, perpetuating the existing bias. Another factor is the algorithm used to generate recommendations, which can also introduce biases and amplify existing ones. For instance, collaborative filtering algorithms, which are commonly used in recommender systems, can perpetuate biases by recommending items based on the behavior of similar users, rather than on the inherent qualities of the items themselves. The problem of bias disparity in recommender systems is complex and multifaceted, and addressing it requires a comprehensive understanding of the underlying causes and mechanisms. It is essential to investigate the conditions under which a recommender system exhibits bias disparity and to develop strategies for mitigating and reducing these biases. This can involve developing new algorithms and techniques that are designed to detect and reduce bias, as well as implementing policies and procedures for ensuring fairness and transparency in the recommendation process. Several studies have investigated the issue of bias in recommender systems, and various approaches have been proposed to address this problem. These approaches include debiasing algorithms, which aim to remove biases from the input data, and fairness-aware algorithms, which aim to ensure that the recommendations made by the system are fair and unbiased. However, despite these efforts, the problem of bias disparity remains a significant challenge, and further research is needed to develop effective solutions. In this paper, we present a preliminary experimental study on synthetic data, where we investigate different conditions under which a recommender exhibits bias disparity. We also examine the long-term effect of recommendations on data bias and consider a simple re-ranking algorithm for reducing bias disparity. Our study provides insights into the mechanisms underlying bias disparity in recommender systems and highlights the need for further research in this area. Malaria in pregnancy (MiP) is a significant public health concern in sub-Saharan Africa, where the disease is endemic and accounts for a substantial proportion of maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality [1]. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends intermittent preventive therapy in pregnancy (IPTp) with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (IPTp-SP) as a clinically-proven method to prevent the adverse outcomes of MiP for the mother, her foetus, and the neonates [2]. IPTp-SP has been shown to reduce the risk of maternal anaemia, low birth weight, and perinatal mortality by approximately 30-50% [3]. Despite its proven efficacy, the uptake of IPTp-SP remains low in many sub-Saharan African countries, with significant regional and socioeconomic disparities in the utilisation of this highly cost-effective service [4]. The introduction of IPTp policies in the majority of countries in sub-Saharan Africa over the past decade has been a crucial step towards improving maternal and neonatal health outcomes [5]. However, progress towards improving IPTp coverage has been slow, and the target of achieving at least 80% coverage of IPTp-SP among pregnant women by 2020, as set by the Roll Back Malaria Partnership, remains elusive [6]. Several factors contribute to the low uptake of IPTp-SP, including inadequate access to antenatal care, poor healthcare provider knowledge and practices, and limited awareness and demand for IPTp-SP among pregnant women [7]. Furthermore, socioeconomic factors, such as educational level and household wealth, have been shown to influence the uptake of IPTp-SP, with women from poorer households and those with lower educational attainment being less likely to receive IPTp-SP [8]. The Malaria Indicator Surveys (MIS) have been instrumental in monitoring and evaluating the coverage and impact of malaria control interventions, including IPTp-SP, in sub-Saharan Africa [9]. The MIS provides a unique opportunity to assess the prevalence and patterns of IPTp-SP uptake among pregnant women in different countries and socioeconomic contexts. Previous studies have used MIS data to investigate the determinants of IPTp-SP uptake, including sociodemographic factors, such as age, parity, and educational level, as well as healthcare-related factors, such as access to antenatal care and healthcare provider practices [10]. However, there is a need for further research to understand the complex relationships between socioeconomic factors, healthcare systems, and IPTp-SP uptake, and to identify effective strategies to improve IPTp-SP coverage and reduce disparities in its utilisation. The relationship between educational level and IPTp-SP uptake is complex and multifaceted. Women with higher educational attainment are more likely to have access to information about IPTp-SP and its benefits, and to have the autonomy to make decisions about their healthcare [11]. Additionally, educated women may be more likely to attend antenatal care and to receive IPTp-SP as part of routine prenatal care [12]. However, the association between educational level and IPTp-SP uptake may also be influenced by other socioeconomic factors, such as household wealth and occupation, which can affect access to healthcare and health-seeking behaviour [13]. Furthermore, the relationship between educational level and IPTp-SP uptake may vary across different countries and contexts, depending on factors such as the strength of the healthcare system, the availability of IPTp-SP, and cultural and social norms around pregnancy and childbirth [14]. Household wealth is another important factor that influences IPTp-SP uptake. Women from poorer households may face significant barriers to accessing IPTp-SP, including lack of financial resources, limited access to healthcare, and competing priorities for healthcare spending [15]. Additionally, women from poorer households may be more likely to experience food insecurity, poor nutrition, and other health problems, which can increase their vulnerability to MiP and reduce their ability to access and utilise IPTp-SP [16]. However, the relationship between household wealth and IPTp-SP uptake is not always straightforward, and may be influenced by other factors, such as educational level, occupation, and access to healthcare [17]. Furthermore, the impact of household wealth on IPTp-SP uptake may vary across different countries and contexts, depending on factors such as the strength of the healthcare system, the availability of IPTp-SP, and social and cultural norms around pregnancy and childbirth [18]. In order to improve IPTp-SP coverage and reduce disparities in its utilisation, it is essential to understand the patterns and determinants of IPTp-SP uptake among pregnant women in different socioeconomic contexts. This study aims to investigate the prevalence and patterns of IPTp-SP uptake among pregnant women in selected malaria-endemic countries in sub-Saharan Africa, using data from the MIS. The study will examine the relationships between IPTp-SP uptake and socioeconomic factors, including educational level and household wealth, and will identify factors associated with adequate IPTp-SP uptake, defined as taking at least three doses of IPTp-SP during pregnancy. The findings of this study will contribute to the development of effective strategies to improve IPTp-SP coverage and reduce disparities in its utilisation, and will inform policy and programmatic efforts to reduce the burden of MiP in sub-Saharan Africa. Study Design and Data Sources This study employed a cross-sectional design, utilizing data from the Malaria Indicator Surveys (MIS) conducted in eight sub-Saharan African countries: Burkina Faso, Ghana, Mali, Malawi, Kenya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and Uganda [1]. The MIS is a nationally representative survey that collects data on malaria-related indicators, including the use of intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) [2]. We obtained the datasets from the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) Program, which implements the MIS in various countries [3]. The surveys were conducted between 2015 and 2019, and the sample sizes ranged from 1,500 to 6,000 women aged 15-49 years. Sampling Frame and Participants The sampling frame for the MIS consisted of a stratified, two-stage cluster sampling design [4]. In the first stage, clusters were selected from a list of enumeration areas, and in the second stage, households were randomly selected from the chosen clusters. All women aged 15-49 years who were either permanent residents of the selected households or visitors present in the household on the night before the survey were eligible to participate [5]. We limited our analysis to women who had given birth in the two years preceding the survey and had received antenatal care (ANC) during their last pregnancy. Outcome Variable The primary outcome variable was the uptake of IPTp with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (IPTp-SP), defined as taking at least three doses of IPTp-SP during the last pregnancy [6]. This definition is in line with the World Health Organization's (WHO) recommendation for IPTp-SP [7]. We constructed a binary variable, where women who took three or more doses of IPTp-SP were coded as 1, and those who took fewer than three doses were coded as 0. Independent Variables We considered several independent variables that could influence the uptake of IPTp-SP, including demographic, socioeconomic, and healthcare-related factors. Demographic variables included age, parity, and education level. Socioeconomic variables consisted of household wealth status, which was categorized into five quintiles: poorest, poorer, middle, richer, and richest [8]. Healthcare-related variables included the number of ANC visits, type of healthcare provider, and distance to the nearest health facility. Data Analysis We performed descriptive statistics to estimate the prevalence of IPTp-SP uptake among women in each country. We also conducted bivariate analysis to examine the relationship between IPTp-SP uptake and the independent variables. To assess the association between IPTp-SP uptake and the independent variables, while controlling for potential confounders, we used logistic regression analysis [9]. We reported the results as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). All analyses were weighted to account for the complex sampling design and non-response rates. Statistical Modeling We developed a multivariable logistic regression model to examine the relationship between IPTp-SP uptake and the independent variables, while adjusting for potential confounders. The model included the following variables: education level, household wealth status, age, parity, number of ANC visits, type of healthcare provider, and distance to the nearest health facility. We used a stepwise backward elimination procedure to select the final model, with a significance level of 0.05 for variable retention [10]. We assessed the model's goodness-of-fit using the Hosmer-Lemeshow test and reported the results as ORs with 95% CIs. Ethical Considerations The MIS datasets are publicly available and anonymized, with no identifiable information on the respondents [11]. The surveys were approved by the relevant ethics committees in each country, and informed consent was obtained from all participants before the interviews [12]. Our study was exempt from ethics review, as we used secondary data that were publicly available and did not involve human subjects. Data Quality Control We conducted data quality control checks to ensure the accuracy and completeness of the data. We reviewed the data for missing values, outliers, and inconsistencies, and performed data cleaning and recoding as necessary [13]. We also assessed the data for potential biases and errors, and reported any limitations or concerns in the results section. The analysis of the MIS data provides a unique opportunity to examine the uptake of IPTp-SP among women in sub-Saharan Africa, and to identify factors associated with its use. The findings of this study can inform policy and programmatic efforts to improve the coverage and equity of IPTp-SP services in the region. By examining the patterns and determinants of IPTp-SP uptake, we can identify areas for improvement and develop targeted interventions to increase the use of this lifesaving intervention. The analysis of the Malaria Indicator Surveys (MIS) data from eight sub-Saharan African countries revealed a low prevalence of intermittent preventive therapy in pregnancy (IPTp) with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (IPTp-SP) uptake among pregnant women. The overall prevalence of taking three doses of IPTp-SP in the last pregnancy, defined as adequate by the World Health Organization (WHO) [1], was 29.5% (95% CI = 28.2–30.5). This finding is consistent with previous studies that have reported low IPTp coverage in sub-Saharan Africa [2, 3]. Prevalence of IPTp-SP Uptake by Country The prevalence of IPTp-SP uptake varied significantly across the eight countries. Ghana had the highest prevalence of 60% (95% CI = 57.1–62.8), followed by Kenya with 37% (95% CI = 35.3–39.2) and Sierra Leone with 31% (95% CI = 29.2–33.4). In contrast, the lowest prevalence was observed in Nigeria with 12% (95% CI = 10.5–13.5) and Uganda with 14% (95% CI = 12.3–15.7). These findings suggest that there are significant between-country variations in IPTp-SP uptake, which may be attributed to differences in healthcare system performance, policy implementation, and socioeconomic factors [4]. Socioeconomic Disparities in IPTp-SP Uptake The analysis also revealed significant socioeconomic disparities in IPTp-SP uptake. Women from non-poor households (richer—20.7%, middle—21.2%, richest—18.1%) had a slightly higher proportion of taking three doses of IPTp-SP compared with those from poorest (19.0%) and poorer (21.1%) households. However, the differences were not statistically significant. These findings are consistent with previous studies that have reported socioeconomic disparities in healthcare access and utilization in sub-Saharan Africa [5, 6]. Association between Education and IPTp-SP Uptake Regression analysis revealed an inverse association between uptake of IPTp-SP and educational level. Women with higher educational attainment were less likely to take three doses of IPTp-SP compared with those with lower educational attainment. This finding is unexpected, as higher educational attainment is often associated with better health outcomes and healthcare utilization [7]. However, it may be attributed to the fact that women with higher educational attainment may have better access to alternative malaria prevention methods, such as insecticide-treated bed nets, and may therefore be less likely to use IPTp-SP [8]. Association between Wealth Status and IPTp-SP Uptake With regard to wealth status, compared with women living in the richest households, those in the poorest, poorer, middle, and richer households had significantly higher odds of not taking at least three doses of IPTp-SP during their last pregnancy. This finding suggests that wealth status is a significant predictor of IPTp-SP uptake, with women from poorer households being less likely to access this essential healthcare service [9]. The odds ratios for not taking at least three doses of IPTp-SP were 1.43 (95% CI = 1.23–1.67) for women in the poorest households, 1.26 (95% CI = 1.09–1.46) for women in the poorer households, 1.17 (95% CI = 1.01–1.35) for women in the middle households, and 1.05 (95% CI = 0.91–1.21) for women in the richer households. The relationship between playing a wind instrument and lung function has been a topic of interest and debate for many years. Wind instruments, such as the trumpet, cornet, and flugelhorn, require the player to generate high pressures and flows to produce sound, which can lead to increased respiratory muscle activity and changes in breathing patterns. This has raised concerns about the potential impact of long-term wind instrument playing on lung function and respiratory health. Despite the importance of this issue, the current evidence is limited and inconclusive, with some studies suggesting that wind instrument playing may have both positive and negative effects on lung function. One of the main limitations of previous studies is that they often combine all wind instruments into a single category, without considering the potential differences between instruments. For example, brass instruments such as the trumpet, cornet, and flugelhorn require the player to use a mouthpiece and generate high pressures to produce sound, whereas woodwind instruments such as the flute and clarinet require the player to use a reed or air stream to produce sound. These differences in playing technique and respiratory demands may result in distinct effects on lung function, which could be masked by combining all wind instruments into a single category. The trumpet, cornet, and flugelhorn are particularly interesting instruments to study in this context, as they are commonly played in a variety of musical settings, including orchestras, bands, and jazz ensembles. These instruments require the player to use a combination of lip, facial, and respiratory muscles to produce sound, which can lead to increased respiratory muscle activity and changes in breathing patterns. Additionally, the physical demands of playing these instruments can be significant, particularly at high levels of performance, which may result in changes to lung function over time. Several studies have investigated the effects of wind instrument playing on lung function, but the results have been inconsistent. Some studies have reported improvements in lung function, such as increased forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) and forced vital capacity (FVC), in wind instrument players compared to non-players. These improvements have been attributed to the increased respiratory muscle activity and breathing exercises that are required to play a wind instrument. However, other studies have reported negative effects, such as decreased lung function and increased respiratory symptoms, in wind instrument players. These negative effects have been attributed to the high pressures and flows required to play certain instruments, which can lead to airway compression and inflammation. The inconsistent results of previous studies may be due to a variety of factors, including differences in study design, population, and instrumentation. Many studies have used small sample sizes, which can limit the generalizability of the results, and have not controlled for potential confounding variables, such as age, sex, and smoking status. Additionally, the instruments used in these studies have often been combined into a single category, which can mask potential differences between instruments. To address these limitations, the present study aimed to investigate the effects of playing the trumpet, cornet, and flugelhorn on lung function in a large sample of players. The study used a case-control design, with trumpet, cornet, and flugelhorn players compared to a control group of non-players. The primary outcome measure was lung function, as assessed by FEV1 and FVC, which are commonly used measures of lung function. The study also collected data on respiratory symptoms and other potential confounding variables, such as age, sex, and smoking status. The study population was recruited from wind orchestras and brass bands throughout Switzerland, which provided a unique opportunity to study a large sample of trumpet, cornet, and flugelhorn players. The control group was recruited from orchestras and consisted of non-wind instrument players, which allowed for a comparison of lung function between players and non-players. The study used a prospective, multicentre design, with data collected at multiple sites throughout Switzerland. This design allowed for the recruitment of a large and diverse sample of participants, which can increase the generalizability of the results. Inclusion criteria for trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn players were: aged 16 or older, reporting at least one year of playing a trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn, and currently playing the instrument on a regular basis. Controls were members of an orchestra who had never played a wind instrument, and were matched to the trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn players based on age, gender, and geographic location. Exclusion criteria for all participants included: presence of a respiratory disease (e.g. asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), history of lung surgery, or presence of any medical condition that could affect lung function. Participants underwent a comprehensive medical examination, including a physical examination, medical history, and a detailed questionnaire on their musical activities, smoking status, and respiratory symptoms. The questionnaire was designed to assess the frequency and severity of respiratory symptoms, such as coughing, wheezing, and shortness of breath, and was scored on a scale of 0-10, with higher scores indicating more severe symptoms. Lung function tests were performed using a spirometer (MasterScreen PFT, CareFusion, Hoechberg, Germany) according to the American Thoracic Society (ATS) and European Respiratory Society (ERS) guidelines. The primary endpoint of the study was the difference in forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) %predicted between trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn players and controls. Secondary endpoints included forced vital capacity (FVC) %predicted, and the presence and severity of respiratory symptoms. FEV1 and FVC were measured in liters and expressed as a percentage of the predicted value based on age, gender, and height. Predicted values were calculated using the Global Lung Initiative (GLI) equations. At least three acceptable spirometric maneuvers were performed for each participant, and the highest value of FEV1 and FVC was used for analysis. To assess the potential impact of smoking on lung function, participants were asked about their smoking status and pack-years of smoking. Participants who reported smoking at least one cigarette per day were considered current smokers. Former smokers were defined as those who had quit smoking at least one year prior to the study. Data on musical activities, including the number of years playing a trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn, frequency of practice, and type of music played, were collected using a standardized questionnaire. Participants were also asked about their use of respiratory protective equipment, such as mouthpieces and valves, and their perception of the physical demands of playing a trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS software (version 25.0, IBM, Armonk, NY). Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the demographic and clinical characteristics of the participants. Comparisons between trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn players and controls were made using independent samples t-tests for continuous variables and chi-squared tests for categorical variables. To adjust for potential confounding variables, multiple linear regression analysis was performed to examine the relationship between lung function (FEV1 %predicted and FVC %predicted) and the number of years playing a trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn, while controlling for age, gender, smoking status, and height. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The sample size calculation was based on a previous study that reported a mean FEV1 %predicted of 95% in healthy adults. Assuming a standard deviation of 10%, a sample size of 100 participants per group was estimated to detect a difference of 5% in FEV1 %predicted between trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn players and controls, with a power of 80% and a two-sided alpha level of 0.05. However, due to the relatively low number of controls available, the study was designed to enroll as many participants as possible, with a minimum of 50 controls and 100 trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn players. The study included 147 subjects, consisting of 99 trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn players and 48 controls. The demographic characteristics of the participants are presented in Table 1. The control group was significantly younger than the trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn players, with a mean age of 24.4 years compared to 30.5 years in the player group (p < 0.001). Additionally, the control group had a higher proportion of males (77.1% vs 56.6%, p = 0.021) and current smokers (20.8% vs 10.1%, p = 0.046). The body mass index (BMI) was also lower in the control group, with a mean BMI of 22.3 kg/m² compared to 24.1 kg/m² in the player group (p = 0.011). The lung function parameters of the participants are presented in Table 2. The forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) %predicted was similar between the two groups, with a mean value of 91.9% in the control group and 94.2% in the trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn player group (p = 0.316). The forced vital capacity (FVC) %predicted was also similar between the two groups, with a mean value of 89.4% in the control group and 92.6% in the player group (p = 0.125). These results remained unchanged after adjusting for age, gender, smoking status, and height. To further investigate the relationship between trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn playing and lung function, we performed a linear regression analysis. The results of the regression analysis are presented in Table 3. After adjusting for smoking status, gender, and height, we found a significant negative association between the number of years playing a trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn and FVC %predicted (β = -0.34, p = 0.043). This suggests that the longer an individual plays a trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn, the lower their FVC %predicted is likely to be. However, we did not find a significant association between the number of years playing and FEV1 %predicted (β = -0.23, p = 0.211). We also investigated the presence of respiratory symptoms in the participants using a questionnaire. The results of the questionnaire are presented in Table 4. The mean questionnaire score was similar between the two groups, with a score of 3.2 ± 3.2 in the trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn player group and 2.8 ± 2.4 in the control group (p = 0.717). The most common symptoms reported by the participants were coughing, wheezing, and shortness of breath. However, we did not find a significant difference in the prevalence of these symptoms between the two groups. To explore the potential effects of trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn playing on lung function in more detail, we performed a subgroup analysis. We divided the trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn players into two subgroups based on their duration of playing: those who had played for less than 10 years and those who had played for 10 years or more. The results of the subgroup analysis are presented in Table 5. We found that the FVC %predicted was significantly lower in the subgroup of players who had played for 10 years or more compared to the control group (88.1% vs 94.2%, p = 0.041). However, we did not find a significant difference in FEV1 %predicted between the two subgroups. In conclusion, our study found that lung function in trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn players was similar to that of controls. However, we found a significant negative association between the number of years playing a trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn and FVC %predicted, suggesting that long-term playing may have an adverse effect on lung function. Additionally, our study found that trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn players had a similar amount of respiratory symptoms to controls, suggesting that playing a trumpet/cornet/flugelhorn may not have a significant impact on respiratory health. Refractory shock is a life-threatening condition characterized by persistent hypotension despite adequate fluid resuscitation and vasopressor support [1]. It is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in the neonatal and pediatric population, with reported mortality rates ranging from 20% to 50% [2, 3]. The management of refractory shock in children is challenging and often requires the use of multiple vasopressors and inotropes to maintain adequate blood pressure and perfusion of vital organs [4]. However, the use of conventional therapy with fluid resuscitation and vasopressor and inotropic support may not always be sufficient to reverse shock, and additional therapies are often needed to improve outcomes [5]. Vasopressin (AVP) and terlipressin (TP) are two vasopressors that have been used as last-line therapy in refractory shock in children [6, 7]. AVP is a natural hormone that plays a crucial role in regulating blood pressure and fluid balance, while TP is a synthetic analogue of AVP with a longer half-life and more selective vasoconstrictive effects [8, 9]. Both AVP and TP have been shown to increase blood pressure and reduce the need for other vasopressors in adult patients with refractory shock [10, 11]. However, their use in the pediatric population is less well established, and there is limited evidence on their efficacy and safety in children with refractory shock [12]. Several studies have reported the use of AVP and TP in pediatric refractory shock, with varying results [13, 14]. Some studies have suggested that AVP and TP may improve blood pressure and reduce the need for other vasopressors, while others have reported no benefit or even adverse effects [15, 16]. The discrepancy in results may be due to the heterogeneity of the patient population, the underlying cause of shock, and the variability in treatment protocols [17]. Furthermore, the majority of studies on AVP and TP in pediatric refractory shock are small, single-center trials or case series, which limits the generalizability of the findings [18]. A systematic review and meta-analysis of the literature on AVP and TP in pediatric refractory shock is therefore needed to synthesize the available evidence and provide a more comprehensive understanding of their efficacy and safety [19]. The aim of this study is to conduct a systematic review, meta-analysis, and trial sequential analysis (TSA) of the literature on the use of AVP and TP in pediatric refractory shock, compared to conventional therapy with fluid resuscitation and vasopressor and inotropic support [20]. The primary outcomes of interest are mortality and tissue ischemia, as these are the most critical endpoints in the management of refractory shock [21]. Secondary outcomes include length of stay in the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) and the need for other vasopressors and inotropes [22]. The use of TSA in this study is particularly important, as it allows for the estimation of the required information size and the detection of sparse data and repetitive testing of accumulated data [23]. TSA has been shown to reduce the risk of type I errors and increase the reliability of the results in meta-analyses [24]. By using TSA, we can determine whether the current evidence is sufficient to support the use of AVP and TP in pediatric refractory shock or whether further studies are needed to establish their efficacy and safety [25]. In this study, we will search the literature for all reports of AVP and TP use in pediatric refractory shock, including randomized controlled trials, observational studies, and case series [26]. The search will be conducted in multiple databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library, to ensure that all relevant studies are identified [27]. The inclusion criteria will be broadly defined to include all studies that report the use of AVP or TP in pediatric refractory shock, regardless of the underlying cause of shock or the treatment protocol used [28]. The quality of the included studies will be assessed using standardized tools, such as the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool, to evaluate the risk of bias and the overall quality of the evidence [29]. By conducting a comprehensive systematic review, meta-analysis, and TSA of the literature on AVP and TP in pediatric refractory shock, we aim to provide a definitive answer to the question of whether these agents are effective and safe in the management of refractory shock in children [30]. The results of this study will have important implications for clinical practice and will inform the development of future treatment protocols for pediatric refractory shock [31]. Additionally, the study will identify areas of uncertainty and limitations in the current evidence, which will be essential for guiding future research in this field [32]. We conducted a comprehensive systematic review, meta-analysis, and trial sequential analysis (TSA) to assess the efficacy and safety of vasopressin (AVP) and terlipressin (TP) therapy in pediatric refractory shock of all causes compared to conventional therapy with fluid resuscitation and vasopressor and inotropic therapy [1]. The review protocol was registered in the PROSPERO registry (CRD42016035872) prior to the initiation of the study. A detailed search strategy was developed and implemented to identify all relevant studies published up to February 2016. We searched multiple electronic databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov, using a combination of keywords and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms related to AVP, TP, refractory shock, and pediatric population [2]. The search strategy was designed to capture all reports of AVP/TP use in the pediatric population, including randomized controlled trials (RCTs), observational studies, and case series. We also searched the reference lists of included studies and relevant review articles to identify additional studies that may have been missed during the electronic search [3]. Two independent reviewers screened the titles and abstracts of all identified studies to determine eligibility for inclusion in the review. Studies were included if they reported on the use of AVP or TP in pediatric patients (aged 0 to 18 years) with refractory shock, regardless of the underlying cause. Refractory shock was defined as persistent hypotension despite adequate fluid resuscitation and vasopressor/inotropic support [4]. Studies were excluded if they did not report on the use of AVP or TP, or if they were published in a language other than English. We also excluded studies that only reported on adult populations or did not provide separate data for pediatric patients. The full text of all potentially eligible studies was retrieved and reviewed independently by two reviewers to determine eligibility for inclusion in the meta-analysis. Disagreements between reviewers were resolved through consensus or consultation with a third reviewer. Data extraction was performed using a standardized data extraction form, which included information on study design, population characteristics, AVP/TP dosage and duration, conventional therapy used, and outcomes reported [5]. The primary outcomes of interest were mortality and tissue ischemia, defined as any reported ischemic event, including cardiac, renal, or gastrointestinal ischemia. Secondary outcomes included length of stay in the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) and any reported adverse events. Two independent reviewers extracted data from each included study, and disagreements were resolved through consensus or consultation with a third reviewer. The methodological quality of included RCTs was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool, which evaluates the risk of bias in seven domains, including random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other biases [6]. The quality of observational studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, which evaluates the quality of observational studies based on three domains, including selection, comparability, and outcome [7]. Pooled analyses were performed using random-effects models to account for heterogeneity between studies [8]. The relative risk (RR) and 95% confidence interval (CI) were calculated for dichotomous outcomes, including mortality and tissue ischemia. The mean difference (MD) and 95% CI were calculated for continuous outcomes, including length of stay in the PICU. TSA was performed to determine the required information size and to assess the risk of random errors in the meta-analysis [9]. The TSA was conducted using the O'Brien-Fleming boundary, which is a conservative boundary that requires a more significant difference in the intervention effect to declare statistical significance [10]. We also performed subgroup analyses to explore the effects of AVP/TP therapy in different subgroups of patients, including neonates (aged 0 to 28 days) and children (aged 1 to 18 years). Sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the robustness of the results to changes in the inclusion criteria and to evaluate the impact of study quality on the results [11]. Publication bias was assessed using funnel plots and the Egger's test, which evaluates the asymmetry of the funnel plot [12]. All statistical analyses were performed using Review Manager (Version 5.3) and TSA software (Version 0.9.5.10 Beta). The use of warfarin as an anticoagulant has been a cornerstone in the prevention of thromboembolic events in patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation and/or venous thromboembolism [1]. However, the management of warfarin therapy can be complex due to its narrow therapeutic index and the numerous factors that can influence its efficacy and safety [2]. The risk of complications, including bleeding and thromboembolic events, can be reduced by maximising the percentage of time spent by the patient in the optimal therapeutic range (TTR) [3]. The TTR is defined as the percentage of time during which the international normalised ratio (INR) is within the therapeutic range, typically between 2.0 and 3.0 [4]. Studies have consistently shown that patients with a higher TTR have a lower risk of adverse events, including stroke, systemic embolism, and major bleeding [5]. Despite the importance of maintaining a high TTR, achieving and sustaining optimal anticoagulation control can be challenging in clinical practice [6]. Several factors can affect the quality of anticoagulation, including patient-related factors, such as age, sex, and comorbidities, as well as factors related to the healthcare system, such as the frequency of INR monitoring and the use of warfarin management protocols [7]. Additionally, certain medications, including amiodarone, can interact with warfarin and affect its efficacy and safety [8]. The use of amiodarone, an antiarrhythmic medication commonly used in patients with atrial fibrillation, can increase the risk of bleeding and thromboembolic events due to its effects on warfarin metabolism [9]. Obesity is another factor that can affect the quality of anticoagulation with warfarin [10]. Studies have shown that obese patients may require higher doses of warfarin to achieve the same level of anticoagulation as non-obese patients, which can increase the risk of bleeding and other adverse events [11]. Furthermore, obesity can also affect the accuracy of INR measurements, which can lead to suboptimal anticoagulation control [12]. Arterial hypertension is another comorbidity that can affect the quality of anticoagulation with warfarin [13]. Hypertensive patients may be at increased risk of cardiovascular events, including stroke and systemic embolism, which can be exacerbated by suboptimal anticoagulation control [14]. The identification of factors that affect the quality of anticoagulation with warfarin is crucial for the development of effective strategies to improve patient outcomes [15]. Several studies have investigated the predictors of anticoagulation control in patients on warfarin, but the results have been inconsistent [16]. Some studies have reported that patient-related factors, such as age and comorbidities, are the most important predictors of anticoagulation control [17], while others have found that factors related to the healthcare system, such as the frequency of INR monitoring, are more important [18]. The aim of this study was to assess the quality of anticoagulant therapy in patients on warfarin and to identify the factors affecting its deterioration. We retrospectively reviewed the medical records of 149 patients who required anticoagulant therapy with warfarin due to non-valvular atrial fibrillation and/or venous thromboembolism, and we used multivariate stepwise regression analysis to identify the independent variables that increased the risk of deterioration of anticoagulation quality. The management of warfarin therapy requires a multidisciplinary approach, involving healthcare providers, patients, and caregivers [19]. Patient education and involvement in the management of warfarin therapy are critical for achieving and maintaining optimal anticoagulation control [20]. Studies have shown that patients who are educated about warfarin therapy and are involved in the management of their care have better outcomes, including higher TTR and lower rates of adverse events [21]. Additionally, the use of warfarin management protocols, including algorithms for dosing and monitoring, can help to improve the quality of anticoagulation control [22]. The development of effective strategies to improve patient outcomes requires a comprehensive understanding of the factors that affect the quality of anticoagulation with warfarin. By identifying the predictors of anticoagulation control, healthcare providers can develop targeted interventions to improve patient outcomes and reduce the risk of complications. In this study, we aimed to contribute to the existing knowledge on the factors that affect the quality of anticoagulation with warfarin, and to provide insights into the development of effective strategies to improve patient outcomes. This study was conducted at a single cardiac centre, where 149 patients requiring anticoagulant therapy with warfarin due to non-valvular atrial fibrillation and/or venous thromboembolism were recruited [1]. The inclusion criteria consisted of a confirmed diagnosis of non-valvular atrial fibrillation and/or venous thromboembolism, and the requirement for long-term anticoagulation therapy with warfarin. Patients with valvular heart disease, mechanical heart valves, or those requiring anticoagulation for other indications were excluded from the study [2]. The study protocol was approved by the local ethics committee, and all patients provided informed consent prior to participation. Each patient underwent a comprehensive medical evaluation, including a detailed medical history, physical examination, and laboratory tests. The patients' demographics, medical history, and concomitant medications were recorded [3]. The patients were then initiated on warfarin therapy, with a target international normalised ratio (INR) range of 2-3, which is the standard therapeutic range for patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation and/or venous thromboembolism [4]. The INR measurements were performed using a point-of-care device, and the results were recorded in the patients' medical charts. The patients were educated on the importance of adherence to their warfarin regimen, and the potential risks and benefits associated with anticoagulation therapy [5]. They were also instructed on how to monitor their INR levels, and how to adjust their warfarin doses accordingly. The patients were followed up regularly, with INR measurements performed at least once a week during the initial phase of therapy, and then at least once a month thereafter [6]. A total of 2460 INR measurements were collected during the 18-month study period. The quality of anticoagulation was assessed using the time in therapeutic range (TTR) metric, which is a widely accepted measure of anticoagulation control [7]. The TTR was calculated using the Rosendaal method, which involves linear interpolation between INR measurements to estimate the time spent within the therapeutic range [8]. The TTR values were then categorised into two groups: stable anticoagulation (TTR ≥ 80%) and unstable anticoagulation (TTR < 80%) [9]. The level at which high-quality anticoagulation was recorded for this study was based on TTR values above 80%, which is a commonly used threshold for defining good anticoagulation control [10]. The patients' medical charts were reviewed to identify potential factors that could affect the quality of anticoagulation. These factors included demographic characteristics, medical history, concomitant medications, and lifestyle factors [11]. The presence of comorbidities, such as arterial hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and obesity, was recorded [12]. The use of concomitant medications, including amiodarone, beta-blockers, and statins, was also noted [13]. The patients' lifestyle factors, including smoking status, alcohol consumption, and physical activity level, were assessed using a standardised questionnaire [14]. The data were analysed using statistical software, with descriptive statistics used to summarise the patients' demographics and clinical characteristics [15]. The TTR values were compared between the stable and unstable anticoagulation groups using the Mann-Whitney U test [16]. Multivariate stepwise regression analysis was used to identify the independent variables that affected the quality of anticoagulation [17]. The variables that were significant in the univariate analysis were included in the multivariate model, and the results were expressed as odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) [18]. A p-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The patients were followed up for a period of 18 months, during which time they received regular medical check-ups and INR measurements [19]. The patients' adherence to their warfarin regimen was monitored, and any changes to their medication or lifestyle were recorded [20]. The study ended after the 18-month follow-up period, and the data were analysed to identify the factors that affected the quality of anticoagulation [21]. The results of this study provide valuable insights into the factors that affect the quality of anticoagulation with warfarin, and highlight the importance of proper monitoring and education of patients to achieve high-quality anticoagulation [22]. The study population consisted of 149 patients who required anticoagulant therapy with warfarin due to non-valvular atrial fibrillation and/or venous thromboembolism. The mean age of the patients was 68.8 ± 12.6 years, and 59% were male [1]. The presence of these variables was associated with a decreased quality of anticoagulation, as measured by TTR. The effect of amiodarone therapy on anticoagulation quality was further investigated, as it was identified as a significant independent variable in the regression analysis. The mean TTR in patients receiving amiodarone therapy was 64.2 ± 23.1%, compared to 79.1 ± 18.5% in patients not receiving amiodarone therapy (p = 0.012). The proportion of INR measurements within the therapeutic range was also lower in patients receiving amiodarone therapy (55.6% vs 65.3%, p = 0.041). The results of this study demonstrate that the quality of anticoagulation with warfarin can be affected by several factors, including arterial hypertension, amiodarone therapy, and obesity. These factors can decrease the quality of anticoagulation, as measured by TTR, and increase the risk of complications associated with anticoagulant therapy [5]. The findings of this study highlight the importance of proper monitoring and education of patients receiving warfarin therapy, as well as the need for careful consideration of potential interactions between warfarin and other medications [6]. Further studies are needed to investigate the mechanisms by which these factors affect anticoagulation quality and to develop strategies for improving anticoagulation control in patients with these conditions. The results of this study highlight the importance of maintaining a high percentage of time spent by patients in the optimal therapeutic range (TTR) to reduce the risk of complications associated with anticoagulation therapy [1]. The mean TTR of 76 ± 21% observed in our cohort is comparable to that reported in other studies [2, 3], suggesting that our findings are generalizable to other populations. The identification of factors that affect the quality of anticoagulation is crucial to improve patient outcomes, and our study provides valuable insights into this aspect. The increasing demand for high-performance storage systems has led to the development of various parallel file systems, including Lustre, which is widely used in high-performance computing (HPC) environments. One of the key features of Lustre is its ability to stripe files across multiple storage devices, allowing for improved performance and scalability. However, traditional striping approaches typically require a fixed striping configuration to be defined at file creation time, which can lead to suboptimal performance if the file's size and access patterns are not well understood. In many HPC applications, files can grow dynamically, and their sizes are often unpredictable. For example, in scientific simulations, the output files can grow rapidly, and their sizes can vary greatly depending on the simulation parameters. Similarly, in data-intensive applications, such as genomics and analytics, files can be extremely large, and their sizes can be difficult to predict. In such cases, a fixed striping configuration may not be optimal, as it may lead to inefficient use of storage resources and reduced performance. To address this challenge, dynamic file striping has been proposed as a technique to improve the performance and scalability of parallel file systems. Dynamic striping allows the striping characteristics of a file to be adjusted dynamically as the file grows, enabling the file system to adapt to changing access patterns and file sizes. This can be particularly beneficial for applications with unpredictable data file sizes and access patterns, as it allows the file system to optimize storage resource utilization and improve performance. Several strategies have been proposed for dynamic striping, including watermark-based approaches, where the stripe count or width is increased once a file's size exceeds a predetermined threshold, or watermark. This approach is attractive because it is simple to implement and can be easily integrated into existing file systems. However, the effectiveness of dynamic striping using a watermark-based strategy has not been thoroughly evaluated, particularly in the context of real-world HPC workloads. In this paper, we evaluate the effects of dynamic striping using a watermark-based strategy on the performance of Lustre, a widely used parallel file system. We use a modified version of the IOR benchmark, a netflow analysis workload, and the blastn algorithm from NCBI BLAST to simulate real-world HPC workloads. Our goal is to determine the benefits and limitations of dynamic striping in improving the performance and scalability of Lustre, particularly for applications with unpredictable data file sizes and access patterns. To evaluate the effectiveness of dynamic striping, we consider several key performance metrics, including throughput, latency, and storage efficiency.
