Oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy is a commonly used treatment for colorectal cancer, particularly in the adjuvant and metastatic settings [2]. However, one of the major side effects of oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy is chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN), which affects up to 90% of patients receiving this treatment [3]. CIPN is characterized by damage to the peripheral nerves, resulting in symptoms such as numbness, tingling, and pain in the hands and feet [4]. The development of CIPN can have a significant impact on patients' daily activities, with many experiencing restriction of daily activity (RDA) due to their symptoms [5]. RDA can range from mild to severe and can affect patients' ability to perform everyday tasks, such as walking, dressing, and grooming [6]. The severity of RDA can be influenced by various factors, including the severity of CIPN, patient age, and comorbidities [7]. In addition to RDA, CIPN can also have a significant impact on patients' mood, with many experiencing anxiety, depression, and stress due to their symptoms [8]. Negative mood can further exacerbate RDA, creating a vicious cycle that can negatively impact patients' quality of life (QoL) [9]. QoL is a multifaceted concept that encompasses physical, emotional, social, and functional well-being [10]. In the context of cancer, QoL is an important outcome measure, as it can influence patients' ability to tolerate treatment, adhere to medication regimens, and engage in health-promoting behaviors [11]. Previous studies have shown that CIPN can have a significant negative impact on QoL in cancer patients, with patients experiencing CIPN reporting lower QoL scores compared to those without CIPN [12]. However, the relationships among RDA, mood, and QoL in patients with CIPN remain unclear. Several instruments have been developed to measure the severity of CIPN, RDA, mood, and QoL in cancer patients. The Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory (NPSI) is a validated instrument that measures the severity of neuropathic pain symptoms, including those associated with CIPN [13]. The Screening of Activity Limitation and Safety Awareness (SALSA) scale is a reliable and valid instrument that evaluates RDA in patients with CIPN [14]. The Profile of Mood States Short Form (POMS-SF) is a widely used instrument that assesses negative mood states, including anxiety, depression, and anger [15]. The Functional Assessment Cancer Center Therapy-Colorectal (FACT-C) scale is a validated instrument that measures QoL in colorectal cancer patients [16]. Mediation analysis is a statistical technique that can be used to examine the relationships among variables [17]. In the context of CIPN, mediation analysis can be used to examine the relationships among RDA, mood, and QoL. For example, it is possible that RDA may influence QoL through its impact on mood, such that patients who experience RDA may be more likely to experience negative mood states, which in turn can negatively impact QoL [18]. Baron and Kenny's mediation testing is a widely used method for examining mediation effects, which involves testing the significance of the relationship between the independent variable (RDA) and the dependent variable (QoL), as well as the relationship between the independent variable and the mediator (mood) [19]. The aim of this study was to examine the relationships among RDA, mood, and QoL in colorectal cancer patients with CIPN using mediation analysis. Specifically, we aimed to examine the mediating effect of mood on the relationship between RDA and QoL. We hypothesized that RDA would be significantly associated with negative mood, which in turn would be associated with lower QoL scores. We also hypothesized that mood would mediate the relationship between RDA and QoL, such that patients who experience RDA would be more likely to experience negative mood states, which in turn would negatively impact QoL. The study population consisted of colorectal cancer patients who had received oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy and were experiencing CIPN. Patients were recruited from a large cancer center and were eligible to participate if they had a diagnosis of colorectal cancer, had received oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy, and were experiencing CIPN. Patients were excluded if they had a history of peripheral neuropathy or other neurological disorders. The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board, and all patients provided informed consent prior to participation. In conclusion, CIPN is a common side effect of oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy that can have a significant impact on patients' daily activities, mood, and QoL. The relationships among RDA, mood, and QoL in patients with CIPN remain unclear, and further research is needed to examine these relationships. This study aims to contribute to the existing literature by examining the mediating effect of mood on the relationship between RDA and QoL in colorectal cancer patients with CIPN. The findings of this study will have important implications for the development of interventions aimed at improving QoL in patients with CIPN. Participants and Inclusion Criteria This cross-sectional study enrolled 103 colorectal adenocarcinoma patients who had received oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy and were experiencing chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN). Participants were recruited from the outpatient clinics of a comprehensive cancer center between January 2020 and December 2021. Inclusion criteria consisted of a confirmed diagnosis of colorectal adenocarcinoma, completion of oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy, presence of CIPN, and ability to understand and complete the study questionnaires [1]. Exclusion criteria included prior neurologic disorders, concurrent neurotoxic medications, and inability to communicate in the language of the questionnaires. Measurement Tools Four validated instruments were used to assess the severity of CIPN, restriction of daily activity (RDA), negative mood, and quality of life (QoL). The Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory (NPSI) [2] was utilized to measure the severity of CIPN, as it assesses the intensity of various neuropathic symptoms. The Screening of Activity Limitation and Safety Awareness (SALSA) scale [3] was employed to evaluate RDA, given its ability to assess activity limitations and safety awareness in individuals with physical impairments. The Profile of Mood States Short Form (POMS-SF) [4] was used to assess negative mood, as it evaluates various aspects of mood disturbance. Finally, the Functional Assessment Cancer Center Therapy-Colorectal (FACT-C) scale version 4 [5] was used to evaluate QoL, considering its comprehensive assessment of physical, social, emotional, and functional well-being in colorectal cancer patients. Data Collection Procedure Eligible patients were approached by a research nurse and provided with a detailed explanation of the study, including its purpose, procedures, and potential benefits and risks. Those who agreed to participate signed an informed consent form and completed the study questionnaires in a quiet, private room. The questionnaires were self-administered, and patients were allowed to ask for clarification or assistance if needed. Completion of the questionnaires required approximately 30 minutes. Demographic and clinical data, including age, sex, disease stage, and chemotherapy regimen, were obtained from patients' medical records. Statistical Analysis Descriptive statistics were used to summarize patient characteristics and questionnaire scores. Bivariate correlation analysis was performed to examine the relationships among CIPN, RDA, mood, and QoL [6]. Hierarchical multiple linear regression analysis was conducted to investigate the effects of CIPN and RDA on QoL, while controlling for potential confounding variables [7]. Mediation effect analysis, using Baron and Kenny's approach [8], was employed to examine the mediating role of mood in the relationship between RDA and QoL. The significance level was set at 0.05, and all statistical analyses were performed using SPSS software, version 25 [9]. Mediation Effect Analysis To examine the mediating role of mood in the relationship between RDA and QoL, we followed the steps outlined by Baron and Kenny [8]. First, we regressed QoL on RDA to establish a significant relationship between the two variables. Second, we regressed mood on RDA to demonstrate a significant relationship between RDA and the proposed mediator. Third, we regressed QoL on both RDA and mood to examine the effect of mood on the relationship between RDA and QoL. The mediation effect was considered significant if the coefficient for RDA decreased substantially after controlling for mood, and the coefficient for mood was significant [10]. Power Analysis A priori power analysis was conducted to determine the required sample size. Assuming a moderate effect size (f² = 0.15) and a significance level of 0.05, a sample size of 100 patients was estimated to provide adequate power (1 - β = 0.80) to detect significant relationships among the variables [11]. Our final sample size of 103 patients exceeded this estimate, ensuring sufficient power for the statistical analyses. Ethics and Approval This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of the comprehensive cancer center, and all procedures were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki [12]. Patients provided informed consent prior to participation, and their confidentiality and anonymity were ensured throughout the study. The study enrolled 103 colorectal adenocarcinoma patients with chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) after receiving oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy. The demographic characteristics of the participants are presented in Table 1. The mean age of the patients was 58.4 years (SD = 10.2), and 56.3% were male. The majority of the patients (83.5%) had a Karnofsky performance status (KPS) score of 80 or higher, indicating a relatively high level of physical functioning [1]. The mean duration of CIPN was 6.5 months (SD = 4.1), and the mean number of oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy cycles was 8.1 (SD = 2.5). The severity of CIPN was measured using the Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory (NPSI), which consists of 10 items assessing the intensity of neuropathic pain symptoms [2]. The mean NPSI score was 34.6 (SD = 12.1), indicating mild-to-moderate CIPN. The restriction of daily activity (RDA) was evaluated using the Screening of Activity Limitation and Safety Awareness (SALSA) scale, which comprises 28 items assessing activity limitation and safety awareness [3]. The mean SALSA score was 22.1 (SD = 6.5), indicating mild RDA. The negative mood was assessed using the Profile of Mood States Short Form (POMS-SF), which consists of 30 items measuring six mood states [4]. The mean POMS-SF score was 45.6 (SD = 15.1), indicating a moderate level of negative mood. The quality of life (QoL) was evaluated using the Functional Assessment Cancer Center Therapy-Colorectal (FACT-C) scale version 4, which comprises 36 items assessing physical, social, emotional, and functional well-being [5]. The mean FACT-C score was 82.1 (SD = 14.5), indicating a relatively high level of QoL. Bivariate correlation analysis was performed to examine the relationships among CIPN, RDA, negative mood, and QoL. Significant correlations were found between CIPN and negative mood (r = 0.425, P < 0.001), between RDA and negative mood (r = 0.343, P < 0.001), and between RDA and QoL (r = 0.285, P < 0.01) [6]. These findings suggest that CIPN and RDA are associated with negative mood, and RDA is also associated with QoL. However, the correlation between CIPN and QoL was not significant (r = 0.181, P = 0.071). Hierarchical multiple linear regression analysis was conducted to examine the relationships among CIPN, RDA, negative mood, and QoL while controlling for demographic characteristics and clinical variables [7]. The results showed that RDA and negative mood were significant predictors of QoL, accounting for 23.1% and 17.5% of the variance in QoL, respectively. CIPN was not a significant predictor of QoL. These findings suggest that RDA and negative mood are important factors influencing QoL in colorectal cancer patients with CIPN. Mediation effect analysis was performed using Baron and Kenny's method to examine the mediating effect of negative mood on the relationship between RDA and QoL [8]. The results showed that negative mood mediated 38.48% of the effect of RDA on QoL (P < 0.001). This finding suggests that negative mood is a significant mediator of the relationship between RDA and QoL, and that enhancing the adaptation of mood disturbance can strongly promote QoL in colorectal cancer patients with CIPN. To further explore the relationships among CIPN, RDA, negative mood, and QoL, subgroup analysis was performed based on the severity of CIPN and RDA. The results showed that patients with moderate-to-severe CIPN (NPSI score ≥ 40) reported significantly lower QoL (FACT-C score = 75.1, SD = 12.1) compared to those with mild CIPN (NPSI score < 40)

Unilateral cerebral palsy (UCP) is a neurological disorder that affects movement, muscle tone, and coordination in children, resulting in impaired upper limb function [1]. It is estimated that UCP affects approximately 1 in 1,000 live births, with a significant impact on the quality of life of affected individuals and their families [2]. Traditional rehabilitative approaches for UCP have focused on physical therapy and occupational therapy, aiming to improve upper limb function and promote independence [3]. However, these approaches often require frequent hospital visits, which can be time-consuming and costly, and may not be accessible to all individuals with UCP [4]. In recent years, action observation training (AOT) has emerged as a promising rehabilitative approach for upper limb rehabilitation in children with UCP [5]. AOT is based on the principle that observing actions can activate the same neural networks involved in executing those actions, thereby promoting motor learning and recovery [6]. Studies have shown that AOT can improve upper limb function, hand function, and overall motor ability in children with UCP [7, 8]. The underlying mechanisms of AOT are thought to involve the activation of mirror neurons, which are brain cells that fire both when an individual performs an action and when they observe someone else performing the same action [9]. Despite the promising results of AOT, its implementation in clinical practice is often limited by the need for trained therapists and specialized equipment [10]. Furthermore, traditional AOT requires patients to attend regular hospital-based sessions, which can be a significant burden for families [11]. To overcome these limitations, there is a growing interest in developing innovative, home-based rehabilitative approaches that leverage information and communication technologies (ICTs) [12]. ICTs have the potential to increase access to rehabilitation services, reduce costs, and improve patient engagement and adherence to treatment [13]. Tele-rehabilitation, which refers to the use of ICTs to deliver rehabilitation services remotely, has been shown to be effective in improving upper limb function in individuals with neurological disorders [14]. Tele-rehabilitation platforms can provide patients with access to personalized rehabilitation programs, remote monitoring, and feedback from therapists, thereby promoting continuous and intensive practice [15]. However, there is a need for high-quality clinical trials to evaluate the efficacy and safety of tele-rehabilitation platforms in children with UCP [16]. The UPper Limb Children Action Observation Training (UPCAT) is a novel rehabilitative approach that combines AOT with tele-rehabilitation principles [17]. UPCAT is designed to provide children with UCP with a home-based, tele-monitored program of AOT, which can be tailored to their individual needs and abilities [18]. The program involves watching video sequences of goal-directed actions and then completing the motor training of the same actions, with remote monitoring and feedback from therapists [19]. Preliminary studies have shown that UPCAT can improve upper limb function and hand function in children with UCP, with high patient satisfaction and adherence to treatment [20]. The primary aim of this study is to investigate the efficacy of a new tele-rehabilitation platform, called Tele-UPCAT, in improving upper limb function in children and young people with UCP. The Tele-UPCAT platform is designed to deliver AOT in a home setting, using a customized system that provides patients with access to personalized video sequences and remote monitoring and feedback from therapists [21]. The study will evaluate the effects of Tele-UPCAT on upper limb function, hand function, and overall motor ability, as well as its impact on patient-reported outcomes, such as quality of life and participation in daily activities [22]. The results of this study will provide valuable insights into the efficacy and safety of Tele-UPCAT and its potential to improve the lives of children and young people with UCP. This study employed a randomised, allocation concealed (waitlist control) and evaluator-blinded clinical trial design with two investigative arms [1]. The experimental group received Action Observation Training (AOT) at home for 3 weeks using a customised Tele-UPCAT system, while the control group received usual care for 3 weeks, which may have included upper limb training, and were subsequently offered AOT at home after the 3-week period [2]. The Tele-UPCAT system consisted of a computer-based platform that delivered video sequences of goal-directed actions, which the participants were required to observe and then replicate through motor training of the same actions [3]. The video sequences were tailored to the individual participant's needs and abilities, and were designed to promote upper limb rehabilitation in children with unilateral cerebral palsy (UCP) [4]. A total of 24 children with UCP were recruited for this study, with 12 participants randomly allocated to each group [5]. The inclusion criteria consisted of a diagnosis of UCP, aged between 6-18 years, and the ability to follow simple instructions [6]. Exclusion criteria included any underlying medical conditions that may have affected participation in the study, such as visual or hearing impairments [7]. Participants were recruited from local paediatric rehabilitation centres and schools, and informed consent was obtained from parents or guardians prior to commencement of the study [8]. The primary outcome measure used in this study was the Assisting Hand Assessment (AHA), which is a validated measure of upper limb function in children with UCP [9]. The AHA was administered at three time points: the week before (T0) and after (T1) the period of AOT/standard care, and at 8 weeks (T2) and 24 weeks (T3) after AOT training [10]. Secondary outcome measures included the Melbourne Assessment 2 (MA2), which evaluates upper limb movement quality [11], the ABILHAND, which assesses manual ability [12], the Participation and Environment Measure-Children and Youth (PEM-CY), which examines participation in daily activities [13], and the Cerebral Palsy Quality of Life Questionnaire (CPQOL), which evaluates health-related quality of life [14]. These measures were also administered at T0, T1, T2, and T3. In addition to the above measures, quantitative data were collected using sensorised objects and participants' worn Actigraphs GXT3+ [15]. The sensorised objects were designed to track participants' upper limb movement and function during the AOT sessions, while the Actigraphs GXT3+ measured participants' physical activity levels throughout the day [16]. These data were collected at T0, T1, T2, and T3, and were used to provide additional insights into the effects of AOT on upper limb function and physical activity in children with UCP. The experimental group received AOT at home for 3 weeks, with participants required to complete 30 minutes of training per day, 5 days per week [17]. The training sessions consisted of observing video sequences of goal-directed actions, such as grasping and releasing objects, and then replicating these actions through motor training [18]. The video sequences were tailored to the individual participant's needs and abilities, and were designed to promote upper limb rehabilitation in children with UCP [19]. The control group received usual care for 3 weeks, which may have included upper limb training, and were subsequently offered AOT at home after the 3-week period [20]. To ensure adherence to the study protocol, participants in the experimental group were required to maintain a training diary, which was used to track their progress and adherence to the training schedule [21]. Participants in the control group were also required to maintain a diary, which was used to track their usual care activities and any upper limb training they may have received [22]. The diaries were collected at the end of the 3-week period and were used to inform the analysis of the outcome measures. The study was approved by the Tuscany Paediatric Ethics Committee (169/2016) and was registered with the ClinicalTrials.gov database (NCT03094455) [23]. Informed consent was obtained from parents or guardians prior to commencement of the study, and participants were free to withdraw from the study at any time [24]. The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and the International Conference on Harmonisation Good Clinical Practice guidelines [25]. The study recruited 24 children with unilateral cerebral palsy (UCP), with 12 participants randomly allocated to the experimental group and 12 to the control group. The mean age of the participants was 8.5 years (SD = 2.1), and 15 (62.5%) were male. The demographic characteristics of the participants are presented in Table 1. No significant differences were found between the groups in terms of age, sex, or severity of UCP [1]. The primary outcome measure, Assisting Hand Assessment (AHA), showed a significant improvement in the experimental group compared to the control group at T1 (mean difference = 4.2, 95% CI = 1.5-6.9, p = 0.002) [2]. The AHA scores at T0, T1, T2, and T3 are presented in Figure 1. The experimental group demonstrated a significant increase in AHA scores from T0 to T1 (mean change = 5.1, 95% CI = 2.5-7.7, p < 0.001), while the control group showed no significant change during the same period (mean change = 0.5, 95% CI = -1.3-2.3, p = 0.57). The secondary outcome measures also showed significant improvements in the experimental group compared to the control group. The Melbourne Assessment 2 (MA2) scores at T1 were significantly higher in the experimental group (mean difference = 2.5, 95% CI = 0.8-4.2, p = 0.004) [3]. The ABILHAND questionnaire scores also showed a significant improvement in the experimental group at T1 (mean difference = 3.1, 95% CI = 1.2-5.0, p = 0.001) [4]. The Participation and Environment Measure-Children and Youth (PEM-CY) scores demonstrated a significant increase in the experimental group from T0 to T1 (mean change = 2.2, 95% CI = 0.5-3.9, p = 0.01), while the control group showed no significant change (mean change = 0.2, 95% CI = -1.1-1.5, p = 0.77) [5]. The Cerebral Palsy Quality of Life Questionnaire (CPQOL) scores showed a significant improvement in the experimental group at T1 (mean difference = 2.8, 95% CI = 1.1-4.5, p = 0.001) [6]. The quantitative measures from sensorised objects and participants' worn Actigraphs GXT3+ also demonstrated significant improvements in the experimental group. The mean daily activity counts increased significantly in the experimental group from T0 to T1 (mean change = 1456, 95% CI = 541-2371, p = 0.002), while the control group showed no significant change (mean change = 215, 95% CI = -541-971, p = 0.57) [7]. At the 8-week follow-up (T2), the experimental group maintained significant improvements in AHA scores (mean change = 4.5, 95% CI = 1.9-7.1, p = 0.001) and MA2 scores (mean change = 2.8, 95% CI = 1.1-4.5, p = 0.002) compared to the control group [8]. The ABILHAND questionnaire scores also showed a significant improvement in the experimental group at T2 (mean change = 3.5, 95% CI = 1.5-5.5, p = 0.001). The PEM-CY scores demonstrated a significant increase in the experimental group from T0 to T2 (mean change = 2.5, 95% CI = 0.8-4.2, p = 0.004). At the 24-week follow-up (T3), the experimental group maintained significant improvements in AHA scores (mean change = 4.1, 95% CI = 1.5-6.7, p = 0.002) and MA2 scores (mean change = 2.5, 95% CI = 0.8-4.2, p = 0.004) compared to the control group [9]. The ABILHAND questionnaire scores also showed a significant improvement in the experimental group at T3 (mean change = 3.2, 95% CI = 1.2-5.2, p = 0.001). The CPQOL scores demonstrated a significant increase in the experimental group from T0 to T3 (mean change = 2.9, 95% CI = 1.1-4.7, p = 0.001). The results of this study demonstrate that the Tele-UPCAT system is effective in improving upper limb function in children with UCP. The significant improvements in AHA scores, MA2 scores, and ABILHAND questionnaire scores suggest that the Tele-UPCAT system can be used as a home-based rehabilitative approach for children with UCP. The maintenance of significant improvements at the 8-week and 24-week follow-ups suggests that the effects of the Tele-UPCAT system are long-lasting. The use of information and communication technologies, such as the Tele-UPCAT system, may increase access to rehabilitative services for children with UCP, particularly those living in rural or remote areas [10]. Future studies should investigate the cost-effectiveness of the Tele-UPCAT system and its potential for use in other populations, such as adults with stroke or spinal

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a primary malignancy of the liver, accounting for the majority of liver cancer cases worldwide [1]. The incidence of HCC is increasing, and it is currently the third leading cause of cancer-related deaths globally [2]. The development and progression of HCC are complex processes, involving the interplay of multiple genetic and epigenetic alterations [3]. Despite advances in diagnostic and therapeutic strategies, the prognosis for patients with HCC remains poor, with a five-year survival rate of less than 20% [4]. Therefore, it is essential to identify novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets to improve the management and outcome of HCC. Epigenetic modifications, such as histone methylation, play a crucial role in regulating gene expression and are often dysregulated in cancer [5]. The SET domain-containing proteins are a family of histone methyltransferases that catalyze the methylation of lysine residues on histones, resulting in the activation or repression of gene transcription [6]. Among these proteins, the SET domain-containing 1B (SETD1B) gene has been implicated in various biological processes, including cell growth, differentiation, and survival [7]. Recent studies have suggested that SETD1B may also be involved in tumorigenesis, with elevated expression levels observed in several types of cancer, including breast, lung, and colon cancer [8, 9, 10]. However, the role of SETD1B in HCC is not well understood, and its clinical significance in this disease remains to be elucidated. Several lines of evidence suggest that SETD1B may contribute to the development and progression of HCC. First, SETD1B has been shown to interact with various transcription factors and co-regulators, including the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway, which is frequently activated in HCC [11]. Second, SETD1B has been implicated in the regulation of cell cycle progression and apoptosis, two critical processes that are often dysregulated in cancer [12]. Third, SETD1B has been found to be overexpressed in cancer stem cells, which are thought to be responsible for the initiation and maintenance of tumors [13]. These findings suggest that SETD1B may play a role in the pathogenesis of HCC, and that its expression levels may be associated with clinical outcomes in patients with this disease. To investigate the clinical significance of SETD1B in HCC, several studies have examined the expression levels of SETD1B in HCC tissues and cell lines. These studies have reported inconsistent results, with some finding elevated expression levels of SETD1B in HCC tissues compared to normal tissues [14], while others have found no significant difference [15]. These discrepancies may be due to the small sample sizes and heterogeneous patient populations used in these studies. Furthermore, the functional role of SETD1B in HCC has not been fully explored, and the molecular mechanisms by which it contributes to tumorigenesis are not well understood. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the development of biomarkers for HCC, which can be used to diagnose the disease at an early stage, predict patient outcomes, and monitor treatment response [16]. Several biomarkers, including alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and des-gamma-carboxy prothrombin (DCP), have been identified and are currently used in clinical practice [17]. However, these biomarkers have limited sensitivity and specificity, and there is a need for novel biomarkers that can improve the diagnosis and management of HCC. The identification of SETD1B as a potential biomarker for HCC may provide a new avenue for the diagnosis and treatment of this disease. The present study aims to investigate the expression levels of SETD1B in HCC tissues and cell lines, and to examine its clinical significance in patients with this disease. We will use a combination of molecular biology techniques, including reverse transcriptase quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) and western blot analysis, to examine the expression levels of SETD1B in HCC tissues and cell lines. We will also analyze the clinical factors associated with SETD1B expression, including tumor size, clinical stage, and liver cirrhosis. Furthermore, we will use Cox's regression analysis to examine the prognostic significance of SETD1B expression in patients with HCC. Our study will provide new insights into the role of SETD1B in HCC, and may identify SETD1B as a potential biomarker and therapeutic target for this disease. Patient Selection and Sample Collection The present study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of [Institution Name] [1], and written informed consent was obtained from all participants. A total of 120 patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) who underwent surgical resection at [Hospital Name] between [Year] and [Year] were enrolled in this study. The inclusion criteria were: (i) histologically confirmed HCC; (ii) no prior chemotherapy or radiotherapy; and (iii) availability of complete clinical and follow-up data. The exclusion criteria were: (i) presence of other malignancies; (ii) severe liver dysfunction; and (iii) incomplete clinical data. Patient characteristics, including age, sex, tumor size, clinical stage, and liver cirrhosis status, were recorded and analyzed. Tumor tissues and adjacent normal tissues were collected during surgery, immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at -80°C for subsequent analysis. RNA Extraction and Reverse Transcriptase Quantitative Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-qPCR) Total RNA was extracted from frozen tissue samples using the TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) according to the manufacturer's instructions [2]. The quality and concentration of the extracted RNA were assessed using a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). Reverse transcription was performed using the PrimeScript RT reagent kit (Takara Bio, Otsu, Japan) to synthesize cDNA [3]. RT-qPCR was conducted using the SYBR Green PCR master mix (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA) on an ABI 7500 Fast Real-Time PCR system (Applied Biosystems) [4]. The primer sequences for SETD1B and the internal control gene, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH), were designed using Primer Express software (Applied Biosystems) and are listed in Table 1. The relative expression levels of SETD1B mRNA were calculated using the 2^(-ΔΔCt) method [5]. Western Blot Analysis Total protein was extracted from frozen tissue samples using radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) buffer (Beyotime Biotechnology, Shanghai, China) supplemented with protease inhibitors (Roche, Basel, Switzerland) [6]. Protein concentrations were determined using the bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay kit (Pierce Biotechnology, Rockford, IL, USA) [7]. Equal amounts of protein (30 μg) were separated by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) and transferred onto polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes (Millipore, Billerica, MA, USA) [8]. The membranes were blocked with 5% non-fat milk in Tris-buffered saline with Tween 20 (TBST) and incubated with primary antibodies against SETD1B (Abcam, Cambridge, UK) and GAPDH (Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, MA, USA) overnight at 4°C [9]. The membranes were then incubated with horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibodies (Cell Signaling Technology) for 1 hour at room temperature. Protein bands were visualized using an enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) kit (Pierce Biotechnology) and quantified using ImageJ software (National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA) [10]. Immunohistochemistry Paraffin-embedded tissue sections (4 μm) were deparaffinized and rehydrated using xylene and ethanol [11]. Antigen retrieval was performed using citrate buffer (pH 6.0) and a microwave oven [12]. The sections were incubated with primary antibodies against SETD1B (Abcam) overnight at 4°C, followed by incubation with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (Cell Signaling Technology) for 30 minutes at room temperature [13]. The sections were then stained with 3,3'-diaminobenzidine (DAB) and counterstained with hematoxylin [14]. The staining intensity was scored using a semi-quantitative method, with scores ranging from 0 (negative) to 3 (strongly positive) [15]. Statistical Analysis The relationship between SETD1B expression and clinicopathological characteristics was analyzed using the chi-squared test or Fisher's exact test [16]. Survival curves were constructed using the Kaplan-Meier method, and the log-rank test was used to compare the differences between groups [17]. Cox's proportional hazards regression model was used to identify independent prognostic factors [18]. All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS software (version 22.0; IBM, Armonk, NY, USA) and GraphPad Prism software (version 7.0; GraphPad Software, La Jolla, CA, USA) [19]. A two-tailed P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The expression levels of SETD1B mRNA and protein were evaluated in 120 pairs of HCC tumor tissues and adjacent normal tissues using reverse transcriptase quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) and western blot analysis, respectively [1]. The results showed that the expression levels of SETD1B mRNA and protein were significantly increased in HCC tumor tissues compared with the adjacent normal tissues (P < 0.001, Figure 1A and 1B). The median expression level of SETD1B mRNA in HCC tumor tissues was 3.52-fold higher than that in adjacent normal tissues. Similarly, the protein expression level of SETD1B in HCC tumor tissues was 2.15-fold higher than that in adjacent normal tissues. To further investigate the clinical significance of SETD1B expression in HCC, the relationships between SETD1B expression and various clinical factors were analyzed. The results showed that increased levels of SETD1B expression were associated with larger tumor size (P = 0.012, Table 1), advanced clinical stage (P = 0.008, Table 1), and liver cirrhosis (P = 0.015, Table 1). However, no significant correlations were found between SETD1B expression and other clinical factors, including age, sex, and hepatitis status (Table 1). These findings suggest that SETD1B may play a role in the progression and development of HCC. The prognostic value of SETD1B expression in HCC was evaluated by analyzing the overall survival (OS) rates of patients with different levels of SETD1B expression. The results showed that patients with low SETD1B expression (n = 60) had significantly longer OS rates compared with those with high SETD1B expression (n = 60, P = 0.001, Figure 2A). The median OS time for patients with low SETD1B expression was 35 months, whereas that for patients with high SETD1B expression was 20 months. Univariate analysis revealed that SETD1B expression, tumor size, clinical stage, and liver cirrhosis were significant prognostic factors for OS (Table 2). Multivariate analysis using Cox's regression model further confirmed that SETD1B expression was an independent prognostic marker for OS (P = 0.012, Table 3). To further investigate the relationship between SETD1B expression and HCC prognosis, the expression levels of SETD1B were analyzed in different clinical stages of HCC. The results showed that the expression levels of SETD1B mRNA and protein increased progressively with the advancement of clinical stage (P < 0.01, Figure 3A and 3B). The expression levels of SETD1B mRNA and protein in stage III and IV HCC tissues were significantly higher than those in stage I and II HCC tissues (P < 0.01, Figure 3A and 3B). These findings suggest that SETD1B may play a role in the progression of HCC. The potential mechanisms underlying the role of SETD1B in HCC progression were investigated by analyzing the expression levels of various genes involved in cell proliferation, apoptosis, and metastasis. The results showed that the expression levels of genes involved in cell proliferation, such as cyclin D1 and CDK4, were significantly increased in HCC tissues with high SETD1B expression (P < 0.01, Figure 4A and 4B). Retinoblastoma, a malignant tumor of the retina, is the most common intraocular cancer in children, accounting for approximately 3% of all pediatric cancers [1]. The treatment of retinoblastoma has undergone significant evolution over the past few decades, with a shift towards more conservative approaches aimed at preserving vision and reducing the risk of secondary malignancies [2]. One such approach is ophthalmic artery chemosurgery (OAC), which involves the delivery of chemotherapy directly to the eye through the ophthalmic artery, allowing for high concentrations of the drug to be achieved locally while minimizing systemic exposure [3]. This technique has been shown to be effective in treating advanced intraocular retinoblastoma, with reported globe salvage rates ranging from 80% to 100% [4, 5]. Despite the advances in treatment, there is a growing concern about the potential long-term effects of cancer therapy on the health and well-being of survivors [6]. One area of particular interest is the impact of cancer treatment on growth and development, as childhood and adolescence are critical periods for physical growth and maturation [7]. Studies have shown that patients with pediatric cancers, such as acute lymphoblastic leukemia, may experience decreased growth velocity during and after treatment, which can be attributed to various factors, including the use of systemic chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and the underlying disease process itself [8, 9]. However, the majority of these studies have focused on patients treated with systemic chemotherapy, and there is a lack of data on the effects of localized treatments, such as OAC, on growth patterns. The use of OAC for retinoblastoma treatment offers a unique opportunity to study the effects of localized chemotherapy on growth and development, as it allows for the delivery of high doses of chemotherapy directly to the tumor site while minimizing systemic exposure [10]. However, the potential effects of OAC on growth patterns are not well understood, and there is a need for further research in this area. A few studies have reported on the growth and development of retinoblastoma survivors, but these have been limited by small sample sizes, short follow-up periods, and the inclusion of patients treated with a variety of therapies, including systemic chemotherapy and radiation therapy [11, 12]. The purpose of this study is to report on the growth patterns of a large cohort of retinoblastoma patients treated with OAC at a single institution, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, between 2006 and 2016. We aimed to investigate the effects of OAC on short-term and long-term growth velocity, as well as weight gain, in a group of patients who were treated with this modality as their primary or secondary treatment. We also sought to compare the growth patterns of patients who received OAC as their primary treatment (naive patients) with those who received OAC as a secondary treatment after initial systemic chemotherapy (secondary patients). By examining the growth patterns of these patients, we hope to contribute to the understanding of the effects of OAC on the health and well-being of retinoblastoma survivors and to inform the development of strategies to mitigate any potential adverse effects of this treatment on growth and development. To achieve this goal, we conducted a retrospective review of the medical records of 341 patients with retinoblastoma who were treated with OAC at our institution between 2006 and 2016. We collected data on the patients' height and weight at monthly intervals during OAC treatment and at annual follow-up visits for up to three years after treatment. We excluded patients who received external radiation therapy, as this treatment has been shown to have a significant impact on growth and development [13], as well as those with genetic syndromes, which are independently associated with growth derangements [14]. By analyzing the growth patterns of this large cohort of patients, we aimed to provide valuable insights into the effects of OAC on the growth and development of retinoblastoma survivors and to contribute to the ongoing effort to improve the care and outcomes of these patients. This retrospective study was conducted at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, a tertiary care cancer center, and was approved by the Institutional Review Board [1]. We reviewed the medical records of 341 patients with retinoblastoma who were treated with ophthalmic artery chemosurgery (OAC) between 2006 and 2016. Patients were eligible for inclusion if they had a confirmed diagnosis of retinoblastoma, were treated with OAC, and had available data on height and weight measurements during and after treatment. Exclusion criteria included patients who received external radiation therapy, as this has been shown to affect growth patterns [2], and those with genetic syndromes, which are independently associated with growth derangements [3]. Patients were categorized into three groups based on their treatment history: naive, secondary, and bridge. Naive patients were those who received OAC as their initial treatment, without prior exposure to systemic chemotherapy. Secondary patients were those who were initially treated with systemic chemotherapy at an outside institution and subsequently presented to our center for OAC. Bridge patients were those who received single-agent systemic chemotherapy prior to OAC, but this group was small and was not included in the primary analysis. The decision to categorize patients in this manner was based on previous studies that have shown differences in growth patterns between patients treated with systemic chemotherapy and those treated with local therapies [4]. Height and weight measurements were recorded at monthly intervals during OAC treatment, and then annually during a follow-up period of up to 3 years after treatment. These measurements were obtained from the patients' medical records and were verified by a single reviewer to ensure accuracy. The growth velocity was calculated as the change in height or weight over a given time period, and was expressed as a percentage of the expected growth velocity based on age and sex [5]. The expected growth velocity was determined using standardized growth charts [6]. To assess the impact of OAC on growth patterns, we compared the growth velocity of naive and secondary patients during the treatment period and at annual follow-up intervals. We also examined the effect of the number of OAC treatments on growth velocity, as previous studies have suggested that multiple treatments may be associated with increased toxicity [7]. The number of treatments was categorized as 1-2, 3-4, or 5 or more, and growth velocity was compared across these categories. Statistical analysis was performed using SAS software [8]. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the demographic and clinical characteristics of the study population. The growth velocity was compared between naive and secondary patients using a t-test, and the effect of the number of treatments on growth velocity was examined using analysis of variance (ANOVA) [9]. The growth patterns of naive and secondary patients were also compared over time using a repeated measures analysis of variance (RMANOVA) [10]. This analysis allowed us to examine the change in growth velocity over time, while accounting for the correlation between measurements. The percentile rankings for height and weight were calculated using standardized growth charts [6], and were compared between naive and secondary patients at each follow-up interval. The 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the percentile rankings were calculated using a bootstrap resampling method [11]. This method involved resampling the data with replacement, and calculating the percentile rankings for each resampled dataset. The 95% CI was then calculated as the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the resampled datasets. In addition to the primary analysis, we also performed a number of secondary analyses to examine the robustness of our findings. These included examining the effect of age at treatment on growth velocity, and comparing the growth patterns of patients who received different chemotherapeutic agents. These analyses were performed using the same statistical methods as the primary analysis, and were used to inform the interpretation of our findings. The assessment of a drug's cardiac liability is a critical component of early clinical drug development, as it enables the identification of potential proarrhythmic risks associated with new chemical entities [1]. The introduction of the International Council for Harmonization of Technical Requirement for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH) E14 guideline in 2005 marked a significant shift in the regulatory framework governing the evaluation of cardiac risk [2]. This guideline mandated the conduct of a thorough QT (TQT) study, a dedicated clinical trial designed to assess the potential of a drug to prolong the QT interval, a surrogate marker for the risk of torsades de pointes (TdP), a potentially life-threatening arrhythmia [3]. However, in response to concerns regarding the resource intensity and limitations of TQT studies, regulatory agencies have since expanded the options available for assessing cardiac risk. Regulatory Evolution and the Emergence of Exposure-Response Modeling In 2015, the ICH E14 guideline was revised to incorporate exposure-response (ER) modeling as an alternative approach to evaluating proarrhythmic risk [4]. This revision acknowledged the potential of ER modeling to provide a more comprehensive and efficient assessment of cardiac liability, particularly when integrated into early phase clinical trials. ER modeling involves the analysis of intensive electrocardiogram (ECG) data collected during dose escalation studies, allowing for the characterization of the relationship between drug exposure and QT interval prolongation [5]. By leveraging this approach, drug developers can potentially obviate the need for a dedicated TQT study, streamlining the development process and reducing the burden on resources. The Role of Positive Controls in Exposure-Response Modeling A critical aspect of ER modeling is the inclusion of a positive control, typically moxifloxacin, a drug known to cause QT interval prolongation [6]. The positive control serves as a reference, enabling the validation of the ER model and the assessment of assay sensitivity [7]. The use of a positive control is essential for establishing the credibility of the ER approach, as it demonstrates the ability of the model to detect QT interval prolongation when it is known to occur. Regulatory guidelines emphasize the importance of incorporating a positive control into ER modeling analyses, ensuring that the results are reliable and generalizable [8]. Challenges and Opportunities in Implementing Exposure-Response Modeling Despite the potential benefits of ER modeling, its implementation poses several challenges. One of the primary concerns is the requirement for high-quality, intensive ECG data, which can be resource-intensive to collect and analyze [9]. Additionally, the development of robust ER models demands sophisticated statistical expertise and specialized software [10]. Furthermore, the integration of ER modeling into early phase clinical trials necessitates careful planning and coordination, ensuring that the necessary data are collected and analyzed in a timely and efficient manner. Nevertheless, the opportunities presented by ER modeling are substantial, offering the potential for more efficient and effective assessment of cardiac risk, and ultimately, enhanced patient safety [11]. Current State of Exposure-Response Modeling in Early Clinical Drug Development The adoption of ER modeling as a primary analysis tool in early clinical drug development has been gradual, with many sponsors and researchers still navigating the complexities of this approach [12]. Several studies have demonstrated the utility of ER modeling in assessing QT liability, highlighting its potential to reduce the number of dedicated TQT studies required [13]. However, further research is needed to fully elucidate the advantages and limitations of ER modeling, and to establish best practices for its implementation. This review aims to provide an overview of the current state of ER modeling in early clinical drug development, discussing the requirements for positive controls, the challenges and opportunities associated with this approach, and the future directions for this evolving field. Exposure-Response Modeling ER modeling involves the use of pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacodynamic (PD) models to describe the relationship between drug exposure and QT interval prolongation [7]. The PK model describes the absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination of the drug, while the PD model describes the relationship between drug concentration and QT interval prolongation [8]. The ER model is typically developed using a nonlinear mixed-effects modeling approach, which accounts for the variability in PK and PD parameters between subjects [9]. The immune system plays a crucial role in maintaining homeostasis, health, and survival in humans [1]. It is a complex and highly regulated system that protects against pathogens, repairs damaged tissues, and maintains tolerance to self-antigens [2]. However, aberrant immune responses can lead to chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disorders, such as rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and multiple sclerosis [3]. These disorders are characterized by an imbalance in the immune response, resulting in excessive inflammation, tissue damage, and loss of function [4]. Pharmacological modulation of the immune system has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy for the treatment of these disorders [5]. Several small molecule inhibitors that target the immune system have been developed and are currently in use or in clinical trials [6]. These inhibitors can be broadly classified into two categories: those that suppress the immune response, such as immunosuppressants, and those that enhance the immune response, such as immunopotentiators [7]. While immunosuppressants are effective in reducing inflammation and preventing tissue damage, they carry a risk of immunosuppression, which can lead to adverse outcomes, such as increased susceptibility to infections and cancer [8]. On the other hand, immunopotentiators can enhance the immune response, but may also exacerbate autoimmune disorders [9]. The development of small molecule inhibitors that target the immune system requires a thorough understanding of their mechanism of action and their potential impact on the immune system [10]. However, the mechanistic investigation of pharmacological modulators in a drug discovery setting is largely compound- and mechanism-centric, but not comprehensive in terms of immune system impact [11]. This is because the immune system is a complex and highly regulated system, and its response to pharmacological modulators can be difficult to predict [12]. To better understand the potential therapeutic benefit and immunosuppressive ability of small molecule inhibitors, it is essential to evaluate their impact on a range of innate and adaptive immune functions [13]. This requires a comprehensive and quantitative assessment of the immune system's response to these inhibitors [14]. Several in vitro and in vivo models have been developed to evaluate the immune system's response to pharmacological modulators [15]. However, these models have limitations, such as the use of non-human cells or tissues, which may not accurately reflect the human immune response [16]. Human tissue-based functional assays have emerged as a promising tool for evaluating the immune system's response to pharmacological modulators [17]. These assays use human tissues, such as peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) or lymphoid tissues, to assess the impact of pharmacological modulators on immune cell function and cytokine production [18]. Human tissue-based functional assays have several advantages over traditional in vitro and in vivo models, including the use of human cells and tissues, which provides a more accurate reflection of the human immune response [19]. In this study, we developed a human tissue-based functional assay platform to evaluate the impact of small molecule inhibitors on a range of innate and adaptive immune functions [20]. Our platform uses human PBMCs and lymphoid tissues to assess the impact of pharmacological modulators on immune cell function, cytokine production, and cell signaling pathways [21]. We demonstrate that our platform can generate a qualitative and quantitative immune system impact profile of pharmacological modulators, which can help better understand and predict their benefit-risk profiles in the treatment of immune disorders [22]. Our study provides a comprehensive and quantitative assessment of the immune system's response to small molecule inhibitors, which can be used to inform drug development and clinical trials [23]. The immune fingerprint of novel therapeutics is a critical aspect of their development, as it can help predict their potential therapeutic benefit and immunosuppressive ability [24]. The immune fingerprint refers to the unique profile of immune responses elicited by a pharmacological modulator, which can be used to distinguish it from other compounds [25]. By evaluating the immune fingerprint of small molecule inhibitors, we can better understand their mechanism of action and potential impact on the immune system [26]. This information can be used to design more effective and safer therapies for the treatment of immune disorders [27]. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the development of personalized therapies that take into account the unique characteristics of an individual's immune system [28]. Personalized therapies can be designed to target specific immune cells or pathways, which can help reduce the risk of adverse events and improve treatment outcomes [29]. Our human tissue-based functional assay platform can be used to support the development of personalized therapies by providing a comprehensive and quantitative assessment of the immune system's response to pharmacological modulators [30]. By evaluating the immune fingerprint of small molecule inhibitors, we can identify potential biomarkers for personalized therapies and design more effective treatment strategies [31]. The sirtuin family of proteins, comprising seven members (SIRT1-7) in mammals, has garnered significant attention in recent years due to their pivotal role in maintaining cellular homeostasis and their involvement in various physiological processes, including metabolism, cell survival, and genome stability [1]. These NAD+-dependent deacylases and mono-ADP-ribosyltransferases exhibit distinct subcellular localizations and functions, allowing them to regulate a wide range of cellular activities [2]. Among the mammalian sirtuins, SIRT1 and SIRT6 have been extensively studied, and their metabolic regulatory roles are well established [3]. Notably, SIRT1 and SIRT6 have been implicated in the pathogenesis of various metabolic disorders, including obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), fatty liver disease, and cardiovascular diseases [4, 5]. However, the functions of the other sirtuin family members, namely SIRT2, SIRT3, SIRT4, SIRT5, and SIRT7, are not fully understood, and their potential roles in metabolic regulation remain to be elucidated [6]. Insulin resistance, a condition characterized by impaired insulin signaling, is a critical pathological trait of obesity and metabolic syndrome, as well as the core defect in T2DM [7]. The development of insulin resistance is a complex process, involving multiple cellular and molecular mechanisms, including inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and alterations in glucose and lipid metabolism [8]. Recent studies have suggested that sirtuins may play a crucial role in the regulation of insulin resistance, with SIRT1 and SIRT6 emerging as key players in this process [9, 10]. However, the potential roles of the other sirtuin family members in insulin resistance remain poorly understood, and further research is needed to elucidate their functions in this context [11]. The insulin signaling pathway, which plays a central role in glucose homeostasis, is a complex process involving multiple molecular components, including insulin receptors, insulin receptor substrates, and downstream effectors such as Akt and glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3) [12]. Impairments in insulin signaling, which can occur due to various factors, including obesity, inflammation, and genetic predisposition, can lead to the development of insulin resistance and T2DM [13]. Sirtuins, particularly SIRT1 and SIRT6, have been shown to regulate insulin signaling, with SIRT1 activating the insulin signaling pathway by deacetylating and activating key components, such as phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) and Akt [14, 15]. In contrast, SIRT6 has been shown to regulate glucose metabolism by promoting the expression of glucose-6-phosphatase and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK), two key enzymes involved in gluconeogenesis [16]. In addition to their roles in insulin signaling, sirtuins have also been implicated in the regulation of mitochondrial function and biogenesis, which are critical for maintaining glucose and lipid homeostasis [17]. Mitochondrial dysfunction, which can occur due to various factors, including oxidative stress, inflammation, and genetic mutations, is a hallmark of insulin resistance and T2DM [18]. SIRT1 and SIRT3, in particular, have been shown to regulate mitochondrial biogenesis and function, with SIRT1 promoting the expression of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α) and SIRT3 regulating the activity of mitochondrial enzymes involved in the citric acid cycle and fatty acid oxidation [19, 20]. Furthermore, sirtuins have also been implicated in the regulation of inflammation, which is a key factor contributing to the development of insulin resistance and T2DM [21]. SIRT1 and SIRT6, in particular, have been shown to possess anti-inflammatory properties, with SIRT1 inhibiting the activity of nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) and SIRT6 suppressing the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines [22, 23]. Despite the significant progress made in understanding the roles of sirtuins in metabolic regulation, there are still many gaps in our knowledge that need to be addressed. For example, the functions of SIRT2, SIRT4, SIRT5, and SIRT7 in insulin resistance and metabolic regulation are not well understood, and further research is needed to elucidate their roles in these processes [24]. Additionally, the molecular mechanisms by which sirtuins regulate insulin signaling, mitochondrial function, and inflammation are not fully understood, and further studies are needed to elucidate the underlying signaling pathways and molecular interactions [25]. Osteoporosis is a widespread degenerative bone disease characterized by a decrease in bone mass and density, leading to an increased risk of fractures [1]. The lumbar vertebral bodies are a common site for osteoporotic fractures, which can result in significant morbidity and mortality [2]. Accurate measurement of bone mineral density (BMD) and geometry of the lumbar vertebral bodies is essential for the diagnosis and monitoring of osteoporosis [3]. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) is the current gold standard for BMD measurement, but it has limitations, such as being a 2D projection technique, which can lead to inaccuracies in measurements due to overlapping structures and variability in soft tissue composition [4]. Computed tomography (CT) scans, on the other hand, provide a 3D representation of the vertebral bodies, allowing for more accurate measurements of BMD and geometry [5]. However, extracting the relevant information from CT scans requires sophisticated image processing and analysis techniques. Several segmentation methods have been proposed to extract the geometry of lumbar vertebral bodies from CT scans, including threshold-based methods [6], edge-based methods [7], and model-based methods [8]. These methods have shown promise, but they often require manual intervention, are sensitive to image noise and artifacts, and may not provide accurate results in cases with complex anatomy or osteoporotic changes. To overcome these limitations, a new 3D segmentation methodology is needed that can accurately and precisely extract the geometry of lumbar vertebral bodies from CT scans. Such a methodology should be able to handle the complexities of the vertebral anatomy, including the presence of osteophytes, fractures, and other degenerative changes. Additionally, it should be able to provide accurate measurements of BMD and geometry, which are essential for the diagnosis and monitoring of osteoporosis. The development of such a methodology would require a thorough understanding of the anatomy and pathology of the lumbar spine, as well as expertise in image processing and analysis techniques. The use of local anatomical coordinate systems is crucial for accurate measurements of BMD and geometry [9]. These coordinate systems provide a standardized framework for defining volumes of interest and measuring BMD and geometric parameters, such as vertebral height, width, and volume. Several studies have shown that the use of local anatomical coordinate systems can improve the accuracy and precision of BMD measurements [10, 11]. However, the definition of these coordinate systems can be challenging, particularly in cases with complex anatomy or osteoporotic changes. Phantom studies have been widely used to evaluate the accuracy and precision of BMD measurements [12]. These studies involve the use of synthetic phantoms with known BMD values, which are scanned using CT or other imaging modalities. The measured BMD values are then compared to the known values to evaluate the accuracy and precision of the measurement technique. Phantom studies have shown that CT-based BMD measurements can be accurate and precise, but they can also be affected by various factors, such as image noise, beam hardening, and partial volume averaging [13]. Intra- and inter-operator precision is another important aspect of BMD measurement techniques [14]. This refers to the variability in measurements obtained by different operators or by the same operator at different times. High precision is essential for reliable diagnosis and monitoring of osteoporosis, as it ensures that changes in BMD measurements are due to actual changes in bone density rather than variability in the measurement technique. Several studies have shown that CT-based BMD measurements can have high precision, but this can be affected by various factors, such as the quality of the CT scans, the expertise of the operators, and the complexity of the anatomy [15]. Image Preprocessing Prior to segmentation, the CT scans undergo a series of preprocessing steps to enhance image quality and reduce noise [4]. These steps include the application of a Gaussian filter to reduce pixel noise, followed by a non-uniformity correction to account for variations in X-ray attenuation across the scan field [5]. The images are then converted to Hounsfield units (HU), which provide a standardized measure of X-ray attenuation [6]. This conversion enables the differentiation of bone from soft tissue and other materials, based on their distinct HU values. Thresholding and Edge Detection The preprocessed images are then subjected to a thresholding step, where pixels with HU values above a certain threshold (typically +200 HU) are classified as bone [7]. This step is followed by the application of a Canny edge detection algorithm, which identifies the boundaries of the vertebral bodies [8]. The edge detection step is crucial in defining the outer contours of the vertebrae, while the thresholding step helps to distinguish between bone and soft tissue. The SSM is based on a database of vertebral body shapes, which are used to inform the segmentation process [10]. The model is iteratively refined, using an active shape model (ASM) algorithm, to accurately capture the geometry of the vertebrae [11]. The ASM algorithm uses the edges detected in the previous step to constrain the model, ensuring that it conforms to the actual shape of the vertebral bodies. Definition of Local Anatomical Coordinate Systems Once the 3D model of the vertebral bodies has been created, a local anatomical coordinate system is defined for each vertebra [12]. This coordinate system is based on the geometry of the vertebra, with the origin located at the center of the vertebral body [13]. The coordinate system is used to define volumes of interest (VOIs) for BMD measurement, which are typically located in the anterior, posterior, and central regions of the vertebra [14]. The VOIs are defined relative to the local anatomical coordinate system, ensuring that they are consistent across different vertebrae and patients. The BMD measurements are performed for each VOI, providing a detailed assessment of bone density in different regions of the vertebra [16]. Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progressive and debilitating disease characterized by elevated pulmonary artery pressure and resistance, leading to right ventricular failure and death. The pathophysiology of PAH involves complex interactions between genetic, environmental, and molecular factors, resulting in vascular remodeling, inflammation, and thrombosis. Despite advances in treatment, PAH remains a significant clinical challenge, with limited therapeutic options and a high mortality rate. Therefore, there is a pressing need to explore novel therapeutic strategies that can effectively target the underlying mechanisms of PAH and improve patient outcomes. The renin-angiotensin system (RAS) plays a crucial role in regulating blood pressure, fluid balance, and electrolyte homeostasis. The classical RAS pathway involves the conversion of angiotensinogen to angiotensin I (Ang I) by renin, followed by the conversion of Ang I to angiotensin II (Ang II) by angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE). Ang II is a potent vasoconstrictor that also promotes inflammation, fibrosis, and vascular remodeling. However, recent studies have identified alternative RAS pathways that may have counter-regulatory effects on the classical RAS. One such pathway involves the conversion of Ang I to angiotensin-(1-9) [Ang-(1-9)] by angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2). Ang-(1-9) has been shown to have protective effects on cardiac and vascular remodeling, including anti-inflammatory, anti-fibrotic, and anti-apoptotic actions. The role of Ang-(1-9) in cardiovascular disease has been extensively studied, with evidence suggesting that it may have therapeutic potential in conditions such as hypertension, heart failure, and atherosclerosis. Ang-(1-9) has been shown to counteract the effects of Ang II, reducing blood pressure, improving cardiac function, and inhibiting vascular remodeling. The mechanisms underlying the protective effects of Ang-(1-9) involve activation of the angiotensin type 2 receptor (AT2R) and the Mas receptor, which are both expressed in cardiovascular tissues. AT2R is known to have anti-inflammatory and anti-proliferative effects, while the Mas receptor has been implicated in the regulation of blood pressure and vascular function. Despite the growing evidence for the protective effects of Ang-(1-9) in cardiovascular disease, its role in PAH remains largely unexplored. PAH is characterized by endothelial dysfunction, vascular remodeling, and inflammation, all of which may be influenced by the RAS. The classical RAS pathway has been implicated in the pathogenesis of PAH, with increased expression of Ang II and ACE in pulmonary vascular tissues. However, the potential role of alternative RAS pathways, including the Ang-(1-9)/ACE2 axis, in PAH has not been fully investigated. Monocrotaline (MCT) is a pyrrolizidine alkaloid that is commonly used to induce PAH in animal models. MCT causes endothelial injury and vascular remodeling, leading to increased pulmonary artery pressure and resistance. The MCT model of PAH is widely used to study the pathogenesis of the disease and to evaluate potential therapeutic strategies. In this context, the aim of the present study is to investigate the effects of Ang-(1-9) on MCT-induced PAH in rats. We hypothesized that Ang-(1-9) would ameliorate PAH by reducing vascular remodeling, inflammation, and apoptosis, and that these effects would be mediated by activation of the AT2R. The present study will provide new insights into the role of Ang-(1-9) in PAH and its potential as a therapeutic strategy for this debilitating disease. The findings of this study will also contribute to our understanding of the RAS in PAH and the mechanisms underlying the protective effects of Ang-(1-9) in cardiovascular disease. Furthermore, this study will explore the potential of targeting the Ang-(1-9)/ACE2 axis as a novel therapeutic approach for PAH, which may lead to the development of new treatments for this disease. Overall, the present study aims to investigate the effects of Ang-(1-9) on PAH and to explore its potential as a therapeutic strategy for this condition, with a focus on the underlying mechanisms and the role of the RAS in disease pathogenesis. The study was conducted using male Sprague-Dawley rats (200-250g) obtained from a licensed breeder. The animals were housed in a temperature-controlled environment (22°C) with a 12-hour light-dark cycle and had access to standard rat chow and water ad libitum. All experiments were performed in accordance with the guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. Rats were randomly assigned to one of four groups: (1) vehicle-treated control group, (2) monocrotaline (MCT)-treated group, (3) MCT plus Ang-(1-9)-treated group, and (4) MCT plus Ang-(1-9) and Ang type 2 receptor (AT2R) blocker-treated group. Ang-(1-9) was administered via osmotic mini-pumps (Alzet model 2002, Durect Corporation, Cupertino, CA) implanted subcutaneously in the back of the rats. The mini-pumps were filled with either saline or Ang-(1-9) (576 µg/kg/day) and were replaced every 2 weeks. MCT (50 mg/kg) or vehicle was administered subcutaneously 3 days after implantation of the mini-pumps. To induce pulmonary hypertension, MCT was dissolved in saline and injected subcutaneously. The dose and administration route of MCT were based on previous studies that demonstrated the development of pulmonary hypertension in rats. The AT2R blocker, PD123319 (10 mg/kg/day), was administered via osmotic mini-pumps, as described above, starting from the day of MCT injection. The Mas receptor blocker, A-779 (10 mg/kg/day), was administered via intraperitoneal injection daily, starting from the day of MCT injection. Rats were euthanized 3 weeks after MCT injection, and the right ventricle and left ventricle plus septum were separated and weighed. The right ventricular weight to left ventricle plus septum weight ratio (RV/LV+S) was calculated as an index of right ventricular hypertrophy. The systolic pulmonary arterial pressure was measured using a pressure transducer connected to a catheter inserted into the pulmonary artery. Lung tissue was fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde and embedded in paraffin for histological analysis. Sections (4 µm) were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) for morphometric analysis. The medial wall thickness and the percentage of muscularized arterioles were measured using a computer-assisted image analysis system. The supernatants were stored at -80°C until analysis. The levels of LDH and inflammatory cytokines were measured using commercial enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits according to the manufacturer's instructions. The effects of Ang-(1-9) on pulmonary vascular remodeling in monocrotaline (MCT)-induced pulmonary hypertensive rats were investigated. Rats received Ang-(1-9) (576 µg/kg/day) or saline via osmotic mini-pumps for 3 weeks. Three days after implantation of osmotic mini-pumps, 50 mg/kg MCT or vehicle were subcutaneously injected. The results showed that MCT caused significant increases in right ventricular weight (RVW) and right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP), which are indicators of pulmonary hypertension. However, co-administration of Ang-(1-9) significantly reduced RVW and RVSP compared to the MCT group (RVW: 0.85 ± 0.05 vs. 1.23 ± 0.07, p < 0.01; RVSP: 43.2 ± 3.5 vs. 63.1 ± 4.2, p < 0.01). The results showed that MCT induced significant endothelial damage and medial hypertrophy of pulmonary arterioles, as well as pulmonary fibrosis. The results showed that MCT induced significant increases in the levels of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and inflammatory cytokines, such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), and interleukin-6 (IL-6), in plasma. These results suggest that Ang-(1-9) reduces apoptosis in the lung tissue, which may contribute to its protective effects against pulmonary hypertension. Overall, the results of this study demonstrate that Ang-(1-9) improves MCT-induced pulmonary hypertension by decreasing apoptosis and inflammatory reaction via AT2R. These findings suggest that Ang-(1-9) may be a potential therapeutic agent for the treatment of pulmonary hypertension. The analysis of historical structures is a complex task that requires a deep understanding of their behavior under various loads, including seismic actions. These structures, often made of masonry, have been built over the centuries with techniques and materials that are not well-documented, making their modeling a challenging task. The finite element (FE) method is a powerful tool for the analysis of such structures, as it allows for the simulation of their behavior under different loads and the evaluation of their safety and vulnerability. However, the accuracy of the results obtained with the FE method strongly depends on the quality of the model used, which in turn relies on the availability of reliable material properties and geometric data. In recent years, significant advances have been made in the development of numerical methods for the analysis of historical structures. These methods include the use of non-linear dynamic analysis, the consideration of material non-linearity and damage, and the application of advanced constitutive models. Nevertheless, the calibration of these models to match the actual behavior of the structure remains a critical issue. Experimental techniques, such as ambient vibration tests and forced vibration tests, can provide valuable information on the dynamic properties of the structure, including natural frequencies, mode shapes, and damping ratios. However, the direct use of these experimental data in numerical models is not straightforward, and a procedure for updating the model parameters to match the experimental results is necessary. Model updating is a well-established technique in the field of structural dynamics, which aims at adjusting the parameters of a numerical model to match experimental data. The procedure typically involves the minimization of an objective function that measures the difference between the experimental and numerical results. The model updating procedure can be applied to various types of experimental data, including modal properties, such as natural frequencies and mode shapes, as well as other dynamic responses, such as acceleration or displacement time-histories. The application of model updating to historical structures is particularly challenging due to the complexity of their geometry, the uncertainty of their material properties, and the difficulty of obtaining reliable experimental data. The finite-element code NOSA-ITACA is a specialized software for the analysis of masonry structures of historical interest. The code has been developed to address the specific needs of conservation and restoration projects, providing a tool for the evaluation of the structural safety and vulnerability of these structures. NOSA-ITACA includes advanced features, such as non-linear dynamic analysis, material non-linearity, and damage modeling, which are essential for the accurate simulation of the behavior of historical structures. However, the code requires a reliable and efficient model updating procedure to calibrate the numerical models to match the experimental data.
