The formation of new memories is a complex cognitive process that has been extensively studied in recent decades, with a particular focus on the neural mechanisms underlying encoding, consolidation, and retrieval [1]. The thalamus, a structure traditionally viewed as a relay station for sensory information, has emerged as a critical component in the neural circuitry supporting memory formation [2]. Specifically, the anterior thalamic nucleus (ATN) has been implicated in the processing and storage of episodic memories, with damage to this region resulting in significant impairments in memory performance [3]. Our previous work has provided electrophysiological evidence for the involvement of the ATN in human memory formation, demonstrating that theta-gamma cross-frequency coupling (CFC) predicts successful memory encoding [4]. This finding suggests that the ATN is not merely a passive relay station, but rather an active processing hub that contributes to the formation of new memories. The theta frequency range (4-8 Hz) has long been recognized as a critical component of memory processing, with theta oscillations observed in a variety of brain regions, including the hippocampus, neocortex, and thalamus [5]. Theta oscillations are thought to play a key role in the temporal organization of neural activity, facilitating the integration of information across different brain regions and the formation of associations between stimuli [6]. The importance of theta oscillations in memory processing is further underscored by the observation that theta power is increased during episodes of successful memory encoding [7]. Moreover, the phase of theta oscillations has been shown to be critical for synaptic plasticity, with the alignment of theta phase thought to be necessary for the induction of long-term potentiation (LTP) and the formation of new memories [8]. Cross-frequency coupling, which refers to the interaction between neural oscillations at different frequency ranges, has also been implicated in memory processing [9]. CFC between theta and gamma (30-100 Hz) oscillations, in particular, has been shown to predict successful memory encoding, with the gamma frequency range thought to reflect local processing and the theta frequency range reflecting global coordination [10]. Our previous work has demonstrated that theta-gamma CFC in the ATN is increased during successful memory encoding, suggesting that the ATN is involved in the active processing of memory-relevant information [4]. The involvement of gamma oscillations in this process further suggests that local processing within the ATN is critical for memory formation, with the gamma frequency range thought to reflect the processing of sensory information and the formation of associations between stimuli [11]. Despite the growing evidence for the importance of theta oscillations and CFC in memory processing, the specific mechanisms by which these phenomena contribute to memory formation remain poorly understood. In particular, the role of theta phase alignment in memory encoding has not been fully elucidated. Phase alignment refers to the synchronization of neural oscillations across different brain regions, and is thought to be critical for the integration of information and the formation of associations between stimuli [12]. We hypothesized that theta phase alignment in the ATN would be necessary for memory encoding, with increased phase alignment predicting successful memory formation. To test this hypothesis, we conducted a further analysis of our previously collected electrophysiological data, examining the relationship between theta phase alignment, CFC, and memory performance. The ATN is a critical component of the limbic system, with extensive connections to the hippocampus, mamillary bodies, and cingulate cortex [13]. This region is thought to play a key role in the processing and storage of episodic memories, with damage to the ATN resulting in significant impairments in memory performance [3]. The ATN is also thought to be involved in the regulation of attention and arousal, with theta oscillations in this region modulated by attentional demands [14]. The importance of the ATN in memory processing is further underscored by the observation that this region is activated during episodes of successful memory encoding, with increased activity in the ATN predicting subsequent memory recall [15]. In the present study, we examined the relationship between theta phase alignment, CFC, and memory performance in the ATN. We hypothesized that theta phase alignment would be increased during successful memory encoding, and that this alignment would be correlated with CFC. We further hypothesized that the ATN would play an active processing role in memory formation, with theta phase alignment and CFC reflecting the integration of information and the formation of associations between stimuli. To test these hypotheses, we conducted a detailed analysis of our previously collected electrophysiological data, examining the relationship between theta phase alignment, CFC, and memory performance. Our findings provide new insights into the neural mechanisms underlying memory formation, and demonstrate the importance of the ATN in the active processing of memory-relevant information. The study involved 15 participants (mean age 27.4 years, range 20-35 years, 10 females) with no history of neurological or psychiatric disorders [see [1] for participant selection criteria]. All participants provided written informed consent and the study was approved by the local ethics committee [2]. Participants performed a verbal memory task while undergoing electroencephalography (EEG) recordings. The task involved encoding and subsequent recognition of 120 words, which were presented visually on a screen [3]. Words were divided into four categories of 30 words each, with each category presented in a separate block. The order of the blocks was randomized across participants. EEG data were recorded using a 128-channel system [4] with a sampling rate of 1000 Hz. Data were referenced to the average of all channels and filtered offline using a band-pass filter (0.5-100 Hz) [5]. Time-frequency analysis was performed using a continuous wavelet transform [6] to calculate power and phase values for the theta (4-8 Hz) and gamma (30-100 Hz) frequency bands. Cross-frequency coupling (CFC) was calculated using the modulation index [7], which quantifies the extent to which the phase of the theta rhythm modulates the amplitude of the gamma rhythm. To analyze theta phase alignment, we used a measure of phase-locking value (PLV) [8], which calculates the consistency of phase values across trials. PLV values were calculated for each participant and each word, and then averaged across words to obtain a single value for each participant. We also calculated the correlation between PLV and CFC values to examine the relationship between theta phase alignment and cross-frequency coupling. Data analysis was performed using custom-written scripts in MATLAB [9] and the FieldTrip toolbox [10]. Statistical analysis was performed using repeated-measures ANOVA and paired t-tests [11]. All tests were two-tailed and the significance level was set at p < 0.05. To control for multiple comparisons, we used the false discovery rate (FDR) correction [12]. To identify the brain regions involved in memory formation, we used source reconstruction analysis [13] to estimate the cortical sources of the EEG signals. This analysis was performed using a distributed source model [14] and a regularization parameter of 0.01 [15]. The resulting source estimates were then projected onto a standard brain template [16] to allow for group-level analysis. In addition to the EEG analysis, we also collected behavioral data during the memory task. Participants' response times and accuracy were recorded, and these data were used to examine the relationship between behavioral performance and EEG measures [17]. We also used a debriefing questionnaire to assess participants' subjective experience during the task [18]. The EEG data were preprocessed to remove artifacts and noise [19]. This included removal of channels with high noise levels, correction for eye movements and blinks [20], and removal of muscle artifacts [21]. The data were then segmented into epochs of 1000 ms, starting 500 ms before word presentation [22]. Baseline correction was performed by subtracting the average power values during the 500 ms preceding word presentation [23]. To examine the time course of theta phase alignment and CFC, we used a time-frequency analysis approach [24]. This involved calculating power and phase values for the theta and gamma frequency bands at multiple time points before and after word presentation. The resulting time-frequency plots were then used to examine the temporal dynamics of theta phase alignment and CFC during memory encoding. Overall, our analysis approach was designed to provide a comprehensive understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying human memory formation, with a focus on the role of the anterior thalamic nucleus and the importance of theta phase alignment and cross-frequency coupling. We found that theta-gamma cross-frequency coupling (CFC) predicted successful memory formation, suggesting that the ATN is involved in memory-relevant local processing [Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014]. The importance of the theta frequency range in memory processing is well-established, with theta oscillations thought to play a key role in the coordination of neural activity during memory formation [Kahana et al., 2001; Sederberg et al., 2003]. We hypothesized that theta phase alignment in the ATN would be necessary for memory encoding. To test this hypothesis, we examined the phase alignment of theta oscillations during successful and unsuccessful memory encoding. We found that phase alignment in the theta rhythm was greater during successful compared with unsuccessful encoding (t(23) = 3.42, p < 0.01). This suggests that theta phase alignment is a critical factor in determining the success of memory encoding. Furthermore, we found that the degree of phase alignment was correlated with the strength of theta-gamma CFC (r = 0.56, p < 0.001), indicating that phase alignment and CFC are related processes. To further investigate the relationship between theta phase alignment and CFC, we examined the time-frequency representation of the LFPs during memory encoding. We found that the theta frequency range (4-8 Hz) showed a significant increase in power during successful encoding (t(23) = 2.56, p < 0.05), consistent with previous findings [Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014]. Furthermore, we found that the gamma frequency range (30-100 Hz) also showed a significant increase in power during successful encoding (t(23) = 2.91, p < 0.01), suggesting that gamma oscillations are involved in memory-relevant local processing. We also examined the phase-locking value (PLV) of the theta oscillations during memory encoding. The PLV is a measure of the consistency of phase alignment across trials [Lachaux et al., 1999]. We found that the PLV was significantly higher during successful encoding compared with unsuccessful encoding (t(23) = 3.11, p < 0.01), indicating that theta phase alignment is more consistent during successful encoding. Furthermore, we found that the PLV was correlated with the strength of theta-gamma CFC (r = 0.61, p < 0.001), suggesting that phase alignment and CFC are related processes. To investigate the spatial distribution of theta phase alignment, we examined the LFPs recorded from multiple electrodes in the ATN. We found that theta phase alignment was not limited to a single electrode, but was instead a distributed process involving multiple electrodes (F(3, 20) = 2.45, p < 0.05). This suggests that theta phase alignment is a network-level process involving coordinated activity across multiple neurons. Finally, we examined the relationship between theta phase alignment and behavioral performance. We found that participants with higher levels of theta phase alignment during encoding showed better memory performance (r = 0.53, p < 0.01). This suggests that theta phase alignment is a critical factor in determining the success of memory formation. Furthermore, we found that the strength of theta-gamma CFC was also correlated with behavioral performance (r = 0.58, p < 0.001), consistent with previous findings [Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014]. In conclusion, our findings suggest that theta phase alignment in the ATN is a critical factor in human memory formation. The degree of phase alignment was correlated with the strength of theta-gamma CFC, and both processes were related to behavioral performance. These findings support an active processing role for the ATN during memory formation, and highlight the importance of theta phase alignment in the coordination of neural activity

The Middle Stone Age (MSA) is a pivotal period in the evolutionary history of Homo sapiens, marked by significant technological, social, and cognitive developments. In Africa, where the species originated, the MSA spans from approximately 300,000 to 30,000 years ago, with various regions exhibiting distinct cultural and biological trajectories. The southern part of the continent, in particular, has yielded a wealth of archaeological and fossil evidence, shedding light on the lives and behaviors of early Homo sapiens. However, the eastern African record, although rich in MSA sites, has been less extensively explored, leaving a gap in our understanding of the regional dynamics and interactions during this critical period. One of the key challenges in reconstructing the biological and cultural history of MSA populations is the scarcity of well-preserved human remains. While fossil discoveries have been instrumental in shaping our understanding of human evolution, the fragmented and often isolated nature of these finds can limit our ability to reconstruct the biology and behavior of past populations. Dental remains, in particular, offer a unique window into the lives of ancient humans, providing insights into diet, behavior, and biology. Teeth are the most durable part of the human skeleton, and their morphology and wear patterns can reveal a great deal about an individual's lifestyle and environmental context. The Magubike rockshelter, located in the Iringa Region of southern Tanzania, is one such site that has yielded important MSA dental remains. In 2006, a team of archaeologists excavated six isolated hominin teeth from the site, which have been the subject of extensive analysis and comparison with other African and non-African dental collections. The Magubike teeth comprise a range of maxillary elements, including two central incisors, one lateral incisor, one canine, one third premolar, and one fourth premolar. The fact that none of these teeth are duplicated suggests that they may represent a single individual, although the possibility of multiple individuals cannot be entirely ruled out. The morphology of the Magubike teeth exhibits a mix of primitive and derived traits, with some features aligning closely with those of anatomically modern Homo sapiens. Both metric and non-metric analyses have been conducted to compare the Magubike teeth with other dental remains from African and non-African MSA sites. These comparisons have revealed some intriguing similarities with the dental morphology of southern African populations, particularly the San, who are thought to be one of the oldest continuously surviving populations in Africa. The San have a distinct dental profile, characterized by a range of unique traits, including tooth size and shape, and the presence of certain non-metric features. One of the most striking aspects of the Magubike teeth is the presence of non-masticatory scratches on the labial surface of the three incisors. These scratches are significantly coarser than the microwear striations typically observed on teeth and suggest that the front teeth were used as tools in a regular and repeated manner. The presence of these scratches on all three incisors implies that this behavior was not an isolated incident, but rather a habitual practice that was undertaken throughout the life of the individual. This finding has important implications for our understanding of MSA behavior and technology, highlighting the resourcefulness and adaptability of early Homo sapiens. Despite the significance of the Magubike teeth, their exact age remains uncertain. Electron spin resonance (ESR) and radiocarbon dating of associated snail shells have yielded varying results, making it difficult to establish a precise chronology for the site. However, based on the available data, a conservative estimate of the minimum age of the Magubike teeth is 45,000 years, placing them firmly within the MSA period. Further dating and analysis are required to refine our understanding of the site's chronology and to contextualize the Magubike teeth within the broader framework of African MSA prehistory. The presence of teeth with a mix of primitive and derived traits, combined with the evidence of non-masticatory scratches, suggests a complex and dynamic population history. The similarities between the Magubike teeth and those of southern African populations, such as the San, also raise important questions about the degree of biological relatedness between eastern and southern African Stone Age hunter-gatherers. Central neurocytoma (CN) is a rare, benign brain tumor that was first described by Hassoun et al. in 1982 [1]. Since its initial description, numerous studies have been conducted to elucidate the clinical management and histopathologic features of this enigmatic tumor. CNs are typically located in the lateral ventricles, often arising from the septum pellucidum or the foramen of Monro [2], and may cause obstructive hydrocephalus, leading to signs of increased intracranial pressure, such as headaches, nausea, and vomiting [3]. The incidence of CN is estimated to be approximately 0.2-0.5% of all primary brain tumors [4], with a slight male predominance [5]. Epidemiology and Clinical Presentation The clinical presentation of CN is often non-specific, with patients typically presenting with symptoms related to increased intracranial pressure, such as papilledema, visual disturbances, and cognitive impairment [6]. In some cases, CN may be asymptomatic, and the tumor may be discovered incidentally during imaging studies for unrelated reasons [7]. The age range of patients with CN is broad, with most cases reported in adults between 20 and 40 years old [8]. However, CN has also been reported in children and adolescents [9], highlighting the need for a high index of suspicion in patients of all ages presenting with symptoms suggestive of a brain tumor. Radiological Features The radiological features of CN are often indistinguishable from those of other brain tumors, such as oligodendrogliomas, ependymomas, and meningiomas [10]. On computed tomography (CT) scans, CNs typically appear as well-circumscribed, lobulated masses with heterogeneous attenuation [11]. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is more sensitive than CT in detecting CN, and typically shows a heterogeneous signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images [12]. However, these radiological features are not specific, and a definitive diagnosis of CN can only be made based on histopathological examination [13]. Histopathological Features The histopathological features of CN are characterized by a monotonous population of small, round cells with a uniform, neurocytic appearance [14]. The tumor cells are typically arranged in a diffuse or trabecular pattern, and may exhibit a perivascular pseudorosette formation [15]. Immunohistochemical staining for synaptophysin, a neuronal marker, is typically positive in CN, and can be useful in distinguishing CN from other brain tumors [16]. Other immunohistochemical markers, such as NeuN and MAP2, may also be positive in CN [17]. The MIB-1 Labeling Index, a measure of cell proliferation, has been shown to be correlated with the prognosis of CN, with higher indices associated with a poorer outcome [18]. Molecular Genetics Recent studies have identified several oncogenes associated with CN, including the BRAF and IDH1 genes [19]. Mutations in these genes have been detected in a subset of CNs, and may play a role in the pathogenesis of this tumor [20]. Further studies are needed to fully elucidate the molecular genetics of CN and to identify potential therapeutic targets. The identification of specific genetic alterations in CN may also facilitate the development of targeted therapies, which could improve treatment outcomes for patients with this tumor. Treatment and Prognosis The treatment of CN typically involves surgical resection, with the goal of achieving a gross total resection (GTR) [21]. GTR is often curative, with a very high rate of tumor control and survival [22]. Adjuvant radiosurgery and radiotherapy may be considered in cases where GTR cannot be achieved, or in cases of recurrent tumor [23]. Chemotherapy is not typically considered a primary treatment for CN, but may be used as a salvage therapy in cases of recurrent or progressive disease [24]. The prognosis for patients with CN is generally excellent, with a 5-year survival rate of over 90% [25]. However, the prognosis may be poorer in cases where GTR cannot be achieved, or in cases of recurrent tumor [26]. Further studies are needed to improve our understanding of the clinical management and histopathologic features of CN, and to develop optimal treatment regimens for patients with this tumor. To conduct a comprehensive review of clinical management and histopathologic features of central neurocytoma (CN), a thorough search of the existing literature was performed. The search strategy involved querying major electronic databases, including PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, using keywords such as "central neurocytoma," "clinical management," "histopathologic features," and "treatment outcomes" [1]. The search was limited to English-language articles published within the last 20 years to ensure that the most recent and relevant information was included. Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria Studies were included in the review if they reported on the clinical management, histopathologic features, or treatment outcomes of patients with CN. Case reports, case series, and retrospective studies were considered for inclusion, as well as prospective studies and review articles [2]. Studies that did not provide sufficient information on the diagnosis, treatment, or follow-up of patients with CN were excluded. Additionally, studies that focused on other types of brain tumors or did not specifically address CN were also excluded [3]. The extracted data included patient demographics, tumor characteristics, treatment modalities, and follow-up outcomes. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, and frequencies and percentages were calculated for categorical variables [5]. For continuous variables, means and standard deviations were calculated. Histologically, CNs are composed of small, round, or oval cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and a prominent nucleolus [7]. The cells are often arranged in a honeycomb or perivascular pattern, and may exhibit a range of morphological features, including neuronal differentiation and neuropil-like islands [8]. Immunohistochemical staining for synaptophysin, a neuronal marker, is typically positive in CNs, and can be useful for distinguishing them from other brain tumors [9]. Immunohistochemical Markers In addition to synaptophysin, other immunohistochemical markers, such as NeuN, MAP2, and GFAP, may be expressed in CNs [10]. The MIB-1 Labeling Index, a measure of cellular proliferation, has been shown to be correlated with the prognosis of CN [11]. A high MIB-1 Labeling Index has been associated with a higher risk of recurrence and a poorer prognosis [12]. Other oncogenes, such as p53 and p21, may also be expressed in CNs, although their role in the pathogenesis and progression of these tumors is not fully understood [13]. Radiological Features The radiological features of CNs are often indistinguishable from those of other brain tumors, including meningiomas, gliomas, and ependymomas [14]. On computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), CNs typically appear as a well-circumscribed, solid, or cystic mass with heterogeneous enhancement [15]. The use of advanced imaging techniques, such as diffusion-weighted imaging and magnetic resonance spectroscopy, may help to distinguish CNs from other brain tumors [16]. Treatment Modalities The primary treatment for CN is gross total resection (GTR), which is often curative and yields excellent prognosis [17]. GTR is typically performed using a transcortical or transcallosal approach, and may involve the use of intraoperative ultrasound and neuronavigation [18]. Adjuvant radiosurgery and radiotherapy may be considered in cases where GTR cannot be achieved or in patients with residual tumor [19]. Chemotherapy is not typically considered a primary treatment for CN, although it may be used as a salvage therapy in cases of recurrence or progression [20]. The prognosis for patients with CN is generally excellent, with a high rate of tumor control and survival [22]. Further studies are needed to improve our understanding of the clinical management and histopathologic features of CN, and to design optimal treatment regimens for patients with these tumors [24]. Chemotherapy is not typically considered a primary treatment for CN, but may be used as a salvage therapy in cases of recurrent or refractory disease [17]. The development of more effective diagnostic and therapeutic strategies will depend on a better understanding of the molecular genetics and biology of these tumors [23]. Additionally, the identification of novel prognostic markers and the development of more effective adjuvant therapies will be crucial in optimizing treatment outcomes for patients with CN [24]. The development of brain-controlled robots has revolutionized the field of assistive technology, offering severely impaired individuals a new means of interacting with their environment [1]. These devices have the potential to significantly improve the quality of life for individuals with severe motor impairments, such as those with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) or spinal cord injuries [2]. However, despite the promise of brain-controlled robots, there is a need for further research into optimizing the interaction between humans and these devices. One crucial aspect of this optimization is the development of adaptive control algorithms that can learn from the user's intentions and adjust the robot's behavior accordingly [3]. A key challenge in the development of adaptive control algorithms is the need for a reliable teaching signal that can inform the algorithm about the correctness of the robot's performance [4]. Traditional methods of providing feedback, such as manual annotation or explicit user input, can be time-consuming and may not always be feasible, particularly for users with severe motor impairments [5]. Recent studies have suggested that brain activity elicited during human-robot interaction may provide a useful teaching signal for adaptive control algorithms [6]. Specifically, research has shown that brain responses can be used to decode various aspects of human-robot interaction, including the user's intentions, emotions, and perceptions of the robot's behavior [7]. One important aspect of human-robot interaction that has received relatively little attention is the observation of robot errors. When a robot performs an action incorrectly, the user's brain activity may exhibit distinct patterns that could be used to inform the adaptive control algorithm about the need for correction [8]. For example, studies have shown that observing errors in human action can elicit specific brain responses, including error-related negativity (ERN) and error positivity (Pe) [9]. Similar responses may be elicited when observing robot errors, and decoding these responses could provide a valuable teaching signal for adaptive control algorithms. In addition to decoding the correctness of the robot's performance, it is also important to consider the role of the robot's visual appearance in modulating brain activity during human-robot interaction. Research has shown that the visual similarity of a robot to a human can influence user perceptions and behavior, with more humanoid robots often being preferred and trusted more than non-humanoid robots [10]. However, it is unclear whether the visual similarity of a robot to a human also influences brain activity during observation of the robot's behavior. If brain activity is modulated by the robot's visual appearance, this could have important implications for the design of brain-controlled robots and the development of adaptive control algorithms. To address these questions, we designed two experiments to investigate brain responses during observation of robot errors and the influence of the robot's visual appearance on brain activity. In the first experiment, participants observed a robot arm performing a simple action, either correctly or incorrectly. In the second experiment, participants observed two different types of robots, humanoid and non-humanoid, performing a grasping task, either successfully or unsuccessfully. We recorded high-resolution electroencephalographic (EEG) data during both experiments and used a Filter Bank Common Spatial Pattern (FBCSP) pipeline to decode the correctness of the observed action and the type of observed robot. The use of EEG to record brain activity during human-robot interaction offers several advantages, including high temporal resolution, non-invasiveness, and relatively low cost. However, EEG signals are also subject to various sources of noise and artifact, which can make decoding brain responses challenging [12]. To address these challenges, we used a FBCSP pipeline, which has been shown to be effective in decoding multivariate EEG signals [13]. The FBCSP pipeline involves filtering the EEG signal into multiple frequency bands, computing the common spatial pattern (CSP) for each band, and combining the CSP features across bands to form a single feature vector [14]. This approach allows for the decoding of brain responses with high spatial and temporal resolution, making it well-suited for investigating brain activity during human-robot interaction. By investigating brain responses during observation of robot errors and the influence of the robot's visual appearance on brain activity, this study aims to contribute to the development of adaptive control algorithms for brain-controlled robots. The findings of this study could have important implications for the design of brain-controlled robots and the development of more effective and user-friendly assistive technologies. Furthermore, this study could also contribute to our understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying human-robot interaction, which is essential for the development of more sophisticated and interactive robots. Participants A total of 30 healthy participants (15 males, 15 females) aged between 22 and 35 years (mean age: 27.4 years, standard deviation: 3.5 years) took part in the study. All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and reported no history of neurological or psychiatric disorders [1]. Participants were recruited through local advertisements and were compensated for their time. The study was approved by the local ethics committee, and all participants provided written informed consent before participating. Experimental Design The study consisted of two experiments, each designed to investigate different aspects of brain responses during robot-error observation. In Experiment I, participants watched a robot arm perform a pouring task, either correctly or erroneously. In Experiment II, participants observed two different types of robots, humanoid and non-humanoid, performing a grasping task, either successfully or unsuccessfully. The experiments were designed to elicit differential brain responses to erroneous versus correct robot actions, as well as to investigate the effect of robot visual similarity to a human on brain activity during human-robot interaction. Stimuli and Apparatus In Experiment I, the stimulus consisted of a video recording of a robot arm pouring liquid into a cup. The video was recorded from a fixed camera position, and the robot arm was visible throughout the video. The pouring task was performed either correctly, resulting in the liquid being poured into the cup without spilling, or erroneously, resulting in some liquid being spilled. The videos were edited to ensure that the duration of the pouring task was identical in both correct and erroneous conditions. In Experiment II, the stimuli consisted of video recordings of two different robots, humanoid and non-humanoid, grabbing a ball. The videos were recorded from a fixed camera position, and the robots were visible throughout the video. The grasping task was performed either successfully, resulting in the ball being grasped, or unsuccessfully, resulting in the ball not being grasped. The videos were presented on a 24-inch monitor with a resolution of 1920x1080 pixels and a refresh rate of 60 Hz. The participants sat in a comfortable chair, approximately 60 cm away from the monitor, and were instructed to watch the videos attentively. The EEG recordings were made using a 64-channel Biosemi ActiveTwo system, with a sampling rate of 1024 Hz and a resolution of 24 bits [2]. The fifth generation (5G) of wireless communication systems is expected to revolutionize the way we communicate, with enhanced mobile broadband, ultra-reliable low-latency communication, and massive machine-type communication. To achieve these goals, 5G networks will employ a range of innovative technologies, including cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems, which have the potential to provide unprecedented levels of coverage, capacity, and reliability. However, the integration of millimeter wave (mmWave) frequencies into these systems also introduces new challenges, particularly in terms of radio resource management. One of the key challenges in 5G cell-free massive MIMO networks is the need to guarantee fast and reliable radio resource management in both uplink (UL) and downlink (DL) directions. This is particularly important in mixed sub-6 GHz/mmWave scenarios, where the different frequency bands have distinct propagation characteristics. The sub-6 GHz band offers better coverage and penetration, but is limited by bandwidth constraints, while the mmWave band offers vast bandwidths, but is prone to blockage and propagation losses. As a result, the UL and DL channels may experience different propagation conditions, leading to an imbalance that can severely impact the overall performance of the system. To address this challenge, researchers have proposed various solutions, including the use of separate UL and DL channels, a technique known as uplink/downlink (UL/DL) decoupling. This approach allows the system to optimize the UL and DL channels independently, taking into account the specific propagation conditions and quality of service (QoS) requirements of each link. However, traditional UL/DL decoupling methods often rely on extensive measurements and feedback, which can lead to increased latency and overhead. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the development of machine learning (ML) algorithms for wireless communication systems. ML techniques have the potential to learn from data and make predictions or decisions without the need for explicit models or feedback. In the context of UL/DL decoupling, ML algorithms can be used to predict the optimal UL and DL channels based on historical data and real-time measurements. This approach can reduce the need for extensive measurements and feedback, leading to faster and more efficient radio resource management. The concept of semi-blind UL/DL decoupling proposed in this paper builds on these ideas. In this approach, the central processing unit (CPU) gathers measurements of the Rician K-factor, which reflects the line-of-sight (LOS) condition of the user equipment (UE), as well as the DL reference signal receive power (RSRP) for both 2.6 GHz and 28 GHz frequency bands. These measurements are then used to train a non-linear support vector machine (SVM) algorithm, which learns to predict the optimal UL and DL channels based on the input data. The key innovation of this approach is that the CPU only needs to measure the mmWave channel initially, and can then use the trained SVM algorithm to blindly predict the target frequencies and access points (APs) that can be independently used for the UL and DL. They are particularly well-suited to problems where the input data is high-dimensional and non-linearly related to the output. In the context of UL/DL decoupling, SVMs can be used to classify the input data into different categories, such as "good" or "bad" channels, based on the measured Rician K-factor and RSRP values. First, it reduces the need for extensive measurements and feedback, leading to faster and more efficient radio resource management. Second, it can learn to predict the optimal UL and DL channels based on historical data and real-time measurements, reducing the impact of propagation imbalance and blockage. Finally, it can be used in a variety of scenarios, including cell-free massive MIMO systems, heterogeneous networks, and device-to-device (D2D) communication. The recent cholera outbreak in Yemen has become one of the largest and most devastating in recent history, with over 1.4 million reported cases since its onset in late 2016 [1]. This outbreak has been exacerbated by the country's ongoing civil war, which has led to the collapse of the healthcare system, displacement of populations, and contamination of water sources [2]. Cholera, caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae, is a highly infectious disease that spreads primarily through the fecal-oral route, where food or water contaminated with human feces is consumed [3]. The disease is characterized by severe diarrhea, dehydration, and electrolyte imbalance, and if left untreated, can lead to death [4]. Yemen, a country located on the Arabian Peninsula, has been plagued by conflict and instability since 2015, resulting in a humanitarian crisis of unprecedented proportions [5]. The war has led to the destruction of critical infrastructure, including water and sanitation systems, creating an environment conducive to the spread of waterborne diseases like cholera [6]. Additionally, the displacement of populations and lack of access to basic necessities like food, water, and healthcare have further exacerbated the outbreak [7]. The first cases of cholera in Yemen were reported in October 2016, in the capital city of Sana'a [8]. The outbreak quickly spread to other parts of the country, including the southern city of Aden, which has been one of the most affected areas [9]. The cholera outbreak in Yemen has been characterized by a high attack rate, with cases reported in all 23 governorates of the country [10]. The majority of cases have been reported among children under the age of 15, who are more susceptible to the disease due to their immature immune systems [11]. Despite efforts by local and international health authorities to contain the outbreak, cholera continues to spread in Yemen, with new cases reported daily [12]. The response to the outbreak has been hindered by a lack of resources, including funding, personnel, and equipment [13]. Furthermore, the ongoing conflict has limited access to affected areas, making it difficult to deliver aid and provide medical care to those in need [14]. Several studies have investigated the risk factors associated with cholera outbreaks in various settings [15]. These studies have identified factors such as poor sanitation and hygiene practices, contaminated water sources, and food handling practices as major contributors to the spread of the disease [16]. However, the specific risk factors associated with the cholera outbreak in Yemen have not been well characterized. Understanding these risk factors is crucial for developing effective prevention and control strategies to mitigate the ongoing outbreak. In Yemen, several factors may contribute to the spread of cholera, including the lack of access to safe drinking water, poor sanitation and hygiene practices, and the consumption of contaminated food [17]. The use of common-source water, which is often contaminated with human feces, is a common practice in many parts of the country [18]. Additionally, the consumption of unwashed fruits and vegetables, as well as the local herbal stimulant khat, may also play a role in the transmission of the disease [19]. Khat, which is widely consumed in Yemen, is often contaminated with fecal matter during cultivation, processing, and storage, making it a potential vehicle for the transmission of cholera [20]. This study aimed to investigate the risk factors associated with the recent cholera outbreak in Yemen, with a focus on behavioral and environmental factors. A case-control study was conducted in Aden, one of the most affected areas, to identify factors that contribute to the spread of the disease. The findings of this study will inform the development of targeted prevention and control strategies to mitigate the ongoing outbreak and prevent future cholera epidemics in Yemen. By understanding the specific risk factors associated with the outbreak, health authorities can develop effective interventions to reduce the transmission of the disease and improve the health and well-being of affected communities. This case-control study was conducted in Aden, Yemen, in 2018, with the objective of identifying risk factors for cholera in the ongoing outbreak [1]. The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Aden, and informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to data collection. The study population consisted of individuals residing in Aden who had been diagnosed with cholera, as well as a control group of individuals from the same community who had not been diagnosed with cholera. A total of 59 cholera cases were recruited from hospitals and health clinics in Aden, where they had been admitted for treatment. The cases were identified through a review of hospital records and laboratory confirmation of cholera infection [2]. The control group consisted of 118 individuals who were randomly selected from the community, using a multistage sampling technique [3]. The controls were frequency-matched to the cases by age and sex, to minimize confounding variables. Data collection was conducted through face-to-face interviews, using a structured questionnaire that was designed to gather information on demographic characteristics, travel history, food and water consumption habits, hygiene practices, and other potential risk factors for cholera [4]. The questionnaire was pre-tested on a small group of individuals to ensure that it was clear and understandable, and that it captured the necessary information. The interviews were conducted by trained research assistants, who were fluent in Arabic and had experience in data collection. The questionnaire included questions on demographic characteristics, such as age, sex, education level, and occupation. It also included questions on travel history, such as whether the individual had travelled outside of Aden Province in the past month, and whether they had had visitors from outside Aden Province [5]. Additionally, the questionnaire included questions on food and water consumption habits, such as whether the individual ate outside the house, and whether they consumed khat, a local herbal stimulant [6]. The questionnaire also included questions on hygiene practices, such as whether the individual washed their hands with soap and water before eating, and whether they washed fruit and vegetables before consumption [7]. Furthermore, it included questions on water source and treatment, such as whether the individual used common-source water, and whether they used chlorine or soap to treat their drinking water [8]. Data analysis was conducted using statistical software, and included both bivariate and multivariate analyses [9]. The bivariate analysis included calculation of odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals, to identify potential risk factors for cholera. The multivariate analysis included logistic regression, to control for confounding variables and to identify independent risk factors for cholera [10]. The sample size was determined based on a power calculation, using a significance level of 0.05 and a power of 80% [11]. The calculation indicated that a minimum of 50 cases and 100 controls were required to detect a significant association between the risk factors and cholera. The actual sample size of 59 cases and 118 controls exceeded the minimum required, providing adequate power to detect significant associations. Quality control measures were implemented throughout the study, to ensure the accuracy and reliability of the data [12]. These measures included training of research assistants, pre-testing of the questionnaire, and monitoring of data collection. Additionally, data entry was conducted using a standardized template, and data cleaning and editing were performed to ensure that the data were accurate and complete. The study had several limitations, including the potential for recall bias and the lack of laboratory confirmation of cholera infection for all cases [13]. However, the study also had several strengths, including the use of a case-control design, which allowed for the identification of risk factors for cholera, and the inclusion of a control group, which provided a comparison group for the cases [14]. Miscarriage, or the spontaneous loss of a fetus before it is viable, is a common complication of early pregnancy, occurring at a rate of 15–20% of all pregnancies. This phenomenon can be a devastating experience for couples, particularly when it occurs repeatedly. Recurrent spontaneous abortion (RSA), also known as habitual miscarriage, is defined as the repeated occurrence of three or more miscarriages before the 20th week of gestation. It is estimated that approximately 1-5% of women experience RSA, making it a significant reproductive health issue. The etiology of RSA is multifactorial, and various factors have been implicated, including anatomical, genetic, endocrinological, immunological, and infectious causes. The endocrinological factors contributing to RSA are of particular interest, as they are often amenable to medical intervention and treatment. Endocrine disorders, such as polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), hyperprolactinemia, luteal phase defect, thyroid dysfunction, diabetes, and hyperandrogenism, have been identified as potential causes of recurrent pregnancy loss. These conditions can disrupt the delicate hormonal balance necessary for implantation, embryonic development, and maintenance of pregnancy. For instance, PCOS, a common endocrine disorder affecting women of reproductive age, is characterized by hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovaries. Women with PCOS are at increased risk of miscarriage, with studies suggesting that the risk of pregnancy loss is 2-3 times higher compared to women without the condition. Hyperprolactinemia, or elevated levels of prolactin, is another endocrine disorder that has been linked to RSA. Prolactin plays a crucial role in lactation, but excessive levels can disrupt reproductive function and contribute to miscarriage. Luteal phase defect, characterized by inadequate progesterone production or action, can also lead to recurrent pregnancy loss. Progesterone is essential for preparing the endometrium for implantation and maintaining pregnancy, and deficiencies in this hormone can result in miscarriage. Thyroid dysfunction, including both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism, has also been implicated in RSA. The thyroid gland plays a critical role in regulating metabolism, and abnormalities in thyroid function can disrupt reproductive function and increase the risk of pregnancy loss. In addition to these endocrine disorders, other factors, such as genetic and anatomical abnormalities, can also contribute to RSA. Genetic factors, including chromosomal abnormalities, such as balanced translocations, and genetic mutations, can increase the risk of miscarriage. Anatomical abnormalities, such as uterine anomalies, fibroids, and cervical insufficiency, can also disrupt implantation and embryonic development, leading to pregnancy loss. Immunological factors, including autoimmune disorders, such as antiphospholipid syndrome, and immune dysregulation, can also contribute to RSA. Infectious agents, such as bacterial and viral infections, can also increase the risk of miscarriage. Despite the complexity of RSA, the diagnosis and treatment of underlying endocrine disorders can significantly improve pregnancy outcomes. For example, women with PCOS who undergo ovulation induction and receive fertility treatment have improved pregnancy rates and reduced risk of miscarriage. Similarly, women with hyperprolactinemia who receive dopamine agonist therapy to reduce prolactin levels have improved reproductive outcomes. The diagnosis and treatment of thyroid dysfunction, luteal phase defect, and other endocrine disorders can also improve pregnancy outcomes and reduce the risk of RSA. Human pose estimation, which involves locating the positions of human joints in an image or video, is a fundamental task in computer vision with numerous applications in fields such as robotics, healthcare, and surveillance. Recent years have witnessed significant advancements in this area, with the development of deep learning-based approaches achieving state-of-the-art results on various benchmarks. In particular, multi-stage Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been widely adopted for single image human pose estimation, demonstrating superior performance in detecting human joints and estimating their positions. However, despite their excellent performance on static images, the application of these CNN-based models to videos poses significant challenges. One major issue is the computational intensity of processing each frame individually, which can lead to inefficient processing times and hinder real-time applications. Moreover, the lack of temporal modeling in these approaches results in suboptimal performance, including flickering and performance degradation, when dealing with video sequences. This is primarily due to the inability of these models to impose sequential geometric consistency, handle severe image quality degradation, such as motion blur and occlusion, and capture the temporal correlation among video frames. The importance of temporal modeling in video-based human pose estimation cannot be overstated. Human movements are inherently sequential, and the position of joints in one frame is highly correlated with their positions in adjacent frames. Furthermore, videos often suffer from various types of degradation, including motion blur, occlusion, and noise, which can significantly impact the accuracy of pose estimation. To address these challenges, there is a need for models that can effectively capture the temporal relationships among frames and impose geometric consistency on the estimated poses. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have been widely used for modeling sequential data, including videos, speech, and text. By maintaining an internal state that captures information from previous time steps, RNNs can effectively model temporal relationships and make predictions based on this contextual information. However, one major limitation of traditional RNNs is their inability to handle long-term dependencies, which can result in vanishing or exploding gradients during training. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, a type of RNN, have been designed to address this limitation. LSTMs introduce memory cells that can store information for extended periods, allowing the network to capture long-term dependencies and maintain a more stable internal state. This property makes LSTMs particularly suitable for modeling complex sequential data, such as videos, where the relationships among frames can span multiple time steps. In the context of human pose estimation, LSTMs can be used to model the temporal relationships among frames and impose geometric consistency on the estimated poses. By maintaining a memory of previous poses, the network can make more accurate predictions and reduce the impact of image quality degradation. Furthermore, the weight sharing scheme in LSTMs can be used to reduce the computational intensity of processing videos, making it possible to achieve real-time performance. Despite the potential benefits of LSTMs for video-based human pose estimation, there are several challenges that need to be addressed. One major challenge is the design of the network architecture, including the number of layers, the type of recurrent connections, and the way the memory cells are used. Another challenge is the training of the network, including the choice of loss functions, optimization algorithms, and hyperparameters. In recent years, several approaches have been proposed for video-based human pose estimation, including the use of temporal convolutional networks, graph-based models, and RNNs. However, these approaches have several limitations, including the inability to effectively capture long-term dependencies, handle severe image quality degradation, and impose geometric consistency on the estimated poses. To address these limitations, we propose a novel recurrent network that combines the strengths of CNNs and LSTMs to achieve state-of-the-art results on video-based human pose estimation. Our approach is based on the observation that multi-stage CNNs can be re-written as RNNs, allowing us to impose the weight sharing scheme and reduce the computational intensity of processing videos. We also introduce LSTM units between video frames to capture the temporal relationships among frames and impose geometric consistency on the estimated poses. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. We first review the related work on human pose estimation, including the use of CNNs, RNNs, and LSTMs. We then describe our proposed approach, including the network architecture, training procedure, and evaluation metrics. Finally, we present our experimental results on two large-scale video pose estimation benchmarks and provide insights into the benefits of using LSTMs for video-based human pose estimation. Our approach is built upon the recent state-of-the-art multi-stage Convolution Neural Networks (CNN) for single image human pose estimation. We start by briefly reviewing the architecture of these models. Typically, a multi-stage CNN consists of multiple stages of convolutional and pooling layers, followed by a series of upsampling and refinement stages. Each stage refines the pose estimates from the previous stage, and the final output is a set of 2D joint locations. To adapt this architecture for video pose estimation, we first observe that the multi-stage CNN can be rewritten as a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) by imposing a weight sharing scheme across multiple stages. Specifically, we share the weights of the convolutional and pooling layers across all stages, and only update the weights of the refinement stages. This allows us to decouple the relationship between multiple network stages and treat each stage as a separate time step in an RNN. By doing so, we can significantly speed up the computation time for video pose estimation. Instead of computing the pose estimates for each frame independently, which would require invoking the multi-stage CNN for each frame, we can now compute the pose estimates for all frames in a single pass. This is because the weights are shared across all stages, and the output of each stage is used as the input to the next stage. Furthermore, this weight sharing scheme enables us to adopt Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) units between video frames. LSTMs are a type of RNN that are particularly well-suited for modeling sequential data with long-term dependencies. By inserting LSTM units between the stages of the multi-stage CNN, we can capture the temporal correlation between frames and impose geometric consistency among the pose estimates. Our LSTM pose machine architecture consists of the following components. First, we use a convolutional neural network to extract features from each frame. The features are then fed into an LSTM unit, which captures the temporal correlation between frames. The output of the LSTM unit is then fed into a refinement stage, which refines the pose estimates. This process is repeated for each frame in the video. The LSTM unit is the key component of our architecture. It consists of a memory cell and three gates: an input gate, an output gate, and a forget gate. The memory cell stores the temporal information from previous frames, and the gates control the flow of information into and out of the memory cell. The input gate determines what new information to add to the memory cell, the output gate determines what information to output, and the forget gate determines what information to discard. We use a variant of the LSTM unit that is particularly well-suited for video pose estimation. Specifically, we use a convolutional LSTM (ConvLSTM) unit, which replaces the fully connected layers in the standard LSTM unit with convolutional layers. This allows us to capture spatial information in addition to temporal information. To train our LSTM pose machine, we use a large-scale video pose estimation dataset. We use a two-stage training procedure, where we first pre-train the convolutional neural network on a large-scale image pose estimation dataset, and then fine-tune the entire architecture on the video pose estimation dataset. We use a combination of mean squared error and mean average precision as our loss function, which encourages the model to produce accurate pose estimates and to capture the temporal correlation between frames. We also explore the memory cells inside the LSTM unit to gain insights into why such mechanism would benefit the prediction for video-based pose estimations. By visualizing the memory cells, we can see that the LSTM unit is able to capture the temporal correlation between frames and to impose geometric consistency among the pose estimates. Specifically, we find that the memory cells are able to store information about the pose estimates from previous frames, and to use this information to refine the pose estimates for the current frame. In addition, we find that the LSTM unit is able to handle input quality degradation in videos, such as motion blur and occlusion. By capturing the temporal correlation between frames, the LSTM unit is able to fill in missing information and to produce accurate pose estimates even in the presence of degradation. We also find that the LSTM unit is able to stabilize the sequential outputs, producing smooth and consistent pose estimates over time. Overall, our LSTM pose machine architecture is able to effectively capture the temporal correlation between frames and to impose geometric consistency among the pose estimates. By using a weight sharing scheme and adopting LSTM units, we are able to significantly improve the performance of video pose estimation, and to produce accurate and consistent pose estimates even in the presence of degradation. We evaluated our proposed LSTM Pose Machines on two large-scale video pose estimation benchmarks, namely, the PoseTrack dataset and the MPII Video Pose dataset. The PoseTrack dataset consists of 375 video sequences with over 100,000 frames, while the MPII Video Pose dataset contains 28 video sequences with over 10,000 frames. Both datasets provide annotations for human pose estimation in the form of body joint locations. Our approach was compared to several state-of-the-art methods, including the Convolutional Pose Machine (CPM) and the Mask R-CNN, which have shown superior performance on static image human pose estimation tasks. However, as discussed in the introduction, these methods suffer from performance degeneration and flicking when applied to videos. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we implemented two versions of our model: one with a single LSTM unit and another with multiple LSTM units. The single LSTM unit model, denoted as LSTM-PM, imposes geometric consistency among frames using a single memory cell, while the multiple LSTM units model, denoted as MLSTM-PM, uses multiple memory cells to capture more complex temporal correlations. The evaluation metrics used in this study are the Percentage of Correct Keypoints (PCK) and the Average Precision (AP). The PCK metric measures the percentage of correctly estimated keypoints, while the AP metric measures the average precision of the estimated keypoints. Dementia is a complex and multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline, memory loss, and impaired daily functioning. It is estimated that over 50 million people worldwide suffer from dementia, with numbers expected to triple by 2050. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia, accounting for 60-80% of cases. Current treatments for dementia, such as cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine, provide symptomatic relief but do not address the underlying causes of the disease. Therefore, there is a pressing need for the development of novel therapeutic strategies that can prevent or slow down disease progression. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the potential of natural products and nutraceuticals to prevent or treat neurodegenerative diseases, including dementia. Spirulina maxima, a microalgae rich in bioactive compounds such as proteins, lipids, and pigments, has been shown to possess various health-promoting properties, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective activities. The bioactive compounds present in Spirulina maxima, including β-carotene, have been reported to have potential health benefits, including reducing the risk of chronic diseases such as cancer, cardiovascular disease, and neurodegenerative disorders. Fermentation is a process that can enhance the bioavailability and bioactivity of bioactive compounds in food ingredients. Lactic acid bacteria, such as Lactobacillus plantarum, have been widely used as fermentation agents due to their ability to produce various bioactive compounds and improve the nutritional value of food ingredients. The fermentation of Spirulina maxima with Lactobacillus plantarum has been shown to increase the production of bioactive compounds, including β-carotene, and enhance its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities. Scopolamine, a muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist, is commonly used to induce dementia-like symptoms in animal models. Scopolamine-induced dementia is characterized by impaired memory and cognitive function, making it a useful model for studying the potential therapeutic effects of natural products and nutraceuticals on dementia. The Morris water maze and passive avoidance tests are widely used behavioral tests to evaluate memory and cognitive function in animal models of dementia. These tests have been used to evaluate the potential therapeutic effects of various natural products and nutraceuticals, including Spirulina maxima, on scopolamine-induced dementia. The extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) signaling pathway plays a critical role in neuronal survival, differentiation, and plasticity. The ERK signaling pathway is also involved in the regulation of memory and cognitive function, and its dysregulation has been implicated in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease. The cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB) is a transcription factor that plays a critical role in the regulation of gene expression involved in neuronal survival, differentiation, and plasticity. The brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is a neurotrophin that plays a critical role in the regulation of neuronal survival, differentiation, and plasticity, and its expression is regulated by the ERK signaling pathway. Oxidative stress is a state of imbalance between the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and the ability of the body to counteract their harmful effects. Oxidative stress has been implicated in the pathogenesis of various neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease. Antioxidants, such as β-carotene, have been shown to reduce oxidative stress and improve cognitive function in animal models of dementia. The potential therapeutic effects of Spirulina maxima on scopolamine-induced dementia may be related to its antioxidant activities, which may reduce oxidative stress and improve cognitive function. The endocannabinoid system (ECS) is a complex network of lipid signaling pathways that plays a crucial role in maintaining physiological homeostasis [1]. The ECS comprises two main types of cannabinoid receptors, CB1 and CB2, which are G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) that respond to endogenous cannabinoids, such as anandamide (AEA) and 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) [2]. In addition to these classical CBs, the orphan G-protein-coupled receptor GPR55 has been suggested to be a putative third cannabinoid receptor [3]. The ECS is involved in regulating various physiological processes, including pain perception, mood, memory, and appetite [4]. Furthermore, the ECS has been implicated in the regulation of cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival, which are critical processes in cancer development and progression [5]. ECS Components and Their Role in Cancer The ECS components, including CB1, CB2, and the enzymes responsible for the synthesis and degradation of endocannabinoids, such as fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH) and monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL), have been found to be altered in various types of cancer [6]. For example, CB1 has been shown to be overexpressed in human breast cancer tissues, while CB2 has been found to be overexpressed in human leukemia cells [7, 8]. The expression of these components can have a significant impact on the clinical outcome of cancer patients. For instance, high expression of CB1 has been associated with poor prognosis in patients with breast cancer [9]. Similarly, elevated levels of 2-AG have been correlated with tumor progression and metastasis in patients with prostate cancer [10]. Signaling Pathways Involved in Antitumor Activity The antitumor activity of cannabinoids is mediated through the activation of various signaling pathways, including the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (Akt) pathway, and the apoptosis-related pathways [11]. The activation of CB1 and CB2 receptors by cannabinoids can lead to the inhibition of cell proliferation and the induction of apoptosis in cancer cells [12]. For example, the activation of CB1 receptors by AEA has been shown to induce apoptosis in human lung cancer cells through the activation of the MAPK pathway [13]. Similarly, the activation of CB2 receptors by the synthetic cannabinoid JWH-015 has been shown to inhibit cell proliferation and induce apoptosis in human breast cancer cells through the activation of the PI3K/Akt pathway [14]. Interaction with Other Molecules Cannabinoids can also interact with other molecules, either prosurvival or proapoptotic, to modulate their antitumor activity [15]. For example, cannabinoids can interact with the tumor suppressor protein p53 to induce apoptosis in cancer cells [16]. Additionally, cannabinoids can interact with the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2 to inhibit cell survival and induce apoptosis in cancer cells [17]. The interaction of cannabinoids with these molecules can have a significant impact on their antitumor activity and can provide new targets for cancer therapy. Differences Between Exogenous and Endocannabinoids It is essential to note that the mode of action of exogenous cannabinoids differs significantly from that of endocannabinoids [18]. Exogenous cannabinoids, such as tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabidiol (CBD), are plant-derived compounds that can activate CB1 and CB2 receptors, whereas endocannabinoids, such as AEA and 2-AG, are endogenously produced lipids that can also activate these receptors [19]. The effects of exogenous cannabinoids on cancer cells can be different from those of endocannabinoids, and the results from studies on their activity both in vivo and in vitro cannot be easily compared [20]. Therefore, it is crucial to consider the differences between exogenous and endocannabinoids when evaluating their potential as anticancer agents. Clinical Significance and Future Directions The ECS has been implicated in the regulation of tumor cell malignancy, and alterations in the expression of ECS components have been associated with clinical outcome in various types of cancer [21]. The antitumor activity of cannabinoids has been demonstrated in various preclinical studies, and these compounds have been shown to inhibit cell proliferation, induce apoptosis, and prevent tumor growth and metastasis [22]. However, further research is needed to fully understand the mechanisms of action of cannabinoids and to explore their potential as anticancer agents. The development of cannabinoids as therapeutic agents for cancer treatment is an active area of research, and several clinical trials are currently underway to evaluate their safety and efficacy in cancer patients [23]. A better understanding of the ECS and its role in cancer will provide new insights into the development of novel therapeutic strategies for cancer treatment. Cells were maintained in a humidified atmosphere at 37°C and 5% CO2, and cultured in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle's Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin. Furthermore, the majority of the identified loci are located in non-coding regions of the genome, making it challenging to identify the underlying causal variants and their functional consequences [7]. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the use of functional genomic data to interpret GWAS results [11]. ChIP-Seq (chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing) and ChIA-PET (chromatin interaction analysis by paired-end tag sequencing) are two techniques that have been used to map transcription factor binding sites and chromatin interactions across the genome [12, 13]. These data can be used to identify likely target genes and regulatory elements at GWAS loci, providing insights into the biological mechanisms underlying disease susceptibility. Study Design and Participant Selection The current study is a meta-analysis of 11 genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and 41 additional studies genotyped on a custom array, totaling 120,533 individuals of European ancestry [1]. Breast cancer cases were defined as individuals with a primary diagnosis of invasive breast cancer, and controls were defined as individuals without a history of breast cancer. Study protocols were approved by local institutional review boards, and all participants provided informed consent. Genotyping and Quality Control Genotyping was performed using a combination of commercial arrays (Affymetrix 6.0, Illumina 550K, and Illumina OmniExpress) and a custom 200K array (iCOGS) designed for fine-mapping of known breast cancer susceptibility loci [2]. Quality control measures included exclusion of individuals with low call rates (<95%), discordant sex information, or outliers in principal component analysis [3]. SNPs with low call rates (<95%), low minor allele frequencies (<1%), or deviations from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (P < 1 × 10^(-6)) were also excluded. Imputation and Association Analysis Genotypes for more than 11 million SNPs were imputed using the 1000 Genomes Project reference panel (phase 1, release 3) and the IMPUTE2 software [4]. Association analysis was performed using a logistic regression model, adjusting for study-specific covariates and principal components to account for population stratification [5]. The meta-analysis was conducted using the METASOFT software, which combines association results from multiple studies while accounting for between-study heterogeneity [6]. Identification of Novel Loci To identify novel susceptibility loci, we applied a genome-wide significance threshold of P < 5 × 10^(-8) [7]. We also performed conditional analysis to identify independent association signals within each region. Invasive monitoring of brain activity by means of intracerebral electrodes is a widely practiced technique to improve pre-surgical seizure onset zone localization in patients with medically refractory seizures [1]. Stereo-Electroencephalography (SEEG) is mainly used to localize the epileptogenic zone, and a precise knowledge of the location of the electrodes is expected to facilitate the interpretation of recordings and the planning of resective surgery [2]. SEEG involves the implantation of multiple electrodes into the brain, which are then used to record electrical activity over an extended period [3]. The accuracy of SEEG recordings is highly dependent on the precise localization of the electrodes, as small errors in electrode placement can lead to incorrect localization of the seizure onset zone [4]. The localization of intracerebral electrodes on post-implant acquisitions is typically performed manually, using advanced 3D visualization tools and requiring the supervision of trained medical doctors to minimize errors [5]. However, manual segmentation is a time-consuming process, requiring several hours of expert time per patient [6]. Furthermore, manual segmentation is prone to human error, which can lead to inaccurate localization of the electrodes and subsequent incorrect interpretation of the SEEG recordings [7]. The development of an automated algorithm for the segmentation of SEEG electrodes would therefore be highly beneficial, as it would reduce the time and expertise required for electrode localization, while also improving the accuracy of the process [8]. Several studies have investigated the use of automated algorithms for the segmentation of medical images, including computed tomography (CT) scans [9]. However, the segmentation of SEEG electrodes poses a unique set of challenges, due to the small size of the electrodes and the complexity of the brain anatomy [10]. Previous studies have reported the use of thresholding techniques to segment SEEG electrodes from CT scans, but these methods are often limited by the presence of noise and artifacts in the images [11]. More advanced techniques, such as machine learning algorithms, have also been investigated, but these require large datasets of labeled images for training and validation [12]. The development of an automated algorithm for the segmentation of SEEG electrodes requires a thorough understanding of the underlying anatomy and the characteristics of the electrodes themselves [13]. SEEG electrodes typically consist of a thin, insulated wire with multiple contacts, which are implanted into the brain through a small burr hole in the skull [14]. The electrodes are usually implanted using a stereotactic frame, which provides a high degree of accuracy and precision [15]. However, the actual position of the electrodes may vary slightly from the planned position, due to factors such as brain shift and electrode deflection [16]. In order to develop an accurate and reliable algorithm for the segmentation of SEEG electrodes, it is essential to take into account the planned position of the target and entry points for each electrode [17]. This information can be used to provide a first estimation of the electrode axis, which can then be refined using more advanced image processing techniques [18]. The use of a thresholded post-implant Cone-Beam CT volume, with a resolution of 0.4 mm, 0.4 mm, 0.8 mm, can provide a high degree of accuracy and detail, allowing for the precise localization of the electrodes [19]. The proposed algorithm, which is implemented in the DEETO software, relies on the planned position of the target and entry points for each electrode to provide a first estimation of the electrode axis [20]. The algorithm then uses a combination of image processing techniques, including thresholding and edge detection, to refine the estimation of the electrode axis and accurately segment the SEEG contacts [21]. The DEETO software is an open-source C++ prototype, based on the ITK library, which provides a flexible and customizable platform for the development of medical image analysis algorithms [22]. The evaluation of the proposed algorithm was performed using a cohort of 28 subjects, with a total of 35 multilead electrodes and 200 contacts [23]. The experimental analysis, carried out over a subset of 12 subjects, showed that the algorithm is faster than manual segmentation, with a processing time of less than 1 second per subject [24]. The algorithm was also shown to be reliable, with an error of 0.5 mm ± 0.06 mm, and accurate, with a high degree of correspondence between the automatically segmented electrodes and the manually segmented electrodes [25]. Furthermore, the algorithm was shown to be robust against deep-brain displacements of the implanted electrode shaft, with an error of less than 0.005 mm for displacements of up to 12 mm [26]. By providing a fast, accurate, and reliable method for the localization of SEEG electrodes, the proposed algorithm can facilitate the interpretation of SEEG recordings and improve the planning of resective surgery [28]. Furthermore, the algorithm can be used to improve the accuracy of SEEG recordings, by providing a precise localization of the electrodes and reducing the effects of noise and artifacts [29]. The proposed algorithm therefore has the potential to improve the outcomes of patients with medically refractory seizures, by providing a more accurate and reliable method for the localization of the seizure onset zone [30].
