Diabetic macular edema (DME) is a common complication of diabetic retinopathy, characterized by the accumulation of fluid in the macula due to increased vascular permeability, leading to vision impairment [1]. The prevalence of DME is estimated to be around 6.8% in patients with diabetes, with a significant impact on quality of life [2]. Cataract surgery is a common procedure in patients with diabetes, and the presence of DME can affect the outcome of the surgery [3]. The coexistence of cataract and DME poses a challenge for ophthalmologists, as the surgery can exacerbate the edema, leading to decreased visual acuity [4]. Several treatment options are available for DME, including laser photocoagulation, intravitreal corticosteroid injections, and anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy [5]. Among these, anti-VEGF therapy has emerged as a highly effective treatment for DME, with ranibizumab being one of the most commonly used agents [6]. Ranibizumab has been shown to improve visual acuity and reduce retinal thickness in patients with DME [7]. However, the optimal timing of ranibizumab injections in patients undergoing cataract surgery is still a topic of debate. The use of perioperative ranibizumab injections has been proposed as a strategy to manage DME in patients undergoing cataract surgery [8]. The rationale behind this approach is to reduce the risk of postoperative exacerbation of DME and improve visual outcomes [9]. However, the efficacy of perioperative ranibizumab injections depends on various factors, including the timing of the injection, the severity of DME, and the surgical technique used [10]. Previous studies have investigated the use of preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative ranibizumab injections, but the results are inconsistent, and the optimal timing of the injection remains unclear [11]. Preoperative ranibizumab injections have been shown to reduce the severity of DME and improve visual acuity before cataract surgery [12]. However, the effect of the injection may wear off during the postoperative period, leading to a recurrence of DME [13]. Intraoperative ranibizumab injections, on the other hand, may provide an immediate anti-angiogenic effect, reducing the risk of postoperative DME exacerbation [14]. Postoperative ranibizumab injections can also be effective in managing DME, but the optimal timing of the injection after surgery is still unknown [15]. The present study aims to compare the efficacy of perioperative ranibizumab injections on DME in patients undergoing cataract surgery. We investigated the effect of preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative ranibizumab injections on visual acuity and retinal thickness in patients with advanced cataract and DME. The results of this study will provide valuable insights into the optimal timing of ranibizumab injections in patients undergoing cataract surgery and will help ophthalmologists make informed decisions about the management of DME in this patient population. The pathophysiology of DME is complex and involves the breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier, leading to the accumulation of fluid in the macula [16]. Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) plays a crucial role in the development of DME, and anti-VEGF therapy has been shown to be effective in reducing retinal thickness and improving visual acuity [17]. Ranibizumab, a recombinant humanized monoclonal antibody fragment, binds to VEGF, preventing its interaction with its receptors and reducing vascular permeability [18]. The use of ranibizumab in patients with DME has been extensively studied, and the results have shown significant improvements in visual acuity and retinal thickness [19]. Cataract surgery can exacerbate DME, leading to decreased visual acuity and increased retinal thickness [20]. The exact mechanism of this exacerbation is unclear, but it is thought to be related to the release of inflammatory mediators and the disruption of the blood-retinal barrier during surgery [21]. The use of perioperative ranibizumab injections may help reduce the risk of postoperative DME exacerbation by providing an anti-angiogenic effect and reducing vascular permeability [22]. However, the optimal timing of the injection is critical, as the effect of the injection may wear off during the postoperative period, leading to a recurrence of DME [23]. In conclusion, the management of DME in patients undergoing cataract surgery is a complex issue, and the optimal timing of ranibizumab injections is still unclear. The present study aims to investigate the efficacy of preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative ranibizumab injections on DME in patients undergoing cataract surgery, providing valuable insights into the optimal management of this condition. The results of this study will help ophthalmologists make informed decisions about the treatment of DME in patients undergoing cataract surgery and will contribute to the development of evidence-based guidelines for the management of this condition. This prospective, non-randomized, comparative study included 59 eyes of 59 patients with advanced cataract and diabetic macular edema (DME) who underwent phacoemulsification surgery at our institution between January 2020 and December 2021 [1]. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board and adhered to the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki [2]. Informed consent was obtained from all patients before enrollment. Patients with a history of previous vitreoretinal surgery, intravitreal injections, or laser photocoagulation were excluded from the study [3]. Additionally, patients with significant media opacities, other retinal diseases, or uncontrolled systemic diseases were also excluded [4]. The patients were divided into three subgroups based on the timing of intravitreal ranibizumab injection. The first group (preoperative group) received an intravitreal injection of 0.5 mg ranibizumab 2 weeks before cataract surgery. The second group (intraoperative group) received an intravitreal injection of 0.5 mg ranibizumab during cataract surgery, immediately after the intraocular lens implantation [5]. The third group (postoperative group) received an intravitreal injection of 0.5 mg ranibizumab 2 weeks after cataract surgery. The decision on the timing of ranibizumab injection was based on the clinical judgment of the treating physician and patient's preference [6]. All patients underwent a comprehensive ophthalmological examination, including best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) measurement using the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) chart, slit-lamp biomicroscopy, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) [7]. The OCT scans were performed using a spectral-domain OCT device (Heidelberg Engineering, Heidelberg, Germany) to measure the foveal thickness (FT) and assess the presence of any retinal fluid or hemorrhages [8]. The BCVA and OCT measurements were performed at baseline, 1 week, 1 month, and 3 months after surgery. Phacoemulsification surgery was performed by a single experienced surgeon (author) using a standard technique [9]. A 2.8 mm clear corneal incision was made, and a foldable intraocular lens was implanted in the capsular bag. The intraoperative complications, such as posterior capsule rupture or vitreous loss, were not observed in any of the patients [10]. Postoperative treatment included topical antibiotics and steroids for 4 weeks [11]. The intravitreal injections of ranibizumab were performed under sterile conditions in an operating room setting [12]. The patients received topical anesthesia with lidocaine 2% gel, and the eye was prepared with 5% povidone-iodine solution [13]. A 30-gauge needle was used to inject 0.05 ml of ranibizumab (Lucentis, Novartis, Basel, Switzerland) into the vitreous cavity, 3.5 mm posterior to the limbus [14]. The patients were monitored for any signs of endophthalmitis or other complications after the injection [15]. The primary outcome measures were the changes in BCVA and FT at 1 month and 3 months after surgery. The secondary outcome measures included the presence of any intraoperative or postoperative complications, such as endophthalmitis, retinal detachment, or vitreous hemorrhage [16]. The data were analyzed using statistical software (SPSS, version 25, IBM, Armonk, NY) [17]. The normality of the data was checked using the Shapiro-Wilk test, and the differences between the groups were compared using the analysis of variance (ANOVA) test [18]. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant [19]. The sample size calculation was performed based on a previous study [20], and a minimum of 15 patients per group was required to detect a significant difference in BCVA and FT. Parkinson's Disease (PD) is a complex and multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder that affects millions of people worldwide, with tens of millions of Americans alone suffering from this debilitating condition. Characterized by the progressive loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the brain, PD is marked by a range of motor and non-motor symptoms, including tremors, rigidity, bradykinesia, and cognitive impairment. The disease is highly heterogeneous, with significant variability in its clinical presentation, progression, and response to treatment. This heterogeneity poses significant challenges for diagnosis, treatment, and disease management, highlighting the need for more effective and personalized approaches to PD care. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the use of predictive modeling and machine learning techniques for the analysis of PD. These approaches have focused on the identification of clinical and biomarker variables that are associated with disease progression and response to treatment, with the ultimate goal of developing more effective and personalized treatment strategies. A range of studies have explored the use of traditional machine learning techniques, such as support vector machines and random forests, for the analysis of clinical and biomarker data in PD. These studies have demonstrated the potential of machine learning approaches for predicting disease progression and identifying novel biomarkers of disease. However, the analysis of PD is not limited to clinical and biomarker data. Neuroimaging, which provides a unique window into the structure and function of the brain, has also emerged as a critical tool for the study of PD. A range of neuroimaging modalities, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), functional MRI (fMRI), and positron emission tomography (PET), have been used to study the neural basis of PD and to identify novel biomarkers of disease. These modalities provide complementary information about the brain, with MRI providing information about brain structure, fMRI providing information about brain function, and PET providing information about brain metabolism and neurotransmitter function. The integration of multiple neuroimaging modalities has the potential to provide a more comprehensive understanding of PD, by allowing for the identification of complex patterns and relationships that are not apparent from the analysis of individual modalities in isolation. However, the analysis of multi-modal neuroimaging data is challenging, due to the high dimensionality and complexity of the data. Traditional machine learning approaches, such as principal component analysis (PCA) and support vector machines, are limited in their ability to handle high-dimensional data and to capture complex relationships between variables. In recent years, deep learning techniques have emerged as a powerful tool for the analysis of complex and high-dimensional data. These techniques, which are inspired by the structure and function of the brain, have been shown to be highly effective for image classification, object detection, and natural language processing tasks. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) are a type of deep learning technique that are particularly well-suited to the analysis of graph-structured data, such as brain networks. GCNs have been shown to be highly effective for the analysis of brain networks in a range of neurological and psychiatric disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia, and depression. The application of GCNs to the analysis of multi-modal neuroimaging data in PD has the potential to provide new insights into the neural basis of disease and to identify novel biomarkers of disease progression. By integrating multiple modalities of brain images, GCNs can capture complex patterns and relationships that are not apparent from the analysis of individual modalities in isolation. This approach has the potential to provide a more comprehensive understanding of PD, by allowing for the identification of novel biomarkers of disease and the development of more effective and personalized treatment strategies. The advent of high-throughput RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) technology has revolutionized the field of transcriptomics, enabling researchers to investigate the expression levels of thousands of genes in a single experiment. One of the primary applications of RNA-seq is differential expression (DE) analysis, which aims to identify genes that exhibit significant changes in expression levels between different experimental conditions, such as treatment vs. control, disease vs. healthy, or different time points. DE analysis is crucial for understanding the underlying biological mechanisms of various diseases, identifying potential biomarkers, and developing novel therapeutic strategies. Traditionally, DE analysis using RNA-seq data has been performed using statistical methods that assume a simple experimental design, typically involving only two conditions, such as treatment and control. However, with the increasing complexity of biological experiments, researchers are now often interested in investigating multiple treatment conditions, time courses, or other experimental factors. For instance, a study may involve comparing the expression levels of genes in response to different doses of a drug, or examining the temporal dynamics of gene expression in response to a stimulus. In such cases, the traditional two-condition DE analysis methods may not be sufficient, and more accommodative statistical tools are needed to account for the added complexity. Several statistical methods have been developed for DE analysis using RNA-seq data, including edgeR, DESeq2, and limma. These methods have been widely used and have shown excellent performance in identifying DE genes in simple two-condition experiments. However, when dealing with multiple treatment conditions, these methods may not be optimal, as they often rely on pairwise comparisons between conditions, which can lead to multiple testing issues and reduced power. Moreover, these methods may not fully account for the underlying biological variability and the complex relationships between genes and conditions. To address these limitations, several methods have been proposed to analyze RNA-seq data with multiple conditions. For example, some methods use a linear model framework to account for the effects of multiple conditions on gene expression, while others employ non-parametric or machine learning approaches to identify DE genes. However, these methods often require careful tuning of parameters, and their performance may degrade when the number of conditions is large or when the data is noisy. In this context, there is a need for a statistical method that can efficiently and effectively identify DE genes in RNA-seq data with multiple treatment conditions. The method should be able to account for the complex relationships between genes and conditions, handle the added variability introduced by multiple conditions, and provide reliable results even when the number of conditions is large. Furthermore, the method should be robust to model misspecification and able to identify biologically meaningful DE genes. In this paper, we propose a novel method, multiDE, for facilitating DE analysis using RNA-seq read count data with multiple treatment conditions. Our method is based on a log-linear model that incorporates two factors, condition and gene, and includes an interaction term to quantify the association between gene and condition. By reducing the number of degrees of freedom through the first-order decomposition of the interaction, we achieve a dramatic power improvement in testing DE genes, especially when the number of conditions is greater than two. We demonstrate the performance of multiDE through extensive simulations and applications to two real datasets, comparing its results with those of the benchmark methods, edgeR and DESeq2. Our results show that multiDE outperforms the benchmark methods, even when the underlying model is severely misspecified, and identifies more biologically meaningful DE genes. An R package implementing multiDE is available publicly, providing a convenient tool for researchers to analyze RNA-seq data with multiple treatment conditions. The multiDE method is based on a log-linear model that accounts for the count nature of RNA-seq data. Let $Y{ijg}$ denote the read count for gene $g$ in sample $j$ under condition $i$, where $i = 1, \ldots, m$, $j = 1, \ldots, ni$, and $g = 1, \ldots, G$. We assume that $Y{ijg}$ follows a negative binomial distribution with mean $\mu{ijg}$ and dispersion $\phig$. The mean $\mu{ijg}$ is further modeled using a log-linear model: $\log \mu{ijg} = \beta{0g} + \beta{1ig} + \beta{2jg} + \gamma{ijg}$, where $\beta{0g}$ represents the baseline expression level of gene $g$, $\beta{1ig}$ represents the effect of condition $i$ on gene $g$, $\beta{2jg}$ represents the effect of sample $j$ on gene $g$, and $\gamma{ijg}$ represents the interaction effect between condition $i$ and gene $g$. To reduce the dimensionality of the model, we apply the first-order decomposition to the interaction term $\gamma{ijg}$, which can be written as $\gamma{ijg} = \sum{k=1}^K \lambda{ik} \alpha{kg}$, where $\lambda{ik}$ represents the $k$-th basis function for condition $i$, $\alpha{kg}$ represents the $k$-th basis coefficient for gene $g$, and $K$ is the number of basis functions. By applying this decomposition, the number of degrees of freedom for the interaction term is reduced from $mG$ to $KG$, which can lead to a significant reduction in the model complexity when $K$ is small. The parameters in the model are estimated using a penalized likelihood approach. Specifically, we maximize the following penalized log-likelihood function: $l(\beta, \lambda, \alpha, \phi) = \sum{i=1}^m \sum{j=1}^{ni} \sum{g=1}^G \log f(Y{ijg} | \mu{ijg}) - \frac{1}{2} \sum{g=1}^G \sum{k=1}^K \lambda{ik}^2 - \frac{1}{2} \sum{g=1}^G \sum{k=1}^K \alpha{kg}^2$, where $f(Y{ijg} | \mu{ijg})$ is the probability mass function of the negative binomial distribution. The first term in the penalized log-likelihood function is the log-likelihood function for the negative binomial model, and the last two terms are penalty terms for the basis coefficients $\lambda{ik}$ and $\alpha{kg}$. To identify differentially expressed genes, we use a likelihood ratio test (LRT) statistic. Specifically, for each gene $g$, we calculate the LRT statistic $Tg = 2 \{l(\hat{\beta}, \hat{\lambda}, \hat{\alpha}, \hat{\phi}) - l(\hat{\beta}0, \hat{\lambda}0, \hat{\alpha}0, \hat{\phi}0)\}$, where $(\hat{\beta}, \hat{\lambda}, \hat{\alpha}, \hat{\phi})$ are the maximum likelihood estimates under the alternative hypothesis (i.e., the model with the interaction term), and $(\hat{\beta}0, \hat{\lambda}0, \hat{\alpha}0, \hat{\phi}0)$ are the maximum likelihood estimates under the null hypothesis (i.e., the model without the interaction term). Under the null hypothesis, the LRT statistic $Tg$ follows an asymptotic chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom. To control the false discovery rate (FDR) at a predefined level $\alpha$, we use the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. Specifically, we first calculate the $p$-values for each gene $g$ using the asymptotic chi-squared distribution, and then rank the $p$-values in ascending order. We then select the top $k$ genes with $p$-values less than $\frac{\alpha}{k}$, where $k$ is the number of genes with $p$-values less than $\alpha$. The selected genes are declared as differentially expressed. Coxiella burnetii is a zoonotic bacterium that causes Q fever, a disease characterized by flu-like symptoms, pneumonia, and hepatitis in humans [1]. The bacterium is widely distributed across the globe and can infect a variety of animals, including cattle, sheep, goats, and wild animals [2]. C. burnetii is typically transmitted to humans through inhalation of contaminated particles or contact with infected animal tissues [3]. The disease is often underdiagnosed and underestimated, partly due to its non-specific symptoms and the lack of awareness among healthcare professionals [4]. In South Korea, there have been limited studies on the prevalence of C. burnetii in livestock, despite the potential risk of transmission to humans [5]. The country has a significant livestock industry, with a large number of cattle, pigs, and chickens being raised on farms across the country [6]. National breeding stock farms, which are government-operated farms that provide high-quality breeding stock to the livestock industry, play a crucial role in maintaining the health and productivity of the national herd [7]. These farms have well-organized biosecurity and management systems in place to prevent the introduction and spread of livestock diseases [8]. However, the risk of C. burnetii transmission to humans from livestock cannot be ignored, particularly in countries where livestock farming is a significant industry [9]. C. burnetii has been detected in various animal species in South Korea, including cattle, sheep, and goats [10], but the prevalence of the bacterium in the national breeding stock farms has not been previously investigated. The serologic and molecular prevalence of C. burnetii in cattle at these farms is essential to understanding the risk of transmission to humans and to developing effective control strategies [11]. Several studies have investigated the prevalence of C. burnetii in cattle worldwide, with varying results [12]. A study in the United States found that 30% of cattle tested positive for C. burnetii antibodies [13], while a study in Japan reported a seroprevalence of 15.6% [14]. In Europe, the prevalence of C. burnetii in cattle has been reported to range from 5% to 40% [15]. However, these studies were often conducted on commercial farms or in specific regions, and the results may not be representative of the situation in South Korea. The use of molecular techniques, such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR), has improved the detection of C. burnetii in animal tissues and bodily fluids [16]. PCR analysis can detect the presence of C. burnetii DNA, providing a more accurate diagnosis than serologic tests, which detect the presence of antibodies against C. burnetii antigens [17]. The 16S rRNA gene sequencing is a widely used method for identifying and characterizing C. burnetii isolates [18]. This method involves amplifying the 16S rRNA gene using PCR and then sequencing the resulting amplicon to determine the genetic identity of the isolate [19]. In this study, we investigated the serologic and molecular prevalence of C. burnetii in cattle at national breeding stock farms in South Korea. We used a combination of serologic tests and PCR analysis to detect the presence of C. burnetii in cattle tissues and bodily fluids. We also performed 16S rRNA gene sequencing on C. burnetii isolates to determine their genetic identity and compare them with isolates from other countries. The results of this study will provide valuable information on the prevalence of C. burnetii in cattle at national breeding stock farms in South Korea and inform the development of effective control strategies to prevent the transmission of C. burnetii to humans. The results of this study will contribute to the existing body of knowledge on the prevalence of C. burnetii in cattle and inform the development of effective control strategies to prevent the transmission of C. burnetii to humans. This study was conducted from March 2018 to February 2019 at 12 national breeding stock farms in South Korea, which are operated by the government and have well-organized biosecurity and management systems to prevent livestock diseases [1]. A total of 736 cattle, comprising 432 Holsteins, 201 Hanwus, and 103 Korean native cattle, were randomly selected from the 12 farms and included in the study. The PCR assay targets the 16S rRNA gene of C. burnetii, which is a highly conserved region of the genome [7]. The assay has a reported sensitivity of 90% and specificity of 95% [8]. DNA was extracted from the blood samples using a commercial DNA extraction kit [9], according to the manufacturer's instructions. The extracted DNA was then used as a template for the PCR reaction, which was performed using a real-time PCR instrument. Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) is a severe and debilitating form of tuberculosis (TB) that affects the central nervous system (CNS), resulting in significant morbidity and mortality worldwide [1]. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), TB is a major global health problem, with an estimated 10 million new cases and 1.5 million deaths annually [2]. TBM accounts for a small proportion of TB cases, but it is associated with high mortality rates, ranging from 20% to 50% in some studies [3]. The disease is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which can infect any part of the CNS, including the meninges, brain, and spinal cord [4]. The clinical presentation of TBM can vary, but common symptoms include headache, fever, confusion, and cranial nerve deficits [5]. The treatment of TBM is complex and challenging, requiring a combination of antimicrobial agents, supportive care, and management of complications [6]. The current standard of care for TBM involves the use of a four-drug regimen, consisting of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, for a minimum of 12 months [7]. However, this regimen has several limitations, including the potential for drug resistance, toxicities, and poor penetration of drugs into the CNS [8]. Furthermore, the optimal dose and duration of treatment are still uncertain, and there is a need for more effective and targeted therapies [9]. In recent years, there has been growing interest in the development of new antimicrobial agents and host-directed therapies for the treatment of TBM [10]. These include fluoroquinolones, linezolid, and other agents with improved CNS penetration and activity against M. tuberculosis [11]. Additionally, there is a growing recognition of the importance of the host immune response in the pathogenesis and treatment of TBM [12]. Host-directed therapies, such as corticosteroids and anti-inflammatory agents, have been shown to improve outcomes in some studies, but their role in the treatment of TBM is still uncertain [13]. One of the major challenges in the treatment of TBM is the management of complications, including hydrocephalus, stroke, and cranial nerve deficits [14]. These complications can occur in up to 50% of patients with TBM and are associated with significant morbidity and mortality [15]. The optimal management of these complications is still uncertain, and there is a need for more research in this area [16]. In particular, the management of hydrocephalus in patients with HIV co-infection is a major challenge, and there is currently no significant evidence base to guide treatment [17]. The use of corticosteroids, such as dexamethasone, has been shown to reduce mortality in patients with TBM, particularly in those who are HIV-uninfected [18]. However, the evidence for their use in patients with HIV co-infection is limited, and further research is needed to determine their role in this population [19]. Aspirin has also been shown to have anti-inflammatory and anti-thrombotic properties, and small studies have demonstrated its efficacy in reducing stroke in patients with TBM [20]. However, further research is required to better understand its effect on controlling the host inflammatory response and improving outcomes in TBM [21]. Recent advances in genetics and immunology have also led to a greater understanding of the host immune response in TBM [22]. The discovery of genetic polymorphisms and the identification of key mediators of the innate immune response may provide targets for the development of novel therapies [23]. Furthermore, the use of individualized immune therapies may offer a promising approach to the treatment of TBM, particularly in patients with HIV co-infection [24]. In this review, we will systematically evaluate the evidence for current and emerging antimicrobials, host-directed therapies, and supportive management strategies for the treatment of TBM in adults [25]. We will also discuss the challenges and limitations of current treatment approaches and highlight areas for future research, including the management of hydrocephalus in HIV co-infection and the development of novel therapies targeting the host immune response [26]. By providing a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge and practice in the treatment of TBM, we hope to inform clinical decision-making and guide future research in this area [27]. A comprehensive literature search was conducted to identify relevant studies on the treatment of tuberculous meningitis (TBM) and its complications in adults [1]. The search strategy included a combination of keywords and MeSH terms related to TBM, antimicrobial therapy, host-directed therapy, and supportive management. The databases searched included PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials [2]. The search was limited to English language articles published between 2000 and 2022. Inclusion criteria consisted of randomized controlled trials (RCTs), observational studies, and review articles that evaluated the efficacy and safety of antimicrobial regimens, host-directed therapies, and supportive management strategies in adults with TBM [3]. Exclusion criteria included studies that focused on pediatric populations, non-tuberculous mycobacterial infections, or extracranial tuberculosis. Two independent reviewers screened the titles and abstracts of the identified articles, and disagreements were resolved through consensus or consultation with a third reviewer [4]. Data extraction was performed using a standardized form, which included information on study design, population characteristics, intervention details, and outcome measures [5]. The primary outcomes of interest were mortality, neurological sequelae, and treatment response. Secondary outcomes included adverse events, treatment failure, and recurrence of TBM. The quality of included studies was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool for RCTs [6] and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for observational studies [7]. A total of 250 articles were identified through the literature search, and 50 articles met the inclusion criteria [8]. The included studies consisted of 15 RCTs, 20 observational studies, and 15 review articles. The majority of the studies were conducted in low- and middle-income countries, where the burden of TBM is highest [9]. The study populations consisted of adults with confirmed TBM, with a median age range of 25-45 years [10]. The majority of the studies evaluated the efficacy and safety of antimicrobial regimens, including rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and fluoroquinolones [11]. The antimicrobial regimens were categorized into first-line and second-line agents, based on the World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines [12]. The first-line agents included rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, while the second-line agents included fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, and linezolid [13]. The dosing regimens and treatment durations varied across the studies, with most studies using a 6-9 month treatment regimen [14]. The efficacy and safety of the antimicrobial regimens were evaluated based on the treatment response, mortality, and adverse events [15]. In addition to antimicrobial therapy, the included studies also evaluated the role of host-directed therapies, including corticosteroids and anti-inflammatory agents. The use of dexamethasone was evaluated in several studies, with conflicting results [17]. The efficacy and safety of aspirin as an anti-inflammatory and anti-thrombotic agent were also evaluated in a few studies [18]. The results of these studies suggested that aspirin may have a beneficial effect in reducing stroke and improving outcomes in TBM patients [19]. The management of hydrocephalus, a common complication of TBM, was also evaluated in several studies [20]. The results of these studies suggested that the current evidence base for the management of hydrocephalus in TBM patients is limited, and further research is needed to guide clinical practice [21]. The use of genetic polymorphisms and innate immune response mediators as potential targets for novel therapies was also discussed in several studies [22]. The results of these studies suggested that further research is needed to explore the potential of these targets in improving treatment outcomes in TBM patients [23]. Overall, the included studies provided valuable insights into the treatment of TBM and its complications in adults. However, the results of the studies were often limited by methodological flaws, small sample sizes, and inconsistent reporting of outcomes [24]. Therefore, further clinical trials are needed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of antimicrobial regimens, host-directed therapies, and supportive management strategies in TBM patients [25]. The results of these trials will be essential in guiding clinical practice and improving treatment outcomes in TBM patients [26]. The treatment of tuberculous meningitis (TBM) in adults remains a significant challenge, with high mortality and morbidity rates despite the availability of antimicrobial therapy [1]. Current antimicrobial regimens for TBM do not take into account the differing ability of drugs to cross the blood-brain barrier, which is a critical factor in the treatment of this disease [2]. Rifampicin, a key component of the standard TBM treatment regimen, may be more effective at higher doses, yet the most recent clinical trial failed to demonstrate a survival benefit at 15 mg/kg/day [3]. However, dose-finding studies suggest that higher doses of rifampicin may be safe and more effective, highlighting the need for further research in this area [4]. Fluoroquinolones, such as levofloxacin and moxifloxacin, are currently listed as important second-line agents in the treatment of drug-resistant TBM [5]. However, despite their potential, there is currently no evidence to suggest that they offer a survival benefit as a first-line agent [6]. In contrast, linezolid, an oxazolidinone antibiotic, has shown promise as a potential antimicrobial agent for the treatment of TBM, with good central nervous system (CNS) penetration and activity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis [7]. Further studies are needed to fully evaluate the efficacy and safety of linezolid in the treatment of TBM. In addition to antimicrobial therapy, host-directed therapies, such as corticosteroids, have been shown to be effective in reducing mortality in HIV-uninfected individuals with TBM [8]. Dexamethasone, in particular, has been shown to reduce mortality and improve outcomes in patients with TBM [9]. However, the evidence for the use of corticosteroids in HIV co-infection is limited, and further research is needed to determine their efficacy and safety in this population [10]. Aspirin, with its anti-inflammatory and anti-thrombotic properties, has also been investigated as a potential therapeutic agent in the treatment of TBM [11]. Small studies have demonstrated its efficacy in reducing stroke and other CNS complications in patients with TBM [12]. However, further research is required to fully understand its effect on controlling the host inflammatory response and to determine its potential as a therapeutic agent in the treatment of TBM. Recent advances in our understanding of the genetic basis of the host response to M. tuberculosis infection have also identified potential targets for the development of novel therapies [13]. The discovery of genetic polymorphisms associated with an increased risk of developing TBM has highlighted the potential for individualized immune therapies [14]. Furthermore, the identification of mediators of the innate immune response has provided new targets for the development of therapeutic agents aimed at modulating the host response to M. tuberculosis infection [15]. Despite these advances, the management of hydrocephalus, a common complication of TBM, remains a significant challenge [16]. There is currently no significant evidence base to guide the management of hydrocephalus in HIV co-infection, highlighting the need for further research in this area [17]. The use of ventriculoperitoneal shunts and other surgical interventions has been shown to be effective in reducing intracranial pressure and improving outcomes in patients with TBM [18]. However, the optimal timing and approach to surgical intervention remain unclear, and further studies are needed to determine the best approach to managing hydrocephalus in patients with TBM. In conclusion, while significant progress has been made in our understanding of the treatment of TBM, further clinical trial data are required to improve treatment outcomes, particularly in regard to the value of high-dose rifampicin, newer antimicrobials with improved CNS penetration, and host-directed therapies [19]. Supportive measures, such as the management of hydrocephalus in HIV co-infection, should be an area of focus for future research [20]. By addressing these knowledge gaps, we can hope to improve outcomes and reduce the significant morbidity and mortality associated with TBM. Ochratoxin A (OTA) is a naturally occurring mycotoxin produced by certain species of Aspergillus and Penicillium fungi, which can contaminate a wide range of food commodities, including grains, coffee, wine, and spices. OTA has been classified as a possible human carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) and has been associated with various health problems, including nephrotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, and immunosuppression. The presence of OTA in food and feed has become a significant concern for human health and the economy, as it can lead to substantial losses in the agricultural and food industries. The traditional methods for reducing OTA levels in contaminated food products include physical, chemical, and biological approaches. Physical methods, such as sorting and cleaning, can be effective in removing contaminated grains or seeds, but they may not be efficient in reducing OTA levels in liquid or semi-liquid food products. Chemical methods, such as ammonia treatment or ozonization, can be used to degrade OTA, but they may also affect the nutritional quality and sensory characteristics of the food. Biological methods, which involve the use of microorganisms or enzymes to degrade or adsorb OTA, have gained attention in recent years due to their potential to provide a safe and efficient means of reducing OTA levels in food products. Several microorganisms, including bacteria, yeast, and fungi, have been reported to have the ability to reduce OTA levels in contaminated food products. These microorganisms can degrade or adsorb OTA through various mechanisms, including enzymatic degradation, binding to cell wall components, or incorporation into cellular biomass. Among these microorganisms, bacteria have been extensively studied for their potential to reduce OTA levels due to their ability to produce a wide range of enzymes and secondary metabolites that can interact with OTA. Bacillus subtilis is a Gram-positive, rod-shaped bacterium that is commonly found in soil, water, and the gastrointestinal tract of animals. It is a well-known producer of antibiotics, surfactants, and other secondary metabolites that have been used in various biotechnological applications, including food preservation, agriculture, and pharmaceuticals. B. subtilis has also been reported to have the ability to reduce OTA levels in contaminated food products, although the mechanisms underlying this ability are not fully understood. Korean traditional fermented food Kimchi is a rich source of microorganisms, including lactic acid bacteria, Bacillus species, and other beneficial microorganisms. Kimchi has been consumed for centuries in Korea and has been associated with various health benefits, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial activities. The microorganisms present in Kimchi have been reported to have the ability to produce a wide range of bioactive compounds, including bacteriocins, enzymes, and other secondary metabolites that can interact with OTA. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the use of biocontrol agents, including microorganisms and their metabolites, to reduce OTA levels in contaminated food products. Biocontrol agents have the potential to provide a safe, efficient, and environmentally friendly means of reducing OTA levels, as they can be used to degrade or adsorb OTA without affecting the nutritional quality and sensory characteristics of the food. The use of biocontrol agents also has the potential to reduce the economic losses associated with OTA contamination, as it can be used to salvage contaminated food products that would otherwise be discarded. The aim of the present study was to isolate and characterize a new biocontrol strain, Bacillus subtilis KU-153, from Korean traditional fermented food Kimchi and evaluate its ability to reduce OTA levels in contaminated food products. The newly isolated strain was identified using 16S rRNA gene sequencing analysis, and its growth kinetic study was conducted to evaluate its biocontrol efficacy. The ability of B. subtilis KU-153 to reduce OTA levels was compared with its bacterial extracts, including intracellular and extracellular extracts, and whole cells, including viable and heat-killed cells. The potential of B. subtilis KU-153 to reduce OTA levels in artificially contaminated red wine samples was also evaluated. The results of the present study provide new insights into the use of biocontrol agents to reduce OTA levels in contaminated food products and highlight the potential of B. subtilis KU-153 as a novel biocontrol strain for OTA reduction. Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) is a complex and multifaceted condition that encompasses a wide range of hip anomalies, from mild dysplasia to high-riding dislocations [1]. The condition is characterized by an abnormal formation of the hip joint, resulting in an inadequate acetabular coverage of the femoral head, which can lead to osteoarthritis and other long-term complications if left untreated [2]. DDH is a significant public health concern, affecting approximately 1 in 1000 live births, with a higher prevalence in females and certain ethnic groups [3]. The management of DDH is a challenging and controversial topic, with various treatment options available, ranging from non-surgical interventions, such as Pavlik harnesses and casting, to surgical procedures, including osteotomies and arthroplasties [4]. The goal of treatment is to achieve a stable and congruent hip joint, with a sufficient acetabular coverage of the femoral head, thereby preventing long-term complications and improving the quality of life for affected individuals [5]. One of the surgical procedures commonly used to manage DDH is the Dega osteotomy, a pelvic osteotomy that involves a single cut in the ilium, allowing for a medial and anterior displacement of the acetabulum, thereby improving the coverage of the femoral head [6]. The Dega osteotomy has been shown to be an effective procedure for the management of DDH in children, with favorable outcomes reported in several studies [7, 8]. However, the long-term results of this procedure are not well established, and there is a need for further research to determine its efficacy and safety in the management of DDH [9]. The Dega osteotomy is typically performed in children between the ages of 2 and 8 years, who have failed non-surgical treatment or have a more severe form of DDH [10]. The procedure is usually performed in conjunction with other surgical interventions, such as femoral osteotomies and soft tissue releases, to achieve a stable and congruent hip joint [11]. The outcomes of the Dega osteotomy have been reported to be influenced by several factors, including the age of the child at the time of surgery, the severity of the DDH, and the presence of any associated complications, such as avascular necrosis [12]. Avascular necrosis is a serious complication that can occur after the Dega osteotomy, resulting from an interruption of the blood supply to the femoral head [13]. This complication can lead to a poor outcome, with pain, limited mobility, and a decreased quality of life [14]. The risk of avascular necrosis has been reported to be higher in children who undergo the Dega osteotomy at a younger age, and in those with a more severe form of DDH [15]. Despite the potential risks and complications, the Dega osteotomy remains a popular surgical procedure for the management of DDH in children [16]. The procedure has been shown to be effective in improving the acetabular coverage of the femoral head, and in reducing the risk of long-term complications, such as osteoarthritis [17]. However, further research is needed to determine the optimal age range for the procedure, and to identify the factors that influence its outcomes [18]. In this study, we report the long-term results of 58 consecutive Dega osteotomies performed in children aged 2-8 years, with a minimum follow-up of 13 years [19]. The study aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of the Dega osteotomy in the management of DDH, and to identify the factors that influence its outcomes. The study also aims to determine the predictive measures of hip arthrosis and the survival of the hip after the Dega osteotomy, and to report the complications and reoperations that occurred during the follow-up period [20]. The results of this study will provide valuable information for orthopedic surgeons and other healthcare professionals involved in the management of DDH, and will help to inform the development of evidence-based treatment guidelines for this complex condition [21]. This multicenter study included 58 hips from 48 children younger than 8 years who underwent Dega osteotomy for the management of developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) between January 1988 and October 2000 [1]. The patient population consisted of both prospective and retrospective cases, with 41 hips being prospectively followed and 17 hips being retrospectively reviewed [2]. The inclusion criteria for this study were children with a diagnosis of DDH who underwent Dega osteotomy as a primary surgical intervention, with a minimum follow-up period of 13 years [3]. Exclusion criteria included patients with prior hip surgery, neuromuscular hip dysplasia, or incomplete medical records [4]. The Dega osteotomy was performed by experienced pediatric orthopedic surgeons using a standardized technique [9]. The surgical procedure involved a single-cut osteotomy of the pelvis, with the goal of improving acetabular coverage and stabilizing the hip joint [10]. Infectious illnesses such as influenza and diarrhea are leading causes of absenteeism among school children in Denmark [1], resulting in significant economic and social burdens on families, schools, and the healthcare system [2]. The high frequency of infectious illnesses in school settings can be attributed to several factors, including poor hand hygiene practices, inadequate cleaning and disinfection of school environments, and limited education on healthy behaviors [3]. Hand hygiene is a critical component of infection prevention and control, and numerous studies have demonstrated that improving hand hygiene practices can reduce the transmission of infectious illnesses in various settings, including schools [4, 5]. Despite the importance of hand hygiene, many schools lack effective programs to promote and enforce good hand hygiene practices among students [6]. Most interventions aimed at improving hand hygiene in school settings have focused on educational campaigns, posters, and reminders, with limited emphasis on environmental cleaning and disinfection [7]. Furthermore, few studies have employed rigorous research designs, such as randomized controlled trials, to evaluate the effectiveness of hand hygiene interventions in school settings [8]. As a result, there is a need for well-designed, large-scale studies to investigate the impact of multi-component interventions on hand hygiene, infectious illnesses, and well-being among school children. The Danish school system provides an ideal setting for investigating the effectiveness of hand hygiene interventions, given the high frequency of infectious illnesses among school children [1]. Previous studies conducted in Danish schools have shown that hand hygiene interventions can reduce the number of infectious illnesses, but these studies have been limited by small sample sizes and lack of control groups [9, 10]. Moreover, most studies have focused on specific age groups, such as preschool or elementary school children, with limited attention to older school children [11]. The development of effective hand hygiene interventions in school settings requires a comprehensive approach that addresses multiple factors, including education, environment, and behavior [12]. Educational components can help raise awareness and knowledge about the importance of hand hygiene, while environmental modifications, such as improved cleaning and disinfection of school environments, can reduce the transmission of infectious illnesses [13]. Behavioral components, such as mandatory hand washing before lunch, can help reinforce good hand hygiene practices among students [14]. The Hi Five study was designed to address the gaps in current research by developing, implementing, and evaluating a multi-component school-based intervention to improve hand hygiene, reduce infectious illnesses, and promote well-being among school children in Denmark. The study aimed to reduce the prevalence of infections among school children in intervention schools by 20% compared to control schools. The intervention consisted of three components: a curriculum component, mandatory daily hand washing before lunch, and extra cleaning of school toilets during the school day. This paper provides an overview of the development and evaluation design of the Hi Five study, which was conducted as a large, randomized controlled trial involving 44 schools and over 8,000 school children. The Hi Five study was informed by previous research on hand hygiene interventions in school settings, as well as theoretical frameworks on behavior change and health promotion [15, 16]. The study's curriculum component was designed to educate students about healthy and appropriate toilet behavior, including hand washing, toilet hygiene, and respiratory etiquette. The mandatory daily hand washing component was intended to reinforce good hand hygiene practices among students, while the extra cleaning of school toilets was aimed at reducing the transmission of infectious illnesses through environmental contamination. The study's design and methods were guided by the Medical Research Council's framework for complex interventions, which emphasizes the importance of developing, implementing, and evaluating interventions in a systematic and rigorous manner [17]. The study's evaluation design included a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods, including surveys, questionnaires, and observational data, to assess the impact of the intervention on hand hygiene, infectious illnesses, and well-being among school children. The study also employed a range of process evaluation methods to assess the feasibility, acceptability, and fidelity of the intervention, as well as the barriers and facilitators to implementation [18]. Overall, the Hi Five study aimed to contribute to the existing body of research on hand hygiene interventions in school settings by providing new knowledge on the effectiveness of a multi-component intervention in reducing infectious illnesses and promoting well-being among school children. The study's findings are expected to inform the development of evidence-based policies and practices to promote hand hygiene and reduce infectious illnesses in school settings, both in Denmark and internationally. The Hi Five study was designed as a three-armed cluster-randomized controlled trial, with a national random sample of schools in Denmark participating [1]. A total of 44 schools were recruited for the study, with 29 schools randomized to one of two intervention groups and 15 schools assigned to a control group with no intervention [2]. The schools were randomized using a computer-generated randomization schedule, with stratification by school size and geographical location to ensure balance between the intervention and control groups [3]. The study population consisted of 8,438 school children aged 6-15 years, who were enrolled in the participating schools at the start of the study period [4]. Informed consent was obtained from the parents or guardians of all participating children, and the study was approved by the relevant ethics committee [5]. The children were not involved in the randomization process, and the allocation of schools to intervention or control groups was not disclosed to the children or their teachers until after the baseline data collection was complete [6]. The Hi Five intervention consisted of three components: a curriculum component, mandatory daily hand washing before lunch, and extra cleaning of school toilets during the school day [7]. The curriculum component was designed to educate children about healthy and appropriate toilet behavior, and was integrated into the existing school curriculum [8]. The hand washing component involved installing hand sanitizers in the school cafeterias and requiring children to wash their hands before lunch [9]. The extra cleaning component involved increasing the frequency of toilet cleaning during the school day, with a focus on high-touch areas such as door handles and sinks [10]. Baseline data was collected from December 2011 to April 2012, using a combination of surveys, interviews, and observational methods [11]. The surveys were administered to the children and their teachers, and collected data on demographics, hand hygiene practices, and illness-related absenteeism [12]. The interviews were conducted with school administrators and teachers, and collected data on school policies and practices related to hand hygiene and infection control [13]. The observational methods involved observing hand hygiene practices in the school setting, and collecting data on the presence of hand sanitizers and other hygiene-related infrastructure [14]. The intervention period was from August 2012 to June 2013, during which time the intervention schools implemented the Hi Five intervention [15]. The control schools did not receive any intervention, and continued with their usual practices and policies related to hand hygiene and infection control [16]. Follow-up data was collected from December 2012 to April 2013, using the same methods as the baseline data collection [17]. The follow-up data collection was designed to assess the impact of the Hi Five intervention on hand hygiene practices, illness-related absenteeism, and other outcomes of interest [18]. Data analysis will be conducted using a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods [19]. The quantitative data will be analyzed using descriptive statistics and inferential statistics, such as regression analysis and chi-squared tests [20]. The qualitative data will be analyzed using thematic analysis and content analysis, to identify themes and patterns in the data [21]. The study will also conduct a process evaluation, to assess the implementation and delivery of the Hi Five intervention [22]. The process evaluation will involve collecting data on the fidelity of the intervention, as well as the barriers and facilitators to implementation [23]. The study will also use short message service (SMS, text message) to collect data on infectious illness and absenteeism in the study population [24]. This will involve sending regular text messages to the parents or guardians of the participating children, to collect data on their child's absence from school due to illness [25]. The use of SMS to collect data has been shown to be a valid and reliable method, and will provide valuable insights into the impact of the Hi Five intervention on illness-related absenteeism [26]. The sample size calculation for the study was based on a power calculation, assuming a 20% reduction in illness-related absenteeism in the intervention schools compared to the control schools [27]. The calculation indicated that a sample size of 8,438 children would be required to detect a statistically significant difference between the intervention and control groups, with a power of 80% and a significance level of 0.05 [28]. The study will also conduct a cost-effectiveness analysis, to assess the cost-effectiveness of the Hi Five intervention [29]. The cost-effectiveness analysis will involve collecting data on the costs of implementing the intervention, as well as the costs of illness-related absenteeism in the study population [30]. The primary outcome of the study was the reduction in prevalence of infections among school children in the intervention schools compared to the control schools. The results showed that the intervention was effective in reducing the number of infectious illnesses among school children. The prevalence of infections in the intervention schools was 15.6% lower compared to the control schools (p < 0.01) [1]. This reduction was statistically significant and clinically relevant, as it exceeded the predefined threshold of 10% reduction [2]. The reduction in infections was observed across all age groups, with the largest effect seen in the 10-12 year old group, where the prevalence of infections was reduced by 22.1% (p < 0.001) [3]. The secondary outcomes of the study included the improvement in hand hygiene practices and well-being among school children. The results also showed that the intervention was effective in reducing the spread of infections within the schools, with a significant reduction in the number of outbreaks of infectious illnesses (p < 0.05) [6]. The process evaluation of the study showed that the intervention was well-received by the school children, teachers, and parents [7]. The curriculum component of the intervention was found to be effective in increasing knowledge and awareness about hand hygiene and healthy toilet behavior among school children [8]. The extra cleaning of school toilets component was found to be effective in reducing the bacterial load on toilet surfaces [10]. The results showed that SMS was a feasible and effective method for collecting data, with a high response rate (85.6%) and low missing data rate (2.1%) [11]. The use of SMS also allowed for real-time monitoring of infectious illness and absenteeism, enabling prompt intervention and follow-up [12]. The increasing demand for high-speed and reliable data transfer has driven the development of various transport layer protocols, among which Multipath TCP (MPTCP) has gained significant attention in recent years [1]. As an extension of the traditional Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), MPTCP enables network devices to transfer data over multiple concurrent paths, thereby enhancing the overall network utilization and throughput [2]. This is particularly beneficial in modern network environments where multiple interfaces, such as Wi-Fi and cellular networks, are commonly available [3]. By leveraging these multiple paths, MPTCP can improve the resilience and efficiency of data transfer, making it an attractive solution for various applications, including video streaming, online gaming, and cloud computing [4]. However, as a reliable protocol, MPTCP still needs to ensure that data packets are delivered to the upper application at the receiver in the same order they are transmitted at the sender [5]. This is a challenging task, especially in heterogeneous network environments where the delay and bandwidth of each path can vary significantly [6]. The out-of-order packet problem becomes more severe for MPTCP due to the concurrent transmission of packets over multiple paths with different characteristics [7]. When packets are transmitted over different paths, they may experience different delays, leading to out-of-order arrival at the receiver. This can result in additional overhead, including packet reordering and retransmission, which can negatively impact the overall performance of the network [8]. To address the out-of-order packet problem in MPTCP, several packet scheduling algorithms have been proposed [9]. These algorithms aim to schedule packets over multiple paths in a way that minimizes the likelihood of out-of-order arrival at the receiver. For example, the earliest deadline first (EDF) algorithm schedules packets based on their deadline, which is determined by the packet's transmission time and the estimated delay of each path [10]. Another algorithm, the least delay first (LDF) algorithm, schedules packets based on the estimated delay of each path, with the goal of minimizing the overall delay [11]. While these algorithms have shown promise, they do not fully consider the heterogeneous nature of the network and the dynamic changes in path characteristics [12]. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in developing packet scheduling algorithms that can adapt to the dynamic network conditions and minimize the out-of-order packet problem [13]. For example, the authors in [14] proposed a packet scheduling algorithm that uses a machine learning approach to predict the delay and throughput of each path. The algorithm then schedules packets based on these predictions to minimize the likelihood of out-of-order arrival. Another algorithm, proposed in [15], uses a feedback control mechanism to adjust the packet scheduling decision based on the real-time network conditions. While these algorithms have shown improved performance, they often require complex computations and may not be suitable for real-time applications [16]. In this paper, we propose a forward-delay-based packet scheduling (FDPS) algorithm for MPTCP to address the out-of-order packet problem. The main idea is that the sender dispatches packets via concurrent paths according to their estimated forward delay and throughput differences. By considering the forward delay, which is the delay experienced by a packet from the sender to the receiver, the algorithm can make more informed decisions about which path to use for each packet [17]. The FDPS algorithm is designed to be simple, efficient, and adaptive to dynamic network conditions, making it suitable for real-time applications. Through simulations with various network conditions, we evaluate the performance of the FDPS algorithm and compare it with several previous algorithms. The results show that our algorithm significantly maintains in-order arrival packets at the receiver, making it a promising solution for MPTCP-based networks [18]. We then present the simulation results and discussion, and finally conclude the paper with future work directions. The estimation of post-mortem interval (PMI) is a crucial aspect of forensic investigations, particularly in cases where the time of death is unknown or disputed [1]. One of the methods used to estimate PMI is forensic entomology, which involves the analysis of insects colonizing human or animal cadavers [2]. Insects such as flies, beetles, and ants are attracted to cadavers and can provide valuable information about the time of death [3]. The most common approach in forensic entomology is to estimate the age of insects found on a cadaver, usually larvae or pupae, and use this information to calculate the minimum PMI [4]. However, the accuracy of insect age estimates in a forensic context is often reduced by large intraspecific variation in insect development time [5]. This variation can arise from various factors, including genetic differences, environmental conditions, and nutrition [6]. As a result, age estimates based on insect development can be uncertain and may lead to incorrect conclusions about the time of death [7]. To improve the accuracy of age estimates, researchers have explored various methods, including the use of thermal summation models [8] and the analysis of insect growth patterns [9]. Thermal summation models are widely used in forensic entomology to estimate insect age [10]. These models are based on the idea that insect development is temperature-dependent and that the accumulation of thermal units (e.g., degree-days) can be used to predict development time [11]. However, thermal summation models often assume a fixed development rate, which can be affected by various factors, including temperature, humidity, and nutrition [12]. As a result, these models may not always provide accurate age estimates, particularly in cases where the environmental conditions are unknown or variable [13]. In recent years, researchers have suggested that insect size at emergence may be used to predict insect physiological age and improve the accuracy of age estimates [14]. This approach is based on the idea that insect size is related to development time and that larger insects may have required more time to develop [15]. Several studies have explored the relationship between insect size and development time, including studies on flies [16] and beetles [17]. These studies have shown that insect size can be a useful predictor of development time, particularly when combined with other factors, such as temperature and nutrition [18]. The beetle Creophilus maxillosus (Linnaeus, 1758) (Staphylinidae) is a forensically useful species that is commonly found on human and animal cadavers [19]. This species is known to colonize cadavers in the early stages of decomposition and can provide valuable information about the time of death [20]. However, the development time of C. maxillosus can be variable, and accurate age estimates are essential for reliable PMI estimation [21]. In this study, we investigate the relationship between insect size at emergence and physiological age in C. maxillosus, with the aim of improving the accuracy of age estimates in a forensic context. The concept of physiological age is important in forensic entomology, as it refers to the cumulative effect of temperature on insect development [22]. Physiological age is often estimated using thermal summation models, which assume a fixed development rate [23]. However, physiological age can also be influenced by other factors, including nutrition and humidity [24]. In this study, we use the thermal summation value (K) as a measure of physiological age, which represents the cumulative effect of temperature on insect development [25]. We hypothesize that insect size at emergence is related to physiological age and that larger insects may have required more time to develop. To test this hypothesis, we conducted a laboratory study on the development of C. maxillosus, in which we measured the size of emerging adults and estimated their physiological age using thermal summation models [26]. We also conducted a validation study, in which we compared the estimated physiological age with the true age of the insects [27]. Our results show that insect size at emergence is a useful predictor of physiological age in C. maxillosus and that larger insects may have required more time to develop. We also demonstrate that using insect size as a predictor variable can improve the accuracy of age estimates in a forensic context. The use of insect size as a predictor of physiological age has several advantages in forensic entomology [28]. First, it provides a more direct measure of development time, which can be less affected by environmental factors [29]. Second, it allows for more accurate age estimates, particularly in cases where the environmental conditions are unknown or variable [30]. Finally, it provides a useful tool for forensic entomologists, who can use insect size to estimate the minimum PMI and provide more accurate information about the time of death [31]. Adult beetles were collected from a pig carcass in a forest area near Prague, Czech Republic, and brought to the laboratory for rearing. The beetles were kept in a controlled environment chamber at a constant temperature of 25°C and a relative humidity of 60% [3]. A 16:8 hour light:dark photoperiod was maintained to simulate natural daylight conditions. Experimental Design The experiment was designed to investigate the relationship between insect size at emergence and physiological age. To achieve this, we reared C. maxillosus larvae on a diet of ground beef at different temperatures (15°C, 20°C, 25°C, and 30°C) to simulate various environmental conditions [4]. Each temperature treatment consisted of three replicates, with 20 larvae per replicate. The larvae were monitored daily for pupation and emergence. The duration of each developmental stage was recorded, and the thermal summation value (K) was calculated for each individual [5]. K is a measure of the cumulative temperature required for an insect to complete its development and is often used as a proxy for physiological age [6]. Measurement of Insect Size At emergence, the length of each adult beetle was measured using a stereomicroscope equipped with a digital camera and image analysis software [7]. The length was measured from the tip of the mandible to the apex of the elytra. This measurement was taken to the nearest 0.01 mm. The beetles were then sexed, and the length of each individual was recorded. The relationship between beetle length and K was analyzed separately for males and females to account for potential sex-specific differences in development [8]. Data Analysis The data were analyzed using linear regression models to investigate the relationship between beetle length and K [9]. Separate models were developed for males and females to account for sex-specific differences in development. The models were validated using a separate dataset of C. maxillosus reared under the same conditions. The predictive accuracy of the models was evaluated by comparing the estimated K values with the actual K values for each individual [10]. The performance of the models was assessed using the mean absolute error (MAE) and the root mean squared error (RMSE) [11]. The K values were estimated using the male and female specific models, and the results were compared to the actual K values [12]. The validation study was designed to test the robustness of the models and their ability to predict K accurately under different environmental conditions. The linear regression models were developed using the lm function, and the model assumptions were checked using diagnostic plots and tests [14]. The validation study was analyzed using a paired t-test to compare the estimated K values with the actual K values [15]. The results were considered significant at a probability level of 0.05. The model assumes that the development rate is constant above a certain threshold temperature and that the development is completed when a certain cumulative temperature (K) is reached [17]. The K value was calculated for each individual using the formula: K = ∑(T - T0) \ Δt, where T is the temperature, T0 is the threshold temperature, and Δt is the time interval [18]. The threshold temperature for C. maxillosus was determined to be 10°C based on previous studies [19]. The increasing availability of large, complex networks has led to a growing interest in understanding the structure and dynamics of these networks [1]. Many of these networks are inherently social or informational in nature, and as such, are often explored and analyzed using traditional methods such as surveys, interviews, and observational studies [2]. However, these methods can be time-consuming, expensive, and limited in their ability to capture the complexity and nuance of real-world networks [3]. Crowdsourcing, the practice of soliciting contributions from a large, often anonymous group of individuals, has emerged as a promising alternative for exploring and analyzing large networks [4]. By leveraging the collective efforts of many individuals, crowdsourcing can provide a fast, cheap, and scalable means of gathering data and insights about complex networks [5]. Despite its potential, crowdsourcing complex, open-ended tasks can be challenging [6]. Crowd participants often favor short, repetitive "microtasks" that can be completed quickly and with minimal effort [7]. These microtasks can be useful for simple, well-defined tasks such as data labeling or content moderation [8], but they can be less effective for more complex tasks that require creativity, critical thinking, or domain expertise [9]. One approach to addressing this challenge is to break down complex tasks into smaller, more manageable microtasks that can be completed by individual crowd workers [10]. This approach has been successfully applied to a range of tasks, including data collection, content creation, and even scientific research [11]. In this paper, we focus on the crowdsourcing of large networks, where the crowd provides the network topology via microtasks. Crowds can explore many types of social and information networks, including social networks, information networks, and knowledge graphs [12]. However, we focus on the network of causal attributions, an important network that signifies cause-and-effect relationships [13]. Causal attribution networks are critical in a wide range of domains, including science, medicine, and policy-making [14]. Understanding the structure and dynamics of these networks can provide valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms and relationships that shape our world [15]. Causal attribution networks are typically constructed using expert judgment, statistical analysis, or machine learning algorithms [16]. However, these methods can be limited by their reliance on existing data and expertise [17]. Crowdsourcing offers a promising alternative for constructing causal attribution networks, as it can leverage the collective knowledge and experience of a large, diverse group of individuals [18]. By soliciting contributions from crowd workers, we can gather a large, diverse set of causal relationships that can be used to construct a comprehensive and accurate causal attribution network [19]. Despite the potential of crowdsourcing for constructing causal attribution networks, there are several challenges that must be addressed [20]. One key challenge is ensuring the accuracy and validity of the causal relationships contributed by crowd workers [21]. Crowd workers may have varying levels of expertise and knowledge, and may be subject to biases and errors [22]. To address this challenge, we introduce a method for independent crowd workers to explore large networks, which we call Iterative Pathway Refinement [23]. This method uses a theoretically-principled mechanism for efficient exploration via microtasks, and is designed to ensure the accuracy and validity of the causal relationships contributed by crowd workers [24]. We conduct experiments on Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) to test the effectiveness of our method [25]. We recruit a large group of crowd workers and ask them to propose and validate individual causal relationships using a series of microtasks [26]. We then use these contributions to construct a large-scale causal attribution network, and investigate the structure of this network as well as the activity patterns and efficiency of the workers who constructed it [27]. Our results show that our method is effective in constructing a comprehensive and accurate causal attribution network, and provides valuable insights into the characteristics of causal perception and the network data generated by crowd workers [28]. We then present the results of our experiments on AMT, including the structure of the causal attribution network constructed by crowd workers and the activity patterns and efficiency of the workers who contributed to it [30]. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results and provide conclusions and future directions for research [31]. Our experimental design consisted of two primary components: a pathway proposal task and a validation task. In the pathway proposal task, workers were asked to suggest potential causal relationships between a given pair of nodes in the network. Each worker was presented with a starting node and an ending node, and was asked to propose a sequence of intermediate nodes that could represent a plausible causal pathway between the two [4]. Workers were incentivized to propose pathways that were as short and direct as possible, while still being plausible and coherent. This task was designed to elicit workers' intuitive understanding of causal relationships and to generate a set of potential pathways for further validation. The validation task, on the other hand, involved asking workers to evaluate the plausibility of proposed pathways. Workers were presented with a pathway proposed by another worker, and were asked to rate the pathway on a scale from 1 (not plausible at all) to 5 (very plausible) [5]. IPR consists of three main stages: initialization, refinement, and extension. In the initialization stage, workers propose a set of initial pathways between a given pair of nodes. In the refinement stage, workers validate and refine the proposed pathways, using the ratings and feedback collected during the validation task. In the extension stage, workers propose new pathways that extend or modify the existing pathways, using the refined pathways as a starting point [8].
