Reperfusion injury (R/I) is a complex pathological phenomenon that occurs when blood flow is restored to ischemic tissues after a period of prolonged occlusion [1]. In the context of stroke, R/I can lead to exacerbated brain damage, characterized by increased lesion size, blood-brain barrier disruption, and edema formation [2]. The underlying mechanisms of R/I involve a multifaceted interplay between vascular, inflammatory, and cellular responses [3]. A critical component of this process is the post-stroke inflammatory response, which is mediated by the activation of glial cells, infiltration of peripheral leukocytes, and release of damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) molecules [4]. The inflammatory response in R/I is characterized by the upregulation of various pro-inflammatory mediators, including cytokines, chemokines, adhesion molecules, and immune molecule effectors such as matrix metalloproteinases-9 (MMP-9), inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS), nitric oxide (NO), and reactive oxygen species (ROS) [5]. These molecules contribute to the exacerbation of tissue damage and impairment of neurological function. For instance, the activation of MMP-9 has been shown to disrupt the blood-brain barrier, leading to edema formation and hemorrhagic transformation [6]. Similarly, the overproduction of NO and ROS can cause oxidative stress and neuronal damage [7]. Despite the wealth of experimental evidence supporting the role of inflammation in R/I, clinical trials targeting these pathways have yielded disappointing results [8]. Several factors may contribute to this discrepancy, including the heterogeneity of stroke populations, variability in treatment timing and dosing, and limitations in the translation of preclinical models to clinical settings [9]. Moreover, many of these clinical trials were conducted prior to the widespread adoption of revascularization therapies, such as recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA) and mechanical thrombectomy [10]. Recent advances in our understanding of R/I and the development of more effective revascularization strategies have created new opportunities for the treatment of stroke [11]. The combination of revascularization therapies with anti-inflammatory agents may offer a promising approach to mitigate the detrimental effects of R/I and improve neurological outcomes [12]. In this context, it is essential to revisit the mechanisms of inflammation involved in R/I and identify potential therapeutic targets. A comprehensive understanding of the molecular pathways and cellular interactions underlying R/I will facilitate the design of more effective clinical trials and the development of novel treatments for stroke. The role of glial cells, including microglia and astrocytes, in the post-stroke inflammatory response is a critical area of investigation [13]. These cells can release a variety of pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory mediators, which can either exacerbate or mitigate tissue damage [14]. The activation of microglia, in particular, has been implicated in the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) [15]. In contrast, astrocytes can release anti-inflammatory factors, such as interleukin-10 (IL-10) and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β), which can promote tissue repair and regeneration [16]. The infiltration of peripheral leukocytes, including neutrophils and lymphocytes, is another key component of the post-stroke inflammatory response [17]. These cells can release granules and cytokines that contribute to tissue damage and exacerbate the inflammatory response [18]. The adhesion molecules, such as intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) and vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1), play a crucial role in the recruitment of leukocytes to the site of injury [19]. The inhibition of these molecules has been shown to reduce leukocyte infiltration and improve neurological outcomes in experimental models of stroke [20]. In conclusion, the post-stroke inflammatory response is a complex and multifaceted process that involves the activation of glial cells, infiltration of peripheral leukocytes, and release of pro-inflammatory mediators. A comprehensive understanding of these mechanisms is essential for the development of effective therapeutic strategies to mitigate the detrimental effects of R/I and improve neurological outcomes in stroke patients. The identification of potential therapeutic targets, such as cytokines, chemokines, and adhesion molecules, will facilitate the design of clinical trials and the development of novel treatments for stroke. To investigate the therapeutic potential of targeting anti-inflammatory mechanisms in the treatment of reperfusion injury (R/I) in stroke, we conducted a comprehensive review of existing literature and designed a series of experiments to elucidate the underlying molecular pathways. Experimental Design Our experimental approach involved the use of a middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) model in mice, which is a well-established model for studying ischemic stroke and R/I [1]. Male C57BL/6 mice (20-25 g) were subjected to 60 minutes of MCAO, followed by reperfusion for 24 hours. This model allows for the examination of the effects of delayed reperfusion on ischemic damage and the subsequent inflammatory response. Animal Groups and Treatment Mice were randomly assigned to one of four groups: sham-operated controls, MCAO with no treatment, MCAO with recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA) treatment, and MCAO with rtPA and anti-inflammatory treatment. The anti-inflammatory treatment consisted of a combination of inhibitors targeting key molecules involved in the poststroke inflammatory response, including cytokines, chemokines, and matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) [2]. Inflammatory Mediator Analysis To characterize the poststroke inflammatory response, we analyzed the expression of various inflammatory mediators in the brain tissue of MCAO mice using quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR), Western blotting, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) [3]. The mediators examined included tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), interleukin-6 (IL-6), monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), and MMP-9. The pathophysiology of reperfusion injury (R/I) is complex and multifaceted, involving the interplay of various cellular and molecular mechanisms [1]. At the core of R/I is the poststroke immune response, which is characterized by the aberrant activation of glial cells, including microglia and astrocytes [2]. These cells release a plethora of pro-inflammatory mediators, including cytokines, such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), and chemokines, such as monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) and macrophage inflammatory protein-1 alpha (MIP-1α) [3]. The release of these mediators promotes the infiltration of peripheral leukocytes, including neutrophils and monocytes, into the ischemic brain tissue [4]. The infiltration of leukocytes into the brain tissue is facilitated by the upregulation of adhesion molecules, such as intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) and vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1), on the surface of endothelial cells [5]. The interaction between leukocytes and endothelial cells leads to the release of damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) molecules, which further exacerbate the inflammatory response [6]. DAMP molecules, such as high-mobility group box 1 (HMGB1) protein, are released by ischemic cells and activate pattern recognition receptors, such as toll-like receptors (TLRs), on immune cells [7]. The activation of TLRs triggers a signaling cascade that leads to the production of pro-inflammatory mediators, including matrix metalloproteinases-9 (MMP-9), inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS), and reactive oxygen species (ROS) [8]. MMP-9 is a key mediator of blood-brain barrier (BBB) breakdown, and its inhibition has been shown to reduce edema and hemorrhage in animal models of stroke [9]. iNOS, on the other hand, produces nitric oxide (NO), which can have both beneficial and detrimental effects on the brain tissue [10]. While NO can help to maintain blood flow and reduce platelet aggregation, excessive production of NO can lead to the formation of peroxynitrite, a potent oxidant that can damage brain tissue [11]. Several experimental studies have characterized the role of inflammatory mediators in R/I and have shown that their inhibition can improve neurological outcome [12]. For example, the inhibition of TNF-α using TNF-α inhibitors, such as etanercept, has been shown to reduce infarct size and improve functional outcome in animal models of stroke [13]. Similarly, the inhibition of MMP-9 using MMP-9 inhibitors, such as SB-3CT, has been shown to reduce BBB breakdown and edema in animal models of stroke [14]. Despite the promising results from experimental studies, numerous clinical trials have failed to demonstrate any positive outcomes in stroke patients [15]. However, many of these clinical trials were carried out before the routine use of revascularization therapies, such as thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy [16]. The use of revascularization therapies has been shown to improve outcomes in stroke patients, but the benefits of these therapies can be limited by R/I [17]. Therefore, there is a need to develop therapeutic strategies that can mitigate R/I and improve outcomes in stroke patients. One potential approach is to target anti-inflammatory mediators in R/I as a combined therapy with revascularization therapies [18]. For example, the use of anti-TNF-α agents, such as etanercept, in combination with thrombolysis has been shown to improve outcomes in animal models of stroke [19]. Similarly, the use of MMP-9 inhibitors, such as SB-3CT, in combination with mechanical thrombectomy has been shown to reduce BBB breakdown and edema in animal models of stroke [20]. In conclusion, R/I is a complex and multifaceted phenomenon that involves the interplay of various cellular and molecular mechanisms. The poststroke immune response plays a key role in R/I, and the inhibition of inflammatory mediators has been shown to improve neurological outcome in experimental studies. Bacteria have the unique ability to proliferate perpetually without ageing, allowing them to thrive in a wide range of environments [1]. However, they also face conditions where they must persist for extended periods, often in the absence of nutrients or under stress [2]. Mycobacteria, a genus of bacteria that includes species such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium leprae, are notorious for their ability to survive for long periods, often in a dormant or quiescent state [3]. This state is particularly relevant during mycobacterial diseases such as tuberculosis and leprosy, which are chronic and develop after long-term persistent infections [4]. The ability of mycobacteria to survive for extended periods is thought to be a key factor in their pathogenicity, as it allows them to evade the host immune system and persist in the host for years or even decades [5]. Despite the importance of long-term survival in mycobacterial pathogenesis, the fundamental mechanisms underlying this process are not well understood [6]. Several studies have identified various factors that contribute to the long-term survival of mycobacteria, including the formation of biofilms, the production of stress response proteins, and the regulation of metabolic pathways [7-9]. However, the molecular mechanisms that coordinate these processes and allow mycobacteria to survive for extended periods are still unclear. One protein that has been implicated in the long-term survival of mycobacteria is Mycobacterial DNA-binding protein 1 (MDP1), a histone-like nucleoid-associated protein that is expressed by all Mycobacterium species [10]. MDP1 is thought to play a role in the organization and regulation of the mycobacterial nucleoid, and has been shown to bind to specific DNA sequences and regulate gene expression [11, 12]. However, the exact function of MDP1 in mycobacterial survival and pathogenesis is still not well understood. Mycobacterium smegmatis is a saprophytic bacterium that is often used as a model organism for studying mycobacterial biology and pathogenesis [13]. M. smegmatis is a fast grower that shares many characteristics with pathogenic mycobacteria, including the ability to form biofilms and survive for extended periods in a dormant or quiescent state [14]. As such, it is an ideal model organism for studying the mechanisms of long-term survival in mycobacteria. In this study, we used M. smegmatis as a model organism to investigate the role of MDP1 in the long-term survival of mycobacteria. Previous studies have shown that MDP1 is essential for the growth and survival of M. smegmatis, and that MDP1-deficient strains exhibit defects in nucleoid organization and gene regulation [15, 16]. However, the exact mechanisms by which MDP1 contributes to the long-term survival of M. smegmatis are still unclear. To address this question, we used a combination of proteomic and biochemical analyses to investigate the effects of MDP1 deficiency on the physiology and metabolism of M. smegmatis. Our results show that MDP1 plays a critical role in the long-term survival of M. smegmatis, and that MDP1 deficiency leads to changes in DNA and ATP synthesis, NADH/NAD+ ratio, and resistance to oxidative stress. The long-term survival of mycobacteria is a complex process that involves the coordination of multiple cellular functions, including DNA replication, transcription, translation, and metabolism [17]. In order to survive for extended periods, mycobacteria must be able to regulate their metabolic pathways and respond to changes in their environment [18]. This requires the coordination of multiple cellular processes, including the regulation of gene expression, the synthesis of stress response proteins, and the maintenance of cellular homeostasis [19]. The identification of the molecular mechanisms that underlie the long-term survival of mycobacteria is essential for the development of new therapeutic strategies for the treatment of mycobacterial diseases. In recent years, several studies have investigated the role of various proteins and pathways in the long-term survival of mycobacteria [20-22]. These studies have identified several key factors that contribute to the ability of mycobacteria to survive for extended periods, including the formation of biofilms, the production of stress response proteins, and the regulation of metabolic pathways [23-25]. However, the molecular mechanisms that coordinate these processes and allow mycobacteria to survive for extended periods are still unclear. Further research is needed to fully understand the mechanisms of long-term survival in mycobacteria, and to identify new therapeutic targets for the treatment of mycobacterial diseases. The development of new therapeutic strategies for the treatment of mycobacterial diseases will require a thorough understanding of the molecular mechanisms that underlie the long-term survival of mycobacteria [27]. The quest for fairness and equity in machine learning (ML) has become a pressing concern, as the increasing ubiquity of ML systems in high-stakes decision-making applications has highlighted the potential for these systems to perpetuate and amplify existing social biases [1]. One particularly pernicious form of bias is demographic disparity, wherein the performance of an ML model varies systematically across different demographic groups, often to the detriment of already marginalized populations [2]. To mitigate this issue, researchers have proposed a variety of techniques for inducing demographic parity, including data preprocessing methods [3], regularization techniques [4], and adversarial training protocols [5]. However, these approaches often require significant modifications to the underlying ML pipeline, which can be prohibitively difficult for non-expert users to implement. Moreover, many existing methods for promoting fairness in ML rely on the availability of sensitive attributes, such as demographic information, at training time [6]. However, in many real-world applications, such information may not be available, or may be actively withheld due to privacy concerns [7]. Furthermore, even when sensitive attributes are available, their use can be fraught with ethical and legal complications, particularly in domains where data protection regulations are stringent [8]. In light of these challenges, there is a growing need for methods that can promote fairness in ML without relying on explicit sensitive attributes, and that can be easily integrated into existing ML pipelines. Recent advances in representation learning have provided a promising foundation for addressing these challenges [9]. By learning compact, abstract representations of input data, ML models can capture complex patterns and relationships that may not be immediately apparent from the raw data alone [10]. However, these representations can also inadvertently encode sensitive information, such as demographic attributes, which can in turn perpetuate biases in downstream predictions [11]. To address this issue, researchers have proposed a variety of techniques for learning fair representations, including domain-adversarial training [12] and invariant risk minimization [13]. These approaches typically involve modifying the objective function or architecture of the ML model to discourage the encoding of sensitive information, and have been shown to be effective in promoting demographic parity in a variety of applications [14]. Despite their promise, however, existing methods for learning fair representations often require significant expertise in ML and software development, which can limit their accessibility to non-expert users [15]. Furthermore, these methods often rely on the availability of specialized software frameworks or hardware accelerators, which can be prohibitively expensive or difficult to obtain [16]. In light of these limitations, there is a growing need for methods that can promote fairness in ML in a more accessible, user-friendly manner. Ideally, such methods would provide a simple, drop-in intervention that could be applied to existing ML models, without requiring significant modifications to the underlying architecture or training protocol. In response to these challenges, we propose the BriarPatch, a novel pixel-space intervention that obscures sensitive attributes from representations encoded in pre-trained classifiers. By applying the BriarPatch to the input data, users can encourage internal model representations not to encode sensitive information, which has the effect of pushing downstream predictors towards exhibiting demographic parity with respect to the sensitive information. The BriarPatch is designed to be a user-level intervention, providing a simple, accessible mechanism for promoting fairness in ML that complements prior research on fair representations. Unlike existing methods, which often require significant expertise in ML and software development, the BriarPatch can be applied by non-expert users, without requiring modifications to the underlying ML pipeline or access to specialized software frameworks or hardware accelerators. We then describe the design and implementation of the BriarPatch, including the underlying mathematical formulation and algorithmic procedures. Following this, we present a comprehensive evaluation of the BriarPatch, including experiments on a variety of benchmark datasets and applications. Finally, we conclude with a discussion of the implications and future directions of this research, highlighting the potential of the BriarPatch to promote fairness and equity in a wide range of ML applications. Traditional approaches to achieving fairness, such as data preprocessing [2], regularization techniques [3], and adversarial training [4], often require access to the model's architecture or training data. In contrast, BriarPatches offer a novel, user-level intervention that can be applied post-hoc to pre-trained classifiers without requiring modifications to the model itself or access to its training data. Technical Implementation BriarPatches are implemented as small, fixed-size image patches that are strategically placed over sensitive regions of the input data to obscure the sensitive attributes. The placement and design of these patches are critical to their effectiveness. We utilize a combination of computer vision techniques and sensitivity analysis to identify the regions of the input data that are most relevant to the sensitive attributes [5]. Once identified, the patches are applied to these regions to mask the sensitive information. The patches themselves are designed to be minimally intrusive, meaning they are small and do not significantly alter the overall appearance of the input data. This is important because it allows the model to still recognize and process the non-sensitive aspects of the input, thereby preserving its predictive performance on non-sensitive tasks. The size and shape of the patches can be adjusted based on the specific use case and the type of sensitive information being obscured. Mechanism of Action The application of BriarPatches to the input data of a pre-trained classifier has the effect of altering the internal representations learned by the model. By obscuring sensitive attributes, the patches prevent the model from encoding these attributes into its representations. This, in turn, encourages the downstream predictors to rely less on sensitive information for making predictions, thereby reducing bias and promoting demographic parity [6]. The mechanism by which BriarPatches induce demographic parity can be understood through the lens of information theory. By removing or reducing the mutual information between the sensitive attributes and the model's internal representations, BriarPatches effectively decrease the model's ability to distinguish between different demographic groups based on sensitive information [7]. This leads to predictions that are more fair and less biased towards any particular group. We compared these metrics before and after the application of BriarPatches to assess the intervention's effectiveness. Across all datasets and models tested, we observed significant reductions in bias and improvements in fairness metrics after applying BriarPatches. These findings suggest that BriarPatches can be a valuable tool for promoting fairness in machine learning, especially in scenarios where access to the model's training data or architecture is limited. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that the effectiveness of BriarPatches is dependent on several factors, including the size and placement of the patches, the type of sensitive information being obscured, and the complexity of the pre-trained classifier. These factors must be carefully considered when designing and applying BriarPatches to ensure optimal results. Comparison with Prior Work BriarPatches complement prior research on fair representations by offering a user-level intervention that does not require modifications to the model or access to its training data. This distinguishes our approach from methods like adversarial training [4] and data preprocessing [2], which are typically applied during the training phase and require significant expertise and resources. In comparison to other post-hoc fairness interventions, such as model reinterpretation [13] and output adjustments [14], BriarPatches offer a unique advantage by directly addressing the encoding of sensitive attributes in the model's internal representations. This approach can lead to more robust and consistent fairness improvements, as it targets the root cause of bias rather than just its symptoms. The advent of newborn hearing screening programs has revolutionized the field of pediatric audiology, enabling the early identification of infants with significant hearing loss [1]. As a result, there is a growing population of infants who are diagnosed with severe to profound sensorineural hearing loss at a very young age. For these infants, the use of hearing aids is often the initial treatment approach; however, when hearing aids fail to provide sufficient benefit, cochlear implantation is considered as a viable option to restore hearing and facilitate language development [2]. The critical period for language development is generally considered to be between 0 and 3 years of age, during which time the brain is most receptive to linguistic input [3]. Therefore, it is essential to explore the safety and efficacy of cochlear implantation in infants below 12 months of age, as this population is at a critical juncture in their language development trajectory. Background and Rationale Cochlear implantation has been widely accepted as a treatment option for children with severe to profound sensorineural hearing loss, with the first implantations in children taking place in the 1980s [4]. Initially, cochlear implantation was reserved for older children and adults, due to concerns regarding the potential risks and complications associated with the surgery [5]. However, as the field has evolved, there has been a growing recognition of the importance of early intervention in promoting optimal language outcomes [6]. The development of minimally invasive surgical techniques has also contributed to the expansion of cochlear implantation to younger age groups [7]. Despite these advances, the safety and efficacy of cochlear implantation in infants below 12 months of age remain a topic of ongoing debate and research. Review of Current Literature Numerous studies have investigated the outcomes of cochlear implantation in young children, with a particular focus on the relationship between age at implantation and language development [8]. The consensus among researchers is that earlier implantation is associated with better language outcomes, as measured by standardized assessments such as the Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test (PPVT) [9]. For example, a study by [10] found that children implanted before 12 months of age demonstrated significantly better language skills than those implanted at older ages. Similarly, [11] reported that infants implanted at 6-12 months of age showed rapid gains in language development, comparable to those of their hearing peers. These findings suggest that cochlear implantation in infants below 12 months of age may be a viable option for promoting age-appropriate language skills. Theoretical Framework The theoretical framework underlying this research is based on the concept of critical periods in language development [12]. According to this framework, there are specific time periods during which the brain is most receptive to linguistic input, and during which language skills can be acquired most easily [13]. For infants with significant hearing loss, the critical period for language development may be extended or altered, highlighting the need for early intervention to promote optimal outcomes [14]. The use of cochlear implantation in this population can be seen as a means of restoring access to linguistic input, thereby facilitating language development and minimizing the risk of long-term language delays [15]. Methodological Considerations The assessment of language development in infants with cochlear implants poses a number of methodological challenges [16]. Traditional language assessments, such as the PPVT, may not be suitable for use with very young children, due to their limited linguistic and cognitive abilities [17]. Therefore, alternative assessment approaches, such as the preferential listening paradigm, have been developed to evaluate the listening skills and language development of infants with cochlear implants [18]. This paradigm involves presenting the infant with speech sounds and objects, and measuring their ability to learn associations between the two [19]. By using this approach, researchers can gain insights into the early stages of language development in infants with cochlear implants, and track their progress over time. Study Context and Significance The present study aims to contribute to the existing literature on cochlear implantation in infants below 12 months of age, by providing safety and efficacy data on this population [20]. The use of a minimally invasive surgical technique, combined with a limited clinical trial design, enables the researchers to evaluate the outcomes of cochlear implantation in this age group, while minimizing the risks associated with the surgery [21]. The findings of this study have significant implications for clinical practice, as they may inform the development of treatment protocols and guidelines for cochlear implantation in infants below 12 months of age [22]. Furthermore, the study's results may contribute to a greater understanding of the relationship between age at implantation and language outcomes, ultimately informing the development of more effective interventions for infants with significant hearing loss [23]. Introduction to Methods The widespread implementation of newborn hearing screening programs has led to the early identification of infants with significant hearing loss [1]. For those who do not benefit from traditional hearing aids, cochlear implantation has become a viable option to restore auditory perception and facilitate language development [2]. The critical period for language acquisition is believed to be within the first few years of life, with evidence suggesting that earlier intervention yields better outcomes [3]. Therefore, it is essential to investigate the safety and efficacy of cochlear implantation in infants below 12 months of age. Participant Selection Infants were selected for this study based on severe to profound sensorineural hearing loss, confirmed through auditory brainstem response (ABR) testing and otoacoustic emissions (OAE) screening [4]. All infants had limited to no benefit from a trial of traditional hearing aids, as determined by audiological assessment and parental report [5]. Informed consent was obtained from parents or guardians, and the study was approved by the institutional review board. Pre-Implantation Assessment Prior to implantation, infants underwent a comprehensive evaluation to confirm their hearing loss and assess their candidacy for cochlear implantation. This included ABR testing, OAE screening, and tympanometry to rule out any middle ear disorders [6]. Additionally, infants were assessed using the preferential listening paradigm to evaluate their ability to learn associations between speech sounds and objects [7]. This paradigm involves presenting infants with paired auditory and visual stimuli, and measuring their looking times to determine if they can differentiate between sounds [8]. Surgical Procedure Cochlear implantation was performed using a minimally invasive surgical technique, which has been employed by our institution for nearly two decades [9]. This approach involves a small incision and minimal tissue disruption, reducing the risk of complications and promoting faster recovery [10]. The surgical procedure was performed under general anesthesia, with careful monitoring of the infant's vital signs and anesthesia depth [11]. Post-Implantation Rehabilitation Following implantation, infants underwent a period of auditory rehabilitation to facilitate language development [12]. This included regular audiological assessments, speech therapy, and parental guidance on how to promote auditory and language skills [13]. Infants were also fitted with a cochlear implant processor and trained to use it effectively [14]. Outcome Measures Language development was assessed using a range of outcome measures, including the Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test (PPVT) [15] and other standardized language assessments [16]. The PPVT is a widely used measure of receptive vocabulary, which involves presenting infants with pictures and asking them to identify the corresponding word [17]. Other measures included the Reynell Developmental Language Scales [18] and the MacArthur-Bates Communicative Development Inventories [19]. These assessments were administered at regular intervals, allowing for the tracking of language development over time. Data Analysis Data analysis involved comparing the language outcomes of infants who received cochlear implants below 12 months of age to those of normal-hearing infants [20]. Statistical analysis was performed using repeated-measures ANOVA and paired t-tests to determine if there were significant differences in language development between the two groups [21]. Additionally, regression analysis was used to examine the relationship between age at implantation and language outcomes [22]. Study Limitations While this study provides valuable insights into the safety and efficacy of cochlear implantation in infants below 12 months of age, there are several limitations that must be acknowledged [23]. The sample size was relatively small, and the study was limited to a single institution [24]. Furthermore, the study relied on parental report and audiological assessment, which may be subject to bias [25]. Future studies should aim to address these limitations by recruiting larger samples and using more objective outcome measures [26]. Surgical Outcomes The surgical procedure for cochlear implantation in infants below 12 months of age was well-tolerated, with no instances of surgical or anesthetic complications reported in our study [1]. This is consistent with previous research, which has demonstrated that minimally invasive surgical techniques can be safely employed in young children [2]. The lack of complications in this age group is particularly notable, given the potential risks associated with anesthesia and surgery in infants [3]. Our findings suggest that, with appropriate surgical planning and execution, cochlear implantation can be safely performed in infants as young as a few months old. Assessment of Listening Skills Pre-implantation assessment of listening skills was conducted using the preferential listening paradigm, which has been widely used to evaluate auditory development in infants [4]. This paradigm involves presenting the infant with two different speech sounds, and measuring their ability to associate each sound with a specific object. Our results showed that all infants in the study were able to learn these associations, demonstrating that they had some residual hearing and were capable of auditory learning [5]. This is consistent with previous research, which has shown that infants as young as a few months old are able to distinguish between different speech sounds [6]. Post-Implantation Language Development Post-implantation language development was assessed using a range of measures, including the Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test (PPVT) [7]. The PPVT is a widely used standardized test of receptive vocabulary, which has been shown to be a reliable measure of language development in children [8]. Our results showed that many of the infants in the study achieved age-appropriate language skills, with mean PPVT scores falling within the normal range [9]. This is consistent with previous research, which has demonstrated that early cochlear implantation is associated with better language outcomes in children [10]. Long-Term Follow-Up Long-term follow-up data were available for all infants in the study, with a mean follow-up period of 5 years [11]. These data showed that the infants continued to make progress in their language development, with many achieving language skills that were comparable to those of their normal-hearing peers [12]. This is consistent with previous research, which has shown that children who receive cochlear implants at a young age are able to catch up with their normal-hearing peers in terms of language development [13]. Our findings suggest that early cochlear implantation can have a lasting impact on language development, and that infants who receive implants at a young age are able to achieve age-appropriate language skills. Comparison with Normal-Hearing Infants Comparison of the language development of the infants in our study with that of normal-hearing infants showed that the two groups followed similar trajectories [14]. Both groups showed rapid improvements in language skills over the first few years of life, with the rate of progress slowing down as they approached school age [15]. This is consistent with previous research, which has shown that language development follows a similar pattern in both normal-hearing and cochlear-implanted children [16]. Our findings suggest that early cochlear implantation can enable infants to develop language skills that are similar to those of their normal-hearing peers. These included the age at implantation, the duration of implant use, and the level of parental involvement in rehabilitation [18]. Testosterone deficiency (TD) is a common endocrine disorder affecting millions of men worldwide, characterized by low levels of testosterone, leading to a range of symptoms including decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, fatigue, and decreased muscle mass and bone density [1]. Testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) has been widely used to treat TD, aiming to restore normal testosterone levels and alleviate symptoms [2]. While TRT has been shown to be effective in improving symptoms and quality of life in men with TD, the optimal duration of treatment and the factors influencing the maintenance of response after treatment cessation remain unclear [3]. The decision to initiate TRT is typically based on the presence of clinical symptoms and low testosterone levels, with treatment individualized to each patient's needs [4]. However, there is limited evidence to guide clinicians on the optimal treatment duration, and the decision to discontinue TRT is often based on patient preference, cost, and potential side effects [5]. Some studies have suggested that long-term TRT may be necessary to maintain symptom improvement, while others have reported that some patients may experience sustained benefits even after treatment cessation [6]. This variability in response to TRT cessation highlights the need to identify predictive factors that can help clinicians determine which patients are more likely to maintain response after stopping treatment. Several studies have investigated the effects of TRT on various health outcomes, including cardiovascular risk, bone density, and cognitive function [7]. However, few studies have specifically examined the factors influencing response maintenance after TRT cessation. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis found that the majority of studies on TRT focused on the efficacy and safety of treatment, with limited data on the long-term effects of treatment discontinuation [8]. Furthermore, the existing literature on TRT cessation is often limited by small sample sizes, variable treatment durations, and inconsistent outcome measures, making it challenging to draw firm conclusions [9]. The potential benefits of identifying predictive factors of response maintenance after TRT cessation are significant. Firstly, it could help clinicians tailor treatment decisions to individual patient needs, minimizing unnecessary treatment and reducing healthcare costs [10]. Secondly, it could enable patients to make informed decisions about their treatment, balancing the benefits and risks of continued TRT against the potential for sustained symptom improvement after treatment cessation [11]. Finally, it could provide valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms of TD and the effects of TRT, ultimately contributing to the development of more effective and personalized treatment strategies [12]. Regular exercise has been proposed as a potential factor influencing response maintenance after TRT cessation, with some studies suggesting that physical activity may help maintain testosterone levels and improve symptoms in men with TD [13]. The mechanisms underlying this potential relationship are not fully understood but may involve the effects of exercise on testosterone production, insulin sensitivity, and body composition [14]. Additionally, longer treatment durations have been suggested to improve response durability after TRT cessation, potentially due to the prolonged exposure to exogenous testosterone and the resulting changes in the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis [15]. To address the knowledge gap in this area, we conducted a prospective study to investigate the predictive factors of response maintenance after TRT cessation in men with TD. Our study aimed to identify the clinical, biochemical, and lifestyle factors associated with sustained symptom improvement after treatment discontinuation, with a particular focus on the role of exercise and treatment duration. By elucidating the factors influencing response maintenance, our study seeks to provide valuable insights into the optimal management of TD and the development of personalized treatment strategies for men with this common endocrine disorder. The relationship between testosterone levels and response maintenance is complex, and several factors can influence the durability of response after TRT cessation. Peak total testosterone (TT) levels during treatment have been suggested to play a role in determining response maintenance, with higher levels potentially associated with a greater likelihood of sustained symptom improvement [16]. However, the evidence is limited, and further research is needed to fully understand the relationship between testosterone levels and response maintenance. In addition to testosterone levels, other factors such as age, body mass index (BMI), and comorbidities may also influence response maintenance after TRT cessation. Older age and higher BMI have been associated with a lower likelihood of response maintenance, potentially due to the effects of these factors on testosterone production and metabolism [17]. Comorbidities such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease may also impact response maintenance, although the evidence is limited and further research is needed to fully understand the relationships between these factors and response maintenance. The clinical implications of our study are significant, and the findings have the potential to inform treatment decisions and improve patient outcomes. By identifying the predictive factors of response maintenance after TRT cessation, clinicians can tailor treatment to individual patient needs, minimizing unnecessary treatment and reducing healthcare costs. Additionally, the findings of our study can help patients make informed decisions about their treatment, balancing the benefits and risks of continued TRT against the potential for sustained symptom improvement after treatment cessation. In conclusion, the predictive factors of response maintenance after TRT cessation in men with TD are complex and multifactorial. Further research is needed to fully understand the relationships between these factors and response maintenance, and to develop personalized treatment strategies for men with this common endocrine disorder. Our study aims to contribute to the existing literature on TRT cessation, providing valuable insights into the factors influencing response maintenance and informing treatment decisions to improve patient outcomes. The study's findings have the potential to impact clinical practice, and the results can be used to develop guidelines for the management of TD. The identification of predictive factors of response maintenance can help clinicians determine which patients are more likely to experience sustained symptom improvement after TRT cessation, allowing for more informed treatment decisions. Participant Selection Men with TD who had been receiving TRT for at least 3 months and had shown significant improvement in their symptoms were eligible for this study [2]. Patients with a history of prostate cancer, breast cancer, or other malignancies, as well as those with severe liver or kidney disease, were excluded from the study [4]. A total of 151 men met the inclusion criteria and were enrolled in the study. Study Design This was a prospective, observational study with a follow-up period of 6 months after TRT cessation. Participants were instructed to stop TRT and were followed up at 1, 3, and 6 months after discontinuation. At each follow-up visit, participants underwent a physical examination, and their TT levels were measured. Testosterone Replacement Therapy Participants had been receiving various forms of TRT, including oral testosterone undecanoate, transdermal testosterone gel, and short- or long-acting testosterone injectables [6]. The type and dosage of TRT were determined by the participants' primary care physicians and were not standardized for this study. However, all participants had been receiving a stable dose of TRT for at least 3 months before enrollment. Outcome Measures The primary outcome measure was the maintenance of response to TRT, defined as the absence of significant TD symptoms and a TT level ≥300 ng/dL at 6 months after TRT cessation [7]. Secondary outcome measures included changes in TT levels, symptom severity, and quality of life over the 6-month follow-up period. Data Collection Participants' demographic and clinical characteristics, including age, body mass index (BMI), medical history, and lifestyle factors (e.g., exercise habits, smoking status), were collected at baseline [8]. Statistical Analysis Descriptive statistics were used to summarize participants' demographic and clinical characteristics. Comparisons between groups (i.e., those who maintained response vs. those who did not) were made using Student's t-test or the chi-squared test, as appropriate [12]. Multivariate logistic regression analysis was performed to identify independent predictive factors of response maintenance [13]. The regression model included variables that were significantly associated with response maintenance in univariate analysis, including TRT duration, peak TT level, and exercise habits. The results of the regression analysis are presented as odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The association between exercise habits and response maintenance was examined using logistic regression analysis, adjusting for potential confounding variables, including age, BMI, and medical history. Quality Control To ensure the quality of the data, all questionnaires and laboratory tests were reviewed by a trained research coordinator, and any discrepancies or missing data were addressed promptly [16]. The study protocol was monitored by an independent data safety monitoring board, which reviewed the data regularly to ensure participant safety and study integrity [17]. Shift work, which involves working outside the traditional daytime hours, is a common phenomenon in modern society. It is estimated that approximately 20% of the working population in developed countries is engaged in some form of shift work, including night shifts, evening shifts, and rotating shifts. While some individuals adapt well to shift work, others experience significant disturbances in their sleep-wake cycle, leading to fatigue, decreased productivity, and increased risk of various health problems, including cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and certain types of cancer. One of the key consequences of shift work is job-related exhaustion, a state of emotional, mental, and physical exhaustion caused by prolonged stress and overwork. Job-related exhaustion is a major concern for employers and employees alike, as it can lead to decreased job satisfaction, increased absenteeism, and reduced overall well-being. The tolerance to shift work varies greatly between individuals, and only some shift workers suffer from disturbed sleep, fatigue, and job-related exhaustion. While factors such as age, lifestyle, and work environment play a role in determining an individual's tolerance to shift work, there is growing evidence to suggest that genetic factors also contribute to the development of shift work intolerance. The genetic basis of shift work tolerance is complex and involves multiple genetic variants that interact with environmental factors to influence an individual's ability to adapt to non-traditional work schedules. Recent studies have identified several genetic variants associated with sleep disorders, circadian rhythm, and response to shift work, highlighting the importance of genetic factors in determining an individual's tolerance to shift work. One of the key regulators of the circadian rhythm is the melatonin system, which plays a crucial role in regulating the sleep-wake cycle. Melatonin is a hormone produced by the pineal gland in response to darkness and is involved in regulating various physiological processes, including sleep, metabolism, and reproductive functions. The melatonin system is regulated by a complex interplay of genetic and environmental factors, and disruptions in this system have been linked to various sleep disorders, including insomnia, sleep apnea, and restless leg syndrome. The melatonin receptor 1A (MTNR1A) gene is a key component of the melatonin system, and variants in this gene have been associated with sleep disorders and circadian rhythm regulation. The MTNR1A gene encodes a G-protein coupled receptor that mediates the effects of melatonin on target cells. The receptor is widely expressed in the brain and other tissues and plays a crucial role in regulating the sleep-wake cycle, as well as other physiological processes. Variants in the MTNR1A gene have been associated with various sleep disorders, including delayed sleep phase syndrome and insomnia, and have also been linked to other conditions, such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. The genetic variation near the MTNR1A gene has also been implicated in the regulation of circadian rhythm and response to shift work, suggesting that this gene may play a key role in determining an individual's tolerance to shift work. Despite the growing evidence linking genetic factors to shift work tolerance, the molecular genetic mechanisms underlying shift work intolerance are not well understood. Previous studies have identified several genetic variants associated with shift work tolerance, but these studies have been limited by small sample sizes and lack of replication. Furthermore, the functional mechanisms by which these genetic variants influence shift work tolerance are not well understood, and further research is needed to elucidate the relationship between genetic variation, melatonin signaling, and shift work tolerance. We used a comprehensive approach, combining GWAS with replication studies, methylation analysis, and gene expression analysis to identify genetic variants associated with shift work intolerance. The human skin microbiome is a complex and dynamic ecosystem, comprising a diverse array of microorganisms that play a crucial role in maintaining skin health and preventing disease [1]. The past decade has seen a significant increase in research focused on characterizing the diversity of taxa present in the skin microbiome, with studies utilizing high-throughput sequencing technologies to catalog the vast array of bacterial, viral, and fungal species that inhabit this environment [2, 3]. While these efforts have greatly advanced our understanding of the skin microbiome, they have also highlighted the need for a more nuanced approach to understanding the functional properties of these microorganisms. One of the primary challenges in studying the skin microbiome is the sheer diversity of taxa present, with estimates suggesting that a single individual can harbor over 1,000 different species of bacteria on their skin [4]. This diversity presents a significant obstacle to traditional methods of functional analysis, which often rely on the use of reference databases to infer the presence of specific metabolic pathways or functional genes [5]. While these approaches have been highly successful in identifying the presence of specific functions, they are limited by the completeness and accuracy of the reference databases used [6]. Furthermore, the detection of a particular pathway or gene does not necessarily guarantee that the associated function is expressed, as this can be influenced by a range of factors including environmental conditions and regulatory mechanisms [7]. In recent years, there has been a growing recognition of the need for a more trait-based approach to understanding the skin microbiome, one that focuses on the functional properties of microorganisms rather than simply their taxonomic identity [8]. This approach has the potential to provide a more nuanced understanding of the skin microbiome, allowing researchers to identify the specific traits that are associated with success in this environment. One way to achieve this is through the use of trait databases, which compile information on the functional properties of microorganisms from a range of sources, including laboratory experiments and observational studies [9]. These databases can provide a wealth of information on the traits of different microorganisms, including their metabolic capabilities, growth characteristics, and environmental tolerances. The development of trait databases for the skin microbiome is a complex task, requiring the compilation of information from a wide range of sources. One of the most comprehensive sources of information on microbial traits is Bergey's Manual of Systematic Bacteriology, which provides detailed information on the characteristics of over 1,000 different species of bacteria [10]. This manual has been widely used as a reference source for microbial taxonomy and systematics, but it also provides a wealth of information on the functional properties of microorganisms. In addition to Bergey's Manual, there are a range of other sources of information on microbial traits, including journal articles and online databases [11]. These sources can provide information on a wide range of traits, including enzyme activity, substrate use, temperature and pH range, and NaCl tolerance. The use of trait databases to analyze the skin microbiome has a number of advantages over traditional methods of functional analysis. Firstly, it allows researchers to focus on the functional properties of microorganisms, rather than simply their taxonomic identity [12]. This can provide a more nuanced understanding of the skin microbiome, highlighting the specific traits that are associated with success in this environment. Secondly, it allows researchers to identify patterns and trends in the distribution of traits across different taxa, which can provide insights into the evolutionary pressures that have shaped the skin microbiome [13]. Finally, it provides a framework for predicting how the skin microbiome may respond to different environmental perturbations, such as changes in temperature or humidity [14]. In this study, we use a trait-based approach to analyze the human skin microbiome, focusing on a database of 971 bacterial taxa that are commonly found on the skin. We use this database to examine the distribution of a range of functional traits, including binary, categorical, and quantitative traits. We compare the distribution of these traits among skin taxa to that of microbial taxa more broadly, using a range of statistical tests to identify traits that are over- or under-represented in the skin microbiome. Our analysis highlights a number of traits that are associated with success in the skin environment, including the ability to grow at warm temperatures, tolerate high levels of NaCl, and exhibit facultative metabolism. We also identify a number of traits that are under-represented in the skin microbiome, including the ability to form spores, produce pigments, and exhibit gliding motility. These findings provide new insights into the structuring principles of the skin microbiome, and highlight the importance of considering functional traits when analyzing microbial communities. To develop a comprehensive trait-based database for human skin bacterial taxa, we conducted an extensive literature review of journal articles and consulted Bergey's Manual of Systematic Bacteriology [1]. Our database comprises 971 human skin bacterial taxa, each associated with a range of functional traits. These traits were categorized into three classes: binary, categorical, and quantitative. Binary traits are those that can be either present or absent, such as the ability to produce spores or catalase [2]. Background and Significance Botulism is a rare but serious disease that can be caused by the ingestion of contaminated food, inhalation of aerosolized toxin, or through wound infection [4]. Current Detection Methods The mouse bioassay is currently the most widely used method for detecting BoNTs, which involves injecting mice with a sample suspected of containing the toxin and observing for signs of botulism [8]. The pathogenesis of cancer cachexia is complex and involves a combination of pro-inflammatory cytokines, hormones, and other factors that contribute to the degradation of muscle tissue. The muscle microenvironment is composed of various cell types, including muscle fibers, satellite cells, and immune cells, which interact to regulate muscle growth, repair, and maintenance. Satellite cells, also known as muscle precursor cells, play a crucial role in muscle regeneration and repair. These cells are normally quiescent but can be activated in response to muscle injury or disease, proliferating and differentiating to form new muscle fibers. However, in cancer cachexia, the function of satellite cells is impaired, leading to a decline in muscle regenerative capacity and contributing to muscle wasting. The transcription factor Pax7 is a key regulator of satellite cell function, and its expression is tightly controlled to ensure proper muscle regeneration. Pax7 is required for the activation and proliferation of satellite cells, but its overexpression can lead to a block in differentiation, resulting in impaired muscle regeneration. Recent studies have shown that Pax7 is overexpressed in the muscles of cachectic mice, and this overexpression is associated with impaired muscle regeneration. The mechanism underlying Pax7 overexpression in cancer cachexia is not fully understood but is thought to involve the activation of pro-inflammatory signaling pathways, including the NF-kB pathway. NF-kB is a transcription factor that plays a critical role in the regulation of inflammation and immune responses, and its activation has been implicated in the pathogenesis of cancer cachexia. We have recently shown that NF-kB-induced Pax7 overexpression impairs the myogenic potential of muscle precursors in cachectic mice, suggesting that lowering Pax7 expression may be beneficial in cancer cachexia. Exercise has also been shown to exert positive effects on cachectic muscles, improving muscle mass and strength, and enhancing muscle regenerative capacity. Exercise has been shown to reduce systemic inflammation, improve insulin sensitivity, and enhance the expression of muscle growth factors, all of which may contribute to its beneficial effects on muscle tissue. Our findings will provide new insights into the role of physical activity in modulating the muscle microenvironment in cancer cachexia, and highlight the potential of exercise as a therapeutic strategy to counteract muscle wasting in this context. The study was conducted on 8-week-old male BALB/c mice, which were randomly assigned to one of four groups: healthy control mice (n = 20), C26 colon carcinoma tumor-bearing mice (n = 20), healthy control mice with access to a running wheel (n = 20), and C26 colon carcinoma tumor-bearing mice with access to a running wheel (n = 20). Mice were housed in a controlled environment with a 12-hour light-dark cycle and had ad libitum access to food and water. The C26 colon carcinoma cell line was obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) and was maintained in vitro according to the supplier's instructions. Tumor cells (1 x 10^6) were injected subcutaneously into the right flank of mice to induce cancer cachexia. Mice were monitored daily for signs of illness, and their body weight and food intake were measured weekly. Tumor growth was measured using a caliper, and tumor volume was calculated using the formula: volume = (length x width^2) / 2. Mice were sacrificed when the tumor reached a volume of approximately 1.5 cm^3 or when they showed signs of distress. To evaluate the muscle regenerative potential after acute injury, we performed a cardiotoxin-induced muscle injury model. Mice were anesthetized with isoflurane, and 50 μL of cardiotoxin (10 μM) was injected into the tibialis anterior muscle. Mice were then sacrificed at 3, 7, and 14 days after injury, and the tibialis anterior muscle was harvested for further analysis. For the exercise protocol, mice were housed in cages equipped with a running wheel (diameter: 11.5 cm, width: 5 cm) for 4 weeks. The running wheel was connected to a computer, which recorded the distance and speed of each mouse. Mice were allowed to run voluntarily, and their activity was monitored daily. The exercise protocol was designed to mimic moderate physical activity, and mice were encouraged to run by placing the food and water at a distance from the running wheel. Muscle samples were harvested and immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen for further analysis. Total RNA was extracted using the TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen), and cDNA was synthesized using the SuperScript III First-Strand Synthesis System (Invitrogen). Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) was performed using the ABI Prism 7000 sequence detection system (Applied Biosystems) to analyze the expression of Pax7, MyoD, and myogenin. The primers used were: Pax7 (forward: 5'-GGGATGATGAGACCGAGTG-3', reverse: 5'-TGCTGGGATAGTGCTGGTG-3'), MyoD (forward: 5'-CTGACGGCGACTCAGATGC-3', reverse: 5'-GGTGCTGGTGGGTGAGGAG-3'), and myogenin (forward: 5'-CTGGAGCGCGGCTATGTC-3', reverse: 5'-GGTGGGTGCAGATGGTGAG-3'). The expression of each gene was normalized to the expression of glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH). Western blot analysis was performed to evaluate the protein expression of Pax7, MyoD, and myogenin. Muscle samples were homogenized in RIPA buffer, and proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE. The membranes were incubated with primary antibodies against Pax7 (1:1000, Abcam), MyoD (1:1000, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), and myogenin (1:1000, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), followed by incubation with secondary antibodies (1:5000, Santa Cruz Biotechnology). The bands were visualized using the ECL detection system (Amersham Biosciences), and the intensity of each band was quantified using the ImageJ software. Muscle histology was performed to evaluate the muscle fiber size and morphology. Muscle samples were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned at 5 μm. Sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and analyzed using a light microscope. The muscle fiber size was measured using the ImageJ software, and the results were expressed as the average fiber size per muscle section. Statistical analysis was performed using the GraphPad Prism software. Data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Differences between groups were evaluated using the two-way ANOVA test, followed by the Bonferroni post-hoc test. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. To investigate the effects of physical activity on Pax7 expression in cancer cachexia, we first examined the muscle regenerative potential after acute injury in C26 colon carcinoma tumor-bearing mice and healthy controls. Mice were subjected to a cardiotoxin-induced muscle injury, and muscle regeneration was assessed at different time points. Our results showed that muscle regeneration was significantly delayed in tumor-bearing mice compared to healthy controls. At 7 days post-injury, muscles from healthy controls had already started to regenerate, as evidenced by the presence of newly formed muscle fibers and a significant increase in muscle weight (Figure 1A). In contrast, muscles from tumor-bearing mice exhibited a marked delay in regeneration, with a significant reduction in muscle weight and a decreased number of newly formed muscle fibers (Figure 1A). We next investigated the molecular mechanisms underlying the delayed muscle regeneration observed in tumor-bearing mice. Our analyses revealed that the delayed regeneration was associated with a persistent local inflammation, as evidenced by increased levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6 in the muscle tissue (Figure 1B). Additionally, we found that the expression of Pax7, a transcription factor that plays a critical role in muscle stem cell function, was significantly upregulated in muscles from tumor-bearing mice (Figure 1C). The overexpression of Pax7 was accompanied by a decrease in the expression of myogenic differentiation markers such as MyoD and myogenin (Figure 1D), suggesting that the impaired muscle regeneration observed in tumor-bearing mice was due to a defect in the myogenic potential of muscle precursors. To verify if physical activity affects Pax7 expression, we hosted control and C26-bearing mice in wheel-equipped cages, allowing them to perform voluntary wheel running. Mice were allowed to run voluntarily for 4 weeks, and Pax7 expression was assessed in muscles at the end of the exercise period. Our results showed that voluntary wheel running downregulated Pax7 expression in muscles from tumor-bearing mice (Figure 2A). The downregulation of Pax7 expression was associated with a rescue of muscle mass and fiber size, as evidenced by an increase in muscle weight and a significant increase in the cross-sectional area of muscle fibers (Figure 2B). In contrast, Pax7 expression remained unchanged in muscles from healthy control mice that performed voluntary wheel running (Figure 2A), suggesting that the exercise-induced downregulation of Pax7 is specific to the cachectic muscle environment. We also examined the effects of voluntary wheel running on muscle inflammation and myogenic differentiation. Our results showed that exercise significantly reduced the levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6 in the muscle tissue of tumor-bearing mice (Figure 3A). Additionally, we found that exercise increased the expression of myogenic differentiation markers such as MyoD and myogenin in muscles from tumor-bearing mice (Figure 3B), suggesting that the exercise-induced downregulation of Pax7 is accompanied by an improvement in the myogenic potential of muscle precursors. To further investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying the exercise-induced downregulation of Pax7, we examined the expression of NF-κB, a transcription factor that regulates Pax7 expression. Our results showed that voluntary wheel running decreased NF-κB activity in muscles from tumor-bearing mice (Figure 4A), suggesting that the exercise-induced downregulation of Pax7 is mediated by a decrease in NF-κB activity. We also found that exercise increased the expression of anti-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-10 in the muscle tissue of tumor-bearing mice (Figure 4B), suggesting that the exercise-induced downregulation of Pax7 is accompanied by an anti-inflammatory response. Overall, our results demonstrate that voluntary physical activity downregulates Pax7 expression in muscles from tumor-bearing mice, leading to an improvement in muscle regeneration and a rescue of muscle mass and fiber size.
