The global population is undergoing a significant demographic shift, with increased life expectancy and a growing proportion of elderly individuals [1]. This phenomenon has led to a rise in the prevalence of chronic diseases (CDs), which can have a profound impact on the overall health and well-being of older adults [2]. CDs, such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer, can affect various aspects of an individual's life, including their physical and mental health, social relationships, and quality of life [3]. One aspect of health that is often overlooked in older adults is sexuality, which is a fundamental aspect of human experience and an essential component of overall health and well-being [4]. Sexuality in older adults is a complex and multifaceted concept that encompasses not only physical intimacy but also emotional connection, intimacy, and sexual desire [5]. However, the sexual health needs of older adults are often neglected, and their sexuality is frequently stigmatized or marginalized [6]. This neglect can be attributed to various factors, including societal attitudes towards aging and sexuality, lack of awareness and education among healthcare providers, and the prioritization of other health concerns [7]. As a result, older adults with CDs may experience a range of sexual health problems, including decreased sexual desire, erectile dysfunction, and vaginal dryness, which can further exacerbate their overall health and well-being [8]. The impact of CDs on sexual function in older adults is a critical area of research, as it can have significant implications for their quality of life and overall health outcomes [9]. CDs can affect sexual function through various mechanisms, including physical symptoms, psychological distress, and social isolation [10]. For example, diabetes can cause nerve damage and vascular problems, leading to erectile dysfunction and decreased sexual desire [11]. Similarly, cardiovascular disease can lead to decreased physical stamina and increased fatigue, making it difficult to engage in sexual activity [12]. Additionally, CDs can also affect an individual's body image and self-esteem, leading to decreased confidence and intimacy [13]. The biological and psychological impact of CDs on sexual function in older adults can be understood through the conceptual model of Verschuren et al. (2010) [14]. This model highlights the complex interplay between physical, psychological, and social factors that influence sexual function in individuals with CDs. According to this model, CDs can affect sexual function through various pathways, including physical symptoms, psychological distress, and social isolation [15]. The model also emphasizes the importance of considering the individual's overall health and well-being, including their physical and mental health, social relationships, and quality of life, when assessing the impact of CDs on sexual function [16]. The existing literature on the impact of CDs on sexual function in older adults is limited, and more research is needed to fully understand the complex relationships between CDs, sexuality, and aging [17]. However, the available evidence suggests that CDs can have a significant impact on sexual function in older adults, leading to decreased sexual desire, intimacy, and overall quality of life [18]. For example, a study conducted by Lindau et al. (2007) found that older adults with CDs reported lower levels of sexual activity and intimacy compared to those without CDs [19]. Another study by Fisher et al. (2010) found that CDs can affect an individual's body image and self-esteem, leading to decreased confidence and intimacy [20]. Cultural and social factors also play a significant role in shaping the sexual health experiences of older adults with CDs [21]. Societal attitudes towards aging and sexuality can influence an individual's perceptions of their own sexuality and their willingness to discuss sexual health concerns with healthcare providers [22]. The concept of modal type theory was first introduced by Fitch [3], who proposed a system of modal logic that could be used to reason about propositions that are not necessarily true, but may become true in the future. Prostate cancer is one of the most common malignancies affecting men worldwide, with a significant impact on public health. The development and progression of prostate cancer involve a complex interplay of genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors. Despite advances in early detection and treatment, prostate cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related deaths in men. Therefore, identifying novel biomarkers and understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying the development and progression of prostate cancer are crucial for improving diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis. The RhoA and ROCK1 genes play a critical role in the regulation of cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, which are key processes involved in cancer development and progression. The RhoA/ROCK1 pathway is a signaling cascade that regulates the actin cytoskeleton, cell adhesion, and motility. Activation of the RhoA/ROCK1 pathway has been implicated in the development and progression of various types of cancer, including prostate cancer. RhoA is a small GTPase that activates ROCK1, a serine/threonine kinase, which in turn regulates downstream effectors involved in cell migration, invasion, and proliferation. Aberrant activation of the RhoA/ROCK1 pathway has been shown to contribute to cancer cell metastasis, angiogenesis, and resistance to apoptosis. Genetic variants in the RhoA and ROCK1 genes may affect the function and activity of the RhoA/ROCK1 pathway, potentially influencing an individual's susceptibility to prostate cancer. Genetic variants, such as single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), can alter gene expression, protein function, and signaling pathway activity. These genetic variations can be used as biomarkers to predict disease risk, progression, and response to treatment. Several studies have investigated the association between genetic variants in other genes and prostate cancer risk, but the role of RhoA and ROCK1 genetic variants in prostate cancer has not been well studied. Prostate cancer is a heterogeneous disease, and the clinical outcome can vary significantly among patients. Biochemical recurrence, defined as a rise in prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels after radical prostatectomy or radiation therapy, is a common indicator of disease recurrence. Clinico-pathological characteristics, such as tumor stage, grade, and PSA levels, are traditionally used to predict disease recurrence and prognosis. However, these factors have limitations, and there is a need for novel biomarkers to improve prognostication and treatment decision-making. The identification of genetic variants associated with prostate cancer risk and progression can provide valuable insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying the disease. These genetic variants can be used to develop novel biomarkers for early detection, prognosis, and treatment monitoring. Furthermore, understanding the genetic basis of prostate cancer can help identify potential therapeutic targets and develop personalized treatment strategies. In this study, we investigated the association between genetic variants in the RhoA and ROCK1 genes and the development, progression, and prognosis of prostate cancer. We aimed to clarify the role of these genetic variants in prostate cancer and explore their potential as novel biomarkers for clinical treatment decision-making. The RhoA and ROCK1 genes are attractive candidates for investigation, given their critical role in regulating cell proliferation, migration, and invasion. Previous studies have shown that aberrant activation of the RhoA/ROCK1 pathway contributes to cancer development and progression. However, the specific genetic variants in the RhoA and ROCK1 genes that contribute to prostate cancer risk and progression are not well understood. In this study, we genotyped six potentially functional genetic variants in the RhoA and ROCK1 genes and investigated their association with prostate cancer risk, progression, and prognosis. Our study provides new insights into the role of genetic variants in the RhoA and ROCK1 genes in prostate cancer and highlights the potential of these variants as novel biomarkers for clinical treatment decision-making. This case-control study was conducted to investigate the association between genetic variants in the RhoA and ROCK1 genes and the development, progression, and prognosis of prostate cancer. The study population consisted of 1699 subjects, including 849 prostate cancer patients and 850 healthy controls. The patients were recruited from the urology department of a tertiary care hospital, while the controls were selected from a pool of healthy individuals who underwent routine health check-ups at the same hospital. The inclusion criteria for the patients included a confirmed diagnosis of prostate cancer, while the controls were required to have no history of cancer. The study was approved by the institutional review board, and all participants provided written informed consent. The patients' clinical and pathological data, including age, prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, Gleason score, tumor stage, and nodal status, were collected from their medical records. The biochemical recurrence (BCR) status was also determined, which was defined as two consecutive PSA measurements of 0.2 ng/mL or higher after radical prostatectomy. The follow-up period for the patients ranged from 12 to 60 months, with a median follow-up time of 36 months. Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood samples using a commercial DNA extraction kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). The DNA samples were then genotyped for six potentially functional genetic variants in the RhoA and ROCK1 genes, which were selected based on their potential functional significance and minor allele frequencies. The variants included rs2410, rs2269736, rs3599, rs3902981, rs6849, and rs10848464. The genotyping was performed using a TaqMan genotyping assay (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA) on an ABI 7900HT real-time PCR system. The genotype and allele frequencies were calculated and compared between the cases and controls using the chi-squared test and Fisher's exact test. The odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated to determine the association between the genetic variants and the risk of prostate cancer. The genotype-phenotype correlation analysis was performed to examine the association between the genetic variants and clinico-pathological characteristics, including PSA levels, Gleason score, tumor stage, and nodal status. To evaluate the prognostic significance of the genetic variants, the Kaplan-Meier method was used to estimate the BCR-free survival rates, and the log-rank test was used to compare the survival curves between the different genotype groups. The Cox proportional hazards regression model was used to assess the independent prognostic value of the genetic variants, with adjustment for clinico-pathological characteristics. The Bonferroni correction was applied to account for multiple testing, and a P-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The patients were categorized into three groups based on the number of risk alleles they carried: 0-1 risk allele, 2 risk alleles, and more than 2 risk alleles. The association between the number of risk alleles and the risk of prostate cancer was evaluated using the chi-squared test and Fisher's exact test. The ORs and 95% CIs were calculated to determine the association between the number of risk alleles and the risk of prostate cancer. To validate the findings, we performed a series of sensitivity analyses, including the exclusion of patients with missing data and the use of different statistical models. We also examined the potential interactions between the genetic variants and clinico-pathological characteristics, including PSA levels, Gleason score, tumor stage, and nodal status. The results of these analyses were consistent with the primary findings, suggesting that the associations between the genetic variants and the risk of prostate cancer were robust and not influenced by potential confounding factors. In conclusion, this study provides a comprehensive analysis of the association between genetic variants in the RhoA and ROCK1 genes and the development, progression, and prognosis of prostate cancer. The findings suggest that the rs2410 mutant allele and the rs2269736 wild allele are risk factors for prostate cancer, and that individuals carrying more than two risk alleles are exposed to a higher hazard of prostate cancer. The study also demonstrates that the risk of biochemical recurrence may be linked to clinico-pathological characteristics and genetic factors, although the associations between the genetic variants and clinico-pathological characteristics were not significant. The results of this study have important implications for the clinical management of prostate cancer and highlight the potential of genetic variants in the RhoA and ROCK1 genes as novel biomarkers for prostate cancer diagnosis and prognosis. Cronobacter species are a group of gram-negative, rod-shaped bacteria that have been recognized as important food-borne opportunistic pathogens [1]. These bacteria have been implicated in the cause of severe infections, including necrotizing enterocolitis, sepsis, and meningitis, primarily in neonates and infants [2]. The most notorious species within this genus is Cronobacter sakazakii, which has been associated with outbreaks of neonatal meningitis and has a high mortality rate [3]. However, Cronobacter species are not exclusively pathogenic, and they can be found in a wide range of environments, including foodstuffs, clinical specimens, and environmental samples [4]. The genus Cronobacter was first proposed in 2007, and it currently comprises seven species: C. sakazakii, C. dublinensis, C. malonaticus, C. turicensis, C. universalis, C. condimenti, and C. helveticus [5]. These species can be differentiated based on their genetic and phenotypic characteristics, including their ability to utilize various carbon sources, their fatty acid profiles, and their susceptibility to different antibiotics [6]. The genetic diversity of Cronobacter species has been studied extensively using various molecular typing methods, including multilocus sequence typing (MLST) and pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE) [7]. These studies have revealed a high level of genetic diversity within the genus, with some species exhibiting a higher degree of diversity than others [8]. Cronobacter species have been isolated from a variety of food products, including powdered infant formula, dairy products, and spices [9]. The presence of these bacteria in food products is a concern, as they can survive in a desiccated state for extended periods and can grow rapidly in the presence of moisture [10]. The ability of Cronobacter species to form biofilms on surfaces has also been recognized as an important factor in their persistence in food processing environments [11]. Biofilms are complex communities of microorganisms that adhere to surfaces and are embedded in a matrix of extracellular polymeric substances [12]. The formation of biofilms by Cronobacter species can make them more resistant to cleaning and disinfection, and can also provide a protective environment for the bacteria to grow and survive [13]. The antimicrobial susceptibility of Cronobacter species has also been studied, and it has been shown that these bacteria can exhibit resistance to a range of antibiotics [14]. The development of antibiotic resistance in Cronobacter species is a concern, as it can limit the treatment options available for infections caused by these bacteria [15]. The use of antibiotics in food animal production has been implicated as a factor in the development of antibiotic resistance in Cronobacter species, and the overuse of antibiotics in human medicine has also been recognized as a contributing factor [16]. In recent years, there has been an increasing interest in the study of Cronobacter species in spices and cereals, as these products have been recognized as potential sources of contamination [17]. Spices and cereals are often imported from countries with limited regulatory oversight, and they can be contaminated with Cronobacter species during processing and storage [18]. The contamination of spices and cereals with Cronobacter species can have significant implications for public health, as these products are often consumed raw or are used as ingredients in a variety of food products [19]. In China, the study of Cronobacter species in spices and cereals has been limited, and there is a need for more research in this area [20]. The aim of this study was to investigate the genetic diversity, antimicrobial susceptibility, and biofilm formation of Cronobacter isolates recovered from spices and cereals in China. A total of 40 Cronobacter isolates were recovered from spices and cereals during 2014-2015, and these isolates were characterized using a range of molecular typing methods, including MLST and O-antigen serotyping [21]. The antimicrobial susceptibility of the isolates was also determined, and their ability to form biofilms was assessed [22]. The results of this study provide new insights into the genetic diversity and antimicrobial susceptibility of Cronobacter species in spices and cereals, and highlight the need for continued surveillance of these products to improve our understanding of the epidemiology of Cronobacter infections [23]. The study was conducted from 2014 to 2015, and a total of 40 Cronobacter isolates were recovered from spices and cereals in China. The samples were collected from various provinces in China, including Beijing, Shanghai, Guangdong, and Jiangsu [1]. The spices and cereals were purchased from local markets and stored at room temperature until processing. A total of 200 samples, including 100 spice samples and 100 cereal samples, were analyzed for the presence of Cronobacter species. The isolation and identification of Cronobacter species were performed according to the protocol described by the International Organization for Standardization [2]. Briefly, 25 grams of each sample were added to 225 mL of buffered peptone water and incubated at 37°C for 24 hours. After incubation, the enriched samples were streaked onto Druggan-Forsythe-Iversen (DFI) agar plates and incubated at 37°C for 24 hours [3]. The presumptive Cronobacter colonies were then subcultured onto DFI agar plates and incubated at 37°C for 24 hours. The colonies were identified as Cronobacter species based on their morphology, biochemical reactions, and molecular analysis. The molecular analysis was performed using the fusA sequencing method, which is a widely used method for the identification of Cronobacter species [4]. The fusA gene was amplified using the primers fusA-F (5'-GGT GGT GAT GGT GAT GGT-3') and fusA-R (5'-CTT TCA GCA CTT TGT TCG-3') [5]. The PCR products were sequenced using the BigDye Terminator v3.1 Cycle Sequencing Kit (Applied Biosystems, USA) and analyzed using the BLAST program [6]. The sequences were compared to the reference sequences in the GenBank database to determine the species of the isolates. Multilocus sequence typing (MLST) was performed to determine the genetic diversity of the Cronobacter isolates [7]. The MLST scheme for Cronobacter species involves the sequencing of seven housekeeping genes, including atpD, fusA, glnS, gltB, gyrB, infB, and ppsA [8]. The primers used for the MLST scheme were described by Baldwin et al. [9]. The PCR products were sequenced and analyzed as described above. The sequences were compared to the reference sequences in the MLST database to determine the sequence type (ST) of each isolate. The O-antigen serotyping was performed using the protocol described by Sun et al. [10]. The O-antigen serotyping involves the use of specific antisera to react with the O-antigen of the bacterial cell wall. The antisera were prepared using the method described by Liu et al. [11]. The isolates were reacted with the antisera, and the results were recorded as positive or negative. The antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed using the broth microdilution method, as described by the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute [12]. The isolates were tested against a panel of 16 antibiotics, including ampicillin, ceftriaxone, meropenem, aztreonam, gentamicin, and ciprofloxacin. The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of each antibiotic was determined, and the results were interpreted according to the guidelines of the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute [13]. The biofilm formation assay was performed using the crystal violet staining method, as described by Stepanovic et al. [14]. The isolates were grown in trypticase soy broth (TSB) at 37°C for 24 hours. The cultures were then transferred to a 96-well microtiter plate and incubated at 37°C for 24 hours. The biofilm formation was measured by staining the biofilm with crystal violet and measuring the absorbance at 595 nm using a microplate reader. The results were interpreted as follows: weak biofilm producer (OD595 < 0.1), moderate biofilm producer (0.1 < OD595 < 0.5), strong biofilm producer (OD595 > 0.5), and non-biofilm producer (OD595 = 0) [15]. The data were analyzed using the SPSS software (version 20.0, IBM, USA). The descriptive statistics, including the frequency and percentage, were used to summarize the data. The chi-square test was used to compare the differences between the groups. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The MLST data were analyzed using the eBURST software (version 3, Imperial College London, UK) to determine the clonal complexes and the population structure of the Cronobacter isolates [16]. The genetic diversity of the 40 Cronobacter isolates recovered from spices and cereals in China during 2014-2015 was investigated using fusA sequencing analysis [1]. The results showed that the majority (23/40, 57.5%) of the isolates were identified as C. sakazakii, while the remaining strains were identified as C. dublinensis (6/40, 15.0%), C. malonaticus (5/40, 12.5%), C. turicensis (4/40, 10.0%), and C. universalis (2/40, 5.0%) [2]. These findings are consistent with previous studies, which have also reported C. sakazakii as the most prevalent species among Cronobacter isolates [3, 4]. To further investigate the genetic diversity of the Cronobacter isolates, multilocus sequence typing (MLST) analysis was performed [5]. The pattern of the overall ST distribution was diverse, with no single ST dominating the population. However, it was revealed that ST148 was the predominant ST, presenting 12.5% within the whole population. This is consistent with previous studies, which have also reported ST148 as a common ST among Cronobacter isolates [7]. MLST also assigned 12 isolates to 7 different clonal complexes (CCs), including CC4, CC13, CC16, CC17, CC72, CC129, and CC143 [8]. These CCs have been previously associated with clinical isolates, suggesting that the Cronobacter isolates recovered from spices and cereals may have the potential to cause disease in humans [9]. The results of O-antigen serotyping indicated that C. sakazakii serotype O1 and O2 were the most two prevalent serotypes, accounting for 40% and 30% of the isolates, respectively [10]. These serotypes have been previously associated with clinical isolates, and their presence in spices and cereals highlights the potential risk of Cronobacter infection from these sources [11]. The antimicrobial susceptibility of the 40 Cronobacter isolates was tested using a range of antibiotics, including ampicillin, ceftriaxone, meropenem, aztreonam, and gentamicin [12]. The results showed that the isolates were susceptible to most of the antibiotics tested, except for ceftriaxone, meropenem, and aztreonam, to which they exhibited resistance [13]. This is consistent with previous studies, which have also reported resistance to these antibiotics among Cronobacter isolates [14]. The emergence of antibiotic-resistant Cronobacter isolates is a concern, as it may limit the treatment options for Cronobacter infections [15]. The ability of the Cronobacter isolates to form biofilms was also investigated [16]. The results showed that 13 (32.5%) of the isolates were assessed as weak biofilm producers, one (2.5%) was a moderate biofilm producer, and one (2.5%) was a strong biofilm producer, while the others (62.5%) were non-biofilm producers [17]. Biofilm formation is an important virulence factor, as it allows bacteria to persist in environments and evade host immune defenses [18]. The presence of biofilm-producing Cronobacter isolates in spices and cereals highlights the potential risk of Cronobacter infection from these sources [19]. The genetic diversity of the Cronobacter isolates recovered from spices and cereals was further investigated using phylogenetic analysis [20]. The results showed that the isolates were divided into several distinct clades, with some isolates forming tight clusters and others being more distantly related [21]. This suggests that the Cronobacter isolates recovered from spices and cereals are genetically diverse, and that they may have originated from different sources [22]. The presence of clinical isolates, such as the C. sakazakii ST4 neonatal meningitic pathovar, in spices and cereals highlights the potential risk of Cronobacter infection from these sources [23]. In conclusion, the results of this study demonstrate that Cronobacter isolates recovered from spices and cereals in China are genetically diverse, and that they may have the potential to cause disease in humans [24]. Therefore, the surveillance of Cronobacter spp. in spices and cereals should be strengthened to improve epidemiological understandings of Cronobacter infections [26]. The proliferation of social media has led to an unprecedented amount of user-generated content, which has, in turn, fueled the development of social media mining techniques [1]. A crucial component of these techniques is the ability to analyze and understand the sentiment and subjective nature of text data [2]. Sentiment lexicons, which are collections of words annotated with their sentiment scores, have been widely used for this purpose [3]. However, the construction of these lexicons is a challenging task, as it requires a large amount of annotated data, which can be time-consuming and expensive to obtain [4]. Recent approaches have addressed this challenge by leveraging pre-trained word embeddings, such as Word2Vec [5] and GloVe [6], which capture latent semantic properties of words [7]. These embeddings have been shown to be effective in sentiment analysis tasks, including sentiment lexicon induction [8]. However, the embeddings obtained by optimizing the performance of a given task, such as predicting contextual words, are often sub-optimal for other applications [9]. This is because the embeddings are biased towards the specific task they were trained on, and may not capture the nuances of other semantic properties [10]. To address this limitation, several studies have proposed methods for adapting pre-trained embeddings to specific tasks [11]. One approach is to use embedding sub-space projection, which involves projecting the pre-trained embeddings onto a lower-dimensional space that is specific to the task at hand [12]. This allows for the capture of task-specific representations that are more relevant to the application [13]. However, most existing methods focus on adapting embeddings for a single task, and do not consider the problem of expanding lexicons that describe multiple semantic properties [14]. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for expanding subjective lexicons for social media mining by exploiting task-specific representations induced via embedding sub-space projection. Our model jointly learns suitable representations and the concomitant predictor for each semantic property, allowing us to expand lexicons that describe multiple properties. This approach enables us to capture the nuances of different semantic properties, and to adapt the embeddings to the specific task of sentiment lexicon induction [15]. The importance of expanding subjective lexicons for social media mining cannot be overstated. Sentiment analysis is a crucial component of social media mining, and is used in a wide range of applications, including opinion mining [16], sentiment-based recommendation systems [17], and social media monitoring [18]. However, the accuracy of sentiment analysis is highly dependent on the quality of the sentiment lexicons used [19]. By expanding subjective lexicons to describe multiple semantic properties, we can improve the accuracy of sentiment analysis, and enable more nuanced and fine-grained analysis of social media data [20]. Our approach is motivated by the observation that different semantic properties, such as sentiment, emotion, and polarity, are often captured by different aspects of word meanings [21]. For example, the word "happy" may have a positive sentiment score, but also convey a sense of emotion or affect [22]. By capturing these different aspects of word meanings, we can create more comprehensive and accurate sentiment lexicons [23]. Furthermore, our approach allows us to adapt the embeddings to the specific task of sentiment lexicon induction, which can improve the accuracy of the lexicons and enable more effective sentiment analysis [24]. The intricate relationship between the immune system and cancer has been a subject of extensive research in recent years, with a particular focus on the role of macrophages in tumor growth and progression [1]. Macrophages are a type of white blood cell that play a crucial role in the innate immune response, acting as a first line of defense against pathogens and foreign substances [2]. However, in the context of cancer, macrophages can have a dual role, either promoting or inhibiting tumor growth, depending on their polarization state [3]. In the case of brain tumors, such as gliomas, meningiomas, and medulloblastomas, the role of macrophages is particularly complex, due to the unique characteristics of the brain microenvironment [4]. Macrophage Polarization and Brain Tumors Macrophage polarization refers to the process by which macrophages acquire specific functional phenotypes in response to environmental cues [5]. The two main types of macrophage polarization are M1 and M2, which are characterized by distinct gene expression profiles and functional properties [6]. M1 macrophages are typically pro-inflammatory and are involved in the defense against pathogens, while M2 macrophages are anti-inflammatory and are involved in tissue repair and remodeling [7]. In the context of brain tumors, M2 macrophages have been shown to promote tumor growth and progression, by secreting factors that support angiogenesis, cell proliferation, and immune suppression [8]. For example, a study by [9] found that M2 macrophages in glioblastoma tumors expressed high levels of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), which is a key regulator of angiogenesis. Tumor-Associated Macrophages and the Tumor Microenvironment Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are a type of macrophage that is found in the tumor microenvironment [10]. TAMs are derived from circulating monocytes that are recruited to the tumor site, where they are polarized towards an M2 phenotype [11]. The tumor microenvironment is characterized by hypoxia, inflammation, and immune suppression, which all contribute to the polarization of TAMs towards an M2 phenotype [12]. In brain tumors, TAMs have been shown to play a key role in promoting tumor growth and progression, by regulating the immune response, promoting angiogenesis, and supporting the invasion and metastasis of cancer cells [13]. For example, a study by [14] found that TAMs in meningioma tumors expressed high levels of matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9), which is a key regulator of tumor invasion and metastasis. Regulation of Neoangiogenesis by Tumor-Associated Macrophages Neoangiogenesis, or the formation of new blood vessels, is a critical step in tumor growth and progression [15]. In brain tumors, neoangiogenesis is regulated by a complex interplay between tumor cells, endothelial cells, and TAMs [16]. TAMs have been shown to promote neoangiogenesis by secreting pro-angiogenic factors, such as VEGF and platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) [17]. For example, a study by [18] found that TAMs in glioblastoma tumors expressed high levels of VEGF, which was associated with increased angiogenesis and tumor growth. In addition, TAMs have been shown to regulate the expression of anti-angiogenic factors, such as thrombospondin-1 (TSP-1), which can inhibit angiogenesis [19]. Circulating Tumor Cells and the Role of Macrophages Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) are cancer cells that have detached from the primary tumor and are circulating in the bloodstream [20]. CTCs are a key indicator of metastatic potential and are associated with poor prognosis in many types of cancer [21]. In brain tumors, CTCs are relatively rare, due to the fact that brain tumors only rarely metastasize [22]. However, the study of CTCs in brain tumors can provide valuable insights into the mechanisms of tumor growth and progression, and can potentially identify new targets for therapy [23]. Macrophages have been shown to play a key role in the entry of CTCs into the bloodstream, by promoting the invasion and intravasation of cancer cells [24]. For example, a study by [25] found that TAMs in glioblastoma tumors expressed high levels of CD163, which is a marker of M2 macrophages, and was associated with increased CTCs in the bloodstream. Future Directions and Therapeutic Implications The study of macrophages in brain tumors has significant implications for the development of new therapeutic strategies [26]. By understanding the role of macrophages in tumor growth and progression, it may be possible to develop new therapies that target the tumor microenvironment and the immune response [27]. For example, therapies that promote the polarization of macrophages towards an M1 phenotype, or that inhibit the function of M2 macrophages, may be effective in inhibiting tumor growth and progression [28]. Additionally, the study of CTCs in brain tumors can provide valuable insights into the mechanisms of metastasis and can potentially identify new targets for therapy [29]. Overall, the study of macrophages in brain tumors is a rapidly evolving field that holds significant promise for the development of new therapeutic strategies. To investigate the role of macrophages in brain tumor growth and progression, we employed a multi-faceted approach, combining in vitro and in vivo experiments, as well as analysis of clinical samples. Our study focused on three types of brain tumors: gliomas, meningiomas, and medulloblastomas, which are known to exhibit distinct tumor microenvironments and immune cell infiltration patterns [1]. Cell Culture and Polarization We isolated macrophages from the peripheral blood of healthy donors and polarized them into M1 or M2 phenotypes using established protocols [2]. M1 macrophages were induced by stimulation with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and interferon-γ (IFN-γ), while M2 macrophages were induced by stimulation with interleukin-4 (IL-4) and interleukin-13 (IL-13). The polarization state of the macrophages was verified by flow cytometry analysis of surface markers, including CD80, CD86, and CD163 [3]. We also cultured brain tumor cells, including glioma (U87 and U251), meningioma (IOMM-Lee), and medulloblastoma (Daoy) cell lines, under standard conditions [4]. Co-Culture Experiments To examine the interactions between tumor cells and macrophages, we performed co-culture experiments using Transwell inserts [5]. Tumor cells were seeded in the bottom chamber, while macrophages were added to the top chamber. The co-cultures were maintained for 24-48 hours, and the conditioned medium was collected for further analysis. We measured the levels of various cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits [6]. Immunohistochemistry and Immunofluorescence We analyzed clinical samples of brain tumors, including gliomas, meningiomas, and medulloblastomas, using immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence [7]. The tissues were stained with antibodies against macrophage markers, such as CD68 and CD163, as well as tumor cell markers, including glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and Ki-67 [8]. We also examined the expression of neoangiogenic factors, including VEGF and platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), in the tumor microenvironment [9]. Flow Cytometry and Cell Sorting To characterize the immune cell infiltrate in brain tumors, we performed flow cytometry analysis of single-cell suspensions prepared from clinical samples [10]. We used a panel of antibodies against immune cell markers, including CD45, CD3, CD4, CD8, and CD68, to identify and quantify the different immune cell populations [11]. We also sorted macrophages and tumor cells using fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) and analyzed their gene expression profiles using quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) [12]. In Vivo Experiments We used a mouse model of glioma to study the role of macrophages in tumor growth and progression in vivo [13]. Mice were injected with glioma cells, and the tumor growth was monitored using bioluminescence imaging [14]. We also depleted macrophages using clodronate liposomes or inhibited their function using pharmacological inhibitors [15]. The effects of macrophage depletion or inhibition on tumor growth and progression were evaluated using histological and immunohistochemical analysis [16]. Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by recurring episodes of intestinal inflammation, which can lead to severe complications such as colorectal cancer and osteoporosis. The exact pathogenesis of UC remains unclear, but it is generally accepted that a combination of genetic predisposition, environmental factors, and an abnormal immune response contributes to the development of the disease. Intestinal epithelial cells play a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of the gut barrier and regulating the immune response to luminal antigens. Disruption of this barrier function and dysregulation of the immune response can lead to the infiltration of inflammatory cells, including neutrophils, into the intestinal mucosa, which is a hallmark of UC. Neutrophil transmigration is a critical step in the development of intestinal inflammation, as these cells can release a variety of pro-inflammatory mediators, including cytokines and chemokines, which amplify the inflammatory response. The transmigration of neutrophils across the intestinal epithelium is regulated by a complex interplay of adhesion molecules, chemokines, and cytokines. Syndecan-1 (SDC1), a transmembrane heparan sulfate proteoglycan, has been implicated in the regulation of neutrophil transmigration and the development of intestinal inflammation. SDC1 is expressed on the surface of intestinal epithelial cells and can interact with a variety of ligands, including chemokines, cytokines, and extracellular matrix components. The role of SDC1 in the regulation of inflammatory responses is complex and multifaceted. On the one hand, SDC1 can act as a co-receptor for various growth factors and chemokines, enhancing their binding to their respective receptors and promoting cell signaling. On the other hand, SDC1 can also act as a decoy receptor, binding to pro-inflammatory mediators and preventing them from interacting with their target cells. The ectodomain of SDC1, which carries the heparan sulfate chains, can be shed from the cell surface in response to inflammatory stimuli, releasing soluble SDC1 into the extracellular environment. This shed SDC1 can then interact with other cells and matrix components, influencing the inflammatory response. The shedding of SDC1 has been implicated in the pathogenesis of various inflammatory diseases, including UC. Elevated levels of soluble SDC1 have been detected in the serum of patients with UC, and this has been correlated with disease activity and severity. However, the exact mechanisms by which SDC1 shedding contributes to the development of intestinal inflammation are not fully understood. It is possible that the shed SDC1 acts as a pro-inflammatory mediator, promoting the recruitment of inflammatory cells to the site of inflammation. Alternatively, the loss of SDC1 from the cell surface may disrupt the normal functioning of the intestinal epithelial barrier, allowing the transmigration of neutrophils and other inflammatory cells. The NF-κB pathway is a key regulator of inflammatory responses, and its activation is a hallmark of UC. The NF-κB pathway is normally kept in check by the inhibitor of κB (IκB) protein, which binds to the NF-κB transcription factor and prevents its translocation to the nucleus. In response to inflammatory stimuli, IκB is phosphorylated and degraded, allowing NF-κB to translocate to the nucleus and activate the transcription of pro-inflammatory genes. The activation of the NF-κB pathway leads to the production of a variety of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), and interleukin-6 (IL-6), which play critical roles in the development of intestinal inflammation. In addition to the NF-κB pathway, other signaling pathways, including the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, have been implicated in the regulation of inflammatory responses in UC. The MAPK pathway is activated in response to inflammatory stimuli and leads to the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines. The interaction between the NF-κB and MAPK pathways is complex and involves the activation of various downstream kinases and transcription factors. Given the complex interplay of molecular mechanisms involved in the development of intestinal inflammation, it is clear that a detailed understanding of the role of SDC1 in this process is essential. The aim of this study is to investigate the impact of cell surface-anchored SDC1 on intestinal inflammation and neutrophil transmigration in UC. By suppressing the shedding of SDC1 from intestinal epithelial cells, we aim to determine whether this can ameliorate the severity of intestinal inflammation and improve the outcome of UC. Our study will provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying the development of UC and highlight the potential of SDC1 as a therapeutic target for the treatment of this disease. Human intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) and cultured in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 μg/mL streptomycin. The cells were grown in a humidified incubator at 37°C with 5% CO2. To establish a model of syndecan-1 (SDC1) shedding suppression, we generated a cleavable resistant SDC1 mutant plasmid using site-directed mutagenesis. The mutant plasmid was designed to prevent the shedding of SDC1 from the cell surface by mutating the cleavage site. The plasmid was then transfected into IECs using Lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer's instructions. The transfected cells were selected using G418 (500 μg/mL) and cloned by limiting dilution. The expression of SDC1 in the transfected cells was confirmed by Western blotting and immunofluorescence microscopy. For Western blotting, the cells were lysed in RIPA buffer and the lysates were separated by SDS-PAGE. The blots were probed with a monoclonal antibody against SDC1 (Abcam) and detected using an enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) kit (Pierce). For immunofluorescence microscopy, the cells were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde and stained with a monoclonal antibody against SDC1 (Abcam) and a fluorescent secondary antibody (Invitrogen). To investigate the effect of SDC1 shedding suppression on neutrophil transmigration, a transwell assay was used. Neutrophils were isolated from the blood of healthy donors using a neutrophil isolation kit (Miltenyi Biotec) and labeled with a fluorescent dye (Calcein-AM, Invitrogen). The labeled neutrophils were then added to the upper chamber of a transwell plate and the transfected IECs were grown on the lower chamber. The plate was incubated for 2 hours and the number of neutrophils that transmigrated to the lower chamber was measured using a fluorescence microscope. To investigate the effect of SDC1 shedding suppression on intestinal inflammation in vivo, a mouse model of ulcerative colitis was used. The mice were treated with dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) (3% w/v) in their drinking water for 7 days to induce colitis. The mice were then injected with a plasmid encoding the cleavable resistant SDC1 mutant or a control plasmid via the tail vein. The mice were sacrificed on day 14 and the colon tissue was harvested for histological analysis. The patients were recruited from the gastroenterology clinic and the diagnosis of ulcerative colitis was confirmed by endoscopy and histology. The differences between the groups were compared using a Student's t-test or a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by a post-hoc test. Matrix factorization has emerged as a powerful tool for recovering missing or corrupted entries in large datasets, with applications spanning collaborative filtering [1], image and video processing [2], and recommender systems [3]. The underlying assumption of matrix factorization is that the data matrix can be approximated as the product of two low-rank matrices, which capture the latent features of the rows and columns. This approximation can be achieved through various techniques, including Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) [4], Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) [5], and Probabilistic Matrix Factorization (PMF) [6]. These methods have been shown to be effective in many scenarios, but they rely on a simple and fixed function, namely the inner product, to model the relationships between the latent features. Recent advances in deep learning have led to the development of more complex and flexible models, which can learn nonlinear relationships between variables [7]. In particular, neural networks have been successfully applied to a wide range of tasks, including image recognition [8], natural language processing [9], and recommender systems [10]. The key idea behind neural networks is to learn a hierarchical representation of the data, by composing multiple layers of nonlinear transformations. This allows the model to capture complex patterns and relationships in the data, which may not be apparent through traditional matrix factorization techniques. The idea of combining matrix factorization with neural networks is not new, and several approaches have been proposed in the literature [11, 12]. However, these methods typically use a neural network to learn the latent features, while still relying on the inner product to model the relationships between them. In contrast, our approach, which we call Neural Network Matrix Factorization (NNMF), replaces the inner product with an arbitrary function learned from the data, using a multi-layer feed-forward neural network. This allows the model to capture nonlinear relationships between the latent features, and to adapt to the specific structure of the data. The NNMF approach can be seen as a generalization of traditional matrix factorization techniques, which can be recovered as special cases by using a linear neural network with a single layer. However, the use of a nonlinear neural network allows the model to capture more complex patterns in the data, and to improve the accuracy of the predictions. Furthermore, the NNMF approach can be easily extended to incorporate additional information, such as graph features or side information, by modifying the architecture of the neural network or the loss function used for training. The optimization of the NNMF model is typically performed using an alternating minimization scheme, where the neural network is optimized for fixed latent features, and the latent features are optimized for a fixed neural network. This approach allows the model to adapt to the specific structure of the data, and to capture nonlinear relationships between the latent features. However, the optimization process can be challenging, and requires careful tuning of the hyperparameters, such as the learning rate, the number of layers, and the number of units in each layer. Despite the challenges, the NNMF approach has shown promising results on several benchmark datasets, outperforming traditional matrix factorization techniques and some recent proposals [13]. The intensive care unit (ICU) is a complex and dynamic environment where critically ill patients receive life-sustaining interventions and meticulous care. Over the past few decades, the ICU has undergone significant transformations, driven by advances in medical technology, changes in patient demographics, and shifting paradigms in critical care medicine. One of the most significant recent developments in the field is the growing recognition of the importance of early recovery from ICU care. The concept of early recovery encompasses a range of strategies aimed at minimizing the duration of ICU stay, reducing morbidity and mortality, and promoting rapid restoration of physical and cognitive function. The Society of Critical Care Medicine (SCCM) has been at the forefront of this movement, leading a large knowledge translation and quality improvement initiative aimed at "liberating" patients from the ICU. This initiative is built around the ABCDEF bundle, a set of evidence-based elements that have been shown to lower ICU stay and mortality, and optimize patient outcomes. The ABCDEF bundle consists of six key components: Assessing, preventing, and managing pain; Both spontaneous awakening trials and spontaneous breathing trials; Choice of analgesia and sedation; assessment, prevention, and management of Delirium; Early mobility and exercise; and Family engagement and empowerment. By implementing these bundled elements, ICUs can create a more patient-centered and recovery-focused environment, ultimately leading to better outcomes and reduced healthcare costs. However, the implementation of the ABCDEF bundle in neurologically injured patients poses unique challenges. These patients often have complex and heterogeneous injuries, requiring specialized care and nuanced approaches to pain management, sedation, and delirium prevention. The neurointensive care unit (NICU) is a high-stakes environment where patients with severe brain injuries, strokes, and other neurological conditions receive highly specialized care. The NICU setting is characterized by a high degree of uncertainty, complexity, and variability, making it difficult to apply generic ICU protocols and guidelines. One of the key challenges in managing neurologically injured patients is the assessment and management of pain. These patients often have impaired communication and cognitive function, making it difficult to assess their pain levels and respond appropriately. Moreover, the use of sedatives and analgesics in the NICU can have unintended consequences, such as prolonging mechanical ventilation, delaying mobilization, and increasing the risk of delirium and other adverse outcomes. The choice of analgesia and sedation protocols is critical in the NICU, as it can significantly impact patient outcomes, including the duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU length of stay, and long-term cognitive and functional recovery. Despite the importance of analgesia and sedation protocols in the NICU, there is a paucity of literature on this topic. Most studies on pain management and sedation in the ICU have focused on general medical or surgical patients, with limited attention to the unique needs and challenges of neurologically injured patients. As a result, there is a significant knowledge gap in this area, making it difficult for clinicians to develop evidence-based guidelines and protocols for managing pain and sedation in the NICU. This systematic review aims to address this knowledge gap by synthesizing the available evidence on analgesia and sedation protocols in the NICU. We will conduct a comprehensive search of the literature, including major databases such as MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library, as well as clinical trials registries and other relevant sources. Our search will focus on studies that have evaluated the effectiveness of different analgesia and sedation protocols in neurologically injured patients, including those with traumatic brain injury, stroke, and other neurological conditions. We will also examine the impact of these protocols on key outcomes, such as time to successful discontinuation of mechanical ventilation, time to early mobility, and long-term cognitive and functional recovery. By synthesizing the available evidence on this topic, we hope to provide clinicians and policymakers with a comprehensive understanding of the challenges and opportunities in managing pain and sedation in the NICU. Our review will highlight the unique challenges of neurologically injured patients and identify areas where further research is needed to inform evidence-based practice. Ultimately, our goal is to contribute to the development of formal recommendations and clinical practice guidelines that can help improve patient outcomes and reduce iatrogenic harm in the NICU. By promoting early recovery and minimizing the risks associated with ICU care, we can improve the quality of life for patients with neurological injuries and reduce the burden on healthcare systems. The systematic review protocol was registered with the PROSPERO database (CRD42017078909) prior to the commencement of the study. A comprehensive search strategy was developed in consultation with a librarian to identify all relevant studies. The following electronic databases will be searched: MEDLINE (PubMed), EMBASE, Cochrane Library, Cochrane Clinical Trials Registry, World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform Search Portal, and the National Institutes for Health Clinical Trials Registry. The search terms will include a combination of Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and keywords related to analgesia, sedation, neurointensive care, and early recovery. The search strategy will be tailored to each database to account for differences in indexing and syntax. The search will be limited to studies published in English, and no date restrictions will be applied. The reference lists of included studies will be hand-searched to identify any additional relevant studies. Unpublished studies, conference abstracts, and grey literature will not be included in the review. The search strategy will be documented in full and provided in an appendix. Study selection will be performed independently by two reviewers. The title and abstract of each study will be screened to determine eligibility, and the full text of potentially relevant studies will be retrieved. The inclusion criteria will be: (1) studies involving adult patients with neurological injury or illness requiring admission to a neurointensive care unit (NICU); (2) studies evaluating the use of analgesia and sedation protocols; and (3) studies reporting on outcomes related to early recovery from NICU, such as time to successful discontinuation of mechanical ventilation, time to early mobility, or ICU length of stay. Studies will be excluded if they: (1) involve pediatric patients; (2) are not published in English; (3) do not report on analgesia and sedation protocols; or (4) do not report on outcomes related to early recovery from NICU. Disagreements between reviewers will be resolved through discussion and consultation with a third reviewer if necessary. The inter-rater agreement will be calculated using Cohen's Kappa coefficient. Data extraction will be performed independently by two reviewers using a standardized data extraction form. The form will be piloted on a sample of studies to ensure that it captures all relevant information. The following data will be extracted: study characteristics (author, year, country, study design), patient characteristics (age, sex, diagnosis), analgesia and sedation protocols (type, dose, duration), and outcomes (time to successful discontinuation of mechanical ventilation, time to early mobility, ICU length of stay, mortality). The quality of included studies will be assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for observational studies. The quality assessment will be performed independently by two reviewers, and disagreements will be resolved through discussion and consultation with a third reviewer if necessary. The results of the study will be combined statistically using meta-analysis if the data are suitable. The decision to combine results will be based on the heterogeneity of the studies, as assessed using the I^2 statistic. If the I^2 statistic is less than 50%, the results will be combined using a fixed-effects model. If the I^2 statistic is 50% or greater, the results will be combined using a random-effects model. The primary outcomes of interest will be time to successful discontinuation of mechanical ventilation and time to early mobility. Secondary outcomes will include ICU length of stay, mortality, and incidence of delirium. Subgroup analyses will be performed to evaluate the impact of different analgesia and sedation protocols on outcomes, as well as the impact of different patient characteristics (e.g. age, diagnosis) on outcomes. After removing duplicates, 4,123 unique studies were screened by title and abstract. Of these, 501 studies underwent full-text screening, and 127 studies met the inclusion criteria. The Cohen’s Kappa coefficient of agreement between the two reviewers was 0.92, indicating excellent agreement. The 127 included studies were published between 2005 and 2022, with 75 (59%) being observational studies, 31 (24%) randomized controlled trials, and 21 (17%) quasi-experimental studies. The majority of the studies (85, 67%) were conducted in adult neurointensive care units, while 25 (20%) were conducted in pediatric neurointensive care units, and 17 (13%) were conducted in mixed adult and pediatric neurointensive care units. The patient population included in the studies consisted of patients with various types of neurological injuries, including traumatic brain injury (43 studies, 34%), stroke (31 studies, 24%), subarachnoid hemorrhage (21 studies, 17%), and spinal cord injury (12 studies, 9%). The median age of the patients was 55 years (interquartile range, 42-65 years), and 63% were male. The analgesia and sedation protocols used in the included studies varied widely. The most commonly used analgesics were fentanyl (55 studies, 43%), morphine (31 studies, 24%), and acetaminophen (21 studies, 17%). The most commonly used sedatives were propofol (46 studies, 36%), midazolam (31 studies, 24%), and dexmedetomidine (21 studies, 17%). The duration of analgesia and sedation ranged from 24 hours to 14 days, with a median duration of 5 days. The primary outcomes of time to successful discontinuation of mechanical ventilation and time to early mobility were reported in 75 (59%) and 56 (44%) studies, respectively. The median time to successful discontinuation of mechanical ventilation was 7 days (interquartile range, 4-12 days), and the median time to early mobility was 10 days (interquartile range, 6-16 days). A stratified analysis of subgroups of interest was conducted to evaluate the impact of the ABCDEF bundle components on the primary outcomes. Cyanobacteria, a diverse group of phototrophic microorganisms, have been gaining attention in recent years due to their potential applications in various fields, including food, pharmaceuticals, and biotechnology [1]. These microorganisms are rich in phytonutrients and pigments, which have been shown to possess antioxidant properties, enabling them to protect cells from damage caused by free radicals [2]. The antioxidant activity of cyanobacteria is attributed to the presence of various bioactive compounds, including phenolics, flavonoids, and phycobiliproteins (PBPs), which have been reported to exhibit scavenging activity against reactive oxygen species (ROS) [3]. Background and Significance Cyanobacteria are widely distributed in various aquatic environments, including fresh water bodies, and have been identified as a potential source of natural antioxidants [4]. The antioxidant properties of cyanobacteria have been attributed to their ability to produce a wide range of bioactive compounds, including carotenoids, phycocyanin, and other pigments [5]. These compounds have been shown to exhibit antioxidant activity, which can help protect cells from oxidative stress and damage caused by free radicals [6]. The use of natural antioxidants from cyanobacteria has gained significant attention in recent years, due to their potential applications in the prevention and treatment of various diseases, including cancer, diabetes, and neurodegenerative disorders [7]. Phytochemicals and Antioxidant Activity The phytochemicals present in cyanobacteria, including phenolics and flavonoids, have been reported to exhibit antioxidant activity [8]. Phenolics are a group of compounds that are characterized by the presence of a hydroxyl group attached to a benzene ring, and have been shown to exhibit antioxidant activity due to their ability to scavenge ROS [9]. Flavonoids, on the other hand, are a group of compounds that are characterized by the presence of a flavan nucleus, and have been reported to exhibit antioxidant activity due to their ability to chelate metals and scavenge ROS [10]. The antioxidant activity of cyanobacteria has also been attributed to the presence of PBPs, which are water-soluble pigments that are responsible for the blue-green color of cyanobacteria [11]. Phycobiliproteins and Antioxidant Activity PBPs are a group of pigments that are present in cyanobacteria, and have been reported to exhibit antioxidant activity [12]. These pigments are composed of a protein moiety and a chromophore, and have been shown to exhibit antioxidant activity due to their ability to scavenge ROS [13]. The antioxidant activity of PBPs has been attributed to their ability to donate electrons and neutralize ROS, thereby preventing oxidative stress and damage to cells [14]. The use of PBPs as natural antioxidants has gained significant attention in recent years, due to their potential applications in the prevention and treatment of various diseases [15]. Freshwater Cyanobacteria of Sri Lanka Sri Lanka is home to a diverse range of freshwater cyanobacteria, which have been identified as a potential source of natural antioxidants [16]. The freshwater bodies of Sri Lanka, including rivers, lakes, and reservoirs, provide a suitable environment for the growth and proliferation of cyanobacteria [17]. The cyanobacteria present in these freshwater bodies have been reported to produce a wide range of bioactive compounds, including phenolics, flavonoids, and PBPs, which have been shown to exhibit antioxidant activity [18]. The aim of this study was to investigate the antioxidant properties of four cyanobacterial species, namely Oscillatoria sp., Lyngbya sp., Microcystis sp., and Spirulina sp., isolated from freshwater bodies of Sri Lanka. Methodology and Objectives The cyanobacterial species used in this study were isolated from freshwater bodies of Sri Lanka, and were identified based on their morphological and molecular characteristics [19]. The total phenolic content (TPC) and total flavonoid content (TFC) of the cyanobacterial species were determined using spectrophotometric methods [20]. The antioxidant activity of the cyanobacterial species was determined using the ferric reducing antioxidant power (FRAP) and 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) radical scavenging activity assays [21]. The PBPs present in the cyanobacterial species were extracted and purified using chromatographic methods, and their antioxidant activity was determined using spectrophotometric methods [22]. The objectives of this study were to investigate the antioxidant properties of the four cyanobacterial species, and to identify the bioactive compounds responsible for their antioxidant activity. Sample Collection and Isolation Cyanobacterial samples were collected from various freshwater bodies in Sri Lanka, including lakes, rivers, and reservoirs [1]. The sampling sites were selected based on their diverse environmental conditions, such as pH, temperature, and nutrient availability [2]. A total of 20 water samples were collected, and the cyanobacterial strains were isolated using the spread plate technique on BG-11 medium [3]. The isolated strains were then purified by repeated subculturing and identified based on their morphological characteristics, such as cell shape, size, and arrangement [4]. Cultivation and Biomass Production The purified cyanobacterial strains, namely Oscillatoria sp., Lyngbya sp., Microcystis sp., and Spirulina sp., were cultivated in 1 L Erlenmeyer flasks containing 500 mL of BG-11 medium [5]. The cultures were incubated at 25 ± 2°C under a 12:12 hour light-dark cycle with a light intensity of 50 μmol/m²s [6]. The biomass was harvested after 14 days of cultivation by centrifugation at 5000 rpm for 10 minutes [7]. The resulting biomass was then freeze-dried and stored at -20°C for further analysis. Extraction and Determination of Total Phenolic Content (TPC) The freeze-dried biomass was extracted with methanol (80%) using a sonication bath for 30 minutes [8]. The extracts were then centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 10 minutes, and the resulting supernatant was used for the determination of TPC using the Folin-Ciocalteu assay [9]. The TPC was calculated using a standard curve of gallic acid, and the results were expressed as milligrams of gallic acid equivalents per gram of biomass (mg GAE/g) [10]. Extraction and Determination of Total Flavonoid Content (TFC) The same methanolic extracts used for TPC determination were also used for the determination of TFC using the aluminum chloride colorimetric assay [11]. The TFC was calculated using a standard curve of quercetin, and the results were expressed as milligrams of quercetin equivalents per gram of biomass (mg QE/g) [12]. Determination of Phycobiliproteins (PBPs) The PBPs were extracted from the freeze-dried biomass using a phosphate buffer (pH 7.0) containing 1 M NaCl [13]. The extracts were then centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 10 minutes, and the resulting supernatant was used for the determination of PBPs using the spectrophotometric method [14]. The total PBP content was calculated using the equations of Bennett and Bogorad [15], and the results were expressed as milligrams per gram of biomass (mg/g). Antioxidant Activity Assays The antioxidant activity of the methanolic extracts was evaluated using the ferric reducing antioxidant power (FRAP) assay [16] and the 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) radical scavenging activity assay [17]. The FRAP assay was performed using a standard curve of ascorbic acid, and the results were expressed as micromoles of ascorbic acid equivalents per gram of biomass (μmol AAE/g) [18]. The DPPH radical scavenging activity was calculated using a standard curve of trolox, and the results were expressed as micromoles of trolox equivalents per gram of biomass (μmol TE/g) [19]. Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) Spectroscopy The freeze-dried biomass was analyzed using FTIR spectroscopy to identify the functional groups present in the cyanobacterial strains [20]. The FTIR spectra were recorded in the range of 4000-400 cm⁻¹ using a FTIR spectrometer [21]. The spectra were then analyzed to identify the presence of specific functional groups, such as N-H stretching bands, which are responsible for the antioxidant activity [22]. Statistical Analysis The data were analyzed using a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by the Duncan's multiple range test to determine the significant differences between the cyanobacterial strains [23]. The results were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) of three replicates [24]. The statistical analysis was performed using the SPSS software (version 20) [25]. Flavonoids are known to have antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties [4], and the high TFC values observed in this study suggest that these cyanobacterial species may have potential health benefits. The phycobiliproteins (PBPs) content of the cyanobacterial extracts was determined using the method described by [5]. The results showed that Lyngbya sp. had the highest total PBPs value of 127.01 mg/g, followed by Oscillatoria sp. (93.45 mg/g), Microcystis sp. (74.21 mg/g), and Spirulina sp. (56.32 mg/g). PBPs are known to have antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties [6], and the high PBPs content observed in this study suggests that these cyanobacterial species may have potential health benefits. The antioxidant activity of the cyanobacterial extracts was determined using the ferric reducing antioxidant power (FRAP) assay [7] and the 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) radical scavenging activity assay [8]. The results showed that Oscillatoria sp. had the highest FRAP value of 39.63 ± 7.02, followed by Lyngbya sp. (29.45 ± 4.51), Microcystis sp. (23.19 ± 3.45), and Spirulina sp. (18.92 ± 2.89). The DPPH radical scavenging activity was also highest in Oscillatoria sp. (465.31 ± 25.76), followed by Lyngbya sp. (248.39 ± 11.97), Microcystis sp. (193.45 ± 9.21), and Spirulina sp. The Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy analysis of the cyanobacterial extracts was performed to identify the functional groups present [10]. The results showed that Lyngbya sp. did not show any N-H stretching band, which is responsible for the inhibition of antioxidant activity [11]. The FTIR spectra of the other cyanobacterial species showed the presence of N-H stretching bands, which may be responsible for their antioxidant activity. The FTIR spectra also showed the presence of other functional groups such as C-H, C-O, and C=C, which are typical of phytochemicals [12]. The active compounds present in the cyanobacterial extracts were identified using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) analysis [13]. The results showed that Lyngbya sp. contained a high amount of fatty acids, particularly linoleic acid and oleic acid, which are known to have antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties [14]. The GC-MS analysis also showed the presence of other phytochemicals such as terpenes and phenolics, which are known to have antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties [15]. The correlation between the TPC, TFC, PBPs, and antioxidant activity of the cyanobacterial extracts was analyzed using Pearson's correlation coefficient [16]. The results showed a significant positive correlation between TPC and antioxidant activity (r = 0.85, p < 0.01), and between TFC and antioxidant activity (r = 0.78, p < 0.05). The results also showed a significant positive correlation between PBPs and antioxidant activity (r = 0.92, p < 0.001). These results suggest that the phytochemicals present in the cyanobacterial extracts, particularly phenolics and flavonoids, are responsible for their antioxidant activity. Overall, the results of this study suggest that Lyngbya sp. and Oscillatoria sp. have high antioxidant activity and may be a potential source of natural antioxidants for use in food, pharmaceutical, and other industrial applications. The high TPC, TFC, and PBPs content of these cyanobacterial species, as well as their antioxidant activity, make them a promising source of phytochemicals with potential health benefits. Further studies are needed to isolate and characterize the active compounds present in these cyanobacterial species and to evaluate their potential health benefits.
